The Śrīkarabhāṣya:
A Vīraśaiva Commentary on the Vedānta Sūtras,
composed by Śrīpatipaṇḍitācārya.
Si. Hayavadana Rāv,
printed at the Bangalore City Press, Bangalore, known as the Mudraksharashala.
Now, in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya, the table of contents for the Pañcapādikā:
First Chapter, First Quarter;
the Section on the One Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) [Introduction].

An investigation into the meaning of the Sūtra: the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta)— preceded by the demonstration that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
The refutation of the embodied soul as the cause of the universe; the section concerning the Inner [Self] (the determination of the locus of the six marks);
and the demonstration that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is of the nature of the Great Liṅga.

The statement that Paraśiva-Brahman, whose essential body is the foremost among the Prābhākara teachers, is of the nature of the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga) by virtue of being the innermost of all; and the determination of the meaning of the term *kapyāsa*.
The section on ether (ākāśādhikaraṇa),
which establishes that the supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, has the nature of the *prasāda-liṅga*; and the section on breath (prāṇādhikaraṇa).
The determination of Śiva’s nature as the mobile liṅga; the section concerning light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa);
the demonstration that Paramaśiva is of the nature of the Śivaliṅga.
The determination of Śiva as being of the nature of the Guru-liṅga; the determination of Gāyatrī as being of the nature of the Guru-liṅga;
the determination of Śiva as being of the nature of the Ācāra-liṅga.
The demonstration that the *Puruṣasūkta* has Śiva as its ultimate referent;
the statement that Hari and Hara are respectively *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; and the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇādhikaraṇa*).
The demonstration that Śiva consists of the nature of the external, desired, and vital *liṅga*;
the demonstration that Śiva is to be meditated upon in three ways as consisting of the nature of the desired, the vital, and the state-*liṅga*.
This is the second quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*).
The section on universal establishment:
the exposition of the doctrine of wearing external signs, and the exposition of wearing internal signs.
The exposition of Paraśiva-Brahman as consisting of ten types of liṅgas; the demonstration that the wearing of the liṅga is Vedic;
and the eight enclosures (aṣṭāvaraṇas) of Vīraśaivism.
The refutation of the eligibility of Śūdras for the knowledge of Brahman;
the removal of the notion that Rudra is inauspicious on the occasion of the offering to Rudra;
and the statement that Śiva, as the Supreme Brahman, is the object of worship while Nārāyaṇa is the worshipper.
The characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa: an exposition on the supreme excellence of observing and wearing [auspicious] marks,
and the definition of a Brāhmaṇa as stated in the Gautama-smṛti.
The removal of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) during the worship of the *liṅga* by those who possess the *liṅga*;
the demonstration that the five Brahma-mantras constitute the nature of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*);
and the demonstration of the Vedic authority (*śrautatva*) for the worship of the *liṅga* performed with the left hand as the locus.

The delineation of the Supreme Lord’s limited nature by virtue of adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, and by means of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) consisting of desire and so forth;
and the demonstration that the wearing of ashes is based on the Śruti.
An exposition on the Vedic nature of wearing rudrākṣa beads;
a statement on the Vedic character of accepting the grace of the water from [the guru’s] feet;
and a demonstration of the Vedic authority for accepting the grace of Śiva.
The ritual for the water used for washing the feet; the demonstration that accepting the grace of Viṣṇu is not based on the Śruti;
and the explanation that the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, assumes a physical body for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
The demonstration of the difference-and-non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman;
the section concerning the state of being a non-eater (atṛtva);
and the description of Paraśiva as the destroyer of all.
The Section on the Cave (Guhādhikaraṇa): An exposition on the Supreme Lord’s abiding within the cave;
the refutation of the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman as that of an original object and its reflection;
and the Intermediate Section (Antarādhikaraṇa).
The demonstration that Paramaśiva is to be meditated upon as being within the center of the eye; the statement that the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is the Person in the Eye (Akṣipuruṣa);
and the presentation of the authority of the Śruti in defining the specific nature of the power (Śakti) belonging to Brahmā as Paramaśiva.
The Section on the Inner Controller: An exposition establishing that Paramaśiva is the object of worship as the inner controller of all,
and a demonstration that Maheśvara alone is the inner controller of everything.
The section concerning the invisible [one] (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa),
which establishes the supremacy of the Supreme Lord; and the section concerning Vaiśvānara (Vaiśvānarādhikaraṇa).
The Third Pāda of the First Adhyāya: An Exposition of the Supreme Śiva as the Object of All Worship in the Form of the Digestive Fire;
The Section Concerning Heaven, Earth, and so forth (Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa).
The demonstration that the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth;
the definition of the nature of the liberated soul; and the distinction of Viśeṣādvaita from Viśiṣṭādvaita.
The exposition on the measurement of the individual soul (*jīva*);
the demonstration of the supremacy of Viśeṣādvaita, which consists of both difference and non-difference;
and the etymological definition of the term "Viśeṣādvaita."
The demonstration of the reality of the world; the section concerning the Infinite (*bhūman*);
and the demonstration that the Supreme Lord is denoted by the term "Infinite."
The Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa):
An exposition of how Paramaśiva, as qualified by the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is denoted by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara);
a demonstration of Paramaśiva’s state of being qualified by that power.
The section concerning the object of the act of seeing;
the description of the supreme Śiva as being black and tawny; the section concerning the small [space] within the heart.
The exposition of the nature of the *dahara-ātman* for the sake of protecting the essence of devotion to Maheśvara;
the context of the non-dual Śiva qualified by the powers of difference and non-difference as taught by Nārāyaṇa;
and the section concerning the imitation (*anukṛti-adhikaraṇa*).
The demonstration that the Supreme Lord, who is the inner self (*daharātman*), is self-luminous and the illuminator of both the gross and subtle aspects of consciousness and matter;
and the establishment of the *Bhagavad Gītā*’s focus on Śiva by means of the sixfold marks of intention (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*).
The section concerning the measured [universe]: the determination that the Supreme Lord possesses a manifested form,
and the determination of the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
The Section on the Deities:
An investigation into the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman;
a presentation of one's own view, preceded by the refutation of objections raised by other teachers regarding the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.
The section concerning those other than Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*),
which refutes the eligibility of Śūdras for the knowledge of Brahman;
and the section concerning trembling (*kampanādhikaraṇa*).
The determination that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is measured by the human heart for the sake of favoring His practitioners;
the section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa);
and the statement regarding the attainment of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is established as the object of meditation in the "Small" (Dahara) and other meditations.
The section concerning the designation of Śiva as Brahman and Puruṣottama; the section concerning the designation of being distinct from other things; and the section concerning deep sleep.
The Fourth Pāda of the First Adhyāya: The Section on the Inferential (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa).
This section establishes that the Supreme Śiva is the object of worship for all, preceded by the refutation of the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause of the world.
The section concerning the cup (Camasādhikaraṇa), the section concerning the inclusion of the number (Saṃkhyopasaṃgrahādhikaraṇa),
and the determination of the appropriateness of accepting thirty-six principles in view of the twenty-five principles.
The enumeration of the thirty-six principles by name;
the section on causality; and the statement that Paramaśiva is the cause of the five great elements.
The section concerning Bālāki;
the refutation of the doctrine of pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita);
and the recollection of the threefold meditations based on the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva), the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), and so forth.
The section on the syntactical connection of sentences;
the stabilization of one's own established doctrine following the refutation of other views;
and the exposition of the theory of the distinction between the conjoined.
The exposition of the Advaita-vādin’s view:
the established doctrine of Viśeṣādvaita, which accords with the Siddhānta of Vedānta intended by all the Śrutis; [this concludes] the Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa.
The exposition of the identity-in-difference between the world and Brahman; the designation of the state of non-dual Śiva as qualified by specific powers;
and the determination of whether Brahman is devoid of attributes or possessed of attributes.
The demonstration that Paramaśiva is the cause of both [the material and the efficient];
the section concerning the interpretation of all [scriptures];
the reconciliation of the doctrine of Viśeṣādvaita—which emphasizes both difference and non-difference—with Paramaśiva.
The first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter:
The section concerning the lack of scope for Smṛti; the refutation of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti.
The section on the refutation of Yoga’s response; the refutation of the Smṛti on Yoga;
the section on the lack of similarity in characteristics.

The demonstration that Paraśiva-Brahman is distinct from all else; the refutation of the Advaita views of the Smārta school—primarily those concerning the illusoriness of the world, the individual soul, and the Lord; and the demonstration that the systems of logic of the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Akṣapādas, Kāpilas, and others lack the determination of the true nature of reality.

The demonstration of the equal conjunction of knowledge and action; the section concerning the non-acceptance by the learned [of other systems]; and the refutation of non-Vedic doctrines such as Jaimini’s [Mīmāṃsā] and the false Advaita.
The section concerning the enjoyer and offspring;
the section establishing that the Supreme Brahman is superior to the universe;
the section concerning the material cause.
The demonstration of the non-difference between cause and effect;
the demonstration that the world is real like a dream; the section concerning designation as something else.
Refutation of the doctrine of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman;
refutation of the Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine originated by Śrīkaṇṭha; the section concerning the observation of the final dissolution (*upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa*).
The demonstration of the Supreme Lord’s power to accomplish the impossible; the section concerning the total pervasion [of Brahman];
and the exposition of the Supreme Śiva, Brahman, as being of both embodied and unembodied nature.
The demonstration that Brahman, though partless, is the cause of the world; the demonstration that Brahman, though partless, is the cause of the world;
and the demonstration that Brahman is endowed with all powers.
Refutation of the doctrine that Brahman is devoid of distinctions;
[the section on] the Supreme Lord creating the world solely for the sake of His own sport,
and the section concerning partiality and cruelty.
The refutation of defects such as partiality and cruelty in the Supreme Lord who is supremely compassionate;
the rejection of the doctrine that the world is illusory; and the section concerning the logical consistency of all dharmas.

And [the nature] of the insentient *pradhāna*, which is the form of Śakti non-different from Paramaśiva, and of the bound soul (*baddhajīva*) as qualified by that [Śakti].

Because the agency for the manifold of dreams belongs to the Jīva only when it is obscured by the bond of Māyā, and because both the bondage and its liberation depend upon the Supreme Lord, the agency for creating dreams does not belong to anyone else.

By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*) obtained through the compassion of the Śiva-teacher, the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) and other such bonds that obstruct the soul's knowledge of Śiva are uprooted; this is the nature of the descent of grace (verse 207).

Furthermore, the descent of grace occurs in six forms, distinguished by degrees such as intense (*tīvra*) or mild (*manda*), across stages beginning with the devotee (*bhakta*) and ending with oneness (*aikya*) (verse 208).

Adhikaraṇa 303: Sāmparāya (The Time of Departure).

At the time of the Vīraśaiva initiation, there is the destruction of meritorious and non-meritorious karma accumulated prior to the Śiva-initiation; following the departure of the vital breath (prāṇotkramaṇa), there is the consideration of the destruction of both natural good and evil deeds subsequent to the initiation (303);
and for those solely devoted to Śiva, there is the attainment of the world of Śiva preceded by the rejection of merit, as well as the attainment of the state of Śiva (307).

Om, salutations to the one whose form is the Liṅga, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe.
To the one known through the Nigamas and Agamas, who bestows perfection upon his devotees. || 1 ||

Śiva alone knows the reality of Śiva, as do Nandin, Viṣṇu, and Kumāra, the son of the Mountain King;

I take refuge in Sadāśiva, the wielder of power, Sukeśa, Caṇḍīśvara, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Śilāda, Kumbhodbhava, the consciousness-filled Vāmadeva, and the venerable Revanāsiddha Guru.

I worship Revana, who is like a wish-fulfilling tree; he is initiated into the investigation of the conduct of the illustrious Śiva, his wings are fully expanded by delighting his own disciples, and he is skillful in tearing asunder irresistible passions such as lust.

The most eminent among those skilled in all the glorious arts, whose wisdom and fortitude were nourished by a preeminent abundance of full compassion from the son of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain (Śiva), shone forth,
resplendent with his focused attention upon the six *liṅgas* maintained by the supreme teacher of the Revaṇa lineage, Siddhārya.
We meditate upon that Lord of Marula, praised by the wise, for the sake of our welfare. || 8 ||
[I bow to] the Siddha known as Ekorāma, whose excellence is renowned, who is the source of immeasurable merit through the arising of his glorious virtues,
who is perfectly served by the wise, whose conduct is praised by the learned, the preeminent teacher of the Dvāpara age,
enriched by establishing the Śaiva tradition which shines through both the rising systems of Vedānta and [Tantra].

Salutations to you, the teacher of the Śiva doctrine. || 10 ||
Adorned with a glorious staff, a topknot, a sacred thread, and a shimmering deer-skin,

This commentary named *Śrīkara*, which reveals the primary meaning of every letter and word of the venerable Sūtras of Vyāsa, removes the cycle of existence, shatters the pride of wicked disputants, destroys all misfortunes, is praised by the wise, and is a mine for awakening to the truth of reality— has been composed through the grace of Śiva.

The Section on the Inquiry:
Now we shall present the Brahma-mīmāṃsā based on the Upaniṣads, consisting of the subject matter, doubt, prima facie argument, final conclusion, and purpose.

The nature of a *bhāṣya* (commentary) consists in its being based upon the words of the Sūtra— words which are refined by the inclusion of scriptural citations (*śruti*) and other materials that are concordant with the Sūtra— and in its illuminating the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introduction (*upakrama*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).

[It is the teaching] uttered from the mouth of a Guru who has been perfected through the purificatory rite of Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*) performed in the eighth month of pregnancy and who instructs others in the meaning of the Śruti.

In the system of those who desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā-darśana*), that which is established as having priority due to its being determined by the necessity of its own nature (*svabhāva-niyama*) is not an object of investigation for a discerning person, because it lacks causal efficacy (*aprayojaka*), like the teeth of a crow; likewise, that which depends on human activity and results in the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), or that which is free from doubt but lacks purpose, such as a jar,
is not an object of investigation because it lacks causal efficacy, like the teeth of a crow.
Is the object [of knowledge] qualified or unqualified, well-known or unknown?
Is there a difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva)—the objects of the notions of "you" and "I," the worshipped and the worshipper—or not?

If there were a difference, there would result a contradiction with hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Just as rivers... and so forth; if there were non-difference, there would be a contradiction with passages such as "Two birds... and so forth.

There would be the consequence of the scriptures being rendered purposeless. For the authority of the scriptures—whether of all scriptures or of some particular scriptures—consists in their primary status;

for the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is indeed characterized by those qualities (*dharma*) such as the desire for a specific object delimited by that [scripture], which are preceded by certain fixed and necessary conditions; and it is immediately after that [qualification] that this [treatise] begins.
For the purpose of destroying the needle-like anxieties in the minds of seekers of liberation who are characterized by numerous doubts such as these,

the supremely compassionate Pārāśarya— the crest-jewel of those possessing knowledge of all scriptures and distinguished by his initiation into the Great Pāśupata [order]— composed this [work], which demonstrates the fruit of the final, eternal human goal from which there is no return.
The aphorism has been set forth:
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (1.1.1).

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word *jijñāsā* (the desire to know), he indicates both doubt and the purpose [of the inquiry]. The doubt is whether Brahman, which is set forth in the Sūtra, exists or does not exist;
for its existence and non-existence are established by such passages as "In the beginning this was Brahman" and "In the beginning this was non-existent."

Herein is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): Brahman does not exist. This is because, like a jar or other such objects, it cannot be an object of perception through the eyes and other senses; because we do not observe living beings possessing knowledge of previous births; and because there is no experience of a person who has gone to the next world returning again—how indeed could a body that has been reduced to ashes return? Therefore, with every effort, one should discharge one's debts.

"One should drink ghee," as seen in such scriptural injunctions. Furthermore, just as a reddish form arises through the specific qualities of lime and turmeric powder, and just as insects arise in cow dung and similar substances, so too do sentient and insentient things arise through the specific qualities of the elements such as earth; their separation from those qualities is their destruction. Therefore, the living being (jīva) is not distinct from the body.
Furthermore—according to the non-Vedic doctrines of other schools, even in the position that the soul exists as distinct from the body, there is no Lord who governs that soul. To explain:

the Veda is threefold, consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), mantras, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Among these, [the injunction] reads: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

The *vidhi-vāda* (injunction) is primary; the *mantra-vāda* (mantra) has as its object the illumination of the meaning to be performed; and the *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) has praise as its object. [Furthermore,] it is the *apūrva* alone that will bestow happiness, suffering, and so forth upon living beings according to their own karma. Therefore, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not possible.

Furthermore: the Upaniṣadic scripture is not to be commenced, because of the absence of both doubt and purpose. For that which is doubted is the subject of inquiry, according to the maxim: "Reasoning proceeds regarding what is doubtful. Now, as for the doubt:
is it regarding the Supreme Śiva-self or the bodily self? It cannot be the former, because [it is stated]: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and "He is indeed One."

"Rudra does not stand for a second; they call Rudra oneness, eternal and ancient"— since the essential nature of the Supreme Śiva is thus ascertained by hundreds of such scriptural passages, there is no second [entity], because the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) illuminates only the embodied self (śārīrātman).

Furthermore—the fruit of the inquiry into that [Brahman] is indeed the knowledge having that as its object; for knowledge is the determination of the object of knowledge. In that case, is Brahman determined by this [inquiry] or not?

If it is determined, there would be a contradiction with hundreds of scriptural passages establishing its indeterminability (*aparicchedyatva*), and there would also follow the consequence of its being non-eternal like a jar. If it is not determined—

There would be the consequence of non-establishment due to the absence of direct realization of the object as it truly is. Nor is there any purpose [in such a view], because liberation would be impossible even through the knowledge of Brahman, given that the inherent indestructibility of both the body and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is understood from such passages as: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black; the two unborn males, the conscious and the unconscious, the Lord and the non-Lord."

Now, one might object: "Since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established by such texts as 'This Self is Brahman' and 'That Thou Art,' while the distinction between them is established by the notion of 'I,' would there not be doubt? If this is asked, the answer is no; for the scriptural texts concerning oneness have only a figurative meaning due to their contradiction with the uncontradicted notion of "I. Nor...

Even with respect to the Supreme Self, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is weak; for even though Brahman is self-luminous, we observe through experience the superimposition of "I am a human being" and so forth by means of the "I-notion" due to the power of beginningless ignorance (avidyā). This is in accordance with the maxim: "Indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived."
If superimposition were impossible, it would follow that liberation could never occur.

Furthermore, because difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory by nature—like darkness and light—it is logical to adopt one side or the other. Therefore: "from which words turn back..."
Furthermore, because [the Upaniṣads] demonstrate that Brahman is not an object of cognition through such passages as "they turn back," the Vedānta scripture is not to be commenced.
This being the position reached, we reply:
the commencement of the Brahmamīmāṃsā scripture, which establishes both duality and non-duality as proven by all the Upaniṣads, is indeed appropriate.

Because the existence of Brahman is perceived through the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception, inference, and scripture. To explain: there is the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*) from the observation of many scriptural passages such as, "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second. Furthermore, in the world, the fact that the sun, moon, seasons, oceans, time, and so forth proceed according to their own specific functions only by virtue of depending upon the Lord (*īśvara*) demonstrates this.

Since it is observed that even those endowed with wealth, grain, knowledge, and other perfect resources do not achieve all their desired goals, while conversely, even those devoid of such assistance are sometimes seen to accomplish tasks considered difficult to perform, this very fact serves as direct perceptual evidence for the existence of an omniscient Lord and for the existence of living beings.

Since in the world one observes that various effects such as chariots, gate-towers, palaces, and walls require a conscious agent, the discerning infer that likewise there exists a Supreme Lord as the creator of this entire insentient phenomenal world, beginning with space.
Just as the color red is produced through the conjunction of lime and powdered turmeric, so too [is the world produced] solely through the conjunction of the four elements, earth and the rest.
The claim that the creation of sentient and insentient things will occur spontaneously is untenable;
for we do not observe the production of animals, birds, wild beasts, and so forth through the mere conjunction of the elements such as earth alone,
so why should there not also be the production of elements characterized by the specific attributes of animals, humans, and the like, within the confines of a single body?
Because the Lord has established even those living secretly in cow dung and similar places, and because even a great king, though endowed with all resources,
is seen to be subject to mental and physical afflictions, old age, death, and poverty,
it follows that there exists a Lord who, like a sovereign, bestows fruits upon living beings in accordance with the meritorious and non-meritorious karma performed in previous births.
It is determined [as follows]:
because it is impossible for an insentient and unprecedented entity to bestow fruits corresponding to the meritorious and non-meritorious actions performed by living beings,
and because we observe that only the actions of paramours, thieves, and others bestow fruits in accordance with those respective actions.
The doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas is also charming only so long as it is not scrutinized.
By this, the theory of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others regarding an insentient cause of the world is also refuted.
In the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat)," the word *asat* teaches subtlety; for if it were otherwise, [the world could not have arisen] from that.

The contradiction with the subsequent statement, "Being was born," would be difficult to avoid. If, by the word "non-existent" (asat) here, one were to accept a state of voidness like that of a sky-flower or a hare's horn, why would the birth of a virtuous person not occur from the son of a barren woman?
Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct; for as the Sūtra says: "If it be argued that it is 'non-existent,' no, because it is a mere negation."
This very point has been elaborated in many ways by Bādarāyaṇa himself.
Furthermore, the commencement of this scripture is justified by the existence of both doubt and purpose:
[the doubt] concerning the nature of the cause of the world, which is described in both the Vedas and the Āgamas and in both the Vedāntas as being characterized by innate and infinite powers.

"I am That"— this [identity] belongs to these two which are beginningless, natural, unproduced, and indestructible by nature; yet they are bound by the noose of illusion (*māyā*), characterized by the activity of a terrible, shoreless, and essence-less saṃsāra, scorched by the fire of the three-fold afflictions, entering and exiting various bodies, distinguished by pride in caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and possessed of desires that are mutually contradictory.
There is doubt because of designations of non-difference, such as "I am Brahman" and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
As for what was stated—that if Brahman possesses attributes (saviśeṣatva), it would be limited—that is incorrect;
for even in the absence of limitation like that of a pot, there are scriptural statements such as "not this, not this," and "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," and so forth.

Determination occurs by means of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because of its suitability; for since the determination of a characteristic has the object of definition (*lakṣya*) as its domain, Brahman is defined by the Vedānta statements through its exclusion from the entire manifold of things—whether homogeneous or heterogeneous, gross or subtle—that do not possess that characteristic. Therefore, an inquiry into it is appropriate.

The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; having known Śiva, one reaches ultimate peace. Having known that Lord, they become immortal. Through the practice of churning with knowledge, the wise man burns away his bonds. Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else. Hara is both the perishable Pradhāna and the imperishable Immortal.

"The one God rules over both the perishable and the imperishable self; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire cosmic illusion (māyā). Free from sorrow, he beholds that Lord who is without desire; having known the God, the Greatness, the Ordainer, one is released from all bonds. Through such passages, by means of the knowledge of Paraśiva-Brahman, the non-dual reality of the six planes (ṣaṭsthala)...

Because the cessation of suffering caused by the noose of *māyā*—which consists of the three innate impurities (*malatraya*)—is preceded by the attainment of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), and because we observe the cessation of innate distinctions in cases such as bees and their larvae or iron and mercury, there is no contradiction with the primary meaning in Vedic texts on non-duality such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Therefore, one should not accept a secondary or metaphorical sense. Just as [in the case of] rivers...

"Flowing into the ocean, they reach their end, casting off name and form; even so, the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high"— since such passages in the Śruti unambiguously teach the relationship between that which is attained and that by which one attains, this scripture cannot be taken as having a figurative meaning.

Because it is improper to claim that numerous scriptural passages—accompanied by the sixfold marks of intentionality (tātparya-liṅga) such as the opening context (upakrama)—have a figurative meaning; for if their primary sense were abandoned, there would be a contradiction with the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.
Nor does the impossibility of superimposition (adhyāsa) entail the consequence of no liberation, since no perceptual scripture enjoining such [non-existence] is observed.

This is because the experience "I am ignorant" characterizes the individual soul (*jīva*) as being bound by the noose of *māyā* and distinguished by the body, senses, and so forth. How, then, can the attribute of having *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) be logically attributed to the Brahman that is pure, undifferentiated consciousness, given such scriptural texts as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and "Brahman is consciousness"? Regarding this [objection]:
Because of the teaching of attributes such as omniscience and wisdom, there is no consequence of [the Self] possessing attributes such as ignorance as it does for the individual soul (jīva).

If one were to admit that ignorance belongs to That [Brahman], it would follow that its status as Brahman is destroyed. If it is argued that when ignorance exists in That, ignorance itself is the means of knowledge [for its existence], this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).

Furthermore, since the scripture states, "For He is without breath, without mind, pure," it is observed that He has no connection with mind or breath; how, then, can error be possible for one who is devoid of these? Moreover, if His lack of knowledge were accepted as being like that of the individual soul (jīva), one would necessarily have to admit another Brahman to remove that ignorance.

If that were so, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of [Brahman] being subject to lack of control. For in such scriptural passages as, "The sage goes to Brahman, the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness; knowing Him alone, one transcends death; the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," its state of being beyond darkness and the fact that knowledge of it is the cause of liberation for individual souls (jīvas) are taught; therefore, [your position] is not tenable.

If it is argued that its state as a living being (*jīvatva*) is merely an illusion, like [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, we say no; for an illusion is possible only when all four categories of objects exist everywhere.
Here, however, because there is an absence of any entity other than Brahman, the occurrence of an illusion is not tenable.
For if another entity were admitted, non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost; if it is not admitted, an illusion cannot be established. It is not like a dream.
The falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) cannot be established by the observation of the successful accomplishment of purposeful action;

for if that were so, it would follow that the injunctions and prohibitions of the scriptures, the instructions of teachers, and so forth, could not be performed, resulting in the undesirable consequence of entering the Buddhist doctrine. Furthermore, [the world] is not non-existent because it is perceived, and because it differs in nature from dreams and the like.
In the second chapter, the doctrine asserting the falsity of the phenomenal world—comparable to a dream or a magical illusion—was refuted in many ways:
"They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord;
produced by mutual dependence, what else could it be but caused by desire? (8)
Holding fast to this view, those ruined souls of small intellect, performers of cruel deeds and enemies of the world, arise for its destruction. (9)
This view has been refuted in many ways in the *Kṛṣṇagītā* by such passages as these.

Furthermore, according to the maxim that "the establishment of a real entity depends upon its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*"), what proof is there for the existence of a featureless Brahman? If it is argued that the Veda (*śruti*) is the proof, then since the Veda itself falls within the phenomenal world (*jagat*), it is false; consequently, the Brahman propounded by it would also be false.

It would follow that [the Veda] is false. If the truth of the Veda is accepted, there is the loss of non-duality (*advaita*); if it is not true, then since there is no other valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of Brahman, Brahman itself would be false, like the son of a barren woman and so forth.
Furthermore, if superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not accepted, there is no sublation of liberation; if it is accepted, [liberation] is by its very nature...

There is no logical consistency in the harmonization of all the Vedāntic scriptures [if based on superimposition]. Nor can ignorance alone be the proof for superimposition, because that would entail the collapse of the self-luminosity [of consciousness]. Nor should it be said that consciousness is qualified by ignorance, as that would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). This is also true for erroneous cognitions such as "I am a living being" or "I am a human."

Because [the soul] is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, as taught in such passages as "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," the Supreme Lord alone is instructed to be the instigator of all actions; for it is said:
"O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings."
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of Māyā.

This is because such instruction is likewise found in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*. If it is argued that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) must be accepted because the sublation (*apavāda*) is seen in the Śruti passage, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth," we say no;
for the Śruti passages beginning with "a mere verbal handle" teach the identity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) with Śiva, since Śiva is the material cause (*upādāna*).
It is not prescribed that [the scriptures] convey falsity;

for the statements regarding "originating from speech" (vācārambhaṇa) serve to demonstrate its non-difference [from Brahman]. They do not lead to the falsity of the world, because the world has Śiva as its true nature.
This is also because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*). For this very reason, the venerable Vyāsa, in order to refute the falsity of the world,

stated in the sūtra "Its non-difference [from Brahman], on account of the words concerning the origin and so forth" (*tadananyatvam ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ*) that the phenomenal world produced from it possesses the same nature as its cause.
As for superimposition (*adhyāropa*), it cannot belong either to that [Brahman] or to something other than it. It cannot be the first, because Brahman is devoid of a body, senses, and so forth.

Nor can it be the second, because in passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), we see the negation of a second entity prior to creation; furthermore, if one were to accept something other than that, it would entail the collapse of pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*).

Because there is no contradiction between them— much like darkness and light— the coexistence of difference and non-difference is logical. For if the body, the embodied soul, and the Supreme Self were identical in essence, worldly transaction would be impossible, and consequently, even for the Advaitins, superimposition (adhyāsa) could not occur.

Furthermore, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does not extend only up to the knowledge of Brahman, for even beyond that, duality such as hunger, thirst, and so forth, as well as ritual action, are still manifested. Nor is a single-sided position tenable:

if non-difference (*abheda*) is accepted, there is a contradiction with scriptural texts on difference such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*); if difference (*bheda*) is accepted, there is a contradiction with scriptural texts on non-difference such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*).

Since non-dualism-in-duality (*dvaitādvaita*) alone is inherent and thus harmonizes with all the scriptures, there is no contradiction with the non-dualistic scriptures such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*); for since non-dualism-in-duality alone is inherent and thus harmonizes with all the scriptures, there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the scriptures, and if one were to accept the authority of only some [select] scriptures...

Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of being outside the Vedic fold like the Buddhists and others; and because, through the passage beginning with "from which" (*yato vā*), the relationship of cause and effect between the world (*prapañca*)—which consists of duality and non-duality—and Brahman is shown, the fulfillment of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) is established. Thus, by the three sūtras beginning with "Āśmarathya [thinks this is] a sign," it is precisely these three views, such as that of difference (*bheda*) and so forth, that are addressed here.

Because it is intended [to be so stated]; for by the sūtra, "But because of the designation of both, like a serpent and its coils," difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) alone is indicated as being non-contradictory. As stated in the Sūtasaṃhitā: "Difference-and-non-difference, as well as non-difference, and difference—these three views are held;
some say everything is eternal, another says this is all impermanent, and yet another..."

Furthermore, in the *Mahimnastava* and other works, there is a reference to the three systems of thought regarding difference (*bheda*) and so forth, specifically concerning permanence (*dhrauvya*) and non-permanence (*adhrauvya*).

If the scriptural passages such as "from which words turn back" were not intended to refer to ordinary souls who lack the grace of the Guru's glance, they would contradict the subsequent statement: "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing from any quarter."

Alternatively, [if the text] were intent on making known its own majesty, there would be a contradiction with many Vedic passages enjoining the realization of Brahman, such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Furthermore: "One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One; this understanding is not to be attained through logic."
Furthermore, because the Śruti and Sūtras— such as "I ask you about the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads" and "Because [Brahman] has the scriptures as its source"—

demonstrate the prohibition of other means of knowledge regarding Brahman, it is appropriate to commence this Mīmāṃsā of Brahman, which is endowed with all the Śrutis and consists of both difference and non-difference.

Here, by the word *atha*, the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is intended. It does not have the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*), as in the cases of "Now follows the instruction on words," "Now follows the instruction on yoga," "Now this is the Jyotis," or "Now this is the Viśvajyotis," because the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not something that can be introduced as a topic. [Objection: But since the word *jijñāsā* indicates investigation (*vicāra*), and since investigation...

If it is argued that there is no possibility of being "subjected" (*adhikṛtatva*) because [the text] is intended to function as a commentary on each respective topic (*pratyadhikaraṇa*), we say no; rather, its status as an instrument (*sādhakatva*) is established by way of expressing immediate succession (*ānantarya*), insofar as it provides the specific qualification of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) required by the injunction (*vidhi*).

For it is impossible for that [opening statement] to have as its purpose the expression of a formal undertaking (*adhikāra*). Now, since statements such as "this is the instruction on words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*) lack a basis in an injunction (*vidhi*), they do not require an undertaking. Furthermore, because an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) cannot be logically connected with the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), it is not for the sake of establishing conformity with the conduct of previous teachers.
The status of being auspicious belongs to the sound alone.
"The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious."

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*). Nor can this be taken as a separate alternative topic (like the opening of the *Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*: "Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary"), because the former subject matter has not been introduced.
For one who is uninitiated, there is no destruction of the three impurities; thus, there is no immediate succession to the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).

Furthermore, it cannot be said that something merely precedes [the inquiry] in an indefinite manner—such as eating or walking at will—because we observe injunctions regarding specific rules (*niyamavidhi*).

It is determined that this treatise on the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra-śāstra*) is preceded by that which is established for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) as the necessary and certain prerequisite for the destruction of the three-fold impurity (*malatraya*). Its subject matter is heard in the Taittirīya recension: [it is] the means for the attainment of that [Brahman] for one who desires the wisdom of Brahman.
To satisfy the inquiry "What [is it]?", he says:

"He who is the bull of the meters, possessing all forms; who was born from the nectar of the meters—may that Indra strengthen me with wisdom. May I become a sustainer of the nectar of the gods. May my body be radiant; may my tongue..."
"Most intoxicated with honey, overflowing abundantly from my two ears; you are the treasury of sacred knowledge (*brahman*), covered by wisdom (*medhā*);
protect what I have heard.
The meaning of this is: He who is Śiva, the bull among the meters (*chandas*), the lord of all sciences.

Because of the Vedic scripture, "The Lord of all sciences"; because of the scripture, "He is the universal form—the entire world-process, for this Rudra is everything"; and he who arose from the Vedas—from the sacred traditions—out of the Immortal, since the Vedas, Upaniṣads, Āgamas, and so forth, are of the nature of the Immortal.

The grammatical alteration of the word order used to express that [meaning] is Vedic; that Indra—Śiva, who possesses supreme sovereignty—may *spṛṇoti*, i.e., may satisfy or strengthen me with *medhayā*, i.e., with wisdom. For it is the power of wisdom that is sought for the sake of realizing Him. He is the sustainer of the gods for the sake of immortality—that is, for liberation.

—May I be one who bears the God; that is, may I be a bearer of the *liṅga* of Śiva, whose form is the God. The meaning is: "May I become a wearer of the beloved *liṅga* of the Supreme Śiva, manifested by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Therefore, the meaning is: "May my body be *vicarṣaṇa*, i.e., free from sin. May my tongue be most sweet with honey (*madhumattamā*).
May she be exceedingly sweet-spoken through my two ears—meaning, may I become one whose collection of causes and effects is fit for the knowledge of Śiva, which is heard extensively;
and for that very purpose, wisdom (medhā) is also prayed for. You are the treasury of Brahman—of Śiva.

The meaning is: "the substratum for perception by those who are not dependent on others. "Covered by *medhā*" means concealed by worldly intelligence; that is to say, its true nature remains unknown to those of ordinary intellect. This is in accordance with the Vedic revelation: "One who has not heard the Vedas does not comprehend that Great One," and "This understanding is not to be attained through mere logic. Thus, it is "heard"—meaning preceded by formal study (*śravaṇa*).

"Protect my devotion, knowledge, and so forth"—the sense is: "preserve them by ensuring their attainment and non-forgetfulness. Regarding the phrase "may I become a bearer of the Divine," this refers to both the wearing of external symbols (*bāhyaliṅga*) and the wearing of internal symbols (*antarliṅga*).
There is a doubt as to whether it is the meditation on the *praṇava* [that is intended]. This is because, in passages such as "Him, the supreme deity among deities;

therefore Śiva is remembered as Deva," and "the youthful one joined with the Goddess, whose body is divine," the word *deva* is seen to be used many times in reference to Paraśiva; thus, [the meditation is] on another deity.

This is because no scripture enjoining such an act is observed, and because there is an absence of traditional practice (ācāra). Since the word *dhāraṇa* is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), its meaning is established as "one who holds the deity. Thus, by means of the passage beginning with "For the sake of immortality—for the sake of liberation—may I become a holder of the deity; therefore, may He [the Lord] sustain me with wisdom (*medhā*)—that is, may He unite me [with it]," and so forth...

From the perception of the term *liṅga* in the phrase "may I become" (*bhūyāsam*), and because the meaning of the injunction is established by the existence of the *liṅga* [as a symbol] therein, it is understood that the wearing of the *liṅga* is mandatory for one desiring spiritual wisdom (*brahmamedhā*).

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "He who is the bull among the Vedas, whose form is universal," the fact that [the *liṅga*] has the *praṇava* as its ultimate referent is also indicated. He...

By the statement "The vowel is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas," its status as the bull of the meters (*chandovṛṣabhatva*) is indicated; by "Oṃ tat sarvam" and so forth, its universal form (*viśvarūpatva*) and other attributes are shown; and by "Thou art the sheath of Brahman," its status as the substratum of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmādhiṣṭhānatva*) is established for that very [syllable]. Thus, its purpose as the prescriber of internal absorption (*antardhāṇa*) is also suggested. [This applies] to the eight limbs of yoga, beginning with restraint (*yama*).
And because the internal meditation (*antardhāraṇa*) of the Vedic [mantras] is what is enjoined.

As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): since the mark of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*), namely "Viśvarūpa," and the uncompounded word "Brahman" cannot possibly refer to a limited entity, and since there is no word-break (*padaccheda*) as "deva-dhāraṇe" [but rather "deva-dhāraṇe"], [it refers to the Supreme].

Because the syntactic connection with "gopāya" (protect) is impossible, and because in the case of "bhūyāsam" (may I be), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) cannot signify an injunction since it expresses a benediction; and because the wearing of external marks has been prohibited by such statements as "having seen one bearing the [external] mark of the discus" (*liṅginaṃ cakriṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā*); [the reference is to the internal mark]: "The entire universe is within the mark, within the vital breaths, and within the mind."
Regarding the passage beginning with "They say the *liṅga* is the *jyotirliṅga*; the ascetic should always meditate eternally on the *liṅga* between the eyebrows;

the *liṅga* is indeed Brahman alone," and so forth—because these texts teach that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, has the form of a *liṅga*, [one should meditate] upon the small, stainless, supreme abode, the pure and spotless lotus of the heart, as described in the Taittirīya, Kaivalya, and other Upaniṣads.

Since the aforementioned passages specify only the wearing of the internal *liṅga* (*antarliṅgadhāraṇa*), and because the wearing of an external *liṅga* (*bāhyaliṅgadhāraṇa*) is not observed even in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*), the Vedic character of the external *liṅga* is not established.
Now, [one might object]: "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe; you are the Brāhmaṇa among the gods; you are [the leader] of the goddesses..."
Because the Śrutis declare that the non-dual Śiva is superior to the universe— stating, for example, "Viṣṇu is the lord of the Brāhmaṇas, the lord of the Kṣatriyas," and so forth—
and because the Smṛtis and Purāṇas of Manu and others, which contradict the Āgamas beginning with the *Kāmika* and ending with the *Vātula* composed by Him, lack authoritative validity.

In the *Yajurveda-saṃhitā*, within the *Tripura-saṃhāra* section— beginning with "Those asuras had three cities" and continuing with "He said, 'I choose this boon: may I alone be the lord of cattle (paśu-pati)'"— [it is shown] that among the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu there is the state of being cattle (*paśutva*), while in Śiva there is the state of being the Lord of Cattle (*paśupatitva*).

Furthermore, because the wearing of Śaiva marks such as the Śiva-liṅga, sacred ash, and rudrākṣa beads is heard of in scripture; because such a relationship is observed in the world between the one worshipped and the worshipper, or the master and the servant; and because the wearing of external liṅgas is seen to be enjoined in passages such as "he establishes the universal liṅga" (sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati), [this applies] to those bound by the nooses of passion, hatred, and so forth.

If it is argued, "What need is there to mention that we, who are devotees seeking liberation yet have attained the state of bound souls (paśu), must wear the chosen liṅga of the Supreme Śiva, which bears the mark of our Lord?"— the answer is no;
for the Āgamas such as the Kāmika taught by Śiva enjoin the wearing of the liṅga for as long as one lives, and certainly not merely for the sake of ritual action.

Because there is no room for such rites; because prohibitions against impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like are seen for one who has been initiated; because it would follow that subsequent rites such as those concerning *sāpiṇḍya* would be rendered useless; because after Śaiva initiation, since the states of being a living person or a deceased spirit no longer exist, there is no purpose for the duties of one's own caste and stage of life (*āśrama*); and according to the maxim: "One should not perform a fruitless action."

Because there would be the consequence of entering into non-Vedic doctrines due to the lack of scope for injunctions and prohibitions; because it is heard in scripture that even the liberated souls—who are the most excellent among those established in Brahman—undertake all ritual acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
and because in scriptural passages such as "Whatever Manu said is medicine," the Smṛtis of Manu and others are seen to be authoritative like medicine, as things to be followed.

Because there is an absence of corroborating evidence from Śruti, Smṛti, Āgama, Purāṇa, or Upabṛṃhaṇa texts regarding a formal initiation (dīkṣā) involving the wearing of sectarian marks (liṅga) for Brahmā and others, [the truth] should be known through the yoga of meditation (dhyāna-yoga) as delimited by faith and devotion (śraddhā-bhakti), according to the Kaivalya Upaniṣad: "Know it through faith, devotion, and the yoga of meditation. Thus, it is specifically the yoga of meditation conditioned by faith and devotion that is intended.

Because [the Lord] is taught as the means for liberation—in such scriptural passages as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for going," and "By knowing Him one passes beyond death; there is no other path for liberation"—and because it is taught that liberation has knowledge as its cause in such texts as "One should desire sovereignty from Īśvara, but one should desire liberation from Janārdana."

Since Janārdana alone is heard to be the bestower of liberation, [the injunction] "he establishes the *sarvaliṅga*" lacks a mandatory force because it ends in the present tense (*laṭ*); furthermore, there would be the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if multiple injunctions were assumed. Moreover, by the meaning of the verbal root in "he establishes" (*sthāpayati*), it is indicated that the intent is the establishment of a stationary (*sthāvara*) *liṅga*; and that *liṅga* is consecrated by the hand, hence it is called *pāṇimantra*.

Furthermore, because there is no purpose in performing external rituals for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has become stainless through the attainment of this goal, the emblems residing in a king— such as the white umbrella— are not seen in his servants; likewise, attributes residing in the Supreme Lord, such as consuming poison or wearing serpents as ornaments, serve as causes of fear [and thus would not be adopted].

Because it is impossible to uphold [such a view], because— just like the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*)— there is an absence of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) despite the practice of all learned Vaidikas (*śiṣṭa*),
because the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) does not lead to the realization of the attributeless witnessing-consciousness (*nirguṇasākṣicaitanya*),
and because the *Kāmika* and other Tantras serve as authority only regarding specific elements such as temple construction, festivals, and consecrations; [the aforementioned conclusion follows].

If it is argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* cannot be enjoined— on the grounds of the maxim of the non-applicability of Smṛti (*smṛty-anavakāśa-nyāya*)— because it contradicts direct perception, Śruti, Smṛti, and established custom, just like the Sāṅkhya Smṛti, we reply:
the doctrine of the wearing of the *liṅga* is indeed established by virtue of being ordained by direct perception, Śruti, Smṛti, Āgama, Purāṇa, and Itihāsa.

The Vedic nature of wearing the *liṅga* is established, just like the *agnihotra* and other rites. Therefore, after initiation (*dīkṣā*), the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is enjoined. In the passage, "He who is the bull among the Vedas, the omniform," the limitation of Śiva for the sake of the devotee’s meditation is appropriate; this is also evident from the *Nārāyaṇīya* section, beginning with "Salutation to the Lord of the Nidhana."
Having stated that the *liṅga* is the self of all, by the phrase "he establishes the *sarvaliṅga*," it is shown that this very [text] prescribes the wearing of the delimited *liṅga*:
"He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings."
That Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.

Furthermore, because of scriptural statements such as "I am facing east," "I am facing west," and so forth in the *Śvetāśvatara*, *Atharvaśiras*, and other Upaniṣads, they say that the subtle body (*liṅga*) resides within the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the mind. This is supported by the *Atharvaśiras*, *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*, *Liṅga Purāṇa*, and others, which state: "In the subtle body is deep sleep; the subtle body is the eternal Brahman. Thus, the term "Brahman" without any qualifying prefix refers to the hands, feet, and so forth.

In the sentence "śrutaṃ me gopāya," when the word "deva" is analyzed as a separate term, it is improper to connect it with the distant word "sopāya" by abandoning its syntactic connection with the words "dhāraṇa" (retention) and "śruta" (heard) which are in close proximity according to the *aparimitādhikaraṇa* principle; rather, it must be connected with the proximate word "brahma" itself, as in "brahmaṇaḥ kośo 'si."

Because a grammatical connection is possible through the modification of case endings, and since the word *dhāraṇa* signifies "union," liberation—which is denoted by the term *amṛta*—could not otherwise be logically established.
"O child! For one whose body is joined with the *liṅga*, there is no rebirth."
Simultaneous knowledge would be established, and from that, one would attain liberation.

Thus, because liberation is taught for that very [state] by the statement in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, and because specific fruits of external objects are prescribed by such passages as "my body is most wise" (*śarīraṃ me vicarṣaṇam*), one who stands in the "beyond-āśrama" (*atyāśrama*) state should always, or at least once, mutter [the mantra]: "all my senses... This is the *Pāśupata* vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu-pāśa*); this is the *Śāmbhava* vow.

In all the Vedas, it is stated by the exponents of the Vedas: "Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice that for the sake of non-rebirth. Furthermore, in the Kaivalya, Atharvaśiras, Kālāgnirudra, Muṇḍaka, Śvetāśvatara, and other Upaniṣads, it is taught that this very knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) should be imparted only to one who is established in the Pāśupata vow, for it is said: "To him these meanings have been declared; they shine forth to that great-souled one."

Furthermore, because of the instruction regarding the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), it is established that only one who is initiated by wearing the *liṅga* possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
Now, an objection may be raised: since no statements enjoining the wearing of the *liṅga* are seen in the *Kaivalya*, *Śvetāśvatara*, and other Upaniṣads...

If it is argued that the Pāśupata vow consists solely in the application of ashes, we say no; for it is taught as an injunction for the application of ashes specifically as an ancillary limb (*aṅga*) for the wearer of the *liṅga* who has been initiated into the Pāśupata [order]:
"For those whose bodies are joined with the *liṅga*, there is no rebirth."
This is the Pāśupata yoga for the cessation of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
The Śruti declares that this Atyāśrama is the essence of all Vedānta;
it is the Liṅga named the Supreme Brahman, which liberates one from the bonds of Paśu.
He who wears [the mark] with true devotion is called a Pāśupata;
through devotion to the three bodies, he bears the Liṅga whose essence is Paraśiva.
He who wanders upon the earth bearing this is called a Pāśupata.
The *liṅga* is Śiva, the *kṣetra* is the body, and their union is the locus of refuge.

Therefore, whoever is endowed with both the external signs and the internal limbs— whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic— he alone becomes one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī). Whoever is endowed with both the signs and the limbs, he indeed is the one who has transcended the stages of life.

Thus, it is established that [the Pāśupata doctrine] refers precisely to that [tradition], because in the *Āditya*, *Liṅga*, *Skanda*, and *Kūrma Purāṇas*, the terms *pāśupata* and *atyāśramin* are designated as synonyms for *liṅgadhārī*.
Furthermore, in the *Sadānanda-upaniṣad* of the *Sāma-jaigīṣīya* branch:
Whether he is capable of making it disappear or not, that best of the twice-born,
having consecrated the Śiva-liṅga given by his guru, should wear it upon his chest.
Thus those who know the Veda understand that it must be maintained by a Brahmin solely for the sake of liberation.
In the Atharvaṇa, in the Aiśvarya-śākhā:

"Whether he be a Brahmin or a Kṣatriya, that wise man who constantly bears the single Liṅga worshipped in the left hand—the one higher than the highest—verily for him is that Supreme Lord attainable; he attains the stainless, divine, supreme equality."
In such mantras as these, it is heard that for those seeking liberation, the meditation upon and the steady concentration (dhāraṇa) on the Supreme Lord alone are to be practiced.
In the Rudrādhyāya,
by the words "The first divine physician has spoken [this] as the superior speaker," it is [the nature] of Paraśiva himself [that is indicated].

It is indicated that [this practice] brings about the cessation of the disease of saṃsāra, which consists of the continuous flow of birth and death. For this very reason, even by the Person of the Veda (Vedapuruṣa), it is taught in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and other Vedas that the wearing of the *liṅga* alone effects liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu-pāśa*). In the Ṛgveda:
"This hand of mine is blessed; this hand of mine is more blessed."
This is my universal medicine; this is the auspicious touch.
This is your mother, this is your father; this life-giving breath has come.
This is your crawling forth; go out for the sake of Subandhu.

By this, the wearing of the *prāṇaliṅga* by the Veda-Purusha is indicated. If it is argued that in the phrase "one who touches Śiva" (*śivābhimarśanaḥ*), the intended meaning is the touching of a stationary *liṅga* (*sthāvaraliṅga*)—this is not tenable as an alternative interpretation, because since the sense "he touches Śiva on all sides at all times" is obtained, such constant touching is impossible [in the case of a stationary object]. This very point is heard in the *Vātūla*:
"Know that for him who always holds in his hand Śiva in the form of a *liṅga*, my own state— the abode of all prosperity— resides in his hand.
This is because it is taught that even an iron ball not yet separated from fire possesses the qualities of burning and illuminating inherent in that fire.

By the mere wearing of the *liṅga*, the attributes of the Supreme Lord—such as being the most blessed (*bhagavattara*) and the universal medicine (*viśvabheṣaja*) for one who performs that [act]—are established.
Thus, in the *Kāmika*:
"With the mantra 'This hand of mine is the Blessed One' (bhagavān), [one should always [worship].'"
"The wearing of the hand as a mark is declared for the Vedic Person.
Thus [it is said]. In the Yajurveda:
"O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, not terrible, and free from the appearance of evil..."
O Giriśanta, look upon us with that most peaceful form of yours.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May he deliver me from death, as a cucumber from its stem, yet not from immortality.
O Soma and Rudra, place all these remedies within our bodies;
be gracious and release from us whatever sin has been committed that is bound within our persons.
The elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of these and other mantras is heard in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is the Liṅga, the bestower of blessings—that Liṅga is declared to be the auspicious form; the [other] form is remembered as the terrible (*ghora*) body."
And among those sinless devotees, the auspicious body of the Supreme Lord shines forth between them;
they are the wearers of the *liṅga*, the perfected ones.
With that most peaceful, bliss-bestowing form in the shape of a *liṅga*, O Lord of the Mountain, shine upon me; protect me with that body.
We worship and we uphold the three-eyed, multiformed Liṅga, the eternal Brahman— fragrant and the increaser of prosperity— so that,
like a cucumber from its stem, we may be liberated from death and attain immortality.
In the first eighth chapter of the Yajurveda, in the section known as the last (praśna),
the wearing of the liṅga is proclaimed for the great-souled males of the Vedas.
O Soma and Rudra, grant us all these remedies for us alone— remedies consisting of the restoration of all vital breaths and states of being.

Whatever sin or misdeed, born of the actions of mind, speech, and body, has been committed—consisting of the impurity of *māyā*—bound within the three bodies (*tanūṣu*) of the triad of existences; [may that be purified].
"Therefore, O Lords, quickly and primarily protect us from this; out of compassion, release us completely and awaken our Lord. Thus [he said].

Regarding *somārudrā*: in the case of a dual compound of deities (*devatā-dvandva*), the rule *somārudrau devatādvandve ca* prescribes the lengthening of the first member; furthermore, the suffix *āt* is applied according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* and so forth. In that very context, two forms of the Supreme Lord are heard in scripture: "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies—one terrible, the other auspicious. Therefore, by means of the words *soma* and *rudra*...

The two forms, Ghorā and Aghorā, have been mentioned. *Yuvam* means "you two. *Viśve*—this word ending in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* (viśvā) means "all" (*viśvāni*). These *bheṣajāni* are the remedies that remove the disease of worldly existence (*bhava-roga*).
*Iṣṭa-prāṇatanūṣu*—in the three bodies (*tanūṣu*), maintain (*dhattam*) for us what is bound within those bodies.
Whatever sin— meaning misdeed— that has been committed, being permeated by beginningless ignorance, may you two primarily remove— that is, liberate us— from that;
[we pray to] the Lord Parameśvara, who is accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful one.

Since the two forms of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who is without a second, are established in such passages as these, both are likewise described here in the mantra "Somārudrau. Soma, accompanied by Umā, possesses a divine and auspicious form consisting of the five Upaniṣads; Rudra [is he who] [destroys] the suffering of worldly existence for his devotees.

He is called Rudra because he causes [evil] to flow away. The meaning is: "O you two, both of you, having assumed the forms of the *liṅga*—such as the *iṣṭa*-liṅga and others—within our bodies, destroy the sin consisting of the three impurities (*mala*) that are delimited by our bodies.
The *liṅga* of Śiva, which is the Universal God (*viśve deva*) to be known by the wise, is worn by all the gods.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing its identity as the Self, it should be worn on the neck, the hand, or the head by sages desiring liberation;

thus it is stated even in the Sāmaveda. For this very reason, the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga—which is the medicine for the disease of worldly existence—and so forth, is mandatory for those seeking liberation. Regarding the Ṛgveda mantra beginning with "pavitraṃ te":
"Rik," he says: "O Brahmaṇaspati, your purifier is spread out.
Therefore, that purifying Śaiva emblem, which is free from ailment, should be worn.
"Brahman" is declared to be the *liṅga*, and Brahmanaspati is the Lord;
for that is renowned as the purifier, and through contact with it, the body becomes pure.
Indeed, one whose body has not been purified by austerity, who lacks the refinement of the unrefined,
and who is devoid of initiation, shall not truly attain the supreme *liṅga*.
For it has been stated by the venerable Reṇukācārya, the wearer of the *liṅga* par excellence, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* (Si-Śi.,
Chapter 6): "As long as a devotee does not wear the *liṅga*, for as long as he maintains his life-breath..."
The eating of dog-flesh, for its part, would be prepared with food.
That body in which the wearing of the *liṅga* is not present is to be known as fruitless, like a living being who has abandoned its corpse.
Therefore, its wearing is prescribed as long as one lives, like the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Just as wood found in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual acts,
so too one who is devoid of the *liṅga* is excluded from all rites.

Thus, because the *Vātula*, *Skānda*, *Liṅga*, and other scriptures demonstrate that a transgression (*pratyavāya*) occurs if one fails to perform it— just as with the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*)—

the obligatory nature (*nityatva*) of wearing the *liṅga* is established. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "may I become," [it means] "may I become wise (*medhāvī*)," "may I become possessed of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasvī*"), and "I alone."
Because an injunction is appropriate in cases such as "the first month" and so forth,

because no authoritative evidence or traditional practice is seen that enjoins the assumption of another deity, and because the three impurities (mala)— āṇava and the rest— residing in the three bodies would not be destroyed if initiation were not performed.
Just as the Vedic nature of fire is established by the authority of all the Vedas,
so too the wearing of the *liṅga* is Vedic, because it is established solely through the Vedas.
"Among the Vedas, Vedānta scriptures, Purāṇas, and Āgamas,
the supreme wearing of the *liṅga* has been proclaimed for the Brāhmaṇa. Beginning thus,
[it is taught] especially in the Taittirīya branch of the Yajurveda, the most excellent of the Vedas.
For those seeking liberation, the wearing of the *liṅga* is declared to be the cause of liberation.
Indeed, he was born from the meters, from all the Vedas, and from the nectar;
Indra, possessing supreme sovereignty, is the three-eyed Lord accompanied by Ambā.
May he satisfy and gladden me with wisdom and insight,
for the sake of attaining the immortality of liberation, within all bodies at all times.
The "bearing of the deity" (devadhāraṇa) is intended for one who possesses the bearing— that is, the holding— of Śiva, the Supreme Self, in the form of a *liṅga*.
Therefore, may my body wander through the world faultless and free from sin;
may my tongue become a faculty of taste that speaks with sweet discourse.
Through my two ears, as a pair of auditory organs, I have shed abundant tears;
for they are indeed the treasury and the very abode of Brahmā and the Lord of Pārvatī.
Just as one in the world is endowed with wisdom and intelligence,
so have I diligently applied myself to learning, hearing, and the other [studies] for the sake of attaining the goal.
Because this corroborative support (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) is heard in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* through such passages as:
"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He might strike me down';
therefore, one should expand the meaning of the Veda by means of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*."
Even if there might be ignorance regarding the meaning of the Vedas when known by oneself,
what doubt could there be for great-souled ones concerning that which has been determined by the seers?

Furthermore, because prohibitions against independently determining the meaning of the Vedas are seen in such Smṛtis as, "Having seen one who bears the marks [of a sectarian] or one who bears the discus," etc., no other purpose is logical. Since these prohibitive Smṛtis lack a basis in direct Vedic revelation, they do not possess prescriptive authority, just like the Sāṃkhya Smṛti.

Because the Vedic injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*) is more authoritative; for when there is a conflict between the two statements, "He offers after sunrise" and "He offers before sunrise," one must accept the prohibition imagined by the Māyāvādins—who are like rogue Smārtas whose roots have been uprooted—just as in the case of different Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*), since we observe the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "wheel" (*cakra*). This applies if it concerns the Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*).

If the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other texts that establish the status of the supreme qualified practitioner as a bearer of the *liṅga* were to be dismissed as invalid, it would result in the doctrine falling into the category of non-Vedic (Vedabāhya) systems.
The wearing of the *liṅga* is twofold, distinguished as being either scriptural (*śrauta*) or non-scriptural (*aśrauta*).
O Śiva, the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*) through the *liṅga* is designated as *śrauta* (Vedic);
the wearing of the heated *liṅga* and so forth is declared to be *aśrauta* (non-Vedic).
For those Śrauta-Vīraśaivas who follow exclusively the path of the Vedas,
there would be a great transgression in accepting a heated liṅga.

Thus, because it is seen in the Siddhāntāgama that for one initiated into the lifelong Agnihotra there is no contradiction with other Śrauta sacrificial initiations, so too the initiation of wearing the *liṅga*— being obtained through an obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*)—
does not involve the commencement of one ritual action within another ritual action.

Thus, this restrictive rule pertains to the *sāvakāśa-dīkṣā* (dīkṣā with scope for other rites). Since Śaiva dīkṣā—unlike the dīkṣās of the Agniṣṭoma and other Vedic sacrifices—is not terminated by each individual performance (*pratiprayoga-apavargitva*), there is no contradiction between it and [Vedic rites], and their combination (*samuccaya*) is therefore logical. Consequently, for Śaivas, the performance of Vedic rituals (*ṛtvanuṣṭhāna*) is indeed mandatory, as both are based on the Śruti. As for the prohibition...
Since this [text] is intended to prohibit other lifelong *dīkṣās* that are forbidden [by scripture], it does not pertain to non-Vedic [rites].

Just as one who has been initiated for the lifelong *agnihotra* retains the entitlement to his own obligatory *upāsana* even during periods of birth-impurity (*jātāśauca*) or death-impurity (*mṛtāśauca*), so too does one initiated into Śaivism [retain his entitlement] even during such periods of impurity.

The state of possessing the qualification for the worship of the *liṅga* alone. For this very reason, in the passage "he installs all *liṅgas*," the word *pavitra* indicates that one who has taken up the *liṅga* possesses the fitness for the qualification of wearing and worshipping it at all times:
"He for whom there is the worship of the Śiva-deity and for whom there is the maintenance of the sacred fire..."
And for celibate practitioners and ascetics, there is no impurity regarding the body.
A woman devoted to the worship of the Liṅga, whether she be in childbirth or during her menstrual period,
becomes ten million times more radiant than the sun, fire, or wind; thus,
the worship of Śiva must not be abandoned even during birth or death impurity.

Thus, because the body that possesses the *liṅga* is designated as pure in such works as the *Pārāśarasmṛtisiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, there is no contradiction regarding the wearing and worship of the *liṅga*.
[Objection: But even if authoritative conduct exists, [this practice] is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it is argued that worship, the wearing of sacred ash (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth performed during times such as menstruation or birth-impurity are improper, we say no;

for [if they were improper], one would have to conclude that the slaughter of sacrificial animals, the eating of their meat, the drinking of *surā* liquor, and the like—performed during the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, *Atirātra*, *Pauṇḍarīka*, and other sacrifices—are likewise improper.
[Objection: But surely, if there were no fivefold impurity (*pañcasūtaka*) for Śaivas, it would follow that they transcend the four castes (*varṇa*).
If it is argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* by followers of the Vedas is unworthy because it entails the acceptance of cooked food and other offerings [prepared for others], we say no;

for impurity is not prescribed during the exclusive worship of one's own chosen *liṅga*, just as menstruation does not affect women during their own *agnihotra* sacrifice, nor the *pauṇḍarīka* ritual.
O Maheśvarī, just as the tongue, though capable of touching syllables, becomes pure on this earth merely by the utterance of mantras; so it is here.
Likewise, Śaivas who are in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) remain perfectly pure for the purpose of worship alone;
they are not subject to the restrictions regarding contact with others—such is the teaching of the Vedas.

Thus, because it is heard in the Siddhāntas, Āgamas, and other scriptures that one possesses the fitness for the worship of Śiva alone, and because— even though the state of being a *preta* or a living soul no longer exists after Śaiva initiation— the Śaiva Āgamas enjoin that Śaivas must perform their respective duties (*kartavyatā*) according to their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), including both prior and subsequent rites; [therefore], in the event of non-performance...
Furthermore, because of the observation of transgression [for non-performance], the performance of all duties prescribed by injunction is indeed mandatory.
Those who, performing the dharma ordained for their own caste,
incessantly worship Śrīkaṇṭha with devotion, are indeed remembered as Māheśvaras.
If men abandon the ritual duties prescribed for their own caste and worship Śiva,
