the Lord does not accept their worship.
The eternal conduct of the castes and stages of life was proclaimed by Śiva in the past;
those who act in violation of these are transgressors of Śiva’s command.
Just as punishment will befall those men who violate the king's command, so indeed shall hell be the punishment for those men who violate Śiva’s command.
Having been commanded by Śambhu through Sāmba, one should worship Śiva even while abandoning [worldly] dharma;
Sthāṇu becomes angry with whoever violates his own command.
He who worships Śaṅkara without abandoning Dharma, which is characterized by Vedic injunction and commanded by Śiva— to him Sāmya becomes gracious.

Knowledge and action are mutually dependent for the production of the fruit, like the blind man and the lame man; therefore, one who is detached [from the fruits] should practice both of them. (Śaṅkarasaṃ 185, 78–83)
Even when knowledge has been perfected, action is still enjoined for the wise;
therefore, one should not abandon action that is free from desire for its fruits.
Good conduct alone serves as an ornament for all;
a man devoid of good conduct is censured in the world.
Maheśvara is pleased by knowledge conjoined with right conduct;
therefore, one should possess both conduct and knowledge until the fall of the body.

As seen in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*, the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, and other such texts, because the performance of ritual action is demonstrated there, one performs the actions enjoined by them— even in the absence of a personal motive— just as servants carry out the orders of a king out of fear of disobeying his command.

Even when there is no purpose for performing ritual acts, those initiated into Śaivism must certainly perform them in order to obey the command of Śiva; for the scriptures state, "Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear the sun rises," and so forth, regarding even the gods such as the Wind and the Sun who possess superior knowledge of Śiva.
Since it is heard that even those who possess complete knowledge perform appropriate actions favorable to the entire world out of fear of violating the command of the Supreme Lord,
what need is there to mention human beings of limited knowledge?
Furthermore, in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
We, including Brahmā and all others, are proclaimed to be bound souls (paśus);
since you are our Lord (pati), Śiva is therefore Pāśupati.
Having spoken thus, all the deities took up the wearing of the Śivaliṅga and other emblems;
therefore, all became Pāśupatas, and for that reason Śiva is Paśupati.
Consequently, Śiva alone is indeed the object of worship for the gods beginning with Brahmā.
Likewise, there were embodied beings wearing vibhūti, rudrākṣas, and liṅgas,
with their lotus-hands bound by rosaries of pure crystal.
Having seen Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, the three-eyed Lord,
who is compassionate toward his devotees, brought about the destruction of the Tripura Asuras along with Ambā.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the sages, such as Gautama and others,
always wear the liṅga, especially upon their heads.
Furthermore, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā of the Skanda Purāṇa: "Hari, having placed the liṅga upon his chest, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā), having placed it upon his head,
both attained their respective stations after worshipping me residing within that liṅga."
Since the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga and other emblems by Brahmā and others is seen in such corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*),

and because even Nārāyaṇa is seen in the world to visibly wear the Śiva-liṅga on his hands, head, and other parts in sacred sites such as Ananta, Padmanābha, and Viṭhaleśvara, there is no occasion for the stain of doubt to arise.

If it is argued that there is no purpose in wearing external marks and so forth, because in passages such as "Know [the Self] through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga," only meditation (*dhyāna*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are designated as the causes of liberation—

[we reply: No, for in the Śruti text, "From meditating upon Him, from joining with Him, and from becoming His true nature, at the end there is the cessation of all illusion (*viśvamāyānivṛtti*)," it is [meditation] that is intended.
Because of the scriptural statement that "through meditation on Hara— meaning internal reflection, through union— meaning conjunction,

and through external concentration, through the manifestation of reality— meaning the direct realization of reality— there occurs the cessation of all illusion," and because there is no authority for restricting the scope of such scripture, [the breath is not the Self] on account of the indicative marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa).

For this reason, because there is a threefold nature of meditation on the Lord, and because that [threefoldness] is applicable here— as stated by the venerable Vyāsa in such passages as "due to the threefold nature of the meditation on the Supreme" (Cennopāsātraividhyāt)— and likewise in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"One should perform mental worship either in the heart or even in the *dahara*."
And likewise with the five-syllabled mantra, the Gāyatrī, the Rudra-hymns, and so forth.
The verbal worship has been described as being performed within the Śiva-natured liṅga that has been worn.
Endowed with faith and devotion, one should perform physical worship according to the prescribed rules, either upon the palm of the hand, in the fire, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Thus, a twice-born man who is a follower of the Vedas, constantly performing the worship of the Lord through the three modes of action, attains liberation; it is not by any other means.

By such statements as these, and according to the maxim that "the great-souled ones have one [resolve] in thought, one in word, and one in deed," we see that [the scriptures] promote mental sacrifices, renunciations, and so forth; for if [the practice) were merely internal concentration, the external limb would be fruitless, and there would follow the undesirable consequence that the impurities of action residing therein could not be destroyed.

Furthermore—just as one who has been initiated by the prior rite of *upanayana* possesses the qualification for performing duties such as the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and the daily worship of the *sandhyā* as prescribed by scriptural injunctions, so too only one initiated by the wearing of the *liṅga* possesses the qualification for the meditation on Śiva.
This is because, like fire, the initiation of the *liṅga* is the primary means for liberation; therefore, [liberation] cannot occur in its absence.
Because, by contradicting the Śruti, Smṛti, Āgama, and Purāṇas cited previously, there would follow the consequence of being outside the Vedic fold (*vedabāhya*).
"One who is intent on the meditation of Śiva, whose limbs are conjoined with the Śivaliṅga,
and who has abandoned everything other than Śiva— he is called a yogin of meditation."
The mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, wearing the linga on the head,
the topknot, the sacred thread, and likewise the sacred ash— this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
Thus, because the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga is seen in the Smṛtis of Manu, Gautama, and others as being ordained by the Vedas,
there is no contradiction for the followers of the Veda. Furthermore, since it is taught that "one should desire liberation from Janārdana," the worship of Nārāyaṇa alone [is required for that].
If it is argued that [meditation on Śiva] is necessary for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), we say no; for there is no such scriptural authority (*śruti*). [The scriptures state:
"Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, for he is the maker of auspiciousness; one should abandon everything else. Knowing Śiva, one attains ultimate peace.
"By knowing that Lord, they become immortal. The perishable is *pradhāna*; the imperishable is Hara."

The one God rules over both the perishable and the imperishable; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and by attaining His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire illusion of the world. For Rudra is one, and no second stands beside Him;
He who is the first of the gods, the Great Seer who transcends the universe—that Rudra, the Will-less One, he beholds, and being freed from sorrow, he perceives the Creator.

Because of the superior authority of Vedic injunctions such as "Through grace [he attains] greatness, the Lord," because Nārāyaṇa lacks the status of being the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, and because Smṛtis that contradict the Śruti lack authority; therefore,
by the logic of water poured before one's eyes, such Smṛtis lead only indirectly through the worship of Śiva.
Because the status of being devoted to the cause of liberation is established [in this teaching]:
"Through a thousand births as a follower of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one becomes a follower of Dvaita;
through a thousand of that doctrine, one attains the Saura doctrine."
By practicing that a thousand times, one attains the state of Gāṇapatya;
by a thousand of those, the Vaiṣṇava state is proclaimed in the world of Bhūḥ.
O highly fortunate one, by a thousand of those Vaiṣṇavas, one becomes Śākta at all times;
by a thousand of those, one is said to be an ordinary Śaiva.
O best of Brahmins, by a thousand of those [lives], one becomes a Vīraśaiva;
by that alone one attains liberation, and not otherwise, even through great effort.

This is also evident from the *Skanda Purāṇa*. It is heard in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* that Śivaśarman and others, who had attained the world of Viṣṇu and achieved identity of form (*sārūpya*) with Viṣṇu, subsequently attained liberation through the worship of Śiva. Furthermore, Vyāsa, after his arm was paralyzed, received the *Śāmbhava-dīkṣā* along with his disciples.

It is heard in that very [text] that he became one entitled to liberation (*mokṣādhikārī*). Furthermore, in the *Mahimnastava*, beginning with "The three Vedas, Sāṅkhya... and ending with "...you are like the ocean of waters," [the author] describes his own system and other systems as being straight or crooked, and thus teaches that Śiva alone is the goal to be attained by all.

In the statement "he establishes all the *liṅgas*," although the verbal suffix is in the present tense (*laṭ*), its status as an injunction is established, just as in cases such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) or "he threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). Nor is there the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the case of multiple injunctions, because, as in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni" (*yad āgneyo 'ṣṭākapālaḥ*), all [the elements] are enjoined since they were previously unestablished; for injunctions apply only to what is not already established.

Because of the Smṛti observation that "even many [are established] by a single effort," because there is no determining factor (vinigamakābhāva) to restrict the sense of "establishes" to the ground alone,
because the Śruti cannot tolerate such a limitation, and because both practices are seen as authoritative;
nor should it be argued that the wearing of the mark (liṅgadhāraṇa) is not established, since the meaning "it protects from manual labor, reflection, and worship" is also possible.

Because it would follow that the word *pāṇi* (hand) is redundant given that the mind (*mānasa*) and other organs are seen to perform worship, the interpretation that "Pāṇimantra" means "that which is consecrated by the hand" is also untenable; furthermore, if one accepts a figurative meaning for the word *mantra*, it would result in a contradiction with the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*. As for the meaning of this mantra, it is found in the twenty-first chapter of the second part of the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*.
It was clearly stated by the Blessed Vedavyāsa:
"The Yajurveda also says that the Liṅga indeed establishes everything. Therefore, one should carry the Great Liṅga while reciting the mantra over the hand according to the sacred formulas.
At the time of initiation, the Guru places the *liṅga* in the hand;
that mantra which he then recollects as Śiva is indeed called the *pāṇimantra*.
Because Maheśvara Śiva is pure, because he is the one who establishes [purity],
and because he purifies men, it is called "the Purifier" (pavitra).
Therefore, one should wear the supreme *liṅga* at all times—
whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even blinking;
whether pure or impure, one should wear the *liṅga* everywhere.
The bearer of the *liṅga*, ever pure, with a concentrated mind, should worship his own beautiful *liṅga* upon the palm of his hand with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
"One should perform the groups of obligatory rites as well as the occasional rites with the intention of offering them to Śiva for the sake of the increase of right knowledge" (Liṅga Purāṇa,
Uttara Bhāga, Chapter 21).
Now, one might object: since one who is dying from the mere poison of a scorpion lacks the capacity to consume *kālakūṭa* poison;
since one fleeing from the delusion of a snake upon seeing a rope lacks the capacity to seize the serpent;
and because there is no evidence for wearing any mark whatsoever—how can there be the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga, ashes, and rudrākṣa beads?
If it is argued that those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not accept [these marks] as they would a king's servant, it is replied:

In this world, the Supreme Lord has prescribed them for His devotees as a mandatory injunction (*nityavidhi*), which generates sin (*pratyavāya*) if not performed, for the sake of attaining union (*sāyujya*) with Him; thus, they consist of the marks of sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the Śiva-linga established within oneself.
Because it is observed that servants accept only those royal insignia prescribed by the king's command,

and because there are scriptural injunctions and teachings in the aforementioned Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth, which enjoin the wearing of the Śiva-linga, sacred ash, and rudrākṣa beads.

Because we observe the acts of supporting serpents and consuming poison, and because we see that all former devotees, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, wore the Śiva-liṅga, sacred ash, and rudrākṣa beads,
a devotee of Śiva and observer of Śiva-vows does so for the purpose of fulfilling the command of Śiva.
One should wear the linga, rudrākṣa beads, and sacred ash as the marks of Śiva.
Just as punishment is ordained in this world for violating the king's command,
so too is the Raurava hell the punishment for violating Śiva’s command.
This is also evident from the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*.
If it is objected: "Since that which possesses attributes (*saguṇa*) is illusory (*mithyā*), how can its worship lead to the attainment of attributeless consciousness (*nirguṇa-caitanya*)," we reply:
"The sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8)

This is because the Kaivalya, Śvetāśvatara, and other Upaniṣads teach that the very meditation upon the qualified [Brahman] (saguṇopāsana) leads to the attainment of the all-witnessing consciousness which is devoid of all qualities to be abandoned; and because the Rudra-sūkta and other texts, such as "With firm limbs, many-formed, fierce," teach the eternity of the body of the Supreme Lord.
Nor should it be said that the authority of the scriptures (āgamas) extends only to the parts concerning the construction of temples, festivals, and consecrations;

for it is determined that [the authority] pertains to all matters such as the *nyāsa* of all mantras beginning with the Gāyatrī, the placement of hands (*karanyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), mudrās, sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and pavilions (*maṇṭapa*),
as well as the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) being restricted solely to one who has received the *śāmbhava* initiation.

Now, an objection may be raised: since it has been taught that "he for whom these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and the eight qualities of the self (*ātmaguṇa*) do not exist does not attain union with Brahman (*sāyujya*) nor residence in the same world (*sālokya*)," and so forth—thereby indicating that all rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* lead to the attainment of the Supreme Lord by way of destroying evil (*durita*)—one might think that [the knower] goes together with both knowledge and ignorance, as stated in the passage: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together, by that [knowledge] he goes."

Furthermore, because of scriptural passages showing the combination of knowledge and action, such as "He who knows Brahman, the doer of merit, and the Taijasa [state]— this Self is to be attained through truth, through austerity, and constantly through perfect knowledge and celibacy" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.5), it is logical that the inquiry into Dharma follows immediately after.

Furthermore, having examined the impermanence of the fruits of action through such passages as, "Just as in this world the world acquired by karma perishes, even so in the next world the world acquired by merit perishes," [the scripture teaches: "A Brahmin, having become disillusioned with worlds acquired by karma, should realize that there is nothing uncreated [attained] by means of what is created," and so forth; thus, one who is peaceful and self-controlled [should seek the Self].

From such passages as these, [the attainment of] peace and so forth is understood, and from such passages as "he does not return again," the eternity of liberation (*mokṣa*) is also understood. Therefore, since the desire for that [liberation] is possible therein, the state of being a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣutva*) is indicated. Consequently, either immediately after this set of four prerequisites, or otherwise, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken. If it is argued that even the wearing of the *liṅga* (ascetic emblem), being a mere ritual action (*karman*), lacks utility for liberation, we say no.

Since the statement "There is nothing uncreated by what is created" prohibits only worldly action (*prākṛta-karman*), [the practitioner] should think: "May I become the sustainer of the immortal gods. Through meditation upon that, through union with it, and through the realization of its true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of universal illusion (*viśvamāyā-nivṛtti*). This is the Śāmbhava vow, which is declared in all the Vedas by those who proclaim the Vedas.

Therefore, one who desires liberation should practice that [meditation], and not [merely] install the *liṅga* for the sake of rebirth; for in the *Taittirīya*, *Śvetāśvatara*, *Kālāgnirudra*, and other scriptures, there is instruction that non-material acts such as the meditation upon and wearing of the Śiva-liṅga are causes of liberation, stating: "The hand is the mantra, the purifier."

It is logical that the natural rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, the *śruti* and *smṛti* passages enjoining them as means to liberation, and the statements teaching the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman immediately following the fourfold prerequisites (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), possess a mediate efficacy toward the goal— just like the statement "Food is Brahman"— according to the maxim of the gross star Arundhatī.

By the maxim "in cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the passage," since the sentence "May I become a sustainer of immortality for the gods" unambiguously defines the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman,
the previously cited scriptural passages— which establish the combination of knowledge and action and the fourfold qualifications— [are thus refuted].
The state of being doubtful is established. In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, the Lord Vyāsa said:
"Do not abandon the Prāṇaliṅga for as long as you live, by way of a solemn vow;
O child, there shall be no further birth for you in the wombs of mothers."
Having thus described the wearing of the *liṅga* by one endowed with the fourfold means of accomplishment (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*),

the injunction for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman is then set forth. This is also stated by the venerable teacher Reṇuka, beginning with "The state of the body and the knowledge of the body," and ending with "These must be performed with effort by the devotee of Śiva."
The same has been taught in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*.
Nor should it be argued that "if liberation is possible through the mere wearing of the *liṅga*, then that alone is sufficient;
what is the use of the effort of investigating the Upaniṣadic scriptures? For [it is said]: "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, it should be heard..."

Because it is heard in such passages as "He should be reflected upon, He should be meditated upon; one should engage in the hearing of the Vedāntas," that even for those liberated from the bonds of *māyā*, the duty of obeying the command of the Supreme Lord must be performed until the cessation of the appearance of *prārabdha* karma; therefore, in the absence of that [obedience], [the following applies].
Because there is an absence of firm conviction regarding the knowledge of the signs and their corresponding limbs,
and because [otherwise] desire, anger, and so forth would find the opportunity to enter the internal organ,
one should spend the time from birth until death in reflection upon the Vedānta.
For the sake of abandoning desire and the like, and for the increase of the knowledge of Śiva.

And because of this traditional authority (*smṛti*): just as the *Sautrāmaṇī* and *Bṛhaspatisava* sacrifices— which lack any independent injunctions as primary rites— attain status as both [independent and subsidiary] by the force of two types of injunctions through their being subsidiaries to the *Agnicayana* and *Vājapeya* respectively, so too there is no contradiction between the wearing of the *liṅga* and the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*).

Nor should it be argued that, like the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, the wearing of the marks (liṅga-dhāraṇa) is also a ritual action (karman) and thus a cause of liberation through a traditional succession;

for this would contradict the direct scriptural authority (pratyakṣa-śruti) cited previously. Furthermore, since hearing [the scriptures] (śravaṇa) and so forth are also ritual actions, they too would consequently be causes of liberation.

It could not be so; for if that were accepted, since the primary cause for the cessation of the bonds of *māyā* would be absent, it would follow that the possibility of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) as a scripture would be precluded. If that were the case, your excellence of scholarship would be nothing but a cutter of its own roots.

Just as the sprinkling of rice (*brīhiprokṣaṇa*) and other such rites are combined for the sake of heaven by virtue of being causes for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) arising from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), so too all previously performed actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice when dedicated to the Supreme Lord, as well as the four means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth,
are combined for the sake of liberation by virtue of being instrumental in the knowledge of Śiva and the wearing of the Śiva-linga.

Now, an objection is raised: since there is no identity of the agent between the scripture on wearing the *liṅga* and the scripture on the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), how can there be a rule of sequence? Is there identity of agent here either through the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgitva*), as in the case of the *Ādhāna* and the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices;
or through the relationship of multiple subordinates prompted by a single principal (*ekāṅgiprayukta-anekāṅgatva*), as in the case of the five *prayāja* offerings?

If it is argued that [the knowledge of Brahman] functions either by depending on the impulsion of another qualification— like the *godohana* vessel and so forth— or by virtue of having a single fruit— like the six sacrifices or the medicinal herbs and so forth— it is replied: this is not so,
because of the previously cited Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other authorities such as the Taittirīya, Śvetāśvatara, Kaivalya, Jābāla, and Kaṭhavallī.

Regarding "nanau": let it be granted that the wearing of the *liṅga* is obligatory; however, among the three types of injunctions prescribed in Jaimini’s Sūtras, which one is adopted here—an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), or an exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*)? It is not an original injunction, like the rule "one sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), because the wearing of the *liṅga* is already established by many Śruti texts such as "Thy purifier is spread out, O Lord of Prayer" (*pavitraṃ te vitataṃ brahmaṇaspate*).

The injunction regarding the wearing of the Śiva-linga, other than the topknot, sacred thread, ashes, and Rudrākṣa beads, is not a restrictive rule (niyamavidhi) like "one threshes rice," because the wearing of those other items does exist; nor is it an exclusive specification rule (parisaṅkhyāvidhi) like "five five-nailed animals are edible," because the duty to wear the linga and the non-duty to wear those other items cannot coexist at one time.

If it is argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* is not Vedic because the possibility of its being a mere cumulative injunction (*samuccaya*) is untenable, we say no; for it is established even by three types of injunctions.

In the passage, "May I become a bearer of the *liṅga* of the immortal gods," there is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). As for the wearing of the *liṅga*, [it is further supported by] the text "the universal *liṅga*... [etc.]...
If it is argued that [the injunction] "he establishes" (*sthāpayati*) and so forth is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) because it is prescribed by many scriptural passages—[we reply:

according to the principle of the relationship between the dependent and the supported (*upajīvya-upajīvaka-bhāva*), all sentences such as "he establishes the *liṅga*" are dependent [on the primary injunction], since the word "bearing" (*dhāraṇa*) does not apply to the fruit [of the action]; [this dependence] is found in the passage: "May I become the bearer of the immortal of the gods. (*amṛtasya devadhāraṇo bhūyāsam*).
Because it is heard that [the Veda] prescribes the wearing [of marks] which has liberation as its fruit, it possesses the status of being foundational; therefore, there is no fault.

Furthermore, it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—preceded by the prohibition of the Tantric branding of the heated linga, trident, drum, conch, and discus—it establishes the Śrauta practice of smearing ashes and the Rudrākṣa.
Because of the hearing of injunctions regarding the wearing of the *liṅga* and so forth;
and there is also an injunction of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*)—
namely, [the injunction] concerning the sacred tuft and thread (*śikhāsūtra*), preceded by the prohibition of Tantric branding with the heated *liṅga*, trident, hand-drum, conch, and discus.

It is established that this is a "mark of Śiva" (*śivalāñchana*), because, like the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣas, the wearing of the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*sūtra*) is heard [in scripture] as belonging to Śiva alone.

This is so because those who know the meaning of all the Vedas— having obtained it through the grace of the Supreme Lord— [interpret] the scriptural injunctions for the wearing of the *liṅga*, such as "He who [is the master] of the meters," and so forth, [in this manner].

[They are] those who proclaim the teachings based on scripture, logic, and personal experience— such as Sarvajña, Vyāsa, Dūrvāsas, Reṇuka, Śveta, Upamanyu, Dadhīci, Kumbhasambhava (Agastya), and others— and who, unlike the Buddhists and other schools, do not rely on logic alone;
[they are those who follow] the path of devotion and ritual action as propounded by both the Nigamas and Āgamas and the Vedānta.

If it is argued that since the meaning of "causality" is already established by the word *atha* itself through its expression of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), why is the word *ataḥ* used? We reply:
because in passages such as "We have drunk the Soma, we have become immortal," there is the scriptural hearing of even the fruits of natural karma being eternal;
and likewise in "Om, the single-syllabled Brahman," "That Sun is Brahman," "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," and "Food is Brahman."

In passages such as "He understood" (*vyajānāt*), since various types of meditations (*upāsanā*) are observed, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is employed to dispel the doubt as to how liberation can possibly arise from wearing the *liṅga* favored by the Supreme Śiva, and to firmly establish its causality. [This is done] while [acknowledging] that the fruit of ordinary karma is impermanent.

Since there exist many scriptural passages such as "The world accumulated through merit perishes," the scripture recited in the context of Brahman— namely, "May I become the sustainer of the immortal gods"— is more powerful than the scripture recited in the context of ritual action (*karma*); therefore, one should meditate solely on Śiva, the maker of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else.
"For Rudra is one; he does not stand for a second. Thousands are remembered as being beyond count, yet they are not seen.

"You are Viṣṇu, the sovereign of the gods and the Brāhmaṇas; you are the sovereign of the Kṣatriyas and the Brāhmaṇas, and you are supported by the Brāhmaṇas"—since, according to such scriptural passages, the worship of Śiva alone is that which is enjoined.

"Indeed, he who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity; he does not reach the higher one and becomes worse off"— since such a scriptural passage declares the sin incurred by abandoning one's own deity,
Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, while Mādhava is that of the Kṣatriyas.
Likewise, Brahmā is for the Vaiśyas, and the Leader of the Gods (Śiva) is for the Śūdras.
The Blessed One Rudra is the Brāhmaṇa, Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya,
Pitāmaha is likewise the Vaiśya, and Purandara is the Śūdra.

This is because the status of Śiva as the deity of the Vedic Brahmins is heard in the *Pārāśarya Purāṇa* and other such texts; and because the intent of the Vedic revelation, "Having come from the waters... (*apām...*), and the Smṛti passage, "The state of immortality is indeed declared to be a station that endures until the dissolution of the elements" (*abhūta-saṃplavaṃ sthānam amṛtatvaṃ hi bhāṣyate*), is determined to be the teaching of immortality as required up to the point of the dissolution of the elements.

Since the maintenance of immortality by the gods is enjoined through its being the uncommon cause [of that immortality], therefore, for the sake of knowing Brahman, whose nature is Paśupati, one must engage in the inquiry into the Vedānta texts:
"He who is of true desires and true resolves—he is to be sought after, he is to be desired to be known; indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, it is to be heard..."

In such passages as "it is to be reflected upon" and "it is to be meditated upon," an injunction for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is heard. Furthermore, because in Vedic texts such as "They consider the cessation of the phenomenal world, the peaceful, the auspicious, the non-dual, as the Fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known," the word *ātman* is seen to denote Paraśiva, it cannot have any other meaning.

In this context—the phrase "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*)—the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*), not in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). This is because an inquiry necessarily requires an object of inquiry. Even if the residual genitive were adopted, the status of Brahman as the object of inquiry would still be taught, since a general relationship must ultimately reside in a specific one. Thus, Brahman is directly [the object].

To abandon the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and instead postulate an indirect object-status by way of a general category would be a futile effort; for if the primary element is accepted, those things required by it are established as a matter of course. In this sūtra, one should not accept the supply of the word "to be performed" (*kartavya*), because [the action] is understood simply from the knowledge of the subject matter and the purpose.

Because human activity is possible [in such cases], and because in our established doctrine (siddhānta) the word-potency is not accepted as residing in that which is connected with an action to be accomplished;

for there is no fault of restatement (anuvāda-doṣa) when there is a restatement of what has not been previously established. But how is the fault of restatement avoided merely by supplying the word "to be performed" (*kartavya*)? [This applies] in cases such as: "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice, for the sake of non-monotony."

Since we observe that even with the suffix *tavya* there is an instance of restatement (*anuvāda*), and since a restatement of what has not [otherwise] been established can be possible— as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*)— without even supplying a word meaning "to be done," there is no need for such a supply in order to avoid the charge of being a mere restatement.

Furthermore, since this *sūtra* has as its purpose the investigation of the principles required for the injunction of hearing (*śravaṇa*), there is no need for textual supplementation (*adhyāhāra*) in order to achieve consistency between the *Śruti* and the *Sūtra*; for the injunction of hearing is not accepted [as being directly stated here].

Because it lacks the characteristics that necessitate the status of an injunction, it is certainly not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). This is because the fact that inquiry is the cause of ascertainment...

This is because that which indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is established by common worldly usage. Nor should it be argued that the status of being the cause of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman has not been established;

for once it is established that mere inquiry is the cause of the determination of the object of inquiry, and that the means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman is the cause of its direct realization, it follows that "hearing" (*śravaṇa*), in the form of knowledge derived from the Vedānta texts after they have been investigated, is the cause of that realization.

Nor is it a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), because there is nothing to be excluded. Nor can inquiry conducted without a teacher be what is to be excluded, for [the scripture] says: "A Brahmin, having examined the worlds acquired through action, should attain detachment; there is no uncreated [world] to be gained by the created. For the sake of knowing that, he should approach a teacher alone, with fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. This is for the purpose of attaining knowledge.
Since it is possible for the prescribed approaching of the teacher (*gurūpasadana*) to serve as a visible means [to knowledge], it is improper to assume an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*). Furthermore,

because the purpose of attaining realization is fulfilled by the inquiry into the Vedānta alone, the exclusion of independent inquiry is already established by the very injunction regarding the approach to the teacher.

This is not an injunction of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā-vidhi*), because there is no possibility of other means being obtained simultaneously [with this one]. Nor can it be said that the purpose is to exclude other activities, such that one must engage in the inquiry into the Vedānta for as long as one lives; for it cannot be maintained that the exclusion of other activities is possible, as that would lead to the same fault [of over-extension] in that very case. Furthermore—

Whether for one who has renounced (saṃnyāsin) or one who has not renounced (asaṃnyāsin), there must be a cessation of other activities. It cannot be the latter case, because it is impossible [to remain without such activity]. Nor can it be the former, because this is already established by the very injunctions prescribing renunciation; for even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is heard that "he who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality," which implies that only one whose activity is directed toward nothing else is the means to liberation.

Since the root *sthā* preceded by *sam* is observed to denote completion in such cases as "the *agniṣṭoma* conclusion" (*agniṣṭomasaṃsthā*), and since the completion in Brahman denoted by the term "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*) consists in the absence of any other activity, this is stated explicitly in the *Atharvaṇa* passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon all other words."
Furthermore, because of the prohibition of other activities, as stated in the Smṛti: "One should spend the time from sleep until death in the contemplation of Vedānta.

Therefore, since the prohibition of other activities is already established by another injunction, one should not accept its prescription here while admitting the threefold defect (traidoṣya). For this very reason, it is said that there is an injunction for another auxiliary factor (sahakāryantara-vidhi) according to the alternative view (pakṣeṇa).
Regarding the third [point], "of one who possesses that, like knowledge and so forth," the most venerable teachers [state] in the *Kaivalyacandrodaya*:

"Nor can there be an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) regarding hearing and the rest, because [the goal] is already attained through no other means; nor can there be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) or an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*), as these are not possible in the case of hearing and so forth."

Thus they say. Therefore, since there is no injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*), there is no need for either figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) in order to achieve uniformity with that [injunction]. Or, even if there were an injunction for hearing, still there would be neither figurative indication nor ellipsis; for in all cases, uniformity between the *Śruti* and the *Sūtra* is merely inferential. Consequently, this [sūtra] is intended to set forth the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*).
In this scripture, the fact that the knowledge of Brahman is the purpose (*prayojana*) because it is desired, and that Brahman is the subject matter (*viṣaya*), is established by the Veda itself.
Since the desired knowledge of Brahman cannot be attained without inquiry (*vicāra*), it is taught that inquiry must be undertaken.
Furthermore, Brahman is not devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*); for its supreme power is heard of as being manifold and inherent (*svābhāvikī*).

From the scriptural revelation that "knowledge, power, and action [are His]," it follows that Brahman, the object of inquiry, is eternally both with and without form. Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, who is accompanied by Umā, who is three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil— the one, all-pervading, wonderful Being, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, consisting of consciousness and bliss, and formless— one should [realize Him].

"the sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness"—because of such designations [in scripture], and because there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the *śruti* [to a specific meaning]. Now, one might object: since only the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman constitutes knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), that alone is what releases one from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu-pāśa*).

But that is knowledge with attributes (*saguṇajñāna*). Because [all] phenomena (*dharma*) are subject to sublation, for it is heard in scripture that "therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this,'" and "O Gārgī, the Brahmins declare that imperishable (*akṣara*) to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," and so forth, through the negation of all phenomena; thus, "It is one only, without a second; there is no diversity whatsoever here."

If it is argued that [the Self is devoid of qualities] because non-duality is taught by such passages as these, and because qualities are denied in the scriptural text, "The Witness is the cognizer, alone and devoid of qualities," we say:
no; for the statement "not this, not this" (neti neti) is intended to negate both the manifest and unmanifest worlds (prapañca) previously established by the preceding statements.

Furthermore, because the attributes of Brahman are not prohibited; and thus says the Sūtra: "For [the scripture] prohibits only the extent of what is manifested in nature, and thereafter it speaks of more. Otherwise, there would be a prohibition even of bliss and other such qualities. Moreover, sentences such as "without a second" form a single syntactical unit with the preceding sentence, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and therefore relate to the process of creation.

Because in the time prior to creation, there is the realization of non-duality and supremacy, and because even the scripture concerning the "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa) refers to the absence of the three qualities such as sattva and so forth—

otherwise, there would be a contradiction with statements such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving"— this was the view of the former teachers, both Vedic and others, such as Revanasiddha and Marulasiddha, at the time prior to creation.

The intended meaning is that because there is no origination of the manifold (prapañca) consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, the scriptural passages concerning non-dual Brahman have that [Brahman] as their sole subject matter.
Thus it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone existed. And likewise in the Atharvaśiras:

"I alone existed first; I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me" (Aitareyaka). According to the principle of uniformity of purport (*gati-sāmānya-nyāya*) found in all the Vedāntas, non-duality (*advaitatva*) must be understood as existing in Brahman at the very time prior to creation.
For it is heard in scripture that Brahman, when intent on creation, becomes manifold through desire; thus says the Śruti:

"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. Furthermore, even the statements regarding non-duality refer only to that time prior to creation, because at that time there was an absence of difference which requires a counter-correlate. Likewise, the statements regarding non-difference, such as "All this has that as its self," [refer to the same].

Passages such as "All this is indeed Rudra," and "The Self alone is all this," are intended to demonstrate the non-difference of the universe from Brahman, who has assumed manifold forms by His own will. Furthermore, the non-difference between cause and effect is established through examples such as clay and the like, as well as by the promise that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all. Thus it is said: "He who knows me, he knows all the gods."
Thus, it is established that in the *Atharvaśiras*, the realization of all knowledge is achieved through the knowledge of the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva*).

If it is asked, "Since *prakṛti*—the material cause of the universe—exists prior to creation, how can there be non-duality (*advaita*)?", the answer is no; for she is non-different from Him, being His power (*īśvara-śakti*), just as the power of a magnet to attract iron is not distinct from the magnet itself.
Just as the power of burning belongs to fire, so too Prakṛti is seen to be non-different from Him; and thus says the Śruti:

"The divine power of the Self, hidden by its own qualities," and "The supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action. Furthermore, this supreme power belongs exclusively to Śiva, according to the Śrutis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and other texts.
This is well-established. Therefore, those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) should not accept the non-Vedic doctrine of the falsity of the world and non-duality (advaita).

For scriptural passages such as "not this, not this" (neti neti) do not merely teach the eternal nature of the partless Brahman through negation; [they also teach His positive attributes], as seen in texts such as "He is the fierce one, multiformed with firm limbs."

For the Śrutis declare the eternity even of the divine, auspicious forms of the supreme Śiva, which are beyond material nature (*aprākṛta*), just as they do for the relationship of subordinate and sovereign established in the *Saṃyuktādvaita-pāñcarātra* and other systems. Nor do we maintain that [the Lord] possesses parts merely by virtue of being the possessor of limbs (*aṅgin*); for that would entail the consequence of Him being a sufferer of pleasure and pain like a living soul (*jīva*), whereas He is all-pervading like space.

Furthermore, [the Advaita view] would entail the subversion of hundreds of scriptural passages such as "He is full" (pūrṇa). For one who asserts an absolute difference between them—like that between a jar and a cloth—there would be the consequence of subverting scriptural texts concerning the proposition and the illustration, such as "By which the unheard becomes heard. Nor can it be the case for one who asserts the falsity of either one, like the rope and the snake, given the scriptural description: "His desires are true; His resolve is true."
Because it would entail the destruction of the infinite, natural, auspicious qualities established by the *śruti*;
because it would entail the destruction of the causality of the origin of the world and so forth as ordained by such *śruti* passages as "From which indeed these beings are born";
and because it would contradict the *śruti* that establishes the proposition that through the knowledge of one, all is known.

Furthermore, because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that the worship of Brahman as both with and without form would be fruitless. Therefore, our final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that we are proponents of the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), which is established by the harmonization of all scriptures regarding the inherent nature of reality. This is evident from such scriptural passages as: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," and "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas," which [affirm] the non-duality of the One.
Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpa*) because he is taught to have uncommon attributes such as omniscience.
The individual soul (*jīva*), being bound by the natural fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), is established by universal experience as possessing limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*).

Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), has the nature of insentience (*acidrūpa*) because it is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the universe beginning with Mahat.
If it is asked how the Supreme Śiva—who is the substratum of all and all-pervading—can possess both a formal (mūrta) and a formless (amūrta) nature, the answer is no;
for by its formal nature, the wind exists in only one part of space, whereas by its formless nature, it pervades the entire world.
Likewise, the Pradhāna is formless in the form of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, Kalā, Ākāśa, and Vāyu, while it is formal in the form of Tejas, Salila, and Pṛthivī.

And since corporeality is also observed [in Him], what more need be said of Paraśiva, who is endowed with infinite powers and is capable of accomplishing even the impossible? For we see many scriptural statements such as: "Salutations again and again to You who are of diverse forms and of universal form."
Due to the state of contraction of His power, Maheśvara is proclaimed in the Vedāntas as being partless and devoid of qualities prior to creation.
Indeed, because of the expansion of his power, the Lord Rudra— who liberates bound souls from their fetters— is proclaimed as the possessor of infinite qualities.
Just as the wind manifests in both embodied and unembodied forms,
so does Sadāśiva shine forth, bestowing grace upon all.
Just as Māyā has the form of the world consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest, so too does Śiva;
"He possesses the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest"—this is the proclamation of the Vedānta drum.
Not knowing this heart of the Vedanta, others, deluded and considering themselves learned, propound a false meaning of the scripture in the world.
Because the Śaiva Āgamas contain such passages as these which censure the views of certain Vedic schools, they are not to be accepted by the learned.

Nor is the contradiction of difference and non-difference—like darkness and light—possible; for does this occur at the same time, or through a difference in time, like day and night? It cannot be the first, because [the categories] such as form and genus, word and meaning, quality and substance, and so forth, [are established as distinct].

In the expression "the jar is dear," because name, form, existence, appearance, and dearness are manifested together, one perceives Nature— which possesses the nature of the unreal, the inert, and suffering— as the cause and effect within the non-dual Brahman, which consists of consciousness, bliss, and so forth; therefore, since that is what is observed, there is indeed nothing that is impossible when it is seen.

The first [position] is untenable because it contradicts logic; for if [the world] were merely an illusion like a mirage in the desert, there would be a contradiction regarding the attainment of objects and the accomplishment of purposeful action.

Nor is the second [position] correct, because we observe both scriptural revelation and experience—such as the Śruti text "Two birds..."—which demonstrate that during the state of saṃsāra, there is a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, [while the teaching] "That thou art" refers to their identity.

Thus, on account of numerous scriptural passages, experiences, and observations such as these, non-duality (abheda) is indeed logical in the state of liberation. Since the scripture "He whose desires are true" establishes that the desires of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman— consisting of creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace— are true, the phenomenal world (prapañca) is not [unreal] like a magical illusion or the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
The reality of the body of empirical usage [is not established],

nor is the possibility of superimposition [justified] by the rule that the reality of the effect follows from the reality of the cause; for it is impossible for Brahman— which is devoid of attributes and devoid of action— to be the object of inquiry.

If it is argued that it is logical for the variegated Brahman (śabalabrahman)—which is the Lord falsely reflected as a superimposed image of the qualities of a primary sentient being—to be the object of inquiry, we say no; for there are scriptural passages such as: "That which the mind does not think, by which they say the mind is known—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship."

Because, by means of demonstrating that [the Self] is not graspable by the organ of speech and so forth mentioned in the preceding sentences, it aims at the praise of Brahman as the witness of all the senses through syntactic unity with the principal sentence; because the meditation on [Brahman] with attributes is established by the opening and other [structural indicators] of the context; and because otherwise, even the [meditations on Brahman with attributes] in the *Garuḍa* and *Māntrika* Upaniṣads would result in impossibility.

If it is argued that the state of being the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, characterized by attributes (saguṇa-brahmatva), is merely imagined (kalpita), then it would follow that the direct Vedic and Vedāntic scriptures, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other treatises on devotion, ritual action, and knowledge— which enjoin such [conceptions]— would be rendered as good as water poured out in vain. This is because there would be no non-imagined, non-ignorant (avidyaka) Lord.
Whose devotion, faith, and trust could there be toward one who is like a counterfeit *sālagrāma*?

How could a Lord fashioned by the imagination, even when propitiated through various kinds of ritual acts, become the bestower of diverse fruits? Furthermore, even injunctions such as "Be one for whom the mother is a god," "Be one for whom the father is a god," and "Be one for whom the teacher is a god" have been abandoned; thus, the state of being beyond discourse has resulted.

Moreover, if consciousness were thus superimposed as being qualified by lordship (*īśvaratva*), there would be no fear even from the Lord, just as there is none from a rope-snake or similar illusions.

Yet, fear is heard of even for those possessing direct knowledge (*aparokṣavidyā*), such as the Sun and others, in passages such as: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises," and so forth. Furthermore, [the scripture states]: "The two unborn ones—the knowing and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord; for the one unborn [soul], while enjoying, lies along with the other."

In such scriptural passages as, "Another unborn [soul] leaves this [body] whose enjoyments have been experienced," the non-born nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is demonstrated; thus, the doctrine that they are merely imagined (*kalpita*) is indeed non-Vedic.
Furthermore, what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates with respect to a featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) Brahman? It cannot be verbal testimony (*śabda*), for...

For both primary denotation (*śakti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) function only when preceded by the delimiters of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiters of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).

Nor can it be established through inference (*anumāna*), because inference functions only when preceded by the delimiter of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), the delimiter of the pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*), and so forth; and since the supporting arguments (*tarka*) for such inference are themselves rooted in pervasion (*vyāpti*), they too must be preceded by the delimiter of the pervaded (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) and other such factors.
Because [knowledge] proceeds from activity; for knowledge devoid of specific qualification lacks the capacity to eliminate doubt, error, and the like.

This is because only a certainty (*niścaya*) that possesses the same mode (*prakāra*) and the same object (*viṣaya*) is capable of eliminating error and so forth. Otherwise, if there were a certainty of a jar as a substance (*dravyatva*), the doubt "Is there a jar in the house or not? would not arise.

God (Īśvara) is the substratum of attributes not sublated by His own [knowledge], or rather, He is the substratum of attributes not sublated by His own knowledge, because He possesses the nature of being a subject (dharmitvāt), like a jar; or because He possesses the nature of being a Self (ātmatvāt), like Devadatta. Attributes such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth are not sublated by the direct realization of Brahman, because they do not reside in anyone other than God, just like Godhood (*īśvaratva*). Nor is there a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) [in this argument].

Because, regarding an entity devoid of intrinsic nature (*nirdharmaka*), the contradiction inherent in stating "my mother is barren" due to the existence or non-existence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhakapramāṇa*) results in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all worldly transactional usage (*sarvavyavahāra*); this very consequence serves as the subverter of the opposing position (*vipakṣabādhaka*).

Thus, in the Śruti passage, "The Self, indeed, should be seen," having first restated the fruit which is the direct realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasākṣātkāra*), [it proceeds] by way of its means...

It is untenable to claim that "listening" (śravaṇa) is enjoined; for since the verbal root *śru* means "to hear," it has sound as its object and thus signifies auditory cognition (*śrāvaṇajñāna*). Furthermore, such cognition cannot be an object of injunction, because auditory cognition is already accomplished simply through the study of the Veda as delimited by the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*). Nor can it be argued [that it is enjoined] because we observe usage such as "he listens to the meaning of the Veda" (*vedārthaṃ śṛṇoti*).

It must be stated that even with respect to the knowledge of meaning (*arthajñāna*), the verbal root possesses a primary denotative power (*śakti*); for since that [knowledge] can be accounted for through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone, there is no need to postulate two separate powers.
Furthermore, in cases such as "he hears the sound of a lute," there is no possibility of suspecting the opposite—that the root lacks power—because the knowledge of meaning is absent.

Or, let it be granted that there is power even with respect to the knowledge of meaning; nevertheless, even that is not something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), because the study of the Veda has already been completed by one who has studied the *Sāṅga* [Veda].
Since the connection between words and their meanings has been understood, [the truth] is indeed known through such statements as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite";
for is it not the case that while there is an initial superficial comprehension, the knowledge characterized by definitive ascertainment is not attained through mere study?
If this is argued, we say no; for even that [ascertainment] is possible, like the worm in the bee-hive.
Because [the Self] is not subject to injunction, as it is attained through the compassionate glance of a Guru preceded by the cessation of innate ignorance;
nor should it be argued that "for this very reason, inquiry is what is intended by the word 'hearing' (*śravaṇa*)," because that would entail a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) for an injunction.
On this point, they say: beginning with "Indeed, it is not for the sake of the husband's desire that the husband is dear," and continuing up to "but for the sake of the Self's desire..."

By the passage ending with "everything becomes dear," the fact that the Self alone is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*)—by virtue of its being the nature of unsurpassed bliss—is stated; and since the conclusion says, "Verily, when this Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known; verily, so much, my dear, is immortality," it follows that knowledge of the Self alone is the means for attaining that [immortality].

Thus, having restated that such knowledge of the Self is "to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), it is determined that, upon the inquiry into its means, the injunction regarding those means is provided by the words "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) and so forth. For, since reflection (*vicāra*) is the unique cause for the knowledge of the Word (*śabda-jñāna*), it is understood that reflection itself is what is enjoined by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*). That...

In the passage beginning with "I ask you about that person known from the Upaniṣads; one who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One; this thought is not to be attained through reasoning," Brahman is established as being cognizable through the Vedas alone.

Since there is an absence of any other means of knowledge regarding Brahman, when the requirement for a means of perception arises in the injunction "it is to be seen," the Vedānta texts themselves are that very means.

And that [mere hearing], if not investigated, does not produce certainty. The resulting meaning is this: the Vedāntic statements, when investigated and accompanied by reflection (*manana*) and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), are the cause of the direct realization of the Self.

Nor is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) ever unobserved in the case of an injunction; for example, in the passage: "Half [of the animal] is measured within the altar (*antarvedi*), half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*)."

[Examples of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) include: that which indicates a specific location, as in "one who has a son born and whose hair is black should establish the sacred fires" (*jātaputraḥ kṛṣṇakeśo 'gnīn ādadhīta*); that which indicates a specific age, as in "the *Ṛk* is recited loudly" (*uccair ṛcā kriyate*); that which indicates the Veda by means of the word *ṛk* and so forth;

that which indicates the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), as in "as many horses as one might receive as a gift" (*yāvato 'śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt*); and [the prohibition] "one should not look at the rising sun."

Since we frequently encounter the indication (lakṣaṇā) of exclusion (paryudāsa) in passages such as "one does not choose a Ṛṣi-lineage," and the indication of being a means to a powerful undesirable result in prohibitions for human ends such as "one should not eat *kalañja*," it is therefore appropriate that the injunction to investigate [the Veda] is based on indication.

Now, an objection may be raised: since even inquiry (*vicāra*) is established in the world as a cause for determining the object of inquiry, why should it be enjoined? This is not so; for even if an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) is impossible here, there is scope for a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). To explain: injunctions are of three kinds—original injunction, restrictive injunction, and exclusive injunction (*parisaṅkhyāvidhi*). Among these, in all three periods of time...
The first type of injunction has as its fruit the attainment of that which was not attained by any other means of knowledge;
for example, in the case of "He sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), sprinkling is not established by anything other than this injunction.

The second type of injunction has as its fruit the fulfillment of the unattained portion of what is already partially established; for example, in the case of "He threshes the rice grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*).

Even in the absence of an explicit injunction, threshing is obtained through the very implication of the husking and cooking of the rice grains, which are the material substance for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); thus, it is not an original injunction (apūrva-vidhi).
However, since one might also obtain the method of tearing with the fingernails through such implication, the injunction is intended to ensure that threshing is the means employed at that time.

The third type of injunction is one where two things are already eternally applicable to a single object, and the injunction results in the exclusion of the other; for example, in the case of "He takes up the horse's halter with the mantra 'They have grasped this rein of Truth,'" the mantra is already eternally applicable to the act of taking up the rein by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*) alone.

Thus, there is neither an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) nor a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*); rather, because the indicative power is non-specific, [the mantra] applies to the horse's halter just as it does to others.

[The word "only" (*eva*)] is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the mantra even to a donkey and its fodder; thus, like the injunction "one threshes rice," it should be understood as a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*). Nor is there an absence of things to be excluded, because the inquiry into the embodied self (*śārīrātman*) is what is to be excluded. Nor is there an absence of the possibility of attaining that [inquiry] as a means to the knowledge that leads to liberation, for [it is said]: "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*)... "two... (*dve*).

Because, from statements such as "in the Brahman [portion]," there is the possibility of its application even at the stage of superficial understanding (*āpātapratipatti*). Nor is it the case that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) applies only when another means is actually established in reality;

for otherwise, since the act of splitting with the fingernails would not be established in the case of *vrīhi* grains intended for the *apūrva*, there could be no restriction. [This is so] because, in some way, that [splitting] is established merely for the purpose of producing rice-grains (*taṇḍulībhāva*).

Let there be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the inquiry into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), on the grounds that the word *ātman* here refers to the knowledge of the Self, which would otherwise result in it being understood as an inquiry into the individual self (*jīvātman*).

For in this context, the word *ātman* is used in such passages as "All this is what this Self is" (*idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā*) and "Verily, when the Self has been seen, heard, thought, and meditated upon... (*ātmani khalvare dṛṣṭe śrute mate*).

By examining the context of passages such as "all this has been known" and "this has been understood," it is understood that [the text] refers to the Supreme Self; thus, in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, the venerable teacher Śaṅkarācārya refuted the view that there is an injunction for the knowledge of the Self in the statement "it is to be heard. However, he did not refute an injunction for inquiry (*vicāra*) with the aim of attaining knowledge; therefore, there is no contradiction.

It is thus determined. Therefore, since there is no obstacle whatsoever to the injunction for inquiry (*vicāra-vidhi*), it stands that this aphorism, *athāto brahmajijñāsā*, has been determined—by means of scriptural authority and logical reasoning—to have as its purpose the triad of qualification, subject matter, and fruit required by the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*). Herein, in order to avoid the charge of being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the scriptures...

And for the sake of establishing human activity, the word "to be performed" (*kartavyā*) must be supplied. By the word *jijñāsā*, "investigation" (*vicāra*) is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). If it is objected: "Is it not proper that there be secondary signification by the word *jijñāsā*? For since the combination of root and suffix lacks independent power, a signification of the whole is untenable"—we say no. By means of the suffix *-san*, investigation is conveyed through a "denotative" (*jahat*) secondary signification.

And by some, it is said that the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) is expressed through *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication) based on its nature (*prakṛti*). Others, however, having accepted that the nature [of the word] refers solely to the knowledge of the established (*siddha*), have stated that even regarding the knowledge of the probandum,
there is only *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication), because when something is presented as already established, its connection with a means of proof (*sādhana*) is untenable.

Since the presence [of the meaning] as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatayā*) is necessary, a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the base (*prakṛti*) is essential; thus, it is precisely these two types of metaphorical indication that are intended by Śambhānanda and Śivārādhya.
On this point, some maintain that there is only a single metaphorical indication within the aggregate of base and suffix, and that there is no metaphorical indication in a sentence.
This is because such usage is observed in instances like *ardham antarvedī* ("half within the altar") and *viṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva* ("eat poison"), where [the literal sense is partially retained].

Nor is there an absence of a possible relationship; for even in the absence of a power (*śakti*) residing in the whole, that [indication] is established through the relationship between the parts (*samudāyin*) and their respective powers. And that [indication] is of the "non-abandoning" (*ajahatī*) type. Furthermore, it is not the case that there can be no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a single entity simply because it cannot be construed with a single action in a single form.

It must be stated that this [position] lacks authoritative evidence (*aprāmāṇika*). Even in the case of "The umbrella-bearers are going" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*), there is no single coreference (*ekānvaya*) based on being an umbrella-bearer or not being an umbrella-bearer, but rather based on being an agent of going; otherwise, it would follow absurdly that "those who go are going" (*gantāro gacchanti*). This is because verbal cognition is necessarily restricted by a delimiting qualifier (*avacchedaka-prakāratā-niyama*). If "being a goer" (*gantṛtva*) were the delimiting qualifier...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) itself would become an indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). Nor is this a desired conclusion; for since there is no connection with the primary meaning, it would follow that one must postulate yet another primary meaning beyond this [indicated meaning]. Therefore, there is not a single uniform mode of connection with a single action; rather, there is only a manifold mode, namely as "possessing an umbrella" (*chatritva*) and "not possessing an umbrella" (*acchatritva*). For this very reason:

Even in the case of the injunction "Let the curd be protected from crows," the connection with the action occurs only by way of the form "crows-ness" (*kākatva*), and not by way of the form "being a destroyer of curd. Nor should it be argued that there would be no connection between the deliberation and the resulting cognition because things presented by a single mental function (*ekavṛtti*) cannot be mutually connected; for those two are presented by distinct mental functions (*bhinnavṛtti*).

This is because, since the primary meaning cannot be the indicated sense (*lakṣya*), two functions (*vṛtti*) are accepted in every instance of non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). Nor is it unestablished for a single uttered word to possess two functions, as this is observed in cases such as "the hamlet and the fish in the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣamatsyau*).

Nor is it the case that the word *gaṅgā* has no function in conveying the bank, because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) culminates there; for it is precisely the culmination of the intended meaning that constitutes the power of conveying a sense. Therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the non-abandoning metaphorical indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) within the whole [of the compound].

In reality, however, the word *jijñāsā* is employed through *tantra* (simultaneous application); therein, by one [occurrence] through *jahallakṣaṇā*, "investigation" (*vicāra*) is conveyed, and by the other, the "knowledge" (*jñāna*) that is desired is conveyed through its primary denotation (*abhidhā*). Thus, nothing is untenable.
Since this is established by a single *lakṣaṇā* alone, two *lakṣaṇās* are not required due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). This applies to the *lakṣaṇā* of the suffix as well.
Furthermore, it has never been observed anywhere.

Moreover, by abandoning the knowledge that was desired and then accepting that very same thing again, there follows the fallacy of "eating one's own vomit. Furthermore, because knowledge possesses a fruit, if it were not possible [to attain it], then its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) would be untenable.

In that context, the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) is precisely the fruitfulness of the means to liberation; even that portion is indicated. Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would contradict the statement that [this meaning] is implied (*ārthika*). Furthermore, it is certain that suffixes denote their own meanings as connected with the meaning of the verbal root. This is understood by means of the word *jijñāsā*.

They state [this] because it contradicts their own treatise: "In a sentence, a single *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) is not possible. Since *lakṣaṇā* consists in a relation with the primary meaning (*śakya*), when the syntactic connection of the primary meanings is sublated, there arises the consequence that only what is presented by the word itself would be the object of cognition. Furthermore, it would be cumbersome to assume multiple powers (*śakti*) for the word; for that which is obtained through effort (i.e., secondary meaning) cannot be the primary meaning of a word."

Even though that which is presented through the relation of denotation (*śakyasaṃbandha*) may be accepted as the object [of indication] by virtue of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), since there is a difference in the primary meanings (*śakya*), there is also a difference in their respective relations; therefore, there is no unity of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Thus, even in cases such as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), it is each individual word alone that indicates excellence (*prāśastya*) and so forth by means of the sentence-meaning, and not the sentence as a whole.

Sometimes it is characterized by a distributed occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*). This is because, given the multiplicity of words, their meanings, and their relations, a single indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is impossible.
And thus—where another entity is indicated by words through a relation with the sentence-meaning, there is "sentence-indication" (*vākyalakṣaṇā*).

Just as in the case of "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*) and so forth, there is a technical usage in the treatises stating that the *lakṣaṇā* (indication) resides in the word distinct from that [meaning]; so too, this being established, even in the present case, there is not a single indication in the aggregate. And for those who claim that its occurrence is possible solely through the relationship between the aggregate and its constituent *śakti*s (denotative powers), how can there be unity? For since the constituents are distinct, their relationship must also be distinct. Nor is it the case that...

The unity of the secondary significations (*lakṣaṇā*) is established by their producing a single cognition; for this is an accepted consequence. This being so, since the object of investigation is presented by either one of the two secondary significations, it would be redundant to admit that it is presented by both.

As for the claim that in the sentence "those with umbrellas are going," the syntactic relation is understood solely through the property of "having an umbrella" (*chatritva*), that is to be reconsidered.

In cases such as "He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks" and "He lays down [the bricks] for the sake of creation," it is the aggregate that is intended to be designated. Furthermore, in the expression "The umbrella-bearers are going," the meaning is that the aggregate of both those with umbrellas and those without are going; nor is there any inconsistency regarding the plural number, because in an instance such as "The hamlet and the fish are in the Ganges," the grammatical correctness of the singular number is established when two distinct functions (vṛtti) are expressed.
Just as in the case of *aditiḥ pāśān*, [the form is] correct due to the multiplicity of its constituent parts;
nor is there an absence of a possible relationship [between the base and the suffix], because of the relationship of non-difference (*abheda*) between the aggregate and its constituents.
Even though there is no difference between those two, the diversity of their respective suffixes is universally acknowledged.

For it is precisely the presentation [of the object] by means of a property distinct from the delimitor of its own denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) that constitutes the cause of being a *lakṣya* (indicated meaning). Nor does this entail a difference from *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication), because even when presented under another form, the primary meaning itself is connected with the action.
This is evident from the empirical fact that in the sentence "Let the curd be protected from crows," there arises a cognition characterized by the mode (*prakāra*) of being a destroyer of curd.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to establish [the meaning] otherwise;

in fact, where the sentence "those with umbrellas are going" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*) is employed for the purpose of conveying the connection with the act of going by way of the form of a collective group consisting of both those with and those without umbrellas, there the simultaneous presentation of both the denoted and the indicated meanings through non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) is unavoidable.

For this very reason, in the *Guhādhikaraṇa* (the section on the cave), in the work of Mañcanapaṇḍita, it was established that in the phrase "drinking the *ṛta*," there is a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) consisting of a collective indication of both the drinking and the non-drinking [entities]. And likewise, in the *Liṅgasamavāyādhikaraṇa*, [it was stated] regarding a group by virtue of its connection with the act of placing [the fire].

It has been stated in the *Kaivalyaprakāśa* that since the primary meaning (*svārtha*) is also included [within the secondary sense], there is no contradiction between two functions (*vṛtti*); this was also explained by Bhaṭṭācārya, the worshipper of Paramaśiva, who said: "The group [of meanings] is indicated (*lakṣya*) by virtue of its association with a limiting adjunct (*upadhāna*). Furthermore, if one accepts both functions for a single utterance on the basis of the intended purport (*tātparya*), [then the following applies].

Because there is a desire for a cognition characterized by the mode "possession of an umbrella" (*chatritva*) due to the presence of the state of being under an umbrella (*chatritva*), the sentence "those with umbrellas are walking" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*) is accepted;
likewise, even as in the case of "the hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), a dual operation of the two functions [denotation and indication] is also accepted—let it be so accepted.
However, this much does not prevent the presentation of both the denotable (*śakya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) meanings in the aforementioned instance through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

This is because it must necessarily be accepted that [the word] is capable [of denoting the primary meaning]. Furthermore, the rejection of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) and so forth would result in the futility of the effort [involved]. This is the general direction of the argument.
