Such being the case, if *ajahallakṣaṇā* were admitted in the present context, there could be no syntactic connection between the investigation (*vicāra*) and the knowledge (*jñāna*)—both of which are presented through a single function (*ekavṛtti*)—in the relation of the subject and the predicate (*uddeśya-vidheya-bhāva*), just as in the case of the rule: "The one who utters *vaṣaṭ* has the first portion of the food" (*vaṣaṭkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ*).

And such a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been demonstrated by the venerable Paramaśivānandārādhya in his *Śivajñānacandrodaya*, stating that "for the sake of knowledge, inquiry must be performed. Nor should it be argued that in the present case only two modes of function (*vṛtti*) are admitted, and not *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication);
for if that were so, it would contradict the explicit mention of *ajahallakṣaṇā*. [As in the examples: "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" and "Fish in the Gaṅgā."
In such instances where two functions (vṛtti) are present, there is no application of the term *ajahallakṣaṇā*.

Let us set aside for now the investigation into whether [the primary meaning] is abandoned (*jahat*) or not abandoned (*ajahat*); even if one accepts two functions, the root (*prakṛti*) cannot be resolved through a single function alone—for instance, the presentation of knowledge as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) cannot occur without [the other function].

The connection [of the object] is by way of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor is "being that which is to be accomplished" merely the state of being an object of desire; for even suffering, though not an object of desire, is something to be accomplished, and even that which is not to be accomplished can be an object of desire—as seen in the intense longing of a man separated from his wife for her who has passed away. Furthermore, the words "desired" (*iṣṭa*) and "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) are not synonyms.

For this very reason, the inference that [the object] is the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of being desired (*iṣṭatva*) is refuted, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has already been stated. Or, even if such an inference of being the probandum were granted, it would still not be applicable in the present context—because of the rule that only that which is presented through a verbal function (*vṛtti*) can be the object of the verbal comprehension of syntactic connection (*śābdānvayabodha*). Otherwise, even in the case of deliberation (*vicāra*), there would be no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

Because it is possible for [the object]—which is presented through inference (*anumāna*) and so forth as being to be accomplished by the knowledge that is desired—to be the object of a cognition through positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Furthermore, there is no independent presentation of the knowledge that is presented merely as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix; for in cases such as "the cow is eternal," figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted in order to achieve the independent presentation of "cowness" (*gotva*).

Therefore, since it is necessary to define knowledge in its state as that which is to be accomplished by its very nature, and because two definitions are thus required, it is logical that the definition of inquiry (*vicāra*) applies to the suffix alone, and not to the entire compound; by this, even the assumption of such a [collective] definition is refuted. By one [definition],...

Since the definition characterized by "investigation" (*vicāra*)— and likewise the definition characterized by knowledge in its state of being the goal (*sādhya*)— is also necessary according to the aforementioned sequence,

rather than assuming two words and accepting figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for both of them, it is far more parsimonious to assume two instances of figurative indication (one for the base and one for the suffix) within a single heard word (*śrutapada*). Furthermore, even the definition characterized by investigation [is not required].

It is appropriate [to apply the suffix] to the aggregate (samudāya), because—according to the reasoning already stated—the suffix indicates that base (prakṛti) or that [base] indicates the suffix, such that one or the other would otherwise be redundant.

As for the claim that the suffix *san* has never been observed to function as an indicator (lakṣaka), that is not so; for instance, in the case of "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), the accusative case-ending [indicates the base].

In the case of "he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnants of the *prayāja* offerings," those who maintain that the third and second case endings (*tṛtīyā* and *dvitīyā*) indicate instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) respectively,

as well as those who maintain that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expresses the sense of an action (*kṛtyartha*), [admit] the indication of an operation (*vyāpāra*) in the sentence "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*).

This is also the case for those who maintain that the verbal suffix expresses an operation conducive to the result (*phalānukūlavyāpāra*) in sentences such as "he knows" (*jānāti*) and "he desires" (*icchati*).

Because there is the cognition of being the locus of knowledge and so forth, and because in such expressions as "it perishes" there is the cognition of being the counter-correlative of destruction, and because it is frequently observed that [words] indicate both the state of being a locus and the state of being a counter-correlative;
this is as seen in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the *Guha* section regarding the verse "the two who drink the Truth."

Furthermore, because in the *Dūrvāsī* [commentary] it is established that the suffix *śatṛ*—which denotes an agent common to both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower (*kṣetrajña*), and which is capable of expressing agency—is used here as a mere indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of being a causal factor (*kārakatva*). Nor should it be argued that although other suffixes may function as indicators, no instance of indication is ever seen for the suffix *san*; for such instances exist in cases like "the dog is about to die" (*śvā mumūrṣati*) and "the bank is about to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*).
Because indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is observed in the mere sense of activity;

for this very reason, in the sūtra *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ samānakartṛkādicchāyāṃ vā*, having raised the objection that an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is required for non-sentient things in cases of apprehension (*āśaṅkā*), [the author] says "or not" (*na vā*).

Regarding the statement in the *Vārttika*, "Because of the observation of activity proceeding from desire due to the equality of causes," it is said that the term is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) for an operation that is the effect of desire; for in an insentient entity, there is neither desire nor its effect. In this regard, the *Bhāṣya* of Patañjali states that according to the *Vārttika*, "Or [it is known] through analogy," the usage is figurative (*gauṇa*) with respect to an operation similar to desire.

This has been explained at length. And Kaiyaṭa, having raised the objection that if that were the case, there would be no usage for something similar to desire according to the maxim "when there is a choice between the primary and the secondary meanings, the operation applies to the primary," resolved it by stating that the maxim regarding the primary and secondary meanings is also accepted in some instances in accordance with the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*).

Furthermore, in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, the venerable teacher Dūrvāsabhagavatpāda accepted figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the expression "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*). Therefore, the claim that there is no figurative indication when the suffix *san* is used is empty of substance. As for the argument regarding the maxim of eating what has been vomited (*vāntabhojananyāya*), that is not correct.

The state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatā*) is not understood through the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) of the suffix because it is characterized by deliberation (*vicāra*); rather, it is understood through the base (*prakṛti*) itself by way of indication.

Since there is no possibility of the "logic of eating vomit" (*vāntabhojana-nyāya*) occurring merely by accepting a difference in the signifier, there is no re-acceptance of what has been abandoned without relinquishing the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished.

As for the claim that the statement regarding "desirability" (arthitva) here is contradictory, that too is not so. When it is said, "Inquiry must be performed for the sake of knowledge," inquiry as the means is enjoined with reference to knowledge as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). In that context, since [knowledge] is already present as something established, there is no expectancy for a means; therefore, only its status as a goal to be accomplished is indicated. Without which...

First of all, only that much is to be indicated by the word’s secondary function (lakṣaṇā) until the verbal connection reaches its completion. Once that has been completed, because an injunction culminates in the engagement of a person, and because such engagement is impossible if it is fruitless, the status of knowledge as a means to liberation is postulated to establish its possession of a result; thus, it is "implied" (ārthika). In this regard, however, from your own perspective:

This is difficult to refute: if [the word "brahman"] were construed as the object (*viṣaya*) of the desire for knowledge (*jñāna-pratyaya-arthecchā*), then since mere knowledge lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus cannot be an object, it would follow that only the knowledge of Brahman— which is the means to liberation— is what is desired, and consequently, [the word "brahman"] would have to be understood according to its Vedic sense.

And thus—this is another seed for the investigation into the suffix (*pratyaya*): namely, that the teachers' statement regarding the implied status of [the suffix] as a means to liberation would otherwise result in its being scripturally explicit (*śrauta*) in the manner already described. Furthermore, as for the argument beginning with "of the suffixes" (*pratyayānām*), that too is not correct; for [the suffix] depends upon an investigation relative to the knowledge of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*).

Because [the inquiry] is connected as a means (*sādhana*). While desire is connected by way of the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), the inquiry is connected by way of the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhya-sādhanabhāva*); thus, there is no difference whatsoever in the denotation of its own meaning as being connected with the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). As for the objection that this contradicts the word *jijñāsā*, that is not so; for when both the root and the suffix are indicative (*lakṣaka*), the entire word [is what conveys the sense].

Because it indicates [the object], its denotation is established; for since the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the cognition—which is the primary meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)—as being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is already virtually stated by the very mention of the indication as "investigation" (*vicāra*), it is logical to mention the indication as "investigation" without explicitly stating that [accomplishment] and without depending on [the word for] investigation. Therefore, there are indeed two indications.
This has been determined by Paramānanda Ārādhya; since it has been accepted by Ekorāma Siddha, Ārādhya Bhagavatpāda Ācārya, and others, this alone is to be properly adopted.
This is the statement regarding Śiva’s nature as the Supreme Brahman.

Now, an objection: by such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born," and "These creatures are born rootless and without support," and "Never was there a time when this world was otherwise," the world's lack of a creator and its beginninglessness are established; therefore, it is not appropriate for it to require a creator. [This applies even] to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

In such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," since sacrificial acts and the like are seen to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as their agent and [the soul] as the recipient of the fruit, and because there is no evidence for the existence of a Lord distinct from the conscious embodied soul— given that no purpose is seen for such a being,

and because it is accepted that the agency belongs to the souls alone through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and because the experience of pleasure and pain is observed in the world [to belong to the soul]— [there is no need for a separate Lord].

Furthermore, if the Supreme Lord were the sole agent, the faults of partiality and cruelty would arise, and His status as Lord would be undermined; thus, no purpose whatsoever is accomplished by the Lord.
Moreover, it is impossible for insentient karma and individual souls to be the givers of results.

If one accepts the existence of an omniscient Lord through the inference: "The earth, sprouts, and so forth possess an agent because they are effects, like a pot," then [one must reconcile this with such scriptural passages as]: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," "In the beginning, this was Brahman alone," "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," "Once born, he became the sole lord of all that exists," and "Om is the single-syllabled Brahman."

"That sun is Brahman; salutations to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, among all hosts. Indra is superior to everything. "Indeed, in the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed—not Brahmā, not Īśāna, nor the waters, nor the Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, nor these two, heaven and earth. Then the Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa desired: 'May I create offspring.'"

Because we observe many conflicting views, such as "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born, from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," as well as "Mind indeed is Brahman," "The eye indeed is Brahman," "The ear indeed is Brahman," "Breath is Brahman," "Ka is Brahman," "Kha is Brahman," "Food is Brahman," and so forth.
If it is asked, "How can Śiva alone possess the nature of Brahman?"—the answer is: no.

For in the injunction, "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," since the Vedic text states that "animals consist of both bipeds and quadrupeds," there arises a doubt as to which are intended by the term "animal"; however, regarding the omentum of the goat (*chāga*), [it is established].
Just as the status of a goat as the sacrificial animal is determined by another scriptural passage stating "of fat," so too should Śiva's identity as Brahman be understood. Therefore,
in passages such as "from which indeed these beings are born," the causality of the origin and so forth of the world is stated as the defining characteristic of Brahman belonging to the Supreme Lord.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, Kālarudra, and others, though delimited by the power consisting of the three *guṇas*, do not possess the status of the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*).

This is because they lack the agency over the birth and so forth of the universe, possessing instead only the agency for each individual [creation]. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras has specified: "From whom the birth and so forth of this [universe proceed]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*).
As stated in the *Brahmottara-khaṇḍa*:
Salutations to that wielder of the Pināka bow, by whose command Viriñci creates the world, Hari protects it, and he who is called Kālarudra destroys it.
Thus, the lordship of Śiva alone has been indicated as the efficient cause (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) of the origin and other states of the world. Furthermore:

"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and Maheśvara as the possessor of Māyā (*māyin*); by His constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded. Here, one should know Māyā as Prakṛti—the causal material—and Maheśvara as the *māyin*.

By the word "vidyāt" (one should know), the dependence of Māyā upon the Supreme Lord is stated. For this very reason, because He has brought Māyā under His control, He is "independent" (svatantra); and it is said that this entire world is pervaded by Him through His constituent parts, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kālarudra, and others.
Likewise, in the *Atharvaśiras*: "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world; those gods asked Rudra, 'Who are you?';

he replied, 'I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing whatsoever other than me'"; by such passages, [the text establishes] Śiva alone as being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time and as the inner controller of all.

The state of being the cause of all, the state of being denotable by all words, the state of being the Lord of all, the state of being the self of all, and the state of being Brahman have been established. In the Kāṇva recension, by the passage beginning with "He who dwells in the earth," etc.,
[it is shown] that [the Lord] is indeed the nature of the eightfold forms (aṣṭamūrti) beginning with the earth.

From the statement that Brahman alone is the creator, it follows that no other deity—such as the one characterized by the conch and discus—is the Lord (Īśvara) by virtue of being the creator of the elements and elemental effects. Nor should it be argued that even Viṣṇu can possess a body consisting of earth and other elements, as well as the status of an inner controller (Antaryāmin), through the etymological derivation of his name; for [his] "eight-formedness" (Aṣṭamūrtitva) indeed...

Because Śiva alone is well-known [as the inner controller], whereas Viṣṇu is not well-known as the inner controller; nor is it proper to assert that both Śiva and Keśava are the inner controllers and possess the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrtitva), because there is no single body for both. Furthermore, if both were independent controllers, the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds would occur simultaneously.

Because [otherwise] there would follow the dissolution of the universe; for in hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "He entered from within to what was more internal, He entered the interval between the quarters; that Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—that Rudra who has entered all beings, let there be obeisance to that Rudra," it is seen that Śiva alone is the self of all and the inner controller of all.

Beginning with "The sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda" and ending with "He who is the Supreme Maheśvara," the dissolution of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— who are denoted by the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*— into Maheśvara is established; therefore, none of the others possess the nature of Brahman.
Furthermore, beginning with "The Lord of all sciences" and ending with "Sadāśiva," his very status as Brahman and his being the one propounded by the Praṇava are stated:
"Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, him, the supreme deity among deities, the Lord..."

"First among lords, we know the God, the Lord of the world, the one worthy of praise"—thus, in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, it is determined that we know the Īśvara as the controller of the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
we do not know the Īśvara in any other way. "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor... [of earth].

"Of the earth, the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu"— thus, in the Ṛgveda, his status as the cause of the world, from Brahmā down to Viṣṇu, is established for him alone. Because it is recited within the context of the Soma section, [it does not refer to the Soma plant].
The term "the Soma-plant" refers to the Supreme [Brahman], because it is impossible for the insentient Soma-plant to be the cause of all things.
And in the *Atharvaśikhā*: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon;
from Him are born this entire universe—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the senses together with the elements; He is not the effect."
Beginning with "The meditator is the cause of causes,

but the object of meditation is Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, eternal in the midst of space, and supreme over all," and concluding with "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the maker of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else."
For those seeking liberation, the worship of Śiva alone is prescribed, preceded by the negation of all other [paths].

"Moreover, He is the Lord of immortality; we know all this to be Śiva alone—pure, stainless, all-pervading, non-dual, the one auspiciousness. They consider the non-dual auspiciousness to be the Fourth (Turiya); that is the Self, that is to be known.
Śiva is non-dual; for Rudra is indeed one, and there exists no second to Him. "Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone is absolute";
"Rudra, the Great Seer, is superior to the universe"—from such scriptural passages, the fact that Śiva is without a second is established, and thus it is certain that Śiva alone is the Supreme.
Furthermore:
Salutation indeed to the one whose form is the universe— the supreme Brahman, who is Truth and Reality, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose vital seed is drawn upward, and who has diverse eyes.

By these and other such passages, the supreme Brahman-nature of Śiva, the blue-and-red one, is declared. "The sage, having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, accompanied by Umā— the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual, the fourth state, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and perfectly tranquil— goes [to liberation]."

Because of the statement, "He is the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness; He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hari, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling Lord," and so forth—which establishes that Śiva is the Supreme Brahman transcending the three forms—no others can possess the status of Brahman, as they lack the nature of being the ultimate cause. As for such passages as "Food is Brahman," these are merely figurative praises.

Furthermore: "All indeed is Rudra; all this is truly Brahman. Whatever there may be in the three abodes—the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoyment—I am Sadāśiva, the witness distinct from them, consisting of pure consciousness alone. In me alone is everything born;
in me everything is established; in me everything goes to dissolution. Therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman."
Because of such statements, just as the words *hasta*, *kara*, and *pāṇi* are synonyms, the words *brahman*, *ātman*, and *śiva* are heard to be synonymous;

for in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, after stating at the beginning, "All this is indeed Brahman, this Self is Brahman, this very Self," and concluding at the end, "They consider the non-dual Śiva to be the Fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known."
In this section concerning the non-dual Brahman (*advitīya-brahma-prakaraṇa*), because the introduction and the conclusion convey a single meaning,

and because it is taught that the Brahman introduced at the outset is non-different from the non-dual Śiva mentioned in the conclusion, it is established that He alone is the Supreme Brahman by virtue of being the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe. Otherwise, [there would be a contradiction] with the Śruti regarding Śiva, Brahman, the Self (*ātman*), and so on.
If one were to accept that each of them is an *Īśvara* based on the teaching that they are the cause of the world, it would result in a plurality of *Īśvaras*,
which would contradict all established doctrines (*sakalamata*) and all the *Śrutis*.
Thus, the teacher Jaimini, who understood the meaning of all the Vedāntas, stated in his *Vedapādastava*:

It has been stated that all Vedic statements have Śiva as their ultimate purport. And likewise, after refuting the evil doctrines of the heretics, the Pāñcarātras, the Buddhists, the Advaitins, and others, even those Vedic masters who had mastered the four Vedas— such as Jyotirnātha, Ghaṇṭānātha, Bhīmanātha, Bhaṭṭabhāskara, and others— who were teachers established in the path of the Vedas, [declared as follows]:
Mahādeva is the God whose feet are worshipped by the entire world; the Veda (Trayī) is the Path that crushes the functioning of evil-minded doctrines.
Whoever speaks ill of either of these two, upon his head I place my foot—I, the conflagration at the dissolution of the disputants.
O assembly of kings!

By such passages, the status of Śiva alone as the Supreme Brahman is established. Therefore, in the scriptural injunction "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*), it is indicated that this refers specifically to the desire to know the essential nature of Śiva.
Likewise, the fact that Brahman is the cause of the universe belongs to Śiva alone; thus, in the collection of aphorisms known as the *Brahma-sūtra*...

This is the conventional usage: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman"; "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else. Here, the term *śivaṅkaraḥ* means "one who makes [the self] auspicious"—this is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus. Therefore, it refers precisely to the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the absolute cessation of bonds (*pāśa*).
This is taught as liberation (*mukti*). Nor should it be argued: "Since [the state] is adventitious and therefore impermanent, how can the attainment of Śiva-nature itself be liberation?
For, according to the analogy of the bee and the worm, we observe that a real worm attains the state of a real bee;
and we observe that water, which is essentially real, attains the state of real pearls after its own [liquid] nature has ceased. Why [should this not be so]?
The wise should understand that this is merely a conceptualization of bondage and falsehood.

Now, one might object: "If it is observed through the force of a general rule (*vyāpti*) that the true cognition of mirage-water is what removes the false cognition of water appearing in a desert mirage, how can a [mere] cognition remove that which is real? This is not so.
For we observe the cessation of a true cognition by a subsequent cognition, of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by the recollection of Śiva, of sin by the recollection of a beloved,
of suffering by [the attainment of] its respective object, of doubt by the determination of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*),
and of the prima facie view by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Now, an objection may be raised: since in passages such as "One unborn female, red, white, and black... the Pradhāna is designated as the cause of the world, and because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that Brahman is subject to modification (vikāritva) in its status as the cause of the world;
therefore, the inquiry should be "the desire to know what is not Brahman" (abrahmajijñāsā), meaning that the inquiry should be directed toward the Pradhāna, which is not Brahman.

If it be argued that [they are the objects of inquiry], we say no—because no Vedic scripture is seen that enjoins the inquiry into them; because the Veda is seen to reject their worship, stating that Prakṛti and Jīva are not to be meditated upon; and because, like the Pradhāna, there is an absence of a power that exists without a substratum.
Furthermore, regarding the scriptures that establish the Pradhāna as the cause of the world, [the principle is applied] as in the cases: "The weapon cuts" or "The ear hears."

Thus, its authorship by someone other than that [Lord] is indicated, as in the case of sentences [composed by different authors]. Since an insentient entity cannot be the cause of the world, and because in passages such as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā," it is seen that Māyā is dependent upon Śiva.
Thus ends the first section, *Jijñāsādhikaraṇa*, in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*.

Having first presented this aphorism for the purpose of defining the primary nature of Brahman— according to the principle that "the establishment of a reality depends upon its definition and its means of valid cognition"— in the section concerning "origination and so forth" (janmādy-adhikaraṇa).
In order to dispel doubts and misconceptions regarding whether Brahman is devoid of attributes or possesses attributes, he states the definition of Brahman, which is to be investigated:
"From which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]. (1.1.2)

Thus it is said: "That from which these beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which they enter when they depart—that you should seek to know; that is Brahman. This is heard in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad]. Its subject matter is as follows: the meaning of the sentence is "they enter" while they are dying, i.e., departing.
Therefore, since Brahman can be the subject of inquiry due to its being doubtful in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), there is a connection by way of objection (*ākṣepasaṅgati*).

Furthermore, connections by way of illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) are possible everywhere. Just as Brahman is to be inquired into because it is doubtful, so too [one might argue] that Brahman does not have the definition [of "that from which the origin, etc., proceed"] because the origin and so forth reside in the world (*jaganniṣṭhatva*).

The connection is with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Here, because it is not possible [to define Brahman] by means of an incidental characteristic (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), the connection is with the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). "That which has birth and so forth as its beginning" is a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound. Here, the word "Brahman" is understood from the previous context, and the pronoun "that" (*tat*) is supplied. Thus: "From which this [world] has birth and so forth."
The analysis of the words: "Janmādi" refers to the fivefold set of functions consisting of creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is that from whom—namely, from that Brahman characterized by natural and infinite powers—the manifestation of this world of sentient and insentient beings arises.
By the word "of this" (*asya*), the state of being an effect belonging to the manifold of sentient and insentient things that have become objects of visual perception is indicated;

and by the phrase "from which" (*yataḥ*), the status of Brahman as the cause of the fivefold cosmic acts beginning with birth is pointed out. Since the fivefold cosmic acts of the supreme Śiva-Brahman, such as the birth of the universe, are established by scripture (*śruti*), the practice of the individual souls (*jīvas*) as His worshippers is enjoined.

It is indeed possible for the cause, Brahman, to both act and not act. In this regard, the Śruti passage beginning with "from which" (*yato vā*) indicates manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and concealment (*tirodhāna*) by the phrase "into which they enter.

If Brahman were already known, characteristics such as being "external" (*taṭastha*) would be untenable; yet if it were unknown, there could be no engagement [with spiritual practice] at all. Therefore, in that case—
One should not raise the doubt as to how the operation of the definition and the object to be defined can occur;

for, in one who has received the Śāmbhava initiation taught by a Guru, there arises a preliminary knowledge (apātajñāna). Therefore, the engagement in the investigation of the definition and the object to be defined for the sake of its ascertainment is not contradictory.

As for the object [of the objection]: causality belongs either to Brahman, the substratum of all, or to the imagined Lord (Īśvara) who is the reflection of the quality of *sattva* superimposed upon that [Brahman]. However, because Brahman—the substratum of all—is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), and because the world is eternal [in its essence], causality is not possible [for Brahman in its absolute state]. [Causality] is possible only for that which is imagined, possessed of parts, and illusory in nature.
This is utterly impossible.

Furthermore, since the world and the individual soul are designated as unborn and eternal in such passages as, "The two unborn ones—the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," and "Never was there a time when this world did not exist," how can the Supreme Lord be the cause? If he were the cause...

Because the Lord, the author of the Sūtras, has refuted the Vaiṣṇava doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) originates from *pradhāna*—on the grounds that it contradicts both Śruti and Smṛti—in the Sūtra "On account of the impossibility of origination" (*utpatty-asambhavāt*), that [doctrine] is not possible. Furthermore, if [the soul] were uncaused, there would be a contradiction with such Śruti passages as "From which indeed these [beings are born]" (*yato vā imāni*). Also, [it would contradict] "In the beginning this was non-existent; from that, indeed, the existent was born; the existent alone... (*asad vā idam agra āsīt; tato vai sad ajāyata; sad eva*).

In such scriptural passages as, "O gentle one, in the beginning this was Being alone; it was neither non-being nor being; it was Śiva alone, the absolute," there is observed a great diversity of conflicting views, arising from the hearing of [doctrines concerning] non-existence as the cause, existence as the cause, and the Supreme Śiva—who is distinct from both existence and non-existence—as the cause.

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: The Supreme Lord cannot be the cause of the world because He is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). If that were the case, would He exist as something distinct from the world, or as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*)? And would He be with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*nirākāra*)? Not the first [alternative], because it would entail the collapse of His omnipresence, given that He is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) and without a substratum (*nirādhāra*).
Furthermore, because it is impossible for jars, cloth, and so forth to arise from potters, weavers, and the like [if Brahman were merely their material cause], the second alternative is not tenable;

for that would entail the consequence of Brahman being limited like a jar, and would result in its being something contained within another. Nor is the third alternative possible; for it is illogical to conceive of partless space and so forth as arising from a Brahman that possesses parts.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of [Brahman] being limited, as in the previous cases. Nor is the fourth [option] possible— since it is impossible for that which is partless to be imagined as having parts— and because it would entail a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "It is without parts, without activity, tranquil, blameless, and motionless."

Furthermore—if one accepts that the world is produced by Paraśiva, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda)—then the world itself would necessarily possess the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss. If that were accepted, the world’s birth and other characteristics, as well as its nature of unreality, insentience, and suffering, would not exist; moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of the world being subject to modification, like clay and other such materials. Furthermore—

Furthermore, as for this twofold causality of Brahman or of Pradhāna: it cannot be the first, because if it were merely instrumental (nimitta), there would be the consequence of contradicting non-dualistic scriptures such as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "All is indeed Rudra. Nor can it be the second, because [the scriptures state]:
"Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second," and "One only, without a second."
Because it is impossible to refute other presiding deities established by such scriptural passages as these, the third [position] is not tenable;

for [the Pradhāna and the deity] possess mutually contradictory natures, like darkness and light. Furthermore, if the Pradhāna is accepted, since it is insentient and non-existent [in the sense of being unmanifest], it is impossible for it to function as both the efficient and material cause, as in the case of a potter and the like.

Because they are mutually contradictory, the coexistence of both is impossible. Furthermore, [the attributes] such as bliss (ānanda) established by scriptural passages such as "He understood that Brahman is bliss," "Indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "It is neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone is absolute."... [and so forth].

Regarding the state of being Brahman, there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*). If it were an option, there would follow the loss of what has been performed and the acquisition of what has not been performed, as well as a lack of systematic order. If it were a systematic option, there would follow the consequence of multiple Brahmans. In the case of a combination, since those attributes such as bliss and so forth are of the nature of qualities (*dharma*), [there is no fault].
The impossibility of [Brahman] being the cause of the world's birth and so forth.

Furthermore, if one accepts that Brahman is a transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) like milk and the like, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the bliss and other attributes inherent in Brahman would perish. If, on the other hand, it were a material cause by way of origination (*ārambha*) like gold and its ornaments, [the same fault would apply].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the cause] undergoing modification (*vikāritva*), as before. If one accepts that the manifold of the world (*prapañca*), such as Pradhāna and so forth—which was previously non-existent—is a phenomenal appearance (*vivarta*) like a snake in a rope, then why would this not also apply to things such as a hare’s horn? Therefore, the production of the world is not established. Thus it is said: "By means of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), the worldless reality is manifested through the world."

Following the reasoning set forth by the ancient teachers, for the sake of the disciple’s understanding and to establish the authority of the Vedas, one may state that the non-conscious Māyā alone is the material cause; for this is possible since the Śruti passage beginning with “the one unborn [female], red, white, and black,” teaches that non-conscious Māyā is the cause of the world.

If it is argued that the causality belongs either to Brahman as superimposed upon primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or to the imagined Lord (*īśvara*) reflected in the quality of *sattva* within that nature,

we reply: our established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that it belongs solely to Paraśiva-Brahman, the six-fold locus (*ṣaṭsthala*) consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, who is the substratum of all.

It is logical that [Brahman] is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world. "I am without hands or feet, possessed of inconceivable power; I see without eyes, I hear without ears; I perceive as one whose form is distinct, and there is no knower other than me, for I am eternally consciousness.
Brahman has space as its body, truth as its self, life as its delight, and the mind as its bliss. Indeed, all these..."

"Beings arise from space alone; they merge back into space. Space, indeed, is the revealer of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self"—by such a collection of scriptural passages, [it is established] even for that which is partless.

By the phrase "independent of external instruments," the all-encompassing agency of Brahman is indicated. In the expression "Brahman whose body is space" (*ākāśa-śarīram brahma*), the word "space" refers to its inherent power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) and not to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), because that which is insentient cannot possibly be the cause [of the universe]. "The true self" (*satyātmā*) means one whose nature is truth, according to the Vedic scripture: "The Real is Truth. (*ṛtam satyam*).

By the word *prāṇa*, the conscious power (*cicchakti*) that is the substratum of the entire universe is designated. He who delights in that is *prāṇārāma*. By the word *manas*, the supreme power (*parāśakti*) is expressed; he whose bliss is in that is [the *manomaya*].
By this, independence from external instruments is indicated. For it is observed that even the partless wind possesses the power to cause trees and other things to tremble.

Furthermore, since the partless *jīva* is seen to bring about the creation of the dream-world, what need is there to mention the capacity of that which is endowed with infinite power to accomplish the impossible? For it is observed that even the embodied sun is capable of conceiving the formless time. [This is] for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees.

There is no fault even in conceiving the manifold world of both the manifest and the unmanifest as belonging to Maheśvara, who possesses a divine and auspicious form like the solidity of clarified butter;
for the Śruti states: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, originating from it, dissolving into it, and breathing in it; one should worship it with a tranquil mind."

It is heard in scripture that the entire world is of the same nature as that [Supreme Lord], because it performs the functions of arising, subsisting, and dissolving from Him—just like the foam, waves, and so forth produced from the ocean. However, the fact that the power of the Supreme Lord, who is the material cause of the world, exists only in a single part of Him is demonstrated by the scriptural text: "All beings are but one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven."

Therefore, just as the wind and other elements are contained within the great ether (*mahākāśa*), the worlds contained within the Supreme Lord have the Supreme Lord as their cause. This is also indicated by the Śruti: "The entire universe is within the Liṅga; there is nothing beyond that which is outside the Liṅga."

By the phrase "from which indeed these beings are born," the causality as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*) of Śiva-Brahman is taught; and by the phrase "into which they pass away," His causality as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇatva*) is not [taught]. Therefore, there is no contradiction in His being both the non-different efficient and material cause; however, He is not a single [identical] cause.
Neither superimposition nor falsity is being predicated [of the Self].

But surely—since by such passages as "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," the non-born nature of the individual soul (jīva) is taught just like that of the Supreme Lord;
and since by such scriptural texts as "From which these beings are born," the Supreme Lord’s...

If it is argued that [the world] has only the five great elements as its cause, we say no; for prior to creation, we observe that living beings existing within themselves like grain in a granary act as agents in emerging outward and so forth. Thus, there is no contradiction between the scriptural passages establishing [the world] as produced and those establishing it as unproduced. [As it is said: "But Māyā, indeed, is Nature..."

"One should know Maheśvara as the possessor of māyā; by his constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded. Indeed, my own eternal portion becomes the individual soul (jīva) in the world of living beings"—from such scriptural and traditional (smṛti) declarations, it follows that prior to creation, the Supreme Lord is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) due to the contraction of his power (śakti), and is thus partless (niṣkala) and actionless (niṣkriya).

The scriptural passages beginning with "It is peaceful" (*śāntam*) refer to the time when [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). The scriptural passages beginning with "He reflected" (*sa īkṣāṃ cakre*) refer to the time of the unfolding of the power of the Supreme Lord, who is oriented toward creation (*saguṇa*). If it is argued that if Śiva-Brahman, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss, were the cause of the world, He would be subject to modification (*vikāritva*) like clay and other such materials—[the answer is: "But [it is] Māyā... (*māyām tu*).

There is no contradiction, as the scriptures beginning with "One should know Prakṛti" teach that Māyā is the material cause (upādāna) of the world and the Supreme Lord is its efficient cause (nimitta).
If it is asked how the inert phenomenal universe can be imagined within the Supreme Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness, the answer is: "Just as a spider emits [its web]," and so forth.
From scriptural passages such as "He grasps," we observe that non-conscious threads are produced from a conscious spider;

what then need be said regarding the Supreme Lord, who is endowed with the power to bring about the impossible? Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect between the insentient and the sentient—the phenomenal world (prapañca) and Paraśiva—as well as their identity, are established by all the previously cited [scriptural] texts, such as "All this is indeed the Self."

Since this is established by Vedic declarations such as, "Brahman is that from which [the world] is born, by which it lives, and into which it dissolves; one should worship It as the Peaceful," it is a ringing proclamation that this alone is the Vedic Siddhānta.
This is so even when the method of superimposition and negation (adhyāropa-apavāda) is accepted, as in: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; It thought..."

"May I be many, may I procreate"—"I, who am one, shall become many, shall procreate"; "The one God, generating heaven and earth"; "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends"; "The Lord of the Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra";
likewise, "the wise one, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Puruṣa who is higher than the high"; "Rudra indeed is all"—and so forth.

Because it contradicts the *bahuśruti* (the abundant sacred scriptures), it would result in its entry into the category of non-Vedic doctrines, like those of the Buddhists. As for the claim that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is possible because it is superimposed (*adhyāsika*), given the impossibility of identity between the insentient and the sentient—that is trivial. To explain: superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is indeed the attribution of the qualities of one thing to another. In that regard—
Is it the superimposition of the manifold of non-self upon the self, or the superimposition of the self upon the non-self? Not the first:
for the illusion of a rope-snake is possible through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a real snake perceived previously;

however, in this case, since one does not admit a real manifold distinct from the Self, and because there is no location other than that [Self], such an illusion is untenable. Nor is the second [the case].

—Because if there were a superimposition of the self upon what is not-self, it would follow that Brahman, whose nature is the superimposed self, is false, and many defects such as insentience (jaḍatva) would consequently arise. Nor should it be argued that "the fact of being previously perceived" alone is the regulating factor;
for, just as in the logic of the seed and the sprout, since each preceding superimposition is the cause of each subsequent superimposition, superimposition is possible.

If that were so, then there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. Furthermore, according to the rule that "that which is perceived in a certain place cannot be superimposed upon it," how could the superimposition of the phenomenal world (prapañca) perceived therein be possible upon that very [Brahman], as in the case of a snake?

Furthermore, since the superimposition of "serpent-ness" upon a rope is impossible, this [your] argument is difficult to avoid as being untenable. Moreover, if Brahman and the phenomenal world were both beginningless,

there would be a contradiction with numerous scriptural passages such as, "From which indeed these beings are born," and there would follow the collapse of the logical principles that establish the necessary sequence between cause and effect.

If one accepts the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) on the grounds of its being an object of perception (dṛśyatva), then it follows that Brahman would also be false, since there is no distinction regarding its being an object of perception. If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because [Brahman] is not accepted as an object of perception—then there would be no experience of Brahman in the world. Furthermore, [Brahman is perceived] because it is the object of the notion of "I" (asmat-pratyaya) and because it is immediate (aparokṣatva).
If it is argued that Brahman is not the object of the notion of "I" because of the contradiction with the statement "due to the well-known nature of the inner self," we say no;

for the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not admitted [in our system]. [Scriptural support: "A certain wise man beheld the inner self and, knowing the Self, crossed over sorrow";
"The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen; it is seen by the keenest intellect"; "Behold Me."

Furthermore, because of scriptural, traditional, and Puranic statements such as, "The wise always perceive all this as the Lord of Yoga, whose essence is Śiva," which establish that Brahman is the object of vision; and because if one were to admit that Brahman is an object of empirical vision, there would follow the undesirable consequence of an error occurring without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhānabhrama*).

Therefore, superimposition (adhyāsa) should not be accepted. Now, if it is argued that the falsity of the world is accepted on the basis of the imagined scripture stating, "By the appearance of Māyā, He makes the Jīva and Īśvara," we say no. For there are such texts as: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord; my very own eternal portion has become the Jīva in the world of living beings. And so forth.
Because this would entail a contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti, and because it is impossible for the non-conscious Pradhāna to possess the agency of the conscious Jīva and Īśvara;

furthermore, it would contradict the Sūtra stating "it would have an end or lack omniscience," and it would lead to the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done.
If it is argued that the Pradhāna's causality toward the world exists by virtue of the Supreme Lord’s existence, we say no—this was already refuted in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa*.

This is because, having accepted the authority of such scriptural passages as "Then He thought" (*tadaikṣata*), the doctrine that the *pradhāna* is the cause of the world has been refuted on the grounds of its being outside the Veda.
Furthermore, as for what is called "falsity" (*mithyātva*)— whether it be non-existence (*asattva*), indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*), or sublation (*bādhyatva*)— it cannot be the first.

Because it would entail the consequence of the Vedas being non-authoritative. Not the second, because it would result in [the self] being mute. Not the third—what is this "sublatability" (*bādhyatva*)? Is it being the counter-positive of a negation at all three times, or is it being removable by knowledge? It cannot be the first: there is no negation of the prior time because [the object] is currently being experienced, nor is there a negation of the present time.

Because the mass of the Vedas exists in the Supreme Lord even during the dissolution (*pralaya*) in a contracted form, there is no negation regarding the future time; nor is the second [alternative] tenable— because for the knowers (*jñānin*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) appears as before,
and because hunger, thirst, and so forth are observed in them.

Nor should it be said that, according to the analogy of a burnt cloth, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) still possesses a connection with the cognition of distinctions such as the body and the senses; for this cannot be asserted in the present case in the same way that a burnt cloth appears as a cloth [yet lacks its functions], such as warding off cold, even though the delusion regarding mirages and the like has ceased, they are still perceived as water.

Because the accomplishment of action is absent, it appears in the world like a mirage of water, since it is incapable of functions such as quenching thirst; likewise, even though the cognition of duality exists for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), bodily trembling, hunger, thirst, and so forth would not be connected [to them]. Just as in the world, even when the staff [of punishment] is destroyed...

If it is argued that, just as the dizziness produced by that [spinning] persists even after the ignorance has been destroyed, so too the body and other effects of that [ignorance] which have already begun (prārabdha) must be destroyed solely through experience (*bhoga*), we say no. This is because ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of its effects, just as threads are the material cause of cloth; therefore, such a position is not tenable. Thus, it is stated in the Dūrvāsīya:
Brahman, bound by beginningless ignorance, is the cause of that time;
through its own ignorance it transmigrates, and liberation arises from the imagined [instructional] words.
Thus, this deceptive scripture, which destroys all greatness,
must be disregarded by the devotees of Śiva because it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti.
Due to the destruction of its fruit, this primary darkness is indeed its result;
for it is precisely that which has been described in order to establish that [ignorance] is to be destroyed by knowledge.

That [universe] is established in a completely different way through the definitions of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*); the statement that it is illusory (*māyika*) is seen in the Purāṇas. Likewise, even regarding the perspective of a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), this is certainly another school of thought.

No report of such [creation] is found anywhere within the revealed scriptures (śruti) as they are currently observed. Passages concerning "the beginning of speech" (vācārambhaṇa) do not imply falsity, because they teach non-difference from that [Brahman], since Śiva is the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa).

If it is argued that the explanatory passages (arthavāda) are for the sake of knowledge, that cannot be so, because the power to perform the creation of the world and so forth is not admitted [in Brahman], nor is there such [power] in injunctions or their greatness.
This superimposition is for the sake of negation alone, for it does not exist in reality;
if it is argued that this is for the purpose of establishing a firm conviction, that is not tenable.
There is no sublation of the primary meaning of the scripture because its efficacy is observed;
even in the case of a magician, it is his agency that is spoken of.
Moreover, the agency of Māyā and the other [factors] is not taught by the Śruti or the Sūtras;
rather, their lack of agency is indeed intended to reveal His supreme majesty.
The superimposition of contradictions and the like is not a logical reason for that [reality];
the claim of its illusory nature (*māyikatva*) in the Purāṇas serves only the purpose of delusion.
Therefore, the discourse on ignorance (*avidyā*) and illusion (*māyā*) is indeed intended for deception.
They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
it has arisen from mutual union and has nothing else but desire as its cause.
In the state of qualified non-duality with God, however, the entire world consists of Śiva;
through knowledge, the conceptualizing intellect dissolves, but not its essential nature.
"One should never entertain the notion of difference because of Śiva being the material cause;
thus, the Vedic doctrine alone is to be followed and no other—so says the Śruti.
Likewise, the theory that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are reflections of ignorance (avidyā) and māyā is also not tenable. For instance:

The embodied self (*śārīra*), which is the object of our cognition, is either consciousness reflected in ignorance (*avidyā*), or consciousness reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or consciousness delimited by ignorance, or consciousness delimited by the internal organ. The Lord (*īśvara*), however, is either consciousness reflected in *māyā*, or consciousness delimited by *māyā*. Regarding both of these, they may be considered either natural (*svābhāvika*) or adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*).

The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of that [Self] is either *māyā*, *avidyā*, or the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), but not the gross body (*sthūlopādhi*), because going to the other world would otherwise be impossible. Since it is said, "This individual soul (*jīva*) has an effect as its adjunct,
while the Lord (*īśvara*) has a cause as his adjunct," the position that the soul is a reflection [of Brahman] is also untenable, because Brahman is formless (*nīrūpa*).
Since *māyā* is an unreal entity (*asat-padārtha*), its reflection could not exist. Nor should it be argued that it is like the reflection of the sky in water;

for according to the maxim that "conception must follow what is observed," a reflection of formless space is impossible. The perception of such a reflection is merely an illusion, since we observe reflections of entities possessing form, such as the sun, in water and other media.

Otherwise, it would follow that even air could have a reflection. According to the rule that there is no reflection of something at a place where it does not exist—just as there is no reflection of the lines on a mirror upon the mirror itself—how can a reflection of the all-pervading Brahman be possible within the all-pervading Māyā? Nor should it be argued that the absence of reflection is untenable because a conjunction between two all-pervading entities is impossible.

Even though the halo of light is conjoined [with the sun], it is perceived in that manner; for according to such scriptural passages and sūtras as "They have both entered the supreme highest cave" and "The two selves have indeed entered the cave," because it is established that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) reside in one place, the position [that they are like] a reflection and its original (bimba-pratibimba) is untenable, since it is impossible for a reflection and its original to be situated in the same location.
Furthermore: Jīva and Īśvara are reflections of Brahman in Māyā and Avidyā respectively;

indeed, liberation for them is the destruction of Māyā and Avidyā. If that were accepted, it would follow that liberation is simply the destruction of Jīva and Īśvara. Consequently, this would result in entering the heretical Buddhist doctrine and constitute self-destruction, which is not the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).

Liberation (*mokṣa*) would result in not being a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*). The individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) would become unreal. If that were the case, no one would undertake effort for the sake of the next world, nor would one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) strive for the sake of liberation. Since the nature of both would be false, there would indeed be only worldly activity (*aihika-pravṛtti*) for everyone; and in the absence of all activity...

There would be the total abolition of all activity; since all injunctions and prohibitions would be equally false, no one would engage in anything at all. This being the case, the path of the virtuous would also be destroyed. Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is unreal as a reflection, [the text] establishes the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*—beginning with "All this has that as its essence" (*aitadātmyam*) and ending with "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*)—and then concludes simply with "That thou art" (*na tat tvam asi*).
One might say: "Like fire reflected in a mirror and so forth, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is simply not possible.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* (e.g., "He who dwells in consciousness..."), because since all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are reflections of one [Brahman], the identity of the individual souls (*jīva*) would result; consequently, the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation, pleasure and pain, and so on, would be untenable.

Therefore, the theory of reflection (*pratibimba-pakṣa*) is also untenable. If it were admitted that consciousness delimited by the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) constitutes the individual soul (*jīva*), then consciousness delimited by jars or cloths would likewise have to be considered the individual soul.
Consequently, the theory of delimitation (*avaccheda-pakṣa*) is also not tenable, as it is beset by the aforementioned defects. [As it is said: "In one way and in many ways..."

The scriptural statement "it is seen like the moon in water" is indeed weak, because the previously cited scriptures are more powerful. For, according to the maxim that "not everything is possible in an illustration," an illustration for the omnipresence of Brahman is found [only in those stronger texts].

Furthermore, by the statement "by means of the appearance of Māyā, He makes the Jīva and Īśvara," the imagined nature (*kalpitatva*) of the Jīva and Īśvara is not established, as they are described as "the Knower and the Unknower."
The statement "the two unborn ones, the Lord and the non-Lord," and so forth, is contradicted by the testimony of the many Śrutis, by reasoning, and by direct experience.

As for the term *māyā*: it is derived from the root *aya* (as in *aya-paya-gatau*), which signifies "to go" or "to reach"; furthermore, the *Nighaṇṭu* states, "the syllable *ma* refers to Śambhu, the Creator, and the Moon.
Thus, in the exposition of the meaning of the *Praṇava*, the letter *a* is Brahmā, and the letter *u*...

And because of the scriptural statement, "Viṣṇu is the letter *ma*, Rudra is [the letter *ra*]," [it follows that] Māyā—the power of Paraśiva—by means of *ābhāsa* (manifestation), which is the same radiance as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), "makes" the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*), meaning she renders them manifest. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting all the Śrutis. There is no fault in the previously mentioned [attributes] such as Truth (*satya*) and Bliss (*ānanda*) being the cause of the world.
This is because they possess the nature of the Supreme Lord and His attributes, just as redness, heat, and light belong to fire.
Therefore, it can be asserted that the world (the *prapañca*) is produced by a creator, like a jar or other such objects.

However, although birth and the rest reside in the world, they cannot be the definition of the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, because they belong to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*).

Nevertheless, the status of being the cause of the world is an extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) of the Supreme Lord because it is taught as such. An extrinsic definition is that which distinguishes [an object] while being distinct from its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Although each of the origination and so forth of the world can individually serve as a definition due to their non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), nevertheless, mere agency of production belongs only to the efficient cause (*nimitta*); therefore, the mention of both origination and maintenance [is necessary].
Regarding the mention of "dissolution" (*laya*): it is never possible for an effect to dissolve into its efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Nor should it be argued that the mention of "origination" and "subsistence" is redundant because the status of being a material cause (*upādānatva*) is already obtained by the mention of dissolution alone. For the status of being a material cause is not stated here as a universal attribute; rather, it is intended to establish non-difference according to the principle of the relationship between the primary substance and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra*). Let it be so with Brahman.

The material cause of the world would have to be one thing, while the presiding agent of its origination and maintenance would be another, just as a potter is distinct from the production of a jar, or as a king is distinct from his continued presence in the kingdom. Thus, the mention of "origination" and "maintenance" is merely illustrative.
However, the definition of its essential nature is that which is established by scripture as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

[The nature of] being reality and so forth. Now, [one might object]: if reality and the rest are distinct from the nature of Paramaśiva, they cannot be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the nature of Paramaśiva; or if they are non-distinct, how can there be the establishment of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), for in all cases the sentence-meaning consists in the relation between word-meanings that have entered into a relationship of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), and such is not possible in the case of non-difference.
If it is argued that "that [inherence] is possible," we say no. Where there is the cognition of word-meanings (*padārtha*), there conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Where a collection of words (*padasandarbha*) is intent upon the cognition of word-meanings, there conjunction is the sentence-meaning. But where a collection of words is intent upon the cognition of an indivisible word-meaning (*akhaṇḍapadārtha*), there that very indivisible word-meaning alone is what is conveyed by the sentence. For example—in this...

In response to the question, "Which one among the circles of light is the moon?", the sentence "The moon is that which possesses supreme luminosity" is intended solely to convey the nature of the moon as an undivided whole. Nor is the qualification by "supreme luminosity" the object of knowledge (*prameya*) to be established by this sentence, because it is already established by other means of knowledge; nor is the qualification by "moon-ness" (*candratva*).

Because the universal *candratva* (moon-ness) does not exist as a single individual; nor is there the qualification of being denotable by the word "moon," since that too has not been perceived; and because it is inappropriate to state such a thing in response to a question concerning the mere nature of a thing.
In fact, this is for the purpose of overturning the rule that sentences everywhere necessarily aim at the connection between the word-meanings as they are heard.

It must be demonstrated that there exists, in some cases, the state of being restricted solely to the word-meaning (*padārthamātraniṣṭhatva*). And this [state] is to be expressed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In that regard, since words in common usage possess the capacity for qualified meanings (*viśiṣṭaśakti*), every word-meaning is indeed "with parts" (*sakhaṇḍa*); nevertheless, there is no failure of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*), because it is possible for a sentence to serve as an example when it is restricted solely to the word-meanings. And thus also:

The words "satya" (truth) and so forth have as their referent the single entity that is Brahman, and the referent of the word "Brahman" is not a qualified entity, because of the thousands of scriptural texts proclaiming non-duality.

If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of the partless [Brahman] through words like 'satya' which denote qualified entities?"— understand that this occurs through their secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

And it is said in the *Śivādvaitaprakāśa*: "The means [of cognition] is indeed a specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*), as in the case of the comprehension of the 'full moon'; yet that [qualification] is not known in relation to the moon because of contradiction. However, in sentences such as 'the Truth' (*satyam*) and so forth, the specific qualification is sublated by words such as 'infinite' (*ananta*) and the like. By this, it is shown that the definition of an "indivisible referent" (*akhaṇḍārtha*) does not apply to things such as an army or a forest. As for armies, forests, and the like—

The argument that “because [sentences] possess the nature of a composite whole, they lack the quality of having an indivisible referent (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), and thus mere indication (*lakṣaṇā*) does not constitute *akhaṇḍārthatva*” has been refuted; for even in that case, there is no dispute regarding the fact that [the sentence] rests solely upon the individual word-meanings.
Now, if through indication the sentences such as "That thou art" were intent upon oneness alone, then by means of just one [word],...

If it is argued that because such a meaning is understood [from a single word], other words would be redundant and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of synonymy, we say no. For there is no contradiction in words possessing distinct capacities being non-synonymous with respect to their primary denotations (*śakyārtha*), yet having a single referent through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have praise as their purpose despite being non-synonymous in their primary meanings. Nor is it the case that...

There is no redundancy because the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are distinct. By the word "real" (*satya*), there is the exclusion of the unreal; by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the exclusion of the insentient (*jaḍa*); and by the word "infinite" (*ananta*), the exclusion of the finite. Thus, in every case, due to the difference in exclusions, there is no tautology.

Now, one might object: "Are the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) also different from Brahman or non-different? In the first case, the scriptural teaching of unity would be untenable; in the second, that very same [objection] applies regarding the redundancy of other words. This is not so, because non-redundancy is established just as in the case of words such as "cause," "substratum," "material cause," or "pervader" with respect to a single entity. For it is not the case that causality and so forth—

It is a distinct property (*dharmāntara*). Thus, although the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are non-different from Brahman, they are not redundant because their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are different.
With this very intention, there is a summary in the *Śivādvaitaprakāśa*:
"That which is undifferentiated yet revealed by multiple non-synonymous words..."
They have attained that one indivisible reality established in the Vedānta.

Thus, it is established that "truth" (satyatva) and so forth constitute the essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) [of Brahman]. Now, if it is argued: "That from which the birth of the first Brahmā, the four-faced one, occurs—that is Brahman"—we say no.

Because it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience. As for the so-called "primacy" of the four-faced Brahmā, does it mean primacy with respect to all effects or with respect to sentient beings? It cannot be the first, because the creation of the elements is mentioned first in the text: "From the Self, space was produced. Nor can it be argued that the creation of the elements occurs only after the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Because there is no evidence for the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha— who possesses the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*)—
prior to the creation of the elements, since his birth is necessarily subsequent to that creation; nevertheless, even if he were the progenitor,

his status as the *lakṣaṇa* (definitional characteristic) of the Brahman to be known would not be established, because [in that case] Caturmukha himself would be dependent on a progenitor, just like Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.

Furthermore, it would entail the consequence of [Viṣṇu] being superior [to Hiraṇyagarbha]. Since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) that Hiraṇyagarbha’s birth is from Viṣṇu alone, [the following scriptural passage is cited]:

"May that God, Rudra, the Great Seer who is prior to and superior to all the gods, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha as he is born, endow us with auspicious mindfulness. The meaning of this is: "The Great Seer..."

Rudra— Paramaśiva— who is the author of the Vedas and is superior to the entire universe of sentient and insentient phenomena by virtue of his omniscience and other attributes, first brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha,
the four-faced one, who arises through his own volition from the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is as follows: may that Śiva, beholding with a gracious eye the purpose of the instruction of the entire Veda, unite even us with a benign initiation—a *smṛti* established by the Vedas, Vedāntas, and Āgamas, which consists of supreme bliss and releases one from the bonds of *saṃsāra*. May he join us with it. This is the intended sense.

"May He who is the source and origin of the gods, Rudra the great seer who transcends all, and who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha—may He endow us with auspicious understanding. By such passages as these, it is understood that Hiraṇyagarbha was produced from Maheśvara; therefore, that meaning is not being enjoined here.

Now, [one might object]: since the *Mahopaniṣad* shows that Nārāyaṇa alone exists prior to creation—stating, "Verily, there was only one Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no waters, no Agni and Soma, nor these two, heaven and earth"—and since it shows him to be the cause of all by stating, "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born, from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born," and so forth; therefore... [atha]... [the objection continues].

Why is it called *brahman*? Because it is understood from such passages as "In this, the qualities are vast (*bṛhantaḥ*)" that He alone possesses fullness of attributes; and because, through the conventional usage of the wise, the attributes such as lying upon the ocean—as seen in "That very Brahman, the supreme of poets, moving within the ocean with the mind"—belong primarily to Him alone. Thus, He is neither being nor non-being, but Śiva.

Thus, [the Lord] alone is absolute; for it is more logical that such statements as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) have Him as their sole purport—just as the identity between the general and the particular is established by the maxim of the goat and the animal.

This is like the word *go*, which, although derived from the etymology "that which goes" (*gacchati*) and thus capable of conveying various meanings, is conventionally restricted (*rūḍhi*) to the meaning "cow."

We reply: although the word *brahman* is applied to the four-faced Brahmā, the *praṇava*, brāhmaṇas, and so forth, it is nevertheless appropriate that the causality of the world's birth and so on belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone, because the term possesses both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*) significance specifically for Him who is distinguished by infinite auspicious qualities.

Even though Viṣṇu is the cause of the world, that [definition] does not constitute the definition of Brahman, because his birth is heard of prior to the creation of the gods and others that occurs after the subtle creation. The birth of Viṣṇu is heard in the Ṛgveda: "Thus born, the great Viṣṇu, knowing the Supreme, protects the third [step]."
The meaning of this is as follows: *asya*—of this Maheśvara; *itthā*—in this manner; *vidvān*—the knower;
*bṛhan*—the Great One, Viṣṇu, Ādiviṣṇu; having been born, *abhipāti*—protects; *tṛtīyam*—the third [abode], Kailāsa.
By the word *bṛhan*, Ādiviṣṇu alone is designated. "I offer salutation to the Great Viṣṇu; to the Great One... [and so forth].

Because of the observation in passages such as "We resort to the benevolent thought of Viṣṇu," one who has approached [the Lord] as the unborn Supreme Lord must not abandon that which is thus present for the sake of imagining something else that is not present, as there is no evidence for such a supposition; thus, some fearful person understands [the Lord] as "unborn. This is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "O Rudra, with that face of yours which is to the south, protect me forever."
Furthermore, because Maheśvara alone is heard in scripture to be unborn (*ajāta*), it is entirely logical that Śambhu is the progenitor of Ādi-Viṣṇu. As stated in the Ṛgveda:

"Soma flows pure, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth, the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu. And: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; all this..."
In passages such as "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him," the fact that Śiva alone is the cause of all is heard;

for the statement "Śiva alone is the absolute" refers to the eternal creation, whereas the statement "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa" refers to the intermediate creation. This has been stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
These three, whose nature is causality, were born directly from Maheśvara;
they are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, including all things mobile and immobile.
Previously, all three were appointed by their father to three tasks:
Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for destruction once again.
Nevertheless, out of mutual envy and desiring to surpass one another,
they gratified their own father, the moon-crested Lord, through ascetic penance.
Having obtained [this power] in its entirety through the grace of the Supreme Lord,
Rudra formerly created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa in another kalpa.
In another kalpa, moreover, Brahmā—the one who consists of the universe—created Rudra and Viṣṇu;
and the Lord Viṣṇu again created Rudra and Brahmā;
and Brahmā again created Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava again created Brahmā.
