Because hundreds of scriptural passages, such as "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling Lord," teach that Brahman is indeed distinct from the three forms; and because in the Nārāyaṇa and other Upaniṣads, Nārāyaṇa is not designated as being beyond the three forms; [and because the state of liberation is described as] "the cessation of the phenomenal world, tranquil, auspicious, non-dual, the Fourth."

Furthermore, because Śiva alone is established as transcending the three forms (trimūrti) in such passages as, "They consider Him to be the Self, He is to be known; Śiva is non-dual," and "The meditator meditates on the Lord; all this that is to be meditated upon—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him," His alone is the status of Brahman. Also, in the *Anuśāsana Parva*:
That Lord created from his right side Brahmā, the source of the worlds,
and likewise from his left side Viṣṇu, for the sake of protecting the worlds.
From the heart [emerges] that which is called Kālarudra.

Because of this instruction, the passage concerning the origin of Rudra has as its purport the origin of Kālarudra; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti which states, "A certain fearful person understands [him] as 'unborn'. Nor does the origin of Viṣṇu refer to an incarnation, for that would contradict the previously cited Śruti: "Viṣṇu thus... and so forth.

Furthermore, in the *Atharvaśikhā*, by the word "but" (*tu*) in the statement "The causeless one, however, is to be meditated upon as the cause," a distinction from what was previously stated is established; this is because it teaches that Śambhu is the supreme cause. [In contrast,] the phrase "Nārāyaṇa existed" (*nārāyaṇa āsīt*), which employs the imperfect tense (*laṅ*) denoting a past action not belonging to the current day, refers to the Lord Nārāyaṇa.

Only the initial origination is being established. Just as in the statement "From Śakti there was Parāśara," and according to the maxim of the goat and the animal, words such as *Sat*, *Ātman*, and so forth—just like the words *Nārāyaṇa* and others—have Śiva alone as their ultimate referent. This is because of the Vedic revelation: "All indeed are Rudras," and because of the statement in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad: "He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, He is Fire, He is the Moon; I am the One."
"I existed in the first month and I shall exist; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me"—from this statement in the *Atharvaśiras*;
and those names of yours, O Govinda, which are indeed great in the world...
These indeed are my names; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus, from the words of Śiva addressed to Kṛṣṇa in the *Harivaṃśa*,

and because Vedic scholars such as Jaimini, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Ācārya, and others have established that Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman in accordance with the purport of the four Vedas; and also by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Sūta-saṃhitā*:

Because the nature of Śiva as the Supreme Brahman is indicated by the essential purport of the Sāma-Veda and Vedānta: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; from him all this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is born. Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts; Hara is the perishable Pradhāna and the imperishable Immortal. The one God rules over both the perishable and the Self."

The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the sacred word—may Śiva be mine; may Sadāśiva be mine. For there is indeed only one Rudra; a second has no place. He who rules these worlds by his ruling powers—he for whom Paśupati is the lord of creatures, both of the four-footed and of the two-footed. [The state] wherein the phenomenal world ceases...

They consider the fourth state to be peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; and because the characteristics of Brahman are designated as belonging to Paramaśiva alone through a multitude of scriptural passages such as, "Obeisance to the Lord of Nidhana," "Obeisance to Him who is near the Lord of Nidhana," "Obeisance to the Subduer of all beings," and "Obeisance to Manonmana," He alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe.
The causality of Śiva regarding the birth and so forth of the universe is unimpeded:
the creation of the entire world is performed by the one named Bhava, who is characterized by the rājasa quality delimited by his own power (śakti);
preservation is performed by the one named Mṛḍa, who is the locus of the sāttvika quality; and [destruction] is performed by the one named Hara, who is delimited by the tāmasa quality.

And while effecting the dissolution of all things, Śiva, having caused the dissolution of *prakṛti*—which consists of the three *guṇas*—into his own power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), shines forth as one alone by virtue of his own inherent power of consciousness. This is stated also in the *Mahimnastava*: "Obeisance, obeisance to Bhava, who possesses abundant *rajas*, for the sake of the creation of the universe. For this very reason, it is said in the Śaiva Āgama:
Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal undiminished power,
and infinite power— those who know the ritual rules call these the six limbs of the all-pervading Maheśvara.
That which they call the station of devotion is said to be omniscience;
that which is named the state of Maheśvara is my satisfaction, O Śāṅkarī.
That grace by which this Name exists is my unrestrained awakening;
that which is called the Life-Linga is declared to be absolute freedom.
That which is called "refuge" is indeed said to be the unimpeded power;
that which is the state of unity situated above is said to be infinite power.
"O Goddess, this locus of limbs is supreme, more secret than the secret.
Thus, since qualities such as omniscience and the rest are possible only for Śiva and not for others, it is established that he alone is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe.
Thus ends the section on "Origin and so forth" (Janmādyadhikaraṇa).
Now begins the section on "Having Scripture as its Source" (Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa).
Having established the definition of Brahman, which is the object of inquiry, he states the means of valid cognition:
"Because it has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt). || 3 ||
The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this aphorism is the statement beginning with, "This is the breath of that Great Being—the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda," and so forth.
The scripture (*śāstra*) refers to the Rigveda and the others. Its source (*yoni*), its cause, is Śiva. This is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*):
"Śiva and Umā alone are the two parents. For this very reason, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Nigamas and Āgamas [is established]. Therefore...

Śiva alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world. Herein lies the connection with the scriptural proposition (*pratijñā*). In passages such as "Śiva and Umā alone are the parents," the status of the Supreme Lord as the cause of the Vedas is shown; and in passages such as "By the word, which is multiform and eternal," His eternity is demonstrated.
A doubt arises as to whether it is logical for Paraśiva-Brahman to be the cause of the *Nigamas* (Vedas) and *Āgamas*.
The divine speech, consisting of the Vedas, was uttered by the Self-existent One at the beginning; it is without beginning or end, eternal, and from it all activities proceed.

Since such Smṛti texts declare the eternity of the Veda, and because if it were produced by the Supreme Lord it would follow that it is human-authored, lacks authority, and is non-eternal; therefore, having reached the position that like the Supreme Lord, the Vedas are unproduced and are uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time, we reply:
Since the claim that the Vedas are self-existent contradicts the Śruti stating that Śiva and Umā alone are their progenitors;
and since the *Caraṇavyūha* contained within the Sāma Veda describes their bodies, lineages (*gotra*), castes (*varṇa*), and so forth;
and because each preceding [Veda] serves as the cause for the knowledge of each succeeding one; and because they possess the quality of being composed of sound (*śabdātmaka*).

Furthermore, since the Supreme Lord is designated as the cause of the five elements beginning with space—through such statements as "from the Self, space was produced" because the Self is the cause of space—how can the Vedas be considered self-existent? Likewise, the Smṛti states:
"Of these eighteen branches of knowledge, which are the paths of Brahman..."
The Śruti declares that Śiva himself, the wielder of the trident, is the primordial creator.
By means of Sadyojāta one obtains the Ṛgveda; by Vāmadeva, the Yajurveda; likewise, by Aghora, the Sāmaveda; and by Puruṣa, the Atharvaveda.
Through his Īśāna face, the Lord of the Universe, the bestower of all perfections, likewise brought forth the Kāmika and other Āgamas.
The power of Śiva, the Supreme Self, whose nature is reflective awareness (vimarśa),
takes the form of the Vedas and Āgamas, illuminating all principles of reality.
Therefore, whoever should conceive a sense of duality regarding the meanings of the Vedas and Agamas will certainly fall, along with a thousand of his kin, into a terrible hell.

Thus, by demonstrating that the Supreme Lord is the author of all sciences, such as the *Īga* and *Āgama*, he manifests— without effort, like a mere breath— the Vedas, *Āgamas*, and so forth, which previously existed within his own self as his own powers (*śakti*), through an external manifestation consisting of the arrangement of phonemes in their respective preceding and succeeding sequences.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that the Vedas, Āgamas, and so forth are non-human (apauruṣeya) and have God as their cause.

Consequently, there is no contradiction between the scriptural passages that establish [the world] as being produced and those that establish it as unproduced. Now, [one might object]: "It is neither existent nor non-existent; Śiva alone is absolute; nothing else whatsoever exists here; there is no diversity here. But this is not so...

If it is argued that the Vedas cannot be eternal because of scriptural declarations such as "there is no second" which negate the existence of a second entity, we say no. This is because in scriptures such as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "All is indeed Rudra," the entire phenomenal world of moving and non-moving things is designated as Brahman itself due to its having Brahman as its material cause; therefore, the aforementioned scriptures do not intend to establish the falsity of the world.

Because even prior to creation, the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), whose nature is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*, exists within the Supreme Lord in a contracted form—like a seed containing a sprout—and because there is no difference between power and the possessor of power; as it is said: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and is innate."

Furthermore, because the Śruti teaches that power (*śakti*) belongs to the Supreme Lord by His very nature through the word "and" (*ca*), it is incorrect [to claim] that the world is illusory (*mithyā*), as there is no such scriptural authority for that.
Now, one might object: since words, cognitions, and actions exist for only three moments, how can the Veda, which consists of words, [be eternal]?
If it is argued that [the Veda] is eternal, we say no; for by the principle that "if the cause is eternal,

the effect is eternal," since the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which constitutes all Vedas in the form of their cause, is eternal, the eternity of the Veda as an effect is likewise beyond dispute.

Furthermore—the word of Maheśvara, who is eternally liberated, whose nature is pure, who is the Buddha, and who is the supreme authority by his very nature, is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The rule that "whatever is of human origin is invalid" applies only to those humans who are bound by the fetters of passion, hatred, and so forth. Moreover, even the Vedas [attain validity] through initiation into the Śāmbhava state...

Having obtained the greatness of Śiva’s grace, these [sages], like poets reciting hymns of praise for the infinite auspicious qualities of the Supreme Lord, extol His supreme majesty through the medium of the characteristics of the Creator (Brahmā) and offer praise with such verses as "Obeisance to the Lord of the worlds" and "Obeisance to the one with golden arms. Therefore, by virtue of being the power whose essence is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Supreme Lord, [they attain this state].

The preeminence of the Vedas and Agamas as authoritative sources for Paraśiva is thus established. Now, an objection may be raised: since passages such as "Becoming indeed the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, Prajāpati created all this—the Ṛks, the Yajus, and the Sāmans"—reveal that even the Four-faced One (Caturmukha) and others are the authors of the Vedas, how can Maheśvara alone be their author?

If this is argued, we say no. For from such scriptural passages as, "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him," it is understood that the Vedas existed even prior to the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha; and since it is seen that the Supreme Lord alone is the instructor of all the Vedas to Hiraṇyagarbha, He alone is said to be superior to all. Likewise...
And there is the Śruti:
"He who is the first among the gods, prior [to all], Rudra the great seer, superior to the universe— may that god, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha being born,
endow us with auspicious mindfulness," and so forth.

This indicates that the state of being superior to the expansion of the sentient and insentient (cid-acit-prapañca) and the status of being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha belong to the Supreme Lord alone.

Now, an objection is raised: since omniscience—defined as the knowledge of all categories of things taught in all the Vedas and Vedāntas—is observed even in Upamanyu, Dadhīci, Gautama, Dūrvāsas, and others, how can it belong to the Supreme Lord alone?

If this is argued, we say no: there is no contradiction, because they possess a certain degree of omniscience obtained through the grace of the Supreme Lord as a result of their worship of Him. Just as there is a difference in illumination despite the fact that a firefly and the sun are identical in being light, so too, since the Śrutis that illuminate all things have the Supreme Lord as their author, it is He alone who [possesses such omniscience].

Supreme knowledge is established; for, compared to those who merely propagate the scriptures, we observe that the authors of the scriptures possess specialized knowledge. Furthermore, omniscience—by virtue of pervading the entire universe and being the inner controller of all—is not possible for anyone else.
Because the sixfold attributes, such as omniscience and so forth, are not shared by anything else.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the authoritativeness of the scripture, omniscience, and other qualities are already established by the previous sūtra through [Brahman's] being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, what is the purpose of this sūtra?

If this is argued, we say no; for since the previous sūtra—by means of the inference "the sprout and so forth have an agent because they are effects, like a pot"—illuminates the authority of Brahman, the possibility exists that this present sūtra was composed by the venerable Vyāsa for the purpose of dispelling that doubt, as he has declared the sūtra: "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

"Śāstra-yoni" means that whose source or authority (*pramāṇa*) is the Śāstras, such as the *Nigamas* and *Āgamas*. Nor should it be argued that there is a fault such as "splitting the sentence" (*vākya-bheda*) in defining another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*); for since a Sūtra consists of mere indications, like a verse in poetry, it is free from faults such as splitting the sentence, and thus it is appropriate to establish another topical section. That...
I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upaniṣads; one who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One. This realization is not to be attained by means of logic.

It is the eternal truth, the supreme Brahman, the Person who is dark and tawny, whose vital seed is drawn up, who has diverse eyes—to that one of universal form, salutations again and again! He is the Lord of primary matter and the Knower of the Field, the Master of the qualities.
Its subject matter consists of such statements as: "The cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra," and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.
It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech; I ask about that Puruṣa who is known through the Upaniṣads, from whom words turn back...

The doubt arises as to whether it is logical that Brahman is to be known through the Vedāntas, given the observation of scriptural passages stating both "they turn back" [from it] (indicating it is not an object) and "it is not an object" [of the senses].
As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): Brahman is not to be known through the Vedāntas, for it is said, "It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech."

This is because of the observation of such scriptural passages as: "That which the mind does not perceive, that by which they say the mind is perceived, from which words turn back, failing to reach it along with the mind—he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere.
Furthermore, [it is established] by the inference: "The phenomenal world has a creator, because it is an effect, like a pot."

When it is argued that the Supreme Lord—defined by the sixfold attributes such as omniscience—is established [by other means], and since He is seen to be the object of other means of knowledge, the Supreme Brahman is not something to be known solely through the Vedānta scriptures; to this we reply: [The following is the response: "But because of the teaching of that which is not already known. (Sūtra 1.1.4) The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the objection raised. It is not the case that the Supreme Brahman is known through other means of knowledge. Why? Because of the teaching of that which is not already known (*aprasiddhopadeśāt*). For the Supreme Brahman, characterized by the aforementioned sixfold attributes, is not known through perception or other means of valid cognition; rather, it is taught here as something previously unknown. Therefore, the Supreme Brahman is indeed the exclusive object of the Vedānta scriptures. Furthermore, the fact that the Supreme Lord is established by other means of knowledge does not contradict His being the exclusive object of the Vedānta scriptures. This is because those other means of knowledge do not reveal the specific nature of the Supreme Brahman as defined by the sixfold attributes. Consequently, the Supreme Brahman is established as the exclusive object of the Vedānta scriptures. Thus, the conclusion is reached. *Note: The text provided contains the initial part of the objection and the opening of the response. The full response includes the sūtra and its commentary.*

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is as follows: Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, is indeed the object propounded by the Upaniṣadic scriptures. This is because we observe the negation of other means of knowledge regarding Brahman in such passages as, "One who does not know the Veda does not conceive that Great One," and "This understanding is not to be attained through logic. Furthermore, this is confirmed by the scriptural text: "I ask you about that which is known through the Upaniṣads."

Furthermore, because [the world] is taught to be knowable solely through the Upaniṣads, the validity of inference is established only as being concordant with the Vedānta scriptures, and not independently; for in the construction of chariots, pavilions, gate-towers, palaces, and so forth, we observe multiple agents. Nor can the oneness of the agent be proven by inference. [This applies to attributes such as] the abiding in Brahman, true resolve, true knowledge, bliss, and so forth.

Since it would otherwise follow that Brahman lacks the capacity for self-knowledge regarding its own nature and attributes, and because it would be impossible for Brahman to be the cause of both the world and [the individual soul], its status as the object of knowledge for the Vedāntas is beyond dispute. Passages such as "from which words turn back" are intended to communicate the majesty of that [Brahman]; otherwise, [the scripture would not have taught] that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of these and other such statements being rendered purposeless.
Now, [it may be argued]:
"The greatness of Agni-Śiva is attributed to the *tāmasa* [scriptures]."
And they know that the majesty of Brahman is even greater among those who possess royal power.
In the Sāttvika kalpas, the majesty of Hari is supreme;
in those very kalpas, those perfected in yoga shall go to the highest goal.

Thus, because the *Matsya Purāṇa* establishes that the Śiva Purāṇas are characterized by *tamas*, and because it is shown— beginning with "From *sattva* arises knowledge" and ending with "That intellect which knows both bondage and liberation, O Pārtha, is *sāttvika*"— that only the *sāttvika* intellect is the cause of liberation.
The greatness of Agni and Śiva is characterized by tamas and causes delusion;
from the very worship of those two, harm will certainly arise.

Thus, from the observation of such statements in the *Pāñcarātra-āgama*, it is established that the Purāṇas which expound the *Śiva-tattva* are characterized by *tamas*. Therefore, if it is argued: "Since those Purāṇas lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*), how can the status of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)—who is their subject matter—as being knowable through the Vedānta be justified?"—the answer is: no, because [the objection holds] only if the Śiva Purāṇas were indeed characterized by *tamas*.
Because there is an absence of direct Vedic revelation [supporting them], and because fabricated, disguised Buddhist statements lack authority;

furthermore—whether on the grounds that the Śiva Purāṇas concern a deity characterized by the quality of *tamas*, were composed by an author (Vyāsa) characterized by *tamas*, or were produced during an occasion of *tamas*—the Śiva Purāṇas are considered *tāmasa*. Not the first [alternative]:

Furthermore, since all the Vedas and Upaniṣads, beginning with the Ṛgveda, would also be found to propound Rudra and Agni, they too would incur the status of being *tāmasa* (dark/ignorant), which would lead to the contingency of their lack of authority and the consequence that they are merely Buddhist scriptures. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable—for then the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other texts spoken by Vyāsa would also be *tāmasa*. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable—for by one who is *sāttvika*...
This is because there is no authoritative evidence for the fabrication of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa by means of *tamas*, nor for the fabrication of the Śiva Purāṇa;
and furthermore, because Vyāsa has merely elaborated the essence of all the Vedas and Vedāntas in the form of the Purāṇas. [Objection: But in the Matsya Purāṇa—
Know from me that these six— the Mātsya, Kaurma, Laiṅga, Śaiva, Skānda, and Āgneya— are characterized by tamas.
"Those scriptures which describe the greatness of Agni or Śiva as being characterized by tamas and causing delusion,
whereas those scriptures which speak of the Lord of the World, Mukunda, the imperishable Viṣṇu, are indeed considered to be sāttvika."
O best of sages, wherever they speak of Umānātha, Śaṅkara, Bhairava, Yama, Durgā, Gaṇapati, or Kāla, those various [mantras] indeed yield tamasic fruits.
Those scriptures which speak of the fivefold worship, the gods, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī, are indeed considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).

Since the *Matsya*, *Hārīta*, *Pāñcarātra Āgama*, and other such texts designate the *Śiva Purāṇas* as being characterized by *tamas*, how can that which they propound—the Supreme Lord—be the Supreme Brahman? For destruction (*saṃhāra*), being an attribute of Rudra, is characterized by *tamas*. How then can its [the Lord's] nature be [pure]?

If it is argued that there is no obstacle [to its authority], we say no; for statements such as "The majesty of Śiva, who is Agni, is of the nature of *tamas* and causes delusion," being spoken in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, and since the *Matsya Purāṇa* is classified within the category of *Tāmasa Purāṇas*, those words lack authority.

Since the *Pāñcarātra-āgama* defines fire as being of a *rājasa* nature through such statements as "Brahmā, Indra, Sūrya, Candra, and Agni are born from *rajas*," and because mutual contradictions are observed between the statements of the *Mātsya-purāṇa* and the *Pāñcarātra-āgamas*, the lack of authority of both is established.

Moreover, through such passages as "For the Brāhmaṇas, fire is foremost among the deities," "As long as one lives, one performs the Agnihotra sacrifice," "Worship him, praise him; we worship Tryambaka," "They seek him within the people, Rudra, beyond [the reach of] thought," "Seizing him with the tongue," and "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity," and so forth, there is indeed the meditation upon Rudra-Vaiśvānara alone.

Because of the observation of injunctions stating "it must be performed," because of the observation of transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from non-performance, and because of the instruction that one attains hell by overstepping the worship of one's own deity— as seen in such passages as "You are Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods and the Brāhmaṇas; you are the lord of the Kṣatriyas"— there is [transgression] upon abandoning the worship of Rudra and Vaiśvānara.

Furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence of transcending the four social classes (*varṇa*). Since these fabricated statements contradict the Vedas, they should not be accepted by those who uphold the Veda. This is because, in such scriptural passages and sūtras as "For whom both Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood are food, and who is the eater, encompassing all that moves and does not move," destruction is specified as an attribute of the Supreme Brahman.

Furthermore, if that were not accepted, it would follow that Viṣṇu is not Brahman; for by such passages as "This Agni is indeed Rudra; these are his two bodies, one terrible and the other auspicious," and "From the non-terrible and from the terrible ones," etc., it is taught that he alone is the agent of creation and maintenance through his non-terrible face, and the agent of dissolution through his terrible face. Thus, it is he alone [who is Brahman].
The status of the Supreme Brahman is established by virtue of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world.

Furthermore, because we observe the prayer for the Supreme Lord’s pure, sattvic body as Śiva in such passages as, "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible and free from the appearance of evil," [the Lord is understood to be] the cessation of the phenomenal world and the peaceful.

Furthermore, because of the teaching that Śiva alone possesses supreme tranquility in such passages as, "They consider the fourth state to be auspicious non-duality; the Lord Parameśvara, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful," statements that establish [Śiva] as being purely *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness) refer exclusively to Kālarudra. This is also true for Kālarudra.
The superiority of Viṣṇu by virtue of being a portion (*aṃśa*) of Śiva is well-known in the Vedic scriptures. Thus says the Śruti:
"That which is Brahman, higher than the highest, that Hari who is higher than the highest, that Overlord who is higher than the highest—may my mind be intent upon Śiva."

In such scriptural passages as "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, manifold," the Supreme Lord's primordial power (*prakṛti-śakti*) is indicated to consist of the three qualities (*guṇas*). Therefore, it would follow that it is untenable for Nārāyaṇa to be Brahman by relying solely upon the quality of *sattva*.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting all Vedic scriptures that enjoin the realization of the non-material Brahman;

for in the Jābālopaniṣad, it is seen that meditation on Rudra with a white body is prescribed for those seeking liberation, as in the passage: "devoted to white meditation. Furthermore, in the Sūtagītā of the Sūtasaṃhitā—
O best of Brahmins, Rudra has the quality of sattva within and tamas without; Viṣṇu has tamas and sattva within, and the quality of rajas without.
O best of Brahmins, both within and without that Prajāpati,
Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are indeed overcome by rajas and tamas.
In the Śivadharmaśāstra:
"One who is endowed with the quality of sattva internally, yet joined with tamas externally, is called 'pure sāttvika'; such is Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world."
One who is joined with tamas internally but endowed with the quality of sattva externally is called "pure-tamas"; such is Viṣṇu himself, the Lord of Śrī.
From this instruction, it follows that he alone possesses superiority even over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.
In the Śivarahasyakhaṇḍa of the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā: "The wise know the ten Śaiva Purāṇas to be Sāttvika."
O best of the twice-born, whatever dharma exists therein is indeed to be trusted by them.
That which is taught as pure *sattva* is indeed the locus of bliss and knowledge;
it is the teacher of wisdom to the yogis, pure and resembling crystal.
"The auspicious Śiva, the sovereign of the Brahmins, never sleeps anywhere"—
thus do the Purāṇas proclaim the auspicious stories of the Brahmins.
O lords of sages, ten Śaiva Purāṇas are indeed devoted to the fault of violence,
and four Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas are tāmasa.
The duties of the Kṣatriyas have been heard; among them, Hari is their deity.
Tamas is Kṛṣṇa, who is indifferent and skilled in deceitful actions.
Sleep, laziness, negligence, and the like are proclaimed to be its qualities. Kṛṣṇa is remembered as Viṣṇu, reclining upon Śeṣa, the deluder of his devotees.
The Brāhma [quality] is indeed associated with the Rājasa [quality], which is esteemed everywhere as the duty of the Vaiśya;
Rajas is known to be the abode of suffering, red in color, and fickle.
Endowed with the three qualities (guṇas), they are indeed both fiery and solar;
therefore, O brahmins, the Purāṇas dedicated to Śiva are truly beneficial for them.
Thus, it is stated that the Śiva Purāṇas alone are of the nature of *sattva*.
Furthermore, if it is argued that there is a connection with another *kalpa* regarding the Śiva Purāṇas, that is entirely inconsistent. For the *Mātsya Purāṇa* states:
"The Purāṇa was first created by Brahmā as the foremost of all scriptures."
Immediately thereafter, the Vedas emerged from his mouths;
there was but one Purāṇa, extending to a vastness of a hundred crores [of verses].
By such statements as these, it is established that the *Brāhma Purāṇa* composed by Brahmā itself was condensed at the end of the Dvāpara age by Vedavyāsa into four hundred thousand verses.
In the *Dharma-saṃhitā*:
In the first and primordial Kṛta age, there was only the Brāhma Purāṇa, which is in accordance with the Śruti;
it was divided into eighteen types by means of ten million variations.
And because of the observation [in the text]: "df 186, p. 78). For this very reason, it is inconsistent to claim that the Śaiva Purāṇas refer to a different *kalpa*.
Now, [one might object] that it is Nārāyaṇa alone who, in the forms of the Fish, Tortoise, Boar, and so forth—
If it is argued that his supreme sattvic nature is established by the observation that he removes the entire burden of the earth, we say no;
for in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* it is said:
"On the eleventh day at midday in the month of Māgha, the Great Dancer [Śiva]..."
Then, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, Śiva consumed the poison.
Having remained that night through the yoga of Śiva, bearing the crescent moon,
he beheld Viṣṇu and the others who were surrounding him, as well as those who serve at his feet.

On the twelfth day, Nīlalohita, Mahādeva— the bringer of fear to all worlds— respectfully issued a command to those who had observed the fast and were prepared for the great feast, for the purpose of drinking the nectar produced from the churning of the ocean.

By such passages as these, the unique deeds of the Supreme Lord— such as the swallowing of the *kālakūṭa* poison, the slaying of the demons Andhaka, Jalandhara, and Tripura, and the lifting of Mount Kailāsa— are observed, as well as the necessity for Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas to observe the vow of Ekādaśī. This has been stated in the *Śivadharmaśāstra*:
The fast on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) is to be observed by both Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas,
since Nandīśa, Viṣṇu, and other leaders have practiced this vow.
"The remaining primary [rite] for the followers of the Smṛtis is fasting on the eleventh day (ekādaśī);
for the Śaivas who walk solely upon the path of the Vedas, the primary [rite] is the evening [offering].
Likewise, in the Siddhāntāgama:
"The Śaiva Ekādaśī is correctly remembered as that which extends through the *pradoṣa* [period];
no other [Ekādaśī] should be accepted by the Śaivas, according to the sole teaching of the Śaiva scriptures. And in the *Vīrāgama*:
O Śivā, for all Vīraśaivas who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti,
the Ekādaśī that correctly pervades the time of Pradoṣa should be accepted.
"Indeed, for all Śaiva vows, the evening [rite] alone is primary;
otherwise, O Goddess, in performing them differently, there would be great transgression.
Furthermore, even though the *Padma Purāṇa* and others have Viṣṇu as their primary focus, therein also...

Would it not follow that those [scriptures] which describe the greatness of Śiva are characterized by *tamas*? For, according to the Gītā statement, "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their domain; be free from the three *guṇas*, O Arjuna," even the Vedas are seen to consist of the three *guṇas*. This applies likewise to the *śruti* passages that propound the three forms [of the deity].

If it is argued that [the Veda] consists of the three qualities (*guṇatrayātmakatva*), we say no. Because of the scriptural vision [of the mantra], "By the word, which is multiform and eternal" (*vācā virūpanityayā*), it is improper for the eternal Veda to consist of the three qualities, since the authority of the revealed injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*) is stronger.
Furthermore, by such passages as "The auspicious, tranquil, immortal Brahman, the source," [it is established that] Śiva resides within the Vedas.
Because of the instruction on the state of supreme *sattva*, the statement that the Vedas consist of the three *guṇas* is intended— according to the distinction of qualified aspirants—
to refer to the worship of the Supreme Lord in His gross, subtle, and causal aspects as taught in the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures; therefore, it is not reasonable to interpret it otherwise.

Furthermore—what is this "tāmasatva" (the state of being characterized by *tamas*)? Is it (1) being produced from the *tamaḥ* quality; or (2) being produced from the *tamaḥ* quality as unmingled with its own other qualities; or (3) being produced from the *tamaḥ* quality as not overcome by others; or (4) being qualified by the state of being produced from the *tamaḥ* quality?
(5) Being authored by one characterized by *tamas*; (6) being taught by one characterized by the quality of *tamas*;

(7) teaching that which has the quality of *tamas* as predominant; or something else—none of these apply in the first case, because the Vedas are the breath of the Supreme Lord, who transcends the three qualities (*guṇa*).

Because it would entail the undesirable consequences [of the world] being impermanent, delusive, and of human origin; and because, since the entire manifold of sentient and insentient things is produced from *pradhāna*—which consists of the three *guṇas*—it would follow that even the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other such texts are *tāmasa*. Nor is it produced by *tamas* alone, for it is unestablished that a single [quality] can be a cause.

Not the second [alternative], because every quality (*guṇa*) produces [an effect] only when conjoined with another quality; thus, being produced by the *tamas* quality unassociated with others is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Not the third [alternative], because: "When there was neither darkness nor day, neither night nor existence, nor non-existence—Śiva alone existed."
Because Śiva, established by such scriptural passages as these, is eternally pure, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is not established [as his source].
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable:
"The son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas."
And also by means of narratives, sub-narratives, verses, and purifications of the ritual rules.

"Being an expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, he composed the Purāṇasaṃhitā"— from this statement in the Viṣṇupurāṇa, it follows that none of the Purāṇas composed by Vyāsa possess a *tāmasa* (dark/demonic) nature; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those Purāṇas favored by you would likewise be *tāmasa*, since the same logic applies to all of them.

The fifth [alternative] is not tenable—because it is well-established in all scriptures that Rudra is the agent of dissolution (*saṃhāra*), and because dissolution is an effect of the quality of darkness (*tamas*)—if you argue thus, it is not so;

for it would follow that Viṣṇu is not the Supreme Lord (*anīśvara*) due to his lack of agency in dissolution, [contradicting] the Vedic scripture: "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours... (*yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*).

Furthermore, because the state of Śiva’s body being characterized by *tamas* is denied, it is not appropriate to attribute a specific association with the *guṇas* on the grounds that the Vedas—by the statement "the Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their domain"—teach the *pravṛtti-dharma* (active duty) which consists of the three *guṇas*. Now, one might object: "In cosmic cycles (*kalpas*) where the *tamas* quality predominates, the Purāṇas composed by Brahmā are characterized by that [quality] and are thus *tāmasa*."

If it is argued that Śiva is also characterized by *tamas* because he is the one to be propounded therein, we say no; for there is no evidence that the Purāṇas composed by the four-faced Brahmā during the *tāmasa* kalpas continue to exist in this current Śvetavarāha-kalpa, nor is there any evidence that the twenty-eighth Vyāsa is currently composing Purāṇas in this very kalpa.
And because it is so heard [in scripture]. As it is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "In that Vaivasvata interval, during the Dvāpara ages, the most excellent Vedavyāsa descended twenty-eight times."

Furthermore, the fact that Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, who exists in the present time, is the author of all the Purāṇas is heard in that very same [text]: "He, who was an expert in the meaning of the Purāṇas, composed the Purāṇa-saṃhitā.
Having identified those eighteen Purāṇas in that very place, the sequence is stated with reference to the order of their origin:

"This [Purāṇa] is indeed known as Vaiṣṇava, following immediately after the Pādma. Thus, all the incarnations such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa who reside in the current kalpa are included, because they originate from the lineage of Raghu and others,
and because events such as the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice occurred within the span of this kalpa.
In considering the relative strength or weakness of the Purāṇas— which expound the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava traditions and were composed by the twenty-eighth Vedavyāsa born in this current Kalpa—
it is useless to introduce the conceptualization of Brahmā as being characterized by *tamas* (darkness) and so forth, since these texts are separated from one another by vast intervals of time.

Now, it has been stated that the authors of the Purāṇas attained their status as such by learning the goals of human life from Brahmā; this is true. In that regard, the contents of the Purāṇas pertaining to past kalpas and the author of the Purāṇas are presented by Brahmā exactly as they were in the Padma-kalpa.
The supreme Lord’s grace toward Mārkaṇḍeya; and those ancient events situated within the current kalpa,

such as the incarnations of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Varāha, as well as the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa poison and the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice— these too exist solely by virtue of belonging to this very kalpa.

These [qualities] are taught by Brahmā and likewise established by the authors of the Purāṇas. When there is mutual contradiction among them, it is pointless to use them as a basis for determining the superiority of one's own preferred Purāṇa. Furthermore, where and how is the presentation of past kalpas—separated by vast intervals of time—as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika) or darkness (tāmasa), etc., relevant?
Thus we do not know [the answer].

Nor is it the sixth [alternative]: for although the terrible body belonging to Rudra is characterized by darkness (*tamas*) due to its nature as a destroyer, the Supreme Lord who possesses that body transcends darkness. And so it is said in the *Kaivalya*:
"Having meditated upon the Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, whose companion is Umā, who is three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil,
the sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, who is beyond darkness.
Although the designation "tāmasa" (belonging to darkness) is observed in cases such as Devadatta, who is characterized by a body and so forth in which the quality of *tamas* predominates;

Nevertheless, in that case, such usage occurs because [the object] is qualified by that alone; however, in the present context, it is not so, because there is scriptural evidence for the existence of many forms belonging to the Supreme Lord which transcend darkness and consist of a non-worldly nature of light. "With firm limbs, the fierce one of many forms, the tawny one..."
In the passage "He is adorned with white gold," the word *śukla* (white) signifies being composed of *sattva*,
as in the expression "red, white, and black" (*lohita-śukla-kṛṣṇā*). Otherwise, according to the view of those who assert the superiority of Viṣṇu,
even the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas and others would incur the status of being *tāmasa* (of the nature of *tamas*), since they would then be understood as propounding a Viṣṇu characterized by *tamas*.

Otherwise, how could Viṣṇu be the destroyer of the Yādavas, Kauravas, Daityas, and others for the purpose of removing the earth's burden? Or how could he, in the form of a great deluder (Mahāmoha) known as a Puruṣa, be the author of the scriptures of the Buddha, Jina, and others, which serve to delude the Daityas?

As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: Having spoken thus to them, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, having produced [this being] from his own body of great delusion (mahāmoha), gave him to them and said this, O best of gods:
"This Māyāmoha will delude all those Daityas;
consequently, they shall become bound, having been cast outside the path of the Vedas.
For indeed, in the absence of its own quality of *tamas*, it would not be possible for it to serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for that which is called Mahāmoha.
Because the body of Mohinī is characterized by *tamas*.

Now, one might object: although Viṣṇu possesses the quality of *tamas* for the sake of his cosmic functions, it is not predominant because it is overwhelmed by *sattva*. Rudra, however, being overwhelmed by *tamas*, is characterized by it and thus acts as the agent of dissolution.
If it is argued that the seventh position—that [the Lord] is the object to be propitiated—should be accepted, we say: "Not so.

For in the case of incarnations such as Nṛsiṃha, which proceed with the sole purpose of destroying enemies, there would follow the consequence of being dominated by *tamas* (ignorance) due to that predominance; furthermore, this is refuted by the fact that Śiva is devoid of *tamas*, which serves as a subverting argument against the opposing view.

Not the latter—[the view that] he who is the agent of dissolution is *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness). For is there some other agent of dissolution for him as well, or not? If there is, then even though he is *tāmasa*, he alone is the most eminent and the dissolver of all, because of his independence. If there is not, then this very one is the *tāmasa* most eminent of all; thus, being *tāmasa* is pervaded by being the agent of universal dissolution and being the most eminent.

The reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). Therefore, Rudra is supreme over all because he is the destroyer of all; by contrast, like the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojaka*), because without the relationship of stronger and weaker, the relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is impossible. For if that which is characterized by *sattva* were subject to sublation, it would be contradictory in relation to destruction. It is said that the weak is everywhere sublated.

Furthermore, according to logic, there is the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), because [the subject] "Rudra is superior to the universe" is not established as a locus (*pakṣa*).
Since inference is dependent upon that [scriptural authority], it does not constitute the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).
In this manner, the quality of being *sāttvika* should be refuted by considering the alternatives in the manner described above. Moreover—

It would follow that the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* and other purāṇas which establish the superiority of Viṣṇu are *sāttvika*, while the *Padma Purāṇa* and others which establish the superiority of Rudra are *tāmasa*;
for in the *Padma Purāṇa*, the superiority of both Hari and Hara is described through its preceding and succeeding sections (*pūrvakhaṇḍa* and *uttarakhaṇḍa*).

If it is argued that being *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness) is intended only for that specific portion [of the Mahābhārata], then by that logic, the same status of *tāmasatva* would follow for those portions of the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Bhāgavata*, and so forth. For instance, in the *Bālakāṇḍa* of the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "O Hero, I see no one other than the wielder of the trident (*Śūlin*) capable of supporting you"; and in the *Yuddhakāṇḍa*: "The Lord of Umā, Paśupati, who is worshipped by all the worlds."
And in the Uttarakāṇḍa, it says: "Is this terrible power of weapons mine, or that of Tryambaka?

Because there is an extensive description of the journey to Kailāsa, the subduing of Rāvaṇa, the favor shown to Indrajit, and so forth, and because of the description of how the destruction of Rāvaṇa was caused by the fire of Rudra, he too is perceived as being of a *tāmasa* nature.

Therefore, if one were to conceive of the Śiva Purāṇas as being characterized by *tamas*, it would follow that they are outside the Vedic fold like Buddhism; so, enough with this excessive elaboration.
Here, in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the term "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) refers to the devotees who are exclusively devoted to the One and have been initiated into the Śaiva path.

The identity-in-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman has been established. This is because such texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" and "Having known the Lord, they become one with Him" declare the establishment of non-difference between the object of worship and the worshipper. In the second section, it is shown that Brahman possesses attributes (saviśeṣatva), and that the world and Brahman are distinct at the time of creation and maintenance, yet [become one] at the time of dissolution.
The non-difference [of the individual soul] from [Brahman], like that of a river and the ocean, has been established. In the third section,

it is shown that the very scripture of the Vedas, Vedāntas, and Āgamas— which teaches both difference and non-difference manifested by the Supreme Lord— is the sole authority for the existence of Brahman.
Thus ends the third section, *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*. Now begins the section on *Samanvaya* (Harmonization):
[the inquiry into] the Vedas and Upanishads manifested from the sixfold Paraśiva-Brahman, which are the source of various deities such as Indra, Upendra, and Candra.

To exclude the charge of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), the fourth section is commenced with the aphorism: "But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the harmony (*samanvaya*) [of all things] in it alone, according to the analogy of the flow of a river. (1.1.4) Since everything is in perfect harmony within that very [Brahman] by way of the analogy of the current of a river, there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Thus begins the fourth section.

By the word "that" (tat), it is the previously mentioned Paraśiva-Brahman of the six planes—who is the substratum of all, the cause of all, and known through the Vedāntas—that is designated. By the word "but" (tu), other means of valid cognition such as perception are excluded. By the word "harmony" (samanvaya), [the exclusion applies] to those statements contained therein that propound [deities] such as Candra, Upendra, Dinendra, and others.

By means of the "method of the coarse Arundhatī" (*sthūlārundhatī-nyāya*), the intended meaning is taught to reside in that very [Brahman] through the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*)— such as the introduction and conclusion. The meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is established by all the Vedāntas, which are endowed with these sixfold marks of purport, after first setting aside other means of valid cognition such as perception.

In this regard, the subject matter consists of the statements of all the Vedas, Vedāntas, and Āgamas: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"; "For Rudra is one, he does not stand for a second"; "Countless thousands are remembered, yet they are not seen";
"The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world; those gods asked Rudra: 'Who are you?'"
He said: "I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me.

He entered into the innermost of the inner—the *Ṛta*, the *Satya*, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, whose seed is drawn up, who has diverse eyes—to him of universal form, salutations again and again! All the Vedas...
Regarding the phrase "that state which they proclaim":

it is the fact that all Vedāntic passages, which enjoin both difference and non-difference, have as their ultimate purport the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is the sixfold locus and the dual cause (both material and efficient) of the entire universe.

There is much doubt as to whether [the Upanishads] are devoted to the worship of various deities such as Indra and Upendra who are remnants of *karma*, or whether they propound *pradhāna* and other principles that serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) of those deities.
As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): in no way is Paraśiva-Brahman the subject taught by all the Vedāntas.

It is possible for them [the Upaniṣads] to be intent upon injunctions; otherwise, if they were intent upon both, there would be the fault of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*). Since the relationship of cause and effect between the world and Brahman is observed, the establishment of Brahman through inference is justified. Therefore, it is not the case that Brahman is to be understood solely through the Vedānta.

Furthermore, it is also appropriate that [the Self] is intent upon the worship of various deities, for we see such scriptural passages as: "Agni is the first among the deities," and "That Sun is Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman. Moreover: "This [Māyā] is manifold, very firm, possessing many sprouts; she herself is differentiated by the qualities (guṇas), and even within the sprouts, she is differentiated by the qualities everywhere."

Furthermore, it is appropriate that [the passage] refers to the Pradhāna, because its status as the source of all deities and its nature as the universal cause are indicated by such statements as: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, who produces many offspring resembling herself, who is the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Thus, it is logical that the text has that [Pradhāna] as its intended object.

Furthermore, since worldly conventions such as "this is a jar" or "this is the letter ṭa" depend upon knowledge transmitted through a lineage of elders, [the Veda] must have as its ultimate purport the established Brahman, which is the substratum of all auspiciousness and from which all calamities are removed.

Since the faults of being purposeless and being dependent [on other means of knowledge] would follow, the Vedāntas are enjoined to have as their purport injunctions and meditations (*vidhi-upāsana*) in order to avoid both those defects. Alternatively, it might be argued that they are established as having ritual action (*karman*) as their purport by way of teaching the agent and the deity. To this we reply:

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: it is logical that the Vedāntas have Brahman as their primary purport and that they are intended for the injunction of meditation upon Brahman.

Therefore, the fault of syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) does not arise; for both types of injunction are observed therein. To illustrate: the purport of texts such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" is directed toward Brahman by means of the sixfold marks of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*), beginning with the introductory context (*upakrama*).

Furthermore, its focus on the method of meditation is observed through the following signs for determining the intended meaning (tātparya): the introduction and conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit,
the explanatory praise (arthavāda), and logical consistency.
Thus, in the Smṛti, it is stated that "hearing" (śravaṇa) refers to the determination of the purport of the Vedānta through means such as the introduction and conclusion [of the texts].
Suffering arises from ignorance, and knowledge is its remover;
hearing all the Vedānta statements is that which brings about such knowledge.

"Listening" (śravaṇa) is the determination of the intended meaning of Vedic statements regarding that which is higher than the highest, by means of the marks such as the introductory context (upakrama) and so forth.
Thus, the opening and the conclusion constitute one mark [of the unity of the subject matter]. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" is the opening.
"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That thou art, Śvetaketu"—this is the conclusion.
Furthermore, "That thou art" is the repetition. And: "I ask you about that person known through the Upaniṣads."

Its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) consists in its being unattainable through other means of knowledge. Its "fruit" is the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one, as expressed in such passages as, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and so forth. This very deity reflected: "Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and differentiate names and forms."
The fivefold cosmic functions—creation, sustenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace—are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*).

Just as in the passage, "My dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known," the examples of clay and so forth are logical arguments (*upapatti*); the same applies elsewhere as well.

In the *Nārāyaṇabīja*: "Smaller than the small, greater than the great" is the introduction (*upakrama*); "For all this is Rudra" is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*); "To him who is the Supreme Maheśvara, to the Lord of Ambikā, to the Lord of Umā, to Paśupati, salutations again and again"—this constitutes the repetition (*abhyāsa*); and in passages such as "Rudra, the Great Seer, is superior to the universe," there is the result (*phala*).

The quality of being "unprecedented" (*apūrvatā*) arises because attributes such as being superior to all are not established by any other means of knowledge. "All are liberated from the supreme death" constitutes the fruit (*phala*). "Thousand-headed" is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "There is nothing whatsoever higher than Him" is the logical justification (*upapatti*).

This should be understood in the same way for all Vedānta texts. Therefore, [the Self is defined] by these three types of definitions: those that differentiate its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and those that are incidental (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*).

It is logical that all Vedāntas establish Brahman. Just as the eye, which is the cause for the direct perception of form, establishes the existence of substance, so too the Vedāntas—though intent upon injunctions—establish the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, the substrate of all.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in their being intent on both [injunction and realization]. As it is said: "This wisdom is not to be attained through mere reasoning."

Since the validity of inference has been refuted by scripture (*śruti*), and since there is no establishment of the oneness of the agent through inference, inference is here enjoined as being authoritative with respect to Brahman:
"The entire world— the various beings, the manifold universe, that which has been born and that which is being born— all this indeed..."
By the passage beginning with "Rudra, to that Rudra let there be homage," his identity with the world is established because he is the material cause of the entire universe.
Starting from "The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā," it continues: "He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Fire, he is the Moon;
he alone is all that has been and all that is to be, the eternal. Having known him..."

By the passage ending with "There is no other path for liberation than [him] who transcends death," having declared that Paraśiva-Brahman consists of all deities, there is seen the teaching that the worship of Him alone is the cause of liberation, as expressed in the mantra beginning with "He who is Rudra in the fire."
Furthermore, because Śiva alone is taught to be the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, it is established that He alone consists of all the deities and so forth.

The worship of various deities according to the distinction between superior, middling, and inferior aspirants (*adhikārins*) is not contradictory. As stated in the *Smṛti*: "The power (*śakti*), which is of the nature of both difference and non-difference, is eternally grounded in Brahman," just like the power of fire.

Because of the teaching that [the Self] is the locus of Brahman, because there is no power without a locus, and because of the non-difference between power and the possessor of power, it is logical that He alone possesses agency and that He is its very essence; thus, the Pradhāna does not possess universal agency.
Furthermore, as is seen in the case of hearing news of the welfare of one's son and so forth, even established knowledge can serve as a cause for activity. Therefore, [the Pradhāna is not the cause].

The activity of the elders alone is the cause of engagement. For it is possible for children to acquire knowledge of established objects through the instructions of their mothers, fathers, and others, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth";
likewise, we observe that those who know the ornaments of poetry [acquire] knowledge of all matters through the instruction of their disciples.
Therefore, it is established that the Vedānta texts possess authority with respect to Brahman.

Now, an objection may be raised: since no purpose for the scriptures is seen in the case of an already established Brahman, it is logical that the Vedāntas are merely subordinate to injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*). Furthermore, the cessation of bonds (*pāśanivṛtti*) cannot be the fruit [of knowledge]; and as for that bond, is it distinct from Him (Brahman) or not?
Furthermore, is it non-different from that [Śiva], true, or false? Not the first, because it would entail the loss of the non-duality of Śiva as qualified by power (*śakti*).

Not the second, because if the bond of *māyā* were real, saṃsāra would persist forever, making liberation impossible; consequently, no one would ever exert effort toward the cessation of *māyā*. For this very reason, not the third. Nor the last—

If it is argued that the activity of the Vedānta scriptures is in every way impossible—because the Supreme Lord is eternally established, making the engagement of those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) untenable, and because there is no inequality between the states of bondage and liberation—then we say: no.
For the bond consisting of the three qualities (guṇatraya) is indeed distinct from the Supreme Lord; therefore, upon its cessation...

There is no possibility of the loss of the non-duality of Śiva as delimited by the innate power of consciousness (*svābhāvikacicchakti*). Even if the bond of *māyā* were real, there is no consequence of the impossibility of liberation, because the doctrine of both duality and non-duality is accepted. Nor is there a lack of evidence for this: "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed; one who desires to become Brahman should practice the knowledge of Brahman."

This is because of the existence of scriptural authorities such as these. Since ignorance (avidyā) causes delusion and is distinct from the power of consciousness (cicchakti), its cessation is indeed possible only through the worship of Śiva. What is called "cessation" is dissolution into that power of consciousness which is its cause; for according to the maxim, "destruction is dissolution into the cause."

If it is argued that because ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the manifold of the moving and the non-moving, its cessation is never possible, and therefore the engagement in *saṃsāra* is possible even for those who know Brahman—this is not so. [For it is said: "One grieves while deluded by a lack of mastery; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself and does not return again. And: "Not so."

This is because hundreds of scriptural passages, such as "He returns again," teach that those who know Brahman possess its very nature and are free from returning [to saṃsāra]. Nor should it be argued that there is no purpose for the injunction because knowledge of that [Brahman] is impossible through a word denoting Brahman alone; for even though the knowledge of the substance to be offered and the deity is accomplished by the mere study of the mantra, at the time of the actual oblation—

Because we see an injunction for application (*prayogavidhi*) in the statement, "It should be recollected by means of mantras," there is likewise no contradiction here with the injunction regarding the Vedānta texts.

If it is objected: "But how can an injunction for application be possible here, given that the injunctions of origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*) are not observed?"—we reply:
No, because [such injunctions are implied] in passages such as, "May I become a sustainer of immortality, O gods."

Since the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) is established without contradiction through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the applicatory injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*)—that "having received initiation for the wearing of the *liṅga* of Paraśiva, one should perceive the Supreme Self"—is logically consistent. [This is supported by the scripture:
"From meditating upon Him, from union with Him, and from the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion; having known God..."
In passages such as "one is released from all bonds," a person qualified for liberation—endowed with meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon Paraśiva—is enjoined.

Therefore, the injunction regarding the performance of the ritual (*prayogavidhi*) is established by the logic of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice: one who desires liberation, having received the *Śāmbhava-dīkṣā* consisting of the wearing of sacred ash (*bhasma*), rudrākṣa beads, and the Śiva-liṅga, should attain the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva, through the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*).
Now, an objection is raised: in such passages as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," an injunction regarding the knowledge of Brahman is not possible;

for this would entail that the changeless Brahman becomes an object of action (*karmakāraka*). Even if an injunction were possible, its status as an origination, attainment, modification, or purification would be untenable. Furthermore, according to the principle of the *saktu* (barley-meal) injunction, [the knowledge] would lead to an independent result.
Just as in the case of "one offers with groats," it is improper to say "one should see by means of the self" by way of a transformation of its causality;
for since Brahman is changeless and without differentiation, an injunction to know Brahman is not tenable—if this is argued, we say no.

For although the three types of injunctions—concerning origin (*utpatti*), application (*viniyoga*), and qualification (*adhikāra*)—are impossible in the case of the Supreme Self who is the substrate of all, [the injunction to know is still valid].

For one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the injunction (*vidhi*) is not contradicted for the sake of the fruit that is liberation. If it is asked, "What injunction is resorted to here?", [the reply is:
all three types of injunctions are to be inferred.
Now, an objection: unlike the establishment of a jar by means of the eye, the establishment of Brahman through the Vedāntas does not occur in that same way, because [the Vedāntas] are independent.

If it is argued that the cognition of an object such as "this is a jar" is established through the conjunction of the eye, and that the authority of words lies in the finality of their intended meaning (tātparya), and therefore it is improper to say that Vedāntic sentences enjoin the knowledge of Brahman or produce valid knowledge of Brahman—this is not so. [For example: "He offers the *samidh* oblation."

Just as, by the force of injunction, both the status of being an injunction for the five *prayāja* offerings and the status of being an injunction for their performance are established from such sentences, so too it is indeed possible for the Vedāntas to possess both the quality of producing valid knowledge regarding Brahman and the status of being an injunction with respect to the knowledge of Brahman that assists toward liberation.

Objection: Since it is observed that the knowledge of Brahman is established through the Vedānta texts alone, there is no purpose for an injunction regarding it; for the purpose of an injunction can arise only from the absence of such knowledge. Reply: This is not so. Even though that knowledge is established by the Vedānta texts as being mediate (parokṣa), the injunction is justified for the sake of attaining immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge of it.

The direct realization of Brahman is not ordained through the knowledge alone produced by the words of the Vedānta; rather, the attainment of that realization comes solely from the knowledge consisting of its worship, obtained through the compassionate glance of a true guru. This alone is the path of the Śruti: "Having meditated, the sage goes to the Source of Beings, the Witness of all, beyond darkness..."
Beyond that, through meditating upon Him, through union with Him, and through becoming His very essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of all cosmic illusion;

know this through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation. One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself; by the practice of churning with knowledge, the wise man burns away the bonds. Having known the God, one is released from all fetters.

Having known Him as the Lord, they become immortal. One should see the Self in the Self alone; Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of space. "Consisting of that, born of that, merged in that"—thus, being tranquil, one should worship. "Worship thus, O Prācīnayogya," and so forth—in such passages, knowledge consisting of the worship of the Supreme Lord is prescribed as the primary cause for the fruit of liberation. And likewise, the Smṛti says:
It should be heard from the statements of the Vedas, reflected upon through logical reasonings,
and constantly meditated upon as the object of meditation for the sake of direct realization.
Knowledge is the discernment of the object, and meditation is the cause of its cultivation;
therefore, through the contemplation of even a worm as a deity, the living soul becomes Śambhu.

By these and other statements, he indicates that *nididhyāsana*— accompanied by meditation (*dhyāna*) which is itself distinguished by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)— is the supreme cause for the direct realization of Paraśiva in his six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*) and for attaining identity with Him.
Therefore, preceded by the prohibition of all rites performed for desire, [one should practice] the Vedānta of both the *Nigama* and *Āgama* as they have issued from the mouth of Śiva.
Since the meditation upon Paraśiva— the supreme reality whose nature is unerring and attained through the purification of the mind resulting from the performance of all duties dedicated to Śiva,

and who is the universal cause of both the creation and sustenance of the entire world as propounded by all the Upaniṣads— is what is to be enjoined, the injunction for the practice of knowledge and meditation through such scriptural passages as "Meditate upon Him" (tad upāsasva) is appropriate only for them. Śiva alone...

In the *Atharvaśikhā*, it is stated: "One should meditate on Śiva, the maker of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else"; thus, the worship of anything other than Śiva is rejected for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Therefore, the cessation of the bonds of the illusion of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-māyā-pāśa*) cannot occur otherwise. [As the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* states: "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara."

"The one God rules over the perishable nature; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*). When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, only then, without knowing Śiva, will there be an end to suffering. From such scriptural passages as these, [it follows] that [liberation comes] solely from the meditation, concentration, and knowledge of Śiva.

The fruit in the form of liberation is thus ordained. Therefore, Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman; he is to be held, known, meditated upon, heard, reflected upon, and worshipped by those desiring liberation. Thus, it is the established conclusion that the Vedāntas are intent upon Brahman and intent upon His worship, according to the purport of the sixfold marks (liṅgas).

Now, if it is argued that—according to the principle "Brahman is real and the world is illusory"—liberation consists precisely in the knowledge of one's own true nature preceded by the knowledge of the world's illusoriness obtained through the investigation of all the Vedāntas, we say no; for this would entail the consequence of being outside of all the Vedas and Vedāntas. What, indeed, is this so-called illusoriness of the world?
[The claim that] the world is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, or that there is a negation of it throughout the three periods of time,

is not the first [position], because the relationship of sublated and sublator is impossible between those two; for the negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is not enjoined by the knowledge of Brahman, as seen in such passages as "All is indeed Rudra" and "All this is indeed Brahman."
Because of the teaching that all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) has Śiva as its essence;

furthermore, according to such scriptural passages as "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else," for liberated souls, it is precisely the noose of Māyā— which is conventionally designated as the world consisting of pots, cloths, and so forth in the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*)— that [ceases].

It is concealed by the knowledge that everything has Śiva as its essence. Through the complete knowledge of the fact that everything has Śiva as its essence—as stated in such scriptural passages as "Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is this entire world"—the cognition of "pot-ness" and so forth regarding a pot, a cloth, or other objects ceases; however, the pot and the like do not cease to exist, because they have Śiva as their essence. Therefore, it is not...

The phenomenal world (prapañca) is to be sublated by the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, its falsity (mithyātva) is untenable. If that [falsity] were accepted, it would follow that the scriptural declaration of "knowing all through the knowledge of one" would be rendered null and void.
It is precisely because the phenomenal world has Brahman as its material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) that the scripture declares the proposition of knowing everything through the knowledge of the One.

For this very reason, such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," "All this has that as its self," and "Rudra is indeed all" teach that everything has Śiva as its essence. Therefore, there is no sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by the knowledge of Brahman. Even for those who know Brahman, such as Janaka and others, worldly activity is observed to proceed exactly as before. For them, [the world does not cease].

[Otherwise] there would be the sublation of phenomenal diversity (*prapañcabādha*), as well as the impossibility of the worldly activities such as maintaining the body for those who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Furthermore: "In the state of undivided non-duality (*akhaṇḍādvaita*), everything is indeed Brahman and nothing else.
Through knowledge, the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*) dissolves, but not its essential nature (*svarūpa*)."

One should never conceive of any diversity whatsoever, because Brahman is the sole material cause; since difference is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), how could it ever arise?
Therefore, the assertion that [the world] consists of mere ignorance (*avidyāmātratva*) is indeed for the sake of delusion.
Thus, the censure of those who maintain that the world is illusory is heard. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Gītā*: "They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord.
Nor is the second position tenable: "These creatures are born without root and without support; never was there a time when the world was not thus."
Because [the world] is established as eternal by such passages as these.

Now, one might object: "In the beginning, this was non-existent; from that, indeed, the existent was born"; and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second, Brahman"—by hundreds of such scriptural texts, [it is shown that] prior to creation...
If it is asked, "Since there is a teaching that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-existent, how can it possess reality throughout the three periods of time?"—the answer is no.

For in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*), the non-existence of the phenomenal world prior to creation is stated because, being incapable of differentiation into name and form, it existed within Brahman in a subtle state. This is further supported by the subsequent statement, "From that, indeed, the existent was born" (*tato vai sadajāyata*).
Furthermore, the world's status as an effect is taught by virtue of its being subject to the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).

Moreover, if one were to accept non-existence (*asat*) for the term "unreal" on the grounds that it is a non-entity like a sky-lotus, why would even the son of a barren woman not be the cause of the world? The restriction "Being alone" (*sadeva*) does not negate the possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*); rather, it excludes the unreal (*asat*).
The negation of its being the cause is due to its being subject to error.

Furthermore, how can there be a negation of having attributes in the Śruti passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"? For here we observe a specific time in the word "in the beginning" (agre) and a specific action in the verb "was" (āsīt).
By the restrictive term "only one" (*ekameva*), the existence of any other presiding agent is excluded;

by the word "without a second" (*advitīya*), Brahman's status as the dual cause of the world—both its material and efficient causes—is enjoined. This is to be understood in the same way in such passages as, "For there is only one Rudra, no second stood beside him. For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe."
Therefore, the secret is that there is no negation [of the world] across the three periods of time.
Now, as for the refutation of the view that the world is merely conventionally real and not ultimately real: if it is argued that this is not so, then what is this?

The nature of conventional truth (*vyavahārasatyatva*) consists of: 1) being cognizable through mere convention; 2) being cognizable through a convention that is subject to sublation; 3) being unsublated within three or four stages of inquiry;

4) being contradicted by the means of valid cognition that reveal reality (*tattvāvedakapramāṇa*); or 5) being the object of a cognition devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). 6) [Or, it is the state of being perceived as such.]
Alternatively, [the definition] might be "being the object of a cognition produced by a defect in the instrument of knowledge.

But this is not the first [option], because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman as well, since Brahman too is accessible through empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*). Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity of the teacher and the disciple remaining silent and ignorant. [As it is said: "Therefore, the desire to know Brahman"; "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

Furthermore, this would result in the scriptures and aphorisms—such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—being like painting on a wall [i.e., rendered baseless]. If it is argued that all these scriptural passages concern Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa*), whereas the attribute-less (*nirviśeṣa*) is not the object of any linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), this is unobjectionable; for the very linguistic usage "it is not an object" presupposes its being an object.
