Furthermore, by establishing that the Vedāntas do not have the indeterminate (nirviśeṣa) as their object, [the definition] becomes favorable to our position, since even those [Vedāntic texts] consist of empirical usage (vyavahāra). Nor is it the case that [Brahman] is cognizable through sublated empirical usage; this is the second [point], because over-extension (ativyāpti) to Brahman would be unavoidable. For every...

Empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is indeed sublated because it is included within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Nor should it be suspected that "being sublated" is a qualifier of "being cognizable through empirical usage"; for if "being sublated" alone were the definition, the remaining terms would be redundant. And this is not an acceptable consequence, as it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the illusory (*prātibhāsika*). Nor [is it correct to say] that [the definition applies] when there is non-sublation by a cognition whose object is other than Brahman...

The refinement "being sublated" (*bādhitatva*) is correct; for if "non-sublation by cognition" were defined as not being the counter-positive of a destruction produced by a cognition, there would be a lack of definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of earlier cognitions which are counter-positives of destructions produced by subsequent cognitions. However, if it were defined as being the object of a cognition whose content is not removed by another cognition, then [the definition applies to] "the pot does not exist."

There is no over-extension [of the definition] to jars, cloths, and so forth, which are objects whose cognition has been sublated by the knowledge "the cloth does not exist," because those cognitions have as their object something other than Brahman; this we shall refute in detail further on.

Furthermore, since even the existence of qualities such as "having a blue back" is of the nature of Brahman, [the definition would fail] in the case of those things sublated by cognitions having that as their object.
The over-extension [of the definition] to silver and other such things is indeed unavoidable; for even those cognitions lack an object distinct from Brahman.
Nor should it be argued that there is no such over-extension because blue, the back [of an object], and so forth—which are not of the nature of Brahman—are the objects of those cognitions;

for in that case, [the definition would fail to apply to] precisely those cognitions whose objects are distinct from Brahman, such as the attributeless nature [of Brahman] (*nirviśeṣatva*) and the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*).

Because, by virtue of negating conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that a definition is impossible even within the merely empirical realm (*vyāvahārika*). Furthermore, it is difficult to establish that attributes such as "being devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣatva*), which possess counter-correlates, are nothing other than the very nature of Brahman, which is itself devoid of counter-correlates. This is because knowledge of the mere nature [of Brahman] has as its object nothing beyond the self-luminous consciousness that is capable of tolerating a thousand superimpositions (*adhyāsa*).

Furthermore, it would lead to the impossibility [of the definition] due to the impossibility of being a sublater (*nivartakatva*). If one were to accept that "subsisting in a cognition whose object is not distinct [from the object]" is the delimiting factor for the status of being a sublater, then, given that the insentient mental mode (*vṛtti*) is what is actually sublated, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that [ignorance] is sublated by knowledge (*jñāna-bādhyatva*). Even if one were to somehow admit that the mental mode possesses the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), [the contradiction remains].

Furthermore, since that which is common to the knowledge of its own nature cannot be the non-delimiting condition for the cessation of knowledge, there would be a contradiction with one's own established tenets; let this suffice for the details. Nor is the third position—that being sublated within three or four stages [of inquiry] constitutes [the definition]—correct, because it would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman itself, which is unsublatable (*abādhyam*).

Indeed, Brahman is certainly unsublatable even within three or four stages [of inquiry]. Nor does being unsublatable within three or four stages constitute [the definition], for if that were so, it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of illusory particulars (*prātibhāsika-viśeṣa*). For there do exist illusory objects—such as a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*), a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*), and the like—which are the objects of long-duration delusions.
Furthermore—this word *kakṣyā* refers either to reasoning (*yukti*), to time (*kāla*), or to a contrary means of valid cognition (*viparīta-pramā*).

It cannot be the first [meaning], because the world (*prapañca*) would be sublated by that single *kakṣyā*—namely, "the world is false because it is visible"—and thus its existence would be impossible. Moreover, the Vedic [scripture] is superior to that [reasoning] and is free from defects; therefore, it sublates the former.
This is because even by following that single reasoning, [the definition] would result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) due to sublation (*bādha*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable—because it would over-extend to the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) object, which is the object of a long-standing error.
Nor is the third—because it is a contradiction (*vyāghāta*) to say that something is both the object of a contrary cognition and yet unsublated. And furthermore...

It is logical that sublation (*bādha*) is the cessation of an object; for in the case of jars and the like, which are removable by hammers and such, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because they possess the nature of being removable by erroneous cognition while not being removable by two or three erroneous cognitions. Furthermore, regarding the state of not being sublated by two or three logical arguments:
Regarding the first alternative—that sublation occurs only when [something] exists—there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, because that too is sublated by reasoning (*yukti*).

Since knowledge and ignorance must have the same object, the knowledge that has as its object that very thing which is the object of ignorance is what removes such ignorance. In the present case, this applies to the ignorance whose object is Brahman.
Cessation occurs through knowledge alone regarding Brahman. To explain: is Brahman visible or invisible?

If it were visible, its falsity would be unavoidable. If it were invisible, the very usage of the term "Brahman" would be abolished, since that [usage] is achievable solely through vision. Furthermore, there could be no cessation of ignorance, because there would be an absence of vision directed toward the same object. Nor is it the case that...

A modification (*vṛtti*) cannot perform the functions of knowledge merely by the superimposition (*āropa*) of the nature of knowledge upon it; for otherwise, it would follow that even fire residing in a *guñjā* seed would possess the power to burn. Nor should it be suspected that the nature of knowledge is primary (*mukhya*) simply because it serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for knowledge;

this is contradicted (*vyāghāta*) by the very fact that the difference between cognitions is established through the relationship of the delimited (*avacchedya*) and the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

Furthermore, there would be the consequence that the pot itself would be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) [of the cognition]. In the cognition "the pot-like cognition," the pot is indeed the delimiting factor.

Moreover, if the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) were to have its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) as the mental modification (*vṛtti*), then Brahman would necessarily be distinct from cognition. Nor is there any common ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) shared by both Brahman and the mental modification, by virtue of which the term could be used in its primary sense in both cases. And...

Because it has been stated that "the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*) is unestablished. Indeed, a "nature of knowledge" that conforms to both the modifications of knowledge and ignorance is not supported by valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇika*). This is because the nature of knowledge would cease upon the cessation of self-luminosity, which pervades it; and furthermore, if that [self-luminosity] were absent in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) devoid of distinctions, it would follow that it is of the nature of ignorance (*ajñānatva*). Nor is the nature of knowledge the capacity to remove ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because by the cessation of its own pervader, there is also the cessation of itself; and because, in the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is compatible with superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it would follow that [the definition] is non-pervasive due to the absence of that [pervader]. Nor can both [activity and cessation] be primary through the pair of activity and cessation, as that would entail the fallacy of assuming multiple meanings. [This is so] because of the appearance of the world in consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

Because the conceptualization [of two distinct cognitions] would be futile; because it would result in the unavoidable conclusion that Brahman is false due to its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*); and because, in order to justify the primary meaning of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) for both knowledge and ignorance by postulating two separate activities—engagement and withdrawal—it would follow that the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) would have its primary meaning applied to both a pot and a cloth. And thus, since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) lacks the nature of knowledge...
Even if Brahman is of the nature of self-luminous manifestation devoid of objects, Brahman would still be rendered insubstantial because it would be its own object;
furthermore, since all instances of consciousness would be non-different from Brahman—which is not their own object—mutual transaction between them would be impossible.
If the mental modification (*vṛtti*) were considered primary knowledge, or if Brahman were both self-luminous and its own object, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of Brahman would be unavoidable.

Taking into account the imagined difference between Devadatta and others in their mutual worldly transactions, it is unavoidable that consciousness (caitanya) must be false by virtue of being an object of consciousness.

Nor can it be argued that being an object of consciousness is not a cause for falsity merely because it coexists with a falsely conceived difference, as this would apply to the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) as well.

Because that is unestablished. It must be stated that while the falsity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is accepted in its qualified form, its essential nature (*niṣkṛṣṭa-rūpa*) is not an object of consciousness.

If that were so, then even knowledge qualified by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) would be false and thus not the primary Seer (*dṛk*); consequently, this would apply to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as well.

Thus, "the state of being an object of perception" has been won by us. If there is a difference [between the qualified Brahman and pure Brahman], then that [qualified Brahman] too, being an object of mental modification (*vṛtti*), is false;

if there is no difference, then because the qualified [Brahman] is false, and because it is non-different from the pure [Brahman], it follows that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is real and Brahman is false—this is a perverse conclusion. Therefore, [it cannot be established] through either the difference or the non-difference of the qualified [Brahman].
The contradictory status of the reality of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) and Brahman—the one being false and the other true—is indeed unavoidable.

Furthermore: does Brahman, devoid of attributes, exist or not? In the second case, there is an entry into the Madhyamaka school. In the first case, having asserted the proposition that "Brahman exists,"...
If there is a difference in the grounds for the application [of the terms], the claim of being without distinction is contradicted. Nor is there a proposition regarding two grounds for application;

for the rebuttal based on their being imagined is invalid, because to say that the proposition "Brahman exists without distinction" does not have a qualified entity as its object would be the ravings of a madman. It exists.

Furthermore, in your view, it is impossible for existence (*sattā*), which serves as the ground for the application of words, to be false. Moreover, if Brahman-hood were merely imagined (*kalpita*), it would follow that the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*) lacks the status of being Brahman. This is because the statement "that in which Brahman-hood is imagined is itself Brahman" is self-contradictory. Finally, a relationship with something imagined is logically impossible for that which is attributeless.

However, if there is no difference in the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of the terms], grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible. The elders have stated that "coreferentiality is the occurrence of words with different grounds for their application in reference to a single object.
This same defect applies even when the ground for the application is a property in the form of a negation (*abhāva*), because negations...

If [the attribute] were not distinct from the essential nature (svarūpa), there would be a loss of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); if it were distinct, there would be a loss of the established tenet (siddhānta). By this, the claim that the "attributeless" (nirviśeṣa) is established by itself even though it is not the object of the proposition and other members of the syllogism is refuted; for it would follow that self-establishment would be unavoidable for all objects that are otherwise difficult to prove. By this, the establishment of the attributeless through scripture (śruti) is also rejected.
Because it is impossible for scripture—which is differentiated by the distinction between root-meanings (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*)—to possess authority in that regard;
and because [such a view] would entail the sublation of the previously mentioned inference based on being an object of sight (*dṛśyatva*).
Furthermore: Is the difference between the false object and Brahman ultimately real (*paramārtha*), or is it not ultimately real? In the first alternative...

By accepting the reality of difference, there is a loss of your own tenet (*siddhāntahāni*). In the second case, the unreality (*mithyātva*) of even Brahman, who is real, becomes unavoidable; for there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that where the difference between two things is false, their identity is [true]. Indeed, when the difference of a pot from itself is false, non-difference is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because both difference and non-difference are false.

It is well that there is no other alternative when two things are in mutual contradiction. If this were so, then why would you—who are impartial toward both difference and non-difference—not accept the falsity of both with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman?

Nor is such a position impossible on the grounds of the superior authority of the scriptures concerning non-difference, for [texts such as] "All this, indeed, is Brahman" and others [are equally authoritative].

Because scriptural texts concerning the non-difference of Brahman from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) exist even here as well. Furthermore—[is] the knowledge of Brahman as devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) itself ignorance or not? In the second case, there is a contradiction with your own established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*). In the first case, however, is it with an object (*saviṣaya*) or without an object (*nirviṣaya*)? If it were without an object, there would be a contradiction with the nature of "knowledge" as you intend it. If it has an object...

There would be the undesirable consequence of the objects being eternal, because an eternal cognition must necessarily have eternal objects. Likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the world of plurality (*saprapañcatā*) persisting even in liberation.

If it is argued that at that time [in liberation] there is no such consequence because the objects have ceased and thus [the cognition] is objectless, then in that case, it would not be a cognition at all.

Because there is a contradiction between being objectless (*nirālambanatva*) and being a cognition (*jñānatva*). Nor can it be argued that the permanence of the object is avoided as in the case of cognitions of past objects and the like; for in that case, by having "pastness" or the like as a qualifier, or by having some [past] thing as its objective support (*ālambana*), the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*) would be contradicted. This is because the permanence of the relation with an object [would otherwise follow].

Furthermore, this is because it would entail the fallacy of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To claim that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is established through experience as being without an object and without a substratum is trivial;
for it is perceived precisely as having a connection [to an object], as in "I know this jar" or "this is a jar.

As for any other consciousness you might favor, it cannot be established except at the time when things like a flower in the sky are established—[which is impossible]. This is the direction of the argument.

Moreover: is it a substance (*dravya*) or a non-substance? If it is a substance, there follows the consequence that it must be a substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*). To argue that this is established like a jar delimited by the moment of its production is trivial; for even there, conjunction with the first moment exists. Furthermore, even if it were a substratum of qualities at some time, that would not preclude its being a non-substratum of qualities [at other times]. This remains true even if qualities are considered merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*).

There would be a contradiction with its being without distinction (*nirviśeṣatva*). Without the material cause of ignorance (*avidyopādāna*), that [distinction] cannot be established for the intellect (*buddhi*). If it were not a substance (*adravya*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being dependent upon a substance. Furthermore, this would contradict such scriptural passages as "In his own glory" (*sve mahimni*). Moreover, because of the connection with a substratum, its state of being without distinction would be destroyed. Therefore, by means of such refuting arguments (*khaṇḍanayukti*),...

The direction [of the argument] is as follows: since even Brahman—which is uncontradicted within the interval between the first and second stages—could potentially be contradicted in subsequent stages, the charge of over-extension (ativyāpti) against it is indeed unavoidable.

Nor is the fourth definition—that of being contradicted by a means of valid cognition that reveals reality (tattvāvedaka)—correct, because [this would apply to] the palate and other such organs, as well as the ears and other sense organs.

Because no contradiction with their own nature is observed in those things manifested by the validity that reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka-prāmāṇya*). Nor can it be argued that there is a contradiction with what is to be known by them (*tatprameya-viruddhatva*); for if reality were revealed solely by the status of being Veda, then even such [Vedic] passages as "In whom the heaven... would have meanings contradicted by other Vedic means of knowledge that reveal reality, such as "Here is no diversity," and thus the proliferation of those objects would not exist.

Because it would follow that [the absence of the world] is merely conventional; and because if the absence of the world were a distinct reality, it would entail duality, whereas if it were false, it would contradict the capacity of the means of knowledge that cognize it to reveal ultimate truth; and because, since one must therefore accept a difference from Brahman, there would be over-extension of the definition to Brahman itself.

Furthermore: in this regard, is the distinction between that which reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka*) and its opposite established or unestablished? If it is unestablished, there is a contradiction with your own statement. If it is established, however, since the object is not established by what is non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*), the distinction—which is within the domain of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—would result in being real; consequently, the conventional nature (*vyāvahārikatva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be destroyed. But if that [distinction] does not exist, then that very [phenomenal world] remains.
There is no contradiction in the statement because it reveals reality; for it was stated previously that while difference is false, non-difference is true.
Nor is the fifth [definition]—being the object of a cognition devoid of causal efficiency—correct; for if that were so, [it would apply to] your own...
Since all activity within the spheres of both worldly and Vedic experience would consequently be as unreal as a flower in the sky,
the very contradiction between your own actions and your own words will act like a punishment to turn you away from your dance, just as one wards off a venomous serpent.
Now, if your intention is this— that by the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the negative particle (*nañ*), there is a lack of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śūnyatva*)— then:

"Absence of the lack of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśūnyatvābhāva*). If that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, which is the root-stalk of all objects. Nor should it be argued that while Brahman as delimited by ignorance (*avidyāvacchinna*) possesses causal efficiency, pure Brahman does not, and that being delimited is accepted as having a merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) status; for in that case, it would follow that the qualified [Brahman] must be removable by knowledge.

Furthermore, if the particularity (*viśe�ṣa*) were also excluded, it would follow that the empire of Nihilism (*śūnyavāda*) prevails; for the qualified object does not exceed its qualifiers and the relation between them. Moreover, there is the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the pure Brahman, which is the object of the final mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), since that Brahman serves as the cause of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) consisting in the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*).

There is a causal relationship between manifestation (*prakāśatva*) and the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*). Furthermore, there is another [causal relationship] between manifestation regarding the non-self (*anātmaviṣaya*) and the cessation of ignorance regarding the non-self. This being the case, your established doctrine is that the manifestation of the essential nature of Brahman (*svarūpaprakāśa*) removes ignorance even without having Brahman itself as its object.

Furthermore: there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of an illusory snake and the like, which has a rope as its substrate and performs causal functions such as fear and trembling; there is under-extension (*avyāpti*) to jars and the like that have perished immediately after arising; and there is also under-extension to those moments produced in the moment immediately preceding a mass-formation (*pracaya*).

Because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not observed in those [dream objects], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to dreams that indicate good or bad fortune and serve as causes for causal efficiency at that time. If, however, one intends to refer to causal efficiency in the conventional sense (*vyāvahārika*), then the fault of circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*) remains. Nor can it be said that the meaning of "causal efficiency" refers to transformations such as bracelets or crowns.

The avoidance of the defect [of over-extension] is impossible; for over-extension occurs in the case of dream-objects, and non-extension occurs in the case of things that have arisen and perished. Now, if it is argued that the avoidance of over-extension is achieved by [defining the cause] as belonging to the same class as that which delimits causality—then there is over-extension in the case of the illusory (prātibhāsika), since such a class does not exist therein. For if that were the case, then in that [illusory object],...

Because it would follow that your conventional usage of silver and the like would be accidental, and because it would follow that there is an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in dreams; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

Nor is it the case that [the object] is the object of a cognition affected by a defect in the instrument (*karaṇadoṣa*); this is the sixth [definition], but it is rejected because it over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Because [the definition] is impossible in the case of jars and the like, which are objects of uncontradicted universal cognition and within the range of unimpaired sense organs; and because the definition is impossible in the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), as it is the object of knowledge produced by unimpaired scripture, such as: "From whom these beings are born," "From the Self, space was produced," and "In whom heaven and earth [rest]."

Now, if you think that even the Veda is rooted in the defect of ignorance, and therefore its non-existence [as a valid means] does not follow, then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, because Brahman is the object of the knowledge produced by such scriptural texts. Nor can it be argued that, since Brahman is not sublated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the knowledge produced by the scripture regarding it cannot be tainted by a defect in its instrument. For [the scripture itself says]: "Therefore, the instruction is: 'Not this, not this'."

Because of such scriptural passages as "Then there was neither non-existence nor existence; there was neither being nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being," which are supported by the agent [the Lord] as previously explained, even Brahman is sublated. For, apart from the negation of Brahman, the scriptures describe another meaning [in those passages], and likewise, apart from the negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), they describe another meaning therein.
Describing it is useless.
Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman, which exists as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), whose reality is known by all means of cognition (*pratyaya*).

Nor can it be intended to mean "being a mode of knowledge," because that would result in under-extension (*avyāpti*) to jars and other such objects, since they [are not modes of knowledge]. Of those...

Because [the world] is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of knowledge; because even though Brahman is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), it functions as the qualifier (*prakāra*) in cognitions such as "the jar exists" (*ghaṭaḥ san*);

and because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) functions as the qualifier in the cognition "the world is in Brahman. Nor is it correct to say that being superimposed (*adhyastatva*) is merely a qualification of the object (*viṣaya-viśeṣaṇa*), for if that alone were sufficient, the remaining [qualifications] would be redundant, and furthermore, it would fail to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika*).

Therefore, as for the claim that the reality of the universe is merely conventional— that is a "Māyāvāda" (doctrine of illusion) in disguise from the Buddhists, according to the ringing proclamation of the Śrauta-Śaivas, because it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience.
Furthermore, in the great Mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), non-dualistic identity with a featureless Brahman is not taught;

for the terms *tvam* and *tat* are designated as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman respectively, both of which possess attributes. Moreover, in passages such as "It thought: May I be many," the Supreme Lord Brahman—the cause of the universe denoted by the word *tat*—is taught to be possessed of attributes.
But surely,

because of the impossibility of oneness between the Lord and the individual soul— just as between a cow and a dog— due to their respective association with the attributes of omniscience and limited knowledge as delimited by *māyā* and *avidyā*.

By means of the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicative function that both excludes and includes), which prescribes both abandonment and non-abandonment, [it is said]: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; "one whose desire is for Brahman should practice the knowledge of Brahman"; "having reached the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form"; and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon. Like Devadatta, [the Self] is conditioned by the adjuncts (*upādhi*) of *māyā* and *avidyā*.
"Having abandoned everything else that brings about auspiciousness, the sage goes by meditating upon the abode of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness;
know this through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation," and so forth.

Because of the teaching that the individual soul attains the state of Śiva through the power of meditation and knowledge consisting of the worship of the Lord, who is like a silkworm spinning its own cocoon; and because, in such scriptural passages as "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," He is described as the impeller of all actions and the bestower of the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya*.
Because this refers exclusively to the Supreme Lord; because it would contradict the opening statement, "He thought, 'May I be many'";
and because it would entail the collapse of the promise that through the knowledge of one, all is known.
Now, an objection: the direct realization of the Supreme Lord cannot be achieved through the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), since that which is visible...

Because, according to the principle that "that which perishes [perishes]," there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its destruction, just like a jar; and because in the absence of that [destruction], meditation would be purposeless.
Furthermore, regarding Paraśiva-Brahman, who is delimited by the sixfold attributes such as omniscience and so forth, [there are] the words Śiva, Sarva, Śaṅkara, Ānanda, Jñāna, Ananta, and so on.

Since terms such as *hasta*, *kara*, and *pāṇi* (hand) are synonyms, is the pure soul (*śuddhajīva*), which beholds the Supreme Śiva whose nature is indivisible consciousness, distinct from Him or non-distinct? It cannot be the first [option], for just as it is impossible for the world of objects such as pots and cloths— which appear through the light of the sun— to be the illuminator of the very sun that makes them manifest.

Because it is impossible for one impelled by Paramaśiva to be the knower of that [Paramaśiva]. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable—because, like the sense organ of sight, there can be no direct perception (sākṣātkāra) of it. If it is argued that the soul's realization of it is established because its nature is knowledge distinct from that [object], we say no; for the soul's status as the agent of that direct perception would require it to consist of a knowledge superior to that [object].
[The opponent argues that the individual soul is either] identical in nature to that [Brahman], or its nature is knowledge inferior to that.

Not the first, because it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience. Not the second, because worship of it would be impossible and because the aforementioned defects would ensue. Not the third, because [the scripture states]: "Two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord."

The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the Ruler of all sciences, and the Sovereign of all beings— since this is established through the authority of such Śruti passages, logical reasoning, and personal experience, His state of being superior [to them] is possible. Nevertheless, because direct realization of Him is impossible— like a lamp situated in the midst of the radiance of the sun— it must therefore be attained through the knowledge of meditation (upāsanā).
If it is argued that the realization of Brahman is not established, we say no;

for just as the realization of the sun is established by the eye alone through its solar rays, so too there is no contradiction in the establishment of the realization of the Supreme Lord for the individual soul (jīva) purified by the guru’s initiation, due to the grace of the Supreme Lord. Otherwise, [one would have to admit] "having known Śiva... [and so forth].

[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "He attains ultimate peace," "He knows Brahman, he becomes Brahman itself," and "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind. Furthermore, the worldly practice of instruction between teacher and disciple would not exist.
Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the purport of all Vedānta texts lies precisely in the meaning previously stated.
Thus ends the fourth section, *Samanvayādhikaraṇa*. Now begins the fifth section, *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa*.

Nor should it be asked how the other sūtras have a purpose, given that the purport of the four chapters is revealed by the four [opening] sūtras; for the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, having raised the doubt that the aforementioned definition of Brahman might over-extend to the Pradhāna and so forth, demonstrates the purpose of the remaining sūtras.

Since it is impossible for the changeless Brahman to be the cause of the creation and so forth of the world, one might raise the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Sāṅkhya and Advaita schools as to whether the causality of the creation and so forth of the world— which is subordinate to Brahman due to the power of Brahman’s existence— belongs to that *pradhāna* by way of the analogy of the magnet and the iron needle, or rather whether it belongs to the *pradhāna* independently. Anticipating this, he refutes their view:
Because of seeing; [the Self] is not that which is not based on scripture.
That which is "without sound"—the insentient *pradhāna* imagined by the Sāṅkhya and Advaita schools—is not the cause of the world.

Why? Because of "seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*); that is, because the status of being the cause of the world’s birth and so forth, preceded by seeing, is observed in the Supreme Lord alone, who is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*). This is the meaning of the sūtra. Its subject matter is heard in the *Chāndogya*: "Being alone..."

"Verily, in the beginning, this was Being alone, one only without a second—Brahman. It thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate,'" and so forth. Elsewhere: "Verily, in the beginning, this was the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking. It thought: 'Let me create the worlds. It created these worlds. Likewise: "She (the Unmanifest) created the worlds. And likewise:

Because a multitude of scriptural passages— such as "The Puruṣa consisting of sixteen parts [reflected] upon his own nature," and "He looked around; He created Prāṇa"— demonstrate that the Supreme Lord is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world preceded by His volition (īkṣaṇa),
there arises a doubt here as to whether the causality of the world and the state of being denoted by the word *sat* belong to the Pradhāna or to Brahman.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: because in passages such as "partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, stainless," the Supreme Lord is taught to be actionless and devoid of modification; and because the world's origination and so forth, as well as the act of seeing (*īkṣitṛtva*), consist of the nature of modified attributes; [and because of the scriptural statement]: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing manifold offspring..."
Of similar form: "For one unborn, being attached, lies along with her; another unborn leaves her after she has been enjoyed. She is manifold, very firm, producing many sprouts;
she is herself divided by the qualities (guṇas), and even in the sprouts she is divided by the qualities everywhere."

Because the Śrutis, such as "She who has the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva," teach that the Pradhāna produces many offspring, the status of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is established— either by its own nature or through the predominance of its existence. Omniscience, characterized by the connection with the powers of knowledge and action, resides in that which consists of the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.
It is established [as the cause]. By the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) stating, "From existence (*sattva*), knowledge is born," its very nature as the cause of knowledge is indicated;

for transformation, like that of clay and so forth, is a property of the non-conscious *pradhāna*, and such a thing is impossible for a conscious being. Thus, the relationship of cause and effect between the world and the *pradhāna* is logical. Therefore, in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone... [the *pradhāna* is intended].
It is that very [Brahman] which is designated by the word "sat" (Being) that is so conventionally expressed. For this very reason, the non-difference between cause and effect is real;
and thus the promise that through the knowledge of one, all is known, is established.
Furthermore: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay is known..."

By such statements as, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth," the identity of form between the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) and the thing illustrated (dārṣṭāntika)—namely, the true lump of clay and its effects—is established. For this very reason, Kapila, Auḍulomi, and others [assert] that the Pradhāna is the cause of the world, on the grounds that it is consistent with the scriptural declarations of the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

[The opponents] establish [this]. Therefore, since it is not tenable for that which is different from Him to be denoted by the word "Being" (sat) nor to possess the status of being the cause of the world, this being the position reached (*prāpta*), we reply. As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because of His deliberation (*ikṣati*), He is not one whose nature is not expressed by scripture (*aśabda*). "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)

For, from the Śruti and Sūtra passages—"Then He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—it is heard that the verb *īkṣati* (He thought/looked) belongs to Śiva alone, who is the Supreme Brahman denoted by the word *Sat*; since it is impossible for the non-conscious Pradhāna to be a thinker (*īkṣitṛ*). [The text continues: "The Ṛta, the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa..."
"Dark and tawny, with upward-pointing vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), the three-eyed one; salutations indeed to the one whose form is the universe.

In such Vedic texts as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "The mind that delights in the breath of the true Self and finds bliss therein," the Supreme Śiva, the omniscient Brahman, is shown to be denoted by the word *sat* (Being/Truth) and to be both the material and efficient cause of the entire universe.

It is heard [in scripture]: "The status of being denoted by the term 'Sat' and the state of being the cause of the world for the Pradhāna—which consists of the equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇas)—is not tenable; for that which is delusive in nature and insentient is indeed the Pradhāna, and since the Pradhāna is designated as inert and delusive in nature in the Tāpanīya and other Upaniṣads."

"The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, is the cause of bondage, existence, and liberation from saṃsāra. One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā; by His constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded"—from such scriptural passages, there is an emphatic statement that Pradhāna and the Supreme Lord stand in the relationship of the governed and the governor.

Furthermore—at the beginning, by the statement "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), the sentience of the material cause is indicated; and by the statement "May I be many" (*bahusyām*), its status as the material cause of the world is shown. This is because of the scriptural revelation: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are innate," which refers to the omniscient Supreme Lord.

The possession of all powers, such as knowledge and action, is indeed established by its very nature. Therefore, the scriptural passages concerning the cause of the world do not refer to the Pradhāna.

As for the claim that the Pradhāna is the cause of the world because of the connection between the initial proposition and the illustrative example, that is worthless, because of [the presence of] the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*).

Because volition is the sole characteristic [of the cause]. Indeed, from the scriptural statement, "All this is Brahman; it originates, dissolves, and breathes in That; one should meditate with a tranquil mind," because of the teaching that "all is Brahman," nothing else can be the cause. If it is argued that omniscience is possible for *prakṛti*—which possesses the power of all knowledge during its state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇas*)—insofar as it is delimited by the quality of *sattva*:

That is inconsistent, because for *pradhāna*, which consists of the equilibrium of the three *guṇas*, there is no connection with the *rajas* and *sattva* *guṇas* through a separation from *tamas*; furthermore, it is accepted that *prakṛti* is the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*. As for the claim that if *paramaśiva*—who is *brahman*—is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the world, he would fall into the state of being subject to modification (*vikāritva*), that is not so.

This is beautiful. Because of the teaching that the bond of *māyā*—which is a portion of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) of Supreme Śiva—is the effect, while Supreme Śiva as delimited by the power of consciousness is the cause, there is no stain of doubt regarding [the Lord's] being subject to modification. Since one who desires to create depends upon *rajas* and *tamas*, there is limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*).
If it is argued that [this consequence] would follow— just as there is an absence of fear regarding the burning power of fire for one who has mastered it,

so too for Paraśiva, who has brought the power of *māyā* under control, the occurrence of defects caused by it is untenable. But surely, [it may be objected], according to such passages as "He is indeed without breath, without mind, and pure," the Supreme Śiva...

If it is asked, "Since the connection of Brahman with a body, senses, mind, and vital breath has been refuted, how can the status of being a seer be possible?"— the answer is no; for just as the sun (prabhākara) is self-luminous without depending on any other means, so too Śiva-Brahman exists independently of any other means such as a body or senses.
Because omniscience is possible [for such a being]. And thus says the Śruti: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper;

He sees without eyes and hears without ears. He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of Him; they call Him the foremost, the Great Puruṣa. "Without hands or feet, I am of inconceivable power; I see without eyes..."
"I hear without ears; I perceive as one whose form is solitary, yet there is no perceiver; I am eternally consciousness"—this is heard in the Śvetāśvatara, Kaivalya, and other Upaniṣads.
Nor is it the case that "there is no other seer, there is no other hearer."

Based on the observation of such scriptural passages, one must state that there is no evidence for the existence of an embodied soul (śārīra) distinct from the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). This is because in such scriptures as "Two birds, inseparable companions, friends; two, unborn, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is explicitly designated; and because in the scripture "There is no other seer but He," [the identity is affirmed].

It is taught that there is merely a negation of the status of being a seer, a hearer, and so forth, for those individual souls (jīvas) such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu who are distinct from Him; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the previously cited Śruti passages that establish the difference between Śiva and the individual soul. Therefore, this alone is the most reasonable position.

Anticipating the objection that— since the Śrutis state, "That heat [tejas] saw," and "Those waters saw," and so forth, and thus the non-conscious water and heat are heard to possess the power of seeing— it would be logical to likewise accept a figurative seeing for the Pradhāna and thereby establish its causality of the origin and so forth of the world— he refutes this as follows:
If it is argued that [the term "Self"] is used in a secondary sense, we say no, because of the word "Self."
If it is argued that the "seeing" attributed to Pradhāna is figurative, like that of water and fire, we say no. Why? Because of the word "Self" (ātman).

Having begun with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and having pointed out through the passage, "It thought—'May I be many,' it created fire," etc., that the cause of both sentient and insentient things, starting with fire, is [the Self], it concludes: "All this has that as its essence; That is the Truth; That is the Self."
Because that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) is designated by the word "Self" (ātman);

furthermore, because it is taught as the Self in its own right through the statement, "All this has that as its essence; that is the Truth; that is the Self," and because such [selfhood] is impossible in the case of the insentient *pradhāna*—which consists of the world of both the sentient and the insentient—even a figurative sense is not tenable.
It is taught that words such as *atpaja* and others denote Paramaśiva, who consists of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Now, one might object: since the word *ātman* primarily denotes the conscious individual soul (*jīva*), it is that [soul] alone which possesses the causality of the world preceded by the act of seeing.

If you say this is not so, [we reply] no; for in the Śruti, "This very deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms,'" we see that the entry is together with the Self (ātman). Furthermore, in the passage, "That Self—Thou art, O Śvetaketu," there is the instruction of the identity of individual souls with the Supreme Śiva, who consists of the entire manifest world of sentient and insentient beings. It is not [otherwise].

The status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as the cause of the world and as the universal observer is untenable; furthermore, this would entail the collapse of the principle that "by the knowledge of one, all is known," since in the passage "I shall manifest names and forms" (*nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi*),
the agency is seen to belong to the Supreme Lord.

Nor should it be argued that the soul possesses some degree of primary causality because it is conscious and because the word "Self" (ātman) is seen applied to it; for scripture states, "The Lord of the principal and the knower of the field, the Master of the qualities, is the cause of bondage, existence, and liberation from saṃsāra," and so forth, as well as, "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings."
Causing all beings to revolve, mounted on a machine by means of Māyā.
Moreover, because even in the Smṛti there is the designation that the individual soul (jīva) is subject to the dependence on the noose of the Supreme Lord’s Māyā.

Now, [it may be argued]: since the word "self" (ātman) is seen to be used for insentient things such as the senses, the elements, and the body, and since in the expression "the bank wishes to fall" (kūlaṃ pipatiṣati), the desire to fall—which is an attribute of a conscious being—is attributed to the bank; [therefore, the self must be insentient].

If it is argued that the status of being the primary creator of the world preceded by [the act of] seeing is possible even for the insentient *pradhāna*, we say no. Just as a servant does not possess total independence even when the word "self" (*ātman*) is applied to him—as in "My self is Somabhadra"—so too the *pradhāna* lacks independence despite the application of the word "self. This is also the case in the expression "The bank wishes to fall."
The desire of the bank to fall is merely a perception arising from the mere state of being on the verge of falling; it possesses no ultimate reality.
Furthermore, since this passage teaches that the conscious Supreme Śiva is the cause of the universe preceded by primary observation (*mukhyekṣaṇa*), even a figurative sense is not possible here.

Furthermore— just as expressions such as "the ear hears" or "the weapon cuts" have as their object a conscious agent, so too the scriptural passages teaching that the Pradhāna is the agent, such as "the one unborn," etc., have as their purport nothing other than the Supreme Lord being the agent. This is just as the word "light" (jyotis) has its primary application to the sacrifice or to fire.
Even though the word "Self" (ātman) may refer to both conscious and unconscious entities, it has its primary application (mukhyatva) specifically in the Supreme Self.
He states another reason for this:
"Because liberation is taught for one who is established in That. (Sūtra 7)

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; Thou art That, O Śvetaketu"—having thus taken up that subtle essence and taught the identity of the conscious Śvetaketu with Brahman by saying "Thou art That, O Śvetaketu," [the Upaniṣad continues]: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body; then he will be merged [in the Absolute]."

Because of the teaching that liberation, characterized by the attainment of Brahman, occurs immediately after the fall of the body— according to the analogy of the bee and the insect— the statement of identity in the sentence "That thou art" does not refer to the primary matter (pradhāna) and the embodied soul. For, according to the Śruti, "As a person's resolve is in this world, so will he become after departing from here," one who is devoted to the insentient pradhāna would only achieve identification with that [insentient state].
There would be a contradiction with the entire scripture that teaches the identity of Brahman and the Self.

Now, [one might object]: just as the word *āgnīdhra* is applied to the priests and others stationed in the *āgnīdhra* hall according to the *āgnīdhra-śālā* maxim, so too the word *ātman* is seen to be used for the primary [Self] even when referring to [the body]; and according to the *sthūlārundhatī* maxim, immediately after meditating upon that [body],...

If it is argued that liberation results from meditation on Paraśiva, we say no; for Prakṛti and Jīva are not the objects of worship. [The scripture states: "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace;
through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through becoming His very essence, there is subsequently, at the end, the cessation of universal illusion—Śiva alone."

Because meditation on anything other than Śiva is prohibited for those seeking liberation by such passages as, "One should meditate on Him who brings about auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else," and because it is taught that only for one steadfast in the meditation on Śiva does liberation occur through the prior cessation of the bonds of Māyā;
just as the sun, which illuminates the entire universe, has no need for the light of a lamp.
Even according to the maxim of the "coarse Arundhatī," it is not logical that the direct realization of the meditation on Supreme Śiva should depend upon the meditation on Pradhāna.
Alternatively, if the insentient Pradhāna were denoted by the word "Sat" (Being), [it would contradict the teaching]: "That thou art, O Śvetaketu."
If it were so, the insentience of Śvetaketu—which is conscious—would be established.

In that case, liberation, consisting in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of bonds, would be destroyed. Furthermore, the futility of the scripture and its status as the prattle of a madman would result, which is undesirable. Therefore, the word "Self" (ātman) here refers exclusively to the sentient Supreme Śiva.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the inherent nature of being a *jīva* cannot possibly cease to exist, it must be understood that in the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the meaning is "you are one who possesses that [nature]" (*tat-prakārakaḥ asi*); or else, it must be stated that there is non-difference between the cause and the effect as qualified by the gross and subtle phenomenal world of consciousness and the unconscious (*cid-acit-prapañca*).
If this is argued, we say no; for even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), dependence (*pāratantrya*) exists, and dependence is a cause of suffering.

This is because the state of being free from fear is taught for the liberated one in such passages as, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness; you do not fear anything from any quarter," and because there would otherwise be no distinction between liberation and worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Having begun with, "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*):

Having stated that the insentient phenomenal world has Brahman as its essence, [the text] refers back to the previously indicated Brahman by means of the word "That" (*tat*) in the formula "Thou art That" (*tattvamasi*).
(Folio 106 and 107 are missing.)

On the eastern petal, there is a virtuous mind; on the southeast, sleep, laziness, and so forth arise; on the south, a cruel mind; on the southwest, a sinful intellect; on the west, play; on the northwest, the inclination toward travel and such; on the north, pleasure and affection; on the northeast, the acquisition of wealth;
in the center, dispassion; in the filaments, the waking state; in the pericarp, the dream state; and in the *liṅga*, [the state of deep sleep].

It is clearly stated that "deep sleep is the abandonment of the lotus [of the heart]; the fourth state (turīya) is within the internal vital-breath (prāṇa) as the mark (liṅga) delimited by the heart-lotus," meaning that all individual souls (jīvas) dissolve into deep sleep there. Furthermore, a Smṛti is also heard: "In deep sleep, there is dissolution in Śaṅkara.
Moreover: "Just as one who is fast asleep does not see a dream in any way, so in this Prāṇa [they become] unified."

"Therefore, from that Self, the vital breaths (prāṇas) settle according to their respective abodes; just as they were here—whether a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a gadfly, or a mosquito—they become so again.
And likewise, [the text states] that the soul in deep sleep is "completely embraced by the conscious Self" (prājña-ātman), thus establishing its denotability by the word *Sat*.

Furthermore, its status as the substratum of the entire circle of living beings is specified [in scripture], as in other Upanishadic passages such as: "That which transcends all, the supreme bliss, pure existence, consisting of consciousness," and so forth; thus, the reality of the Pradhāna and others is asserted as being that of the Existent (Sat).
As it is said in the scripture: "Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]," this refers even to the Supreme Śiva, the Brahman.
Because we observe the manifestation and concealment of the gross and subtle phenomenal world of consciousness and unconsciousness;

and furthermore, because another scriptural passage states, "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña), he knows nothing external and nothing internal," [showing that] in the state of deep sleep, the individual souls [are joined] together with their own internal organs.

It is established that Paraśiva is denoted by the word "Sat," transcends all, is omniscient, and is the controller of all, due to the perception of his entry into Brahman. Therefore, pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita), which reveals the illusory nature of the world and the individual soul— like a snake superimposed on a rope— is [the doctrine] of the one for whom the insentient Pradhāna is primary.

Furthermore, even Sāṅkhya, which teaches that the *pradhāna* is the cause of the world, should not be accepted by those seeking liberation, because it contradicts the previously cited Śruti and Smṛti texts.

Since the *pradhāna* lacks the status of being the cause of the world, [the authority of] Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, and others— who are conditioned by its three qualities (*guṇas*)— [is likewise untenable].
In response to the doubt, "What is the status of those scriptural passages that enjoin [Brahman] as the cause of the world?", he says:
"Because of the uniformity of their purport" (1.1.11).
The final goal (*gati*)— the culmination of all Vedānta texts that establish the causality of the universe for Brahmā, Indra, Upendra, Candra, Dinendra, and others,
as well as those teaching both difference and non-difference— is in the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sat*) and who transcends the three forms (*mūrtitraya*). Of that...

"From the commonality"— the meaning is "from the concordance. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the scriptural passages that enjoin the Pradhāna as the cause and those scriptural passages that establish various deities, such as Brahmā, as the cause.

Just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self (ātman) all vital breaths (prāṇas) proceed, each to its respective station; from the vital breaths the gods (devas), and from the gods the worlds. Verily, in the beginning, this [world] was only the Self, and nothing else whatsoever existed, not even a non-existent thing. He thought, "Shall I now create the worlds? and he created these worlds.
From this very Self, space was produced; from this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs. [The Upanishad says:

"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form. "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born. "Verily, in the beginning, there was only Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā."

There was no Ishana, nor waters, nor Agni and Soma, nor these two, heaven and earth. Then indeed, the Purusha Narayana desired, "May I create the progeny. This Purusha Narayana—rootless and without support—is that which these progeny are born from;
he is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Narayana.
Thus, the concordance of such scriptural passages with the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman denoted by the word *Sat*, is indeed not contradictory.

"The entire world, the beings, the manifold universe—whatever has been born and whatever is being born—all this is indeed Rudra; let there be salutation to that Rudra. "The gods, having gone to the heavenly world, asked Rudra: 'Who..."

He said, "I am He; I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future. There is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me. Beginning with the words, "He entered from within to the innermost," [it continues]: "Salutations again and again to Him who is Rudra, the Blessed One, and who is Brahmā; salutations again and again to Him who is Rudra, the Blessed One, and who is Viṣṇu."

"Salutations, salutations! and so forth; for in the *Atharvaśiras*, words such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Candra, and Dinendra are established as denoting Paraśiva. In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "The Lord, the Supreme Master, accompanied by Umā," it continues: "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable."

"The Supreme Sovereign; He alone is Viṣṇu, He is the time of the vital breath, He is Agni, He is the Moon. He alone is everything that has been and all that is to be, the eternal. Because of such passages, there is the teaching that Śiva alone is the Self of all. "Śiva is non-dual, the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; they consider Him the Fourth; He is the Self, He..."

In such scriptural passages as, "One should know [Him]; one should meditate upon Īśāna; all this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is produced from Him," it is taught that He alone transcends the triad of forms and is the cause; thus, these attributes are not predicated of any other.

Now, one might object: what is the status of those Purāṇic statements which establish that the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others are the cause of the world during certain intermediate dissolutions (*avāntara-pralaya*)? We reply: it is not so, because [the scripture] says, "Entering by means of this living self (*jīva*), let me manifest names and forms."
The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.

Thus, since his status as the controller of all is seen in the Śrutis and Smṛtis by virtue of his pervading all beings, his agency belongs solely to the Supreme Lord Paraśiva, who exists as their inner ruler (antaryāmin).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction, because— like Viśvāmitra and others— he possesses the power of creation and so forth obtained through the worship of Paraśiva.
Therefore, it is established that the Śrutis which teach that all the deities are the cause of the universe have as their ultimate purport the Supreme Śiva.
Nevertheless, among the names of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, those of Bhava, Sarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva are the primary ones.

For instance: "The Seasons, Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny," "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"—by such passages, [Śiva] is denoted by the word *bhava*.
Since the verbal root *bhū* has the meaning of "existence" (*sattā*), he is called *bhava* because he exists eternally (*sadā bhavati*) everywhere; this refers to Paraśiva alone.

Because it is the material cause of all, the nature of Being (*sat*) is observed throughout the phenomenal world of moving and non-moving things, as in "the pot is Being, the cloth is Being. Furthermore, its status as the destroyer of all is shown by such passages as: "Salutations to the Subduer of all beings, salutations to the One who transcends the mind, salutations; for whom both the Brahminhood and the Kshatriyahood are but the boiled rice," and so forth.

It is taught that He alone is denoted by the word *śarva*. This is because of the verbal root *śṛ*, meaning "to injure. Furthermore, His status as being denoted by the word *īśāna* is established by scriptural passages such as, "He rules over these worlds with His ruling powers," and "The Lord of all sciences, the Lord of all beings," which declare His role as the controller of all; for the verbal root *īś* has the sense of "ruling" (*śikṣā*).
"Of whom Paśupati is the lord of creatures—both four-footed and two-footed;
from the golden-haired trees, homage, homage to the Lord of Creatures! Homage, homage to Umāpati, to Paśupati!
By such [mantras], [he is worshipped] as the sovereign lord of the bound creatures (paśu), such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and others, who are fettered by the noose of Māyā.

The state of being denoted by the word Paśupati [is established]. "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the individual soul (kṣarātman). Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyā).
He is the Lord of Pradhāna, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Master of the Guṇas, and the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra. One beholds that Will-less One."

Because the cessation of all bonds of *māyā* is shown through the very worship of Paraśiva in passages such as, "The element [of consciousness] free from sorrow, through clarity [of mind], [attains] the greatness, the Lord," and so forth,

[the word *rudra*] refers to that which dissolves (*drāvayati*) Rudra— who consists of the bonds of *māyā* and who is the cause of the state of being a bound soul (*paśu*) for devotees such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
It is denoted by the word *rudra* because of the teaching that it cannot be overcome by other lights, as stated in such passages as:

"The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. That is the light of all lights, which the gods worship" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.10). It is denoted by the word *ugra* (the fierce) for the same reason.
He is denoted by the word *bhīma* because of the teaching that He is the cause of all fear, beginning with the passage: "From fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth.

Now, why is the Blessed Lord Maheśvara called *bhagavān*? Because devotees worship Him through knowledge, and He, in turn, bestows grace, creates and emits speech, and, having renounced all objective states (*bhāvān*), [attains] self-knowledge and the sovereignty of yoga.

Because he is magnified in the great [Veda], he is therefore called the Blessed One Maheśvara; thus, due to the designation in the *Atharvaśiras* as one whose excellence of knowledge and sovereignty is unsurpassed, he is denoted by the term Mahādeva.
Therefore, these eight names belong primarily to Paraśiva alone; hence, Śiva alone is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe.
Furthermore, he states another reason: "And because it is so stated [in scripture]. (12)

"Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is contained within him; all desires are contained within him. This is the Self (Ātman), free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desire is truth and whose resolve is truth.
He is to be sought after, He is to be known. In the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]: "He has no lord whatsoever in the world..."
He has no presiding deity, nor is there any mark of Him. He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; He has no progenitor, nor is there any overlord of Him.
He is the supreme Great Lord among lords, and the supreme Divinity among divinities.

"May we know the Lord of lords, the first among all, the God beyond, the Ruler of the world, the one worthy of praise"— by such passages, the omniscience, the status as the controller of all, the status as the substratum of all, and the status as the object of worship for all are heard [in scripture] regarding Maheśvara, the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," [the nature] of the Brahman that is to be known...

Having pointed out attributes such as being the cause of all through its possession of all powers, and having refuted the view that the *pradhāna* is the cause of the universe by means of the sūtra "Because of [the act of] seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on the Śruti" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*), it is established that Śiva, who is Brahman, possesses the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) through the contraction of his own power, and the state of possessing qualities (*saguṇatva*) through the expansion of his power.

By introducing the commonality of the states of existence (*gati-sāmānya*), it has been explained that all Vedāntic statements— which establish both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*)— are indeed directed toward the Supreme Cause alone. Therefore, in the remaining portion of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā,
the fruit [of the inquiry] is the meditation upon the supreme Śiva— the substratum of all and the cause of all— in terms of both his having parts (*sāvayavatva*) and being partless (*niravayavatva*).
And it is thus determined.

But [an objection is raised]: how can there be a presentation of one and the same thing as having both parts and being partless—qualities whose natures are mutually contradictory like darkness and light?
If it is argued that [these qualities] belong to Paraśiva, we say no—for it is said: "It became both the existent and the non-existent;
the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and unconsciousness, the true and the untrue; the true became the true—the supreme *ṛta* and *satya*."
Salutations indeed to the one of universal form, the Brahman, the Puruṣa, who is dark and tawny, whose vital seed is drawn up, and who has diverse eyes.

Salutations to that one who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; the singular, all-pervading Lord, wondrous, formless, consisting of consciousness and bliss; the Supreme Lord and Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed one.

Because the supreme Brahman, Śiva, is designated as both having form and being formless—just like the wind—in passages such as, "The blue-throated one is tranquil; these two are the forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless," both [attributes] are indeed appropriate.
As the previous teachers have stated: "We are proponents of the authority of the Śruti; we do not hold logic in high regard."

"Sattva" is the state of being fit for the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Asattva" is the state of being unfit for the differentiation of name-and-form, yet becoming an object of subtle vision obtained through the compassionate glance of a true guru. This is to be understood from such passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born," and so forth, starting with the first mantra of the *Sāmaveda*: "And [I praise] your austerity... and so on.

Having praised [Rudra] with the mantra ending in "karmādhipataye namaḥ" (Salutation to the Lord of Action) and the verse "virūpākṣo 'si," one should say: "I take refuge in you; O Sūta, I shall perform this [rite]; may it prosper for that purpose; may it be accomplished through you.

Since there is the instruction that all Vedic rites must be performed solely under the authority of Rudra's command, all Vedic practitioners should act in this very manner at the commencement of every rite.
And elsewhere: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
the overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities.
And: "He has pervaded [all], being pure, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, clean, unpierced by evil"—thus [is described] the state of being both formed and formless.
It is heard in scripture that "the presiding over karma" and so forth are the attributes of the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore: "He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere; who dwells in the heart-cave of all beings;
who is all-pervading—that Blessed One is therefore Śiva, who is omnipresent. [And: "The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed one..."
"Having meditated upon the blue-throated, tranquil one—the witness of all, beyond darkness—the sage goes to the source of speech.

From such scriptural passages, because marks such as being beyond darkness, being the witness, being omnipresent, and being the inner ruler of all are understood to be attributes unique to Paraśiva, there can be no reference to anything else. Likewise, the Smṛti also says:
"A follower of the Vedas should perform all rites dedicated to Śiva;
a follower of Tantra should perform all rites dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, [this refers to] the relationship of worshiper and object of worship characterized by all the Vedāntic statements that enjoin both difference and non-difference.

This is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Among those [texts], according to the maxim of the "coarse Arundhatī" (*sthūlārundhatī-nyāya*), some sentences demonstrate liberation such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and *sāmīpya* (proximity); some are devoted to the worship of Śiva;
and some are devoted to rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which consist of the gross worship of Paramaśiva.

Some [passages] enjoin the Dahara-vidyā, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, and others, which consist of the subtle worship of the Supreme Lord. Their distinction arises from the difference in results due to the difference in the qualifications of the aspirants. According to the analogy of the ocean and its currents, all Vedāntic statements establish Paraśiva alone, whether by a direct or an indirect path. Nevertheless...

Immediate liberation belongs only to those who worship Śiva. For those who worship Indra, Upendra, and others who are partial manifestations (aṃśa) of Him, provided they are free from desire, liberation comes through the worship of Śiva as the fruit of merit accumulated over many births.
Thus it is said in the Śivagītā:
"Devotion to Śiva arises through merits accumulated over ten million births;
by that alone one attains liberation, and not otherwise even in ten million births. Thus it is said in the *Mahimnastava*:

The Vedic triad, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and the Vaiṣṇava—these are the diverse systems that have branched out, each claiming, "This is supreme; that is the beneficial path. Such is the variety of inclinations among those who follow various straight and crooked paths.
"You alone are the one to be approached by men, like the ocean for waters. Thus,
for those who worship various deities such as Sūrya, Gāṇeśa, Viṣṇu, and others, Śiva alone will grant their respective fruits, acting as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of each of those deities.
And so it is said in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"For I am indeed the enjoyer of all oblations and the bestower of all fruits;
having become the body of all deities, I am the self of all, abiding in all."

Therefore, the doctrine of those who maintain that Brahman is a featureless pure consciousness (cinmātra) should not be accepted by seekers of liberation, because it contradicts the Śruti and the Sūtras;

for in those [latter] systems, there is the teaching of attributes such as being the cause of the world preceded by ultimate, primary perception (īkṣaṇa) on the part of the Brahman that is the object of inquiry.

Even the status of being the witness of all, which is propounded by the Upaniṣads, is not ultimately real; nevertheless, they call it "conscious" (cetana), but that too is charming only so long as it is not investigated. Consciousness, by definition, consists in being characterized by the quality of sentience (caitanya).
Therefore, due to the absence of the quality of seeing (īkṣaṇa), its insentience is established, just like that of primordial matter (pradhāna).
Furthermore—for one who maintains the doctrine of Brahman as mere light devoid of attributes—even luminosity itself is not possible.

Luminosity, however, is a specific category of entity that effects the suitability for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of both self and other. Since it is impossible for a featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) reality to be the illuminator of both self and other, it would necessarily be insentient (*jaḍa*), just like a jar or similar objects. Even if [you argue] that both [self- and other-luminosity] are absent...
If it is argued that it possesses luminosity (*prakāśatva*), we say no—for that luminosity is nothing other than its very capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Moreover, if that which possesses capacity is endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*), there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of the doctrine of the attributeless (*nirviśeṣavāda*). If it is argued that some attribute must be accepted because of the authority of the Vedas (*vedaprāmāṇya*) and so forth, then [the same objection applies].

Since attributes such as omniscience, omnipotence, lordship over all, and the possession of true resolve are also enjoined by the Śruti, they must all be accepted. For causality consists in being characterized by specific powers conducive to particular effects; and that [causality] is to be defined solely through its effects. Of the particular effect...
If the world of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*) is false, then its causality is likewise devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony all have as their object only that which possesses specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), the reality of the world (*vastutva*)—for one who asserts the reality of things—is also without proof. Therefore, the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) alone is the cause of both [the origin and the dissolution] of the universe.
It is established that Brahman is the object of inquiry. Thus ends the section on "Iksati" (I.1.5–12).
For the person of the highest qualification, the knowledge of Brahman extends only up to the point of "Iksati" (according to the *Śivādvaitamañjarī*).
The Section Concerning that Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) || 6 ||

One might raise the objection: "Let there be no status as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world for Brahmā and others who are the agents of intermediate creation; rather, let Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Avyākṛta—who are delimited by the collective gross, subtle, and causal bodies—be the causes of the world's origin and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of the repetition. (1.1.13)

The subject matter of this [section] is heard in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], beginning with "From that very Self, space was produced," up to "Different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss.
Here, a doubt arises as to whether the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) denotes the embodied soul (śārīra) or the supreme Śiva himself.
