This is because it illuminates the abundance of both types of attributes; because here, in the passage beginning with "Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman," the inquiry and response regarding the knowledge of Brahman are established specifically for Bhṛgu; and because, starting from "From which indeed these [beings arise]," the definition of Brahman as the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe is taught here in the statement "Seek to know That; That is Brahman."

This is because of the teaching on its having parts in passages such as, "From the earth come herbs; from herbs, food; from food, the person (puruṣa); that very person consists of the essence of food," and so forth; and because, by virtue of existing within the five sheaths beginning with the one made of food, it is the individual soul (jīva) alone for whom the nature of consisting of the five sheaths is appropriate.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: here, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the embodied self (*śārīra*). This is because the text indicates that the one consisting of bliss is the embodied self by stating, "Of this [self], the one consisting of bliss is the embodied self. Furthermore, the one consisting of bliss is recited within the context of the secondary selves, beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*).

Furthermore, there is the observation of a prayer for purification: "May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified. Since the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies "modification," this refers to the transmigrating embodied soul (*śārīra*) who is bound by the noose of *māyā* and delimited by the limbs of renunciation, enjoyment, and yoga.

Because unsurpassed bliss is impossible [in the individual soul], and because the supreme Lord's unsurpassed bliss is heard in the scripture stating "Bliss is Brahman," they explain that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)— which is its effect— is indeed the embodied soul (*śārīra*).

In the Śruti text, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless," the state of being devoid of body (*aśarīratva*) and the state of being distinct from pleasure and pain are predicated of Paraśiva-Brahman;
therefore, its consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is not possible.

Now, an objection is raised: for the sake of easily understanding Paraśiva alone as the cause of the world, the text begins with "Food is Brahman" and concludes with "Bliss is Brahman," thereby teaching both the nature of being composed of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) and the state of being the cause of the universe. Therefore, this is not a section concerning the individual soul (*jīva*).

If this is argued, we say no; for an Īśvara distinct from the individual soul (jīva) lacks scriptural authority. This is because, through such passages as "Entering by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms" and "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," there is an indication of non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman, similar to the expression "This is that Devadatta. Furthermore, the status of being the cause of the world—preceded by the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) as indicated in the scripture "It thought (tadaikṣata)"—[belongs to the same entity].

This is entirely appropriate for the conscious soul (*jīva*). The statement, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," describes the defining characteristic of the soul's nature as distinct from the insentient (*acid*). Therefore, in the scriptural text, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it is taught that for the soul, liberation consists precisely in the knowledge of its own true nature.

Furthermore, according to the maxim of the moon and its branches (*śākhā-candra-nyāya*), for the purpose of indicating the true nature of the Self (*ātman*), the gross body is first indicated as "the person consisting of food" (*annamayaḥ puruṣaḥ*); then, by way of being contained within that, the sheath of vital breath (*prāṇakośa*) which supports the gross body is indicated as "another inner self consisting of breath" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā prāṇamayaḥ*), "another inner self consisting of mind" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā manomayaḥ*), and "another inner self consisting of consciousness" (*anyo 'ntara ātmā vijñānamayaḥ*).

Having pointed out that the mind is included within that [annamaya], and having described the consciousness (vijñāna) contained therein as the intellect (buddhi) according to the analogy of a ladder, and having pointed out the individual soul (jīvātman), which is included within all, as "another inner self consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), because the conclusion refers to that very same entity, the Brahman introduced at the beginning in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" is indeed the individual soul.

It has been taught that liberation is precisely the knowledge of its (Brahman’s) true nature, and that this [knowledge] itself is composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Now, an objection is raised: since it is taught in the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support" that Brahman is the tail, and since being a tail is impossible for that which is partless, Brahman must be something distinct from the one composed of bliss.

If this is argued, we say no; for, beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and concluding with "Brahman is the tail, the support," the introductory and concluding sections possess a single characteristic mark. Thus, the anthropomorphic form of Brahman is established by its very nature. Therefore, the designation of Brahman in terms of a head, wings, and a tail is appropriate.
Just as the limbs of the body consisting of food (*annamaya-śarīra*) [are distinct], Brahman is likewise remembered as "the tail, the support" (*pucchaṃ pratiṣṭhā*),

being the undivided substratum for its own non-distinct limbs of *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda*, and thus consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). This refers to that which was introduced at the beginning with the words, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavidāpnoti param*).

Having established that Brahman is "truth, knowledge, and infinite" by means of a definition that excludes all other things, and having designated it with the word "Self" in the passage "From this very Self," its status as the Self is demonstrated through its being the Self of all;
subsequently, regarding the one referred to by the word "Self" in the passage "There is another inner Self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), [the text proceeds].

Since [Brahman] has been brought forward [in the preceding sections], it follows that by the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), Brahman itself—which is not distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*)—is being designated as "consisting of bliss.
To this, we reply: "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*).
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Here, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Śiva alone. Why? Because of repetition (*abhyāsa*). Repetition means hearing [the term] again and again. Since it is observed that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is used many times in the Vedāntas specifically for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, and not for any other, this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Having introduced the one consisting of bliss, [it says]: "He is indeed essence (*rasa*)."

On account of its being designated as "taste," for it is only by obtaining this [taste] that one becomes joyful; for who indeed could inhale or who could exhale if this bliss did not exist in the ether? For he alone causes one to rejoice. This is the inquiry into bliss: one attains this Self consisting of bliss, knowing that bliss is Brahman, that Brahman is bliss.

"He understood," [it is said]. And in another Śruti—“The one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed the enjoyer of bliss; bliss is Brahman itself”—the word "bliss" is determined to refer specifically to Brahman, that is, Śiva. Furthermore, beginning with the passage, "This is the inquiry into bliss," [the text proceeds] from human beings up to Prajāpati.

Having taught that the excellence of bliss increases a hundredfold at each stage, it is established that the state of being the supreme bliss— the "one bliss of Brahman"— belongs exclusively to Śiva, who is Brahman; [this is so] for the sake of the embodied self, who is delimited by the three bodies characterized by the three impurities (mala).
Since it is impossible for anything other than Śiva to possess unsurpassed bliss as its crowning feature, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed Śiva.
The description of the head and other limbs of the blissful Brahman is solely for the purpose of the devotee’s meditation.
"He who says 'Haṃsa, Haṃsa'—the one named Haṃsa is Sadāśiva."
As long as one perceives it in the form of a bird, one should contemplate it in that very form.
Furthermore, because the Supreme Brahman Śiva is designated as having the form of a swan (*haṃsa*) in such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*),
the conceptualization of His limbs is not contradictory;
for the *ānandamaya* is the innermost of all, beginning with the *annamaya*, in accordance with the understanding of the listener.

Because the teaching proceeds from one to the next as being the Self, culminating in the *ānandamaya*, and because it is impossible to discern the primary Self (*mukhyātman*) as the *ānandamaya* without first having knowledge of the secondary Selves beginning with the *annamaya*, the discernment of the secondary Selves is not contradictory; for the purpose of awakening one to the primary Self, it follows the analogy of [pointing out] the star Arundhatī by means of a coarse object, and the analogy of a continuous flow before one's eyes.
Because they are insentient (*jaḍatvāt*), the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sequence ending with the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, and *manomaya* has the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*).

Because he is sentient (*cetanatvāt*), the *vijñānamaya* is the individual soul (*jīva*) who abounds in consciousness (*vijñāna-pracura*). The *ānandamaya* is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) who abounds in bliss (*ānanda-pracura*).
"Having touched a cow, a horse, fire, or a Brāhmaṇa, one should touch water," according to the Āpastamba Sūtra. Furthermore:
"Having touched a woman in her menses, fire, a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, a devoted wife, a corpse, impure things, or an outcaste Brāhmaṇa (brahmabandhu), one should perform a bath."

Thus, in the *Vṛddha-Śātātapa*, because of the instruction on the coexistence (*sāhacarya*) of pure and impure objects, the fact that they belong to a single context (*prakaraṇaikatva*) is not a defect. This is as stated in such scriptural passages as: "When all [the elements] have dissolved during the time of deep sleep, one who is overcome by darkness attains the nature of bliss," and so forth; [this refers] to the Supreme Lord consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) in deep sleep.

There is no contradiction, because the embodied soul has dissolved along with the noose of darkness— which constitutes the obstacle to the direct realization of that [Self]— and therefore a prayer for its cessation is appropriate;
this is seen from such scriptural passages as, "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," and so forth, just as a pot is made of clay.

Thus, on the basis of such passages, the doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of the blissful one (*ānandamaya*) is not supported by scripture. [Scripture teaches: "He who rules over knowledge and ignorance is another; the one God rules over both the perishable and the immortal selves"; "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct"; "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends"; "Two Brahmans are to be known—the higher and the lower"; and "The eternal among the non-eternal."

The conscious one has entered within the conscious beings as the teacher of men; the Illusionist creates this entire universe, and within it, another is bound by illusion. When he beholds the other, the Lord who is enjoyed, the Master of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Lord of the Guṇas, the Ruler of all sciences, and the Sovereign of all beings— The provided text consists of verses from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (4.6–9). Here is the translation of those verses: "The conscious one has entered within the conscious beings as the teacher of men; the Illusionist creates this entire universe, and within it, another is bound by illusion. When he beholds the other, the Lord who is enjoyed, then he becomes free from birth and death, from old age and grief, and attains immortality. "He is the Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Lord of the Guṇas, the Ruler of all sciences, and the Sovereign of all beings."

Since hundreds of scriptural passages— such as "Paśupati is the lord of those who are bound (paśus)," "He who, dwelling within the self, of whom the self is the body," and so forth— establish the mutual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman,
the activity of entering and exiting various bodies belongs only to the transmigrating embodied soul (śārīra), and not to [Brahman].
The state of being Brahman is thus established.

However, in such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" and "That thou art," the identity of the soul—which is established by its own nature—with the Supreme Lord through the practice of meditation upon Him is taught, according to the analogy of the bee and the insect; otherwise, [this would not be possible].
This would entail a contradiction with scripture, reasoning, and personal experience.

Furthermore, since scriptural passages such as "The material nature and the individual soul are not to be meditated upon" express censure regarding meditation on the embodied soul, liberation does not come through knowledge of the individual soul's own nature. Rather, as it is said: "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace," and "The knower of Brahman attains [the Highest]."

However, since the Śruti states, "But having known Him alone, one goes beyond death; there is no other path for the journey," and because liberation is declared to result only from the individual soul's (*jīva*) meditation upon the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the doctrine that the individual soul is Brahman— just like the doctrine that the primal matter (*pradhāna*) is Brahman— is non-Vedic.

Based on the verse, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs the ritual acts," the word *vijñāna* does not denote the intellect (*buddhi*). This is because it is impossible for the insentient intellect to be the agent of action; for a word that expresses a quality (such as *dharma*) can also be a designator of the substratum (the *dharmī*), just like words such as "cow" and so forth. Therefore, regarding the word *vijñāna*:
Because it grasps the substratum (*dharmin*), it denotes the individual soul (*jīva*).

Furthermore, in the passage "both consciousness and non-consciousness," the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) teaches the conscious being characterized by the attribute of consciousness. Likewise, in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*: "He who dwells in consciousness..."

In place of the passage found in the Kāṇva recension, the Mādhyandinas clarify that the individual self (jīvātman)— which is designated by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) in the Kāṇva Śākhā reading— is the one who "dwells in the self. Furthermore, the neuter gender of the term *vijñānam* is intended to signify its nature as a real entity (*vastutva*).

Thus, the *paramātman* consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), which is distinct from and internal to the living self (*jīva*) consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), is understood through the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an agent, according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. For this very reason, it is heard in scripture that consciousness itself is the agent of sacrifices and other rites, as in: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts. Therefore, one should not accept the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a passive state (*bhāva*).

Now, an objection may be raised: since the individual soul (*jīva*) is conscious, it is logical that it possesses the causality of the universe as indicated by such scriptural passages as, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"; therefore, if the Supreme Lord, who is the cause, cannot be identical with the individual soul, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural texts as, "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me evolve names and forms."

If this is argued, we say no. Because qualities such as having true desires and true resolves—established by scriptural texts such as "He whose desires are true" and "Whose resolve is true"—are impossible in the individual soul (jīva), who is bound by the three-fold suffering and possesses only limited knowledge, that soul cannot be the cause of the world. Furthermore, [the scriptures state] that prior to creation, as in the passage "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," there was an absence of the distinction between name and form, and [the desire to become many] as in "May I be many."

The status of being the dual cause of the universe’s origination is specified for the Supreme Lord alone, who is denoted by the word "Sat. Furthermore, it is entirely logical that during dissolution, He is the agent of the differentiation of names and forms through His own entry into the bound souls contained within Himself, since they are His own parts; for meditation upon the attributeless [Brahman] is impossible.

In passages such as "The tail, the foundation, is Brahman," "This tail, the foundation, is the Atharva-Angirasas," and "The tail, the foundation, is the Great One," the Supreme Lord is taught as having parts for the purpose of meditation according to the differences among qualified aspirants. Even though the meditation involves parts, the fruit is precisely the attainment of the partless [Brahman]. Likewise...
In the section on isolation (*kaivalya*), beginning with "Accompanied by Umā" and ending with "Having meditated, the sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all,
beyond darkness," they declare the attainment of the fruit of meditation on the partless [Brahman] for one who has been a meditator on the qualified [Brahman]. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

In response to the doubt that—because it is read within a section containing a series of suffixes such as *mayaṭ* in "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so on—the suffix in "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) must also have the sense of a modification (or product), just like "a pot made of clay" (*mṛnmayo ghaṭaḥ*), he says:
"If it be argued that [it does not mean Brahman] because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of abundance. (1.1.14)

If it is argued that because the suffix *mayaṭ* in *annamaya* and the others has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), it is likewise appropriate for it to have the sense of a modification in *ānandamaya*, we say no. Why? Because of abundance (*prācurya*). This is because Brahman is abundant in bliss.
[The suffix in *annamaya*] refers to being composed of food.

Since the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen in such instances as "the sacrifice consists mostly of stalks (*aṃśu*)," "the sun consists mostly of rays," "the village consists mostly of Brahmins (*vipra*)," and "the tree consists mostly of birds (*vihaṅgama*)," where it carries the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), here too by the term *ānandamaya*,
the Supreme Lord alone— who is abundant in bliss— is denoted; for [the text] begins with, "This is the inquiry into bliss."

Having described how the bliss increases by a hundredfold at each successive stage, from a distinguished human up to Prajāpati, the bliss of Brahman is then practiced as being without superior through the statement, "That is one bliss of Brahman. Therefore, it is established that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).

Now, an objection may be raised: even if the suffix *mayaṭ* is accepted as signifying abundance—as in "the sacrifice consists of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*)—it is still not possible for [Brahman] to be other than the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because, if there is an abundance of bliss (*ānanda*), the scarcity of suffering is necessarily implied; and since it is the individual soul alone that is the locus of pleasure and pain, it would follow that [Brahman] is nothing but the soul. Therefore, it is more appropriate to take the suffix as signifying a modification (*vikāra*). This is especially so given the opening statement, "consisting of food" (*annamayaḥ*).
Because the suffix *mayaṭ* is observed in common usage to signify a modification— as in "made of clay," "made of wood," "made of silver," "made of copper," and so forth—

and because it is also observed in the Veda to signify a modification— as in "the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood," "the *sruva* spoons are made of *śamī-wood," and "the girdle is made of *darbha-grass"— it is possible in both ways that the state of being "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) itself.
If it is argued thus, we say no: for "abundance of bliss" (ānandapracuratva) means the possession of profuse bliss.

And that consists in being characterized by the absolute absence of suffering at all three periods of time; since this is impossible for the individual soul (jīva), who is distinguished by the three types of affliction (tāpa), it cannot be composed of bliss (ānandamaya). This is because, if one were to admit that a conscious entity undergoes transformation like clay and other material substances, [it would follow that it is subject to change].
There would be the consequence of contradicting the Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* does not have the sense of "modification.
Furthermore, he states another reason: "And because that cause is designated [as Brahman]. (1.4.15)
For who indeed could breathe, or who could live, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? For he alone causes bliss;

thus, because he is the cause of bliss for all living beings, he is designated as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). In the world, only one who is learned makes another learned, only one who possesses wealth makes another wealthy, and only the self-luminous sun and other luminaries illuminate others.

In the same way, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) bestows his own bliss upon the Supreme Lord and all living beings during deep sleep, thereby gladdening them. Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is not anyone other [than the Supreme Lord]. This is because the Supreme Lord, who consists of bliss, is designated as and proclaimed to be the cause of that bliss of the living beings. [Regarding] the bliss of the living beings...

Or rather, it is because that [Brahman] is designated as the cause of that bliss which is by nature [blissful]. When that *ānandamaya* is the cause of the bliss of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is the cause of that [bliss]; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
Now, an objection: since Brahman is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), its being "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and its being the bestower of bliss are untenable.

Following the principle stated by the former teachers— that "the non-proliferated (niṣprapañca) is explained through superimposition and negation"— and because one must accept that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is true only in the sense of mere conventional usage, the state of consisting of bliss (ānandamayatva) must be accepted as being merely figurative.

If it is argued thus, we say no: what is called "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*) is either (1) the state of being an entity that does not persist beyond a certain time, or (2) the state of being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, or (3) the incapacity to be defined as either existent or non-existent.
It cannot be the first, because [the definition] would apply to any entity whatsoever that does not persist beyond a certain time.

Because we accept [the existence of] jars, cloths, and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*) in part; furthermore, there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because the *prakṛti* described as "the cow is without beginning or end" persists throughout all time.
If one intends to mean the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) delimited by persistence at a different time, then even the second moment [would be included].
By establishing its non-duration through the fact of existing at a different time, it would be the very momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) accepted by the Vaibhāṣikas that is proven;
however, it would not be falsity (*mithyātva*) in the sense of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in its own place and time.
Thus, there would be a contradiction with one's own tenets as well as an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of the illusory (*prātibhāsika*).

Not the second [alternative], because since a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) consisting of both existence and non-existence is unestablished, that which is distinct from it is likewise unestablished. Nor is it distinctness from both that which is delimited by existence and that which is delimited by non-existence, because this would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to both the existent and the non-existent; for, according to the cognition "one is not two," it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Nor is it [distinctness] while being distinct from that which is delimited by existence...

[It is] the state of being different from that which is delimited by non-existence (*asattva*). This is because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) due to anything delimited by existence being different from some other thing delimited by existence.

Nor is it correct to intend [the definition] as "that which possesses a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by existence," and so forth; for even so, [this would fail] in the case of that which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*).
Because it would over-extend to Brahman. Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension precisely because [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*);

for that would entail the consequence that the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) would not be properties of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). If, on the other hand, you mean "being different from the nature of existence" (*sadrūpabhinnatva*), that too is not tenable;

for by taking another instance of existence as the referent, one would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Even if one intends to mean "being different from every instance of the nature of existence," [the fault remains] with respect to each individual [instance].

As long as it is [defined] by the mutual exclusion of whatever has the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*), that same fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) remains. Now, suppose it is held that what is intended is the mutual absence of a universal delimited by the nature of existence—this too is flawed because it overextends (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman. Furthermore, if it is [defined] as the aggregate (*kūṭa*) of mutual absences delimited by their respective properties, each having as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) all things whatsoever that have the nature of existence—[then the following applies].

Because, according to your own view, since all existing entities (*sad-rūpa*) are unestablished, the collection of differences (*bhedakūṭa*) having them as counter-correlates is likewise unestablished;

furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to Brahman and to the illusory (*pratibhāsika*). Nor can it be defined as "being distinct from Brahman while being different from the non-existent" (*asadvilakṣaṇatva*), because the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) is unavoidable.

Furthermore, because of the cognition "the jar exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth, it is not logical for jars and the like to be of a nature different from existence; thus, the definition [of Brahman as that which is different from existence] is impossible.

Nor can it be argued that this is sublated by perception through the Śruti text, "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*), on the grounds that [perception is more authoritative than scripture], as in the cases of "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) or "The sun is... [and so forth].

In such cases as "The sacrificial post [is the self]," "One should sacrifice with Soma," "The sacrificer is a *kṛṣṇala*-weight [of gold]," "The cake is on one potsherd," and "That thou art," we observe hundreds of times that even those Śruti texts which contradict direct perception subvert their own stated propositions.

Now, an objection may be raised: if there were non-difference between "Being" (*sat*) and the jar, then—just as in the case of the words "jar" and "kalaśa"—grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible; likewise, if there were difference...

Just as in the case of "the pot" and "the cloth," grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is simply impossible. Therefore, this cognition takes identity (*tādātmya*) alone as its object between "Being" (*sat*) and the "pot. And that [identity] consists in having a non-different existence while being distinct. Consequently, if it is argued that the difference of the pot and so forth from Being is established by cognition, we reply to this as follows:

If identity (*tādātmya*) consists in having a non-different existence while being distinct, then after the sublation "this is not silver," there would follow the cognition "this is silver," because the cognition of the qualifier does not sublate the cognition of the qualified.
[Objection: But when that identity which was cognized in "this is silver" is negated by "not," how...

If you argue that there is a cognition of identity [between the shell and silver], then abandon the inclusion of difference within the meaning of the term "identity. For if the cognition "this is silver" were to have identity as its object by way of direct contact, then the cognition "this is not silver" could not have it as its qualifier (*prakāra*).

Even when there is identity or a relation of being a part of the same locus, a relationship of sublation (bādhyabādhakabhāva) exists; on the contrary, because it takes the form of corroboration by another means of knowledge, it actually brings about the strengthening of the cognition. Otherwise, cognitions such as "possessing color" and "possessing the inherence of color" would be mutually...

Because it would entail the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). Nor is this a desired consequence, as it would constitute an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and contradict the doctrine of identity (*tādātmya*).
Only an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) possesses a reality distinct from that of its locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is different from the locus; any other [absence] is not so different.
Therefore, the statement "the absence of silver is not different from the locus" contradicts the cognition "this is not silver."

Furthermore, since there is no negation of the state of having an identical existence (*abhinnasattākatva*) with the word in the case of a verbal cognition (*śābdabuddhi*)—arising from the word itself—it is likewise impossible to negate it in the case of a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhi*). Nor should it be argued that even in the latter, such [identity] is presented by virtue of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words;
for if that were so, it would follow [absurdly] even in the case of the statement "Brahman is without attributes" (*nirviśeṣaṃ brahma*).

Furthermore—this cognition is a cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), not even a cognition of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because of the cognition "this is not silver. If it were of the nature of negating identity of existence (*abhinnasattākatva*), then the cognition "the form is not a pot" would likewise be so;
and in that case, according to that [opponent's] view, at that time the cognition "the pot is blue" would not occur.
Furthermore— even if one denies that [the object] possesses an identical existence (abhinnasattākatva)— since there is no denial of the non-difference residing in the object before one,

or of the relation that delimits its desirability (iṣṭatāvacchedaka-saṃsarga), an action prompted by error would be unavoidable. For the possession of the delimiter of desirability and so forth cannot, by virtue of being uncontradicted, prevent purposeful activity.

Nor is it the case that the negation of having an identical existence (*abhinnasattākatva*) alone is what negates non-difference. For if that were so, having an identical existence would itself be non-difference; thus, there would be a contradiction with the qualification "while being different" (*bhinnatve sati*). Regarding the term "having an identical existence," what is meant by "having an identical existence"? Is it "possessing existence" (*sattāvatsattākatva*)? [This cannot be,] because the possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) is prescribed in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), and [therefore] the sense of possession...

In accordance with the usage "the man has a staff" (*daṇḍavān puruṣaḥ*) or "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), there is no contradiction in the fact that [the staff] possesses an existence distinct from itself by way of being a separate entity. Nor is it appropriate to say that identity (*tādātmya*) is the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matup*); for in this case, identity cannot enter into the definition of the locus (*āśraya*) or its characteristics, since the primary existence (*prathamasattā*) cannot be established as identical [to the staff] without the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of another existence.

Furthermore, if the existence (*sattā*) that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the pot were false, it would constitute a contradiction of your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). For the status of being a substrate, when connected with another entity, does not deviate from that [existence];
nor is "possessing existence" non-different from existence itself, because it is impossible for the possessive suffix (*matup*) to signify non-difference. Otherwise, [the following would occur]:

Otherwise, it would follow that the staff and the person are non-different. Furthermore, if the difference between the pot and space were of the nature of a relation with existence (*sattā*), it would entail the undesirable consequence of the identity of the insentient and the sentient. Nor can it be argued that, for this very reason, the "difference from the pot" is simply the relation of non-difference with existence within existence; for that would result in a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*). [This is because] identity resides in the pot...

Furthermore, by abandoning the relationship with existence (*sattā-sambandhatva*), one falls into the maxim of "the dawn at the broken shed" (*ghaṭṭakuṭīprabhātanyāya*). Even if one attempts to establish that "possession of existence" (*sattāvattva*)—which constitutes the state of having an identical existence—is present in some cases through non-difference and in others as a substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatayā*), this too lacks universal applicability (*ananugama*).

Moreover, it has already been stated that a *bahuvrīhi* compound is untenable because non-difference cannot function as the possessive suffix-meaning (*matvartha*). This is because [the two cognitions] of blue and [the cognition] of identity...

Furthermore, because it is impossible to conceive of a difference in form between the two cognitions "the jar exists" and "the cloth [exists]" unless they are based on identity (*tādātmya*). Moreover, in this way, according to your view, such expressions as "the jar is a cloth" or "the taste is a jar" would be unavoidable; for it is illogical that there should be no such cognition between two things that are non-different and possess non-different existence. Indeed, it is not the case that something remains unknown even when its reality is present.

You tell us that this very [identity] is its regulator; nor should you say that because there is no such cognition as "the pot is the cloth," identity itself does not exist, for you cannot deny that the difference between the pot and the cloth consists in their having the existence of Brahman as their being. If, even so, you still deny it, then—

On account of parsimony (*lāghava*), why not simply say that mere difference (*bhinnatvamātra*) alone is the determinant for the cognition of co-referentiality (*samānādhikaraṇapratīti*), while the absence of cognitions such as "the pot is the cloth" is due to the absolute non-existence of difference in any way whatsoever? However, if— because it is impossible to deny what is established by perception and other means— the mere fact of difference cannot be the determinant for such cognition, then...

Since it is impossible for you to abandon your own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), you must set aside its identity (*tādātmya*) and instead abandon the very notion that it is the regulator of the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Alternatively, if the deviation from concomitance (*anvayavyabhicāra*) between the regulated and the regulator were to be removed by postulating another regulator, such as their inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*), then—
Let this restrictive factor consisting of identity—which is like the hair on the neck of a goat—be abandoned; for it is precisely from that [identity] that such a cognition is logically established.
Now, if the existence of the substrate were to differ from the superimposed jar and cloth, then indeed it would differ.

"Also by means of the quality and the possessor of the quality. Furthermore: if identity (*tādātmya*) were manifested in the cognition "the cloth exists," then it would necessarily be manifested in the cognition "this is silver" as well.
And if that were so, no one seeking silver would ever act toward a mother-of-pearl shell when identity—composed of the very difference between the desired object and its locus—is known;
for the knowledge of the difference from the desired object acts as an obstacle to purposeful action (*pravṛtti*). Nor is it the case that...

It must be stated that the cognition of having a non-different existence (*abhinnasattākatvajñāna*) is itself the motivator [of action]. For if activity and cessation were to occur simultaneously, their opposing causes would mutually obstruct one another, making the occurrence of any effect whatsoever unavoidable. This is because, if the cognition of having a non-different existence were the motivator, [the aforementioned contradiction would follow].
Furthermore, at that time, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one who seeks a jar would engage in activity toward a cloth.

If, in order to avoid this, another qualification—namely "having the same mode of existence" (*abhinnasattākatva*)—is added, then since that [qualification] is itself unknown, it could not be the motivator of action; for if it were, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, on the other hand, it is known, then it would be unavoidable at the very moment of engaging in activity.
Moreover, it is undisputed that the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) is the cause of the qualified cognition of a desired object present before one.

Even for those who maintain that error consists in the nature of direct witness (*sākṣin*), some utility must be attributed to this [non-apprehension], since they observe that activity occurs even when there is the cognition: "These two—the desired object and the object present before one—are distinct."
And likewise, according to your view, how could there be either engagement or withdrawal through an error that contradicts the non-apprehension of the difference that is required for action?
Moreover, in this way, even such cognitions as "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire" and "on the mountain there is smoke pervaded by fire" [would be problematic].

If [the cognition] were to apprehend identity by virtue of being a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇapratīti*), it would take as its object the difference between smoke and that which is pervaded by fire. And thus, no inference would arise; rather, it would simply be obstructed. Furthermore, just as there is the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) "I cognize this as silver," there would likewise be [the after-cognitions]: "I cognize this as different from silver" and "I cognize this as having an existence distinct from silver."

The reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I know" might also occur at some time; for that which has been known is never not subsequently apprehended. One might even perceive: "For such a long time, the cognition of the difference from silver occurred, and now it has ceased due to sublation. Furthermore, there would be no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) from the sentence "This is silver," because it would arise from an invalid cognition (*ayogyajñāna*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. Therefore, it is not the case that "it is not a jar."
The establishment of its being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent follows from the force of cognition itself.

Nor can it be argued that "if it were existent, it would not be sublated; if it were non-existent, it would not be cognized," for such an argument—based on the apparent inconsistency of cognition and sublation (*khyātibādhānyathānupapatti*)—actually proves the opposite. For sublation is the cognition that "it does not exist," and that [cognition] would establish precisely its non-existence.

Manifestation (*khyāti*) also exists as an acceptance (*astīkāra*); that too would establish existence (*sattā*) itself. Consequently, the object would be established as consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, rather than being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

[Objection: But surely, because of contradiction, one cannot establish that it consists of both the existent and the non-existent; therefore, by implication, it must be distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

If you say that it will be established—then this [thesis] also would not be established, precisely because of contradiction. For just as the nature of being both existent and non-existent is contradictory, so too is the nature of being distinct from both existent and non-existent; for those who know the principles of logic maintain that when two things are mutually exclusive, there is no room for a third alternative. Indeed, no object is found that is distinct from both a jar and a non-jar. This is because everything that is different from a jar [is necessarily a non-jar].

Because it is subsumed under the state of being non-existent (aghaṭatva). If it is argued that there is a non-perception [of the jar] as being excluded from both categories [existence and non-existence], then the impossibility of being excluded from both categories is equally applicable here as well, because everything distinct from existence is subsumed under non-existence.
Now, if it should be suspected that the word "existent" (sat) refers to a specific kind of existence, then [the jar would be] something distinct from some particular form of existence.
The fact that being distinct from both the real and the unreal is possible even in the case of another real entity means that our own desired conclusion is indeed established.
Now, you yourself have stated that non-existence is established through sublation (*bādha*), and that is precisely what constitutes being distinct from the real;
for it is equal in its lack of contact with any real object. Furthermore, even pervasion (*vyāpti*), while establishing existence, [establishes it] in relation to existence...
Thus, by way of its being distinct from the non-existent (*asad*) and by its pervading that [non-existence], it establishes its distinction from the void (*tuccha*).
And if it is argued that even a contradiction regarding an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can somehow be resolved, this is merely the prattle of delusion;
for even if a thing lacks existence in one locus due to sublation (*bādha*), its existence in another locus remains entirely unimpeded.

It is common knowledge that in some cases, when a thing has already been established as real, something similar to it is what is negated; therefore, sublation (bādha) would only establish existence. Furthermore, even cognition (pratīti), by being designated by the term "manifestation" (khyāti), reveals that very same existence, for it has been said that "consciousness alone is the refuge in accepting the reality of an object. And thus, [the object] is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent.

The effort to pacify the contradiction between being distinct from existence and being distinct from non-existence by means of that [reasoning], based on the non-perception of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is a confusion caused by the sight of a "goat's udder" (a non-existent thing) leading to a frantic rush for milk.
As it has been said here: "Existence and non-existence are either attributes of an entity or its own nature. It is not the first [alternative], because at the time of non-existence..."

Because it would entail the consequence that the category of "entity" (padārtha) exists [independently]. For an impermanent property cannot subsist without a substratum; and if it were an eternal property, its existence as a contingent property would be contradicted. Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because there is a contradiction in a single thing having the nature of both being and non-being. If it is argued that there is no contradiction due to the difference in time, we say no; for the property arises from the convergence of causes, not from the essential nature [of the thing] itself. Not so.

Nor can non-existence become existence through a difference in time; for it is impossible even for that which is non-existent to have existed prior to this [present], since that which lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) cannot possess a delimiting time. Therefore, whatever is non-existent at any time is non-existent at all times, and whatever is existent is always existent.

That too is incorrect, because there is no fault in either of the two positions. Nor does it follow that, since an impermanent property cannot exist without a substratum, the property in the form of "existence" (sattā) must necessitate a substratum even at a time when it is non-existent;
for at that time, since the property in the form of existence itself is absent, there is no impossibility of its existing without a substratum. Otherwise, [the same consequence would apply].

Because the term "destruction of its own substratum" would entail the consequence that color and other qualities— which are the counter-correlates of destruction— would exist in the jar; and because, even in your own view, there would be the consequence that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, which do not exist at the time of liberation, would still project ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, if it is argued that the non-existence [of a property] is untenable without a substratum, then let this same logic be applied to the case at hand. By this, the contradiction with non-existence regarding the subject being existent (*sattva*) is largely refuted; for since existence is absent at that time, it cannot be a property thereof. Otherwise, [the same would apply to] a subject characterized by blackness...

Because, in the absence of being a substratum possessing the quality of redness—which is contradictory to that [darkness]—it would follow as a consequence that darkness and redness reside in two separate substrata. If being a property of that [substratum] were constituted by the time of the destruction of darkness, then the same would apply elsewhere; otherwise, it would be a substratum of existence.
This is not so, because it is easy to state [the reason]. Now, one might object: "Non-existence (*asattva*) is indeed a property (*dharma*), just like existence (*sattva*).
How can this [non-existence] subsist without a substratum? And thus, in the state of non-existence, there would follow the consequence of the existence of a substratum.

[We reply: This would indeed be the case if non-existence were something distinct from absence (*abhāva*); but it is not so. Therefore, it is simply absence itself, and that has time, space, and so forth as its locus.

Thus, since the desire for a substratum has been pacified, how could it imply the existence of a counter-correlative for its sake? Otherwise, what would be the status of "existence" and "non-existence" as you intend them? For even those two are merely forms of existence and non-existence within the two-fold nature of being, according to the recollection of the root-meaning [of the verb *as*]. Indeed, this was stated by you when you were unaware of the contradiction.
The reality of an absence is established by the mere existence of its counter-positive, even if that counter-positive is devoid of actual being.
By this, the doubt as to how counter-positiveness can subsist without a substratum is also dismissed;
for while counter-positiveness regarding non-existence cannot be established without a substratum, it is sufficient for it to have existed at a prior time.
If its arising were [the same as that], then it would simply be that very arising.

In reality, however, properties such as pastness and futureness reside only in entities that do not exist by way of their own nature (svabhāva), and not in those that do exist; for conceptual construction follows the dictates of experience.
Contradiction and non-contradiction must also be established solely in accordance with experience.

Thus, when pastness and so forth lack a substratum because they are non-existent, there would be no status as an object of cognition, nor the state of being an objective factor (*karmatva*) of cognition. Likewise, for jars and the like, which serve as the objective factors in acts such as arising, there could be no causality.

Furthermore, ignorance (*avidyā*) would have to possess the status of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) to its own cessation, because a counter-correlation cannot exist without a substratum (*āśraya*).
In reality, however, since the world is non-existent, it cannot serve as a substratum for counter-correlation;

consequently, because the world itself is the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in all places and times, it follows that every single entity whatsoever must serve as its substratum.

Thus, enough of this elaboration. Therefore, the phenomenal world does not possess even a merely conventional reality. Consequently, the Supreme Lord’s nature as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed intrinsic.
Nevertheless, because in the verse "Brahman is the tail, the support," the embodied self (*śārīra*) is designated as the substratum of Brahman—

Since she [Māyā] is distinct from that [Brahman], there is a contradiction in her being the cause of the birth and so forth of the world due to her independence; therefore, suspecting that this "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is merely the embodied soul (śārīra), he says: "And it is proclaimed as being exactly that which is described in the Vedic mantra. (1.1.16)

In this context, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the Supreme Lord. For, beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and concluding with "He who knows Brahman— truth, knowledge, infinite— as hidden in the secret cave of the highest heaven, he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman," [the text] teaches that only those who know Brahman attain the fulfillment of all desires.

Having demonstrated that this very Self is the cause of the entire complex of gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities through the passage beginning with "From that indeed, from this Self, space was produced," and having taught its status as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) through the passage beginning with "Having created that, He entered into it," [the text continues] with "There is another inner Self consisting of vital breath" (prāṇamaya).

Having thus established that [the Self] is within the five sheaths (*kośa*), and because the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is taught there as the primary Self— since the opening and the conclusion possess a single characteristic— the Supreme Śiva alone, who was introduced in the Vedic verse "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," is the one consisting of bliss; thus, "another inner Self is the one consisting of bliss."

And regarding this, they explain as follows: Since the mantra and the brāhmaṇa stand in a relationship of the dependent and the supported, it is logical that they have a single meaning. In the sentence "Brahman is the tail, the support," the word *brahman* signifies the *praṇava*;
thus, the Supreme Lord is taught to be its substratum, its object of exposition, and its very essence. Now, [it may be objected]: "Oṃ, that is Brahman..."

If it is asked: "Since the *praṇava* itself is taught to be the Supreme Brahman by virtue of being the self of all through such passages as [the one beginning with] 'ityādi', how can its having that [Brahman] as its substratum and so forth be taught?"—[the answer is: because, starting from "The Lord of all sciences" (*īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām*) and ending with "Sadāśiva Om," the Supreme Lord alone is taught to have the nature of the *praṇava*, as in [the passage]: "That sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda... (*yo vedādau svaraḥ proktaḥ*).
From the passage beginning with these words and ending with "He who is beyond that is Maheśvara," it is understood that Śiva alone is the object denoted by the *praṇava*.

Therefore, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is designated as being of the nature of the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*) and consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), according to such texts as:
"For who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale, if this ether were not bliss? and so forth.

The nature of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is understood to be that of the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*). Therefore, because it is seen that this one [bliss] is of Brahman— as in the statement "He knew bliss to be Brahman," which teaches that unsurpassed bliss has Brahman as its substratum and that bliss is identical with Brahman due to the instruction on its being the cause of both the self and the world— there is no difference between bliss and Brahman.

The aphorism "consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" was taught by Vyāsa. Now, an objection may be raised: since the word *ānanda* (bliss) is seen to be used many times in reference to Brahman alone, it is appropriate that it refers to Him;
however, since the word *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) is not seen to be repeated in reference to Brahman, how can it refer to Him? This is not so—

Just as in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," the word *jyotis* refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, so too there is no fault here in the word *ānanda* referring to the *ānandamaya*,
given that the concluding passage states: "This is that Bhārgava-Vāruṇī knowledge, established in the highest heaven."

It is beyond dispute that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the Supreme Lord, because he is seen at the conclusion of the Varuṇa-vidyā to be of the nature of Brahman—the very essence of the power of consciousness whose form is the supreme ether, which is another synonym for it.
Now, [an objection is raised]: "Having departed from this world and having approached this self consisting of food (*annamaya*)," and so forth.

If it be argued that—in passages such as these—the worship of one's own sheath of food (*annamaya-kośa*) and the others is what is enjoined here for those seeking liberation, because the scriptural texts referring to the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth separately denote sentient beings, thereby illuminating the gradual liberation of the meditator who has departed from the body—this is not so. For in hundreds of scriptural passages, such as "The individual soul (*jīva*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*) are not objects of worship," the worship of the individual soul by itself is expressly forbidden. Rather, [it is as follows:]...

There is no contradiction, because [the scripture] teaches the liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*) for living beings within that Brahman known as Paraśiva— who transcends the fivefold manifestation (*pañcavyūha*) beginning with Sadyojāta, who consists of the ladder-like path to Kailāsa leading through Paramaśiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, and who is the essence of the presiding deities of the five sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with the *annamaya*.

Therefore, it is taught that the cause even of the blissful one (ānandamaya), who is Sadāśiva and whose substratum consists of the self made of food (annamaya) and so forth, is Brahman known as Paramaśiva; He is its "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā).
Because of the identity between Sadāśiva and Paraśiva, the designation of the blissful one as Brahman is justified. Thus, the blissful one—
It is established that it is none other [than Brahman].

Having raised the objection—given the teaching in the passage beginning with "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" that the Virāṭ-Puruṣa consists of all gross bodies, why should he alone not be the cause of the world's birth and so forth?—it is stated: "none other."
He refutes [this objection]: "Not the other, because it is not possible. (Sūtra 17)
The other—the Virāṭ Puruṣa, distinct from Paramaśiva—is not composed of bliss (ānandamaya). Why? Because of impossibility.

For, by such passages as "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'; He performed austerity; having performed austerity, He created all this," there are described prior to creation attributes such as volition (*īkṣaṇa*), the nature of creation, and being the cause of creation.
The meaning of the Sūtra is that the Virāṭ Puruṣa, who consists of the gross phenomenal world, is impossible [as the cause].

Furthermore, because in passages such as "From Him the Virāṭ was born," the Virāṭ Puruṣa is seen to have been produced from Paramaśiva, and because the creation of the Virāṭ Puruṣa is accomplished through a body.

The impossibility of [the soul] being the subject of the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) prior [to creation] should be understood. In the Śruti, the word *tapas* refers to the act of seeing. Therefore, it is established that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is none other than Supreme Śiva, and not another;
for from Him were produced the progenitors of the world.
With water he released living beings upon the earth; through the plants, he entered men and cattle,
as well as all moving and unmoving creatures.

Thus, in the passage from the Mahānārāyaṇīyopaniṣad, the status of being the cause of the world is attributed specifically to Hiraṇyagarbha. Furthermore, in the opening statement—"The seers perceived him within the ocean; Prajāpati moves within the womb"—it is understood that he alone has entered into all things. This is confirmed by the conclusion of that same passage: "The Ordainer [created] the sun and the moon."

Having raised the objection that the state of being composed of bliss (*ānandamaya*) belongs to that very [Hiraṇyagarbha] alone— since his status as the universal cause is established by such passages as "He fashioned the heaven, the earth, the intermediate space, and then the light" (*yathāpūrvamakalpayat*), and since his existence prior to creation is shown by such passages as "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists"— it is said:
He refutes [this objection]: "And because there is a designation of difference" (Sūtra 1.3.18).

"Who is the first among the gods, appearing in the east, Rudra the great seer who transcends all—may he, beholding the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) as it is being born, endow us with auspicious mindfulness. Thus, in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad: "He who is the first among the gods and their source, Rudra the great seer who transcends all..."

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad as well, the causality of Hiraṇyagarbha is taught to belong to Śiva alone, in the passage beginning: "He generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning. Furthermore, in the Śvetāśvatara, [the text reads]: "The unborn, out of fear, takes refuge in you, O Rudra; with that face of yours which is auspicious, protect me forever," and "Rudra is indeed one, he does not stand for a second," and so forth.

Since attributes such as being unborn and being without a second are heard in scripture as belonging to the Supreme Lord alone, it is most appropriate that Parashiva alone is the referent of the terms Prajapati and others mentioned in the previously cited scriptural passages;
this is because of the abundance of those attributes [in Him]. "Designation by difference" (bhedavyapadeśa) means the designation of difference.

Because of the distinction made between Hiraṇyagarbha—who is the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of individual souls—and Paraśiva, based on their respective states of being produced and unproduced, the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) here is not Hiraṇyagarbha.
Furthermore: "He is indeed rasa; for having obtained this very rasa, one becomes blissful."

It teaches the distinction between Hiraṇyagarbha, who consists of the aggregate of all individual souls, and the Supreme Lord. Now, an objection may be raised: how can the words "another" (*anya*) found in such passages as "There is another inner self consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) establish that [Hiraṇyagarbha] is distinct from [the Supreme Lord]? And how can anything other than the one "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) be Brahman?
If it is argued that this is not tenable, we say no—

for it is precisely the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) who is established as being distinct from the one consisting of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*), which is Hiraṇyagarbha in the form of the aggregate of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*).

Because no other basis for establishing the status of Brahman is seen, and because the fault of infinite regress would follow if one were to accept something other than that [Brahman], it is established that the *ānandamaya* is indeed Paraśiva himself.
Since it is impossible for the attributeless Supreme Lord to be the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe, [the relationship is understood] by the analogy of the magnet and the needle.
In response to the doubt that causality could only belong to that which has been superimposed as primary by virtue of its existence, he says:
"And because of the desire [of the Lord], there is no dependence on inference. (1.1.19)
Although in such scriptural passages as "Prajāpati desired: 'May I procreate offspring,'" and "In the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed;

from Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born, from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born," it is understood that Pradhāna—consisting of the three guṇas—as well as the four-faced Brahmā and others, are the causes of the world; yet...

Regarding the Supreme Lord's status as the cause of the universe, there is no dependence on inference or logical reasoning; for that [dependence] pertains to the scope of intermediate creation, such as that of Pradhāna and other [principles]. Thus, it is also indicated that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, acts as the agent of intermediate creation in his capacity as the Self of all, including Pradhāna, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth.

Regarding the passage "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching," this is because we hear that the agency in the creation of names and forms belongs to Paraśiva— who, as the Self of all, including Pradhāna and Hiraṇyagarbha, is woven through the entire universe— when it says: "Entering with this living self (jīva), let me evolve names and forms."

Furthermore: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. Having emitted that, He entered into it Himself. "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara. "By His constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded.
"The Lord of the qualities of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña is the cause of bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra. "Rudra is indeed one alone."

They stood for the second [time]; they rule over this fourth world, the world that is to be ruled; they would cause to be born him who rules all worlds by means of his ruling powers, the supreme powers. "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings," and so on, in hundreds of such scriptural passages.

It is established that He alone is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because the attributes of being the independent creator of all, the controller of all, the inner ruler of all, the omniscient one, and so forth, are declared to belong exclusively to Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, and are not shared by any other. Furthermore, the status of Pradhāna and others as the cause [of the universe] has already been refuted in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.
It should be understood that, because of the context of the primary subject, this has been refuted once again for the purpose of elaborating upon the commonality of the states of existence (*gati*).
Regarding this matter, he states another reason: "And because its manifestation [is taught] in this [world]. (20)

The meaning is that the scripture teaches—that is, establishes—the union of this individual soul (*jīva*) with this supreme Śiva consisting of bliss, and by implication, the union of both the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as well; it teaches their identity, like that of the ocean and the sea-salt, according to the verse:
"Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean disappear, casting off name and form, so too... [the wise cast off name and form upon reaching the Supreme].

"The wise one, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. In such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "That thou art," and "I am Brahman," liberation is taught as the attainment of that very state. In this Upanishad, at the outset in the statement "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," both the quality of being known and the quality of being attained are predicated of Brahman.

Since the individual soul (jīva) is taught to possess both the quality of being an object of knowledge and the status of being an attainer, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is that because of the difference between the individual soul and Brahman— characterized by the relationship of worshiper and worshipped, pervasiveness and smallness, and omniscience versus limited knowledge— the attainment of the state of that [Brahman] is possible.
Now, an objection: the cessation of that which is inherent cannot occur at all times, according to the analogy of the bitter taste of the nimba fruit.
Even if such cessation were admitted, it would be merely adventitious and impermanent, like the heat of water;
therefore, liberation itself would likewise be non-eternal.
If this is argued, we say no—for in cases such as the bee and the worm, or the water in a pearl-oyster shell, we observe the complete cessation of what is natural;
thus it is established that the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) alone is Vedic.
Furthermore: "For when he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode..."

He finds [fear]—then he becomes filled with fear; for when he perceives even a slight difference within this [Self], then fear arises for him. Thus, in the state of liberation, when he perceives within this Supreme Śiva, who consists of bliss, any other difference in the form of non-identity, then, due to that fear born of [separation from] birth, he does not turn back. When...

When, during this time of meditation upon the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), one perceives identity with Him, then one is liberated from the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Now, an objection may be raised: "If the one consisting of bliss is Brahman, why should the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the others not also be Brahman, according to the maxim of 'half-old woman' (*ardhajaratīnyāya*)? This is not so; for it is said: "This person indeed consists of food," and "From that very one, who consists of the essence of food... [the subsequent sheaths arise]. Thus, the status of Brahman belongs specifically to the one consisting of bliss.

There is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). From this very self consisting of breath, there is another inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya*). From this very self consisting of mind, there is another inner self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
From this very self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—thus [it is described] as being the innermost of all and unsurpassed.
Furthermore, because it is designated as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) itself, its identity with anything other than Brahman is not established.

Some deluded persons superimpose the error of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) upon Brahman, just as one might superimpose the appearance of a snake onto a rope. This is like the case of one who has attained the state of a living soul during the stage of liberation, [yet perceives] the necklace on the neck of Brahman through the reconnection of discernment (*viveka*).

They claim that liberation is simply the knowledge of one's own true nature. However, because this view contradicts scripture, logic, and experience, it should not be accepted by seekers of liberation who follow the Vedas.
[This applies to] those who follow the Smṛtis, those who have fallen away from all [Vedic] systems, and those who attempt to prove the unreality of the world.
One should avoid those who wander the path of courtesans and those heretics cursed by great sages such as Durvāsas, Gautama, Vyāsa,
and Dadhīci; one should avoid those heretics who harbor exclusive hatred toward Śiva.

Thus, according to the words of the ancient teachers. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such [scriptural] passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," which establish from the very beginning that Brahman is the object to be known and the goal to be attained, as well as with the statement, "He enjoys all desires together."

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the fact that the devotees of that [Brahman] have attained all their desires. Moreover, if one were to superimpose error upon the omniscient Brahman, it would entail the collapse of His omniscience and other attributes. As it is said: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord."
Furthermore, this would contradict hundreds of scriptural passages such as these, which is not pleasing to the wise.

On this point, some prattle that the scripture teaches the connection of this individual soul with this Brahman consisting of bliss—namely, the relationship of being a subordinate part—and thus assert that qualified non-dualism alone is the primary doctrine. This [they say].
Because it is non-Vedic, it is not to be accepted by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

This is because the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*), such as Bhaṭṭabhāskara and others who composed the Vedic Mīmāṃsā, disregarded it as utterly unworthy of being considered even as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) when establishing their own doctrines. Furthermore, it contradicts the statement that [the doctrine] is "qualified non-duality" (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), for the qualified...
Furthermore, because it is difficult to define and because it is false (*mithyātva*).

As for what is called a "qualified entity" (*viśiṣṭa*), is it merely the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, or is it something distinct from them? It cannot be the first, because since the three [elements] are multiple, non-duality (*advayatva*) would be impossible; for instance, [one would have to say], "these are the staff, the person, and the relationship."

This is because a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), being a qualified cognition, does not have an object distinct [from its constituents]. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable:

since the Supreme Self in its nature as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) would be different [from the qualified entity], the qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) of the intended Supreme Self remains unestablished; for it is admitted that a man with a staff is distinct from the bare man. Otherwise, [the distinction between them could not be maintained].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that either the cognition "the man with a staff" would apply to a solitary man, or the cognition "a solitary man" would apply to a man with a staff; for a qualified entity distinct from the triad [of relation, relatum, and counter-correlate] would have to be either qualified by this very staff or qualified by a staff distinct from it.

Not the first [alternative], because it is not established that [the qualified] is distinct from the triad [of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation]; for even the qualifier constitutes part of the body of the qualified. Nor the second—furthermore, if the man with a staff were something other [than the constituents], then, being produced without the well-known causal complex of semen, blood, and so forth, he would necessarily be false, like a pillar or a man [seen in an illusion]. And if he were unproduced, he would be eternal, and thus [the cognition] would persist even when the staff is removed.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition "the man with a staff" [arising where only the staff exists]. Since the qualified entity is eternal, and since the qualified entity is distinct from the triad [of body, senses, and intellect], it follows that only the self as qualified by the body and so forth could be the cause of pleasure, pain, and the like;
thus, the fact that the isolated self possesses qualities such as pleasure and pain would not be established. This is because [the self] is other than the triad.

Furthermore, the qualified entity is refuted by non-perception; or, if it were perceived, it would be indistinguishable from a post or a person. Moreover, if there were no difference between the three [the staff, the person, and the qualified entity], it would follow that the staff and the person are identical, because of the rule that what is non-different from that which is non-different from something else must itself be non-different from that thing—just like the single cognition of oneness directed toward three distant trees.
Since even the cognition of oneness regarding the three objects of perception is an error, it follows that the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) itself lacks epistemic validity.

Therefore, because the qualified entity— being difficult to define in terms of existence or non-existence relative to its qualifier, the qualified, and their relation— is illusory, one must accept the non-duality of Śiva alone as the ultimate reality.

For this very reason, the foremost Vedāntins accept that the Supreme Lord is the cause of both the origin and the sustenance of the universe. Consequently, in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, the venerable Vyāsa declared in the sūtra, "The effect is not different from its cause; it is non-different from it, on account of such terms as 'originating' (*ārambhaṇa*)," that the effects referred to in the scriptural passages concerning "originating through speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) are non-different from their cause. Therefore:
The doctrine of "qualified non-duality" (viśiṣṭādvaita) is attractive only to those who are ignorant, much like the term "Brāhmaṇa-Śūdra.

Furthermore, even the relationship between qualifier and qualified is difficult to define. To begin with, being a "qualifier" cannot consist in generating a cognition of exclusion (vyāvṛtti-buddhi), because that [quality] is possible even for the "qualified" and so forth.
Furthermore, it is impossible for a staff or other such instruments, which have multiple causes, to be the uncommon cause of that [consciousness] alone. For in this case, one must discern:

what is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), what is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and what is the relation (*sambandha*)? First of all, it cannot be said that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the qualifier and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the qualified.

In that view, if the atomic souls (*aṇujīva*) were one, it would follow that there is only a single soul; if they were many, it would be impossible for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as qualified by those many souls, to be non-dual—just as one who is qualified by a staff is not the same as one qualified by an earring, because there is a distinction between the forms of being qualified by a staff and being qualified by an earring. And if there were no distinction between those two [forms], [the aforementioned fault would remain].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that a person possessing earrings (kuṇḍalin) would be perceived as "possessing earrings" even when the earrings are absent.

Furthermore, if one accepts a difference in the qualified based on the difference in the qualifiers, how could there be "qualified non-duality" (viśiṣṭādvaita) regarding the Supreme Self, which is qualified by infinite individual souls?

Furthermore, a relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) must be stated, because it is impossible for that which is unrelated to function as a qualifier. First, there is no relation of inherence (*samavāya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because they are separately established (*yutasiddha*). Nor is there a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), because such a relation consists of two distinct essential natures.

Because the relation consists of its relata, it is impossible for the relation and the relata to be one and the same. Furthermore, if a relation consisting of two essential natures (*svarūpa*) were to reside in itself, it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); for it is impossible for the two essential natures to reside in themselves, nor is it possible for them to reside in something else. Therefore, [there is no such relation] between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*).
