It is not a relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), nor is it a relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sambandha*). For if one were to admit a conjunction that pervades the whole, there would follow the consequence of non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) due to their becoming identical;

furthermore, since both are partless, a non-pervasive conjunction is impossible. If, in that case, one were to admit spatial divisions based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the following would apply:]
Furthermore, because even the connection with one limiting adjunct would require a further connection with another limiting adjunct, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Moreover, if one were to admit the existence of both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absence within the same locus delimited by "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), it would follow that the contradiction between existence and non-existence has been cast aside, and it would result in the conjunction being proven illusory (*mithyātva*). Therefore, regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme [Self]...
Since no relation can be established— given that neither the relation of qualifier and qualified nor the relation of impeller and impelled is possible—

the consequence of a non-duality (*advaita*) consisting of the Supreme as qualified by the individual soul (*jīva*) simply does not arise. Therefore, it is established that only the qualified non-duality (*viśeṣādvaita*), which is proven by all the Śruti texts, bestows liberation free from rebirth.
However, some say that in the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," the term "tail" means like a tail—

that is, the support or ultimate resort, the substratum of all worldly bliss. This is because, in the statement "That is one bliss of Brahman," the bliss of Brahman alone is designated as being superior to all others on the royal road.
There is no contradiction with my own established doctrine, which maintains the position of qualified non-duality (*viśeṣādvaita*).
Thus ends the section concerning the "Consisting of Bliss" (*ānandamayādhikaraṇa*).
Now begins the determination of the sixfold marks, the section on the intermediate [state]. (7)

Having established the nature of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) of Śiva— the Supreme Brahman— who is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, who is delimited by the sixfold attributes such as omniscience, who is all-pervasive, and who, like the wind, possesses both form and formlessness; [the author proceeds] for the sake of delivering all devotees, [describing] Him who dwells in the Great Kailāsa that transcends the entire cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

He begins another section of the work to establish that Sadāśiva— who possesses a non-material, divine, auspicious form consisting of the five Upaniṣads and who is surrounded by his devotees— is the primary body of the golden one:
now follows the demonstration that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is of the nature of the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga).
The one within [is Brahman], because of the teaching of its attributes. (Sūtra 21)
The subject of this is seen in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:

"Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun, with a golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his fingernails; just as the lotus flower is like the seat of a monkey, so are his eyes; from him rises [the sound] 'ud'."

He indeed rises above all evils; for he who knows this rises above all evils. Both the Ṛk and the Sāman are his joints (*geṣṇau*); therefore he is called the *Udgītha*, and for that very reason he is the singer (*udgātṛ*), for he is their singer.
He rules over those worlds that are beyond that [sun] and over the desires of the gods. This is with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*). Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).
Now, as for this person who is seen within the eye—that indeed is the Ṛg, that is the Sāman, that is the Yajus, that is the Brahman.

Its form is the same as the form of that [other person]; its two joints are the two joints of that; its name is the name of that. Here a doubt arises: [is this] an excellence attained through the preeminence of knowledge and the excellence of ritual action?
Is this a particular deity, or Nārāyaṇa, or Paraśiva himself?

As for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): the Person designated as the object of all worship within the solar orb and in the eye is not Maheśvara. Why? Because of the scriptural statement of his having a body, beginning with "having golden hair" (*hiraṇyaśmaśru*).
I am without hands or feet, yet possessed of inconceivable power;

I see without eyes and hear without ears. Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable, I am all-pervading like space and full. I am space, wind, light, water, and earth—the sustainer of the universe.

In hundreds of such scriptural passages, the negation of the Supreme Lord Śiva’s being a self-abiding substratum or possessing parts is observed; for instance, because of the teaching that he resides within the sun and within the eye in the texts "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye," it is more appropriate to understand these as referring to another deity. If one were to accept that the Supreme Lord possesses form for the sake of the meditation of his devotees—
The experience of suffering is designated as being like that of a living soul due to its possessing a body according to its own will.
Furthermore, the Person who is to be meditated upon in the solar orb and in the eye is indeed Nārāyaṇa;
for attributes such as having lotus-like eyes and possessing two eyes are appropriate only for him. In the Sāṅkhya-smṛti...
Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lotus throne, situated in the center of the solar disc, always to be meditated upon—
wearing armlets, makara-earrings, and a diadem.
He is golden-hued, possessing a body made of gold, and bearing the conch and the discus.
By such statements, the Blessed One, the great sage Kapila Ācārya, has designated attributes such as residing within the solar orb and being golden as belonging to Nārāyaṇa alone.
Furthermore, if [the passage] were intended to refer to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), the use of the dual number in the word "eyes" (*akṣiṇī*) would be contradicted.

Moreover, since his eyes are described as being like a lotus with petals like a monkey's buttocks (*kapyāsa-puṇḍarīka*), which implies a resemblance to a lotus comparable to the low seat of a monkey, it follows that this passage cannot in any way refer to the Supreme Lord; to this we reply:

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: "Because of the teaching of His attributes within" (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*). The Person heard of as being "within" the sun and "within" the eye—namely, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye"—is indeed Paraśiva himself. Why? Because of the teaching of His attributes; for those attributes belonging to that Great Lord (*maheśvara*) which are taught here [in other passages] are present in this statement.

Because of the instruction. For example, in the passage: "His name is 'Ud'—he has risen above all evils; indeed, he who knows thus rises above all evils," having first shown that "his name is Ud," one hears of his attributes as being free from all blemish; therefore, it is that very [Self] which is meant.

It also provides the etymological explanation for the Person in the Eye. Furthermore, in passages such as "The Self which is free from evil," the state of being devoid of all blemish is heard to belong to the Supreme Lord alone.

Likewise, in the statement regarding the Person in the Eye—"That is indeed the Ṛg, that is the Sāman, that is the Yajus, that is the Brahman"—it designates Him alone as having the nature of the Ṛg, Sāman, and so forth.

Furthermore, in such passages as, "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded," many attributes exclusive to the Supreme Lord are specified.

For the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees, there is no possibility of even a trace of suffering for Śiva— the all-pervading Supreme Brahman— despite his possessing a divine, auspicious form characterized by attributes such as golden hair and beard; for he consists of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which transcends the three guṇas and is dominated by pure sattva.

Furthermore, since those possessing the power to arrest water or fire are not seen to possess the power to obstruct [the Lord], what more need be said regarding the Supreme Lord, who is endowed with all powers and has brought the power of *māyā* under His control?
Therefore, even while in connection with a body, the Blessed Śruti itself establishes His freedom from all sins.

It is not possible for Nārāyaṇa to exist within the eye of the sun (Prabhākara), because the sun is well-known from the Śrutis and Smṛtis as being the primary body of Śiva, who possesses eight forms (Aṣṭamūrti). As stated in the Rudrādhyāya: "He who glides along, blue-necked and crimson; the cowherds have seen him, and the water-carriers have seen him," and so forth. Who... [is he]?
Becoming the intensely red Rudra, who dwells within the solar orb, he descends; that is, he proceeds to accomplish [his function] at both sunrise and sunset.
There, those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas worship the Puruṣa-Rudra manifested therein. And so says the Smṛti:
"He who resides in the center of the solar orb, accompanied by Ambā, is the medicine for the cycle of worldly existence."
I bow to Śiva, the imperishable one, who has a blue neck and deformed eyes.
The sun is the primary body of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
therefore, the yogi should always meditate upon Sadāśiva within it.
The yogi should meditate incessantly upon Sāmba, who wears the crescent moon, whose eyes are like the sun, and whose pair of lotus-eyes are in full bloom.

Since such passages in the *Gautama*, *Bṛhat-Śātātapa*, and other texts specify that the Supreme Lord alone resides within the solar orb, it is not logical to interpret them as referring to anything else.
Furthermore, in the *Jñānayoga-khaṇḍa* of the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, the venerable Vyāsa states:
The supremacy of the Supreme Lord has been clearly stated.
Having personally understood this meaning of the Vedas, one should declare it;
one should expand upon the meaning of the Vedas by means of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas.
This is because such Smṛtis establish the prohibition against one knowing the meaning of the Veda by oneself.
Alternatively: "In the midst of the sky, within the blazing, most beautiful, full solar orb renowned for its hundred thousand yojanas..."
The Lord, the creator of all the worlds, whose form is like gold,
with golden beard and hair, and likewise with golden nails.
His eye is like that of a monkey and other such beings; he has a blue neck and three eyes;
from the cowherd boy up to the most renowned sages, he possesses half the body of Ambikā.
With such reverence, the yogi should meditate upon Maheśvara as being none other than himself.
Thus it is stated in the Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
[He is] situated in the center of the solar orb, beloved of Viṣṇu, immutable,
with vital seed drawn up, three-eyed, and the cause of all causes.
He whose beard and hair are golden, who is endowed with golden nails,
and who thoroughly drinks up the water (ka) with his rays is Prabhākara.
That which is indicated by the word "kapi" by those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāntas is declared by ultimate yogis to be "āsaṃvikasana" (the blossoming of existence).

Therefore, for the sake of protecting the universe of both conscious and unconscious beings, he manifested out of compassion like the interior of a lotus, beautified by the pair of eyes that are like blossoming forest flowers.
The yogi should meditate upon Mahādeva, the omnipresent Lord who wields the trident, whose excellent eye of fire is closed like a bud, and who is the cause of the world's birth and other states.

Because, by such statements as these, it is shown that Śiva alone resides within the solar orb; and because, in the statement of the venerable Nīlakaṇṭha Bhagavatpāda—"The lotus is like the sun; thus are the two eyes"—the two eyes of that Supreme Lord, consisting of the sun and the moon, are seen to be both expanded and closed for the sake of favoring the world.

The "third eye" has been explained as follows: *kaṃ* means water; that which drinks [water] with its rays is *kapi*, meaning the sun. By that [sun], it is *āsam*, meaning *āsitaṃ*, which signifies "blossomed. Just as a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) shines, so too does [the eye] of Maheśvara.

There are two eyes. However, the third eye does not have the nature of being closed like a blossomed white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), but rather is like a closed white lotus; with this intention, the dual number in the word *akṣiṇī* (the two eyes) does not imply the absence of a third eye. [For example,] when addressing a Brahmin who has three sons, one says "two... [sons].

When it is said, "He has two sons who are like fire," the mention of the number "two sons" is not intended to exclude other sons, but rather to emphasize the similarity of those two sons to fire; this should be understood in many such instances in common worldly usage. Furthermore, because the unique attributes of Paramaśiva, such as being golden and so forth, are impossible in the case of Nārāyaṇa.

If it is argued that, according to the principle "in cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the passage" (*sandigdheṣu vākyaśeṣāt*), the remainder of the passage is accepted here because the subject of the sūtra is doubtful—[we reply: in the *Mahopaniṣad*, it is clearly stated in the explanatory sentence, "This sun indeed shines as this orb," that having pointed out the orb of the light-maker (the sun), [it refers to] "he who is in this... [and so forth].

Having taught the radiance of the solar orb with the words, "In the orb, the light shines," and having pointed out the maker of light who presides over that orb with the words, "The person who is in this light of the orb," and having further indicated the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) with the words, "This golden person within the sun," [the text continues] with "The sun is indeed splendor, vigor, strength, and fame," and so forth.

Having described the majesty of that Prabhākara and having designated him as the Lord of Beings with the words, "He who is this Person, he is the sovereign lord of beings," then, in response to the inquiry "What kind of Person is he?", [the text says]: "Obeisance to the one with golden arms, to the golden-colored, to the golden-formed, to the Lord of Gold, to the Lord of Ambikā, to the Lord of Umā."
"Salutation again and again to Paśupati"—thus [the hymn] concludes.

In the Śatarudrīya, attributes such as being golden-hued, being the commander of the army, and so forth—as established by scriptural texts such as "Salutation to the golden-hued one, to the commander of the army"—are not found in any other [deity]. Therefore, [this hymn] establishes that [Lord Śiva] alone is the Supreme Brahman.

Because we observe such usage in the world as "a woman with lotus-eyes" (*kamalalocanā nārī*) and "a man with lotus-eyes" (*kamalākṣaḥ puruṣaḥ*), it follows by the maxim that when there is a mutual contradiction between a general gender and a specific gender, the interpretation must be determined according to the specific gender; and because a Smṛti that contradicts Śruti lacks authority.

Furthermore, because the Sāṅkhya tradition has been refuted by the venerable Vyāsa in the section on "The Non-occurrence of Smṛti" (*Smṛty-anavakāśa-adhikaraṇa*) due to its non-Vedic nature, it is established that the golden person who is the object of meditation in this Udgītha-vidyā is none other than Paramaśiva.
Those who, abandoning Mṛtyuñjaya, worship another deity...
Having entered the mouth of death, they are born again and again.
Even poor food is called a meal of milk-rice for one who has not seen the feet of Śiva; likewise, that supreme state of Viṣṇu is so called by one who has not seen the feet of Śiva.

Since the worship of deities other than Śiva is explicitly rejected in such Smṛtis, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that Śiva alone is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation, directly present at all times in locations such as the solar orb and the eyes.
Furthermore, in such Śrutis as "This Āditya is Brahman," even the Maker of Light [is identified as Brahman].
In response to the doubt that the golden person within the sun—who is taught to possess the nature of Brahman—is indeed the sun itself, [the Sūtra] says:
"And because of the declaration of difference, he is another. (2.1.22)
The person who is heard within the eye of the sun (*prabhākara-cakṣus*) is indeed distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) that identifies with the body of the sun.

Why? Because of the designation of difference. This is because in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, there is a designation of difference between the sun and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). [This distinction applies] to all living beings, such as Āditya, Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, and others, who are souls bound by the fetters of *paśu* and *pāśa*.

The status of being the Supreme Brahman is not tenable [for others]. By such passages as, "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," it is Paramaśiva alone who is designated here as the Inner Controller of all. He who dwells in the earth...

"He who dwells within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within; he who, dwelling in water, is within water, whom water does not know, whose body is water, who controls water from within"— and so forth.

The state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the eightfold form consisting of earth and the rest, and the nature of possessing those eight forms, belong to Him alone and not to others, because such a thing is impossible for them. Furthermore: "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is no other whatsoever distinct from me. He entered into the space within the space; He entered into the space within the quarters; He is I.

In the Atharvaṇa Śruti, through such passages as "I am the eternal and the non-eternal, the manifest and the unmanifest, I am Brahmā and non-Brahmā, I am the eastern and the western," the fact that Rudra, the Supreme Brahman, is the self of all—including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kāla, Rudra, and others—and is the inner controller of all, is firmly established; for it says: "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the herbs, Rudra who is in all..."

And because there is such designation in passages such as, "He entered the worlds; let there be obeisance to that Rudra," and because the characteristic marks (liṅgas) such as immortality (amṛtatva), which are unique to Paramaśiva, are not shared by any other, [it is said in the Jābāla Upaniṣad], which is intended to praise the Śatarudrīya: "These indeed are the names of the Immortal."
Thus, because the term "immortal state" (*amṛtapada*) is designated as referring to Śiva, it is established that the Person within the eye and the sun is indeed Paramaśiva himself.
Scriptural passages such as "That sun is Brahman" are merely figurative, similar to the statement "Food is Brahman," which refers to the sacrificial vessel.

In common worldly usage, there is no fault [in such expressions], because words denoting the body convey the meaning of the embodied being. This is evident from such scriptural passages as: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. Thus, in these and other texts, it is shown that the sun and other luminaries [shine] by the light of the Supreme Lord.

The state of being manifest has been clearly stated. In passages such as "From fear of Him the wind blows," we observe that the wind, the sun, fire, Indra, death, and so forth, engage in their respective functions out of fear of the command of the Supreme Lord; therefore, the inherent Brahman-nature of the sun and other individual souls (*jīvas*) is not being taught here.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the *Subālopaniṣad*, beginning with "He whose body is the self, whose body is water, whose body is the unmanifest," and continuing with "This is the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God,
Nārāyaṇa," establishes that Nārāyaṇa is the self of all.

Since terms such as Rudreśvara, Maheśvara, Parameśvara, Śiva, and so forth are appropriately explained only as referring to Nārāyaṇa, and because the Nārāyaṇa-upaniṣad designates him alone as the supreme cause, no other being possesses the status of the Supreme Brahman. If it is argued that this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), like saying "Yajñadatta was born" or "the pot was destroyed," we say no.

Because, by virtue of context and other factors, they possess a different meaning. If it is argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the word "body" (*śarīra*) regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that words denoting a body denote the possessor of the body, [we reply] that this is not so, because the term is qualified as being other than a derivative word (*niṣkarṣaka*). Furthermore, [this applies to] words denoting attributes inseparably connected (*ayutasiddha*), such as "the white cloth" or "the blue lotus."
If it is argued that, because the primary meaning is understood within the context of the words, Brahman— which reveals the unmanifest— is denotable by all words;

and that since Brahman is the material cause of the entire world of sentient and insentient beings, it is denotable by all words, just as the earth, which is the material cause of jars and other things, is denoted by words such as "jar"— then [we reply]:

To this we reply: Is the intended pervasion (vyāpti) a specific one—that whatever is conventionally designated as denoting a body is a denoter of a body—or is it a general one? Not the first, because of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the word "body" (śarīra) itself.
Nor should the qualification "provided it is not a derivative term other than [the primary] word" be added; for [the status of being] "other than a derivative term" [is problematic].

Because it is impossible to state [what that difference is]. Is it (1) being different from that which denotes a specific [quality], or (2) being different from that which denotes a body, or (3) denoting a qualifier alone? Not the first, because even the word "body" denotes a body qualified by "bodiness. Not the second, because [such a thing] is unestablished; for even in your own view, the word "body" [denotes a body qualified by bodiness].
Because [the term "body"] denotes the Lord who is the denotable object of all words. For this very reason, the third alternative is not tenable:

since the word *śarīra* (body) also denotes a body qualified by "bodiness" (*śarīratva*), it is impossible for it to denote the qualifier alone; thus, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was. Nor is there a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) such that "whatever denotes a body at the time of conjunction does not denote a non-body."

Regarding the pervasion [of the term "body"], since the word "body" does not apply to jars and the like—following the definition of a body stated in the Nyāya-śāstra as "that which possesses the movement of the final parts of the body and serves as the substratum for experience and the sense organs"—the status of being the Lord's body is not established. Nor should it be asserted that being a body consists merely in being subject to control; for if that were so, the word "servant," which denotes one who is controlled by his master, would [inappropriately] apply to the master as well.

Because there is a deviation [from the rule] due to the absence of the capacity to denote a master (*svāmin*). Nor can being "governed by one who has entered within" be the definition of being a body (*śarīratva*), because there is a deviation in the case of a wooden statue or similar objects governed by a craftsman who has entered within. Nor can "inseparability" (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) be added as a qualification of the governor, because the word "within" (*antaḥ*) would then be redundant. And it should not be argued that this much alone is sufficient as a proof.
Because there is a deviation [in the inference] with respect to words such as "hand," which denote hands and the like that are governed by Devadatta who is not established separately;

nor is being a word for a mode (*prakāra*) that is not established separately [a valid reason], because there is a deviation in the case of words such as "color" (*rūpa*), since they lack denotative power over pots and the like.
By this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that words denoting modes not established separately denote the substratum of those modes (*prakārī*)—is refuted.

Because it is impossible to define "being a mode" (*prakāratva*), because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of words denoting properties such as "pot," and because the previously mentioned defect would recur even if "not being a non-expressive word" (*aniṣkarṣapadatva*) were added here as a qualification.
[Objection: But since words such as "pot" constitute the subject (*pakṣa*) and words such as "god" or "human" constitute the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)...

If it is argued: "How can there be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti) when 'denoting a body' is the probandum, since even words such as 'body' are equivalent to the subject (pakṣa) because they denote Īśvara"?—it is not so; for the cognition of deviation acts as an obstacle specifically with respect to the apprehension of the pervasion itself.

Otherwise, if it were established that being an effect entails being produced by a body, then once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped in the case of a jar or similar objects, the fact of being produced by a body would also be proven for a sprout and the like. This is because the locus of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), such as a sprout, would be treated as equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus a supersensible body could be postulated [as its cause]. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all fallacious reasons based on deviation.

If the term "body" (*śarīra*) were included in the pervasion (*vyāpti*), it would be redundant within the pervaded portion (*vyāpya-bhāga*), resulting in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the probans (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). Furthermore, since all terms denote the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*), there is no locus of deviation (*vyabhicāra-sthala*); thus, by this very fact, the inclusion of the term "body" would be irrelevant for the purpose of excluding such cases. This remains true even if terms such as "earth" (*pṛthivī*) and so forth were to denote a body.

Because there is no subverting argument against the contrary position (vipakṣabādhaka) regarding the view that [the term] extends only as far as the embodied soul; nor does the impossibility of primary denotation in the case of Brahman serve as such a subverting argument. For even if one were to postulate a separate independent power—as is done in the case of words like "cow" which have multiple meanings—the primary denotation remains possible, and thus the establishment of a qualified power [of the word] is not achieved. Nor is this an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti).
Because it would result in a deviation from your own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Furthermore: just as you, who maintain that words possess the power to denote mere objects (*padārtha*), have abandoned the idea of a word's power residing in the object as qualified by its relation to an action (*kāryānvita*)—even though you had previously accepted it at the time of linguistic usage—once you realized that such a meaning could be obtained through other means; so too [is the case here]. Even though it was accepted by you...
The specific power of all words to denote the Self as qualified by the body must be abandoned because it is cumbersome and because it is not otherwise obtainable;

otherwise, even the power [of words] to denote that which is connected with an action would not be abandoned. Furthermore, just as it is postulated that words denoting the body extend up to the embodied one (the Self), why is it not likewise postulated that words denoting the embodied one also denote the body?

It is postulated [that Viṣṇu is denoted by all words] because he is seen to exist in such a manner within the states of gods, humans, and so forth; for the result—namely, the establishment of primary grammatical coreferentiality (*mukhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—is the same in all non-dualistic statements.

If it is objected: "But is it not heard in the Purāṇas that Viṣṇu is the denotable object of all words? We say no, because of the scriptural statement: "From whence words turn back... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4).

Furthermore, since even the exclusion of expressibility (*vācyatva*) in Brahman is established by direct scriptural testimony (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), it should be understood that by these very same arguments, the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— that words denoting attributes extend as far as the substratum of those attributes— is refuted. Moreover, in the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*, the statement "whose body is the self" (*yasyātmā śarīram*) does not enjoin [the self] as being a body.

According to the maxim that "the connection with the word *yat* (that which), being first mentioned, and so forth, is the characteristic of the subject (*uddeśya*), while the word *tat* (that) and the particle *eva* (only/itself) are the characteristics of the predicate (*upādeya*)," the power of the injunction is obstructed. Nor is it the case that [the sentence] "That which is dedicated to Agni is the eight-potherd [cake]"...

Thus, its status as an injunction is appropriate because its purpose is to convey what is already known from common worldly experience, and because there is no other thing to be enjoined. In this case, however, since the injunctive portion—

"This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal"— is present, both parts [of the sentence] would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) if they were to enjoin multiple objects in their own presentation, due to the connection with the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning redundancy (*jāmitā*).

Just as "He performs the *upāṃśuyāja* between [the two offerings]" functions as an injunction, so too, because of its connection with the explanatory passage (arthavāda)— "If you, O Yājñavalkya, do not know this Sūtra and that Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*),
and yet drive away the Brahman-cows, your head shall fall off"—
the state of being the Inner Controller is something to be known and thus an object of injunction. And so, it is obtained from another source.

The state of being a body (*śarīratva*) is what is being restated (*anuvādya*); however, that [state] is not well-known in common worldly usage, because the status of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) is absent in the case of earth and other such elements.

Rather, it is merely the state of being controlled (*niyamyatvamātra*). And that has been stated to be insubstantial because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāritva*). In reality, however, the injunction regarding the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmitva*) in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa pertains only to Śiva, who is denoted by the term "Immortal" (*amṛta*), and not to anything else.

It was stated previously [that this belongs] to Viṣṇu. However, because the word *amṛta* is determined to denote Rudra by the Jābāla statement concerning the Śatarudrīya—namely, "These indeed are the names of the Immortal"—and because the passage begins with, "Tell me what one should recite to attain immortality; Yājñavalkya replied: 'By the Śatarudrīya,'" [the former interpretation prevails].
If it is argued that the statement "He is the inner self of all beings" prescribes the status of inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) for Viṣṇu alone, we say no;

for by such passages as "He entered into what is within the interior" and "He who is Rudra in the fire," it is established that Rudra alone is the supreme Brahman as the inner ruler. This is because he is corroborated by many Vedic scriptures, and because even Viṣṇu has Rudra as his body. Thus:
For the exponents of Brahman say: "That which one does not offer to a deity is the Vasordhārā. Agni is a Vasu; this is his stream.
Viṣṇu is a Vasu; this is his stream. With a verse addressed to Agni and Viṣṇu, he offers the Vasordhārā; verily, by means of their respective portions, he satisfies these two.
He thereby supports this very oblation, making it possessed of a foundation; whatever desire he has when he offers it, that he secures and attains.

Agni, indeed, is Rudra; he has two bodies: one is terrible, the other is auspicious. When he offers the Śatarudrīya, he pacifies with it that body of his which is terrible; when he offers the Vasordhārā, [he pacifies] that body of his which is auspicious.
"He gratifies that body with that [offering]"—so it is heard in the *Yajussaṃhitā*. Therein, he supports [the argument] by means of the word "gratification.

In this regard, since Agni and Viṣṇu do not possess a portion of Rudra’s body, how can Rudra’s body be gratified by an offering of the *vasudhārā* intended for both deities? This is because it would involve the contradiction of employing what has already been employed elsewhere (*viniyuktaviniyoga-virodha*). As it is said in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*:
"O Brahman, your fierce form consists of water and the moon;
O Brahman, your auspicious forms consist of the sun, Viṣṇu, and the sacrificial fire. Thus [it is said].
In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "The Lord, the Supreme Master, accompanied by Umā," it continues: "He alone is Viṣṇu, together with Prāṇa..."
"Time, fire, and that moon—he alone is everything, whatever has been and whatever is to be, the eternal"; by this [passage], the fact that Śiva alone is the self of all is established.
"The universe, the past, the world, the manifold, that which has been born in many ways and that which is being born—all this is indeed he."
It is also clearly stated in other scriptural passages such as, "Rudra, let there be homage to that Rudra.

Now, if it is argued that the body of Śiva (śivātanūḥ) is distinct from Agni and Viṣṇu because of the difference in names established by worldly usage through the use of different words, we say: not so; for [the word] śivā [is used] together with those two.
If it is accepted that the body is distinct [from Rudra], how can the gratification of Rudra’s body be established through the offering of the *vasudhārā*?

This is because it would involve the contradiction of employing what has already been employed (*viniyukta-viniyoga-virodha*), because the mantra would have no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*), because it would contradict the indicative power of the mantra (*mantra-liṅga-virodha*), and because it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
If, however, non-difference is accepted, there is no fault whatsoever. Otherwise, [as in the case where] one pours curds into heated milk, that...

Just as there is a distinction between rituals due to the quality of the substance—such as in the case of "The *āmikṣā* belongs to the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* belongs to the Vājins"—there would also follow a distinction between rituals due to the quality of the deity, and thus even a distinction between the *vasudhārā-homa* [offerings] would result. This is because the unseen merit (*apūrva*) arises from the result, and since both the substance and the deity are equally integral to the essential nature of the ritual. Indeed, this Agni is Rudra.
Although such passages as these are *arthavādas* concerning the *vasudhārā* [rain of wealth], according to the principle of the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇanyāya*),

since there is an absence of both corroboration by other means of knowledge and contradiction thereof, it is accepted that *mantras* and *arthavādas* possess authority regarding their own literal meaning; for otherwise, one would have to abandon the fact that they refer to extremely transcendent objects, and a praise without a basis would be impossible.

It is established that because the praise of Agni and Viṣṇu occurs precisely through their being the bodies of the most excellent Rudra, the praise of the offering of the stream of wealth (vasudhārā-huti) occurs by means of them. Furthermore, even Viṣṇu has the nature of being the body of Rudra;
this is stated in the *Īśvaragītā* within the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"For he who is Nārāyaṇa, the infinite, the imperishable Lord of the worlds—
he is this supreme form of mine that performs the task of protection.
And in that very same place, there is the speech of Viṣṇu:
"And know me, O Grandfather, as that other eternal form of his, the source of the universe, designated by the name Vāsudeva.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is not denotable by all words. And thus is the formal argument: all those things under dispute...
Those words denote Viṣṇu, because they are distinct from that which is delimited by the property of being words denoting Viṣṇu as established for both parties,
like a jar. Nor is this argument unproven (aprayojakatva), because if all words were denoters of Viṣṇu, it would follow that all words are synonyms.
Nor can there be non-synonymy based on a distinction of specific capacities, because it has already been stated that such specific capacities are impossible;
therefore, enough with this excessive detail. Consequently, the state of being within the eye and the sun is not possible for any other [deity].
Thus ends the seventh section, the *Antaradhikaraṇa*.
Now follows the demonstration that Paramaśiva consists of the *prasādaliṅga*.

Thus, having raised the objection that there might be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the term "Brahman" to other things due to its association with names, forms, and so forth, he states the section on Ākāśa (the Ether). 8.
It is space, because of its characteristic mark. (Sūtra 23)
The subject matter of this [passage] is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said;
"For indeed, all these beings arise from space alone, they merge back into space;
for space is greater than these, space is the ultimate resort. Here, by the word "space" (ākāśa), the elemental space (bhūtākāśa) is meant.

It is doubted whether Paramaśiva is intended [to be denoted]. Why? Because both are indicated by the scripture (*śruti*). Nevertheless, since the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) has a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*)—both in common worldly usage and in the Vedas—just like the word "lotus" (*paṅkaja*), there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) for it to refer exclusively to Paramaśiva. [Therefore,] in abandoning the primary meaning...

Furthermore, this would result in a contradiction with the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning "seeing"), and there is a lack of evidence [for such a claim]. This is because in passages such as "From space, air [arises]," space alone is designated as the cause of the universe; and because in passages such as "Space is Brahman," "The Self is space," and "If that space were not bliss," space itself is taught to be Brahman; and [because of the scriptural statement] beginning with, "From which indeed these beings are born."

The status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, as prescribed by the Śruti, is understood to belong to Ākāśa alone; for this is clearly stated in such passages as, "All these beings, indeed,
arise from Ākāśa alone," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "In the beginning, this was the Self alone."

Since the status of being denoted by the term "Sat" (Being) and "Ātman" (Self), as established by such scriptural passages [as *satyam jñānam anantam brahma*], belongs to that alone, the statement in passages such as "from the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ sambhūtaḥ*) that space is born from the Self is merely figurative. By the etymological derivation "it pervades (*āpnoti*), therefore it is the Self (*ātman*)," its denotability by the word "Ātman" is beyond dispute. Therefore, space alone is the supreme cause of all.
When the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that [the term] refers to Brahman, we reply:

"It is Ākāśa, because of its characteristic marks. Here, Ākāśa is directly identified as Śiva himself, because of his characteristic marks—that is, because of the characteristic mark of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe; the meaning is that it is not the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
Therefore, because of the designation of its being produced by the Supreme Lord in such passages as, "From this very Self, space was produced," [it follows that] space—
[as described in] "Space, wind, light, water, and earth, the supporter of the universe; that which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the abode of the universe"— [is indeed the Supreme].

Because of the description of the Supreme Śiva as the Self as being distinct from the five great elements through such statements as, "There is no earth for me, nor water, nor fire, nor wind, nor space," and because conscious attributes—such as being the cause of the universe preceded by the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*)—are impossible in the insentient elemental ether (*ākāśa*), [the Supreme Self is not the ether]. This is also evident from the scriptural passage beginning with, "From ether, air... and so forth.
It is heard in scripture that the causal state of Paraśiva, whose nature consists of the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna, has entered into that [Ākāśa].
Furthermore, by the statement: "Indeed, all these beings arise from Ākāśa alone," [this is established].
By the phrase "they merge into space as its instrumental cause" (*nimittakāraṇatvaṃ ākāśaṃ pratyastaṃ yanti*), its status as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇatva*) is also expressed.

Therefore, since the marks of the Supreme Lord—consisting of being the dual cause (instrumental and material) of the universe—cannot possibly exist in the insentient elemental ether, [the passage] in the Śruti: "Greater than the earth, greater than the atmosphere, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds... [is intended to refer to the Supreme Lord].

Because the Supreme Brahman Śiva is designated as the cause of all and the ultimate resort through His independence from anything else, there are signs such as His "truthful resolve" found in the opening passages: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; It thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and 'He desired, "May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so forth.
Because the connection [of the term "ether"] with the elemental ether is impossible, it is established that Supreme Śiva alone is denoted by the word "ether.
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the ether (*ākāśādhikaraṇa*). Now follows the determination of Śiva’s nature as the mobile *liṅga*.
Now begins the section concerning Prāṇa (the vital breath). 9.
Now, one might object: "Since there is a contradiction between the opening and the conclusion regarding the ether being the Supreme Brahman, let the ether not be Brahman;
however, because the vital breath (prāṇa) is designated as the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, let it be Brahman. To this doubt, he says:
"For this very reason, the vital breath [is not Brahman]. (Sūtra 24)

In the *Chāndogya*, the subject matter is recited as follows: having introduced the topic with "O Prastotṛ, that deity which is inherent in the Prastāva—what is that deity?", he replied, "It is Prāṇa. For indeed, all these beings merge into Prāṇa alone and emerge from Prāṇa; this is the deity inherent in the Prastāva. Regarding that...

"If you, being ignorant, should sing [the Udgītha], your head shall fall off. Here, there arises a doubt as to whether the word *prāṇa* mentioned in the teaching on the Udgītha refers to the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) or to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), because characteristics of both are perceived.
[For example: "The mind, O gentle one, is fastened to *prāṇa*; *prāṇa* is the life-force of *prāṇa*"; and "Indeed, all these beings..."
"They enter into breath alone; they emerge from breath alone. For indeed, from breath these beings are born; once born, they live by breath; at death, they enter into breath. "Homage to you, O Vāyu!
You alone are the perceptible Brahman. One should desire to know him. One should know the speaker: it is breath alone that is the conscious self (*prajñātman*) within this body.

"He grasps it and causes it to rise up. Indeed, when a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath (prāṇa), the eye merges into the vital breath, the ear merges into the vital breath, and the mind merges into the vital breath. When he awakens, the living being is born again from the vital breath itself.
By hundreds of such direct scriptural statements, it is established that the elemental vital breath alone is the cause of all things.

If it is argued that because the Prāṇa is established as being supreme in hundreds of Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, and because we observe the term "Prāṇa" used there to refer to the elemental air, it follows that this very [air] is the Supreme Brahman itself—
then it is replied: here, by the word "Prāṇa," Paraśiva alone, who consists of six planes (ṣaṭsthala), is designated.
As before, here too, because of the observation of an abundance of *paramaśiva-liṅgas*,
the state of being the object of the actions of the dissolution and emergence of beings as delimited by the attributes of *paramaśiva* is seen in the remainder of the passage:
"When a person sleeps, then speech merges into breath," and so on.

In the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), which is devoid of all activity, although the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) persists, because the activity of the person (puruṣa) has ceased, it is in no way possible for the insentient prāṇa to exercise control over all the senses during the waking state or to enter into the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra) during deep sleep; therefore, regarding the word "prāṇa"...

The supremacy of Paramaśiva is beyond dispute. Likewise, in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad—beginning with "The Lord, the Supreme Master, accompanied by Umā," and continuing with "He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, He is Fire, He is the Moon," and so forth—the very nature of Paramaśiva as the Self of all is indicated; therefore, by the word *prāṇa* here, no other [deity] is denoted.
Thus ends the ninth section concerning the vital breath (prāṇa). Now begins the tenth section concerning light (jyotis), which establishes that the Supreme Śiva is of the nature of the Śivaliṅga.

Having established that Paraśiva-Brahman is of the nature of the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*) by virtue of being the innermost Self of all— through the sūtra *antastaddharmopadeśāt* (I.1.20)— and having pointed out that He is the Grace-Liṅga (*prasāda-liṅga*) by virtue of being within the ether— through the sūtra *ākāśastalliṅgāt* (I.1.22)— the sūtra *atha eva prāṇaḥ* (I.1.23) [establishes] that very same [Brahman] as having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its primordial material cause.
Having taught the nature of the *caraliṅga*, he then demonstrates, by means of three sūtras, the *śivaliṅga*, the *guruliṅga*, and the *ācāraliṅga*:
"Because of the mention of the feet in the light [passage]. (Sūtra 25)

The subject matter of this [passage] is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest worlds—that indeed is this very light which is within this person. Here, by the word "light" (jyotis), another deity such as Vaiśvānara, Sūrya, Candra, or others [is not meant].

The doubt arises as to whether that which is being described is the light itself, or the Supreme Lord who illumines the manifold world of sentient and insentient beings, both gross and subtle, beginning with the Sun (Prabhākara). This is because there are numerous marks (liṅgas) supporting both interpretations.

Nevertheless, it is more appropriate for the Sun, the Moon, and other luminaries to possess the quality of being "light" (jyotiṣṭva), since we observe that the light of the Sun and others serves to dispel darkness.

Likewise, it shines by the word "light" (*jyotis*), because of the designation of light as consisting of radiance, splendor, and so forth. It is not possible for the Supreme Brahman—which is devoid of distinctions and consists of the *śivaliṅga*—to shine in a primary sense, since the celestial limits (*dyumaryādā*) mentioned in the Śruti are established only for those [entities]. This is because [the Supreme Brahman] is the Self of all and the substratum of all.
Since there is no contradiction with the limit of heaven (*dyumaryādā*) in every respect for the cause of all things, what was stated previously alone is consistent.

Now, one might object: because of the designation of the "Supreme Light" in the passage, "The light beyond heaven shines," and because created lights do not possess such a nature, it is Brahman alone—by virtue of its omnipresence—who possesses the limit of heaven.

If it is argued that [the term "light"] is designated thus because of its propriety and because it serves the purpose of the devotee's meditation, and not because it refers to the triply-transformed light (*trivṛtkṛta-jyotis*),
we say no; for in such scriptural passages as "Agni is the first among the deities" and "That sun is Brahman," [it is used in this sense].

Because it is observed that the meditation on Vaiśvānara and other lights serves a specific purpose, and because the Śruti states, "Let me make each of these threefold," thus showing that the light of the *trivṛt* is indivisible, it exists within the space of the world. Since that alone is primary, it does not have any other meaning. It is the light of Vaiśvānara and the rest that shines everywhere.

The two divine sounds (*paradivyaśabda*) are taught for the purpose of meditation by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Therefore, there is no contradiction with the internal distinctions. For it is impossible to conceive of a distinction of being "only a span in size" (*prādeśamātra*) regarding the Supreme Brahman, which is Śiva, the Linga, and the substrate of all. [This is stated in the passage: "In the worlds beyond all, unsurpassed and supreme."

The mention of the "light" (jyotis) in passages such as "Vaiśvānara," which refers to the fire in the form of an effect, indicates that it has the Supreme Self as its ultimate referent, even though there is no scriptural mention of specific locations.

Now, one might object: since in the passage, "This indeed is that light which is within this person (puruṣa)," the gastric light is taught to be the supreme light and the Supreme Self, the word "light" (jyotis) here too must refer to the Supreme Self.

If this is argued, we say no; for here only similarity (*sārūpya*) is taught. Furthermore, as in the Śruti passage: "His head is *bhūḥ*, for the head is one, and this syllable is one," the fact that the gastric fire (*kaukṣeya-tejas*) refers to elemental fire (*prākṛta-tejas*) is beyond dispute, because it is taught there as having parts (*sāvayavatva*). This is its vision: "wherein this [light] is in this body..."

One perceives heat through touch; this is its scriptural description: when one covers the ears and hears, as it were, a roar, as it were, the sound of a blazing fire. One should meditate upon this as "that which is seen and heard. He who knows this becomes beautiful to look at and famous. Thus [ends the section on] heat and sound.

Because it is impossible for attributes such as seeing and hearing to belong to Paramaśiva; or else, in the passage "the light beyond heaven," that which is indicated as residing within the person might be the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni). In any case, the position of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is not established.

If this is argued, it is replied here: by the mention of "light," it is precisely the Brahman of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*), whose nature is the Śiva-liṅga, that is designated by the word "light. Why? Because of the mention of "feet" (*caraṇa*); the meaning is, because of the mention of "quarters" (*pāda*). [As stated in the scripture: "Such is His greatness; greater than this is He."

In the preceding statement, "The Puruṣa; one foot of His is all beings; three feet of His are the immortal in heaven," by the phrase "one foot of His is all beings," the manifested glory consisting of the entire universe is designated as a single portion of the Light that is Paramaśiva. By the phrase "three feet of Him are the immortal in heaven,"...

In the phrase "of the four-footed," the immortal three-footed state—characterized by its connection to the celestial realm (*dyus*), consisting of eternal sovereignty, and representing the causal manifestation (*kāraṇa-vibhūti*)—is indicated. This is because the word *dyu* denotes the ether (*ākāśa*);
thus, although it is possible for the sun and other luminaries to exist within the ether—as in the scriptural passage, "The light beyond the heaven"—[the term here refers to the Supreme].

Since it is impossible for anything else to possess unsurpassed luminosity, and because accepting such a thing would entail the faults of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing an irrelevant topic, the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to Brahman alone.
"The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Him alone..."

"Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined. "In the supreme golden sheath, there is the stainless, partless Brahman, pure, the light of lights—that which the knowers of the Self know. "The gods worship Him, the light of lights, as the immortal life-force. By hundreds of such scriptural passages, [it is established that] this belongs to Paramaśiva alone.
Because it establishes the state of being the supreme light. Furthermore, in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the nature of the supreme light is taught as belonging to the Supreme Lord alone;
for although the quality of being bounded by heaven might be possible in the case of an effected light, this passage occurs within a context concerning Brahman.
It is in no way possible for the effects of light—such as the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and the sun—to possess a connection with all heavens and to be the innermost self of all.
[Objection: But surely, according to the Śruti text, "By that splendor kindled, the sun shines," it is only the perceptible light grasped by the eye [that is meant].

If it is argued that the word "light" (jyotis) is understood here [from the previous context], we say no; for there is no such determining factor (vinigamaka). This is because this term is seen used elsewhere as well—for instance, in passages such as "he sits by the light" (vācaivāyaṃ jyotiṣāste) and "may the mind enjoy the light" (mano jyotirjuṣatām)—where it does not refer to that which illuminates the gross and subtle expansion of the sentient and insentient (cid-acit-prapañca). That [which is meant here] is the illuminator of the gross and subtle world of the sentient and the insentient.

It is understood through the analogy of light. Even for the partless Supreme Brahman, meditation upon it as having parts within regions such as the heart for the sake of the devotee’s worship is not contradictory; for both aspects of Brahman are its own inherent nature, as seen in the scriptural statement: "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman."

Furthermore, having shown the heart-lotus with the words "the stainless, pure lotus of the heart," and so forth, [the text continues] up to: "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil, the sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness."

Since the meditation on the Supreme Lord as possessing parts is taught as a means for attaining the partless witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), the practice of meditating upon the light prescribed in the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad as a symbol is likewise not contradictory. This is because, while the digestive fire, the sun,
and so forth are not seen to possess four feet, all the attributes mentioned in the scripture are possible when the reference is to the Supreme Lord.
The fact that the word *jyotis* (light) refers to that [Supreme Reality] is beyond dispute.
Now follows the determination of Śiva’s nature as both Guru and Liṅga:
in the Śruti passage, "Gāyatrī indeed is all this," the deity Gāyatrī is shown to be the self of all and to possess four feet.

Anticipating the objection that "it is precisely that [the eye] which is designated here by the word 'light' because of its connection," he says: "If it be argued that it is not so because of the mention of the meters, we say no; for there is a scriptural teaching regarding the fixing of the mind in that way, and there is indeed a corresponding vision. (2.3.26)
Having established the Supreme Brahman known as the Śiva-liṅga by means of the word *jyotis* in the preceding sūtra,

[the author] now teaches the Guru-liṅga through the Gāyatrī mantra, which consists of the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of Paramaśiva. Beginning with the Gāyatrī in the passage, "The Gāyatrī is indeed all this," he [identifies] that very [Gāyatrī] with the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, and so forth.
This very point has been stated in the Ṛgveda verse beginning with "Tāvānasya mahimā" (Such is His greatness),

which, after pointing out attributes such as its being the self of all, establishes the word "Brahman" for that which is designated by the term "Chandas" (the Veda) with the words "Yadvai tadbrahma. Therefore, it is the Supreme Śiva mentioned in the preceding Sūtra who is designated here, and no other.

*Tena*—thus, because of the teaching regarding the fixing of the mind (*ceto'rpaṇa*), that is, because of the statement concerning the concentration of the mind, it is not merely the *gāyatrī* meter that is taught here by the word "Gāyatrī. Since it is impossible for a mere metrical *gāyatrī* to be the self of all, it is the Supreme Śiva alone who is taught here as the Gāyatrī upon whom the mind is fixed. [This refers to] Brahman.

The meaning is that the contemplation of the similarity between Paraśiva and the Gāyatrī is taught for the sake of attaining the fruit [of liberation]. And such a similarity is possible, for the four-footed Brahman—expressed in the text, "One foot of him are all beings; three feet of him are the immortal in heaven"—shares its fourfold nature with the four-footed Gāyatrī. Furthermore, the Gāyatrī is seen to be four-footed in certain instances.

The meaning is as follows: "For such is the observation," because in other places—both external and internal, in locations such as the young lotus, the sun, and the eye—the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman is observed through the form of a *liṅga* (symbol) consisting of parts, and in the form of atoms and so forth; thus, "observation" means that it is seen. [In the case of] *kaivalya*:

Beginning with the passage, "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure," and having established the lotus of the heart as the abode of the Supreme Self through such statements as, "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil, the sage goes [to Him]," [the text describes] the Supreme Lord.
It has been established that form consisting of parts is the object of meditation for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). In the Yajurvedic branch,

beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Nidhana" and ending with "This is the purifier, the mantra for the hand, the universal mark (*sarvaliṅga*) of Soma and Sūrya," [the text] describes the *liṅga* as being identical in nature to the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, the Śruti, at every step, establishes [this truth] preceded by salutations in order to manifest that [Śiva] is to be worshipped by all.
Therefore, the worship of the Śivaliṅga must necessarily be performed even by Vedic Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.
"Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being; one beholds Him who is free from desire."

By the passage, "The realm free from sorrow, through serene faith, [one attains] the Greatness, the Lord," it is seen in many other places that meditation upon the Supreme Lord in His atomic (subtle) form is also taught. Therefore, in the Śruti text, "Gāyatrī indeed is all this," it is not the Gāyatrī limited merely by syllables that is taught as being the Self of all, but rather...
Brahman alone, which is the cause of the universe delimited by the Gāyatrī, is designated here as "all this.
Now follows the determination of the Gāyatrī’s nature as consisting of Guru and Liṅga.
But [an objection may be raised]:
We worship that most excellent *bhargas* of the divine Savitṛ, which impels our thoughts toward the sphere of Dharma and its purpose.
If it is argued that since this [verse] is seen in the *Smṛti* to refer to the Sun, how can it be said to refer to Śiva? We say no;

for the word *bharga* is conventionally established (*rūḍhi*) in the sense of Śiva by virtue of the *Nighaṇṭu*, and because the status of being the deity Sūrya and others in the phrase "the desirable [light] of Savitṛ" is not intended as its primary meaning, given that [verses] such as "Agni as a messenger" and "To which Rudra?"—as stated by Baudhāyana in the context of the *Grahayajña*—are what is intended to be expressed.

Because the word *vareṇya* (excellent), being relational, requires a correlate, it generates a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the proximate word *savitṛ* (the progenitor). Likewise, because the word *yat* (which) is a qualifying term, it requires a substantive that shares its gender, case-ending, and number; and since the word *bharga* possesses those same characteristics, [it fulfills this requirement].

Because it is suitable as being connected with that [word *bharga*]. In this regard, since the connection of the sentence "We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of Savitṛ" is possible— wherein "that which is the splendor (*bharga*) of the neuter [Savitṛ]" would impel the intellects toward objects such as Dharma— it follows otherwise that the word *yat* (which) would lack syntactic connection without the supply of a substantive, and the supply of words is a secondary (inferior) method for this mantra.

If the reference were to the splendor of the sun (*sūryatejas*), it would lack the status of being the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); furthermore, if the word "most excellent" (*vareṇya*) were taken to denote the splendor of Brahman, it would contradict the genitive form of the word *savitṛ*. If one intends to express the state of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*), the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is already accounted for; thus, since there is no distinctness [between the two], even the genitive of relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) cannot be applied.

The word *savitṛ* in the locative case is not intended [here], but rather the term for Śiva, who is its presiding deity (*adhideva*), because He alone is the impeller of primordial wisdom (*anādiprajñā*). As it is stated in the *Mantropaniṣad*: "When there was neither darkness nor day, neither night nor what exists nor what does not exist—Śiva alone was the sole one; that is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent of Savitṛ, and that is wisdom."

"Therefore, from Him the ancient [path] has issued forth. And in the Gītā: "I take refuge in that very same primordial Puruṣa, from whom the ancient activity has issued forth. As for the meaning of the words in the Smṛti: [the name] Savitṛ is derived from the root *pūñ*, meaning "to bring forth," thus He is the progenitor of all living beings; and because He "shines" (*divyati*), He is called Deva.

Because He shatters all sins, Bharga is Hara; may He impel our *dhiyaḥ*—our intellects—toward their objects, such as Dharma and the like. Of that Bharga, the *vareṇyam* (most excellent) nature is superior to the universe, golden in form, as stated in the Śruti: "This golden person who is within the sun," and "He who moves about, blue-necked and deep red."
"We worship [the Lord] as qualified by [attributes] such as having a blue throat. This was stated by Vyāsa in the *Vyāsagītā* within the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"I take refuge in that supreme reality, the auspicious Savitṛ who is most excellent;
I take refuge in you, O Virūpākṣa, whose very nature is the worlds Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ."

Nor is there the fault of abandoning the conventional meaning of the word *savitṛ*; for, compared to abandoning the conventional meaning of a mantra-word, the abandonment of the conventional meaning of a word in a Smṛti statement is more commendable. This is because, in that [Smṛti] view, it has already been stated that the conventional meaning of the word *savitṛ* found in the mantra would result in the impossibility of its being a knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Furthermore, the word *vareṇya*, which possesses a relational referent, would have its intended meaning disregarded.
The single defect here is that [the interpretation] is the same for both Śruti and Smṛti.
Regarding this, some provide the following word-arrangement (*padayojanā*) for the words contained in the Gāyatrī mantra:
"That *bhargas*—the Supreme Śiva—who is in the midst of the shining *deva*, the Sun (*savitṛ*), may he [illuminate] our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*)."

May [the Sun] impel—urge forward—the intellects whose objects are Dharma and so forth; that is to say, may he impel the most excellent (*vareṇya*), the one worthy of being chosen, the one worthy of worship. "We meditate upon (*dhīmahi*) Brahman"—this is the syntactical connection to be understood here. In this context, the intermediate word "in the midst" (*madhye*) must be supplied after "of Savitṛ," because such is seen in another Vedic text: "He who is within the sun, golden..."
"A person is seen," and so forth.

Others explain that even for the Prābhākara, there is the view of being a worshipper of Śiva in this mantra: "That Bharga, who is Paramaśiva, may he impel (prerayati) our intellects (dhiyaḥ)—the faculties of understanding whose objects are dharma and so forth. That [is the meaning].

That is the meaning; there is no fault here because it is Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). We meditate upon—that is, we contemplate—the most excellent (*vareṇya*), that which is worthy of being chosen or worshipped, of Savitṛ, the Sun; [namely] Paramaśiva. Who is self-possessed? One who has conquered anger. Who is radiant? One who is free from malice.
Of whom, when his wrath is aroused in battle, do even the gods stand in fear?
"I wish to hear this" (*etadicchāmyahaṃ śrotum*)—

since such a transposition of gender is observed in works such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* (1.4), what need is there to mention that transpositions of gender, voice, and so forth are permissible in the Veda, which is regarded as the word of the Lord?

Others, disregarding the maxim that "conventional usage (rūḍhi) sets aside etymological derivation (yoga)," rely on an etymological derivation whose power is unimpeded by conventional usage— like a word that is mute— and describe the term *bharga*, which is conventionally established as referring to Śiva, as applying to the non-Śiva, the Aparameśvara, just as words such as *gopa* or *paṅkaja* can denote a donkey or moss respectively. Otherwise...
Because if one were to assume a different meaning, it would result in a contrary fruit for the meditation on the *gāyatrī*.
Furthermore, there would be the risk of a failure in the accent, as in the case of [the story]: "Indra’s enemy [was killed] due to a mistake regarding the accent.
This has been stated by Haradattācārya, the author of the Vedāntabhāṣya on the four Vedas:
"O sinless one, if your primordial supreme splendor were indeed the stainless state of Śrīkaṇṭha and Bharga, it would certainly be acutely accented (ādyudātta);
therefore, by virtue of the lexicon stating that words ending in 'da' [denote the sun], I understand that he is none other than Śiva himself, situated within the orb of the sun. Thus.
O Śrīkaṇṭha! If even your primordial, sinless (anagha), and supreme Bharga-pada (the state of Bharga) were to become [merely] "tejas" (light/heat), then—

given that the mantra "bhargo devasya" and so forth is established as having an udātta accent on "bharga"— there would certainly arise a violation of the perceived phonetic sequence (*śrūyamāṇa-svara-bhaṅga*), because while the syllable is inherently udātta due to its being a *preraka* (impelling force), the vowel following the letter *ga* would be heard as *anudātta* according to the rules of residual accentuation (*śiṣṭa-svara*).

If the word *bharga* ends in the vowel *a*, then when the vowel following the letter *bha* is *anudātta*, it becomes *anudātta* by the rule of the remaining accent (*śiṣṭasvara*); subsequently, when an *udātta* is followed by an *anudātta*, the resulting audible tone is *svarita*. Therefore, [the word] ends in *a*. For this reason—namely, because of the cause of its being *udātta*—I understand from the authority of the lexicon (*kośa*) and the science of semantics (*abhidhānaśāstra*) that it ends in *a*.
Therefore, Śiva alone is the one situated within the orb of the sun.

Furthermore, in the Maitrāyaṇīya recension: "We meditate upon the splendor (bhargas) of the god; Savitṛ is indeed the god—I contemplate him whose name is Splendor. Likewise: "O Rudra, those who discourse on Brahman call this [deity] by the name of Splendor."

In another Śruti passage as well, having introduced the question, "Who is Savitṛ? What is Gāyatrī?", it is understood that even here, the very first foot [of the mantra] consists of *bhūḥ*, the second foot consists of *bhuvaḥ*, and the third foot consists of *svar*; thus, it is the *adanta* (ending in 'a') alone that is taught.
Therefore, the notion that "the god Savitṛ is our [father]" is contrary to all perceptible Śrutis. As for the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, however—

Even though it refers primarily to the sun, there is no fault, as it denotes Paraśiva in its primary sense. Nevertheless, because it is a Smṛti text of the Sāṃkhya school, it is to be accepted only by the Tantrikas.
Furthermore, in such contexts as "Bharga of the god, to the Śikhā for Rudra-soul, Vaṣaṭ," and so forth.
The state of being supreme to Paraśiva has been clearly stated; indeed— as water that has fallen from the sky goes to the ocean— so it is.
The salutation of all the gods goes toward Keśava.

If it is argued that because Nārāyaṇa is seen to be the sovereign lord of all deities in such passages as these, he alone is the referent of the word *bharga*, we say no; for in the *Pañcaśīrṣopaniṣad*, there is an application (*viniyoga*) [of this mantra] to the initiation (*upanayana*) characterized by the five heads—
that is, to the Three-eyed Supreme Śiva, in whom [the mantra] is led upward— and because such an application is observed at the beginning of that [text].

This is because it is established as being dedicated to that [deity] with the words "for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvaraprītyartham*). Furthermore, since the power whose essence is Gāyatrī is non-different from the power of Paramaśiva, the attributes of the Supreme Lord abound herein.

The one denoted by the word *bharga* is none other [than the Supreme Lord]. Furthermore, the Smṛti text stating that "the salutation of all the gods goes toward Keśava" is not to be accepted, because it is recited within the section concerning Sāṃkhya Smṛti;
for it has been refuted by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Smṛtyanavakāśa* (Non-occasion for Smṛti) Adhikaraṇa.
The gravity of the meaning is appropriate according to the specific application (*viniyoga*). If it were intended for another deity different from that [Gāyatrī], [the mantra would be]:

"Endowed with three eyes whose radiance is white like pearls, crystal, sapphire, and gold; joined with a crescent moon; holding the *gāyatrī* [rosary], the boon-granting gesture, the fear-dispelling gesture, the goad, the whip, the radiant skull-bowl, the mace, and the conch..."
I worship her who bears a pair of great lotuses in the form of wheels with her hands.

Thus, the contradiction between the meditation on Gāyatrī and the [scriptural] statement regarding Śiva is difficult to avoid. If it is asked, "If Gāyatrī is denoted by the word *bhargas*, how is her status as Sāvitrī well-known?"—the fact that even the maker of light (the sun) possesses the nature of Śiva has already been stated previously through the use of the word *savitṛ* in such passages as "He who rises... Furthermore, [the hymn] begins: "Today, with homage, [I offer] a song of praise to you, Rudra, the protector of heroes..."

In the Vedic revelation of the Sāmaveda, because the salutation and hymn to all the deities in the *vidhiṣṭanā* [mantra] are designated as referring to Paraśiva, and because in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad* it is taught that He alone is the Self of all— stating "He is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa"—
Nārāyaṇa does not possess lordship over the salutation; otherwise, there would be the contingency of contradicting the Śruti.

Because the Vedic injunction (*śrautavidhi*) is more authoritative, the sovereignty over the wealth entrusted to ministers and others in the world belongs to Śiva alone without obstruction. Regarding the application (*viniyoga*) in the *upanayana* [initiation], some propose an alternative meaning, namely that "one leads (*nayati*)" means "one causes to reach (*prāpayati*). That is inconsistent, because in the preceding sentence there is the term "five-headed" (*pañcaśīrṣa*), and in the subsequent one, "for the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*."

Thus, because of the hearing of attributes not shared by any other [deity], the fact that the word *bharga* denotes Rudra and its ending in the letter *t* are established as being in accordance with the Śruti within the context of the Gāyatrī. Therefore, it is proven that the status of being the subject matter of the Gāyatrī and the connection with the celestial realm belong to him alone.
Now follows the determination of Śiva’s nature as the *ācāraliṅga*.

Having thus established that the Supreme Lord has the nature of the *guruliṅga* by virtue of being the subject matter of the Gāyatrī, he states his nature as the *ācāraliṅga* through another aphorism:
And because the designation of the quarters beginning with "the elements" (bhūta) is appropriate only in this way. 27.

In this context, it is Paraśiva himself—who is taught in the Gāyatrī mantra as having the nature of the Guru and the Liṅga—who is conventionally designated as the Ācāra-liṅga. Why? Because the designation of the quarters (pādas) beginning with "beings" (bhūta) is logically possible [only for him]. For such a designation of the quarters beginning with "beings" is not logically possible for the Gāyatrī, which consists merely of a sequence of syllables.

The Śruti text, "These are the five Brahma-puruṣas," is consistent with the preceding context of the Supreme Brahman, Śiva; for instance, as an ancillary to the meditation on Paraśiva, who is of the nature of Gāyatrī,
delimited by the lotus of the heart.

For the purpose of prescribing the meditative visualization (*vyūha*) of the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta, there is the scriptural passage: "Of this very heart, there are five openings for the gods," and so forth; therein it is heard: "These indeed are the five Brahma-puruṣas. Thus, the five Brahma-puruṣas, beginning with Sadyojāta, who are the limbs of the meditation, [are to be meditated upon] within the apertures of the small lotus (*dahara-puṇḍarīka*).

Because it is stated that those who abide [in these] possess the nature of the five Brahmans, their connection with the Supreme Brahman is understood even in the case of the small apertures (*daharacchidra*).
Beyond the arrays of the five Brahmans— Sadyojāta and the others— who preside over the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the five elements (*bhūta*), lies the Supreme Brahman.

He is called Paraśiva; he alone is the liberator from the bonds of the bound soul (paśu) and is to be worshipped by all. If [the text] were restricted solely to the Gāyatrī, then the contradiction regarding the five Brahma-puruṣas being of the nature of Brahman—which are its limbs—would be unavoidable.
Therefore, because of the connection with the five Brahmans within the cavities of the heart, those five Brahmans situated therein...
Due to the existence of the relationship with Paramaśiva, the scriptural mention of the five Brahma-puruṣas is justified.
Within the lotus of the heart reside the five Brahma-puruṣas, beginning with Sadyojāta, situated at the eastern, southern, western, northern, and upper faces.

Therefore, it is established that in the Gāyatrī passage, Brahman alone is what is being expounded; and in the Jyotis passage, because of its connection with the celestial realm (*dyu*), that very same [Brahman] is recognized. This is so because the designation of the elements and so forth as "feet"—that is, as constituent parts—is logically applicable to Brahman, and because it is indeed appropriate. Thus, by the word "Gāyatrī," that which is delimited by the Gāyatrī is [meant].
The meaning of the sūtra is that Brahman alone is being spoken of.

Now, one might object: even in the Puruṣasūkta, it is stated that Nārāyaṇa alone possesses the fourfold division of parts, beginning with "beings," in the verse, "All beings are one foot of him; his three feet are the immortal in heaven. Therefore, [the sūtra] should refer to him as well.

Because it illuminates His connection with the day, because the passage beginning with "I know this great Puruṣa" points to Him alone as being beyond darkness, and because passages such as "There is no other path for going" teach that knowledge of Him alone is the cause of liberation, it is logical that He alone is the intended referent.

[Objection: But since Rudra is also designated by the word "Puruṣa" in such passages as "Puruṣa indeed is Rudra," why should [the Puruṣa-sūkta] not have him as its referent? [Reply: No, because in the passage "Hrī and Lakṣmī are his two wives; day and night are his two sides," we observe the mark (liṅga) of being the husband of Lakṣmī, which is unique to [Viṣṇu] and not shared by others. In the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa, this is the [established] position.
"Accompanied by Viṣṇu, speaking poetic wisdom like Uśanas," and "This is the vow of the Puruṣa, the final one of Vārāha.
