This is indeed the Saṃhitā called Vaiṣṇavī; by employing this, one pleases Viṣṇu—thus, through the designation of it as the Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā, [it is used] on the occasion of assigning the respective deity-mantras among the eighteen great propitiatory rites (mahāśānti) of the Atharva-veda, specifically in the Vaiṣṇavī rite.

This is because the *Puruṣasūkta* is enjoined for the propitiation of Viṣṇu in the *Vaiṣṇava-śānti*, is enjoined in various ways for the worship of Nārāyaṇa in the *Smṛtis* of Śaunaka, Bodhāyana, and others, and is treated according to the method of explaining the meaning of the *Puruṣasūkta* in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts.

If it is argued that, by the observation of the hymn of praise to Nārāyaṇa, it is also logical that the *Chāndogya*, which elucidates its meaning, is likewise devoted to him alone— then, regarding the demonstration that the *Puruṣasūkta* is devoted to Śiva, it is said here: the *Puruṣasūkta* also [is devoted to Śiva] by means of the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya*), such as the introduction and conclusion.

It is indicated as being solely devoted to Śiva; for the word "Puruṣa" is established as referring to Śiva by hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "Rudra is indeed Puruṣa," "The Puruṣa who is dark and tawny," "I am the ancient Puruṣa," and "I am the Puruṣa, the Lord. Furthermore, the term "Īśāna" is conventionally used for Śiva. Moreover, regarding the status of Śiva and Keśava as Puruṣa and Prakṛti respectively—

In the *Sāmānyarudrasūkta*, established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and *Āgamas*, it is said that the single Śakti of the Supreme Lord became fourfold for the sake of specific purposes: "Bhavānī in [the matter of] enjoyment, Viṣṇu among men, Kālī in anger, and Durgā in battle. Thus, in the *Ādityapurāṇa*, these are the words of Śiva addressed to Viṣṇu.
"You are Prakṛti, O best of gods; I am Puruṣa, there is no doubt.
Everything consists of you and me, having the nature of the unmanifest Puruṣa.
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The one named Puruṣa is the eternal, complete embodiment of Sāmba."

"It is proclaimed in the Veda that Vāsudeva is the supreme power (parā-śakti). Thus it is stated in the Gītā: "Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti). And in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Prakṛti is Viṣṇu the Supreme; Puruṣa is Śiva the Supreme."

Furthermore, within the *Asurakāṇḍa* and other sections contained in the *Śivarahasyakhaṇḍa*, Nārāyaṇa’s female form, Śiva’s male form, and the origin of their respective teachers and creators of the worlds are elaborated upon in many ways.
Therefore, the word "Puruṣa" in the opening statement, "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," refers to Śiva. [This is established] by means of the sacrifice...

Even by the intermediate statement, "The gods performed the sacrifice," it is understood that the focus is precisely upon Him; for in the Śruti text, "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu," Nārāyaṇa is designated as being of the nature of sacrifice. [The phrase] "by means of sacrifice" refers to the instruments such as the sacrificial animal which are denoted by the word "sacrifice" and consist of Viṣṇu; and "sacrifice" refers to the worship of Paraśiva.

In the Vedic revelation, "The Hotṛ-priest of the sacrifice, the King, Rudra... the status of the Supreme Lord as the Master of Sacrifice is clearly demonstrated. In the Ṛgveda as well, it is explicitly stated through such passages as, "I praise Rudra, the Lord of songs, the Lord of the sacrifice, who possesses water and food. Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Those twice-born who perceive Mahāviṣṇu in the form of sacrifice within the sacrifice—
knowing that Mahādeva alone is primarily the God of Sacrifice and no other— they indeed attain true knowledge. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, among the eight forms (*mūrti*) of the Supreme Lord, the sacrificer (*yajvan*) is designated as one of His forms.
As stated in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"The sky, fire, earth, wind, moon, sun, and water..."
"And the initiated one—thus, O Lord of Gaurī, are your eight forms in sequence.
Furthermore, the status of being the performer of sacrifice, the enjoyer of sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, and so forth, belongs to Him alone;
for all Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra* are seen to have Rudra as their ultimate goal (*śeṣatva*), as He is the one of eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*).

Because the fire of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is a single limb [of His body], and because the Supreme Lord exists within the orb of fire as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*), no other [fire] can be the presiding lord over all rituals such as the *agnihotra*. As stated in the *Yajurveda*: "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies—one terrible and the other auspicious. And: "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants..."
And likewise in the Smṛti:
"One should meditate upon Rudra, surrounded by flames, situated in the midst of the circle of fire,
endowed with his ten digits (kalās), and bearing the Śakti and the Svastika."

Thus, because Rudra is seen to have fire as his essence and to be the inner controller within the circle of fire; furthermore, by the permission of Śiva, the gods perform the immolation of the sacrificial animal and consume only what remains after Śiva, using the sacrificial materials such as the *puroḍāśa* cake. Likewise, in the Yajurveda: "O Lord of Animals, this animal is for you today..."

"I bind [thee] at the beginning of the well-performed rite, in the midst of it; grant thy approval for the excellent sacrifice; may we sacrifice; may this oblation be acceptable to the gods. This is because it is remembered many times in such passages as "This Soma belongs to the one with matted hair" (*ayaṃ somaḥ kapardinaḥ*). Furthermore, in the first mantra of the Sāmaveda, beginning with "Austerity is thine and muttering is thine," it refers to the Lord of Action (*karmādhipataye*).

At the conclusion of the word "namas," having established that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*) of all Vedic rituals by means of the mantra "virūpākṣo 'si," and having offered praise, [one says]: "I take refuge in you; I shall perform this work woven together by you; may it be successful for that purpose; may it be accomplished from that. Thus, because all Vedic rituals are to be performed with the permission of Rudra...
From the hearing of the injunctions, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is the primary deity of all Vedic rites such as sacrifices and the like.
Furthermore, in another Śruti it is said: "O Rudra, this dog is your animal; enjoy it; O Rudra, this is your portion."
The meaning of the phrase "by Svasrāmbikā" is as follows: *Ākhu* means one who digs everywhere;
it refers to Viṣṇu in the form of the Great Boar (*mahāvarāha*). O Rudra, that [Viṣṇu] became your sacrificial animal (*paśu*) in the form of a boar.
That animal was [consumed] by *Svasrā*—by *Ambikā*, Pārvatī—who is co-naturally established as the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvābhāva-sahaja-siddhānuṣyūtā*).
"Enjoy together"—that is, partake. "To you"—the meaning is that this is your sacrificial portion (*yāgabhāga*). Likewise, in the *Vṛddha-Śātātapa*:
[He saw] the Great-Souled One, the destroyer of Hiraṇyākṣa, in the form of a mouse.
I [saw] him in the form of the sacrificial animal, that very Yajñavarāha.
O Lord of Gods, Viśvanātha, Sadāśiva, together with Pārvatī,
please graciously accept Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.

Thus from the Śramaṇa. This very same repetition is found in the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "They sprinkled that sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass; the Puruṣa born in the beginning—by him the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis sacrificed. Its meaning is as follows:

they sprinkled the "sacrifice"—Viṣṇu, who consists of the essence of the sacrifice—upon the "sacrificial grass," that is, at the *savana* (pressing), for the purpose of immolation (*ālambhana*), pouring [the water] over him at the beginning.

—The gods, beginning with Brahmā, the Sādhyas, and the ṛṣis, sacrificed to the Puruṣa who existed prior to creation, using Rudra as the sacrificial animal (paśu); the meaning is that they sacrifice [to him] even now. As stated in the Skānda Purāṇa: "I myself sacrificed to that very Puruṣa, the Lord, by means of that very sacrifice. Likewise, in the second book of the Bhāgavata:

It has been taught in that very manner; for this reason, He is well-known in the world as Ādivarāha (the Primeval Boar). The phrase "of solar hue, beyond darkness" expresses His unprecedented nature. That He is of solar hue means He is golden; this golden nature was clearly stated in the *Antaradhikaraṇa*. Furthermore, in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "accompanied by Umā" and ending with "beyond darkness," it refers to Him alone.

Since the state of being beyond darkness (*tamaḥparatva*) is intended to be expressed, the fruit of the knowledge of Him is taught in the statement: "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here. In this context, the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) is designated as referring to Paraśiva in the *Jābāla* and other Upaniṣads.
Therefore, by the principle of the uniformity of the goal (*gatisāmānya*), it is established through the sixfold marks that the *Puruṣasūkta* has Paraśiva alone as its ultimate referent.
This is to be known.

Furthermore, it is fitting that Śiva, who is the self of all, possesses a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, and a thousand arms. [As stated: "To the one with a thousand eyes, the bountiful one; thousands [of forms] in a thousand ways [arise] from your two arms."
By the Rudra-hymn beginning with "The weapons," the possession of a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, and so forth, is attributed specifically to Rudra.

Now, one might object: since the Śruti states, "Prajāpati moves within the womb," Nārāyaṇa alone is designated as the progenitor of Brahmā; and since it is said, "One should seek liberation from Janārdana," he alone is the bestower of liberation.
If it is argued that Śiva cannot be the subject of the *Puruṣasūkta* because [the hymn] is appropriate [for Viṣṇu], we say no;

for even in other Vedic texts such as, "Rudra, the great seer, who is superior to the universe, generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning," it is Śiva alone who is designated as the primary progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha. Furthermore, in the *Atharvaśikhā*, it is stated that Śiva is one...
"One should meditate upon Him who brings about auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else"—thus, "bringing about auspiciousness" means precisely the bestowing of liberation (*mukti*).

And that belongs to Him alone and not to another, because [any other] is inauspicious (*aśiva*). Then, without knowing Śiva, there will be no end to suffering; but by meditating, the sage goes to the Source of Beings, the Witness of all, who is beyond darkness; having known Him, he transcends death.

"There is no other path to liberation. Having perceived that Lord, the adorable Puruṣa, the deliverer, one attains ultimate peace. "The wise who perceive Him abiding within themselves—for them there is eternal peace, and not for others. Since such scriptural passages establish that Śiva alone is the bestower of liberation, [it is said]: "For the sake of the sacrifice, let there be a way; for the sake of the lord of the sacrifice, let there be a way."
Since it is withdrawn into Paramaśiva, the Lord of Sacrifice, it is understood that the Puruṣasūkta is declared to be Śiva’s own:
"A Vedic scholar who has mastered the Vedas, wearing the horizontal triple-tilaka, should constantly mutter the Rudra and the Puruṣasūkta for the sake of pleasing Rudra."
Thus, because it is recited together with the Rudrasūkta.
Now, [one might object]: in the statement "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," there is the concluding mention of a unique characteristic, namely, being the husband of Lakṣmī.
If it is argued that, by virtue of this observation, the word *puruṣa* occurring in the introductory sentence must also refer exclusively to Viṣṇu, we say no;

for its usage is justified through its general denotative power (*sāmānya-śakti*) alone. Furthermore, the status of being the husband of Gaṅgā and the husband of Pārvatī—established by the two statements "Hrī and Lakṣmī are his two wives" and "Day and Night are his two sides"—is appropriate for Śiva alone. As it has been said:
In the Skanda Purāṇa: As the Gaṅgā fell from Rudra’s head with great force onto the summit of the Himālaya, Sadāśiva, overwhelmed by her weight, spoke to her.

"Be modest; having found me here, do not behave with excessive pride toward this man, the best of men, the source of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the rest. Having bowed to that Mahādeva, she thereafter remained devoted to him with piety.
"Because she is united with the matted locks (*jaṭā*) through modesty (*hrī*), she is called *Hrī* by the wise. Thus it is said. In the Rudrayāmala:
"The supreme power *Māheśvarī* is seated upon the circle of her lap."
From that spark of splendor, Mahālakṣmī— renowned as Śyāmā and enchanting to all— was born in ancient times, along with millions of Lakṣmīs and Vāks.
The millions of deities, beginning with Hari and Brahmā, have arisen from the splendor of Śiva.
"Furthermore, those who are always devoted to that [place] are indeed liberated from these [sins]. Thus it is said.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "By the word *hrī*, there is the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of all sins."
Lakṣmī is renowned as Gaurī; she is Mahālakṣmī, the Great Sovereign.
And the status of Śiva, the Supreme Self, as the Lord of the Fortune of the Gaṅgā is well-known throughout the three worlds as a common attribute, as enjoined by the Vedas.

"Therefore, his right side attains equality with the day, while his left side is always the Goddess; thus it attains similarity with the night for Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Hrī and the river Bhramarā are both wives of Śiva’s Dharma;
and Gaṅgā is the daughter of the Mountain, the Himālaya."
"Even by those scriptures capable of establishing the status of Gaṅgā as the Lord's wife, through such titles as 'the Lord of the two mothers' (dvaimātura) and so forth.
Now, if it is argued that in the Vājasaneyaka it is recited: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are His two wives"—what of it?

This is because the word *śrī* also ultimately resolves into being the *hṛllekhā*, which is recited in the same context; nor can the reverse be maintained, for the word *hrī* is never seen to be used for Kamalā (Lakṣmī), whereas the word *śrī* is used for Lakṣmī in the *Āyuṣyasūkta*:
"They call me Śrī, Lakṣmī, Umā, Ambikā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Jayā, and Indrasenā."

Because the application of the mantra "hrīśca te" has been observed in the case of Gaurī, and because its employment in the worship of Gaurī— who is studied in the Sāmaveda and other branches— during the *grahayajña* sacrifice is stated in the *Mṛtparṇavā* and other texts, it is certain that the word "hrīḥ" refers to Gaurī. Therefore, in accordance with what was heard first, the phrase "Lakṣmī and [the others] are the wives" [is interpreted accordingly].

"Seated upon his lap is the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara, known as Mahālakṣmī, dark-hued and enchanting to all. Thus, it is precisely this supremacy of Lakṣmī, who is Ambikā seated on Śiva’s lap as stated in the *Śivapurāṇa*, that is intended.
Even though this hymn is employed in the worship of Nārāyaṇa and so forth by virtue of its being devoted to him, there is no contradiction whatsoever in its being devoted to Śiva.

This is because, by the force of the direct scriptural statements (*abhidhāna-śruti*) in mantras such as "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord," it is universally accepted that these mantras—which actually refer to deities like Agni—are employed during the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) for the worship of those specific planetary deities; they are employed at the time of offering worship to Mars and the others, and are frequently employed for recitation (*japa*) and other rites intended to please them. Otherwise—
One should worship the giver of wealth, who possesses universal forms, with the Puruṣasūkta;
or else, a devoted person should worship him with the two Nārāyaṇa hymns.
Since in such passages the status of being "either one" (anyataratva) is established even through other applications (*viniyoga*), the *Liṅgapurāṇa* also states:
"The sky is the head of that omnipresent Lord, the supreme abode (*parameṣṭhin*); the space is His navel;
the moon, sun, and fire are the eyes of the wielder of the Pināka bow; and the directions are His ears."
Then the Vedas were born from his mouth, and Vāyu was born from his breath;
indeed, the Brahman was born from his face, as was the Lord, the blessed Brahmā.
From the two arms of the Great-Souled Pinākin came Indra and Viṣṇu; from his thighs came the Kṣatriyas, from his thighs the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras.

Thus, because it has been explained by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa as being devoted to Śiva, likewise in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as well, its devotion to Him alone is determined due to the abundance of marks (liṅga) of the Supreme Lord. Now, [an objection may be raised]: "A quarter of Him consists of all beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven. In this regard—
In response to the objection— arising from the recognition of a connection with the sky in the passage "the light beyond the sky shines" (*paro divo jyotirdīpyate*)—
as to how both sentences can have the Supreme Lord as their subject given that the latter specifies being "beyond the sky," he says:
If it be argued that this is not so because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. || 28 ||

That which was previously indicated by the locative case in the mantra—"A quarter of Him is all beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven"—as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is further taught as being beyond the sky by the ablative case in the phrase, "The light that shines beyond this heaven. Moreover, in the sentence "the light that shines beyond this heaven,"...

If it is argued that the recognition of the Supreme Lord through the *jyotiḥ* passage is not possible because of the teaching of His being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the world and His being distinct from the world, we say no. Why? Because there is no contradiction in either case;
for even though both a change in grammatical case and a change in meaning are possible, there is no contradiction in the recognition of the Supreme Lord.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction between the preceding, following, middle, or subsequent parts [of the statements]. Just as in examples such as "the peacock on the top of the palace" (*saudhāgre mayūraḥ*) and "the peacock beyond the top of the palace" (*saudhāgrāt parato mayūraḥ*), by means of these two sentences, the very same "beyond-ness" (*paratva*) of the sky (*div*) is recognized; so it is here.
Furthermore, for that which is all-pervasive like space (*vyoman*), there is both a state of being distinct from the world and a state of being within the world.
This is possible only for the Supreme Lord: "The Self, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, is hidden in the cave of this creature;
He whose face, head, and neck are everywhere resides in the heart-cave of all beings."
That Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.

In passages such as "Space, wind, fire, water, and the earth that sustains the universe," the fact that Paraśiva is distinct from the world and yet is its inner controller (antaryāmin) has been clearly stated with a voice as resonant as a bell.
Therefore, the pervasive Paraśiva possesses the nature of the sixfold liṅgas, beginning with the Mahāliṅga and ending with the Ācāraliṅga.
It is appropriate for the worship of the devotee who possesses his final body.

Therefore, Paraśiva alone is the supreme light, self-luminous and independent of any other means of realization, which illuminates the entire expanse of the gross and subtle sentient and insentient universe as distinguished by His own unique portion.
Thus ends the tenth section, concerning Light.
Now begins the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which establishes that Śiva consists of the external, beloved *liṅga* of the vital breath. 11.

Having previously established that Śiva— the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, the subject of all Vedāntas, and whose nature is unsurpassed bliss— possesses the character of the sixfold *liṅga*, [the author] now, by means of another section (*adhikaraṇa*), establishes that very same Śiva possesses the character of the external *iṣṭa-liṅga* (worshipped *liṅga*) to be meditated upon by all seekers of liberation.
He shows this:
"The vital breath [is Brahman], because it follows [the same reasoning] in that way. (Sūtra 1.1.29)
The subject matter of this [passage] is heard in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, within the narrative of Indra and Pratardana:

"Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through battle and manliness"—thus it is recorded. In that [narrative], it is heard: "He said, 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātmā); him [know as such]...'"

"Meditate upon me as life, as immortality. Likewise, later on: "Now, indeed, it is breath alone, the conscious self, which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise up. Similarly: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker. And at the end: "This very breath is the conscious self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal. In this regard:

In the *Pratardana-vidyā*, a doubt arises as to whether the object of worship is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the embodied self denoted by the word "Indra," or indeed the Supreme Lord. Indra’s statement, "Know me alone," is a mark indicating his status as a deity and thus refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, [the text states], "Having taken hold of this body, he makes it rise."

Because of the unique characteristic of being the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it refers to the object that is the *prāṇa*; and because of the hearing of a multitude of attributes belonging to the supreme Śiva-liṅga, such as "bliss," "undecaying," and "immortal," it is indicated that this is indeed the external *iṣṭa*-liṅga presided over by a digit (*kalā*) of Supreme Śiva bestowed through the compassion of the Guru.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: Here, the Supreme Lord is not indicated in every respect. For there is the hearing of attributes peculiar to the elemental air—such as "I am the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the conscious self (*prajñātman*"; "as such, [know] me as life and immortality," and "the vital breath alone, as the conscious self, having grasped this body, causes it to rise"—and because in both common worldly usage and in the Vedas, [these terms refer to] the air situated within the body.

Because the state of being the vital breath (*prāṇatva*) is established as primary, the word *prāṇa* here denotes the vital air itself. Alternatively, since the word *indra* is well-known to refer specifically to the individual soul (*jīva*), the word *prāṇa*, which stands in grammatical apposition with it, is also applied to that very same entity; thus, by the word *prāṇa*, Indra himself is denoted here.

This living being (jīva) designated as Indra, having been told by Pratardana, "Choose for yourself that boon which you consider most beneficial for a human being," instructed him to meditate upon himself, saying, "Meditate on me," thus teaching that meditation upon one's own self is the most beneficial thing. Therefore, [it refers] to either the elemental vital breath (bhūta-prāṇa) or the living being (jīva).
If it be argued that [the object of meditation] in the Pratardana-vidyā is the vital breath (prāṇa), we reply: "The vital breath [is Śiva], because of the concordance [of the context].
Here, "vital breath" refers specifically to the external liṅga presided over by a digit (kalā) of Paramaśiva. Why? Because of the concordance [of the attributes] as in the case of the Jyotis-vākya.

Brahman alone is indicated; likewise, because the word "prāṇa" follows from and leads to the understanding that it has Paraśiva as its ultimate referent. This is evident from the opening statement, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self; meditate on me as life and immortality," and from the intermediate passage, "He who would know me—his world is not destroyed by any deed, neither by the killing of a mother nor by the killing of a father."

For, by such passages as "Neither by theft nor by killing," the destruction of all actions—both good and evil—is seen in the realization of Paramaśiva. Likewise, even in the concluding portion, qualities such as bliss are heard as indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the nature of Brahman-Paramaśiva, in the words "blissful, undecaying, immortal. Therefore, [this cannot refer to] the unconscious wind.

Since qualities such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are impossible [in the external vital breath], the term "prāṇa" here teaches only the external *prāṇa-liṅga*—the subtle body delimited by the gross body and presided over by a portion (*kalā*) of Paramaśiva;
it does not have as its referent the all-pervading, full Brahman. This is because the subsequent sentence states: "In this very body, prāṇa dwells."

It has such a lifespan because of its designation in grammatical apposition with the word "āyus" (lifespan). If it were restricted to being merely elemental air (*bhūtavāyu*), there would be a contradiction with the attributes established by the previously cited scripture—such as the destruction of all sins, bliss, immortality, and freedom from old age—for [the scripture] states: "He indeed causes him to perform good deeds whom He intends to lead forward; He indeed causes him to perform evil deeds whom He intends to lead astray."

Furthermore, because these attributes—established by such scriptural passages as "Him they seek to drive out from these worlds," "He is the guardian of the world, He is the lord of the world, He is the sovereign of all"—are possible only for Paramaśiva; and likewise in another Śruti:
"He who is the bull of the Vedas (Chandas), whose form is the universe, who arose from the nectar of the Vedas—he is Indra."

May [the Lord] protect me with wisdom; may I become a vessel for the immortality bestowed by the gods; may my body be most discerning, my tongue most sweet, and through my two ears may I hear much. You are the treasury of Brahman, covered by wisdom; protect what has been cooked for me. Thus, through the wearing of the supreme Śiva-liṅga whose essence is Indra, there is the direction toward liberation. May there be auspiciousness.
"O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.
With firm limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods"—thus, in the Śruti, [the term] "lifespan" refers to the duration until the end of the gross body.
Because of the designation of the installation of the *paramaśivaliṅga*, the word "prāṇa" refers directly and exclusively to the *paramaśivaliṅga*.

An objection may be raised: [Is this not like] in the Pratardana-vidyā, where, through grammatical coreferentiality with the word "Indra" in the statement "Know me alone," [the self is identified with Indra]?

If it is argued that because the attributes of the all-pervading Brahman—such as "bliss" and "undecaying"—are specified, the instruction is intended solely for a particular type of living being (*jīvaviśeṣa*), and therefore how can the mere mark of the vital breath (*prāṇaliṅga*) limited by the gross body be accepted? We say: no, because [the text] states, "Know Me alone," and so forth.

Indeed, it is the very body of Indra that is being taught; however, it is specifically the sign (liṅga) of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the locus for the soul (jīva), that is pointed out for the purpose of the devotee’s meditation. Through such statements as "He is the lord of the world, He is the protector of the world, He is the ruler of the world," the intent is directed toward the signs of His nature as the all-pervading cause of both the creation and destruction of the universe. "I am the Prāṇa, the self of wisdom (prajñātman)... [taṃ...]
By such passages as "Meditate on me as life, as immortality," it is determined that the external vital breath (*prāṇa*), which consists of the desired marks, is not the Self.

It is impossible in any way for Indra’s body, Indra’s vital breath, or Indra’s individual soul (*jīva*) to be the object of meditation for those seeking liberation, nor can they be the Supreme Brahman. And this has been clearly stated in the concluding sūtra of this section.
By Bādarāyaṇa.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:

"If it be argued that [Brahman is not taught here] because of the instruction concerning the Self of the speaker, [we reply] no, for there is an abundance of references to the connection with the inner self (adhyātma) in this [section]. (2.1.20)

"Know me alone; I am the vital breath (prāṇa), the self consisting of intelligence (prajñātman). Meditate upon me as life and immortality"—since at the beginning of this passage there is the manifestation of a specific characteristic of the individual soul (jīva), and since even in the conclusion—"blissful, undecaying, immortal"—the attributes such as bliss and so forth are appropriate to the individual soul.

If it is argued that because the opening and the conclusion possess a single characteristic—namely, that here Indra, the speaker, is taught as one's own self, and therefore Indra alone is denoted by the word "prāṇa"—we say:
no; why? Because in this [passage] there is an abundance of references to the connection with the inner self (adhyātma). For in this sentence...
The meaning is that there exists an abundance—that is, an abundance of the internal connection, which is the connection with Paramaśiva.

For instance, in the opening passage, "That which you consider most beneficial for humanity," and so forth, the teaching is given that the worship of Him alone is the "most beneficial" as the means to liberation; likewise, in other Śrutis, it is said: "Having known the Lord, they become immortal."

"Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace; Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else. By knowing Him alone, one transcends death; there is no other path for the journey. Since such passages teach that liberation is obtained through the worship of Paramaśiva, He is the object of worship for humanity as the most beneficial of all.

It is indeed a characteristic mark of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-liṅga). Even in the middle [of the passage], it is stated that "He alone causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from these worlds;

He alone causes him to perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward"—thus, the quality of being the instigator of all actions is heard as a characteristic mark of the Supreme Lord alone. And at the conclusion, it says: "Just as..."

Just as the rim is fixed upon the spokes of a chariot wheel and the spokes are fixed upon the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed upon the powers of consciousness (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the powers of consciousness are fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa).
This very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), which is blissful, undecaying, and immortal; thus the attributes of Supreme Śiva are established. This...

"He is the lord of the world, the sovereign of all"—thus it is Paramaśiva alone who is understood. Now, one might object: since it is taught that Indra possesses the nature of *prāṇa* (vital breath) through such statements as "He slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ," "Vital breath is indeed strength," and "Indra is the king who rules over the world," [is he not the subject here? [The answer is: No, because of his possession of power (*balavattvāt*). By means of rain...
Because it nourishes the proliferation of the conscious and the unconscious, that very [breath] is conventionally designated as "prāṇa.

Therefore, statements such as "being the most beneficial" and so forth should be construed as referring to that [breath]. Since it was said to Pratardana, "Know me alone," it might be suspected that what is being taught here is simply meditation upon oneself. To this doubt, he says:
But the instruction is based on the vision gained from the scriptures, as in the case of Vāmadeva. (Sūtra 31)

Indra instructed [Naciketas], "Know me alone as the Supreme Lord, who am denoted by all words because I am the self of all, according to the scriptural vision: 'Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms.
This is just as Vāmadeva [declared his] state of being the self of all through such statements as, "I was Manu and the Sun," and so forth.

The meaning is that he taught it to his own [disciples] in that same manner. Furthermore, in the Śruti passage, "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else," the absence of anything other than Śiva is observed for those devotees who have attained the state of Śiva through the worship of Śiva, just like the worm in the bee-hive. Therefore, in the Daṇḍaka forest, by the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva...

Śrī Rāma is indeed all; Rudra is truly one alone, for there is no second to stand beside him. Śiva alone is to be meditated upon as the maker of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else. One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti (primordial nature) and Maheśvara to be the wielder of Māyā; by his constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins, do not grieve.

Having been thus instructed by the knowledge of Śiva, which is the essence of all the Vedāntas, Vāsudeva taught Arjuna during his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa through such statements as "I am everything" and "That Great Soul, who is my very own eternal portion existing as the individual soul in the world of living beings, is exceedingly difficult to find. Just as he taught with the vision that Śiva is the Self, so too was the instruction of Indra given to Indra.

It is not contradicted by its being the Brahman that is Paraśiva; and that Brahman is clearly stated in such passages as, "He who knows that Brahman becomes Brahman itself. For this very reason, in the statement "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self," only the external sign of Prāṇa permeated by a portion (kalā) of Paramaśiva is taught.
Because one’s own worship is the cause of sustaining the life of devotees, that very [worship] is determined by the term "prāṇa" (life-breath) in the Vedas and Āgamas;
as in such passages as: "I am the prāṇa, the self of wisdom; meditate upon me as longevity and immortality."

Having raised the doubt as to whether there is any other object of worship because of the mention of external signs (*liṅga*) such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he says: "Now, the demonstration that Śiva is to be worshipped in three ways—consisting of the desired [form], the vital breath, and the sign (*bhāvaliṅga*):

If it be argued that [Śiva is not the subject] on account of the signs of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), we say no; because of the threefold nature of the meditation, and because that [threefold nature] is applicable here due to its being resorted to. (Sūtra 32)

"I am the vital breath (prāṇa), the self of intelligence; worship me as life and immortality. Since in such statements as "As long as the prāṇa dwells in this body, so long is there life" and "The prāṇa is indeed strength," there is here instruction and indication solely of the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) and the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), which are limited and conditioned by the gross body.

If it is argued that there is no worship of Paraśiva, who is the cause of both [creation and dissolution] of the universe and the all-pervading supreme reality, we say no; for that is precisely what we accept. Why?

Because of the threefold nature of worship (*upāsātraividhyāt*). This refers to the three modes of worship—namely, as the body, as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and as the state of being (*bhāva*)—according to the maxim of the "gross star" and "Arundhatī" (where one first perceives a gross object to eventually reach the subtle).

The meaning is that [this practice] is resorted to because it is a means for the direct realization of Paraśiva—the sixfold, complete state non-different from the inner self—and because it is useful. In the introductory statement, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self; as such, meditate on me as life-span and immortality," and so forth, there is meditation upon the *iṣṭaliṅga* (the chosen symbol) due to the abundance of attributes belonging to the primary *liṅga* as delimited by the gross body.

In the middle—because of the abundance of characteristics belonging to the *prāṇa*, such as being the cause of all actions in the statement "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," there is the meditation on the *prāṇa* as the *liṅga*.
At the conclusion—it is just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes, and the spokes are fixed upon the hub; even so, these elements and their qualities [are fixed].
"Entrusted in the elements of wisdom, the elements of wisdom are entrusted in the vital breath; this very vital breath is the self consisting of wisdom," and so forth.
Because of the abundance of qualities characterized by the state [of being], the meditation upon that which possesses those characteristics is enjoined.
If [the text] were intended to refer to something other than Paramaśiva, there would be the consequence of contradicting the consideration of the preceding, succeeding, and intermediate passages.
Therefore, no other meaning is logical here.

Regarding this, some say that in the passage beginning with "upāsātraividhyāt" (due to the threefold nature of meditation), the intent is the meditation upon Brahman as non-distinct from Prāṇa and Jīva.
For example: "Now, indeed, it is Prāṇa alone, the conscious self (prajñātmā), which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise."

Thus, it is the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) alone that is taught here, because the sustaining of the body is the primary function of the vital breath. In the "Dialogue of the Vital Breaths" (Prāṇasaṃvāda), having introduced the vital breaths beginning with speech, the text teaches through the passage starting with "the most excellent vital breath said to them," that the vital breath possesses consciousness and is the object of worship for all.

Furthermore: in the passage "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," because the attributes of cause and effect such as speaking and so forth belong to the individual soul (jīva), it is that very soul which is being taught. Since its nature is consciousness (caitanya), its being the "self of wisdom" (prajñātman) is also appropriate. By the words "blissful, undecaying," and so forth, its identity with the attributeless Brahman is indicated.

Thus [it is said]. Nevertheless, a threefold classification of meditation here as being without distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not tenable, because this is a context concerning the Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahma*). Having begun with "Know me alone," and having stated, "You are the vital breath, the conscious self;
meditate upon me as life and immortality," it concludes: "This very vital breath is the conscious self, blissful, undecaying, and immortal."

Thus, because the attributes such as being the unique bliss of Paraśiva are established in Śiva through both the opening and the conclusion [of the text], and because it is impossible to assign the ten states consisting of the elements and the vital breath (prāṇa) to anyone other than the Supreme Lord;
for in the *Kaivalya[-Upaniṣad]*, by the passage beginning "He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa," the terms Viṣṇu, Prāṇa, and so forth [refer to Him].
Because [the term] is designated as a synonym for Paraśiva;
and because, in passages such as "Prakṛti and Jīva are not to be worshipped," the worship of Jīva and others has been refuted,
and since the worship of the attributeless Brahman is impossible, this [text] is intended solely for the worship of the qualified Brahman, Paraśiva.

It is determined that there are three kinds of worship. In such passages as, "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self. Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyā)," the phrase "through meditation" (abhidhyānāt) refers to the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the phrase "through union" (yojanāt) refers to the worship of the *iṣṭaliṅga*.

By the phrase "from the state of reality" (*tattvabhāvāt*), the worship of the *bhāva-liṅga* is clearly stated. By the sentence "having taken hold of this body, it causes it to rise," the attribute of *prāṇa* is taught; for even the activity of *prāṇa* is dependent upon Paramaśiva. Why? Because: "No mortal lives by *prāṇa* or by *apāna*; rather, by another..."

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "In whom these two depend, they live. Furthermore, by the statement, "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," the attribute of the individual soul (jīva) is shown. Also, in passages such as, "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here" and "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," [the nature of the Self is revealed].

Because the embodied soul, which is distinct from speech and the other faculties, is sustained by dependence on Brahman, its worship consists of the nature of sustaining (*dhāraṇā*), honoring (*arcana*), and offering (*arpaṇa*).
Thus, the words *jīva* and *mukhyeṣṭa* are synonyms, just as the words *ghaṭa*, *kumbha*, and *kalaśa* are.
Indeed, that Brahmin or Kṣatriya who constantly sustains the *liṅga* offered in his left hand—which is the beloved [form] higher than the highest—[attains liberation].
Only by him is that stainless Supreme Lord attainable; he attains the supreme, divine state of equality.

"If that [life-force] is abandoned, one should not eat; rather, one should even relinquish the vital breaths"—thus, in the *Sadānanda-Upaniṣad* of the *Sāma-Jaiminīya* branch, the primacy of the life-force (*prāṇa*) as the characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*) is indicated. Likewise, it was also pointed out by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Śaṅkara-Saṃhitā*:
Then, having brought about the descent of power (śaktipāta) into the body of the disciple by means of his own vidyā,
and having placed the life-force (prāṇa) of the disciple into the Śiva-liṅga of the sacred seat (pīṭha),
and having established that liṅga within that [disciple's] life-force, it then becomes a *prāṇaliṅga*.
Having given that *liṅga* to his disciple who was endowed with faith and devotion, he said:
"Do not abandon this *prāṇaliṅga* for as long as you live, by way of a solemn vow.
My child, there shall be no further rebirth for you within the wombs of mothers. Thus [he spoke].
Likewise, in the Siddhāntāgama and in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi:
"Having taken the life-force of the disciple, one should deposit it there in the liṅga. (22)
One should establish that very linga within the life-force of the son with single-minded devotion.
Having done this, the preceptor should place the liṅga into the hand of the disciple. || 23 ||
This *prāṇaliṅga* of yours is indeed to be sustained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Never, nor anywhere, should you separate it from the body.
If, through negligence, the linga falls from the body onto the surface of the earth;
"Quickly release your vital breaths for the attainment of the perfection of liberation. (25) Thus it is stated.

Furthermore, it is likewise indicated in another Vedic scripture: "He is indeed the breath of the breath. Moreover, in yet another Vedic scripture, the Supreme Lord's nature as consisting of the three marks (*liṅga*) is taught.
Having faces, heads, and necks everywhere, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, that Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.
It always bestows through austerity the desired vigor;
they say that is the mark of the mind within the vital breaths.

Those who know the Lord— who is graspable through meditative absorption, called "the nestless," the auspicious one who brings about both existence and non-existence, and the creator of the emission of the *kalās*— they have cast off the body.

Because hundreds of such scriptural passages establish the practice of the three-fold meditation on the desired state of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and because here too—through the examination of the introduction, the conclusion, and the intermediate references—the determination is made that the sole purport is Supreme Śiva; and because other [deities] are not seen to bestow liberation; and because this is a context concerning Supreme Śiva.
No other meaning is prescribed here. Therefore, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that by the word "prāṇa" in this context, the Supreme Śiva-Brahman alone is denoted.
Thus ends the eleventh section, the Prāṇādhikaraṇa.

Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter, titled "Samanvaya," in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* by the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya, the preeminent leader of the host of ascetics of the glorious Nirābhāsa Vīraśaiva tradition.
The Second Pāda of the First Adhyāya: The Section on "Established Everywhere" (Sarvatra-prasiddhi-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

In the first quarter (pāda), having established that Paraśiva-Brahman is the cause of both the origin and dissolution of the universe, the subject propounded by all the Vedāntas, omniscient, omnipotent, eternally satisfied,
and the supreme state of Paramaśiva— and having further [established this] regarding certain words whose indicative marks (liṅga) are not explicit—
In the doubt as to whether [the term] denotes Brahman or conveys some other meaning, the second quarter of the chapter is commenced for the purpose of understanding its primary sense:
"Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere" (1.2.1).

In the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka of the Yajur-Āraṇyaka: "That small, stainless lotus which has become the supreme abode, situated in the middle of the city; within that also is a small space, free from sorrow—that which is inside it is to be meditated upon. Having thus pointed out the rule for the contemplation of the Jyotir-liṅga, [the text describes] the true nature of that reality...

Having clearly stated, "The vowel is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and is established at the end of the Veda; he who is beyond that which is dissolved into primordial nature is Maheśvara," and so forth, [the text] teaches the universal nature of the Supreme Brahman as the Liṅga through such passages as "Obeisance to the Lord of Nidhana," and concludes with,
"This establishes the universal Liṅga of Soma and Sūrya."
"The *pāṇimantra* is purifying"—this is heard as its subject matter.

Now, one might object: "Since the meditation on external symbols (*bāhyaliṅga-upāsana*) was already established in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the section concerning the vital breath (*prāṇādhikaraṇa*), for what purpose is this [repeated]? This is not so; for in the first section, it was introduced by way of defining the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*).
Something has been briefly examined. In the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*, it was established that there is indeed an injunction for the meditation on the threefold marks (*liṅga*).

Here, however, for the sake of clarity, we shall establish the wearing of external marks (*bāhyaliṅgadhāraṇa*), just as in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa*—where, despite the refutation of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world, it is refuted again by the argument "because there is no distinction, as in the case of the *camasa*," and so forth.
This exposition of the doctrine regarding the wearing of external marks refers to Soma and Sūrya; for in this context,
as well as in the preceding section, the words "Soma" and "Sūrya" denote the Moon and the Sun respectively.

Because of the praise of Prabhākara seen here, and because of the subsequent indication of the praise of the five Brahma-puruṣas who establish the one Supreme Śiva, there arises the doubt as to whether the object of worship here is Prabhākara or the Supreme Śiva.

The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), however, is as follows: "The entry into the path of Tantra for those who have fallen away from the way of the Śruti [is untenable]. For, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the section distinguishing between the Tantric and the Vedic, the Pāśupata and other Āgamas are rejected—just like the Pāñcarātra and others—due to their lack of being rooted in the Vedas; and because Dharma has as its sole root the word that is the means of valid cognition consisting of injunction (codanā). If one were to accept their authority...
"O King, he who does not relinquish this which is indeed a purifier becomes one who has no share in speech, and no share in the celestial vault (nāka).

Regarding this, there is a verse: 'He who, like a friend, has abandoned his own kin—there is no share for him even in speech; though he hears, he hears in vain, for he knows not the path of righteous action. Because of such contradictions with the Śruti, [the Sūtra states] "because the scripture is its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

This is because of such scriptural passages and sūtras as, "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," and "This understanding is not to be attained through reasoning," which establish that Brahman is what is propounded by the Vedānta.
Therefore, the Tantras and Āgamas have no authority whatsoever in establishing Dharma and Brahman. Consequently, he establishes all the lingas.
In this context, the wearing of one's own preferred sectarian marks (liṅga) is not appropriate; rather, by virtue of the preceding section, it is stated here:
"At dawn he is Brahmā himself, at midday he is Maheśvara, and at evening he is Viṣṇu—the Sun-god who is the embodiment of the Triple Veda."
Thus, because the *Smṛti* establishes that Prabhākara consists of three forms, the meaning obtained from the passage "this [is] of Soma,

[and] of Sūrya" is as follows: for all Vaidikas, he places upon his hand the *pāṇimantra*— the consecrated mark or sign (*liṅga*) of Soma, who is Śiva, and of Sūrya, who is Prabhākara— upon the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

Since the worship of Prabhākara alone is primary, the statements establishing Nārāyaṇa found in the preceding section— beginning with "The thousand-headed one"— as well as the statements beginning with "Sadyojāta" and so forth found in the subsequent mantras and sections, are designated as having Prabhākara as their sole referent. Therefore, it is logical that they have him as their sole referent.
Furthermore, because of the teaching of the identity with all things (sarvātmakatva) of that which consists of the Śiva-liṅga through the mantra "Nidhanapataye namaḥ" and so forth,
the word "etad" (this) in the phrase "etatsomasya sūryasya" cannot be joined with a word that refers back to the previously mentioned salutation to Soma and Sūrya.

Because of the rule "namas-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam-vaṣaṭ-yogācca" [Pāṇini 2.3.16], which prescribes the use of the genitive case instead of the dative due to the absence of these particles in the dative form, and because of the natural force of the word "sthāpayati" (he establishes), it is intended here that the object is the *liṅga* placed upon the ground. [The mantra] "pāṇimantraṃ pavitram" [is recited] with the hand.
If it is argued that because the meaning is connected with the phrase "the consecrated hand-mantra," the wearing of external marks is in no way appropriate, we say:

No. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "Because of the teaching well-known everywhere" (*sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*), [this applies] everywhere—in the Vedas, Vedāntas, Āgamas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas.

The meaning is that because Brahman— which is well-known in the *Hāsa* and other scriptures as being of the nature of Paraśiva with six locations— is taught here, beginning with the words "the small, stainless" (*daharaṃ vipāpmaṃ*) and ending with "he establishes the universal liṅga" (*sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati*), as an object of meditation through external and internal dhāraṇā, and is thus established [as such]. This refers to the injunctions for wearing the ashes (*vibhūti*), Rudrākṣa beads, and the Śivaliṅga.
The claim that the Śaiva doctrine is not to be accepted by the Vedists because it is rooted in the Tantras and Āgamas is charming only when left unexamined.

Why? Because [the Śaiva doctrine] is well-known in the Vedas, Vedānta, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas; and because the Śiva-Āgamas, such as the Kāmika, possess authority equal to the Vedas—either due to the identity of their author or because they are rooted in the Vedas. Thus, the Śaiva doctrine is [valid] as it is expounded by both.
It is indeed Vedic. As it is stated in the Siddhāntāgama:
"Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative and are not to be undermined by logical arguments."
O great sage, the Veda is the primary authority for all systems such as Sāṃkhya and the rest;
it is certain that their validity is derived from following the Veda.
O great sage, the Pāñcarātra, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga systems abide within a single portion of the Veda; however, the Śaiva doctrine consists of the Veda itself.
"O Great Sage, because it follows all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra is superior to the Sāṃkhya and other systems that reside only in a portion of the Vedas;
because it follows all the Vedas, it is always authoritative like the Veda itself."
Furthermore, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"Just as the Lord Maheśvara is the author of the divisions beginning with the Kāmika, so too is the son of Satyavatī the author of the eighteen Purāṇas."
By such statements, the authority of the Purāṇas spoken by Vyāsa was established by the great sage Sūta, just like that of the Śiva-āgamas such as the Kāmika.
Therefore, in that very same [work]:
The Lord of the World proclaimed this Great Tantra, consisting of two parts and four chapters, as the sole means for achieving Dharma and liberation to the daughter of Himavat.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the Śiva Āgamas serve as the means for attaining both Dharma and Brahman.

Furthermore, like the Vedas and Vedānta, some Śiva Āgamas prescribe the Pati, Pāśa, and Paśu categories, as well as the construction of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and pavilions (maṇṭapa) for rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; while others expound upon the worship of Śiva.

Some [texts] expound upon the wearing of ashes, rudrākṣa beads, and the śivaliṅga; others expound upon temples, festivals, and consecrations. For instance: "Indeed, these are the creatures—both bipeds and quadrupeds—over whom Paśupati is the lord of creatures, both of the four-footed and the two-footed."
Thus, from such statements as "Therefore, Rudra is the lord of creatures," and "Having known the God, there is the casting off of all fetters;
through the practice of churning by means of meditation, the wise man burns away the fetter," [it is established] in the perceptible Vedas and Vedāntas.
From the *Darśana* [of Rāmānuja], there arises the ringing proclamation of the Vedic character of the Śaiva Āgamas, which establish the three categories of Pati,
Pāśa, and Paśu; and likewise of the Pāñcarātra Āgama, which relies upon the technical terminology of the three categories of Cit, Acit, and Īśvara.
Because it lacks a foundation in Vedic technical terminology, it is non-Vedic. Furthermore,

[it is non-Vedic] because all mantras— such as those of the Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Chāndogya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Śrīsūkta, Ṣaḍakṣara, Tryambaka, Gāyatrī, and so forth— are [in the Veda] prescriptive of the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa) and of meditative visualization (dhyāna).

For the sake of prosperity, one must not neglect the rules regarding the secondary marks (*avaraliṅga*)—such as Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Śaunaka, and others—which prescribe the rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration and festivals; for this is established by the *Yajurveda* and the *Atharvaveda*, such as the *Bṛhajjābāla-upaniṣad*, which states: "Agni is ashes," and so forth.

Because it contains the exposition of the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta within the Yajurveda, and because it establishes the practice of wearing the Śiva-linga as proven by such Vedic texts as "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not cause suffering," "He who is the bull among the meters, the universal-formed one," and "Soma and Rudra," [it is said: "Worship him; praise him."

Furthermore, since the Agamas share the same purpose as the Vedas by virtue of enjoining the worship of Śiva based on the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*, which itself elucidates the meaning of the Mantras, the Vedic character of the Agamas is established beyond dispute. Therefore, it is proven that the wearing of the *liṅga* prescribed therein is likewise [Vedic]. Thus, in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*:
Indeed, in the past, I manifested the auspicious Pāśupata vow,
which is the most secret of secrets, subtle, the essence of the Vedas, and intended for liberation.
This Pāśupata conduct is to be practiced by those seeking liberation;
the Pāśupata is recorded as being threefold: Tantric, Vedic, and Mixed.
The wearing of heated marks such as the linga and the trident is considered Tantric;
the wearing of the linga, rudrākṣa beads, and sacred ash is Vedic.
They worship Ravi, Śambhu, as well as Śakti, Vighneśa, and Janārdana with equanimity; for that indeed is the Miśrapāśupata.

"For those seekers of liberation who are solely devoted to the path of the Vedas, the Śrauta and Pāśupata [systems] should be accepted; the Tantrika [system] mixed with other traditions should not be accepted.
And likewise in the Smṛti:
Whatever treatises are seen to be current in this age that are contrary to the path of the Vedas, their foundation is indeed characterized by tamas.
The fact that Śiva is the presiding deity of the Brahmins is sung in the Śrutis and Smṛtis;
therefore, the exclusive worship of Śiva should be performed for as long as one lives.

Thus, from this scriptural testimony, it is clear that there is no other form of worship; for both [the Vedas and the Āgamas] are appropriately designated as "Nigama" and "Āgama" by virtue of their relationship as primary and auxiliary limbs. Furthermore, the internal wearing of the *liṅga* is established—

Having established the existence of the *bhāvaliṅga* through the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* with passages such as "the small, stainless one" (*daharaṃ vipāpmam*), and having pointed out the universal nature of the *liṅga* through passages such as "salutation to the upward-facing one" (*ūrdhvāya namaḥ*), the wearing of the external *liṅga* is enjoined by the statement concerning the "all-*liṅga*" (*sarvaliṅga*).
It has been explained. The passage beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Nidhanas" and ending with "This [is] of Soma, of Sūrya" is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

Since there is no *ca* particle there to prescribe a combination, and since there are no words in the dative case to prescribe acts of obeisance, and because the opening and conclusion refer to Paramaśiva, the reference to Soma and Sūrya in the middle portion [must also be understood as referring to him].

Because consistency [otherwise] would be impossible, the meaning is as follows: "everyone" (sarvaḥ) refers to every person; "all" (sarvam) refers to the *liṅga* of Śiva—which exists within the solar orb of the Sun and is the beloved form of Paraśiva—composed of five threads and obtained through the compassionate glance of a true Guru. By the phrase "he establishes all *liṅgas*" (*sarvaliṅgaṃ sthāpayati*), it means that he maintains [or upholds] it.
Having pointed out the installation of the *liṅga*, in response to the inquiry as to what constitutes the locus for that installation of the *liṅga*,

it is ordained that it be worn on the hands and so forth due to the specific characteristic of the term "pāṇimantra-pavitram. By the phrase "the *pāṇimantra* is pure (*pavitram*)— because it protects through being held in the hand and through meditation and worship"— the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is [implied as] the supreme purity.

Just as in the case of [the rule regarding] the *yajñopavīta*, its status as something to be worn at all times is established by prescribing its purity at a time when impurity—such as that resulting from ritual cleansing (*śauca*) or sipping water (*ācamana*)—might otherwise occur. Furthermore, there is no fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here, similar to the injunction: "The cake for Agni is on eight potsherds.
As it has been said:
Whoever always holds in his hand Śiva in the form of a *liṅga*,
for him my perfected state— the abode of all prosperity— remains established in his very hand.

Thus it is stated in the Vātūla[-tantra]. Likewise, in the Laiṅga[-purāṇa], the meaning of this mantra was clearly declared by the Blessed Vyāsa: "In the Vedas, in the collections of scriptures, in the Purāṇas, and in the Āgamas, the wearing of the liṅga is proclaimed as the supreme duty of a Brāhmaṇa."
Having begun thus, [the scripture] states:
"The Yajurveda also declares that the *liṅga* indeed establishes everything;
therefore, one should hold the great *liṅga* while consecrating it with the mantra on the hand."
At the time of initiation, the Guru places the *liṅga* in the hand;
that mantra which he recollects as Śiva is indeed called the *pāṇimantra*.
Because it is the purifier of Maheśvara, because it establishes Śiva,
and because it sanctifies human beings, it is called "Pavitra" (the Purifier).
Therefore, at all times— one whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, or even opening and closing one's eyes— one should maintain the supreme liṅga.
Whether pure or impure, one should wear the *liṅga* everywhere;
the wearer of the *liṅga* is always pure, possessing his own beautiful *liṅga*.
"Concentrated, one should worship [the deity] upon the palm of the hand with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

One should perform the regular (nitya) sets of rites as well as the occasional (naimittika) ones with the intention of offering them to Śiva, for the sake of the full increase of right knowledge. Thus it is said.

The exposition of Paraśiva-Brahman as consisting of ten kinds of *liṅgas*—furthermore, regarding the mantra "Salutation to Nidhanapati": *nidhana* refers to the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) of moving and non-moving beings; its *pati* is the Lord, the agent, which is to say, the substratum of all absorptions. To Him, "Salutation" (*namaḥ*) is uttered. It is the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañcopaśama*).

"They consider the fourth state to be peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known—'Auspicious and non-dual,'" according to the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*. This is also an indication for the *Sītībhūta* [state]. By this, the reality of Śiva as the partless (*niṣkala*) cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe is taught. "Salutation to the one who is the end of the lords of death."
By this statement, the agency of destruction belonging to Kālarudra and others—who are the causes of the dissolution at the end of an intermediate kalpa—is indicated.

Furthermore, in the subsequent passage, "Salutation to the Subduer of all beings, salutation to Manonmanā," the role of destroying all beings, including Viṣṇu and the rest, is heard; as is seen in such texts as, "Viṣṇu alone is the great being."
In passages such as "The gods follow Hari as he seizes Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, and the other beings— the Lord of the universe,

the Bull among thoughts," there is the quality of being the destroyer of beings such as Viṣṇu and others; and in passages such as "Lord of all sciences, Sovereign of all beings," there is the quality of being the presiding lord over all knowledge.
And his sovereignty over all beings is likewise taught.

In the passage, "Homage to the Upper One, homage to the Upper Liṅga," it is Sadāśiva himself who is taught as characterized by being essentially the pure power of Māyā that transcends everything beginning with Mahat.
2) "Obeisance to Hiraṇya, obeisance to Hiraṇyaliṅga"—

here [the deity is] Śiva as delimited by the power of ignorance (avidyā-śakti), which consists of the great darkness (mahā-tamas) that is the aggregate of the three qualities (guṇa-traya) situated in the western wheel.
3) "Obeisance to Suvarṇa, obeisance to Suvarṇaliṅga"— here...
The *prāṇaliṅga*, which consists of a portion of consciousness (*citkalā*) delimited by the power (*śakti*) of the *rajas* [quality] following the *śikhācakra*, is now determined.

4) Regarding the mantra "Salutation to the Divine One (*divyāya*), salutation to the Divine Liṅga (*divyaliṅgāya*)," this refers to one's own chosen *liṅga* (*sveṣṭaliṅga*) as delimited by the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), which consists of the abundance of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) that have entered the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāracakra*).

5) Regarding "Salutation to Bhava; salutation to Bhavaliṅga," the Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga), which is delimited by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) consisting of the pure internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) situated in the wheel of command (ājñācakra),
is heard [in this passage].

6) Regarding "Salutation to Śarva! Salutation to the Liṅga of Śarva!", the *prasāda-liṅga*—which is delimited by the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) that conforms to the principle of space (*vyoma-tattva*) situated in the Viśuddha-cakra—is described here.
7) Regarding "Salutation to Śiva! Salutation to the Liṅga of Śiva!"... [the *anugraha-liṅga* is described].
The mobile *liṅga* is said to consist of the wind-principle (*pavanatattva*) residing in the *anāhata-cakra*, delimited by the primordial power (*ādi-śakti*).

8) Regarding "Salutation to Jvala; salutation to the flaming *liṅga*," here the *Śiva-liṅga*—which consists of the fire-principle (*tejas-tattva*) residing in the *maṇipūraka-cakra* and is accompanied by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)—is designated.

9) Regarding "Salutation to the Self (ātman), salutation to the mark of the Self (ātmaliṅga)," the guru-liṅga as delimited by the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), which consists of the water-principle (jalatattva) situated in the svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra, is explained here.
10) "Salutation to the Supreme (parama), salutation to the supreme liṅga (paramaliṅga)."

In this context, the *ācāraliṅga*—characterized by the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) whose nature is earth and which resides in the foundational wheel (*ādhāracakra*)—is being described. By the statement, "this establishes the *sarvaliṅga* of Soma and Sūrya," it is meant that one establishes the *liṅga*-form body of Śiva, who is Soma and resides within the solar orb (*sūryamaṇḍala*), consisting of these ten kinds of *liṅgas*. This refers to the Earth.

Therefore, the nature of one’s chosen *liṅga*— which has the hand as its locus and consists of ten types of *liṅgas*— as being composed of the five *brahmans* and the thirty-six *tattvas*, is now described.
This is the demonstration of the Vedic character of the wearing of the *liṅga*.
Furthermore, the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga is heard of in the Vedas, Vedānta, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Āgamas, and so forth.
In the Yajurveda:
"O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious."
With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we attain that life span ordained by the gods.

The sacred foot, spread out, ancient; by which, when purified, one crosses over evil deeds—purified by that pure, sanctifying [foot], may we cross over sin and the enemy. The door of the world, radiant, sacred, luminous, shining, full of splendor, pouring forth in many ways the stream of immortality—may that foot be ours.
"May he establish me well in the world; I take refuge in Varuṇa, the golden-horned one.
The purifying one, who dwells in the light, the all-seeing, who is the Purifier—may He purify me. May the divine beings purify me," and so forth;
by such passages, the wearing of the *liṅga* by all the gods is taught.

And in the Sāmaveda: "The Śaiva-linga, which is to be known by the learned as the Viśvedeva, is worn with faith and devotion by all the gods; for the sake of self-realization, it should be borne on the neck, in the hand, or on the head by sages desiring liberation. He who bears that supreme, pure, stainless, and sorrowless linga within his body [attains the goal]."
He attains liberation—the supreme, divine, eternal, and ancient Śaiva state, which is to be known through the Vedas and is the immeasurable essence of the gods, O Śambhu.
And in the Atharvaṇa: "For the realization of the Supreme Self, [one should meditate upon] the Śāmbhava Liṅga, the destroyer of time, within the bodies."

One desiring liberation should wear it. The Śiva-liṅga, the God of gods belonging to Śaṅkara, should always be worn by great and most great sages, whether they be silent ones (maunibhiḥ) or yogins. By wearing the Śiva-liṅga, one attains union with Brahman (sāyujyam) and residence in the same world as Him (salokatām);
through that, one attains all desires and does not return again, does not return again. Thus it is said.

Likewise, in the Vedāntas: "May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and all my senses and strength be nourished. All is the Upaniṣad of Brahman. May I not repudiate Brahman; may Brahman not repudiate me. May there be no repudiation of me, and no repudiation of myself, for one who is devoted to the Self and intent upon the Upaniṣads."
"May those dharmas be in me; may they be in me—[the dharmas] of him who is the bull among the Vedas (*chandasa*), the one of universal form," and so forth.
Whether the best of the twice-born possess the power of internal retention (*antardhāraṇa*) or lack such power, the Śiva-liṅga, having been consecrated by the Guru, is placed upon the chest.
Those who know the Vedas understand that it should be maintained by Brahmins solely for the sake of liberation.
Having placed both [hands] upon the throat, the hands, and the head, and reciting that purifying mantra for the hands,
the Brahmin or Kṣatriya who constantly bears that single Liṅga worshipped with the left hand— the supreme among the supreme—
attains that very Supreme Lord, the stainless one, and reaches divine, supreme equality.
These are the corroborative statements (*upabṛṃhaṇa-vākyāni*) pointed out by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*:
"Having fashioned [an image] of gold, silver, stone, or even copper,
a twice-born man should wear an unbroken *liṅga* made with five threads," and so on, beginning thus.
"By the mantra 'This hand of mine is the Blessed One,' the wearing of the *liṅga* in the palm is always prescribed; so says the eternal Ṛgveda."
O best of gods, may we with devotion hear of the auspicious Supreme Śiva;
may we with our eyes behold the auspicious Sadāśiva in the form of the Liṅga.
May we, being satisfied, constantly perform the auspicious sacrifice according to the rules;
as long as life shall endure, may there be well-being and what is beneficial for the gods.
With our bodies and with constant devotion,
we duly install the Śāmbhava Liṅga named Svasti, as does Indra, Vṛddhaśravas.
May Pūṣan, the Viśvedevas, Tārkṣya, and likewise Viṣṇu,
as well as Bṛhaspati, bestow the supreme lordly power of the Liṅga.
The *caraṇa* is declared to be the *liṅga*, pure and the destroyer of sin;
because it leads (*nayati*) or causes one to attain (*prāpayati*) the moving (*caraṃ*) living soul (*jīva*) to the Supreme Self (*parātmā*), it is so called.
It is the pervasive (*vitataṃ vyāpakam*), eternal (*nityaṃ*), ancient (*purāṇaṃ*), and everlasting (*śāśvataṃ*) Brahman.
By means of which mark, being purified, one shall cross over all evils.
By means of that pure sign, being purified,
may we indeed cross over the enemy— the āṇava, māyīya, and kārmika impurities.
It is the door for the world—that is, for the world of devotees—and the means for attaining it;
for it is radiant, self-luminous, pure, and the purifier of the worlds.
It is luminous, radiant, and shining by virtue of its nature as consciousness;
endowed with the quality of greatness, it is celebrated as the Great (Mahat).
The "foot" (caraṇa) is declared to be the *liṅga* because it is the cause of the world's dissolution;
it is the stream of nectar, distinguished by the various stages of liberation such as *sālokya*.
O gods, may that [merit] which is being milked in many ways be especially ours; may you always grant us a dwelling of well-being in this world and in our bodies day after day.
May he, out of affection, grant the wearing of the *liṅga* by all through the *Pavamāna-anuvāka*, which is the sole medicine for the disease of worldly existence.
Because it is sung with the Yajus, therefore the auspicious Pāśupata is pure;
it is like the purifying wind, perfectly cleansing and free from all evil.
May she, who dwells in the three worlds with the linga as her purifier and is expert in the knowledge of Śiva, being herself purified, purify me.
Because it purifies all living beings, the Liṅga is called pure;
the golden Liṅga is declared to be Maheśvara, whose form is the universe.
I take refuge with my mind and speech in that imperishable Varuṇa, whose emblem is borne upon his horn-like head, the eternal devotee of Śiva.
"Grant me a sacred ford," thus was he entreated by the personifications of the Vedas;
[he who is] Brahman, the soul of all, eternal, and existing in the form of the *liṅga*.
Then, [I perceived] my own divine Upanishadic limbs in particular:
the bodies, both gross and subtle, as well as the organs of knowledge and action.
Abiding everywhere and at all times in the form of signs such as existence (bhāva) and so forth,
may they constantly nourish [all beings] with the wealth of supreme bliss.
Therefore, may I never reject Him, nor ever fail to worship Him;
may the Brahman who is the eternal Liṅga not abandon me, nor may He spurn me.
May that Brahman be ever-present within my own self, the body; "anirākaraṇam" (non-rejection) means complete non-repudiation.
May those qualities known as sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads that exist in the Upaniṣads abide in me eternally; may they always abide in me.
And so forth. Furthermore, in that very context, the fact that non-performance produces sin is observed:
"The body of one in whose gross physical form the wearing of the *liṅga* is not found should be known as fruitless, like a living being who has abandoned its body."
Just as wood found in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual acts,
so too one who is devoid of the *liṅga* is excluded from all ritual acts.
One should avoid like an outcaste that person on whose chest there is no linga, on whose neck no rosary of rudrākṣa beads, and on whose forehead no lines of sacred ash.
A Brahmin should not, even in his mind, transgress the wearing of the *liṅga*;
since it is ordained by the *Śruti*, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
Lord Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas;
therefore, according to the teaching of the Vedas and Vedānta, the wearing of his liṅga must be performed by the Brāhmaṇas.
Just as the marks of a master are to be worn by a servant upon the earth,
so too is the wearing of the *liṅga* and other signs always prescribed for a devotee.
In the hand of Anantapadmanābha is the wearing of the liṅga;
likewise, in Pāṇḍuraṅga, the head of Viṣṇu bears the wearing of the liṅga.
Since it is well-known and ever perceived by men, what more need be said?

Since the wearing of the *liṅga*, which is the very nature of the Supreme Brahman consisting of Paraśiva in the six locations (*ṣaṭsthala*), is observed [in scripture] through such passages, the wearing of that very *liṅga* is enjoined by the "Sarvaliṅga" statement.
To this point, he states another reason:
And because the intended qualities are applicable [to Brahman]. || 34 || 2 ||

The meaning is that the qualities intended here—such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and others—which are to be adopted for the purpose of meditation, are "established" (*upapatti*), that is, they are logically consistent with Paraśiva-Brahman. This is known from such passages as: "Ṛta and Satya are the Supreme Brahman, the Person who is dark and tawny, whose seed is drawn upward, the three-eyed one; salutations indeed to the one of universal form."

Because of hearing that teaching. And in another Śruti passage: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; one should meditate with a tranquil mind. Now, a person consists of volition (kratu); as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here. He should form a resolve: 'I am composed of mind, have vital breath for my body, am of the nature of light, possess true resolve, and have space for my self.'"

In passages such as "the creator of all" and "possessing all desires," because it is intended to describe the Supreme Lord— who is the self of all— as having a limited form consisting of vital breath (*prāṇa*) for the sake of the devotee's worship, and as possessing [attributes] such as the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), his nature as the self of all is taught here by the mantra for the hand (*pāṇimantra*) beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of the End" (*nidhanapataye namaḥ*).

Because the term "purifier" (*pavitra*) refers specifically to that [liṅga] by virtue of its being located in the hand—even though it is thus delimited—it does not follow that the worship of another [deity] is enjoined here.
Now, one might object: since in other Purāṇas the liṅga is described as a limb subordinate to the Supreme Lord, [the word] *caraṇam* (foot) must mean the *pavitra*.

If it is argued that since such scriptural passages are conventionally established as referring to the feet [of Viṣṇu], and since even among those born of mixed castes outside the Vedic fold (vedabāhya-saṅkaraja) the marks of ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the Śiva-liṅga are observed, how can these be considered Vedic (śrauta)? To this we say: no;
for in the Liṅga Purāṇa, following the description of the origin of the Jyotir-liṅga—
Then, with a joyful mind, Nārāyaṇa prostrated before Maheśvara and spoke to the Lord who dwells within the liṅga and bears the liṅga.
If affection has arisen, and if something is to be given to us both,
then the coiled serpent shines like a pedestal beneath a linga.
Above that, the earth appears like a seat, shaped like the leaf of an ashvattha tree;
situated upon it is the Great God, in the form of a most magnificent light.
O Mahādeva, grant us such a *liṅga* as this, which is the cause for uprooting our pride, and indeed bestow initiation upon us both.
