"By means of its retention, its meditation, and the prescribed method of its worship,
we shall certainly attain happiness pertaining to both this world and the next."
Having heard those words, the eternal Viśvanātha [bestowed] a linga made of sapphire upon Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and me.
Having presented a linga made of ruby, he caused him to receive initiation;
thereafter, the Lord bestowed upon him unwavering devotion.
Having placed the Liṅga of Hari upon my chest and I, the Grandfather (Brahmā), upon my head,
with a delighted mind, supreme faith, and great joy;

Because, through such passages as these, it is shown that the Supreme Lord alone possesses the form of the *liṅga*. Furthermore, in the Siddhāntāgama: "The *liṅga* consisting of light, which formerly existed [as the source] of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, was unlimited; by whom could it be fully comprehended?"
The pedestal is the supreme Śakti, and the Liṅga is Paraśiva himself;
through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the entire universe is called the Liṅga.
The eternal Śruti declares that the Lord’s status as supreme over all, which arises from His own nature as the Liṅga-form, is such that He has no likeness among other gods.
That into which Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods dissolve and into which they go—
that is the supreme Liṅga, Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
How can the similarity between the supreme self, which is devoid of any form like an image,
and the deities who possess the forms of images be asserted?

This is because it is shown [to be so] by such passages as these. Vyāsa and Gautama state that the words fabricated by the rogue Dadhīci under the pretext of a curse lack authority here, as they are contrary to the Śruti.
If that were the case, then what of the lingas installed by Viṣṇu at Pāṇḍuraṅga, Rāmeśvara, Śrīśaila, and other such places?
Therefore, even for Viṣṇu, supremacy over all is not tenable; if that were accepted, it would result in the heretical doctrine of the Buddhists.

Furthermore, if the word *caraṇa* were taken to mean "foot," there would arise the contradiction of attributes such as omnipresence and self-luminosity—which are established by the scriptural texts concerning the *caraṇa*—being attributed to him.
Due to the abundance of attributes belonging to the Supreme Lord, this [term] refers exclusively to the Supreme Lord, just like the words "space" (*ākāśa*), "breath" (*prāṇa*), and so forth.

That by which the world is moved (*caryate*) and consumed (*bhakṣyate*) is *caraṇa*; this also implies "staying" (*sthiti*). Alternatively, it means that which leads the moving soul (*cara*) to liberation (*mokṣa*), according to the Vedic revelation: "He alone causes one to perform good deeds. This amounts to saying it is the cause of origination, maintenance, and dissolution.

Because it exists for that purpose, the word *liṅga* denotes the *caraṇa*. The synonymy of the words *liṅga* and *caraṇa* is well-established by such statements as, "That wherein and by which all that is moving and unmoving dissolves (*līyate*) and is understood (*gamyate*).
Now, the eight enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) of Vīraśaivism:
Ash, rudrākṣa beads, the liṅga, the guru, the mantra, as well as conduct,
water from the feet, and the prasāda— these indeed are the eight enclosures of Śiva.

Due to the absence of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the Vedic Śiva-āgamas mentioned above, the eightfold enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*) of Śaivism—which are auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—are in no way possible for them. This is because those who are non-Vedic lack the purificatory rites of the Śaiva fire.
Furthermore, the wearing of the ashes from the Śaiva fire, as established in the *Jābāla* and other Upaniṣads, is not prescribed for them.

Because they lack the topknot (śikhā) as prescribed by the injunctions— starting with the passage "one face on the topknot" (*śikhāyām ekam ekāsyam*)— the wearing of rudrākṣas is not possible for them. Furthermore, since the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī-mantra*) is recited within the context of the Śruti,
they are not included among the four types of castes mentioned in the Vedas, and they are excluded from the eighteen castes mentioned in the Smṛtis.

Furthermore, that [liberation] is also not possible because of the unfitness for instruction in those mantras even through the process of transposition. How can the Vedic ritual procedure for *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other consecrations be justified for those who are outside the Vedas and devoid of the *upanayana* sacrament? In the absence of that [sacrament], there is also an absence of the *liṅga*, since [the status of being a devotee] arises from the wearing and worship of it.

How can the attainment of the state of Supreme Śiva, preceded by the destruction of all sins, be logically established? For [your position] does not accept the status of the Brāhmaṇa as the teacher, which is established by such scriptural and traditional texts as: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed all the deities" and "Among the castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the Guru."

Even the fourfold grace of the holy waters at the feet of the Guru is not possible; it is understood to be like [the juice of] a gourd grown in a vessel of clarified butter. Likewise, in the Siddhāntāgama, it is stated:
"The Āgama is said to be the body of the Śivaliṅga."
The Śruti declares that consciousness belongs to the liṅga, while the Vedānta proclaims it to be the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Because they are devoid of those purificatory rites (saṃskāras), the state of being a *liṅgin* (one possessing the marks) does not exist for them at all times.
This is the refutation of the Śūdras' eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Furthermore, how could there be the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self (*liṅgāṅgaikya*) as established by the meaning of the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)?
In the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, regarding those outside the Vedic fold, it is stated in the sūtra:
"Because of the reference to sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) and because of the mention of their absence"— referring to Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
who are established [as such] by the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas.
Since the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) has been prohibited [for others], what need is there to mention others? Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct.
Now, one might ask: how can Rudra be the Supreme Brahman? [Is it not] like Nirṛti and the other deities mentioned in the *Āpastamba Sūtra*?
If it is argued that this is because of the designation [in the scripture] of him as an inauspicious deity in the passage, "having touched water after the oblation to Rudra," we say no;
for there is no evidence for such a view, and it would result in the undesirable consequence of [the scripture] being harsh toward the Vedic revelation.
[As stated: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords, him, the supreme deity among deities, the first lord among lords..."
"Let us know the God from of old, the Lord of the world, the one worthy of praise; Rudra is indeed one, he does not stand for a second.

"Incalculable thousands [of forms] are remembered, yet they are not seen. "Rudra is superior to all, the great seer, Śiva, the non-dual"—from these and hundreds of other such scriptural passages, Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is taught to be the deity who has no equal or peer.

Furthermore, because the attributes such as lordship over all deities are taught as belonging to him alone, and because it is impossible for his servants—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—to be worthy of worship in his presence, the sprinkling of water around [the sacrificial ground] is prescribed for the purpose of Rudra’s disappearance. This is stated in the Yajurveda: "He sprinkles water around for the sake of Rudra's disappearance. Nor...

Because of its inclusion in the section on *niṛti* and so forth, there is a sense of inferiority; for in the Āpastamba Sūtra— "Having touched a cow, a horse, fire, or a Brāhmaṇa, one should touch water"— the teaching regarding the superior and inferior cows, horses, and fires occurs within a single context.
Because the words *śva*, *yuvan*, and *maghavan*—which denote both superior and inferior [meanings]—are mentioned together in a single sūtra;
furthermore:
"A woman who is menstruating, fire, a cow, a Brahmin, and likewise a wife devoted to her husband..."

"Having touched a corpse, an impure thing, or a *brahmabandhu*, one should perform a bath. Even in the *Vṛddhaśātātapa*, because of the mention of cows and Brahmins in association with a menstruating woman (*rajasvalā*), there is no fault regarding the context;
therefore, that [Brahmin] alone possesses the status of a Brahmin (*brahmatva*).
Now, regarding Śiva as the object of worship (the Supreme Brahman) and Nārāyaṇa as the worshipper:
having raised the objection that the definition of Brahman stated here might over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to Nārāyaṇa, [the author] refutes it:
"But because of impossibility, he is not the embodied soul" (Sūtra 1.2.3).

In this context, however, the word "tu" (but/however) signifies certainty: the previously mentioned wearing of the Śiva-liṅga must necessarily be performed by those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who are practitioners of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). It is not the bodily [form]—referring to the previous section beginning with "thousand-headed," which describes Nārāyaṇa as characterized by having a thousand heads and so forth, in the form of a physical image.

Because of the designation; because signs such as "lying upon the ocean" and "the source of all prosperity in the ocean," and so forth, are appropriate for Him alone; and because of the use of the words *acyuta* and *hari*, which denote Him—therefore, the embodied one (*śārīra*) consisting of the form of Nārāyaṇa is not the object of worship here. Why? Because it is untenable.

Beginning with "Salutation to Nidhanapati" and ending with "He establishes the universal liṅga," this section demonstrates that the Śiva-liṅga is the object of all forms of worship consisting of meditation (dhyāna) and concentration (dhāraṇā), by establishing its nature as the Supreme Brahman through the presentation of its being the Self of all, preceded by salutations at every step. [This applies] to that which consists of form...
Because those attributes are impossible for Viṣṇu, it is established that the Liṅga alone, which possesses an incomparable form, is the object of all worship. As stated in the Śaiva tradition:
"The Liṅga consists of Śiva and Śakti; it is of the nature of consciousness and is the supreme Lord."
It is the eternal object of meditation and concentration for the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
In this, the entire world, consisting of both the moving and the stationary, dissolves;
yet at the time of creation, it proceeds from that eternal Brahman, which is the Liṅga.
Thus, through this etymological derivation, the greatness of the *caraliṅga* is stated to be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman.
Because it is established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and *Āgamas*, its wearing, worship, and so forth are Vedic (*vaidika*).
Since there is no Vedic injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*) for the worship of the form of Viṣṇu, such as the *Sālagrāma* stone and others, their status as Tantric (*tāntrika*) is established.
Furthermore, because attributes of the Supreme Lord such as being the "Lord of the Universe" (viśvapati), which are mentioned in that specific context, are impossible in Nārāyaṇa;

and because in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "to the Lord of animals," "to the Lord of trees," and "to the Lord of worlds," the sovereignty over all the worlds is established for Śiva alone—as in: "For Rudra is one, a second does not exist..."—[Nārāyaṇa cannot be the subject].

Because the status of being the Lord of the world has been refuted for anyone other than Rudra by the mantra "He rules over the worlds with his ruling powers," and because it is heard that he alone possesses supremacy over the universe in the passage "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," Viṣṇu and the others who possess bodies do not possess the status of being the object of worship for all.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of those scriptural passages enjoining the worship of Nārāyaṇa?", it is replied: Just as in such Śrutis as "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," the nature of Brahman is taught to Śvetaketu and others who are practitioners of the meditation on Brahman,
so too, having taught the Brahman-nature of Nārāyaṇa, [the text proceeds] with the passage beginning "resembling the interior of a lotus bud."

Having pointed out that lotus of the heart with the words "In its center is the flame of fire," and having indicated the nature of the individual soul (jīva) with the phrase "the flame of fire," it is then ordained that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is situated within that very flame as its inner controller (antaryāmin), and thus He is to be meditated upon, by means of the passage beginning with "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Indra."

It is determined that [the Supreme Self] is denotable by all words such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and so forth, which are forms of its own manifestation. Likewise, in other Śrutis as well, it is heard that Rudra—who is beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Kālarudra—is the cause of them and is denotable by those very words. [He is described as] the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual, and the Fourth (turīya).

"In the *Māṇḍūkya*, it is held that 'He is the Self; He is to be known. In the *Atharvaśikhā*, it says: 'One should meditate upon the Lord who transcends all; this entire world—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra—all these are brought forth from Him,' and [describes] the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated one."
Beginning with the words "He is the Tranquil One," and continuing with "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hari, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-Ruler;

He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, Fire, and the Moon; He alone is everything that has been and that is to be, the Eternal," and so forth, the establishment of His being denoted by all words is confirmed; thus, no other entity can be established as the object of worship here.
Or rather, I am Hari himself, the omniscient Supreme Person;
the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Beginning thus: "The great-souled Maheśvara, whose seed is drawn up, who has diverse eyes, whose form is the universe,
the blue-necked one, who beholds [all], the destroyer of sins."
Since this has been stated by the Blessed Lord Vādarāyaṇa in the *Dhyānayoga-prakaraṇa* of the *Sūta-saṃhitā* with the words "ityādi" and so forth, the Vedic [scripture] has no other purpose.
Furthermore, in another Smṛti:
"Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed Hari, the lord of great yogis,
revealed his supreme sovereign form to Pārtha. Thus it is said in the Vāmana Purāṇa.
"Then that Hari, the immutable Self, the enemy of Mura, revealed to the gods his own sovereign form (liṅga) resting within the lotus of his own heart. Thus it is said.
Also in the Gītā: "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the region of the heart of all beings. So it is stated in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas.
That Nārāyaṇa is the worshipper and Śiva is the object of worship has been heard with the resonance of a bell.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
"And because of the designation of action and agent. (Sūtra 4.1.36)
Nārāyaṇa is not the one to be worshipped here—why? Because of the designation of object and agent [in the mantra]: "Salutation to Brahman; may there be retention for me, may there be non-removal;
may I be the retainer; what is heard by my ears, let that not depart from me;
for such-and-such, Om. Thus it is stated in the previously mentioned Nārāyaṇa-mantra.

This is because of the designation of Nārāyaṇa as the performer of the ritual of worship consisting in the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga denoted by the syllable *oṃ*. For those seeking liberation who follow the Vedas (*śrauta*), the worship consisting of the attentive practice of wearing, worshipping, and offering to the supreme Śiva-liṅga both externally and internally is indeed mandatory. This begins with the words: "He who is the bull among the Vedas, whose form is the universe... and so forth.

The passage ending with "Protect what has been heard by me" is likewise heard [in scripture]. Furthermore, by the statement "resembling the interior of a lotus bud," the heart-lotus (*dahara-puṇḍarīka*) of Nārāyaṇa, who is the subject under discussion, is taught; and by the subsequent statement ending with "the Supreme Self is situated there," the Supreme Lord is designated as residing within that [lotus]. Thus, Nārāyaṇa is established as the meditator and the Supreme Lord as the object of meditation.

The agency of action (*karmakartṛtva*) is attributed to Paramaśiva; therefore, it is established that Śiva is the object of worship for Nārāyaṇa. Now, one might object: even in the absence of scriptural authority or traditional practice enjoining the meditation on another deity—as in the Vedic text, "Salutation to Brahman; may there be support for me"—[Śiva is accepted] as the representative of Nārāyaṇa.

If it is argued that since the wearing of the conch and discus is established in the Pāñcarātra system, why should this [text] not be intent upon that very practice? We say no—because by the term *anirākaraṇam* (non-rejection), what is rejected (*nirākaraṇam*) is the world of phenomena (*heyaprapañca*) which is to be abandoned;

that which is not so rejected is *anirākaraṇam*. Since this yields the sense that Brahman is that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*), [the text refers to] the word and the characteristic marks of Brahman.

And because they are synonymous, the accomplishment of wearing the *liṅga* follows from the sense of the text without any obstacle. Likewise, the wearing of the conch (*śaṅkha*) is not something to be enjoined, as there is no evidence for assuming such a burdensome meaning.
Now, [we shall discuss] the definition of a Brāhmaṇa.
The mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, wearing the linga on the head,
the topknot, the sacred thread, and likewise the sacred ash— this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
One should abandon like an outcaste that person who has no mark on his forehead, no rosary of rudrākṣa beads around his neck, and no six-syllable mantra in his mouth.
One should not transgress, even in thought, the practice of smearing ashes and the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),
for since these are ordained by the Śruti, one who abandons them becomes fallen.

Thus, because it is heard in the *Smṛtis* of Gautama, Śātātapa, Gāruḍa, and others that the wearing of the *liṅga*, the *tripuṇḍra*, and so forth constitutes a characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa, and that their transgression gives rise to sin; furthermore,
because the wearing of the *liṅga* is established by the *Śruti* as being the most excellent of all through the Tantric injunctions.
Furthermore, since there is no purpose for Vedic [injunctions] in this context, it is not logical to accept both types of injunctions.
"Those who revile the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself;
those who wear it with devotion wear Him Himself."
Thus it is stated in the *Jābāla* and likewise in the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad*. Alternatively, from the passage beginning with "The Lord [should apply] by means of the rules for the *tripuṇḍra*"—

which constitutes the answer to Sanatkumāra’s question— and following the statement "one should draw three horizontal lines," there is the teaching that the three lines consist of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*, which are themselves the essence of the three Vedas.
Furthermore, since the identity with Rudra, Maheśvara, and Sadāśiva is established, it is certain that the wearing of the *liṅga* must be enjoined as both necessary and a cause of supreme merit.

Now, one might object: just as there are injunctions for the wearing of the discus in passages such as "having seen one who bears the *liṅga* or the discus," so too [is there an injunction] for the wearing of the *liṅga*.

If it is argued that because prohibitions are observed, how can there be acceptance based on Śruti, we say no: just as the light of a lamp and the like do not illuminate within the light of the sun, so too the Tantric injunctions and prohibitions do not shed light upon the Śrauta injunction. Since these prohibitions lack a basis in the Veda, their authority should not be questioned.

Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that because this prohibition is tantric in nature and is read within the context of the section on the branding of the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅkana*), its purpose is to prohibit the wearing of heated sectarian marks (*taptaliṅga*). [The scripture says: "One should meditate upon the Lord;
He is to be meditated upon. All these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—are produced from Him. You...
"Viṣṇu is the lord of the gods and the Brāhmaṇas; you are the lord of the Kṣatriyas. For among the gods I am a Brāhmaṇa, and among humans you are a Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Brāhmaṇa;

for he who sacrifices beyond his own deity [incurs sin]," and so forth—in such Vedic passages [is established] that Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the fact that otherwise there is transgression.
Because it is so heard [in scripture]. Smṛti also states:
"Since Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, he is known to have originated from their *piṇḍa*;
thus he must be understood as belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, otherwise he would not be a Brāhmaṇa."
Born from the body of Rudra and having gone to dissolution in the ground of Rudra,
he does not recognize his father, just as the son of a courtesan does not recognize his own father.
The Blessed One Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa; therefore, one born from that *piṇḍa* should be known as a Brāhmaṇa—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Therefore, even for renunciants, a son should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite;
however, on the anniversary of the death of his mother or father, he should not perform the *pārvaṇa* if [the specific conditions are not met].

"Like Buddhists, Mlecchas, and others, he should be shunned; he would be fallen in his own world," and so forth—by such statements, the fact that the birth of a Brāhmaṇa is caused by the *rudra-piṇḍa* (the funeral offering to Rudra) and that his deity is Rudra is specified.
Therefore, the wearing of marks (*lāñchana*) and other such signs belonging to other deities is not to be prescribed for Brāhmaṇas.
One should not dwell for even a single day where the body is not marked with the sign of the wheel;
if one should remain there, that great sinner becomes as if he had killed a thousand Brahmins.
If one wears the Sudarśana, the destroyer of one's lineage, out of ignorance, delusion, or even sport,
one should perform a bath with one's clothes on upon seeing it.
Just as wood found in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual purposes,
so too is a Brahmin marked with the discus excluded from all rites.

Since prohibitions against this are seen in such works as the *Śātātapa*, *Gāruḍa*, *Śaṅkha*, and *Viṣṇu-smṛti* through these and other passages, it is logical that [the text] refers specifically to the wearing of the *liṅga*. This has been stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
Salutations be to you, O Brahman, the great-souled Teacher;
for this universe, being produced, is indeed subject to death, and thus must be refuted by you.
Brahman is non-repudiation, for it is the ancient cause;
that which is non-repudiation is indeed the sustaining support, according to the best of teachers.
Renowned in the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas, and heard by me through my ears— may I become the sustainer of that God who is the cause of all.
The gods, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others who are well-known and likewise remembered,
are all rendered powerless by Death, the enemy of all.
"Let these be rejected by me; they must never be worn.
O gods, may I not become one who wears them while sinking into the water."
They are unable to strike me as I am sinking in the ocean of death;
this *liṅga* of mine is above, so take refuge in both it and me.

Thus, in the verse beginning with "anirākaraṇa," the preeminence of the wearing of all three—the *bhūti* (sacred ash), the *rudrākṣa* (beads), and the *liṅga*—is established by itself through the word "om. Just as in the passage "May I become wise; I alone was first," the optative mood (*liṅ*) in the form of a benediction is prescribed here in the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Raising the doubt as to whether the wearing of an image [of Śiva] might be intended, since the *Jābāla*, *Kālāgnirudra*, and other Upaniṣads illuminate the meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon Śiva, he says:
"Now follows the demonstration of the supreme excellence of both the vision of the *liṅga* and its wearing."
|| 37 || Because of the distinction in sound. || 5 ||

Beginning with "Salutation to the Upward One" (*ūrdhvāya namaḥ*) and ending with "The mantra of the hand is purifying" (*pāṇimantraṃ pavitram*), the text establishes that the *liṅga* alone is the self of all; therefore, the worship of the embodied forms of deities such as Nārāyaṇa is not to be performed here.
Why? Because of the specific wording of the sūtra: "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādyasya yataḥ*), which defines the Brahman that is the object of inquiry.

Because the state of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe— as declared by scriptural authority and the aphorisms beginning with "from which indeed these beings are born"— is indicated by the very word *liṅga*.
[It is so called] because therein and by means of which all that is moving and unmoving dissolves (*līyate*) and is known (*gamyate*).
Therefore, the Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman, the cause of all, and imperishable.

And because of this traditional teaching (*smṛti*): that in which the manifold universe of moving and non-moving beings is joined together and dissolves again at the time of creation, and from which it emerges—that *liṅga*, the substratum of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, is designated as the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in the Purāṇas, the wearing of the *liṅga* and its worship are heard of in many ways.
In the Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Skanda-purāṇa: "Having become Rudra, one should worship Rudra; one who is not Rudra should not worship Rudra.
He who is united with the liṅga of the vital breath (prāṇa) is Rudra; of this there is no doubt."
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths;
humans are superior even to animals, and among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among Brāhmaṇas, the learned are superior; among the learned, those whose intellect is fixed on sacrifice;
among those whose intellect is fixed on sacrifice, the performers [of rites]; and superior to them are the renunciants (saṃnyāsins).
Among them, the wise are best; among them, the worshippers of Śaṅkara are best;
and among them, O fortunate one, those who are united with my liṅga as their own body are the most excellent.
A man who possesses knowledge of the six additional stages (ṣaṭsthala) regarding those attached to the limbs of the Liṅga is superior to him;
there is no one more exalted than he, and he is indeed myself—of this there is no doubt.
The gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and the sages, such as Gautama and others,
always wear the liṅga specifically upon their heads.
Hari, having placed the Liṅga upon his chest, and Pitāmaha (Brahmā), having placed it upon his head,
both attained their respective stations after propitiating me, who am established within the Liṅga.
Wherever one devoted to Śiva remains, his body in contact with the *liṅga*, for even a moment or half a moment, that place is called a field of Śiva (*śivakṣetra*).
Those men who dwell in difficult regions but remain attached to the Liṅga as their limb,
being liberated from all sins, shall go to the supreme goal.
That mortal who follows behind a person who is devoted to the meditation on the *liṅga* and who is attached to the *liṅga* as his body shall also attain liberation.
O Śikhivāhana, the water used for washing the feet of a mortal who bears the *liṅga* should be worn for the sake of purifying sins and ignorance.
Wherever the wind goes after touching the body of one who is solely devoted to the *prāṇaliṅga*, the mortals situated there are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
He upon whose head fall the dust particles from the feet of one who has attained oneness with the Śiva-liṅga for the duration of a Yuga is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Whether it be food or even mere water that is given to one who bears the *liṅga*,
that food is equal to Mount Meru and that water is comparable to the ocean.
Seeing that best of the twice-born performing the union of the *liṅga* and the body, Ravi thought:
"Having pierced my orb, he will depart from this place and go to Śiva."
Merely by the sight of those who possess a connection between their bodies and the Śiva-liṅga,
human beings, as well as beasts, birds, wild animals, and the like, attain liberation.
By such statements as these, because the superiority of perceiving the *liṅga* and its retention is established, the retention of a physical form (*vigraha*) is not enjoined.
Furthermore, in the statement "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," it is taught that Brahman is superior to Nārāyaṇa.

Just as the *prayājas*—understood from sentences such as "He offers the *samidhs*" read within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa—are known to be auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, so too is the heart, which is read within the context of Nārāyaṇa, said to be related to Nārāyaṇa. [As stated: "The Self, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, is hidden in the cave of this [heart]."

"By the grace of the Creator, the man free from sorrow beholds that Lord, the Greatness, who is devoid of desire"—since at the beginning [of this passage], words such as "Lord" (*īśa*), which primarily denote Śiva alone, are explicitly mentioned; and thus, the praise of Śiva, who is established by birth, is intended to be the ultimate purport of the injunction. "Rudra, the Great Seer, is superior to the universe. He...

The repetition is stated to have the following purpose: because the abundance of Śiva is mentioned even in the middle with the words "He is the Supreme Maheśvara," and because there is a description of the praise of the abundant Śiva at the end as well, with the words "Salutation indeed to the one with upward-flowing semen, the three-eyed one, whose form is the universe";
and because characteristics such as being superior to the universe are unique to Him alone, He is called "the unprecedented" (apūrva).
The fruit [of the meditation] is indicated by the passage ending with "all are completely liberated from supreme death.

It is understood that the purpose of the *arthavāda* in the section beginning with "thousand-headed" (*sahasraśīrṣam*) is the praise of Nārāyaṇa. This is supported by the statement: "There is nothing else higher than Him. Thus, through the intended meaning of the entire section—

Because there is the comprehension that Śiva is the ultimate subject, there can be no other intent. Furthermore, the *Sahasraśīrṣā* hymn alone is not the introduction here, because the attributes such as being the Lord of Umā found in the concluding hymn would be inconsistent with Nārāyaṇa. Moreover, in the introductory mantra "smaller than the small," the fact that the Lord resides in the cave of the heart of all conscious beings is established.

Having taught that through His grace alone all beings attain liberation from suffering, and having demonstrated His nature as the source of the activity of creation and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "The seven vital breaths arise" and ending with "Everything is filled by the Puruṣa," [the text continues] with "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth," and so on.

Having commenced with a praise of the Dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*), and having established the qualification for its worship among ascetics (*yati*) through the passage beginning with "The supreme is placed in the cave," [the text] prescribes liberation as the fruit for its worshiper with the statement, "All are completely liberated from the highest immortality."

Having designated the locus for its worship with the words "the small, free from evil," and so forth; having pointed out Maheśvara’s status as the object of worship therein with the words "that sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda," and so forth; and having demonstrated the preeminence of the unique attributes of Paramaśiva by showing that the worship concerns specific qualities through the words "Ṛta and Satya";...

In that arthavāda-praise, having established Nārāyaṇa alone as the primary qualified candidate by virtue of his being a special worshiper, a lord of ascetics (yatīndra), and the foremost among Śiva’s devotees— introducing Nārāyaṇa therein with the passage beginning "Nārāyaṇa,
the great object of knowledge" and so forth, and then [describing him] with the passage beginning "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" and so forth—

Having designated that lotus of the heart, by the statement "the Supreme Self is situated in the center of its crest," the existence of the Supreme Lord within that lotus of the heart is taught; then, having offered praise to the orb of light with the words "this sun indeed shines as this orb," [the text continues] "he who is within the sun..."
By the phrase "the golden person" (*hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the abiding of Rudra as the Supreme Brahman within that solar orb is established;

thereafter, having demonstrated the attributes such as being the Lord of All belonging to Maheśvara—who is to be meditated upon by means of the five Brahma-mantras—his state of being both manifest and unmanifest, like the wind and other elements, is designated by the passage beginning with "Salutation to the one with golden arms" (*namo hiraṇyavāhave*). And so says the Smṛti:
"The great sage Padmagarbha, having realized the singular knowledge of Śiva, taught it to Vasiṣṭha by means of the ascetic Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, there is the word of Śiva in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O fair-faced one, there is no devotee superior to Nārāyaṇa for me;
he formerly attained the state of being my wife, the state of being my bull, and the state of being Bāṇa. Thus spoke Śiva to Aśvatthāman.
"Just as I am to be worshipped by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied action,
therefore no one other than Kṛṣṇa is dearer to me.
And in the Saurasaṃhitā:
Having himself realized the meaning of Śiva’s supreme reality, Śiva spoke thus to Viṣṇu; and Viṣṇu proclaimed it to the one born from the lotus-womb.
Caturmukha [taught] it to Vasiṣṭha; Vasiṣṭha likewise to Śakti;
Śakti to Parāśara; and Parāśara to Vyāsa.
By such statements as these, [it is shown] that Nārāyaṇa and the Supreme Lord possess the relationship of worshiper and object of worship, and disciple and teacher; and furthermore,
by the mark of Nārāyaṇa’s capacity for the contemplation of the jyotir-liṅga delimited by the small space (dahara), which is not shared by any other.

"Whatever is seen or even heard in this world, both within and without—all that is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa and remains established therein. Thus, because these attributes such as being the ultimate reality and all-pervasiveness belong to the Supreme Lord, it is appropriate to offer praise to Nārāyaṇa as the supreme goal, just as in the statements "That art thou, O Śvetaketu" and "Thou art Brahman," which establish the identity of the individual self with the Absolute. This is due to His being the material cause of all and His being the inner controller of all.

The state of being the self of all and being denotable by all words is appropriate for the Supreme Lord alone. "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world; those gods asked Rudra, 'Who are you? He replied, 'I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future. There is nothing whatsoever other than me,' beginning thus... [and so on].

For in the *Atharvaśiras*, beginning with "He indeed is the Lord Rudra, who is Brahmā, who is Viṣṇu, and who is Maheśvara," and in the *Kaivalya* Śruti, "He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa," there is the designation of Him alone as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*).
Furthermore, in the *Muṇḍaka*, *Māṇḍūkya*, *Chāndogya*, *Kaivalya*, *Taittirīya*, and other Upaniṣads, [the same applies] to Paraśiva.

Since it is stated that [the Lord] is to be meditated upon as small, let that [smallness] be appropriate for Him alone. In response to the doubt that— because it is a contradiction for the pure Supreme Lord to reside in the impure left hand, and because it would subvert all [other] marks— wearing the *liṅga* on the body is not enjoined, he says:
And because of Smṛti. || 6 ||

If it is argued that the wearing of the *liṅga* on the hand is not mentioned in any way in the statement "He establishes all *liṅgas*; the mantra of the hand is pure," we say no—why? Because of the *Smṛti*:
"The Dharma of Manu [prevails] in the Kṛta age, the Gautama-smṛti in the Tretā age... [and so forth].
In the Dvāpara age, Śaṅkha and Likhita [were the authorities], and in the Kali age, the Smṛti of Parāśara.

The meaning is that, according to the Smṛtis of Manu and others well-known for the four ages beginning with Kṛta as indicated in such [scriptures], and according to the Smṛti enjoining the wearing of the Śiva-liṅga by Brāhmaṇas, the wearing and worship of other deities must not be accepted by those who follow the Veda. For instance, in the Manusmṛti:
"All [the sages] beginning with Akṣapāda, with supreme joy,
bear the Śiva-liṅga day and night upon the fire of their foreheads.
In that same work, in the description of the yogins of meditation:
"Being intent on the meditation of Śiva, with his limbs conjoined to the Śivaliṅga,
and having abandoned everything other than Śiva— he is called a yogin of meditation. Thus it is stated in the Gautama-smṛti.
The mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, wearing the linga on the head,
as well as the rudrākṣa and sacred ash— this is the characteristic mark of a brāhmaṇa.
"Whether one is unable or indeed able to internalize the *liṅga*,
one should wear the external *liṅga*, because it is certain that [the external] has that same form.
Thus it is stated in the *Śaṅkhasmṛti*.
Just as an insect certainly becomes a bee through union with a bee,
so too a human being always becomes Śiva through union with Śiva.
"One should worship with vigilance the *liṅga* held in the left hand;
the twice-born should always wear it on the head, the heart, and the throat.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Pārāśara-smṛti*.
For those beings who have died in Kāśī—whether they be ascetics or wearers of sectarian marks—they attain the very state of Brahman; indeed, the state of a preta does not exist for them.
For one who worships the Śaiva Liṅga and for one who maintains the sacred fire,
as well as for forest-dwellers and ascetics, there is no period of ritual impurity (sūtaka) affecting their bodies.
"He who worships the Śiva-liṅga, which is identical with Śiva, upon his hand and so forth,
has liberation in the palm of his hand by the grace of Śaṅkara. Thus it is said in the Anuśāsana Parva.

"O best of the Bharatas, what do the Brahmins say regarding the eternal worthy recipient (pātra)—whether it be one who is not a Brahmin but bears the marks (liṅgin), or a Brahmin who does not bear such marks? Thus, in response to Yudhiṣṭhira’s question:
"Having recognized good conduct, whether in one who bears the marks or in another..."
"O Great King, they say that both of these are ascetics who deserve gifts. Thus spoke Bhīṣma.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "In the Vedas, in the collections of Śāstras, in the Purāṇas, and in the Āgamas..."
"The wearing of the *liṅga* is declared to be supreme for the Brāhmaṇa. Beginning thus, it continues:
"The Yajurveda also says, 'Indeed, the *liṅga* establishes everything.
Therefore, the great *liṅga* should be worn with the mantra 'pāṇimantra'. Such is heard in the scriptures.
Now follows the demonstration that Paraśiva-Brahman possesses the nature of the six *liṅgas* within the six stages beginning with *aikya* (oneness),
according to the Siddhāntāgama:
"O fair-faced one, among the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, for the followers of the Vedic path..."
The wearing of the linga has been declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments.
The power of consciousness (cic-chakti) is called Nidhana because it is the principle that presides over dissolution;
since she is a limb of Maheśvara, her status as his consort is established.
Kālarudra is the lord of dissolution and the sovereign of the universal withdrawal;
his nature as the "End-maker" (Antaka) and the "Destroyer" (Hantṛ) is attributed to Śiva alone.
Because the principles beginning with Mahat move toward the upper region,
the Pradhāna is celebrated by the scriptural statement, "to that which is above."
In the statement "to the Ūrdhvaliṅga," Sadāśiva is thus declared;
likewise, in the statement "to Hiraṇya," the causal limb (kāraṇāṅga) is proclaimed.
By the statement "the golden linga," they declare the linga of existence;
by the statement "to the golden one," the subtle body is awakened.
By the statement "the golden liṅga," they declare the prāṇa-liṅga;
by the statement "salutation to the divine one," the gross body is perceived.
In the phrase "to the divine liṅga" (divyaliṅgāya), one's own chosen liṅga is prescribed; likewise, the state of identity is proclaimed by the word "Bhava" (bhavāya).
In the mantra "bhavaliṅgāya," there is likewise the Great Liṅga;
in the mantra "namaḥ śarvāya," the place of refuge is proclaimed.
The *prasādaliṅga* is declared to be in the place of the word *śarva-liṅga*, O Śivā;
indeed, the *prāṇaliṅgi-sthala* is proclaimed by the word *śivāya*.
In the phrase "to Śivaliṅga," the mobile liṅga (caraliṅga) is indicated;
in the phrase "salutations to Jvalāya," the place of grace (prasādasthala) is spoken of.
In the mantra "To the blazing liṅga," the Śiva-liṅga is likewise remembered;
and in the mantra "Obeisance to the Self," the state of Maheśvara is likewise [remembered].
In the statement "for the sake of the self's mark," that which is called the "mark of the Guru" is described;
the stage of the devotee (bhaktasthala) is fully explained by the statement "for the sake of the Supreme."
This is declared to be the sign of conduct (ācāra-liṅga) by means of the term "supreme sign" (parama-liṅga);
it belongs to Soma, who dwells within the orb of Mitra.
The *liṅga* of Soma-Pārvatīśa, which removes the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*),
should always be installed within the bodies of all devotees by the Guru.
Because it is the most purifying among all purifying things, it is called "the Purifier";
therefore, one should always wear the *liṅga* with the mantra "as large as the palm of the hand."
Having placed the *liṅga* in his hand at the time of initiation, the Guru protects (*trāyati*) the devotees through contemplation (*manana*) and worship (*pūjana*); according to this etymology,
that *liṅga* is called the "Hand-mantra" (*pāṇimantra*), the eternal Brahman.
The demonstration that the five Brahma-mantras are of the nature of the thirty-six principles (tattvas):
"In ultimate reality, the nature of the thirty-six principles is always expressed by the mantras known as the five Brahmans; this very nature belongs to that Liṅga."
Salutations be to you, whose nature is that of Sadyojāta and who are the principle of the elements (bhūtatattva);
salutations to you, Sadyojāta, Śarva, and the principle of water (jalatattva).
Salutations to You who, in every state of existence, possess the form of the Great Liṅga and the embodiment of Fire;
likewise, salutations to You who, beyond existence, possess the nature of the element of Air.
Homage to you, Bhava, who take the form of space, the wielder of the trident!
Homage to you, the source of existence, the moon, the principle of fragrance!
Salutation to you, Vāmadeva, to Rudra, to the essence of taste;
salutation to you, Jyeṣṭha, to the form of Śiva, to the essence of form.
Salutation to you, the most excellent one in the form of Hara, the principle of touch;
salutation to you, Rudra, Vāmadeva, the principle of sound.
Salutation to Kāla, to Śarva, and to the one whose self is the principle of the anus;
salutation be to you, the secret principle, the beginning of the Kalavikaraṇa [and other Rudras].
Salutations be to you, the reality of the feet, the transformer of strength;
salutations to strength, to peace, and salutations to you, the reality of the hands.
Homage to you, whose form is the essence of speech, the subduer of strength;
homage be to you, the self of the nose, the tamer of all beings.
Salutation to Mamonmanā, the formidable one, whose essence is the principle of the tongue;
let there be salutation to the non-terrible ones (Aghoras), and salutation to you, the essence of the eye.

And let there be salutation to the terrible ones; salutation be to you, the principle of the skin. And salutation to those more terrible than the terrible; salutation to you, the principle of the ear.
And I bow to all; salutations to you, the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva). And salutations to all the Śaivas; salutations to you, the principle of mind (citta-tattva).
Salutations to you in the forms of Rudra; salutations to you, the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva).
Let there be salutations to Tatpuruṣa; salutations to you, the principle of mind (manas-tattva).
Salutation to Mahādeva, to Soma, to the essence of life;
salutation to that Rudra, the Terrible, who is the form of primordial nature.
Salutation to you, the Lord, the Great Lord, the principle of passion (rāgatattva);
salutation to the one whose nature is all knowledge, the self of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Salutation to the Lord; salutation to the one whose self is the principle of *kalā*;
salutation to the sovereign of all beings, who takes the form of *niyati*.

Salutations to you, the sovereign lord of Brahmā; salutations to you, the principle of Time (kālatattva). Salutations to you, the sovereign lord of Brahmā; salutations to you, the principle of Māyā (māyātattva).
Salutations again and again to you, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the Self, and to Brahman;
salutations to the one whose form is Śiva, who is with Ambā, and who bears the body of Sadāśiva.
Salutations to the one whose nature is Sadāśiva, who is the essence of Śakti;
salutations again and again to you, O Oṃkāra, who are the essence of Śiva-tattva.

The state of being with parts (sakalatva) and the state of being partless (niṣkalatva) of the Supreme Self, who is the Liṅga consisting of the thirty-six principles, are declared according to the subsequent Śruti.
"Therefore, the *liṅga* should always be worn, as long as one lives, like the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
Thus, the wearing of the *liṅga* on the hand and other parts of the body is not contradictory.
Furthermore, [this applies] to that which, by virtue of being an instrument, is devoid of any other independent injunction.

Just as the Sautrāmaṇī and Bṛhaspatisavana sacrifices are established through the combined force of both [the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* and the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*] by virtue of being subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the Agnicayana and Vājapeya respectively, so too here, in the Nārāyaṇa Anuvāka, having commenced with "daharaṃ vipāpam" and having established the wearing of the internal liṅga (*antarliṅgadhāraṇa*) consisting of the contemplation of the light-liṅga (*jyotirliṅgānusandhāna*), [it concludes with] "nidhanapataye namaḥ."
Beginning with these words and ending with "the hand-mantra is purifying," since the external worship of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is also established,

the success of both [internal and external worship] through the force of both [scriptural authorities] is as clear as the ringing of a bell. This establishes that acts such as the worship of the *liṅga* based on the left hand are indeed scripturally sanctioned (*śrauta*).

As for the claim that it is impossible for the followers of the Vedas (*śrauta*) to perform the rites of bearing and worshiping the Supreme Lord with the left hand because of its inferiority—that is trivial. For such an assertion would entail the absurd consequence of [the followers of the Vedas] being like onions (*śuṇṭha*). This is because the Vedic text, "One may drink from the hollowed palms (*añjali*) or from a vessel that is not broken," prescribes the *añjali* formed by joining the hands.

Since the left hand is observed to possess a Vedic status as an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the *brahmayajña*, the libations to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), and as an ancillary to the act of salutation (*namaskāra*), there is no occasion for impurity [to arise from its use].
Therefore, because it is established by the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other authorities, the wearing of the hand-symbol (*pāṇiliṅga*) and its worship are indeed established for those who follow the Śruti.
Therefore, it is stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*: "By the wearing of the *liṅga* alone, the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is warded off;
not otherwise, even through great effort over hundreds of millions of births."
Those in the world who wear the *liṅga* are celebrated as devotees; others are declared to be bound souls (*paśu*). Therefore, one should practice the Pāśupata [path].
Even the gods, such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and sages such as Gautama,
were freed from the state of being bound (paśutva) solely through the wearing of the liṅga.
Thus it has been said.
Now, by virtue of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, the Supreme Lord [appears] in the form of the three desired lingas.
Regarding the determination of limitedness:

in response to the objection that since it is impossible to conceive of a specific small location for the omnipresent Supreme Lord, the meditation on the "small" (*dahara*) and so forth must refer to another deity, he says:

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the object of knowledge] because of its having a small abode and because of designations to that effect, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like the ether. || 39 || 7 ||

"Arbhakaukastvāt" means "because of having a small abode"; that is, because its state is such that it has a small dwelling place (*okaḥ*). This is because of the specific designation of a limited internal and external space in the passages, "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" and "establishing all marks; the mantra is the purifier of the hand," and because of that description. Of that...

And because of the designation of being limited in extent. Since it is designated as being limited in extent by such passages as, "Thin like the awn of a grain of wild rice, yellowish, shining, and resembling an atom," and "The hand is the mantra, the purifier," which describe it as residing within the flame of fire and having the hand as its locus in the form of a *liṅga*, the omnipresent Supreme Lord is not what is taught here—if this is argued, we say: no, for thus...

Because the all-pervading Śiva, who is Brahman, is worthy of bestowing grace upon devotees, He is perceived as a subtle light-liṅga within the heart-lotus (dahara-puṇḍarīka) which has the form of a cave, and as a gross liṅga in the form of the five-syllabled mantra upon the palm of the hand; thus, He can be meditated upon in both gross and subtle forms.
Because practices such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) are possible [in this context], he provides an illustration for that: "And like space.

Just as space, though all-pervading, appears limited through delimitation by such things as lattices, needle-eyes, and apertures, so too the Supreme Lord, by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the gross, subtle, and causal bodies, exists in the form of the three desired signs.
The meaning is that [the Self] is limited by itself yet all-pervading; by this much, there is no loss of its omnipresence. Likewise, it is heard in other scriptural passages:
"The Person is indeed the size of a thumb, for he rests within the thumb."
The Lord, the master of the entire world and the consumer of all, is pleased.
Having contemplated the stainless and pure lotus of the heart, in its center [one perceives] that which is luminous, free from sorrow,
inconceivable, unmanifest, and infinite in form.
Auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman.
The size of the tip of a hair, situated in the center of the heart,
the Viśvedeva, the Jātavedas, the most excellent one—
those wise ones who behold him abiding within themselves, for them [there is eternal peace].
Peace is eternal for them, but not for others.

Whether he is capable of internal concentration or incapable of it, that best of the twice-born should wear upon his chest the Śiva-liṅga— known as the Śāmbhava, denoting the Supreme Brahman— which is worn both internally and externally,
consecrated and bestowed by the Guru.
Thus those who know the Veda understand that it should be maintained by a Brahmin solely for the sake of liberation.
Having placed [the hand] upon the throat, the hand, and the head, he recites this purifying mantra for the hand:
"This is my blessed hand; this is my most blessed one.
This is the universal remedy for me; this is the auspicious touch."
"This is your mother, this is your father; this life-giver has arrived.
This is your path forward; move out for Subandhu.
Thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that the all-pervading [Self] is limited [in its manifestation].
Demonstration that the wearing of ashes is based on the Śruti:

Now, one might object that because no injunction for the wearing of ashes is found in the Śruti or Smṛti as being a primary limb (*aṅga*) of the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon the wearing of the Supreme Lord, it cannot be considered Śrauta; rather, it would merely be a matter of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

This would result in a succession of blind men. If it were to be undertaken based on a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), would it be obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)?

Not the first, because no transgression (*pratyavāya*) is observed for its non-performance. Not the second, because no specific occasion (*nimitta*) is heard of in scripture. Not the third, because there is no injunction specifying a qualified agent (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) such as "one desiring cattle" or "one desiring a son" should wear ashes. [Objection: There is indeed an injunction.
If that were so, how could its prohibition be tenable? For a prohibition is impossible regarding what has been enjoined.

Since injunction and prohibition are mutually contradictory in nature—like darkness and light—it is impossible for them to possess equal force. However, due to the abundance of prohibitory statements in the Smṛtis and Sūtras, it is established that the prohibition itself possesses superior force.
For instance, regarding the initiation into virtuous conduct (*saccaritradīkṣā*), there is the statement of Gautama: "One should not stand upon ashes, chaff, potsherds, or impure things.
And in the *Āpastamba Sūtra*: "If one stands upon ashes or chaff, the foot must be washed."
Having touched incense-fire, lamp-oil, ashes, bone, or a menstruating woman,
a Brāhmaṇa should enter the water with his clothes on.

If it is argued that because a prohibition is seen in the *Śaṅkha-smṛti*—namely, "The *āgneya* bath is with ashes; the *vāyavya* bath is known to be with cow-dust"—and because this is specified as a means for bathing, there must be an injunction for it, [we reply: its purifying nature applies only to the act of bathing itself; otherwise, the prohibitive statements would be contradicted.

If it is argued that [the practice] is indeed enjoined in every respect because the *Atharvaśiras* prescribes the wearing of ashes with mantras—beginning with "Agni" and ending with "one should take the ashes and rub them over the limbs"—then [we reply]:
even that is this *Pāśupata* vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (*paśu*). Thus, it is stated therein.

If it is argued that because the wearing of ashes is seen to be a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the Pāśupata vow being prescribed there, it is not taught as a universal practice, and therefore it is not to be accepted as Vedic (*śrauta*),
we reply to this: in the Ṛgveda— "The triple life-span of Agni, the triple life-span of Kaśyapa..."

"Whatever triple life-span belongs to the gods, may that same triple life-span be mine. Thus [it is said]. In the Jābālopaniṣad: "Those who revile this ash, the light, and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they indeed revile Śiva himself; but those who wear it with devotion, they wear Him alone."
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "One should wear ashes consecrated with the mantra 'Mā nas toke.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is the Sāman, the middle mark is the Yajus, and the lower mark is the Ṛk directly; therefore, the triple-mark (puṇḍra) is the threefold life-span. Thus it is said.

"One should not be negligent regarding prosperity"—this is heard in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka* of the *Yajurveda*: "He is free from passion, free from evil. In this context, "one should not be negligent regarding prosperity" does not mean being intent on sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), because the preceding sentence states: "Having brought pleasant wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny."

Because it is observed that the procedure for collecting wealth—which consists of the characteristics of ordinary sovereignty—is taught [in the context of the word *bhūti*], the term *bhūti* refers exclusively to ashes. In the Bodhāyana Sūtra: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*);
for it is known from scripture: 'One must not neglect the *bhūti* (ashes).'"
In the Mānava Purāṇa:
"Having kindled the fire with ashes, you should cover your body [with them],
and wear the Tripuṇḍra on the forehead, the heart, and both arms."
One must never be negligent, and likewise maintain mindfulness of the syllables of the world.

Thus it is heard [in scripture]. In the Sāma-Śāṇḍilya Śākhā: having taken the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) with the left hand and properly covered it with the right hand using the *raudra-mudrā*, one should consecrate it five times or once with the five Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*. Then, [one applies it] with "Īśāna" on the head, "Tatpuruṣa" on the face, and "Aghorebhyaḥ" [on the heart].

The procedure for this is heard in many ways, beginning with: "Having consecrated the heart with 'vāmadevāya', the waist with 'sadyojātaḥ', and the feet with the *praṇava*, [one consecrates] the entire body," and so forth; and also in the *Sāmamaitreya* recension:
"Having drunk liquor and having gone to the wife of one's guru..."
Having committed theft and having committed the murder of a Brahmin.
Covered in ashes and lying on a bed of ashes,
one who recites the Rudrādhyāya is liberated from all sins.

Thus, it has been established that even for great sins such as the drinking of liquor, the wearing of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*) alone is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). In the *Atharvaśiras*, beginning with "Agni is ash" and ending with "The mind, these eyes—ash," the all-pervading nature of ash is taught; thereafter, one should take up the ash with the mantra beginning with "Agni."
"One should wipe [the body] and touch the limbs," so it is said. Furthermore, regarding the failure to do so, a transgression is heard in the *Vṛddha-Śātātapa*:
"He on whose forehead there is no ash, on whose neck no rosary of Rudrākṣas, and in whose mouth the five-syllabled mantra does not reside—one should abandon him like an outcaste."
And in the Māruḍasmṛti:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for gods and Brahmins; a circle is for kings and Vaiśyas;
a half-moon is for Śūdras; and for others, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka)."
Śātātapa says:
One should never, even in jest, draw the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay;
otherwise, one is tormented by the instruments of Yama's servants in that very shape.
"A person who bears the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the goad, the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, or circular forms,
is purified by the mere wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes.
One who is marked on the body with the conch, the discus, and other weapons of the deities [is likewise purified]."
By the mere wearing of the triple mark with ashes, a person is purified.

By such statements as these, the Gautama Smṛti establishes that for those lowest of Brāhmaṇas who wear the conch, the discus, and the vertical *puṇḍra* marks, the application of sacred ash (*bhasma*) alone is the expiation, and nothing else. In the Jābāla [Upaniṣad]:
"Now listen attentively to the conduct: having taken the ash with the mantra beginning with 'Agniriti' and having rubbed it over the limbs..."
One should touch it and apply the *tripuṇḍra* above; this is the duty (*dharma*) of Brāhmaṇas. Thus says the Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Sandhyā performed without the *tripuṇḍra*, and *japa* performed without the *tripuṇḍra* [are fruitless]."
A śrāddha performed without the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is proclaimed to be demonic.
"A learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) even in his mind;
since it is ordained by the Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen.
Thus, the wearing of ashes is established by numerous Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas.
Its being the subject matter of Vedic injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*) is beyond dispute.

Now, after the rule for the wearing of ashes has been established in various ways through such passages as "Sanatkumāra questioned the Lord Kālāgnirudra," at the conclusion of the *Kālāgnirudra Upaniṣad*:
"Whether he be a learned student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic, whoever applies the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) with ashes becomes purified from all major and minor sins;
he is as one who has meditated upon all the gods; he is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)," and so forth.

If it is argued that the application of the rule for the wearing of ashes (*bhasmadhāraṇa*) does not fall under the category of obligatory injunctions (*nityavidhi*) because its fruit is declared and because a transgression (*pratyavāya*) is prescribed for its non-performance—this is not so; for even in cases such as "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" and "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the obligatory Agnihotra, Jyotiṣṭoma, and so forth are likewise declared to have fruits. Thus, those [obligatory rites] too [would be subject to the same logic].

It would not be the subject of an obligatory injunction (*nityavidhi*). If it is argued that the status of rites such as the *agnihotra* as obligatory injunctions is beyond dispute because of scriptural statements regarding the sin incurred by non-performance— such as "He who extinguishes the sacred fire [commits a sin] toward the gods"—
then for those who never develop faith in the Vedic ashes:

"It is certain that they do not possess the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). Thus, because the *Jābāla* [Upaniṣad] shows that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in failing to perform them, it is established that these rites are the subject of obligatory injunctions (*nityavidhi*). Therefore, the prohibition of ash established by the previously cited Smṛti refers specifically to ash found on bones, potsherds, and the like.
The prohibition "one should not apply [it]" does not intend to forbid the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes;

for the wearing of ashes is enjoined by many Smṛtis, such as those of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, as well as the Jābāla, Manu, Yājñavalkya, Gautama, Śātātapa, Skanda, Liṅga, Śaiva, Kūrma, and others.

Furthermore, its status as Śruti is established because it is proven by numerous Purāṇas and Itihāsas. Regarding the demonstration of the scriptural authority (*śrautatva*) of wearing Rudrākṣas, it is stated in the Kātyāyana Śākhā: "Indeed, those Rudrākṣas are those which the Vedas wear."

"Therefore, the gods uphold them; he who goes, stands, eats, sleeps, or opens his eyes while wearing them, overcomes all sins and, having become Rudra, becomes like Rudra. Thus it is said in the seventh Brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhajjābāla Upaniṣad:
"In the wearing of auspicious Rudrākṣas, there shall be great power."
"That which is the size of an *dhātrī* fruit is declared to be the best. Thus it is said.
In the *Saṃvarta-smṛti*:
"In bathing, giving, recitation (*japa*), fire-offering (*homa*), the *vaiśvadeva* rite, and the worship of the gods..."
Likewise, at the time of expiation, during a śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation.
"Whatever Vedic rite a Brahmin might perform out of delusion without wearing Rudrākṣa beads, he does not obtain the fruit thereof. Thus it is said.
Long ago, when my eyes were opened due to the affliction of Tripura, drops of water fell from them upon the earth; those became the Rudrākṣas.

For it is seen in the *Śāṇḍilya-śākhā*, included within the *Kramāmnāya*, that there is a prescription for the wearing of Rudrākṣas stating: "By being born [with them], and by seeing or touching them, one obtains the fruit of giving away a thousand cows; by wearing them, one becomes purified from the great sins (mahāpātaka) and minor sins (upapātaka), such as killing a Brahmin, killing a cow, and stealing gold."
Furthermore, its status as Śruti is determined by hearing of its greatness in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, the *Itihāsas*, and other such texts.

Now, regarding the statement that the acceptance of the grace of the water from the feet (*pādodaka*) is Vedic—even in the *Śiva Purāṇas*, it is said: "My food offering (*naivedya*), the remains of the garland (*nirmālya*), and likewise the water [offered] are unworthy for me," and so forth.

Because Śiva himself stated that the grace of the water from his own feet (pādodaka-prasāda) must not be consumed, and since the fruit of Śiva-worship is solely its prasāda, the prohibition of that prasāda effectively implies a prohibition of the worship itself.
It is said by the sages that what is offered to Viṣṇu is pure and fit to be eaten.
But having consumed the remains of offerings (nirmālya) belonging to others, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
The auspicious water from the feet of Viṣṇu removes untimely death, destroys all diseases, and pacifies all sins.
The water of the Śālagrāma stone is especially destructive of sins;
it serves as a daily expiation for the sins committed since birth.

If it is argued that, because the injunctions for receiving the grace of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet are seen in such Smṛtis as these, the worship of Viṣṇu and so forth alone is prescribed for all followers of the Vedas—
it is replied: [the same applies] to the worship of Śiva, the water from Śiva’s feet, and the grace of Śiva, just like the Agnihotra and other rites.

Because it is enjoined by the Vedas, Vedāntas, Āgamas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, it possesses the status of being Vedic (*śrauta*) and is to be accepted as such. Since Tantric injunctions are observed, the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites pertain specifically to those qualified for the Tantras.
Because Śiva is Brahman, he is to be worshipped by Brahman. This has been stated in the *Chāndogya* Upaniṣad, in the *Prapada-brāhmaṇa*:
"He approaches the Brāhmaṇa," it says. In the Yajurveda: "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all;
the overlord of Brahman, the overlord of the sacred word—may Śiva be mine, Sadāśiva Om. And in another Śruti:
"This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa; therefore, Brāhmaṇas have Soma as their king; Soma is ours."

Because the identity of Mahādeva with the Brāhmaṇas and his status as their sovereign are established in such Vedic texts as, "Soma alone is the king of the Brāhmaṇas; 'He is our king,' so say the Brāhmaṇa subjects," and so forth, Mahādeva alone is the fit object for seeking refuge and for propitiation by the Brāhmaṇas, since they are supported by the Brāhmaṇas. As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor of the letters in both their direct and reverse orders;
specifically, one should go for refuge to Rudra as the Lord of the Brāhmaṇas.
And in the *Manusmṛti*:
"Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, Mādhava of the Kṣatriyas,
Brahmā likewise of the Vaiśyas, and the Leader of the Gods (Indra) of the Śūdras. Thus it is stated in the Pārāśarya Purāṇa.
The Supreme Lord is the most excellent among all the gods;
for a relationship is appropriate between two who are both most excellent, but not with one who is otherwise.
Therefore, a relationship with Śiva alone is indeed fitting for the Brahmin.
All the gods are of mixed origin, while Purandara is a Śūdra;
the Grandfather (Brahmā) is a Vaiśya, and Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya.
The Blessed One Rudra is the Brāhmaṇa, the highest of all;
for Rudra, who is of the nature of Brahman, his status as a Brāhmaṇa is not born of any cause.
In this world, it is indeed the Brāhmaṇa who always seeks refuge with a Brāhmaṇa;
no one else—the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, or even the Śūdra, nor those of mixed caste—does so.
Therefore, a twice-born Brāhmaṇa should always approach the Great Brāhmaṇa, the Lord, by means of the Veda as his path, and not anyone else.
"He who does not fall into confusion regarding Virūpākṣa, the best of the twice-born, who is the self of all selves—for him there is no doubt in this world. Thus [it is said].
The Śruti also says: "He who indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity, but does not reach the higher one."
"He incurs sin and becomes worse.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "Those who, having abandoned their own deity, worship another deity..."
They should be known as heretics, excluded from all ritual acts.
"One who is not a portion of a god does not give food; one who is not Viṣṇu is not a lord of the earth;
one who is not a Ṛṣi does not compose poetry; and one who is not Rudra is not a reciter of the *krama-pāṭha*.
Thus, in the Dharmaśāstra, it is stated that a Brāhmaṇa who recites the Veda is a portion of Rudra. Therefore, for those seeking liberation...

For those following the Vedic path, worship of that [liṅga] alone must be performed. Since the Śiva-liṅga is established by the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas through such [mantras] as "Obeisance to Nidhanapati," it alone possesses the status of being Vedic;
whereas because the Sālagrāma stone and others are primarily Tantric in nature, they possess only the status of being Tantric.
The worship of the *liṅga* and so forth is also established in all the Vedas. In the Ṛgveda: "O Rudra, for the sake of your glory the Maruts offer praise;
that which is your beautiful and wondrous birth, and that station of Viṣṇu which was established as supreme—by that you protect the secret name of the cows."

The meaning of this is: O Rudra, that beautiful and wonderful (*cāru citram*)—meaning the manifold manifestation (*janima*), such as jewels, gold, silver, stone, coral, and so forth—which has appeared as your *liṅga*; for the sake of your glory (*śriye*), the Maruts—the gods—placed it near you (*upa-mam*);
"upa" means near, and "mam" refers to that which possesses *lakṣmī* (splendor). Thus, it is "upama."

The station of Viṣṇu, characterized by the fortune that bestows all gifts, has been established as his sovereignty. You, possessing the name which is the secret—the mystery—of the cows, that is, of the Vedas, protect—that is, you guard—it. The expansion of this [passage] is found in the Parāśara Purāṇa:
Having worshipped with devotion a beautiful and variegated Raudra-liṅga made of pure stone, Mahāviṣṇu attained the supreme state.
And she is celebrated as Lakṣmī, the beloved of Mahāviṣṇu;
having worshipped and honored whose linga, it is to be adored by all sentient beings.
"Brahmā, the creator of the entire world, [attains his status] indeed through the worship of his *liṅga*.

Likewise, in the Yajurveda: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he release us from death, as one releases a cucumber from its stem, while remaining in immortality. In another Śruti: "Worship him, O Priyamedhas, worship him well!"
In such scriptural passages as "Worship! Let them worship, O sons! And again, worship with boldness! Worship! Worship forth!

the Supreme Lord's status as the one to be worshipped and the gods' status as the worshippers are heard. Therefore, it is established that the worship of Śiva is the subject of the obligatory (nitya) injunction. He who destroys the three cities [Tripura] is *Punarnam*, meaning Sadāśiva.
And regarding the sin incurred by failing to perform that [rite], it is heard in the *Ṛgveda*: "They seek him within the people, Rudra, beyond [the reach of] thought;
they seize the one with the tongue as his weapon. Here, "in the people" (*jane*) refers to those situated among the people—the singular being used for the class (*jātāvekavacanam*).
"Beyond" (*paraḥ*) means the supreme (*utkṛṣṭam*) Rudra; the inversion of word order (*vacanavyatyaya*) therein is a Vedic license (*chāndasaḥ*). "Within" (*antaḥ*)—

Those worshippers who, with *manīṣā*—that is, intentionally and with prior reflection—seek [the Self] within the small ether (*daharākāśa*), those people seize—that is, they consume—the food consisting of the various modifications of *saṃsṛti*.
The sense is that those who eat without the propitiation of Rudra are merely consuming excrement with their tongues. As it has been said:
In the Vṛddha-Śātātapa: "Those who do not desire Śiva, accompanied by Bhavānī,
within [themselves], undoubtedly lick excrement with their tongues."

"Therefore, one should worship Śiva, the Great God, endowed with devotion. Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'they desire within,' since only a mental activity is observed, how can this refer to external worship? This is not so; for "what one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs through action. Thus, what is in the mind is [ultimately expressed externally].

"Of the great-souled ones, one [mode of worship] is through speech and one is through action"—thus, because the Śiva-pūjā is taught by means of the mind, speech, body, and actions according to the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas; and by the statement "desiring within," external Śiva-pūjā is also established by implication. Furthermore, in the Āpastamba Sūtra:

"Therefore, we study; one should study while wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*), saying: 'We worship Rudra for the sake of his goodwill. Because the supreme *liṅga* of Śiva is established [in the body] by means of the sacred thread, its worship and so forth are also established by implication. As stated in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*:
"The Great God, established in the Veda, accompanied by Ambā, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel..."
Day after day, people afflicted by the delusion of false doctrines will, out of ignorance, fail to worship the Lord in the *liṅga* under such names as Śiva, Rudra, and so forth.
Since this is well-known in numerous Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇa, and Itihāsa texts such as these, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga alone is the duty enjoined for those who follow the Śruti.
He who, disregarding Vedic rites, performs only those actions prescribed by the Smṛtis...

"Whatever one performs out of delusion, one is not tainted by merit"—this statement from the *Manusmṛti* contradicts direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Therefore, practices such as the five-fold worship (*pañcapūjā*) established in the Smṛtis—such as those directed toward Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara—are to be accepted as non-Vedic (*aśrauta*). As it has been said:
In the *Pārāśarya*: "Those who, having abandoned the Lord Śambhu, worship another deity,
fall undoubtedly into a most terrible hell."
In the Śivagītā:
"Having abandoned such a God as Him, he who serves another deity is indeed like one who,
having left the Ganges, longs for a mirage."
The demonstration that the acceptance of Śiva’s grace is established by the Vedas:

through such passages as "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the bestower of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else," the Vedic nature of the worship of the Śivaliṅga and its universal acceptability are indeed established by the Śruti. Therefore, [this applies] to the grace of Śiva.
Even though there are prohibitions regarding the Tantras, it is proper to accept them because the Vedic injunctions are more powerful.
Furthermore, in the *Saura-saṃhitā*, Lord Vyāsa clearly stated in a dialogue with Jaimini:
"My remains from offerings (*nirmālya*), the water from my feet, flowers, and leaves are unfit [for ordinary consumption]."
Thus it was spoken by the Lord—so say some great seers.
"O Lord, tell me truly how it is that they speak thus."
To Jaimini, who had thus questioned him, he replied:
"O Jaimini, those who are cursed by Vīrabhadra and are averse to devotion to Śiva fall within the scope of the words of the God of gods."
Those who are devoted to deities other than Śambhu, those who have not been initiated, those whose actions are impure, and those whose intellects are fixed on doctrines other than Śambhu’s;
"For them, those fourfold favors of the Lord are not appropriate.
In that very context, the word of the Lord is: "My used remains of offerings (nirmālya), the water from my feet, the flower, and the leaf—"
It expands, in due order, upon dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
O Goddess, through the service of my *naivedya*, one attains that state which would otherwise require thousands of *ekādaśī* fasts and ten million emaciations of the body.

Since the procedure for accepting Śiva’s grace (*prasāda*) is shown in that very [text] by such passages as "thus," the grace of Śiva must indeed be accepted by the devotees of Śiva; thus, because the prohibition concerns those who are not devotees, there is no contradiction between the injunction and the prohibition.
In the *Kāmika*:
Everything experienced by Śiva is designated as *nirmālya*;
it is intended to be of two kinds—*bhojya* (to be consumed) and *dhārya* (to be worn)—and is further considered to be of six types.
The property of the deity, the substance belonging to the deity, the food offering (naivedya) that has been presented,
the substance for Caṇḍa cast outside, and the remains of the offering (nirmālya)— these are remembered as the sixfold [categories].
The property of the gods consists of village lands and the like, as well as four types of male and female slaves;
gold, silver, gems, and so forth are recorded in tradition as the wealth of the gods.
Whatever substance is mentally intended for Śiva is called *naivedya*;
likewise, garlands, perfumes, food, drink, and so forth that have been enjoyed by Śiva [are also offered].
That which has been offered to a consecrated *liṅga* by gods, sages, or men is called *nivedita*. It is the food offering (*naivedya*) that has been presented.
