That is called "fierce substance" (caṇḍadravya), offered during the morning twilight;
it is said to be of six kinds, including leaves and flowers cast outside.
"When a self-manifested Bāṇaliṅga made of moonstone is situated in the heart,
it is said that the merit of a hundred sacrifices is gained from consuming the remains of Śambhu’s offerings.
And in the Dharmaśāstra:
In the case of a self-manifested (*svayambhu*) linga, one made of bamboo, one made of gems, one fashioned from silver,
or a linga consecrated by a perfected being (*siddha*), there shall be no appointment of a *caṇḍa* attendant.
One should consume the pure remains of Śambhu’s offerings without negligence;
however, having consumed the remains of another's offerings, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"He who is celebrated as the one and only Rudra in all the Vedas—from him a Vedic practitioner should always eat food that has been consumed by Śiva alone. Thus [it is said].
In the Ṛgveda: "O most auspicious Rudra, take this from us; may we partake of it through your most healing remedies."

"May I drive away my hatred from my father," and so forth. The meaning of this is: O Rudra, having partaken of those most peaceful (*śantamebhiḥ*)—that is, most blissful (*sukhatamaiḥ*)—remedies (*bheṣajebhiḥ*) given by you, which are remedies against the fear of *saṃsāra* and the causes for its removal; thus is the construction. I, who have worshipped you, my father... [text continues].

"Free from hatred"—meaning one whose ego (*ahaṃkāra*) has departed; therefore, "free from sin," I have become so. The meaning is: "favor me. This is because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*): "Śiva himself is my father. Thus it is stated in the *Ṛgveda Upaniṣad*.
"Everything that exists in this world, whatever moves within the universe, is pervaded by the Lord.
By renouncing it through Him, you should enjoy; do not covet the wealth of anyone.
This is its meaning: "All this" refers to the world consisting of stationary things, and "whatever moves within the universe" refers to the world consisting of moving things.

And the entire collection of living beings is to be inhabited by the Lord (Īśāvāsya)—according to the Śruti: "It is to be inhabited by the Lord" (īśena śivaliṅge āvāsyaṃ). Therefore, you should eat with that which has been relinquished by the Śiva-liṅga, namely the *prasāda* remaining from what has been consumed;

for among those who follow the Śruti, there is a prohibition against the *prasāda* of deities other than the Supreme Lord, as expressed in the mantra: "O greedy one, whose wealth would you covet? (gṛdhraḥ kasyasvid dhanam).
It is thus prescribed. Likewise, in the Yajurveda: "O Rudra, in your guidance (*praṇīti*), that which Manu, the father, worshipped—both the *śam* (peace) and the *yoḥ* (well-being)—that [we] obtain.

O Rudra, in your guidance—that is, in your worship—the father, who is the cause of the world's birth and so forth, and who is Manu, consisting of the mantra, [worshipped] that which is *śam*, the bestower of happiness, and *yoḥ*, which is described as distinct from it.
I have obtained this prasāda, both cooked and uncooked;
may we eat this prasāda which has been enjoyed by you.
As stated in the Jābāla Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāma Veda: "One should eat what has been eaten by Rudra, drink what has been drunk by Rudra, and accept what has been given by Rudra."

"One should smell [it] and eat what has been taken by Rudra; therefore, Brahmins with tranquil minds eat only the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) and consume only the *nirmālya*. Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The disciplined and the peaceful indeed eat only that which has been eaten by Rudra."
"For they smell only what has been smelled, and they drink only what has been drunk.
Thus [it is said]. In another section of the Yajurveda: "By Rudra, food is nectar; indeed, the gods, desiring to eat, and the Vedas desire [it] through Rudra.
By Rudra—that is, by the Lord—food is eaten; therefore, food is nectar, [that is,] grace."

The meaning is "they desire. In the Kāṇva recension [it says]: "If one should eat what is eaten by Atri, O Gopsātama—if one has eaten sin—eat the pure, eat the evil; he goes downward. He who has three cows is *triguḥ*, that is, the Three-eyed One (*trilocana*). *Psātam* means "eaten"; the root *psā* means "to eat. Thus, *atrigupsātam*.

If one should eat what has been offered to a non-Lord (anīśvara), he eats sin; he goes downward, meaning he falls into hell. Likewise, it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "He who eats, chews, and swallows food without having first offered it to Śambhu [is a sinner]."
"He eats dog-flesh and consumes the *sūtra*, and he both chews and protects.
Now, the procedure for the water for the feet (*pādodaka*) according to the *Bodhāyana-śākhā*: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the water for the feet of Mahādeva."

Having established the Lord Mahādeva— the auspicious, pure, infinite, unborn, and desired one— with the *Śrīrudra* hymn, with the *pavitra* (sacrificial ring), and with the hundred-streamed and thousand-streamed [mantras], and having consecrated him with the two verses beginning with "All is indeed Rudra" (*sarvo vai rudraḥ*),
and having sprinkled water upon his head, he should cause [the disciple] to consume [the remainder] with the mantra "Truth is the Cosmic Order" (*ṛtaṃ satyam*). Regarding this, Jābāla says:
Having washed the feet of the Blessed One, having filled a conch shell, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice, and having offered the *caru* oblation,

one should consecrate it with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge"; then, performing the sprinkling on the head with the mantra "kadrudrāya", one should drink the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*) with the mantra "ṛtaṃ satyam".
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā it is said:
"The worship of Śiva should be performed immediately after the worship of the fire;
thereafter, one should oneself eat pure food offered to Śiva."
In the Śivadharmottara-śāstra:
"One who eats a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, food, drink, or medicine without having offered it to Śiva immediately becomes a sinner. Thus it is said.
In the *Śātātapa-smṛti* it is said: "Fire has a terrible form, while the *liṅga* is called Aghorā;
therefore, having first worshipped the *liṅga*, one should thereafter worship the fire."
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"He who performs the Prāṇāgnihotra by the grace of Śiva alone obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices; there is no doubt about this."
Uttering the praise of Śaṅkara with every morsel of food, one should be known as always fasting and liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
In the Vedas, it is sung that Śiva is the God of the Brāhmaṇas;
therefore, he is present in the Prāṇāgnihotra as well as in the Soma sacrifices and others.

"In the Pārvaṇa rite, in the Vaiśvadeva, and likewise in the Śivāgnikaraṇa, one should perform the rites according to the procedure for Śiva’s grace (Śivaprasāda), and not otherwise. Thus it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "He who, at the time of the Śrāddha, offers with devotion the remnants of what has been eaten by Śiva to the ancestors and the deities..."
"By that very same rice-ball mixed with sesame seeds, the ancestors remain well-satisfied for ten million kalpas. Thus it is said in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
"The middle rice-ball, offered to those in the forms of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, bestows sons."
"What need is there for further talk? The offering of Rudra (rudranirmālya) is declared in the Vedas.
Thus [it is said]. In the Yajurveda, in such scriptural passages as: "O Paśupati, I bind this animal for you today at the beginning of the well-performed rite;
consider it with favor, let us sacrifice with a good sacrifice; may this oblation be pleasing to the gods," and so forth.
Because everything, including the form of the sacrificial animal, is designated as a grace (*prasāda*) of Śiva:
"O Fathers, take up the embryo, the boy with the lotus-wreath;
that which here is the essence of man, the wife consumes it."
Thus, because the *Āpastamba Sūtra* teaches that the birth of a Brāhmaṇa is caused by the *rudra-piṇḍa*, and because the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* states:
"One should desire many sons who follow the mantras of Śiva."
They uplift their lineage, just as a rope with a jar draws [water] from a well.

Since this is established by such sources as the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Āgamas, the consumption of the water of Śiva’s grace (prasāda) is a duty enjoined for those following the Śruti. Furthermore, the ringing proclamation of the Śaiva Siddhānta is that prohibitory statements regarding this refer either to "Caṇḍa" substances or to those who have not received Śaiva initiation. This is because, if one were to accept only the injunctions of Tantric Smṛtis that prohibit Śiva-prasāda, [the aforementioned scriptural authority would be contradicted].

Otherwise, it would follow that the Vedas, Vedāntas, Smṛtis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, previously mentioned, would be rendered as good as water poured out in libation (i.e., discarded).
Therefore, because of the consequence of being outside the Vedic fold, the previously stated view alone is correct.
Furthermore, in the fourth skandha of the Bhāgavata:
Do Brahmā and the other gods, besides you, not know that what is called Śiva is actually inauspicious, since they scatter him in the cremation grounds with matted hair and beard,
and carry him on their heads like a head-splitting, excellent Piśāca adorned with garlands, ashes, and human skulls?
"Released from his feet.
Thus it is said in the *Rāmāyaṇa*:
"There, the celestial sages (*devarṣi*), the *gandharvas*, and those dwelling upon the surface of the earth..."
"They touched the water fallen from the limbs of existence (bhavāṅga), thinking it to be pure.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"That [water] emerged from the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks, [carrying] bones like gravel..."
Having flooded [the earth], he led those sinful sons of Sagara to heaven.

Thus, since the injunction for accepting the prasāda of Śiva is seen in the *Bhāgavata*, *Rāmāyaṇa*, and *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, and because the prohibition of accepting the prasāda of Viṣṇu is seen in the eleventh skandha of the *Bhāgavata* through such statements as "I would not even use the light of a lamp offered [to You]," it is indeed the prasāda of Śiva [that is intended].
He is to be accepted by the Vaidikas.
Now, [it may be objected]: in the fourth book of the Bhāgavata it is said:
"Adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, and ornaments used by You..."
May we cross over your illusion, O servants who feed upon leftovers!

If it is argued that even the injunction for accepting the grace of Viṣṇu is seen in such passages as these, we reply: since there is no Vedic injunction regarding the acceptance of that grace of Viṣṇu,

and because of this statement and the qualifying term "those who eat the leavings" (*ucchiṣṭabhojina udāsāḥ*), [the practice of] having horizontal marks, vertical sectarian marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the branding of the heated discus (*taptacakrāṅka*), and so forth— [is rejected].

It is to be accepted only by the followers of the *Pāñcarātra* and other Tantras, not as food fit for Vaidikas. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering redundant such statements from the Eleventh Canto as "Do not covet the offering presented [to the deity]," as well as the words of the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad* which were previously elaborated upon.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A follower of the Vedas should always accept the remains of offerings (nirmālya) consumed by Śambhu;
he would not do so even with his life-breaths at his throat for food consumed by Viṣṇu. Thus it is said.
In the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*:
"The food of Mādhava must not be eaten under any circumstances by the best among the Vaidikas;
one should, however, eat without negligence the food that has been partaken of by Sadāśiva."
In the Śāṇḍilya-smṛti:
"The food of Mādhava (Viṣṇu) must not be eaten by those who follow the Śruti and desire liberation;
rather, that which has been partaken of by Śiva should be eaten, according to the sole instruction of the Śrauta injunctions."
Śātātapa says:
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Vaiśya, one who with a deluded mind eats the food of one residing in the temple of Viṣṇu shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

By such statements, it is determined that the scriptural passages prohibiting the grace (*prasāda*) of Viṣṇu refer to the primary [Vedic] sense, whereas the prohibitions against the grace of Śiva refer to other than the primary [Vedic] sense. Furthermore:
"In the case of a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative."
But when there is a conflict between two scriptural statements, the specific injunction is declared [to prevail].

According to this principle, because there is an abundance of statements regarding the acceptance of Śiva’s grace, it is not logical that [the texts] have any other meaning. Is the lack of authority for those statements— which define the supreme qualified recipient of Śiva’s *nirmālya*— due merely to the existence of prohibitions,
or rather due to their being established as having no other possible purpose?

Not the first [alternative]; for if that were so, since one would observe mutual contradictions within the established scriptures— due to differences in stages of life (*āśrama*), caste (*varṇa*), age-cycle (*yuga*), Vedic branches (*śākhā*), place, time, and person, as well as following the distinctions between general and particular entities— it would follow that the entire scripture is invalid.

And [the prohibitions] of those such as Āpastamba who prohibit renunciation (saṃnyāsa), who prohibit women and Śūdras from reciting the Vedas, who prohibit non-violence (ahiṃsā) in general, who prohibit agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and so forth,
who prohibit libations (tarpaṇa) performed with one hand, and who prohibit marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle (mātula) and other such matters.

If it is argued that the scripture possesses some degree of authority because of the existence of such statements, then it would follow as a consequence that [the opponent] is entirely outside the Vedic fold.

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for, as in the case of the offerings made at sunrise or before sunrise, this is merely according to the principle of "not disparaging" (*na-dvitīya-na-hi-nindā-nyāya*).

This is because the prohibitory statements regarding the grace of Śiva found in various Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other texts are established as having another purpose— namely, their intent being to praise rituals such as the Agnihotra. For instance, the authors of the Smṛtis and others, while establishing the necessity of performing rituals like the Agnihotra and intending to offer praise for them, [uttered those prohibitions].

The orientation toward ritual action preceded by its censure has indeed been established. By the authors of the Purāṇas, beginning with Śiva, who demonstrate the necessity of accepting Śiva’s grace, it is taught that eating food other than Śiva’s grace is like eating dog-meat; this is set forth along with the requirement for expiation and the subsequent avoidance of contact with such persons.

Censure has been expressed regarding the wearing of non-ascetic marks (*aliṅgadhāraṇa*) and so forth; likewise, there is no intention to censure in either case, but rather the intention is solely for praise. Therefore, this systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) must certainly be adopted; otherwise, there would be the consequence of mutual contradiction. Consequently, by the principle of "not-censuring" (*na hi nindā nyāya*), the prohibitive statements therein [are to be understood as praise].
Because there is no such intention [to deceive], all scripture is indeed authoritative, distinguished by the specific qualifications of its respective practitioners as previously stated.
Now, one might object: "In that case, does it not follow that even the Buddhist scriptures possess authority? We say: No, because they lie outside the Veda.

Since the worship of Śiva, the practice of devotion to Śiva, the inquiry into the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), and the water of Śiva’s grace are all established in the Vedas and Vedānta, the Śaiva scriptures are of the nature of the Veda. Furthermore, according to the intended meaning of our Master,
the Pāñcarātra and other such systems are also "apparent Vedism" (prātibhāsika-vaidika), as they consist of descriptions of the meaning of the Śrutis.

Thus they are called. Therefore, there is a distinct difference in the Buddhist scriptures. Regarding the invalidity of the Vedas, the intent of the Buddhist scripture is solely to prohibit them, just as the drinking of liquor is prohibited; it is like the rule that one should not look upon Viṣṇu at the time of twilight (pradoṣa). As stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should not look upon Hari at twilight, especially on the thirteenth lunar day."
If one should see [the sun] through negligence, there is a loss of twelve years' worth of merit.
And in the Skanda Purāṇa: "If one should look upon Hari at dusk, or if one should look upon him through negligence, four things of his perish: life-span, wisdom, fame, and strength."
The fact that the practice of beholding Viṣṇu at the time of dusk (pradoṣa), his worship, recollection, and the acceptance of the grace of his foot-water (pādodaka) and so forth,
is to be adopted outside of the Śruti, because it is not based on the Śruti— enough with this elaboration.
[Now follows] the statement that the Supreme Śiva, who is none other than Brahman, assumes a physical body for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.

Fearing that if Śiva, the omnipresent Supreme Brahman, were to assume a body for the sake of showing grace to his devotees, he would be subject to pleasure and pain—just like embodied beings such as Nārāyaṇa and others—the Sūtra refutes this:
"If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment [of pleasure and pain], we say no, because of the difference in nature. (40) 4.4.8.

If it is argued that the Supreme Lord—who is a wish-fulfilling tree for His devotees and who assumes divine, auspicious forms at His own will—undergoes the experience of pleasure and pain like an individual soul (*jīva*), we say no. Why? Because of the difference in nature (*vaiśeṣyāt*). [The Upaniṣad says: "Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this creature; the one free from sorrow beholds Him, the desireless Creator."
In the passage "By grace [I know] the greatness of the Lord," there is the teaching that He transcends the *praṇava* (Om) and is to be meditated upon within the lotus of the heart of all;
and in passages such as "The Lord of all sciences," there is the teaching of His unique attributes, such as being the sovereign of all knowledge. Salutations...

Furthermore, because attributes such as having a body composed of light are taught in passages beginning with "To him whose arms are golden" (*hiraṇyabāhave*), [the Lord] is not the individual soul (*jīva*).

Therefore, since this highlights a distinct excellence, even though the individual soul and the Supreme Self are one in consciousness, their qualities of omnipresence and atomicity, and their respective lack and presence of dependence on a body, remain distinct; thus, the Supreme Lord never shares the status of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain like the individual soul.

It is possible [that the soul experiences pleasure and pain]. However, just as one who relies on the science of fire-suppression has no fear of burning, how can it be consistent for one who has mastered *māyā* to be an experiencer of pleasure and pain created by *māyā*? Therefore, the author of the Sūtras taught the term "vaiśeṣya. *Vaiśeṣya* is simply *viśeṣa*; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (to form an abstract noun). This is so in another mantra, "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*).

Furthermore, since the individual soul's state of being an enjoyer of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and the Supreme Lord's lack thereof are thus indicated, the mutual distinctness of the two is firmly established.
Moreover, [the Lord's] connection with a body assumed by His own will is not the same as the individual soul's connection with a body produced by karma.

This is a distinction. Therefore, by means of the sixfold marks of purport—beginning with the opening statement "smaller than the small"—it is indicated that even the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad teaches Paraśiva; thus, in this context, Nārāyaṇa is designated as the worshipper and Paraśiva as the object of worship.
Demonstrating the nature of difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman:
Now, [consider] such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," "That thou art," "I am Brahman," and "This Self is Brahman."

If it is argued that because of the teaching of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, their innate difference—which consists of mutually contradictory natures like those of a jar and a cloth—can never cease, we say no;

for if there were no difference between the *jīva* and Brahman, it would entail a contradiction with scripture, experience, and reason. Furthermore, the very commencement of the sacred scriptures [would be impossible].

It may be so; for while there is a designation of difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in such passages as "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends... the knower and the ignorant, the two unborn ones, the Lord and the non-Lord," etc., non-difference is logical because their oneness is taught in the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*). This is provided that the authority of even a single portion of the Śruti is accepted.

Because it would follow that [the Veda] is outside the pale of the Vedas— just like Buddhism and other systems— and because there is a lack of authoritative evidence for such a claim, as well as mutual contradictions among the Śrutis;
this is like the shortness and length of a coiled snake versus a straightened snake, or the pervasiveness and limited extent of the sun’s radiance versus its orb.

Although the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are one in their nature as consciousness (*cit*), there is indeed neither contradiction nor conflict between difference and non-difference, because their respective natures—atomicity (*aṇutva*) and omnipresence (*vibhutva*)—are mutually opposed. Therefore, the difference between the individual soul and the Lord during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and their non-difference in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) are taught to be like that of the bee and the insect. Thus says the Śruti: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
Just as the flowing rivers disappear into the ocean, casting off name and form,
even so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high.
By these and other such passages, he clearly teaches both difference and non-difference.
This alone is the view of the author of the Sūtras, established through the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedānta texts; this is the ringing proclamation.
[End of] the section on being the Eater (the consumer). 2.
It demonstrates that Śiva is the Supreme Brahman by showing that he is the object of worship for Nārāyaṇa and others, as well as their cause and their nourisher:
|| 41 || "He is the Eater, because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving. || 9 ||
Its subject matter is seen in the Kaṭhavallī:
"For whom both Brahminhood and Kshatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who indeed knows where he is? Thus it is said.

In this context, a certain eater is designated, indicated by the rice of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings—characterized by the Brahmin and Kṣatriya classes and distinguished by death as the condiment. Regarding him, a doubt arises: is he fire, the Pradhāna, the earth, the individual soul (jīva), or the Supreme Lord?

[The opponent argues: "Fire is the eater of food; it is other than the two [fire and breath] that perform austerity; [it is the one] who eats the single unborn [nature] which is red, white, and black. And so on.

"Indeed, these beings are born from this; once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten, and it eats the beings; one of these two eats the sweet fruit of the *pippala* tree. All this, indeed, is Brahman; because it is born from that (*taj-ja*), dissolves into that (*tal-la*), and breathes (or moves) in that (*tad-ana*), therefore it is called *tajjalān*. One should meditate upon it with a tranquil mind"—from such is the vision of the Śruti. Therefore, "born from that" is *taj-ja*; "dissolves into that" is *tal-la*; and "breathes (or moves) in that" is *tad-ana*. Thus, it is *taj-ja*, *tal-la*, and [the rest].
The word "ca" (and) implies "that [Brahman], its food, and its waters"— the elision of the intermediate members being a Vedic usage— and the word "iti" indicates the reason; thus,

the meaning is that one who is tranquil should meditate upon Brahman as the entire phenomenal world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, which is the substratum of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: In hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Another, not eating, looks on," "Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, stainless, the witness of all, beyond darkness," and so forth, [it is established that] Śiva— the Supreme Brahman, an ocean of compassion, the refuge of all auspiciousness— is devoid of both the state of being an enjoyer of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-bhoktṛtva*) and partlessness (*niṣkalatva*).

For his nature as a destroyer consists in seizing the life-force (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the root of that is indeed anger; for delusion (*moha*) is the basin for that quality of abandonment which is anger, and its source-nature (*prakṛti*) is darkness (*tamas*);
because darkness is shrouded by ignorance (*ajñāna*), the sequence is ignorance, darkness, delusion, and then anger.

This is possible; for there is no evidence to postulate qualities such as non-existence (*asattva*) and so forth—which are the general characteristics of the individual soul (*jīva*)—in the Supreme Lord, who is distinct from them. Furthermore, this would entail the contradiction of previously cited scriptures stating that He is "without parts" (*niṣkalam*) and so on.

Therefore, it is appropriate that these qualities belong only to Viṣṇu and others in their capacity as the embodied self (*śārīrātman*). As for that Viṣṇu, his nature is characterized by sleep, in which the quality of darkness (*tamas*) predominates.

Because, due to an excess of delusion in the stories of the *Skanda-purāṇa* and other texts, he rolled about for a long time in the cremation ground of Vṛndāvana, and because he remains even today in Vṛndāvana in the form of the black *tulasī*, let him be the destroyer of those possessed of inauspicious qualities; as it is said in the *Sūtagītā*:
O best of Brahmins, Rudra has purity (sattva) within and darkness (tamas) without;
Viṣṇu has darkness within and purity without, while passion (rajas) exists on the outside.
"O best of Brahmins, within and without that Prajāpati,
Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are indeed overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Thus it is stated in the Śivadharmaśāstra.
Endowed with the quality of sattva within, yet joined with tamas without;
united with pure sattva, Śaṅkara is the benefactor of the world.
Endowed with the quality of rajas internally and possessed of the qualities of sattva externally,
yet joined with pure tamas, he is Viṣṇu himself, the Lord of Śrī.
"Brahmā, joined with the quality of *rajas*, is eternally present within both the external and the internal.
Beyond the three forms (*trimūrti*), Śiva is omniscient, pure, and stainless.
Thus, they consider the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), the peaceful, the auspicious, and non-dual as the Fourth (*turīya*); that is the Self, that is to be known.

By such passages as these, the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu and Śiva’s status as the cause of causes who transcends the three *guṇas* are taught; thus, in no way is his [Śiva’s] role as the destroyer of the universe possible, and that [role] belongs to Viṣṇu and others alone.
This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
To this we reply: "The Eater [is the Supreme Lord], because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving. Here, the Eater is directly Paraśiva himself. Why?

Because of the mention of the moving and the unmoving; that is to say, because of the scriptural statement regarding the eating of the world, which consists of the sentient and the insentient. This is because every living being is perceived as being eaten by him, with death serving as the condiment.
The mention of "Brahman and Kṣatriya" is for the purpose of illustration.

Since it is impossible for individual souls (jīvas) such as Nārāyaṇa—who possess only limited knowledge and are submerged in the cycle of birth and death—to be the destroyer of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of the moving and the non-moving, the "Eater" (attā) here is none other than Paraśiva. [He is] the cessation of the phenomenal world...

They consider the fourth state to be peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known. "Homage to the Lord of Destruction, homage to the Great Devourer. "As a spider emits and withdraws [its web]," "He who swallows all these worlds," and "From which indeed these beings are born"—in hundreds of such scriptural passages.

Since the state of being the cause of the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings is seen to belong to the Supreme Lord alone, it is not possible for deities such as Vandyā and others. The Śruti passage, "The other, not eating, looks on," indicates merely the denial of being an enjoyer of the fruits of karma; therefore, there is no contradiction. [Regarding the verse] "But Māyā..."

Because [the scriptures] declare that he has mastered *māyā* in passages such as "One should know Prakṛti and Maheśvara as the wielder of *māyā*," and because they describe his transcendence of darkness (*tamaḥ-paratva*) in the section beginning with "Accompanied by Umā" and ending with "beyond darkness," and because he exists even during the dissolution (*pralaya*) as its witness in passages such as "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed."

Moreover, the state of being a remainder is observed; by the statement, "Neither existent nor non-existent, Śiva alone is absolute," the intrinsic reality of existence and non-existence—consisting of the bound soul (*paśu*) and its fetters (*pāśa*)—is not negated. This is because the beginninglessness of the world is designated in such Vedic passages as: "These creatures are born from that which is rootless and supportless; never was there a time when this world was otherwise. And thus:

Smṛti states: "For the conscious Self alone, by the power of its will, manifests the entire collection of objects externally, even though they reside within it, without any material cause, just like a yogin."
By the term "without substrate" (*nirupādāna*), his status as the dual cause of the universe—like a spider—is indicated.

Therefore, Śiva is taught to be "absolute" (*kevala*) by virtue of the fact that the phenomenal world is contracted within his own self. Consequently, it is fitting that he alone possesses the power of universal withdrawal (*saṃhartṛtva*).
Furthermore, he states another reason: 42. And because of the context. || 10 ||
Because the context concerns Brahman as defined by unique attributes (asādhāraṇadharma) such as "The wise one is neither born nor dies" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18),

and because in the passage "Who indeed knows where he is? (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14), there is an observation of a multitude of attributes belonging to the Supreme Lord, such as its being difficult to know and the statement "Having realized the great, all-pervading Self, the wise man does not grieve" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.2.12).
Furthermore, there is no evidence for abandoning the subject under discussion and accepting a non-contextual one.
The quality of being the destroyer of all, which is mentioned in the section concerning the Supreme Lord, is not applicable to anyone else.

Just as [the attributes of] being the agent of creation and sustenance [belong to Him], if one does not accept [Him] as the agent of destruction, [the scripture states]: "Rudra is indeed one; He did not stand for a second."

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of contradicting such scriptural passages as these; moreover, there would be the consequence of undermining the preeminent majesty of Brahman. Since, in passages such as "From which indeed these beings are born," even the act of dissolution is taught as being dependent upon Him, there is no room for the stain of doubt. Therefore, it is established that the Eater is none other than Paraśiva.
Thus ends the second section, concerning the Eater (attṛtva). Now begins the third section, concerning the Cave (guhā).

Having thus established that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the destroyer of all, he refutes the view of those who maintain the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is that of the original object and its reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*) by means of another section:
"The two selves have entered the cave, for that is seen [in scripture]. (Sūtra 1.2.11)

"The two who drink the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme realm—the knowers of Brahman call them shade and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and the three *Nāciketa* rites"—this is the subject matter found in the *Kaṭhavallī*. [The opponent's position:
In the scriptural text, "The other, not eating, looks on," the Supreme Lord is [the one referred to].

Because of the negation of being an enjoyer [in other contexts]. Since there is the designation of being an enjoyer in the passage "the two who drink the *ṛta*," it is understood that here the state of being an enjoyer belongs only to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Because of its sentience and because of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman, there is no mutual contradiction between them, as in the case of shadow and light.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) possess mutually contradictory natures, it is appropriate that only these two have entered the cave of all beings. Because the relationship between cause and effect is primarily centered on the intellect, the embodied soul (*śārīra*) is established as being distinct from it.
Now, [one might object]: "When a man has died, there is doubt regarding him; some say 'he exists,' and others say 'he does not exist.'"
Because of the scriptural statement, "Instructed by you, I have known this," it is not proper to accept the position that the two are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*).

Even though the coexistence of the individual soul and the Lord is seen in the mantra "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), in the passage "The other, not eating, looks on" (*anaśnannanyo abhicākaśīti*), the Supreme Self is intended; for it is said:
"And that which you see as distinct from merit and distinct from demerit, distinct from this cause and effect... (*anyatra dharmādanyatrādharmādanyatrāsmātkṛtākṛtāt*).

Because by the phrase "drinking the *ṛta*," the teaching is given that only the Supreme Lord is the enjoyer of the fruits of action, and because the indicative mark of localized nature is seen in the words "in the world of good deeds" (*sukṛtasya loke*), [the following is established]. By the dual number in "drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*), the drinking of those two is taught. Since that [drinking] is impossible for the intellect (*buddhi*), which is insentient by nature, the position that the intellect and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are the two is not tenable.
If this is argued, we say no;
for in the sentence "The umbrella-bearers are going," men who both possess and do not possess umbrellas are accepted as being "umbrella-bearers.
Likewise here too, although there are two—one drinking and one not drinking—they are both designated as "the two drinkers" with reference to the omnipresent Lord.

If it is argued that the passage "The existence of [the soul] in one part of the world of merit is not possible" establishes that there is no transgression of the observation of karma, and that in the statement "He does not increase by action nor does He become less," the Supreme Lord is designated as the witness of good and evil deeds—therefore, it is only the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) that are being taught here; [Response: This is not so. For the Supreme Lord alone is the subject under discussion in this context, as is evident from the introductory statement, "He who dwells in the self (ātman) and controls the self from within. Furthermore, the term *ātman* is used here to denote the Supreme Self, as seen in such passages as, "The self of whom the body is the dwelling place" (*śarīraṃ yad avasthitam*), and "He who dwells in the earth and controls the earth from within. Moreover, the phrase "He does not increase by action nor does He become less" teaches that the Supreme Lord is eternally immutable. And the statement, "He is the bridge for the performance of sacrifices so that these worlds may not perish," shows that He is the support of the entire universe. Therefore, because the Supreme Lord is the subject of the discourse, it is He who is referred to by the word *ātman*. As for the objection regarding the impossibility of the soul's existence in one part of the world of merit, that is resolved by the fact that the soul is dependent upon the Supreme Lord. Thus, the Supreme Lord alone is the one being taught here.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*):

Here we reply—those two who have entered the cave are indeed the two selves, for that is seen from scripture. It should be understood that Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) are the two who have entered the cave. Why? Because they are "the two selves" (*ātmānau hi*); the word "hi" (indeed) signifies that both are indeed selves, as in the phrase "drinking the *ṛta*" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*).

Thus, from the hearing of the experience of the fruits of karma, one Self is established; it is logical that the second [entity] mentioned is also indeed a Self. He provides the reasoning for this with the words "because of the observation of that" (*taddarśanāt*). The meaning is that when a number is heard, in common worldly usage, only a thing of the same kind is observed there. For in the world, when it is said, "A second to this cow must be sought," it is a cow alone [that is sought].

A second [entity] is sought, neither a horse nor a man. Likewise here too, because of the commonality of being the Self (*ātmatva*), the individual self (*jīva*) and the supreme Self (*paramātman*) are to be understood [as distinct]. That the Supreme Lord is "measured by a span" (*prādeśamātra*) and has entered the cave of all beings (*sarvabhūtaguhāpraviṣṭatva*) is not contradictory.
As stated in another Śruti:
The Blessed Lord has faces, heads, and necks everywhere; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings; he is all-pervading; therefore, the auspicious Śiva is omnipresent.

Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being. Having thus known the form of the Supreme Self—dwelling in the cave, partless, and non-dual; hidden in the cave, situated in the depths, ancient—whoever knows that Self deposited in the cave in the supreme ether, seek the Self that has entered the cave.

Thus, there is no contradiction, because hundreds of such scriptural passages teach that although the Supreme Lord is omnipresent, He enters into a specific limited space within the heart-cave for the sake of being meditated upon by His devotees. Furthermore, the fact that He initiates the world of the well-performed deeds is appropriate for both [the individual soul and the Supreme Lord], even when they occupy only one part [of the body], just as the term "umbrella-bearer" applies to one who holds only a portion of it.

The mutual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), like that between shadow and sunlight, is not contradictory; for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is indeed the enjoyer of bliss. This is because the scriptures—such as "He whose delight is in the true Self and the vital breath, whose pleasure is in the mind" and so forth—declare that he who delights in the Self experiences the bliss of his own nature, which is perceivable by the mind alone. Furthermore, this is evident from the statement: "The other, not eating, looks on."

The denial of being the enjoyer of the fruits of karma is also logically consistent. Therefore, due to the equality of their enjoyment, a distinction in the enjoyer arises—according to the maxim of the master and the servant—and a distinction in the object of enjoyment is likewise appropriate. For it is said: "Of the eternal, He is the eternal; of the conscious, He is the conscious. There are two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknowing, the Lord and the Unlord, upon the same tree. Of the person...

"Immersed [in ignorance], he grieves, deluded by his own powerlessness; but when he beholds the other, the beloved glory of the Lord, he becomes free from sorrow"—and so forth. Thus, in the Śrutis, the eternally liberated and omniscient nature of the Supreme Lord, as well as the attributes of being bound by delusion and grief produced by beginningless ignorance, are established.

Although a distinction between the two is established by their respective observations, nevertheless, because the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) are one in their nature as consciousness (*cit*),
and because non-difference is seen in such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the individual soul and the Supreme Lord are understood as those who have entered the cave,
in accordance with statements such as "by which one sees and hears," through their association with the intellect (*buddhi*) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In response to the doubt that, because the known Supreme Lord is designated with attributes such as being the "Beholder," the state of "dwelling in the cave" must belong to both the intellect and the Supreme Lord, he refutes this by another reason:
"And because of the qualification" (Sūtra 1.2.12).
Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot.
He reaches the end of the journey— that supreme abode of Viṣṇu— which is difficult to see, hidden, entered into deeply, placed in the secret cave, situated in the abyss, and ancient.
"Having known the God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow"—

this statement, by specifying the attributes of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) through the metaphor of the chariot and the charioteer, and because of the specific qualification regarding the activity or non-activity of entering and exiting many bodies in such passages as "the wise one is neither born nor dies."

Furthermore, because it is observed that through the knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Lord, the individual soul (jīva) is liberated from joy and anger, it is said that the individual soul and the Supreme Lord have both entered the cave.
However, since a reflection and its original object cannot coexist in one place, [the analogy of] Śiva and the jīva as the original object and its reflection [does not apply].
Thus ends the section on the Cave (guhādhikaraṇa).
Now begins the section on the Intermediate One (antarādhikaraṇa) || 4 ||

Having taught that the omnipresent Supreme Lord resides within the cave of the heart by demonstrating that Paramaśiva is to be meditated upon in the center of the eye, [the author] now shows him in another location through a different scriptural passage:
45. On account of the intermediate state. || 13 ||

The subject of this [discussion] is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "This person who is seen in the eye—He said, 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman. Even if one pours clarified butter or water into this [eye], it goes only along the eyelashes," and so forth. Here, is this person within the eye the person who is a mere reflection (chāyā-puruṣa), or is it the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)?

The doubt arises as to whether [the person in the eye] is the presiding deity of the senses or the Supreme Lord. Why? Because it is taught that he is perceived as something visible, being well-known as "the shadow-self, the person who is a reflection," and as "this person who is seen in the eye. For he, while seeing form with the eye, is present within the eye; thus [it is said].

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is also attained; by the remainder of the sentence, "This is the immortal, fearless Brahman," the Supreme Lord is indicated. Furthermore, that which is seen as the person in the eye is also seen as the Sun, who is the deity presiding over the eye.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: because the embodied knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is seen to have entered the sense-organ of sight during the experience of the world, and because he is denoted by the word "Self" (*ātman*) due to his connection with the mind, it is he who is being taught.
Alternatively, the sun is what is enjoined, based on the observation of the scriptural statement: "By its rays, this [sun] is established in this [eye]."

Because signs such as immortality are impossible in relation to the deity presiding over the eye, and because a specific location is indicated, the Supreme Lord is not the object of meditation here. To this we reply: "The Inner One is [the Supreme Self] because of the appropriateness. The "Inner One" is the Person situated within the eye; he is indeed the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the appropriateness [of the attributes].

Because of the logical consistency [of the attributes]. Since qualities such as being the Self, immortality, and fearlessness are predicated of the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, and since those same qualities are heard of here in relation to the Person situated in the eye, it is taught that he is not anyone else.
"They consider the cessation of the phenomenal world, the peaceful, the auspicious, the non-dual, to be the Fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known."
"Śiva is non-dual, the eternal, the truth, the supreme Brahman;

these indeed are the names of this immortal one," and so forth—because such teachings regarding Śiva alone are found in the Taittirīya and Māṇḍūkya [Upaniṣads]. The terms Śiva, Brahman, and Paramātman are synonymous, like the words *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*.
It is enjoined: "Śiva alone, the maker of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon, having abandoned everything else"; "Rudra is one alone; he does not stand with a second";

"Innumerable thousands [of Rudras]"—and by such scriptural passages as "Rudra, the great seer, who transcends the universe," it is shown that the attributes of being supreme over all and being the object of worship for all are attributed to him alone. Thus it is remembered, and no other is seen.

The person within the eye is Mahādeva himself. Although there is the scriptural statement, "Even if one pours clarified butter or water into this [eye], it flows away along the eyelashes," the locus of the eye is free from all stains of defect. They call him "the one in whom all things meet" (*saṃyadvāma*); for indeed, all desires meet in him, and all lovely things meet in him, who—
"He who knows this is indeed the Giver of Desirable Things (*vāmanī*), for he leads all desirable things; he leads all desirable things for one who knows this.
He is indeed the Shiner (*bhāmanī*), for he shines in all worlds; he shines in all worlds for one who knows this.
Because such attributes as "the center of all desirable things" are designated here, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is to be meditated upon as being within the eye.
Thus it is said.
To the objection—how can Śiva, who transcends all and is omnipresent, be the "Person in the Eye" (akṣipuruṣa)?—the Sūtra replies:
46. And because of the designation of his location and so forth. (1.2.14)

Having established that the Supreme Lord possesses the eightfold form (*aṣṭamūrtitva*)—beginning with earth and ending with the embodied self (*śārīraka*)—through the passage "He who dwells in the earth," etc., [the text] further establishes His abiding in the eye through the Śruti:
"He who dwells in the eye, yet is within the eye; whom the eye does not know; whose body is the eye;
who controls the eye from within; He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Thus, the eye is also His locus.
Therefore, the meditation on the eye is established as valid, just like the meditation on the heart and so forth.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Since meditation is characterized by specific names, forms, and qualities, and since these are absent in that which is all-pervading like space, how can there be meditation upon it?
This is not so; for through such descriptions as "Its name is 'Ud' (Rising)" and "It has golden earrings," [the scripture teaches] even that which transcends ordinary qualities.

Because Maheśvara is designated by names, forms, and qualities, and because He is Śiva, the Brahman endowed with all powers who bestows the fruits of worldly prosperity and the supreme good (abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa), it is possible to speak of His two-fold form. In the state of liberation (kaivalya), the heart-lotus is stainless...
Having pointed out the heart-lotus with the words "pure" and so forth:

[one should meditate upon] that one, all-pervading, wonderful Lord, who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; who is consciousness-bliss, formless, and accompanied by Umā; the Supreme Lord, the Master, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil.
By such statements as these, because a single entity— like the wind— is designated as both partless and possessing parts,
[the author] demonstrates the authority of the Śruti in defining the specific nature of the power (*śakti*) of Paramaśiva-Brahman; and in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad]:
Salutations indeed to the one whose form is the universe—the Puruṣa who is *ṛta*, the supreme *satya*, the Supreme Brahman, the dark-throated, the one with upraised semen, and the three-eyed.
*Ṛta* is that which transcends the mind; *satya* is that which transcends speech; "supreme" means beyond the three forms consisting of the three *guṇas*.

By the statement "Brahman," the partless nature, lack of limbs, and so forth of Paraśiva are taught; then, by the words "the Person dwelling in the city" (puruṣaṃ puriśayaṃ), "black and tawny" (kṛṣṇapiṅgalam), "having fire as seed" (kṛśānuretastayā) thus being one whose vital energy flows upwards (ūrdhvaretasam), "three-eyed" (trilocanatayā) thus having diverse eyes (virūpākṣam), and "universal-formed" (viśvarūpam) due to being the cause of both the worlds, His nature as possessing parts and limbs is described. Therefore...
The fact that the supreme Brahman, Śiva alone, possesses both form and formlessness, as established by such scriptural passages as "These two are the forms of Brahman," is thus proven.

Therefore, the worship of these two as being related as limb and possessor of limbs (aṅga-aṅgin) is what is enjoined. Since the goal cannot be accomplished without the means, it is logical to prescribe the worship of specific locations such as the eye for the purpose of attaining Him.
He states another reason:
"And precisely because it is designated as being distinguished by pleasure. (Kārikā 15)

The person within the eye is Śiva himself. Why? "Precisely because of the mention of that which is distinguished by bliss. By the word "precisely" (eva), it is indicated that no doubt should be entertained here. It is heard at the beginning of the passage that Brahman is "that which is distinguished by bliss" (*sukhaviśiṣṭa*), namely Śiva; the meaning is that it is that very same one who is mentioned here. [As stated: "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman..."
Because at the beginning [of the passage], "Brahman," the state of Brahman as characterized by bliss is demonstrated.
Now, one might object: in the sentence, "But the teacher will tell you the path," there is no observation of a context concerning Brahman;
for the word *ka* is conventionally used in the sense of sensual pleasure, and the word *kha* is well-known to mean space (*ākāśa*), given the opening of the passage.

If it is asked how the preeminence of bliss (*sukha-viśiṣṭatva*) in Brahman is established, it is said in reply: Having heard the statement regarding the Gārhapatya and other sacrificial fires—"Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman"—Upakośala said: "I understand that Prāṇa is Brahman, but I do not understand what Ka is, nor what Kha is."

Regarding the statement "I perceive," this has already been explained. In the sentence, "That which is indeed *kaṃ* (bliss) is the same as *khaṃ* (space), and that which is *khaṃ* is the same as *kaṃ*," because the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* are designated in a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*), the word *kaṃ* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) here in the sense of bliss.
Nevertheless, by virtue of being an established symbol (*adhiṣṭhita-pratīkatva*), the word "Brahman" is applied to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
Although the word *kaṃ* is conventionally established as denoting the specific pleasure derived from the objects of the senses, the words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ*, which denote each other,
are understood here as referring exclusively to Brahman, whose nature is bliss. In this context, by the repetition "Brahman is *kaṃ*, Brahman is *khaṃ*, Brahman is *khaṃ*,
Brahman is *kaṃ*," the word *kaṃ* is enjoined by means of the word *brahman*.

Bliss, as a quality, is also to be meditated upon just like the possessor of the quality; therefore, at the beginning of the Śruti passage, Brahman is indicated as being characterized by bliss. Having previously concluded—after the Gārhapatya and other fires had each declared their own greatness—that "O Upakosala, this is that [Self] of yours, and from this comes both knowledge and the knowledge of the Self"— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the logical flow of the preceding section.)

It teaches that the Supreme Lord is the ultimate goal. In the statement, "But the teacher will tell you of the way," the promise to declare the way alone precludes the intention to speak of anything else. This is as when it is said, "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus"—referring to the knowledge of the Person situated behind the eye.

Having ascertained that he alone is free from the mire of sin, [the text] points out his very nature as Brahman. Then, having established that the Supreme Lord under discussion resides in the eye and possesses qualities such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*), and having begun with the words "I shall describe the path of those who know Him," it says: "This person who is seen in the eye—He is your Self."
Because of the designation [of the person] as "thus he spoke" (*hovāca*) without limitation, it is established that the person within the eye is the Supreme Lord.
Anticipating the objection that the attributes taught here might over-extend to the *chāyā-brahman* (the reflected self), he refutes this by means of another reason:
And because the scripture declares the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. || 48 || 16 ||

Furthermore, the person within the eye is Śiva alone; why? Because of the description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads. "One who has heard the Upaniṣads" (śrutopaniṣatka) means one by whom the Upaniṣad—the knowledge of Brahman—has been heard and practiced. The meaning is: because of the description of his path, which consists of the route beginning with light (arcirādi), as stated in the passage: "Those who know thus, and those who in the forest [practice] faith and austerity... and so forth.

Those who worship thus attain the light itself; from the light they go to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight, and from there, having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they are born in the sun. This indeed is the abode of the vital breaths; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is the supreme goal; from this they do not return again.

This very same [teaching] is here designated as the "Knowledge of the Person in the Eye. Having begun with the words, "Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him or not, they pass into the flame," it continues: "From the sun to the moon, from the moon to the lightning;
there a person who is non-human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman; by this [path]..."
"Those who proceed in this manner do not return to this human whirlpool"— thus, by means of this supreme path, the Brahman-hood of the Person in the Eye is taught.
"Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice."
There, people who know Brahman go to and come from that Brahman.
And thus, in the Smṛti, the attainment of Brahman is proclaimed. Therefore, the person within the eye is not the reflection of a person.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
"Because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other. (Sūtra 1.2.17)

In this context, the other [beings], such as the shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*) and so forth, are not the person within the eye. Why? Because of instability and because of impossibility. "Instability" means that for the meditator, there is no presence of another person who could produce a shadow in every eye;
furthermore, "impossibility" means that qualities such as immortality cannot exist in a shadow-person. This is the meaning.

Now, it may be objected: whenever a person approaches the eye, the reflection of that person is seen in the eye, and when he has departed, it is no longer seen. Since the scripture, in the passage "This person who is in the eye," teaches the meditation on the person seen in one's own eye, one should look at the region of his neck during that meditation.

If it is argued that one perceives a certain person near the eye and therefore the meditation is upon a specific region of the eye belonging to that shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*) alone, we say no; for attributes such as immortality and so forth, which are the qualities of Supreme Śiva, are impossible in a shadow-person. [The text continues: "established in the eye."

Furthermore, because the attributes of a person (puruṣadharma), such as creation, maintenance, and dissolution, are impossible in a deity, [the Supreme Self is established]. In passages such as "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises," the dependence of the sun and other celestial bodies upon the Supreme Lord is taught.
In the Mahānārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad: "The Person is the size of a thumb, resting within the thumb."

In the Śruti passage, "The Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased," it is specifically designated that the Supreme Lord alone resides within the eye as being the size of a thumb;
therefore, it is in no way possible for anyone other than Him to be the object of worship within that [eye].

But surely—since in passages such as "Water and earth are the eaters, and fire and wind are the eaters," the wind also is understood to be an enjoyer, it is possible that the status of being an object of meditation in the space of the thumb-sized [heart] taught in the context of the Prāṇāgnihotra belongs to the vital air (prāṇavāyu) alone; moreover, its status as the enjoyer of the five oblations is also understood. Therefore, it is not [the case that the Supreme Self is meant].
If it is argued that the Supreme Lord alone is the object of worship here, we say no; for even if the vital air (prāṇavāyu) is understood to be the enjoyer,
attributes such as being the sovereign of the entire universe and being the enjoyer of the world of moving and non-moving beings cannot reside in an insentient entity.

Because the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) cannot exist [independently]; for, from such scriptural teachings as "You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter within me, O Rudra," it is understood that even the state of being the enjoyer of the five oblations by means of being the substratum of the vital breaths is dependent upon Maheśvara. Therefore, the status of being worshipped in a specific location the size of a thumb is [dependent on Him], and thus [He is] the thumb-sized one.
It should be understood that this well-known meditation is obtainable through the glance of the teacher and concerns those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Thus ends the fourth section, the *Antaradhikaraṇa*. [Now begins] the *Antaryāmyadhikaraṇa* (Section on the Inner Ruler). || 5 ||

Having taught that the all-pervading, auspicious Supreme Brahman is to be meditated upon as dwelling within the eye, [the author] demonstrates through another section that it is to be meditated upon as dwelling within everything: 50.
[The Lord is] the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) with respect to the deities, the worlds, and so forth, because of the declaration of His attributes. (2.1.18)

The subject of this [Upanishad] is stated in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa: "O Kāpya, do you know that Inner Ruler who rules from within this world and the other world, and all beings? Having begun thus, it continues:
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who..."
"He who dwells within the earth and controls it—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Following this [section] concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*), there follow:

"He who [dwells] in all worlds" concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*); "He who [dwells] in all Vedas" concerning the Vedas (*adhiveda*); "He who [dwells] in all sacrifices" concerning sacrifice (*adhiyajña*); "He who [dwells] in all beings" concerning beings (*adhibhūta*); "He who [dwells] in the vital breaths," and so forth; and "He who [dwells] in the self" (*adhyātma*).
Thus, regarding this internal self, a certain inner controller (*antaryāmī*) who governs from within is heard of in scripture.

Is he to be understood here as a specific presiding deity of the earth and other elements, or as some yogi endowed with powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, or rather as the Supreme Lord? A doubt arises as to whether he is something distinct [from these] or not.

Because the aggregate of cause and effect is heard in scripture as residing in a deity—through such passages as "He whose abode is the earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind"—it is logical that this deity possesses the capacity for control. Since it is impossible for the bodiless Śiva to exercise control, the position that the deity itself is the self is appropriate; or [the deity might be] some perfected being (*siddha*) or a yogin.

Through the possession of the eightfold sovereign powers (aṣṭaiśvarya) beginning with atomization (aṇimā), there would be both the state of entering into all things and the state of being their controller.
The individual soul’s (jīva) entry into the senses of all beings for the sake of experiencing the fruits of its own karma is not contradictory.
Because it undergoes transformation into the forms of the Great Principle (mahat), ego (ahaṃkāra), and so forth, the pervasiveness of primordial matter (pradhāna) is established.
It is appropriate that the Virāṭ Puruṣa penetrates all beings by virtue of being the cause of the appropriation of all volitions;
likewise [it is appropriate] for the Supreme Lord in passages such as "Rudra is superior to the universe."

Because of the designation of being superior to the universe (*viśvadhikatva*), it is in no way possible for [the Self] to have entered into the manifold world (*prapañca*) consisting of both conscious and unconscious things that are of the nature of modifications (*vikārātmaka*). Therefore, it follows that the state of being the self of all and the state of being the controller of all belong only to one who is distinct from that [world].
This being the position reached, we reply: "The Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) with respect to the deities, the worlds, and so forth, [is Brahman], because of the designation of its attributes."

He who is designated as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*) with respect to the deities and so forth is none other than Paramaśiva. Why? Because of the designation of His attributes (*taddharmavyapadeśāt*).

For the attributes of that Supreme Lord—such as being distinct from the presiding deities of the earth and others, entering into the gross and subtle worlds, being the controller, being the cause, and being immortal—are [designated].
"Because of designation" means "because of instruction.

Now, one might object: since it is impossible for the changeless Brahman to possess qualities such as being a controller, it must be the Lord alone—reflected in the quality of *sattva* within the *pradhāna*, which is superimposed upon the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman and is thus illusory—who [possesses these qualities].

If it is argued that [the attributes] such as being the controller of all [belong to the individual soul], we say no; for in the scriptural passage, "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," the attributes of being the controller and so forth are attributed specifically to Śiva—who is denoted by the word 'immortal' (amṛta) and is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—since it is impossible for that which is illusory (mithyābhūta) to be the controller of everything. As is seen in the world...

Furthermore, because a reflection is never observed to possess agency, it is not tenable for the Lord reflected [in the soul] to possess universal sovereignty, the status of being the universal controller, and so forth. Therefore, it is established that Śiva alone possesses the qualities of being the inner ruler of all and the universal controller.
Now, one might object: [is it not the case that] these attributes such as being the controller belong to someone other than the Supreme Lord, who is unconditioned by such attributes?

If it is asked, "Why should it not be the Supreme Brahman?"—we say no; because that would entail the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because there is a lack of evidence for its existence, and because there would be no purpose for such a being in the world. Furthermore, if one were to accept that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), like a stone and the like. Therefore, that very [Brahman] possesses both the state of having attributes (*saguṇatva*) and the state of being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇatva*).

At the time of the contraction of power (*śakti*), there is the state of being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇatva*); at the time of its expansion, there is the state of possessing attributes (*saguṇatva*).

Therefore, the qualities of being the cause of both [the creation and dissolution] of the entire universe, being the self of all, entering into everything, and being the controller of all, are appropriate for Mahādeva alone, the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Likewise, in another Śruti: "He who is Rudra in fire, he who is in the waters..."

"In the plants, that Rudra who has entered all beings—to that Rudra let there be homage. All that exists, the world, the manifold, what has been born in many ways and what is being born—all this indeed is Rudra; to that Rudra let there be homage.
Thus it is said in the *Taittirīya*. And in the *Atharvaśiras*: "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world. Those gods..."
They asked Rudra, "Who are you? He replied, "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future;

there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me. Since such passages demonstrate that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses attributes such as being the inner controller of all, it follows that no other can be the Supreme Brahman.

The state of being the inner controller of all (*sarvāntaryāmitva*), the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmatva*), and so forth, are possible in every respect; otherwise, there would even be a contradiction with the context.

For the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), who is as all-pervasive as space, his transcendence over the universe (*viśvādhikatva*) and his immanence within the universe (*viśvānupraviṣṭatva*) are not contradictory.

The term "the immortal Inner Controller" (*antaryāmyamṛta*) refers to Śiva himself by means of the word "immortal. This is because of the Jābāla Śruti statement: "These indeed are the names of the Immortal. Furthermore, the repeated use of the word "immortal" in each successive section constitutes an emphatic repetition (*abhyāsa*).
In the *Atharvaśiras*, it is stated: "He who is the Blessed One Rudra and he who is Brahmā," and so forth.

Just as the repeated use of the word "Bhagavat" refers to Śiva— who is the essence of all and a mine of infinite, divine, auspicious qualities— it is indicated that the repeated use of the word "Amṛta" for Paramaśiva in the Jābāla Upaniṣad is intended to establish its conventional meaning.
In response to the doubt that it is possible for the *pradhāna*, which is superimposed and illusory in nature, to be the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all,
he refutes that view and establishes that the status of being the inner controller of all belongs to Maheśvara alone.
51. And it is not based on memory, because there is no mention of its attributes.

The Smārta [view]—that the Pradhāna, which consists of the aggregate of the three *guṇas*, reflected through the quality of *sattva*, is what is denoted by the term "Inner Ruler" (*antaryāmin*)—is untenable. Why? Because there is a description of attributes not belonging to it: "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower."

The meaning is that [the Pradhāna is not the subject] because of the observation of the remainder of the sentence and because of the impossibility of attributes such as being the Self or the seer. By the word "that" (tat), the Pradhāna is denoted; "not that" (atat) means that which is different from the Pradhāna, namely Paramaśiva. The meaning is "because of the mention," that is, the designation, of those very attributes belonging to Him, such as immortality and so forth.

The sense is that because there is no mention of the *pradhāna* among the primary attributes [of the Lord], the *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhya and Advaita is not the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*).
But surely, it is said in the Smṛti: "It is unreasoned, unknowable, as if entirely asleep," and "the one unborn..."?

If it is argued that, because the Śrutis beginning with these words teach that *pradhāna* is the cause of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), its causality, its status as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*), and so forth are appropriate for *pradhāna* alone—by way of the analogy of the magnet and the needle through the power of the existence of Brahman—that is not so; for [the Śrutis state]:
"He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate'; having created that, He entered into that very thing," and so on.

Because it is heard in scripture that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe independently of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), [we know this from such passages as]:

"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā; the perishable is Pradhāna and the imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over them by means of the perishable self; He is the Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas."

Furthermore, because the Supreme Lord is designated as the cause of bondage and liberation, as well as the sustainer and binder within saṃsāra, and so forth, even the Lord reflected therein does not possess the status of an inner controller (antaryāmin). This is because that which is reflected is insentient and unreal.

The scriptural conception of the relationship between original and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*) regarding Brahman and *pradhāna*, which are both formless, is as charming only when left unexamined as a painting on the wall of the sky. Therefore, the doctrine of the non-dualists is indeed the doctrine of non-duality.
And so says the *Smṛti*:
Bound by beginningless ignorance, that Brahman, which is the cause of time, transmigrates through its own ignorance; liberation [is attained] from the imagined statement.
Thus, this deceptive scripture, which destroys all greatness,
must be disregarded by the devotees of Śiva because it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti.

This [ignorance] is primary in the Kalāpa and other systems; indeed, it is primarily darkness (tamas), for it was described as such precisely for the purpose of establishing that it is destroyed by knowledge.
In the investigation of knowledge and ignorance, that [agency] is established in an entirely different way;
however, according to the position of the magnet, its agency is said to be directed by that [magnet].
Since the scriptural passages such as "He thought" (Tadaikṣata) demonstrate that the primary agency belongs to Him,
it is not tenable for the Pradhāna to possess agency merely by virtue of its proximity to Him.
Even regarding the perspective of a magician, this other opinion is certainly held;
however, no mention of it exists anywhere within the revealed scriptures (Śrutis) as they are currently observed.

The statements concerning "commencement through speech" do not lead to the falsity of the world, because they reveal its non-difference from That [Brahman] and because the world has Śiva as its true nature.
If it is argued that the descriptions of the creation of the world and so forth are merely figurative (arthavāda) for the sake of knowledge, that is not correct;
for such [creation] is not accepted [as real], and it does not pertain to the greatness of the injunctions.
If it is argued that [the attribution] is for the sake of negation, then there is no superimposition in reality;
if it is argued that it is for the sake of establishing a firm cognition, that is not tenable.
There is no sublation of the primary meaning of scripture because its effects are observed;
however, in the case of a magician, agency resides in Brahman.
Furthermore, the agency of Māyā and the other factors is not taught by the Śruti or the Sūtras;
rather, their lack of agency is indeed intended to reveal His (the Lord's) greatness.
For whom is the illusory nature (māyikatva) described in the Purāṇas not a cause for understanding the contradictory meaning? It is established there for the purpose of delusion.
They say that this world is without truth, without foundation, and without a Lord;
it has arisen from mutual union, and what else could it be but the product of causes and effects?
But when undivided non-duality manifests, the entire world is seen as consisting of Śiva;
through that knowledge, the conceptualizing intellect dissolves, yet not by way of its own essential nature.
"One should never entertain the notion of difference anywhere, because Śiva is the sole material cause. In this world, the doctrine of non-dual difference is consistent with all the Vedas;
that alone is declared to be Vedic—such is the drumbeat of Vedānta."
Therefore, the established conclusion is that Maheśvara is the inner controller of all.
Anticipating the objection that because the individual soul (jīva) is conscious, it is more logical for the attributes such as being the "seer" to belong to it alone, he refutes this:
52. "And the embodied soul [is not the inner controller], for both [Vedas] teach him as distinct. (20)

Here too, the word "no" (na) is understood from the previous context. They do not declare the embodied being—the individual soul (jīva)—to be the inner ruler (antaryāmī). Why? Because both [recensions] study him as distinct. For both the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas study this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) as separate from the inner ruler: the Kāṇvas read, "He who dwells in the intellect" (yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan), and [the Mādhyandinas read], "He who dwells in the self" (ya ātmani tiṣṭhan).

The Mādhyandinas [hold] that because the terms *vijñānātman* and *ātman* are synonyms for the individual soul (*jīva*), it is taught that the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*) is indeed the Supreme Śiva, who is other than the individual soul. Therefore, it is established that it is not possible for the individual soul, the Virāṭ-puruṣa, Pradhāna, and so forth, to be the Inner Ruler.

Now, an objection is raised: the scriptural text, "There is no other seer but He," rejects any self other than the Supreme Lord as a seer, a hearer, a thinker, or a knower; therefore, two distinct seers cannot logically exist within the body. To this, we say: No.

Because of the designation of the coexistence of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in the mantra "Two birds... (*dvasuparṇā*), the prohibition of another presiding agent in the scriptural text "There is no other seer than He" (*nānyo'to'sti draṣṭā*) is appropriate. For, by the passage "Where there is, as it were, duality," the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is first established during the state of transmigratory existence; whereas [by the passage] "But where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what... (*yatratvasya sarvam ātmaivābhūt tat kena...*) [the non-difference is shown].

By the statement, "What should one see, and by what should one see? What should one speak, and by what should one speak? it is understood that in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), because of the knowledge that everything has Śiva as its essence, the cessation of saṃsāra is realized. Therefore, the relationship of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is logical. Consequently, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is described as the regulator of all and the inner controller of all.
Thus ends the fifth section, concerning the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). Now begins the sixth section, concerning the Invisible (Adṛśyatva).

Now, in order to establish the supremacy of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) and to refute the claims that the individual soul (jīva) and others are Brahman or its own self-propelling agent, the state of Paramaśiva as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all has been established; and for the purpose of further establishing His very supremacy, [the following is set forth].
He demonstrates that the possession of qualities such as invisibility belongs to another subject through a subsequent section:
