53. That which possesses qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman], because of the statement of its attributes. (21)

Its subject matter is seen in the *Atharvaṇa*: "Now, the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and immutable—which the wise perceive as the source of all beings," and so forth.

Here, the doubt arises as to whether the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) characterized by qualities such as invisibility is the embodied soul (*śārīra*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*), or the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*). For in passages such as, "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring similar to herself," it is established that primordial matter— consisting of the three *guṇas*— is the source of beings because it produces many offspring.

Since the word *yoni* denotes a cause (*nimitta*), the "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) must be the conscious self (*vijñānātman*). It is not possible for the stainless Supreme Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, to undergo transformation into the form of earth and other elements like clay and so forth, as in the scriptural passage: "As a spider emits [its web]."

If it is argued that the fact that the conscious spider is seen to create and withdraw the wheel of threads—which are themselves unconscious—establishes that the nature of consciousness is the cause of the manifold of both the conscious and the unconscious, we say no. For a conscious spider alone is not the cause of the thread and cloth; rather, it is observed that its body itself is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of those things.

Likewise, the body of a person alone is the cause of hair, nails, and so forth. Therefore, attributes such as invisibility and the like are appropriate here for the *pradhāna*. If it is argued: "How can *prakṛti* be the source of beings, given that the remainder of the passage beginning with 'He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving' illuminates the abundance of attributes belonging to Paramaśiva"?—[the answer follows].

It is explained as follows: Now, regarding the "higher [knowledge]" by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained—in passages such as "that which is invisible," etc.—the word "Imperishable" first makes known the Pradhāna, characterized by attributes such as invisibility;
then, in the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable," that which is heard to be higher than the Imperishable will be the Omniscient and All-knowing One.

Therefore, since it has been argued that the Pradhāna—denoted by the word "akṣara"—is the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), we reply: here, the source of beings characterized by qualities such as invisibility is indeed the Great Lord (*maheśvara*). Why? Because of the statement of His attributes.
This means because of the declaration of many attributes belonging to the Supreme Lord, such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and so forth. It is not [the Pradhāna].

The Pradhāna is taught to be denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) and to possess the causality of the world; as introduced [in the passage]: "As a spider emits and withdraws [its thread], as herbs arise from the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe arise here from the Akṣara."

Because it is recognized here as being the very cause of the world— referring to that which is "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*) and "all-perceiving" (*sarvavit*), whose austerity consists of knowledge, and from whom this Brahman, name, form, and food are born— and because attributes such as omniscience are impossible in the case of the non-intelligent *pradhāna*, [the text refers to the Supreme Self] by the words, "higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ*).

From the context, it is taught that there is nothing higher than the Imperishable (akṣara), the source of beings (bhūtayoni). This is because the Imperishable under discussion is designated as the source of beings in the passage: "He who knows the true Puruṣa, the Imperishable—he has truly spoken that knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, in another Śruti text: "The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā..."

"Having meditated upon the three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil one, the sage goes to the source of beings, the all-witnessing, beyond darkness"—because of such teachings regarding attributes like being the source of beings belonging to Śiva alone, the "source of beings" (bhūtayoni) is none other than Him.
Furthermore: "Two sciences are to be known," as the knowers of Brahman say—namely, the higher and the lower—in this statement.

Having pointed out the lower knowledge characterized by the Ṛgveda and other scriptures, the text then teaches that Brahman— Paramaśiva— is the object of higher knowledge through the passage beginning, "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained.
It is further specified that these two types of knowledge, distinguished as higher and lower, result respectively in the fruits of worldly prosperity and supreme liberation.

By the passage beginning with "And the three sciences would have to be asserted," the fact that the Supreme Lord alone is the source of all beings has been established. Furthermore, in passages such as "O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? the promise of knowing everything through the knowledge of one thing is set forth. (The two kinds of injunctions to be known here have been indicated. Thus, there is the promise of universal knowledge through the knowledge of a single entity.
This is possible only in the case of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, because such a proposition is impossible in the case of the insentient *pradhāna*. Furthermore,

having introduced the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) as the primary subject— stating that "He taught the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son"— the text proceeds to describe the higher [knowledge] through the division of the higher and the lower.

Having shown that this knowledge consists in the attainment of the Imperishable, he points out its nature as the science of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). For the lower science of ritual action (*karmavidyā*), characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, introduces the commencement of the science of Brahman for the purpose of praising the science of Brahman:
"For these boats in the form of sacrifice are unstable; that which is called the eighteenfold [Veda] is inferior, in which ritual action prevails."

Having expressed censure through such passages as, "Those fools who rejoice in this [worldly life] go again and again to old age and death," one who has thereby become dispassionate possesses the qualification for the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). As it is said: "A Brahmin, having examined the worlds acquired through karma, should attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created. For the sake of realizing that..."
He teaches this through such passages as, "One should approach the Guru alone, with fuel in hand, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman.
Therefore, it is established that the Source of Beings (*bhūtayoni*), characterized by qualities such as invisibility, is Maheśvara.
To provide further reason for this point, he says:
54. And because of the distinction and the designation of difference, it is neither of the other two. || 22 ||

Here too, Śiva alone is the source of beings, and not the other two—namely, Prakṛti and the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the mention of distinctive attributes and because of the designation of difference.
"Distinctive attribute" and "designation of difference"—the meaning is "by means of these two.
For it is said: "Divine, indeed, is that formless Person; he is both external and internal, for he is unborn."
For it is without breath and without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable.

By such statements as these, distinction (*viśeṣa*) is taught; for attributes such as divinity and so forth are impossible in either the individual soul (*jīva*) or primordial matter (*pradhāna*), other than the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, there is a designation of difference, as in "higher than the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*), where the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) refers to the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) in the form of a bond (*pāśa*).

Therefore, because of the designation "beyond all modification" and "higher than the high," there is a distinction made between the fetter (*pāśa*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Consequently, the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) is not the other [the individual soul]. Alternatively, the phrase "higher than the Imperishable" may refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), while "higher than the high" may refer to Paraśiva; however, due to this designation of distinctness, it is understood here that the Supreme Lord alone is intended.
Furthermore, he states another reason: 55. And because of the presentation of form. || 23 ||

Here too, Śiva alone is the source of all beings. Why? "And because of the presentation of form. Form means a body consisting of limbs; the meaning is that [Śiva is the source] because of the presentation of such a form. Having taught the distinction of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, from the individual soul and primordial matter by the words "higher than the high Imperishable," [the text continues] with "From Him is born the vital breath... and so forth.

Having demonstrated that the Supreme Lord is the cause of all things, including the vital breaths and so forth, [the text] shows His very nature as the universal form through such passages as: "Fire is His head, the sun and moon His eyes, the quarters His ears, and the Vedas are His uttered speech; the wind is His breath, the universe His heart, and from His feet the earth arose—for He is the inner Self of all beings."

Since attributes such as being the cause of all and being the inner ruler of all are impossible for both the individual soul (jīva) and primordial matter (pradhāna), the presentation of a form is not possible for them.
If it is asked, "How can there be a presentation of a form for the Supreme Lord, who possesses qualities such as invisibility?"—the answer is: no, because of the context.

Because of the reference back to the subject at hand by the word "this" (eṣa), the scripture—stating, "From this is born the vital breath; this is the inner self of all beings"—teaches that it has the source of all beings as its very object. Furthermore, its possession of both form and formlessness, like that of the wind and so forth, is indeed its inherent nature.
Moreover:

Having previously taught that [the Self] is the cause of everything from the vital breath (prāṇa) down to the earth, by means of the passage beginning with "From this is born the vital breath," and having then pointed out its status as the cause of the fuel-sticks and so forth, by means of the passage beginning with "From him comes fire, whose fuel is the sun" and ending with "And from him come all herbs and juices," [the text continues] with "The Person alone is all this, action... and so on.

The scripture teaches that the source of all beings is the Self of all: "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of creation. He supported the earth and this heaven—whom as a god shall we worship with our oblation?
In this Vedic passage, by the phrase "arose in the beginning," the birthlessness of Mahādeva, whose body is the three worlds, is indicated.

Because the vital breath (prāṇa) abides within all beings by its very nature, the presentation of all forms—such as "The Person alone is this universe, [and] action," and so forth—is the means for the realization of Paramaśiva; such is the established conclusion (rāddhānta). Therefore, the source of beings (bhūtayoni), denoted by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara), is indeed the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the sixth section, "The Section on Invisibility" (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa). Now begins the seventh section, "The Section on Vaiśvānara."

Having pointed out that Maheśvara, who is superior to all, is the cause of the universe and possesses such attributes as being superior to all, the author demonstrates through another section that He alone is to be worshipped by all in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*):
56. *Vaiśvānara*, [is the Lord], because of the specific common term. (24)

The subject matter of this [text] is recited in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? Starting from "You indeed meditate upon this very Vaiśvānara Self; tell us that," and having introduced the connection of qualities such as space, the sun, and so forth, while setting aside each individual meditation, they present [the Self] as the head and other parts, and declare: [ChU 5.18.1] "He who meditates on him as one-footed loses his feet. [ChU 5.18.2] "He who meditates on him as two-footed becomes two-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.3] "He who meditates on him as three-footed becomes three-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.6] "He who meditates on him as six-footed becomes six-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.7] "He who meditates on him as seven-footed becomes seven-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.8] "He who meditates on him as eight-footed becomes eight-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.9] "He who meditates on him as nine-footed becomes nine-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.10] "He who meditates on him as ten-footed becomes ten-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.11] "He who meditates on him as eleven-footed becomes eleven-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.12] "He who meditates on him as twelve-footed becomes twelve-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.13] "He who meditates on him as thirteen-footed becomes thirteen-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.14] "He who meditates on him as all-footed becomes all-footed himself. [ChU 5.18.1] "Verily, he who meditates on him as Vaiśvānara, knowing him thus, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, in all selfs. Such is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara. [ChU 5.18.2] "But he who meditates on him as not thus, his food is limited... he does not eat food in these worlds, in these beings, in these selfs. [ChU 5.18.1] "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the Self that is within all. That which is the breath in the mouth is the head of this Vaiśvānara Self; that which is the eye is the right side; that which is the mind is the middle; that which is the ear is the left side; and the vast space is the trunk. [ChU 5.18.2] "Fire is his head, the sun and moon are his eyes, the directions are his ears, the revealed Vedas are his speech, air is his breath, the world is his trunk, the earth is his foundation. [ChU 5.18.1] "In this way, O Śvetaketu, you meditate upon this Vaiśvānara Self as the eater of food, as the consumer of food. [ChU 5.18.2] "And whatever is eaten here, whatever is drunk, by that he is satisfied. And what is his exhalation and inhalation, that is the food of the breath; and what is the breath's food, that is the food of this [Self]. [ChU 5.18.1] "When one eats food, when one drinks water, then he satisfies this [Self]. And when he is satisfied, then this [Self] is satisfied, and through its satisfaction, all these worlds are satisfied. [ChU 5.18.1] "This is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara, O Śvetaketu. Meditate upon it, my dear. [ChU 5.18.2] "And whoever departs from here without knowing this Vaiśvānara Self, his worlds are consumed by thieves. [ChU 5.18.1] "But whoever departs from here knowing this Vaiśvānara Self, his worlds are not consumed by thieves. [ChU 5.18.2] "This is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara, O Śvetaketu. Meditate upon it, my dear. [ChU 5.18.1] "And whoever departs from here knowing this Vaiśvānara Self, his worlds are not consumed by thieves. [ChU 5.18.2] "This is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara, O Śvetaketu. Meditate upon it, my dear. Meditate upon it, my dear. [ChU 5.18.1] "And whoever departs from here knowing this Vaiśvānara Self, his worlds are not consumed by thieves. [ChU 5.18.2] "This is the knowledge of Vaiśvānara, O Śvetaketu. Meditate upon it, my dear. [ChU 5.18.1] "And whoever departs from here knowing this Vaiśvānara Self, his
But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and is the measure of all,

eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Of this very Vaiśvānara Self, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the brilliantly radiant), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (the multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (the manifold-pathed), the trunk is *bahula* (the expansive), and the bladder is indeed...
"His wealth is the earth, his feet are the earth, his chest is the sacrificial altar, his body hair is the *barhis* grass, his heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, his mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire,

and his mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire," and so forth. Regarding this passage, there are many conflicting interpretations as to whether the word "Vaiśvānara" refers to the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), the deity presiding over that fire, or the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
"They are seen: this is the Vaiśvānara fire which is within the person, by which this food is cooked—namely, that which is eaten;
its sound is heard when one covers the ears and listens. When he is about to depart [from this world], he no longer hears that sound. By such passages, the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) is designated.

This is because of the hearing of the use of words common to both; for instance, in such passages as "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the universe and of the days," the deity Agni is perceived. Furthermore, since the use [of the term] is possible when that deity is understood through its sovereignty—as seen in the hymn of praise beginning with "May we abide in the good will of Vaiśvānara, for he is the king and the glory of all beings"—[the term applies to the Supreme Self].

Furthermore, because in such passages as "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," the status of being the giver of the fruit [of the rite] is heard through [Vaiśvānara's] being the deity of the sacrifice; and because of the specific use of the word "Self" (ātman); and because at the beginning [of the section], the word "Self" is heard in the question, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"—it is indeed Vaiśvānara who is taught by means of the word "Self."
Because the state of being an enjoyer is observed through the proximity of Vaiśvānara, the individual self (jīvātman) is also taught [in this context].

This is because the word "Vaiśvānara" is conventionally established as referring to the elemental fire, in the sentence: "One meditates upon the self as Vaiśvānara, who is the measure of a span and all-pervading."

If it is argued that the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, who is all-pervading, cannot in any way be denoted by the word "Vaiśvānara" because of being restricted to a specific location measured by only a span (prādeśamātra),
we shall reply: "Vaiśvānara [is the Supreme Lord] because of a specific common term," as stated here.

Vaiśvānara is indeed Maheśvara himself; why? Because of a specific term among common terms. Among common terms, there is a specific term [found] in such passages as the introduction: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? and "You are currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara; tell us about that," and so forth.

Because of the use of the term "Brahman," which is unique to Paramaśiva, and because that [status] is impossible for the elemental fire and so forth, Vaiśvānara is Śiva himself. Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) applies to both the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, while the word "Vaiśvānara" applies to the digestive fire and others.

It is common to all three; nevertheless, a distinction is observed. By such statements as "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is Sutejas," the reference of both the terms *ātman* and *Vaiśvānara* to the Supreme Lord is established. It is Śiva alone, the Supreme Brahman, who is intended here.

Because attributes such as having the sky as its head and so forth are possible; and because, in passages such as "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves," it is logical that the Supreme Lord, who is all-pervading, is the enjoyer of the fruits resting upon all worlds. Thus, indeed, all his evils are consumed away.
In such passages, the capacity to destroy all sins is appropriately attributed to the Supreme Lord alone.
Since there is an abundance of attributes belonging to Brahman in the introduction, conclusion, and other parts, it is established that Vaiśvānara is none other than Brahman.
To demonstrate another reason for this point, he says:
57. "That which is being remembered would be inference. || 25 ||

Here too, Paramaśiva alone is called Vaiśvānara, as in the passages: "Agni is the head, the eyes are the moon and sun," and "Agni is the mouth, the sky is the head," and so forth; since the universal nature (*sarvātmakatva*) of the Supreme Lord is thus proclaimed, Vaiśvānara is not distinct from the Supreme Lord. Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed...
"In the passage beginning with: 'The well-shining [breath] is the eye, the omniform;
the breath is the manifold path; the trunk is the abundant; the bladder itself is wealth; the earth itself is the two feet; the chest is the altar;
the body hair is the sacrificial grass; the heart is the Gārhapatya fire; the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; the mouth is the Āhavanīya fire.'"
Because the word *vaiśvānara* is established as referring to Paramaśiva:
"Salutation to Him, the Self of the worlds, whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the sun, and whose ears are the quarters."

Thus, the Smṛti also teaches that [Vaiśvānara] has the Supreme Lord as its referent. The form described in the Smṛti, which is being remembered, may serve as an inferential mark (*anumāna*) for understanding this. The word "iti" signifies a reason; because it is an inferential mark in this way, it is therefore determined that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Lord.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason:

"58. If it be argued that [the Self] is not [the eater] because of its being within and because of sound and so forth, we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [otherwise] it would be impossible, and they also study this as the Puruṣa. (26)

Now, an objection is raised: Vaiśvānara is not the Supreme Lord. Why? Because of the word and other reasons, and because of his abiding within. First, as for the word: the term "Vaiśvānara" does not refer to the Supreme Lord, because it has its primary application to the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni).
By the word "and others" (ādi), the triad of fires is indicated, such as "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire. Furthermore, that which is eaten...

Furthermore, by the passage beginning "The first [portion] that comes should be offered as an oblation," the status of being the locus for the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) is proclaimed;

for these reasons, Vaiśvānara is indeed the digestive fire within the stomach (*jāṭhara*). Moreover, because of its being established within: "He knows him as established within the person"—since scripture declares that Vaiśvānara is established within, and this [quality] belongs to the digestive fire.

If it is argued that [this is] possible—[we reply: no, because there is instruction for meditation upon Maheśvara as delimited by the gastric fire through the instruction for [identifying Him with] the vision [of the sun];
and because [such identification] is impossible in the case of attributes such as having heaven as His head.
The meaning is that [the fire] cannot exist in the mere digestive fire alone. Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins study this very Vaiśvānara as a person;
they study this Vaiśvānara as a person, they speak of him as a person. "This Agni Vaiśvānara is the person;
he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara thus—as a person, established within the person."
Since the Supreme Lord is the Self of all, his being "of the form of man" (*puruṣavidha*) and his being "situated within the man" (*puruṣe 'ntaḥpratiṣṭhita*) are both entirely appropriate.
By some, even in the reading *puruṣavidham abhidhīyate*, this same meaning is indicated. [This applies] to the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*).

The state of being shaped like a person (puruṣavidhatva) is not possible [in the literal sense]. However, because the Supreme Śiva is the self of all, everything is non-contradictory for the purpose of the devotee’s meditation.
Now, even if the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) cannot possibly consist of the three worlds, [the same applies] to that which resides both externally and internally.

Because the elemental fire is seen to have a connection with the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), its nature as consisting of the three worlds is possible. In passages such as, "He who by his light extended over this earth and heaven, and the two worlds and the intermediate space," the fact that the deity whose body is that [fire] has the heavenly world as a constituent part is established through its possession of sovereign power. Therefore, it is not [the case that...].
If it is argued that [the Vaiśvānara] is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), we say no;

for in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Rudra who is in the fire," the Supreme Śiva alone is designated as having the Vaiśvānara and other limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and thus here it is not the gastric Vaiśvānara nor any other.
Furthermore, with regard to the position that [the Self] is the Supreme Lord, he teaches another reason:
59. "For this very reason, it is neither a deity nor an elemental being. (27)

If it is argued that because the mantra-text shows the third elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*) to consist of the three worlds, its connection with the bodily parts— as in "the head itself is *sutejas*" and so forth— is appropriate precisely for that [fire], and that this is consistent due to the possession of sovereignty by the deity whose body it is;

We reply: "Devatābhūtam" (the deity and the elemental being) is a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*). Neither of these two is denoted by the word *vaiśvānara*. For this very reason—namely, for the reasons previously stated, such as the fact that the attributes of having heaven as the head and so forth are inconsistent in both cases—the meaning is that [neither is the referent]. Furthermore:

Since the elemental fire— consisting of redness, heat, and light— and its presiding deity possess sovereignty attained through the worship of Paraśiva, they lack the status of being the "Self" (ātman) and the state of being the Lord of All; therefore,
it must be understood that the designation "Vaiśvānara" belongs exclusively to Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who has been established as such.
Regarding this point, he further presents the opinion of the Teacher (Jaimini): "60. Jaimini [holds that] there is no contradiction even with direct [perception]. (28)

Jaimini considers it not contradictory that the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, is denoted by the term Vaiśvānara; for in the scripture it is stated, "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies—one terrible and one auspicious"—and thus Agni is directly designated as being of the nature of the Supreme Lord.

In the preceding section, the worship of Paramaśiva was taught as delimited by the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), in accordance with its being established within [the body] and so forth. Now, it is indicated that there is no contradiction even in worshipping [Him] directly as the Supreme Lord, without the use of a symbol (pratīka). Furthermore—[He is] "of human form" within the person.

In the phrase "established within," the fact that this Supreme Lord possesses limbs is indicated by the word *puruṣa*, while His being without parts is indicated by the expression "established within. Through the preceding and following context, it is taught that the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara. [The etymology is: He is both *viśva* (all) and *nara* (man), or he is the *nara* of all (*viśveṣāṃ naraḥ*), or all men (*viśve narāḥ*).

Or, [the term] *vaiśvānara* may mean "belonging to Viśvanara," for *viśvanara* is indeed *vaiśvānara*. Here, the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) is used in its primary sense, as in the cases of *rākṣasa* or *vāyasa*.
Furthermore, the word *agni* (fire) will also refer to the Supreme Lord alone, by virtue of His possessing qualities such as being the foremost (*agraṇī*).

And the conceptualization of Him as the *gārhapatya* fire and so forth, as well as His being the locus for the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*), belongs to the Supreme Lord alone because He is the Self of all.
It is now being determined.
In response to the doubt as to how a statement concerning the omnipresent Supreme Lord can be consistent with His being "measured by a span," the author presents the view of another teacher:
61. "On account of manifestation," says Āśmarathya. (Sūtra 27)

The dimension of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who is all-pervasive, is taught to be the measure of a span (*prādeśamātra*). Why? Because of manifestation. It is Paramaśiva himself who, for the sake of the worship of his devotees, manifests in specific locations such as the heart and the eyes with the measure of a span.
The Blessed One has faces, heads, and necks everywhere; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings; and the Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.

Āśmarathya explains that because the all-pervading [Brahman] is designated as having limited dimensions in the Śvetāśvatara and other Upaniṣads for the purpose of providing a focus for the devotee's meditation, the scriptural mention here of being "the size of a span" is likewise appropriate.
Regarding this point, he further shows the view of another teacher: 62. Bādari [holds that the soul exists] because of remembrance. (30)

Beginning with the passage, "The small, free from evil, dwelling in another's abode," and continuing with "like the interior of a lotus," [the text] describes how Śiva-Brahman, who is omnipresent, resides within the cave of the heart; how he consists of a flame of fire; how he is denoted by all words;
and how, by his own will for the sake of crossing over the worlds, he dwells in locations such as the heart measuring only a span (prādeśamātra). Thus, he is "measured by a span."

Thus, Bādari considers it to be so by way of the mind (*manas*). Just as rice and other grains measured by an *āḍhaka* are called "an *āḍhaka*," so too the Supreme Lord, perceived within a space of the measure of a span (*prādeśa*), is determined to be "the span. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the omnipresent [Lord] being limited.
"He who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara, who is of the measure of a span and all-pervading,

eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves"— since in such passages the meditation on Vaiśvānara as being of the measure of a span, from the head down to the chin, is designated, there is no contradiction in the Supreme Śiva-Brahman being of the measure of a span.
Therefore, Jaimini maintains that the scriptural statement regarding the person of the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*) is justified by virtue of his attaining that size;
the author of the Sūtras demonstrates this as follows:
"On account of attainment, so [says] Jaimini, for thus he shows. (Sūtra 31)

The meaning is that another scriptural passage is shown regarding Vaiśvānara’s being the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*). In the Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa: "In this world, the gods have indeed attained a well-known [state] that is the size of a span; thus I shall speak of them, and thus I shall cause them to be attained as the size of a span. He said, pointing to the head: "..."
Pointing to the eye, he said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as 'The One of Excellent Splendor' (sutejas).

Pointing to the two nostrils, he said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as 'The One of Diverse Paths' (pṛthagvartman). Pointing to the space within the mouth, he said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as 'The Abundant One' (bahula). [He pointed to] the principal waters.
Pointing [to the chin], he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara, the Wealth. Pointing to the chin, he said:
"This indeed is Vaiśvānara, the Foundation. Here, by the word *cubuka*, the lower part of the jaw (the chin) is indicated.
And by [stating] that the sun possesses the quality of "splendid light" (*sutejas*) and so forth, [the text teaches] the Vaiśvānara who consists of the three worlds.

It teaches the attainment of the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*) of the Supreme Lord by correlating the constituent parts beginning with heaven and ending with the earth with the bodily parts of the self beginning from the head down to the chin. In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is taught that heaven has the quality of "good light" (*sutejas*);
thus, by means of this specific quality of having a universal form (*viśvarūpatva*), a certain distinction is indicated.
Beginning with "The chest itself is the altar, the body hair the *barhis* grass, the heart the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind the *anvāhāryapacana* fire,
and the mouth the *āhavanīya* fire," and concluding with "One who knows thus offers the *agnihotra*," this passage defines the chest and other parts of the practitioner as the altar and so forth.

The scriptural statement that [the Self] is "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) teaches this on account of its possession of all branches (sarvaśākhā). Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for the all-pervading [Self] to be delimited.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
64. And they declare this [Self] to be in this [body]. || 32 ||

Furthermore, in this body, Nārāyaṇa, Jābāla, and others declare this all-pervading Supreme Lord to be present, saying: "You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as Rudra; nourish me with that food. And: "May Śiva enter me, not for burning"; "The Lord, the Master of the entire world, the consumer of the universe, is pleased."

The meaning is that in such passages, they consider the Supreme Lord to be the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) by virtue of being delimited by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) of the worshipper, and to be limited to the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*).
Furthermore: "This infinite, unmanifest, infinite Self is established in the *Avimukta* (the Unreleased); in what is that *Avimukta* [established]?"
"It is established"—in the *varuṇā* and in the *nāsī*. "What indeed is the *varuṇā*, and what is the *nāsī*?
In this regard, it wards off (*vārayati*) all evils pertaining to the senses in the *varuṇā*, and it destroys (*nāśayati*) them in the *nāsī*;
having thus explained [the names], they further inquire: "And what is its location? It is precisely that junction which exists between the eyebrows and the nose.

Since the junction between this world and the next occurs [there], and because even in the Jābāla Upaniṣad the Supreme Lord is designated as being measured by the span of a cubit (prādeśamātra), it is established that Vaiśvānara— presented here as being limited to the size of a cubit by means of the gastric fire— is none other than Śiva.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Vaiśvānara-adhikaraṇa,
in the *Śrīman-nirābhāra-vīraśaiva-yati-vraja-parivṛḍha-śrīmat-sadāśiva-brahmendrasarasvatī-sthāpita-vaiyāsika-brahma-mīmāṃsā-sūtrārtha-prakāśaka*.
The second quarter of the first chapter, titled "Samanvaya," in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya;
now begins the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya.
The Section Concerning Dyubhvādi (Heaven, Earth, etc. || 1 ||

Of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman— who is a mine of infinite jewels of auspicious qualities, who is delimited by the sixfold attributes such as omniscience, who is the non-different material and efficient cause of the universe, and who is supremely compassionate—
there is [the authority] of certain Śrutis through the purport of the sixfold marks of intention (liṅgas), beginning with the introduction (upakrama), within the two previously mentioned quarters.

Having established the concordance (*samanvaya*) here as well, the third section (*pāda*) is commenced by the venerable Vyāsa in order to uproot the thorns of doubt regarding indistinct scriptural statements; namely,
the demonstration that the Supreme Śiva is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, as taught in the Brāhmaṇa.
65. That which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word. || 1 ||

The subject matter of this [Upaniṣad] is recited in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "That in which the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space are woven, together with the mind and all the vital breaths—know that alone as the one Self; cast off other words; this is the bridge to immortality. Here, the reality heard of as the substratum of heaven, earth, and so forth, is the Supreme Lord.
It is doubted whether [the subject] is that [Self] or something else.

Here, it is more appropriate to understand this as referring to the primary elemental air (pradhāna-kṣetrajña-bhūta-vāyu), because the primary [air] is the cause of the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
This is because the primary [air] is designated as all-pervasive in the scripture: "It is infinite, boundless, and indeed a mass of consciousness."

Because of the designation by the word "Self" in the Śruti passage, "Release other words; this is the bridge to the Immortal," and because the embodied soul is seen to be the locus of what is to be experienced, it is also faultlessly established that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the support of all.
[As stated: "Vāyu, O Gautama, is indeed that thread; by Vāyu, O Gautama, as the thread, this world and the other world..."

Furthermore, all beings are woven together [in it], as established by the Śruti regarding Vāyu being the substratum of all. Moreover, since the status of Vāyu as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not in any way possible— given that the Supreme Lord is designated as "superior to the universe" and so on in such Śruti passages as "Rudra is superior to the universe"— [Vāyu cannot be that abode].

When it is argued that [the Self] is possible [to be the support], we reply: the support of heaven, earth, and so forth is [the Self] because of its own word; "heaven and earth" refers to heaven (*dyu*) and earth (*bhū*), and that which has these two as its beginning is "heaven-earth-and-so-forth."

"Day, earth, etc. refers to heaven, earth, the intermediate space, the mind, the vital breaths, and so forth. Its "abode" (āyatana) means its locus; the meaning is that it is the Supreme Lord. Why? "On account of the word itself" (sva-śabdāt). This means because of the hearing of the word "Self" (ātman)—that is, the word "Self" which is the designator of Brahman itself—as in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self" (tamevaikaṃ jānatha ātmānam).
"The cessation of conceptual proliferation, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual—this they consider the fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known.

Here too, it is understood that the word "Self" (ātman) refers to Śiva. Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is not anything other [than Him]. Furthermore: "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. [This refers to] the Puruṣa.

"Verily, this entire universe is action, austerity, and Brahman, the supreme immortality; Brahman alone is this immortality in the east, Brahman in the west, Brahman in the south and in the north. Space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports all—whatever is the supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe," and so forth, in hundreds of such scriptural passages concerning Śiva.

Since the designation of being "beyond all" and the "substratum of all" belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone, it is established that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is Maheśvara. Furthermore, because the existence of a "far shore" for the bridge is logically possible, the state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is distinct from the Supreme Lord.

To address the doubt that [the Self] might be something that comes into being, he states another reason: 66. Because it is designated as that which is to be approached by the liberated (muktopasṛpya). || 2 ||

By the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (setu), only the universal substratum is taught, not [the bridge] characterized by having a further shore and so forth. Here too, the state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so on belongs to Paramaśiva alone. Why? Because of the designation as that which is to be approached by the liberated (muktopasṛpya).
That which is to be approached and attained by the liberated is "muktopasṛpya. This is an expression where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary focus.

The meaning is that there is a designation of being "approachable by the liberated" (*muktopasṛpyatva*) from that [scriptural passage]. Alternatively, there is no difficulty in the reading *muktopasṛpyatvavyapadeśāt*, which means: because that which is to be approached and attained by the liberated is indicated here. When the seer perceives the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person—

"Brahma-yoni. Then, "the wise one, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains supreme equality"—here, having taught the attainment of the same form as Śiva for the worshippers of Paramaśiva, [it continues]: "The fifteen Kalās have returned to their foundations, all the deities to their respective deities, the actions, and the self consisting of consciousness, all into the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]."
They become one. Just as rivers [merge], having reached Rudra—[note:

pages 270 and 271 are missing]—the attainment of the state of Śiva, preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), is indeed what is meant by the passage beginning with "they call him equal to Rudra."

It is taught that this is liberation. According to the maxim, "Censure does not intend to censure; it is engaged in praising that which is worthy of praise," the censure of another's doctrine here does not produce demerit (*pratyavāya*), because it is impossible to establish the superiority of the knowledge of Śiva through *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) without refuting the opposing position. Furthermore, regarding the censure of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*)...

Because [the teaching] is prescribed as being conducive to the establishment of reality, and because a prohibition applies only to that which is other than what has been prescribed; and because individual souls (*jīvas*) do not constitute a portion of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), since in passages such as "It thought:

May I be many" (*tadaikṣata bahu syām*), the Lord is seen to be the cause of the souls who are His own parts and were previously latent within Him, like a father and his sons. As it is said: "When all desires that dwell in His heart are released... (*yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye'sya hṛdi sthitāḥ*).

"Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains the Brahman. The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen"—by such passages [it is shown] that through the grace of Paramaśiva, for those who worship Him, there is the attainment of the state of Śiva, preceded by the absolute cessation of bonds.
Because of the designation that "liberation occurs," it is established that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) alone.
67. It is not inference, because of the absence of words denoting that [inference]. || 3 ||
That which is inferred is *anumāna*; thus, the *pradhāna* propounded in the Sāṃkhya tradition is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

Why? Because of the absence of its word (*atacchabdāt*). For in such passages as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," there is an absence of any term that denotes the *pradhāna*, since the insentient *pradhāna* lacks omniscience and other such qualities.
Because all phenomena are non-existent [independently], it is Supreme Śiva alone who is accepted here as the cause of all and the substratum of all.

Although the *pradhāna* cannot be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth because it is insentient, and although such a status might be suspected for the *jīva* because it is sentient, [the author] says:
68. And [the word] *prāṇabhṛt* [is also used]. || 4 ||
The individual soul (*jīva*), though it is a living being (*prāṇabhṛt*), is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth. Why? Precisely because of this word [“Self”].

For although the individual soul, as a living being, is seen to possess the nature of consciousness and to be denoted by the word “Self,” it is nevertheless said: "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind;
it is subtler than the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold."

Since the individual soul (jīva) is designated in hundreds of scriptural passages—such as "The soul is to be known as a part," and "Two unborn ones, the knower and the unknowable, the Lord and the non-Lord"—as being possessed of limited knowledge and finite dimensions, it is impossible for the soul to be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; therefore, it cannot be the referent of that term [the Supreme Self]. Consequently, [the abode] must be Śiva alone, who is all-pervading and endowed with every power.
The state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
He states another reason: 69. Because of the designation of difference. || 5 ||
Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, is not the living being (prāṇabhṛt). Why? Because of the designation of difference. There is a designation by way of distinction;
therefore [it is said]:
"Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words; He is indeed the bridge to immortality. [And: "On the same tree..."

"The person, submerged [in the world], grieves through lack of mastery, deluded; but when he perceives Him who is worshipped as another, the Lord, then he, freed from sorrow, attains His majesty. Because in such passages as "Two birds, inseparable companions...

there is a designation of natural difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman through attributes such as being the knower and the object of knowledge, the individual soul, which possesses limited knowledge, does not [attain the Lord].
The state of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is appropriate [for the Supreme Self].
He states another reason for the position of the Supreme Lord: "On account of the context" (Sūtra 1.3.70).
Because the introduction to the scriptural passage begins with the proposition that "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known?",
and because the knowledge of everything becomes possible through the knowledge of Paraśiva, who is the material cause of the entire universe; [the reference is] not to the individual soul (jīva).

Just as the sentences such as "He offers the *samidh* oblation," which are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), have the New and Full Moon sacrifices as their purport,

so too all Vedāntic statements found within the context of the Supreme Lord that teach difference and non-difference have the Supreme Lord as their purport. This is evident from such scriptural passages as, "There is not the slightest diversity here."

If it is argued that because Brahman is understood as being free from all conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) preceded by the negation of everything, and because the Upanishads have that alone as their purport through the sixfold marks of intention found in their openings, conclusions, and so forth—this is not so; for it contradicts many scriptural passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower," which [affirm] duality. [This is so] despite the negation of all difference...

Furthermore, because it indicates the knowledge that everything has Śiva as its essence; for we see no purpose in a knowledge of the non-dual and undifferentiated that is devoid of the world (*niṣprapañca*), since such knowledge lacks the power to release one from the bond of *māyā*. In this Upaniṣad, he [imparts] that knowledge of Brahman...

Having introduced the knowledge of Brahman as "the foundation of all sciences," and having first presented two types of knowledge— distinguished as the higher and lower— which establish the activity of the single knowledge of Śiva as the answer to the question, "O Venerable One, when one thing is known, all this becomes known"?— at the outset...

Having stated that the fourteen branches of knowledge are "lower knowledge" (*aparavidyā*), and then beginning with "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained," and having established— through the passage ending in "from the Imperishable the entire universe arises here"— that its defining characteristic is being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, [the text] describes its very nature with the words "He who is all-knowing," and so on.

Having deprecated the path of active worldly involvement with the words, "For these are rafts, they are not firm," and so forth, [the text continues]: "Those who possess austerity and faith, dwelling in the forest, peaceful, wise, and living on alms—being free from passion, they depart through the door of the sun to where the immortal, immutable-souled Person dwells. In this passage, the terms "immortal" (*amṛta*) and "Person" (*puruṣa*) are used in their specific, non-common [technical] senses.
It has been established that [the two] denote Śiva.
In the passage, "The perishable is *pradhāna*, the immortal-imperishable is Hara," the word *akṣara* is determined to refer to Paraśiva.

Having stated, through such passages as "By whom one knows the imperishable, true Puruṣa," that [Paraśiva] is the cause of the creation of the individual soul (*jīva*), that [imperishable] is what must be understood.

Having indicated that He is to be known through the words "Know Him as the gentle one" (*saumyam vidhi*), and having stated that He is to be known through the Vedāntas by means of the passage beginning with "Taking up the bow of the Upaniṣads" (*dhanur gṛhītvopaniṣadam*), [the text proceeds] with the knowledge of the supreme Śiva, whose nature is gold, through such passages as "When the seer sees the golden-colored one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman."

Having taught the state of attaining identity with Supreme Śiva preceded by the cessation of merit and demerit, it is understood from the passage beginning with "Just as rivers" and ending with "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" that this is a section concerning Supreme Śiva through six types of indicators (*liṅga*);
for the word *Īśvara*, which denotes the object of knowledge, is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of Śiva. [This applies even] to the one of golden color; salutations...
Furthermore, because [the Lord] is seen as the ultimate referent in passages such as "To him with golden arms" (*hiraṇyabāhave*),

it is established that only the knowledge of Śiva— the cause of the universe, superior to the universe, and the controller of the universe— is the cause for destroying the bonds of worldly existence (*bhavapāśa*).
Therefore, [the world] is like a snake imagined upon a rope, being a product of ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus subordinate.

It should be understood that the doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman as free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-brahmādvaitavāda*) is non-Vedic, because no Vedic scripture is seen to enjoin it. Furthermore, in another Śruti it is said, "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, for he is the maker of auspiciousness," which shows the abandonment of meditation on anything other than Śiva; and [it says], "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace."

Because it is declared that the knowledge of Śiva alone is the cause of ultimate peace; because liberation is heard of as resulting from the knowledge of Śiva alone in the statement, "Having known the Lord, they become immortal"; and because it is established that for those solely devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, all sins are destroyed through the practice of churning with knowledge—according to the statement, "The wise man burns away his bonds through the practice of churning with knowledge"—liberation results from the worship of Him alone.
The Sound of the Bell: Since this Upaniṣad primarily treats the manifold attributes of Paramaśiva, it is established that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is indeed Paramaśiva himself.
He states another reason for its referring to the Supreme Lord:
71. An exposition of the supremacy of qualified non-duality (viśeṣādvaita), which consists of both difference and non-difference:
"And on account of abiding and eating. (Sūtra 7)

For this reason also, a living being is not the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; why? Because of "abiding and eating" (*sthityadanābhyām*). Abiding and eating constitute "abiding-and-eating. By means of these two [the genitive dual]: "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. Of them, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6).

In the passage "He shines forth," the individual soul's status as the enjoyer of the fruits of karma is taught, while in the phrase "the other, not eating," the supreme Lord's state of remaining indifferent is taught. Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, is the Great Lord alone.
Now, an objection is raised: in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second for him," [is this not contradicted?]

If it is argued that because non-duality is established by first negating all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman found in mantras such as "Two birds... is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), we say no;
for this contradicts the scriptures (*śruti*) that establish non-duality and those that establish the absence of attributes (*nirguṇa*) prior to creation.

Because of the absence of the manifoldness (prapañca) of both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta), [the Upaniṣads] refer to the state beyond time. All scriptural passages concerning differentiation refer to the period subsequent to creation, as in: "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone was the absolute";
"I alone existed first"; "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone"; and "Being alone, my dear, [this was in the beginning]."

Because, according to the principle of the uniformity of the various scriptural passages (*gatisāmānyanyāya*), the non-duality of Brahman prior to creation is established in all Vedānta texts; and because in passages such as "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*), we hear that Brahman, when intent on creation, becomes manifold through desire; [and this applies] after the time of creation.

Since Brahman is observed to possess qualities (saguṇa), it is not logical that [the term "Nirguṇa"] has any other meaning. Thus says the Smṛti: "Prior to creation, Mahādeva is praised in the scriptures as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) by those who know the truth, due to the contraction of his power."
At the beginning of creation, due to the abundant majesty of the Supreme Lord's power,
He is celebrated as possessing auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the like.
Therefore, the reconciliation of the non-dual (advaita) scriptures occurs after creation;
however, the realization of the non-dual scriptures is said to pertain to the state prior to creation.
Now, due to the distinction of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, Sadāśiva possesses attributes (*saguṇatva*);
however, because he is witnessed by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), his state of being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇatva*) is established.
"Therefore, He is celebrated in the Vedas as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).

Thus, in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, through the passage beginning "The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā," the embodied nature, the state of tranquility, and the possession of attributes of Brahman are taught. At its conclusion, [it speaks] of that very same [Brahman] as the witness of all, beyond darkness...

In the passage beginning with "parastāt" (beyond), its partlessness, freedom from qualities (*nirguṇatva*), and so forth are taught. Witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) is not a quality, for the Śruti declares: "The witness is the cognizer and is without qualities.

Now, one might object: since the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is the cause of the world, exists prior to the creation by Maheśvara, how can there be non-duality (*advaita*)? If this is asked, the answer is no.

—Because in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "The divine power of the Self is concealed by its own qualities," and "The power of the Supreme is heard to be manifold indeed, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action," we see that His power is non-different from Him. There is no natural separation between power and the possessor of power. Therefore...

Since Paramaśiva is the substratum of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is the ultimate cause of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and since He is non-different from it by virtue of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), He is established as the non-distinct efficient and material cause (*abhinnanimittopādānakāraṇa*).
[Objection: But surely, because the term "non-duality" (*advaita*) conveys the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, in the absence of duality—

If it is argued that there is no purpose for the word "viśeṣa" (particularity) because non-duality (*advaita*) cannot be perceived [otherwise], we say no. This is because the word "non-dual" conveys merely the negation of difference, and since the reality or unreality of difference has not been established, the word "particularity" is specified. By this, even if there is identity of genus between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, [the distinction remains] among insentient things such as stones, clods of earth, wood, and so forth.

Just as there is a difference in their essential natures, so too, despite their unity in the genus "consciousness," a real difference between the two is taught because of the perception of mutually contradictory attributes— such as atomicity and omnipresence, or limited knowledge and omniscience— as existing separately.

The etymological definition of *viśeṣādvaita*: "Viśva" (the universe) and "śeṣa" (the Residue/Supreme) are the two "viśeṣas"; the non-duality (*advaita*) of those two is *viśeṣādvaita*. In this context, by the term "non-duality," the cessation of the natural difference of the individual soul (*jīva*)—like that of a worm within a bee—is taught. One who should say, "Haṃsa, Haṃsa."

This is because the word *viś* is clearly taught as a synonym for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in Vedic texts such as "in the all-seeing sky, in the wind, in the Supreme Self" (Nirukta 2.14), and because the definition of Brahman as the cause of the universe is indicated by the word *viś* through its etymological derivation from the root *vā*, meaning "to produce. By the word *śeṣa*, [the following is meant:]...

The individual soul (*jīva*) is designated as a portion of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), based on scriptural declarations such as "as sparks from a fire"; and by the term "non-duality" (*advaita*), the state of union (*sāyujya*) between the individual soul and Brahman established in scriptures such as "just as rivers [merge into the ocean]" is taught.

Now, regarding the demonstration of the reality of the world: if the world and individual souls were false—like everything superimposed upon a rope—it would follow that the Vedic scriptures, the Purāṇas, and other texts which enjoin prohibitions and injunctions [regarding them] would themselves be outside the Veda. In our view, all knowledge is indeed real. Furthermore, in that regard:

Since the cognition of similarity is ultimately real, even the cognition of a rope as a snake is true; for without similarity, that [illusory] cognition would be impossible. Furthermore, because the constituent parts of the [rope] exist here as well through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), the cognition of nacre as silver is also true. However, due to the greater number of nacre-parts, no such practical usage occurs.

Since even the two sets of visual causal conditions that perceive two moons—when the eyes are pressed by a finger or similar object—are real, the cognition of two moons is also real; for when the cause is real, the effect must also be real.
Due to being obscured by a *pittadoṣa* (bile disorder) located in one's own eye, the whiteness residing in the conch shell is not perceived.

The rays emerging from one's own eyes strike a conch shell smeared with gold; because they are extremely subtle, they are perceived by the eyes themselves. Therefore, even the cognition in the form "the conch is yellow" is indeed real.
Due to contact with various locations, those respective cognitions arise. Because of extreme rapidity, there is no perception of the intervening space.

Therefore, even the cognition of a circle of fire (alātacakra) is real. Due to the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), since portions of the other elements exist within each single element, the fact that the portion of space is predominant does not prevent the attainment of the object "water. Therefore, even the cognition of a mirage (marumarīcikā) is real, because the ignorance (avidyā) that serves as its cause is real.

Even dream-cognition possesses reality. According to the logic of the seed and the sprout, when the cause exists, the effect is real. Furthermore, because it indicates auspicious and inauspicious results, and because the cognition experienced during the dream remains established even upon waking, dream-cognition is not false; for it is just like the waking world.

Because [all things] are dependent upon the Supreme Lord; even the knowledge of a magician is true, because the gems, mantras, herbs, and so forth that cause it are real, and because the cognition therein is also uncontradicted;
for the knowledge of all objects presented to the intellect is ultimately real.
Furthermore, because the various objects that serve as the causes of error are themselves real, all cognition is indeed true.

If it is argued: "By the force of the pervasion (vyāpti) that 'whatever is perceived has perished,' since the objects existing within the phenomenal world (prapañca) constructed by beginningless ignorance are false, why would the objects in the previously mentioned examples not also be false?"—the answer is no.

There would be no experience of Brahman; moreover, Brahman itself would be false, like the phenomenal world (prapañca), because it would be the object of a cognition produced by a cause that is false and unreal, just as the phenomenal world is. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is appropriate. [This is so] because of the etymological derivation: "That which is not *vidyā* (knowledge) is *avidyā*," and that which is such is *māyā*.

If it is argued that since Māyā is the material cause of the world, how can its effect—the phenomenal universe—be real? Do not say so; for in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Know Māyā to be Prakṛti and the Great Lord to be the wielder of Māyā," and "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," Māyā is established as the power (*śakti*) of Brahman.

Because of the designation [of the two as one], and because of the non-difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*), like the moon and its moonlight, if the power were to perish, it would follow that Brahman characterized by that power would also perish; consequently, one would fall into the view of those who deny the existence of God (*nirīśvaravāda*).
Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is the substratum of the entire phenomenal world, beginning with heaven and earth, which constitutes His own manifestation.
The Section on the Grounds || 2 ||
Now follows the demonstration that the Supreme Lord is denoted by the word *bhūman*.

For the purpose of revealing the objectless supreme bliss of one who possesses the knowledge of Paramaśiva— the mine of infinite jewels of auspicious qualities— and who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), he says:
72. [The Self] is the Infinite, because it is taught as being superior to the serene faith (samprasāda).

The subject matter of this [passage] is found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "The Infinite (bhūman) alone is to be sought after," "Venerable sir, I wish to know the Infinite," and "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite;
but where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite. Here, that which is to be established by the word "Infinite" (bhūman) is [the Self].

The doubt is whether it is the vital breath (prāṇa) or the Supreme Lord. Since the word *bhūman* is heard with an abstract suffix—according to the rule "there is elision of the final vowel of *bahu*, and *bhū* replaces *bahu*"—it indicates abundance (*bahutva*). When there arises a specific desire to know what constitutes that abundance, the answer is "the vital breath is greater than hope," because the vital breath was mentioned immediately prior. Thus, [the opponent argues] it is the vital breath.

It appears that "the ground" (bhūmi) is meant; for thus have I heard from those like the Blessed One: "One who knows the Self crosses over sorrow. Therefore, O Blessed One, I am in sorrow; may the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of sorrow.
Because of the abundance of marks indicative of Brahman, it appears that the Supreme Lord is intended. Consequently, a doubt arises here.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, is as follows: here, by the word "the Great" (*bhūman*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is intended. This is because it is indicated by the questions and answers between Nārada and Sanatkumāra that the vital breath is Brahman. For instance: "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than name? "Speech is indeed greater than name. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than speech? "Mind is indeed greater than speech."

Furthermore, by means of the question and answer—"Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than name? and "Yes, indeed, that which is greater than name," continuing thus down to "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*)—it is the vital breath alone that is grasped here.
Beyond the vital breath, however, no further question or answer is heard. [The text continues: "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than the vital breath?
and "Yes, indeed, that which is greater than the vital breath"—but it is the vital breath itself [that is the subject].

Having taught in detail, beginning with "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed greater than name and so forth up to hope," and having authorized the one who perceives the vital breath by saying, "You are an over-speaker; you are an over-speaker," and "One should say, 'I am an over-speaker,' and not deny it," [the text continues]: "But he indeed is an over-speaker who over-speaks by means of the Truth."

Having taught that the one who observes the vow of *prāṇa* is an "exceeding speaker" (*ativādin*), [the text] proceeds through a succession beginning with truth to show that *prāṇa* alone is considered the "Fullness" (*bhūman*). Since the teaching of "Fullness" is directed toward that very [prāṇa], it is logical that *prāṇa* alone is denoted by the word *bhūman*.
Furthermore, the definition of "Fullness" established by the statement, "where one sees nothing else," is specified as belonging to that very [prāṇa].
Since the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is observed even in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the definition "he sees nothing else" is appropriate.

And so the Śruti, having demonstrated the state of deep sleep—which is devoid of the activity of all [other] causes—through such passages as "he does not hear, he does not see," [states]: "In this city, the fires of the vital breaths alone..."

The phrase "it is awake" establishes that even in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by the fivefold functions, remains in a waking state; thus, sleep is indicated as being primarily constituted by the *prāṇa*. This is not inconsistent with the bliss (*sukha*) specified in the scriptural passage, "That which is the Infinite (*bhūman*), that is bliss," because of the Vedic revelation, "The *prāṇa* indeed is the immortal. Furthermore, as for that which... [yo vai]... [is the Infinite].

"The Plenum is that which is immortal"—thus, it is appropriate that immortality is predicated of that [Plenum] alone. For, by such statements as "Prāṇa is the father, Prāṇa is the mother, Prāṇa is the brother, Prāṇa is the friend, Prāṇa is the teacher, Prāṇa is the Brāhmaṇa," it is taught that Prāṇa alone is the self of all. Furthermore, [the text] says, "He makes Prāṇa itself the self of all"; thus, it is of Prāṇa alone [that this is said].

It teaches that He is the cause of the world; therefore, because there is no contradiction with the context regarding the desire to know the Self— as seen in the statement, "Therefore, he who knows the Self crosses over sorrow"— if one were to argue that, by means of the sixfold marks of purport, the *bhūman* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and not the Supreme Lord.

It is said: The "Fullness" (bhūman) is indeed the Supreme Lord, because it is taught as being beyond the state of serene confidence (samprasāda). Why? Because it is taught as being beyond the state of serene confidence. Serene confidence is so called because in this state the nature of the individual soul (jīva) becomes perfectly tranquil; it refers to the state of deep sleep. And since in that state the vital breath (prāṇa) remains awake, the word "serene confidence" is used here to denote the vital breath.
Therefore, "after that" means after the instruction concerning *prāṇa*.

Some say: "The *samprasāda* is the individual soul (*jīva*); [the instruction follows] above that. However, immediately after the instruction concerning *prāṇa*, the text says, "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth"; by the word "but," it declares that speaking about *prāṇa* is not transcendental speech.

By stating that the doctrine of the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is denoted by the word "Truth" (satya), is the "highest speech" (ativāda), he teaches the state of abundance (bhūmā). Furthermore, because liberation is taught through the knowledge of the Self in passages such as "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow," and because it is impossible for the insentient vital air (prāṇavāyu) to bestow liberation, the word "Self" (ātman) refers to the Supreme Śiva.

Because this is established by numerous scriptural passages— since liberation is taught to be attained through the knowledge of Paraśiva alone in many such texts as "Knowing Śiva, one attains ultimate peace" (*śivaṃ śāntim atyantam eti*) and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*)— and because [Paraśiva] is subsequently described as the Self in the passage beginning with "Now,

therefore, the instruction on the Self" (*athāta ātmādeśaḥ*), [the Self is Paraśiva]. Furthermore, [this is so] because of the attributes found in such statements as "where one sees nothing else" (*yatra nānyat paśyati*).

Because of the impossibility [of such qualities] in the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and because of the abundance of contextual indications (*prakaraṇa-liṅga*) in the passage, "I am he, O Venerable One, who grieves; may the Venerable One carry me across to the further shore of grief," that which is denoted by the word *bhūman* is indeed the Supreme Lord himself.
He states another reason for the position of the Supreme Lord:
73. And because of the logical consistency of the doctrine. || 9 ||

Because, through such passages as "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else," attributes such as the absence of all worldly activity prior to creation are established in relation to Paramaśiva; this very point is the indicator for those whose souls are liberated. As stated in the previously mentioned *adhikaraṇa*: "Thus the knower, freed from name and form, [reaches] that which is higher than the high..."

By the passage beginning with "He approaches the divine Person," the attainment of *sāyujya* with Śiva— preceded by the absolute cessation of the bonds of the pure individual soul (*jīva*) who meditates upon Brahman— is established through the analogy of a river merging into the ocean. Therefore, for those souls that have attained the state of Śiva, there is both liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*).
The negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is logical through the knowledge that everything has Śiva as its essence.

But an objection may be raised: since the statement, "Until I am liberated, then I shall attain [union]," describes the experience of the phenomenal world for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) until the point of disembodied liberation (videhamukti), how can there be a negation of the phenomenal world for those who possess the knowledge of Śiva and are liberated while living?
If it is argued that [rebirth] occurs, [we reply]: for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who worship Śiva,

even though the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) still exists— like a camphor lamp placed in the midst of a fierce heat— the supreme Śiva, whose nature is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), exists as the Self of the universe due to the presence of the knowledge that everything is of the nature of Śiva.
It becomes an object of perception; likewise, scriptural passages such as "this arises from that" are heard.
Therefore, the experience of those who know Brahman—the *jīvanmuktas*—is observed to be "I am Brahman.
According to the maxim that "nothing is impossible for what is perceived," it is not reasonable to interpret this in any other sense. [This applies] to Brahman.
Since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has non-different efficient and material causes, it is entirely appropriate to perceive its identity with that [Brahman]. Furthermore,

in another scriptural passage such as "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?", there is the absence of the conventional worldly behavior of the natural phenomenal world for those who possess the knowledge that all is of the nature of Śiva, just as described previously.
Because it is understood as the nature of the liberated soul (*muktajīva*). That which is indeed the *bhūman* (the Infinite) is bliss; thus the blissfulness of the *bhūman* has been shown.
Furthermore, that which is heard in the scripture, "That which is indeed the *bhūman* is immortal," is immortality, which is an attribute unique to Paraśiva.
Moreover: "In what, O Venerable One, is He established? "In His own majesty. "All this is indeed the Self; from the Self [it all proceeds]."

Prāṇa— because by the passage beginning with "From the Self, space," the attributes such as being established in its own majesty and being the cause of all are predicated of that very Paramaśiva; thus it is established that the one denoted by the term "Bhūman" is indeed Paramaśiva.

If it is asked, "How can the existence and non-existence of phenomenal activity be possible for the one Supreme Śiva?"—the answer will be clearly stated later by the venerable Vyāsa himself in the sūtra: "As in the world, [His] isolation consists solely of sport. This concludes the section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). 3.

Now, having taught the supremacy of Paramaśiva, who is Brahman and distinguished by the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the author explains in another section that he is denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable):
[The text continues: ...Having thus established the superiority of Paramaśiva, who is Brahman, over all else, he states in a subsequent section that he is designated by the term *akṣara*.
74. [Brahman is] the Imperishable, because it supports everything up to the end of space. || 10 ||
The subject of this is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "In what, indeed, is space woven like warp and woof? He replied:

"O Gārgī, that which the Brahmins call the Imperishable (akṣara) is this very thing—it is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, and it is without shadow. Here, by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara),...
There arises a doubt as to whether the *praṇava* is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

For in such passages as "The *oṃkāra* alone is all this," the *praṇava* is shown to be the self of all; and because the word "syllable" (*akṣara*) is well-known in common usage to mean a phoneme—as in "the traditional collection of syllables"—and also because of another scriptural passage stating, "The single-syllabled Brahman is *om*."
If it is argued that because the *praṇava* is designated as being identical with Brahman, its denotability by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) is appropriate;

whereas because of the scriptural statement, "The Person is called akṣara," the denotability of the individual soul (*jīva*) by the word "akṣara" is also appropriate; therefore, the denotability of the Supreme Lord by the word "akṣara" is not tenable—then [we reply]:

We reply: "The Imperishable (Akṣara) [is Śiva], because of the support of all things up to the ether. Here, that which is denoted by the word "Imperishable" is indeed Śiva. Why? Because of the support of all things up to the ether; that is to say, because of the sustaining of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which extends from the earth up to the ether and is brought forth by His own power. As it is said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, and that which is between these two..."

Regarding the space that is pointed out as the substratum of the entire manifold of transformations— beginning with the statement, "These two, heaven and earth, what has been, what is, and what will be, are said to be woven like warp and woof in space alone"— when Gārgī asks, "In what, then, is that space woven like warp and woof?", [the answer is given] by the passage beginning, "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas call this the Imperishable (akṣara). In this [Imperishable], [space is woven].

By the statement of Yājñavalkya ending with "O Gārgī, in the Imperishable (akṣara), the ether (ākāśa) is woven like warp and woof," the support of everything up to the ether for that Imperishable is determined; [as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad]:
"The perishable is Pradhāna, the immortal Imperishable is Hara; the one God enters the perishable self and the ether."
