"Air, fire, water, and earth, the sustainer of the universe; that which is the supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe"—since in such other scriptural passages as these, the Supreme Lord alone is taught as being primarily denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) and as the support of everything up to the ether, this cannot possibly apply to anything else. Furthermore, as for that which...

"Oṃkāra indeed is all this. Even that [statement] in the Śruti describes the syllable *praṇava* as being the self of all for the purpose of praising it as the means for realizing Brahman. In that context, because of the abundance of attributes belonging to the Supreme Lord and because of the context of the Supreme Lord, it is He alone who is denoted by the word "Akṣara" (the Imperishable).
Siddham.
This is the demonstration that Paramaśiva is qualified by Śakti.
Having raised the objection that [the reason] "because he supports everything up to the ether" is over-extended (*ativyāpti*) to the Pradhāna, he refutes it:
75. And that [is so] because of the authoritative instruction. || 11 ||

That steadfastness (dhṛti) can belong only to Śiva, the Supreme Brahman. Why? Because of the "ruling" (praśāsana). For in such passages as, "O Gārgī, by the ruling of this Imperishable, the sun and moon stand held apart," the ruling of Paramaśiva alone is heard; for it is impossible for the insentient Pradhāna to exercise such ruling. Furthermore, in another Śruti:
Because [the text] beginning with "The Lord of all sciences" designates the quality of being the controller of all as a characteristic of Paramaśiva;

for it is improper that the Pradhāna should always possess such governance. By this, the qualified nature of Brahman, the substratum of all, is taught, since the support of the universe is impossible for that which is devoid of attributes.

Since the scripture states, "His power is heard to be indeed manifold," and because this teaches that power is inherent (*svābhāvikatva*), it is never possible for Brahman to be devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*). Even though power and the possessor of power are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddhatva*)—as in the case of the statement "fire burns"—there is still a conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) between them; thus, [power] is not non-existent.

Or, regarding the statement "the dharmas exist as eternal," there is no contradiction because we observe that even when there is no actual separateness, there is an uncontradicted conventional usage of separateness. As it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Śiva is directly of the nature of consciousness, while Śivā consists of truth and bliss. Furthermore: "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second."

Since the non-duality of the Supreme Lord has been established within the teaching of the world, it is beyond dispute that Paramaśiva alone, as qualified by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), is denoted by the word "Imperishable" (*akṣara*).
He states another reason:
76. And because of the exclusion of other states. || 12 ||
For this reason as well, the support of the limit of space belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, and not to the Pradhāna or other such principles. Why?

Because of the exclusion of the nature of others (*anyabhāvavyāvṛtteḥ*). This means that because the properties of others—such as the Pradhāna—are excluded, and because its opposite is heard in scripture. As it is said: "That, O Gārgī, is this Imperishable; it is unseen but seeing, unheard but hearing..."

Regarding the statement, "heard by the ear, known by the mind, [and] cognized," the characteristics of the Supreme Lord, such as being the seer and so forth, are not possible for the Pradhāna because of its insentience. Therefore, the Supreme Lord is that which is denoted by the word "Akṣara" (the Imperishable).
The Section Concerning the Object of the Act of Seeing (Īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa) || 4 ||

In order to establish that Śiva—the Supreme Brahman, who transcends the means of knowledge such as perception and who bestows grace upon all—becomes perceptible to his devotee through His extraordinary compassion, he presents another topical section: 77. *Īkṣatikarmavyapadeśātsaḥ* (Because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing).

The subject matter of this is heard in the *Praśnopaniṣad* of the Atharvaveda: "O Satyakāma, this syllable *oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, by means of this very abode, the knower follows after one or the other. Beginning thus, it continues: "But he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures—he, in the heat [of fire], [reaches] the sun..."
[The passage continues: "He is perfected. Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil;

led up by the Sāman chants, he goes to the world of Brahman. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the person who is heard of as the object of meditation is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) or someone else.

In that context, the one to be worshipped is not Paramaśiva, but rather Hiraṇyagarbha alone; for it is seen here that the attainment of his world is what is intended, as expressed in the passage: "He is led by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman. Furthermore, the word "Supreme" (*parama*) can appropriately apply to him when he is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*), and he is also denoted by the term "Person" (*puruṣa*). Alternatively, it may be Nārāyaṇa; for [it is said]: "They always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu..."

If it is argued that, because the term "the wise" (*sūrayaḥ*) is established as referring specifically to the experience of the learned, and because the word *praṇava* also primarily denotes that [experience], it is actually Hiraṇyagarbha— the collective totality of all individual souls (*sarvajīvasamaṣṭyātmaka*)—
who is enjoined here as the object of universal worship; therefore, in no way is the worship of Paramaśiva enjoined here.

We reply: On account of the designation of the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati-karma-vyapadeśāt*), that person to be meditated upon here is indeed Śiva. Why? Because in the supplementary passage—"He sees the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond the mass of living beings"—the one to be meditated upon is designated as the object of the act of seeing; therefore, the meaning is that he is indeed Paramaśiva.

If it be objected that—in the passage "He is led up by the Sāman chants to the world of Brahman"—the word *brahman* is conventionally used for the four-faced [Brahmā], and therefore why should the meditation here not be upon him? We say no. For in the Śruti text, "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings (*jīvaghana*)," the term *jīvaghana* refers to Hiraṇyagarbha, who presides over all individual souls.

Therefore, that which is beyond [the self], namely the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the object of vision (*īkṣaṇa*), is taught to be the very same one who is the object of meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*). The qualification "the Supreme Person" (*paraṃ puruṣam*) is possible only if Paramaśiva is understood;
for there is nothing else higher than Him—"There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; He is the pinnacle, He is the supreme goal."

Because, in such passages as these, there is a designation by the word *puruṣa* of the absence of any entity distinct from Him; or else, because the unique attributes of Paramaśiva— as indicated in the Śruti passage, "The wise man attains through the syllable Om that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme"— are impossible for Hiraṇyagarbha and others.

Regarding the phrase "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*), the "world of Brahman" refers to the realm of Paramaśiva, which is indicated as the goal to be attained by his worshippers. Furthermore, after the distinction is made that the syllable *oṃ* is both the higher and the lower Brahman, the subsequent instruction that one should "meditate upon the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*) establishes that it is indeed Paramaśiva who is determined here to be the object of meditation.

May the Lord of Brahmā, the Sovereign of Brahmā, the auspicious Brahmā, be ever propitious to me—Sadāśiva. The letter *A* is Brahmā, the letter *U* is Viṣṇu, and the letter *M* is the Destroyer of Time; therefore, they call the *Oṃkāra* the *liṅga*. In hundreds of scriptural passages, such as "Salutation to Tārā," the nature of the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahmā, as being identical with the *praṇava*, is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and at their conclusion.
In passages such as, "He who is beyond that which is merged in Prakṛti is Maheśvara," the state of being supreme to the *praṇava* is also indicated.
Therefore, it is appropriate that he alone possesses both the nature of the *praṇava* and supremacy over the *praṇava*. This is according to the text:
"Just as a snake is freed from its skin, even so is he freed from evil."
They explain that for the worshippers of Paramaśiva, there is liberation through the sequence beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world), preceded by the cessation of all sins.

In the statement "higher than this mass of individual souls (*jīvaghana*) and higher than the highest," because of the instruction that the object of meditation is "higher than the *jīvaghana*— that is, Hiraṇyagarbha, who consists of the aggregate of individual souls"— the position of Hiraṇyagarbha is not intended here.

If it is argued that here only the side of Nārāyaṇa is designated, we reply: since the Śruti states, "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all brought forth," there is the designation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kālarudra, and the others as being the first-born living beings (*prathamajīva*) and as being produced by Paramaśiva; therefore, they lack immortality, fearlessness, and sovereignty over the world.

If it is asked, "Since Nārāyaṇa is designated as the 'soul of all' and the 'final resort' in such passages, how is it not possible for him to be the object of meditation?"—it is replied: [in the context of the passage] beginning with "from this mass of living beings... (etasmājjīvaghanāt).
From *jīvaghana*—the Hiraṇyagarbha who is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of individual souls—to the "higher" (*para*), that is, the most excellent Nārāyaṇa;

even higher than that is the "Supreme Person" (*puruṣam param*), the Supreme Brahman, who dwells within the city (*puri*)—that is, within the small lotus of the heart—as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Therefore, because the instruction states that the worshiper shall "directly behold" Him, Nārāyaṇa is not the object of worship here.

In passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality," the attributes of Brahman are ascribed to Nārāyaṇa—who is a devotee of Paramaśiva—in a figurative sense, similar to the case of Śvetaketu and others; thus it is taught that "that which is higher than Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in another Vedic scripture it is said: "Brahman is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than that which is higher than the highest."

"O Lord, may my mind be of auspicious resolve regarding that which is higher than the highest"—thus the Personages of the Vedas pray that their mental resolve be fixed upon the Supreme Śiva, who transcends both Brahmā and Viṣṇu. In the phrase "that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," that abode which is superior to and more exalted than Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman denoted by the name Śiva; that is the abode.
It is understood that the wise—the learned ones who worship Supreme Śiva—always see [Him], meaning they directly perceive Him. And so says the Smṛti:
"Above Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa is the supreme, which remains as the ultimate residue."
The wise always behold that eternal state known as Śiva.
Therefore, seekers of liberation must understand that the state of Śiva alone is superior to that of Nārāyaṇa.
Now, regarding the description of the dark-brown (kṛṣṇapiṅgala) complexion of Paramaśiva:
furthermore, while it is appropriate for Nārāyaṇa to be the soul of the universe, this is due to his being a portion of the power (umā-śakti) of the Supreme Lord.
Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa, Vāsudeva is the supreme Prakṛti;
the single power of the Supreme Lord becomes fourfold at the time of its application:
as Bhavānī in enjoyment, as Viṣṇu among men, as Kālī in anger, and as Durgā in battle.

In such passages, his status as a portion of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) is clearly stated. Therefore, regarding the phrase "Ṛtaṃ Satyam," *Ṛta* and *Satya* are beyond the reach of speech and mind; he is Virūpākṣa by virtue of having three eyes, and Kṛṣṇapiṅgala because his nature is variegated through the power of the Praṇava in the form of Umā.
The supreme power known as Praṇava is remembered as the innate nature of Śiva;
beyond that is the Supreme Brahman, Maheśvara, who transcends the universe.

Since the *Smṛti* declares that the *praṇava* consists of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*), and because of the instruction, "He beholds the Puruṣa who dwells in the city, the Supreme Brahman which transcends all," it is established that the Puruṣa indicated here as the object of that vision is none other than Śiva himself.
The Section Concerning the Small One (Daharādhikaraṇa) || 5 ||

To demonstrate another scriptural section concerning Maheśvara—who transcends the entire phenomenal world of moving and non-moving beings, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—for the purpose of delivering his devotees from saṃsāra, [the author] states: 78. "The small [ether] [is Brahman], because of the subsequent [scriptural statements]. (1.3.14)

The subject matter of this [discussion] is seen in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, a small lotus-palace, within it is a small ether; that which is inside that is what one should seek, that indeed is what one should desire to understand," and so forth. Here, the object heard as being denoted by the word "small" (*dahara*) may be the elemental ether, the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Lord.
Thus there arises a doubt.
Here, the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone is denoted by the word "dahara" (small), because that alone is well-known.
Its smallness is relative to its dwelling place, just like the space contained within the eye of a needle.

In passages such as, "As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it," there is a designation of [the heart] as the substratum of heaven and earth and as being comparable to space, based on the unity of space in its nature as vacuity and the distinction created by its internal and external states.

It is not contradictory for that which pervades all, namely space (*ākāśa*), to be designated by the term "small" (*dahara*) because of its entry within [the heart]. Furthermore, it is also not contradictory for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be designated by the term "small. This is evident from such passages as, "Now, that which is small within this city of Brahman (*brahmapura*)," where the "city of Brahman" refers to the body of Brahman, the Supreme Śiva, and the soul is its self.
This is because of the scriptural vision:
"The soul is to be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided a hundredfold, within the hearts of all embodied beings."

In passages such as "Thus the self consisting of consciousness is to be known," the individual soul (*jīva*) is designated as having a small dimension; therefore, it is conventionally referred to by the term *dahara* (the small). Furthermore, the comparison with the ether (*viyat*) and other such descriptions indicate the distinctness of the individual soul from Paraśiva. Consequently, both the individual soul and the elemental ether may be denoted by the word *dahara*.

If it is argued that [the quality of] "pervading all" is possible [for the individual soul], we reply: the "small" [ether] is the Supreme Lord himself because of the subsequent [reasons]. Here, the small ether is indeed the Supreme Lord;
why? Because of the subsequent reasons found in the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣa*). For instance, [it is so] because of that which was declared as the object of inquiry.

Having begun with, "If they should say to him regarding the small ether (daharākāśa): 'What is there in it that should be sought after, or what should one desire to understand? and having taught the answer to this inquiry through the words beginning with, "He should say: 'As large as this [outer] ether is, so large is this ether within the heart,'" because of its being compared to the ether;

Because it is designated as having heaven, earth, and so forth as its locus, it is impossible for the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) to be the object of all meditation. Likewise, qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), which are specified in passages such as "That Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true," do not [belong to the elemental ether].
[These qualities] belong to the elemental ether and the individual soul (jīva).

Furthermore, having taught that the fruits of actions are impermanent by stating, "Just as here on earth the world acquired through action perishes, even so there in the hereafter the world acquired through merit perishes," [the text continues]: "Now, those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these truths..."

Because it is established that the small ether (*daharākāśa*) under discussion has bliss as its fruit—based on the statement, "He obtains all desires; he has freedom of movement in all worlds"—its nature as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is indicated.
Therefore, the small ether, which is compared to the ether and serves as the substratum for heaven and earth, [is the Supreme Lord] due to the previously stated reasons.
Thus it is established that [the goal] is Paramaśiva.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
79. "On account of the movement and the word; for thus is the mark seen. (Sūtra 1.3.15)

This is an elaboration of the [sūtra] "To the subsequent [texts]. Furthermore, in the passage concerning the small [space], having designated the Supreme Lord— the subject under discussion— as "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) with the words, "All these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it," [the text speaks of] the daily [attainment] of that [world] by the individual souls denoted by the word "creatures."

The "going" (gati) being mentioned leads to the understanding that the destination—the external space—is Brahman. With reference to both the "going" and the term "Brahmaloka," the dual number was used by the authors of the Sūtras in the expression "by the two words denoting going.
For it is observed that, in the state of deep sleep every day, the individual soul (jīva) goes to Paramaśiva.
In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad: "This is that Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), resplendent like ten million suns, by whom all this is pervaded.

Its activity is eightfold: on the eastern petal there is a mind inclined toward merit; in the southeast, sleep, laziness, and so forth arise; in the south, a mind for cruelty; in the southwest, the intent to sin; in the west, play; and in the northwest, the inclination toward movement and the like."

In the north (saumya) there is delight in pleasure; in the northeast (īśānya), the acquisition of wealth; in the center, detachment (vairāgya); in the filaments (kesara), the waking state; in the pericarp (karṇikā), dreaming; and in the linga, deep sleep (suṣupti).
Thus, it is firmly established that this is indeed the journey to the supreme Śiva-linga, which consists of the space within the heart (daharākāśa).
The words *liṅga* and *brahman* are synonyms, just like the words *ghaṭa*, *kumbha*, and *kalaśa*.
This is evident from the fact that [the Lord] dwells daily in the world of Brahmā named Mahākailāsa, which shines with the luster of infinite jewels.
This alone is to be accepted. In this context, it is stated by the phrase "going to the world of Brahman day after day" that this itself is the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

By the word *ca* ("and"), the principle of the "Niṣāda-sthapati" (the chief of the Niṣādas) is also indicated for the purpose of accepting the *karmadhāraya* compound. Furthermore, it is taught in the *Śivagītā*: "And because of the absence of that [state] during deep sleep, the individual soul (*jīva*) has attained the state of Śaṅkara."
Therefore, it is established that the small ether is the Supreme Śiva.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"And because its support and greatness are perceived in this [ether]. (Sūtra 1.3.16)
Because of the scriptural statement, "This is the bridge, the upholder," which indicates the greatness of its nature as sustenance (*dhṛti*),
and because the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is perceived in this passage, the small ether is indeed the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, beginning with the words, "In this, there is a small ether within," [the text] describes it through its similarity to space.
Having taught the concentration on all things and having spoken of the Self in that very context,

and having demonstrated its distinction through qualities such as being free from evil, the text declares its steadfastness within that same uninterrupted section: "Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded."

By the term "support" (*vidhṛti*), because of its association with the word "Self," the sustaining of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth by Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is taught. Therefore, the support of the universe is not possible for anyone other than the Supreme Lord, just as there is a bridge that supports a flow of water.

It is for the very purpose of preventing the confusion of the excellence of the fields that this Self is the supporter of these worlds—divided by distinctions such as the internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth—as well as of the castes and stages of life; it is the dam (*setu*) for the sake of non-confusion, that is, for the sake of non-mixture. Thus, in this context, the scripture points out the greatness of the small one (*dahara*), characterized by its power of supporting. As stated in another Śruti:
The upholding of the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings is heard to belong to the supreme Śivaliṅga alone:

"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart"; likewise, "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Supporter, for the sake of the non-confusion of these worlds."
Therefore, none other than the Supreme Lord is denoted by the term "dahara.
He now shows another reason for the conclusion that Śiva is non-dual, qualified by the powers of difference and non-difference as taught by Nārāyaṇa:
81. And because of common renown. || 17 ||

The term *dahara* (the small) is well-known as referring exclusively to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). This is because we observe that the Supreme Lord is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in such passages as, "Ether, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form," and "All these beings, indeed, arise from ether alone. Therefore, the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) here is the Supreme Lord.

Although the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well-known to denote the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), nevertheless, because it is taken as a point of comparison in the statement, "As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart," it cannot be the case that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the elemental ether. Therefore, that which is denoted by the term "small" (dahara) is not the other [the elemental ether].
But is it not said: "That small, sinless lotus which has become the supreme abode, situated in the middle of the city—within that also is a small sky;
free from sorrow, that which is within it is to be meditated upon"?
And in the Kaivalya [Upaniṣad], having taught the small lotus of the heart as "the stainless, pure lotus of the heart," [it speaks of] that which is in its center.

By the passage beginning with "the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil," the worship of the Supreme Self (paramātman) is indicated. If it is argued that there arises a contradiction between the mutual Śruti texts because the Supreme Lord is taught here as the "small ether" (daharākāśa), we say no; for [this refers to] the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa)...

Because qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva) and others belong to the Supreme Lord, they cannot possibly exist [in anything else]. By the term "the small ether" (daharākāśa), the primordial nature of the ether of consciousness (cidambara-prakṛti) is expressed. Since there is no difference between power and the possessor of power (śakti-śaktimatoḥ), there is no mutual contradiction with the scriptural texts.
[This is known] from such passages as, "Brahman has the ether as its body," "whose self is truth, whose delight is life-breath, and whose joy is the mind," and so forth, regarding the Supreme Lord.
Because of the teaching that [the Goddess] has consciousness as the ether of her body;
furthermore, in the *Kūrma-purāṇa*, Vṛṣabha asks:
"Who is this blessed Goddess who constitutes half the body of Śaṅkara?"
Tell us who ask you exactly how Śivā Satī, the daughter of Himavat, [perished].
The Tortoise said: This secret knowledge is the very liberation of living beings;
it is known as the Void (Vyoma), the supreme limit, whose nature is wisdom and which is intensely longing for the Transcendent (Ati).
Intrinsic and rooted in that, the stainless radiance is like that of the sun;
the single power of Maheśvara, through its association with manifold limiting adjuncts, [appears as many].
In his presence, she plays with both supreme and inferior forms;
behold, she performs all this work, this entire world.
The wise declare that for the Lord there is neither effect nor instrument;
by means of this supreme [power], the God enjoys the bliss of his own self.
By her, this entire world is pervaded and supported;
she is the one Śakti, while Śiva alone is called the Possessor of Śakti (Śaktimān).

Those who contemplate reality, the yogis, declare that there is a difference between power and the possessor of power from the perspective of ultimate truth, yet they perceive their non-difference as well.
In that very place, the words of the Goddess are as follows:
"Know me to be the supreme Śakti, who rests upon Maheśvara;
I am non-dual, imperishable, and one, whom those seeking liberation behold."
I am indeed the self of all beings, the auspicious one dwelling within all; I am the embodiment of eternal sovereignty and wisdom, the source of all activity.
Possessing infinite and boundless majesty, she is the one who carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra.

Since Nārāyaṇa, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, has explained the context of the non-duality of Śiva as qualified by the powers of difference and non-difference through such passages, the fact that the Supreme Lord is of the nature of the "small" (the *dahara*) and resides within the small is not contradictory.
He states another reason:
82. If it be argued that he [is the one referred to] because of the reference to another, we say no, because of impossibility. || 18 ||

If it is argued that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the individual soul (jīva), because in the sentence "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman," the word *brahman* refers to—that is, designates—the other [i.e.,] the individual soul, we say no; for such a thing is impossible.
The meaning is that attributes such as "having true resolves" (*satyasaṅkalpa*) and so forth are impossible in the case of the individual soul.

Furthermore, by the force of the complementary passage—"Now, that serene being (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form; this is the Self"—it is the individual soul (jīva) alone that is understood here.
This is because in another scriptural text, the term "serene being" is used to designate the embodied self as delimited by that state of deep sleep.

If it is argued that here [the individual soul] alone is designated, and furthermore that "rising up from the body" is a characteristic mark of the living soul (jīva), and therefore the living soul itself is what is denoted by the term "small ether" (daharākāśa) here—
[we reply: it is said that the living soul, which is delimited by the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and so forth, exists within the small ether.

Otherwise, it would contradict the comparison with space. Since there is instruction regarding the soul's attainment of the Supreme Lord preceded by its emergence from the body, this is not a section concerning the individual soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, because it is a section concerning the Supreme Lord, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is denoted here by the term "dahara" (the small).
He states another reason: 83.
"If it is argued that [the soul] exists because of the answer, then its nature must be manifested. (19)

If [it is argued that the reference is] to the subsequent [passage], then in the later passage of Prajāpati—"That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand"—the attributes such as having true resolves are taught of the Self denoted by the word *jīva*; therefore, "that is what one must seek... [and so forth].
Because [the text] specifies that very [Self] through such expressions as "it is to be desired to be known" (*vijijñāsitavya*), which refer to the desire to know, the seeking, and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Dahara-vidyā* and subsequently in the *Prajāpati-vidyā*, it is said: "This person who is seen in the eye; this is the Self;
he who moves about being honored in a dream; this is the Self; and that wherein he is soundly asleep, serene... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1–4).

In passages such as "This Self does not know the dream," since it is precisely the individual soul (jīva) who is subject to the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep that is being taught here, and because it is that very soul whose attributes—such as being free from sin—are taught in this context;
[this refers to] the attributes of immortality and so forth established by the statement, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."

If it is argued that the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) is the individual soul (*jīva*) because of that very teaching, we say no. In the phrase "but [he is] one whose nature is manifested," the word "but" (*tu*) serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, even based on the subsequent passage of Prajāpati, the suspicion that it refers to the individual soul is not tenable;
for here, the individual soul is intended as one whose true nature has become manifest, as expressed in the text: "Having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form."

In the concluding statement, "it is accomplished," the Supreme Lord alone is the subject taught as possessing attributes such as being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) through the manifestation of the state of Brahman for the liberated soul (*muktajīva*).
Since the liberated soul, by virtue of being Brahman, lacks the status of being a [limited] individual soul (*jīvatva*), the teaching of the attributes of Brahman is entirely appropriate. Likewise...

In such scriptural passages as, "The knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high; the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the identity of the liberated souls with Brahman is indicated. Likewise, the Smṛti says: "The Great Lord is completely full within and without, and everything is that."
The most excellent of scholars should practice this for the sake of attaining supreme bliss.
The realization "I am Śiva" is indeed the cause for attaining the state of Śiva;
it is not mere knowledge nor mere conduct—it is one endowed with such realization who becomes Śiva.
Knowledge is the discernment of reality, and meditation is the cause for its cultivation;
therefore, once Mahādeva is known, the wise person should become engaged in meditation.
One should become endowed with uninterrupted concentration directed toward Śiva;
for in that way, his very nature arises, just as it does from the constant contemplation of a worm or an insect.

"By being pierced by the glance of the Guru, a human becomes Śiva, just as iron attains the state of gold through the infusion of mercury. Now, an objection is raised: if the small ether (daharākāśa) were the Lord (Īśvara), then the reference to the individual soul (jīva) in the passage beginning with "Now, this serene one" would be purposeless.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "84. And the reference is for another purpose. (Sūtra 2.3.20)

The reference to the individual soul (*jīva-parāmarśa*) has another purpose— it is intended to establish the non-difference from Brahman; for the reference to the soul, as understood from the remainder of the sentence, "Having attained the nature of the supreme light, he manifests in his own form," is that which is to be reached through the process of merging (*upasampatti*).

It refers to the Supreme Lord alone; for that [liberation] is impossible without reference to the individual soul (jīva), yet the reference to the individual soul is not for the purpose of propounding the individual soul itself. 85. "If it be argued that on account of the scriptural mention of smallness, [the Lord cannot be meant], that has already been answered. (Sūtra 21)

If it is argued that because the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, is heard to be "small" in passages such as "In this small space within the heart," and since it is impossible for the all-pervading One to possess the smallness of a "dahara" (the small), it is more appropriate that the term *dahara* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone— this is not so. For in the sūtra *Arbhakaukastvāt* ("Because of the smallness of the abode"), by means of the analogy of the ether, [it is shown that] the Supreme Lord [assumes smallness] for the sake of the meditation of His devotees.
The state of being limited has already been explained.

Now, one might object: since the scriptural passage, "This person is seen in the eye," begins by referring to the individual soul (jīva) as it exists in the waking state, and because the experience of the waking state and so forth is appropriate to the individual soul, it must be that very soul which is denoted here by the term *dahara*. To this we say: no.

This Self is free from evil, ageless; day and night do not cross this bridge of His, nor does old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor merit, nor demerit. All evils turn back from it, for this world of Brahman is free from evil.
Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even one who is blind becomes non-blind, one who is pierced becomes unpierced, and one who is afflicted becomes non-afflicted.

It causes affliction; therefore, having crossed this bridge, even at night one arrives as if it were day. For this world of Brahman is indeed "once-for-all illumined" (*sakṛdvibhātaḥ*)—thus, because of the abundance of references to Brahman and the Self in the remainder of the passage, it is stated that this is not a different context. Furthermore, regarding the exposition of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]...
This is because it is logically consistent as a means of establishing the Supreme Self, according to the analogy of the moon seen through a tree branch.

Furthermore, in another Śruti passage—"One should see the Self in the Self alone; Śambhu [is] in the midst of space; Śiva alone is to be meditated upon"—and similar texts, the fruit of liberation is prescribed for the knowledge of meditation (*upāsanā*).

Therefore, one should worship the Śiva-tattva—characterized by qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth—as enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, preceded by the renunciation of prohibited and optional actions performed with desire, and endowed with one's own duty (*nijadharma*) free from longing.
Now, an objection may be raised: since no primary indicative mark (*mukhyaliṅga*) establishing the Śiva-tattva is seen in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, how can it be understood as referring to that?
This is stated as follows: in the *Taittirīya*, beginning with "the small, stainless [space]" and ending with "He who is beyond is Maheśvara";
and in the *Kaivalya*, beginning with "the lotus of the heart, free from passion and pure" and continuing with "accompanied by Umā," and so forth.

Because the worship of Paramaśiva is established without doubt, it does not have any other object as its domain. Likewise, in the Gītā [18.61]: "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His Māyā, as if they were mounted on a machine."
Go to Him alone as your refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. (18.62)
Thus it has been established. The section concerning imitation (Anukṛtyadhikaraṇa) [ends]. 6.

Having established that the all-pervading Supreme Lord possesses the nature of the "small" (dahara) self, the author demonstrates through another section of the work that He alone is self-luminous, independent of any other means of proof, and the illuminator of both the gross and subtle realms of the sentient and insentient.
86. And because of the imitation of that [action]. || 22 ||

In the Muṇḍakopaniṣad it is heard: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. Here, the entity heard of as the illuminator of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) is the question: is it a particular kind of physical light (tejoviśeṣa) or the Supreme Lord (parameśvara)?

There is doubt. If it is argued that here a particular kind of fire (*tejo-viśeṣa*) alone is being taught—because fire is well-known as a powerful illuminator, and because we observe that a weak thing is overcome by a superior light—therefore, it is not the Supreme Lord; [then the answer follows:]

We reply: On account of imitation (*anukṛti*), that specific light (*tejoviśeṣa*) which is the subject to be established here is the Supreme Lord alone. Why? Because of imitation; "imitation" means emulation. That which is called "shining after" is expressed in the passage, "everything shines after Him as He shines.
For one light does not shine while another light is shining. Therefore, [the subject] is that which appears as light.

It is logical that everything, including the sun, the moon, the stars, and so forth, shines in accordance with the Śiva-tattva. By the phrase "tasya ca" (and of him) in the Sūtra, the quality of being the illuminator of all—which is intended by the fourth quarter of the scriptural passage cited as the subject matter, namely, "by his light all this shines"—is appropriately attributed to Śiva alone, as it is he who is self-luminous. That very [quality] belongs to the luminaries...
And this is well known from such passages as "the light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7). Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*) and the pronoun "that" (*tat*):
"In the supreme golden sheath, there is the stainless, partless Brahman;
that pure one, the light of lights, which the knowers of the Self recognize. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.9)
Thus, it is understood that it is appropriate to take the subject at hand as Paraśiva-Brahman alone;

the meaning is that Paramaśiva is indeed golden (*hiraṇmaya*), consisting of light (*jyotirmaya*), and consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). This is evident from such passages as: "Salutation to Hiraṇya, salutation to Hiraṇyaliṅga, salutation to Hiraṇyabāhu, to the golden-hued, to the golden-formed," and so forth.

This is well known as belonging to Paramaśiva himself. In that supreme sheath (kośa), the space within the heart (daharākāśa), which is higher than the sheaths beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya), it is said: "Brahman is the tail, the support. That Brahman which serves as the support is firmly established there; and He is stainless (viraja), free from the three impurities (mala), partless (niṣkala), devoid of bonds (pāśa), pure (śubhra), free from innate defects, and [the light] of lights.
The meaning is that it is the illuminator of the luminaries such as the sun, and this is established by the experience of the wise.
Regarding the position of the Supreme Lord, he states another reason: "87. And moreover, it is recorded in Smṛti. (23)
I am indeed that which is subtler than the subtle; I am likewise the Great One, this manifold universe.
I am the Ancient One, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord; I am the Golden One, I am the very form of Śiva.
Thus, in the Kaivalya and other Upaniṣads, the nature of Paramaśiva alone as consisting of light is recorded. Furthermore, the word "api" (also) serves as a conjunction;
likewise, in the Gītā: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that."
That supreme abode of mine, having gone to which they do not return.
That splendor which, residing in the sun, illuminates the entire world,
and that which is in the moon and in the fire— know that splendor to be mine.

Thus, it is taught that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, being self-luminous without dependence on any other means of realization, is the illuminator of the entire expanse of the gross and subtle sentient and insentient universe which is interwoven with Himself.
Therefore, He does not have anything else as His object.

Demonstrating that the Bhagavad Gītā has Śiva as its ultimate purport through the sixfold marks of intention (*ṣaḍvidhatātparyaliṅga*): Now, one might object that in the Gītā, by the statement "Know that splendor to be mine," Nārāyaṇa alone is taught to be the Supreme Brahman as the illuminator of all; and by the words "The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, O Arjuna," [it is shown that he is the inner controller].

If it is argued that its abiding within the small space (dahara) as prescribed by the sentence is appropriate for him alone, and not for Śiva— since a contradiction with the context is seen here, and therefore Nārāyaṇa alone is taught in this passage— we say no.
Because the meaning of the *Gītā* also reveals Paramaśiva through the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introduction and conclusion;
for beginning with "The Lord of all beings" and ending with "Go to Him alone as your refuge," its focus on Śiva is established. [Objection:
By stating "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in Me alone," and so forth, its focus on Viṣṇu alone has been indicated.

This is not to be doubted; for if the meditation on the "small" (dahara) were intended to refer to Viṣṇu, it would contradict the many previously cited Śrutis such as those from the Taittirīya and Kaivalya Upaniṣads. Furthermore, by the subsequent passage, there is a separate injunction for the meditation on Viṣṇu accompanied by the specific mode regarding the fruit. As it has been said:
Hear again from Me the supreme word, the most secret of all secrets. Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
You shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins, do not grieve.

In such passages, the non-difference between these two—Śiva and Keśava—as the object of worship and the worshipper, is to be understood through the logic of the Sūtra: "But by the vision of the scripture, there is instruction [of identity], as in the case of Vāmadeva.
Furthermore, because Viṣṇu is also a portion (aṃśa) of Śiva, the worship of Viṣṇu brings about the gratification of Śiva.

It is taught that the statements prescribing liberation through the worship of Viṣṇu serve as a cause for liberation by means of generating devotion to Śiva, according to the analogy of the "gross Arundhatī" (where one first points to a nearby star to help find a distant one). In the *Īśvaragītā* of the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, Śiva is heard to say: "This supreme form of mine is called by the name Nārāyaṇa."
Abiding as the self-nature of all beings, she is peaceful and designated as the Imperishable.

"Therefore, this great yogi, my devotee, the supreme person, is indeed to be worshipped and saluted for the sake of generating my pleasure. Thus, having received the Gītā scripture from the Lord, Kṛṣṇa taught it to Arjuna solely by virtue of His command. In that very [text]:
Śiva said: "This knowledge has been spoken by me for the benefit of those who take refuge in Brahman;
it should always be given by you to disciples whose minds are tranquil."
"Even the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the son of Devakī,
personally and directly bestowed this supreme [knowledge] upon Arjuna.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is the object of worship here.
The Section on the Measured [Object] (Pramitādhikaraṇa) || 7 ||
By means of another section, he demonstrates the presentation of the form of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is the illuminator of the expansion of the conscious and the unconscious:
88. "He is known from the word alone. (Sūtra 1.3.24)
The subject of this [Upanishad] is heard in the Kaṭhavallī: "A person the size of a thumb dwells in the middle of the self;

he is the ruler of what has been and what is to be; therefore, he is free from fear. And: "The person the size of a thumb is like a smokeless light; he is the ruler of what has been and what is to be; he alone is today, and he is tomorrow; this indeed is that."
Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether the person (puruṣa) heard of as being the size of a thumb is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).

Here, on account of the instruction concerning the measurement of a thumb’s breadth, it should be inferred that it is the individual soul, because it possesses limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Furthermore:
"He is the universal form, consisting of the three qualities, having three paths; the lord of all, he moves about according to his own actions, [the size of] a thumb..."
Then Yama forcibly extracted from the body of Satyavat a person the size of a thumb, who was bound by the noose and possessed of a form resembling the Sun, yet endowed with volition and egoism.

If it is argued that because the Śrutis and Smṛtis such as these teach that the *aṅguṣṭha*-measure refers to the body alone—and because of the designation "He stands in the middle of the self," which indicates His existence within the body—the *aṅguṣṭha*-measure of the *jīva* is established in every respect—it is replied: here, the *puruṣa* who is *aṅguṣṭha*-measure is indeed the Maheśvara. Why? Precisely from the word itself—that is, from the word "Īśāna" (the Lord).
The meaning is that Maheśvara is directly perceived and ascertained. The particle *eva* (only) is for the purpose of excluding others.

This is because in other scriptural passages such as "Lord of all sciences," the term *Īśāna* is heard as referring exclusively to Paramaśiva; for the body cannot possess lordship. This is so because [Maheśvara] possesses universal sovereignty as taught in the scripture: "Of the past and the future."

Because [the attributes] are untenable in the case of the individual soul (jīva); because in another scriptural passage—"That which has been and that which is to be, and who is the Lord of immortality"—He alone is heard of; because there is no consistency for the context of "This indeed is That" in any other than the Supreme Lord;
and because in such passages as "All is indeed Rudra," He alone is heard of as being the self of all moving and non-moving things; and because Brahman is what is being inquired about here.

"Tell me that which he sees, other than what has been and what is to be. [The Sūtra says: "On account of the word itself," because by the scriptural statement of the name itself, the Supreme Lord alone is designated as the primary subject in this context; for [the text] begins with "Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the Lord of the Universe," and continues with "to the Lord of All, to Sadāśiva, to the illustrious Mahādeva."
By the passage ending with "namas," [the Lord] is established as the Supreme Lord in the Yajur and Sāma Vedas;

and in the Atharva Veda, in the text "Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, in the midst of the ether," it is precisely He who is established as the Lord of all. For the Puruṣa is thumb-sized, indeed residing within the thumb.

"The Lord of the entire world, the Sovereign, the All-enjoyer, is pleased"— since the Great Upaniṣad (*Īśāvāsya*) thus specifies that the thumb-sized being is the Supreme Lord himself, it cannot be anyone else.
Now follows the determination of the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
In response to the doubt as to how the all-pervading Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, can be of the size of a thumb, he says:
"But [the thumb-size is] with reference to the heart, because the qualification [of the scripture] is for human beings. (Sūtra 1.3.25)
The word "tu" (but) here serves to dispel doubt. With respect to the heart— that is, with respect to the location of the heart—
the Supreme Śiva, who pervades all like space, appears in the form of a luminous liṅga of the size of a thumb, delimited by the heart, for the sake of bestowing grace upon the practitioner.

The state of being the size of a thumb is thus established. For it is heard in scripture: "The Person is the size of a thumb, and he dwells within the thumb. If it is asked how there can be such a restriction to the size of a thumb when the lotus of the heart varies in dimension across bodies such as those of elephants and gnats, the text replies to this:

The remainder [of the argument] is that "because the scripture has humans as its qualified subjects. In the sixth section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Pūrvatantra*, under the heading "Action for the sake of a fruit," an objection was raised that even animals and the like possess qualification for rites performed for the sake of heaven, on the grounds that the scriptural injunction "one who desires heaven" applies to them. This objection was refuted by restricting the scope of the term "one who desires heaven," since animals and the like lack the requisite capacity.

Having established that the scripture pertains to human beings, and having reached the position that it therefore entitles all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) was reached that the entitlement belongs to the three [upper] castes alone, because of the scriptural hearing of the connection with the sacred fires only for those three: "In every spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn, a Vaiśya."
Furthermore: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should attain detachment, realizing that 'there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created.
For the sake of knowing That, he should approach a Guru alone—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman—with fuel in hand."

"One who is desirous [of results], capable, learned, and not excluded by the scriptures is qualified for Vedic ritual"— since this is indicated by the Śruti and the Sūtras, the scriptural injunctions regarding initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth have as their subject matter the characteristic qualification of human beings, defined by capacity and desire. Therefore, that which you consider to be most beneficial for a human being...

In such passages, because the teaching concerns that which is most beneficial for human beings alone, and because qualities such as having desires and so forth are impossible in the case of animals and other beings, and because of the excellence of their bodies— namely,
that only humans possess a heart-lotus the size of a thumb— it refers to them alone.

The eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Therefore, the supremely compassionate Supreme Śiva attains a nature delimited by the very size of the human heart, according to the injunctions of the scripture of worship (*upāsanā-śāstra*).
This is like the space within a jar, which possesses the dimensions of the jar, or the space within the small cavity (*daharākāśa*) delimited by the measure of a thumb.
The Supreme Lord’s possession of that measurement is not contradictory;

there is no fault because the statements teaching a "thumb-sized" soul refer to the liberated soul (*muktajīva*). In such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the attributes of Brahman are taught of the liberated soul by virtue of its identity with Brahman.
It is consistent. Furthermore: "The Person, the size of a thumb, the inner self, is eternally seated in the hearts of people;
one should draw him out from one's own body with patience, as a reed from its sheath. One should know him as bright and immortal. Thus, there is no contradiction in his being the size of a thumb.
The Section on the Deity (Devatādhikaraṇa) || 8 ||
An investigation into the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman:
Having thus established the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman, [the author] states that the gods possess such eligibility—90. *Tadupary api vādarāyaṇaḥ sambhavāt* (2.3.26).

The subject matter of this [section] is heard in the third chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Of those among the gods who awakened to this, they themselves became that; likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings.
Because [the Vedas] have human beings as their primary authority, this present section follows by way of connection with that [preceding discussion].
Here, there arises the doubt as to whether or not the gods possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

On this point, the gods do not have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman; for in passages such as, "That which you consider most beneficial for a human being," the worship of Paraśiva is presented as the most beneficial specifically for humans.
Because of specific designations, because of the purposefulness [of rituals], because the scripture has humans as its qualified subjects,

because the gods lack bodies composed of the five elements (pañcīkṛta-vigraha), and because we observe that only one characterized by a gross body is entitled to perform acts such as praise and meditation— as seen in passages such as "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra."

If it is argued that the state of possessing a body is predicated of the gods, we say no; for those things which fall within the scope of injunctions (*vidhi*) cannot be coherently applied elsewhere. Even if they possess bodies, qualities such as being qualified for Vedic ritual—defined by scripture as "one who is desirous, capable, learned, and not excluded by scriptural prohibition"—are not possible for them.
This is because of the teaching regarding the identity of the state of the gods and the Supreme Lord. In passages such as, "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world;
those gods asked Rudra," it is declared that the heavenly world itself is the station of Rudra, the Supreme Self, and the station of the gods as well.

Furthermore, in passages such as "He attains self-sovereignty" (*svārājyam āpnoti*), the attainment of self-sovereignty by even liberated souls is heard. Moreover, in passages such as "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," the absence of other means of knowledge is taught. Since the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), which is the cause for the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), is not seen in the Vedic scriptures, [initiation] is the requisite means.

Since it is a logical principle that "without [the performance of rites], the goal cannot be accomplished," it follows that for gods who are devoid of ritual acts such as the application (*upanayana*), the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman is not possible in any way. To this we reply: "Above them, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains their qualification] because of the possibility. That is to say, above those humans, for those who are higher than them.

Bādarāyaṇa maintains that even the gods residing in the heavenly world possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Why? Because of the possibility. For in the *Ārṣeya-śiras*, there is the inquiry of the gods regarding Rudra—"Who are you?"—and his reply, "I alone existed first," and so forth; thus, both the desire for knowledge on the part of the gods and the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman by the Supreme Lord are established.

Because it is so observed. In that very same context, in another passage—beginning with "Then the gods did not see Rudra; those gods meditated upon Rudra"—the worship of the Supreme Lord as the object of the gods' devotion is heard in scripture. Furthermore, by the passage beginning "Whosoever among the gods awakened," there is the teaching that even the gods possess the nature of Brahman through their desire for the knowledge of Brahman.
The qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is not contradictory.

In the passage, "The gods indeed went to the heavenly world" (devā ha vai svargaṃ lokam agaman), by the word "heaven" (svarga), based on the context of the current section, there is intended the world of Śiva-Brahmā, which is superior to the worlds of the gods such as Hiraṇyagarbha.

The state of being superior to the world is designated [for them]. Even though gods and others are always possessed of enjoyments, because they perceive defects such as impermanence in those objects of enjoyment, detachment and the like, as well as the desire for liberation consisting of unsurpassed bliss, are possible.
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra.

Since the gods are designated as possessing physical forms (*vigraha*) in such sources as mantras, *arthavādas*, *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, and *āgamas*, and since their status is established by the *brahmasūtras*— which are self-evident and uncontradicted— and because they are themselves the very embodiments of the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāntas,
it is determined that the scriptural injunction regarding the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) has as its object only those humans who possess limited knowledge. Or rather:
"Maghavat indeed dwelt as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) for one hundred and one years with Prajāpati.

And in such passages as "Bṛgu Vāruṇi approached his father Varuṇa, saying: 'Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman,'" the practice of brahmacarya and other disciplines is seen for the purpose of acquiring the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, by virtue of belonging to the same lineage as Bhṛgu and others, by being naturally distinguished by the sacred thread (*yajñasūtra*),

and by possessing innate knowledge of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), the qualities such as learning (*adhitva*) which constitute the grounds for eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are indeed possible. Since the Vedas possess authority through their explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the gods, by having physical bodies, possess that capability.

It is established that even the contradiction regarding the literal consistency of quality-stating passages (guṇavāda) such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" and "Fire is the remedy for cold," as well as the contradiction in explanatory passages (arthavāda) such as "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra," does not exist in their own literal sense, because there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and no prior establishment [of the contrary] by another authority.

Because of the possibility of consistency; since there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement that [the deity] is "thumb-sized" when understood in relation to one's own thumb, it is logical that [this scripture] possesses authority.
Now, an objection: since only words ending in the dative case denote deities, and those [words] are insentient, how [can they be the self]?

If it is argued that there is no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman [on the part of the gods], we say no; for since embodied deities denoted by words ending in the dative case have been established [as existing], their qualification for the knowledge of Brahman is possible.
Anticipating an objection regarding the existence of embodied forms for the gods, he refutes it as follows:
91. If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding action, we say no, because we observe multiple activities [occurring simultaneously]. || 27 ||

Now, an objection is raised: since the gods lack a physical body, they would have no entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, such a body must be admitted. If that were the case, then in the performance of ritual action as well, they would assist merely by being present through their embodied form—just like the officiating priests and others—and yet that is not possible, because a single body cannot be in multiple places at once.

If it is argued that because simultaneous presence is impossible, accepting that the deity possesses a physical body would entail a contradiction regarding the deity’s capacity to assist in the ritual action, this is not a fault. Why? Because we observe multiple activities;
for even though the gods possess bodies—just like Saubhari and others—even when a single god has many bodies, [he can act in various ways].
Because simultaneous pervasion of bodies is seen in the Śruti;

for instance, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, in the Śākalya-brāhmaṇa, after beginning with "Then Vidagdha Śākalya asked him: 'How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? and having replied, "Three and three hundred, and three and three thousand," etc.
In response to the question "Which are these?", it is stated that these very [beings] are the Great Ones (*mahiman*), and that these are indeed the thirty-three gods; thus,
having explained the inclusion of the three thousand and six hundred gods within the thirty-three gods,
[it is further shown that] even among those thirty-three, six are included in six, three in three, two in two, and [finally] one in the god whose nature is wind.
The Vedic scripture, by declaring their inclusion [within the sacrifice], demonstrates that a single wind possesses a manifold nature.

Therefore, even though the gods possess embodied forms, there is no contradiction whatsoever in their being of various kinds due to the injunctions regarding their participation as constituent parts of the ritual action.
Also in the Smṛti:
"O bull among the Bharatas, having attained the fruit [of yoga], a yogin may indeed create many bodies for himself and perform great deeds with all of them."

For, by such statements as "he may enjoy sense-objects through some [bodies] and perform severe austerity through others," it is established that even for the lords of yogis, the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies through the power of yoga— by means of sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest— is taught.

How could one suspect that those with subtle (taijasa) bodies—the gods whose perfection is established from birth—possess multiple simultaneous cognitions? A single person is not fed simultaneously by many who are feeding him;
nor is a single person saluted simultaneously by many who are saluting him.
In this way, there is no contradiction in the ritual act wherein many people simultaneously relinquish their respective substances, directed toward a single deity possessing a physical form;
for [this holds true] upon accepting that deities such as Brahmā possess physical forms.
Anticipating the objection that because the bodies [of the gods] are impermanent, the Veda that expresses them must also be impermanent, he says:
92. "If it be argued that [the Veda is non-eternal] because of sound, no; because [the world] originates from this [Veda], on account of perception and inference. (2.1.28)

Granted that there may be no contradiction regarding ritual action (*karman*), a contradiction is observed in the word—the Veda. If one accepts that the gods possess embodied forms (*vigraha*) like those of ourselves and others, it would follow that they are subject to birth and destruction. Therefore, if one accepts that a deity with an impermanent body is the referent of the eternal Veda, there would be a contradiction between the word and its meaning.
Because there is no eternal relationship [between the Veda and its deities], there is a contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal.
Furthermore, if one accepts the non-eternality of the gods such as Indra and others as propounded by the Śruti, then the Veda that propounds them would likewise be of human origin and non-eternal.

If it is argued that this would result in the abandonment of the Vedic injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, and that there would be a contradiction regarding many matters—such as the failure to establish those rituals enjoined by them—we say: no, there is no such contradiction. Why? Because [the world] originates from that.
For it is precisely from the mass of the Vedas, which expresses the eternal forms residing in deities and others, that the manifold universe (*prapañca*) of deities and so forth arises.
The meaning is: because it is heard that [the world] has arisen from the Source (*prabhava*). How is this understood?
By means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

Perception refers to the *Śruti* (revealed scripture), and inference refers to the *Smṛti* (traditional scripture). According to their respective order, the *Śruti* [states] that creation was preceded by sound (*śabda-pūrvā*).
It points this out; and thus says the Śruti: "With 'these,' Prajāpati created the gods; with 'they have flowed forth,' humans;
with 'drops,' the ancestors; with 'beyond the filter,' the cups; with 'the swift ones,' the stotra; with 'all,' the śāstra;
with 'for good fortune,' other creatures. Likewise, [it is said] by such passages as, "He, through the mind, entered into union with speech," and so forth.
In various places, creation preceded by sound is taught.
Smṛti also states:
"The eternal Speech, without beginning or end, was emitted by the Self-existent One."

"In the beginning, [the world] was divine and consisted of the Veda, from which all activities proceed. And: "In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned the names and forms of beings, as well as the setting in motion of their actions, solely from the words of the Veda."

Therefore, since the eternity of the Veda and the non-eternity of the gods and so forth are understood through the cited passages, there is no contradiction. Even though individual instances (*vyakti*) are non-eternal, because the form (*ākṛti*) is eternal and that alone is the meaning of the word, the relationship—just as in the case of "cow" and so on—is established as innate (*autpattika*); thus, there is no contradiction regarding the word.
Furthermore, according to the principle that "whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech and performs through action," just as a teacher,

for the sake of teaching his pupils, first recalls the scripture held in his mind and subsequently instructs the students on its meaning; or just as a potter, at the time of making a jar, [recalls] the specific form from the word "jar."
Just as one creates a jar or similar object after having contemplated it within the mind, so too the Supreme Lord, at the time of creation,
recollects the specific forms from the Vedic words such as "Indra" residing in His own heart,
and subsequently creates Indra and the others; thus, there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning words.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"And for this very reason, there is eternality. (93.29)
The eternity of the Veda is indeed established by such means as the remembrance of its author.

Having raised the doubt that it might be non-eternal due to its connection with non-eternal things, [it is shown that] because the Vedas teach the creation of gods and others as delimited by specific forms (*ākṛti*), and because a form is the meaning of a word, and because of that [form],...

He concludes that because [the universal] is eternal, impermanence cannot be based on its connection with something impermanent. Precisely because the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of the word, the eternity of the Veda is not contradicted.

Some have said that the eternity of the Veda and the Lord consists in their persistence through the state of the intermediate dissolution (*avāntara-pralaya*). [As it is said: "By speech, which is manifold and eternal..."

This is inconsistent because it would result in a contradiction with such scriptural passages as these. Furthermore, since the Vedas are eternal by virtue of being the power of the Supreme Lord’s self-reflection (*vimarśa-śakti*), if they were false, it would follow that one has entered the heretical doctrines outside the Veda (*veda-bāhya-pāṣaṇḍa-mata*). Moreover, [the scripture states]: "He chooses the composers of the mantras," and "The hymn of Viśvāmitra comes into being."

Although Viśvāmitra and others are the authors of mantras, the eternity of the Veda— consisting of both mantra and brāhmaṇa— is taught by recalling the specific forms denoted by names such as "Viśvāmitra" when they are used in those respective Vedic words;
for Brahmā creates [the world] by recollecting the meanings of Vedic terms such as Indra and the like.

Because he lacks the capacity to understand the meaning of the mantras that have not been studied, he creates the entire manifold of moving and non-moving beings— such as Viśvāmitra and others— again after the daily dissolution. Therefore, both his authorship of the mantras and the eternity of the Veda are established.
Anticipating the objection that since Indra and the other deities possess different names and forms in every kalpa, how can the Veda be their authoritative source, [the author] says:
94. "And because their names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even though there is a recurrence [of creation], as is seen from scripture and tradition. (2.1.30)

Because all Indras possess identical names and forms across all kalpas, even if a succession of Indras is admitted in the cycle of rebirth, there is no contradiction; this same principle should be understood to apply to Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, and the others as well.

[Objection: "But even if the universal (*ākṛti*) is the referent of a word, since all universals and individuals are destroyed at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), there is no evidence for the production of individuals possessing those same universals upon [re-]creation; thus, the contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal remains as it was. [Reply: This is not so, because the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless. At every creation, an entity is produced that possesses exactly the same universal as before, not one that is different. At the time of dissolution, everything...

An object perishes as nothing more than a residue of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); there is no destruction without a trace (*niranvayadhvaṃsa*). Since the existence of objects designated by those very names is observed—just as in the case of cognition—the presence of latent impressions is accepted. And from these impressions, a creation arises with identical names and forms, not one characterized by difference. This identity of name and form is [attested] in the Śruti.

It must be accepted on the basis of both scriptural vision and traditional remembrance: "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as before, as well as the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space, and likewise the gods. "He who first ordains the Brahman and indeed bestows the Vedas upon him—that God, who is the light of self-knowledge, [should be sought by] the seeker of liberation..."
There is the Vedic revelation beginning with, "I take refuge [in Him]," and so forth. There is also the Smṛti:
"In the beginning, He created the waters alone; into them He infused His seed.
That became a golden egg, radiant like a thousand suns."
"He created Brahmā first and bestowed the Vedas upon him," and so forth.

Furthermore: "Just as one who has fallen asleep sees no dream whatsoever, so when he becomes one with this prāṇa alone, speech enters into him together with all names, the eye enters into him together with all forms, and the ear [enters into him together with all sounds]."

The mind merges together with all sounds; it merges together with all thoughts. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a fire, even so from this Self the vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge, each to its respective station, and from the vital breaths...
In the Vedic revelation as well,
it is described that just as frogs and other creatures emerge from clay, the subsequent cosmic manifestation possesses names and forms identical to those of the manifestation of the previous kalpa;
this occurs even when, during deep sleep, the conventional usage of the dream and waking manifestations has dissolved.
Just as in the case of the conventional usage of prior awakening, so too should it be inferred for the creation and dissolution within subsequent kalpas.
With the connection of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he states another opinion:

95. *Madhvādiṣvasambhavādanadhikāraṃ jaiminiḥ* || 31 || (Jaimini [holds that there is] no entitlement [to knowledge] because of the impossibility [of certain things] in the case of Madhu and so forth.)
Jaimini maintains that gods have no entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman. Why?
Because their entitlement is impossible in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations. In the passage, "That sun is the honey of the gods;

it is called 'honey' because it is like honey due to being the food of the gods," the heavenly world itself is the horizontal cross-beam of that honey, and the intermediate space is the cake, for [it belongs] to the sun.

Because honey remains [there], there is the superimposition that "that very thing is honey and *apūpa*. By such statements as "red, white, black, and hidden," the Madhu-vidyā and others—which have the attainment of the solar orb as their fruit—are restricted [to those within the orb], because there is no one other than Āditya and the rest [within the orb]. This is because one cannot simultaneously be both the object of meditation (*upāsya*) and the meditator (*upāsaka*). And thus:

If one were to accept that [the person within the sun] has the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), then by virtue of there being no distinction in its being a form of knowledge, it would follow that [the person within the eye] also possesses that qualification. However, since qualification is impossible in that case, it is likewise impossible in the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, [the text asks]: "Which of these two should one worship? and subsequently mentions the five [fires] which have the sun as their support.

Having begun with "The *amṛtas* [are] Rohita and the others," and having taught that the five groups of gods— the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas— subsist respectively upon each of those *amṛtas*, [the text continues]: "He who knows this *amṛta* thus, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, becomes satisfied by seeing this divine *amṛta* with Agni as his mouth."
By these and other such passages, [the text] shows that those who know the nectars (*amṛta*) upon which the Vasus and others subsist attain the majesty of the Vasus and others.

But how could the Vasus and others themselves—being subsistent upon the nectars of other Vasus and so forth distinct from themselves—know [those others], or what majesty of Vasus and others distinct from themselves could they desire to attain? Likewise, "Fire is one quarter; Wind is one quarter."

In meditations upon the nature of deities such as, "The sun is a foot, the quarters are a foot, Vāyu is the absorber, and the sun is Brahman—this is the instruction," and so forth, they have no qualification [for those specific meditations]. Likewise, [in the passage], "These two are Gautama and Bharadvāja;
this one is Gautama and this one is Bharadvāja; these two are Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni; this one is... and so on.

In the meditative knowledges (*ṛṣyupāsyavidyā*) concerning the seers— such as "This one is Viśvāmitra, this one is Jamadagni, these two are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa, this one is the son of Vasiṣṭha, this one is Kaśyapa, Atri is speech," and so forth— there is no entitlement for those very seers themselves. Therefore,
since the deities are in every way incapable of having an entitlement to the Madhu-vidyā, they cannot have an entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
It is understood that [the soul] comes into existence.
Regarding this, he states another reason: 96. And because of its existence in light. (Sūtra 32)

Since we observe scriptural statements indicating that even the gods possess the qualification for worshiping the supreme Śiva— who is the light of lights— as His unique and exclusive object of worship, saying, "The gods indeed meditate upon Him as life, as immortality," it is understood that their lack of qualification for other forms of worship, such as that of the Madhu-vidyā, is established by logic.

Furthermore, since the terms for deities such as the Sun and the Moon exist in common worldly usage only with respect to the visible orbs themselves, and since these orbs lack a physical body— being insentient like a lump of clay—

the same applies to fire, wind, and so forth. Moreover, because the *mantras* and *arthavādas* have other purposes [and do not intend to describe the literal nature of the gods], [they cannot be taken as evidence for their corporeality].
Because they lack authority regarding their own [benefit], the gods do not possess embodied forms. For this reason as well, Jaimini considers that the gods have no entitlement [to Vedic rites].
Thus, he refutes the objection raised by the teacher Jaimini regarding the eligibility of the gods for the knowledge of Brahman:
97. Let it be developed; for Bādarāyaṇa says "it exists. || 33 ||

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Although the gods lack eligibility for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations, the teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that they do possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.
For there exists a conscious deity, possessing a physical form and distinct from the orb [of the sun], who identifies with that orb; the meaning is that this is established in the Purāṇas.
