Even though the Vasus and other deities lack qualification for the Madhu-vidyā, their qualification for the meditation upon Brahman residing within the lotus of their own hearts is not contradicted; for it is possible that in another kalpa, the Vasus and others may attain the state of Brahman. [The supreme reality] named Śiva consists of both the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) aspects.

Brahman is prescribed as the object of worship for the gods. Beginning with the passage, "This sun is the honey of the gods," Brahman—abiding in various states of effects characterized by names and forms such as Āditya and Vasu—is taught as the object of worship. Now...

Thereafter, by the passage beginning "He rises upwards; by this very [path] he rises, he does not set," the Brahman consisting of the cause, which has entered as the inner self within the subtle Āditya, is taught as the object of meditation. In that context: "He who, having thus become one of the Vasus, beholds this very nectar through Agni as his mouth, is satisfied."

The fruit consisting of the attainment of the state of Vasu and so forth is stated [in the passage]: "Indeed, the sun neither rises nor sets for him; it remains as perpetual day for him who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman. Thus, the fruit of attaining Brahman is taught.
Therefore, the qualification of the gods for the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations is possible.

Furthermore—although the gods lack the qualification for the worship of deities mixed with [human] gods, nevertheless their qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is indeed possible. For the absence of qualification in one instance does not entail a lack of qualification in all instances; otherwise, it would follow that Brāhmaṇas and others who are unqualified for the Rājasūya and similar sacrifices would also be unqualified for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
As for what was stated—that [the term "light"] refers to the luminous body—there is indeed an answer to that:

although words such as "Āditya" and so forth are applied to the luminous body, they nevertheless refer exclusively to the deities presiding over them, signifying those respective divine selves. For it is possible for the gods, by virtue of their sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), to abide in the form of light.
And there is the capacity to assume various forms and act accordingly. For it is heard in scripture:
"Indra, having become a ram, carried off Medhātithi, the son of Kaṇva" (*Vāṣka-mantra-upaniṣad*); and it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The Sun, having become a man..."
"He indeed approached Kuntī. Thus, presiding deities are accepted for clay and other such materials, as seen in passages such as "The clay spoke" and "The waters spoke.
But [it may be objected]: since the Mantras and Arthavādas lack the intention to convey their own literal meaning, the same must apply to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas which are based upon them.

If it is asked, "How can there be the establishment of a literal meaning (vigraha) given that such is not the case?"—no; for here too there is indeed an answer: the meaning is that even those [scriptures] possess authority regarding matters that are not sublated. Even in the case of explanatory passages (arthavādas), the authority of the comprehension of meaning produced by the power of the words' own expressive capacity remains entirely unimpeded, provided there is no sublation. This is because the purpose is not achieved by that alone.

If it is argued that the assumption of syntactical unity with an injunction is for the sake of making [the passage] subordinate to that injunction, we say no; for by this much, there is no possibility of sublation of the intermediate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*). If that were merely an appearance, even the praise would not exist.
For this very reason, even in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as the praise of Vāyu, one must accept the uncontradicted meaning through restatement (*anuvāda*).
The status of being subordinate to praise (*stutiparatva*) is accepted [as the purpose].

However, in reality, just as the explanatory passages concerning heaven (*svargārthavāda*) possess authority by way of establishing the fruit required by the injunction (*codanā*), so too do those passages that establish the embodied form of the deity. For instance: "Indra, being satisfied, [endows] him with progeny..."

Upon careful consideration of such passages as "he satisfies with animals," and by application of the *rātrisatra* principle, the propitiation of the deity alone is postulated as the function (*vyāpāra*) of the ritual acts;
however, that which is called *apūrva*—which is equal to the Self and beyond the scope of other means of knowledge—is not fit for such postulation. Nor is [the result] already bestowed...

The deity does not consume the oblation, because that would contradict perceptible reality. If there is no consumption, how can there be satisfaction? And if there is no satisfaction, how can [the deity] be pleased? To this it must be said: even for one who does not eat, pleasure is possible through the mere act of renunciation directed toward them.

Just as when someone most worthy of honor is absent, yet in the context of honoring those who are present, one first sets aside some betel or other offering for him and gives it to him; then, once the worship of the present ones has been performed, he hears of it— even though he himself received nothing— and by the mere fact of his initial renunciation for his own sake, he [considers himself honored].

Thinking himself honored, he becomes pleased. Likewise, it is not contradictory that the gods also experience pleasure when oblations are cast into the *āhavanīya* fire with them as the intended recipients. In this same way, the pleasure resulting from the performance of salutations and other such acts should be illustrated.
Nor is there an impossibility of the gods being pleased even by non-sentient objects like the cups (*graha*), because there exist presiding deities for them.

Because it is possible [that He grants fruits], in reality the Lord who dwells within all (*sarvāntaryāmīśvara*) alone is the bestower of all fruits; therefore, His pleasure alone is postulated [as the cause]. For this very reason, it is said in the *Gītā*:
"Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith..."
Whatever firm faith he possesses, that very faith I make steadfast for him.
"Endowed with that faith, he strives for its propitiation;
and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone.
Therefore, it is established that because deities possess consciousness and embodied form, they have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
9. The Section on Excluding the Śūdras (Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa).
Now follows the refutation of the eligibility of Śūdras for the knowledge of Brahman. [Objection:
Because of the hearing of the word "Śūdra" in the Vedic text, "O Śūdra, I indeed think that you know it," [it might be argued that they are eligible]. This refers to what was mentioned previously.

Having raised the objection that Śūdras also possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)— on the grounds that it is generally declared that human beings are qualified [for Vedic study] and because a specific location within the heart, the size of a thumb, is shown to them— the author says:
98. For it is indicated by his sorrow upon hearing that [the Buddha] was disregarded, and by his fleeing at that time. (34)

The subject matter of this [passage] is recounted in the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Alas, O Śūdra! Let it be with you and those very cows," [the teacher replied]. "Bring them back, O Śūdra! You would have made me speak through this very mouth. In this context, the addressing of the disciple by the teacher with the word "Śūdra" in the phrase "Alas, O Śūdra! is appropriate. Therefore, in this case—
It is now considered whether or not there is eligibility for Śūdras in the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā).
There is eligibility for Śūdras in the knowledge of Brahman, because even in the Śruti, the word "Śūdra" is seen used as a form of address.
[For example: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn, a Vaiśya."

If it is argued that because the connection with the sacred fires (*agni*) is seen here only for those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), therefore only they possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for this knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), we say no;

for the desire for liberation (*arthitva*) and other such qualifications are possible even for *śūdras*. [This is so] provided one does not abandon the principle that human beings are the qualified subjects [of Vedic injunctions].

Because there is a designation of qualification for the gods, it follows as a prima facie argument that just as there is qualification for the three higher castes, there must likewise be qualification for a Śūdra; for even though he lacks qualification for rites accomplished by fire due to the absence of the *āhavanīya* fire,
qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*) is possible, just as it is for the gods and others, despite the absence of initiation (*upanayana*) and similar rites.

The section concerning the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) of gods and others. Now, an objection may be raised: "Since they have spontaneously manifested the Vedas and know the meaning of the Vedas, only they are eligible. This is not so; for even Śūdras can attain knowledge through means such as listening to the Purāṇas. This is according to the logic of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (niṣādasthapati-nyāya).

Furthermore, because the possibility of being qualified for the reception of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) exists [for them]. Therefore, if it is argued that the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman is possible here for a Śūdra by taking the word "Śūdra" in its primary sense—it is replied: there is no qualification for a Śūdra for the knowledge of Brahman, even though the gods lack the rite of initiation (upanayana).

There is no contradiction regarding his eligibility [to teach], because he has attained the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas through specific meritorious deeds, because he possesses the status of a Brahmasūtra (the thread of Brahman) which is established by its own nature and is non-sublatable, because he has a body of light, and because of his connection with the heavenly world.

Since the initiation (*upanayana*), which is the cause for eligibility to study the Vedas, pertains only to the three higher castes, and since the Upaniṣadic scripture is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the Veda; and because of the prohibition, "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice"; and because there is no logical justification for the mention of the word "Śūdra" in the Saṃvarga-vidyā in the fourth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—that mention is not a valid indicative mark (*liṅga*).

This sūtra— "Because of the hearing of that disregard by him, and because of his running away at that time, it is indeed indicated"— is intended to explain that the gender [of the word *liṅga*] refers to the subject under discussion.
That is to say, because of the hearing of that disregard by this Kṣatriya Jānaśruti— namely, the hearing of the disregard shown toward that Haṃsa— [the fact of being a Śūdra] is indicated.

That sorrow which arose is indicated by the word *śūdra*. Because he then ran toward Raikva due to that sorrow—in order to make known his own omniscience through [the name] "Raikva"—Jānaśruti ran toward Raikva with that sorrow; thus Jānaśruti is called *śūdra*.
Since the primary meaning is impossible here, the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is accepted. In this context, [it refers to] King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa.
Once, as some swans were flying over his palace in the form of a line of flight, one swan said to another, "This Jānaśruti is a man of great fortune. To him, the other replied, "Who is this wretch?
Raikva is far superior even to him. Upon hearing this, grief arose in Jānaśruti; by that very [grief]—

Having observed the gift of a chariot, cows, gold, and so forth brought by Śoka, Rāma said: "O Śūdra Jānaśruti, let this gift that has been brought belong to you alone; I will not teach with such a meager gift.
This is the summary of the meaning of the narrative to be understood.
Moreover, because the study of the Vedas is absent, there is no attainment of that knowledge which is established by it;

therefore, the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, *Itihāsas*, and so forth, serve to explain the meaning of the Śruti. Consequently, even the entitlement to hear them is not enjoined for Śūdras independently. However, as for the knowledge produced by hearing them—

The fruit is the removal of all sins. Since Vidura, Dharmavyādha, and others were born from portions of the gods, their eligibility for liberation through the knowledge arising from hearing the Purāṇas is not contradictory.

[Objection: "Let Jānaśruti be a Śūdra in the primary sense; why resort to an inferior figurative interpretation? To this, [the author] says: 99. "And because his status as a Kṣatriya is understood from the subsequent indicative mark concerning Caitraratha. (Sūtra 3.4.35)

Nor, in this case as well, can Jānaśruti be considered of the Śūdra caste; for, following the present context, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the subsequent Saṃvarga-vidyā consisting of his being mentioned alongside Abhipratārin Caitraratha, who is well-known to be a Kṣatriya—since, as a general rule, those of equal status are mentioned together. Indeed, at the commencement of Jānaśruti’s meditation...

Pautrāyaṇa was one who gave with faith, a liberal giver, and one who prepared much food. He had lodgings constructed everywhere, thinking, "Thus people will eat from me from all sides. Having thus taught the nature of a donor and the practice of providing various kinds of cooked food, he [said] in their midst:
"Even as he was rising, [Raikva said], 'O Kṣattṛ, in the broth of the sheep'"—thus the urging is taught. At its conclusion, it says, "This is his wife, this is the village in which he dwells";

these are indeed the Raikvaparṇas by name among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he lived for him—thus his status as a donor of many villages is taught. Therefore, by these qualities, [the excellence] of Jānaśruti [is established].

Kṣatriyahood itself is made known. Now, a religious student begged for alms from Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni while they were being served food; thus, by virtue of his connection with the priest named Kāpeya, Abhipratārin is taught to be a Kṣatriya, a descendant of Citraratha. Furthermore, the fact that the Kāpeyas had the descendant of Citraratha as their domestic priest is well-known in the Śruti. By this [it is established].
"The Kāpeyas caused Citraratha to sacrifice with this two-night rite. For generally, among those of the same lineage, it is indeed those of the same lineage who become the officiating priests.
[Objection: But surely, Abhipratārin's status as a Caitraratha arises from his connection with Citraratha and the Kāpeyas; therefore, [the text] does not...

If it is argued that he is a Kṣatriya, we say no; for in the supplementary passage, "A certain lord of the Kṣatras named Caitrarathi was born," he is designated as a Kṣatriya by virtue of being born in the lineage of Citraratha and being a lord of the Kṣatras. Similarly, later on, Abhipratārin is taught to be a Kṣatriya because he was associated with a Brāhmaṇa, Kāpya. Likewise, [he is so designated] because of one Brāhmaṇa.
It is understood that Jānaśruti was also a *kṣatriya*. Therefore, the address "O Śūdra" is appropriate only for a *kṣatriya*.
One might suspect, however, that according to the principle of the "chief of the Niṣādas," a *śūdra* also possesses the qualification to hear the Upaniṣadic discourse on Brahman.
He refutes [this], because of the misapprehension of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the desire for their non-existence. (36)

Even here, there is no eligibility for Śūdras to the knowledge of Brahman; why? Because in the context of the instruction on the knowledge of Brahman, there is a reference to purificatory rites such as initiation (*upanayana*). "He initiated him; 'Teach me, O Venerable One,' thus he approached. "Devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, seeking Brahman—'He indeed will tell us all that,'" they [said]. Thus they...

Because of the teaching that initiation (*upanayana*) is a constituent part of the knowledge of Brahman, as seen in the passage beginning, "With hands weary from toil, they approached the Blessed Pippalāda," and so forth, a Śūdra therefore has no entitlement [to such knowledge].
Now, one might object: in passages such as "Having initiated them... and so on, there are instances where even those who have not been initiated, and even those who are uninitiated, [are mentioned].

If it is argued that initiation (*upanayana*) is not mandatory because the *Vaiśvānara* section designates [the students] as being qualified [for it], we say no; for a prohibition presupposes a prior possibility of occurrence. Since only twice-born (*dvija*) individuals who have already undergone initiation—such as Prācīnaśāla and others who were initiated by Śiva—are qualified, the prohibition applies specifically to King Aśvapati, who was the instructor of their own particular knowledge.

It should be understood [that he was not initiated] because of his inferior caste; the meaning of the scriptural passage is that King Aśvapati spoke to those sages, such as Prācīnaśāla and others, without having first initiated them.
Now, one might object: "In that case, should initiation not be assumed for a Śūdra as well? To this, he says: "And because of the mention of the absence of that [initiation]."
There is no sin whatsoever for a Śūdra, nor does he deserve the purificatory rites (saṃskāra).
The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he is of a single birth—so says the Smṛti.

The meaning is that this is because of the statement regarding the absence of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as initiation (*upanayana*), and so forth. "Sin" (*pātaka*) refers to that which arises from the lack of distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten. The implication is that a "once-born" (*ekajāti*) is one who lacks initiation.
If it is argued that there exists an injunction stating, "One should cause a *niṣādasthapati* to perform a sacrifice," [the answer is no].

It is established that, because the hearing and instruction of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) in the Śruti and Smṛti are prescribed exclusively for the three twice-born classes who have been distinguished by the sacrament of initiation (upanayana), the eligibility of a Śūdra for the knowledge of Brahman is never possible.
On this point, he states another reason: 101. "And because activity proceeds when there is a determination of its non-existence. (37)

For this reason as well, there is no eligibility for a Śūdra; for the instruction proceeds only when the absence of Śūdra-status has been determined, as is indicated by the designation: "O gentle one, a non-Brāhmaṇa does not deserve to carry the sacred fuel; bring it, for you have approached me with truth. Thus, Satyakāma Jābāla, whose father had died, [was instructed].
Having approached Gautama, he said, "I wish to enter upon the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). Gautama asked him, "What is your lineage?

Jābāla replied, "Even my mother does not know; I myself do not know. Having heard this, Gautama concluded that such truthful speech is impossible for one who is not a Brahmin, and thus determined his lack of Śūdra status.

It is established that a Śūdra has no qualification [for Vedic study], because we see in the narrative accounts that [the sage] accepted only the service [of the Śūdra]. Now, one might object: even if initiation (*upanayana*) is impossible for him, the exclusion from the utterance of the *brahman* (Veda) is merely occasional rather than universal; it does not apply at all times.
For even though initiation is impossible for a child, one should not have him recite the *brahman*, except in certain cases.
Because the rule for the utterance of the *brahman* is prescribed specifically during the pouring of the *svadhā* offering, it is logical that this [utterance] occurs only occasionally.

Consequently, for an uninitiated *śūdra* at rites such as the *pākayajña*, there would be an exclusion of the utterance of the *brahman*. However, this does not constitute a prohibition against his eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Thus he says: "It is impossible [to say otherwise]."
102. Because of the prohibition of hearing and studying [the Veda], and because of Smṛti. || 38 ||

For this reason as well, there is no entitlement for a Śūdra. Why? "And because of Smṛti. This means that according to Smṛti, there is a prohibition—meaning a strict ban—on his hearing the Veda, on its study, and on the two purposes resulting from it, namely the knowledge of its meaning and its practical performance. For instance, [the Smṛti states]: "Now, if he should overhear the Veda, [his ears] are to be filled with molten tin and lac..."

Regarding the instruction for a Śūdra concerning the study of the Vedas and so forth, it is heard [in the scriptures]: "If he utters [the Veda], his ears are to be filled; if he retains it, his tongue is to be cut out; and if he masters it, his body is to be cut asunder.
Furthermore, regarding a Śūdra's hearing of the Veda: "Upon his ear, heated [iron] should be applied with diligence."
The king should fill the vessel merely by the utterance of that [mantra].
One should then swiftly cut off his tongue due to that act of holding [the forbidden object];
this is declared to be the rule for causing the destruction of the body.

Thus, traditional scripture (smṛti) is also observed. Therefore, since the injunctions for hearing the Veda, studying the Veda, and performing the rites according to the meaning of the Veda are possible only for the members of the three higher castes who are distinguished by sacraments such as initiation (upanayana), it is the established conclusion (rāddhānta) that they alone possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.

If it be objected that, since Vidura, Dharmavyādha, and others are seen to possess knowledge of Brahman, there can be no prohibition against Śūdras having the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman—we say no; for they were portions of the gods.
For those who are born as portions of the gods, one should not cause distinctions of caste to be made.
Just as in the case of Vāmadeva and others, for one whose consciousness is established in its own nature at all times,
the distinction of castes is merely imagined for his sons, kinsmen, and so forth.

In such passages, because Vidura and others are designated as being free from distinctions of caste by virtue of their status as *kāraṇapuruṣas* (causal persons), their Śūdra-hood is merely figurative. Nevertheless, it is ordained that they possess only the right to hear the Purāṇas and Itihāsas in the presence of their guru along with those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). It is not [the case that they have other rights].
The qualification for the study of the Vedas and Vedānta based on direct perception. Section on "Trembling" (Kampanādhikaraṇa). 10.
The investigation concerning the incidental topic has concluded. Now he demonstrates the connection with the meaning of the primary statement: 103.
On account of trembling. (Sūtra 39)
Having demonstrated at the beginning of the Kaṭhavallī that the all-pervading Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, assumes the dimensions of the human heart for the sake of favoring his practitioners—
[it says]: "Whatever exists in this entire world, having issued forth, vibrates by means of Prāṇa."
A great terror is this raised thunderbolt; those who know this become immortal.

Thus, the subject matter is recited in the sixth chapter of the Kaṭhavallī: "The doubt here is whether the cause of the trembling of the world is the vital breath (prāṇa), or a thunderbolt (aśani), or the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). In the statement 'the prāṇa makes that which has issued forth tremble,' it is heard that this entire world, once produced—that is, 'issued forth'—trembles with the prāṇa as its instrumental cause. Regarding the word *prāṇa*, [it may refer] to the vital air...

Since the Supreme Lord, who is the trusted authority for the world, cannot be the cause of the shaking of the universe, and because He alone is designated as Brahman in such passages as "Salutations to you, O Vāyu;
you indeed are the perceptible Brahman," there is no contradiction here in teaching that the meditation on Prāṇa alone leads to liberation. Furthermore: "He conquers death again..."

In the Śruti passage, "He who knows thus," the fruit of liberation for the knowledge of Vāyu is clearly stated. Alternatively, in the passage, "A great terror, a raised thunderbolt," since it is heard that lightning, clouds, and rain are produced when the thunderbolt— Vāyu itself— manifests in the form of Parjanya, it is logical that the term "thunderbolt" (vajra) also indicates the wind that is the cause of the lightning bolt.
If it is argued that, because the primary characteristic of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is not seen here in any way, the Supreme Lord alone is not being taught—

this is answered by [the principle of] figurative interpretation (kalpanā). Here, the cause of the trembling of the universe is indeed the Supreme Lord himself, based on the verbal root *ejṛ*, meaning "to tremble."

The meaning is "because it has the sense of causing to tremble. The word *prāṇa* is heard in reference to the Supreme Lord; the Supreme Lord's status as the cause of the trembling of the entire universe arises from His being the Ruler. Out of fear of His command, we all turn away from what is forbidden and proceed toward what is enjoined. "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear of Him the sun rises."

In such passages as "From fear of him, fire, Indra, and death as the fifth run away," the quality of being the cause of fear in the wind and other elements is taught to belong to the Supreme Lord alone.
Furthermore, in such passages as "The Ruler of all sciences, the Lord of all beings," the status of being the controller of the universe is attributed to Him alone.

It is appropriate that [the Lord] is the cause of fear for the world upon being seen; for it is heard that "the face of a king is terrifying" and "it is auspicious," and thus even the one whose form is auspicious is a cause of fear due to his role as the ruler of the world. Because he is the material cause of all, it is fitting that he is denoted by the word *prāṇa*; for he alone is Viṣṇu, as in such passages as "He is the *prāṇa* of *prāṇa*" and so forth.

It is heard [in scripture]. Moreover, because it is understood from the introduction, the conclusion, and the intermediate references that this constitutes a context concerning the Supreme Lord, it does not have any other object as its subject matter.
That indeed is semen, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.
In it all worlds are supported; no one whatsoever transcends it.

Thus, in the introductory statement, the Supreme Lord alone is taught. Furthermore, this quality of being the impeller—expressed in the words "the entire world trembles at the breath"—is appropriate for the Supreme Lord alone, and not for the mere air (vāyu). For it is well known from another scriptural passage:
"No mortal lives by means of either the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna);
rather, they live by something else upon which these two depend.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, later on:
Out of fear the fire blazes, out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra, Agni, and Death as the fifth run their courses.

By such statements as these, it is determined that this is a section concerning the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), due to the abundance of His attributes. The designation of the term "thunderbolt" (*vajra*) is appropriate for the Supreme Lord alone, because of the commonality of being the cause of both fear and security. Furthermore, the declaration of the fruit of immortality (*amṛta*) in passages such as "those who know this become immortal" refers exclusively to the Supreme Lord; for it is said, "having known the Lord, one becomes immortal."

"Having known Śiva, one attains peace; beholding the supreme Brahman, one goes [to liberation], not by any other cause"—since in such passages the knowledge of Śiva alone is specified as the cause of liberation, immortality is nowhere enjoined as resulting from the knowledge of Vāyu. In that context, at the conclusion, [the question is asked]: "Tell me that which you see as other than what has been and what is yet to be."
Since it has been stated that [this power] belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, it is established that the quality of being the cause of the trembling of the world does not belong to anyone else.
The Section Concerning Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa) || 11 ||

In another section, he establishes that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who has been presented as the object of meditation in specific locations such as the small lotus of the heart, is the goal to be attained:
104. *Jyotirdarśanāt* (Because of the vision of light).

In the *Chāndogya*, within the Prajāpati-vidyā of the fifth chapter, it is recorded: "This serene being (samprasāda), having risen from this body and having reached the highest light (paraṃ jyotiḥ), becomes that supreme person (uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ). Here, a doubt arises as to whether the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to the well-known light of the sun and so forth, or to Nārāyaṇa or Paraśiva.
In this context, the word "light" (*jyotis*) does not denote Paramaśiva, because that term primarily refers to radiance (*tejas*).

Since in the sūtra *jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt* (I.1.24), the word "light" is seen to abandon its primary meaning in favor of being a cause for the "feet," the same logic applies here: it is not tenable for it to denote the Supreme Lord. Why?

Because of the absence of a cause, it is also impossible for the Supreme Lord to be the cause for attaining liberation. For in the section concerning the channels (*nāḍīkhaṇḍa*), beginning with "These channels of the heart are imperishable," and in the scriptural passage starting with "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays," it is specifically the maker of light (the sun) that is designated as the means for attaining liberation.

Furthermore, this is also appropriate for Nārāyaṇa; for in passages such as "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self," the supreme light to be attained by the liberated is designated by the term *puruṣottama*.
This is because the word *puruṣottama* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that very sense. Therefore, it refers to him alone.

When it is argued that it is possible for Śiva to be denoted by the term "supreme light" (*parañjyotis*) as being in grammatical apposition with the word "Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*), we reply: "Now, we shall establish that Śiva, who is Brahman, is the Supreme Person—on account of the vision of the light. Here, why is it that the supreme light is Śiva alone? Because of the scriptural vision [to that effect]. Ya...
Since the text begins with "The Self is free from evil" and shows that the Supreme Śiva alone is the subject consistently maintained throughout,

there is no contradiction here in attributing to the Supreme Lord the state of being denoted by the term "Supreme Light," the status of the Highest Person, and the state of being the goal attained by the liberated. It is precisely this Supreme Lord, characterized by attributes such as freedom from evil, who is to be sought after here.

Because of the initial proposition; because of the subsequent connection [in the text]: "I shall explain this further to you in this way"; and because, in such passages as "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless," there is the instruction on the attainment of light by means of bodilessness.

Furthermore, because of the qualifying attributes of the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*), it is the Supreme Person alone who is indicated here. Since this is a context concerning Brahman, it is not logical for the state of being attained by the liberated to belong to the Sun. This is evident from such passages as, "The wise one attains Brahman here; he goes to the divine Person, higher than the high," which describe the non-return [to saṃsāra] for those seeking liberation.

Because the attainment of Paramaśiva is observed [in scripture], it is not possible for even Nārāyaṇa to be the one attained by the liberated. This is because the attainment of Paramaśiva by the liberated is seen in such passages as, "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace," and "Having known the Lord, they become immortal. Furthermore, the term *puruṣottama* is also applicable to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), as he is superior to all *puruṣas*.

He is "supreme" (*parama*) because he is superior to those who possess bodies (*śārīra*). Furthermore, even in the *Brahmamedha-kalpa*, the word *puruṣottama* is seen to be used as a synonym for the Supreme Śiva, who is the goal to be attained—as in the phrase "to envelop Puruṣottama"—just as the words *hasta*, *kara*, and *pāṇi* are synonyms for the hand. This is evident from such passages as "The Lord (*īśāna*) of all sciences... and so forth.

The Supreme Light is indeed Paraśiva, who is the regulator of all sciences beginning with the Vedas, the source of all prosperity, and the abode of the Puruṣa. "That Brahman which is higher than the highest, Hari who is higher than that which is highest, and the Sovereign Lord who is higher than that which is highest—may my mind be intent on Śiva. Śiva is non-dual, the Fourth (Turiya).

In such passages as "They consider Rudra, the great seer, to be superior to all," because there is a designation of superiority over the individual souls (jīvas) such as Nārāyaṇa who are denoted by the word *puruṣa*, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that Paramaśiva alone is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*). If it is argued that the word *puruṣottama* has a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) only for Viṣṇu, [the answer is: in the *Harivaṃśa*, with respect to Kṛṣṇa...
The word of the Supreme Lord:
"O Govinda, those names of yours which are indeed great in the world, they alone are my names; no deliberation should be made in this matter."
Thus, from the observation of this scriptural statement, it is established that He alone is denoted by the term *Puruṣottama*.
This concludes the section concerning the designation as being distinct from other entities (*arthāntaratvādivyapadeśādhikaraṇa*). 12.
105. Space [is distinct from the Self], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth. || 41 ||

The subject matter of this passage is recited in the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "That which is called 'space' (ākāśa) is indeed the revealer of name and form; that within which they are, is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self. Here, as to whether the space taught as the revealer of name and form is the elemental space (bhūtākāśa), the individual soul (jīva), or the Supreme Lord (parameśvara): [this is the inquiry].

Thus there is a doubt: Is it the ether (*ākāśa*), because the word "ether" is conventionally established in that sense, and because it is possible for it to be the source of the differentiation of names and forms by virtue of providing space—as in such passages as, "All these beings indeed arise from the ether alone," where the causality of the universe is designated specifically for it? Or could it be the individual soul (*jīva*) as well?

"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva), I shall manifest names and forms"— since the entire collection of modifications is thus manifested as name and form, such manifestation is impossible for the changeless Supreme Lord;
yet, because we observe His manifestation of names and forms, and because He is of the nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), it follows that [the agency] belongs to those two alone.

If it is argued that what is being stated is the fact of being denotable by the word "space" (ākāśa), we reply: here, why is it that Śiva alone is the one denoted by the word "space"? Because of the designation of his being the "interior of things" (arthāntaratva) and so forth; that is, because of the designation of his being the interior of all objects and categories.

This is to be understood from the designation and description of the inner self (antarātman) within the expansion of the conscious and unconscious (cid-acit-prapañca), both gross and subtle, which consist of name-and-form (nāma-rūpa). For it is impossible for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) and other such entities— which are distinct from the Supreme Lord— to possess attributes such as being the Self (ātmatva) and immortality (amṛtatva), and because that would contradict the context (prakaraṇa).
It is established that [the Self] is none other than Brahman because of the abundance of the marks of Brahman.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being something else (arthāntaratva), namely the section on deep sleep (suṣupti). || 13 ||
106. [The Self is distinct from the body] because of the difference between deep sleep and departure. || 42 ||

The phrase "because of designation" (*vyapadeśāt*) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. The subject matter of this [sūtra] is seen in the sixth chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*:

"This person (*puruṣa*), consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), who is within the vital breaths (*prāṇeṣu*), the light within the heart (*hṛdyantarjyotiḥ*), being common (*samānaḥ*), traverses both worlds. Here, the one "consisting of consciousness" is the embodied self (*śārīra*) delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), [and not] the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
Or is it so? This is the doubt.

Here, the individual soul (jīva) alone is denoted; for, by means of the introduction, the conclusion, repetition, reference, and so forth, the subject matter proceeds concerning the soul alone. This is because of the context of the embodied self in the passage, "He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths," and because of the statement, "He indeed is that great unborn one."

Because even in the concluding summary, "This is the Self," we observe that this [Self] is not refuted; and because in the middle section as well, the designation of its abiding within the heart is seen in the statement, "This space within the heart"; and because in these considerations of the beginning, middle, and end, no words are observed that establish the Supreme Lord as the subject, it refers only to the individual soul (jīva) which persists through the three states.
If it is argued that "because it exists, that very [Self] is what is being propounded here," we reply:

In the Śruti passage, "Which is this Self? It is that which consists of consciousness," the liberated soul (*muktajīva*) is propounded—like a worm inside a bee-cocoon—and not the bound soul (*baddhajīva*). Why? Because [the characteristics described apply] in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and in the state of departure (*utkrānti*).

The meaning is that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established twice by means of differentiation. First, regarding deep sleep, it is said: "In this state, this person is completely embraced by the Intelligent Self (*prājña*); he knows nothing external, nor does he know anything internal. Here, by the term *prājña*, Paramaśiva is indicated as distinct from the individual soul.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that here the *jīva* is the *puruṣa*, because it is possible for him to possess both external and internal consciousness within the body, because he is the lord of the body, and because his attributes are seen through the sixfold marks such as the introduction and conclusion? Therefore, the *jīva* alone is what is denoted by the word 'Prājña' here. [Reply: No. By the word 'Prājña', Paramaśiva alone is established here. He who...

This [Self] rests within the space of the heart; for attributes such as omniscience and universal lordship, as indicated by scriptural passages beginning with "He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, the master of all," cannot possibly belong to anything else.
Likewise, at the time of departure, the embodied self, mounted by the conscious Self (the Prājña), goes forth uttering sounds.

The Supreme Lord is taught as being distinct from the embodied self. To begin with, in the opening section, there is no mention of the attributes of the embodied self in the passage: "He who is this, consisting of consciousness, among the vital breaths. Furthermore, after referring to the attributes of the embodied self, it is pointed out that its state of being one with Śiva is like that of a worm within a bee. Likewise, in the conclusion as well: "He indeed is the Great, the Unborn..."

The term "Self" (*ātman*) here refers precisely to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), as indicated by attributes such as being unborn and so forth. Consequently, there is a question at every step: "Tell me that which is beyond this for the sake of liberation alone," and there is a repeated response: "He remains untouched by it, for this person is unattached. This difference in phrasing makes known the intent of the passage to be non-duality. [It is] untouched...

It is established that this passage does not refer to the embodied soul (*śārīra*), because it is designated as being intent on teaching the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) who is distinct from the body and the senses, as shown by the statement: "Not followed by merit, nor followed by evil, for then he has crossed over all sorrows."
Regarding the position of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), he states another reason: 107.
"Because of the words 'Lord' (pati) and so forth. (Sūtra 43).

Furthermore, this is indeed a presentation of Paramaśiva, because in this context words such as *pati* (Lord) and others, which designate the Supreme Lord, are observed. It is heard [in scripture]: "The ruler of all, the sovereign of all, the lord of beings, the protector of beings," and so forth; as well as "the overlord of Brahmā, the overlord of Brahman, for the sake of the Lord of creatures (*paśūnāṃ pataye*)."

In passages such as "to the Lord of trees" and "to the Lord of worlds," the status of being the sovereign of all is well-known to belong to the Supreme Lord alone. Thus, since attributes of this kind— such as being the Lord of all— are never observed in the individual soul (jīva), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is Paramaśiva alone who is taught here.

Thus ends the section on deep sleep (*suṣupti-adhikaraṇa*) in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* by the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya, the preeminent leader of the multitude of ascetics of the illustrious Nirābhāsa Vīraśaiva tradition.
The third quarter of the first chapter, titled "Consistency" (*Samanvaya*).
Now begins the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*. Section One: On that which is inferential (*Ānumānikādhikaraṇa*).
At the commencement of this treatise, having taught the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) for the sake of those seeking liberation attaining the fruit that is free from rebirth,

and having stated the definition of the world’s birth and so forth as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the scripture in order to establish the reality of that Brahman according to the principle that "the nature of a thing is established by the fact of its being established," [the author proceeds].

Having demonstrated, in the fourth sūtra, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntic texts regarding Brahman by showing the non-contradiction of scriptural passages concerning difference and non-difference— which possess mutually contradictory natures— and having raised the objection that the aforementioned definition of Brahman would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to the Pradhāna,

[the author] proceeds from "Because of seeing, it is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*) up to "Because of the uniformity of the way of approach" (*gatisāmānyāt*), establishing [the Pradhāna's exclusion] by its lack of scriptural basis (*aśabdatva*).
In the first pāda, the doctrine that *pradhāna* is the cause of the world was refuted by means of Vedāntic passages.

In the second and third pādas, having established the concordance (*samanvaya*) of passages containing indistinct, distinct, and indistinctly distinct marks of Brahman with Brahman through the medium of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), [the author] addresses certain branches of the Vedic tradition...

In response to the doubt as to how the state of being "not based on scripture" (*aśabdatva*) can be established for that [Pradhāna], given that words demonstrating its status as the cause of the world through Pradhāna are actually observed, the fourth quarter (pāda) is commenced:
the demonstration that Supreme Śiva is the object of worship for all.

108. "If it be argued that for some [it is] even inferential, we say no; because [the text] shows the apprehension of what was presented through the metaphor of the body, and [scripture] further demonstrates this.
The subject matter of this is taught in the *Kaṭhavallī*:
"Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind."
"The intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind (manas), and the Great Self (mahān ātmā) is superior to the intellect;

the Unmanifest (avyakta) is superior to the Great, and the Puruṣa is superior to the Unmanifest. There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. Thus [it is said].

Here, a doubt arises as to whether that which is taught as being "greater than the Great" and designated by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) refers to the Pradhāna of the Sāṅkhya system, or rather to the embodied self (śārīra).
Based on the context of the preceding and following passages, it is the Pradhāna alone that is asserted here. In the Sāṅkhya treatise...

Since the terms "the Great" (mahat), "the Unmanifest" (avyakta), and "the Person" (puruṣa) are well-known in the context of the three principles (tattvas), it is established that they are recognized here [in this text] as those very same things; therefore, it is not tenable to claim that this [text] is not based on scripture (aśabdatva). Furthermore, terms such as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta), "Prakṛti," "Pradhāna," and "Māyā" are observed in the Veda itself.

If it is argued that because there is no restrictive rule stating that the Vedāntas have their systematic unity (*samanvaya*) in Brahman alone, and since the status of *pradhāna* as the cause of the world is established by Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning in the Smṛtis of Kapila and others, therefore that [pradhāna] itself is what is being propounded here—
We shall explain this with the words "that which is inferential," and so forth.
"Inferential" (*ānumānika*) means that which is derived from inference; thus, *pradhāna* is meant. This [doctrine] is also well-known among certain followers of Vedic schools (*śākhins*).

If it is argued that the claim of its being "not based on the Word" (*aśabdatva*) is unestablished because *pradhāna* is understood by the term "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*), we say no; for [it refers to] the body.
Because that which was presented and established in the preceding verse by means of the metaphor of the chariot is here grasped by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
Now, as to how the word "unmanifest" can refer to the body, he says: "And it shows."
When the preceding series of statements is carefully considered, it shows by way of propriety that the word "unmanifest" (avyakta) indicates the assumption of a body:
"Know the self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot."
Know that the intellect is the charioteer and the mind is the reins;
the senses they call the horses, and their objects are the paths over which they range.
The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer.

Having begun with "He reaches the end of the path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," and having thus proclaimed it, the text— in response to the inquiry "What is that abode of Viṣṇu?"— shows the goal higher than the senses under discussion, starting from "Higher than the senses" and ending with "That is the limit, that is the supreme goal."
In this passage, the senses, their objects, the mind (*manas*), and the intellect (*buddhi*), which were previously introduced, are mentioned by their own specific names within this sentence.

Previously, the Self (*ātman*) was taught using the word "Self"; later, it is referred to by the word "Person" (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, the intellect, which is spoken of as "the Great One" (*mahat*) in the subsequent sentence, was already grasped by the word "intellect" itself in the preceding sentence. The intellect is of two kinds.

The intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha and the intellect of those such as ourselves [are distinguished]. According to the scriptural vision, "He who first ordains the Brahmās," the intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha, which arose at the beginning, is superior to the intellects of those such as ourselves;
therefore, it possesses greatness (*mahattva*). In the preceding [verse], the two were indicated by being unified; here, they are presented separately.

Discrimination: In the former instance the word is "body" (śarīra), and in the latter it is "the unmanifest" (avyakta). It should be understood that, by the process of elimination, these two have the same meaning. In the phrase "that supreme abode of Viṣṇu," the sense of the ablative case alone is determined. Likewise, in the Brahmamīmāṃsā:
That which is the supreme station of Viṣṇu is indeed [the supreme station] of all embodied beings;
for what else could be the supreme station except for Mahādeva accompanied by Ambā?
Because it is seen thus:
"This meaning of the Veda is known by oneself; therein they declare there is ignorance.
One should augment the meaning of the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
Thus, because the designation "knowledge of the meaning of the Veda" is made only by way of such supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) and so forth, no other [subject] is what is being propounded here.
Furthermore: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
it is seen, however, by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect."
Having thus taught in this passage the unfathomable nature of Śiva, who is superior to Nārāyaṇa, [the text] prescribes yoga for the sake of attaining Him:
"The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self consisting of knowledge;
he should restrain knowledge in the Great Self; and he should restrain that [Great Self] in the Peaceful Self."

This is what is being taught: one should restrain speech within the mind—meaning that, having abandoned the activity of the external senses such as speech and so forth, one should abide in the mind alone. One should hold that mind, which is oriented toward the conceptualization of objects, within the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is denoted by the word "knowledge" and whose nature is determination—by avoiding the defects of discursive thought (*vikalpa*). One should then [restrain] that intellect as well...

One should enter into the Great Self as the enjoyer, or into the supreme intellect, by means of attaining subtlety. And one should establish that Great Self within the peaceful Self, the Supreme Person, whose synonym is Śiva, in the ultimate state. Therefore, by examining the beginning, the conclusion, and the middle [of the text], it is established that Sāṅkhya is the primary subject matter.
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that, because there is no other possibility, Paramaśiva alone is enjoined as the object of all worship.
Now, to address the objection: "How can the gross body, which is fit to be designated by the term 'manifest' (*vyakta*), be denoted by the term 'unmanifest' (*avyakta*)," he says:
109. But that [mind] is subtle because of its fitness [for it]. || 2 ||

The word "tu" (but) serves to dispel doubt. The verb "shows" (*darśayati*) is to be supplied. He shows that the subtle cause of the elements, which constitutes the gross body, is indicated by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Why? Because it is worthy of that term; that is, because it is fit to be designated by the word "unmanifest. This is according to the usage of the term "prakṛti" (primordial matter), as in the expression "the Soma pressed by the cows."
The designation [of the Self] as a modification is appropriate.
He shows another reason for its being subordinate to Paraśiva: "110. Because it is dependent on that, it has purpose through that. (Sūtra 3)
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the Sāṃkhyas accept that the *pradhāna* is precisely the subtle state of the world, we say no.

Why? Because of its dependence on Him—that is, its dependence on the Lord. It is the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas that the independent unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the cause of the world; however, in our established conclusion (*siddhānta*), that which is designated by terms such as *māyā* and *avidyā* is presided over by the Lord.

[The term *avyakta* refers to] the *pradhāna* as the cause, because of their absolute difference. [Objection: But surely, in its prior state, the subtle world—which is the seed of names and forms not yet manifested—is fit for the designation "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and the Self (*ātman*) is of that same nature.
If it were understood that the body possesses the fitness for the term "unmanifest" (avyakta), then the Sāṅkhya doctrine alone would be taught.
If it is argued that the prior state of the entire phenomenal world—consisting of both the subtle and the sentient—is prescribed as *prakṛti*, we reply:
it is impossible to assert that the inert *pradhāna* is the cause of the world by virtue of being a power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord.

Anticipating the objection that the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) would be redundant—since the production of the world is possible from the Supreme Lord alone as the presiding cause over primordial matter (*pradhāna*)—it is stated that it is "purposeful. This means it serves a specific purpose. The unmanifest, in the form of a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), is necessary for the Lord. [As it is said: "But [the Lord projects] *māyā*..."
"One should know Prakṛti as Māyin and Maheśvara [as the controller]"—thus the dependence of Māyā upon the Supreme Lord is heard in scripture.

Furthermore, the status of being the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, as presented by Māyā, is dependent solely upon the Supreme Lord who has brought Māyā under His control. This is just as in the case of the injunction, "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," where the terms such as "Vāyavya" occurring within the scope of the injunction [refer to the deity].

The relationship of words with their meanings is established by means of injunction (*vidhi*). However, for these sentences qualified by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; one approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity"—there is no primary authority (*mukhya prāmāṇya*). This applies to statements such as "Vāyu is the swiftest deity," and so forth.

Just as there is a coherence of subordinate sentences through the praise of the nature of Vāyu, so too it is not contradictory that passages teaching that Māyā is the cause of the world are intended as praise, while simultaneously making known the Supreme Lord who presides over it. Nor does this imply that if the term *avyakta* refers to *avidyā*, then the sense organs and other effects must also be [considered] its transformations.

It should not be asked how, given that the word "those" (*tat*) refers to what is possible as material cause (*upādāna*), only the body is understood; for those [other things] are established by their own specific terms, and thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*), it is the body that is proven. There is another interpretation of the two sūtras:
the body is to be known as twofold—the gross (*sthūla*) and the subtle (*sūkṣma*). In the preceding statement, neither of these two was included under the term "body."

That which is subtle and is subsequently described by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) because it possesses that quality must necessarily be accepted. This unmanifest, which is the basis for all living beings and constitutes the state of the great deep sleep, is called "space" (*ākāśa*) by some, "illusion" (*māyā*) by others, and "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*) by still others.

In this very Imperishable (akṣara), O Gārgī, space is woven like warp and woof. Thus, in the Śruti, it is designated as "space"; in the mantra "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," it is designated as "Māyā"; and in the Śruti "That which is beyond the Imperishable," it is designated as "the Imperishable. That same [entity] is called the Unmanifest (avyakta) which is beyond the Great (mahat). Within that, the gross...

That which is perceived here is subtle—that which will be described further on in the passage: "In the transition to another body, it moves enveloped [by the elements]. Both of these bodies, being indistinguishable [in nature], were previously described as a chariot; however, here the subtle one is explained by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

Because the subtle body is worthy of being designated by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*), and because the bondage and liberation residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) depend upon it, its transcendence over the individual soul is taught. Therefore, the supremacy of Paramaśiva beyond the unmanifest is indicated.
He is the Lord of both Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*); as Paśupati, the Master of Māyā, he creates this universe, and none other than him exists within Brahman.

"He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance regarding that which is to be known—he is another; the one God rules through the two selves, the perishable and the imperishable"—thus it is heard in such passages. Therefore, it is established that this is a context concerning the Supreme Lord.
He states another reason for the position that it refers to the Supreme Lord:
111. And because [the Lord] is not stated to be an object of knowledge. || 4 ||

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas, having accepted that liberation results from the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, have stated that even *prakṛti* must be known for that purpose. However, nothing has been stated here that is useful for such knowledge, since there is merely the hearing of the word "the Unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Therefore, the Unmanifest is not the *pradhāna*, because the Wise One speaks thus—if this is argued, we say no.
This is because the present section concerns direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Now, it may be argued that the statement "because [the Unmanifest] is not mentioned as being knowable" is inconsistent, since later on, that which is denoted by the word "Unmanifest" is indeed stated to be knowable:
"That which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, and likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless..."

"Having perceived that which is without beginning or end, greater than the Great (mahat), and eternal, one is liberated from the jaws of death. Now, in this context, however, it is the Pradhāna—devoid of desire and other qualities—which is determined in the Kapila scripture to be "greater than the Great. That very [Pradhāna] is designated here as the object to be perceived. Therefore, if it is argued that the Unmanifest (avyakta) is indeed the Pradhāna, it is replied: "There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa."
Since the Supreme Lord alone is designated here as being superior to all in the Śruti, it is taught that He alone is to be perceived, and not any other.
Furthermore, he shows another reason in support of the position that the Supreme Lord is intended:
If it be argued that [the Self] speaks, we say no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context. || 5 ||

If it be argued that, because in passages such as "The one unborn female, red, white, and black," the causality of the world is heard to belong to the *pradhāna*—which consists of the three qualities (*guṇas*)—in a figurative sense, therefore the *pradhāna* alone is taught here as the object to be perceived (*nicāyya*), we say no. For it is the Wise One (*prājña*), the Supreme Lord, who is determined here as the object to be perceived. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). For [the following attributes] belong to the Wise One...
The context here is seen from both the opening and the conclusion: "The Ruler of what has been and what is to be," "The person the size of a thumb,

smokeless like a light," "The person the size of a thumb stands in the middle of the self," and "There is nothing higher than the person"— this refers to the person delimited by the heart within all beings.

In order to prevent the misconception that [the Self] is a different deity, the text designates the term "Īśāna," which is unique to Paramaśiva, and declares His absolute supremacy by stating, "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; He is the pinnacle, He is the supreme goal. Furthermore, it indicates His nature as the Self beyond the reach of sight and other senses by stating, "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth."
Since it is said, "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind," and because the meaning of this arises from the instruction on yoga for the sake of that realization—
stating that "one is liberated from the mouth of death"— and because the fruit of liberation from death is heard for those who know this,
it is established that this is a section concerning Paramaśiva.

Even in the *Kāpila* (Sāṃkhya) treatise, there is no designation of *nirvāṇa* through the knowledge of *pradhāna* alone; for that [liberation] is seen to result from the knowledge of both the insentient *prakṛti* and the sentient *puruṣa*. If it is argued that this is not a section concerning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), we say no, because here the release from the mouth of death is specifically taught as resulting precisely from the knowledge of the nature of the sentient and the insentient. Thus him...

"Having known [this], one transcends death; beholding it, one goes to the supreme Brahman"—thus, in all the Upaniṣads, it is intended that the possession of attributes such as sound and so forth belongs only to the wise Śiva. Therefore, it is established that it is impossible here to assert that the Pradhāna is the object of knowledge or is denoted by the word "Unmanifest."
He states another reason:
113. "And for these three alone there is such an introduction and a question. (6)
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "unmanifest" (avyakta), nor can it be the object of knowledge (jñeya).

This is because, in the Kaṭhavallīs, the introduction of the three— the fire, the embodied soul, and the Supreme Lord— as being "unmanifest" due to their power as the granters of boons, and the subsequent discussion of the question, are proclaimed as being directed toward them alone.

Regarding that [topic], first there is the question concerning fire: "O Death, you are indeed the foremost among those; you know the fire that leads to heaven. Explain that to me, for I am full of faith. Then there is the question concerning the individual soul (*jīva*): "There is doubt regarding this person after death—some say 'he exists,' others say 'he does not exist. May I be instructed by you in this knowledge. These occur elsewhere.

"Tell me that which you see from Dharma"—this refers to the Supreme Lord. The reply, "He told him about that Agni who is the source of the worlds," as well as "the bricks he used, how many there were, and how [he built them]," refers to Agni. [Then follows: "Behold, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman."
And how, O Gautama, does the self become after having undergone death?

"Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body; others pass into inanimate matter, according to their action and according to their knowledge. This refers to the subject of the individual soul (jīva).

In passages such as "The wise one is neither born nor dies," this [teaching] is seen to have the Supreme Self as its subject matter; for no such question and answer regarding the Pradhāna is observed here. If it is argued that the Pradhāna is not mentioned because it was not asked about, we reply: Is this question concerning the Self—"When a man has died, there is doubt as to whether he exists"—the very same as that [other] question? Or is it something else?
The word "from dharma" (dharmāt) is drawn back again; or rather, is this a new question raised that is different from the previous one?

This question concerns the Self. If it were said that it is drawn back once more, it would be because a non-difference between these two questions—one concerning the Self and the other concerning the Supreme Lord—is possible.

One might explain that only two questions concerning Vaiśvānara and the Self can be stated here, and not the presentation of three questions; thus, one might argue that this other, unprecedented question is being raised. Therefore, just as there is no fault in assuming a question beyond the act of giving, so too is there no fault in the absence of a formal question.

If it is argued that there is no fault because the introduction of the primary subject is appropriate, we reply: due to the influence of the opening of the discourse, we do not assume any question here based on the distinction of the granting of boons. For in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, from the commencement of the granting of boons until its conclusion, the discourse is seen to proceed as a dialogue between Mṛtyu and Naciketas.

It is said that Death granted three boons to Naciketas, who had been sent by his father. With the first boon, Naciketas chose his father’s goodwill; with the second, the knowledge of the sacrificial fire; and with the third, the knowledge of the Self, as expressed in the verse beginning "whatever they say regarding the deceased. Since this is the presentation of the knowledge of the Self among the boons, [the phrase] "if other than dharma" refers to this context here.

Thus, this other unprecedented question might be raised; however, in that case, the proposal of a conceptualization of the question based on a distinction in the nature of the giver of the boon would be impossible.

Now, one might argue that this is indeed an unprecedented question because of the difference between the questioner and the subject to be questioned; yet, even previously, the question concerned the individual soul (*jīva*).

"This is the third boon among boons," [it is said], because a doubt is seen there; for the embodied self (śārīra) is within the scope of dharma and so forth. Thus, the question "not other than dharma" is appropriate. Since the conscious self (prājña) is distinct from dharma, the question "other than dharma" is stated. Furthermore, the character of the questions is not the same.
It is observed that the former [passage] concerns the existence and non-existence [of difference], while the latter concerns a reality distinct from the attributes (dharma).

Therefore, since there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna), the question in the latter is not a mere continuation of the former; if this is argued, we say no, because although there is a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman during the state of bondage, their identity is taught in the state of liberation, just as in the case of the bee and the worm.

The distinction between questions should not be understood as arising from a distinction in the subjects asked about. Here too, the answer to the question "Is there anything other than dharma?"—namely, "The wise one is neither born nor does he die"—teaches the non-difference (*abheda*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva by means of the negation of birth and dissolution. Likewise:
He by whom both the end of dream and the end of waking are perceived—
the wise man, having realized that great and all-pervading Self, does not grieve.

Thus, having established the cessation of grief for the individual soul (*jīva*)—who experiences the manifold world of waking and dreaming—through the realization of its specific attributes of greatness and omnipresence, it is taught that the soul which has merged into Brahman is non-different from the Supreme Lord.
For the established doctrine of Vedānta is that the severance of grief results from the knowledge of the Wise One (*prājña*). Likewise, later on, "that which is here... [is further explained].

"Therefore, what is there is here; what is here is there. He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity"—thus the identity of the liberated individual soul (*muktajīva*) and the supreme consciousness (*prājña*) is taught. Likewise, beginning with "O Naciketas, choose another boon superior to the inquiry into the existence or non-existence of the embodied self," even though he was being tempted by Death with various desires, [he remained firm].

When Naciketas did not waver, then Death, by demonstrating the distinction between the fruits of worldly prosperity and the supreme good, and by showing the distinction between knowledge and ignorance, [spoke to him]: "I consider you, Naciketas, to be one who desires wisdom; desires do not lead you astray."

Praising their question, "Many have desired [to know this]," he spoke as follows: "The wise man, having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that God is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave, seated in the depths, and ancient, abandons both joy and sorrow."

Thus, even here they explain that there is non-difference between the embodied soul and the Supreme Self in the state of liberation. Furthermore, since there are no questions or answers concerning the *pradhāna* in this Upaniṣad, the *avyakta* is not the *pradhāna*.
He states another reason:
114. And like the Great [Self]. || 7 ||

Just as the Sāṃkhyas do not accept that the word "mahat" (the Great) in the Veda— found everywhere in such passages as "The Self greater than the intellect," "Having known the Self as the pervasive Great One," and "I know this Person, the Great"— refers to the second principle called *buddhi* (intellect), so too [is it here].
The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is not accepted as the primary principle (*pradhāna*), which is not under discussion, by means of Vedic terms for the unmanifest.

Therefore, it is established that the word "unmanifest" refers only to the body under discussion, and thus the absence of scriptural authority (*aśabdatva*) regarding the *pradhāna* is proven. Now, [one might object]: from the supplementary passage, "This is that head; for this is a ladle (*camasa*) with its mouth downward and its base upward," the head is the ladle.
How, then, is the determination made here? To this he says: 116. "Because it begins with light; for thus some [scriptural texts] record. (Sūtra 1.1.24)

Based on such scriptural passages as "That which is the red form of fire," and because the section begins with light (*jyotis*), the intermediate material cause consisting of fire, water, and food is denoted by the word *ajā* (the unborn). Certain followers of particular recensions (*śākhins*) likewise record that redness, whiteness, and blackness belong to fire, water, and food respectively; for the word *ajā* denotes a thing that is devoid of birth.

It is logical that [the word *aja*] denotes Paramaśiva. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. Now, one might object: "In the opening of the *Jyotiḥ* passage, *prakṛti*—consisting of the fourfold multitude of beings such as those born from sweat—is intended here by the word *ajā*, and it should be understood as the cause of the world, consisting of the three *guṇas*. To this we say: no.

The Sāṃkhya doctrine that the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is the cause of the world [is rejected]. According to the principle of the uniformity of all Vedānta texts (*sarvavedāntapratyayanyāya*) and because of the recognition of the red and other colors well-known in other recensions—namely, "That which is the red color of fire is the color of heat; that which is white is the color of water; that which is black is the color of food"—it is precisely heat (*tejas*), water (*ap*), and food (*anna*) that are intended here.

Because the words *lohita* and so forth are common [to both meanings], and because those words are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to specific colors and are thus used figuratively (*bhākta*) to denote the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and because there is no doubt due to the absence of ambiguity, the primary mantra is not investigated here according to the logic of the conclusion (*nigamana*).
In this very context, the exponents of Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) begin by asking, "What is the cause, Brahman? and then state:

"Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the divine Self, hidden by its own qualities. From the opening of this passage, it is understood that Māyā, the power of Paramaśiva, is the generator of the universe. Furthermore, in the remainder of the passage, [it says] "But Māyā..."

From the scriptural understandings of "one should know Prakṛti" and "the one who presides over each womb," it follows that she never possesses independence. This *ajā* (the Unborn) is called *prakṛti* because she has Paramaśiva as her cause;
she is indeed the power (*śakti*) of Maheśvara, whose name and form (*nāmarūpa*) are unmanifest, existing in the state prior to name and form.

It is declared in the mantra; regarding its modification, it is stated that it possesses a threefold nature in a threefold form. But how can it be said that the source of fire, water, and food is the unborn (aja) in a threefold form consisting of the three colors?
Nevertheless, even in the Taittirīyaka, her independence is declared, provided she is graced by the Supreme Lord.

Having established the Supreme Lord as the cause of the universe by beginning with "Smaller than the small, greater than the great," and continuing with "From Him the seven vital breaths arise," etc., [the text] points to the "one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*) at the time of teaching His identity with that which is produced from Him. Therefore, through a consideration of what precedes and follows:
It is ordained that the causality of the causal nature consisting of fire, water, and food arises through the grace of the Supreme Lord;
therefore, the Sāṅkhya doctrine that it is established independently is not tenable.
Now, since the origin of fire, water, and food is heard [in scripture], and because a conventional etymological derivation (*yoga-ruḍhi*) is impossible, how can they be denoted by the word *ajā*?
To address this point of apprehension, he says:
"117. And because of the instruction through metaphorical designation, there is no contradiction, as in the case of honey and so forth. (2.3.10)
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel an objection. There is no inconsistency regarding the term "unborn" (*ajā*); why? Because it is taught as a metaphorical designation (*kalpanopadeśāt*).

The nature of being "unborn" is attributed to that which consists of fire, water, and earth. Just as in the world, one man abandons an already-enjoyed she-goat while another pursues her, so too [is there] in the case of abandonment and enjoyment.

This is for the purpose of establishing the equilibrium of *prakṛti*, which consists of fire, water, and earth, and serves as the material cause for the aggregate of effects and causes. Just as in the case of honey and so forth— where, for example, in passages such as "The sun is indeed honey to the gods" and "One should meditate on speech as a cow"—

there is a figurative attribution (*kalpanā*) of honey and other things to the sun and so forth, likewise there is no contradiction in the figurative attribution of the nature of a non-born female goat (*ajā*).
If it be argued that here the causality of *prakṛti* for the phenomenal world is taught independently, we say no; for [the scripture] says:
"The Vedas, sacrifices, seasons, and vows—the past and the future—these the gods proclaim.
From Him the Illusionist (*māyin*) creates this entire universe, and within Him another is held fast by illusion."

Thus, because at the commencement of creation, it is taught that the Supreme Lord alone, as qualified by Māyā, is the cause; furthermore, it is logical that it is the insentient Prakṛti alone—distinct from the Supreme Lord—that dissolves into Paramaśiva in the state of liberation, and not the conscious power (cicchakti). And so says the Smṛti:
The entire universe is his power, while Maheśvara is the possessor of power;
for power is of the same nature as the possessor of power and is never distinct from it.
The identity of these two is eternal, like that of fire and its power to burn;
for there is always an absence of distinction between a power and that which possesses the power.

Thus [it is said]. Here, because it is non-separately established from the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), there is no contradiction in the fact that the causality residing in the Supreme Lord belongs to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) denoted by the word "Unborn" (*ajā*).
Now, an objection is raised: in passages such as "The one Unborn, indeed, lying along, enjoys," the independent single individual soul (*jīva*) is shown to have entered into *māyā*.

If it is argued that because there are designations of a single individual soul (*jīva*) possessing independence and being the liberator from *māyā*, the Supreme Lord cannot be the cause of bondage and liberation, we say no. For it is stated: "The one God rules over the perishable and the immortal souls; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and by becoming His true essence, there occurs at last the cessation of the universal *māyā*."

Thus, it is established that there is no other way, because by means of this— through the wearing of the three marks such as the *iṣṭa* and so forth— the liberation of living beings from *māyā* has been firmly established.
This concludes the section on the inclusion of the number (the *Saṃkhyopasaṃgraha-adhikaraṇa*).
With respect to the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), it is indeed more appropriate to accept thirty-six principles.
Thus, having refuted the independent causality of the *pradhāna* for the world, [the Sūtra] refutes the twenty-five principles:
1.1.8: "Not even because of the inclusion of a number, on account of the diversity [of things], and because of the excess."

The subject of this is recited in the sixth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "That indeed is the light of lights, the life of life, which they worship here as immortality.
