Immediately following that, [it says]: "In whom the five classes of beings and the ether are established—him alone I consider to be the Self; knowing him as the immortal Brahman, I become immortal. This refers to the vital breath (prāṇa).

"Those who know the breath of the breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of the mind—they have perceived through that the ancient, supreme Brahman. In this mantra, I consider that immortal Self—the support upon which the five classes of beings and the ether are dependent—to be the foundation. Thus, one who knows Brahman shall become immortal.
"I shall become immortal. In this context, the "five five-people" (pañca pañcajanāḥ) are those established by the Sāṅkhya school:
"Root-nature is unevolved; the seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are both nature and evolutes;
the group of sixteen is only evolute; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolute."

Thus, the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) have been summarized. Alternatively, there may be the doubt: "Are the five categories, beginning with *prāṇa*, established by the Veda? In this doubt, the conclusion reached is that they are indeed principles (*tattva*). By the expression "five-fives," the number twenty-five is stated; for the word *jana* is used here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the principles.
Since the *pradhāna* is not even mentioned as a primary entity among the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, it follows that it is not "non-scriptural" (i.e., not supported by scripture).

To this we reply: Even the claim that the *pradhāna* possesses scriptural authority based on the mention of the number twenty-five in the cited Śruti passage is impossible. Why? Because of their diversity; that is, because of the various intermediate numbers [within that total].

Because it is impossible to establish five groups of five due to the absence of a common defining property (*anugamaka-dharma*), he states another objection to the acceptance of the number twenty-five even if some degree of similarity exists: "And because of excess" (*atirekāt ca*). This is because space, the Puruṣa, time, and so forth are in excess of the five classes of beings (*pañcajana*).
It is taught that because the number thirty-six is established, there is no comprehension of the number twenty-five.

For instance, since it is certain that the word *pañcajana* occurs as a single compound with its qualifier, the word *pañca* (five), which is a part of that compound, cannot be construed with another word *pañca*; therefore, there is no perception of the number twenty-five.
If it be asked, "Since the principles (tattvas) beginning with Time (kāla) are not seen here, how can the enumeration of thirty-six principles be established?

[the answer is: In the Vṛddhajābālopaniṣad, after first defining the three categories of the bound soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), and the Lord (pati), and then establishing the Supreme Brahman Śiva as the agent of the five cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya), he spoke again:

"What are the thirty-six principles (tattvas)? He said to him: "Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, the three qualities (guṇas), and the twenty principles beginning with Earth, which are the substrata of name, form, and activity, and are mutually distinct. When the Supreme Lord enters into Śakti, who is distinct from [His] aspect as the Seer, as described in the Vṛddhajābālopaniṣad, then..."

The [states] called Prājña, Taijasa, and Miśra arrive; this is because they are designated as the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) in their uncontracted state. Since this is seen very clearly in the *Śvetāśvatara*, *Nārāyaṇa*, and other Upaniṣads, it has been elaborated upon in many ways in the first section of the second chapter in accordance with the Śruti and Āgama. Therefore:
In this context, it is appropriate to accept only the thirty-six principles.
Thus, once the perception of any other number has been refuted, he states what is intended by the term *pañcajana*:
"119. Or rather, the vital breaths and so forth, because of the specific statement of the text. (Sūtra 1.4.12)

The five—vital breath (*prāṇa*), eye, ear, food, and mind—are denoted by the word "five people" (*pañcājana*). Why? Because of the remainder of the passage; for in the subsequent mantra it says: "The breath of breath, and the eye of the eye... and so forth.
Those who know the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of the mind.

Thus, the five beginning with *prāṇa* are called "the five people" (*pañcajana*) because of their sequential order. If that is so, how can the word *jana* be applied to *prāṇa* and the others? And how is the application of the word *jana* possible for the *tattvas* and so forth in the Sāṃkhya system? [The answer is: It is established in both cases alike; however, due to the specific context of proximity in the sentence, [the meaning is determined].

Only the five vital breaths (prāṇas) are taught here. Although the word *pañcajana* is well known as denoting human beings (*puruṣa*), its application by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to the vital breaths and so forth—which are related to them—is not contradictory in this context.
Furthermore, the word *puruṣa*, which is a synonym for the word *mānuṣa* (human), is understood to refer to the vital breaths. These, indeed, are the five...

Regarding the term *brahmapuruṣāḥ*, there is the Brāhmaṇa passage: "For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the father, the vital breath is the mother," and so forth. Furthermore, due to the force of the compound, the conventional meaning (*rūḍhatva*) of the whole is not contradictory. If it is asked, "How can a conventional meaning be assumed when there has been no prior usage? it is replied:

For when a word with a secondary meaning enters into proximity with a word whose primary meaning is present, its referent is understood through that association. Just as in such cases as "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "he cuts the sacrificial post," or "he prepares the altar," so too here,
the status of the word *pañcajana* as a proper name is understood from its occurrence within a compound and from its subsequent explanation.
In the case of those [terms] mentioned in proximity with the remainder of the sentence, such as "prāṇa" and so forth, which require a designation, [the term *pañcajana*] will apply to them.
By some, gods, ancestors, gandharvas, asuras, and rakṣases have been explained as the "five *pañcajanas*";
by others, the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth have been accepted; and in another place, it says "by the *pāñcajanya* [army]."

The word "viśaḥ" (the people) is heard as an alternative application for the term "pañcajanaḥ. Even if that [meaning] were included here, there would be no contradiction; however, the author of the Sūtras does not accept the number twenty-five here, because the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth are shown in the supplementary passage to be distinct from that [number], even though among the Mādhyandinas food is recited among the vital breaths and so forth.

Since food is not mentioned among the breaths and so forth in the text of the Kāṇvas, how can it be maintained that the "five people" (pañcajana) consist of the breaths and so forth? To this he says: "Because for some, when food is absent, light [takes its place]. (Sūtra 1.4.13)

For some of the Kaṇvas, even in the absence of food, the number five is completed by means of light (*jyotis*). Since "that indeed is the light of lights" was mentioned as the subject in the preceding sentence, how could this light—being recited with equal status for both [groups]—be understood by some as being preceded by the number five found in the corresponding mantra? It could not.

Regarding the phrase "of some": he says it is due to a difference in desire. For the Mādhyandinas, because they accept the five classes of beings (*pañcajana*)—such as *prāṇa* and the rest—as recited in the same mantra, there is no need for the light (*jyotis*) mentioned in another mantra.

For the Kāṇvas, however, because that [light] is absent, there arises a desire [to include it]. And due to this difference in desire, even though the mantra is the same, [the inclusion of] the light...

[The opponent argues: "There is acceptance and non-acceptance [of the texts]. Thus, there is no established scriptural authority [for the Pradhāna]. Therefore, it is already established that the Pradhāna is not based on scripture (aśabda);

because of the specific instruction, nothing else can be the cause. [The reply is: In the Taittirīyaka, the creation begins with ether (ākāśa), whereas in the Chāndogya, it begins with fire (tejas). Thus, a variation regarding the effects is known. By means of this variation regarding the effects, Brahman—which is the cause of the universe—is also [indicated].
It is understood that it can be stated that what is consistently apprehended in all the Upaniṣads is intended as the Real (Sat).
To resolve the contradiction regarding the cause, the author of the Sūtras has here provided this solution:
even though there is a diversity of views concerning the effect, the creation of ether and so forth is not intended [as the primary subject]. It is not [the case that the cause is intended].
For it is here that the detailed account of the creation of ether and so forth is intended to be established. Therefore, there is no contradiction with that [other scriptural passage].

Indeed, no human goal (puruṣārtha) is seen or heard of that is tied to creation; nor can such a thing even be imagined. This is because, upon examining the beginning, middle, and end, the text is seen to have the Supreme Lord as its ultimate purport. By means of food...
"O gentle one, seek the root of water through its sprout; O gentle one, seek the root of fire through its sprout;

O gentle one, seek the root of Being through its sprout"—from this, it is understood that the world, characterized by birth and so forth, is presented for the purpose of declaring the non-difference between cause and effect by means of illustrations such as clay and the like.

Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction between the Supreme Lord being the cause of the world and such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," he offers a rebuttal: 122. On account of the drawing together [of the contexts]. (Sūtra 1.4.15)

In the passage "Non-being indeed was this in the beginning," because there is an attraction (*ākṣepa*) to the "Being" previously under discussion, this [text] does not have non-existence as its cause.

For instance, having refuted the doctrine of non-existence with "He becomes non-existent indeed," and having determined the nature of Being with "If one knows that Brahman exists," and having taught the creation from that [Being] with "It desired," [the text] concludes by declaring "That is Truth."

Thus [the section] has been concluded. "On this point, there is also this verse" — thus a verse concerning *prakṛti* (primordial matter) has been cited. In that context, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) cannot be accepted by means of the word "non-existent" (*asat*), because that would entail abandoning the subject under discussion and assuming something not under discussion. Even though the word "non-existent" exists [in the text],...

Because even that which previously existed can have figurative usage in the absence of the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), this is to be inferred everywhere from the manner in which things are designated. This applies even to such passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name-and-form," and "He, the Overseer, entered here unto the very tips of the fingernails."

Because [the Self] is drawn forth by virtue of having entered into phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*). However, if one were to perceive the grammatical derivation of that which is without a presiding overseer (*niradhyakṣa*), then subsequently, by what [term] could that which is connected to phenomenal expansion be grasped by the pronoun "He" (*saḥ*) which follows in the context? It is heard in scripture that the Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), enters [into the world]. [This refers to] Him who has entered into the body.
Because it is designated as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), as in: "Seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind.
Furthermore, this world which is being perceived is known to have an agent; thus it is understood that it was so even at the time of the first creation, according to the maxim:
"For there is nothing indeed that is impossible when [the cause] is observed. "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*)."

In passages such as, "Having projected name-and-form, having emitted that, He entered into that very thing," sovereignty (*adhipatitva*) is likewise taught. Regarding the expression "was projected" (*vyākriyata*), the verbal suffix denotes the reflexive-passive construction (*karmakartari*); this should be understood with reference to the excellence of the manifestation within the established Supreme Self, even though—as in the expression "the field is being harvested by itself"—[the agent is already present].

There is no contradiction in [the Lord] being the distinct agent; or rather, this *lakāra* (verbal suffix) should be understood as denoting the object (*karman*), as in expressions such as "the village is gone to" (*gamyate grāmaḥ*). Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the Supreme Lord being the cause of all things, nor is there any contradiction regarding the causal Paraśiva-Brahman due to any conflict with the process of creation.
The Section Concerning Bālāki || 5 ||
Now follows the refutation of the doctrine of Śuddhādvaita (Pure Monism).

Having thus rejected the Sāṅkhya view which maintains that *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the cause of the universe, [the author proceeds] with the refutation of that which establishes *pradhāna* as the cause of the universe through its proximity to the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) Brahman. Always...
He refutes the doctrine of pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita), which emphasizes the identity of the individual soul and Brahman:
123. *jagadvācitvāt* || 16 || [Because it denotes the world.]

In the *Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa*, within the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, it is seen [stated] after beginning with "I shall tell you about Brahman": "O Bālāki, he who is indeed the maker of these persons, and whose work this is—he indeed is to be known.

Here, there arises a doubt as to whether that which is to be known is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). In this context, it is the vital breath alone that is being designated.
Why? Because of the observation that "his indeed is that action," since action, which is of the nature of motion, has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its substratum;

and because in the supplementary passage, "Then he becomes onefold in this very *prāṇa*," the word *prāṇa* is heard; for the term *prāṇa* is conventionally established in the primary sense for the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*). And those [deities] which were previously mentioned by Bālāki with respect to the sun—

The individual souls (*jīva*) have been described in such passages as "the person in the moon" and "the person [in the eye]"; for them also, *prāṇa* is the presiding controller, because they are specific states of *prāṇa*. This is established by another Vedic text which asks, "Which one is the single deity? and answers, "It is *prāṇa*; they call him Brahman, he is Āditya. Alternatively, the embodied soul (*śārīra*) is determined [as the subject], since it is said, "He whose work this is."

Because the instruction regarding actions characterized by merit and demerit is possible, and because the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) as the enjoyer—which was previously introduced in passages such as "the Sun is the Person"—is established, the designation of these persons as "the agent" is appropriate; furthermore, a characteristic mark of the individual soul is seen here. For example: "As a master enjoys his own [wealth], so do these..."
"Just as [people] eat the merchant, even so this conscious self (prajñātman) eats by means of those selves;

even so these selves eat this self. Having thus addressed Bālāki—who was intent on knowing the Person—by calling out to a sleeping man, and having shown that he did not wake up from it but woke up when struck with the hand, Ajātaśatru spoke.

If it is argued that because a living being distinct from the vital breaths and so forth is established here, and because such [a distinction] is impossible in the case of the Supreme Lord— who has cast off all bonds of karma— and furthermore, because no marks indicative of the Supreme Lord are seen here, one must conclude that either the vital breath or the living being alone is intended here, we reply as follows.

In this context, the Supreme Lord alone is to be understood as the presiding controller of the individual soul (*jīva*). Having commenced with the instruction "I shall tell you of Brahman," when Bālāki presented various persons residing in the sun and other objects, Ajātaśatru rejected those [identifications] with the words "Verily, you have been speaking falsely to me," and so forth; then, he himself [proceeded to describe] these persons...

He who said, "He is the agent of this action," therein [establishes] that this refers primarily to Brahman; for the agency of the Puruṣa and His independence are logically possible only for the Lord (Īśvara). Furthermore, in such passages as "The Lord of all sciences" and "Paśupati is the Lord of these creatures," the status of being the controller of all belongs to Śiva alone, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Because of the establishment [of this meaning], there is no inconsistency in using the word "karma" (action) there; for the word "karma" signifies the world, as it is derived from the sense that "it is being made" (*kriyate*), and thus refers to the world.

Since the agency of the Person (*puruṣa*) is already established by the very statement that he has created the world, [the text] intends to make known that the persons taught by Bālāki as objects to be known are not Brahman.
The separate mention of the persons is according to the logic of the "Brahmin-wanderer" (brāhmaṇaparivrājaka) maxim.
If it is objected that because the individual soul (jīva), abiding in its state of rest, is conscious, its independent agency as the creator of all is being taught—this is not so;
for, by the logic of "the cow and the bull" (gobalīvarda), it is intended to show that the persons described by Gārgya as being Brahman are distinct from Brahman.
"Not the other, because of the separate designation.
Having raised this doubt again, he refutes it:
"If it be argued that it is not so because of the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained. (Sūtra 1.1.17)
If it be argued that this passage— beginning with "Just as these [servants] wait upon the merchant" and concluding with "then he becomes one with this very breath"—

is not intended solely for the meditation on the all-pervading Brahman, because the concluding portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) manifests the characteristics of the limited individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital air (*prāṇa*), that has already been refuted in the previous section, the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*.

In the *Pratardana-vidyā*, the meditation on the three marks, such as being the desired (*iṣṭa*), has been explained. Likewise, here too, this should be understood through the introductory statement, the concluding summary, and the intermediate reference. This is because in the introduction, "I shall tell you of Brahman," there is seen an opening with the Supreme Brahman; and in the middle, in the phrase "of whom that is the work," there is the mention of the agency over the entire universe.

Because of the specific instruction regarding that very [Self], and because in the concluding passage—"Having removed all evils, he who knows thus attains the pre-eminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings"—there is the hearing of a fruit that is unsurpassed; therefore, it is not reasonable to assume that the text has any other purpose. Furthermore, in the passage "For the mind, my dear, is bound to Prāṇa," the word *prāṇa* [refers to the Supreme Self].

The state of being Brahman is taught here. Therefore, in this context, the meditation on the three genders should be understood as non-different from Him. Nor is the matter already settled by the discussion concerning Pratardana;
for there, the word "karma" was not established as denoting the universe, and thus there remains the doubt that it might have another referent.
Furthermore, because it is possible [that the Upanishads teach Brahman], he states another reason:
"But Jaimini [holds that they] have another purpose, on account of both the question and the answer; and so also some [others]. (1.1.18)

The teacher Jaimini considers the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in this section to be for another purpose—that is, for the sake of understanding Brahman. Why? Because of the question and the answer. First, regarding the question: through the awakening of one who has fallen asleep, it is heard that the subject of the inquiry is distinct from the embodied soul (*śārīra*), which is differentiated from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, the object of the subsequent inquiry is shown to be distinct from the embodied soul.

"O Bālāki, where was this person sleeping? Where indeed did he become thus? Whence has he come back?"—this is the question and the answer as well. "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this very breath (*prāṇa*). O gentle one, he becomes merged with Being (*sat*); from this Self, all the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) [arise]."

It is heard in scripture that "they settle according to their respective abodes," indicating that during deep sleep the individual soul (*jīva*) attains Śiva; and it is also heard that the world, beginning with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), is born from Brahman, thus establishing His status as the cause of the universe. Therefore, through the knowledge of the Supreme Lord, the identity of the individual soul with Him is taught. Moreover, some, such as the Vājasaneyins, state this in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru.
They declare the living being (*jīva*) to consist of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) to be distinct from it.

Furthermore, in response to the question, "Where was this person consisting of consciousness then? Whence did he come? the answer, "He lies in that space (*ākāśa*) which is within the heart," shows that the word *ākāśa* is well-known to denote Brahman.
And because there is uniformity regarding all Vedānta texts, the same conclusion holds here as well. Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is that which is to be known.
This concludes the section on the "Connection of the Sentences" (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa). 6.
Regarding the stabilization of one's own established doctrine after first refuting the views of others:

having raised the objection as to how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, given that they are taught in the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa* as being each exclusively denoted by their own respective words, he says:
126. Because of the connection with the sentence. || 19 ||

The subject matter of this [text] is seen in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with: "He said: 'Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self (ātman) the husband is dear,' and so on, up to: 'Verily, it is not for the sake of all that all is dear, but for the sake of the Self all is dear; the Self, indeed."
"Verily, Maitreyī, this Self (ātman) is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon;

verily, by seeing, hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing this Self, all this is known. Here, a doubt arises as to whether this [Self] indicated by being "to be seen" and so forth is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). It is the individual soul, the cognizing self (vijñānātman), that is treated here.

Why? Because of the force of the introductory statement (*upakrama*), wherein the manifold world consisting of husband, wife, children, cattle, wealth, and so forth, is designated as dear because it exists for the sake of the Self.

Furthermore, in that very same passage, starting with "Not indeed for the sake of the husband," etc., there is an introduction regarding the enjoying individual soul (*bhoktṛ-jīva*), and in the middle [of the text] as well, this...
"Great, infinite, and boundless, this very aggregate of consciousness, arising from these elements, perishes after them;

there is no consciousness after death"—since this teaches that [the self] arises from its own constituent elements within the body, it indicates that this very [self] is what is to be seen. Likewise, [it says]: "By what, my dear, would one know the knower?"

Since the section concludes with a statement identifying the agent [of action], it is the embodied self (śārīra) alone who is taught. Therefore, because we observe Maitreyī’s question at the beginning—"Is there immortality through ritual action accomplished by wealth?"—it follows that this section does not teach anything other than that [embodied self].
This being the position reached—
It is stated: the Puruṣa who is taught here as the object to be seen is indeed the Supreme Lord. Why?

Because of the syntactical connection (*vākyānvaya*). For the sentence, through its opening, conclusion, middle portion, and internal reference, is consistently harmonized (*samanvaya*) with Śiva alone, the Supreme Brahman.

Having heard from Yājñavalkya that "there is no hope for immortality through wealth," meaning there is no hope for liberation through ritual action accomplished by means of wealth, Maitreyī asks about the means to liberation:
"What should I do with that by which I might not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows."

Immediately following the questions, the knowledge of the Self (*ātman*) is taught through the passage beginning with "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," and so forth. For no one accepts that liberation results from the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord who is "to be seen," as indicated by the phrase "by the seeing of the Self, my dear. Thus, from the hearing of the word "Self" and from the resulting knowledge, the previously promised "knowledge of all things" is established. This is evident from the introduction.

This is because we see Maitreyī’s question, "Is there immortality through action that is accomplished by wealth? and because we see the concluding statement, "Indeed, this much alone is immortality. Therefore, even the difficult passage at the end—"When, indeed, the Self is seen, heard, reflected upon, and realized, all this is known; herein one should know [the Self] according to its true nature"—is established.

It leads one to the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the instruction regarding the Self alone, which is the means to immortality, concerns the Supreme Self (paramātman) exclusively and not the individual soul (jīva).
Now follows the exposition of the doctrine of the distinction between the two [the individual and the Supreme] as conjoined.

Furthermore, since there is an introductory reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the passage beginning with "O, [he is] not [the master]," how can the statement teaching that through the knowledge of one thing all is known be understood as having Brahman as its subject?

Moreover, because the text "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower" establishes that the embodied soul (*śārīra*) is unproduced, its being produced from Brahman is impossible. Therefore, by the knowledge of Brahman—
Anticipating the objection that the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*) is untenable, [the Sūtrakāra] says:
127. "On account of the establishment of the initial proposition, Āśmarathya [holds it to be] a sign. (20)
Furthermore, since the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known"—expressed as "When the Self is known, all this becomes known;
all this is what this Self is"—is established, the indicative mark (liṅga) [of the wheel] is shown;
and because the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are absolutely distinct, the statement regarding the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is not contradicted.

Since, in passages such as "from which indeed these beings are born," it is understood that these individual souls (*jīvas*) are likewise produced from Brahman— just like the five elements— and since one must admit a mutual difference between cause and effect, their identity is not possible. Therefore, the statement of the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one is justified, just as in the case of curd and milk.

Therefore, Āśmarathya considers that the introduction of the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of apprehending the aspect of difference between the two; for, by means of such statements as "of whom the Self is the body," the fulfillment of the promise of knowing everything becomes possible. This is because in worldly experience—such as the perceptions "I am thin" or "I am fair"—there exists a mutual distinction even while they appear as one.

The proponent of difference (*bhedavādī*) maintains that the introduction of the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between the connected and the unconnected— like the relationship between a limb and its possessor— based on the observation of the singularity of the *darbha* grass.
Now follows the exposition of the Advaita position.

Having thus taught the view of those who maintain an unconnected difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—like that of a jar and a cloth—as well as the view of those who maintain a connected difference—like that of a limb and its possessor—the [author] states the doctrine of pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*):
128. "Because it will depart with such a nature," says Auḍulomi. (Sūtra 21)

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that for the individual soul (*jīva*) who is about to depart—that is, one who is casting off the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of its own ignorance—there is no departure from Brahman because it is eternally non-different from Brahman, just as the space within a jar is non-different from the great space (*mahākāśa*); therefore, through the knowledge of Brahman, there is the knowledge of everything. Alternatively:
Just as when the illusion of a snake superimposed on a rope ceases, only the rope remains, so too,
after the cessation of the illusion of the individual soul (jīva) superimposed upon one’s own Self, the Self alone remains; this is what Auḍulomi maintains,
based on hundreds of scriptural passages such as "That thou art."

Because of the instruction on the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman— illustrated by the relationship between an object and its reflection, or like the space within a jar and the great space (*mahākāśa*)—
and because the state of being a *jīva* is merely superimposed (*āropita*), and because no superimposition is observed apart from its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
in reality Brahman alone is established as free from delusion; thus, one should perceive it through the cognition of non-difference.
Some followers of Advaita maintain that the soul undergoes transmigration (*jīvopakramaṇa*).
This is the doctrine of Viśiṣṭādvaita, which accords with the established conclusions of Vedānta intended by all the Śrutis.
Thus, having demonstrated the validity of these two views based on specific portions of the Śruti:
He demonstrates the view of the primary Vedānta siddhānta intended by all the scriptures:
129. "On account of abiding, so [says] Kāśakṛtsna. (2.3.22)

This alone is the intention of the author of the Sūtras. Since the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) remains established through the non-contradiction between the Śrutis on difference, such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), and the Śrutis on non-difference, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the introduction here of the individual soul (*jīva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the difference-and-non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman; thus says the one who knows the purport of all the Śrutis.

The preeminent proponent, Kāśakṛtsna, maintains this view. Therefore, it should be understood that the third position, established by all the Śrutis, is the ultimate truth. "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the supreme light, manifests in its own true form; as a river [merges], so the sage goes after meditating."

Know that the source of all beings is reached through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation; thus the knower of Brahman attains it—this is the section concerning the cup (Camasādhikaraṇa). II.3.2.

Now, one might object: "Since the Pradhāna is taught here as the cause of the world, and since it is characterized by a threefold nature that persists throughout the entire context under discussion, its introduction here is also appropriate. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it: "115. It is not so, because there is no distinction, as in the case of the *camasa* [cup]. (Sūtra 2.3.7)
Furthermore, the proponent of the Sāṅkhya doctrine (Kāpilavādī) states that it is not possible for primordial matter (*prakṛti*) to be inexpressible by words. Why? Because of the wording of a mantra.

Regarding the passage, "The one unborn female, red, white, and black," a doubt arises as to whether the word "unborn" (*ajā*) teaches the *pradhāna*, or the intermediate *prakṛti* consisting of fire, water, and earth established in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, or perhaps the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). Here...

"Unborn" (*ajā*) means that which is not born; this refers precisely to *prakṛti* as established in the Sāṃkhya system, which, by virtue of consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is "red, white, and black. It is *prakṛti* itself in its state of equilibrium among these qualities that is taught here.
If it is asked, "Since the word 'unborn' primarily denotes a she-goat, why should it not refer to that?"—the answer is no, because of the context of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Because it is impossible for that [individual soul] to possess the qualities of producing abundant offspring—as in the passage beginning "producing many offspring"—and of having a course consisting of red, white, and black; and because, in the verse "One unborn being, taking pleasure, lies by her;
another unborn being leaves her after she has been enjoyed," this refers to the bound individual soul (*baddha-jīva*).
Since it is observed that the experience of pleasure and pain is distinguished by the enjoyment of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*),

and since liberation consists in the cessation of the bonds of *māyā* through the discernment (*viveka*) of one who has completed his enjoyment— thereby demonstrating a designation distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*)— it follows that the "Unborn" (*ajā*) here must be the Pradhāna itself. Therefore, the Pradhāna is not "non-scriptural" (*aśabda*).

Therefore, since the status of *pradhāna* as the cause of the world is established by scripture (*śruti*), and thus the Sāṅkhya system (*kāpila*) is Vedic—this being the position reached—we reply: there is no understanding [of the term] based on its dependence upon *pradhāna*. Why? Because of non-distinction. The word *ajā* (unborn), meaning "that which is not born," can be applied elsewhere as well; for qualities such as redness and so forth are inherent in other things as well, by whatever means.

Furthermore, because it is possible to include all things—such as the unborn (*aja*) and so forth—within [the category of] "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*), and because there is no reason for a specific determination [of the subject], it is the doctrine of the followers of Kapila (*kāpila-vāda*) alone that is taught here. This is like the case of the *camasa* vessel; for just as in the mantra, "The *camasa* has its opening below and its base above," it is not possible to know specifically which *camasa* is being referred to.

Since qualities such as having a downward opening can occur in other things as well in some way or another, there is likewise no determination of the *pradhāna* even in the case of the "Unborn" mantra. Therefore, the *pradhāna* is not based on scripture (*aśabda*).
This concludes the section concerning its being the cause. 4.
Now, regarding the determination that Paramaśiva is the cause of the five great elements:

having raised the objection that the causality of Brahman with respect to the five great elements is untenable— since the scriptural passage "From the Self, space [arose]" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ*) establishes that only space is produced from Brahman— the author says:
121. And because it is stated that [the Lord] is designated as such in the case of space and so forth by virtue of being their cause. || 14 ||

This [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of providing a complete resolution to the reconciliation of Paraśiva-Brahman established by the first three quarters [of the sūtras]. Now, it may be objected that the aforementioned reconciliation is not possible, because the very authority of the Vedāntas is difficult to maintain due to mutual contradictions. To illustrate: regarding the Self...

"In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], it is said: 'Ether was produced. In the Chāndogya, it is said: 'He created that fire. In the Muṇḍaka, it is said: 'He created these worlds,' and 'From this [Being] is born breath, water, light, death, and the waters. Thus, there is mutual contradiction. Even regarding the nature of the cause, in the Chāndogya it is said: 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone'; while in the Aitareya, it is said: 'In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone.'"

Therefore, since it has been argued that "concordance is not tenable," we reply: the author of the Sūtras will resolve the discordance regarding the sequence of creation and so forth—which pertains to the effects—in the passage beginning with "There is no discordance regarding the ether because there is no scriptural statement [to the contrary]," by means of the order of succession. Here, however, it is stated simply that there is no discordance regarding the cause. And...

The word "but" (tu) expresses the removal of doubt regarding the same meaning. There is no contradiction in the fact that space and the rest are effects of the Supreme Lord; why? Because He is described exactly as He is taught. Just as the Lord is described as the cause in one Vedānta text—being omniscient and the Lord of all—in that very same manner He is described in relation to space and the rest.

It is taught that there is no contradiction because it is stated even in another branch [of the Veda]. In the passage "May I be many," the conscious Supreme Self is declared to be the cause of all modifications. Furthermore, by the words "He created all this, whatever exists here," the text teaches that prior to creation, the Creator is the cause of the entire universe. And as for the passage "When there was darkness"—it refers to Śiva alone.
The term "kevalaḥ" (the absolute) refers to the reality denoted by the word Śiva, which is called Brahman as the cause that exists prior to the universe.
That Brahman, whose characteristics are known as the cause, is heard of with those same characteristics in other Upaniṣads as well—
in such passages as "one only, without a second" and "the Self alone was this in the beginning"— where the Supreme Lord is established as the cause of all.

In such passages as "He who knows the Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and their non-distinction in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*) are established.
Now, an objection may be raised: since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory by nature—like darkness and light—one of these two positions must be rejected.
If it is argued that [the doctrine] must be determined as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), we say no; for there is no evidence for the authority of only one portion of the Śruti.
Furthermore, if one side were accepted, it would entail the consequence of the other portions of the Śruti being non-authoritative.
Moreover, the contradiction—like that between sleep and waking, darkness and light, fire and water—is not to be perceived as insurmountable.
The acceptance of the mutual contradiction between difference and non-difference must be due to one of the following: the contradiction in reality, the absence of a cause,
its irrationality, its non-existence, the lack of evidence, the lack of fruit, the lack of understanding, the lack of distinction,
or the absence of a single scriptural authority.

The first [alternative] is not tenable: because in such passages as "That which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe," there is the relationship of substratum and superstratum between the world-complex (prapañca), consisting of duality and non-duality, and Brahman;

in such passages as "Everything shines only after Him who shines," there is the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator; and in such passages as "The witness of all, beyond darkness," there is the relationship of the witnessed and the witness.
In such passages as "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," is the causality of the world and its subsequent entry [into it] observed?
Or rather, is there the experience of knowledge and ignorance in the individual soul (*jīva*), the nature of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) in primordial matter (*prakṛti*),

the state of the three worlds and the three stages of existence in the evolved effect (*vikṛti*), or the eternality and non-eternality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) according to the followers of Kaṇāda?

This is because we observe that the earth and wind possess neither heat nor cold; that Maheśvara is the Lord of Half-Woman (Ardhanārīśvara); that in figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) there is the nature of both abandoning and not abandoning [the primary meaning]; that in the Sāṃkhya and Advaita systems the Witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) consists of both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*); and that a human being is characterized by both merit and demerit, while a firefly possesses both light and darkness.

Not the second [alternative]: for even prior to creation, in passages such as "When darkness... and so forth, the Supreme Lord, who is self-luminous, is characterized by the material cause (prakṛti) of darkness; and in passages such as "From which indeed these...", non-dual Śiva is the cause of the birth and other states of the dualistic world. This is just like the relationship between attribute and substratum, as expressed in such texts as "His supreme power is indeed manifold."
Just as between a gem and its radiance, there is an inherent distinction of natural power; the absence of which implies the absence of creation.

If one were to accept the falsity of both Māyā and the phenomenal world—as one would with a sky-lotus or a hare's horn—then, like the statement "my mother is barren," the contradiction with direct perception would be unavoidable.

Furthermore, since the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is declared in passages such as "Two birds... (*uta dvā suparṇā*), and since non-difference is declared in hundreds of scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), it is logical to accept both difference and non-difference. To accept only one side would result in the contradiction of the scriptures.
Nor is the third [position] tenable: "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind," and "This subtle *jīva* is seated within the heart."
The individual soul (jīva) is a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts; yet it is all-pervading like space and without parts.
Having realized the Self as great and all-pervasive, the wise man does not grieve.
Full within and full without, he is like a jar filled with water submerged in water.
Empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky.
"Then [there is] that which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, one, all-pervading, consciousness-bliss, formless, and wonderful"— in such passages,

although the identity of consciousness between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is declared, there remains the contradiction of their respective dimensions, namely atomicity (*aṇutva*) and omnipresence (*vibhutva*). This is just as, even when two snakes are one in being, they possess mutually contradictory dimensions consisting of shortness and length.

Because the radiance of the sun and the solar orb which serves as its locus both possess the nature of light, they are one in their luminosity; nevertheless, they possess mutually contradictory attributes consisting of pervasiveness and limitedness.
Likewise, even according to the analogy of a cloth that is both contracted and expanded, the coexistence of difference and non-difference is established.

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, because of the mutual distinction between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca)—the effect and the cause—as established in both scripture and aphorism: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real"; "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates, dissolves, and breathes in That; one should meditate with a tranquil mind"; and "The non-difference of that [effect from its cause] follows from such terms as 'originating' and so forth."

Because of the designation of both difference and non-difference through the illustration of clay and so forth, and likewise in the *Atharvaśiras*, beginning with "There is nothing whatsoever other than Me," and continuing through the first section with "I alone am the light; I am all; he who knows Me knows all," and starting from "He who is Rudra is the Blessed Lord, as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu."

The non-difference of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—the collection of effects such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Kālarudra, and others—from the causal Śiva has been determined in the second section: "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hari, He is Indra; He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, He is Fire; He alone is everything that has been and that is yet to be; He is the eternal Law (ṛta), He is Truth (satya)."
Furthermore, because in the *Kaivalya*, *Taittirīya*, and other Upaniṣads, the phenomenal world of effects is declared to be non-different from its cause, Paraśiva;

nor is there a fifth [alternative]: in passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," one perceives that the individual soul (*jīva*), though distinct from Brahman, attains identity with It through the practice of meditation upon It. Thus, the validity of both difference and non-difference is not contradictory.

Nor is the sixth [alternative] correct; for in such passages as, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara," and "From Him is born Prāṇa, mind, and all the senses; He rules over both knowledge and ignorance, while He is other than these," the relationship of ruler and ruled between the phenomenal world (prapañca), which consists of duality and non-duality, and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is seen to be without contradiction.

Not the seventh— [the view that] "by the practice of churning through meditation (*dhyāna*), the wise man burns away the bond," or "this Self is indeed to be attained through truth, austerity, right knowledge, and perpetual celibacy," and so forth; [this is not the case] because [liberation is attained] by means of the performance of dualistic practices such as meditation and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

Because it shows that the fruit is the attainment of the state of Supreme Śiva, who is absolute non-duality (paramādvaita). Now, one might object: "If dualistic rituals are indeed the cause for attaining the non-dual Brahman, what is the use of this laborious inquiry into the scriptures of the Upaniṣads? To this we say: No; for it is through the destruction of evil (durita) by means of rituals performed without desire for fruits [that the mind becomes fit].

This is because they serve as the means for attaining Brahman according to the maxim of "the gross Arundhatī" (where one first perceives a nearby bright star to locate the fainter Arundhatī). Accordingly, the Smṛti states:

beginning with "He who has these forty-eight sacraments... and ending with "...he goes to union with and the same world as Brahman," it teaches that rites such as *garbhādhāna* lead to the attainment of Brahman by way of destroying sin. Therefore...

There is no contradiction in the relationship of the means and the end between ritual actions, which are the means of propitiation, and the Supreme Lord, who is the object of propitiation. Nor does this contradict the scriptural statement regarding the fruits of the stages of life (*āśrama*), for not all of these [actions] result in worlds of merit.
This remains true even though the fruits of actions performed with desire are independent [of the Lord].

For those who perform actions free from desire, there arises the supreme human goal, which is liberation from the three impurities beginning with *āṇava*. Otherwise, in the absence of the performance of action, there would be an absence of purification of the mind; in its absence, there would be no arising of knowledge;
and in its absence, the consequence would be the impossibility of liberation. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is pleasing to the wise.

Having bowed, [the author] says: In order to ward off the harsh arguments of those who are averse to the Vedas and Vedānta along with their auxiliary sciences (sāṅga), the Blessed Vyāsa, the crest-jewel of the omniscient, presented two views—dualism and non-dualism—in two sūtras under the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter: "Bādari [holds it to be] non-existence; Jaimini [holds it to be] existence."

Having demonstrated the supreme reality through the authority of a portion of the Śruti, Bādarāyaṇa— by means of the sūtra "Therefore [it is] twofold, like the twelve-day sacrifice"— designates his own intended view, which is the essence of the meaning of all scriptures, as the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (bhedābheda).

Nor is the ninth [alternative] tenable—for in the dualistic system (*dvaitamata*), it is impossible to attain oneness with Brahman that is free from rebirth, just as a river cannot become one with the ocean. In the non-dualistic system (*advaitamata*), however, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the state of possessing qualities (*saguṇabrahmatva*) and lordship (*īśvaratva*) are merely imagined (*kalpita*), like a snake in a rope; thus, [the status of] the scriptures of devotion (*bhaktiśāstra*)...

The two previously mentioned views should not be adopted, as this would result in the abandonment of the Vedic scriptures that establish injunctions and prohibitions, as well as the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and so forth; for [these texts] state: "One who grieves while deluded does so through lack of mastery," and "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and so on.

The fact that the individual soul (jīva) is an experiencer of suffering due to being bound by *māyā*, and that its identity with Paramaśiva is realized through the knowledge of Him, is established [in the scriptures]. Likewise, in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Accompanied by Umā" and ending with "Beyond darkness," it is shown by means of devotion, meditation, and worship of the Lord endowed with qualities (*saguṇeśvara*).

Because it teaches the attainment of Brahman as the witness devoid of qualities (nirguṇa-sākṣi-brahma), and because— in contrast to all other systems— it possesses the complete presence of the three sections consisting of devotion, action, and knowledge,

and because it points to liberation-in-union (sāyujya) like a river merging into the ocean, and because it follows both types of scriptural revelation, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference. It is not [the case that they are contradictory].

It should not be argued that even in the Advaita system, devotion (*bhakti*), ritual action (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth are observed; for if the Lord of Māyā (*avidyeśvara*) is non-existent and merely imagined, whose devotion, faith, and trust could they possibly be directed toward—any more than toward an artificial *sālagrāma*? Furthermore, how could an imagined Lord, like a snake superimposed upon a rope, be one who is worshipped through all ritual actions?

Nor is it the case that the tenth [member] bestows all desired fruits— just as the sprinkling of rice grains is combined with heaven by virtue of being a cause for the *apūrva* (unseen potency) arising from the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), so too are all practices such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) [combined] by virtue of being instrumental causes for liberation.

They are combined within the non-dual Brahman with its distinctions. Therefore, like the relationship between the Āghāra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they exist as subsidiary and principal; or like the five fore-offerings (pañcaprayāja), they exist as multiple subsidiaries prompted by a single principal.

The reconciliation of difference and non-difference is established in every respect— whether by their dependence on the impulsion of distinct injunctions like the *godohana* vessel, or by the unity of fruit as in the case of the six sacrifices— since there is no contradiction whatsoever; for in the mantra "Two birds," we hear of the association between Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) as delimited by knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

For those established in the doctrine of Śuddhādvaita (Pure Non-dualism), there is no contradiction because they accept the phenomenal world of duality within the non-dual Brahman; thus, there is no conflict between difference and non-difference in a single locus. Nor is there a contradiction if both [aspects] are intended as the primary meaning, since the sentences such as "He offers the *samidh* oblations" serve as injunctions for both the five *prayāja* offerings and their performance as the means.
Just as the Sautrāmaṇī and Bṛhaspatisava sacrifices— which lack independent injunctions—

attain their status as both [independent rites and subsidiary parts] through the force of both [types of evidence] by virtue of being subsidiaries to the Agnicayana and Vājapeya respectively, so too is it with the Upaniṣadic passages such as "The Self, my dear, is to be seen."

Furthermore, because both the status of being a means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman (*brahmapramāpakatva*) and the status of enjoining the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñānavidhāyakatva*) are possible; and because, in every section beginning with "Therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), both difference and non-difference are indicated through the presentation of prima facie views and established conclusions (*pūrvapakṣa-siddhānta*);
moreover, having demonstrated his own position that both are to be enjoined by means of the analogy of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha-yajña*).

Regarding the sūtra "Because it is possible as in the case of the twilight" (sandhyavad upapatteḥ), since both systems are established by means of the illustration of the time of twilight, the ringing proclamation is that the view of Kāśakṛtsna— which emphasizes both difference and non-difference— is indeed the primary system.

Taking as his authoritative basis the intermediate statement, "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭan*), etc., wherein the Supreme Self is described as residing within the individual self (*vijñānātman*), Āśmarathya maintains that the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established; thus he resolves the contradiction with the non-dualistic scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

[The former] refutes [the objection] by means of similarity. Auḍulomi, however, taking as his authoritative source such scriptural statements as "There is no diversity here" and "Not this, not this," teaches that the appearance of the dualistic phenomenal world is non-contradictory within non-dual Brahman, like the appearance of a snake in a rope.
Kāśakṛtsna, on the other hand, [teaches this] through an investigation based on a comprehensive reflection upon the beginning, middle, and end of all the Vedāntas.

By means of the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), one should understand that [the Lord] indeed possesses both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*). This alone is to be known as the primary doctrine of Vedānta. [This concludes] the Section on Primordial Matter (*prakṛty-adhikaraṇa*). 7.

Having thus established the non-contradictory difference-and-non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, he now declares the difference-and-non-difference between the world (jagat) and Brahman: "The demonstration of the difference-and-non-difference between the world and Brahman..."
130. And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. 23.

Therefore, the subject matter of this [enquiry] consists of such scriptural passages as: "From this very Self, space was produced," "The one God, generating heaven and earth," "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra—they are all born from Him," and "He thought: 'May I be many.

In the aphorism *janmādyasya yataḥ* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2), it is stated that being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman; that is what is now investigated.

Although it would have been more appropriate to present this [topic] immediately after the *janmādi-sūtra*, nevertheless, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is placed at the conclusion of the "Harmonization" (*samanvaya*) because it is easy to state that the Vedāntas—which convey the sixfold marks of purposiveness—contradict the inference that establishes mere efficient causality (*nimittatva-mātra*). This is how it should be understood. Nor is it the case that...

The section concerning birth (*janmādhikaraṇa*) would be rendered purposeless. Here, Brahman is taught to be merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*), like a potter and so forth; for in passages such as "He thought" (*sa īkṣāñcakre*), we observe that He is the creator of the world preceded by reflection, which highlights His distinction from material causes such as a lump of clay or a potter. Thus, [if this were the case], the Supreme Lord’s status as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) would not be established.

Furthermore, because it would follow that [the Self] is subject to modification like clay and other such materials, it is not possible for a single entity to be the cause of both [the material and the efficient].

In the world, potters, weavers, and others are seen to be the transformers (*pariṇāmin*) of jars, cloth, and so forth; moreover, the accomplishment of the fruit of an action is observed to be rooted in a cause that is distinct from the effect itself. [This applies likewise] to the cause of the universe.

Because, like clay and other materials, there would be a transformation [of the Lord], His status as the Supreme Lord would be destroyed, and [His action] would be purposeless; therefore, the Supreme Lord is understood to be the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
Furthermore, in passages such as "partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless," He is described as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).

Since the status of being both cause and effect is denied of the Supreme Brahman, it is understood that He is the cause through *vivarta*— an illusory manifestation consisting of the appearance of another form while not abandoning His own essential nature, like a rope appearing as a snake; otherwise, [such causality would be impossible] for the causal Supreme Śiva-Brahman.
Consequently, the world, being of the nature of an effect, would necessarily possess parts, impurity, and insentience.
Therefore, the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be merely figurative.

Furthermore, the scriptural passages enjoining the world's causality would imply that Brahman is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) or the cause of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-kāraṇa*).
When it is argued that [the Lord] must be accepted as such, it is replied:

here, the fact that Paraśiva alone is the cause of both the origin and the sustenance of the universe is stated; for in hundreds of scriptural passages, such as "As the spider [spins its web]," the status of being the non-different instrumental and material cause is demonstrated by means of illustrative examples.

If it were accepted that [Brahman] is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*), then its establishment as the material cause (*kāraṇa*) and its status as the substratum of the world (*jagad-adhiṣṭhānatva*) would not be taught.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "Prakṛtiśca Brahma," its nature as the efficient cause is also indicated. Why?

Because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); [this is possible] only by virtue of being a single, non-different cause that is both the efficient and the material cause.

"Because of the consistency with the proposition and the illustration as heard. This means: non-contradiction, non-opposition, and harmony between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the proposition is: "Have you asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? And here, by the knowledge of one [thing]...

The knowledge of all is taught; and that is possible only if [the world] is the material cause (*upādāna*). This is because there is no distinction between the material cause and its effect, and because it is possible to know everything through a cognition whose nature is that of the material cause.

For if there were a difference between the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause, as in the case of a chariot, a city gate, or a palace, the knowledge of all through a single cognition would be contradictory.

As for the illustration: "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'"—this is seen to concern only the material cause (*upādāna*).
Likewise, "by means of a single nugget of gold, all that is made of gold would be known," and so on.

"Just as by means of a nail-cutter, all iron would be known"—this is the proposition (*pratijñā*). "In the same way, [the question] 'O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? is the proposition.
"Just as plants grow from the earth" is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "When the Self, which is the inner controller, is seen, heard, and reflected upon... [is the conclusion].

Having made the proposition that "when this [Self] is known, all this is known," he provides the illustration: "Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds, but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, [the sound is grasped]."
Furthermore, regarding the designation of the non-dual state of Śiva as qualified by a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣaviśiṣṭaśivādvaitapadanirdeśa*):

in the section on "origination" (*janmādhikaraṇa*) based on such scriptural passages as "from which indeed these beings are born," the author of the Sūtras has indicated the non-duality of Śiva as qualified by a specific power, rather than [the non-duality] of a Brahman devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣabrahmaṇaḥ*).

Because the relationship of cause and effect is impossible; because no perceptual scripture exists that establishes [Brahman] as the material cause through illusory transformation (*vivarta*); and because it contradicts the scriptural statements regarding the initial proposition and the illustrative example, this view should not be accepted by those seeking liberation. For in the passage "from which indeed these... (*yato vā imāni*), it is the power of the Supreme Lord alone [that is intended].
Although it has been indicated that the Supreme Lord is both the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world, nevertheless,

there is no separation between them as there is between a lump of clay and a potter. For in the Śruti text, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," the innate nature of the Māyā-power residing in the Supreme Lord is pointed out, just as the power of burning is innate to fire.
Therefore, it is certain that Brahman is never without attributes.
In this examination of Brahman’s state of being both without attributes and with attributes,
[the author] refutes the view that it is exclusively a cause without attributes.
131. And because of the teaching on covetousness. || 24 ||

Since both agency (*kartṛtva*) and material causality (*upādānatva*) are predicated of Paraśiva-Brahman, its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) through the desire expressed in "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*), and its status as the material cause are understood from the phrase "May I become many" (*bahusyām*). Therefore, it is not possible for Brahman to be devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) or merely the efficient cause.
Now follows the demonstration that Paramaśiva is the cause of both [the individual soul and the world]: 132. And because both are directly taught [in scripture]. 25.

But surely, how can his status as the material cause of the universe be established, given that the Śruti—"Rudra, the great seer, superior to the universe, beholds Hiraṇyagarbha being born"—declares that the Supreme Lord, having by His own will created Hiraṇyagarbha as the creator of the world, beholds him out of compassion? [The answer is: "Know Māyā to be Nature... [and so forth].

In passages such as "One should know... and so forth, the Pradhāna is recorded as having the status of material cause (*upādānatva*); likewise, in passages such as "From that the Virāj was born; from the Virāj, the Puruṣa," its nature as primordial matter (*prakṛtitva*) is observed. Anticipating the objection that the Pradhāna alone possesses the status of being the material cause of the universe by virtue of denoting primordial matter, [the author] refutes this:
In the Vedāntas that are directly perceptible, it is traditionally taught (*āmnāyate*) that Śiva-Brahman is the cause of both the manifestation and the dissolution of the universe.

Through the statement, "All these beings, indeed, arise from Ākāśa alone and return into Ākāśa," his status as both the instrumental and material cause is well-established by virtue of being the cause of origin and dissolution. This is also stated in another Śruti:

In passages such as "The Lord of all sciences," his status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is established; and by the passage "All is indeed Rudra," his status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is recorded through his being the very nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-svarūpatva*). Likewise, in the *Śatarudrīya*, beginning with "Salutation to the golden-armed one" and ending with "to the lord of the *kuluñcas*," his sovereignty over the universe is shown. Following that, [the text continues with] "Salutation..."

By the passage ending with "to Parṇyāya and to Parṇaśadyāya," its nature as the universal self (*viśvātmakatva*) is designated. Furthermore, in another Śruti text—“Brahman was the forest, Brahman was that tree; Brahman stood presiding over the worlds, upholding them”—both aspects are perceived. And in the *Atharvaśiras*, beginning with “I alone existed first,” and so forth...

Since both the fact that [the Lord] is the self of the entire universe and His sovereignty over the universe are established through direct perception in the first and second sections, the status of the Supreme Lord as the cause of both aspects of the world is proven.
He states another reason as follows:
133. Because of self-activity and transformation. || 26 ||
For this reason as well, Brahman possesses both the status of efficient cause (*nimitta*) and material cause (*upādāna*). Since "self-activity" (*ātmakṛti*) refers to activity belonging to the Self,

and because such activity is observed in common with the state of being an agent, [the text] "He made Himself by Himself" (*tad ātmānaṃ svayam akuruta*) shows that the Supreme Lord, who is denoted by the word "Self," possesses the status of agent through "Himself" (*svayam*) and the status of object through "Himself" (*ātmānam*).
The establishment [of Śiva] as the object of the act [of realization] is achieved through its being taken up as the object.

Now, one might ask: "How can the Self, which is Śiva already established from before, be the object of an action? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of transformation" (pariṇāmāt)—[referring to] that whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, which is untainted, and which is a mine of infinite auspicious qualities.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction in Maheśvara—who serves as the efficient cause—being the material cause (*prakṛti*) and thus the soul of the universe, because he undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) into the form of the phenomenal world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities;
[the opponent replies: "But surely, transformation is precisely the attainment of another state preceded by the abandonment of one's own original nature, as in the case of milk turning into curd."

If it is argued that for the eternally pure Maheśvara, there would be destruction of his essential nature and the consequence of possessing qualities of modification due to his being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), we say no; for even when acting as the material cause (*upādāna*) while being the instrumental cause (*nimitta*), he is untouched by modification and the like. This is because it is established that the Supreme Lord’s causal agency consists in his being the material cause of the world through the power of *māyā*, while the *māyā* itself undergoes transformation into the form of the universe.

Since it is heard in passages such as "one should know [it] as Prakṛti" that Māyā, which is non-different from Him, is that which is governed, and the Supreme Lord is the governor, it is established that the causality of both the universe and its opposite belongs to no other.
He states another reason:
134. And indeed, it is also called the source (yoni). || 27 ||

For this reason as well, the Supreme Lord alone is the material cause (*prakṛti*). For indeed, He is designated by the word "womb" (*yoni*), which is a synonym for *prakṛti*, in such passages as: "The wise behold Him as the womb of all beings," and "Having meditated on the Creator, the Lord, the Person, the womb of Brahman, the sage goes to the womb of all beings. Therefore, He possesses both the nature of being the material cause and the efficient cause.
And thus it is established that [the source] belongs to the Supreme Lord alone. In common usage, the word *yoni* is seen as a synonym for *prakṛti* (primordial matter), as in the statement:

"The earth is the *yoni* of herbs and trees. Furthermore, even in the case of a woman's womb (*strīyoni*), there is indeed its status as the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the embryo by way of its constituent parts;
elsewhere, however, the word *yoni* is also seen to denote the locus of abiding (*sthityadhikaraṇa*), as in: "Thy *yoni* is Indra... [RV 2.38.8].
Regarding the phrase "niṣade akāri," although its status as a synonym for *prakṛti* (primordial matter) is understood from the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*), nevertheless,
in passages such as "as a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]," it is seen that Śiva alone is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
The Section on the Basis for All Explanations. 8.
Now follows the reconciliation of the doctrine of qualified non-dualism (viśeṣādvaita), which emphasizes both difference and non-difference, with Paramaśiva:
"By this, all [other doctrines] have been explained, indeed, have been explained. (Sūtra 28)

The subject matter here is the speech of Uddālaka to Śvetaketu in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Bring a fruit of the Nyagrodha tree. "Here it is, venerable sir. "Break it open. "It is broken, venerable sir. "What do you see here? "These tiny seeds, venerable sir. "My dear, break one of these open. "It is broken, venerable sir. "What do you see here? "Nothing at all."
"Lord," [he said]. "O gentle one, from this very subtle atom (aṇiman) stands this great banyan tree.

Thus, by means of the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), do the Vedas and Vedāntas—which teach both ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman—establish the Supreme Śiva of the six planes (*ṣaṭsthala-paraśiva*), or do they establish the embodied soul (*śārīra*), or are they intent upon the doctrine of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇuvāda*)?

Thus, a doubt arises: since the Supreme Lord alone is taught to be "superior to the universe" in passages such as *viśvādhiko rudraḥ*, it is not possible for Him to be the object of the Vedāntic means of knowledge that pervade the universe.
It is more appropriate that the Śatarudrīya and other such texts recited in the previously mentioned ritual context (*karmaprakaraṇa*) have the individual soul (*jīva*) as their subject matter.

Because, if [the Self] were intended as the Supreme Lord, there would be a contradiction with the context and the purpose [of the passage]; furthermore, because the Smṛtis, Āgamas, and so forth have various deities as their objects. Moreover—even though the doctrine of the Pradhāna has already been refuted by such [Sūtras] as "On account of seeing, not that which is non-scriptural" (BS 1.1.5)—in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad],...

Because we observe statements that demonstrate the inclusion of the gross world within the subtle reality (*sūkṣmatattva*), the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) characterized by atomic nature is logical. Beginning with "Bring a fruit of the banyan tree" and ending with "The banyan tree stands," a scriptural illustration of the prior state of the universe is heard. In that illustration, there is nothing whatsoever [present].
Thus, because of the mention of the word "atom" (*aṇu*), the doctrine of atoms whose nature is void appears as the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Therefore, since it is argued that the Vedāntas cannot possibly have Brahman as their primary purport in any way—this being the position reached—we reply: even if the Vedāntas have various deities as their purport, [they do so] through primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) or through indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

And by means of the exclusion of what is not that (atadvyāvṛtti), [the term] becomes a means of valid knowledge (*pramāpaka*) for Paraśiva-Brahman. This is because, according to the principle of uniformity of purport (*gatisāmānyanyāya*) found in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "I ask you about that Person known through the Upaniṣads," "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," and "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," all the Vedāntas [converge upon this single reality].

This is because it is established that [the text] teaches Brahman. Even though they are recited within the context of ritual action (*karma-prakaraṇa*), the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Śatarudrīya*, and others do not have any other purpose. According to the maxim that "the sublation of context by an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not to be prevented," it is indeed proper for the context to be sublated by an indicative mark.

"To the Lord of beasts, to the Lord of trees, to the Lord of the worlds"—because of the abundance of such marks of Brahman, as in "He who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going," this [passage] does not have another subject matter.
Furthermore, wherever in the Vedas, Vedāntas, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth, attributes such as being the cause of the world [are found], [it refers to Brahman].
The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that in each respective instance, what is being propounded is precisely the supremacy of Paraśiva-Brahman as the six-fold locus (*ṣaṭsthala*).

Furthermore, even though the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and so forth may appear to have various deities as their objects, everything is entirely consistent because they are all harmonized within Paramaśiva according to the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*).

By this—namely, by the realization of the Self through the manifestation of its own true nature—the claim that "everything becomes known through the knowledge of one" is fulfilled; thus, the positions such as those of the atomists (*paramāṇuvāda*) are explained as being refuted precisely because they contradict the promise of the knowledge of all.
Furthermore, if atoms and the like were the cause, then even upon the realization of the Self, everything would not be known, because the Self would not be their material cause (*upādāna*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement "not anything," which establishes the non-manifestation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). Furthermore, the state of being atomic (*aṇutva*) attributed to Brahman is a figurative designation based on its subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*). Consequently, in the Vedāntas, Brahman alone is understood to be the cause of the world. The repetition of the word "explained" (*vyākhyātā vyākhyātā*) indicates the completion of the chapter. By this—
By establishing that Brahman, together with its attributes, is the non-different efficient and material cause of the phenomenal world,
all the various theories regarding the authority of specific portions of scripture— such as those of the Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, Pāñcarātras, and others—

as well as the doctrine of the falsity of one or another [of the three natures], the doctrine of the universal falsity [of the world], and the doctrine of primary non-difference, have been explained and resolved.

The meaning is that they have been refuted. There is a concordance between the characteristics of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, it is established that only that [Veda] is Vedic, and nothing else.
Thus ends the eighth section, "The Topic on the Explanation of All."
