Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter, titled "Samanvaya," in the Śrīkarabhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya, the preeminent leader of the multitude of ascetics of the glorious Nirābhāsa Vīraśaiva tradition.
The first chapter is completed.
Now, [the second chapter] in the Brahmamīmāṃsāsūtra composed by the venerable teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda—
The First Pāda of the Second Adhyāya in the Śrīkara Bhāṣya.
The Section on the Absence of Opportunity for Mindfulness (Smṛtyanavakāśādhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

In the first chapter, having established— in accordance with all Vedānta— that [the Lord] possesses innate omnipotence, omniscience, and the causality of all things, [the author] refutes the Sāṃkhya tradition by means of the rejection of Smṛtis, logic (tarka), and other doctrines that contradict the Vedānta.

He begins the second chapter in order to demonstrate that He alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world. Although the status of the Pradhāna as the cause of the origin of the world has already been refuted on the grounds of its being non-scriptural in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, he speaks [next] out of the apprehension that there exists scriptural authority in the form of Smṛti for its being the cause of the world.
If it is argued that this leads to the fault of leaving no room for memory, we say no, because otherwise there would be the fault of leaving no room for memory.
If it is argued that by not accepting *pradhāna* as the cause of the world, there would follow the defect of leaving no room for the *Smṛtis*—

meaning the defect of the lack of authority of the *Smṛtis* of the Sāṃkhya and others— that is not so; for if one does not accept Śiva-Brahman as the cause of the world, there would follow the defect of the lack of authority of other *Smṛtis*, such as those of Manu and others.

Nor is there a lack of a determining factor; for the Smṛtis of Manu and others, being rooted in the Veda, possess authority due to their strength, whereas Sāṅkhya and other systems that contradict the Veda lack authority due to their weakness—this is the meaning. In the first pāda of this chapter, the contradiction with Smṛti, Tarka, and so forth is refuted; in the second, [the contradiction] with those doctrines...

The state of being wicked is established [in the first section]. In the third, the contradiction with scripture regarding the earth and other elements as causes is refuted; in the fourth, the contradiction with scriptures that teach the individual soul (*jīva*) and the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is refuted. In the statement, "He who in the beginning supported with his knowledges the seer Kapila when he was born, and beheld him as he was being born," [the author establishes] Kapila's excellence in knowledge.

Because it is seen to be the most excellent; and because the Veda states, "Whatever Manu said is medicine," thereby indicating that Manu’s words possess the status of a primary injunction like a medicinal drug; and because this demonstrates their mutual contradiction—whether it be the primacy of the Sāṅkhya and other systems, or that of Manu and others.
It is doubted whether the Upaniṣadic statements follow the Smṛtis of Sāṅkhya and others, or the Smṛtis of Manu and others.
The Vedic statements concerning the cause of the world are applicable only to the Pradhāna.
Even if one has personally understood the meaning of the Veda, there may still be ignorance regarding it;
therefore, a wise person should cause that meaning to be grasped through the Smṛtis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas.

Thus, according to this restrictive rule (*niyama*), since the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas* do not depend upon the *Sāṃkhya-smṛti*— which, though composed by the supremely authoritative Great Sage Kapila, is a means for attaining results that are not fully complete and which produces only the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) such as the *Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa* and *Soma* sacrifices—

it follows that the *Sāṃkhya-smṛtis* composed by the Great Sages, which primarily establish the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause, possess primacy. This being the position reached [by the opponent]—

We reply: It is incorrect to claim that the understanding of the meaning of the Vedānta must follow the Smṛti of Kapila because, in the Śruti passage "the seer born as Kapila," Kapila is designated as supremely authoritative due to his excellence in knowledge.
For even Viṣṇu [is so designated] in such passages as "that one supreme form of Viṣṇu."

Because there is no proclamation of his superiority over all others, it follows as a consequence that the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta must be in accordance with the *Buddha-pāñcarātra-āgama* composed by him.
Furthermore, [he is not the author] because he is established in unimpeded knowledge within the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*.

Because Bṛhaspati is described as being superior to all others, there would arise the contingency of determining the meaning of the Śruti according to the Lokāyata Smṛti composed by him. Furthermore: "This [universe] was then enveloped in darkness, unknown, and without distinguishing marks," [and so on]. This would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis.
It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and as if entirely fallen asleep.
Then the Lord Svayambhū, the unmanifest, who dispels darkness and whose power operates through the great elements and other principles, appeared, making this world manifest.
He who is beyond the grasp of the senses, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal,
who consists of all beings and is inconceivable— he himself shone forth.
Desiring to bring forth various kinds of creatures, he, having meditated, first created water alone;
into that he cast his seed.
By this much [of the passage], the causality of Kālarudra with respect to Brahmā and all others is established through the power of Māyā, whose nature is darkness (*tamas*).
"When that was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent [quality] of Savitṛ; and from that, ancient wisdom issued forth."
One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti (Nature) and the wielder of Māyā to be Maheśvara;
from him, as its constituent part, this entire universe has arisen and is pervaded.

I take refuge in that God who, as the Self, illumines the intellect, whom the seeker of liberation approaches for shelter—He who ordained Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him; he who beholds Hiraṇyagarbha being born—may that God endow us with auspicious mindfulness. All that has come to be...
"Whatever manifold world has been born, and whatever is being born— all this is indeed Rudra.
Since the causality of Paraśiva is established by such direct Vedic revelation, the authority of the Sāṅkhya Smṛti— which is based on the Vedas only through inference— is not valid.
Furthermore: "The goal which all the Vedas proclaim, which one should meditate upon as the Lord to be meditated upon—this entire world is Brahman;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the senses are produced from Him. He is not the cause of causes;
He is the meditator, the meditator of meditators, and the cause that is to be meditated upon."

"Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of All, Śambhu—the one auspicious Śiva—is to be meditated upon alone in the midst of space; having abandoned everything else, [he is] the maker of auspiciousness," and so forth in the Śrutis.
Devotion to Śiva arises through merits accumulated over ten million births.
Whatever meritorious deeds, such as sacrifices and charitable works, a human being performs;
Having renounced desires according to the prescribed rule with the intention of offering everything to Śiva,
a man becomes very firm through the grace of Śambhu.
Then, terrified, the lords of the gods flee, abandoning their obstacles;
by that, service rendered to the Moon-crested Lord comes to pass.
Knowledge arises for one who listens, and through knowledge alone one is liberated.
What is the use of saying more here? For one whose devotion to Śiva is firm, [liberation is certain].
"Even one seized by multitudes of great sins and minor sins is liberated," and so forth;

thus, in the *Śivagītā* and many other Smṛtis, the supreme person Śiva is established as the object of worship, and all ritual actions— whether prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*), by tradition (*smārta*), or obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)— are shown to be forms of his adoration.
This has been demonstrated;

moreover, it is stated in such scriptural passages as: "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas; Pradhāna is the perishable, and Hara is the immortal and imperishable. Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire cosmic illusion (viśvamāyā). And so forth.
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest consisting of the three qualities was produced from Him"— thus even in the Smṛtis, His very status as the controller of Pradhāna is recorded.
And in the case of a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative.
But when there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, it is better to follow the Veda.
From the observation of such principles of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya, it is indicated that the primacy belongs exclusively to the Smṛtis of Manu and others which follow the [Vedic] Smṛti;
for even though the insentient Pradhāna, consisting of the three guṇas, is incapable of being the cause for the manifestation of the sentient individual soul (jīva).

Anticipating the objection that the causality of mahat, ahaṃkāra, and so forth— well-known from the Smṛti of Kapila— is established by virtue of their proximity [to Brahman], he refutes it: "And because the others are not perceived" (Sūtra 2).

Furthermore, because other non-conscious entities such as *mahat* and *ahaṃkāra* are not perceived [as ultimate causes], and because in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Āgamas— such as "From the Self, space was produced," "From this, the vital breath is born," and "From the Imperishable, the universe arises here"—
it is seen that Supreme Śiva alone is the cause of *mahat* and *ahaṃkāra*, unlike non-conscious things such as a pot.
The status of *pradhāna* as the cause of the *mahat* and subsequent principles is in no way possible;

rather, it is logical that the very words of Manu and others— whose authority is established by the Śruti in the passage, "Whatever Manu said was medicine"— which constitute a remedy for the world, are what serve the purpose of the Vedānta.
The Section on the Reply Concerning Yoga. 2.

Having raised the objection that even if the Pradhāna cannot independently be the material cause of the world, it might be possible through the direction of Īśvara, he refutes the system of Yoga which prescribes such a view:
By this, Yoga is refuted. || 3 ||

Even though there is a distinction between Sāṅkhya and Yoga regarding independence and dependence, since even in the *Hiraṇyagarbha-smṛti* (the Yoga scripture) the predominance of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the material cause is taught, by this very refutation of the Sāṅkhya-smṛti,
the Yoga-smṛti is also answered— that is, rejected— such is the meaning of the portion of the sūtra.

In passages such as "All is indeed Rudra," "All this is certainly Brahman," "All this has that as its self," and "When one thing is known, O Venerable One, all this becomes known," the fact that Brahman is the very self of the world is indicated.
For if [Brahman] were not its material cause, it would be impossible for it to have that as its self, as seen in such texts as "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning."

Since the *Hiraṇyagarbha* is remembered as being superior to all, and since yoga-knowledge— along with its means for attaining the fruits of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)— is elaborated upon in hundreds of Śrutis such as the *Śvetāśvatara* through passages beginning with "having made the body even and holding it three fingers high," one must consider whether, in accordance with the Smṛti on Yoga, the Pradhāna is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the phenomenal world or Brahman.

There is a doubt: while it may be logical that the *pradhāna* is the material cause (*upādāna*) and the Lord is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), as in the case of clay and the potter, if the Supreme Lord were the material cause of the world,
it would be difficult to avoid numerous defects such as being subject to modification and destruction, just like clay and other such materials.

Now, one might object: since the preponderance of Yoga is observed in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* as the cause for the fruits of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and since even in the Śaiva Āgamas such as the *Kāmika*, which illuminate the meaning of the Vedas, it is taught that "having opened the door-panel of the mantras consisting of both the primary (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) forms,
one should break open the door to liberation"— [how then can Yoga alone be the means?].
When the vital breaths move through the middle channel, steadiness of mind arises by abandoning all thoughts with an attentive consciousness.
With a self that is serene and free from conceptual construction, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
"The wise man should practice the cessation of the vital breaths," and so forth in the Upaniṣads; "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind," and so forth in the Smṛtis.
"The state which is attained by the Sāṅkhyas is also reached by the Yogins."
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct.

If it is argued that, because the *Bhagavadgītā* teaches that yoga effects the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*), liberation from sin, and so forth, it is therefore appropriate to determine the meaning of the Vedānta in accordance with the *Hiraṇyagarbha-smṛti*,

which prescribes such [yoga]— we reply: Yoga is established in the Śrutis, Āgamas, and other texts as a means for attaining both Dharma and Brahman, and as a means for the restraint of the mind (*manonirodhaka*).
Furthermore, although [the clay] is primary by virtue of being practiced by the learned (*śiṣṭas*), it is not tenable that the effect is derived from that which is its primary material cause;

for, through the knowledge of one thing, as stated in the passage: "O gentle one, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name;
'clay' alone is the reality. Thus, by the knowledge of one [cause], [all effects are known].
Because it contradicts all the Vedāntas which establish the propositions and illustrations for the doctrine that [the self] is consciousness alone;

and because: "That meaning which is found in the Smṛtis, Āgamas, and Purāṇas but is contradicted by the Smṛti should be understood as the meaning of the Tantras, and it is censured by the exponents of the Veda."
Thus, from the perspective of the Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya systems:
"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā;
this entire world has arisen from that which constitutes His limbs and pervades it."

For in such passages as "His power is heard to be indeed manifold, like that of a spider," the Supreme Lord is designated as the non-different efficient and material cause. As for the objection that if the Supreme Lord were the material cause, He would be subject to defects such as mutability— just as clay and the like are— that is incorrect.

Since the power of the Supreme Lord is accepted as being subject to modification as a material cause—just like the individual soul’s power—the Supreme Lord, who possesses that power, cannot logically be subject to transformation or modification. If, on the other hand, He is accepted as being merely an efficient cause (nimitta) like a potter, the contradiction with such scriptural texts as "that into which they enter when they depart" becomes unavoidable. Therefore, Yoga, like the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, [is not authoritative].

[The Sāṃkhya view] has been refuted. If it is asked, "What then is the status of the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures?", [the answer is: their systematic consistency with the Vedānta is appropriate, provided there is no contradiction with the Vedānta.
This concludes the section on "Not being of a different nature" (Na vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||

Anticipating the objection—"Since Paraśiva-Brahman is established as being distinct from everything else, how can it be logically consistent for the Lord, who transcends the three *guṇas*, to be the cause of the world which consists of those same three *guṇas*?"—the author says:
"Not so, because of its difference [from the world]; and its being such [as the cause] is known from scripture. (2.1.4)

If it is argued that because Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) while Pradhāna consists of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*), it is Pradhāna alone that can possibly be the material cause (*upādānatva*) of the world—both sentient and insentient—which is composed of the three qualities, we say: no; for its being so is from scripture. That is to say, both its being the material cause and its being the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatva*) are established by the Word (*śabda*).
"Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its web], and as herbs arise from the earth,
so does the universe arise here from the Imperishable"— from such Vedic words, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is the cause of both the manifestation and the withdrawal of the world.

In the Śruti text beginning with "ajāmekām" (the one unborn), there arises a doubt because the Supreme Lord's status as the cause of the world is not explicitly understood. In this Śruti, the causality of the Pradhāna—characterized by the three qualities (guṇas) and comprising both the conscious and the unconscious—is indicated without ambiguity. This is because in the world, the production of the conscious from the conscious and the production of the unconscious from the unconscious are observed to be its inherent nature. [Thus it is said: "Rudra is the source of the universe..."

In such passages as "the Great Seer, the Lord of the Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña," his distinctness from the world is proclaimed even while he is described as the controller of the universe. Manu also says:
"This [world] was then enveloped in darkness, unperceived, and without distinguishing marks."
It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and as if entirely asleep.
Then the Blessed Lord, the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū), who is unmanifest, made this manifest.
Thus, it is demonstrated that even for the Four-Faced One (Brahmā) and others, the Pradhāna exists as a cause characterized by darkness (tamas).
Therefore, in accordance with the Yoga-smṛti which establishes that the Supreme Lord is solely the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa)...
If it is argued that the ascertainment of the meaning of Vedānta is thus established, we reply:
according to the Śruti, "As the spider emits and withdraws [its thread]," the production of non-conscious threads and cloth from the conscious spider is demonstrated;
likewise, the production of non-conscious hair and nails from the conscious person is shown. This is also seen in the verse, "The one unborn female... (ajāmekām).

Because the status of being the primary cause, which is rooted in the Vedas, is logically established for Brahman; and because in passages such as "But Māyā is indeed Prakṛti" and "The Lord of the Field (Kṣetrajña)," it is taught that Śiva alone is the controller of Pradhāna.

Therefore, [the world] does not possess the nature of insentience, impurity, non-sovereignty, suffering, or the composite nature of consciousness and unconsciousness, as is the case with the phenomenal universe [if it were caused by Pradhāna].

It should be understood that the status of being the cause of the four-faced Brahmā and others—who have *pradhāna* as their primary material cause—as stated in the *Manusmṛti*, is specified for the Lord alone who presides over that insentient *pradhāna*.
Now, one might object: "In the Śrutis and Purāṇas, it is said, 'Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa,' 'Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa,' and so forth."
Because the status of being the cause of the four-faced one (Brahmā) is taught [to belong] to Nārāyaṇa. Furthermore:
"The waters are called 'nārāḥ'; the waters are indeed the offspring of Nara. Since they were his primordial abode (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa."

Thus, the word *Nārāyaṇa* is intended [as the subject] later on. In its conclusion, it says: "One should know that Supreme Person, golden-hued and accessible through one's own intellect," thereby attributing qualities such as being golden-hued to Him alone. Furthermore:
"Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lotus-throne in the center of the solar disc, is to be meditated upon at all times."
Wearing armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, and a crown, adorned with necklaces, possessing a golden body, and bearing the conch and discus.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has arisen from Viṣṇu;
I am the source of the entire universe as well as its dissolution.
I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
Nārāyaṇa is the fulfillment of the world, the eternal Self without a second.

Thus, the status of being the cause of the world’s birth and so forth is clearly taught in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other texts. If it is argued that for this very reason Nārāyaṇa is intended [by the author] to be the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha and others as stated in the Manusmṛti—that is incorrect, because [the scripture states]:
"When there was darkness, neither day nor night existed..."
Neither being nor non-being, he is the absolute Śiva alone;
from that Imperishable has issued forth the venerable and ancient wisdom of the knower.
"He who is the first of the gods, situated in the east, Rudra, the great seer, superior to all— who beheld the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) being born;
he who ordains the Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him— to that God, the light of self-knowledge,
I, seeking liberation, go for refuge," and so forth.
For in the Mahānārāyaṇa, Śvetāśvatara, and other Upaniṣads, it is indicated beyond doubt that Śiva alone is the cause of Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest.
Furthermore: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; all this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is He."
This has been elaborated in many ways in numerous texts such as the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Atharvaṇaśikhā*, beginning with the words "they are fully produced" (*samprasūyante*).
Likewise, in the *Bhārata*, which is equal to the Vedas, in the *Anuśāsana Parvan*: "He created from his right limb Brahmā, the source of the worlds."
Likewise, from his left side, the Lord [created] Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the world.

"In the heart is that which is called Kālarudra, the cause of the dissolution of the universe. Thus it is elaborated in many ways in the Śaiva Purāṇas: "They consider the cessation of phenomenal expansion, the peaceful, the auspicious, and the non-dual as the Fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known," and so forth. This is also found in the Māṇḍūkya and other Upaniṣads.

The state of being beyond the three forms (mūrtitraya) and the state of being the cause of the cause have been established as belonging to Him alone. Since the causality of the three forms is observed in Nārāyaṇa in such passages as "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa," it should be understood that [the former two states] refer to the intermediate creation.
These three, whose nature is causal, were born directly from Maheśvara for the sake of the creation,
maintenance, and dissolution of the universe of moving and non-moving beings.
Formerly, all three were appointed by their father to three tasks:
Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for destruction.
Nevertheless, out of mutual envy and desiring to surpass one another,
they propitiated their father, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance.
In a former kalpa, Rudra created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa;
then, in another kalpa, Brahmā, who is identical with the universe, created Rudra and Viṣṇu.
And the Lord Viṣṇu created that Brahmā again;
and Brahmā [created] Nārāyaṇa again, and Bhava [created] Brahmā again.
Thus, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā of the Śiva-purāṇa, the creation during the intermediate kalpas has been demonstrated.
In the conclusion of the Manusmṛti:
"He placed the moon in his mind, the quarters in his ears, Viṣṇu in his stride, and Hara in his strength."
One should know Agni as the deity of speech, Indra of evacuation, and Prajāpati of procreation.
"One should know that Supreme Person (puruṣa) who is the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, golden-hued, and accessible to the mind in deep sleep"—thus it has been taught.
"I am indeed that which is subtler than the subtle; I possess that."
I am the Great One; I am this manifold universe.
I am the Ancient One, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord; I am the golden one, I am the form of Śiva.

Salutation to the one with golden arms, the leader of armies, and the lord of the quarters; salutation to the golden one, salutation to the one whose mark is gold, salutation to the golden-hued one, salutation to the one whose mark is the celestial realm, salutation to the one with golden arms, to the golden-colored one, to the one of golden form, to the lord of gold, to the lord of Ambhika, to the lord of Uma, to the lord of creatures—salutation, salutation! Truth.

"Truth indeed is Rudra; we know that Puruṣa, we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us"—since in hundreds of such scriptural passages (śruti) it is seen that Śiva alone possesses the nature of being golden (*hiraṇmaya*) and is denoted by the word *Puruṣa*, the statements in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa that contradict the Śruti [are invalid].
It should be understood that, because they are rooted in delusion like the Buddhist and other scriptures, it is not logical for them to serve as supplements to the Veda.
Regarding the word "composed by Manu" (manupraṇīta), [it is said]:
"O best of Brahmins, Rudra has goodness within him, but darkness on the outside."
Thus, it is conventionally described as referring to Kālarudra, who is established in the Purāṇas as being characterized by the external quality of *tamas*.

Furthermore, in such passages as "O my vital breaths, disputing for the sake of what is better, the earth said," "the waters said," and so forth, the possession of consciousness by insentient entities such as the earth is heard; likewise [it is taught] regarding rivers, oceans, mountains, trees, and the like.

Since even non-conscious things are described as conscious in the Purāṇas, one might suspect that there is no difference between Brahman and Pradhāna; therefore, [the Sūtrakāra] says: "But there is a designation of the presiding deities, because of distinction and because of following after. (Sūtra 5)

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. It has been taught that the capacity to initiate speech—established by such scriptural passages as "Earth spoke"—belongs only to the deities presiding over earth and the other elements. Why? Because of specific designation and because of following [the deity]. In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, it is said: "Come, let me [enter] these three deities... all the deities indeed disputing for the sake of superiority..."
Having understood that the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) was attained by those gods, Agni, becoming speech, entered the mouth;
Āditya, becoming the eye, entered the eyes; Vāyu, becoming the breath, entered the nostrils—and so on.
From such passages in many *Śrutis*, it is understood that it is indeed the presiding deities (*abhimānidevatā*) of speech and the other senses who are intended to be expressed.

Therefore, [the Lord] must be distinguished from the insentient *pradhāna* and other such principles. Furthermore, in passages such as "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters," etc., it is stated that Rudra alone possesses the status of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the earth and the deities presiding over them.
Consequently, [He alone possesses] the qualities of being the self of all, being distinct from all else, being the controller of all, and being the cause of all.
It is not possible for the other [view].
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"But it is seen" (sūtra 6).

The word "tu" (but/however) is for the purpose of refuting non-Vedic reasoning. [From this] the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born; from whom these beings are born; through fear of whom the wind blows; both consciousness and unconsciousness [proceed from him]. Even so, these elements (*bhūtamātrā*) are deposited in the sense-perceptions (*vijñānamātra*), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the senses. A person is immersed in the same tree [of existence] due to a lack of mastery (*anīśayā*).

"He grieves while being deluded; the knower of the Self transcends grief. In such passages as "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," the status of being the cause of all and so forth is seen to belong to Śiva alone. By virtue of being endowed with diverse and manifold powers and by acting as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, there arises from Him—though He is conscious—the production of insentient things such as hair, nails, and teeth among sentient beings. [The text continues: "The insentient..."

The production of sentient beings such as scorpions and other insects from cow dung, wood, and the like; the production of worms and other creatures within honeybees; and the attainment of the form of bees by worms through the agency of insects—all this is understood [from scripture]. Therefore, its status as the dual cause of the world is established.
The refutation of the Advaita doctrine of a specific Smārta school, which primarily maintains the falsity of the world, the individual soul, and the Lord:

Having thus refuted the two Smārta systems consisting of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which establish the distinction between the world, the individual soul, and the Lord, the Advaita doctrine of a specific Smārta school, which primarily maintains the falsity of the world, the individual soul, and the Lord, is now refuted.
If it be argued that it is non-existent, we say no, because it is a mere negation. (Sūtra 7)
But there is no second to it, nor is there anything diverse here;
even if the lord of elephants were to die with a rabbit's horn, let this world exist;
even if a lotus were to grow within a circle of blazing fire, let this world exist.
"There is no effect of illusion and the like, nor is there illusion, for there is no fear;
as the blueness in the sky exists [only in appearance], so shall the world become real.
Thus it is stated in various Śrutis and Smṛtis.

If it is argued that the world, consisting of sentient and insentient entities, is non-existent because one observes fallacious statements purporting to demonstrate the unreality of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—just like the horn of a hare—and that it is therefore illusory; we say no, because this is a mere negation. Even at the time of dissolution (pralaya), it is merely a negation of the gross state of the world. Even during dissolution...

The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the phenomenal world exists in the Supreme Lord in a subtle form, like a seed and its sprout, it arises again at the time of creation through His divine play (*līlā*).
"As the Creator fashioned it in the beginning, the world acquired through karma perishes; the world acquired through merit perishes."

Because in such scriptural passages as "Two birds, united, friends," "The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord," and others, the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is declared; the world was never otherwise than this. Furthermore, because in such passages as "Not even the slightest thing else exists," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "Brahman is one only, without a second," [the unreality of the world is also taught].
From hearing false doctrines, there arises the doubt as to whether this world, consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, exists eternally or does not exist at all.

[The truth is: "There is no diversity whatsoever here"; "Now follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this'"; "That which does not exist in the beginning and at the end, does not exist in the present either";
"Brahman is Truth; the world is illusory; the individual soul is indeed Brahman and nothing else."
This individual soul (jīva) has the effect as its limiting adjunct; the Lord (īśvara) has the cause as his limiting adjunct.
Having abandoned the state of being both cause and effect, pure, perfect consciousness remains.
Through superimposition and negation, the non-conceptual reality is conceptually elaborated;
this meaning has been devised in sequence by those who know the truth for the sake of instructing disciples.
Thus, based on the Śruti, Smṛti, the tradition of the ancient teachers, and the principles of logic, it is established that the world is illusory (mithyā).
If this were not so, the contradiction with the aforementioned harmony of Śruti and Smṛti would be unavoidable.
To this, we offer the following reply: "By means of superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda), the world devoid of manifoldness (niṣprapañca) is described as manifold."
The unreality of the world should not be taught according to the logic devised by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*),

because such a view is not seen in the perceptible scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) that prescribe the method of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*). This is because [the scriptures] speak of creation,
maintenance, and dissolution, as in the passage beginning, "From which indeed these beings [are born]," and so forth.

In the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is indicated that even in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of sentient and insentient beings exists in a subtle form within the Supreme Śiva—who is a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*)—just as seeds of grass and other plants exist in a dissolved state in the earth during the summer season. This is further clarified by the subsequent sentence: "From that, indeed, Being (*sat*) was born."
Furthermore, because of the teaching on re-creation; and thus says the Smṛti:
"In Śiva—the supreme cause, whose nature is truth, knowledge, wealth, and bliss—the web of the moving and unmoving world lies like seeds absorbed in the earth during the summer."
Abiding in a subtle form, he again emerges outwardly in a gross state according to his own respective desire; such is the liberated soul, no longer subject to rebirth.

It should be understood that statements such as "Being only, my dear, this was in the beginning; there was nothing else whatsoever" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), which indicate the non-existence of the world, refer to the state of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). This is because the subsequent statement, "He thought:

'Let me create the worlds'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), teaches creation. Furthermore, statements indicating duality, such as "Two birds" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), have as their subject matter the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Everything became the Self alone—by what means could one see whom? and so forth;
such statements describe the experience of the realized sage characterized by a specific state of supreme *samādhi* filled with the bliss of Śiva.

Therefore, the non-dualist (*advaita*) doctrine, which imposes superimpositions (*adhyāropa*) contrary to the *Śruti*, the *Sūtras*, and other authorities, is to be disregarded. Consequently, Brahman is...

Like a rope-snake, although the world—consisting of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth—appears during the state of saṃsāra due to the power of ignorance (avidyā), it is nevertheless unreal because it is sublated by the experience of the knowledge that directly realizes one's own true nature, preceded by the discernment of the tenth man.
[Sūtra 2.1.8: "Because of the undesirable consequence that [the cause] would likewise [cease to exist] upon dissolution, [your theory] is inconsistent."

Because at the time of dissolution (*apīti*), there would be the same consequence as in the case of the bodies of frogs and other creatures which, though consisting of the single element earth, reappear during the rainy season; likewise, since the universe— comprising both sentient and insentient entities— exists within Brahman in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) during dissolution, its reappearance follows from such scriptural passages as "He thought" (*sa īkṣata*).

Because of these [scriptural] demonstrations, the false doctrine that the world, the individual soul, and the Lord are distinct is inconsistent and illogical. Now, one might object: since it is understood from such passages as "Brahman alone, without a second" and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self," that prior to creation there was only Brahman; and since it is also stated in "where he sees nothing else" and "everything became the Self alone" that [the Self] is everywhere— [The response follows: ... And this is logical because of the instruction that excludes [any real] difference. Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar nature arise, so too, O gentle one, do various beings emerge from the Imperishable. This serene being, having risen up from this body—
"Having attained the supreme light, he becomes established in his own true form"; "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "That thou art";

"I am Brahman"; "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; "As rivers flowing with water..."—in such scriptural passages, the liberated soul [is described] by way of the relationship between that which is to be attained and that which causes attainment.

If it is argued that liberation— characterized by the attainment of Brahmanhood preceded by the cessation of the natural state of being a *jīva*— is like space, and is the intended primary conclusion of all Vedānta scriptures, Smṛtis, Sūtras, Purāṇas, and so forth, that is inconsistent;
for it is impossible for a *jīva* who has attained a state of inherent difference to become Brahman, just as it is impossible for that which has coldness as its inherent nature [to become hot].
Furthermore, although water may become hot through contact with fire, it is observed that its coolness returns even before a watch (yāma) has passed;

likewise, although the individual soul (jīva) exists as delimited by the nature of difference, and Brahmanhood may thus be possible for the individual self, it is not permanent because it is adventitious. Difference is not destroyed. Therefore, difference is conditional (aupādhika), while non-difference is inherent (svābhāvika).
It should be understood:
just as the state of being an image and the state of being a reflection are imagined in the sun,
so too are the state of being the individual soul (jīva) and the state of being the Lord (Īśvara) imagined in Brahman.
This individual soul (jīva) has its limiting adjunct (upādhi) in the effect; the Lord (īśvara) has his limiting adjunct in the cause.
Having abandoned the state of being both cause and effect, the one characterized by perfect awakening (pūrṇabodha) remains distinguished [as the Absolute].

Thus, in the scripture, it is taught that both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are constructed by māyā and are unreal. Therefore, because an inherent difference cannot cease, [the following contradiction arises] with respect to those scriptural passages that establish duality and non-duality, as well as those concerning the goal and the seeker, such as: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form."
Thus, this very [knowledge]—

which is preceded by the cessation of *māyā* and *avidyā* taught through the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (partially inclusive and partially exclusive indication) found in the words of Devadatta, and which effects the realization of the non-duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—
is proclaimed as the cessation of innate difference, like the cases of the bee and the worm, or the iron and the mercury.

It has been clearly taught [in such passages as]: "Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating"; "One is ignorant and the other is wise;

indeed, one unborn [soul] lies down with her whom he enjoys, and another unborn [soul] leaves her once her enjoyment has been experienced"; and "From which these beings are born; the wise one is neither born nor does he die," and so forth.
For in these and other texts, the teaching regarding creation is given in accordance with the soul's experience of the fruits of its prior karma. Otherwise, [it would not be so].

Because an unequal creation is logically untenable; furthermore, there would be the unavoidable consequence that the Vedas, Vedāntas, Āgamas, and so forth— which enjoin the worship [of Brahman] as the means for attaining Brahman through karma, devotion, and dispassion— would be rendered purposeless, since [the world] would exist merely as the reflection of the original image (bimba) in the form of individual souls (jīva) and the like.

If it were designated as being imagined through *māyā*, it would follow that liberation—like a jar or other such objects—is subject to destruction, which would result in liberation not being the ultimate goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*).

Furthermore, this contradicts scriptural passages such as "The Knower and the Unknower," which establish that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are unproduced. Moreover, if the embodied self were already Brahman even prior [to realization], it would contradict the statement, "Having reached the highest light. This applies equally to the stainless one (*nirañjana*).

If one accepts the postulation of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā* for Brahman— which is eternally free, partless, unsurpassed, and self-luminous— then its non-duality (*advaita*) is lost. Furthermore, if the difference from Brahman were unreal even prior [to such a postulation], like a snake in a rope, [the postulation of *māyā* would be redundant].
How can the authority of the great Mahāvākyas such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), which enjoin the realization of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, be justified?

Furthermore, it would entail the consequence that both teacher and disciple must remain silent. Moreover, since Brahman has already attained its own nature as Brahman, the attainment of that state would be like grinding what is already ground; consequently, hearing, reflection, and other such practices would be rendered futile. [This is] like cutting off a tail that has already been cut, or severing what is already severed.

According to the maxim, "In the ear, a dog is indeed a dog, not a horse nor a donkey," it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that although the Supreme Self— which is of the nature of knowledge and bliss, eternally liberated, and self-luminous— is concealed by its own ignorance, its self-luminosity is never lost. This is just as the existence of duality in the waking and dreaming states, and non-duality in deep sleep, are established by the universal experience of all beings.

Likewise, difference persists until the attainment of Śiva-hood, which is difficult to prevent; therefore, there is no contradiction in the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, just as [there is none] between a river and the ocean.
Through superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda), the world of manifoldness (prapañca) is explained away as being without manifoldness; otherwise, this principle would be transgressed.

Because the absence of the arising of knowledge would entail the consequence of the non-existence of liberation, and because one observes the experience of ignorance within the self in the form "I am ignorant," both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are unreal, like a reflection and its original, being fashioned by *māyā*. When analyzed according to the etymology of *māyā*— namely, that which is measured (*mīyate*) by it is *māyā*— it is found to be so.

In response to the objection that— since the falsity [of the world] is accepted due to its contradictory nature as both existent and non-existent, and as consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness— the origination and so forth of the world created by Him must be merely an illusion, like a dream or a magical trick, he says:
And it is not so because of the absence of an illustrative example. || 9 ||

Since the falsity of *māyā*, the unreality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), and even the possibility of an opponent's objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding these are not found in the perceptible Vedantic texts— and because no mention of an illustrative example is seen anywhere—

the doctrine of the world's falsity (*jagan-mithyātva*) is not at all tenable; for [the scriptures state], "From which indeed these [beings arise]," and "As a spider emits [its thread]," and so forth.
Since the Śrutis unambiguously designate Brahman as the cause of the world's birth and so forth, that alone must be accepted by the followers of the Vedas,
in accordance with the Advaita scriptures which state that [the world] consists of an inconceivable construction resembling a dream or a magical illusion.

Even if one accepts the analogies of the world as a dream or a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), because *māyā* is non-inert (*ajaḍa*) by nature, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of Brahman is thereby indicated. Consequently, there is no contradiction with one's own scriptures which enjoin that Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*). Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that *māyā* is false based on the etymological derivation "that which goes toward (*ayati*) *ma* (Śiva)," for *māyā* is that which attains (*prāpnoti*) the auspicious (*śiva*).

By way of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*): Māyā is the innate power residing in Paramaśiva, as seen from such scriptural passages as "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold" (*parā'sya śaktirvividhaiva śrūyate*) and "But Māyā is Nature" (*māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ*).
Furthermore: "That which is the unmanifest cause, eternal, consisting of both being and non-being..."
That person who is distinguished in two ways is celebrated in the world as Brahman.
Thus, in the *Manusmṛti*, it is said that one naturally attains Maṃ— the auspicious, supreme Brahman;
this eternal state of being established in Brahman is called *Māyā* in the world.

Thus, in the Śiva-āgama, the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti is established as certain. Furthermore, the substance of the dream-multiplicity is not perceived even during the waking dream; however, because an object seen on a previous day exists on the following day as well, [it is said]:
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "The world of one who performs ritual action perishes."
Furthermore, because the status of being an enjoyer of the fruits of actions in this and the next world is pointed out by the Śruti and is observed in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and so forth;

and because no scripture is seen that ordains the attainment of heaven or hell as a result of virtuous or non-virtuous acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice or the killing of a Brahmin performed in a dream— that scripture is charming only so long as it is not critically examined.
Because in the world, reflections of sentient beings, humans, deer, the sun, the moon, and so forth cannot possess sentience;
because elephants, horses, and the like fashioned from clay, stone, cow dung, and such lack the capacity for actions such as walking by their own power;
and because the innate consciousness of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is understood through scripture, reasoning, and direct experience.

That delusive scripture which asserts that both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are mere reflections of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is not to be accepted by those who seek the ultimate truth (*pāramārthika*).
Likewise, in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*, Vyāsa spoke these words to Dūrvāsas:
"Bound by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), [the soul perceives] Brahman as its cause through time."
They transmigrate due to their own ignorance; liberation [is attained] through the imagined statement.
Thus, this deceptive scripture, which destroys the greatness of the Self,
should be disregarded by the devotees of Śiva because it contradicts the Śruti and the Smṛti.
This [ignorance] is primary in the case of the Kalāpas and others; it is darkness (tamas) because it is turned away from the fruit.
Indeed, that very [nature] has been described for the purpose of establishing its quality of destroying knowledge.
Even in the case of a magician, his authorship [of the illusions] is merely what he himself claims;
there is no mention of such a thing anywhere in the revealed scriptures (śruti) as they are actually observed.
Therefore, because the Supreme Lord is the cause of the world, the reality of the world remains unimpeded.
As long as knowledge has not arisen, ritual actions must be performed;
until then, the world appears as real, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
As long as Brahman— the non-dual substratum of all— has not been born [i.e., realized],

so it is stated in the words of the Śruti and the ancient teachers; for until that point, the appearance of the world through ignorance is admitted, just like the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, up to the limit of the experience of the knowledge of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*).
Anticipating the objection that the practice of the truthfulness of Vedic scriptures and rituals might still be possible, [the author] refutes it:
"And because of the defect in their own position" (10).
If one accepts that the world appears only during the state of cognition—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—then two faults would arise:

first, the impossibility of the lineage of teachers of the non-dual scriptures (*advaita-śāstra*), and second, the occurrence of the fault of depending on dualistic actions such as hunger and thirst after that [realization]. Therefore, the doctrine of the falsity of the world (*jagan-mithyātva-vāda*) is not tenable.

This is logical. Regarding the acceptance of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon Brahman—as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is it upon Brahman itself, or upon the primary [reflection], which is the appearance of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)? It cannot be the first, because Brahman is changeless (*nirvikāra*). It cannot be the second, because that [appearance] is insentient (*jaḍa*). Nor can it be the third, because it is imagined (*kalpita*).
Furthermore, how could the status of being a reflection be possible for Brahman, which is all-pervading and partless?

If it is argued that [the reflection of Brahman] is like the reflection in the sky, that is incorrect. In the world, it is observed that only space as delimited by clouds, stars, and so forth, undergoes reflection; for space itself is not perceived due to its dissimilarity with darkness and light. Furthermore, if formless things were to reflect, why would wind, time, and the like not also do so? Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct. As Śuka said: [text fragment].

There would be the consequence of universal liberation; if that were so, there would be no experience of ignorance such as "I am immersed [in suffering]. Furthermore, the production of bodies consisting of both sentient and insentient matter would not be possible. Therefore, the doctrine of the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not tenable.
This concludes the demonstration of the lack of certainty regarding the true nature of reality in the systems of logic and philosophy of the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Akṣapādas, Kāpilas, and others.

If it is argued that, although superimposition is not observed in the perceptual scriptures (*pratyakṣika-śruti*), superimposition must nevertheless be accepted because it is indicated by the sublation [of error] in the scripture concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa-śruti*), he replies:
"Because reasoning is unstable, if it be argued that it may be inferred otherwise, even so there would be the consequence of the impossibility of liberation. (Sūtra 1.1.11)

If it is argued that because the systems of logic—namely those headed by the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Akṣapādas, Kapilas, and others—are unstable, and because they lack any definitive determination of the true meaning due to being corrupted by the fault of mutual contradiction, the reality must therefore be inferred otherwise; [we reply:

such statements as "the clay alone is real" are merely fallacious utterances, and thus the falsity of the world, the individual soul, and the Lord [is established], just as [one might falsely infer] that "the mountain possesses fire."

If you argue that [the Self] is to be inferred according to the logic of "from smoke" and so forth, even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-liberation—as in the case of the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Buddhists, and others—and the consequence of the absence of liberation consisting in the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), which is established by many Śruti texts such as "Just as rivers... Therefore, from whence this... [text continues].

Regarding the passage beginning with "The serene one does not return again," which establishes Brahman as the cause of the universe, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world is understood therein. If it is argued that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) must be accepted according to the logical principle that "when X exists, Y exists," that is incorrect; for this is contradicted by such scriptural passages as, "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend Him, the Great One," and "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning."
They declare that there is ignorance regarding the meaning of the Veda when one understands it by oneself alone;
one should augment the meaning of the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

For it is taught in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and other such texts that one who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the Ṛṣis through reasoning (*tarka*) that does not contradict the *Vedas* and the *Śāstras* knows Dharma, and no other: "He who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the Ṛṣis with reasoning that is not in conflict with the *Vedas* and the *Śāstras*, he knows Dharma, and no other. Thus, even in these works, the refutation of personal whims, the transformations of one's own intellect, and fallacious reasoning is enjoined.

For, when following reasoning rooted in human intellect, one observes that no final certainty can be established, as there is the possibility that such reasoning might be refuted by the reasoning of other persons who are more skilled in sophistry (kutarka) at other times and in other places.
[This applies to] the systems of Mithyā-dvaita, Śūnya-advaita, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Bauddha...
In the sūtra "Because the scripture has no other source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*), the Blessed Vyāsa taught that the authority for the scripture consists precisely in its nature as the Veda.

If one were to accept the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which has Brahman as its material cause, there would arise the contingency of contradicting those scriptural passages that establish the identity of the world with Brahman, such as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "All is indeed Rudra. This will be discussed further below.

In the sūtra "tadananyatvam ārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ," the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa has clearly taught that the scriptural passages concerning "originating from speech" (vācārambhaṇa) serve the purpose of refuting the doctrine of the world's falsity by establishing that the phenomenal universe, which has Brahman as its cause, is identical in essence with Brahman. Therefore, there is no stain of doubt.
Since the passages beginning with "Speech is its origin" (vācārambhaṇa) teach non-difference from That,
they do not imply the falsity of the world, because the world has Śiva as its true nature.

Thus it is specified in the Skanda Purāṇa. For in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "Having known Śiva, one goes to the ultimate peace," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," it is declared that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation. This is also evident from the realization of one's own true nature through the discernment of being the tenth, as in the statement, "You are the tenth."

If it is argued that [the Lord] is the cause of liberation, that is inconsistent. The *pradhāna* is the perishable, while Hara is the immortal and imperishable. Through meditation on Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of universal illusion (*viśvamāyānivṛtti*).
"Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, the Sage goes to the source of all beings;
know that through the yoga of knowledge, characterized by faith and devotion, the wise man burns away the bonds through the practice of meditation and the dissolution of mental constructs.
This is established by the observation of hundreds of such scriptural passages, as well as by statements such as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."

It is determined that only the knowledge produced by *upāsana* (meditative worship) is the cause of liberation. Knowledge alone, like the knowledge of medical science and the like, possesses no value as a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). As long as knowledge arises, action must be performed; thus, [action continues] only until the production of knowledge.
As for the statement that the performance of ritual action (*karmānuṣṭhāna*) follows from the appearance of a dualistic world, that is charming only so long as it is not critically examined.
For the simultaneous conjunction of knowledge and action is indeed established in such scriptural passages as, "Knowing this, one offers the *agnihotra*," and others.
Just as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in the world;
therefore, one should remain possessed of good conduct and knowledge until the fall of the body.
The blind man is burned without seeing, and the lame man is burned even while seeing;
likewise, knowledge and action are mutually dependent, like the blind and the lame.
Just as a bird cannot traverse the expanse of the sky with only one wing,
so too liberation is not accomplished by the path of knowledge alone.

In such Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama texts, the injunction for the performance of dualistic rituals is taught even after the attainment of knowledge. Therefore, just as in the analogy of the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the knowledge of the world's falsity through the knowledge of Brahman is untenable. Furthermore, even in the state of non-duality, the application of the statement "I am non-dual" is not logically possible.

Since the injunctions regarding their bathing, twilight rituals (*sandhyā*), vertical and horizontal sectarian marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and *tiryakpuṇḍra*), and the conduct appropriate to their caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramācāra*) are seen in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the claim that these do not exist would result in the denial of direct perception—like saying "my mother is barren.
Furthermore, under the doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaitapakṣa*), is that [Brahman] with attributes (*saguṇa*), without attributes (*nirguṇa*), or both? Not the first.

If one accepts [the Lord] as possessing attributes (*saguṇa*) and as having four faces (*caturmukha*), it would be logical for Him alone to bear the marks of the *kamaṇḍalu* and so forth; it would not be appropriate for the necessity of applying vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), horizontal marks (*tiryakpuṇḍra*), or the worship of Śiva, Keśava, and others.
Even so, the consequence of the collapse of non-duality (*advaita*) is unavoidable. Nor is the second [position tenable], because the worship of that [qualified deity] is impossible. Not...

The third [position] is untenable because it entails the collapse of one's own doctrine (*svamatabhaṅga*). Furthermore, in non-duality (*advaita*), the relationship between the taught and the teacher is not logically possible; for we observe the report "I am dead" even regarding one who is actually dead. How can the realization "I am non-dual" be determined in the case of non-duality? It is only duality that accounts for the possibility of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). If one accepts that [non-duality] is merely conventional (*vyāvahārikamātra*), [then the doctrine fails].
That which is to be designated as "duality for the sake of conventional usage" (vyāvahārikadvaita) must be accepted, because conventional usage is impossible within absolute non-duality (advaita).

If one were to accept the non-duality of Brahman [as the ultimate reality], then since that [duality] would be an attribute of it, the doctrine of Brahman with attributes (saguṇabrahmavāda) would be unavoidable. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct.
The Section Concerning What is Not Accepted by the Learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa) || 4 ||

The refutation of non-Vedic doctrines such as Jaiminīya-Mithyādvaita and others: Since Brahman is understood to be complete and devoid of distinctions from such scriptural passages as "All-pervading like space and full" and "Partless, actionless, and tranquil," does the causality of the world belong to Pradhāna in accordance with that [understanding], or...?
Anticipating the objection that [the existence of] atoms and so forth is logical, he says:
"By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned are also explained. (12)

By this—the refutation of the previously mentioned views of false non-duality (*mithyādvaita*), void non-duality (*śūnyādvaita*), and those of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others—it is also established that there are "those not accepted by the learned" (*śiṣṭāparigraha*).
Here, "those not accepted by the learned" (*śiṣṭāparigraha*) refers to those who are both learned (*śiṣṭa*) and unaccepted (*aparigraha*).
The "learned" (*śiṣṭa*) are those proficient in the scriptures and practices of Jaimini, which primarily concern deities ending in the dative case.

Those who propound the non-distinction between the bound and the unbound; those who are unrestrained and devoted to the false doctrines concerning the Veda, the world, the individual soul, and the Lord;

and even the non-Vedic schools such as the proponents of false duality, void-nonduality, Jainism, Buddhism, and Lokāyata—all these have been explained by the Vedānta-smṛtis, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and other texts by the most eminent masters established in the Vedas and Vedānta.
Because of its omnipresence like space, its lack of distinction, and its nature as pure consciousness (*cinmaya*), and by such logical principles—

as well as from statements such as "the world accumulated through karma perishes"— it is shown that karma is the creator of the universe, since both the world and the individual soul (*jīva*) are understood to have karma as their cause. Furthermore, in passages such as "He makes the one unborn [Māyā] into the individual soul and the Lord by means of the appearance of Māyā," it is [shown that] Māyā [is the cause].
The causality of the phenomenal world (prapañca), including the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), appears [in scripture]. Therefore, there is doubt.

On the one hand, in passages such as "without eyes, without ears, without hands, without feet," the all-pervasiveness, partlessness, and the status of Brahman as the material cause (upādānatva) of the universe are established as logical. Alternatively, in the passage "having examined the worlds," since it is understood that the worlds have karma as their cause...
A living being is born through karma and grows through karma;
by karma they are dissolved. Therefore, the world has karma as its essence.
The universe is born through Māyā, it grows through Māyā, and it dissolves through Māyā;
therefore, the world consists of Māyā.

By such statements as these, they declare that the phenomenal world (prapañca) consists of action and is composed of māyā; therefore, that [view] is also logical. For in passages such as, "In Him there is neither effect nor cause, and neither one equal to Him nor superior to Him is seen," it is understood that Brahman is devoid of distinctions, being free from the nature of cause and effect and so forth. In every respect...

When it is argued that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, cannot be the cause of both [the creation and dissolution] of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the author extends the argument by citing scriptural authority: "Know that very thing to be Brahman which the mind does not think, and by which they say the mind is thought"—in such passages from the Upanishads, the rejection of inference is taught. As it is said: "Just as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web]."

Because the Śruti, following such faulty examples as these, designates the Lord as the cause of both aspects of the world, it is established that insentient matter (*jaḍa*), karma, *pradhāna*, atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, do not possess the causality of both aspects of the world.
This is evident from passages such as "the *pradhāna* and the Knower of the Field" (*pradhānakṣetrajña*), which refer to the Veda, the individual soul (*jīva*), karma, *pradhāna*, and the like.

Dependence upon the Supreme Lord is heard in scripture. In both worldly custom and the treatises, it is shown that the punishment for those characterized by wicked deeds such as theft is the administration of justice by the master, not the deeds themselves.
Furthermore, in the Purāṇas it is said: "That which is performed as dharma or adharma by whatever cause may become dharma [or the opposite]," and so forth.

The experience of contrary results from their actions is observed in those who committed sinful deeds such as the killing of their fathers, like Kāṭaka and Koṭa, and in those who performed meritorious deeds such as sacrifices, like Dakṣa and others. Furthermore, all the Śruti passages beginning with "from which words turn back, not having reached it along with the mind" are intended solely to make known the majesty [of the Lord]. Therefore, even by Brahmā, the majesty of Śiva cannot be [fully described].

He awakens; your path is past, and your majesty, which cannot be reached by speech or mind, is described with trepidation even by the Śruti through the exclusion of what is not that—thus is taught his possession of an inconceivable majesty. Therefore, [it is established] by such Śruti passages as "for him there exists neither effect nor instrument" that this refers to Mahādeva, the Supreme Brahman, Śiva.

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of making known its greatness. By this, the section concerning the enjoyer and the offspring (Bhoktrāpattyadhikaraṇa) [is concluded], which deals with the nature of being empty and the nature of not being empty. 5.

The establishment of the Supreme Brahman as being superior to the universe is found in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa of the Kāṇva recension, beginning with "He who dwells in the earth, whose body is the earth," and continuing through "He who dwells in consciousness, He who dwells in the self, whose body is the self."

In response to the objection that— since Śiva, the Supreme Self, is designated as having eight forms (aṣṭamūrti)— the state of being an enjoyer of pleasure, pain, and liberation, which reside in the individual soul (jīva), is possible for the Supreme Lord who is characterized by the body of the jīva, just as it is between a body and its embodied occupant— he says:
If it be argued that there is no distinction because of the eater’s becoming [the food], it may be so, as in the case of the world. 13.

Because of the designation of the soul and the Lord as body and embodied in the statement, "Whose self is the body"; because of the consequence of being an enjoyer—that is, the consequence of the transmigratory pleasure and pain residing in the individual soul; and because of their non-distinction, [it would contradict] such scriptural passages as, "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating," which establish the states of bondage and liberation for the individual soul and the Lord respectively.
Just as space, despite being all-pervading and the cause of all things, remains established as free from the stain of defects belonging to the entire world created by itself; so too the Supreme Lord,
although established as the cause of all, the body of all, and the inner controller of all.
He is distinct from the stain of all defects.

From the passage beginning with "whose body is the earth" up to "whose body is the Self," it is heard that He is characterized by bodies consisting of both sentient and insentient beings. Or [it is said]: "He is without eyes, without ears, without hands or feet; He is bodiless."

In such scriptural passages as, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches him who dwells [therein]; for he is bodiless, mindless, and pure," his state of being without a body (aśarīratva) is taught. Therefore, a doubt arises:
if the Supreme Lord lacks a body and so forth, how can his status as the Lord of all, his omniscience, and [his other attributes] be maintained?

This is logical: since the distinction between the attributes of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—established by such scriptural passages as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*)—is merely figurative, like that of a body and its possessor, it follows that pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in the individual soul actually belong to the Supreme Lord alone.
Therefore, the status of the individual soul as a worshiper and the Supreme Lord as the object of worship is not possible.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is the body of the Lord of Pārvatī;
because they are bound by the fetters of ignorance, the unenlightened do not know this.

In the Śaiva, Skānda, and other Purāṇas as well, it is taught that He alone has the universe as His body. Therefore, since the Lord is designated as distinct [from the world], it is not proper to rely upon a bodiless, attributeless Supreme Self. This being the position reached, we reply: in such scriptural passages as, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless," and so forth, [the elements] beginning with air...

Thus, its nature as both with form and without form has been taught. The capacity of the formless wind to cause trees to tremble and uproot them is observed. Likewise, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad it is said: "Without hands or feet, swift and a grasper; I see without eyes, I hear without ears; there is no knower other than Me, for I am eternally consciousness."

"I alone am to be known by all the Vedas; I am the author of the Vedānta and also the knower of the Vedas. For me there is neither merit nor sin, nor is there destruction; there is no birth, body, sense organs, or intellect. Thus, in the Kaivalya [Upaniṣad], Śiva’s omniscience, omnipotence, causality of all things, and sovereignty over all are established through his independence from body and sense organs.

Therefore, there is no stain of doubt here; for since it is taught that Brahman possesses innate power in the statement, "His power is indeed heard to be manifold," the doctrine of a qualityless Brahman is not tenable.
Consequently, in the Vedānta scripture, beginning from "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" and ending with "Non-return, on account of the word," [this remains the case].

Indeed, its distinctiveness is clearly observed. For instance, in the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), Brahman is designated as the object of the desire to know for a specific person. Furthermore, in the aphorism "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]" (*janmādy asya yataḥ*), it is taught that He is the cause of the world's birth, sustenance, and dissolution, and the one who is established by the scriptures. And in the aphorism "But that [is established] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*), it is that very same [Brahman] who is [the subject].

Furthermore, because it has been established through the harmony (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedāntas, its possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) alone is logical; for in that which is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), qualities such as the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and so forth are impossible. This is just like [the passages] "One should meditate on speech as the cow" and "The Yajus is its head, the Ṛk is its right wing, the Sāman is its left wing," or "Food is Brahman," and so forth. Its...

The status of being a body is merely figurative and pertains solely to the subject of his worship. Even in the doctrine that the Supreme Lord assumes a body, there is no attainment of pleasure, pain, or the like, because that body is not produced by karma and because he is independent. This applies to the terms Brahmā, Īśvara, Śiva, Mahādeva, Śaṅkara, and so forth.

It should be understood that these are merely synonyms, just like the words *ghaṭa*, *kumbha*, and *kalaśa*. This is because in such passages as "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," the non-produced nature (*ajanyatva*) of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is heard; and because of the scriptural statement regarding the "appearance" (*ābhāsa*), "By means of the appearance of Māyā, He makes the Jīva and the Īśvara," [it is clear that] at the time of creation, through Māyā—which is of the nature of the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord—...
The intention is that the Supreme Lord manifests the state of being both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) by His own will;

therefore, agency is taught as belonging to Him alone, because power (*śakti*) is non-different from Him and thus not a separate entity. Consequently, what was stated previously is indeed correct. Some refer to this very doctrine of non-dualism-with-a-distinction (*advaita-viśeṣa*) as "qualified non-dualism" (*viśeṣādvaita*).
They declare that "Seshvaradvaita" (Non-dualism with God), "Shivadvaita" (Non-dualism of Shiva), and "the doctrine which is the essence of all the Vedas" are synonymous terms.
This concludes the section on the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* (The Topic of Commencement).

The demonstration of the non-difference between cause and effect [is established] because, in such scriptural passages as "Of the eternal, He is the eternal; of the conscious, He is the conscious," "O dear one, these creatures have Being as their root," and "Two birds, inseparable friends, one being ignorant and the other Lord," the Jīva and the Īśvara are seen to be unproduced; thus, even though they lack falsity (mithyātva), [they are not different from Brahman].

Anticipating the objection that since no scripture is seen asserting the reality of the world, and since the scripture concerning "originating from speech" (vācārambhaṇa) leads to the understanding of the world's falsity, that [position] alone is logical, he says:
"Its non-difference [from Brahman] [is established] on account of the words concerning 'originating' and so forth. (2.1.14)

Regarding their non-difference: according to the principle that "there is no difference between power and the possessor of power," one must accept the non-difference between the manifestation of their own power-aspect and the empowered Supreme Śiva, through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti established by logic; that is, they are non-different as cause and effect, like clay and a jar. Why?
From such scriptural passages as "The modification is a verbal handle, a name;
'clay' alone is the truth," "Rudra is indeed all," "The Truth, the Real, the Supreme Brahman," "As a spider [spins its web]...
from that [it arises]," and "He who is peaceful," etc., it is taught that the phenomenal world (prapañca), which has the power of Brahman as its material cause, is of the very nature of Brahman.

By this, it should be understood that the meaning indicated by the Sūtra is as follows: the Advaita view—that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is superimposed upon Brahman and is therefore false, like a snake on a rope;

the Dvaita view—which accepts a difference between the world and Brahman like that between a jar and a cloth; and the Viśiṣṭādvaita view—which accepts a difference between the two as being conjoined, like that between the body and its possessor—are all refuted. Khaṃ.

In passages such as "Air, fire, water, and earth, the sustainer of all," and "That which is the Supreme Brahman," the distinctness of Brahman from the world of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*) is heard. Furthermore, by such texts as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "All this is indeed Brahman," His being the self of the world consisting of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is also revealed. Therefore, [He is] the cause...
The doubt arises as to whether this is so or not.

In the passage, "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," there is the mutual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Furthermore, through such statements as, "From the Self, space was produced," the world and Brahman are characterized by the relationship of effect and cause.

And their mutual difference has been demonstrated. How can there be non-difference between Brahman—which consists of reality, consciousness, and bliss—and the phenomenal world—which consists of unreality, insentience, and suffering?
Since the emergence of worms and the like is observed in honey and other such substances, there is no non-difference between cause and effect.

If it is argued that the distinction between threads and cloth is established through the difference in the accomplishment of purposes and the accomplishment of functions, and that if cause and effect were non-different, the worldly practice of experiencing the fruits of pleasure and pain—both in this life and the next—would not exist due to the identity of the world and Brahman, and therefore the non-difference of the world and Brahman is untenable; [Response: [This objection is refuted by the following:]... (The remainder of the argument follows).

We shall explain: "Are you so conceited? Did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?
