Having kept in mind that the entire phenomenal world has Śiva alone as its sole cause and that the effect is non-different from the cause, [the text speaks of] the nature of the cause.

When it was proposed that through the knowledge of Paraśiva there arises the knowledge of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) which is its effect, the disciple—who did not understand that the whole has Śiva as its sole cause—raised an objection: "O Blessed One, how can that instruction [be possible]? He questioned how the knowledge of one thing could result in the knowledge of another through the knowledge of the Self. [This concerns] the phenomenal world.

Observing that the Supreme Self alone is the sole cause, the Teacher first teaches—on the basis of what is established by common worldly experience—that the effect is non-different from its cause, as in: "My dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known;
the modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the reality is simply 'clay'. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–5)

Just as jars, bowls, and other objects produced from a single lump of clay are known through the knowledge of that [clay], because their substance is not distinct from it, so too the world, having Śiva as its material cause, is known through the knowledge of Śiva; this is the intended meaning of the *ārambhaṇa* scripture.

In this context, having raised the doubt that the effect is a distinct substance from its cause based on the view of those who maintain a first cause, [the author] demonstrates the non-difference between cause and effect through common worldly usage by means of the passage beginning with "vācārambhaṇam. The word *ārambhaṇa* means that which is begun, grasped, or touched; here, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. It is [grasped] by means of speech (*vācā*), that is, by means of what is preceded by speech.
"By means of usage" (vyavahāreṇa) means by means of a cause.
Usage consists of activities such as fetching water, preceded by sentences such as "one should fetch water with a jar.
For the sake of accomplishing that usage, there is a modification characterized by a broad base, belly, and so forth, produced from that clay substance.

A particular configuration and the name "jar" and so forth, which are induced by that [configuration], are perceived. For the sake of accomplishing specific practical functions such as carrying water, the substance clay itself undergoes a change of state and acquires another designation;
therefore, it is taught that even the jar and the like are nothing but the substance clay, which alone is real. "Clay alone..."

Regarding the statement "truth," the claim that there is non-difference between cause and effect, and that the effect is false like a rope-snake, is incorrect. For the non-difference of those two—cause and effect—is not established, since the identity of a real entity (satya) and a false entity (mithyā) is logically impossible. If that were the case, either Brahman would be false or the world would be real. Furthermore, as for those who [hold that] the effect...

Accepting the ultimate reality [of non-duality], they assert that while the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is adventitious (*aupādhika*) and their non-difference is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), both of these— [difference and non-difference]— are intrinsic in the case of the insentient (*acid*) and Brahman. For them, since there is no other entity distinct from Brahman to serve as an adjunct (*upādhi*), and because [Brahman] is partless and all-pervading...

Due to the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), even the very nature of Brahman, which is Paramaśiva himself, would undergo transformation into a form that is to be abandoned (*heyākāra*). Furthermore, when ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) is destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), would the soul perish or not? If it were to perish, liberation (*mokṣa*) would consist in the annihilation of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-uccheda*); if it does not, [then the soul remains].

If ignorance were destroyed, there would follow the undesirable consequence of liberation for this [individual soul], because its state as a *jīva* would persist as something distinct from the nature of Brahman.

Therefore, is this delusion of ignorance Brahman’s or that of someone other than it? It cannot be the first, because they are mutually contradictory like darkness and light, and because one who is ignorant lacks the status of being Brahman. Nor can it be the second.
Because it is impossible for there to be another consciousness [within it], and because accepting a second consciousness would contradict one's own scriptures;

therefore, just as the spider (ūrṇanābhi) places its own effect— the web of threads— within itself in a subtle form unfit for the differentiation of name and form during its causal state, and [manifests it] during its effected state...

He manifests [the world] in a gross form suitable for the differentiation of name and form; likewise, the Supreme Lord, having established the universe—composed of consciousness and unconsciousness—within Himself in a subtle state during the period of dissolution, reveals it at the time of creation as having a gross nature. Therefore, the non-difference of cause and effect is established.

The demonstration that the world is real is not tenable as being non-different from its cause, because— unlike a jar or a cloth— the difference between the accomplishment of the object and the accomplishment of the function between cause and effect is established. Therefore,
regarding the phenomenal world...
Having admitted that the world is superimposed upon Brahman, one must also admit the non-difference between the substrate and the superimposed;
for [the world] is perceived when [Brahman] is present. (Sūtra 1.1.15)

The word *bhāva* denotes the existence of the cause; the word *upalabdhi* denotes the existence of the effect; and the word *ca* is taught as signifying the existence of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of those two. "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; thou art That."

In such passages, since the world is seen to consist of creation, maintenance, dissolution, manifestation, and grace—all of which are dependent upon Brahman—superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not tenable. Furthermore, because of the teaching that "this world has That as its essence" (*aitadātmyam*), the phenomenal universe—which is the effect of Brahman—is of the nature of Brahman, and because living beings likewise attain the true Brahman; moreover, in the world...

Furthermore, since the lump of clay, which is the cause, is perceived when the effect such as a jar exists, and because there is recognition of the jar as being essentially clay— namely, "This jar is indeed clay"— it is logical that the effect and the cause are non-different.
He now demonstrates the reasons for the reality of the world:
And because [the existence] of another [is established] through the existence [of this one]. || 16 ||

From such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone," it is established that the effect is non-different from its cause; for the entire manifold world, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, exists within the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, which is its cause. In the world, all these things, such as jars, bowls, and the like—
In its prior state, it appears as consisting solely of clay; therefore, there is no contradiction in the reality of the world.
Furthermore, he states another reason for the reality of the world:

"If it be argued that [the world is unreal] because of the designation of it as non-existent, we say no, because [that designation refers] to another attribute, as is clear from the remainder of the passage. (1.1.17)

If it is argued that because of the designation of non-existence—since the Śruti states, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent"—the phenomenal world (prapañca) is designated as non-existent prior to creation like the horn of a hare, and therefore the world consisting of consciousness and the unconscious, though appearing in Brahman like a snake in a rope during the present time, does not exist at all; [we reply: no, for [it exists] by way of another attribute (dharma).
How can there be a designation of non-existence based merely on being distinguished by the attribute of subtlety? From the remainder of the passage.

Because in the subsequent sentence, "From that, indeed, Being was born," the gross state following creation is mentioned; therefore, in the statement "In the beginning, this was non-existent," it means that prior to creation, this world was non-existent—that is, it existed in a subtle state. Hence...

The meaning is that after creation, "Being" (Sat) was born from that [Brahman], meaning it came to possess a gross state. Having established that the phenomenal world has Brahman as its illusory material cause (*vivartopādāna*)— according to the principle that "illusory transformation" (*vivarta*) consists in assuming the nature of another while not abandoning one's own essential nature, like a snake in a rope— is the falsity of the world not thereby proven?

If it is argued that this is logical, that is incorrect. For in the Śrutis it is stated, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," and "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here"; and in the world, it is known that everything such as pots and bowls did not previously exist in the clay. Therefore, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is non-existent, like the horn of a hare.

If it is argued that this is logical, we say no. Just as a single body undergoes the states of childhood, youth, and old age, the distinction between the subtlety and grossness of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is taught as being determined by differences in time. Therefore, the word "non-existent" (*asat*) indicates its subtle nature, while the word "existent" (*sat*), distinct from that, indicates its gross nature. Consequently, regarding the phenomenal world—
The reality and non-difference from Brahman are well-established.
He states another reason for the refutation of falsity:
"On account of reasoning and other scriptural texts" (Sūtra 1.3.18).

By reasoning: just as a tortoise, by its own power and according to its own will, extends its limbs such as its feet outward and then withdraws them back into itself, so too does Paramaśiva, at the time of creation,
manifest [the universe] externally by means of the differentiation of names and forms.

Because it is established by such reasoning as "during dissolution, [Brahman] conceals within its own self the phenomenal world consisting of both consciousness and the non-conscious, which is non-different from itself," and by other scriptural passages as well, such as: "In the beginning, this was indeed nothing at all; that, being non-existent, thought: 'May I be';
and "At that time, this was indeed undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form."

This is because of such scriptural passages as those containing the words "non-existent" (asat) and "manifested" (vyākṛta). It is clearly taught that during the state of dissolution the phenomenal world is contracted, and at the time of creation it expands.
Having thus established the reality of the world, [the author now] provides an illustration regarding the non-difference of cause and effect by means of two sūtras.
He shows [the answer]:
"And like a cloth" (paṭavat ca) || 19 ||
Just as a cloth is seen to exist in two distinct states— the state of contraction at one time and the state of expansion at another— so too, the cause is the state of Paramaśiva contracted by Śakti,
while the effect is the state expanded by Śakti. Just as there is non-difference between the cloth when it is rolled up and when it is spread out, so it is here.

There is non-difference between cause and effect, as in the case of clay and a jar. Now, an objection may be raised: "In the example of clay and a jar, the clay and the jar are distinct, because they are objects of distinct cognitions;
therefore, that reason [of being objects of distinct cognitions] is inconclusive (vyabhicāra), like the case of a jar and a cloth. This is not so, because of the substance of the clay.
The form characterized by a broad base, belly, and so forth is the cause for the conventional usage "this is a jar.

The connection of that very [jar] with another state that serves as its counter-correlative (pratiyogi) is the cause for the conventional usage "the absence of the jar. In this regard, because the state of the two shards is its counter-correlative, it is that very state of the jar which serves as the cause for the conventional usage "this [jar] does not exist. Nor is there anything distinct from that.

No such thing as the "absence of a jar" is perceived, nor is it even postulated, since the practical usage of "absence" is established by that much alone. Therefore, just as clay— though non-existent in its specific form as a jar—
is not contradicted in its nature as clay even when it undergoes transformation into the forms of a jar or a bowl through one of its own aspects, so it is with Śiva.
Even though there is a transformation into the form of the world by means of a single portion of its own power, the non-difference of the world from [Brahman] is not contradicted.
Anticipating the concern that the non-difference between cause and effect—which are mutually distinct—might jeopardize worldly transactional practice, he says:
"And as in the case of the vital breaths and so forth" (Sūtra 2.1.20).
Just as the single wind, through the differentiation of its functions such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, assumes various effects consisting of name and form (*nāmarūpa*),

even so Paraśiva alone, though appearing in the form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of the conscious and the unconscious by the power of His own Śakti, remains non-different [from Himself]. Furthermore— just as...

Just as a Śiva-yogin, at the time of meditating on Paramaśiva, performs the contraction of the vital winds such as prāṇa and apāna through breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, and performs actions such as expansion during the period of worldly activity; in the same way, the Supreme Lord performs the expansion of the universe at the time of creation and its contraction at the time of dissolution.
Therefore, it is established that the world, which is of the nature of an effect, is non-different from the supreme cause, Paraśiva.

And because of this non-difference, the promise that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all, becomes established. This concludes the section concerning the teaching [of non-difference]. (Sūtra 7)

Having thus demonstrated that his own intended position is the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*)— since the doctrine of the distinction between the world and God and the doctrine of the falsity of the world have been refuted— he now refutes the doctrine of those who maintain the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmavāda*).
Because of the designation of [the Self] as other [than the body], there would follow the defect of not performing what is beneficial and so forth. (Sūtra 21)

Because of the designation as Brahman—that is, because the individual soul (jīva), which is other than Brahman, is designated as being Brahman itself—there follows the contingency of faults such as the non-performance of what is beneficial. "Non-performance of what is beneficial" refers to the failure to provide garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, which are the means of attaining desired ends;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is included the provision of things like tigers that bring about the undesired. Such is the contingency of these faults.

Therefore, the doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is Brahman is not tenable. This is because in such passages as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is designated, whereas in such scriptural texts as "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), their non-difference is indicated. Thus, there arises the doubt: is there a difference between the two, or not?
This is because the scriptural passages that teach a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman have as their purport the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for in such texts as "He who worships another deity [thinking] 'He is one and I am another,' he does not know; he is like a beast," and "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity," the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman is heard.
Just as the state of being an image and the state of being a reflection are imagined in the sun,
so too are the states of being the individual soul (jīva) and being the Lord (īśvara) imagined within the one Brahman.

In this context, since the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established through the analogy of the original object and its reflection, and since their relationship as cause and effect is taught in passages such as "From which indeed these beings are born," and because the unity of cause and effect is indicated in the scriptural text concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that there is no Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from the individual soul.

It is explained: just as in such statements as "Food is Brahman, breath is Brahman, yonder sun is Brahman," the status of Brahman attributed to the individual soul (jīva) is merely figurative. If the identity of the soul with Brahman were established in a literal sense, then everything that constitutes the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired by souls would have to be accepted as belonging to Brahman alone.
If that were so, since the independent Brahman is capable of creating a desired manifold, the creation of an undesired manifold would be untenable.
As for what was said regarding the perception of the dirtiness of a face in jewels, swords, mirrors, and so forth—
This must be examined: when will defects such as smallness and impurity—which are adventitious—be destroyed?
If it is argued that they perish upon the removal of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a sword, then does the reflection, which is the locus of that smallness and so forth, persist or not?

If it persists, then because the *jīva*, which corresponds to it, would also persist, there follows the undesirable consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*). If it perishes, then [the same applies] to that very [reflection].

Liberation would consist in the annihilation of one's own nature through the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, if the *jīva* were identical with Brahman, then omniscience, universal lordship, and the status of being the controller of all would belong to that [individual soul].
[This concludes] the refutation of the Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine originating from Śrīkaṇṭha.

Raising the objection that, although the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are one in essence due to their nature as consciousness (*jñāna*), the distinction between them is perceived through the difference of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), and therefore the scriptural texts that establish their difference must refer only to a distinction based on limiting adjuncts— the author says:
Moreover, [the self is] distinct, because of the teaching of its differentiation. || 22 ||
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of certainty.

Brahman is something distinct from and superior to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) that is the source of internal, external, and celestial sufferings. Why? Because of the designation of difference [in scripture]. [For example: "The Self, indeed, should be seen."

Because of the designation of mutual difference between the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and the Supreme Self, Śiva, as expressed in passages such as, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon; then, my dear, one becomes merged with Being," the view that the individual soul alone is Brahman is not tenable. This is because there are [scriptural statements] that establish the reality of the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman.
Do the Śruti texts have as their object a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), or do they have as their object a superimposed difference (*āropita-bheda*)?

Not the first, because it is impossible for a living being (*jīva*)—who is by nature non-different from itself—to perform that meditation. Furthermore, does Brahman know him or not? If it does not know him, there is a loss of its omniscience and the consequence of its being insentient (*jaḍatva*). If it does know him...

One would have to recognize the suffering of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is non-different from oneself, as one's own suffering—consisting of internal and other forms of pain. If this were the case, the unavoidable consequence would be the attribution of the defects known as "failing to do what is beneficial" and "doing what is harmful" to Brahman.

Nor is the second alternative tenable; for even there, under the view that the ignorance belongs to the *jīva*, the same logical difficulties resulting from the previously mentioned alternatives remain unchanged.

On the view that Brahman is ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is impossible for Brahman— which is self-luminous by nature— to be the witness of ignorance or to perform the creation of the world and so forth caused by it.
If it is argued that "the light [of Brahman] is concealed by ignorance," then since concealment consists in the cessation of light, [Brahman could not be its witness].

Since the very nature [of Brahman] is self-luminous, the cessation of that nature would mean the destruction of its own essence; thus, thousands of defects such as the loss of essential identity have already been pointed out. Therefore, just as copper and gold exist within their respective generic classes of inert metals, the natural distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established within the generic class of consciousness (*cij-jāti*). Nevertheless, through contact with the sapid (non-conscious) element...

Just as the attainment of unimpeachable gold-nature occurs preceded by the cessation of the copper-nature, so too for the conscious individual soul (jīva), through the worship of the Supreme Lord and by virtue of His grace, unimpeachable Śiva-hood is established.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with statements such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) which enjoin the identity of the individual soul and the Lord.
Furthermore, since the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is indicated as being natural in the sūtra "But the difference [is] additional" (B.S.

2.1.22), and because non-difference is designated in the sūtra "Non-difference from that" (B.S. 2.1.20), it is understood even by children that the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) alone is the one approved by the author of the sūtras.

Now, one might object: since difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory in reality, and because it is impossible for natural difference to cease, the doctrine of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*)—which postulates both difference and non-difference—is alone the most consistent fourth position.
For, as in the view of difference-and-non-difference, here too all the Vedas are seen to be harmonized through the relationship of subordinate and principal.

Like the sun and its heat, like the moon and its moonlight, like dharma and its possessor, like a quality and its substrate, and like a staff and its bearer, [the Lord] is established as distinct. In this regard, Viśiṣṭādvaita has been demonstrated as his own intended position by Śrīkaṇṭha Śiva, the foremost of the Śaivas and the author of the *Brahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya*. In that work, it is established that liberated souls possess the status of being the husbands of Gaurī.
The identity [of the individual soul] with that [Supreme Self], preceded by the refutation of attributes such as being the cause of the world and being the inner controller of all,
has been elaborated through the five similes beginning with "Just as the rivers flow" (*yathā nadyaḥ syandamānāḥ*),
which is based on the scriptural texts concerning the glory of the three quarters (*tripādvibhūti*) and the glory of absolute liberation (*kaivalyavibhūti*).
It is argued that liberation characterized by union with Śiva (śivasāyujya) is not accepted; therefore, this [other view] alone is logical. To this we reply:

the claim that difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory in reality is charming only so long as it is not investigated, for difference and non-difference are both demonstrated in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Āgamas, Sūtras, and other authoritative texts.

Furthermore, because the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming and the non-distinction in the state of deep sleep are established by the experience of all, it is likewise stated in the Śiva-āgama:
"Deep sleep alone is indeed superior, even to internal creation and dissolution."
At the time of creation there is differentiation; at the time of dissolution, non-differentiation is taught.
Thus, because the individual soul (jīva) is seen to be characterized by both knowledge and ignorance, there is no contradiction in reality. "Even a crow, having reached Mount Meru, becomes golden;
likewise, having attained Śiva through devotion, the soul becomes Śaṅkara."
From this statement, it follows that the prior state of things is not perceived;
likewise, through meditation on Śiva, the individual soul does not undergo rebirth.
Just as water found within a mother-of-pearl shell certainly becomes a pearl in the world.
Indeed, a living being endowed with devotion becomes Śiva and not otherwise;
just as copper, through the process of alchemical transmutation, certainly becomes gold.
Through the piercing glance of the Guru, the individual soul becomes Śaṅkara.

Because of the observation of many such examples in the scriptures and through experience, there is no contradiction, as the inherent distinction [between the Lord and the individual soul] is set aside.

This is because the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa contains such statements as, "He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the self," and "Whose self is the body," which establish that the Supreme Lord possesses eight forms (aṣṭamūrtitva).

There would be contradiction with many scriptural passages such as, "It is indeed without breath, without mind, pure; for it dwells bodiless," and so forth. For in the passage, "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; I see without eyes, I hear without ears," the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, is understood to possess all powers by virtue of His independence from the body and the senses.

Since there is no observation of Śruti, Sūtra, or other authoritative texts that establish qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita*), the acceptance of a relationship between part and whole would entail the unavoidable consequence that the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited. Furthermore, it is taught that Brahman is full within and full without, like a full jar; thus, its fullness is declared even in places distinct from that [limited body]. Therefore, that doctrine is to be disregarded.

Furthermore, because Brahman is designated as having both form and formlessness—like the wind—for the purpose of meditation, as seen in passages such as "Brahman has two forms indeed; [it has] all faces, heads, and necks," and so forth; and because it was explained at length in the *Jīvamukhyaprāṇaliṅgasūtra* that three modes of meditation on the Supreme Lord are taught for the sake of the devotee's worship.

"At the time of the final end, they all, having reached the supreme immortality, are liberated in the world of Brahman; he who knows that which is hidden in the supreme, imperishable heaven attains all desires together with the Stainless One and reaches supreme equality"— in such numerous Śrutis, [the fruits] beginning with Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and Sāyujya constitute the vibhūti of the three-quarters of Paramaśiva.

Furthermore, because one observes the manifestation of liberation (*kaivalya*), which consists in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the natural state of being a living soul (*jīva*),

all scriptures that establish the fourfold liberation are indeed authoritative. The manifestation of power as an effect (*kāryavibhūti*), consisting of the sovereignty of established beings such as Indra, is exemplified by such injunctions as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

And the causal manifestation (*kāraṇa-vibhūti*), which consists of the sovereignty over the world of the four-faced Brahmā attained through the perfection of Haṭhayoga—this is for those who possess the qualification [for liberation].

This is because of the observation of such scriptural passages as: "Know that [the Self] is attained through the yoga of faith, devotion, and knowledge, perfected by penance over many births and accompanied by self-restraint, tranquility, and other virtues, consisting of service to the Guru, the Cares (the Lord), and the Īśvara."

But surely, in the Subālopaniṣad it is said: "This one, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the sole god, is Nārāyaṇa"—thus the state of being the self of all bodies and the inner controller of all belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone.
[We reply: This refers only to Paramaśiva; for it is said: "Rudra indeed is everything; he is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa; he who is Rudra in fire, he who is in water, he is within... [and so on].

In such scriptural passages as "He entered into the space between," and in such Smṛti texts as "O Arjuna, the Lord of all beings dwells in the region of the heart," it is taught that the state of being the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all belongs to Śiva alone; for the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrtitva) is not seen anywhere else than in Nārāyaṇa, according to the Subāla-Upaniṣad and the Kaṇva and Mādhyandina recensions.
He provides an illustration for the difference in nature between the individual soul and Brahman:
"And because of [the case of] stones and so forth, that is untenable. (2.3.23)

"And like a stone, etc."—by means of the illustrative example of things of a different genus, such as stones, the impossibility of that [identity] is shown; the meaning is that the previously mentioned state of being Brahman, established by such scriptural texts as "This Self is indeed Brahman," is impossible and unattainable for the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, because it is eternally established as its very nature...

Just as the heterogeneous examples such as stone and so forth establish a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, so too is a homogeneous difference established. Just as there is a naturally established mutual difference among insentient things such as iron, stone, wood, trees, and shrubs,
likewise there is a natural mutual difference between the two sentient beings of the same genus, the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*), just as [it exists] in the earth.

Just as the difference between diamond, lapis lazuli, agate, topaz, emerald, and coral is seen, so too is the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) perceived. "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one attains immortality. [The perishable...]

The Pradhāna is the immortal and imperishable Hara; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through becoming His true essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (māyā). There are two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord; [the individual soul] is completely embraced by the conscious Self.
He is the eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of many. Indeed, there are two Brahmans.
When one perceives the higher and the lower among those things to be known—that which is cherished by the Lord, who is other than these—the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati) is the ruler of all creatures;
Rudra, the Great Seer, is superior to all, the sovereign of all sciences. We worship Tryambaka.
This mantra of the hand, which establishes the presence of Soma and Rudra in every mark, is the purifier of nectar.
Through such scriptural passages as "May I become the sustainer of the gods," the mutual distinction between the intrinsic natures of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is demonstrated.
If there were non-difference between the two, defects such as the impossibility of [Brahman] being the cause of the world in its forms of benefit and harm, as previously described, would follow.
The Section Concerning the Observation of the Bringing Together (Upasaṃhāra-darśana-adhikaraṇa) || 8 ||
This demonstrates the Supreme Lord’s power to bring about the impossible;

for even in the concluding statement "That thou art," there is a reference to Brahman as non-different from the individual soul (jīva), and because it would be impossible to negate that difference if the individual soul and Brahman were essentially distinct by nature, like a stone and a clod of earth or wood and a piece of timber.
Anticipating the objection that the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) belongs to Brahman alone and is merely superimposed, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, he says:
"If it be argued that [Brahman does not become the world] because we see [the material cause] withdrawn [into itself], we say no, for it is like milk. (Sūtra 2.1.24)

Since the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is seen in the opening statement, "Brahman is one, without a second," and also in the concluding statement, "That thou art" (tattvamasi), if one were to admit an innate difference between the two— as expressed in the intermediate passages through examples such as stone, clods of earth, and wood— then [the doctrine of] innate difference [would be contradicted].
If it is argued that cessation is not possible— as in the case of water and so forth— we say no;
for just as milk undergoes transformation through the cessation of its own nature into the form of curd by virtue of contact with buttermilk and other substances,
so too does the individual soul [undergo transformation] through the state of devotion accompanied by hearing, reflection, and so forth.

The attainment of Śiva-hood preceded by the cessation of innate individuality (jīvatva) is not at all contradictory. Since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is understood from such passages as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), while their non-difference is established in passages such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), a doubt arises as to whether that distinction is innate or adventitious.

That difference is merely adventitious, for it is impossible for an essential nature (svabhāva) to cease; even in cases such as water, where the essential nature is obscured by heat and the like, that very essential nature remains after a lapse of time. Otherwise, if one does not accept the scriptural declarations of non-difference, there would be the consequence of being non-Vedic—like the "half-old woman" maxim—with respect to the majesty of the Supreme Lord.
If it is argued that the cessation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is possible, we say no;

for we observe the birth of humans from humans and the birth of animals from animals, and thus it is more logical that [the appearance] is merely adventitious (*āgantuka*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. This being the position reached—
It is explained as follows: just as in the world, through the contact of milk with buttermilk and other substances,

there is the manifestation of the accomplishment of its transformation into curd— preceded by the cessation of the milk-nature established by its own essence— so too [is it] in the case of a bee born from the species of insects.
[It is] the attainment of a form identical to one's own, preceded by the cessation of the state of being a worm, which is distinct from its own species;
likewise [it belongs to Him who is] capable of both effecting and not effecting, endowed with all powers, affectionate toward His devotees,
the bestower of the fruits desired by His devotees, the refuge of all sciences, whose desires are true, and whose resolve is true.

Furthermore, [the attainment of one's own true nature by Paraśiva’s devotee], preceded by the cessation of the natural state of being a transmigrating soul (jīva) and characterized by freedom from rebirth—
this is established for Śiva in such Vedic scriptures as "The God alone, generating heaven and earth," and so forth.

Since it is heard in scripture that [the Supreme Lord] is the cause of the birth and so forth of the diverse world— such as space, wind, fire, and water— by way of being independent of external instruments,
and since it is observed that insentient hair and nails arise from a sentient person, and sentient scorpions and the like arise from insentient cow dung, therefore, of that Supreme Lord...
The capacity to bring about the impossible has been established.
In this regard, he shows an illustration: "And as in the world, [the gods and others do so]. (25)

Just as in the world, for those such as gods, sages, and perfected beings whose powers are limited and circumscribed, [the Lord]— through His own grace— first removes the ignorance, poverty, and other defects residing in the person who is His support,

and then bestows the splendor of liberation (*kaivalya*) consisting in the attainment of Himself, preceded by the removal of their status as ordinary living beings (*jīvatva*) and the conferral of the wealth of knowledge and His own natural devotion.

In such scriptural passages as these, and in the *Smṛti* which states, "Indeed, Śiva alone, the God, by the power of His will, manifests the multitude of objects existing within Him externally, without any material cause, just as a yogi does," it is heard that the Supreme Lord possesses infinite powers (*śakti*) characterized by the joining together of the accomplishment of what was previously impossible.
Therefore, there is no stain of doubt regarding the excellence of its greatness. This concludes the section on the consequence of total dissolution (Kṛtsnaprasaktyadhikaraṇa). 9.

Having thus established that the Supreme Lord possesses the power to grant the attainment of one's own Self, preceded by the cessation of His inherent state as a *jīva*, [the text proceeds] with the demonstration of the nature of Paraśiva-Brahman as consisting of both the manifest (*mūrta*) and the unmanifest (*amūrta*).
[The Sūtra] demonstrates that [Brahman] consists of both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta):

"If [Brahman were to transform entirely], there would be the consequence of its being completely exhausted, or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that it is partless. (2.1.26)
In the Vedāntas, is Brahman partless or possessed of parts? If it is partless, there follows the consequence of its being entirely consumed [in creation];

for if Brahman is all-pervasive, it would entail becoming limited during the creation of the universe. If it is possessed of parts, there is a contradiction with the scriptural term "partless," and the consequence of the invalidation of those Śrutis that establish its partlessness.
Therefore, because the Supreme Lord is autonomous, one must accept that He possesses both a formal (mūrta) and a formless (amūrta) nature.

[He is] the one whose self is Truth, who delights in vital breath, whose mind is bliss; who is without breath, without eyes, space-like, inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite consciousness, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman, accompanied by Umā.

From hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Tranquil One with the blue throat, the Sage goes to the Source of Beings," it is evident that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses both a manifest and unmanifest nature; and that through the worship of the manifest Śiva, one attains the fulfillment of all desires and reaches the partless Witness. Thus, His status as the cause of the universe [is established].
There is a doubt as to whether [Brahman] is partless or possesses parts.

Because those [scriptural passages] that establish Brahman as partless and those that establish Brahman as possessing parts are mutually contradictory—like darkness and light—both are indeed invalid. If both types of scriptural testimony were accepted...
There would be the consequence of the abolition of established order. Therefore, when it is argued that the status of Pradhāna or atoms as the cause of the world is logical, we reply:
because Śiva is independent, his nature as both manifest and unmanifest is logical. [Just as one may say] "one offers the oblation after sunrise" or "before sunrise."

Just as the performance of both [offerings] is established by the principle of "the accomplishment of both" (*ubhayasiddhi*) based on scriptural authority such as, "One should sacrifice with *yava* grains or one should sacrifice with *vrīhi* grains," so too here,

because we observe scriptural injunctions prescribing both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), both must indeed be enjoined. Even if there is predominance of only one part of those two, it would result in the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratī*) maxim.
The consequence of the invalidity of the Śruti would be difficult to avoid;

for [if Śiva were merely a part], he would have to reside as a constituent limb within the great Kailāsa and other non-material divine abodes, bestowing upon his devoted worshippers the threefold eternal auspicious manifestations such as *sālokya* and the rest.

It bestows upon those who worship the indivisible mass of consciousness (*cidghana*)—which is itself and free from all stains such as defects—the attainment of its own nature, which consists of the glory of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*). Therefore, both types of worship have been described. This is because, according to the principle that "when X exists, Y exists," the Purāṇas show that gods and others experience suffering through the assumption of a body.

If it is argued that for devotees who have attained the three types of liberation—such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and so forth—the experience of suffering upon assuming a body is unavoidable, we say no; for they possess a causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*). The experience of ordinary suffering and the like belongs only to those who possess bodies formed by meritorious and sinful karma. For those who are non-material (*aprākṛta*) and assume forms by their own will, there is no such restriction.

As it is seen in the Śruti: "When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa who is the source of Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, attains the stainless state of equality.
And by such statements as: "He is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech; from him words turn back, together with the mind, not having reached Him."

In response to the objection that, since Śiva is established as being beyond the reach of mind and speech, one should not admit that he possesses a body, the Sūtra says: "But on account of scripture, because [the Lord] has sound as His source" (2.1.27).

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). [This is supported by] such scriptural passages as: "I ask you about that person known through the Upaniṣads," "The supreme Brahman, the *ṛta* and the *satya*," "Smaller than the smallest," "We worship Tryambaka," "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One," and "The Self of this living being is hidden in the cave. In these and other texts, Śiva is the Supreme Brahman.

Because it is rooted in the Word (*śabda*), because the Veda is its authority, and by the force of the scriptural passages enjoining both [aspects], His nature consists of being partless, being the object of all worship, being distinct from all else, being the substratum of all, and so forth.
[Objection: But how can a single entity possess both difference and non-difference, both form and formlessness, both reality and unreality, and both knowledge and ignorance?

If it is argued that the relationship of cause and effect, as well as pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, or the state of being pervaded and not being pervaded, is untenable due to the contradiction of entities, this is charming only so long as it is not investigated; for these are established by both worldly experience and the Veda. In the world, [such relationships are seen] between clay and a jar, between a lamp and its light, between the moon and its moonlight, and between the sun and its heat.

Furthermore, there is both difference and non-difference between power and the possessor of power. Primordial matter (pradhāna) is formless in its causal state and possesses form in its state as an effect. Wind, by virtue of having parts, occupies only a portion of space, yet by virtue of being partless, it pervades the entire universe.

The snake perceived by direct perception is real, whereas the snake superimposed upon the rope is unreal. Pots and other objects are real insofar as they consist of clay, but unreal in their forms such as having a conch-like neck.
Objects like mountains depicted in a painting are unreal, while only those mountains that are capable of causal efficiency are real, as is the case with a firefly.

The state of being manifest and unmanifest; the possession of knowledge and ignorance by the individual soul (jīva); the sentience of a body within a single human frame and the insentience of its nails, hair, and teeth; the simultaneous presence of gods, lords of yogis, and others throughout all worlds; and [the presence] of space within its effects such as air, fire, water, and earth.

Both fullness and non-fullness are observed. And in the Veda it is shown: "Consciousness and unconsciousness, truth and untruth—[all] became the Truth. Therefore, because He possesses all powers and is independent, everything is without contradiction. "I am without hands or feet, yet I possess inconceivable power; I see without eyes..."

"I hear without ears; I perceive as one whose form is solitary, yet there is no knower of me"—by such passages, even in the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), his possession of all powers is heard of through his independence from the body, senses, and so forth. Therefore, it is Brahman alone, though possessed of parts, who is the cause of the creation and other processes of the diverse universe.
Regarding the demonstration that Brahman, though partless, is the cause of the universe,
[the author] speaks in response to the doubt: "How can Brahman, which is partless, possess parts and be the cause of the phenomenal world?"
And likewise in the self; for indeed, [the qualities] are manifold. || 28 ||

Just as various diverse constructions of the waking world— such as elephants, horses, and so forth— are observed during the time of dreaming by the power of one's own mind within the partless individual self (*jīvātman*) which is characterized by limited powers;
in the same way, [these are seen] within the supreme Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is characterized by all powers and is partless, through the power of His own *māyā*.
The conception of a manifold and diverse universe is thus established.

Furthermore, in the conscious Person (puruṣa), there are seen various insentient qualities such as hair and nails; likewise, among heterogeneous elements like water and fire, there are seen heterogeneous powers such as heat and so forth. [This is] darkness (tamas).

Since fire and water, though possessing mutually contradictory natures like light and darkness, are seen to coexist without contradiction in the ocean, and since the digestive fire is observed within the human body, nothing is impossible for Śiva, who transcends the world and possesses every supreme majesty.
As it was said by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa:
How can the agency of creation and so forth be attributed to Brahman, who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and stainless by nature?
To this question [the reply is]:
"The powers of all entities are within the domain of inconceivable knowledge;
therefore, those powers of being, such as creation and so forth, belong to Brahman."

"O best of ascetics, they exist through austerity, just as heat exists in fire. And the Śruti says: "What was the forest? What was that tree from which heaven and earth were fashioned? O wise ones, you ask with your minds; I declare to you from my mind: Brahman was the forest, Brahman was that tree. O wise ones, I speak this to you from my mind.
Because even in the Śruti and Smṛti it is seen that the partless Supreme Śiva alone is the agent—as in the text, "Brahman, upholding the worlds, presided over them"—that alone is logical.
[An objection: If the partless and qualityless Brahman is the cause of the world, then, like the individual soul (jīva), he must be subject to Māyā.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And because of the defect in one's own position" (sūtra 29).

Indeed, according to the maxim of the iron needle [being drawn out by its own magnetism], because of the defect in the non-dualist position— which teaches that the cause of the world-prakṛti is Brahman devoid of qualities due to the power of its existence—
and because of the defect of a partless prakṛti being the cause of the world, as well as the impossibility of purely insentient matter being the cause of the world.

Even if one accepts that the Pradhāna is the cause of the world through its proximity to Brahman—using the analogy of a magnet and a needle—the Brahman’s state of being devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣatva) is undermined. Since that power is dependent upon it, its possession of qualities (saguṇatva) is unavoidable.
Furthermore, it is impossible for the partless Pradhāna to undergo transformation into the diverse forms of the universe, such as the Mahat and so forth.

This has been accepted even by the Sāṃkhyas; likewise, Kaṇāda and others have also accepted that the world arises through the transformation of the form of the universe via the conjunction of partless, indivisible, spaceless, and insentient atoms (*paramāṇu*). Nevertheless, because an insentient entity cannot possess independence, its status as the cause [of the world] is untenable.
This is established by the very meaning of the word *brahman*. Therefore, the defect in your own position is unavoidable.
Since, according to the etymology "that which measures (*mā*) is *māyā*," *māyā* is understood to be like the horn of a hare;
thus, there would be a contradiction between the natures of reality and unreality in *māyā* and *brahman*, the former being insentient and the latter sentient.

In response to the objection that—since [the world] is mutually distinct from Brahman like a jar and a cloth, its connection [with Brahman] is impossible; since it is therefore impossible for Brahman to be the cause of the world; and since it is impossible for the changeless [Brahman] to possess a nature consisting of *māyā*—the theory that *māyā* is superimposed upon Brahman like a snake on a rope is the appropriate one—it says:
And by seeing that, she becomes endowed with everything. || 30 ||

"All these" refers to the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), which is distinguished by all powers such as the creation of the world and so forth. "From the vision of that" means from the vision of that Brahman, the Supreme Śiva; the meaning is because it is established by the Vedas, as in: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold."
"Intrinsic are His knowledge, power, and action; one should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the wielder of Māyā (māyin) as Maheśvara.

In such scriptural passages as "Indra, by means of Māyās, assumes many forms," the Supreme Lord—who is omnipresent and partless—is established as possessing all powers by His very nature. Therefore, Brahman is never at any time devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa).

He is the material cause of the world consisting of the three *guṇas*. Because he is characterized by two powers, his *māyā* is a distinct power (*bhinna-śakti*) and his *cit-śakti* is the non-distinct power (*abhinnā-śakti*). Thus, Śiva—autonomous, capable of effecting the impossible, and non-dual—remains of one and the same nature throughout the three periods of time. Of him...

If there were no distinction [between Brahman and the world], its status as the cause of the universe would be impossible. Thus, since it is observed that He possesses inherent power and is the cause of all things, the doctrine that this [world] is superimposed and false is not tenable.
This is the demonstration that Brahman is characterized by all powers.

To the objection that if Brahman is accepted as the cause of the world by virtue of possessing all powers, then defects such as being subject to modification and transformation—like clay and other materials—would necessarily follow, [the Sūtra] says: "If it be argued that this is not so because [Brahman] is devoid of organs, we say that has already been answered. (3.2.31)

If it is argued that because Brahman is devoid of instruments (*vikaraṇatvāt*)—as stated in passages such as "It has neither eyes nor ears, neither hands nor feet"—meaning it is devoid of the means consisting of a body, senses, and so forth, the status of Brahman as the cause of the world is not possible, then the answer to that has already been stated: "Because it is based on the Word (Śruti), and [the Lord's powers] are indeed manifold," and so on. For Brahman, the Veda is the sole authority.

Indeed, Brahman’s capacity for all effects is logically established precisely because of its lack of a body, sense organs, and so forth. And thus, the scripture is an authoritative source regarding the Blessed One: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears. This is also evident in such passages as, "Supreme is his power; all beings are but a foot of him," and so on.

The nature of Paraśiva, who possesses manifold and infinite powers, is described as being both identical with the universe through a single portion of his own power and inherently distinct from the universe. And in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"Of him whose ever-increasing desires for the universe are most wondrous..."
Salutations to Him who is distinct from all the worlds, in whose single fragment of power the entire path is fully contained— Him whom those who know the paths call the Lord of the Path.
Thus it has been shown. Therefore, Paramaśiva alone—who is the Lord of all and endowed with all powers—is that which must always be taken as refuge by those seeking liberation.
This concludes the refutation of the doctrine that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*).

If Brahman, which is without distinction and without modification, were the cause of the world, it would follow that it is subject to modification; therefore, having raised the objection that the causality of the world belongs only to Brahman as qualified by *māyā*, [the author] refutes it:
"No, because [the world-creation] has a purpose" (Sūtra 32).

Based on the scriptural vision that "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent," it is impossible for Brahman to ever be devoid of attributes, because it possesses a purpose; for in such passages as "from which these beings arise," the purpose of the creation and so forth of the world is seen to reside in Brahman alone.

Because [the scriptures] state, "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra," and so forth, it is understood that Brahman possesses a purpose. Furthermore, in such passages as, "May I become the sustainer of the immortal gods," and "He establishes all signs; the mantra is the purifier of the hand," [it is shown that He acts] for the sake of delivering His devotees from the gross, subtle, and causal bodies.

Because it is designated as having the purpose of sustaining [the self] in the form of the *liṅga* (subtle body) characterized as "desired," "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), and "state" (*bhāva*). It is "possessing a purpose" (*prayojanavān*) because it has a superior application (*prayojana*). Due to that state, the purpose is the superior application—that is, the conjunction—as the object of supreme love; it is the sustaining [of the self] in the form of the "desired" and other *liṅgas* within the gross and other bodies.

It is possible [that someone might resort to Him], yet according to the maxim that "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose," if there were no purpose for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), no one would resort to Him. Furthermore, for all devotees, a purpose consisting of results pertaining to this world or the next is not tenable if there is no distinction in the attainment of the fruit. Therefore:

The doctrine that Brahman is the cause [of the world] as qualified by Māyā—like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope—is indeed charming only so long as it is not investigated. For it is impossible for the insentient, unreal world, which is a reflection of Māyā, to be the cause of the universe, just as a reflection in water [cannot be the source of the water].

Furthermore, in such passages as "Without parts, actionless, tranquil... from this [Brahman] the vital breath is born," the state of being actionless is clearly indicated, [thus precluding such a causal role]. Regarding the birth of the world and so forth:

A doubt arises as to whether the causality belongs to the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣa-brahman*) or to the variegated [Brahman] endowed with attributes (*saviśeṣa-śabala*). Causality regarding the birth and so forth of the world is never possible in the case of Brahman as pure consciousness devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa-cinmātra*), because it is changeless (*nirvikāratva*), actionless (*niṣkriyatva*), and devoid of power (*niśśaktikatva*). Therefore, [causality belongs] to the Lord (*īśvara*) who is the variegated [Brahman] fashioned by the superimposed *māyā*.
When it is argued that its status as the cause of the world is thus established, the author states the final conclusion:

"Not so, because [the Lord] possesses a purpose. Since the scripture declares, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold," it is possible for Brahman to possess attributes; why? Because He possesses a purpose.

Since it is possible for the Brahman with attributes (*saviśeṣa-brahman*) alone to be the subject matter of all Vedāntas and to serve as the purpose— namely, the granting of all desired objects to gods and humans—
that doctrine of the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādin*) should be disregarded by those who uphold the doctrine of the Self (*adhyātmavādin*). To explain:

How can those who maintain that reality is devoid of distinctions state, "This is the means of valid cognition for the indistinct reality," given that all means of valid cognition have as their object reality possessed of distinctions? Furthermore, that convention established within one's own circle— that [reality] is proven by one's own experience— is also refuted by the self-witnessing experience of [the Self] as possessing distinctions.
Because all experiences have as their object something characterized by some particularity— as in the thought "I saw this"—
an experience that is being experienced as possessing particulars remains indeed with its particulars even when it is being abstracted as "indeterminate" through some fallacious statement;
for it persists as qualified by those unique, non-essential particulars distinct from pure existence (sattā) which serve as the grounds for such abstraction.
Therefore, since other specific qualities are excluded from an entity that is already distinguished by certain specific qualities, a qualityless entity is never established anywhere;
for consciousness is both characterized by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

Since the knower is perceived as having the nature of illuminating objects, and since there is indeed a specific experience during sleep, intoxication, and fainting, we shall establish this more thoroughly in its proper place. Furthermore, the many specific attributes such as eternality and so forth, which are accepted by [the opponent] themselves, certainly exist; and it cannot be established that these are merely the bare substance.

Even though there is an acceptance of the mere entity (*vastumātra*), since we observe disputes regarding its specific modes (*prakārabheda*) and since one's own position is established through the specific modes one favors, those who follow valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) must state that the entity is indeed qualified (*saviśeṣa*). In the case of words, however, their capacity for denotation is specifically directed toward an entity that is qualified.
Because it functions in the form of words and sentences; for a word-status arises through the conjunction of a stem (*prakṛti*) and an affix (*pratyaya*).
Due to the distinction between the meanings of the stem and the affix, it is inevitable that the word itself conveys a specific meaning.
Furthermore, the differentiation of words is based upon the differentiation of their meanings. This applies to that which consists of a collection of words...

Since a sentence, by virtue of expressing the specific relations between multiple word-meanings, lacks the capacity to convey a reality devoid of attributes, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a reality without attributes.

Furthermore, perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is divided into the categories of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), possesses no validity with respect to a reality devoid of attributes.

Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) has a qualified object precisely because its object is characterized by multiple categories such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) likewise has only a qualified object, because it serves as the cause for the subsequent recognition (*pratisandhāna*) of an object as qualified by those very categories experienced within itself. This is what is called non-conceptual cognition.
An entity is apprehended as being devoid of some particular attribute, but not as being devoid of all attributes;

for such a thing is never observed to be apprehended, nor is it logically possible. Indeed, every cognition arises in the form "this is thus" by virtue of some particular attribute. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct.
The Supreme Lord creates the world solely for the sake of His own divine play (*līlā*).
Anticipating the objection— "For what purpose does Śiva, whose nature is supreme bliss and who is partless, act as the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe?"— the author says:
But as in the world, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport. || 33 ||

It is determined that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, at times manifests the playful sport of *līlā*, while at other times he abides in absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) by himself; just as in the world, at times through the play of a great king who possesses the preeminence of all sovereignty, fortitude, heroism, and prowess, and who is the sovereign lord of all the circles of lands surrounded by the seven continents.
Furthermore, it is observed that there is both the initiation of activity and occasional remaining in silence; moreover,

just as for all sentient beings the movement of the vital breaths such as prāṇa and apāna occurs by virtue of their own nature, so too might the Supreme Śiva, who is the root of supreme bliss, follow after the effects such as the birth of the universe by his very nature.

It is beyond reproach that Śiva— who has attained all desires and whose very nature is supreme bliss— engages in the activity of initiating the world’s creation and other functions through his own divine play (līlā), and that he remains in that state by himself from after the dissolution until the next creation.
The Section on Inequality and Cruelty (Sūtra 10).

The refutation of defects such as partiality and cruelty in the Supreme Lord, who is supremely compassionate: [it is shown that] even though Paraśiva— who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and untainted (*nirlipta*)— is accepted as the cause of the world, there is no fault, because the creation of gods,
animals, humans, and so forth, in superior, inferior, and middling states, occurs in accordance with the respective merits and demerits (*dharma*) of beings, such as health and disease.
Anticipating the objection that defects such as partiality and cruelty are unavoidable—just as they are for a bound soul—the Sūtra states:
"Partiality and cruelty [do not apply] because [the Lord] has regard [for other factors]; for thus He shows. (2.1.34)

The objection that the Supreme Lord would be subject to partiality and cruelty because we observe living beings in the world experiencing pleasure and pain is not tenable; why? Because He is dependent—specifically, dependent upon the merit and demerit performed by the living beings. For the Śruti demonstrates this very point through its illuminating declarations.

Although it may be conceivable that Śiva, the Supreme Person, being possessed of his inherent power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), can be the cause of the birth and so forth of the diverse and manifold universe even though he is partless,
nevertheless, through his creation of gods, animals, humans, and others— ranging from the highest to the middling and the lowest— he appears to exhibit partiality, like a bound soul (*baddhajīva*).

It would follow [that Paraśiva is subject to faults]. If it is argued that because the qualities of heaven, hell, pleasure, pain, and so forth are manifested within sentient beings, the defects of Paraśiva such as cruelty (*nairdhṛṇya*) need not be avoided, we reply: "No, because of dependence.
Since the bodies of the gods and others being created depend upon the karma of the individual souls (*jīva*), an unequal creation is unavoidable.
Indeed, the Śrutis demonstrate that the lives of gods and others depend upon their respective karmas: "One who performs good deeds becomes good;
one who performs evil deeds becomes evil; one becomes virtuous through virtuous action; one becomes sinful through sinful action. And likewise, it was stated by Vyāsa:
He is merely the instrumental cause in the act of creating those things to be created,
since the powers of the objects to be created are indeed the primary causes.
It has been said that it is merely a sign; nothing else is required.
O best of ascetics, by its own power, a thing is led to its true state as a reality.

By these and other such statements, it has been declared that the cause of the diversity among gods and others is precisely the power of the past karma of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) being created;

thus, the refutation of the doctrine of the world’s falsity is established. Furthermore, Śiva’s dependence upon merit and demerit is logically consistent with respect to intermediate creation, but not with respect to the primordial creation.

Since there would be an absence of merit and demerit for living beings, the defects of partiality and cruelty would indeed be unavoidable if the attributeless Brahman were the creator. Therefore, raising the objection that it is more logical for this illusory world to have as its cause the illusory, variegated (śabala) Brahman, he says:

If it is argued that [the distinction between souls] does not exist because of the non-distinction of karma, we say no; for [karma] is beginningless, and this is both logically consistent and observed in experience. || 35 ||

If it is argued that prior to creation there can be no karma for living beings because of their lack of differentiation— since at the time of dissolution the entire manifest world of sentient and insentient things perishes and thus karma is also destroyed— we say no, because [karma] is beginningless. Due to the uninterrupted succession of cycles of creation and dissolution according to the analogy of waves in a stream, the manifest world is indeed beginningless.

Because the karmas of living beings performed during a previous creation remain in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) even during the dissolution, like a state of sleep, it is logical that they manifest again at the time of a new creation, as they depend upon the meritorious and sinful actions performed by those beings. Furthermore, this is observed to occur again at the time of dissolution; through the will of the Supreme Lord, [the world] attains a subtle state. Therefore...

The adherence to the reality of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is unavoidable. If it is asked: "How is the existence of individual souls (*jīvas*) in Brahman in a subtle state prior to creation logically established? And how can the inequality of creation be said to depend upon the prior karma performed by those souls?"—the answer is:
because [this process] is beginningless, according to the analogy of the waves in a continuous stream, both the souls and their performed karmas [are eternal].

Thus, non-distinction is also logically established by its beginninglessness; for at that time, the existence of the individual souls (jīvas) in a subtle form is possible, just as seeds exist in the earth during the summer season. Likewise, it is accepted that their karmas also exist in this same manner.

If this were not accepted, the faults of the destruction of what has been done (kṛtanāśa) and the acquisition of what has not been done (akṛtābhyāgama) would ensue. Therefore, regarding the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas)...
Furthermore, the beginninglessness of those respective actions is unavoidable. Therefore, the reality of creation is taught as being in the form of a continuous stream;

for, by establishing the beginninglessness of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) in the verse "The Knower and the Unknower" (*jñājñau*), the beginninglessness of their respective actions is also established by implication.

Now, one might object: let it be granted that both the individual souls (*jīva*) and their respective actions (*karman*) are beginningless; nevertheless, it is precisely because Paraśiva fashions the bodies of the souls that those various actions become possible. Since insentient actions must have a sentient agent as their purpose, it follows by implication that the Lord alone must be the cause of those respective actions. [This is so] because, like deep sleep, the souls experience the bliss of absorption into their own self.

How could there be a creation consisting of further entry into a body that is the locus of all afflictions? Therefore, he is merciless. If it is argued that creation exists because, in the absence of souls entering bodies, they would lack the attainment of their own grace and liberation from all afflictions, even so—

If it is asked, "Why is His own glory, consisting of auspicious liberation (*kaivalya*), not bestowed at one and the same time upon all *kṣetrajñas* by means of His grace so that they may be released from the bonds of all karma?"— the answer is: although Śiva is supremely compassionate and capable of granting liberation to all *kṣetrajñas* simultaneously, [He does not do so].
Just as a sovereign of the earth, in accordance with his own command and following the ripening of an individual's karma,

effects the severing of their bonds; even a lord in the world does not, without his own punishment, make one who transgresses his command a recipient of his favor— even if that person is his own son— so too is the Supreme Lord.

Without the preservation of the merit and demerit performed by the individual soul (*jīva*), [the Lord] does not bestow His own attainment. Just as the Sun (*prabhākara*) causes only those lotuses favorable to blooming to open by the spreading of His own radiance, so too does the Lord [act]. Is it not stated in such scriptural passages as, "He indeed makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead to the higher world," and so forth?

If it is argued that because the Supreme Lord alone is heard in scripture to be the controller of the individual soul (jīva), there is nothing whatsoever to be done by the soul, and therefore the defects of partiality and cruelty would accrue to Him—that is incorrect. For although individual souls lack the omniscience and omnipotence of the Supreme Lord, they possess consciousness; consequently, they possess limited knowledge and limited agency.

It arises by its own will; therefore, the experience of karma performed according to one's own will belongs only to individual souls (*jīva*). Just as in the world humans and others engage in their respective activities in accordance with the light of the sun, so too do the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) perform various actions according to their own karma, under the power of the existence of the Supreme Lord. Having meditated...

"The sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness"—thus the venerable Śruti demonstrates his status as the witness of all, like the sun. Therefore, he is untainted by the stain of defects. Consequently, it is established that the beginninglessness and the dependence upon the Supreme Lord of the individual soul, the world, and karma are proven, just as [the Lord ordains] the sun and the moon.
In such Vedic passages as "In the beginning He fashioned [the world]; the wise one is neither born nor does he die," and so forth, it is stated:
"The Self, the Great Lord, is of the nature of truth and knowledge, infinite and all-pervading;
His very portion resides in the hearts of living beings in the world of souls."
Just as sparks arise from fire through contact with wood,
so too do the portions of the Great Lord arise from the connection with beginningless karma.
Endowed with beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), he is celebrated as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
and the devotion to Śiva is for all people at all times and in every respect.
While she exists, whatever mortal is liberated—
provided his mind is devoted to Śiva— is liberated, even if he be an outcaste.
Thus it is indicated in the *Śivagītā Upaniṣad* that both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are indeed beginningless, and likewise in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*. Therefore, he is not tainted by any blemish.
This concludes the section concerning the compatibility of all attributes (*sarvadharmopapattyadhikaraṇa*).

Scriptural passages enjoining actionlessness, such as "partless," "actionless," and "quiescent," have as their object the foundational Brahman (*adhiṣṭhāna-brahman*). One must accept that scriptural passages such as "whose desires are true" and "whose resolves are true" refer exclusively to the variegated Brahman (*śabala-brahman*) reflected through *māyā*.
If this were not the case, then due to mutual contradiction, the consequence that all the Vedāntas would lack authority would be unavoidable; in response to this doubt, he says:
"And because all attributes are possible [in Brahman]. (36)

In the passage "But for the world, [it is] mere sport" (*lokavattu līlākaivalyam*), it is established that at one time the purpose of Brahman is sport (*līlā*), while at another time He remains in Himself; thus, there is no contradiction with attributes such as omniscience, which are established by such scriptural texts as "He who is all-knowing, he who knows all," "Salutation to Vāmadeva," and "For Him there exists neither effect nor instrument."
The state of time as the play (*līlā*) of the Supreme Lord refers to the state of the contraction of His own powers (*sva-śakti-saṃkoca*) regarding attributes such as actionlessness (*niṣkriyatva*).

Therefore, all attributes—whether qualified (*saguṇa*) or unqualified (*nirguṇa*)—are established as belonging to the one Supreme Śiva alone. "Rudra is indeed one; there is no second for him," and "Brahman is indeed one, without a second."

Because such scriptural passages declare the oneness of Brahman; because that which is imagined as being variegated by *māyā*—like a reflection of one's own face—possesses existence; because there can be no reflection of that which is all-pervading and partless;
and because attributes such as the opening of the eyes, which reside in the reflection of one's own face, must belong to oneself alone.

It is established that the curses of Gautama, Dadhīci, Vyāsa, and others— which contradict direct perception, the Śrutis, and the Smṛtis— and which are favorable toward Śiva, are to be disregarded and not relied upon by devotees of Śiva.
Some men, resorting to Advaita, are like cats.
Those who are deluded proclaim the equality of others with Rudra.
Those lowest of Brahmins who were cursed by Dadhīci and Gautama will descend into the Kali age as revilers; such men shall be excluded from the community.
Cursed by Dadhīci, Vyāsa, and Dūrvāsas, those lowest of the twice-born in this world fall into the ocean of hell by resorting to the view that the universe is illusory.
And by establishing the falsity of the Lord of the world and of all living beings,
they will abandon their state of devotion and go to the abode of Yama.
A person who proclaims "I am Brahman" while devoid of devotion to the deities goes to a most terrible hell for an inexhaustible period of time.
Since the doctrine that the world is illusory has been refuted in the Skanda, Laiṅgya, Kūrma, and other Purāṇas,
it is beyond dispute that seekers of liberation should take refuge in the Vedāntic teaching that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the cause of the world's birth and so forth.

Thus ends the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics, which establishes the nature of both difference and non-difference.

The first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, which is devoted to the refutation of contradictions and consists of thirty-six sūtras divided into eleven topical sections (adhikaraṇas), beginning with "Smṛti has no scope" (Smṛty-anavakāśa), is completed.
The Pañcapādikā is completed.
The Pañcapādikā for the sake of the middling practitioner. The Śivādvaitamañjarī commentary on the Śrīkaṇṭha Bhāṣya.
Now begins the second quarter of the second chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya.
Introduction to the Second Quarter.
