In this first chapter (pāda), the opposing views— namely those of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Vaiśeṣika, Advaita, and other schools— are refuted for the purpose of establishing one's own position, which is the doctrine of non-dualism-within-dualism (dvaitādvaita) as established by all the Vedāntas.
In the section concerning "Iksati" (Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa), the primacy of Pradhāna as the cause of the world is rejected on the grounds that it is not taught by the Vedas.

The fact that Brahman is the cause has been established; however, here, in response to the objection that it is more logical for *pradhāna* (primordial matter) to be the cause of the world based primarily on fallacious reasoning, this [objection] is refuted once again by demonstrating its consistency with sound logic. Thus, there is no fault of redundancy.
By means of this refutation of the wicked doctrines of the Sāṃkhyas and others, [the path is cleared] for those seeking liberation.

Because this chapter strengthens the steadfastness of those established in the pure Vedic path, it has a topical connection (*saṅgati*) with the preceding chapter on the non-contradiction of the Vedas.

Furthermore, since the establishment of one's own position— preceded by the removal of contradictions regarding the harmony (*samanvaya*) of all Vedānta texts— was already accomplished in the previous chapter, there is a relationship of mutual dependence (*upajīvyopajīvaka-bhāva*) between these two successive chapters.

Since it is impossible to know one's own position and established doctrine in the absence of a refutation of opposing views, it is explained that the first section (pāda) serves as a necessary foundation (*upajīvya*) by virtue of being the cause for establishing one's own position. Precisely because they are devoted to the refutation of opposing views,
the essential connection (*sārasaṅgati*) of all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) has been taught.
The Section on the Impossibility of Creation (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

Regarding the objection that, according to the final sūtra of the preceding section (*sarvadharmopapatteśca*), it is established in the Siddhānta that the attributes such as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and possessing qualities (*saguṇatva*) are possible through the contraction and expansion of the power (*śakti*) of Paramaśiva, and that the Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) could likewise be the cause of the contraction and expansion of those attributes:
The intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) for this [section] consists in its initiating a formal discussion (*adhikaraṇa*) for the purpose of refuting that [position]. In this regard,

the result— determined by both the opening and the conclusion— is the harmonization (*samanvaya*) of the doctrines of difference-and-non-difference established by all the Vedānta texts, preceded by the refutation of fallacious arguments that contradict the Veda.
And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, inference is not valid; and because of [the nature of] activity. (1)

The Pradhāna, which is established through inference as the cause of the world, cannot be the primary cause. Why? Because of the impossibility of design—since it is impossible for the insentient Pradhāna, which lacks knowledge of itself or others, to be the cause of the world's creation. Furthermore, because of the activity of the insentient.
Furthermore, because effort itself is untenable, the Pradhāna cannot be the cause of the world. This is due to its lack of volition.

Since Sāṃkhya is respected by the learned for its conformity with Vedānta, there arises a doubt as to whether the Pradhāna’s status as the material cause of the world mentioned therein is based on valid cognition or on delusion.
The status of *pradhāna* as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is indeed rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are both nature and evolute;
the group of sixteen is evolute only; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor evolute."

Thus concludes the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. That which is called *mūlaprakṛti* (primordial nature) consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which are composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion; whose effects are lightness, illumination, motion, support, heaviness, and obstruction; which are entirely beyond the senses; which are distinguished solely through their effects; which do not exceed nor fall short [of one another]; and which have attained a state of equilibrium.

The substances. And that primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of the equilibrium of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is one, itself insentient, exists for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of many sentient beings, is eternal, all-pervading, constantly undergoing transformation, and is not a modification of anything else, but rather the ultimate cause itself.

The seven beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are its transformations and are also the primal natures (prakṛtis) of others: the Great Principle, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and the five subtle elements—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. These are respectively the sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa [forms of ego].

Among them, the vaikārika is sāttvika and is the source of the sense organs and so forth; the bhūtādi is tāmasa and is the cause of the subtle elements (tanmātras), which in turn are the causes of the gross elements.

The *taijasa* (fiery) is *rājasa* and is the sustainer of both. The five great elements beginning with space (*ākāśa*), the five organs of cognition beginning with hearing (*śrotra*), the five organs of action beginning with speech (*vāk*), and the mind (*manas*)—these sixteen are exclusively modifications (*vikāra*).
The Person (*puruṣa*), however, because it is without measure (*niṣparimāṇa*), is neither the material cause (*prakṛti*) of anything nor a modification (*vikṛti*) of anything; for this very reason:
The Self is devoid of objective qualities (*nirdharmaka*), consisting solely of consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), eternal, inactive (*niṣkriya*), all-pervading, and distinct in each body.

Because it is changeless and inactive, agency and enjoyership are not possible for it. Nevertheless, even though such is the reality, the deluded [claim] that the consciousness of the Puruṣa arises merely through the proximity of Prakṛti and Puruṣa.

Having superposed the agency of *prakṛti* upon *puruṣa*, and having superposed the redness of a hibiscus flower upon a crystal gem, they think, "I am the agent, I am the enjoyer. Thus, from ignorance comes bondage (*bhoga*), and from the knowledge of reality comes liberation (*apavarga*). This very point they establish through perception, inference, and authoritative testimony (*āgama*). In that regard:

Regarding those categories of reality established through direct perception, there is no ground for dispute with you. Furthermore, scripture (*āgama*) is authoritative because it is demonstrated to be rooted in the knowledge of omniscient beings such as Kapila.
Moreover, [it teaches] that the general characteristics of *prakṛti* consist precisely of the threefold suffering and delusion, such as internal and other afflictions.

Because the primary cause (pradhāna) is observed to be inherent in the manifold world (prapañca), it alone is appropriately the material cause (upādāna) of the universe; for whatever is inherent in something is its material cause, as in the case of a jar and so forth. According to the principle that the attributes of the cause are transferred to the effect, the attributes of insentience, suffering, delusion, and so on, which reside in the primary cause, are present in the manifold world.
Since that very [pradhāna] is the material cause of the world because of its luminosity, this being the position reached, it is resolved as follows:
In the section concerning the lack of scope for Smṛti, the Sāṅkhya scripture was refuted;

and in the section beginning with "And because of the impossibility of construction," [it was shown that] since your proposed pradhāna is insentient, it cannot be an "inference" (anumāna) in the sense of that which is inferred.
The state of being the cause of the manifold diversity consisting of various types of both conscious and unconscious entities is not possible. Why?

Because of the impossibility of such an arrangement (*racanānupapatti*). Since they are insentient, they lack mutual awareness; thus, the arrangement of the diverse and manifold world is impossible. For example, in the world, [the construction of] pavilions, gate-towers, ramparts, and so forth—

Because we observe the construction of pavilions and the like, and because this demonstrates the commencement of such effects through the superintendence of a conscious being, it is not taught that the insentient *pradhāna* is the independent material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.
The two occurrences of the word "and" (*ca*) serve to aggregate the lack of invariable concomitance (*anaikāntyam*); for whiteness is not invariably concomitant [with being a product].
"Cowness and so forth are pervaded by causality. This means:

let it be that qualities such as whiteness, even when co-present [in an effect], do not possess causality; however, substances such as gold, which are themselves co-present in their effects, certainly possess the pervasion of causality. For existence (*sattva*) and the other [qualities] are also substances that are co-present in their effects.

Nor should it be argued that [the qualities] are excluded from being causes; for while *sattva* and the others are attributes (*dharma*) of substance, they are not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of substance itself.
Furthermore, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are merely specific modifications of the nature of substances such as earth, acting as the causes of lightness, illumination, and so forth.
They are not perceived as being conjoined with effects by way of being substances like clay or gold. And thus, *sattva* and the others are indeed called "qualities" (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, that which was asserted—the fact that the world has a single root—in order to establish the fixed nature of its cause, is also untenable because *sattva* and the other qualities (*guṇas*) are manifold. For this very reason, the fixed nature of the cause is not established; for according to their doctrine, the *pradhāna* is nothing other than *sattva* and the others in a state of equilibrium. Thus, due to the multiplicity of causes, there is an infinite regress.

The situation remains exactly the same. Furthermore, their status as established entities cannot be proven through their being infinite; for if all three were indeed infinite, they would be omnipresent, and since there would be no deficiency or excess, disparity could not be established. Consequently, the commencement of an effect would be impossible.
Therefore, for the very purpose of initiating an effect, their finitude must necessarily be accepted.

An objection is raised: "But surely, in the case of chariots and the like, the fact of being presided over by a conscious agent is clearly observed; therefore, everything other than those [examples] has been made the subject of the proposition (pakṣa).
Anticipating this, he says: "If it be argued that it is like milk and water, [we reply] that even in that case... (Sūtra 2).

If it is argued that just as milk existing in the udders moves independently, so too the insentient *pradhāna* acts independently as the cause of the world, beginning with the *mahat* and the *ahaṃkāra*, the meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that even in those cases of milk and water, there is no independence because they are impelled by the Supreme Lord.

Here there is another meaning as well: it has been stated that the creation of the diverse world is impossible for the insentient *pradhāna*, but that is not so, because activity is observed to occur like that of milk and water. For instance, when milk transforms into the state of curd, a succession of transformations—from its initial movement onwards—occurs spontaneously, independent of anything else.

Thus it is established. And just as water released from a cloud, though possessing a single taste, is seen to assume various forms upon reaching the coconut, the palm, the mango, and other trees; so too, the primary cause (pradhāna), which by its very nature undergoes transformation, even when unguided by another and remaining in a similar state of transformation during the period of dissolution (pratisarga), [assumes diverse forms] in the state of creation (sarga).
The diverse transformation caused by the inequality of the *guṇas* is thus established. As it has been said:

"By way of transformation, like water, due to the specific differences in the substrates of each individual *guṇa*. If it is argued that this very unmanifest (*avyakta*) proceeds independently of anything else—

We say that this applies there as well. As for the examples of milk, water, and so forth that were pointed out, even in those cases, activity is not possible without the superintendence of the Intelligent One (prājña). The intention is that those too have been made the subject of the previous argument.
[The Rudra who is in the fire...]

Since the status of being the impeller of all through the state of inner controller (*antaryāmin*) is established as belonging to the Supreme Lord alone in passages such as "In the waters" (*apsu*), it is determined that even the flowing, moving, and transforming of milk and water is dependent upon the Supreme Lord; for an insentient entity lacks independence.
He states another reason: "And because of the non-establishment of exclusion and because of independence. (3)

In the system of the followers of Kapila, because there is no establishment of a distinction— since they do not accept the existence of a Lord who is distinct from *pradhāna* as its impeller— and because [the latter] is independent due to its autonomy, the creation of the manifold world (*prapañca*) by *prakṛti* would occur at all times; and since that [world] has *pradhāna* as its material cause...

Because it would follow that there could be no dissolution of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) consisting of the sentient and the insentient; and because Paraśiva, being omniscient, is observed to possess knowledge of time. Thus, it is logical that he possesses the play (*līlā*) of creating the universe at certain times while remaining in a state of silence, and at other times remains in a state of absolute isolation (*kevalāvasthā*). This is not possible for *pradhāna*, which is devoid of intelligence.
Furthermore, because it lacks the capacity for knowledge of time—like the analogy of the blind and the lame—the state of being the cause of the world is never tenable.

Moreover, if [Prakṛti] were to undergo transformation independently of the superintendence of a Lord whose will is true, it would follow that there could be no state of dissolution apart from creation; thus, Pradhāna, when not presided over by the Intelligent One (Prājña), cannot be the cause.

When it is presided over by the Wise One (prājña), the establishment of the order of creation, re-creation, and various emanations is achieved through His power of true resolve (satya-saṅkalpa). Even though it is presided over by the Wise One, He has attained all desires, is perfectly complete,
possesses unsurpassed and infinite bliss, and is faultless and stainless.

One should not argue that this same defect applies [to the Sāṃkhya view] because there would be no cause for the regulation of creation and dissolution, and because it would follow that the Creator is merciless in creating an unequal world; for even though He is perfect, His activity is possible for the sake of sport (līlā), and as the Omniscient One,
He possesses the specific causes for the distinctions of creation and dissolution in the form of His perception of primordial nature (prakṛti) as it undergoes particular transformations.

Furthermore, it is because the very actions of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) establish the arrangement of the diverse creation. Now, one might object: "If all states are accomplished solely by the meritorious and sinful actions of the *kṣetrajñas*, what is the use of a Lord as a presiding director? Nature (*prakṛti*) itself, conditioned by the performed actions consisting of merit and demerit, [is sufficient]."

It will transform in such and such a manner according to the specific arrangement corresponding to human purpose; likewise, it is observed that the specific transformation of food, drink, and so forth—which become causes of pleasure or pain when they are either corrupted by poison and the like or nourished by special medicines—depends on the conditions of place, time, and state. Furthermore:

If you argue that the established order of creation and dissolution, as well as the unequal creation of gods and others and the state of liberation, are possible only for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) which possesses the power of transformation in all its modes— then you are ignorant of the nature of meritorious and non-meritorious karma. For the nature of merit and demerit is to be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*).

The scripture (*śāstra*) is the mass of syllables known as the Veda, which has no beginning or end and whose recitation is uninterrupted. Furthermore, it cannot tolerate even the scent of defects such as negligence, which might arise from a lapse in the oral tradition. And merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*), consisting respectively of actions that propitiate the Supreme Person and those contrary thereto, are dependent upon His grace and His restraint.

And he says that pleasure and pain are the fruits thereof. Thus Bhaṭṭācārya states: "By the desire for the fruit, they seek to please the Self with their actions; 'Being pleased, He is sufficient for the fruit'—such is the limit of the scripture. And so says the Śruti:
"The navel of the world sustains the universe—the performed sacrifice and the pious work, the manifold, that which has been born and that which is being born."
And thus it was said by the Blessed One himself:
"Since from Him the activity of beings proceeds, and since by Him all this is pervaded,
a person attains perfection by worshipping Him through his own duty."
"I hurl those hateful, cruel, and most base of men, the inauspicious ones, perpetually into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence"—thus [it is said].
That Blessed One, Mahādeva, has attained all his desires; he is omniscient, the Lord of all, and one whose resolve is ever-true.

Engaged in divine play (līlā) consistent with His own majesty, He established the duality of actions by designating "these actions are right" and "those actions are wrong"; then, having generally bestowed upon all individual souls (kṣetrajñas) the appropriate bodies, senses, and so forth for their worship, as well as the power to govern them, He revealed the scripture that makes His own command known.
For the purpose of withdrawing them, [the Supreme Lord] remains having entered within as the inner self (antarātman) and as the permissive director (anumantṛ).

However, the individual knowers of the field (kṣetrajña), possessing powers bestowed by Him, having their causal bodies and so forth assigned by Him and resting upon Him as their support, themselves undertake meritorious and non-meritorious actions according to their own will. And from that—

Knowing one who performs meritorious deeds to be a follower of his own teaching, he causes that person to prosper through virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; and one who transgresses the teaching, he joins with the opposites thereof.
Therefore, objections regarding a lack of independence or other such deficiencies find no ground.

Compassion (*dayā*), indeed, is defined as the inability to endure the suffering of others, regardless of one's own self-interest. Yet, even when directed toward one who is intent on transgressing one’s own teachings, it does not conduce to virtue; on the contrary, it brings about impotence. In such a case, restraint alone is the virtue. Otherwise—

Because it would follow that the subjugation of enemies and such acts would lack merit; rather, by the mere cessation of his resolve to prevent others from following his own teaching and by not taking account of the infinite offenses committed against him throughout beginningless and endless kalpas due to their engagement with evil objects, he himself proceeds toward the increase of unsurpassed bliss. As it has been said:
To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love,
I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.

Thus, the Pradhāna is not the cause of the world. Anticipating the objection that the insentient Pradhāna might be the material cause of the universe by its own independence— since it is observed that objects such as grass eaten by a cow undergo transformation into the form of milk and so forth— the author says:
And because it does not exist elsewhere, [the soul] is not like grass and such. || 4 ||

If it is argued that—just as grass and other substances transform into the form of milk and so forth without depending on any other external cause—it is possible for the insentient *pradhāna* likewise to transform into the manifold forms of the great principle (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), and so on; we say no. For how can it be logical for even grass to possess such transformation independently?

And because it does not exist elsewhere: since grass and other substances existing in the belly of a bull cannot undergo transformation into the form of milk [on their own], if one were to admit that they transform independently, it would follow as an absurd consequence that the grass and other things eaten by all animals would likewise transform into the form of milk. Therefore, it is only through the impulsion of Paramaśiva that grass and the like transform into the form of milk.

The state of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) is thus designated. If it were admitted that the *pradhāna* undergoes transformation by itself, the consequence would follow that it has no need for the *puruṣa*. If the insentient *pradhāna* could spontaneously accomplish the purpose of the *puruṣa*, it would follow that objects such as jars could spontaneously perform the function of drawing water. Even if it were [admitted] that the *pradhāna* is presided over by intelligence (*prajñādhiṣṭhita*), the *pradhāna*...

If it is argued that [the Pradhāna] accomplishes the purpose of a conscious being, then it is entirely dependent upon God, because an insentient entity cannot, by its very nature, undergo transformation through a desire for an object that accords with the intention of a conscious being; thus, the Pradhāna is not in reality the material cause of the world.
He then presents another reason:
If it is argued that it is like a man and a stone, even so [the objection remains]. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "like a man and a stone": just as in the world the operation of the senses toward their objects occurs due to the proximity of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), and just as the movement of iron needles and the like occurs due to the proximity of magnets,
so too does the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) assume the form of the world beginning with the *mahat* (intellect) through the proximity of Supreme Śiva.
If it is argued that transformation occurs [due to the presence of the Puruṣa], even so, there follows the consequence of the impossibility of liberation from the defects (doṣas). To explain:
if the Pradhāna is impelled by the Puruṣa, there is a contradiction with your own tenet that the Pradhāna is independent;
for if it were an immutably constant (kūṭastha) entity, its status as such would be lost, since it is impossible for something to be an instigator without its own activity.
For even a cripple possesses the activity of speech.

The activity of a magnet is merely its proximity to iron. Since the proximity of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* is eternal, it cannot constitute an activity. If even that which is eternal were to constitute an activity, there would be faults such as the non-cessation of the activity of *pradhāna*.
They must be observed. Therefore, due to its proximity to that [Puruṣa], the Pradhāna cannot possess independence either.

Although the Puruṣa, whose nature is pure consciousness, is inactive, and the Pradhāna is likewise devoid of the power of vision, nevertheless the insentient Pradhāna proceeds to act due to the proximity of the Puruṣa; for so it is observed.

Due to the proximity of a lame man who lacks the power of locomotion but possesses the power of sight, the blind man—who lacks the power of sight but possesses the power of activity—is impelled by that consciousness and proceeds. Iron moves due to the proximity of a magnet.
In this same way, the creation of the world proceeds, brought about by the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. As it has been said:

If it is argued that "the union of both is like that of the lame and the blind—the purpose of the Puruṣa being perception and the purpose of the Pradhāna being isolation—and from that [union] creation is produced," the reply here is: "Even so.
Even in this way, the impossibility of the activity of the Pradhāna remains exactly as it was; for even in the case of the lame man, who lacks the power of locomotion...

There are thousands of specific instances, such as the vision of the path and its instruction, which occur only occasionally; even a blind sentient being proceeds by understanding those instructions. Similarly, there is the movement toward a magnet by iron and so forth; however, for the Puruṣa, who is devoid of action, this is not the case.
Such transformations would be impossible. Since mere proximity is eternal, there would be the consequence of an eternal creation;
and since [the soul] would be eternally liberated, there would be an absence of bondage and consequently an absence of liberation. Therefore, *pradhāna* is not the cause.
He states another reason:
Because the status of being the principal [member] is untenable. || 6 ||

Furthermore, since the three *guṇas* existing in a state of equilibrium at the time of dissolution cannot enter into a relationship of mutual subservience (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) without the impulsion of the Lord, the creation of the world consisting of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* manifestations would be impossible;
for it is precisely from the relationship of mutual subservience, based on the relative superiority and inferiority of the three *guṇas*, that such creation occurs.
You maintain that the activity of the world proceeds according to the specific qualities (*guṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) for each individual;

however, during the state of dissolution (*pratisarga*), because the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* exist in a state of equilibrium, there is an absence of mutual superiority or inferiority among them. Consequently, since the relationship of primary and subordinate cannot arise, the evolution of the world is not possible. Nevertheless...
If inequality were admitted [as a primordial state], it would follow that creation is eternal; therefore, the *pradhāna* is not the material cause of the world.

Furthermore, it is impossible for the three *guṇas* to function with equal predominance. Rather, in a creation characterized by *sattva*, the *sattva* quality is predominant while the other two are subordinate; the same applies to creations characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Anticipating the objection that "it is precisely the Pradhāna, characterized by various natures according to the difference in time, that is inferred," he refutes it:
"And because [the Pradhāna] would be devoid of the power of cognition in such an inference. (7)

Otherwise— even if it were admitted that the Pradhāna is inferred as being characterized by various inherent natures— it could never be the material cause of the world, because, being insentient, it is devoid of the power of cognition; and due to the absence of the power of cognition, it is incapable of knowing specific times.
It is possible.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
"Because even when [the cause] is admitted, the object is absent" (sūtra 8).
Even if it is admitted— that is, even if one accepts that the insentient *pradhāna* undergoes transformation independently without being presided over by an intelligent principle—

the production of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is untenable because the *pradhāna*, being insentient, lacks a purpose, such as the goals of enjoyment (*bhoga*) or liberation (*mokṣa*). Even if the existence of the *pradhāna* is accepted on the basis of inference, [the *pradhāna*]...
It should not be inferred [that the *pradhāna* exists] because there is no purpose for it.
For it is said, "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s seeing and for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *pradhāna*";
thus, the purposes of the *pradhāna* are intended to be the experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) of the Puruṣa. And those two are not possible for the Puruṣa.
For that which consists solely of the essence of consciousness— being inactive, changeless, and stainless, and therefore by that very fact eternally liberated in its true nature—
neither enjoyment, which consists in the perception of *prakṛti*, nor liberation, which consists in separation from it, is possible. Yet, for such a being,
there arises the possibility of enjoyment in the form of perceiving pleasure through a specific transformation, due to the proximity of *prakṛti*.

Since the proximity of *prakṛti* is eternal, liberation could never be established. However, it is logical that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is devoid of any personal motive, is the creator of the world through his divine play (*līlā*). Since play is impossible for the insentient *pradhāna*, its status as the cause of the world is untenable.
He states another reason: "And because of contradiction, it is inconsistent. (9)
And because of contradiction—furthermore, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is inconsistent and untenable because it contradicts all the Vedānta texts. This system of the Sāṃkhyas is internally contradictory;
for instance, [they maintain] that *prakṛti* is a distinct category, is an object of perception, and is an object of enjoyment.
Having accepted the Puruṣa as the enjoyer, the presiding controller, the seer, and the witness of Prakṛti,
and asserting that even its liberation (kaivalya) is to be attained through Prakṛti alone acting as the means,
they declare that because its nature consists solely of eternal, changeless consciousness, it is a non-agent and that liberation is its very own nature. Therefore...
Thus, they say that the practice of the means for liberation and liberation itself belong to *prakṛti* alone.

They further maintain that the activity of creation and so forth, as well as the purpose of human experience and liberation, proceed from *prakṛti* through mutual superimposition, due to the proximity of the changeless and indifferent *puruṣa*.
Because the composite is for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth,
because of superintendence, because of the state of being an enjoyer, and because of activity for the sake of isolation, the Puruṣa exists.
And from the opposite of that, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established,
as well as his isolation, neutrality, and state of being a seer, due to his lack of agency.
The evolution of Pradhāna proceeds in such a manner for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.

Having said this, they spoke as follows: "Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate; rather, it is *prakṛti* (primordial nature), which has various substrates, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated."
Therefore, through its respective conjunctions with those [guṇas], the unconscious *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were conscious;
and although the guṇas are the actual agents, the indifferent [Self] likewise appears as if it were the agent.

"For the sake of the Puruṣa's seeing, and likewise for the sake of the Pradhāna's isolation (kaivalya), there is a conjunction of both, like that of the lame and the blind; from this [conjunction] arises creation.
Thus, [attributes such as] being a witness, being a seer, and being an enjoyer belong to the eternally changeless, non-agent, and indifferent [Puruṣa].

It is not possible for that which has isolation (*kaivalya*) as its sole nature; nor can even an error rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) occur for such a being, because both superimposition and error are modifications (*vikāra*), and these two cannot belong to *prakṛti*, since they are attributes of consciousness (*cetana*). Superimposition is defined as the attribution of the qualities of one thing to another. And that...

The nature of consciousness is subject to modification; however, superimposition and the like cannot occur in the Puruṣa merely through proximity to Prakṛti. If they could occur despite its being changeless, it would follow that they must occur eternally.

Furthermore, the fact that proximity (*sannidhi*) is not a cause [of action] has been established in the section beginning with "not because of having different characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). If it is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated, how can it be said to be beneficial to the eternally liberated *puruṣa*? For they say: [The relevant verse: "The primordial nature is not for its own sake, nor is the *puruṣa* for his own sake; rather, the union of the two is for the sake of both. (SK 21) And: "The purpose of the *puruṣa* is fulfilled by the manifestation of the difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the *puruṣa*; once this has occurred, the primordial nature ceases its activity toward that *puruṣa*. (SK 35) And: "The primordial nature, though insentient, acts as if sentient for the sake of the *puruṣa*; she is like a cow for her calf, or like a mother for her child. (SK 57) And: "The primordial nature, though devoid of consciousness, appears as if conscious through the reflection of the *puruṣa*, just as the moon appears to move when reflected in moving water. (SK 39) Thus, it is explained that although the primordial nature is insentient, it functions as if it were sentient for the sake of the *puruṣa*. It is stated: "The primordial nature is for the sake of the *puruṣa*. (SK 56). Therefore, even though the *puruṣa* is eternally liberated, the primordial nature is said to be beneficial to him. This is what is meant. And: "The primordial nature does not act out of self-interest, nor does the *puruṣa* act out of self-interest; rather, their union is for the sake of both. (SK 21) And: "The purpose of the *puruṣa* is fulfilled by the manifestation of the difference between the intellect and the *puruṣa*; once this has occurred, the primordial nature ceases its activity toward that *puruṣa*. (SK 35) And: "The primordial nature, though insentient, acts as if sentient for the sake of the *puruṣa*; she is like a cow for her calf, or like a mother for her child. (SK 39) Thus, it is explained that although the primordial nature is insentient, it functions as if it were sentient for the sake of the *puruṣa*. This is what is meant. And: "The primordial nature does not act out of self-interest, nor does the *puruṣa* act out of self-interest; rather,
Through various means, she who is beneficial acts for the sake of that man who is ungrateful and devoid of virtue; though she herself possesses merit, her efforts for his sake are rendered fruitless.
Likewise,
they say: "Prakṛti, having been seen by a particular Puruṣa according to her own true nature,
withdraws from that Puruṣa at that very moment."
Just as a dancer ceases from her dance after showing herself to the audience,
so does primordial nature (prakṛti) cease from its activity after manifesting itself to the person (puruṣa).
It is my conviction that there is nothing more delicate than primordial nature (prakṛti);
once she has been seen by the Puruṣa, thinking "I have been seen," she does not present herself for sight again.
Thus, that which is "unseen" (asaṅkhyāta) is as follows: because the two Puruṣas are eternally liberated and changeless, the one [the Puruṣa] never sees nor superimposes [the other];

nor does it see its own self, because it is insentient. Since the seeing of the Puruṣa’s own self is [equivalent to] seeing itself, it does not superimpose [itself], because the Puruṣa lacks the modification consisting of the act of seeing.

Because of this possibility, it is said that "seeing" is merely proximity (*sannidhi*). It has already been stated that because proximity is eternal, there would follow the consequence of eternal seeing. Furthermore, even a temporary proximity distinct from one's own nature is not possible for that which is eternally changeless. Moreover, if seeing in the form of one's own proximity were the cause of liberation, then it would also be the cause of bondage.

If it were that very same [proximity], then bondage and liberation would both be eternal. If it is argued that false perception (*ayathārthadarśana*) is the cause of bondage and the perception of one's own nature as it truly is (*yathāvatsvarūpadarśana*) is the cause of liberation, then since both types of perception do not exceed the nature of mere proximity (*sannidhāna*), there would necessarily be the consequence of both occurring at all times. If that proximity were non-eternal, then...

A cause for that [proximity] must also be sought, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, wishing to avoid this fault, one were to claim that this "proximity" is merely the existence of its own nature (*svarūpasadbhāva*), then, because that nature is eternal, bondage and liberation would likewise be eternal. Therefore, due to such contradictions, the system of the Sāṃkhyas is untenable.

Even for those who assert that Brahman— which is immutably eternal, devoid of distinctions, and pure self-luminous consciousness— is the witness of ignorance and thus participates in the unreal states of bondage and liberation, there remains an inconsistency; for, according to the reasoning already stated, the superimposition of the status of being the witness of ignorance and so forth is impossible.

However, this is the distinction: the Sāṃkhyas maintain a plurality of puruṣas for the sake of establishing the fixed order of birth, death, and so forth; since they do not accept even that [plurality], there is an even greater lack of consistency. As for the disparity mentioned regarding the distinction between the ultimate reality and non-reality of *prakṛti*, that is incorrect.

Whether [the witness-consciousness] be ultimate (pāramārthika) or non-ultimate (apāramārthika), it is untenable for pure consciousness— which is eternal, changeless, self-luminous, and of a single essence— to possess a witnesshood that is distinct [from itself]; however, if it were ultimate, it would be even more inconsistent, since one would have to admit that it is an object of perception and subject to sublation.

Even in the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bhedābheda-vāda), the inconsistency has already been stated previously: that this very nature belongs to Brahman as the possessor of the adjuncts, and thus the connection with the adjuncts and so forth is untenable.
This concludes the section concerning the "Large and Long" (mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa). 2.
Having thus refuted the Smārta view, he refutes the Vaiśeṣika and Naiyāyika views: "Or [the world] is like the large and the long from the short and the spherical" (2.2.10).

If it is argued that, according to the principle that "the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect," the world— being derived from the Lord whose nature consists of knowledge and bliss— must possess those same attributes, [we reply: from two atoms that are short and spherical,
which are respectively shorter and more spherical than other great atoms, [a larger atom is produced].

Just as something long and characterized by transformation arises possessing a twofold quality, so too is it appropriate for the Lord— who consists of knowledge and bliss— to be the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of both sentient and insentient entities, which are respectively of the nature of suffering and insentience; for the world is established as being essentially composed of both the sentient and the insentient.
There arises a doubt as to whether the cause is the atom (*paramāṇu*) or Brahman.

According to the principle that "the qualities of the cause produce qualities of the same kind in the effect," it is not logically possible for the world (*prapañca*), which is insentient and of the nature of suffering, to be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss.

Since atoms and the like are insentient, it follows that it is logical for atoms themselves— acting through the impulse of God in accordance with the karma of sentient *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls)— to be the cause of the world by way of the sequence of dyads, triads, and so forth; this being the position reached, we reply:
Like the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause, the Vaiśeṣika theory of atoms—which relies primarily on fallacious reasoning—is also untenable.

Just as their claim that a large and long dyad (dvyaṇuka) arises from two atoms is inconsistent, everything else they accept is likewise illogical. [This includes] the view that dyads and so forth arise from atoms in a gradual sequence.
The meaning is that this [theory] is also inconsistent, just like the doctrine of the creation of the world.

To explain: the constituent parts, such as threads and the like, produce a composite whole by joining with one another through their respective sides; likewise, atoms too, by joining with one another through their respective sides...
They would be the producers of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; otherwise,

since atoms lack any distinction of spatial parts (*pradeśabheda*), even when a thousand atoms are conjoined, there would be no dimension (*parimāṇa*) exceeding that of a single atom, and thus [the resulting object] would remain minute (*aṇutva*).
Nor should it be argued that even atoms possess parts through their own parts, and those [parts] in turn through their own parts, leading to an infinite regress;
for the difference between a mustard seed and a mountain consists in the smallness or greatness of their constituent parts.
If an atom were likewise to have infinite parts, then, due to the equality of having infinite parts, there would be no distinction between a mustard seed and a mountain.
If there is no distinction of spatial parts among atoms, then no expansion exceeding the dimension of a single atom can arise;
for if the difference between a mustard seed and a mountain is not established at all, what can be done? If this is asked, let the Vedic position be accepted.

As for the interpretation offered by others, that this [sūtra] is intended solely to refute the objections raised against the doctrine of Brahman as the cause—that is inconsistent and merely redundant; for, having already refuted the defects alleged by opponents against the doctrine of Brahman as the cause in the preceding section (pāda), it is precisely in this section that the refutation of the opposing position is carried out. From the conscious Brahman...
Furthermore, the impossibility of the world's origination has been elaborated upon in the sūtra "na vilakṣaṇatvāt" (Sūtra 2.1.4). Therefore,

the intended meaning of the sūtra is that, just as the production of the large and long from the short and the spherical is untenable, everything else accepted by that [opponent] is likewise inconsistent.
The Section Concerning the Atom Not Being the Cause of the World (Sūtra 2.2.16–17).
To address what is inconsistent here, he says: "In either case, there is no action; therefore, that [action] is absent. (11)
Whether it be the Supreme Brahman Śiva or the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) who impel the atoms—
in either case, that is, on both sides, motion (calana), which is the action of the atoms, is not possible;
for since both the individual soul and the Supreme Lord are partless, [there can be no motion] of these partless individual souls.

Because there is no relation of conjunction with partless atoms, and because there can be no impelling force between the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Lord when they are unrelated, that [conjunction] is absent; thus, due to the absence of motion, there is an absence of mutual conjunction among the atoms. And so it is said:

The emergence of the world, beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and triads (tryaṇuka), is not possible. For in the theory that atoms are the cause, the production of the world is held to occur through the sequence of dyads and so forth, preceded by their conjunctions generated by motion residing in the atoms. In that regard, the initial [motion] residing in the atoms—which serves as the cause for the production of the entire world—...

It is accepted that [certain motions] are caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa). Specifically, the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the initial motion of atoms and the internal organ (manas) are caused by the unseen force.

This action residing in the atoms—whether caused by an *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) inherent in themselves or caused by an *adṛṣṭa* inherent in the Self—is impossible in either case. For an *adṛṣṭa* produced by the performance of merit and demerit by the *kṣetrajña* (the conscious soul) cannot possibly reside in an atom; and even if it did reside there, it would follow that creation would occur at all times.

It is not possible for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the self to be the cause of the production [of motion] residing in atoms. If, on the other hand, action arises in atoms due to contact with the self possessing the unseen force, then, because that stream of the unseen force is eternal, there would follow the consequence of an eternal creation.

But surely, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is capable of producing a fruit by depending upon its ripening (vipāka)—for some unseen [karmas] ripen at that very moment, some in another birth, and some at a later time; therefore, because it depends on ripening, there is no consequence of [the cause] producing [the effect] at all times. This is not so.

The simultaneous destruction of all things produced by various types of actions performed at different times and places by infinite selves— without prior convention— and their remaining in an unripened state for a period of two *parārdhas*, is not logically consistent.
Nor can it be due to the conjunction of atoms with a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) instigated by the will of God, because an inferentially established God does not exist.

Because this has been established in the [sūtra] "On account of having the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt), there is therefore an absence of the view that the origin of the world is preceded by action residing in atoms.
He states another reason:
And because of the acceptance of inherence, there would be an infinite regress due to its being on the same footing [as the related entities]. || 12 ||
Furthermore, in the Nyāya school's view, because the inherence (*samavāya*) between the threads and the cloth is accepted as being equivalent—

since the relation of inherence is equal to the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*)— just as a further relation must be admitted for the conjunction between a jar and a cloth, so too a further relation must be asserted for the inherence between the threads and the cloth.

In this way, another third relation must also be intended for that [relation]; and thus, because of non-termination—the consequence of an infinite regress. Some [hold] that the Naiyāyika position is incorrect, and it is also inconsistent due to the admission of inherence (*samavāya*). Why?

Because of this parity, there would be an infinite regress; for just as inherence, like the whole, the genus, and the quality, requires another factor to establish it, that further establishing factor would likewise require yet another, and thus, due to this infinite regress, the position is simply untenable.

This is what is meant: that relationship which is the cause of the cognition "here" (iha-pratyaya) among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and exist in the relation of container and contained (*ādhāra-ādheya*) is accepted as inherence (*samavāya*). If inherence is accepted as that which accounts for the absence [of separation] in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth—which are perceived as not existing separately—then [the same must apply] to inherence itself.

Because of that similarity, one must search for a cause for such a state; yet for that [cause] as well, the same would apply, leading to an infinite regress. If it is postulated that the nature of inherence (*samavāya*) is its inseparability from those [entities], then this very nature should be postulated for the genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) themselves, rather than accepting an unseen inherence and then asserting that this is its nature.
It is explained that it is logical to [consider the relation] as being imagined. This same fault applies whether inherence (samavāya) is eternal or non-eternal.
He states another fault regarding its eternality:
"And because it exists eternally" (sūtra 13).

Since inherence (*samavāya*) is a relation, if the relation were eternal, then its relatum—the world—would also necessarily be eternal; this is inconsistent because [the world] is not eternally existent. Furthermore, atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal, because they exist at all times and are observed [to do so].

Furthermore, there would be the contingency of creation occurring even during the period of dissolution (*pralaya*). Nor can it be argued that creation occurs only at certain times and not always due to the impulsion of God (*īśvara*),
because— as previously stated— it is impossible for the partless God to act as an impeller, given the absence of a conjunctive relationship (*saṃyoga*) with partless atoms (*paramāṇu*).
He states another reason: "And because it possesses form and so forth, there is a reversal [of the nature of the self], as seen [in experience]. (14)

Furthermore, in the view of the Naiyāyikas, because it is accepted that the atoms of earth, water, fire, and air are characterized by color, taste, smell, and touch, the opposite would follow—namely, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of defects such as impermanence and having parts. Why? Because [these qualities] are observed in things possessing color and so forth.

Since jars and other such objects are observed to be impermanent and composed of parts, it follows that if atoms were likewise impermanent, they could not serve as the cause of the world, beginning with dyads (*dvyaṇuka*). This is because the four types of atoms— those of earth, water, fire, and air— are [endowed with] color, taste, smell, and touch...
This is because we observe that things such as jars, which possess form and other qualities, are non-eternal and are produced by other causes of a similar nature.

Indeed, an unperceived object being postulated in accordance with what is observed cannot be restricted to whatever specific feature one personally desires. Or rather, it is on the basis of conformity with observation that atoms are postulated as possessing form and other qualities.

For this reason as well, [the theory] is inconsistent. Now, if—out of a desire to avoid this fault—it is not admitted that atoms possess color and other qualities, then it is not logical for them to be the cause of the world.
Regarding this, he states another reason:
And because there would be a fault in either case. (15)

Not only is there a fault in the admission that atoms possess color and other qualities; even if they were devoid of color and so forth, since the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of its cause, earth and the other elements would be devoid of color and the rest. If, out of a desire to avoid that [consequence], one admits that they possess color and so forth, then the previously mentioned fault arises. Thus, because of the fault in both cases, the theory is inconsistent.
Therefore, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is untenable.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
"And because it is not accepted [by the world], there is absolute disregard for it. (16)

Although the position of the Kāpila Yoga and other systems has been abandoned because it contradicts both scripture (*śruti*) and logic (*nyāya*), there is nevertheless partial acceptance of it by Vaidikas such as Manu and others who maintain the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). On the other hand, the position of Kaṇāda is not accepted by the learned authorities (*śiṣṭas*) such as Manu and others, because it stands as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and is inherently untenable.
It should be understood that those seeking liberation must be absolutely indifferent [to them]. This concludes the section on the aggregate (samudāyādhikaraṇa). 4.
He refutes the Buddhist position:
"Even if the aggregate were caused by both [self and other], that [result] would not be obtained. (17)

There, the Buddhists are of four kinds: those who assert the existence of both cognition and objects, those who assert the non-existence of both, those who assert the existence of cognition alone, and those who assert the non-existence of that [cognition]. First, the view of those who assert the existence of both is refuted. Their position is shown as follows:
Earth is merely an aggregate of fragrance-atoms; water is a collection of taste-atoms;

fire is a multitude of form-atoms; and air is designated as a collection of touch-atoms. Bodies, whether sentient or insentient, as well as jars, cloths, and so forth, which belong to those respective classes, are likewise nothing but aggregates of atoms.
Like a sky-lotus, space is an absolute non-existence at all times. The individual soul (*jīva*) consists of a continuum of cognition accompanied by afflictions;

God (*īśvara*) possesses the nature of a continuum of cognition free from afflictions. Furthermore, the aggregate is twofold, distinguished as external and internal: the external consists of earth and so forth.
The internal [world], consisting of mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), is such that the entire universe is merely these two aggregates. To explain:
for the external aggregate, atoms (*paramāṇu*) are the cause; and these are of four kinds—earthy, watery, fiery, and airy.
For the internal aggregate, the five aggregates (*skandha*) are the cause: form (*rūpa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*).
When examined, sound, touch, and so forth are the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha). The manifestation of these is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).

The suffering produced by them is the aggregate of sensation (vedanāskandha). Names such as "Devadatta" are the aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha). The latent impressions (vāsanā) of these are the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāraskandha). They maintain that from the accumulation of these, the composite whole arises.
The doctrine of the four elements established in that system is refuted.

Even if one accepts an aggregate of atoms consisting of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), that [aggregate] cannot be attained; that is, the attainment of such a collection is impossible. This is because, according to that system, there is no [connection] between the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).
Because [the self] is impermanent by virtue of being a momentary continuum of cognitions, it is impossible for it to be the agent of the conjunction of momentary atoms; therefore,

the Vaiśeṣika is a "partial nihilist" (ardhavaināśika), since he establishes the extremely rapid destruction of the body and so forth through the distinction of atoms while nevertheless accepting the permanence of the self, whereas the proponent of universal momentariness (sarvakṣaṇikavādī) is a "complete nihilist" (pūrṇavaināśika).

It is now being determined. Therefore, following the refutation of the partial nihilistic view of the Vaiśeṣikas, the full-scale nihilistic view—which has now come to mind—is being refuted. Thus, this intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) should be inferred.
In that regard, first, as for the established scriptures of the Buddha-muni, there are the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, Yogācāras, and Mādhyamikas.

For both the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas, cognition and all objects other than it are momentary and truly existent. However, this is the distinction: for the Vaibhāṣika, objects such as jars are directly perceived; for the Sautrāntika, however, it is cognition itself that arises in the form of jars, cloths, and so forth, and by means of that form...
They maintain that imperceptible objects such as jars are understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding this, since the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas do not differ in their assertion of the existence of external objects, their views are treated as one for the time being; it is then doubted whether that position is rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or in error (*bhrānti*), even though both sets of attributes [of the two schools] are present.
Because [the world] is manifest and because it is established by perception contrary to the Vedas.

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: they accept external objects consisting of the collection of atoms of the elements and their derivatives—such as earth and so forth—as well as internal objects in the form of mind and mental factors, all of which are established by perception and inference. Others, however, [deny] external objects.

They assert that all things, beginning with the earth, are to be inferred through consciousness. Others, however, maintain that consciousness alone is ultimately real and devoid of external objects, while the external world is like the objects in a dream.
All three of these [schools] declare that the entity they themselves accept is momentary.
He does not accept the existence of a self, space, and so forth, as having their own intrinsic nature, distinct from the aforementioned primary elements, derived matter, mind, and mental factors.
Others, however, assert the emptiness of all things. Among them, those who maintain the existence of external objects are first refuted; they hold the following view:

The atoms of earth have the nature of color, taste, smell, and touch; those of water have the nature of color, taste, and touch; and those of air have the nature of touch. These [atoms] aggregate in the form of earth, water, fire, and air. And from these elements, such as earth and the rest, there arise the aggregates of bodies, sense organs, and objects. In that regard:

When it is argued that the continuum of consciousness itself— mounted upon the conceit of being a grasper residing within the body— subsists as the self, and that from this alone all worldly transaction proceeds, the following is stated in response: "Even though the aggregate has both [parents] as its cause, there is no attainment of that [self]."

The established conclusion (siddhānta): Regarding this aggregate accepted by the proponent of the aggregate— which is an aggregate consisting of the elements such as earth and so forth, having atoms as its cause, and which is an aggregate consisting of the body, sense organs, and objects, having earth and so forth as its cause— in that aggregate which has both types of causes:

The attainment of that [result] is not possible; the meaning is that the production of a composite whole consisting of the world is not possible. Because atoms and the primary elements such as earth are admitted to be momentary, when do these momentary-perishing atoms and elements ever act in combination, when do they ever combine, and when do they become objects of cognition?
When do [things] come to serve as the basis for conventional transactions such as abandonment and acquisition? Who is this conscious self? Which object does it touch?

At what time would it experience which object consisting of consciousness? Or who would acquire at what time which object already known? For the creator perishes once created, and that which was created perishes; likewise, the knower perishes once the object is known.

And how could one person experience what has been seen by another, or how could one person grasp an object known by another? Since you do not admit that [the self] is a distinct entity, such conventional transactions and the like cannot be established on that basis. Furthermore, it will be demonstrated later that the self is precisely the referent of "I" and that it is indeed a knower; therefore, that doctrine is rooted in delusion.
Regarding this, he states another reason:
"If it is argued that [the formation of aggregates] is established because of their being mutually dependent, we say no, because they lack a cause for the state of aggregation. (18)
If it is argued that the state of being an aggregate and so forth is established through the mutual causality of the [twelve] factors beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), this is what is meant:

although all phenomena (*bhāva*) are momentary, nevertheless all of this is rendered possible by ignorance. For ignorance is, by definition, a perverted cognition (*viparītabuddhi*) whose object is such things as permanence in regard to what is momentary; through that [ignorance], the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) known as attachment, aversion, and so forth [arise].

They arise. From that comes the consciousness characterized by the blazing of the mind; from that come the mental factors called "name" and the material substances beginning with earth called "form"; from that comes the sixfold sense-faculties called the "six bases"; from that comes the body called "contact"; from that come sensation and the others; and from that, once again, ignorance and the rest arise.

As it has been stated: this beginningless cycle of rotation, consisting of ignorance and the rest, is mutually rooted. And thus, everything—this entire collection of primary elements such as earth and so forth, as well as their derivatives—is not possible without [this cycle]. Therefore, since the existence of these collections and so on is established, [the opponent] concludes as follows:

To this, the reply is: "No, because they are not the cause for the state of being an aggregate. This is not tenable, because these factors, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), are not the cause for the state of being an aggregate of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), such as earth and so forth. Indeed, ignorance—which consists of the cognition of stability and so on regarding what is unstable—and the passion, hatred, and other factors caused by it, do not have a momentary entity that is a distinct object as their basis.

They function as the cause for the aggregation [of atoms]. For the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, for instance, does not become the cause for the aggregation of the object—the shell and so forth.
Furthermore, since one who possesses the notion of stability regarding what is momentary has perished at that very moment, for whom could passion and the like arise?

It is established that for those who do not accept a single, stable substance as the substratum of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), even the continuity of those formative forces cannot be postulated.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
And because the preceding ceases when the succeeding arises. || 19 ||

Furthermore, on the view of momentariness, the production of the world is not tenable, because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment, the preceding moment has already perished. Consequently, it is impossible for that [preceding moment] to serve as a cause for the subsequent moment. If non-existence were to function as a cause, then everything would arise everywhere and at all times. If it is argued that being "located in the preceding moment" is precisely what constitutes causality, then in that case, only a specific [entity]...
The momentary existence of a jar is the cause of all subsequent moments— whether they consist of cows, buffaloes, horses, walls, or anything else.
Even if it were maintained that only a cause belonging to the same class [as its effect] exists in the preceding moment, nevertheless,
for all jars existing in subsequent moments across every location, there would be only a single jar existing in the preceding moment acting as their cause.
There would have to be a cause. Now, if you think that "one" is the cause of "one," even so, it is not known which one is the cause of which one.

If you say that the momentary jar existing in a certain location is the cause of the subsequent jar-moment only when it is related to that same location, do you maintain that the location is permanent? Furthermore, [this does not apply] to an object in contact with the eye and other sense organs.
It should be understood that because it is non-existent at the time of the arising of cognition, it is impossible for any object whatsoever to be the objective domain of that cognition.
He refutes this further by means of another reason:
If it were non-existent [at that time], there would be a contradiction of the proposition; otherwise, there would be simultaneity. (20)
It has already been stated that if an effect were to arise even in the absence of a cause, then everything would arise everywhere and at all times.
Not only would there be a contradiction regarding production, but your own thesis would also be undermined.
Furthermore, you maintain that the four conditions—the dominant, the cooperative, the objective, and the immediately preceding—are the causes for the arising of consciousness.

Thesis: The dominant factor is the faculty (*indriya*). Now, if—in order not to contradict the thesis—it is asserted that while the moment of the jar itself still persists, another moment of the jar arises, then it would follow that both the cause and the effect, the two moments of the jar, would be perceived simultaneously. Yet they are not perceived in such a manner.

Furthermore, the thesis of momentariness would be abandoned in this way. If it is argued that momentariness remains established [even so], then the simultaneity of the sensory contact and the cognition would follow as a consequence.
He shows yet another reason:
The non-attainment of analytical and non-analytical cessation [is established] because there is no interruption. || 21 ||

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the destruction of material objects such as jars and cloths preceded by intelligence, brought about by means such as the throwing of stones. Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the destruction of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as earth and so forth, by their own nature due to the power of time. Of these two cessations...

Non-attainment means non-occurrence. Why? Because there is no interruption. In the Buddhist doctrine, since it is accepted that each preceding atom acts as an independent cause for each succeeding atom, and because insentient atoms lack the capacity to discern specific points of time, [the desired result does not follow].

Because a discontinuity in the continuum of atoms is never possible, both creation and dissolution are untenable in the Buddhist view. Thus, the arising of what is non-existent has been refuted; now it may be said that the total destruction of what is existent without leaving a trace is also not tenable.

According to those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), there are two kinds of destruction: first, that which is gross, consisting of the cessation of a similar continuum (*sadṛśasantāna*) which occurs immediately after the impact of a hammer or other such causes and is capable of being perceived; and second, that which is subtle, occurring at every moment, imperceptible, and characterized by the absence of any continuity (*niranvaya*). Both of these are likewise [momentary].
It is designated by the two terms "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). These two are not possible; why?

Because there is no interruption. For that which exists, an interruption without a trace (*niranvaya-viccheda*) is impossible. And this impossibility is because what is called the arising and destruction of an existing thing is merely the attainment of another state.

However, by us—who establish that the effect is non-different from its cause on the grounds that substance alone, as conjoined with various states, is one and stable—this non-difference has been demonstrated in the section titled "Tadananyatvam" (Non-difference from That). If it is argued that because the extinction of a lamp is seen to be a destruction without any residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), destruction elsewhere must also be inferred to be without residue, we say no; for this is not the case with jars, bowls, and the like.
Since it has been determined that the destruction of an existent substance is merely its transition into another state— based on the observation of the persistence of substances such as clay—

then, because non-perception is also possible in the case of a lamp and similar objects due to their transition into a subtle state, the hypothesis of a transition into another state must likewise be applied there.
It is determined that this is because it is logical.
Furthermore, he shows another reason: "And because there would be a fault in either case" (2.2.22).

Furthermore: regarding the series of atoms constituting jars, cloths, and so forth, whether they possess stability for some time or momentariness—in both cases, there is a fault in either alternative. In the case of stability, there is the fault of abandoning one's own tenet, because the Buddhist doctrine maintains momentariness. In the case of momentariness, [there is the fault] of jars and the like...

The capacity to perform functions such as carrying water would not exist. Therefore, since faults have been demonstrated in both positions, the Buddhist doctrine is untenable. It has been stated that for those who maintain the theory of momentariness, the arising from the non-existent (*tuccha*) and the subsequent lapse into non-existence of what has arisen are possible; yet, there are faults in accepting either of these two modes.
If [the effect] were to arise from the void (*tuccha*), the effect would necessarily be of the nature of the void. For whatever arises from something is observed to be of the nature of that thing;
for example, jars, bracelets, crowns, and so forth, produced from clay or gold, are observed to be of the nature of clay or gold. And the world is not of the nature of the void.

This is accepted by you, yet it is not perceived. If there were the destruction of an existing thing without any residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), then after a single moment, the entire world would necessarily become non-existent. Furthermore, if the world were to arise from that which is subsequently void, it would itself be of the nature of the void, as just described. Therefore, since there are faults in both cases, origination and cessation cannot occur in the manner asserted by you.

[Objection: According to the Buddhist doctrine, atoms are indeed momentary; however, jars, cloths, and the like—which consist of a continuum of those [atoms]—are certainly stable. Even so, if you argue that the performance of functions such as carrying water is possible for jars and the like, then:

If one were to accept the distinctness of those continua in relation to atoms, then one would have to accept that objects such as jars and cloths are produced from atoms through the sequence of dyads and so forth;
and if this were the case, it would result in entering the position of the Naiyāyikas, which would constitute a deviation from the tenets of the Buddhists.
Having refuted the Buddhist position that the four primary elements are merely aggregates of atoms, [the author] now refutes the emptiness of space:
"And because there is no distinction in the case of space" (2.2.23).

Furthermore, since the existence of all individual knowers (*kṣetrajña*) is perceived in space (*ākāśa*), and because this perception is indistinguishable and equal [for all], one must accept that space, like the four elements which consist of perceptible aggregates of atoms, is likewise an aggregate of supersensible atoms— according to the analogy of water reaching up to the knees. And thus:

Indeed, the acceptance of emptiness (*śūnyatva*) is untenable. In order to establish the stability of external and internal entities, the insubstantial nature of both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) has been refuted. In that context, the insubstantiality of even the element of space (*ākāśa*), which the Buddhists enumerate as insubstantial along with those two, is also rejected.
Furthermore, it is not tenable for space (*ākāśa*) to be indefinable (*nirūpākhyatā*).

This is because, like earth and the other elements which are accepted as being of the nature of positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*), space is also established by uncontradicted cognition (*abādhitapratīti*).
Nor can it be said that space is merely the absence of earth and the other elements, for such a claim cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*).

If space were the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), the mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), or the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of earth and the other elements,

then the cognition of space would still be untenable. For if prior and posterior non-existence were space, then while earth and the other elements exist, the cognition of space would be impossible, and the world would consequently be devoid of space.

Even if mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) were space, since mutual non-existence resides in its respective objects, there would be no cognition of space in the intervals between them. Furthermore, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not possible for earth and the other elements. Moreover, because it has been established that non-existence is a particular state of an existing entity, even if space were of the nature of non-existence, [the aforementioned objection does not apply].

There is no contradiction in the fact that the space existing within atoms possesses form and is thus visible, because it is endowed with form through the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) demonstrated by the instruction on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). Therefore, the doctrine of the voidness of space is indeed charming only so long as it is not investigated.
Having thus refuted the five elements as conceived by the opponents, [the author now addresses] the nature of consciousness as a momentary continuum (*jñānasantāna*).
Now he refutes the established doctrine of the Buddha school, which takes the form "of living beings," with the following: "And because of recollection" (2.2.4).

The permanence of living beings is undeniable, as evidenced by the observation of memory— the recollection on subsequent days of objects experienced on previous days. If one were to accept that consciousness consists merely of a stream of cognitions,
then because the streams of cognition experienced on previous days would have perished during states such as deep sleep, there would be no subject capable of remembering them.
Nor should it be argued that those successions of cognitions (*jñānasantāna*) arising on subsequent days will possess the capacity for recollection;

for it is impossible for one person to remember objects experienced by another. Therefore, it is illogical for the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) to consist of a succession of cognitions. Thus, the stability of the object under discussion is indeed established.

Recollection (*anusmaraṇa*) is the cognition of an object previously experienced; recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the cognition of an object [in the form] "this is that very same thing. Thus, the entire range of entities experienced in past time is recognized. And yet, as you [the Buddhists] do not [admit] identity in the case of flames and the like—as in the thought "this is that same lamp-flame"—so too identity is not experienced [in the case of the self].

It cannot be said that this delusion of unity is based on similarity, because a single cognizer who undergoes such delusion is not admitted [to exist]. For one person does not subsequently connect what has been experienced as either unity or similarity by another.
Therefore, the delusion of unity is based on the experience of similarity residing in objects belonging to different times.

By those who speak thus, the oneness of the knower must necessarily be accepted. Furthermore, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a difference even among objects of knowledge such as jars, as we do in the case of flames and the like, by which we might postulate that recognition is based on similarity. As for what is also said—that the momentariness of jars and other things is established through perception and inference—[that too is untenable].

Perception, which has as its object a present thing, makes its own object known by way of excluding it from things that are not present, just as blue is distinguished from yellow. Thus, the present is established as being a distinct entity from the past and the future. In this regard, inference also [establishes this], because [the present] possesses causal efficiency and existence.

A jar and so forth are momentary; for that which is non-momentary, such as a rabbit’s horn, is incapable of causal efficiency and is therefore non-existent. This is because of the existence of the final moment of the jar. The existences of the preceding moments of the jar have perished, because they are existences of jar-moments, just like the existence of the final moment of the jar. And this [momentariness] is established through the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect, and so forth.
This has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, the exclusion of the present object perceivable by direct perception from what is not present does not imply that the present thing is a different entity;
rather, it merely indicates its connection with the present time. And it is not by that much alone [that it becomes a different entity].
The state of being a distinct entity is established because that very thing can be connected with a different time.
