As for the two reasons stated for momentariness—namely, existence (*sattva*) and causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*)—they are contradictory, as they prove the opposite of what is intended. For by virtue of existence or causal efficacy, a jar or similar object is [established as] enduring.

It can indeed be said that whatever is non-momentary is non-existent and incapable of performing a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), just like a rabbit’s horn. Furthermore, the capacity for causal efficacy would actually prove non-momentariness itself; for it has been stated that because a causal operation is impossible for that which perishes in a moment, the capacity for causal efficacy cannot exist [in such a thing]. This applies likewise to the final moment of a jar.

Because destruction is observed to arise from a cause, other moments of the jar as well must possess stability due to the occurrence of their own causes. Nor should it be argued that hammers and the like are not causes of destruction, but rather causes for the production of a dissimilar continuum such as shards;
for it has already been established that the very attainment of the state of being shards constitutes the destruction of jars and the like.

Even if one accepts that [the jar] is distinct from the arising of the potsherds, the mallet and other such instruments possess only the nature of being causes of destruction. To claim that the mallet and so forth are the cause of the potsherds is incorrect. Therefore, the stability perceived through recognition cannot be denied by any means, since it concerns the identity of an object related to both prior and subsequent times.

By asserting that recognition has a different object [than its own nature], one would have to assert that even cognitions of blue and so forth have as their objects something other than blue and so forth.
Furthermore, for those who maintain the momentariness of both the knower and the known, the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*)— [which is required for inference]— is impossible.

Even the presentation of reasons preceded by a thesis such as "momentary" and so forth is not tenable for you, because the speaker perishes at the very moment the thesis is commenced; for it is not possible for others, who do not know what was commenced by another, to bring it to completion. Therefore, the Vedic scripture is logical.
He refutes it again by another reason: "Not from the non-existent, because that has not been observed" (2.2.26).
The arising of subsequent streams of cognition from a preceding stream of cognition that has perished during sleep is not possible when it is non-existent;
why? Because it is never observed. For instance, a perished lump of clay and the like lack the capacity to produce a jar or similar objects.
Thus far, these are the common [objections] raised against the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas, who both maintain the existence of external objects.

Regarding the objections stated therein—specifically, that because an object with which [the cognition] is associated does not persist at the time the cognition arises, it is impossible for any object to be the objective domain of cognition—the Sautrāntika counters this: the non-persistence of the object at the time of cognition is not the reason for its not being the objective domain of cognition; rather, it is precisely its being the cause of the arising of the cognition [that constitutes its being the object].

[The object] is that which is the objective domain of cognition. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence that the eye and other [senses] would also be objects of cognition; for we accept that only that which is the cause of cognition by imparting its own form (*svākāra*) is the object of cognition. Even though an object has perished after imparting its own form to the cognition, it is inferred by means of the form such as blue (*nīla*) residing in the cognition. And it is not...

If it is argued that the form of each subsequent cognition is established by each preceding cognition—since if a cognition of blue exists, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that no other cognition could arise, and therefore the variety of cognitions is produced solely by the object—it is said in reply: "No, because what is non-existent has never been seen. This form of blue and so forth which is perceived in cognition— [The remainder of the passage continues: ...is not produced by an external object, because such an object is not perceived; rather, it arises from internal latent impressions (vāsanā). Furthermore, since the object is not perceived at the time of the cognition, its causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not established. Moreover, if the form were produced by an external object, then all cognitions would have to be identical in form, as the external object remains the same. Therefore, the diversity of cognitions is due to internal causes alone. Thus, the form of blue and so forth perceived in cognition is not derived from an external reality.

An aspect cannot belong to an object that has perished and is non-existent, because it has not been perceived. Indeed, when a substratum (dharmin) has perished, the transfer of its property (dharma) to another object is never observed. Even a reflection and the like belong only to something stable;
moreover, even in those cases, it is not the mere property that is transferred. Therefore, the diversity of cognition is caused by the diversity of the object.
It occurs precisely because [the cause] persists at the time of the cognition. Therefore, it should be understood that the Buddhist position is inconsistent.
Anticipating an objection regarding the acceptance that even a perished entity can produce an effect, he says:
"And in this way, there would be the accomplishment [of effects] even for those who are indifferent. (26)

Even so, if that which has perished were still capable of producing an effect, then all effects would be accomplished even for living beings who are indifferent and devoid of activity. Therefore, this is incorrect. Likewise, if one accepts momentariness, the arising of the non-existent, and causeless destruction, then [the same absurdity follows] even for those who are indifferent and not exerting themselves.
The accomplishment of all aims would be possible; for it is through effort and other means that the attainment of the desired or the cessation of the undesired is achieved.

However, if all entities were subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇadhvaṃsa*), then among all things, neither the preceding object nor its specific qualities—such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like, or knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth—would persist in any subsequent state. Consequently, nothing could be accomplished through effort and other such means.

There is something [to be said]. If this were so, since all accomplishments would be established by means of a non-cause (*ahetu*), then even for those who are indifferent, both the fruits of this world and the next, as well as liberation (*mokṣa*), would be established.
Therefore, the doctrine of the Buddha is the work of an incarnation of Viṣṇu created to delude the Asuras.
It must be rejected in every way by the followers of the Veda.
This concludes the section on Non-existence (Nābhāvādhikaraṇa). 5.
Having thus refuted the doctrine of the Buddha, [the author] now refutes the Jīveśvara-vāda, which is called "crypto-Buddhist" (pracchanna-bauddha):
"It is not non-existence, because [the world] is perceived. (2.2.27)
The non-existence of the phenomenal world of sentient objects— consisting of the five great elements as delimited by the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—
means either its emptiness, like a rabbit's horn, a sky-lotus, or the son of a barren woman, or its falsity, like the world-appearance in a dream.

Not the first—the non-existence [of the world]. The non-existence of the phenomenal world consisting of the conscious (jīva and Īśvara) and the unconscious, its emptiness (*śūnyatva*), is not possible. Why? Because of perception; for the establishment of objects occurs through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If emptiness were accepted like that of the son of a barren woman and so forth, there would be no perception by direct experience.

Having thus refuted the Buddhist doctrine that maintains the self (*ātman*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*) or designation (*abhidhāna*), [the author] now rejects the Vasiṣṭha doctrine— which maintains the self (*jīva*) and Brahman are cognition (*prajñāna*) or designation (*abhidhāna*)— preceded by that refutation.
There exists a relationship of dependence between the doctrine of consciousness (*vijñānavāda*) and the doctrine of cognition (*prajñānavāda*).

The subject matter of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is the doctrine of those who maintain that Brahman alone is consciousness and life— the doctrine of non-dualism without difference (*nirviśeṣādvaita*)— which holds that "Brahman is real, the world is illusory, and the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed Brahman and nothing else," and according to the logic of that system, there is no entity distinct from one's own self. Even though [this view] was refuted in the preceding section (*pāda*) as being the opponent of our own established doctrine by means of scripture (*śruti*) and other authorities, [it is here addressed again].

Furthermore, because this is a refutation primarily through reasoning (*yukti*), there is no fault of tautology. Since that scripture exists as a source of authority for a portion of the revealed word (*śruti*), it is doubted whether its doctrine is based on error or on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: "Everything has become the Self alone; then by what and whom could one see? By what and whom could one speak? Not here... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1].
Because in passages such as "There is no diversity whatsoever," the non-existence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is demonstrated, just like the son of a barren woman; and because,
although blue color and so forth appear through delusion in cases such as the blueness of the sky, a mirage in the desert, or a snake in a rope, when examined,
they are found to be non-existent throughout the three periods of time— so too, although the phenomenal world appears to the deluded through their own ignorance, [it is nonetheless non-existent].

When it is argued that, through the vision of discrimination, the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-existent in all three periods of time—just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—we reply with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "The *jīva* is indeed Brahman and nothing else. That [previous argument] is incorrect, because there is no non-existence, for [the soul] is perceived (*upalabdheḥ*).
It is impossible to assert the non-existence of an object distinct from one's own self. Why? Because it is perceived.

The specific object of the knowing self is established through the apprehension of cognition in the form of producing fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). For it is precisely in this way that all worldly people understand: "I know the jar"—thus, by means of the meaning of the verbal root *jñā*, which is accompanied by both an object and an agent, appearing as an immediate manifestation witnessed by the whole world.
They explain that those who attempt to prove that mere consciousness alone is the ultimate reality become objects of derision for the whole world;
furthermore, it has already been stated previously that such scriptural passages as "everything became the Self alone" refer to the state of Śiva’s absolute isolation (kevalāvasthā).

If that were not the case, since the phenomenal world exists by virtue of its nature as the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there would be a contradiction with many scriptural passages such as "Two birds...

(*dvā suparṇā*), and there would follow a contradiction with direct perception— like saying "my mother is barren"— regarding [the experience of] learning, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and so forth, which occur in the world through the power of previously performed meritorious and sinful deeds.

It is difficult to refute [this]. From merit comes heaven, and from sin comes hell; for this very reason, in such passages as "the world of the doer of merit perishes" and "the world acquired through action perishes," the reality of the world is taught.

Furthermore, if the world were non-existent, would it be a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*), a subsequent absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), or a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)?

The first [alternative] is not tenable—because in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born," the subtle state of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) during dissolution and its gross state at the time of re-creation are described, just like childhood, youth, and so forth. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable—because in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was the Existent alone," even during dissolution, according to the principle that "destruction is absorption into the cause," [the world remains].
The first [position] is not tenable, because of the teaching that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) exists as having the nature of reality (*sat*).

Nor is the third, because the phenomenal world is observed to consist of the accomplishment of purposeful activity (*arthasiddhi-kriyāsiddhi*). Nor is the fourth, because [the world] is seen in such passages as: "That which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe," and so forth—just as the four elements exist in space (*ākāśa*).

Because of the designation of Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as the substratum and the superstratum, one might raise the following objection: "Since the son of a barren woman is not perceived, whereas the phenomenal world is established by universal experience, even if the world exists, its falsity is established—just like a dream. To this, he says:
And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and so forth. || 28 ||

It would not be possible to assert the falsity of the waking world by means of examples such as dreams and magical illusions. Why? Because of the lack of homogeneity (*vaidharmya*); that is, because there exists a difference between the world of dreams and magical illusions and the waking world.
[For] after awakening, the world of dreams and magical illusions is [seen to be] non-existent through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The falsity [of the dream world] is established because it is sublated; however, since no such sublation is observed for the waking world, its falsity is not established.
Furthermore, regarding the meritorious and non-meritorious actions performed in dreams, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice or the killing of a Brahmin—

Because there is no attainment of heaven, hell, and so forth [based on dreams], and because it is observed that the fruits of good and evil deeds performed in the waking state are obtained here and in other worlds, the similarity of this world to a dream is in every way untenable.
Furthermore, due to the dissimilarity between dream-cognition and waking-cognition, it is not logical to assert that waking cognitions are devoid of objects.

For dream-cognitions and the like are produced by sense organs impaired by defects such as sleep and are sublated; waking cognitions, however, are the opposite of those, and thus they cannot be equated with them. Furthermore, if all cognitions were devoid of objects, even the object you seek to establish would not be established, because the inference itself that proves the absence of support would likewise be devoid of an object.

If that [knowledge] possesses an object, then because the possession of knowledge is not invariably concomitant [with being devoid of an object], it is all the more impossible to establish its being empty of objects.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the scriptural passage, "To whom everything has become the Self alone," establishes that even the waking world is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman—that is incorrect; for even while the world is real, [it is not perceived] by one who is asleep.

Just as a person is devoid of knowledge of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), so too for one who has dissolved into Brahman, although the phenomenal world exists, it is logical that he is devoid of the knowledge of his own cognition and the knowledge of the phenomenal world, due to the absence of mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
By this, the sublation (*bādha*) of the phenomenal world is not being asserted. However, for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*):
The state of being devoid of knowledge of self and others is like that of deep sleep, fainting, and so forth, due to the experience of the bliss of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
However, because worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is observed upon waking again, it is not possible for this state to be sublated by the knowledge of Brahman.

By the word "and" (*ca*), the process of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavāda*)—as in the case of a rope-snake and similar examples—is indicated; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [other such instances are included].

Even the scriptural examples of a city of Gandharvas, a magician’s net, and so forth, are refuted. Otherwise, if one accepts the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) as being like a dream and the like, the unavoidable consequence would be an entry into the Buddhist view due to the faults of the destruction of what has been done (kṛtanāśa) and the acquisition of what has not been done (akṛtābhyāgama); this should be understood by the discerning.
Furthermore, he refutes it by means of another reason: "There is no entity, because it is not perceived" (29).

In the doctrine of non-dualism without attributes (*nirviśeṣādvaita*), if one accepts the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of examples such as dreams or the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, then the existence—that is, the reality—of the attributeless Brahman does not exist; why?
Because it is not perceived. According to that view, since [the world] is ultimately unreal, the Vedas and Vedāntas lack the status of being valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
That doctrine should not be accepted by those seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Not only is the existence of a featureless Brahman impossible; why? Because it is not perceived anywhere.
For the existence of a Brahman that is devoid of agency, devoid of object, and consisting of pure consciousness is not possible.

Since it is not found thus in the Vedas and Vedāntas, and according to the maxim that "the statements of those who propound falsity are themselves false," their own school accepts that the Vedas and Vedāntas are false;
how, then, can the reality of the Brahman taught by those false Vedas and Vedāntas be established? [Especially] in the case of a Brahman devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa).

Because it is impossible for [the world] to be established by the Vedas and Vedānta, and because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than those to prove the existence of Brahman, the falsity of that non-differentiated Brahman— along with the manifold universe of worlds, individual souls, and the Lord as taught in those scriptures— is unavoidable. Therefore, like the doctrine of the Buddha which consists of mere consciousness, the Advaita doctrine as well is charming only so long as it is not subjected to critical inquiry.

Since both [schools] accept the falsity of the phenomenal world consisting of the universe, the individual soul, and the Lord, as well as the doctrine of non-duality (advaita), it is certain that the two are equal.
[This concludes] the demonstration of the reality of the dream-phenomenon.

Moreover, even the reality of dream cannot be denied, because the dream-phenomenon is real, because the dream also has the Supreme Lord as its cause, because the latent impressions (vāsanās) of that [dream] persist even in the waking state,

and because it is taught— according to the principle that "the dream is accompanied by the latent impressions of the waking state"— that the dream also has the latent impressions of the waking state as its cause.
This is because [the dream] is established by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous lives, even when one perceives objects not seen while awake.
Furthermore: "He who sees a black man in a dream will live for six months;
likewise, he who sees a person of Time (*kālapuruṣa*) wearing red garments in a dream [will die immediately]."
And he who especially perceives a city of the Gandharvas;
Within six months, he reaches the world of Yama; of this there is no doubt.

Thus, from the observation of many scriptural traditions and from the manifestation of the experiences of all people according to the methods of the *Svapnādhyāya* (Treatise on Dreams), its truth is established. This concludes the section [dealing with] the impossibility [of the dream state] in every respect. 6.
Having thus refuted the doctrines of Vasiṣṭha and Yama— which, by contradicting the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), propound a dry Vedāntic non-dualism devoid of distinctions—
he now refutes the doctrine of Sāndīpana, known as the "non-dualism of emptiness" (*śūnyādvaita*), which is a philosophy of self-destruction (*svātmahanana*).
Now follows the refutation of the doctrine of Sāndīpani, known as the Non-dualism of Voidness (śūnyādvaita):
"And because it is altogether untenable" (30).
The doctrine of the universal voidist— which is characterized by the falsity of both cognition and its object—

is utterly incoherent, because it contradicts all means of valid cognition, such as perception, inference, scripture, tradition, and authoritative testimony, and because it is logically untenable in every respect. This applies equally to the doctrines of *vijñāna* (consciousness) and *prajñāna* (wisdom).

Because it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience, both of those [views] are not to be accepted due to a lack of foundation. Since this [work] is commenced for the purpose of refuting that doctrine— arising from the doubt as to why consciousness (*prajñāna*) and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) might not both be void— it is called *Mithyādvaitaprakāśikā*.

Because those two treatises stand in the relationship of primary and subordinate (aṅga-aṅgin), there is a logical connection between the preceding and succeeding sections consisting of the relation of the dependent and the dependent-upon (upajīvya-upajīvaka).
Since the scriptures state, "Ka is Brahman," "Kha is Brahman," and "Ākāśa is the Self," the doubt arises as to whether that doctrine is based on valid authority (pramāṇa) or on error (bhrānti).

Indeed, the doctrine of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavāda*) alone is the ultimate goal (*sāndīpanakāṣṭhā*) equivalent to the teaching of the Sugata. Momentariness and other such tenets were taught through provisional acceptance and other means in accordance with the intellectual capacity of the disciples. [The truth is that] consciousness and all external objects do not exist; emptiness alone is reality, and liberation is simply the attainment of non-existence. Such is the case.
Like [the arguments regarding] the Buddha and others, this refers to the intention of Sāṃdīpa; for that alone is logical. Since the void is neither caused nor producible, it is established by itself;
therefore, a cause must indeed be sought for it from its own nature. And that [void] does not arise from either existence or non-existence.
First of all, the arising of anything from existence is never observed; for a jar or the like is not produced without the prior destruction of the lump of clay and so forth.

Nor is production from non-existence possible. For if a jar or the like were produced from non-existence when the lump of clay and so forth have perished, it would itself be of the nature of non-existence. Likewise, production from self or from another is not possible.

If it were produced from self, there would follow the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and a lack of purpose. If it were produced from another, [it would follow that] the production of one thing [would arise] from another...

Because there is no distinction in their "otherness," it would follow that everything could arise from everything. Since there is an absence of birth itself, there is likewise an absence of destruction; therefore, emptiness alone is the reality. Consequently, birth, destruction, existence, and non-existence are merely illusions. Furthermore, since an illusion cannot occur without a substratum, there must be a substratum for the illusion.

One must rely upon some ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*). For just as the occurrence of an error is possible even if the defects, the locus of those defects, and the cognizer are not ultimately real, so too the occurrence of an error is possible even if the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not ultimately real;
thus, it follows that emptiness alone is the reality. To this [objection], [we reply]:
We reply: "Because it is untenable in every respect. The universal emptiness intended by you is not possible.

Do you assert that everything is existent, or non-existent, or otherwise? In no way can the voidness you intend be established, given the words "existence" and "non-existence" and their corresponding cognitions in the world.
Since it has been established that an existing entity itself is the object of its particular states,

he who asserts that "everything is empty" necessarily asserts that "everything exists. By asserting that everything which exists possesses particular states, your intended notion of "insubstantiality" (tucchatā) is not [established].
It is established from some source or other.

Furthermore—by one who wishes to establish emptiness itself after having apprehended it through some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the truth of that very means of valid cognition must be admitted. If that were not true, everything would be true; thus, in every respect...

Furthermore, universal emptiness is untenable. Therefore, those who seek the ultimate goal of liberation should not, in any way, accept the doctrine of Sāndīpa— who asserts that the nature of reality consists of insentience and self-destruction— as maintained by the Buddhists.
Regarding this point, he states another reason: "And because of momentariness" (31).

Because Sāndīpani’s doctrine asserts that consciousness (*cit*) arises momentarily and independently within the space of the elements— like a flash of lightning from a stone-fire or a streak of lightning— without a root cause, his view should not be accepted.
For if it were to arise by itself from itself in an instant without a root, then [the same would apply] to everything else.

Because it is momentary, it perishes. If that were so, then whether by its own inherent capacity or by following the body, according to the principle that "in the absence of a cause, there is no effect," the cognition, being an effect, lacks its own capacity for its own production; for nowhere in the world does an effect arise in the absence of its cause.

Because no production of effects is observed [from such a cause], and because in your own scripture you do not accept the persistence of knowledge independently of the body, sense organs, and so forth. If it is argued that there is capacity through the pursuit of a body, then since you do not accept an Īśvara as the cause of the world who is distinct from his own knowledge, from what would the body, sense organs, and so forth arise?

If one does not accept the emergence of both knowledge and its object [from the self], there would be the consequence of contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), due to the contradiction with the notion of "I," just as in the statement, "My mother is barren. Furthermore, according to that view, if one accepts the identity of knowledge and the body,
then since the separation of knowledge and the body is observed when everyone's body falls away or during sleep, [that identity would be untenable].
"Contradiction with scripture, logic, and experience is difficult to avoid.
Having known the Self as the individual soul (jīva), like a snake [mistaken for] a rope, one would carry fear.
But if it is known that 'I am not the jīva, I am the Supreme Self,' then one becomes fearless. Thus it is said.

Just as the proponents of Advaita declare that liberation occurs without dependence on meditation, concentration, and the like— by following the dry non-dualism consistent with the opinion of Vasiṣṭha and by means of the instruction of "I am the individual soul, which is Brahman alone," like a rope-snake— at that very moment of [realizing] the sublation [of the world].
The bodiless exists always; it is eternally free from the body.
This alone is eternal liberation; otherwise, it is a cause of delusion.
Thus, following the *Bṛhad-Vāsiṣṭha*, which is a preeminent tantra outside the Veda, the adherents of the Sāndīpa doctrine prattle on:
"The elemental ether (ākāśa) called the body exists eternally because it lacks a root;
liberation is merely the ascertainment of the voidness of the knowledge consisting of the body, due to its momentariness."

By the principle that "in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect," since the knowledge whose nature is Brahman is admitted to be eternally void due to the absence of its root, the voidness of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is its object is established by implication. Therefore, through the certainty of that scripture— using the state of pure deep sleep as an illustration— that "I am never [this]" is established.

Although the notion of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya) exists through such qualities as being a speaker, an agent, an enjoyer, a knower, and a rememberer, it has been established by the Guru’s instruction— using examples such as the waking from a dream of an elephant or a lion—
that at every moment, all such notions of "I" and the like are empty.

Furthermore, in this view, the identity of the body and the self is asserted, as is the self's lack of prior or subsequent births; it is also stated that the living being is produced from the union of semen and blood, like the emergence of an insect from cow dung. Therefore, since there is no difference between this doctrine and the Buddhist doctrine, [the latter] is superior.
This scripture should be disregarded by those who desire Vedic [rituals], because, like a stone or inert space, it is devoid of utility;
thus, no fruit whatsoever is logically established by the ascertainment of its existence through such meditation.
Furthermore, for those devoid of knowledge of that doctrine, there is a return to rebirth, as they are like those who have fallen from a mountain peak.
Not the first [alternative], because knowledge is admitted to arise spontaneously like lightning from a cloud and thus perishes by itself;

therefore, the application of a scripture for its sake is not tenable. Furthermore, since the non-destruction of the entity produced by itself is a property of that very self and is independent, and because of the admission of the identity of the body and the self through the union of semen and blood—

Because you accept the production of the individual soul (*jīva*), it follows as a matter of course that the destruction of one's own body is itself one's liberation; thus, a contradiction with your own words is unavoidable. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable—for if there were no returning [to rebirth], the engagement of both teacher and disciple in your scripture would be impossible.

If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of being as ignorant as animals; therefore, this doctrine is charming only when left unexamined, as it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience. In the section concerning the ether (*ākāśa*) based on its characteristic marks, [it is stated] that the word *ākāśa*—derived from the etymology "that which shines forth from all sides" (*ā samantāt prakāśate*)—[denotes Brahman].

It should be understood that because words such as "wind," "ether," "light," and "sun" are established as referring to Brahman by virtue of possessing marks of Brahman—such as being the cause of the world—the passages beginning with "What is Ka? What is Brahman? do not have any other subject matter. This concludes the section on the impossibility [of multiple qualities] in one [Brahman]. (Sūtra 7)
Having thus refuted the doctrine of Sāṇḍilya, who asserts universal emptiness, he now refutes the Jaina doctrine, which is similar to it:
"Now follows the refutation of the Jaina doctrine:
Not so, because [the attributes] cannot coexist in one [substratum]. (2.2.32)

The Jains assert that the phenomenal world possesses existence, non-existence, the nature of both existence and non-existence, and the nature of being distinct from both existence and non-existence at one and the same time.

This is not possible, because it is impossible for real, contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence to coexist within a single phenomenon at a single time. There would be no contradiction if these were accepted as occurring at different times.

Because it relies upon doctrines contrary to the Vedas, there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) between the preceding and following sections by way of the relationship of the supported and the supporter (*upajīvyopajīvakabhāva*), which serves to refute the former view and establish the latter.
Here, a doubt arises as to whether the opinion of the "Direction" (*dig-*) school is based on valid authority (*pramāṇa*) or on delusion (*bhrānti*). Of that [opinion] as well...
Because it is accepted by people of many regions;

for they indeed believe that this entire world, consisting of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living things (*ajīva*), is without a Lord (*nirīśvara*). And that [world] consists of six substances (*ṣaḍ-dravya*).
Those substances are known as *jīva*, *dharma*, *adharma*, *pudgala*, *kāla*, and *ākāśa*. Among these, the *jīvas*...

They are of three kinds: bound, those perfected in yoga, and liberated. That which is called *dharma* is a specific substance pervading the universe that serves as the cause of motion for things possessing movement. *Adharma* is likewise pervasive, serving as the cause of stability. That which is called *pudgala* is a substance characterized by color, odor, taste, and touch; it is of two kinds: in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*)...

And that which consists of their aggregation is a specific substance composed of air, fire, water, earth, and body. Space (*ākāśa*) also consists of a single infinite number of points (*pradeśa*). Among these, the substances distinct from atoms (*aṇu*) are subsumed under the five "existential bodies" (*astikāya*): the existential body of living beings (*jīvāstikāya*), the existential body of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), and the existential body of rest (*adharmāstikāya*).
The soul-substance (pudgalāstikāya) and the space-substance (ākāśāstikāya). The term *astikāya* is applied to a substance that exists in multiple locations.

They also include another compendium useful for the liberation of living beings: the categories of soul (jīva), non-soul (ajīva), influx (āsrava), bondage (bandha), stoppage (saṃvara), and shedding (nirjarā).

It has been grasped. And that [spiritual path] consists of right knowledge, vision, and conduct. Among these, the soul (jīva) possesses the attributes of knowledge, vision, bliss, and energy. The non-soul (ajīva) is the entire collection of objects to be enjoyed by the soul. Influx (āsrava) consists of the sense organs and so forth, which serve as the instruments for such enjoyment. Bondage (bandha) is of eight kinds.

There are four types of obstructive karmas (*ghātikarma*) and four types of non-obstructive karmas (*aghātikarma*). Among these, the former obstructs the innate qualities of the soul—namely knowledge, perception, vigor, and bliss;
the latter serves as the cause for the body, its configuration, the identification with it, its duration, and the resulting pleasure, pain, and equanimity.

Nirjarā is the means to liberation, consisting of austerity as understood from the teachings of the Arhat. Saṃvara is the restraint of the senses, which takes the form of meditative concentration (samādhi).
Liberation, however, is the manifestation of the innate nature of the self for one whose afflictions, such as passion and the like, have ceased.
Furthermore, the atoms that serve as the causes of earth and so forth are not of four kinds, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; rather, they possess a single nature.

The distinction between earth and the other elements is produced by transformation (*pariṇāma*). And every category of entity—whether existent or non-existent, eternal or non-eternal—is such that it may be said:
"it may exist," "it may not exist," "it may both exist and not exist," "it may be inexpressible," or "it may both exist and be inexpressible."

"There may be existence, non-existence, and the inexpressible; there may be both existence and non-existence, and the inexpressible"—thus, because the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) applies everywhere, every category of entity consists of substance and modification (*dravya-paryāya*).

They establish that it possesses existence, unity, permanence, and so forth by way of its substantial nature, while the opposite is established by way of its modificational nature. And as for modifications:

The specific states of a substance; and since these possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, everything—such as existence, non-existence, and so forth—is logically consistent. To this, it is replied: "Because [these] are impossible in one [thing]. This is not tenable. Why?
Because of the impossibility [of opposites] in one [thing]: because contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence cannot exist simultaneously in a single entity, like shadow and light.
This is what is meant: [it is impossible] for a substance...

Furthermore, because the specific state denoted by each respective qualifying modal term (*paryāya-śabda*) constitutes a distinct category (*padārtha*), the coexistence of contradictory properties within a single entity is impossible. To illustrate: it is not possible for that which is qualified at one time by a specific state such as existence (*astitva*) to be simultaneously qualified by its opposite, non-existence (*nāstitva*), and so forth.

Furthermore, how can impermanence—which is the substrate of specific modifications known as arising and destruction—and permanence, which is the opposite of that, both inhere in that same substance? Moreover, how can distinctness—which is the state of being the locus of contradictory properties—and non-distinctness, which is the opposite of that, both inhere in it? It is just as [the properties of] "horseness" and... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].

This is the meaning: it has already been stated that if one accepts both difference and non-difference according to a distinction of time, there follows the consequence of abandoning one’s own philosophical position (*svamatabhaṅga*). It has also been stated previously that the worldly linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of "exists" and "does not exist" among speakers is based on the existence of universals (*jāti*) and so forth. But how can the single Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Śiva, be the self of all?
If it is argued that this is what is stated by the *śrotriyas*, [the reply is:

because Maheśvara possesses true volition (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) as delimited by unique attributes such as omniscience, which is the cause of the expansion of the sentient and insentient world; for although individual souls (*kṣetrajñas*) are distinct by nature, [they are united] like the bees and the worm.

The established conclusion of all Vedānta is that liberation consists precisely in the attainment of Śiva-hood— which is eternally auspicious in nature— preceded by the cessation of the state of being an individual soul (jīvatva) through meditation, concentration, and worship of Śiva.

Furthermore— since the six substances, beginning with the soul (jīva), lack the status of being a single substance and its modes (paryāya), it is difficult to establish unity and plurality within them by way of their substantial oneness and their modal nature. Now, if it should be argued that these six substances exist in such a manner through their own respective modes and their own respective natures— even so:

To claim that "everything is non-conclusive" involves a contradiction with one's own tenet, because there is an absence of mutual identity [between the thesis and the reason]. Therefore, this Jaina doctrine is not tenable.
In the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world] without being presided over by a Lord (īśvara), the previously mentioned defects remain exactly as they were.
The Jainas (Kṣapaṇakas) establish that the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) possess a dimension equal to the dimension of the body; this too he refutes:
"And thus, there would be non-universality of the self" (3.2.33).

If this is your position, it follows that the self would be non-omnipresent (akātsnya). For your established doctrine is that the living being (jīva) consists of innumerable spatial units (pradeśa) and possesses the same dimensions as the body. In that case, when the self residing in a body such as that of an elephant enters the body of an ant, which is of smaller dimensions, it would follow that it is non-omnipresent because it would occupy only a small portion of space.

Furthermore—if it were admitted that the soul possesses a size equal to that of the body—it would follow that, because it could not exit the body, the soul would reach the next world together with the body. Therefore, the subtlety of the soul must be admitted, as the sizes of bodies are not fixed. 34.

If subtle living beings residing within the bodies of mosquitoes and the like were to obtain the bodies of elephants and such through the power of karma, they would not be able to pervade the bodies of those elephants because of the smallness of the soul. Likewise, if gross living beings residing within the bodies of elephants and the like were to obtain the bodies of mosquitoes and the like through the power of karma, [the same difficulty would apply to] the body of the mosquito and so forth.
Because there would be no room due to their extreme smallness.

Anticipating the objection that— since souls, like a tuft of cotton, are admitted to possess parts, they could undergo contraction in the bodies of mosquitoes and so forth, and expansion in the bodies of elephants and so forth— he refutes this:
And even by way of figurative interpretation there is no absence of contradiction, because of [the necessity of] transformation and so forth. (35)
Regarding the argument from "succession" (*paryāyāt*): there is no contradiction because contraction and expansion are accepted as occurring through the sequence of bodies.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction regarding the entry into the bodies of elephants, horses, sons, daughters, horses, and so forth, [the response is: even so, since individual souls (*jīva*) would possess parts, the defects of being subject to modification and destruction—just like jars, cloths, and the like—would necessarily follow; this is what is taught.
Furthermore, in order to refute that view, he states another reason:
"And because of the permanence of the final state and the permanence of both, there would be no distinction. (36)
Since the soul's final dimension, attained in the state of liberation,

remains fixed thereafter due to the absence of assuming another body, and since both that liberated self and its dimension are eternal, that very dimension must be the soul's natural (svābhāvika) one; this was also the case previously.

Therefore, there would be no distinction [between different selves]. Consequently, the claim that the self has the same dimensions as the body is entirely inconsistent; thus, this doctrine, which lies outside the Veda, should be understood by the discerning. *Patyadhikaraṇam* (The Section on the Lord). 8.

Having refuted the doctrine of Kapila, who maintains that the Pradhāna is the cause based on inference, he [establishes] the supremacy of Paśupati Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, according to the Raudra and Pāśupata Tantras which accept the authority of certain portions of the Śruti.
Since the view that [Brahman] is the cause of both the sentient and insentient world has not been accepted, he now refutes those doctrines:

"Because of the lack of consistency in the case of the Lord [of the Śaivas], there is the appearance of the Śaiva doctrine, as well as the Raudra, Pāśupata, Gāṇapatya, and Saura [doctrines]. (Sūtra 2.2.37)

In the preceding section, it was stated that the doctrine of the Kṣapaṇakas is inconsistent because existence and non-existence cannot coexist simultaneously in a single locus due to their mutual contradiction; likewise, [in this section], it is argued that [the opponent's view] is untenable because being the material cause (*upādānatva*) and being the agent (*kartṛtva*) are contradictory in a single locus. Thus, by way of this illustrative analogy (*dṛṣṭānta-saṅgati*), the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerns that which is independent and characterized by all powers.

The connection with the established conclusion (siddhānta) is justified by the sequence of resolving contradictions, because this section is commenced for the purpose of proving that Śiva’s status as the cause of both the origin and the dissolution of the universe is possible.

For the Lord—Paśupati Śiva, the Supreme Brahman—it is not possible for Him to be merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) by way of impelling the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the world; why? Because of inconsistency (*asāmañjasyāt*). For there are scriptural passages enjoining that the Supreme Lord is the cause of both [the material and efficient causes] of the world, such as: "As a spider emits and retracts [its thread]," and so forth.

Since there is no such concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts as described above, the primacy belongs to the pure Sāttvika Śaiva doctrine which establishes the Lord of Beings, Śiva, as the cause of both the origin and dissolution of the universe;
and not to the Śaiva-like doctrines that are mere semblances, nor to the mixed, Raudra, Pāśupata, Gāṇapatya, Saura, or Vaiṣṇava systems.

Because it is taught that this Supreme Power (parā-śakti)— which is manifold, very firm, possesses many sprouts, and is itself non-different from the qualities— is the cause of the three forms [of the Lord] in such passages as these; and because Nārāyaṇa is shown to be Brahman in passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa is the highest reality," and because the Sun is also shown to be Brahman in passages such as "This Āditya is Brahman."
In the mantra "We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages," the term *gaṇapati* refers to the Lord of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the rest;

for in their respective scriptures, the status of being supreme over all is attributed to Vighneśvara. Furthermore, in the Purāṇas, during occasions such as the destruction of Tripura, he is designated as one who is worshipped by the three forms [of the Supreme Deity]; thus, the status of being the cause of the universe belongs to him, not to those previously mentioned.

When it is argued that [the power of creation] belongs only to Śakti and the others, we reply: in such scriptural passages as "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra— they are all brought forth," "One should meditate on the Lord,
who is to be meditated upon," and "Obeisance to the Lord of all sciences, the subduer of all beings," [it is clear that Brahman is the source].

Because its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is established by virtue of being the producer of that [world], and its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established through its dissolution into that [Brahman],
the causality of powers (*śakti*) and so forth pertains only to intermediate creation.
Furthermore, since there can be no power without a substratum, the causality residing in the power [must ultimately reside in the substratum].
This is established by the very sense of the word "capable. In the *Śaivavāyavīyasaṃhitā* it is said:
"These three, whose nature is that of causes, were born directly from Maheśvara for the sake of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe of moving and non-moving beings."
All three were appointed by their father to three tasks:
Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for destruction;
yet, out of mutual jealousy, they each sought to excel one another.
Having propitiated that father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity,
Rudra formerly created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa in another kalpa.
In another kalpa, however, Brahmā—who is composed of the universe—became Rudra and Viṣṇu;
and likewise, the Lord Viṣṇu again created Brahmā.
Furthermore, Brahmā [worships] Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava [worships] Brahmā.
From such scriptural indications, it is understood that the status of Nārāyaṇa and others as the cause of the universe is not established as beginningless.

Their status as Brahman—such as in the passage "Food is Brahman"—is merely figurative, as has been elaborately demonstrated in various ways in the *Janmādhikaraṇa*. Nevertheless, among the three forms [of the deity], the superiority of Rudra alone is unavoidable, for it is said: "Rudra is superior to the universe."

"O best of Brahmins, in the Śrutis it is said: 'The Great Rishi is higher than the highest; that [Brahmā] is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than the highest; the Supreme Lord is higher than the highest,' and so forth.
Rudra possesses sattva within and tamas without;
indeed, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are overcome by rajas and tamas respectively."

And because the *Sūtasamhitā* teaches the gradation among the three forms [of the Lord] by means of such passages as [the verse beginning with] "ptyādi"; and in the *Śātātapa*: "In the Vedas and in the Purāṇas, wherever Śakti [is mentioned], [there He is] Janārdana."
"The greatness [of others] is imagined out of delusion; that is declared to be tāmasa. And in the Gautama-smṛti:
"The Śaiva dharmas, the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and likewise the Smṛtis..."
The internal forms of the sattvic nature possess validity at all times, just like the Vedas.
The Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas, as well as the Śrutis and Smṛtis,
always possess an internal nature characterized by tamas, serving merely for the purpose of excretion.

Therefore, it has been stated that the Viṣṇu Purāṇas should not be studied by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Since Rudra is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas and is himself a Brāhmaṇa, his status as the deity of all deities is unavoidable.
Furthermore: "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies—one terrible and the other auspicious"—thus [it is said] regarding that Rudra of yours.

In the *Taittirīya*, it is declared that Śiva possesses two forms, one peaceful (*śānta*) and one unpeaceful (*aśānta*); furthermore, the protection of devotees is described through his *aghora* body, as well as through the Raudra school of the *Pāśupata* Tantra, which is marked by the heated liṅga seal, and the [other] *Pāśupata* Tantra, which is marked by the seals of the heated trident and *ḍamaru* drum.
The superiority of the Śaiva doctrine, as defined by the wearing of the Śrauta Śivaliṅga, is undeniable. In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:

"Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, who is accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful, the sage goes to the Source of Beings, the Witness of all, beyond darkness."

Thus, by the description of Śiva as being characterized by perfect tranquility (*praśāntatva*), the transcendence of darkness (*tamaḥparatva*), and his distinctness from the three forms (*mūrtitrayavilakṣaṇatva*), the predominance of pure *sattva* in the Śiva doctrine is taught.
"They consider the cessation of phenomenal expansion (*prapañcopaśama*), the auspicious (*śiva*), the non-dual (*advaita*), as the fourth; that is the Self, that is to be known."
Because it is likewise illustrated in the *Māṇḍūkya*; and in the *Siddhāntāgama* and the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"O Agastya, tiger among sages, you who have reached the further shore of all the Āgamas;
I shall speak the Siddhānta which brings about the knowledge of Śiva—listen with reverence."
O Agastya, the established doctrines are known in many ways due to differences in preference; they are endowed with diverse practices and set forth different meanings.
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative; they should not be refuted by logical arguments.
O great sage, the Veda is the primary authority for all systems such as Sāṃkhya and the rest;
it is certain that their validity is established through following the Veda.

O Sage of great intelligence, because it follows all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra is superior to the Pāñcarātra, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, as well as to the Sāṃkhya and other systems that abide only in certain portions of the Vedas.
That which is proclaimed as the Śaiva Tantra, known as Siddhānta and spoken by Śiva,
is always an authoritative means of knowledge like the Veda, because it embodies the meaning of all the Vedas.
The Āgamas have been proclaimed in many ways by Śiva, the Supreme Self,
according to their divisions as Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula.
Among those, the Śaiva Tantra is determined to be fourfold:
the Vāma, the Dakṣiṇa, the Miśra, and that known as the Siddhānta.
The Vāma system is characterized by power (śakti), while the Dakṣiṇa is of the nature of Bhairava;
the Miśra is devoted to the Seven Mothers, and the Siddhānta is in accordance with the Vedas.
By such statements as these,
[the author] sets forth the established doctrines proven by the twenty-eight Āgamas, beginning with the Kāmika, which are concordant with the dharma of all the Vedas—
in the *Kāmika*:
"For Śiva alone, the Lord, like a yogin, may manifest the multitude of objects existing within himself externally by the power of his will, without any material cause. And in the Siddhāntāgama:
Just as a tree exists in the form of leaves, flowers, and so forth,
so does the one Śiva shine forth in the form of the earth and other elements.
Just as a cloth produced from threads is considered to be composed of threads,
so too the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, having arisen from Śiva, is Śiva alone.
Through the expansion of his own power, Śiva exists as the soul of the universe;
he appears as a cloth does when it is spread out, rather than remaining in the form of a rolled-up bundle.
By such statements as these, [the text establishes] Śiva’s status as the dual cause of the universe:
"Just as by meditating on a bee, a worm always becomes a bee, so too by meditating on Śiva, the individual soul (jīva) becomes Śiva; not otherwise."
Thus, because the doctrine of both duality and non-duality has been established, the twenty-eight Śiva-āgamas, beginning with the Kāmika, possess authority just like the Vedas.
The son of Satyavatī is the author of the eighteen Purāṇas.
Just as the Lord Maheśvara is the source of the various divisions beginning with the Kāmika;

Thus, because the authority of the Purāṇas has been established by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Sūtasamhitā* through the illustration of the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, [the present case] is like the refutation of Smṛtis such as those of the Sāṃkhya— which contradict the Smṛtis of Manu and others that are concordant with the Vedas— within the section on "Smṛti having no scope" (*smṛty-anavakāśa-adhikaraṇa*), in favor of those Smṛtis that are concordant with the Vedas.

Thus, because of the designation by such Śrauta-Śaiva teachers as Revanasiddha, Marulasiddha, Ekorāmasiddha, Udbhaṭārādhya, Vemanārādhya, and others: "Obeisance again and again to the one with the golden arm, the golden-colored, the golden-formed, the Lord of gold, the Lord of Ambikā, the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Paśus."

Because in passages such as "Salutation to you, the members of the assembly and the lords of the assembly; salutation to Paśupati, the lord of the worlds," etc., Śiva alone is taught to be the Lord of all; and because in this sūtra [Sūtra 1.2.3], "From the words 'Lord' (pati) and so forth," the attributes such as being the Lord of creatures (paśupatitva) are primarily established as belonging to Śiva alone; therefore, [the objection] in the sūtra "On account of the inconsistency of the Lord" (patyurasāmañjasyāt) [is refuted].

Some say that it is improper for Śiva, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), who is distinct [from the individual soul], to be the cause of both the creation and destruction of the universe, because this contradicts the Vedas and is therefore not authoritative; yet even that is not contradictory.
To this point, he states another reason:
And because a relationship [between the two] is untenable. || 38 ||

If one were to accept that Śivetara, Nārāyaṇa, and others are the cause of the world and the Lord of Paśus (Paśupati), [one would contradict] the golden nature and the status of being the Lord of Umā established by such scriptural passages as: "Obeisance again and again to Hiraṇyabāhu, the Lord of Paśus," "The Ruler of all sciences, the Lord of Brahmā, Brahmā— may Śiva be mine," and "Rudra is indeed all."
Furthermore, the status of being Paśupati (the Lord of Creatures) and the causality of the origin and so forth of the universe are not possible for those other than Śiva.
Therefore, the doctrines of the Śrutyaikadeśins, Miśras, and others are to be disregarded by the followers of the Veda.
[Salutations to] Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara.
One should worship with single-minded devotion and place one's own chosen deity in the center.

If it is argued that this view alone is necessary because of the observation of such scriptural statements, that is incorrect; for no direct Vedic or Smṛti texts enjoining that view are observed, it is contradicted by the experience of devotees, and according to that view,
the Lord who is the cause of the world's origin and so forth is admitted to be illusory, whereas [the truth is] the foundational Brahman.

Because it is designated as being without distinction and because it entails many defects such as the acceptance of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) which contradicts the Vedas, that doctrine is not to be accepted.
At the beginning of creation, the three eggs (*aṇḍatraya*) were born from the power of Śambhu (*śāmbhavī-śakti*).
O high-minded one, within the sattvic egg which resembles pure crystal.
From that [egg], Vāṇī and Rudra were born, endowed with the quality of sattva;
from the rajas-dominated egg consisting of blood, Śrī and Brahmā were born.
Therefore, those two, whose limbs were red in color and who were endowed with the quality of rajas,
were enveloped by darkness within the cosmic egg of darkness, which resembled a dark cloud in appearance.
Umā and Viṣṇu have both arisen from Him; therefore, these two possess the quality of darkness (tamas).
The Supreme Śakti, however, transcends the qualities (guṇātītā) and is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
"Śiva-natured, dependent on Śiva, and the illuminator of the universe of the conscious and the unconscious"—

thus, because the *Śaktipurāṇa* designates that the cosmic egg (*tamaṇḍa*) arose from the ocean of Nārāyaṇa, [the practices of] drinking liquor and consuming meat found in the Śākta Āgamas and the Pāñcarātra Āgamas are [to be understood as] like those of the Rākṣasas and others.
I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who is born from Śiva and Keśava;
he is Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff, and the beloved of Viṣṇu.
By such reasoning— as in the principle that "the qualities of the cause are transmitted to the effect"— it is established that although Bhairava is born from the seed-vitality (*vīrya*) of Śiva,

his dark complexion, his drinking of wine, his fondness for meat, and so forth, as well as his engagement in activities such as the killing of living beings, are justified by his having Viṣṇu as his material cause (*upādāna*). Therefore, even that [conduct] is not something to be enjoined.

Because they accept doctrines such as the consumption of red sandalwood and the remnants of food— which are contrary to the Vedas— and because they assert that the Sun-god is merely possessed of parts and designate him as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*),
[the author] states another reason for their refutation:
And because a substratum is untenable. || 39 ||
If one accepts that the Lord— who is the reflection of Māyā upon a substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) distinct from Brahman— is the cause of the origination and so forth of the world,
then the status of the substrate is untenable; for according to your view, since the substrate-Brahman is accepted as being devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa),
the Vedas and Vedāntas would be inapplicable to it, and consequently, activity toward Brahman would be impossible.

Its falsity is established by implication, like that of a rabbit's horn; for in their view, since the individual soul (*jīva*), Brahman, and the Lord (*īśvara*) are not admitted, the impossibility of a substratum (*svadhiṣṭhāna*) arises. This is because the status of the Supreme Lord as the substratum of the entire manifest world of sentient and insentient beings—established by such scriptural passages as "He entered into the innermost of the inner" and "Rudra who is in the fire"—would otherwise be untenable.
Because it is untenable and impossible.
Furthermore, according to that view,
since the manifold world— including the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth— is superimposed upon the Brahman which is its substratum, the performance of religious duties would be impossible.

Furthermore, according to that view, because two distinct forms of consciousness are admitted, Brahman could potentially be ignorant; consequently, the Vedānta texts which enjoin His omniscience would be untenable, and spiritual activity would be impossible.
Moreover, in the Pāñcarātra system, there are scriptural passages such as "He whose body is the earth" and "He whose body is the self," and so forth.

In accepting the relationship of part and whole between the world and the Lord, we observe the worldly convention that the whole is subtle while the part is gross; for it is said: "Air is the self of fire, and earth is the sustainer of the universe; that which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, is the great abode of the universe."

Thus, the impossibility of [the soul] being the substratum of all things, as established by such scriptural passages, is logically consistent. Furthermore, since it is impossible for a subordinate part (aṅga) to be both the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) and the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) of its principal (aṅgin), if one accepts the relationship of part and whole, then qualities such as attachment, aversion, pleasure, and pain residing in the parts that constitute the nature of the individual soul (jīva) would inevitably belong to the principal, namely the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).

If that were accepted, it would contradict all the Śrutis. For this very reason, the Pāñcarātra doctrine, which is outside the Veda, is even more untenable. By this, the refutation of Dvaita is established by implication, since both [the Advaita and the Pāñcarātra] are Vaiṣṇava traditions.
Furthermore, because the Vaiṣṇava systems such as Dvaita-Bhāgavata and Pāñcarātra accept that the Cause of the Universe possesses a body, [they are refuted].

He refutes the claim that the doctrine of the Vaidikas—that the causal agent of the world, Nārāyaṇa, possesses parts (sāvayavatva), and that even in the state of liberation, souls attain bodies with some slight difference [from Him] as a means for the practice of devotion—is inconsistent: The Vaidikas maintain that because of scriptural designations, the causal agent of the universe, Nārāyaṇa, is possessed of parts; and they hold that even in the state of liberation, individual souls attain bodies that possess some slight distinction from Him, serving as a basis for the practice of devotion. He now refutes this as being untenable.
If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of [the necessity of] experience and so forth. (Sūtra 40)

If it is argued that Nārāyaṇa possesses a body and sense organs because the world exists for his purpose—just as it does for the individual soul (jīva)—we say no; why? Because of [the mention of] enjoyment and so forth.

For in passages such as "He who has neither hands nor feet, yet is swift and a grasper," the independent Lord, the cause of the universe, is taught to be the agent of all things without dependence on a body or sense organs; thus, unlike the individual soul, the Supreme Lord has no need for the purposes of self-conception and the like.

The dependence on a body, sense organs, and so forth must not be admitted. Here, by the refutation of the body and sense organs of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the refutation of the dualistic and qualified-monism (*viśiṣṭādvaita*) schools is established; and by the teaching regarding "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) and so forth, the refutation of the doctrines of illusory monism (*mithyādvaita*) and nihilistic monism (*śūnyādvaita*), which purport to establish the attributeless nature of the Supreme Lord, is likewise taught. Therefore:

The primary intention of the author of the Sūtras is that those seekers of liberation who possess discernment through the study of the Vedas and Vedānta must accept precisely the Vīraśaiva doctrine as propounded by both the dualist and non-dualist schools.
As stated in the Siddhāntāgama:
The Vīraśaiva doctrine, which reconciles dualism and non-dualism, is the sole arbiter for liberation;
it is the essence of the conclusions of all Vedānta and the bestower of success in all aims.
Because it has been thus specified, that alone is supreme; this is the "bell-fault" (*ghaṇṭā-doṣa*).

Furthermore, if the Lord, who is the cause of the world, is established as possessing a body, then—by the consequence of being limited and corporeal like a jar or similar objects—his status as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the corporeal *pradhāna*, the individual soul (*jīva*), air, and space would be undermined.

This is not tenable. For it contradicts such scriptural passages as, "Thou art indeed That, and That art indeed Thou; there the vital breaths do not depart, but are absorbed right there," and because the states of being both formed and formless cannot coexist in one place, his status as the Lord (Īśvara) is untenable.
Now, [one might argue] that for Śiva, who is the Supreme Brahman, [the scriptures state]: "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny..."

If it be argued that, because of the designation of having a body in such passages, an inconsistency similar to that [of the Sāṃkhya] would follow, that is incorrect. For Śiva possesses a body that is a manifestation of his divine play (*līlā*). Even in the absence of a physical body and so forth, since the scriptures declare him to be the cause of all—stating, for example, "without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper"—and since, like Nārāyaṇa, birth as a natural attribute is impossible for him, he does not possess a body for the sake of some specific effect.

There is no stain of suspicion regarding fault in Śiva, whose form is auspicious play. But surely— since the performance of the five-fold worship (pañcapūjā) of Āditya, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Gaṇanātha, and Maheśvara reveals that everyone is a Śaiva, how can he be excluded?
The sun is the primary body of Śiva, the Supreme Self;
within the Ādityahṛdaya, Rudra shines as its controller.
"Situated in the center of the solar orb, accompanied by Ambā, he is the medicine for the world. This is seen in the *Skanda*, *Liṅga*, *Kūrma*, and other Purāṇas.
Furthermore, in the verse: "I bow to him whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; I bow to the beloved of Mukunda," his [divinity] is indicated.

From the description of him as having eyes like the sun, Sūrya is a Śaiva. Ambikā is his wife, Vighneśvara is his son, and Viṣṇu is his devotee; thus, it is undeniable that they are Śaivas. Viṣṇu’s devotion to Śiva is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The state of being Bāṇa, the state of being a bull, the state of being a wife, the form of Ghoṇa,
the state of being a worshipper, and the state of being a friend of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
"Therefore, Nārāyaṇa attained [the status of] the foremost among devotees. Thus it is said. In the Śaiva [scriptures]:
"Gopālaka bore the Liṅga upon his head with devotion."
"O, what doubt can you have regarding the wearing of the *liṅga*?
O people, let those whose understanding of existence has been fashioned by the removal of delusion behold the power of the nectar of Pāṇḍuraṅga! Thus [it is said].
Also in the Śaṅkara-saṃhitā:
"Having placed the Liṅga upon his chest, Hari, and upon his head, Pitāmaha (Brahmā), having worshipped me residing within the Liṅga, both attained their respective stations. Thus it is said.
From this vision of Viṣṇu, his status as a devotee of Śiva is established. In the *Vīrāgama*, within the description of the ten types of Śaivas, it is stated:

"O Goddess of the gods, the Vaiṣṇava is proclaimed as a general Śaiva, due to the performance of the five crest-initiations (*śikhā*) and the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* mantra beginning with 'Bharga'."
O Great Goddess, through the reconstitution of the ashes arising from the Rudra-piṇḍa, the wise one [attains] the former Śaiva [state], while the Saura is proclaimed as the latter.
Because he is established in the form of Sāmba situated in the center of the solar mandala,
because he is a limb of that eight-rayed [sun], and because of his devotion to the previous rites.
The ritual procedure for the fivefold worship (pañcapūjā) is thus declared to be the Miśra-śaiva tradition.

If it is argued that since the systems of the Sauras and others have been established as being included within the Śaiva system by such statements, how can the refutation of those [other] Śaivas be justified? We reply:
no, because [the scriptures state], "Śiva alone, the bringer of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon, having abandoned everything else," and "Rudra is one alone; he did not stand for a second."

Because the Śaivas alone are seen in the Śruti to possess the injunction for the worship of Śiva through such passages as these, whereas the Sauras and others lack devotion to the supremacy of Śiva, do not accept that Paśupati is the cause of both the creation and dissolution of the universe, and because there is no Vedic injunction prescribing his collective worship, their refutation is unavoidable. Trilocana.
Because the branding with the heated *liṅga* favored by the Śivācāryas is non-Vedic— just like the Pāñcarātra and other such systems—

and because, despite the absence of [the specific] Śaiva practices, there is an acceptance of Śiva as merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) as in the systems of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, and because there is no adoption of the relationship between limbs and the whole (*aṅgāṅgitva*) as in the non-Vedic Pāñcarātra and similar schools.

It is not possible for there to be equality with Vīraśaiva, who are distinguished by the wearing of the *prāṇaliṅga*. As it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The mark of the *liṅga* and the mark of the *bhaga* are to be accepted by both Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas; nevertheless, that which belongs to Rudra is declared to be the most superior of all."
This is because of such scriptural observation. Marking with the *liṅga* is superior to marking with the wheel that consists of the *bhaga*.

Since the *Śrīcakra* has the form of a *bhaga*, and since the *bhaga* is recognized as the *svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra* in all Vedāntic philosophy, it is unavoidable that the *cakra* is designated by the term *bhaga*. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is correct.

Since it is impossible for anything other than Paśupati, who is Śiva, to be the cause of the world, and in order to refute systems of thought other than the Paśupati doctrine, he states another reason:
"They would be either finite or non-omniscient. (Sūtra 41)
In passages such as "Viṣṇu alone is the great being, [who becomes] manifold beings in various ways," Viṣṇu’s status as a *bhūta* (being) is established;

whereas in passages such as "The Lord of all beings," Śiva is established as their master by virtue of being the controller of all beings. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of "and. Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa and others, distinct from Paśupati, possess finitude like individual souls (*jīva*) and lack omniscience.

Upon seeing them, their status as the cause of the world’s birth and so forth is not tenable; for in such scriptural passages as "A certain one, fearing, takes refuge in Him who is unborn and all-knowing," and others, qualities such as being unborn and true belong to Śiva alone. Thus, in the first chapter, terms such as "Lord" (pati) and so forth were taught in reference to Paraśiva.

In order to refute the Vaiṣṇava and other doctrines which accept the authority of only certain portions of the Śrutis while disregarding others, a new section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been commenced with the sūtra: "On account of the lack of consistency in [the doctrine of] the Lord" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*). This is because some mixed Śaivas (*miśraśaiva*), by resorting to the Advaita doctrine, at times assert an equality between Śiva and Keśava.

Furthermore, because it establishes the falsity of the Lord who is the cause of the world, that [position] is untenable. Some men, resorting to non-dualism like cats, being utterly deluded, proclaim the equality of others with Rudra.
Thus, in the Sūtasamhitā, within the Sūtagītā as well, that censure is seen:
"Those born from the *rudra-piṇḍa* and dissolved into the realm of Rudra do not recognize their father or their progenitor, just like the sons of a prostitute."
The Vedas are but Dravidian songs; the sages are Toṇḍala and others;
there is only censure of Śiva, devotion to Hari, and skill in cooking.
Due to the curse of Dadhīci and Bhṛgu, those devoted to Viṣṇu on the surface of the earth became intent on reviling Śiva and were possessed of wicked conduct.
Having embraced heretical views, they indeed enter the hells— those who deny Śiva,
who is superior to the universe, the divine of the Brāhmaṇas, and higher than the highest.
Those of deluded minds and evil deeds, even though they call themselves Vaiṣṇavas, disparage Mahādeva— who is established in the Vedas, who is with Ambā, and whose crest is adorned by the half-moon.
Day after day, people afflicted by heresy will, out of delusion, fail to worship the god Śiva, known by names such as Rudra and others, within the *liṅga*.
People afflicted by heresy will, out of sheer delusion, mark their own bodies with symbols such as the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Because such [texts] as the Śaiva, Liṅga, and Skanda Purāṇas teach that Vaiṣṇavas are heretics due to the power of the curses of Dadhīci and Bhṛgu, their doctrine is to be disregarded.
Furthermore, in this sūtra, the refutation of duality and the refutation of non-duality are both treated on the basis of the authority of certain portions of the Śruti.

In the Vaiṣṇava systems such as the Bhāgavata and Pāñcarātra, because the Lord who is the cause of the world assumes a body, He possesses finitude and perishability, just like a jar or a cloth. For the proponents of Advaita, since they accept that Brahman is devoid of attributes and acknowledge the existence of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) preceded by superimposition— like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope— there follows the consequence of His being non-omniscient.

And because of this explanation, the previously stated doctrine—which relies on the authority of fallacious reasoning devoid of reflection upon the preceding and succeeding parts of the Vedic texts—is refuted.
[Objection: "Indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; there was neither Brahmā nor Īśāna. 'I know this Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman'... [Thus it is said.]
From such passages as "The great Puruṣa, sun-colored, beyond darkness; knowing Him alone, one becomes immortal here;

there is no other path for going," found in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, the Puruṣasūkta, and others, as well as from the Bhagavad Gītā's statement "Vāsudeva is everything," it follows that [liberation] results only from the knowledge of Nārāyaṇa who has become Brahman.

If it is argued that being the cause of the birth and so forth of the world is appropriate for Him alone because He is the means to liberation, we say no. For [the scripture] states: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; all this is Brahman; from Him are born Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the senses. Furthermore: "He is not the cause of causes; He is the meditator, the cause of causes, and the object of meditation."
"Endowed with all sovereignty, the Lord of all, Śambhu—the one Śiva in the midst of space—is to be meditated upon as the bringer of auspiciousness.

Since in hundreds of such scriptural passages (śruti) it is Śiva alone who is designated as being distinct from the three forms (mūrtitraya), as the cause of causes, and so forth, it is not appropriate for anyone else to be the cause of the birth and other states of the world. This is also evident from such texts as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," and so on.

The scriptural passages such as "Brahman is food" are merely figurative. In the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter, under the section titled *Sarvatra-prasiddhy-adhikaraṇa*, the intended meaning of the *Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad* is established;
and in the first quarter of that same chapter, under the section titled *Jyotiś-caraṇa-adhikaraṇa*, the intended meaning of the *Puruṣasūkta* is established.

However, according to the perspective of the Śāstras, it is stated in the Sūtra, "But the instruction is like that of Vāmadeva," that the purport of the Bhagavad Gītā is clearly established as being centered on Paraśiva-Brahman by means of the sixfold marks of intentionality (*ṣaḍvidha-tātparya-liṅga*). Thus: "He thought, 'May I be many';
He made Himself manifold"; "Rudra indeed is all"; and "By the Lord is all this pervaded, whatever exists in this world."

If it is argued that because Śiva alone is designated as the dual cause (material and efficient) of the world in passages such as "the world [is born from Him]," neither of the two [alternative] positions is tenable— and thus there is no contradiction with the Pāñcarātra and other texts which enjoin Nārāyaṇa as the cause of the world— that is incorrect. For it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
When the sage Sānanda delivered the denizens of hell from their suffering,
