Bhānu’s son, out of anger, went to Mount Kailāsa.
There, having beheld the Lord of All accompanied by Ambā and having bowed down again and again,
he, filled with sorrow, spoke his joyful account.
Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Rudra asked Nārāyaṇa:
"For the sake of filling the world of Yama once again, [what shall we do]?"
"Compose scriptures that revile men for the sake of achieving delusion.
Having heard that, Hari likewise composed the Buddha-scripture.
The Pāñcarātra, the Cārvāka, the Aghora, and likewise the Kṣapaṇa;
similarly, Rudra Mahādeva is present for the filling of the realm of Yama.
"With devotion, he composed the Śākta, Kāpālika, Miśra, and Pāśupata Tantras— delusive scriptures that lie outside the Veda. Furthermore, in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
In ancient times, for the purpose of deluding the Dānavas, Keśava and Śiva [revealed] the Pāñcarātra, the Kāpāla, the Yāmya, and likewise the Lokāyata.
The Buddha, Jaina, and Cārvāka systems have produced infinite scriptures;
therefore, those such as the Pāñcarātra and others are indeed outside the Veda.
One should never touch the scriptures, even when one's life-breaths have reached the throat.

Because of such scriptural testimony. Furthermore, the Pāñcarātra and other Āgamas composed by the demons (danuja) for the purpose of deluding the world and filling it with their doctrines possess no authority. Moreover, in the Śivarahasya-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, it is said:
"The wise know the ten Śiva Purāṇas to be Sāttvika."
The duties which exist therein are to be trusted by the best of the twice-born.
That which is taught as pure *sattva* is indeed the locus of bliss and knowledge;
it is the *vidyā* instructed to yogis, resembling pure crystal.
"The auspicious Śiva, the sovereign of the Brāhmaṇas, never sleeps anywhere"—
thus do the Purāṇas proclaim these auspicious stories of the Brāhmaṇas.
O lords of sages, the ten Śiva Purāṇas are devoted to the fault of violence,
and the four Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas are tāmasa.
The duties of the Kṣatriyas have been heard; among them, Hari is the presiding deity.
Darkness (tamas) is black, indifferent, and skilled in deceitful actions.
Sleep, laziness, negligence, and so forth are its fivefold tamasic aspects;
sleep, laziness, negligence, and the like are proclaimed to be its qualities.
Kṛṣṇa is remembered as Viṣṇu, the one who reclines upon Śeṣa, and the deluder of his devotees;
these duties of the Kṣatriyas have been declared by the Brahmins.

From such observations, it is evident that Brāhmaṇas follow the Śiva-proclaimed Nigama and Āgama scriptures, characterized by the wearing of the *liṅga*, sacred ash, the crest-mantra (*śikhā-mantra*), meditation, crystal rosaries, and so forth; for it is said:
"The Śiva-liṅga, the crest-mantra, meditation, and indeed the rudrākṣa [rosary]..."
The application of the vibhūtis and the six mudrās are thus proclaimed.
Thus, because of this established conclusion, that alone is logical.
Furthermore, regarding the [Vedic] statement: "The gods follow Hari and Hara;
they follow Him, the Lord of the universe, the Bull of prayers," in the Śruti—
Even by the high-souled Viṣṇu, who was born with the limbs of a fish, a tortoise, a boar, a man-lion, a man, and so forth, death was eventually attained.

Thus, in the *Smṛti*, it is stated that Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, and others are finite; and in the *Sūtasaṃhitā* and *Sūtagītā*, it is said, "Indeed, Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa are overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*. Because of this designation of being enveloped by *tamas*, some maintain that the omniscience of Nārāyaṇa is established only by implication (*arthāt*).

This too is established as being non-contradictory, because it negates the status of being the dual cause of the universe for those such as Nārāyaṇa—who are distinct from Paśupati—yet who are characterized by birth and death shrouded in darkness (tamas). Thus ends the section on the impossibility of origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa). || 9 ||

Regarding the refutation of the *Pāñcarātra* and other systems by relying on their status as being authoritative only for a single portion of the Veda: why would the *Pāñcarātra-āgama* be [rejected] by the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is established by such Vedic texts as "That Viṣṇu is the one supreme" and "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," and who possesses absolute sovereignty over all? How [could this be]?
Anticipating the objection that [this view] contradicts the Vedas, he refutes it: "Because of the impossibility of its origination" (Sūtra 42).
Because it would entail the birth or production of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) from the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*),

which contradicts scripture, logic, and experience, the *Pāñcarātra Āgama* scriptures that prescribe the origin of the *jīva* must not be accepted by the Vaidikas under any circumstances. [Otherwise,] the *kṣetrajñas* would be like the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*).

If one accepts that [the individual soul] originates from the Supreme Self, then, by the same logic, it would follow that the souls are subject to destruction; consequently, liberation—which consists of attaining a state of similarity (*sārūpya*) with Nārāyaṇa as taught in those scriptures—would not be possible.
Thus, the question arises: is the *Pāñcarātra* scripture, which designates the soul as being produced, based on valid authority (*pramāṇa*), or is it rooted in error?
There is doubt.

The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is as follows: because it was composed by Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman; because it is devoted to Him; because it makes known the means for attaining the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*); and because it is superior to [the teachings of] Manu and others, the Pāñcarātra Āgama taught therein [is authoritative].

The authority of the Vedas is established; and their system is as follows: from Vāsudeva, who is the supreme cause, Saṅkarṣaṇa is born as the individual soul (jīva). From Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna arises.
From that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) named Aniruddha comes forth. These four are the manifestations (vyūhas) of the Lord of All. Thus it is said.
Therefore, that scripture is irrefutable.
Furthermore, because it is observed that all Brāhmaṇas employ [the fruits of] their actions— such as sacrifices, ancestral rites, and gifts— in dedication to Kṛṣṇa.
Of all the various atonements that consist essentially of ascetic practices and ritual acts,
the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme among them all.
Whatever I do with body, speech, mind, or the senses, whether through bondage of the self or by the very nature of *prakṛti*,
I offer it all to the Supreme, to Nārāyaṇa.

Because such statements as these teach that all ritual actions must be preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu and that they constitute the worship of Viṣṇu; because we observe the practice of uttering "Śrī Govinda, Govinda" during the formal resolve for every action; and because Viṣṇu is declared to be the primary deity at the *śrāddha* ceremony, and at Gayā, at the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu...

"May it be given. By this, because it indicates the dedication specifically to Viṣṇu through the formula "May the illustrious Janārdana be pleased," and because the injunction for the recitation of the twelve names beginning with Keśava— such as "Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda"— for the purpose of effecting purification of the body has been extensively elaborated upon in various ways in the Smṛtis.
In the ritual attendance for the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana):
Nārāyaṇa, who dwells eternally in the center of the orb of the sun, seated upon a lotus throne;
adorned with armlets, crocodile-shaped earrings, and a crown; wearing a necklace, possessing a golden body, and bearing the conch and the discus—He is to be meditated upon.
O wielder of the conch, discus, and mace; O Acyuta, whose abode is Dvārakā;
O Govinda, O lotus-eyed one, protect me who have come to you for refuge!
Thus, from the observation of the prayer to Nārāyaṇa within the solar maṇḍala:
"Obeisance to the divine one who is the essence of the Brahmanas, and to him who is for the welfare of cows and Brahmanas;
obeisance again and again to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, who is for the welfare of the world."
Thus, having performed the remembrance of Govinda,
just as water fallen from the sky goes to the ocean,
so too does every prostration to the gods go toward Keśava.

By this statement, it is established that among all acts such as salutations performed for other deities, Keśava alone is the primary object of intent; furthermore, since it is observed that the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* mark made with Vaiṣṇava clay must be applied by everyone every morning, and because one does not accept the *liṅga*, holy water, or consecrated offerings (*prasāda*) from any source other than the Śālagrāma.

Furthermore, since in the systems of the Smārta-Vaiṣṇavas and others, instruction is received from the Rāmāyaṇa alone, and since the recitation of the *Viṣṇu-sahasranāma* is the primary object of contemplation for all, it is stated that all Brāhmaṇas are indeed devoted to Viṣṇu.

Since the Yajurvedic scripture states, "Rudra is indeed cruel," and thus designates Rudra as being characterized by *tamas*, it follows by implication that the Śiva Āgamas composed by him, as well as the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas that propound them, lack authority due to their *tāmasa* nature. Likewise, in the Śāṇḍilya Smṛti:
All those scriptures which declare Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, to be the highest of all, are indeed considered to be of the nature of sattva.
The scripture that speaks of Prajāpati, Kṛśānu, and likewise the goddess Sarasvatī as being supreme,
is declared to be rājasa.
Any scripture that declares the supremacy of the Liṅga, Vāmadeva,
or Umāpati as being the highest is proclaimed to be tāmasa.
Thus it has been clearly stated.

Furthermore, since it is heard in the scriptures that after the offering to Rudra in all sacrificial rites and the like, one must "touch water," this very fact serves as the primary illustration for demonstrating Śiva’s tamasic nature and inauspiciousness.

Since it is taught in passages such as "From Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born" that Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the world's origin and so forth, and because the Pāñcarātra Āgama composed by Him is therefore superior, it follows that all Brāhmaṇas should accept only that [Pāñcarātra]; to this, we reply: [The following objection is raised: Since it is taught in passages such as "From Nārāyaṇa, Rudra is born" that Nārāyaṇa is the cause of the world's origin and so forth, and because the Pāñcarātra Āgama composed by Him is therefore superior, it follows that all Brāhmaṇas should accept only that [Pāñcarātra]. To this, we reply:
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: the Vaiṣṇava doctrine propounded in the Pāñcarātra Āgamas is not to be enjoined for the followers of the Vedas.
Why? Because those [Āgamas] are primarily based on Tantric principles.
This is evident from such Smṛti texts as: "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord; the Wise One is neither born nor does he die. And so forth.

Because the beginninglessness of the individual souls (jīvas) is taught, the doctrine of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas—which proclaims doctrines external to the Vedic scriptures regarding the origin and so forth of the soul—would become non-Vedic, like the doctrine of Buddha. Is the preeminence of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas due to their being composed by Nārāyaṇa? Or...

The first [definition]—as that which reveals the secret conduct (*gūḍhācāra*) and dharma of the Vaiṣṇavas—is not correct, because it over-extends (*ativyāpti*) to the Buddhist scriptures (*buddhāgama*) and so forth. Nor is the second [definition] correct, because it would entail the fallacy of granting authority (*prāmāṇya*) to texts such as the *Kūcimāra*.
For it is said: "In the case of Smṛtis, Tantras, and Purāṇas, whatever matter contradicts the Śruti..."
But the meaning of the tantra is to be understood as something censured by the Brahmins and others.
Thus, from the observation of the *Pārāśara-vyavasthā*, if that [position] were accepted, the consequence of being beyond the four castes (*varṇa*) would be unavoidable. Furthermore,
because the name of Viṣṇu is remembered at the commencement of all rites in certain *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, the superiority of Viṣṇu [is established].
Is [the supreme being] the status of the *parabrahman* or the primacy of a Vedic deity?
Not the first, because in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," "Rudra is indeed the eternal, the ancient," "There is only one Rudra;
he does not stand for a second," and "They speak of the oneness of Rudra," it is Śiva alone who is [described].
Because the status of being supreme over all is established [for Viṣṇu], no other possesses supremacy over all.
Furthermore: "Among the gods you are a Brāhmaṇa, and among humans I am a Brāhmaṇa;
indeed, a Brāhmaṇa approaches a Brāhmaṇa; you, Viṣṇu, are the sovereign lord of the gods and the Brāhmaṇas."

In the Yajur and Sāma Vedas, it is taught that Śiva is of Brahminical nature and is to be worshipped by Brahmins; for instance, through such passages as "The Lord of Kṣatriyas, among Brahmins [he is] to be worshipped by Brahmins alone as the most trustworthy one, O Mahādeva," it is declared that Śiva is a Brahmin and is the object of worship for Brahmins.
"This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin; therefore, Brahmins have Soma as their king; Soma is ours..."
In passages such as "Soma alone is the king of the Brāhmaṇas; 'O Brāhmaṇas, we have a king,' so say the subjects," the Brāhmaṇahood and the lordship over the Brāhmaṇas of Śiva are taught.
(In the Kūrma Purāṇa...)
The Brāhmaṇa is the teacher of the letters in both their direct and reverse orders;
specifically, one should take refuge in Rudra as the Lord of the Brāhmaṇas.
In the Pārāśara Purāṇa: "The Supreme Lord is the most excellent among all castes;
for a relationship is appropriate between two most excellent parties, but not with another."
Therefore, the connection of the Brahmin is indeed joined with Śiva alone;
the mixed castes are all the gods, while Purandara is the Śūdra.
Pitāmaha is the Vaiśya, Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya,
and the Lord Rudra is the Brāhmaṇa— the highest of all.
The Brahminhood of Rudra, who has become Brahman, is not born of any cause;
indeed, he is eternally the Brahmin in the world, and it is toward the Brahmin that one should seek refuge.
Neither the other [castes]—the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, nor the Śūdra, nor those of mixed birth—are so;
therefore, by the singular path of the Veda, one is always a twice-born Brāhmaṇa.

One should understand the Great Brāhmaṇa as Īśāna and none other—the Self who has become the soul of all, Virūpākṣa, the best of the twice-born. For him who does not fall into confusion regarding this, there is no sin; of this there is no doubt.
Thus it is said. Likewise, in the Yajurveda: "He who indeed sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity;

he does not reach the higher deity and becomes worse off. The meaning of this scriptural passage is that he who, having bypassed his own deity, sacrifices to another deity, does not reach the supreme deity and becomes worse off. People do not desire him within.

"Those who, by means of their higher intellect, grasp Rudra with their tongue— that is, Śiva accompanied by Bhavānī— do not desire him within the tortoise, as supported by this scriptural statement; rather,
they undoubtedly grasp only the *purīṣa* (the earth-element) with their tongue."
A Brāhmaṇa should always approach the Supreme Lord, the Great Brāhmaṇa, the Sovereign, through the Śrauta and Smārta rites and through constant right conduct.
For that reason, the best among theists, the Brahmin, should always regard Viṣṇu and all others as subordinate; he should never regard them as primary.

For those who have attained their caste by birth and likewise for those in the stages of life (āśramas), Mahādeva alone is to be worshipped preeminently for the sake of spiritual perfection; there is no other.
"For the sake of attaining that [state], the eternal Mahāviṣṇu is to be worshipped by all"—
by such passages in the Skanda Purāṇa, the Brāhmaṇahood of Śiva alone is understood.
"Neither one who is not a portion of the gods gives food, nor does one who is not Viṣṇu become a lord of the earth."
No one who is not a seer composes poetry, nor does anyone who is not Rudra recite the Krama-text.
Thus, in the Skanda Purāṇa, the Brahminhood of a Brahmin who is a portion of Rudra is stated by virtue of his reciting the sequence of the Vedas;

the Kṣatriyahood of Viṣṇu is stated by virtue of his being the lord of the earth, as in the verse: "No one who is not Viṣṇu is a lord of the earth. Furthermore, it is said: "Viṣṇu is fond of ornaments, and Śiva is fond of consecration."

Thus, because it is heard that the incarnations such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were born into the Kṣatriya lineage; because in the world one observes the use of terms such as Govindarāja, Varadarāja, and Raṅgarāja for the forms of Viṣṇu; and furthermore, because the word *varman* is employed in the auspicious festivals and other rites prescribed in the Pāñcarātra Āgamas, [it follows] regarding Viṣṇu...
The status of a Kṣatriya is inescapable.
Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, while Mādhava is the deity of the Kṣatriyas;
likewise, Brahmā is the deity of the Vaiśyas, and the Leader of the Gods (Indra) is the deity of the Śūdras.
Thus, in the *Manusmṛti*, Viṣṇu’s status as the deity of the Kṣatriyas is clearly stated.

Now, one might object: since the word "Īśvara" is heard in reference to Viṣṇu at the sites of Veṅkaṭeśvara and Viṭaleśvara, and since his birth in a Brāhmaṇa family is mentioned in the context of his incarnation as Paraśurāma, how [is he the deity of the Kṣatriyas]?

If it is argued that the status of being a *kṣatriya* is being taught [here], we say no; for Veṅkaṭeśvara’s status as Viṣṇu is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*), since attributes such as the serpent ornaments and so forth are manifested in his [manifested] form, while in the original form (*mūlavigraha*) they are absent— just as a rope appears as a snake, it is nothing more than a mere appearance.
Furthermore—the word *Īśvara* is used because of the sight of a Śiva-liṅga beneath his hand.

Since Viṭṭhaleśvara Viṣṇu is seen wearing a Śiva-liṅga on his head, the word *Īśvara* is determined there by means of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound (*īśvarasya liṅgam*). [This applies also] to Viśvāmitra, who was born from a portion of Rudra.

It is observed that even one born as a Kṣatriya attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism, as in the case of Paraśurāma, who was born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa; whereas one born as a Brāhmaṇa performs the duties of a Kṣatriya through his occupation, as seen in the case of Vyāsa. And it is established in the *Harivaṃśa* that this [change in status] was caused by the transposition of the *caru* offerings dedicated to Rudra: [The text continues with the verses: "O Brāhmaṇa, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two gods, Rudra and Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni became a Kṣatriya and you became a Kṣatriya. "O best of Brāhmaṇas, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two gods, Rudra and Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni became a Kṣatriya and you became a Kṣatriya. "O best of Brāhmaṇas, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two gods, Rudra and Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni became a Kṣatriya and you became a Kṣatriya. "O best of Brāhmaṇas, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two gods, Rudra and Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni became a Kṣatriya and you became a Kṣatriya. "O best of Brāhmaṇas, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two gods, Rudra and Viṣṇu, the son of Jamadagni became a Kṣatriya and you became a Kṣatriya. "O best of Brāhmaṇas, because of the transposition of the *caru* offerings of the two
In ancient times, due to a reversal of the sacrificial oblations (caru) between the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava rites of Bhṛgu,
the portion of Viṣṇu indeed took birth on earth as the son of Jamadagni.
Viśvāmitra, the son of Kuśika and descendant of Gādhi, who possessed portions of Śiva,
begot a son whose nature consisted of austerity, knowledge, and tranquility.
"Having attained equality with the Brahman-sages, he has gone [to that state].

Therefore, Śiva possesses the nature of a Brāhmaṇa, the lordship over Brāhmaṇas, and for that very reason, supreme excellence—[as it is said]: "The Brāhmaṇa born from the *piṇḍa* of Rudra [worships] Rudra, the all-pervading Lord of all."
Through delusion alone he does not recognize his father, just like the son of a courtesan.
One should know that the son who hates his father has seed elsewhere;
one should know that he who constantly hates Brahmins has his seed in the lowest place.

This is seen in the Skanda Purāṇa with these and other words. Therefore, because Rudra is a Brāhmaṇa and because he is the cause of the origin of Brāhmaṇas, the public proclamation is that those who hate Rudra are to be excluded from the Brāhmaṇas. "The ancestors take up the embryo, a boy wearing a lotus-garland; when the man here says 'it exists,' the wife eats it."

In the *Āpastamba-Gṛhyasūtra*, it is heard that the Brāhmaṇa is the cause of the *rudrapiṇḍa* (the rice-ball for Rudra), as expressed in the phrase "he becomes one who conforms to the assembly of men.
Now, if it is argued that by the mention of the Vasus and others, only the eleven Rudras are intended here, we say no.
It is logical that they are designated as Rudras precisely because they are portions (*aṃśa*) of Īśvara, since there is no difference between a part and the whole.

According to the principle of the original and its transformation (*prakṛti-vikṛti-nyāya*), their manifestation occurs in rites such as the *śrāddha* in that same manner. Therefore, it is established that Rudra alone is superior to Viṣṇu and the others.
The second [position] is not tenable—namely, that Nārāyaṇa alone existed, and neither Brahmā nor Īśāna existed—for in such passages as "From Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born;

from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born," we do not see Nārāyaṇa as the cause of the cause in the same manner as Śiva. Furthermore, in the statement "Nārāyaṇa alone existed," the term *eka* (alone) refers to the primordial Viṣṇu, just as in the phrase "Parāśara was the first [to exist]" (*āsīt parāśaraḥ*).
The state of being born from Paramaśiva is thus taught. Likewise, in the Ṛgveda: "Viṣṇu, knowing thus the supreme one, having been born, great, protects the third.
The meaning of this is: Viṣṇu, the knower (vidvān) who knows in this manner the supreme Maheśvara, [is born] from Viṣṇu.
The state of being a knower of Paramaśiva is well-known in another mantra: "O Viṣṇu, you know the divinity of the Supreme.
Such is Bṛhadviṣṇu; the qualification "Bṛhat" (Great) refers to Viṣṇu as one who transcends the other forms, such as the Vyūhas and Avatāras.
Thus, it refers to Viṣṇu who is beyond all other manifestations.

In another mantra as well: "I offer salutation to the great Viṣṇu; O Viṣṇu, we resort to your great benevolence," and so forth. Being born from Him, that Ādiviṣṇu himself directly protects Kailāsa, the third world situated above the realms of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Therefore, it is established that [the Lord] is born from Ādiviṣṇu, the unborn Maheśvara.
"O Rudra, some fearful person approaches you saying, 'I am unborn'; protect me forever with that face of yours which is to the south.

Since by this mantra from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* the state of being unborn is established for Śambhu alone, his status as the cause of causes is proven. [It is not the case that] Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa.
Sentences such as these have as their subject matter Rudra in his intermediate state (*avāntarakāla-rudra*).
Starting from the passage, "These three causal selves were born directly from Maheśvara," it continues:
"And likewise, the Lord Brahmā was created again by Viṣṇu."

Furthermore, in the *Vāyusaṃhitā* it is observed that through such passages as "Brahmā [was born] from Nārāyaṇa, and Bhava again from Brahmā," various intermediate distinctions have been extensively elaborated across different *kalpas* due to the grace of Paramaśiva; yet, by the act of [the text stating] "Nārāyaṇa alone existed," his [oneness] is established.

The state of being born from the Supreme Lord has been taught; however, in that context, he is not seen to be the cause of the three forms (mūrtitraya). In other Vedic scriptures, the status of being the cause of the universe as well as the cause of the three forms is specified for Śiva alone. In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "The exponents of Brahman say: What is the cause?"

Brahmā, beginning with the question "From where were we born? and establishing through a series of questions and answers that Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman, [declares]: "When there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone existed."
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; from it has issued forth the ancient wisdom.
Since Śiva alone is established by such passages as these, through His existence prior to the entire universe and as the referent of the Gāyatrī mantra;
and since His status as "superior to the universe" (viśvādhika) is taught in such texts as, "He who was the first among the gods, Rudra, the great seer, superior to all"; and in the Atharvaśiras—

One should meditate upon Īśāna, who is to be deeply contemplated. All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—are produced from Him, as are all the senses together with the elements. He is not a cause among causes; rather, He is the meditator and the object of meditation. Śambhu, the one Lord endowed with all sovereignty, is the auspicious Śiva alone in the midst of space.

Since the Śrutis, such as "One should meditate on Him alone who brings about auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else," designate Him alone as the cause of all causes, and because no Śruti is seen that establishes Nārāyaṇa as the cause of all causes or as being superior to the universe, it is not in any way tenable that Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman. [He is] Īśāna.

By the passage beginning with "of all sciences" (*sarvavidyānām*), Śiva’s role as the protector is established; furthermore, in such scriptural texts as "Salutation to the Lord of Death, salutation to the Subduer of all beings, salutation to the Great Devourer," His very nature as the cause of the dissolution of all things is observed.

Therefore, His status as the Supreme Brahman is beyond dispute. [As stated in the Vedānta-sūtras: "From which [Brahman] the birth and so forth of this [universe proceed]," and "From which indeed these beings [arise]."
Furthermore, in passages such as "from which [all beings] are born," it is stated that being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman.

Nor is the third [option] tenable, because for those who follow the Vedas, Virūpākṣa is designated there as the presiding deity of all ritual actions (*karmādhidevatā*), following the opening of the first mantra of the Sāmaveda, "And penance is yours, and recitation is yours," and concluding with, "Obeisance to the Lord of Action" (*karmādhipataye namaḥ*). Thus, it is said: "You are Virūpākṣa."

At the commencement of every action, the remembrance of Śiva alone is appropriate. Thus it is stated in the Śaiva Purāṇa: "A follower of the Vedas should perform all actions with Śiva as the objective; whether one is impure or pure, or even if one has reached any state whatsoever."
"He who remembers Virūpākṣa is pure both externally and internally"—thus it is heard in scripture. And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Whether pure or impure, in all states and at all times..."
Whoever indeed remembers Virūpākṣa becomes as pure as Vaiśvānara.

Thus it is heard: because they are rooted in the Śruti, just like the Smṛtis of Manu and others, the various statements enjoining the recollection of Śiva at the commencement of all rites possess the status of being enjoined (or authoritative).
However, because they lack a basis in the Veda, the Smṛtis that prescribe the dedication to Viṣṇu at the commencement of rites [do not possess such authority].

Its weakness is like that of the Smṛtis of the Sāṅkhya and other schools. Having remembered that the day, the weekday, the lunar mansion, the conjunction, and the karana— all are composed of Śiva, the follower of the Veda should perform his ritual action.
Thus, in the *Smṛti*, it is heard that the days, weekdays, lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and so forth, are composed of Śiva. And likewise, the *Śruti* says:
"The entire world, the beings, the universe—wondrous, born in many ways, and whatever is being born—all this is indeed Rudra; let there be obeisance to that Rudra."
In hundreds of such scriptural passages, it is heard that "everything has Śiva as its essence.
Furthermore, at the commencement of a Śrāddha rite:
"The Great Lord Maheśvara, the Sovereign (Īśāna), exists in the form of the ancestors."
May the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva, be pleased.

Thus, the obligation to perform the *śrāddha* rite has been taught as a means of pleasing Śiva and as an act of worshiping Śiva. Likewise, in the conclusion—through the passage beginning with "Salutation to Vāmadeva"—the dismissal of the Brahmins is heard to be preceded by the remembrance of Śiva; [thereby establishing consistency] between the introduction and the conclusion.
Because it is seen that [the ritual] is ultimately dedicated to Śiva, the central portion of it must likewise be dedicated to Him alone. Accordingly, the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* states:
"One should perform occasional *śrāddha* rites with devotion for the sake of pleasing Śiva;
one should do so with everything prescribed for one's own home, with the intention of worshipping Śiva."
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "He who offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) with true devotion at the site of Gayārudra,
having uplifted seven generations of his lineage, is glorified in the world of Śiva."

Because, in that context, the instruction begins with "Īśāna, Viṣṇu, Kamalāsana, Kārtikeya, the triad of fires, Arka, and Rajanīśa," etc., the feet of Īśāna alone are taught first; and because of the statement in the Bodhāyana Sūtra, "May [the offering] given at Gayā reach all the feet, beginning with the feet of Śrī Rudra," the entire Śrāddha ceremony is indeed for the propitiation of Śiva alone.

If it is argued that, because of the statement "of Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, the protector of the śrāddha," he alone is taught as the protector of the śrāddha and therefore he alone is the giver of the fruit of the śrāddha— this is not so.
Viṣṇu is mentioned here by virtue of his office as the presiding deity over the host of the Viśvedevas and others, just as [the king] is designated in the royal treasury.
Viṣṇu’s role as their protector is specified like a command to his servants. In the Skanda Purāṇa, after the paralyzing of Vyāsa’s arm, Viṣṇu says to Vyāsa:
"Indra is the performer of sacrifices, and Vākpati (Bṛhaspati) is the author of the Vedas."
"I alone am the creator of the world; my creator is Maheśvara.

By this statement, the supreme preeminence of Śiva alone is taught. This is because the Śruti text, "Rudra who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who is in the plants—Rudra who has entered all beings," teaches the abiding presence of Rudra alone as the presiding deity of the waters and other elements.
At the time of bathing as well—one should perform the bath after recollecting Rudra, the presiding deity of the water, with the Vāmadeva mantra. Likewise, in the Śātātapa [Smṛti]:
"With the mantra 'Vāmadeva,' [one should remember] Sadāśiva, the lord of the waters."
One should always perform the ritual bath with mindfulness for the cessation of all sins.
Since the prayer to Śiva at the time of bathing is seen in such passages as these, that alone is appropriate:

"I bow to the immutable Śiva, who dwells in the center of the solar orb, who is accompanied by Ambā, the medicine for the world, the blue-throated, the three-eyed. Thus it is stated in the Gautama-smṛti.

"The sun is the primary body of Śiva, the Supreme Self"— thus it is taught in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* that the sun resides within the solar orb and constitutes the primary body of Śiva. Therefore, it is established that Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman.

But surely, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "This golden person within the sun" and continuing with "His eyes are like a tawny lotus," there is the teaching of two eyes for the person manifested in the solar orb; thus,
by such statements as "He who always dwells in the center of the solar orb is to be meditated upon," [the identity] of Nārāyaṇa [is established].
If it be argued that because of the teaching regarding His abiding within the solar orb, He alone is the one denoted by the word *bharga*, we say no;

for this was refuted in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "On account of the teaching of His attributes within" (1.1.20). Furthermore, in the *Nīlakaṇṭha-bhāṣya* and in the *Dhyāna-yoga-khaṇḍa* of the *Sūta-saṃhitā*, Śiva is established as the one who abides within the solar orb.

Because of the instruction regarding the meaning of that mantra—in the statement, "His eyes are like a lotus with a yellowish-white interior" (*kapyāsaṃ puṇḍarīkamiva*)—it has been demonstrated in many ways that by the phrase "the sun (*kapi*) drinks water (*kaṃ*) with its rays," it is established by implication that the third eye is in a state of being closed (*mukulīkṛta*), just like a lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) that has been opened by it. In the *Śatarudrīya*: "He who glides forth... (asau yo'vasarpati).

By the passage beginning with "The blue-necked, the crimson-hued," it is established that Śiva alone resides within the solar orb. Furthermore, because the Vedic text—"Today we offer praise to you, Rudra, the skillful one; to the lord of heroes, we pay homage"—is heard as an injunction for the dedication of all devotional hymns, praises, and salutations to Śiva, all obeisance to the gods [is ultimately directed toward him].
Because statements such as "it goes toward Keśava" contradict the Vedas, they do not possess the status of being authoritative injunctions, just like the words of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti.
Furthermore, in the sentence "by means of the five-headed initiation," [the reference is] to Maheśvara, who possesses three eyes and is distinguished by five heads.

Since the application (*viniyoga*) has been established for the *sandhyāvandana* rite, it is logical that all words in the passage should be construed according to that application. However, within that specific context, because the word "Bharga" is explicitly stated to refer to Rudra by the phrase "the splendor of the god, of the nature of Rudra," and according to the maxim that "in a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative," [the former prevails].
The meaning of the sentence must be construed in accordance with the meaning of the scripture.
On this point, some say that just as goods presented by a minister are subject to the king's authority, so too salutations and other acts offered to Viṣṇu are subject to Śiva’s authority.
Just as an ornament such as a crown brought by thieves should not be worn by those very thieves, so too is the salutation to the gods [not to be performed by those who have stolen it].
Just as all rivers and the like indeed enter into the ocean,
so too does the salutation of all the gods certainly enter into Mahādeva.
"It is not possible for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others to always maintain both [the mūrdhābhiṣeka and the smārta ācamana]";
thus it is heard in the Skanda Purāṇa. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Now, in the Viṣṇudharmottara, immediately after the definition of the smārta ācamana, it says: "Now, with Keśava and the others," and so forth.
If it is argued that the *purāṇa*-prescribed sipping of water (*ācamana*) is established as something to be performed by those following the Vedic tradition, we say no;
for the Vedic *ācamana* is declared to be that which is to be performed continuously during sacrifices and the like,
whereas the *smārta* *ācamana* is to be known as that which pertains to those who rely upon *smārta* (tradition-based) rites.

Thus, based on the recollection in the Gautama-smṛti, it should be understood that the sipping of water (ācamana) using names such as Keśava is indeed tantric. If it is asked, "Why should even Vaidikas and Smārtas not perform ācamana with Keśava and the other names at times such as the voiding of urine?"—the answer is no; for Brāhmaṇas have Śiva as their deity.
The sipping of water (ācamana) should indeed be performed with the names of Śiva;
at times such as the Brahma-yajña, the Vedic ācamana is prescribed;
and at times such as the Soma sacrifice, the Śrauta ācamana is enjoined.
In the Smārta rites such as the Sandhyā, the worship of the Smṛti has been declared.
At the time of voiding urine and other excretions, the ancient tradition prescribes sipping water (ācamana);
a wise person should perform this twenty-five times while reciting the names of Śiva and other mantras.

Thus, based on the observation of the *Smṛti* of Vṛddha-Śātātapa, that [the former] alone is logical. The vertical *puṇḍra* and so forth are not to be accepted by the followers of the Vedas (*vaidika*), because they belong to the Tantras. As it is stated in the *Pārāśara Purāṇa*:
"The triple-line mark (*tripuṇḍra*), the smearing with ashes (*uddhūlana*), and so forth, should be known as the emblems of the Śruti."
Neither the vertical *urdhvapuṇḍra* and so forth, nor the horizontal *tripuṇḍra*, are mentioned in the Śruti.
In the Śātātapa [Smṛti]:
"If one should ever apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with clay even in jest,
he is tormented by the instruments of that same shape by the servants of Yama."
And in the Gāruḍa-smṛti:
"The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is for gods and Brahmins; a circle is for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
the half-moon is for Śūdras; and others [should wear] the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka)."
And in the Sūtasamhitā and the Brahmagītā: "People afflicted by heresy, acting out of sheer delusion, apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead, or a circular or semi-circular mark."
People afflicted by heresy will, out of sheer delusion, mark their own bodies with symbols such as the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
In the Viṣṇusmṛti:
"Just as wood found in a cremation ground is unfit for all ritual acts,
so too a Brahmin marked with the discus is excluded from all ritual acts."
One should abandon like an outcaste that person on whose forehead there is no mark of ash, on whose neck no rosary of rudrākṣa beads, and in whose mouth the five-syllable mantra does not reside.
In the Gautama-smṛti: "The mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, wearing the *liṅga* on the head,
the *śikhā*, *rudrākṣa*, and sacred ash— these are the characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa."
If a Brāhmaṇa born of noble lineage and learned in the scriptures should wear the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* mark,
the king shall place him upon a donkey and banish him from the kingdom.
If a learned Brahmin of noble birth wears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*,
one should avoid such a Brahmin as one would a jar defiled by the remnants of liquor.
Furthermore, O Gautama, even the rule for expiation regarding that is heard:
"A man who has applied the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* with clay and worn circular leaf-shaped marks is purified simply by wearing the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes."
When the body is marked with conch shells, discs, and other weapons of the deities,
a person is purified merely by wearing the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made of sacred ash.
"The body of that man who is free from disease is burned by fire;
yet, O twice-born, he is purified by the ash merely through the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads.
Thus it is said in the Sāma Śākhā.
Having drunk liquor, having gone to the wife of one's guru,
and having committed the theft of gold and the killing of a Brahmin;
Covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes,
and reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus, through numerous Śrutis and Smṛtis, the greatness of wearing ashes, Rudrākṣas, and the Liṅga has been elaborately expounded in many ways throughout all the treatises.
Now, one might object: since the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, which supplement the Vedas, do not propound the path of non-Vedic Tantras...

If it is argued that the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and other marks are Vedic because they are like the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* made with ashes, we say no; for it is stated in the *Pārāśara Purāṇa* or the *Dharmaśāstra*: "That meaning which contradicts the Śruti is to be understood by the wise as the meaning of the *Tantra*, and not as the meaning of the Veda."

From such scriptural testimony, even though the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and other such practices are mentioned in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, they are not to be accepted by the followers of the Veda, because—despite being recorded in those texts—they lack a basis in the Veda and are contrary to it.
[As it is said: "In Gauḍa there is learning, in Cola there is austerity, and in the region of Kāśmīra there is compassion."
In the noble land, there is virtuous conduct; in Kerala, however, there is the accomplishment of mantras.

If it is argued that— since the *Pārāśara Purāṇa* thus establishes the supreme excellence of the customs of the Āryāvarta region, and since practices such as the worship of the name Keśava, the vertical *puṇḍra*, and the *sālagrāma* are frequently observed in that region— therefore the custom of that region alone is pleasing to the wise— that is incorrect. For in that very same [text]:
One should practice the virtuous conduct well-established in the Middle Country and other such regions;
however, even there, one should not practice that which contradicts the Smṛtis or the Mantras.
In all countries, whatever conduct is prescribed by Smṛti or Śruti, and which is not prohibited, that is authoritative; of this there is no doubt.

If it is argued that even though names such as Keśava and others are not mentioned in the Vedas, they should nevertheless be practiced like the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), that is incorrect. For the injunction regarding the sacred thread is established by the mantra "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier" found in the *Gṛhyapariśeṣa*, which lacks any contradiction with the Śruti, and is also seen in the *Brahmopaniṣad*.
In the same way, since names such as Keśava and others are not established by the Śruti, their Tantric nature is unavoidable.

However, because the Śiva-liṅga is established by the Śruti, its fitness for Vedic worship is logically justified. In the Yajurveda branch, beginning with "Obeisance to Nidhanapati," it says: "This [liṅga] of Soma and Sūrya, which resides in all liṅgas, he installs."

From the mantra beginning with "pāṇimantraṃ pavitram" up to its conclusion, the Śiva-liṅga is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman, the object of all worship; thus, through salutations at every step, its nature as the Self of all is heard:
"In this, at the time of the end, the entire universe, both moving and unmoving, dissolves."
At the time of creation, it goes forth from that; therefore, the liṅga is higher than the highest.
Thus, through etymological derivation from the *Liṅga-purāṇa*, it is established that the *liṅga* possesses a preeminent and great majesty.
Therefore, because it is established by both the Śrutis and the Purāṇas, the *liṅga* is indeed Vedic.
In contrast, because it lacks a basis in the Vedas, the worship of the deity in the form of Viṣṇu’s image and the *sālagrāma* stone is purely Tantric.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu’s status as a worshipper of the Śiva-liṅga is heard in the Ṛgveda:

"O Rudra, for the sake of your glory the Maruts offer praise; for that beautiful and wonderful birth of yours which you established as the supreme station of Viṣṇu, by means of that you protect the secret name of the cows. Thus it is stated in the Brahmakaivarta Purāṇa.
"Having first worshipped with devotion a beautiful stone linga of Rudra,
Hari indeed attained that foremost Vaishnava state, which is most difficult to obtain and higher than the highest.
Thus it is stated in the Parashara Purana.
Having worshipped with devotion a beautiful and variegated Raudra-linga made of pure stone, Mahāviṣṇu attained the supreme state.
And that prosperity (lakṣmī) has been declared to be difficult to attain even for Mahāviṣṇu;
and as for the Liṅga, which is to be worshipped and honored by all sentient beings—
this and more has been elaborated in many ways throughout the section on the "Establishment of the Teaching Renowned Everywhere" (sarvatra-prasiddhopadeśādhikaraṇa).

Now, as for what was stated—that Rudra and the Āgamas and Purāṇas composed by him and expounding his doctrine are *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness)—that is incorrect. For in the Śruti: "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies, one terrible and the other auspicious (*śiva*)," it is established that Rudra, who is the Supreme Brahman, acts as the destroyer of the universe through his terrible form, while [he sustains it] through his auspicious form.

It is established that [Brahman] is both the cause of the world and its nourisher. If it is argued that Rudra possesses the quality of *tamas* because destruction is a cruel attribute and he is the agent of destruction, whereas Viṣṇu possesses the quality of *sattva* due to his nourishing the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), we say no;

for if he were not the agent of destruction, the consequence would be a lack of a Supreme Lord (*nirīśvaratva*). This is because [the scripture states]: "From whom indeed these beings are born... and so forth.

One should not entertain doubt on this account, for in Vedic passages such as "Both Brahman and Kṣatra become his food," the dissolution [of all things] is intended to be described as an attribute of Brahman. Furthermore, in the *Sūtasaṃhitā*, within the *Sūtagītā*, it is taught that even Kālarudra possesses superiority over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others: "O best of Brahmins, there exists Rudra... [and so forth].
"O lords of sages, ten Śaiva Purāṇas exist with Sattva within and Tamas without; and four Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas are Tāmasa.
The Dharma heard in them is for Kṣatriyas, and their presiding deity is Hari."
Tamas is black, indifferent, and skilled in deceitful acts; through negligence and other such factors, it manifests in five ways as the quality of darkness (tāmasa).
Sleep, laziness, negligence, and so forth are proclaimed to be its qualities.
Kṛṣṇa is remembered as Viṣṇu, who reclines upon Śeṣa and deludes his devotees.
This much has been shown in the first chapter of the Sambhava-kāṇḍa within the Śivarahasya-khaṇḍa. The Śruti also says:

"The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful"—thus in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad; and "the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual"—thus in the Māṇḍūkya as well, regarding Śiva too.
Because he is designated as the most *sāttvika*, his status as supreme over all is heard [in scripture]; therefore, there is no possibility of the taint of being *tāmasa*.
This has been elaborated upon in many ways in the section concerning "having this as its source" (*śāstrayonitva*), and is thus summarized here.
Regarding the performance of sacrifices, by the rule stating that one should touch water after the oblation to Rudra, [it is implied] that Rudra is a *tāmasa* deity.

As for the statement that this very [example] is the primary illustration regarding the status of inauspicious deities, that is incorrect; for it would result in an absurdity regarding the Vedic texts. For in the Yajurvedic revelation, it is explicitly stated that the sprinkling of water is for the purpose of concealing Rudra:
"He sprinkles water around, for the concealment of Rudra. Furthermore, in the Skanda Purāṇa, Vyāsa said—
The three-eyed Lord with Ambā is the sovereign of all the deities;
therefore, he is called Mahādeva by those who know the Vedas.
For this very reason, its non-duality is established by the Vedic revelation: "It is indeed one alone."
An oblation is not accepted by his servants, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others,
in order to establish the transcendence of Rudra, the Supreme Self.

"In all sacrifices and oblations, for the sake of attaining the power of invisibility (antardhāna) from Rudra, the touching of water to the Nīlakaṇṭha who wields the trident is prescribed. Thus it is said; likewise in the Kūrma [Purāṇa]:
Having duly honored and fed the lord upon the ground,
one should then dismiss him, just as the ritual of worship for servants is performed.
Likewise, having offered an oblation with devotion to Rudra Mahādeva, the bestower of the fruits of all sacrifices, for the sake of attaining his disappearance from view;
"The touching of water is prescribed, and thereafter the worship of the Deity.
Furthermore, the absence of Śiva’s grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other deities is heard in the *Mantropaniṣad*, beginning with:
"Of him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither equal nor superior to him is seen," and so on, up to "one."
By such passages as "Thus Rudra did not stand for a second," his very non-duality and other attributes have been taught.
Now, if it be argued that because [this passage] is read within a section concerning Nairṛtas, Rākṣasas, and so forth, Śiva must also be considered inferior, that is incorrect.
For in the Āpastamba Sūtra, by the rule beginning with "Of fire, cows, and Brāhmaṇas," the touching of fire, cows, Brāhmaṇas, and others [is prescribed].

Since the rule for bathing is heard [in the scriptures] upon touching an outcaste, an impure substance, or a woman in her menses, and because they are recited in a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*), there is no fault of a single context (*prakaraṇa*). Likewise, the Smṛti also states:
"A cow, fire, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), an outcaste, and a woman in her menses..."
Likewise, having touched a Brahmin in name only (brahmabandhu), one should enter the water with one's clothes on.

Thus, from this observation, the impurity of all [others] is shown to be without foundation; therefore, the supreme preeminence of Śiva alone is beyond dispute. Furthermore, in the Sūta-saṃhitā: "Difference-and-non-difference, as well as non-difference, and difference—these are the three views."

"One person says everything is eternal (*dhruva*), another that it is all non-eternal (*adhruva*), and yet another that it consists of both eternity and non-eternity"— since this triad of views is thus designated by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Mahimnastava* starting from the passage "The proof of the proposition [is established] through the mark," according to the sequence of difference and non-difference, even the Vedic followers of Jaimini and others find the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) untenable.

Since the Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine is to be disregarded, and since even Vedic scholars such as Bhaṭṭabhāskara and others have established that only the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) is ultimately real—

because the Viśiṣṭādvaita is not included within the three systems of thought established by the Vedas regarding difference and so forth— it is indeed unavoidable that the Viśiṣṭādvaita is Tantric in nature.

Furthermore: "Indeed, animals are of two kinds—bipeds and quadrupeds; therefore Rudra is the lord of animals. He rules over them as Paśupati, 'Lord of Animals,' over both the quadrupeds and the bipeds.
Having understood that Brahmā and the others are "animals" (*paśu*) from such passages, [one should worship] the God...

Because it is clearly taught that Māyā constitutes a "bond" (pāśa) through such passages as, "The abandonment of all bonds occurs when the afflictions (kleśas) are exhausted; by the practice of churning with knowledge, the wise man burns away the bond," and because the Supreme Lord's status as the "Lord of Beasts" (paśupati) is explicitly taught in such [mantras] as, "Obeisance, obeisance to the Lord of Beasts."

The Śaiva scripture, which expounds the three categories of Paśupati, Pāśa, and Padārtha, is Vedic because it is rooted in the Vedas. Conversely, the Rāmānuja doctrine, which primarily employs the technical terminology of Cit (consciousness), Acit (the unconscious), and Īśvara (the Lord), is non-Vedic because it lacks a basis in the Vedas; this is a proclamation as clear as the ringing of a bell.

Since it is established by such Vedic texts as, "The gods indeed desire to eat food that is nectar [offered] to Rudra," and "The Vedas desire that which is devoted to Rudra; you should eat [that]," it is beyond dispute that the grace of Śiva is to be accepted by followers of the Vedas (*vaidika*),
whereas the grace of Viṣṇu is to be accepted by followers of the Tantras (*tāntrika*), because the latter is primarily tantric in nature.

It is improper to cremate those whose bodies have already been cremated, for as seen in such passages as "There is no burning of what is already burnt, nor cooking of what is already cooked," the re-burning of the burnt is prohibited; if one were to accept [such a practice], initiation (*dīkṣā*) would be rendered utterly futile.
Furthermore, if cremation were accepted, would it be by means of a Smārta fire, or by means of a Vaiṣṇava fire associated with the initiation involving the bearing of the *śakra* [mark]?
Not the first [alternative]: for if cremation with the *smārta* fire were accepted, then even for one initiated into Vaiṣṇavism, there would be the state of a *preta* like that of a bound soul;

furthermore, since his ancestors would thereafter enter the worlds of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, and even the fourth generation could attain the heavenly world (*svargaloka*), this would contradict the scriptures that prescribe the attainment of *sārūpya* (likeness) with Viṣṇu for those initiated into Vaiṣṇavism.
There would be the consequence of futility; initiation would be fruitless because there is no application for the Vaiṣṇava fire that has arrived with the wearing of the discus.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the Vaiṣṇava fire is recited in the sections of the Pāñcarātra Āgama, and therefore its burning [of the body] as well...
Its status as Tantric is indeed unavoidable.
As stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Yāmala, and my own Arhata [system]..."
"And other such [systems] as these are for the purpose of delusion.
Likewise, in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "The Kāpāla, the Lākula, the Vāma, and likewise the Pāñcarātra..."
These should not be practiced by those seeking liberation, as they are in contradiction with the path of the Vedas.
In the *Pārāśara Purāṇa*:
"Regarding the discernment of dharma, adharma, and so forth, all scriptures spoken by human beings, such as the *Pāñcarātra* and others, are not authoritative; this is the established conclusion."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"If the Pāñcarātra and other paths have their root in the Veda, they are to be known as authoritative through the Tantras; they are never independent."

Furthermore, because this is seen repeatedly in the *Sūtasamhitā*—specifically in the passage stating that "those who have fallen from the path of the Vedas enter the path of Tantra"—that opinion must be disregarded.
Now, one might object: "But surely, in the *Uttarabhāga* of the *Padmapurāṇa*, it is stated in the *Mahopaniṣad* that 'this wearing of the wheel (*cakra*) and other [marks] has been taught'."

Because it is heard that the wearing of the conch, the discus, and so forth is established by many Vedic scriptures (*śruti*), and because the statements in the Purāṇas that follow the *Pāñcarātra* Āgamas and other such texts possess authority; likewise, in the *Pārāśara Purāṇa*:
"That which has been taught in accordance with the Tantras, one should abandon."
A twice-born man who is devoted to the Veda should diligently study either the Purāṇas or the Dharmaśāstras.
Having said this, anticipating the question of how one should know whether something conforms to the Tantras, he says:
"Whatever matter in the Purāṇas or the Dharmaśāstras contradicts the Śruti,
that is to be understood as the meaning of the Tantra at all times by the best of the Vaidikas."
The Smṛtis and the Purāṇas, headed by the Mahābhārata,
are determined to possess authority because they follow the Vedas.

Furthermore, because there is no direct Vedic injunction (*pratyakṣavidhāyaka-śruti*) for the presence of marks such as the discus (*cakra*), and because in the Śruti text "The foot is pure" (*caraṇaṃ pavitram*),

a different application is observed— just as the mantras beginning with "O door of fragrance" (*gandhadvārā*) are seen to have different applications yet are accepted as being consistent with their respective contexts— if the word "foot" (*caraṇa*) were intended to mean the "discus," [that would be untenable].

And because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*mānābhāvāt*). There is a lack of authoritative evidence because such lexicographical statements as "The foot is the purifier, the discus, the gate to the worlds, the Sudarśana," and so forth, lack a foundational source; likewise for such [passages] as "Austerity, the sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), the name, the mantra, and the sacrifice as the fifth."

Since the statements of the *Pāñcarātra-āgama*, which prescribe the five tantric sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*), lack a basis in the Veda, it is beyond dispute that the Vaiṣṇava doctrine is tantric. As it is said in the *Śiva-purāṇa*:
"Rudra is the fire Sviṣṭakṛt; thus they daily perform the rite of oblation (*homakriyā*)."
If even Rudra, the Lord of Creatures, does not desire the ritual for animal sacrifice,
and if the wise Brahmins abandon that Goddess who embodies the Śrī Rudra, the Gāyatrī mantra endowed with the word *bharga*, how indeed can they be Vaiṣṇavas?
Because of such designations, the Viśiṣṭādvaita-Vaiṣṇava doctrine based on the Pāñcarātra Āgamas— which prescribes the origination of the individual soul (jīva)—
is not to be accepted by those who follow the Vedas.
He states another reason for that doctrine being outside the Veda:
And that [mind] is the instrument of the agent. (43)

Regarding the statement, "From Saṅkarṣaṇa, that which is called Pradyumna, the mind (manas), was born," it is not possible for the instrument—the mind—to be produced from the agent—the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because the ignorant individual soul lacks the capacity to create the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). From the passage, "From this [Brahman] are born breath, mind... it is heard in scripture that the origin of the mind proceeds from the Supreme Brahman alone. Therefore...
They explain that the authority of this system (*tantra*) is also refuted because it propounds a meaning contrary to the Vedas (*śruti*).

Alternatively, [they argue] whether the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) produces the mind (*mānasa*) by being qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or unqualified; it cannot be the first, because according to their own view, even that internal organ is admitted to be produced by the living being (*jīva*), [and thus there would be a mutual dependence between] the internal organ and the living being.

Furthermore, because of the absence of a body, sense organs, and so forth, as well as the lack of its own capacity, there would follow the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to multiplicity if one were to accept a body and other such factors for the activity of the individual soul’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable— if one accepts that it is produced by the mind through its own capacity— [the same faults would apply].

Why could the body, the senses, and so forth not be the cause of the birth and other states of the world? If that [body, etc. were the cause of the world’s birth and so on, there would be no purpose for the Lord of the world. Furthermore, because we observe the experience of ignorance in the individual soul (jīva) in such forms as "I am ignorant," there would arise the contingency of contradicting the scriptural statement, "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower. Moreover, while that [ignorance] exists, [the existence of] attributes such as "truthful resolve" in Him [the Lord]...
And because they are not perceived [as such]. Therefore, the Pāñcarātra doctrine, which establishes that the mental [self] is produced from the individual soul (jīva), is untenable.

Now, in response to the objection that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the other three are not of the nature of individual souls, but rather are indeed Lords (īśvara) whose very essence is consciousness—just like Vāsudeva—the author says:
Or, if consciousness and the rest do exist, there is no negation of them. || 44 ||

By the word "or" (*vā*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is overturned. Since consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the "beginning" (*ādi*) are the Supreme Brahman, and since Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha also possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, there is no negation of that [status]. This means there is no negation of those two—the contradiction between their doctrines and the contradiction with the scriptures; the meaning is that the contradiction is not refuted. In any case whatsoever...

It should be understood that the prohibition of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas— which are outside the Veda— is likewise uncontradicted, because in the Śrutis the origination of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman is not observed in the manner of [the production of] jars or cloth, nor is the mind seen to be the cause of that soul.
Furthermore, even in the Pāñcarātra Āgama, it is stated that for liberated souls who have attained identity of form (sārūpya) with Viṣṇu...

The status of being the cause of the mind is thus asserted. Therefore, even though Saṅkarṣaṇa and the other three have attained the state of Nārāyaṇa, they are not designated as the cause of the mind like the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
For if those were included, it would entail the existence of an infinite number of Lords, leading to an infinite regress.

It would follow that those statements which teach the superiority of Vāsudeva would be rendered invalid. Furthermore, since Sāṃkhya and Yoga do not accept the causality of Saṃkarṣaṇa and the other three in that manner, if one were to admit the lordship of the triad beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa, there would be no purpose for Vāsudeva,
as the task would be accomplished by one alone.

There would be a loss of the established tenet of the Pāñcarātra Āgama, which maintains that the Blessed One alone is Vāsudeva, the ultimate reality; furthermore, if Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others— who are not the Supreme Lord—
are designated as equal to Vāsudeva, then their origination from Vāsudeva cannot be admitted.
Therefore, the contradiction with the Pāñcarātra Āgamas, which enjoin that [the Lord] is produced from Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, is unavoidable.

Since no Śruti is observed that enjoins the Brahmanhood of Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others—unlike [the cases of] ether, prāṇa, and so forth—it is appropriate to regard their system as outside the Veda. My devotee...

If, following the Tantric principle that "he is superior to me," one establishes that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are superior [to the individual soul], there arises a contradiction regarding their being produced by him (the soul) or being his worshippers. Furthermore, it is not possible for the mind to have them as its cause if they are inferior to it. Therefore, in every respect—
The Pāñcarātra doctrine should not be respected by those possessed of discernment, because it contradicts scripture, reason, and personal experience.
Now, one might object: "Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata..."
O royal sage, know that these various forms of knowledge indeed represent diverse philosophical views.
"These [views] have become authoritative and are not to be refuted by logical arguments.

Thus, in the *Bhārata*, the *Siddhāntāgama*, and the *Pārāśarasmṛti*, the systems beginning with Sāṃkhya are established as authoritative. If it is argued that the Pāśupata system is superior to those because it is taught as being equal to them, we say no.
Likewise, although the term *pāśupata* refers to ten types of Śaiva traditions— both Vedic and Tantric— the meaning appropriate to the context is here specified.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* and the *Bhārata*, the distinction between the Śaiva and Pāśupata doctrines is set forth.
Furthermore, the superiority of the Śaiva system over the Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and others has been correctly taught:
"The Āgamas have been proclaimed in many ways by Śiva, the Supreme Self, according to their divisions as Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. Thus it is said.

The mutual distinction between the Śaiva and Pāśupata [systems] is established as being like that between a jar and a cloth. Furthermore: "O great sage, because it follows all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra is superior to the Sāṃkhya and other systems which abide in only a single portion of the Vedas."
Thus, in that very [text], they explain that the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata,

and other systems are inferior because they abide in only a single portion of the Veda, whereas the Śaiva doctrine is superior because it consists of the entirety of the Veda. This is also stated in the *Mahimnastava*:
The triple Veda, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and that of Viṣṇu—these are the various divergent systems, each claiming, "This is the supreme; that is the beneficial path."
Because of the diversity of tastes among men who follow various straight and crooked paths, you alone are accessible to all, like the ocean to all waters.

Thus, because all systems— such as Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and others, whether following a straight or a crooked path— are taught to be one with Śiva according to the analogy of rivers merging into the ocean, it is a ringing proclamation that the Śaiva system is superior to all other systems.
Furthermore, what is said in the *Anuśāsana-parvan* of the *Bhārata*, which is equal to the Vedas: "O best of the Bharatas, who among the eternal Brahmins is a worthy recipient?
Is it a Brahmin who bears the sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), or even a Brahmin who does not bear such marks?"
Thus, in response to Yudhiṣṭhira’s question:
"O Great King, even having recognized good conduct through outward signs and other means, they say that alms should be given; both of these are considered ascetics."
Thus, from Bhīṣma’s reply— which indicates either that those Brāhmaṇas who bear the *liṅga* are the primary recipients of gifts or that Brāhmaṇas other than them are the recipients—
it is established by implication that the Śaiva doctrine characterized by the wearing of the *liṅga* is the most excellent of all. For this very reason:

Because they are opposed to the Śaiva doctrine, which consists of all the Vedas, the Sāṃkhya and other systems have been refuted here by the Blessed Pārāśarya (Vyāsa). Nevertheless, since the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Pāñcarātra were composed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Nārāyaṇa respectively, they are of human origin; whereas [the Śaiva system] was propounded by Paśupati, who is the Supreme Brahman.

The Pāśupata scriptures are non-human in origin and possess authority equal to the Vedas. If it is argued that certain portions of these scriptures contradict the Vedas because they indicate only the efficient cause (nimitta), then by parity of reasoning, those portions of the Veda themselves— such as "He desired," "He reflected"— which likewise show only the efficient cause, would also result in being invalid.
Furthermore: "O Sage, are these [systems]—Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, Veda, and Pāñcarātra—intent upon a single reality, or are they intent upon separate realities? By such questions, [the author asks]:

Are Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, Veda, and Pāñcarātra devoted to one principle, or are they devoted to the exposition of distinct principles? If they are exponents of a single principle, what is that single principle? But when...

Since these [scriptures] teach distinct principles and are intent on propounding mutually contradictory meanings, and because conceptual alternatives regarding a real entity are impossible, one must accept only a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For while human-authored works are characterized by speaking of mutually contradictory things, those that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) have all defects such as error eliminated by their non-human nature.
Valid authority is difficult to find. And Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman, known through the Vedas.

By such [scriptural passages] as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "Rudra is indeed all," it is determined that Śiva—the one reality designated as the Supreme Brahman—is the universal self, known through the Vedānta.
Furthermore— in the Śiva-proclaimed Nigamas and Āgamas— it is taught that the Supreme Brahman, designated as Mahādeva,
who is both with and without form and is replete with the sixfold sovereign powers (ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya),
is divided into the categories of Hiraṇmaya, Sūkṣma, Vyūha, and Vibhava. In the Vīrāgama:
For that is the Brahman of the Brāhmaṇas who perform sacrifices under the name of Mahādeva;
it is the great scripture containing all the Upaniṣads, which brings about the knowledge of Śiva.
Mahādeva, the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra, was worshipped by his devotees according to their respective capacities through ritual action preceded by knowledge.
For that which is the cause of the supreme, subtle, and manifold manifestations—
such as the state of being Ardhanārīśvara and others— is known as the "playful manifestation" (*līlāvibhava*).
The five eternal manifestations (vyūhas), beginning with Sadyojāta, have been proclaimed;
their respective five locations, such as Vibhakta and the rest, have likewise been described.
It is both with parts and without parts, subtle, golden-hued, and free from disease;
like space, it is completely pervasive and endowed with all sovereign powers.
The independent support of the universe, known by names such as Śiva and Rudra,
the Great Lord (Maheśvara) accompanied by Ambā, who is endowed with the eternally conscious power of awareness.

By such passages as "Ṛta, Satya, Para-Brahman, Puruṣa, Kṛṣṇapiṅgala," and so forth, the auspicious forms characterized by the divine play (*līlā*)—such as being half-male and half-female (*ardhanārīśvara*)—established by the Śruti, are designated as the *vibhava* [manifestations].
These are taught within the five Brahma-mantras, beginning with Sadyojāta, as the fivefold emanation (*vyūha*) starting with Sadyojāta. *Namo...*

By means of the mantra "To the golden-armed one, to the golden-hued one," the Supreme Brahman known as Mahādeva— whose essential nature is a body composed of light and who is endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers— is explained.
The Blessed One has all faces, heads, and necks; he dwells in the secret cave of all beings; and because the Blessed One is all-pervading, Śiva is therefore omnipresent.

In this regard, it is accepted that Paramaśiva alone possesses the nature of being everything (*sarvamayatva*), the state of being the inner controller of all (*sarvāntaryāmitva*), and the quality of pervading all (*sarvavyāpakatva*). Therefore, there is no difference whatsoever between the Veda and the Āgamas; consequently, the Pāñcarātra doctrine—which prescribes the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such views contrary to the Veda—should not be followed by those who desire the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
It must be heard.
Furthermore, he states another reason: "And because of contradiction" (sūtra 45).

Furthermore, there is a specific contradiction: while the doctrines of the Sāṅkhyas and others contradict certain parts of the Vedānta by asserting that *pradhāna* is the cause of the world and so forth, the Pāñcarātra doctrine contradicts the Vedānta in its entirety, as seen in such passages as: "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," and "The non-conscious [nature], which exists for the sake of another, is eternal and constantly undergoing transformation."
The field of those engaged in action, consisting of the three qualities, is said to be the form of Prakṛti.
The relationship between that [prakṛti] and the person (puruṣa) is one of pervasion;
indeed, it is determined to be ultimately beginningless and endless.

Thus, since the eternity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established everywhere in the Vedas and the Āgamas, it should be understood that the Pāñcarātra doctrine— which prescribes the origination and so forth of the *jīva*— is based on delusion, as it contradicts all the Vedāntas.
Vāsudeva is the supreme reality, the immutable cause of all;
the individual soul, known as Saṅkarṣaṇa, is born from him.
From Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna—whose form is volition—is born as his mental son;
from him is born the one named Aniruddha.
"The syllable *haṃ* arises"—thus the triad of emanations (*vyūha*) is proclaimed.

Such is the procedure heard in the *Pāñcarātra-āgama*. Therefore, that scripture is not to be accepted as satisfactory without critical inquiry. For it asserts the birth of the unborn *jīva*, like a jar or other objects, and the causality of the limited-knowledge *jīva* with respect to the mind.

In the system of the Pañcarātra, the notion that the mind has become inert possesses the agency of the "I-maker" (ahaṃkartṛtva) leads to an unavoidable contradiction with such Vedic scriptures as, "It is neither born nor does it die.
Now, [one might object] that in the Puṣkara-saṃhitā of the Pañcarātra—
That [tradition] in which they worship the fourfold self as something to be performed,
using their own names handed down through tradition, is the Āgama of the Brāhmaṇas.
Because from this scripture, that supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva— the non-dual state of equanimity— is attained through action preceded by knowledge.
Because, by such statements as these, Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are also designated as having forms that are bodies manifested by the will of the Supreme Brahman.

Just as in the Śaiva Āgamas, here too they explain that after attaining the *vibhava* (manifestation) through worship, one attains what is beyond the *vyūha*, namely that which is called Vāsudeva. The *vibhava* refers to the group of manifestations such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth.

The manifestation (vyūha) consists of those known as Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. It has been established that the subtle form, which possesses the sixfold sovereign powers (ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya), is called Vāsudeva and is the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, it is not contradictory to designate the presiding deities of the principles of the individual soul (jīva), mind (manas), and ego (ahaṃkāra) by the terms "jīva" and so forth.
If it is argued that this is just as Brahman is designated by terms such as "space" (ākāśa) or "vital breath" (prāṇa), we say no;
for, unlike the Śaiva system, the emanations (vyūha) such as Vāsudeva lack a foundation in direct Vedic revelation.
Furthermore, if Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others were considered to be the Lord (Īśvara), it would result in a contradiction with their own scriptures which enjoin that they are produced from Him.

If one were to accept their causality while also accepting their lordship (īśvaratva) in accordance with their own scriptures, an infinite regress would result due to the consequence of falling outside the Vedic fold (*vedabāhya*). This is because the Śruti passage, "The Unborn is born in many ways," declares that the Supreme Lord assumes a form created by His own will through His own volition (*svasaṃkalpa*).

If it is argued that there is no contradiction in [the Lord] being born from Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and so forth, that is incorrect. For the Śruti, such as "He desired: 'May I be many,'" also intends to establish that Brahman is the cause of both the world and the individual soul; furthermore, terms such as Saṃkarṣaṇa are not seen in that context, and if they were accepted, there would be a lack of consistency between the preceding and following passages.
Just as in the case of the terms "ether" (ākāśa), "vital breath" (prāṇa), and so forth, the Śruti does not designate the words Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others as referring to Brahman.
Thus, the authority of that scripture appears like a painting on the wall of the sky.
[This was done] by Keśava and Śiva for the purpose of deluding the Asura Tripura.
The Buddha, the Jaina, the Cārvāka, the Pāñcarātra, and the Mudgala.
Therefore, false scripture should not be heard by those who desire liberation.
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the Pāñcarātra, in the Buddhist [teachings], and likewise in the Kaula systems..."
And those who have been initiated with faith are the lowest of Brahmins in this world.

In the *Vāyusaṃhitā* of the Śaiva tradition: "Whether in the Buddha, the Jina, the Pāñcarātra, or even in the Lokāyata, he who is initiated becomes immediately fallen; there is no doubt in this matter."
By such statements as these, the Buddha-pañcarātra scriptures are taught through conceptual constructs for the purpose of deluding the rākṣasas:
"Whether a householder, a celibate student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
whoever desires to attain perfection for the sake of the splendor of the body of the deity..."
Such works belonging to the *Pāñcarātra* tradition are not to be accepted by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Therefore,

through a comprehensive examination of the beginning, end, and middle of all the Vedānta scriptures and Āgamas, it is understood that the doctrine of non-dualism (*advaita*) alone is the primary established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of Vedānta, as seen in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* Sūtra.

By establishing that [Brahman] is the cause of both aspects of the world, the dual nature of the world and the Lord as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) is shown, while their non-dual nature through the designation of being the material cause (*upādāna*) is also demonstrated.

Furthermore, in the sūtra "Because of the designation of being approached by the liberated" (*muktopasṛpyavyapadeśāt*), [the distinction between] the individual soul and the supreme Brahman is addressed.

From the designation of the relationship between that which is attained and that which attains, it is established by implication that the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman possess both difference and non-difference. [This is evident from such scriptural passages as:
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; "That thou art"; "I am Brahman"; "That indeed is Thou, and Thou indeed art That";
"He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"; and "As rivers flowing merge into the ocean, losing their name and form."

Likewise, because the scriptures— such as "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high"— indicate that the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman possess both difference and non-difference, that very [doctrine] must be accepted.
