Thus concludes the work composed by the venerable Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpādācārya, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics.

In the Śrīkarabhāṣya, which elucidates the meaning of the Brahmamīmāṃsā-sūtras of Vyāsa— the systematizers of the doctrine of qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita) characterized by both difference and non-difference—

The second chapter, which consists of forty-five sūtras beginning with "There is no inference" (nānumānam) and so forth, and which is divided into eight topical sections (adhikaraṇas), is concluded; this being the section that sets forth the resolution of contradictions.
Now begins the third quarter of the second chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya: The Section on Space (Viyan-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||
In the first quarter (pāda), the doctrines of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Logicians (Tārkika), Advaita, and others— which contradict the Śruti—
were refuted because they do not accept that Brahman, as the substratum, is the cause of both the world and its manifestation;
this was done by demonstrating the mutual contradictions among the Śrutis regarding the world.

In order to refute the doubt that it is inconsistent for Brahman to be the cause [of the world], the third pāda is commenced. "The ether [is not produced] because it is not mentioned in scripture. (Sūtra 1)

In the two preceding chapters, by means of the refutation of those who hold pseudo-scriptural views (*śrutyābhāsa*) and those who prioritize mere reasoning (*yukti*), it has been demonstrated that all Vedānta texts are non-contradictory with respect to Brahman.
Since these two chapters resolve mutual contradictions among the scriptures, they constitute the internal consistency (*saṅgati*) of the book. Now, [the following...]

In order to demonstrate the absence of even a trace of defects such as mutual distraction, the manner in which the entire range of sentient and insentient things—regarded as the effects of Brahman—is produced is clarified:
"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only without a second; that Brahman thought, 'May I be many; may I procreate.'"

In the section concerning creation, beginning with "It created fire," the origin of fire and the other elements alone is recorded in the scripture. However, because the birth of ether and air is heard of in such passages as "From this Self, space was produced" and "From this [Self], breath is born," a doubt arises here as to whether or not the ether (viyat) is produced.
Because in such scriptural passages as "Space is Brahman," "The Self is space," and so forth, space alone is established as being Brahman;

and because in passages such as "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is within them is the Self," its status as the inner controller of all and its instruction as the Self are likewise pointed out—in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Since the teaching of creation pertains only to fire (*tejas*) and the other elements, the partlessness [of the Self] is not possible;
thus, it follows that the statements in the Taittirīya and other texts prescribing the origin of that [Self] are merely erroneous. This being the position reached:
We shall explain [the following].

"The ether is not [produced], because it is not heard [in scripture]. [Objection: The ether—namely, space—is unproduced, like Brahman, because it is partless. [Reply: This is not so. Why? Because it is not heard [in scripture]. For nowhere in the scriptures is its unproduced nature heard; thus, the ether is produced.

Furthermore, the state of being the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmatva*) is not enjoined in every respect. Passages from the Śruti such as "Space is Brahman," "The ether is the Self," and so forth, possess only a figurative sense—just like "Food is Brahman," "Prāṇa is Brahman," "Mind is Brahman," "Consciousness is Brahman," "Bliss is Brahman," "The single-syllabled *om* is Brahman," and "Yonder sun is Brahman. [The word] "space" (*kham*)...

Since it is taught in such scriptural passages as, "Air, light, water, and earth, the supporter of the universe; that which is the supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe," that Śiva is Brahman as distinct from space (ākāśa), it is not logical to interpret [the term] in any other sense.
Furthermore— in passages such as "Space, indeed, is the bringer-out of names and forms"—
the word *ākāśa* refers to Brahman, based on its etymological derivation as "that which shines (*kāśate*) everywhere (*ā*).
This is because we observe in the Smṛti that "the Śruti is a speaker of truth," and thus [the meaning] of statements such as "Food is Brahman" [must be understood accordingly].

If it is asked how this is figurative, [the answer is that] in passages such as "He who is Rudra in fire, he who is in the waters, he who is in the plants," they explain that Śiva-Brahman, by virtue of being the essence of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) and as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all, is denotable by all words.
He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Fire, he is the Moon; he alone is everything that has been and that is yet to be.

In passages such as "The eternal one" and "All this is indeed Rudra," the fact that everything has Brahman as its essence and is non-different from it— by virtue of being an effect of Brahman— is clearly taught in the sūtra, "Because of the words concerning origin and so forth, [the world] is non-different from That. Furthermore, in the previous chapter, under the sūtra "Ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks," it was established.

It has already been stated previously that words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and others refer to Brahman because they possess the characteristics of Brahman. For instance, although it is heard in passages such as, "From which indeed these beings are born," and "Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks by the thousands fly forth and into that very same [fire] they enter," that living beings (*jīvas*) are born from Brahman, nevertheless, because they are partless (*niravayava*), [they cannot be produced in the manner of material effects].

Just as it was shown that [the origination] is figurative, so too, in response to the doubt that the origination of space in the statement "from the Self, space was produced" is likewise merely figurative, he says:
"But it exists. (Sūtra 2.3.47)

The word "tu" (but) serves to indicate certainty. There is the origination of space from existence. For in such scriptural passages as, "From this very Self, space was produced," the origination of space is heard of, just like that of a jar and so forth.

However, even though it is beyond the senses like the individual soul (*jīva*), its [origination] is untenable because it is insentient; for [the scripture says], "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "The two—the knower and the ignorant."
In passages such as "Two unborn ones, the Lord and the non-Lord," since there is no evidence from other scriptural authorities for [the non-Lord] being a living soul (jīva),

and because we do not observe any teaching that it is not produced from Ākāśa, its production from that [Ākāśa] is not precluded— even though it is partless— just as in the case of the mind, the vital breath (prāṇa), and so forth.

Having raised the objection that because the scriptures declare the immortality of both air and space—based on the scriptural statement, "The atmosphere is the immortal of air"—the texts teaching the origin of space must be taken in a figurative sense, [the author] refutes this:
"Because of the impossibility of a figurative sense, and because of the word. (Sūtra 3)

If it is argued that because the *Chāndogya* teaches the creation of fire and the other elements in the passage "It created fire" (*tat tejo 'sṛjata*), and because it is not possible for those scriptural texts showing the origin of space—such as "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*)—to be taken in their primary sense, it is therefore proper to assume they are figurative; we say no. Why? Because of impossibility and because of the [scriptural] word. From the Self, space...

Because the scriptural statement "He was born" (*sambhūtaḥ*) cannot be taken in a figurative sense, and because of the [scriptural] word itself—given that hundreds of such scriptural passages are seen, such as "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night;

Śiva alone was the sole one," "Rudra alone existed, there was no second to stand with him," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one without a second"—it is established that the production of space (*ākāśa*), like that of a jar and so forth, is indeed primary. [The rest of the passage concerns] the perishable...

Because in passages such as "The one God, Hara, rules over the primary cause (pradhāna), the immortal, and the imperishable self" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 1.10), it is established that the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Brahman; therefore, even the word "immortal" found in the scriptural statement, "The air and the intermediate space—that is the immortal," must refer to Brahman because it possesses those characteristic marks, according to the Sūtra: "It is the ether [Brahman], on account of its characteristic marks" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.3.41). Thus...

In this regard, concerning the statement "This very one is Prāṇa," there is no stain of doubt because it has been extensively demonstrated in the preceding chapter that passages containing the marks of Brahman are intended to convey Brahman as their subject; otherwise, the contradiction with such scriptural texts as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" would be unavoidable.

Having raised the objection—given that space is designated as Brahman in passages such as "Space is Brahman," and given the scriptural teaching of the origin of space in "From the Self, space was produced," how can [the designation of Brahman] be taken in its primary sense?—he says in response to that:
"And it may be so for one [term], like the word 'Brahman'. (Sūtra 4.3.4)

Even though in passages such as "Space is Brahman" space is presented as being Brahman, the origination of space in the statement "From the Self, space was produced" is indeed primary. Why? Because it is like the word "Brahman. Just as in cases such as "That sun is Brahman" or "Food is Brahman," the word "Brahman" is used figuratively with respect to the sun and so forth, which are effects, whereas it is used in its primary sense with respect to that which is the cause.

Just as the term *brahman* has its primary sense in reference to Brahman, so too the designation of the single element ether (*ākāśa*), which is an effect, by the word *brahman*—as in the expression "ether is Brahman"—is merely secondary. Furthermore, if one were to accept that [ether] is partless and unproduced, then atoms and the like would also have to be eternal. Therefore, the production of ether is not precluded.
He states another reason for its being non-eternal:
|| 50 || "There would be a loss of the proposition because of the exclusion from words. || 5 ||

If it is argued that since the *Chāndogya* (6.2.3) teaches the creation of fire and the other elements alone in the passage "It created fire," there would be a contradiction with other scriptural texts if the production of ether (*vyoman*) were also accepted—[we reply: there is no loss of the initial proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*), because ether is not an effect of Brahman, owing to its difference from Brahman, that is, its being distinct from Brahman. [As stated in the Chāndogya: "By which [Brahman] the unheard becomes heard..."
A contradiction with the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known" (as expressed in the passage beginning with *śrutaṃ bhavati*) would arise [if Brahman were not the cause];
therefore, its being produced from Brahman must be accepted.
Furthermore: "All this has this as its self," "Rudra is indeed all," and "All this is indeed Brahman."

Because hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Obeisance to the one with upward-flowing vital energy, to Virūpākṣa, obeisance, obeisance to Viśvarūpa" teach that Brahman is the self of all, it is impossible to assert that ether (*viyat*) is distinct from Him.
Now, if it is asked: "Once it is established that [ether] possesses an origin, how is the resolution of the aforementioned contradiction achieved?"—it is replied:

For in the Chāndogya, only the origin of fire (*tejas*) is heard, and not its position as the third; however, in the Taittirīyaka, it is heard that "from ether comes air, from air comes fire," thus establishing fire as the third. Consequently, since there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between those two statements, according to the Taittirīya scripture, Brahman created fire after having created ether and air.
It is maintained that the Chāndogya Śruti is interpreted [in this way]; therefore, there is no contradiction between these two scriptural passages.

As for what was stated—that the Taittirīyaka’s teaching on the origin of ether is figurative because of the absence of causal materials, or because of its inference of eternality due to its all-pervasiveness—that is incorrect, with the intention of showing that Brahman itself, as revealed in the Śruti, is the causal material of ether.
He refutes [the opponent's view] by means of a counter-inference (pratyanumāna):
"But as far as there is modification, so far there is division, as in the world" (Sūtra 6).

The word "tu" (but) is intended to dispel the doubt regarding the impossibility of the origination of space; for, while a division is observed among all classes of modifications, no such division is observed in Brahman, which is itself a modification. It is like the worldly case: just as in the world, having stated "all these are the sons of Devadatta," by speaking of the birth of some among them, the birth of all would be implied.

It is just like that. This being so, the statement "the wind and the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—that is the immortal" is intended merely to indicate that they endure for a long time, similar to the gods.
Furthermore, ether, the directions, time, the mind, and atoms have their existence dependent on something else.

Furthermore, against the proponent of the production of space (*ākāśa*), the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason "omnipresence" (*vibhutva*) as stated by the opponent should also be understood, because [space] possesses divisions that have the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as itself, just like a jar, a bowl, and so forth.
Now, one might object: the production of air (*vāyu*) is not heard in the *Chāndogya*, whereas it is indeed heard in the *Taittirīyaka*. And thus:
As before, in order to resolve the contradiction between these two statements, it must be said that the origin of air is figurative. This concludes the section on Mātariśvan (the Wind). 2.

Furthermore, by the statement "Moreover, this deity that never sets is Vāyu," and because the dissolution of Vāyu is denied, there arises the doubt that it is eternal; he refutes this doubt by means of an extended application (atideśa):
"By this, Mātariśvan is explained. (Sūtra 7).

The meaning is that by this explanation of the origination of ether (*viyat*), air (*vāyu*) is also explained as being produced from Brahman delimited by ether. The meaning is that even if air were eternal, the same objections would apply, such as the failure of the initial proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*) through the knowledge of one thing alone. Furthermore, the denial of the dissolution (*laya*) of air should be understood as relative; because it is an extended application (*atideśa*), it need not require a separate formal connection (*saṅgati*).

The separate mention of air (mātariśvan) from ether (viyat) is for the purpose of referring back to air, as it was previously mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad in the context of the origin of air—despite the doubt that might arise there—even though the Taittirīya Śruti, by the principle of "the remainder of the sentence" (vākyaśeṣa) and the principle of the "harmonization of attributes" (guṇopasaṃhāra), establishes that "from ether, air [is born]. Thus he said: "From that [ether], fire [arises]."

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the statement "This deity that never sets is Vāyu" is intended as a praise, because it occurs within a section concerning meditative worship (upāsana). Therefore, the fact that Vāyu is produced remains entirely unrefuted.
Anticipating the objection that even Brahman must have an origin from some cause—just as Ākāśa and Vāyu do—the author says the following:
But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is logically untenable.

The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of restriction. The impossibility of the existent Brahman—that is, the impossibility of its origination—is due to its lack of logical consistency (*anupapatti*). It is taught that the origination of Brahman is impossible because there is no other cause for it.

As stated in such passages as: "O gentle one, when there was being alone, there was neither day nor night, neither existent nor non-existent; Śiva alone was [all]" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 4.18), and so forth. Prior to this [creation],...

Because of the hearing of the restrictive statement that "there is only one [Lord] of creation," the persistence of anything other than Him is not possible. Furthermore: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; all this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is produced from Him; and He is the meditator of the causes, together with all the senses and the elements."

But the Cause is that which is to be meditated upon. Since it is declared of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, that "Śambhu, the Lord of all, endowed with all sovereignty, the one auspicious Śiva who makes all auspicious, is to be meditated upon in the midst of space, having abandoned everything else," and since he is designated as being without cause and as the cause of causes, it is not tenable for him to possess equality with ether and air. Or rather:
The Upanishads declare that the unmanifest (avyakta), mahat, ego (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, space, wind, and so forth, have Brahman as their cause.
Likewise, is another cause for that [Brahman] itself perceived? If it is argued that from the Śruti, "In the beginning this was non-existent (asat);

from that, indeed, the existent (sat) was born," the existent arises from the non-existent—that is incorrect. How can the existent arise from the non-existent? If the existent arises only from the existent, the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya) would result.

It is established that the origination of Brahman is not tenable, because the promise of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is possible only in the case of Śiva, the supreme cause, and because the entire phenomenal world, which is distinct from Him, is not seen to arise from Him.
The Section on Light (Tejo’dhikaraṇa) || 3 ||
Having thus established that ether and air are produced from Brahman, [the author] now demonstrates that fire and the other elements also have Brahman as their cause:
"Fire [is born] from this, for so [the scripture] says. (Sūtra 9)

In the *Chāndogya*, in the passage "It created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*), fire is taught to have Brahman as its cause; whereas in the *Taittirīyaka*, in the passage "From air, fire" (*vāyoragniḥ*), fire is taught to be produced from air. Consequently, a doubt arises as to whether fire has its own respective preceding cause or whether it has Brahman as its cause.

If it is argued that because the sequence of causality is taught in the passage, "From space comes air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth," it is not possible for fire and the other elements to be directly produced by Brahman—then it is replied:

in the passage, "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath (prāṇa)," the status of being the cause of all things such as the vital breath, as well as the status of being the support of all, [is established].

Furthermore, since the state of being entirely devoid of specific characteristics (*vilakṣaṇatva*) is observed in Brahman alone, it is untenable for the insentient air (*vāyu*) to have Brahman as its cause. In the passage "From air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*), it is understood that the cause is indeed Brahman as delimited by air. This is also evident in such passages as "Rudra who is in the fire" (*yo rudro 'gnau*).

Since the quality of being the inner controller of all is specified in reference to that very [Brahman], it is established that He alone is the cause of everything. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the Chāndogya and the Taittirīya Upaniṣads. Nor is this ablative case used for the sake of indicating sequence; for that would entail the necessity of supplying the word "immediately after" (anantaram), as in the phrase "fire immediately after air."

Furthermore, since the ablative case is seen in the sense of a cause in passages such as "from the Self [arose] space" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ*) up to "from earth [arose] plants" (*pṛthivyā oṣadhayaḥ*), it is entirely inconsistent to ask why the ablative is used here in the sense of sequence. Nor is there any contradiction in one instance being born from Brahman and in another being born from air; for air itself is born from Brahman.

Since the meaning of the Chāndogya passage is that fire is produced from Brahman which has attained the state of air (*vāyu*), there is no contradiction in the statement "from air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*) having this same sense. Thus ends the section [on the origin of fire]. 4.
Having thus demonstrated that fire is also produced from Brahman, he states in another section that water as well is produced from Brahman: || 55 || "Water" || 10 ||

"Water [arose] from that," for it is thus that [the text] continues. Because water and earth follow immediately after fire, and because water and earth are present in the mind immediately after the statement that fire is produced from air, two sections are commenced according to the sequence of connection characterized by proximity in the intellect (*buddhi-sannidhi*). Thus, he created that.

Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a contradiction between the statement beginning with "Thus" (*ityādi*), which establishes that [the earth] is produced from Brahman, and the statement "From fire, water," the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—similar to the previous case—is that there is indeed a contradiction. To refute the partial final conclusion (*ekadeśasiddhānta*) that there is no contradiction because water, by its very nature, prevents fire and therefore cannot be produced from it, [the author] says: "Water [is produced] from fire; for... (*āpastejaso jāyante | hi*).
The meaning is that the Śruti declares that water is produced from fire in that manner.

Even though there is a relationship of the burned and the burner between water and fire when they have been made tripartite (*trivṛtkṛta*), there is no contradiction between them when they are not so made. The resolution of the contradiction is to be understood as before.
The Section Concerning the Earth as the Subject Matter. || 5 ||
Having thus stated that water has Brahman as its cause, [the author] demonstrates that earth is produced from it:
"Earth [is produced from water], because of the context, the nature [of the elements], and other scriptural passages. (Sūtra 2.3.11)

It is heard in scripture: "Those waters thought, 'May we become many, may we procreate,' and they created food. Regarding this, there is a doubt: because it is well-known, does the word "food" (anna) refer only to boiled rice and the like? And thus, since rice, barley, and so forth, as well as the boiled rice produced from them, are denoted by the word "food" both through etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), [the question arises whether] in some cases it is produced from food, and in others from earth.

Regarding the apparent contradiction between these two scriptural passages—"The herbs [arise] from the herbs" and "Food [arises] from the herbs"—wherein the former suggests that food is produced by the earth and so forth, we reply:
here, the word "food" refers to the earth itself and not to rice and other grains. Why? Because of the context, the form, and other scriptural statements.

This is because the context concerns the origination of the great elements, beginning with "It created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*); and because of the scriptural statement, "That which is black is of food," which indicates that the black form is concordant with earth and serves as a signifier of its earth-nature; and because in the same section it says, "From water, earth," and "That which was the solid mass of the waters condensed became the earth. Thus, regarding the earth...

The meaning is that this is because there exist other words establishing [the earth] as something produced. At that time, during the process of creation, whatever solidification—that is, the state of becoming dense—there was of the waters, that was struck together; that solidification became transformed into a manifested self. That very [solidification], in the form of the transformation of the waters into a solid shape, became the earth; such is the meaning of the Śruti. And thus, regarding food such as rice and so forth...
It is established that there is no contradiction because [the world] does not have water as its material cause (*upādāna*), but rather has earth and the other elements as its material causes.

Thus, first of all, the lack of contradiction among the scriptural passages concerning the great elements (*mahābhūta*) according to the order of creation has been demonstrated. Furthermore, through such passages as "He who dwells in the earth, whose body is the earth," and so forth, [the existence of] Śiva in the various recensions (*śākhā*) such as the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina...

Because it is taught that the Supreme Brahman has all beings, beginning with the earth, as its body; because it is impossible for [Brahman] itself to be the cause of its own body; because if its body were non-eternal, it would follow that it is equal to the individual soul (jīva); and because nothing other than that [Supreme Brahman] can be the cause of all things, [the earth and so forth...]

If it is argued that it is not possible for each preceding factor to be the cause of each succeeding one while also having Brahman as their ultimate cause, we say no; for in passages such as "Rudra who is in the fire," the inner controller-ship (*antaryāmitva*) of Śiva is demonstrated, and statements such as "He who dwells in the earth" are intended solely to demonstrate His inner controller-ship of all things, just like the statement "Food is Brahman."

This is an instruction regarding the nature of being a body, but not a literal conceptualization of having a physical body. Why? Because even the elements such as earth and so forth, by the analogy of the contraction and expansion of a cloth, remain identical with Brahman even during dissolution; thus, there is no loss of the status of having eight forms (aṣṭamūrtitva).
As it is said in the Śaiva [scriptures]:
From Maheśvara and Mahāśakti, there was born a person named Īśāna, whose nature is that of a bird;
from him arose the one of great strength known as Pavana.
From that Aghora was born the fire that consumes all;
from that was born Vāmadeva, whose essence is water and who is a treasure-house of compassion.
Therefore, the earth-natured one, whose form is Sadyojāta, bestows auspiciousness;
from that all medicinal herbs arise, and from them food is produced in due order.
Therefore, Sadāśiva is the creator of all beings, both conscious and unconscious, who have come forth from Him, by virtue of being their inner controller (antaryāmin).
First, the Lord of Gods produced the fivefold [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta in a subtle form, and likewise the gross phenomenal world.
Thus, by virtue of this scriptural vision, it is established that the status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world belongs to Him alone and not to another.
This concludes the section [beginning with] "From His brooding over" (Tad-abhidhyāna-adhikaraṇa). 6.

In response to the doubt that in passages such as "from ether, air," the status of being the successive cause might belong not to the insentient elements but to the deities presiding over them, he presents another topical section:
|| 57 || "But from the meditation on Him alone [proceeds], because of His characteristic mark. || 12 ||

Now, based on those elements, another matter is investigated through the logical connection of the relationship between the support and the supported: is there a doubt as to whether the deities presiding over the great elements proceed independently in the production of elemental derivatives, or whether they do so under the direction of Īśvara?

Since the independence [of the elements] is heard in such passages as "From space, air," etc., regarding the production of their respective effects, they are indeed independent; thus, there is a contradiction between the scriptural texts teaching that Brahman is the creator of all and the scriptural texts concerning the creation of the elements.
To this, we reply:

That Supreme Self, having first willed through meditation consisting of the vision directed toward each respective effect, creates every effect by presiding over its respective cause; why? Because of His characteristic marks (*liṅga*), namely, the mark of being the controller of all, as indicated by such passages as "He who dwells in the earth" and so forth.
The meaning is "because it is so heard. Regarding "in the earth"—that is, in the deity presiding over it. The intention is as follows:

since words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) are conventionally established in the sense of the mere element (*bhūta*) alone, to take them as referring to the deity would entail the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, the independence of the deities who preside over the elements is heard in such passages as "from ether, air" (*ākāśād vāyuḥ*). Nor are they [the deities] water.

The phrase "they saw" (*aikṣanta*) is a mark indicating that the words beginning with *tat* refer to deities, because that act of seeing resides in Brahman as delimited by those [deities]. Thus, there is no evidence whatsoever for the independence of the deities.
This concludes the section on the reversal (*viparyayādhikaraṇam*). 7.
Having thus stated that the five great elements have Brahman as their cause, he demonstrates that they are dissolved back into Brahman alone: "But the reverse order is also logical. (2.3.13)

Thus, while investigating the order of the origination of the elements (*bhūta*), the order of their dissolution (*layakrama*)—though already present in the mind—is now examined by way of incidental connection (*prasaṅga*). The purpose of this investigation is the knowledge of the difference and non-difference between the world and Brahman.
Precisely because it is incidental, the order of the dissolution of the world is set forth in this section (*pāda*). In that regard, [what is the order] of the elements?
There arises a doubt as to whether the process of dissolution follows the very same order as the scriptural account of origination, or whether it occurs in a different manner.

In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, it is heard that the origination of the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth occurs prior to space (viyat) and the other elements, as stated: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, mind, and all the sense organs. However, in the Atharvaśikhā, [the order of the dissolution of] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra... [is described differently].
Since there is a mention of the elements and the sense organs [in the order of space and so forth], the previously stated order of creation is not tenable; this being the position reached, we reply:
the previously stated order of creation is indeed tenable, for "the mind, my dear, consists of food; breath consists of water."

Regarding the statement "Speech consists of fire" (*tejomayī vāk*): since it is heard that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are of the same nature as the elements (*bhautika*), they are included within the elements; thus, there is no requirement for a separate order [for them]. The simultaneous origination of Brahmā and the others with the elements is because they have those elements as their form;
since they have the fire-like elements as their form, they are included within them. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the previous sequence.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural vision [in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad], "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" Śiva alone is the direct progenitor of all beings. By demonstrating the production of conscious living beings (jīvas), his status as the cause of the unconscious is established by implication. This is stated in the Atharvaśikhā:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra—they are all produced from Him, as are all the senses," and so forth.
Because [the scriptures] show that Brahmā and others are the causes of both sentient and insentient things, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Sadāśiva is the embodiment of sound; Maheśvara is the embodiment of touch;
Rudra is directly the embodiment of fire; Janārdana is the embodiment of taste."
Gandhamūrti and Caturvaktra—these are the five forms;
indeed, these beginning with Sadāśiva abide in the state of the five Brahmans.
The acts of creation and so forth are not attributed to them because they exist as His inner rulers;
for it is certain that the entire process of the world's birth and so on belongs to Śiva alone.
Therefore, by His will, they [re-emerge] again into that supreme cause,
like the contraction of a cloth or its expansion.
Furthermore, they declare that its manifestation occurs perfectly through His will.

From this scriptural statement, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that Śiva alone causes the phenomenal world (prapañca), which was withdrawn within Himself, to become latent during the dissolution (pralaya).
This concludes the section concerning the intermediate consciousness (antarāvijñānādhikaraṇam). 8.

Since the scripture "From this [Brahman] is born Prāṇa" teaches here, at the outset, the creation of the vital breath, the sense organs, and so forth from Brahman as Paramaśiva, there exists a contradiction with the Taittirīyaka passage— which, being based on the scripture "From the Self, space was produced," teaches the initial production of the five elements; therefore, [the opponent] objects.

If it is argued that between [the body] there is first consciousness and then the mind in succession because of their respective characteristics, we say no, because there is no distinction [between the two].
If it is argued that between the intermediate state (*antarā*) and the ether (*ākāśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*)— the senses and the internal organ—

are produced in succession because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the Śruti, "From this [Self] is born breath (*prāṇa*)," since the creation of the five elements is taught in that text immediately after the creation of breath and so forth, we say no; for that [text] is non-specific (*aviśeṣāt*).
Since the scripture (śruti) establishes only their origination and does not establish their sequential order,

and since the vital breaths, the sense organs, and the internal organ are elemental in nature, they arise only after the origination of the five great elements; such is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra.

The sense organs are called "consciousness" because they are the means for accomplishing consciousness. As for what was stated—beginning with "From this [Brahman] is born Prāṇa"—it is taught that everything is an immediate effect of Brahman. Therefore, the claim that by this sentence the direct origination of everything from Brahman is established through the indication of the mark of meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*) is untenable.

Since this sentence is intended to convey a specific sequence, a sequence is perceived here for all [the elements] as well. First, regarding ether and the others, the sequence established by other scriptural passages is perceived here too. Furthermore, because they are mentioned together in the text, it is understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that *vijñāna* (discriminative cognition) and *manas* (mind) also arise in sequence between the gross elements (*bhūta*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
If it is argued that this [statement] is not intended to establish the origination of everything from Brahman alone because of its being a mere "support" (*uttambhana*), we say no;
for there is no distinction. By the phrase "from this is born breath," there is no distinction made between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and mind (*manas*), as well as ether and the other elements;
thus, for all of them, the relationship consisting of direct origination is what is expressed by the phrase "from this is born."
Since the elements from breath down to earth are not distinguished [in this context], that alone (the dissolution itself) is what is to be enjoined, not the sequence;

furthermore, because it would contradict the sequence established in other scriptural passages, this is not intended to teach a sequence. For another sequence is perceived starting from "earth dissolves into water" up to "it becomes one with darkness. This refers to the previously mentioned sequence of the origin and dissolution of the elements.

This is not contradicted by the order of creation [described] in the case of Indra. Thus it is established that there is no contradiction by any statement with those passages concerning the creation of the elements.
This concludes the section on the dependence on the moving and the non-moving (Carācara-vyapāśraya-adhikaraṇa). || 9 ||
In passages such as "from space, air," it is understood that space and the others are themselves the indirect causes.
To address the doubt that the designation [of Brahman] as their cause might be absent because Brahman is merely the substratum for them, he says:
"But that designation [of Brahman as the cause] would be based on [the world of] moving and non-moving beings; it is figurative, because [Brahman] exists when they exist. (1.1.15)
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.

The designation by various specific words based on all moving and stationary beings is figurative (bhākta); that is to say, it applies to a single part of the denoted object. [This refers] to Brahman, which is the qualifier of all things.

Because it is not the object of means of valid cognition such as perception, which grasp objects as possessing qualifiers (*prakāra*), and because prior to hearing the Vedānta there is no cognition of the qualified (*prakārī*), and because the final determination [of the meaning] is preceded by the cognition of the qualified, those various words in common worldly usage are designated as being either metaphorical (*bhākta*) or non-metaphorical (*abhākta*) with respect to that single part of the denotable object which is the mere thing itself. Alternatively:

Fearing that the designation of Brahman by words such as "splendor" (*tejas*) and so forth—words understood to denote merely those respective entities—might be figurative (i.e., non-primary), it is stated: "But [the designation] rests upon the moving and the unmoving. This means that the designation resting upon the moving and the unmoving refers to the words denoting them; that is, words denoting the moving and the unmoving.
Why is it that the primary devotee of Brahman alone [attains this]? Because all words are permeated by the nature of Brahman;

for, according to the scripture concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*), the denotative capacity of all words is such that they are permeated by that very nature. As it is said: "That Deity reflected: 'Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*')."

"Name-and-form are the explanations [of the world]. Thus, because Brahman, being of the nature of that [name-and-form], is conceived as having entered into all things for the sake of their differentiation into name and form, the designation of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth by words such as "the sun" (*āditya*)—as in "The sacrificial post is indeed the sun" or "The sacrificer is the grass-bundle" (*prastara*)—is not primary (*mukhya*), due to the impossibility [of such identity]. This is similar to the case of "The platforms are shouting."
Since men merely occupy beds and such things, their being denotable by those words is secondary;

however, because Brahman enters into the phenomenal world as its very self, its being denotable by those words is primary, just as it is primary for the Self when it has entered bodies such as those of Brāhmaṇas to be denoted by the words "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth. Otherwise—

Since purificatory rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) terminate in the body alone, they cannot constitute a purification of the self; for if there were a scriptural declaration of a fruit for one whose purification pertains to the self, that declaration would be for the sake of another, and injunctions such as "a Brahmin should sacrifice" would become purposeless. Therefore—

It is a well-known proclamation that the primary denotation of the word "That" (tat) belongs to Brahman, who is Supreme Śiva as delimited by the phenomenal world consisting of the stationary and the moving;
this is the section concerning the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa). 10.

To dispel the doubt that—on the basis of Vedic texts such as "From which indeed these beings are born"—the individual soul (jīva) might arise from Brahman just as ether and the other elements do, [the Sūtra] states: "61.
The Self [is not produced], because of the scriptural statement of its eternity, and because of those [scriptures]. (2.3.16)

The embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) is not produced. Why? Because of the lack of scriptural authority; for in the scriptural accounts of creation, there is no mention of the production of individual souls (*jīva*), as seen in such passages as "the Knower and the Unknower" (*jñājñau*). The subtle meaning is that their eternity is declared by those very scriptures. While the production of the entire universe, beginning with space (*viyat*), from the supreme Brahman has been stated, the question now arises whether the soul (*jīva*) likewise undergoes production or not.

There arises a doubt: what is correct? That [the soul] exists. Why? Because the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known" is logically consistent, and because the oneness [of the Self] is determined prior to creation. Furthermore, there are scriptural passages stating that the individual soul (jīva), like space and other elements, is subject to origination.
"From which the progenitor of the world was born, by water he released living beings upon the earth; Prajāpati created the creatures.

"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being (sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. Since there is thus a statement regarding the origin of the conscious world, the origin of the individual soul (jīva) is also understood [from it]. Nor should it be argued that [this is not so] because Brahman is eternal.

Since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is understood through such passages as "That thou art," the soul must be eternal. However, since the identity of ether and the other elements with Brahman is also understood from such passages as "All this has that as its self" and "All this, indeed, is Brahman," it follows that those too must be eternal. Therefore, when it is argued that the soul, like ether and the rest, must be produced, the following is stated in reply:

"Not the Self, because of the scripture. The Self is not produced; why? Because of the lack of scriptural statement. For the prohibition of the soul's production is heard in such passages as, "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "The two, the knowing and the unknowing," and so forth. Furthermore, the eternity of the Self is understood from those very scriptures: "He is the eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious, the one among the many... and so on.

[The Self] "grants desires; He is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient; He is not slain when the body is slain," and so forth. Therefore, the Self is not produced. How, then, is the proposition that by the knowledge of one, all is known, to be justified? It is justified in this way: because the individual soul (jīva) is also an effect [of Brahman].

And because of the non-difference between cause and effect. If that were so, then, like ether and the rest, the soul would have to be admitted as something subject to origination. This is not so, it is said. For what is called "being an effect" is simply the attainment of a different state by a single substance; this indeed applies to the soul as well. However, there is this distinction: the soul does not undergo such a transformation as the insentient ether and other elements do.

The modification of the individual soul (*jīva*) is characterized by the contraction and expansion of knowledge; that of ether (*viyat*) and the other elements, however, is characterized by a change in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). This very production, characterized by a change in essential nature, is denied in the case of the individual soul.

This is what is meant: having established that the objects of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the controller possess distinct natures; having negated [in the enjoyer] the arising and so forth belonging to the object of enjoyment and established his eternity;

and having negated in the controller both the arising and so forth belonging to the object of enjoyment as well as the state of being the locus of non-human goals (apuruṣārtha) belonging to the enjoyer.

Having established His eternity, faultlessness, omniscience at all times, the possession of true resolve, His lordship over the lords of the senses, and His lordship over the universe, it has been demonstrated that in all states, both the conscious and the unconscious are subject to Him, while He is their controller. Therefore, at all times—

Brahman is entirely full because it is the illuminator of both conscious and unconscious entities (*cidacidvastu*). It can never possibly acquire those attributes [of the objects it illumines]. Even in its subtle state, it remains as the illuminator of the conscious and unconscious entities withdrawn within itself. Therefore, duality is eternal. In the state of liberation, according to the analogy of the bee and the insect...

The attainment of Śiva-hood preceded by the cessation of the innate state of being a *jīva* is clearly taught in such passages as, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Therefore, because the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman in the bound state and their non-difference in the liberated state are both accepted, there is a harmonious reconciliation (*samanvaya*) of all the Śruti texts. For example:

Since Śiva is designated as the dual cause of the universe—both its material cause and its efficient cause—by virtue of being the natural manifestation of His own power, just as it is said that "the spider creates and withdraws [its web]," non-dual duality alone is possible. Difference is established through the state of being the effect, while non-difference is established through the state of being the material cause; this holds true for both the state of the effect and the state of the cause.

They declare both the difference and non-difference between the world and the Lord. In the state of being an effect (*kāryāvasthā*), however, there is non-difference because [the world] is a transformation of His own power (*svaśaktipariṇāmitva*), and difference because He is its controller (*svaniyāmakatva*). Even in the causal state (*kāraṇāvasthā*), there is non-difference because [the world] is contained within Him, and difference because it is permeated by His activity, like grass and other plants in the summer heat.

Because it exists in a subtle form, its distinctness from itself is established by all the Vedāntas. In the passage "Being alone, my dear," it is shown that at the time of dissolution, the entire manifold consisting of consciousness and non-consciousness exists as having Brahman as its essence, while subsequently, by virtue of being the ordainer of creation, its distinctness from that [Brahman] is also established.

It is explained as follows: regarding the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat); from that, the existent (sat) was born," the term *asat* refers to the fact that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—consisting of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*)—exists in a subtle form. Furthermore, by the phrase "from that, the existent was born," it is shown that Brahman, being interwoven with the subtle-form phenomenal world, is the cause of the gross phenomenal world.
It is thus designated.

In that regard, when that which exists in the state of a cause attains the state of an effect, there occurs for the insentient portion— which was devoid of sound and other qualities in its causal state— a modification consisting of a change in its own nature by way of possessing sound and other qualities for the sake of experience.

And for the conscious portion (cidaṃśa) to become the enjoyer of specific fruits of action, there occurs a modification in the form of an expansion of knowledge corresponding to those fruits. In the Controller, who is characterized by both aspects, there occurs a modification in the form of being characterized by those two aspects in that particular state.
A modification consisting of the attainment of another state from the causal state is common to both the two modes and the possessor of those modes (prakārin). Therefore...

Thus, with reference to the modification consisting in the attainment of different states by a single entity, the proposition that "by hearing the unheard" constitutes the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is established; this is illustrated by the examples of clay and so forth, introduced by the words "Just as, my dear," and so on.
These [examples] intend to refer to the connection with and separation from various bodies, which cause the contraction and expansion of such knowledge.
The scriptural passages stating that the individual soul (jīva) undergoes birth and death, such as "Prajāpati created the creatures," and so forth,
intend to convey that there is no change in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), just as there is none in the insentient portion. Furthermore,
there are scriptural passages such as "Of the eternal among eternals, of the conscious among conscious beings," which support this view.

The intended undesirable modifications are of two kinds: those consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathātva*) and those consisting of the contraction or expansion of knowledge (*jñāna*). "This indeed is that great, unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, Brahman," and so forth, are the scriptural texts concerning the Supreme. Likewise, there is the determination of the oneness of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is eternally filled with both conscious and unconscious entities, prior to creation.

Because there is no differentiation between name and form, it is logically consistent [to say] that "in the beginning this was undifferentiated; it was differentiated by means of name and form. For, by means of the presence or absence of the differentiation between name and form, they speak of multiplicity and unity.

Whether they assert that the state of being a *jīva* is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), or those who say it is produced by an ultimate limiting adjunct, or those who maintain that Brahman— which is pure Being (*sanmātra*) by nature— exists itself in a threefold form as the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller;
all of these [theories] concern the power of ignorance, the power of the limiting adjunct, and the powers of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller.

They establish that even during the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the determination of oneness at that time is possible precisely because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*). This is shown by the two sūtras: "Inequality and cruelty [do not apply to God] because He is dependent [on other factors]" and "[The Lord is not the cause of inequality] because of the non-differentiation of karma," which [demonstrate] the distinction between individual souls (*jīva-bheda*) and the respective stream of their karmas.

And because [the world] is admitted to be beginningless. There is this much distinction: for one [view], by means of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), Brahman itself becomes deluded; for the other, by means of a beginningless, ultimate adjunct (*upādhi*), Brahman itself is bound.
Since there is no other entity distinct from the adjunct and Brahman, for the latter, Brahman itself transforms into various diverse forms.

And although the limited portion lacks the status of an enjoyer, it experiences undesirable fruits of action; because [the Lord] is omniscient, He perceives the enjoyer as non-different from His own Self and thus experiences them Himself. For us, however, because [the Self] consists of the contraction and expansion of its own powers, it remains at all times in both the states of cause and effect.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that [Brahman] abides as an ocean of immeasurable and noble qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*), from which even the scent of all defects has been cast out;

and it is entirely consistent that the non-human goals and the transformations of essential nature residing in the conscious and unconscious entities— which constitute its modes— [belong to them alone].
The Topic on Knowledge. 11.

In response to the doubt as to what the reason is for ether and the other elements being produced while the living beings (jīvas) are unproduced, he says: "Therefore, [the self] is a knower. (Sūtra 2.3.17)
The individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed consciousness (*jña*), having the nature of a knower and not the nature of an insentient entity. Therefore, its being produced is impossible.

Since it is observed in the *Smṛti* that only insentient things such as jars are admitted to be produced, and since space (*ākāśa*) and so forth arise precisely because they are insentient, whereas the soul does not arise because it is sentient—this is the subtle meaning.

It has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is not produced, like space and other such entities. In connection with that, the true nature of the soul is now examined. Is its nature insentient by essence—like a stone according to the Sugatas—with consciousness as a merely adventitious quality? Or is knowingness itself its very nature? Which of these is correct?

How is it that [the self] is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)? It is so because it is heard thus [in scripture]. For in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, in place of the Mādhyandina recension which reads, "He who dwells in the self" (*ya ātmani tiṣṭhan*), the Kāṇvas read, "He who dwells in consciousness" (*yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan*). Likewise, from the passage, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute karmāṇi tanute 'pi ca*), the fact that the agent, the self, has the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpatva*) is understood. But another [says]:
If it is admitted that the individual self (jīvātman) possesses knowledge and the status of being a knower as its inherent nature, then it would follow that, being all-pervading,

it would be perceived everywhere at all times; furthermore, actions would become purposeless, and consciousness would not be perceived even though the self exists during states such as deep sleep or fainting— despite the presence of the necessary causal conditions for a waking person.

Because the arising of knowledge is observed [only occasionally], knowledge is not its essential nature (*svarūpa*), nor is it the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Consciousness (*caitanya*) must necessarily be accepted as adventitious, and the all-pervasiveness (*sarvagatatva*) of the self (*ātman*) must also be accepted, because effects are perceived everywhere due to the admission that the self is present everywhere; for if the effect could be produced merely by the movement of the body [to the location of the object], there would be no need for such universal presence.

Furthermore, there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the conceptualization of [the soul's] transmigration. Scripture (*śruti*) also demonstrates the absence of knowledge at the time of deep sleep:
"Indeed, I do not now know myself as 'I am this,' nor these beings. Likewise, it is so in the state of liberation.

He shows the absence of [ordinary] cognition with the words, "There is no consciousness after death. As for the usage of the term "the nature of cognition" (*jñānasvarūpa*) and so forth, it is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), based on cognition being an attribute unique to that [Self]. This being the position reached, we reply:
For this very reason, this Self is a knower; its essential nature is that of being a cognizer, neither is it mere cognition nor is it insentient by nature.

Why? For this very reason; that is to say, on the basis of scripture alone. By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), the scripture under discussion—namely, the scriptural passage "The Self [is not born] because of scripture"—is referred to. Likewise, in the Chāndogya, within the speech of Prajāpati concerning the nature of the liberated and unliberated selves, it is said:
"Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self; by the mind alone he beholds these desires and rejoices, which are in the world of Brahman."

"Satyakāma, whose resolve is true, does not remember this body as something newly produced; even elsewhere it is said, 'The seer sees no death. Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka, having asked 'Which is the Self?', it is replied:
'This person who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart. And likewise: 'O Maitreyī, by what means can one know the Knower?'"

"One should know that this person indeed knows; for thus he is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the perceiver, the doer—the person whose essence is consciousness. "In this very way, these sixteen parts belong to this all-seeing one. This concludes the section on departure and movement (utkrāntigatyadhikaraṇa).
As for what was said—that if its nature as a knower were innate, it would follow that being omnipresent, it would be perceived everywhere at all times—to that it is replied:
"Departure, going, and coming. (18)

"The world accumulated through karma perishes; the world accumulated through merit perishes. From such scriptural passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "When merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world," it is understood that for living beings there is *utkrānti*—the departure from the body—and *gati*—the journey to the worlds of heaven or hell—and *āgati*—the return to the earthly world after the enjoyment of the fruits of merit and demerit.

[The soul's] return [to the body]. From hearing these [scriptural passages], the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed atomic (*aṇu*), because if it were all-pervading (*vibhu*), its movement would be impossible; such is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra. This section is commenced for the purpose of refuting the position of the Dvaitavādins, the Kṣapaṇakas, the Tārkikas, and others, who accept the all-pervasiveness of souls. "This atomic Self [is to be perceived] with the mind... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12].

It should be understood that doubt arises because of the establishment of both atomicity and omnipresence for the individual soul (jīva), who is designated by the previously mentioned quality of being a knower, in such passages as "He, indeed, is this great unborn Self" (*sa vā eṣa mahān aja ātmā*).
While in passages such as "This great unborn Self," the omnipresence of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is indicated, elsewhere [it is said] "the universe... [is the Self].
Since it is declared that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) "pervades the entire world" (*bhuvanam abhyabhavān*), one might conclude that its atomicity is impossible; to this we reply:
This [Self] is not all-pervading, but rather this Self is indeed atomic. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching of its departure, going, and returning.
First, the departure is heard in scripture: "By that very light, the self departs—either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body.
Furthermore, the going is stated: "All those who depart from this world go to the moon alone. And likewise, the returning:
Since the scripture states, "From whichever world he returns again to this world for the sake of action," thereby demonstrating the soul's departure to the other world,

and because its omnipresence would make separation from the body impossible, one must accept that the soul possesses the quality of being minute, as indicated by the scriptural passage, "The soul is atomic. As for those scriptural passages expressing omnipresence, such as "He is indeed this great, unborn one," [they refer to the soul's pervasion through its connection with the all-pervading intellect].

It should be understood that this refers to the state of being the Supreme Self (*paramātma-paratva*). This is because hundreds of scriptural passages are seen, such as: "The Self, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great, is hidden in the cave of this creature; that which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe," and so forth.
Moreover—
Situated in the middle of the blue lotus, it is radiant like a streak of lightning;
slender like the awn of a wild grain, yellow, luminous, and resembling an atom.
Within the center of that crest, the Supreme Self is established.
In this passage, the essential nature of the three principles—Paśu (the bound soul), Pati (the Lord), and Pāśa (the bond)—is clearly taught.
By the designation of the term "dark cloud" (*nīlatoyada*), *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, is taught as the form of the bond.
Up to the words "resplendent like a streak of lightning" and "resembling atoms," [the nature] of the individual soul (*jīva*), denoted by the word *paśu*, is described.

The nature of that reality has been taught as being subtle like the awn of a grain of wild rice (*nīvāra*). By the phrase "situated at the tip of its crest," the *Śiva-tattva*, which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), is taught. By the passage, "He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hari, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruler," [the nature] of Śiva, who is distinct from the individual soul, [is taught].
It has been established that [the Supreme] is expressible by all words and transcends the three forms (mūrti). Likewise, in the *Māṇḍūkya*:
"They consider the fourth state to be the cessation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual; that is the Self, that is to be known. And:
"One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; this entire universe is Brahman; He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, and He is Agni."

"Having meditated upon that very Moon, which is all that has been and that which is to be, eternal, one transcends death; there is no other path to liberation. In such passages as "All is indeed Rudra," the distinction of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, from the three forms [of the Trimūrti], His being denotable by all words, and the state of one who is established in Him [are affirmed].
And because there is an instruction regarding the teaching of liberation, the omnipresence and other attributes do not belong to the other [the individual soul].
He states another reason for the refutation of the individual soul's omnipresence:
"And by its own self, in the latter two" (Sūtra 2.3.19).

The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis. Although departure (*utkrānti*)—in the form of separation from the body—is somehow possible even for an eternal self and mind, movement and return (*gatyāgatī*) are not possible in any way;
therefore, its atomicity alone is logical.
Regarding this, he states the reason once more:
"If it be said that [the soul] is not atomic because of scriptural statement to that effect, we say no, because of the context of the other. (2.3.20)

If it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) is not atomic because, after introducing the jīva with the words "this which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," the text states "he indeed is this great unborn Self," and thus the scriptural mention of greatness implies it is not minute—[we reply]: no, because of the context of something other [than the jīva]; for in that passage, the subject under discussion is the Supreme Self (prājña), who is distinct from the jīva.
Although the jīva was introduced at the beginning, it is nevertheless stated: "He whose Self is known and realized by him... and so forth.
Since the Supreme is being established in the middle [of the context], this greatness belongs to that which is connected with the "Being" (Sat), and not to the individual soul (jīva).
Furthermore, he states another reason:
"And because of the word for itself and its measurement" (Sūtra 2.3.21).

The word "aṇu" itself is heard directly [in scripture]: "This is the subtle self (aṇu ātmā) into which the vital breath has entered fivefold. Having extracted the measure (māna), that is, the standard of measurement (unmāna); having extracted a substance similar to an atom (aṇu), the state of being measured by that is heard with respect to the individual soul (jīva).

"Of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, and that again divided into a hundred parts"—thus even the conventional usage of "the size of a hair-tip" is observed. Therefore, this self (*ātman*) is indeed atomic (*aṇu*).
Now, if it be objected that if the self were atomic, a sensation pervading the entire body would not be possible, [the author] says in response to this doubt:
67. There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood.

Just as sandalwood situated in one part [of the body] produces coolness throughout the entire body, so too it is logical that the *kṣetrajña*, though situated in a single location, is the experiencer of pleasure and pain in all limbs—just as in the case of the sandalwood in one spot.

The location and the state [of the soul] are perceived through direct observation; therefore, in response to the doubt as to in which part of the body the soul resides, he states the specific location:
"If it be argued that there is a distinction in its location, no, because it is admitted [to be in the heart]; for it is in the heart. (Sūtra 23)

If it is argued that the particular state [of fragrance] in the case of a drop of yellow sandalwood and the like arises from its specific location on a particular part of the body, whereas such is not the case for the Self (ātman), we say no; for even the Self is admitted to reside in a specific part of the body. Indeed, the residence of the Self in the region of the heart is heard in scripture: "For the Self is in the heart; there are one hundred and one channels therein. Likewise, having introduced the subject with "Which is the Self? [the text continues].

"This which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart"— this is stated to demonstrate that the Self resides in a specific location; the example of sandalwood is shown for this purpose, but it does not imply that sandalwood itself requires a specific location.
Furthermore, by means of another reason, he explains how that which exists in only one part performs an effect that pervades the entire body:
"Or [it is] due to its quality, as in the world" (sūtra 24).

The word "or" (vā) is intended to exclude other opinions. The Self exists pervading the entire body by means of its own quality, knowledge. Therefore, like light—for example, the light of gems, the sun, and so forth, which, though residing in one place, is seen to pervade many places—so too is the knowledge of the Self, which resides in the heart.

It functions by pervading the entire body. It is determined that the operation of knowledge—which belongs to the knower and stands in the place of light—outside its own substrate is possible, like the radiance of a gem.
Now, it was stated that the self is merely knowledge; how then can it be said that knowledge possesses qualities distinct from its own nature?
Anticipating this objection, he says thereon:
"The distinction [of the soul from the body] is like that of odor; and so he shows. (Sūtra 25)

Just as there is a distinction between the earth and its quality, smell, which is perceived as belonging to it, so too the Śruti demonstrates the establishment of the distinction between the Self and knowledge— which is cognized as a quality of the knower— by stating:
"From the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails, this person indeed knows," thus indicating that the individual soul (jīva) has the heart as its abode.
Having designated [the self] as having an atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇatva*), its pervasiveness throughout the body is also conventionally described.

Anticipating the objection— "Since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is taught in such passages as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*), why should the soul not also be all-pervasive (*vibhu*) like Brahman?"— he says:
|| 71 || Because of the separate instruction. || 26 ||

"Rudra, the great seer, is the Lord of all beings, superior to the universe; he is the master of Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the Lord of the Guṇas, and the cause of the bondage, maintenance, and liberation from worldly existence. In such passages as "Two birds... and others, [it is established that] the relationship between the individual soul (Jīva) and Brahman is that of the governed and the governor, that the world and the soul are distinct from [Brahman], and that [Brahman] is the cause of the soul's bondage and liberation.

Because of the separate teaching in such passages as "the state of being an enjoyer or a non-enjoyer of saṃsāra," it is established that omnipresence belongs only to that which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva).
Anticipating the objection that in passages such as "He who dwells in consciousness," consciousness itself is designated as the Self, he says:
But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that name, as in the case of a wise man.

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. Because that quality is its essence—that is, because the quality of consciousness is its essence—the self is designated as "consciousness. Consciousness alone is its essential quality. Just as the bliss of the Prājña is its essential quality, and thus the Prājña is referred to by the word "bliss," for if this bliss did not exist in the space [of the heart], it would not be so.
"Ānanda is Brahman"—thus he understood. For bliss is indeed the essential quality of the wise one (prājña). That is the singular bliss of Brahman;

"knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere. Or, as in the case of "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," the wise one (vipaścit) is designated by the word "knowledge" (jñāna). [He is] together with...
In passages such as "He who is all-knowing by means of the wise Brahman," it is understood that this is a quality consisting of the refinement of knowledge belonging to the conscious one (prājña).
He states the justification for this again:
And because it is manifested as the very nature of the self, there is no fault in perceiving it.

Because of the scriptural vision that "this person consisting of consciousness, who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths, being common [to all], moves through both worlds," there is no fault in designating the self by means of that [consciousness], since it persists as long as the self exists. This is seen from such passages as: "Just as flowing rivers disappear into the ocean."
Having likewise abandoned name-and-form and the divine [elements],
the fifteen constituents (kalās) have returned to their foundations, and all the deities have returned to their respective divinities.
The karmas and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

In hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "This serene being, having arisen from this body and having attained the supreme light, manifests in its own true form," [it is taught] everything up to disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), which consists in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the inherent nature of being a transmigrating soul (*jīvatva*).

For one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and is steadfast in Śiva-yoga, meditation on Śiva, and knowledge of Śiva, the designation of "atomicity" (aṇutva) is not contradictory, because even during the times of meditation and absorption on Śiva, their state as a pure individual soul remains— like a camphor lamp placed in the midst of a fierce heat.

The sense is that for those established in knowledge, there is the observation of rising again after samādhi— like a sleeping person— until the completion of the prārabdha karma; for if the all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) of the individual soul (jīva) were accepted,
the coexistence of atomicity (aṇutva) and pervasiveness would be impossible, making the relationship between the jīva and Brahman like that of a river and the ocean.
The contradiction among the scriptural texts that establish [the soul] as both the attainer and the attained would be difficult to avoid.

Furthermore, even the Lord’s status as the inner controller (antaryāmin) and so forth would not be possible. If it is argued that the soul’s atomicity is merely due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), that is inconsistent with such passages as: "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord... and so on.
Because it is taught that the soul exists even prior to the creation of the elements due to its being unborn, it is therefore determined that the atomicity of the soul is its inherent nature.
As for the argument that because there is an absence of cognition during deep sleep and other states, cognition cannot be an attribute invariably connected to the soul's essential nature—
To this he replies:
"Because, while it exists, its manifestation occurs, like virility and so forth. (29)

The word "tu" (but) here is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Since one's own consciousness—which exists even during states such as deep sleep—is manifested during states such as waking, it is logically established that it is an attribute inherent to its very nature (*svarūpānubandhidharma*), just like masculinity (*puṃstva*) and so forth. For example, although the specific faculty of masculinity exists during childhood, it remains unmanifest.

When manifested in youth, that state of being possessed of [the body] does not become merely occasional for the person. For the fact of the body consisting of the seven constituents (dhātus) is invariably connected to its very nature; this is because the body's essential character is designated as "the body consists of the seven constituents, the three impurities, the two origins, and is composed of the four kinds of food. Thus, even during states such as deep sleep, the referent of "I" (ahamartha) shines forth.

This has already been stated. The fact that existing knowledge has objects as its domain is perceived even in the waking state. Furthermore, these attributes of the self, such as being a knower and so forth, have already been established. Therefore, the nature of the individual self (jīvātman) exists prior to the state of deep sleep (prājña). And this self is of atomic dimension (aṇuparimāṇa). Nor does the statement "after death there is no consciousness" mean that [the self ceases to exist].

It is said that for the liberated one there is an absence of knowledge; rather, having arisen from these elements, he perishes after them. Thus, the perception of birth, death, and so forth—which in the state of transmigratory existence is caused by conformity with the elements—does not exist for the liberated one. This is as described in the passage beginning with "as rivers flowing," where, in the state of liberation, [the self] is like water merging into water.

Because it is seen that the pure soul attains that [state], and because of the consistency with such scriptural passages as: "The seer sees neither death nor disease nor suffering from it; the seer sees everything and attains everything in every way," and "Not being born again, remembering this body, he rejoices, beholding these desires with the mind."
Therefore, the atomicity and the nature of being a knower of the *jīva* are not contradictory.
Now, regarding the doctrine that knowledge is the self (*jñānātmavāda*), he states the refutation of its omnipresence:
"Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other. (Sūtra 3.2.30)

Otherwise, under the view that [the self] is omnipresent and under the view that it consists of mere consciousness, perception and non-perception would necessarily occur simultaneously, or there would be a fixed restriction to one or the other; that is, perception alone would be constant, or non-perception alone. What is meant by this is as follows: in the world, regarding the current perception and non-perception of the self—

The cause would have to be of the nature of cognition and omnipresent. Whether it be through perception alone, or non-perception alone, or both being the cause, it would follow that both must exist at all times and in all places. If it were through perception alone, there would never be non-perception of anything anywhere; if it were through non-perception alone, there would never be perception of anything anywhere. This is our position.

Because the self resides only within the body, its perception occurs only there and not elsewhere; thus, the established rule is maintained. Even for those who hold that perception depends on the instruments (the senses), since all selves are omnipresent and therefore always conjoined with all instruments, and since there is no restrictive rule regarding the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, the aforementioned defect remains the same. Therefore, what was stated previously alone is logical.
The Section on the Agent (Kartradhikaraṇa) || 13 ||
