In response to the doubt that— since scriptures such as "This Self is Brahman" teach that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) alone is Brahman, agency and so forth are untenable for him, whereas agency and so forth are tenable only for the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which serves as his limiting adjunct (upādhi)— it is said:
In order to refute the non-dualist view that asserts the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*tajjīvabrahmavādakādvaita*), he says:
"The [Self] is an agent, because the scriptures have purpose. (Sūtra 3.4.31)

It has been stated that this self is the knower and that its dimension is atomic. Now, it is considered whether it is that very self which is the agent, or whether, while being itself a non-agent, it merely attributes the agency of the insentient *guṇas* to itself. What is reasonable here? That the self is indeed a non-agent. Why? Because the self is a non-agent, and agency belongs to the *guṇas* alone.

It is heard in the treatises on the inner self (*adhyātmaśāstra*). For instance, in the *Kaṭhavallī*, by stating "the living being (*jīva*) is neither born nor does it die," and so forth, all things such as birth, old age, and death—which are attributes of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—are negated; furthermore, agency (*kartṛtva*) in actions such as killing is also negated.

"If the killer thinks he kills, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither kills nor is killed. (Gītā 2.19) The meaning is that one who perceives the Self as the killer does not know the Self. And so it was said by the Blessed One himself:
It is said that the soul's (jīva) true nature is non-agency, whereas the conceit of agency is a delusion:
"All actions performed in every way by the qualities of material nature,
the self whose mind is deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer.'"
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities (guṇas),
then Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause in the agency of both cause and effect.
"The Puruṣa is said to be the cause of the experiencing of pleasure and pain.

Therefore, the Puruṣa alone possesses the quality of being an experiencer (bhoktṛtva), while agency (kartṛtva) belongs solely to Prakṛti. This being the case, we reply: "The [Self] is the agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. Why is it that the Self alone is the agent and not the Guṇas? Because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless.

For scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" and "one seeking liberation should meditate upon Brahman" enjoin the very enjoyer of the fruits—such as heaven and liberation—in the state of agency. Indeed, when that which is insentient is the agent, no other [sentient being] can be enjoined. It is called a *śāstra* because of its teaching (*śāsana*); and teaching consists of instigation (*pravartana*). And the capacity of the scripture to instigate [is established].
By way of generating awakening; for the insentient *pradhāna* cannot be made to awaken.

Therefore, the meaningfulness of the scriptures would only be possible if the conscious enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) were the agent. As it has been said: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer. And as it was stated in the passage beginning with, "If he thinks himself the slayer... and so forth.

It is stated that the non-agency of the self regarding the act of killing is heard in scripture; this is said because, due to the eternity of the self, there is no possibility of its being slain. Furthermore, as for the statement beginning with "The actions performed by nature," which records that agency belongs to the *guṇas* alone, that refers to the self's agency in worldly activities.

Since [agency] is produced by the association with the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and is not inherent to its own nature, it is stated—through the discrimination between what has been attained and what has not—that agency belongs to the qualities alone. And thus it is said in that very same place:
"The cause of this [self] in births from good and evil wombs is attachment to the qualities."
Likewise, having accepted the agency of the self in that very context,
it is said: "This being so, he who, due to his unrefined intellect, perceives the isolated self as the agent— that person of dull wit does not see."
The locus, the agent, and the various instruments,
as well as the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth factor therein.

Thus, since the agency of the self is dependent on everything from the locus (the body) up to fate, he who considers the self alone to be the agent does not see; the meaning is that he is a fool. To provide further reason for this point, he says:
Because of the teaching on appropriation and because of the teaching on the wandering [of the Tathāgata]. || 32 ||

Having introduced the subject with "Just as a great king," it is taught that the agency regarding the grasping and relinquishing of the vital breaths belongs to [the Self], in the passage: "Having taken hold of these very vital breaths, he moves about within his own body according to his will.
Regarding the claim that agency belongs only to the intellect (*buddhi*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the text here refutes the agency of the intellect.
78. And because of the designation [of the agent] in the action; for if it were not so, there would be a reversal of the grammatical instruction. || 33 ||

Furthermore, because consciousness (vijñāna) is designated as the agent in worldly and Vedic activities—according to the statement, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs actions"—it is by the word "consciousness" that the agent is designated. If it is argued that here there is no designation of the Self, but rather of the internal organ, the intellect (buddhi), then in that case there would be a reversal of the grammatical reference. [The reference] would be to the intellect.

Because it is an instrument, there would have to be an indication using the instrumental case, as in "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*). Thus, in the passage, "By means of consciousness, he takes up consciousness from these means of knowledge," one does not perceive that the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses both the status of an instrument and that of an agent.
If the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) were designated as the agent, then his agency would also be possible during states such as deep sleep and the head-impact [of death].

Therefore, since that [agency] is impossible for the individual soul (jīva) whose nature is that of Brahman, the objection arises that agency belongs only to its internal organ (antahkarana). To this, he says: "As in the case of perception, there is no restriction" (79. Upalabdhivadaniyamaḥ || 34 ||).

Just as in the Advaita system, since the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of Brahman, which consists of consciousness, it is logical that agency belongs solely to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). However, the claim that because agency resides in that [organ], the soul is without agency during states such as deep sleep due to the non-perception of that [agency] at those times, is inconsistent. This is like the case of perception: for example, in the case of a scholar who is habituated to expounding all the scriptures.

In the absence of the presence of a disciple, the capacity for the act of teaching that specific knowledge is contracted. Likewise, it is not contradictory that the individual soul (jīva) possesses universal agency through its conjunction with the insentient internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, while in the absence of such conjunction, that power is contracted. It is therefore incorrect to claim absolute inactivity based on that alone. Consequently, there is no restriction that [the Lord] must be the agent at all times.

This is possible; nevertheless, agency remains unavoidable. Furthermore—just as chariots, palaces, and the like possess the capacity for agency even when their power to act is constrained by the nature of their constituent parts and instruments, so too do living beings possess the inherent power of agency even when they are dissociated from the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and so forth.

Even if there is no manifestation of the power of agency residing in itself, the power of that agency is not precluded from the *jīva*; for if that [agency] were not admitted in the *jīva* alone, the contradiction with numerous *śruti* passages enjoining the agency of the *jīva*, such as "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating," would be difficult to avoid. Therefore, [agency does not belong] to the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

It should be understood that agency is untenable [for the individual soul]. For if the power of agency were present in the *jīva* even during states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it would follow that it possesses independence; and one might ask: why should it not possess knowledge of itself and others even while asleep? To this doubt, he says:
|| 80 || Due to the reversal of power. || 35 ||

If it is argued that the agency belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone—because in deep sleep there is an absence of cognition, and because we observe a contraction of the power to know oneself and others during the state of movement (waking and dreaming)—we say no. Why? Because of the reversal of powers (*śaktiviparyayāt*). For in such scriptural passages as, "When everything has dissolved at the time of deep sleep, one who is overcome by darkness attains the nature of bliss," it is shown that [the powers reside] in the Self during sleep.

Due to the power of the Supreme Lord’s form as Māyā, which is most insentient, there occurs a reversal of the individual soul's (jīva) capacity; because of this concealment (tirodhāna), agency is untenable for the intellect (buddhi). This is just as in the world, the nature of fire (vaiśvānara) is temporarily concealed by gems, mantras, and the like, or as the nature of cold water is [concealed] by contact with the sun, fire, and so forth.
Just as the coldness inherent in [water] is obscured by the covering of a rain-cloud, and just as the radiance of the sun is obscured [by clouds],

so too is the self-knowledge and knowledge of others of the *jīva* obscured by the power of the bonds (*pāśa*) of Paraśiva through the contraction of its own power; yet, by that much alone, the qualities residing in itself remain unique and not shared with anything else.
It is reasonable to say this.

Furthermore, if the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, then since it would be impossible for anyone other than the agent to be the enjoyer, the power of enjoyment would also belong to that [intellect] alone;
thus, the Self’s power of enjoyment would be lost. And consequently, enjoyment would accrue to the intellect alone.

If there were an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a self, [the opponent would object] that their accepted position is indeed that "the person exists because there must be an experiencer. Furthermore, if the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, the capacity of being an instrument would be contradicted;

yet the capacity of being an instrument cannot be denied, since in the world it is observed that only an agent accompanied by instruments performs an action, and this applies to the intellect as well.

Another instrument would have to be postulated; and thus there would be a dispute over mere names, since you too admit that agency belongs only to one distinct from the instrument. He states another reason for refuting the agency of the intellect:
And because of the absence of meditative absorption (samādhi). || 36 ||
If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, then it would also be the agent in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that serves as the means to liberation.
Yet, that absorption is capable of concentrating the *prakṛti* by means of the thought, "I am other than *prakṛti*. Therefore, the Self alone is the agent;
for what is called "absorption" arises through the grace of Śiva.

At the time of experiencing the direct realization of the self-luminous Supreme Śiva, which severs the bonds of ignorance through the yoga of Śiva, one transcends the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— being liberated from the activities of the body, senses, mind, and vital breath— and follows the Śiva-tattva, the supreme space that illuminates the supreme light, free from phenomenal proliferation and devoid of affliction.

Having immersed oneself in the ocean of intense bliss, even in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which transcends both knowledge and ignorance, one does not forget that [bliss]. Like a camphor lamp placed in the midst of a scorching sun, it remains free from conceptualization and mental construction, characterized by the form of Śiva.
Its unsurpassed nature is established by all the Vedas. This is so because the individual soul lacks agency regarding merit and demerit.
Because of the absence of meditative absorption (samādhi), that [knowledge] is absent;

know that through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga. By intense contemplation of That, by union with That, and through the realization of the true nature of reality, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyā).
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill,
the wise man burns away the fetters through the practice of churning with meditation.
Verily, the Self, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
The same [objections] should be stated regarding the siddhas such as Revanasiddha, Marulasiddha, and Ekāmasiddha, who are established by many such Śrutis.
There would be no instruction on liberation in the form of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahmaikya*) established by Śrutis such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Furthermore, because the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient and perishes at the time of liberation, there would follow the absurd consequence of the self's own destruction.
Now, if it is admitted that the Self is an agent, one might object that its agency would never cease; to this he says:
"And as the carpenter, in both ways" (Sūtra 3.2.40).

Even though the Self is endowed with the instruments such as speech and so forth, it acts only when it wills; for the Śruti also declares accordingly: "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs with action. But when it does not will, then it does not act;
just as a carpenter, despite the presence of tools such as an axe and the like, acts or refrains from acting according to his own will, so it is here.

If the intellect (*buddhi*), which is insentient, were the agent, it would always remain an agent because there would be no cause for regulating its desire for enjoyment and so forth. Therefore, they explain that agency belongs neither to the intellect nor to primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Since desire is an attribute of the sentient, agency over all things belongs only to the sentient individual soul (*jīva*), as is logically consistent, just like a carpenter. For example, a carpenter...

An agent of action exists in both ways, in both forms; likewise, the individual soul (*jīva*), by its own will during the states of waking and dreaming, while characterized by gross and subtle bodies, performs worldly and Vedic activities and experiences the pleasure and pain of sense objects. During the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), however, it is devoid of the activities of the body and the senses.

He experiences supreme bliss established in the power of the fetter (*pāśa-śakti*), which is of the nature of supreme Śiva-tamas. Therefore, it is established that agency belongs only to the conscious individual soul (*jīva*).
This concludes the section on dependence on another (*parāyattādhikaraṇa*). 14.
If the agency belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone, then its independence—just like that of the Supreme Lord—is established by implication.
Therefore, in response to the doubt as to how there can be a distinction between the two, he states their relative gradation:
"But [the soul's activity is] from the Highest, for so scripture declares" (Sūtra 2.3.40).

In this regard, the agency of the ignorant soul in performing meritorious and non-meritorious deeds arises from another, namely, from the impulsion of Paraśiva. Why? Because of scripture (*śruti*); for there is the scriptural statement: "He indeed causes one to perform good action. Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses no independence. Here, as to whether the agency of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) belongs to it independently or is dependent upon the Supreme Self—that Supreme Self being Śiva—[it is dependent].
Or is it Nārāyaṇa? This is the doubt. For if [the soul] were dependent upon the Supreme Self, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would result in being purposeless.
Indeed, only one who is capable of initiating activity or cessation through his own intellect becomes a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
Therefore, his agency exists by virtue of independence. Furthermore—
Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge, the soul of the universe, and the supreme refuge;
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, and Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Self.

Beginning with these words and ending with "Nārāyaṇa remains pervading all that is within and without," there is established the supreme self-nature of Nārāyaṇa—his being the Self of all, his being the inner controller of all, and his being the all-pervader—along with the scriptural teaching: "I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss."

Because it is designated as such even in the *Gītā*, and because the word "Nārāyaṇa" lacks conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for Śiva, the disappearance of the *ṇatva* [nasalization] in a figurative designation (*gauṇavyapadeśa*) would be unavoidable. Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that agency belongs either to the individual soul (*jīva*) or to Nārāyaṇa, the following is stated in reply:

In the phrase "but from another" (*parātu*), the word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. His agency arises from another—that is, from the Lord who is distinct from the individual soul—due to what cause? From scripture (*śruti*). [The scriptures state: "The one God rules over the perishable Pradhāna through the perishable self";
"The Lord has entered within all beings as the ruler of people"; and "He alone is indeed good."

"He makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from this world; indeed, He makes him perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward"—thus [it is said]. "He who, dwelling within the self, is internal to the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. In such scriptural passages, [the attributes of] Śiva [are described].

Because of the scriptural teaching that He is the controller of all, the agency of both the individual soul (jīva) and Nārāyaṇa is not tenable. As for the claim that— beginning with "The thousand-headed God" and ending with "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all that is within and without"—
it is Nārāyaṇa alone who is taught to be the inner ruler of all and so forth, that statement is incorrect.
Now, regarding the demonstration that the term *nārāyaṇa* denotes Śiva:
this has already been extensively elaborated upon in the *Sarvādhikaraṇa* by means of the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*).
As for the absence of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) of the word *nārāyaṇa* for Śiva—
O you who are the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, O Śivā, the accomplisher of all goals,
O refuge, O Goddess Tryambakā, O Nārāyaṇī, homage be to you!
Regarding the statements such as "Nārāyaṇī is of the nature of sound," if it is claimed that Pārvatī is Nārāyaṇī, that is incorrect;

for nowhere else is she seen to be used in that way, and because in instances such as "Rudrāṇī, the wife of Rudra" and "Indrāṇī, the wife of Indra," the suffix clearly indicates the status of being a wife. [The term *nārāyaṇa* means] one whose abode or place (*ayana*) is *nāra*, which is a collection (*samūha*) of men (*nara*).

If it is argued that the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* in the word *nārāyaṇa* is precluded by its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), we say no; for like Viṣṇu, the term is also a conventional designation (*rūḍhi*) for Śiva. Since such usage is possible through both etymology and convention—as in the cases of *bādarāyaṇa*, *uttarāyaṇa*, and *rāmāyaṇa*—what more need be said regarding its conventional status? He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Agni, and he is the Moon.
"Thus all that has been and all that is to be is eternal"—so says the Kaivalya Śruti.
"Whatever names are indeed great for you, O Govinda, in this world, those very same are my names; no deliberation is needed here."

Thus, from Śiva’s words to Viṣṇu in the *Harivaṃśa*— "This supreme form of mine is called Nārāyaṇa"— and from the observation in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and the *Īśvaragītā*, according to the principle that "the qualities of the cause are transferred to the effect," and from the Vedic declaration, "O son, you are indeed my own self under the name of 'son'," although the term *Nārāyaṇa* is firmly established for Śiva, Viṣṇu is likewise [his manifestation] by virtue of being a portion (*aṃśa*) of him.
This is appropriate. Furthermore, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The *āra*s are to be known as the poor, while the *nārā*s are indeed the Lord of Wealth (*Dhanādhipa*). Because He desires that wealth through friendship, He is truly Nārāyaṇa, Śiva."

Thus, since the substitution of *ṇ* (ṇatva) is observed in usage for Śiva as a distinct [form], the doctrine that the *ṇatva* is entirely sublated is indeed charming only when left unexamined. Furthermore, in the Gītā, by such passages as "The Lord of all beings through His Māyā... seek refuge in Him alone, O Bhārata," the status of Śiva alone as the controller of all beings is indicated.

If it is argued that the title "Lord" (Īśvara) without any prefix belongs to Him alone because it is not established for others, and because Kṛṣṇa himself, through such statements as "I am seated in the heart of all," teaches his own status as the inner controller of all and other attributes of Supreme Śiva by virtue of his sovereignty— therefore, [the title] is appropriate for him alone from the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*)— [we reply:]...

In the sūtra, "Or [it is] instruction [given] as in the case of Vāmadeva," it was already pointed out previously that Kṛṣṇa’s instruction on the attributes of Brahman from the perspective of the vision of the scripture (śāstradṛṣṭyā) is not contradictory, just like that of Vāmadeva.
Now, it was argued that in this way, the futility of the scriptures concerning injunctions and prohibitions would follow; to that, he says:
But [the Lord] is dependent on the effort performed [by the individual], because otherwise prescribed and prohibited acts would be rendered meaningless, and for other such reasons. (Sūtra 3.2.39)
The Lord, depending upon the actions performed by the *kṣetrajña* (the embodied soul), bestows happiness and suffering upon them;

this is because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions of the scriptures would be rendered purposeless, and so forth—meaning there would be no contradiction [with reason]. Otherwise, the authority of the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions would be lost, since in all actions, the person [is the agent].
The Inner Ruler, the Supreme Self, impels [the individual soul] by granting His permission, having regard for the effort and exertion already performed.
Without the permission of the Supreme Self, its activity would not be possible. Why is this so?
Because of the non-futility of prescribed and prohibited injunctions, and so forth. Here, the word "and so forth" includes favor, restraint, and other such factors. As it is said:
In the case of property held in common by two parties, the transfer of ownership to another cannot take place without the consent of one of them;

yet, if that other's consent is given, it is as if the act were performed by oneself, and thus the result accrues to that very person alone. Furthermore, it has already been established that even for one who has the power to turn others away from evil deeds, to give consent to such acts brings about a state of cruelty.

If it is objected that this is untenable—namely, that [the Lord] himself causes good and evil deeds to be performed through the desire to elevate and the desire to cast down, as stated in the texts: "For he alone makes him perform good deeds whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds; he alone makes him perform evil deeds whom he wishes to lead down"—it is said in reply: this is not so.

This is common to all. However, for one who proceeds established in extreme favorability toward the Supreme Person, the Lord Śiva, favoring him, himself generates an inclination toward the most auspicious actions that are the means for attaining Himself. And for one who [proceeds] in extreme unfavorability...

Established [in this state], he proceeds; by restraining that [mind], he generates an aversion toward actions that lead to lower rebirths and are opposed to his own attainment. As it is also said in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*:
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds."

"Thinking thus, the wise, endowed with devotion, worship Me. Beginning from this point: "To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me."
"Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
Likewise:

"Untruthful and without foundation, they say the world is without a Lord," and so forth, ending with: "those who hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, the envious ones"—having said this:
"These hateful, cruel, lowest of men, I cast into the cycles of worldly existence..."
"I perpetually cast the inauspicious ones into asuric wombs alone," so it is said.
Likewise, it was stated by the Blessed One himself in the *Śivagītā*: "Now, what is the use of much speaking? The world was created by me alone."
"By me alone it is constantly protected, and by me it is also withdrawn. Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"In the center of the heart, [one should meditate upon] the Lord of the Universe, Jātavedas, the most excellent, who is the size of a hair-tip."
Those wise ones who perceive that Self attain eternal peace, and no others.
I alone preside over every womb; by me was all this, consisting of fivefold elements, created in the beginning.
Having perceived me—the Lord, the Person, the adorable God—one attains unto me, the ultimate peace.
In whatever form those mortals worship me alone,
in that very form, being pleased with them, I grant their desire.
Whether by the prescribed method or even without it, those who worship me with devotion—to them I grant the fruit, for I am pleased; of this there is no doubt.
Moreover, even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion,
he is to be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.
Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not defiled by any ocular defects,
so too the one inner self of all beings is not defiled by any of the sufferings of the world.
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.
O mighty-armed one, those who are not my devotees and are devoid of faith in me,
they indeed desire fruits pertaining to this world, the next world, and so forth.
For it is held that the fruit of action is perishable, limited, and subject to degrees of excellence.
Those lowest of men who perform actions without understanding them enter the wombs of insects and into the jaws of death again and again.
For any embodied being whatsoever born among the various classes of living beings.
Devotion to me arises through merits accumulated over ten million births;
that very devotee of mine, endowed with faith, attains knowledge.
Even after performing various karmas for hundreds of millions of births,
you must then renounce them all and fully take hold of my power.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give,
and whatever austerity you practice, O Rāma, perform that as an offering unto Me.
"Therefore, O best of the Raghus, there is no devotion greater than that toward me. Thus ends the section on the portions (aṃśādhikaraṇa). 15.

Now, having refuted the Advaita position— which establishes that the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman itself by means of proving the soul's being impelled by Brahman— he proceeds to refute the doctrines that the soul is unreal (*alīka*), that there is only one soul, or that it is a reflection (*pratibimba*), all of which are included within that [Advaita] system: Thus, having refuted the Advaita doctrine— which establishes the very nature of the individual soul as being a portion of Śiva (*śivāṃśatva*)— by means of the reason that the soul is impelled by Brahman, and by means of the proof that the soul is directly Brahman itself, he now refutes the doctrines of the unreality of the soul contained therein, the oneness of the soul, and its being a reflection.

The Lord is a partial incarnation (aṃśa), because of the various designations [of his forms], and also because some scriptural passages record him as having the nature of a fisherman, a hunter, and so forth. (Sūtra 2.3.42)

Having previously established that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic, a knower, and possesses agency dependent upon Paramaśiva, they now declare that the oneness of the soul, the identity of the soul with Brahman, the unreality of the soul, and the soul’s status as a reflection are untenable, because they are non-Vedic.
Just as from a well-kindled fire thousands of sparks of similar nature issue forth, even so,
O gentle one, various states of being are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also pass away.

Because hundreds of scriptural passages such as "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti" declare that individual souls (jīvas) are portions of Brahman, the doctrine of the oneness of the soul is not tenable; for there is a designation of multiplicity, as in the passage "Two birds... where the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is designated, and because otherwise there would be a designation of non-difference in such scriptural texts as "That thou art."

One must indeed accept both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. The individual souls are indeed parts (*aṃśa*) of Brahman and not something other than it, as this is seen in the Śruti. Nevertheless, some—namely, certain followers of the Atharva Veda—record that Brahman possesses the nature of fishermen and woodcutters;
thus, they record a constant distinction between the individual soul and Brahman based on the relationship of master and servant.

They say: "The Brahmadāśas, the Brahmadāsas—these gamblers are indeed Brahman," and so forth. By such scriptural passages, they establish that even in the state of liberation, for the liberated souls who have attained similarity with Brahman (*brahmasārūpya*), servitude, dependence for the sake of service (*kaiṅkarya*), and so on, are established without contradiction; this is the view of the Sūtrakāra [Bādarāyaṇa] regarding those who belong to certain Vedic branches (*eke śākhinaḥ*).

This is because [the scripture] specifies this by virtue of [the jīvas] abiding in only one portion of the Veda. While the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the object of service (*śeṣin*) of the Supreme Lord is appropriate for bound, pure *jīvas* during the state of *saṃsāra*, such dependence and so forth must not be accepted for liberated *jīvas* during the state of liberation, as it would be a cause of fear; as stated in such scriptural passages as "Just as rivers... and so on.
Because of the instruction regarding the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between difference and non-difference; for it has already been stated previously that we are proponents of the authority of the Śruti and do not rely excessively on mere reasoning (*yukti*), since [the truth] is established through Śruti, reasoning, and direct experience in the *Jijñāsā* and subsequent sections.

Furthermore, because this has already been established in many ways previously, it is indicated that even in the Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita systems, since there is no complete reconciliation with the Śruti, their reconciliation with all the Śrutis is merely figurative, as they rely on the shadow of the theory of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda). This is the case for the logicians and others who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference.

Because it lacks a comprehensive synthesis of all the scriptures, like the systems of the Buddhists and others, that doctrine is utterly untenable. Now, a doubt arises as to whether this individual soul (*jīva*) is entirely different from the Supreme, or whether it is the Supreme Brahman itself under delusion, or whether it is Brahman delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), or whether it is a part of Brahman; for there are conflicting scriptural statements.
Doubt:
But surely this matter has already been settled in the sūtra *tadananyatvam adhikantu bhedanirdeśāt* (II.1.14). True!

That very point was raised as an objection due to the conflict between scriptural texts concerning multiplicity and unity, and was then specifically established by demonstrating that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman.

It is being determined: for as long as the soul's status as a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman has not been established, so long will the soul's non-difference from Brahman and Brahman's superiority over it remain unestablished. What, then, is the prima facie position?
That they are absolutely distinct. Why? Because of the scriptural indication of difference in such passages as, "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord," and so forth.

Furthermore, scriptural passages asserting the non-difference between the knower and the unknown are figurative, as they convey a contradictory meaning—much like saying "one should sprinkle with fire.

Nor is the view that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman tenable. For the word *aṃśa* denotes a portion of a single entity; if the jīva were a portion of Brahman, the defects inherent in the jīva would accrue to Brahman. Moreover, the jīva is not a fragment of Brahman.
Thus, the status of being a part is established; for Brahman cannot be divided into parts, and otherwise the previously mentioned defects would follow.
Therefore, it is difficult to establish that something entirely distinct from it could be its part.

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is simply Brahman itself appearing through delusion. Why? Because of such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*).
This is because of the teaching that Brahman is one's own self. As for those [scriptural passages] that speak of multiplicity,

since they merely restate objects established by perception and other means of knowledge, they are shown— just like perception and the rest— to be contained within ignorance by those scriptural texts which, being otherwise unestablished, are devoted to the teaching of non-duality.

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman itself as delimited by beginningless limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Why? Precisely because of the teaching regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self. Nor can it be said that this limiting adjunct is imagined through delusion, for that would result in the impossibility of the established order of bondage, liberation, and so forth. To this objection, it is replied: "It is a part of Brahman."

Why? Because of the designation of difference and because of the designation otherwise, as oneness. For the designation is seen in both ways. First, the designation of difference is seen through such terms as "the creator" and "the created," "the controller" and "the controlled," and "Brahman" and so forth. Furthermore, some record that [Brahman] possesses the nature of fishermen, gamblers, and others: "The fishermen are Brahman... and so on.
"The Brahman-servants, these Brahmans are gamblers"—thus the followers of the Atharvaveda study that even the *dāśas* (servants) and *kitavas* (gamblers) are [forms] of Brahman.
Therefore, the meaning is that non-difference is designated by virtue of [Brahman's] pervading all living beings.
Thus, in order to establish the primacy of both designations, it must be accepted that this individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman.
Nor can the designations of difference be explained away (*anyathāsiddhatva*) by claiming their objects are already established through perception and other means;

for [the distinctions] such as being created by Brahman, being governed by Him, being illumined by Him, being subservient to Him, and so forth, are not within the scope of perception and the like, and thus they are not otherwise established. Therefore, [the scriptural texts] speaking of the creation of the world and so on—

[The Upanishads] are intent upon teaching an unreal object by way of restating distinctions established through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor [is it possible for them to teach] the creation of ether and so forth preceded by the resolve to become many, nor the entry [of Brahman] into that [creation] in the form of a living being (*jīva*), based on a contemplation of the Self as being non-different from Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, partless and of a single essence.
The differentiation of diverse names and forms; the state of being a partaker of pleasure and pain caused by the experience of infinite objects produced thereby;

the state of being the inner ruler (antaryāmitva) by remaining therein as the non-enjoyer and governing it; the contemplation of one's own identity with the causal Brahman while existing as the individual soul (jīva); liberation from saṃsāra; and the scripture that teaches this.
It is taught that one must wander while performing [actions]; for if that were so, it would result in the fallacy of being like the incoherent prattle of a madman.

Furthermore, the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not tenable, precisely because it contradicts the previously mentioned designations such as being "governed" (*niyāmyatva*) and so forth. For it is not the case that a single person, such as Devadatta, [is simultaneously both the ruler and the ruled].

The relationship of controller and controlled and so forth is established through distinctions such as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body and other factors. Therefore, in order to justify both designations, it must be accepted that this individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman.
Consequently, for one who relies on the path of the Vedas, [the inquiry] primarily concerns what is known as the "harmonization of all the Śrutis."
It is thus determined that the doctrine of both duality and non-duality (Dvaitādvaita) alone must be accepted. Even in the Smṛti it is said:
"Śiva is real, the world is real, and the individual soul is real by its very nature;
their non-difference is also real, like that between a worm and a bee."
Because of such traditional authority (*smaraṇa*), that alone is delightful. Anticipating the objection that—

since scriptures such as "This Self is Brahman" teach that the individual soul (*jīva*) itself is Brahman, the scriptural passages concerning difference, such as "The slaves are Brahman, the servants are Brahman," must be taught as being merely imagined (*kalpita*), like a snake in a rope— he says:
Now follows the demonstration of the plurality of individual souls (jīva).
[Sūtra 41: On account of the wording of the Mantras.
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial nature) and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā;
from Him, who has become its constituent part, this entire universe has arisen and is pervaded.

Furthermore, from the wording of such Vedic mantras as, "One foot of Him are all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven," it is shown that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Śiva, that Māyā is the material cause (prakṛti), and that the entire universe arises from the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as delimited by that [Māyā] and constitutes His body. Therefore, the individual soul, the person, is a minute fraction of the limbs of Paramaśiva, the possessor of Māyā.
Furthermore—the word *pāda* (foot) denotes a part. The plural form in the phrase "all beings" (*viśvābhūtāni*) is due to the multiplicity of living entities.

In both the mantra and the sūtra, the singular form in the word "part" (*aṃśa*) intends to refer to the genus. Likewise, in the passage "Because of the scriptural declaration of the Self," the singular number also intends to refer to the genus: "The eternal among the transient, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many."
From such scriptural passages as these, the multiplicity of selves— which constitutes their difference from the Lord—

is understood by those capable of knowing the true nature of the self, even though all selves are one insofar as they consist of the nature of consciousness; and that there is no confusion [of experiences] among them, despite their lack of physical contact, will be explained immediately hereafter.
Furthermore, he will speak of the multiplicity of selves. Therefore, the doctrine of the non-duality of the self is untenable.
To this point, he states another reason:
"Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti. (Sūtra 42)
The Supreme Lord (Maheśvara) is the infinite, all-pervading Self, whose nature is truth and knowledge;
the world of living beings is but a portion of Him, residing within the hearts of all creatures.
Just as sparks arise from fire through contact with wood,
so too are those known as the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) joined with beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus it is said in the Śivagītā:
"In the world of living beings, a portion of My very self exists as the eternal individual soul;
O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all creatures."
Causing all beings to wander, mounted upon a machine by means of his illusory power.

Thus, in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*, the fact that individual souls (*jīvas*) are portions of the Lord (*īśvara*) and their plurality is taught. Furthermore, in the Taittirīya recension as well, the plurality of souls is observed in such passages as, "From which indeed these beings are born," and so forth. Therefore, the doctrines asserting the unreality of the soul, the oneness of the soul, and the identity of the soul with Brahman are indeed untenable.
Now, the demonstration that Śiva is beloved by Viṣṇu:

Indeed, because the *Puruṣasūkta*— which establishes [the identity] of Viṣṇu— is seen with the statement, "All beings are but one foot of him," and because in the *Kṛṣṇagītā* it is stated, "A portion of Myself alone am I in the world of living beings," thereby indicating that individual souls (*jīva*) are His own portions, [it follows that] Hari [is the Supreme].

If it is argued that because the syllable *oṃ* is prescribed as the first thing to be uttered during the recitation of the Vedas and Vedānta—thereby enjoining the remembrance of Viṣṇu—and because the *Kapila-smṛti* states, "All Vedic sentences are indeed remembered as the names of Hari," the individual souls (*jīvas*) must therefore be portions (*aṃśas*) of Viṣṇu; we reply: no, because this contradicts the many previously cited Śrutis and Smṛtis, and because [the status of the soul] has been established in the first section of the first chapter (*pūrvādhyāya-prathamapāda*) based on the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Because asserting that the referent of the term *jīva* possesses a portion of all living beings would contradict all the scriptures; for the scripture states, "Viṣṇu alone is the one great being, while the various beings are manifold," implying that it is a deity who enters into the excellent bodies of Viṣṇu and others.
Having entered into inferior bodies such as those of humans, he becomes a human being.

Thus, since Viṣṇu’s status as the individual soul (jīva) is understood even from the Śruti, and because Viṣṇu’s transcendence of the three forms— unlike that of Śiva— is not observed in the perceptible Śrutis; and because Śiva, being the Self of all, is denotable by all words, it would follow that the word "Viṣṇu" is also accepted as a synonym denoting Śiva.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the world-deluding form [of Viṣṇu]— distinguished by the conch, the discus, and the vertical *puṇḍra* marks— to be the Supreme Being, it is stated that individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed portions of Śiva.
In the mantra "Hari Oṃ," because the word "Viṣṇu" is indicated at the outset, the Veda is said to have Viṣṇu as its essence.
That which is delightful when not investigated [is as follows]: "All is indeed Rudra," "Śiva and Umā alone are the ancestors," "The Lord of all sciences," and so forth,
in hundreds of scriptural passages.

"The Veda is Śiva, Śiva is the Veda; the student of the Veda is Sadāśiva; there is no one other than Rudra who recites the Krama-text. Since such Smṛti texts reveal that qualities such as being the soul of all, being the source of all the Vedas, and being the controller of all the Vedas belong to Śiva alone, it is not logical for others to possess them. Therefore, in the sentence "Hari, O... [the reference is to him].

The utterance of Śiva alone— who is denoted by the word "Hari," who is qualified by Viṣṇu, and who is expressed by the syllable *oṃ*— is taught. For in the Smṛti passage, "The vowel which is at the beginning of the Vedas," the Vedic injunction for the utterance of the unqualified *oṃ* alone at the beginning and end of the Vedas is heard.

Beginning with "The syllable *om*— this is all," and concluding with "Thus, he who knows this enters by means of the self into the self— the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), auspicious, non-dual"— the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad establishes, as the primary purport of all Vedānta, that Śiva is the essence of the *praṇava*.
It has been pointed out that [the Lord] is both denoted by the meaning of the *praṇava* and transcends the *praṇava*.
Likewise, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], it is said: "May Brahmā, the overlord of Brahmā, the auspicious Śiva, be mine; Sadāśiva Om.

Here, the letter *a* is Brahmā, the letter *u* is Viṣṇu, the letter *m* is the destroyer of Time (Kāla), and the half-measure (*ardhamātra*) is Paramaśiva; therefore, [one should meditate upon] the syllable *Oṃ*.
Regarding the statement "they call it the *liṅga*," its nature as being composed of the *praṇava* is clearly taught even in the *Sāma-śruti*:
"Brahmā is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than that which is higher than the highest;
may that Supreme Lord, who is higher than the highest, grant that my mind be fixed on auspicious resolve (*śivasaṅkalpa*)."

Thus, based on the evidence of the Śruti, it is indeed appropriate to utter the name of Śiva, who is of the nature of the Praṇava, above that of Viṣṇu; for the Śruti states: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self in the household. Furthermore, because of the scriptural direction: "Obeisance to the Blessed Rudra-Viṣṇu; protect me from death," and because of the Smṛti evidence: "To Śiva in the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu in the form of Śiva," this [mantra] belongs to me.
Since it is heard in the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and in the *Īśvaragītā* that "the supreme form is called Nārāyaṇa," there is no contradiction in Viṣṇu being the body of Śiva.
At the time of her deployment, by the gracious favor of Śiva, the power of Śiva became fourfold:
Bhavānī for enjoyment, Durgā in battle, Kālī in wrath, and Viṣṇu among men.

Thus, because the *Sāma-śākhā* teaches that Viṣṇu is a portion (*aṃśa*) of Pārvatī; because of the list of the one hundred and eight names of Śiva which states, "Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff, the beloved of Viṣṇu";

and because of the statement in the *Skanda-purāṇa*, "I bow to the one whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; I bow to the beloved of Mukunda," [Viṣṇu's] status as the beloved of Śiva is established.

And that state of being beloved by Him has been pointed out. Therefore, it is appropriate that Śiva, whose essence is the *praṇava*, is permeated by the word "Viṣṇu," just as the moon is permeated by its own moonlight. His state of being dear to Viṣṇu is established from hearing such statements from the Purāṇas, including those of Vyāsa and Skanda, which say: "I meditate upon Kālabhairava, who was born from Śiva and Keśava."

[This is] without obstacle. If it is argued that because the state of Śiva as the husband of Gaurī alone is accepted as primary, the utterance of that [name] alone is prescribed at the beginning and end of the Vedas; [we reply: for in both worldly and Vedic usage, such as "the woman [embraces] her lover as if dear," there is an illumination of the inherent nature of women and men—specifically of a man and a woman who belong to another—to be the locus of supreme mutual love.

Just as in sacrifices and other rites, when Indra is invoked, he is designated as "the paramour of Ahalyā" because he was the one who caused her joy even while he was Śacī’s husband; likewise, because Śiva is the object of Viṣṇu’s love,
and because Viṣṇu is a portion (aṃśa) of Gaurī— and since there is no difference between a part and the whole— the word *Hari* is uttered at the beginning and end of the Vedas, [which is] *Oṃ*.
This is correct.
Regarding the objection that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were a part of Brahman— being a single portion of it— the defects residing in the soul would logically belong to Brahman itself, he says:
"But the Supreme is not thus, like light and so forth. (Sūtra 2.1.43)
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. Just as light and so forth [are parts] of the sun, so the individual soul (jīva) is a part of the Supreme Self (paramātman).

For example, just as in the case of entities qualified by "cowness" and so on—such as cows, horses, white, black, and the like—the qualifiers such as "cowness" are their parts; or just as for an embodied being such as a god or a human, the body is a part. In that same way [the soul is a part of the Self].
Being a part (*aṃśatva*) consists in being a single portion of a single entity. Indeed, the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of a single qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is precisely a part.
Accordingly, discerning people designate a qualified entity by saying, "this is the qualifying part" and "this is the qualified part.
Even though the qualifier and the qualified stand in the relation of part and whole, a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is observed. Thus...

The relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), as well as their difference in essential nature (*svabhāva-bheda*), is thus established; this is expressed by the statement, "The Supreme is not like this. Just as the individual soul is of such a nature, the Supreme is not of that same nature; for indeed, just as light is of a different nature from the luminous object, so too [is the Supreme] from that which stands in the place of light.
The meaning is that Śiva, as the possessor of parts (*aṃśin*), is distinct from his own part (*svāṃśa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and is even a different entity (*arthāntarabhūta*).

Thus, designations of difference proceed by relying on the distinction in essential nature (*svabhāvavailakṣaṇya*) between the individual soul and the Supreme caused by the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyatva*). However, designations of non-difference [apply] to qualifiers that are incapable of existing independently.

They are established as primary by relying on their extension to the substantive (the inner self). In such passages as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman," just like the words "That" and "Brahman," the words "this" and "Self" also refer to the Inner Controller of the individual soul (*jīvāntaryāmī*).
He also cites a *smṛti* [text] regarding the absence of suffering in the Lord despite the suffering of the individual soul:
And they remember it as well. || 44 ||
In that regard, that which is the Supreme Self is remembered as the Truth, devoid of qualities;
it is not smeared by fruits [of action], just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
He who is the other, whose self is karma, is joined with both liberation and bondage.
That this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is the body of the God of gods—
beings do not know this truth because of the weight of their sins.
Thus, through the relationship of light and its possessor, and through the relationship of power and its possessor, the state of part and whole exists between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—
just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads abroad,
so too does this entire universe constitute the power of the Supreme Brahman.

The meaning is that they remember the Lord’s state of being free from suffering despite the suffering of living beings. By the word "ca" (and), the scriptural passage beginning with "One of them eats the sweet fruit of the pippala tree, while the other looks on without eating" is indicated.
Thus, since being a portion of Brahman, being impelled by Brahman, and possessing knowledge are common to all, [the distinction remains].

Anticipating the objection as to how the scriptures can justify the permission for some to study the Vedas and reflect upon their meaning while excluding others, and likewise the permission for some to see or touch [the scriptures] while excluding others, he says:
The granting of permission and the avoidance [of certain acts] are like [the rules regarding] light and so forth in relation to the body. || 45 ||

Although all beings possess a single uniform nature by virtue of being portions of Brahman and so forth, they are nevertheless distinguished as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the like— just as fire, for example, despite its uniform nature as fire, is brought from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) but avoided when coming from a cremation ground; and just as food and other things are permitted for a *śrotriya* but forbidden for one who has been accused of a crime.
It is answered:

"But even so, since the conscious agent is one across all bodies, one might object that the dharma and other qualities which are the causes of action, delimited by Devadatta’s body, would not be known by means of Yajñadatta’s body. Anticipating this, he says:
And because there is no continuity, there is no confusion [of actions and their results]. || 46 ||

Even though the individual souls (*jīvas*) possess a uniform nature by virtue of being portions of Brahman and so forth, there is no confusion of experiences because they are mutually distinct and, due to their atomic dimension (*aṇutva*), are separate in each body. Furthermore, the absence of confusion of experiences among the *jīvas* has been stated both in the doctrine that the *jīva* is the illusory Brahman (*bhrāntabrahmajīvavāda*) and in the doctrine that the *jīva* is Brahman as conditioned (*upahitabrahmajīvavāda*).

Furthermore, there is no confusion of the attributes of relation and so forth between the limited self of Devadatta, who is the agent, and the continuity of Yajñadatta’s body; for even among those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who have attained knowledge of Brahman,

until the final liberation of the disembodied state (*videhamukti*), the individual souls (*jīva*), being atomic in nature, remain distinct due to the differences in their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body.

Because [the experience] is delimited, there is no confusion. Even though there exists the enjoyment of *prārabdha* karma consisting of pleasure and pain—just like a bound individual soul (*baddhajīva*)—there is no commingling [of experiences], and through the excellence of the knowledge of Śiva, a distinction from the pure bound souls of transmigratory existence is possible.
As it is said in the Śivāgama:
This triad of living beings is traditionally taught through the divisions of the bound, the pure, and so forth;
[the first] being devoid of initiation from a guru and lacking devotion to Śiva.
But one who possesses the conceit of being his own agent is called a bound soul (paśu);
however, having received the supreme initiation from a Guru, he becomes endowed with the three types of service (kaiṅkarya).
Endowed with excellent qualities such as peace and the like, desiring liberation, free from passion,
possessing an intellect dependent on Śiva, and being a devotee— he is known as the pure soul (śuddhajīva).
Endowed with the bliss of the majesty of Śiva-yoga and Śiva-knowledge,
like a pure camphor lamp placed in the midst of a fierce sun,
[he dwells] in the form of Śiva, the supreme form, which possesses the radiance of ten million suns.
But one whose mental fluctuations have dissolved is known as a liberated soul (muktajīva).
"One who is free from passion and hatred is called a *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living)"—thus it has been clearly taught.

Now, one might object: even in the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is an illusory Brahman, the regulation of experience and so forth are possible due to the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Anticipating the objection that [things] do not arise from themselves, he says: "And it is merely an appearance. (47)

For that whose nature consists solely of the manifestation of an indivisible single essence, the cause for establishing the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) through the concealment of its own nature is merely an appearance (ābhāsa). It has already been established that for that whose sole nature is light, the concealment of light is nothing other than the destruction of light. Alternatively, the reading may be "ābhāsa eva" (merely an appearance).

If that were the case, the reasons would be fallacious; furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "By the word 'and' [the Self], He implies a separate self," "The Impeller and the Impelled," "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Unlord," and "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit. For [this distinction] exists only when there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi) imagined through ignorance (avidyā).
Since it is admitted that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) conditioned by all adjuncts (*upādhi*) is one, the confusion of experience remains exactly as it was.

Furthermore, if it is accepted that individual souls (*jīva*) are reflections in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then because the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is never observed to exist in the same place, [the two would not be found together]. [As it is said: "The two have entered the cave, in the highest supreme abode."

Furthermore, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "The two who have entered the cave" (*guhāṃ praviṣṭāv ātmānau*) and the specific *Guha-adhikaraṇa* of the Sūtras, that [position] is charming only so long as it is not critically examined. Even in the doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman conditioned by a real limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), when there is a distinction between limiting adjuncts...
Anticipating the objection that "the arrangement will come about through the power of beginningless unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which serves as the cause," he says:
|| 93 || "Because there is no restriction regarding the unseen. || 48 ||

Furthermore, since even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which serves as the cause for the succession of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), would have no regulating cause by virtue of residing in the very nature of Brahman, there would be total lack of order; moreover, through the connection with these limiting adjuncts and the unseen forces,
the destruction of the very nature of Brahman would be possible.

Furthermore, according to the Advaita view, since all individual souls (*jīvas*) are omnipresent and thus exist within their own respective bodies which serve as their reflections, there would be no restriction regarding *adṛṣṭa*—that is, due to the absence of a restrictive rule for merits and demerits (*puṇya-pāpa*). Consequently, there could be no established order such that some experience poverty while others enjoy sovereignty. Therefore, the souls must be atomic (*aṇu*).
One must accept both plurality and the inherent distinctness of each individual body.

[Objection: But surely, intentions and the like—such as "I shall attain this fruit," "I shall take this," "I shall do this," and "I shall not do this"—being restricted to each individual self, will serve as the causes for the observed regularity in their respective applications.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And likewise in the case of intentions and so forth. (49)

Even in the case of intentions (*abhisandhi*) and so forth, which are accomplished through the conjunction of the mind common to passion, hatred, and the like, there would likewise be no such restriction;
consequently, there would be no established rule that some living beings possess passion while others possess hatred.
Therefore, even regarding intentions and the rest, which serve as visible causes, [the same principle applies] as has been stated.

The meaning is that there is no fixed rule regarding the cause [of action]. Now, since the scriptures—such as "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," and so forth—declare the absence of independence in living beings (jīvas), it follows that the Lord alone is the enjoyer of the fruits of the merit and demerit performed by the jīvas.
If it is argued that his role as the impeller is dependent upon karma and that karma is beginningless, then [the conclusion remains] because of their lack of independence.

If it is argued that the status of being the enjoyer of the fruits of both prescribed and prohibited actions belongs only to the other [the individual soul] because it is the impeller of both karma and the living being (jīva), we say no—for although the individual souls lack omniscience like the Lord, they do not possess insentience like jars or cloths since they are objects of knowledge;
and although they are dependent on the Lord like a king’s servant, their agency in performing actions according to their own will is possible. Therefore, it is they alone [who are the enjoyers].

The state of being the enjoyer of the fruits of merit and demerit is unavoidable; for there are hundreds of scriptural passages such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," "The world acquired through karma perishes," "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brāhmaṇa should attain detachment," and "Speak the truth, practice dharma."
A limited agent and a limited knower, possessing a bound body from time immemorial—
the creation beginning from the act of observation up to the entry [into the body] is fashioned by the Lord;
the creation of the phenomenal world of waking and so forth is fashioned by the individual soul (jīva).

The agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) is also clearly taught in such Smṛtis. Furthermore, even though the activities of sentient beings— such as beasts, birds, wild animals, insects, and so forth— are possible through their being permeated by the light of the Sun, this does not entail a loss of their agency.

Similarly, even though God is the controller, there is no contradiction in the fact that individual souls possess some degree of agency by virtue of their being conscious entities. Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of contradicting the declarations of the previously cited scriptural texts. Therefore, there is no contradiction between the scriptural passages that prescribe agency for both the individual soul and the Lord.

Anticipating the objection that—since individual souls (jīvas) are limited by virtue of being portions (aṃśas) of Brahman, and since there is non-difference between a part and the whole—the systematic distribution of pleasure and pain for that [Brahman] alone would be established—he says:
"If it be argued that [the distinction is possible] due to the difference in locations, we say no, because of their inclusion within [the one]. (Sūtra 2.3.50)
Even though the nature of Brahman is one and indivisible, it is connected with various kinds of limiting adjuncts (upādhis);

thus, the state of confusion remains exactly as before. Even if the connection were through distinct spatial locations, since every location would be a part of Brahman, the suffering resulting from the connection with each respective location would belong to Brahman itself.

Therefore, the doctrine that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman under the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is indeed charming only so long as it is not critically examined; for this contradicts the scriptural injunction, "From which these beings are born," and "Two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower,
the Lord and the Unlord," as well as the sūtra beginning with "Because of the impossibility of origination" (BS 2.3.9), which was already established by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa.

Because of the teaching that individual souls (*jīvas*) are unborn, and because of the teaching that they are parts of Brahman through such passages as "A part [of Me], on account of the various designations," etc., those souls who have entered into Brahman at the time of dissolution— being non-imagined and distinct by their very nature— are designated as "parts of Brahman" merely by virtue of their re-manifestation at the time of creation.

Because of the acceptance [of the Self] expressed by "Thou art," the relationship of part and whole— as between a limb and its possessor— is not tenable. Just as in the world, it is taught that the son is a part of one's own self— according to the saying, "The Self indeed is the name of the son"— when a son is born, produced as a thread running through the mother’s womb in a white form that has entered the bodies of men bound by various prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Likewise, in our view, since it is accepted that during dissolution (pralaya) the individual soul (jīva), having emerged from Brahman, is indeed a portion (aṃśa) of Him by virtue of being external to Him, there is no contradiction with the Śruti and Sūtra passages teaching [the soul's] being produced or unproduced. Therefore, the soul's status as an enjoyer, established by such Śruti texts as "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit," is not contradictory. For this very reason, [it exists] in a specific location...

By virtue of the non-difference between the part and the whole, the doctrine that the Supreme Śiva, as Brahman, is the experiencer of pleasure and pain because individual souls (*jīva*) are His parts, has been refuted. This is because, according to Vedic injunctions such as "He entered into the innermost of the inner," "Having entered within, He is the ruler of people," and "The Lord of all sciences," [Brahman exists] as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the individual souls.

Because it is accepted that [the Lord] is the controller of the individual soul (jīva), it is determined that the experience of the desired and undesired fruits resulting from the karma performed by the individual soul does not belong to the Lord.
Thus concludes the work composed by the venerable Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpādācārya Svāmī, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics.

In the Śrīkarabhāṣya, which elucidates the meaning of the Vaiyāsika Brahmamīmāṃsā Sūtras that establish the doctrine of Viśeṣādvaita, this is the second chapter titled "The Refutation of Contradictions."
The third chapter, consisting of fifty sūtras and divided into thirteen sections beginning with "viyat," is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter of the second book in the Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya.
The section concerning the vital breath as the offspring. || 1 ||

In the first quarter (pāda), having resolved the mutual contradiction between the scriptural passages that enjoin the produced nature and the unproduced nature of the entire group of five elements beginning with ether— which are effects of Brahman— it is established that although the individual soul (*jīva*) is an effect of Brahman, it is by its very nature unproduced due to its consciousness, possesses innate difference, and has that [consciousness] as its essential nature.
Since its status as a *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body) is established by implication, its investigation is conducted here in the final section (*caramapāda*).

For, from such passages as "Brahman has space as its body, whose self is truth, who delights in the vital breaths, and whose bliss is the mind," it is understood that Śiva, who is Brahman, possesses a natural *liṅga-śarīra* consisting of mind and vital breath; and this applies to individual souls (*jīva*) as well.

It is beyond dispute that [the soul] possesses a produced nature characterized by the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra). Therefore, in response to the doubt that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—like that of a river and the ocean—is in no way possible except through the destruction of the subtle body, he says:
"And likewise the vital breaths" (tathā prāṇāḥ). || 96 || 1 ||

Just as the five great elements (pañcamahābhūtāni) are born from Brahman, so too is it established that the vital breaths and the sense organs have Brahman as their cause, because of such scriptural passages as, "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs. In this section (pāda) as well, regarding the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a mutual [contradiction] among the scriptures...

It should be understood that, according to the opponent's position (*siddhānta*), the consistency of Brahman is not established because of contradiction and the resulting lack of authority [in the texts]; whereas, according to our own position, the consistency is established because they possess authority through non-contradiction. In the section concerning the origin of the five great elements—beginning with "From the Self, space was produced"—there is no mention of the origin of the vital breaths, sense organs, and so forth; for these sages were at the beginning...

Regarding the statement, "These beings are indeed the ṛṣis," and "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the ṛṣis," and so forth—the existence of the vital breaths and the sense organs prior to creation is observed; therefore, their non-produced nature (ajanyatva) is indicated beyond doubt. However, in passages such as "From this [Brahman] the vital breath is born," the vital breaths and other elements appear to be effects of Brahman. Therefore, is the production of the vital breaths and so forth logical or not?
This is what is being considered: Is there a contradiction due to the absence of a deciding factor? The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says "just like the individual soul":

just as the individual soul is not produced, so too the sense organs are not produced; just as the scriptural statement regarding the production of the soul is figurative, so it is understood that the scriptural statement regarding the production of the sense organs is also figurative.

Likewise, the phrase "the vital breaths" (prāṇāḥ) extends the same designation to the vital breath itself. What, then, is the scriptural authority for this? In the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," they ask, "What was there then? [The reply is: "In the beginning, those sages (ṛṣis) were indeed the existent. They ask, "Who are those sages? [The reply is: "The vital breaths are indeed the sages.
Thus, the existence of the sense organs prior to the creation of the world is heard in scripture through the word "vital breath."

Because of the plural number, it is determined that these are indeed the sense organs (*indriya*). Nor can this scriptural passage be interpreted as referring to their long-term endurance—like the passage, "The wind and the intermediate space, this is the immortal; this deity, namely the wind, does not set"—because of the statement, "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*).

Because it is heard that the vital breaths (prāṇas) remain even at the time of the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world; and those passages speaking of their origination are to be interpreted like those speaking of the origination of the individual soul (jīva). This being the position reached, it is replied: "So also the vital breaths."

The vital breaths (prāṇas) arise in the same manner as ether and the other elements. Why? Because in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," "Rudra is one alone; he does not stand for a second," and "When there was darkness, Śiva alone existed," the persistence of Śiva alone prior to creation is determined; and because the origin of the senses is heard [in scripture] in the statement, "From Him is born the vital breath."

Because an antecedent state is impossible; nor can the theories regarding the production of the sense organs be assimilated to the theory of the production of the Self, for we observe scriptural texts that negate the production of the Self and others that declare its eternity. Even in the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is the Supreme Self alone, denoted by the word *prāṇa*, that is indicated. [This is so] because of the text: "All these beings..."
"They enter into breath alone and emerge from breath alone"— since the word "prāṇa" is well-known to refer to the Supreme Self,
this was elaborated upon in various ways in the section titled *Prāṇas tathānugamāt* (Sūtra 1.1.28). Furthermore,
the word "ṛṣi" in the phrase "The ṛṣis are indeed the vital breaths" is appropriately applied to Śiva, the omniscient one.
He has not been born among insentient sense-organs;
for it is seen in the *Śvetāśvatara* that "Rudra, the great seer, is prior to and superior to all," and in the *Taittirīya* that "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all."
In response to the doubt as to how the scriptural statement using the plural number, "The vital breaths are the seers" (*ṛṣayaḥ prāṇāḥ*), is to be understood, he says:
"Because a figurative sense is impossible, and because of the prior mention of that [the one]. (Sūtra 2.4.9).

The plural form [of the word *rudra*] is figurative (*gauṇī*), because it is impossible for that very Supreme Self, Śiva, to have multiple referents; for we observe that scripture teaches His abiding in that state prior to creation. Furthermore: "Obeisance to the Rudras who are on earth, those who are in the intermediate space, and those who are in heaven; their food is the wind, and the rain is their pressing-stone—to them, ten..."

"Ten to the east, ten to the south, ten to the west, ten to the north, and ten upward—to them I bow; may they be gracious to us. Him whom we hate and him who hates us, him I deliver into your power. Thus, in the Śatarudrīya, [it is taught] that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses a playful and auspicious form (*līlā-maṅgala-vigraha*) which exists within the elements such as earth and in the directions such as the east.

There is no stain of doubt because the plurality [of the elements] is established; for in various passages such as "From this, the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," the origin of those five great elements and the sense organs, beginning with the vital breath, is heard, and thus the origin of the sense organs is indeed primary. In a single sentence, a single word may in some instances be secondary.

The sense is that, in some cases, the primacy [of the individual soul] would be impossible. If the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) were eternal, there could be no "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one," as established by such scriptural passages as: "Venerable sir, when one thing is known, all this becomes known.
This is because [the knowledge of all] occurs through the knowledge of Brahman in its causal form.

For the purpose of establishing the proposition that all cognitions have the form of effects, it is proven that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the sense organs (*indriyas*) are also produced from Brahman;
as stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*) and "It created fire" (*tat tejo 'sṛjata*), and so forth.

In response to the doubt that these [elements] might arise from something else, he states— on the basis of their origination being observed in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad— that their being produced from Brahman is indeed primary:
"Because speech is preceded by that" (Sūtra 3).

The elements of fire (*tejas*), water (*ap*), and food (*anna*)—which constitute the nature of Brahman—are denoted by that word. Since it is taught through the passage, "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire," that speech, together with breath and mind, is established as having the nature of fire, water, and food; thus, the scriptural teaching of their origin is demonstrated. Therefore, because of the existence of such scriptural teachings of origin, [Brahman is the cause] of creation.
Because the sense organs did not exist previously, it is stated that they, like the five great elements, are produced and impermanent;

therefore, there is no contradiction with the Śruti texts. For in the Śruti passage, "In the beginning this was indeed unmanifest; it became manifest through name and form," there is the very absence of the creation of ether and so forth, which are the objects of speech consisting of name and form.

Because of the scriptural teaching and because there is an absence of functions such as the organ of speech at that time, and because hundreds of Śrutis— such as "When [there was] darkness, Śiva alone was the absolute"— declare that prior to creation Śiva abides as pure essence alone, the status of being produced, as stated in Śrutis such as "From this, the vital breath (prāṇa) is born," is non-figurative for the vital breath and other faculties. Or rather, [this applies] even to the state of liberation.

The fifteen *kalās*— namely, *karma*, *vairāgya*, *guru*, *careśvaratva*, *śeṣatva*, *kaiṅkarya*, *pāratantrya*, *bhūtadayā*, *anugraha*, *jñāna*, *aiśvarya*, *tapaḥ*, *śakti*, *bala*, and *vīrya*— have dissolved into *videhamukti*.
