All the presiding deities have likewise returned into their respective source-deities (*pratidevatā*).
The karmas and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

As it is said in the Śruti: "Just as rivers [merge into the ocean], he who knows the Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; no one ignorant of Brahman is born in his lineage; he crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil; released from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. Because this passage teaches that in the liberation of *sāyujya* (union), there is the attainment of the reality of Śiva preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), like rivers merging into the sea.

Because of the non-existence of a subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), he is therefore not a non-Vedic person. [This is understood] by means of the passage: "Brahman has space as its body, whose self is truth, who delights in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and whose bliss is in the mind. Here, "delighting in the vital breaths" (*prāṇārāma*) means that this Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, sports everywhere among the vital breaths; "whose bliss is in the mind" (*mana-ānanda*) refers to one for whom bliss resides in the mind.

Because He does not depend on external sense organs—which are transformations of *prakṛti* produced by karma consisting of the three *guṇas*—but rather possesses a divine, auspicious form that is His very nature of true knowledge and bliss, the eternity of that *liṅga-śarīra* is unavoidable. [As it is said: "With steady limbs, He of many forms is formidable; may He be auspicious with His ears."
"The one who praises with steady limbs and bodies"— the venerable Śruti itself is the authority in this matter. Therefore,

it should be understood that only the subtle bodies (liṅga-śarīra) of living beings— which are composed of the elements and their derivatives, produced by karma, and characterized by the nature of the asuras— are subject to origination and dissolution even in the state of liberation.
The Section on the Seven Courses of Existence. 2.

Thus, having established that the individual soul (jīva) and the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) are born from Brahman, in response to the inquiry as to what those principles qualified by them are, he describes the nature of their constituent bodies and the principles qualified by them in another section:
And because the sevenfold course has been specifically distinguished, the hands and other [limbs] remain [fixed]; therefore, it is not thus.

If it is argued that there are only seven sense organs because the Śruti states, "From him the seven senses and the seven breaths arise," and because the departure for the next world is specified [in that context], and thus the sense organs are only seven—namely, the five cognitive organs beginning with hearing, the single organ of speech, and the single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—[the reply is: "But the hands and so forth exist; therefore..."
The hands and other limbs are not like this—the hands, feet, anus, and genitals remain in the body along with the living soul as long as it remains;
when the soul has gone to another world, they go to that other world with it.
As stated in the Śruti: "When he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the vital functions (prāṇas) depart after it."

Because it is heard in scripture that all the sense organs go to the next world along with the individual soul (*jīva*), for this reason it is not the case that there are only seven sense organs; rather, the meaning is that there are eleven sense organs. Furthermore, the single internal organ is called "mind" (*manas*) because its nature is doubt, and "intellect" (*buddhi*) because its nature is ascertainment.

Because of the traditional teaching that "the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises from the principle of self-conceit (abhimāna-tattva)" and that "the mind (citta) consists of memory," there is no excess in the number [of principles]. It is heard in scripture that "from him the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) arise," referring to the seven sense organs. In some places, eight are mentioned:
"eight graspers (grahas) and eight over-graspers (atigrahas)," where the sense organs are the graspers that bind the person like a sacrificial animal.

The meaning is that "excessive graspings" (*atigrahas*) refer to objects such as the senses, because they draw them away through the arising of passion and so forth. In the passage, "There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in the head and two downward ones," the anus and the generative organ are included with speech, making nine;

in the passage, "There are indeed nine vital breaths in a person, and the navel is the tenth," there are ten; and in the passage, "There are indeed ten vital breaths in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh," the self is the eleventh.

Thus, in some places thirteen organs are heard of, while in others eleven; regarding this, it is considered whether those organs might indeed be only seven. When there is such a conflict of scriptural statements (*śrutivipratipatti*), a doubt arises: what is the conclusion? That they are seven. Why? Because of the specific qualification of their movement in the passage: "These seven worlds in which they move."

"Movement" (gati) refers to the wandering through the worlds together with the living being as it is born and as it dies; therefore, only seven are mentioned. [The text says: "These seven worlds, in which move the vital breaths (prāṇas) that dwell in the cave and are deposited—seven and seven. This repetition is intended to refer to the distinction between different persons. And because they are specifically qualified, those vital breaths possess movement by their very nature.
"When the five senses, together with the mind, come to rest, and the intellect no longer stirs—that, they say, is the supreme goal.
Thus, the supreme goal is the departure for the sake of liberation, having abandoned wandering within the body; in this way, [it occurs] together with the individual soul (*jīva*).
Because only seven [organs] are heard of as undergoing birth and death, and because they are specifically qualified as "the knowers" (*jñāninaḥ*) in the state of yoga,
the instruments of the individual soul (*jīva*) are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose, mind, and intellect—
these seven indeed are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) located in the head, while two are directed downwards, and so forth.

Since there is no mention of speech, hands, feet, anus, or the organs of evacuation and movement in the passages defining the fourteen vital breaths (*prāṇas*), it follows that the designation "vital breath" applied to them is merely figurative, based solely on their providing a very slight assistance to the individual soul (*jīva*). To this, we reply as follows.

But since [the hand and so forth] exist, it is not thus. There are not seven sense organs, but rather eleven, because the hand and others also serve as instruments for the experience of the living being (jīva) who resides in the body, and because their functions are distinct. For a difference in function is indeed observed in the case of the hands and so forth, just as in the case of the ears and other senses—namely, grasping and so on. Therefore, they certainly exist. Thus, it is not the case that "the hands and others do not [exist]."

The meaning is that one should not think [of them] as being thus [separate]. It is the mind alone that, through its distinct functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and reflection (*cintā*), is designated by the terms *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *citta*. Thus, there are eleven faculties.
Therefore, in the statement, "These ten are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh," the word *ātman* denotes the mind.
The eleven faculties and the five objects of the faculties are said to be taijasa;
the ten deities are said to be vaikārika.
"And here, the mind is the eleventh.

Thus, the number of sense-faculties established by the Śrutis and Smṛtis is fixed. Assertions of a higher number are intended to refer to the different modifications of the mind, while designations of a lower number occur in various contexts [due to specific purposes].

They are impelled by specific effects such as the intended act of going and so forth. Furthermore, the word "tu" (but) here serves to exclude the possibility of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) being seven; for, through the passage beginning with "The hand, indeed, is a grasper," the vital breaths are heard of as distinct from the hands and other limbs. Thus, while the number seven might be possible, [the text establishes] that they are more than seven.

Even if there were a difference [in number] or if they were established as seven, the number seven could be included within the number eleven residing in the sense organs, since it is possible for a smaller number to be included within a larger number; therefore, one should not think thus. The meaning of the Sūtra is that there are exactly seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*).

Although one hears of a list numbering thirteen— consisting of the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the single mind, while setting aside the eleven organs— and including the heart, ego, vital breath (prāṇa), and so forth; nevertheless,

Since these two are merely distinctions within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they do not result in an increase in the total number; thus, the conclusion that there are eleven sense organs (*indriya*) is beyond reproach. As for the statement "there are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head," the designation of "seven" does not establish them as sense organs;

rather, through the teaching of the "breaths," it indicates that those same four sense organs are counted as seven solely on account of their different locations. Therefore, [the number remains eleven].

There is no contradiction with reality. The statement, "Indeed, there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in a person, and the navel is the tenth," intends the body in its human form and does not intend the [actual] vital breaths; thus, the absence of contradiction is established.
Now, one might object that the preceding and subsequent explanations of this Sūtra are inconsistent with the passage, "Seven vital breaths come forth..."

Because the sevenfold nature of the nose, tongue, eye, ear, skin, mind, and speech is understood; because they are specifically qualified as "those located in the head"; because the particle *ca* (and) in the Sūtra would be inappropriate due to the lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) between these two reasons; and because of the restrictive enumeration: "Those which are indeed the seven located in the head are the prāṇas, and not others. For this very reason...
If it is argued that the explanation of the subsequent sentence is also inconsistent, then we shall explain the pair of preceding and subsequent sentences otherwise:
at the time of death, those who accompany [the deceased] possess the status of sense organs (indriya) precisely because they serve as the instruments for experience; and thus they...

Because of the scriptural statement that "all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) depart following the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*)," and because it is heard that only the seven [breaths] beginning with the sense of smell depart along with the individual soul (*jīva*), there are only seven senses. If it is objected: "Since the word 'all' is heard, how can it be said that only seven are heard to depart?"—to this he replies by means of a qualification: [The text continues: "But those seven which have the mind as the eighth... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7). By this specific qualification, it is established that the departure of the seven alone is intended. Therefore, the number of senses is seven. Furthermore, the term "vital breaths" (*prāṇas*) here refers to the senses, because they are the instruments of the vital breath; for the senses are so called because they are the channels through which the vital breath functions. Thus, the conclusion is that the senses are seven. Alternatively, one might argue that since the word "all" is used, all the senses must depart. To this, he says: "But those seven which have the mind as the eighth... This shows that the word "all" is used in a restricted sense, referring only to those seven which have the mind as the eighth. Therefore, the senses are indeed seven. Moreover, the word "vital breaths" (*prāṇas*) is applied to the senses because they are the instruments of the vital breath; the senses are designated as such because they are the pathways for the activity of the vital breath. Consequently, the number of senses is seven. Or again, the word "all" may be understood as referring to the totality of the senses belonging to the body, whereas the mention of the "seven" refers specifically to the senses of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, the number of senses is seven. "It becomes one; then it does not see, does not smell, does not sleep, does not speak, does not hear, does not think, and does not touch"—so they say. Furthermore, because only the seven natural [organs] beginning with sight are specifically mentioned, the word "all" refers only to those natural ones, just as in the expression "all Brāhmaṇas should be fed," the word "all" [refers only to the invited Brāhmaṇas].

The phrase "just as [the case] of the uninvited Brahmins" is intended to dispel such a doubt. However, in that state where the eye is the locus of the agent, that very person is denoted by the term *cākṣuṣa* (the visual one). When the person exists having abandoned the pervasion of objects such as form and so forth, he becomes a knower of name and form. [He is] one [and the same] in the heart and in the eye.

The meaning of the scriptural passage is that people say, "He does not see those standing at his side. However, the meaning of the subsequent statement is that even the hands and other limbs, in addition to the seven [organs], are heard of as being agents of bondage. Through such passages as "The hand, indeed, is a grasper," the nature of grasping and binding attributed to the hands and so forth would not be possible without their accompanying the soul. All [of them...].

Furthermore, because of the specific scriptural statement that "the vital breaths (prāṇas) depart," and because it is heard that all the sense organs (indriyas) depart, the vital breaths are eleven in number and possess the quality of departing. Nor does the word "all" refer here merely to the seven vital breaths mentioned in the context; rather, the direct scriptural statement (śruti) is more authoritative than the contextual indication (prakaraṇa).

The term "all" refers to those who are the subject of the action. In the statement "All Brāhmaṇas are to be fed," since it is impossible to feed every single Brāhmaṇa, the word "all" is understood to refer to those Brāhmaṇas who have been invited; this is pointed out as being like the previous case. Therefore, it is established that there are exactly eleven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) that depart.
The Section on the Atomicity of the Vital Breath (Prāṇa) || 3 ||

Now, an objection is raised: "The departure (utkrānti) of the sense organs is not possible, because they are all-pervading (vibhu) due to being produced from the undivided ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). In response to this objection, he provides a refutation by means of another topical section: || 100 || "And they are atomic (aṇavaḥ). || 5 ||

Because the Śruti declares that "these vital breaths (prāṇas) are atomic and the sense organs (indriyas) are limited," there is the designation of atomicity for the prāṇas and indriyas; yet, because of the scriptural hearing of their infinity in the passage, "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite," there is [the claim of] all-pervasiveness (vibhutva). Therefore, a doubt arises as to whether they are atomic or all-pervasive. It is not so.
If it is argued that the minuteness of the sense organs is established, and that since the sense organ of touch located in the body would otherwise be incapable of perceiving cold,

heat, softness, and other tactile qualities throughout the entire body— and because this would contradict the previously cited scriptural texts— it is therefore logical that they are all-pervasive (vibhu), we reply as follows:

"And they are atomic by nature. Although the sense organs are atomic, the word "and" (ca) indicates that they remain atomic even in their state as effects. According to the principle that "the self conjoins with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object; from this, perception arises," although all the sense organs are subtle, their pervasiveness is not understood because of their contact with objects.

Therefore, there is a contradiction with scripture. If the sense organs were merely all-pervasive, then the sight and touch of Viśveśvara residing in Kāśī would be possible even for those dwelling on the Setu.
Furthermore, this is because of scriptural statements regarding their departure and so forth, such as: "When the prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after it."
Because they are described as being limited in size; because they are not perceived by bystanders during their departure from the body and other such states;
because the sense organs, such as the ear, lack the capacity to perceive sounds located in distant places;
and because of the experience of rapid movement toward objects such as sound, according to the analogy of a needle passing through the petals of a lotus.

It is determined that the sense organs of living beings are indeed minute. As for the scriptural mention of their infinity, as in the passage, "Now, he who meditates upon those [prāṇas] as infinite," this is intended to refer to the great abundance of effects belonging to the objects of meditation, which serve as qualifiers of the prāṇas to be meditated upon.

In response to the objection that even in those scriptural passages which describe the soul’s activity of entering and exiting many bodies, there is also instruction regarding the departure of the sense organs, and thus the statement prescribing the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as primary is justified, he says:
And he is the most excellent. || 6 ||

In the dialogue concerning the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*), beginning with "When the principal breath departs, all the vital breaths depart," the *mukhyaprāṇa* (the chief vital breath) is determined to be preeminent as the cause of the body's maintenance and as the substratum of all the sense organs.
Furthermore, because the activity of the *prāṇa*-wind is observed even when all other senses have ceased during deep sleep, [it arises] from this [breath].

Furthermore, because the Śruti states "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*) and shows that the vital breath arises even before all the sense organs, they say that the mind is a sign within those vital breaths; and because the Śruti indicates that the mind, which is the support of all the sense organs, also has the vital breath as its support, it is stated in the Smṛti as well: "The mind is the lord of the senses, but the vital air (*māruta*) is the lord of the mind."

Furthermore, since the wind (*māruta*), which is of the nature of *prāṇa*, is understood to possess supreme preeminence, it is unavoidable that *prāṇa* is superior even to the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in the injunction regarding the primacy of the departure of *prāṇa*.
Now, [one might object]: "In the passage, 'That One breathed, windless, by its own power (*svadhayā*) at the time of dissolution,' [it is shown that]... [the One is the support of all].

If it is argued that because the existence of *prāṇa* is heard [in scripture], the hearing of its birth in the passage "from this, *prāṇa* is born" must be figurative—just like the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*)—we say no; for this would contradict the scriptural determination of Śiva’s existence prior to creation in such passages as "He is neither existent nor non-existent, He is Śiva alone. Therefore, in the passage "from this, *prāṇa* is born," [the birth] of *prāṇa*...

Because its origination is heard to be similar to that of the earth and other elements, and because there is no denial of its origination; and because in the passage "It breathed, windless" (*ānīd avātam*),
it is not the preeminent vital breath (*prāṇa*) that is intended to be spoken of, but rather the existence of the one Supreme Śiva-Brahman alone is declared—
since it is heard right there that "it was windless" (*avāta*)— and because the same reasoning applies as in the preceding case.
It is established that the formulation of a separate *yoga* (sūtra) is for the sake of the subsequent inquiry. Thus ends the section concerning the activity of air (*vāyu*). 4.

Even though the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the most excellent of all, there may arise the doubt that it is either the air (*vāyu*) itself or the activity of touch residing therein that constitutes its true nature; this doubt he refutes by means of another section:
"It is neither air nor activity, because of the separate instruction. (Sūtra 7)

"Vāyu" (wind) and "kriyā" (activity) constitute "vāyukriye"; [the latter] does not mean the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, because of this separate instruction—in the Śruti passage, "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; ether, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe"—there is a separate designation of the origin of wind and the vital breath, and thus they are not one and the same.
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is as follows:

Regarding this preeminent Prāṇa, is it merely the air that is the second among the great elements (mahābhūta), or is it its activity in the form of vibration, or is it the air itself having attained some particular state? On this point of doubt, the initial position (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is simply air; for that which is Prāṇa...

Because of the designation "the wind" (*vāyu*), or because the status of being *prāṇa* is not well-known for mere wind, and because the word *prāṇa* is well-established in reference to the functions of wind such as inhalation and exhalation;
furthermore, in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad], having begun with "One should meditate on Brahman as the mind" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*), [it describes] the Brahman whose form is the mind...

If it is argued that, because speech, hand, eye, and ear constitute the four feet, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the fourth foot of Brahman— and that "by means of the wind as its light, it shines and heats"— wherein "shines" means it becomes manifest and "heats" means it exerts itself in its own activity— this is so because, by describing the vital breath as distinct from the wind, a state of differentiation is established.
Since those two scriptural passages are mutually contradictory, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) must be the activity of the sense organs. To this we reply:

the meaning is that *prāṇa* is neither the activity of air, nor air itself, nor the activity of the sense organs. If it is argued that *prāṇa* is distinct from the activity of the sense organs because it is taught separately from them, we say no; for there is no difference between a function (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses the function (*vṛttimat*).
If it is asked how the contradiction with the scriptural statement, "That which is prāṇa is vāyu," is to be resolved, it is replied:
it is indeed the Great Vāyu itself, existing in the form of the fivefold self such as prāṇa and so forth, that is called "prāṇa. Thus, [it is] a modification—
They explain:

moreover, because of the separate designation of air and breath from that very same source in the passage, "From this [Self] is born space, air," breath is not merely the activity of air. For the activity of fire and the other elements is not designated separately from them.

It is taught as a substance. However, the statement "that which is prāṇa is vāyu" is for the purpose of making it known that prāṇa is merely vāyu having reached a different state, and not a distinct principle (*tattva*) like fire (*tejas*) and so forth. Furthermore, since prāṇa vibrates even during inhalation and exhalation, the conventional usage of the word *prāṇa* is established for a substance possessing action, and not for action alone. This is proven.

Is this prāṇa, being a modification of air, a distinct element like fire, or—given the separate designation of prāṇa and air—is the prāṇa produced by something else? Anticipating this doubt, [the Sūtra] says:
"But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught together with them and for other reasons. (2.4.8)
This *prāṇa* is not a specific element (*bhūta-viśeṣa*), but rather a specific instrument of the living being (*jīva-upakaraṇa-viśeṣa*), like the eyes and other senses.

And it is understood from the disciples and others along with the instruments, the sense organs; for this *prāṇa* is taught together with the eyes and the rest. Indeed, in the dialogues concerning *prāṇa* and similar contexts, its teaching alongside them is appropriate only if it belongs to the same class as they do.
Among the organs comprised by the term "prāṇa," its specific designation is understood through the word "ādi" (and so forth).

Alternatively, because of its specific mention in passages such as "this which is the chief prāṇa" and "this which is the middle prāṇa," the prāṇa exists in the heart in a form corresponding to that of fire (tejas).
Abiding in dependence upon the individual soul (jīva), through the functions of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth,
and by way of the paths of iḍā and piṅgalā in the form of exhalation and inhalation,
it repeatedly goes out and then enters back into itself in succession.

Thus, in the Yogaśāstra, the true nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) has been clearly taught. Therefore, it should be understood that the prāṇa arises from the quality of rajas within the five elements by the will of the Lord.
Furthermore, because the prāṇa is enumerated among the sense organs, such as the eyes, in all the Śrutis.

Furthermore, due to its association with the sense organs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is conventionally described as being material (*bhautika*), like the eyes and other senses. This is supported by such scriptural passages as:
"The sustainer, being sustained himself, sustains; the one God is seated in many ways"; and "Thou alone hast entered into many;
thou art the knot of the vital breaths, O Rudra, enter me as the destroyer. Thus [it is said] regarding the *prāṇa*.

The support is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of dispelling the aforementioned doubt. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not possess independence like the individual soul (*jīva*); rather, it is like a minister in relation to a king, like horses in relation to a charioteer, or like the senses in relation to the vital breath.
Because it is superior [to them], the aforementioned defect does not apply. Furthermore, this is so even though the vital breath is produced from the *rajas* quality of the five elements.
Furthermore, because its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is air, it is conventionally designated as being included within air. Likewise, in the *Vātulāgama*:
"The self (*ātman*) is to be known as consisting of ether (*ākāśa*); the vital breath (*prāṇa*) likewise consists of air;
the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) consists of fire (*tejas*); and the mind (*manas*) consists of water (*jala*)."

Thus it has been correctly taught. [An objection is raised: "If this [prāṇa] is also an instrument like the eye and other organs, then like them, it must also possess an activity consisting of service to the individual soul (jīva). Yet that [activity] is not observed. Therefore, this cannot be an instrument like the eye and so forth. To this doubt, he says:
And there is no fault because of non-performance; for thus [the scripture] shows. || 9 ||

It is called an instrument because it is an instrument by virtue of being an agent; it is "without action" because of the absence of such agency. Furthermore, the defect that is raised—namely, that this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is devoid of specific actions in the form of services rendered to the individual soul (*jīva*)—does not exist, since the Scripture demonstrates its activity in the form of specific services, such as the sustaining of the body and the senses.

"Whose departure makes this body appear most wretched—that one among you is the best. Having said this, and having shown that even upon the departure of speech and the other [organs] the body and the senses remain intact, whereas upon the departure of the *prāṇa* there is a loosening of the body and the senses; therefore, [he is the best] by way of being the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*.

This *prāṇa*, existing in fivefold form, assists the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of sustaining the body and the sense organs; thus, its status as an instrument (*upakaraṇatva*) is established, just like the eyes and other senses.
Furthermore, precisely because *prāṇa* is not a [sensory] organ (*akaraṇatvāt*), it does not lack an object of action (*kāryābhāva*). How then, with respect to the Self (*ātman*)?

If it is asked, "How is the maintenance of the body accomplished by Prāṇa, given that the function of sustaining the body—which is unique and not possible for the other sense organs—is its very nature of being helpful? we reply:
Indeed, the Śruti demonstrates the uniqueness of Prāṇa regarding this stated function in the Dialogue of the Vital Breaths (Prāṇasaṃvāda).

Having determined the preeminence of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), that most excellent breath said to them: "Do not fall into delusion; it is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this body (bāṇa). Thus, the Śruti also [speaks of] protecting the body (bāṇa)—the nest situated within the physical frame—by means of the vital breath.

For the Prāṇa indeed speaks thus: "Another [is] a nest of many impurities. Thus the Śruti also states that the Prāṇa protects the house called the body by its presence and then enters into sleep. Furthermore, the Śruti says: "The Prāṇa itself, being the conscious self (prajñātman), having taken possession of this body, illumines it. This indicates another function of the Prāṇa: its role as the illuminator of the body.

Therefore, the primacy of the vital breath (prāṇa) is unavoidable. Now, one might object: "In this way, since there exist various vital breaths such as [the individual] prāṇa and others due to differences in name and function, how can the established position that 'the prāṇa is indeed one' be justified? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
The fivefold activity [of the breath] is designated as being like that of the mind. || 10 ||

Just as, despite the difference in the functions of desire and so forth and the resulting difference in their effects, desire and the rest are not entities distinct from the mind—because of the scriptural statement: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind"—so too, [it is said]: "Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, and ana—all this is indeed prāṇa."
From this statement, it is understood that the apāna and the others are merely specific functions of the prāṇa itself, and not separate principles.
Furthermore, the prāṇa has four functions known as exhalation, inhalation, the movement of the entire body, and departure (from the body).
[The udāna] distributes the essences of food and other substances consumed equally throughout all the limbs—these five [functions] constitute its fivefold activity.

Although there is a fivefold difference in its functions depending on the eyes and other organs, the causal Prāṇa-vāyu is one and the same. Even though the insentient Prāṇa lacks the existence of a transformation into the form of an effect, there is no contradiction in its capacity for action, because Paraśiva— who is characterized by that Prāṇa and whose very nature is indicated by it— exists.

If it is argued that, based on the hearing of such scriptural passages as "the life-breath of the life-breath," and because the scripture stating "as he departs" indicates that the life-breath (*prāṇa*) is subtle since it is the cause of departure, [we reply: no, for its very greatness is understood through its pervasion of all bodies;
moreover, that which is atomic in form cannot be pervasive, as it is said: "He is equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe."

Anticipating the objection that the doctrine of atomicity is inconsistent with the scriptural teaching on departure (*utkrānti*), he says: "And [the self] is atomic" (Sūtra 2.3.11). This is because the designation in scripture [indicates otherwise]. || 106 || 11 ||

The claim that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) possesses a great dimension because of scriptural passages such as "Everything is established in the vital breath; indeed, all this is enveloped by the vital breath," and so forth, is incorrect. Rather, it is not contradictory to hold that the vital breath, while residing in the heart in the form of the subtle individual soul (*jīva*), attains a vast dimension through its functions such as inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*). Regarding its greatness:

Because the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is observed through numerous scriptural statements, logical arguments, and the evidence of experience— such as "When he departs, all the vital breaths depart"— and because its departure would be impossible if it were merely of the size of the Great Soul (*mahat*), it is determined that the *prāṇa* is atomic (*aṇu*). As for the scriptural passage, "He is equal to these three worlds," that refers to the totality of all air.
There is no contradiction with the internal wind.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural vision: "Brahman has space as its body, the true self as its nature, the vital breaths as its delight, the mind as its bliss, is enriched by peace, and is immortal."

It should be understood that the scriptural declaration of its greatness refers to the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), which is manifested through the power (*kalā*) of Paraśiva, consists of the five non-material Brahmas, and governs all individual souls (*sakalajīva*). This is because immortality is attributed to it, making departure (*utkrānti*) impossible,
and because it is not produced by the material quality of *rajas*.
The Section Concerning Light and the Other [Elements] (Jyotirādyadhikaraṇa) || 5 ||

It has already been refuted that the Pradhāna, being insentient, can be the cause of the universe; therefore, how can it be logically maintained that the life-force and the sense-faculties, which are themselves non-conscious, initiate their own respective activities spontaneously? Rather, it must be established that Maheśvara alone impels the sense-faculties in accordance with the karma performed by the individual soul (jīva).
Anticipating this doubt, he states [the solution] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"But the presiding over fire and the other elements is by him who possesses breath, because of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the vital breath. (Sūtra 1.4.12)

The word "tu" (but/then) here signifies certainty. Why are the sense organs, such as the eye, the abodes—that is, the dwelling places—of the luminaries, namely the deities such as the Sun? Because of their being so declared in scripture (*āmananāt*). For in the Śruti passage, "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth," there is the declaration (*āmanana*) of those deities, such as the Sun, in relation to locations such as the mouth.

From the description of their entry, it is established that the deities, beginning with the Sun, act as impellers of the senses either by being the inner rulers (*antaryāmin*) of Paraśiva along with the living soul (*jīva*) which possesses vital breath (*prāṇa*), or else independently. Why? From the scriptural statement: "He who rules the sun from within—he is your Self, the inner ruler, the immortal. "Viṣṇu alone is the one great Being; he has become the various beings in manifold ways."

This is established by the force of such scriptural passages as "The Lord of all beings," which demonstrate that Maheśvara alone, as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all deities including Viṣṇu who preside over the senses, impels the senses in accordance with the karma performed by the individual soul (jīva). This is the subtle meaning.

The origin of the most excellent vital breaths from Brahman, as well as their specific magnitude resulting from its transformation, has already been explained; furthermore, the fact that those vital breaths are presided over by deities such as Agni was established incidentally through the sūtra: "But there is designation of the presiding deities because of distinction and common association. And [this applies] to the individual soul as well.

The presiding nature (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) over these means of one's own enjoyment is well-known in the world; it is also established by such scriptural passages as: "In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths (*prāṇa*), he moves about at will within his own body.
Likewise, in this context: "The Sun, becoming the eye, entered the two eyes; there, by means of the eye, one sees forms."

In such scriptural passages as these, the question arises whether the presiding over the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by the individual soul (*jīva*) other than the Supreme Lord, and by deities such as Agni, is dependent upon itself or dependent upon another.
In this regard, [the texts state]: "One sees forms with the eye," and "The Sun, having become the eye, entered into the eyes."

Based on scriptural revelation and observation, it is only the individual soul (*jīva*), the sun, and so forth that are the impellers of the vital breaths and the sense organs. If Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, were their impeller, it would follow that He is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); consequently, the individual soul could not be the enjoyer. If that were the case, there would be no heaven or hell consisting of pleasure and pain—which are the fruits of meritorious and sinful actions—for the individual soul.
When it is argued that [the soul] is the impeller of the vital breaths and so forth, we reply:
"The presiding over light and so forth" means that together with the living soul (jīva) which possesses the vital breaths,
there is the presiding over the objects of the vital breaths by the deities of light and so forth— such as the sun, fire, wind, and others— because of the scriptural teaching concerning them.
It arises from the *āmanana* (contemplation) of Śiva, the Supreme Self. *Āmanana* means contemplating with direct orientation (*ābhimukhyena*).

And that [contemplation] occurs solely through the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the Supreme Self. "Om! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. That is the Imperishable. That most excellent splendor of Savitṛ—wisdom has issued forth from him.

In Vedic texts such as "purāṇī" (the ancient one), by phrases like "savitur vareṇyam" (the most excellent [light] of Savitṛ—the Sun), which describe the Supreme Lord as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of the Sun and as the impeller, the meaning is that it is solely through His will that all the presiding deities of the sense organs are motivated. Why? From scripture (śabdāt).

This is because the scriptures teach that the functioning of the sense organs such as the feet, of the presiding deities such as Viṣṇu, and of the individual soul (jīvātman) in their respective tasks is dependent upon the contemplation of the Supreme Person, Śiva. As stated in the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa: "He who dwells in fire, yet is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is your Self."

The Self is the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), the Immortal; He who dwells in the wind, who dwells in the sun, who dwells in the self, who dwells in the eye—by such passages, His state as the Inner Ruler of all and His role as the Controller of all are taught. "He who is in the fire, He who is in the waters; through fear of Him the wind blows, through fear of Him the sun rises; through fear of Him Agni and Indra [and Death] run on."

Death runs as the fifth. There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand held apart," and so forth—[these are] [scriptural passages concerning] Śiva.

The state of being the inner controller of all, the cause of fear for all, the illuminator of all, and the support of all has been clearly taught. Therefore, it is demonstrated that it is logically untenable for beings such as individual souls (jīvas) and Viṣṇu to independently impel the vital breaths and the senses.

But surely, since it is stated—in the passage beginning, "He indeed carried speech as the first [offering]; when it was released from death, it became fire"—that speech and the others attain the state of fire and the rest, the state of being fire and so forth must consist precisely in being presided over by those [deities]. Therefore, there exists a relationship of presider and presided-over between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the deity.
Anticipating the objection that [the self] is thus produced, he says:
"And because of its eternity. (108) || 13 ||

Since all things are eternal by virtue of being presided over by Paraśiva, and since they are fixed as being intrinsically connected to His own nature, His lordship over them through His mere will is unavoidable. This is established by such passages as: "Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became both the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," which refer to Śiva, the Supreme Person.

It is recorded in the Smṛti that He who is independent and distinguished by His own inherent power of consciousness possesses the essential nature of entering into all conscious and unconscious entities as their controller.

Therefore, it is established that the status of being the regulator of the vital breaths, the senses, and the deities, as well as the state of being their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*), belongs to Him alone and not to any other.

If it is argued that since Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the controller of the individual soul (jīva) and others, it is understood that He alone is the agent; and therefore, the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit performed by the individual soul must also belong to Him alone—this is not so. For, in the impelling of the senses and other organs, the individual soul alone always possesses the sense of independent agency, and thus the experience of the fruits of karma produced by those senses belongs to the soul and not to the other.

Furthermore—since Śiva, by presiding over the senses and their bases as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of deities such as Prabhākara and Viṣṇu, is capable of impelling those senses in accordance with the karma performed by the individual soul (jīva), the Lord does not become the enjoyer of the fruits of that karma. As it is said: "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit, while the other is the unborn one... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).

"The other, the unborn, having enjoyed her, lies with her as she is enjoyed; he leaves her once her enjoyment is finished. Thus the venerable Śruti also teaches in that very manner. Therefore, there is no stain of doubt.
This concludes the section concerning the designation of those [organs] as the senses (ta indriyāṇi tadvyapadeśādhikaraṇam).

The demonstration that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) are superior to the sense organs is based on the teaching of their identity in the Śruti: "Ah! All this is indeed its form and name; all these, beginning with speech, became its form; they became the fivefold form of this very *prāṇa*. Thus, the scripture instructs the unity of the *prāṇa* and the sense organs.
Anticipating the objection that the vital breaths (prāṇas) might themselves be sense organs, [the Sūtrakāra] says:
"Those [other breaths] are sense organs because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one. (Sūtra 2.4.14)

In the passage, "From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs," the vital breath and the sense organs are perceived as distinct principles (tattva). However, in the Śruti text, "Come, let us assume his very form; thus they all assumed his very form," it is understood that the sense organs possess the nature of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). Therefore, are the vital breath and the sense organs one, or...
Or is there a distinction? This is the doubt.

It is appropriate that the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is an organ (*indriya*), because even though the mental organs are mentioned separately in the passage "From this [Self] the vital breath is born," those two are not different principles (*tattva*). Indeed, all these...

Since the scriptural statement "the forms are the self" (rūpamasāma) is more powerful, it might be argued that it is logical for the vital breath (prāṇa) to be an instrument; to this, it is replied: "These are the senses.

This means that the vital breath is a distinct principle from the senses. The reason for this is stated in the phrase "because of its designation as such," while the other part of the sūtra provides the supporting argument.

He explains: those other than the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), namely speech and the rest, are called the "vital organs" (*prāṇendriya*) in their primary state, but they are not the [chief] *prāṇa* itself, because of the teaching of its distinctness in such passages as, "From this, *prāṇa* is born.
Now, if it is argued that this designation of difference is equally applicable to the sense organs and the mind (*manas*), we say no; for the mind—

This is because the traditional teaching that "there are six sense organs" (ṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi) accepts that the mind (*manas*) and the [other] sense organs do not constitute separate principles (*tattva*). Nor, in the present context, does the scriptural statement "But he [the breath] alone... imply an acceptance that the sense organs are not distinct principles from the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the complementary passage regarding the sense organs states:
"All these became its forms; therefore they are called 'breaths' (*prāṇa*). Thus, in the case of the sense organs...
Because it is established that the word "prāṇa" is used figuratively, the sense organs (indriyas) are admitted to be distinct principles (tattva).

Indeed, the term "eye-organ" (cakṣurindriya) is not seen to be figurative when applied to something other than the sense organs themselves. Therefore, all these [organs] belong to this very [principle].

By the statement "form came into being," it is seen that the activity of the sense organs is dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), not that they constitute its function. Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of a distinction, the section concerning the sense organs such as speech is concluded; for in a separate section—beginning with "Then they spoke to this breath within the mouth"—the breath is heard to be distinct from the sense organs.

It is taught that the sense organs possess the function of vital breath (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, in the passage stating, "Then speech and the others said to this *prāṇa* in the mouth," it is taught that the *prāṇa* and the sense organs are distinct principles. Why?
Because of the indication of the experience of their difference; for even when the sense organs have dissolved during deep sleep, the activity of the *prāṇa* is observed. Therefore...
Thus it is established that there is no contradiction with the cited statements.

Moreover, because that designation [of "prāṇa"] applies only to the other vital breaths (prāṇas) distinct from the chief one, the term *indriya* is applied specifically to the eye and the rest, together with the mind, as in such passages as: "The ten and one senses, and the five objects of the senses."
Therefore, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed distinct from the "best" one; nevertheless, they are not included among the sense organs.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 110 || "Because of the scriptural teaching of their difference and because of their distinct characteristics. || 15 ||

On account of the strength of numerous scriptural passages such as "From this [Self] is born the vital breath" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*), even though there is an experience of the dissolution of the mind into the causal body—just like the dissolution of the sense organs during deep sleep—the status of the mind as a sense organ is not tenable; for the Smṛti texts stating "the sense organs have the mind as the sixth" (*manaḥ-ṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi*) are weaker [in authority]. Furthermore, [scripture declares]: "The mind is the lord of the senses, but the vital air is the lord of the mind; the mind is superior to the senses."

The distinctiveness of the mind [from the vital breaths] is established by the observation of many Smṛtis consistent with such scriptural passages (Śruti). They declare that the mind is the internal indicator (liṅga) within the vital breaths, because hundreds of Śruti texts— such as "May my self consisting of food, my self consisting of vital breath, my self consisting of mind, my self consisting of consciousness, and my self consisting of bliss be purified"— teach that the mind exists as something superior to the vital breaths.

Furthermore, because the Sāṅkhya and Yoga treatises describe the arising of the mind from one half of the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the arising of the organs of cognition from the other half, and because they indicate the arising of the vital breath (prāṇa) from the rajas-quality portion of the five subtle elements and the arising of the organs of action from the other half, it follows that the self (ātman) is conjoined with the mind.

According to the principle that "the sense organ [is known] by means of the mind, and the object by means of the sense organ," the mind's status as a sense organ is merely figurative because it pervades all the sense organs. Therefore, the superiority of both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind over the sense organs is beyond dispute.
This concludes the section concerning the fashioning of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtikḷptyadhikaraṇa*).

The establishment of Śiva, the Supreme Self who performs the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), as the cause of the creation of the moving and the unmoving: [Objection] Since it is understood from such passages as "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists" and "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā is born," that Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, and others are the causes of the world, [it follows that Śiva is not]. From this [Supreme Self], the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is born...

In response to the doubt as to how the status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world—established by such scriptural passages as these—can belong to Śiva alone as the Supreme Brahman, he states [the solution] in another section: "16.
But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching. (Sūtra 2.4.16)

From the Supreme Self, Śiva, who performs the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), alone arises the creation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) consisting of the moving and non-moving worlds, through the fashioning of designations and bodies. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching (*upadeśa*): "That Deity thought" (*seyaṃ devataikṣata*), which refers specifically to the Supreme Self, Śiva.

In the *Janmādhikaraṇa*, it has been explained extensively in accordance with statements from the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā* and other sources that, because the scripture teaches [the Lord] as the creator of the body consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
those scriptural, traditional, and Puranic passages which prescribe Hiraṇyagarbha, Viṣṇu,
and others as creators have as their scope only the intermediate creation (*avāntara-sṛṣṭi*).

This has been explained in detail. Furthermore, the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that Paramaśiva alone, abiding within the bodies of Hiraṇyagarbha, Viṣṇu, and Kālarudra, performs the creation and other functions of the universe consisting of the mobile and immobile.
Previously, it was taught that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the cause of air and the other elements by virtue of being their inner controller (antaryāmin).
By the passage beginning with "One should meditate on Īśāna, who is to be meditated upon," His very status as the cause of Brahmā and the others is designated.

Nevertheless, regarding the creation of other [lower] beings, His status as the cause of the entire world—consisting of both the mobile and the immobile—by virtue of being its inner controller (*antaryāmin*) has not been stated there.
Therefore, it was determined in this other section (*adhikaraṇa*): "I alone am that Rudra who is in fire, who is in the waters... and so forth.

"First indeed I existed; and there was no other whatsoever distinct from me," and "He entered into the innermost of the inner," and so forth—because in these passages there is the teaching of attributes unique to Śiva, such as being prior to all things and being the inner controller of all. Also, by such [Vedic] texts as, "The Creator fashioned the heavens and the earth and the intermediate space according to the former [order]."

Because Hiraṇyagarbha is understood to be the cause of the world, and because in passages such as "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa," Nārāyaṇa is seen to be the cause of the four-faced one and others; and because in passages such as "That Fire thought, 'May I become many, may I procreate,' and it created Water," and "Thus the Waters thought, and they created Food," the deities presiding over the elements such as Fire are [intended].
Because of the designation of causality in such passages as "From Consciousness alone all these beings are born," and because the soul's authorship of the elements is indicated therein,
there arises a doubt as to whether Śiva, or Hiraṇyagarbha and others, is the cause of the birth and so forth of all beings and the world.
Because in passages such as "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose," the word *prajāpati* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring specifically to Hiraṇyagarbha;
and because in passages such as "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa," Nārāyaṇa alone is shown to be the cause of all.
Furthermore: "Entering by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms."

Because it is heard that the soul is the agent [of creation], the supreme deity did not indeed intend, "Let me differentiate names and forms in my own form," but rather intended so through the form of the individual soul (jīva), which is its own part, as stated in the words, "by this living self. Therefore, Hiraṇyagarbha and others alone are the cause of the world's birth and so forth.

[Objection: In that case, just as in the expression "having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, I shall enumerate it," the use of the first-person verb form (*vyākaravāṇi*) and the verb "to enter" (*praviśati*), whose action resides in the agent, would be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). [Response: It is not so. In that instance, there is a difference in nature between the king and the spy, and thus [the usage] is figurative; here, however, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is also a part of [the Supreme Self] and is therefore of the same nature [as the Self], it is [so] in that form.
Since both the entry and the prophecy pertain to the Self alone, there is no risk of [the term] being merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Nor is this instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) one characterized by association (*sahayoga*), because when a case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is possible, it is improper to employ a case-ending based on a mere accompanying word (*upapada-vibhakti*). Furthermore, the instrumental case cannot denote the instrument (*karaṇa*) here, because [Brahman] is the agent (*kartṛ*) of both [the entry and the prophecy].

This is because the individual soul (jīva) lacks the status of being the most effective agent (*sādhakatama*) with respect to both the entering and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*). Nor can it be argued that the agency of the soul terminates merely in the act of entering, while the differentiation of names and forms belongs exclusively to Brahman;

for by means of the suffix *-ktvā*, the identity of the agent is clearly perceived [between the two actions]. This remains so even though the soul, as a part of [Brahman], is identical in essence with it.
The phrase "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) is a reference [to the Self] as something external, for the purpose of excluding other forms.
Therefore, this differentiation of names and forms has Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent; hence: "The naming and the detailed unfolding of the forms of beings and their activities..."
In the beginning, he created the gods and others from the very words of the Veda.

In such Smṛtis, within the context of creation by the Four-faced One (Brahmā), the differentiation of names and forms is proclaimed; therefore, since it might be argued that this differentiation of names and forms belongs either to the individual soul (jīva), or to Hiraṇyagarbha as the collective totality, or to Nārāyaṇa who is their cause—this being the position reached—we reply: [The following section follows: We declare: ... [as per the subsequent sūtra].
The fashioning of names and forms is threefold.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view. "The fashioning of names and forms" refers to the differentiation of name and form;

for it is taught that the differentiation of name and form belongs to that very Supreme Brahman which performs the tripartition, as seen in the passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

That which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) is Śiva alone—the witness of the great dissolution and the cause of all. His primacy is established by his being unsublated throughout the three periods of time, as seen in such scriptural passages as, "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman.
Furthermore, the status of being the cause of the creation and so forth of the internal worlds is not possible for any other; [for example,] the golden egg in the midst...

"The ocean first came into being through the power of Rudra; in that [ocean], Brahmā and Viṣṇu are born, as is Jātavedas"— since this Śruti passage teaches that Paramaśiva, having produced the egg of light (*tejo'ṇḍa*) by means of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), subsequently effects the creation of the four-faced one and others, it follows that Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest possess causality only through the process of tripartition.
This is not tenable. For even in the *Atharvaṇa-śikhā* it is said: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the sense organs together with the elements—they are all produced from Him;
Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty, is the Lord of All, in the midst of space.
And in the first section of the *Atharvaśiras*: "He said: 'I alone existed first, and I exist now.'"

"And I shall become [all this]; there is nothing other than me. Beginning with "He entered from the interior into the interior," and ending with "He who knows me alone knows all"—having thus taught that I am denoted by the word 'all' because of having entered the entire expanse of the sentient and insentient (cid-acit-prapañca)—and in the second section, [it is stated] that Rudra is he who, precisely due to that prior entry, is...

Beginning with "Obeisance again and again to that which is the Blessed One and Brahman; he who is Rudra is the Blessed One, and he who is Viṣṇu—to him obeisance again and again," it is established that He alone is appropriately denoted by all such terms as Brahman, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, Indra, Vināyaka, and so forth. In the Manusmṛti—
In the beginning, he created the waters alone; into them he cast his seed.
That became a golden egg, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns.
In that [egg], Brahmā himself was born, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Water is called "nārāḥ," for water is indeed the offspring of Nara.
Since they alone are his abode, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
"Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest; from the unmanifest arises the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). Within the egg are the three worlds and the earth with its seven continents. Thus it is said in the Śiva Purāṇa.
The form of the deity known as Rudra is born as a physical manifestation;
by him, who identifies with that supreme form, his vital energy is cast into the fluid.
Then a divine egg came into being, possessing the radiance of a thousand rays;
Viṣṇu himself entered therein through the majestic power of my Śakti.
Furthermore, at my command, he obtained the name Nārāyaṇa;
and in this regard, they cite this verse concerning Nārāyaṇa:
The subtle essence of water is to be known as *rasa*; *rasa* is proclaimed to be *nara*. O Brahmin, *nara* is the supreme cause of *nara*, and *nara* is considered to be Śiva himself in person.
The abode of Nara has been declared; for that reason, he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
O tiger among men, even Brahmā entered into the form of fragrance.

Furthermore—in another Śruti as well—Rudra, who presides over fire (tejas), emits the waters and deposits his seed within them. Viṣṇu, accompanied by the principle (tattva) [of water], enters into them; thus, because the waters are the abode of the water-principle born from Rudra, Viṣṇu is taught the name Nārāyaṇa, for "nara" means water and "nara" means Rudra. In the Vedāntas, he is established as existing even prior to Hiraṇyagarbha.

It is precisely within the subtle *liṅga-śarīra* produced from the subtle elements that the designation "functioning" (*vṛtti*) occurs in the gross egg (*aṇḍa*) composed of the threefold [elements]; it is not taught that Hiraṇyagarbha and others are in every respect the cause of the threefold egg.

Furthermore, the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) is taught as belonging specifically to one who performs the threefold composition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*). By this [it is shown] regarding the individual soul (*jīva*)...

For it is understood from the text that there is a single agent: "Having entered by means of the Self, let me evolve name and form, and let me make each of them threefold, threefold. However, this process of triplication is not possible for the four-faced Brahmā while he is still within the cosmic egg;
rather, the cosmic egg is produced from the fire, water, and food that have already been triplicated. And [the egg] belongs to the four-faced one.

The origin is recorded in the Smṛti: "In that egg was born Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds. Therefore, it is understood that the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) belongs to Śiva alone, and the differentiation of names and forms (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa), which has the same agent, also belongs to him alone. How then is the phrase "by this living self" (anena jīvena) to be reconciled? It is through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), meaning "by the self who is the living self" (ātmanā jīvena).

The Supreme Brahman itself, having the individual soul as its body, is denoted by the word "jīva. Just as in the passages, "That Fire thought; it created the waters," and "Those waters thought; they created food," the Supreme Brahman itself is denoted as having fire and the other elements as its body.
By such texts as "He who is in the fire," its status as the inner controller of all is clearly taught. Its nature as the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrtitva) [is likewise established].
This is well known in the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas as belonging to Him alone.

Therefore, this differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Brahman Himself, who has Hiraṇyagarbha—the aggregate of individual souls—as His body. And thus [the text says]: "Having entered, let me differentiate names and forms."

In this context, both "entering" (*praviśati*) and "expounding" (*vyākaroti*) refer to the Supreme Person alone. Furthermore, the identity of the agent for both entering and expounding is logically consistent. Moreover, the instruction regarding the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākriyā*) is appropriate within the context of creation performed by the Four-faced One (Brahmā). Now, the meaning of the passage beginning with "Then that deity... is as follows:
"I shall evolve name-and-form; I shall create the diverse creation of gods and other beings, as well as their designations.

For that purpose, I shall make each of these—fire, water, and food—which have not yet reached mutual conjunction and are incapable of specific creation, tripartite (trivṛt) so as to acquire that capacity. Therefore:
This differentiation of names and forms is the work of Śiva alone, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Now, it might be argued that because the differentiation of names and forms shares a single agent with the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa), it must therefore have the Supreme Self as its agent; however, this cannot be maintained.

Because it is also possible for the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent; for the method of tripartition is taught with respect to the souls created by the four-faced Brahmā at a time subsequent to the creation of the cosmic egg.
As it is said: "Just so, my dear, each of these three deities, upon reaching the person, becomes threefold."

"Understand that from me": "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts. That which is its coarsest portion becomes feces; that which is middling becomes flesh; that which is finest becomes mind," and so forth. Likewise, in the preceding passage as well:
"That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat (tejas); that which is white is the form of water (āpas); that which is black..."

By the passage beginning with "Of that food," the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is demonstrated in the fire, sun, moon, and lightning created by the Four-faced One (Brahmā). Furthermore, the tripartition is heard in scripture as occurring after the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*):
"This divinity, having entered these three divinities through this living self (*jīva*), differentiated their names and forms."
"He made each one threefold"—regarding this, he states [the following]:
"The definition of the nature of the tripartition:
'Flesh and so forth are terrestrial, according to the scripture, as are the other two. (1.2.17)
In the preceding [passage], there was a doubt that Hiraṇyagarbha and others possess the status of being the cause of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*);

therefore, to exclude such over-extension (*ativyāpti*), [the text] states that even in intermediate creations and so forth, Śiva— the Supreme Brahman— has entered the bodies of individual souls (*jīva*) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and Viṣṇu by means of the passage beginning with "having entered with this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya*).
The agency of that [Brahman] has been established. In response to the inquiry as to what this tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is, this Sūtra is commenced.

The meaning of the Śruti is as follows: "The compound means a collection. These three deities, having become tripartite, reach the body of the person; each individual deity, characterized by fire and so forth, exists in the form of the three products of tripartition.

"It turned about" (avartata) is the second meaning of the Vedic text. For instance, when earth—in the form of rice, barley, and so forth—is eaten by a person, three effects exist within the body: excrement, flesh, and mind. Likewise, for water that has been drunk, there are three effects: urine, blood, and vital breath (prāṇa); and for [substances] such as clarified butter, which are illuminated by fire and the like, [there are corresponding effects].

The three effects are bone, marrow, and speech. Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is well known as an effect of air, it is designated as an effect of water merely because its existence is dependent upon water. Similarly, although the mind (*manas*) is healthy when one eats food, it is considered an effect of that [food] only insofar as it provides well-being; and although speech (*vāk*) is an effect of fire, it is so designated due to the commonality of being conducive to knowledge.
It is thus designated. In this way, the very process of existing within the body in the form of the three effects is the internal tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*);

this is what the author of the Sūtras states with the words "flesh, etc."—referring to that which was previously mentioned as concerning the deities and others created by Caturmukha after the creation of the cosmic egg.
The instruction regarding the tripartition—that "He made each one threefold"—is untenable;

for in the passage, "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," since flesh and mind are designated as being subtler and finer than feces, they would necessarily follow the nature of their causes, resulting in the undesirable consequence that they are composed of water and fire. This same objection applies to the passage, "Water, when drunk... as well.
Furthermore, because urine and breath would then follow as being respectively gross and subtle, they would consequently have to be classified as earthen and fiery; yet this is not accepted.

For flesh is held to be earthen. Like excrement, both flesh and the mind are held to be earthen—that is, composed of earth—since the discussion begins with the statement, "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold. And according to the literal expression, the same applies to the other two: water, when drunk...

In the two parallel passages, "the fire consumed" (*tejo 'śitam*) and so forth, the transformations are intended according to the literal wording. From the word, "the water drunk is divided threefold," one understands that the transformation into three parts belongs to the water alone; likewise, from the word, "the fire consumed is divided threefold," one understands that the transformation into three parts belongs to the fire alone. Therefore, [the results are] feces, flesh, and mind.

Furthermore, this is because it contradicts the remainder of the passage: "The modifications of earth are urine, blood, and breath; the modifications of water are bone, marrow, and semen; speech consists of fire. Therefore, the manner of triplication described by the statement, "He made each of them threefold," is not demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten... If that were the case [i.e., if the former were being illustrated by the latter], then...

Furthermore, because the mind, the vital breath, and speech are all subtle (*aṇīyas*) and thus composed of light (*taijasa*), the scriptural statement "the mind, my dear, consists of food" (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*) and so forth would be contradicted. Indeed, even prior to the creation of the cosmic egg, when the triply-transformed (*trivṛtkṛta*) elements such as earth and the others have reached the person, the transformation of each one into three parts is described by the passage beginning with "The food that is eaten... (*annaṃ aśitam...*). And this occurs even before the creation of the egg.

There must be a threefold compounding (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) of fire, water, and earth, because they lack the capacity to initiate an effect when not so compounded. For it is only when they are mutually conjoined that they possess the capacity to initiate an effect;
and that very process is what constitutes "threefold compounding. Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, as they had not come together in their entirety.
"Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent, those [principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with the Undifferentiated (aviśeṣa) produce the cosmic egg.
For this very reason, [the scripture says]: "Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), he differentiated name and form; he made them tripartite..."
The sequence of the text, "He made each one threefold," is set aside by the sequence of meaning;

for the demonstration of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) regarding fire, the sun, and so forth— which exist within the cosmic egg— is intended for Śvetaketu, who is situated inside the egg, since it would be impossible for him to demonstrate the tripartition of things existing outside the egg.

This [distinction] is made with respect to the effects of the triply transformed [elements], such as fire, the sun, and so forth. It might be argued: since each of the triply transformed substances—food, water, and heat—is composed of all three (heat, water, and food) and thus possesses a threefold nature, how can they be designated by a single form as "food," "water," or "heat"?
Anticipating the objection that [the soul] is reborn, he says:
"But on account of its excellence, there is that designation; indeed, there is that designation. (2.3.18)

*Vaiśeṣyam* is the state of being specific (*viśeṣabhāva*). The word *viśeṣa*, like the word *vikāra*, refers both to the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). In this context, however, it refers to the substratum; the state of being specific (*vaiśeṣyam*) is the nature of having a preponderance (*ādhikyarūpa*). Because of the tripartite process (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), even though each [element] possesses three forms, there is a designation as "food" and so forth in each respective case due to the preponderance of food and the rest.
The repetition indicates certainty and the conclusion of the chapter.

Furthermore, since the activity of air is observed here in the form of going, contracting, expanding, and so forth, as well as in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and others, and since the activity of space is observed through its providing room for the other four elements distinct from it; [the existence of all five elements is established].
If it is asked how the state of being merely a threefold combination (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is tenable given that [the body] is established through universal experience, [the answer is:
by the mere teaching of the three elements, the remaining two elements are indicated by implication through the logic of *kaimutika* (how much more so).

Therefore, there is no contradiction even with the view that the body consists of all five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), as was shown in the determination of the origin of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

When the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya) arise from the subtle elements that have not yet undergone quintuplication (apañcīkṛta-sūkṣmabhūta), although the process of the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) of the three qualities (guṇatraya) is present everywhere,
the internal organ is produced from the sattvic half of the collective totality (sāmaṣṭi) of the subtle elements, while the other half is distinct from it.

The emergence of the pentad of the organs of knowledge occurs in that same manner; likewise, from the aggregate of the five subtle elements, by means of half of the *rajas* quality, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) arises, and by the other half, the pentad of the organs of action emerges. Just as there is scriptural designation of a thing as being "of the nature of" a particular quality due to its predominance, so too here, in the gross body, it is designated as such due to the predominance of the [gross] elements.
The conventional usage of the term "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) is not contradicted.

If it is objected that there is no transference of the three qualities (guṇatraya) during the production of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, we say no; for the fact that the mind, the sense organs, and the like consist of the three qualities is established by the universal experience of all people across different times. The qualities of the cause [are present] in the effect.
And because of the principle that "they pass over";

however, some say that in the passage "having entered with this living soul" (*anena jīvenānupraviśya*), the living soul (*jīva*) is the agent of entry, while the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is the agent of the fashioning of names and forms. In their view, there is a contradiction with scripture, [as seen in the passage] "having created that... (*tatsṛṣṭvā*).

"It entered into that very [Being]; having entered it, it became the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat)"— since this demonstrates that both the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) and the entry mentioned in conjunction with it have the Supreme Self as their agent,
a common agency (*samānakartṛkatva*) [between the two actions] is not possible.

The Advaitins assert that because the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality non-different from the Lord (*īśvara*), its entry [into the body] is merely figurative; however, this is inconsistent, because it contradicts both perception and the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures. Furthermore, if the individual soul and the Lord were both imagined—like an imagined elephant and a horse—it would be impossible for them to possess consciousness, and consequently, they could not possess agency. Moreover, in the case of a reflection and its original, [they cannot occupy] the same location...

And because [any other cause] cannot be established. For in such scriptural passages as "From which these beings are born," the status of being the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of both sentient and insentient things is not possible for anyone distinct from the Supreme Lord. In the passage, "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of the bondage, sustenance, and liberation from saṃsāra," [it refers to Him who is distinct from] all individual souls.
And because it is understood that the power of concealing [the self] and bestowing grace depends upon the Supreme Lord,

for the sake of those devotees who possess their final bodies, there is the removal of the agency of conceiving the body, senses, and so forth— which serve as the cause for rebirth— in all times and in all states.

By the expansion of the consciousness of dependence on Śiva, through the state of being without support— according to the analogy of the bee and the worm— the attainment of Śiva-hood, preceded by the cessation of one's natural status as a limited individual soul (jīvatva), is established; thus, the essential purport of all Vedānta, which establishes the doctrine of non-dual duality (dvaitādvaita), is here summarized.
