Thus ends the section comprising the seven adhikaraṇas beginning with "Prāṇa" in the second chapter, titled "The Refutation of Contradictions," of the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* composed by the venerable teacher Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of holy ascetics.
Thus ends the fourth quarter, consisting of eighteen sūtras, beginning with "Prāṇa";
the second chapter is completed.
Now, [this work] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda...
In the Śrī Karabhāṣya on the Brahmamīmāṃsāsūtra, the third chapter.
First Pāda:
The Section on the Attainment of That [State] in the Interval. (Sūtra 1)

In the preceding chapter, the contradiction regarding Śiva— the Supreme Brahman whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), who possesses all powers, who is distinct from everything, who is the cause of the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, and whose form is a playful and auspicious manifestation— being the cause of the world’s birth and so forth, was refuted. Therein, in the first quarter (*pāda*), [the views of] Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and...

In the first [pāda], having first resolved contradictions regarding the creation and dissolution of the elements, the attributes of the individual soul (jīva), such as its eternity, were demonstrated.

In the fourth [pāda], having taught the nature of the vital breaths and the senses and their origination from Paramaśiva, the manifestation of the names and forms of all things was demonstrated. In the first pāda of this chapter, [the nature] of the jīva...

The deliberation on the departure from and return to other worlds is explained [in the first chapter]. In the second, there is the discussion concerning the definition and nature of Paramaśiva. In the third, the specific qualities for his worship are presented.
In the fourth, the duties of the four stages of life, beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*), are defined.
An investigation into the soul’s coming and going between worlds:
the Supreme Lord, who is supremely compassionate, out of affection for all living beings,
brought about the production of the triple-layered cosmic egg which serves as their support, and through His entry into it, performed the differentiation of names and forms.

In the context of the statement "He has done," a doubt arises as to how it is possible for the individual soul (*jīva*)— given its lack of form due to being of the nature of the body, its having entered into the Lord (*īśvara*), its being beyond the senses, its being an object that cannot be perceived, and so forth— to have performed [these acts]. To this, he says:
|| 114 || [The soul] is enveloped by the subtle body (aṇu) during its transition into another state, as established by both questions and explanations. || 1 ||

At the time of entering that interval—the moment of reaching another world—the individual soul (*jīva*), accompanied by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) in its atomic form, departs from this world for the heavenly realm by way of smoke and other paths, such as fuel, sacrificial cake, curd, milk, soma juice, and clarified butter—things offered into the fire and denoted by the term "the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). Why is this so? Because it is established through both questions and answers. Do you know this?
"How is it that in the fifth oblation water comes to be called 'man'?"—this is the question. "In this way, indeed, in the fifth oblation water comes to be called 'man'"—this is the answer.
By both this question and this answer, [it is shown] for those who are engaged in actions out of self-identification...
It has been taught that living beings possess the activity of entering and exiting numerous bodies.

This is also an illustration for those who have committed evil deeds. Since many scriptural passages are seen stating, "He alone causes the doer of good works to act," etc., it is implied by the sense that the Supreme Lord leads [beings] to worlds of merit or demerit in accordance with the karma performed by the individual soul.

Therefore, the essential meaning indicated by the aphorism is that the sovereign power of liberation— consisting in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of birth and death and the termination of the state of being a bound soul produced by one's own conceit, merit, and demerit— must be accomplished.

Because the identity of the embodied self with Brahman is established in such passages as "This Self is Brahman," "I am Brahman," "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," and "Thou art indeed That"; and because its movement to and from heaven and other realms is taught in such texts as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "The world acquired by merit perishes; the world acquired by action perishes."
It is considered whether there is going to and coming from the next world or not.

The soul's attainment of the next world is untenable; why? Because it is of the nature of Brahman, because agency resides only in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and because its state of being devoid of activity is established by the absence of the mind during sleep, fainting, and so forth; thus, it is not born [again].

For it has been taught in the Śruti, "Or he dies," and in the Smṛti, "This is indestructible, this is unburnable," and so forth, that his nature is distinct from birth, death, suffering, and the like. Furthermore, according to the logical principle that sound, cognition, and action endure for only three moments—
Since it is observed that even actions performed by the internal organ perish in this very life within just three moments,

and since at the time of the final breath there is the dissolution of the specific elements such as earth— which constitute the body— into the gross elements (*mahābhūta*s), it follows that the scriptural teaching of the soul’s complete departure to and return from the next world is untenable; such was the position reached.
We explain:

because in the *Māṇḍūkya*, within the section on Paramaśiva, the statement "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*) is designated as referring to the Praṇava whose essence is Śiva, even when establishing the status of the individual soul (*jīva*), the doctrine that the individual soul is identical with Brahman is not tenable. [For it is said: "Rudra is indeed all," and so forth.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is taught to be one with the eightfold form of Śiva— in passages such as "the earth is his body," "the waters are his body," and "the self is his body"— his status as Brahman is not contradictory, just as in the case of [the Upaniṣadic statements] "That Sun is Brahman," "Ka is Brahman," and "Kha is Brahman. This is in accordance with scriptural texts such as "I am Brahman" and "Thou art That."

By illuminating the primary meaning of all the Vedāntas through the presentation of both duality and non-duality, these [scriptures] establish that the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the worshiper, attains Śiva, who is the object of worship; likewise, in accordance with other observed analogies such as "Just as rivers...
and so forth, the relationship of the attained and the attainer between the individual soul and Brahman is clearly taught. Of those two, one [eats] the *pippala* fruit...

In the verse, "One eats the sweet fruit while the other looks on without eating," because the transmigrating nature and its absence are understood in the case of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), there is no contingency of the destruction of his omniscience— just as a teacher does not lose his status as a learned man simply because he lacks the physical eye when he is not acting as an instructor— likewise [in the state of deep sleep].

This is not tenable. If the individual soul (*jīva*) were the agent and [the self] were not beginningless, there would be no contradiction with the scriptures that teach the going and coming between this world and the next. Even if actions perish within three moments, the scripture concerning going and coming remains uncontradicted because [actions] produce a latent impression (*apūrva*) that yields future results.

In the Vedas and Vedāntas, it is possible for the substance of curd, which has entered into a subtle state, to undergo transformation into the form of a divine body; therefore, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā (the knowledge of the five fires), such a question and answer are recorded. It is said that Pravāhaṇa of Pañcāla [questioned] Śvetaketu Āruṇeya.

He asked about the destination of those who perform ritual actions and the manner of their return, as well as the path of the gods—specifically: "Do you know how, at the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'? Then, in answering this final question, he described the heavenly world as a fire and [placed] within that very fire...

"The gods offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation King Soma arises," and so forth—by this passage, it is shown that the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the living being, designated as "gods," cast the substance called "faith" into the heavenly world, which is conceived as fire;
and that faith transforms into the form of an immortal body known as King Soma, and that immortal body [is discarded] at the end of the physical life.
They cast the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) into Parjanya, who is conceived as fire; and that body, thus cast therein, becomes rain.

And those same vital breaths cast that rain into the Earth, which is conceived as fire; and that [rain], once cast therein, becomes food. And those same [breaths] cast that food into the Person (*puruṣa*), who is conceived as fire; and that [food] therein becomes semen.
"That [water] indeed becomes that very thing; they pour it into the woman who has been conceived as fire, and that which is poured there becomes the embryo.

Having said this, he declares: "Thus, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be designated by the word 'person' (puruṣa). The meaning is that when the fifth oblation has been offered in this manner, the waters become expressible by the term "person. This being stated...

It is thus stated that even in the preceding oblations, it is the subtle forms of the waters themselves that continue to persist and now assume the form of a person. For this very reason, it is understood from both the questions and the answers that the individual soul (jīva) travels from place to place together with the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) which serve as the cause of the body.
Therefore, based on the observation of scriptural injunctions that the fruit of knowledge is identical to the fruit of action,

it is explained in the Vedāntas that seekers of liberation must perform rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma— when performed as offerings to Śiva— without desire for rewards, since these acts serve as the cause for attaining Śiva by way of purifying the mind.

Now, an objection may be raised: since it is stated that "the waters assume human form," one understands from this that the waters undergo a transformation into the shape of a person; therefore, it follows that the departing soul is embraced by those waters alone. How then can it be said that the soul is embraced by the subtle elements of all [five] gross elements?
To address this doubt, he says:
But [the predominance of one element] is due to its being composed of three [subtle elements] and its greater abundance. || 2 ||

The word "tu" (but) here is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Since it has been established that water initiates the body through the process of triplication—as stated in the passage, "He made each of those threefold"—it is determined that the initiation of the body does not belong to water alone.

This is because sacrificial fuel, the *puroḍāśa* cake, and so forth possess the nature of earth (*pārthivatva*), while curd, milk, and so forth possess the nature of water (*āpyatva*), and clarified butter possesses the nature of fire (*taijasatva*).

If it is argued that this is untenable because the sacrificial materials are tripartite— consisting of the three elements in the form of "fieryness" (*taijasatva*) and thus being of three kinds, such that the statement "the waters become manlike" is incorrect— the answer is that the term "waters" (*āpaḥ*) is used here simply because among the sacrificial materials water is the most abundant. Thus, the word "water" refers to both the earthy and the watery [components].

Therefore, there is an abundance of water among the constituent elements. Consequently, it is clearly taught through the question and answer, "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, water comes to be called 'man'? The meaning of this scriptural passage is as follows:

Regarding the manner of the birth of the embryo through the sequence of the five fires: when one asks, "Do you know how the waters, having been offered as oblations into the fifth fire in the form of a woman, become [the fetus]?"—referring to the fifth oblation—[the answer is: "I do not know. Thus it is said concerning the fifth oblation.
"The waters become human-speeched"—this is the reply.

Its meaning is as follows: in this world, the oblations of fuel-sticks, sacrificial cakes, clarified butter, curds, and so forth, which have been offered into the fire by the sacrificer, are, together with the sacrificer, offered into the fire known as the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) by means of the path beginning with smoke and accompanied by the conducting deities (*ativāhika-deva*). Thus they are offered.

These transform into the form of a divine body. Having enjoyed the pleasures of heaven for some time, that divine body, upon the exhaustion of its merit, becomes liquefied like butter. That liquefied body is then offered as an oblation into the fire known as Parjanya by the *ātivāhika* deities. It then transforms into the nature of water. That water—

In the fire whose nature is earth, the *ātivāhika* body is offered as an oblation; it then transforms through the medium of plants into the form of grains such as rice and barley. That grain is offered as an oblation into the fire that is the human being in the form of food. That food transmutes into the form of semen. That semen is offered as an oblation into the fire that is the woman. That semen then pervades [the womb] in the form of the body situated within the embryo.
Thus, the production of the embryo is described through the sequence of the five fires in the form of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman;
for since the individual soul (*jīva*) is conscious, the vital breaths and sense organs would have no purpose during its departure to and arrival from the next world.
Anticipating the objection that one's own meritorious and non-meritorious actions go along with the self alone, he says in response to that: "And because of the departure of the vital breaths. (3)

In such scriptural passages as, "When he has departed, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him," the journey of the soul (jīva)—which departs enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma)—to the heavenly world along the path beginning with smoke, together with the vital breaths and so forth, is recorded. Therefore, it is implied by the sense that even the sacrificial materials go along with the soul. For even in places such as heaven, in the absence of the means consisting of the vital breaths and so forth, [the soul could not exist].

Because the enjoyment of the respective worlds [in the afterlife] cannot be accomplished [by actions that perish immediately], what was stated previously remains unrefuted. Even though actions in the world perish after three moments, the enjoyment of the next world is established by their producing unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*), just as the hearing of a sentence and so forth do.
Likewise, the Smṛti also states:
When the karma performed by a living being is exhausted in just three moments,
a result known as the "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) always arises, just like food and other such things.
"By means of those [elements], beginning with *prāṇa*, the living soul (*jīva*), having gone to heaven and other realms and experienced the fruits—
those fifteen types of experiences, both auspicious and inauspicious—
enjoys the world of mortals again by means of the sixteenth part. Thus it is said.
Except for this—
when the Lord acquires a body or departs from it, he carries away the six senses, including the mind, which remain established in their own nature.
Having taken these, it departs just as the wind carries scents from their source.

Thus, since movement is impossible for that which is without a substrate, it is established that the departure to the next world must be accepted as occurring through the specific conjunction of the self with its own substrate—the mind, the vital breath, the sense organs, and so forth—at the time of death, according to the Śruti: "Speech merges into fire; the eye merges into the sun; the mind merges into the moon. At the final moment...

Having raised the objection that the departure of the senses and other faculties to the next world along with the individual soul (jīva) is untenable—since scripture speaks of their dissolution into the presiding deities of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sense organs—the author refutes this:
"If it be argued [that they do not depart] because of the scriptural statement regarding their going to Agni and so forth, we say no, because that is figurative. (Sūtra 4).

Since, at the time of the separation of the living being from the gross body, there is the scriptural designation of the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other faculties into the deities presiding over them— such as fire (*agni*), wind (*vāta*), the sun (*āditya*), and the moon (*candra*) in the passage beginning "When this person has died, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, sight into the sun, and mind into the moon"— it follows that they do not depart along with the living being.

If it is argued that the scriptural teaching regarding the departure [of the senses] cannot be otherwise, we say no; for it is figurative, as it serves to indicate their distinctness [from the Self]. Thus: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself";
"The vital breaths do not depart from there, they are merged right there"; "Fire is established in my speech, speech in the heart, the heart in Me, I in the Immortal, and the Immortal in Brahman."

This is because [the passage] has as its subject matter the disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) of a Śiva-yogin who is free from attachment, aversion, and so forth, as established by such scriptural texts; otherwise, the contradiction with numerous other scriptural passages, such as "When he departs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows after him," would be unavoidable. Furthermore, there is the designation [of the soul] together with hair and the like that do not perish, as in: "The herbs [become] his body-hairs, the trees his hair."
The scriptural statement regarding the dissolution of the eye and other organs is determined to concern the sequential departure of the presiding deities; for in the Śruti passage,

"In this very fire the gods offer faith," it is observed that only faith (*śraddhā*) is offered into the first fire, known as the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), [and not substances such as] curd, milk, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that it is inconsistent for the world of heaven (dyuloka) to be the fire into which oblations are offered, [the Sūtra] says:
"If it be argued that this is not so because it is not heard of in the first [case], we say no, for it is those very [fires] that are intended, on account of the appropriateness. (5)

As for what was stated—that it is understood from the question and the answer that the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by subtle waters mixed with other elements—that is not tenable; because in the first oblation concerning the fire of the heavenly world, there is no scriptural mention of water being the substance to be offered, as it says: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith (śraddhā)."

If it is argued that faith alone is indeed heard in the scripture as the object to be offered, and that faith is well known as a particular modification of the mind belonging to the living being (jīva), and therefore water should not be offered there—[we reply]:
no, because those very waters are designated by the word "faith" in that context. Why? [Because of] the question.

Because a reply is appropriate [only if they are the same]. In the reply to the question, "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?", water is indeed mentioned at the outset as the substance to be offered into the fire of the heavenly world under the name of *śraddhā* (faith). If, in that context, the word *śraddhā* did not denote water, then the question would be one thing and the reply another, which would be inconsistent.

It may be so; however, the concluding summary of the response—"Thus, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"—indicates that *śraddhā* (faith) is indeed of the nature of water (*aptva*). Furthermore, the manner introduced in the question—"Do you know how...?"—is concluded by the word "thus" (*iti*) in the phrase "at the fifth [oblation]. [The sequence is: *śraddhā*, King Soma, rain, food, semen, and [the self].

For it is thus concluded that "the waters indeed have human speech. Furthermore, the Vedic usage of the word *śraddhā* (faith) with reference to water is observed in such passages as: "He leads forward the waters," and "The waters, indeed, are faith"; and "They offer faith as an oblation; from that oblation King Soma arises. Thus, it is only the transformation of the waters themselves into the form of Soma that is logically consistent. Therefore...

It is thus established that the individual soul (jīva) migrates enveloped by waters mixed with other elements. Therefore, it is the water itself—when offered in the form of curds, milk, and so forth—that is figuratively designated by the term "faith" (śraddhā).
But [an objection may be raised]: since in this context both the question and the answer refer specifically to water, it must be the performers of ritual actions alone [who are meant].
It has not been heard that [the sacrificial fires] go to heaven. To the question of how it is possible for the materials of the oblation to go along with them, he says:
"If it is argued that this is because it has not been heard, we say no, because those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* are known [to go]. (6)

As for what was further stated—that the meaning "the individual soul (jīva) goes enveloped by water" is understood from this sentence—that is not tenable, because the jīva is not mentioned in this sentence. For here, it is faith and the other elements in their specific states that are heard as being offered in sacrifice, but not the jīva enveloped by them. If this is your objection:

That is not so, because those who perform sacrifices and other rites are perceived [in the text]. Later on, it says: "Now, those here in the village who worship with the thought, 'Sacrifice and meritorious works, and what is given,' they pass into smoke; from smoke into night; from night into the waning half of the month;
from the waning half of the month into the southern progress of the sun; from the southern progress into the year; from the months... [and so forth].
From the world of the fathers to the world of the fathers, from the world of the fathers to the sun, from the sun to the moon—this is King Soma, the food of the gods;

the gods consume it. Having dwelt there for as long as their merits endure, they then return again by this very same path: as they came, they return to space; from space to air; having become air, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud.

Having become a cloud, it rains; from that [rain] arise here rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, beans, and so forth—and it becomes that very thing again. Thus, according to the Śruti, those performers of *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrifices and public works) who desire fruits devoid of the knowledge of Brahman become kings of the Soma in the heavenly world, having attained the fruit of their good deeds through a body composed of nectar.

Immediately after the enjoyment of that fruit, having returned to the world of mortals with one part remaining, they enter a womb. Here too, because of the recognition through the term "King Soma" in the passage, "In the fire of the heavenly world they offer faith; from that oblation King Soma arises," it follows that in those questions and answers as well, [the soul] is enveloped by water.

The individual soul (*jīva*), which is a constituent part consisting of that [water], is taught as being "the waters. Since the word denoting the body—which has as its sole essential nature the qualification of the soul—ultimately refers back to the soul itself as the qualified entity, it follows that the soul departs enveloped by them.
Now, even if it be granted that performers of ritual action go to the heavenly world, nevertheless, their enjoyment of that world is not established there. That...

In the Śruti passage stating "the gods consume [him]," it is established that those who have gone to heaven, whose actions are enveloped by divine bodies consisting of nectar, are consumed by the gods; since it is impossible for those performers of ritual action to experience enjoyment once they have been consumed by the gods—as if by tigers and other predators—the term "Soma, the King" does not refer to the individual soul (jīva). This is because it is illogical for the jīva to be the object of such consumption.
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"In the five stages beginning with 'devotion' (bhakta) and ending with 'refuge' (śaraṇa), duality is established; in the stage of 'oneness' (aikya), non-duality is established.
[Sūtra 7: "Or rather, it is figurative, because of the knowledge of the Self; or else, He shows it as such."

The word "but" (*pā*) sets aside the objection. If it is argued that this [self] is not the individual soul (*jīva*), because we see that King Soma—the food of the gods—is what the gods consume, and thus [the self in question] must be that [Soma], we reply: this state of being consumed is merely figurative;
it is taught that, by virtue of not knowing the Self, [the soul] exists as an instrument for the gods.
Moreover, because those who perform sacrifices and other rites do not know the Self, they exist as instruments of enjoyment for the gods both here and in the hereafter.

By performing worship through sacrifices and the like in this world, they serve [the gods]; having attained that world granted by the gods who are pleased by such worship, they become an instrument of enjoyment for them, sharing the same enjoyments there, just as a beast is for its masters. Thus is he [for the gods].

Thus the Śruti shows that those who do not know the Self serve as instruments for the gods. Smṛti also shows that those who know the Self attain Brahman, while those who do not know the Self become objects of enjoyment for the gods, as in the words: "Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods;
my devotees come to me too. Therefore, the intention is that the individual soul (jīva) serves as food for the gods.
The statement regarding [the gods] being "eaten" is therefore figurative. For it is heard in scripture that for the gods, satisfaction itself is the act of eating:
"Indeed, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar," so it is explained.
Therefore, those who perform good deeds but are devoid of knowledge of the Śiva-principle attain the status of servants to the gods; whereas he who [knows otherwise]—
"He who worships a deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like an animal to the gods," so it is declared in the Śruti.
Also in another Śruti: "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity, but does not reach the higher one."
From the scriptural observation that "one becomes worse," it follows that he who worships a deity other than Śiva— such as Upendra and others—

through sacrificial rites and the like, is distinct from Indra and the rest; [thinking] "I am other than Candra, Upendra, and so forth," he worships Māyā as Prakṛti and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā (māyin).
This entire world is pervaded by that which arises from His constituent parts.

Thus, whoever abandons the realization that living beings such as Brahmā, Upendra, and others are portions of Śiva—established by the Śruti—and worships them with a sense of duality, does not know the reality of Śiva. Just as a beast of burden, such as an ox, assists through plowing and other labors, so too [does he serve].

Even one engaged in ritual action (*karmaṭha*) benefits like a beast, performing the offering of oblations (*havis*) to Indra and the other gods in this world, and likewise performing service for them in the next world. Thus, by virtue of being merely a "beast of the gods," practitioners of ritual action become food for the gods; however, it is not as with tigers and the like that the gods consume the flesh, blood, and so forth of those performers of rituals. Therefore, in those respective worlds...
Because they partake of the nectar (*amṛta*), they do not consume flesh. The ultimate meaning here is as follows:

for those performers of action who are attached to fruits, there is the attainment of enjoyment in that world; whereas for those of virtuous action who have offered [their deeds] to Śiva, having attained purity of mind through the destruction of sin, [they attain liberation] by means of hearing, reflection, and meditation, aided by faith, devotion, dispassion, and so forth.
The attainment of the state of Śiva is thus determined by such scriptural passages as: "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the bestower of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else," and:
"Those people who, thinking of no other, worship me with devotion."
For those who are constantly devoted to Me, I provide for their well-being and security.

In such Smṛtis, non-dual devotion (*ananyabhakti*) is taught as the cause for Śiva’s grace, whereby one attains identity with Śiva; nevertheless, devotion must still be practiced. Likewise, in the Śaiva tradition, Vyāsa spoke to Śiva:
"O Sāmba, although upon the disappearance of duality you are 'I' and I am not 'you'."
For a wave is indeed oceanic, yet the ocean is not merely a wave.

Thus it has been correctly taught. Therefore, the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is as follows: because the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) exists for devotees within the five stages beginning with devotion (*bhakti*) and ending with refuge (*śaraṇa*), there is the attainment of non-duality (*advaita*) through the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—like that of a river and the ocean—as established by hundreds of such scriptural texts as "The Lord and the soul... and so forth, wherein Śiva and the soul stand in the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper, and master and servant.
Nevertheless, the state of both difference and non-difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) remains unimpeded, according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves.

Therefore, the resultant meaning demonstrated is that those who know the Self are instruments of the Supreme Lord, while those who do not know the Self are instruments of the gods; thus, in every respect, the bound soul, being completely enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), [attains] heaven and so forth.
It is established that [the soul] proceeds. This concludes the section concerning the passing away of what has been performed (Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇa). || 2 ||

Since the individual soul (jīva) descends to the world of mortals while still possessing residual karma, one might ask: "Granted that those who have performed meritorious deeds go to the heavenly world, how is it that they return from there after having experienced its enjoyments? In response to this doubt, the author demonstrates the manner of that return through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
Upon the exhaustion of the performed [karman], one who possesses a residue (anuśaya) returns by the same way and not by that way, according to what is seen and what is remembered. || 8 ||

When there is the exhaustion—that is, the destruction—of the merit performed with the aim of heaven upon the completion of its results, [the soul returns] by that same path by which it went from here toward the heavenly world; or else, by another path? The suggestion that it might be by another path is rejected as being without foundation. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that it returns by that very same path. [The soul returns] possessing residual karma (anuśaya).

Being "remnant" (śiṣṭa)—meaning one who possesses the accumulated karma remaining after what has been experienced—he returns to the world of mortals and attains a birth corresponding to that [karma] in accordance with his actions. Why? Because of "perception and tradition," which means because of Śruti and Smṛti.
For those who perform only the rites of *iṣṭāpūrta* and *datta*, [he returns] by way of the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*) beginning with smoke, in accordance with the fruits of their karma.
Having experienced the enjoyments of heaven, the return at that very moment is declared;

for in such scriptural passages as "having dwelt there until the exhaustion of their merit, they return again by this same path," the soul’s return after the conclusion of its enjoyment is designated, whether through the exhaustion of all karma or by means of a specific karma.
It is doubted whether [the soul] descends.

It is logical that there is a return upon the exhaustion of all karma. *Anuśaya* is the remainder of karma that has not yet been experienced; and that remains no longer when the enjoyment of the entire store of karma has been completed. Having dwelt there until the exhaustion of its momentum (*yāvat-saṃpātam*), it then follows this very same path...

Furthermore, immediately following the scriptural statement "they return again," it says: "Having not reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here, from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of karma.
Moreover, in passages such as "as this [person] reaches space, from space to air," and so forth, there is no mention whatsoever of the persistence of residual karma.

Regarding the scriptural passage "until the falling together" (*yāvatsampātam*), it is explained that *sampāta* refers to the aggregate of karma; thus, "until the falling together" means not exceeding that aggregate. Since it is stated that the soul dwells there and experiences that [result], one might conclude that the soul descends only at the conclusion of the enjoyment of the fruits of all its karma. To this, we reply:
The individual soul (jīva), possessing latent tendencies (anuśaya) and having residual karma, descends back to the mortal world. Why? From both Śruti and Smṛti:
"When their merit is exhausted, they enter the mortal world;
and when there is residual good karma, having returned again to the world of beings, they perform action once more."
Out of delusion, he performs [actions] again at the time of his end, and thus he repeatedly resorts to the heavenly worlds and other realms.

Furthermore: "Those here whose conduct has been pleasant are likely to obtain a pleasant birth—a Brahmin birth, a Kṣatriya birth, or a Vaiśya birth; whereas those here whose conduct has been foul are likely to obtain a foul birth—a dog birth, a pig birth, or a Caṇḍāla birth."

Regarding those who have descended [to earth], it is heard in scripture: "Among those who have descended from that world, those of pleasant conduct—meaning those of pleasant deeds—attain a pleasant womb, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa or others; whereas those of foul conduct—meaning those of despicable deeds—attain a foul womb, such as that of a dog, a pig, or a Caṇḍāla. Thus, for those who have descended, there is merit.

Smṛti also states: "The castes and stages of life, being devoted to their own duties, after experiencing the fruits of their actions in the hereafter, are then—by the remainder of those fruits—reborn with distinctions of place, caste, family, form, lifespan, learning, wealth, conduct, and intelligence;
and by the remainder of the fruit of action, [they obtain] birth, form, caste, strength, intellect, wisdom, and possessions."
He undertakes the performance of dharma, thinking: "That [dharma] proceeds as easily as a wheel in both worlds.

The phrase "until the exhaustion of its momentum" (*yāvat-sampātam*) refers specifically to those particular karmas that have begun to yield their fruit. The statement "whatever he does here" also refers to that same category. This applies to those whose fruits have not yet been experienced and for whom no atonement has been performed.
Furthermore, the destruction of actions through the experience of the fruits of other actions is also untenable.

Therefore, having gone to that world, they return again with their residual karma (*sānuśaya*) "as they went and not as they went"—meaning they return by the same manner of ascent and by a different manner. For the ascent was [by way of] smoke...

And because the world of the ancestors and so forth would not be reached otherwise, [the soul] does not depart immediately; for if it were not so, the experience of pleasure and pain upon being reborn would not be possible.
Therefore, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that the soul returns accompanied by residual karma (anuśaya). This concludes the investigation into the meaning of the word "conduct" (caraṇa).

Now, as for the claim that those who perform Vedic rituals return [to this world] according to the Śruti text "those of pleasant conduct," that is inconsistent; for in such Śruti passages as "by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," it is taught that through the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya), there is liberation characterized by non-return. Regarding the phrase "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*): [it refers to those whose conduct is auspicious].

Anticipating the objection that [the term "foot"] might refer solely to devotion to the purity, sipping of water, bathing, twilight prayers, and so forth as enjoined by the Smṛti, he says: || 122 || "If it be argued that [it refers to the foot], no; Kārṣṇājini holds that it is for the purpose of indicating [all such practices]. || 9 ||

Regarding the terms "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*) and "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇa*), Kārṣṇājini maintains that the word *caraṇa* (conduct) is intended to indicate merit and demerit; for the word *caraṇa* is well-known in both worldly usage and the Veda as referring to the performance of virtuous rites such as those prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti. Indeed, the practice of Śrauta and Smārta rites according to good custom is what is celebrated as *caraṇa*.

"By that alone there shall be purification of the mind, and from that they go to the supreme state"— thus says the Śruti. With a concentrated mind, I shall declare for you that which is approved by the *Caraṇa-Śruti* of one who has taken up the *liṅga*, and which is well-known in the *Smṛtis*, *Tantras*, and *Purāṇas*.
The Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti, which rests upon the obligatory and occasional rites.
A twice-born man, free from desire, should establish a connection between the liṅga and his own body;
through the performance of prescribed duties, purification of the mind will certainly arise.
Through the purification of the mind, devotion arises; that devotion is unswerving.
Through it, knowledge is born and the ignorance of the self is destroyed.
Therefore, liberation [arises] from that; one should properly perform the action prescribed by the injunctions.

By such passages, it is clearly taught even in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* that the word *caraṇa* refers to the conduct prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) and the Smṛtis (*smārta*). Indeed, worldly people consider *caraṇa*, *ācāra*, *śīla*, and *vṛtta* to be synonyms. And in the Veda: "Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, not others."

The other good deeds that we have performed should be emulated by you. Speak the truth, practice righteousness, do not drink liquor, do not eat *kalañja*, do not go to another's wife, and do not speak falsehood; thus he establishes the mark of all [virtues].
In such Vedic passages as "The hand-mantra is purifying," "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may I become the sustainer of immortality;

may my body be full of discernment," and so forth, the performance of virtuous deeds consisting of [ritual] conduct is for the purpose of purifying the mind, which serves as the foundation for devotion to Paramaśiva.
It is designated as such. Therefore, by the word *caraṇa*, which denotes right conduct (*sadācāra*), there is meant that which consists of the conduct prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis;

this is considered to be for the purpose of indicating the rites (*karma*) of the Śrutis and Smṛtis, which lead to the supreme state—designated as the eternal abode of auspiciousness, free from rebirth, unsurpassed, incomparable, and supreme. By the word *caraṇa*, which expresses the meaning of right conduct, [the aforementioned is intended].

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that, according to the theory of non-exclusive indication (*hyajahallakṣaṇā*), ritual action is enjoined as having the Vedic and Smṛti-based conduct as its constituent parts.

Now, regarding the excellence of such conduct: surely, by the mere performance of Vedic rites, [one does not attain the goal] in the same way as one attains it through the performance of optional Smṛti-based rites which serve as causes for pleasure and pain.
Anticipating the objection that, if there were a designation of returning [to this world], all the Vedas would be as purposeless as human compositions and so forth, he says in response to that:
"If it be argued that they are purposeless, no; because they depend upon that. (Sūtra 10)

If it is argued that, just like the performance of Smṛti-based optional rites (*kāmyakarma*), the practice of Śruti-based rites would also result in rebirth and worldly prosperity as their fruits— and thus, since both are equal in this regard, the Śruti-based rites would be rendered purposeless— the answer is no, because [the Smṛti] is dependent upon that [Śruti]. Just as the commands of a minister are made manifest in accordance with the command of a king, so too does the Smṛti follow the meaning of the Śruti.

According to reason, since the *smṛti* is dependent upon that [the Veda], there is no contradiction in the superiority of the Veda. Furthermore: "If one seeks to understand the meaning of the Veda by oneself, a great transgression would occur;
therefore, a wise person should cause the meaning of the Veda to be grasped through the *smṛtis*, the *tantras*, and the *purāṇas*."
Thus, because restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) are observed even in the Smṛtis regarding the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda; moreover:
"A man devoid of right conduct becomes censured in the world;
therefore, a wise man should possess right conduct until the fall of the body."
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct; indeed, the scriptures do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct.
For even the ritual acts prescribed by the Vedas do not purify one devoid of right conduct, nor does a teacher purify one who is devoid of right conduct.

From such statements as these, since it is taught that only those qualified for the Smārta rites are qualified for the Śrauta rites, the relationship between the two is that of the subsidiary and the principal (*aṅga-aṅgitva*) according to the maxim: "When X exists, Y exists. Therefore, even though there exists a distinction between superior, middling, and so forth, between the two, their cause of liberation is through a traditional succession; this is the intention of the teacher Kārṣṇājini. Hence, the *Caraṇa-śruti* [is established].
It is conventionally described as being for the purpose of indicating karma.
Furthermore, it is through the ritual action prescribed by the Vedas alone— according to the maxim of the "gross Arundhatī"—
that it serves as the cause for the purification of the mind and, subsequently, for the knowledge of Vedānta.
If you do not accept that this [knowledge] has as its fruit the unsurpassed supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), which results in non-returning, then [the scripture says]:
"A Brahmin, having examined the worlds acquired through action, should arrive at detachment; there is nothing uncreated [that can be attained] by means of what is created."
For the sake of realizing that, he should approach a teacher alone— one who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman— with fuel in his hand.

"Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality. "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. "Knowing the Lord, they become immortal. "From meditating upon Him, from uniting with Him, and from becoming His true nature, there follows at last the cessation of all illusion. "Knowing Him alone, one attains immortality."
The contradiction with hundreds of non-human (apauruṣeya) scriptural passages, such as "There is no other path for going," would be difficult to avoid.
Following his own preference, he demonstrates the intention of another teacher and then states his own view:
"Good and evil deeds alone are what is denoted by the word 'conduct' (caraṇa)."
"But Bādari [holds that it consists] only of good and evil deeds. || 11 ||

In the passage "those of pleasant conduct" (ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ) and "those of foul conduct" (kapūyacaraṇāḥ), the word *caraṇa* denotes *sukṛta* (good deeds) and *duṣkṛta* (evil deeds) by its primary power (*śakti*). This is because the term *carati* is used for actions— as in "he performs a meritorious act" (*puṇyaṃ karma ācarati*) or "he performs a sinful act" (*pāpaṃ karma ācarati*)—
and because there is a separate mention [of conduct] from [the acts themselves].

This is because it is logical to apply the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), as the subject matter is established by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) and by Vedic revelation inferred from established custom (*ācāra*).

Since a primary sense is possible, it is not proper to resort to a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, the teacher Bādari maintains that "good and evil deeds" alone are what is denoted by the word *caraṇa*. In this regard, the view of Bādari alone is his own position.

However, it is accepted that the result of the twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and other rites—enjoined by *śruti* inferred from *ācāra*—is the fulfillment of eligibility for other ritual acts. Alternatively, since a principal rite devoid of its auxiliary parts cannot produce a result, Vedic action produces results only when accompanied by *ācāra*. Therefore, one must accept that the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*) functions through non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*).
It is thus determined. Therefore, it is established that those who descend do so while still possessing latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*).
This concludes the section concerning those who perform undesirable actions and the like. 3.
Having experienced great suffering in hell, those who have committed evil deeds obtain a sinful birth according to the specific nature of those actions;
likewise, while the performance of sacrifices, public works, and gifts leads the virtuous to the attainment of the heavenly world, for those who have committed evil deeds—
In response to the doubt as to what their destination is, he says:
"And it is heard [in scripture] regarding those who perform undesirable acts and so forth. (12) || 125 ||
Regarding those who perform undesirable acts and evil deeds, although there is the scriptural statement that they see Yama (Vaivasvata) according to the instructions of his messengers, nevertheless,

because of the Vedic vision stating, "All who depart from this world go indeed to the moon," the attainment of both meritorious and non-meritorious worlds occurs through the gateway of the lunar orb for both of them. Thus...

The experience of hell by evildoers cannot be prevented; for in the Śruti, there is instruction regarding the movement of those who perform both desired and undesired deeds to the lunar orb. Thus, it is considered whether or not evildoers, like doers of good deeds, have an experience of heaven.

Since the scripture states, "All who depart from this world go indeed to the moon," and thus describes the destination of all performers of both meritorious and non-meritorious deeds without distinction, it follows that both types of persons experience heaven; to this we reply:

Although the Śruti states, "All those who perform undesirable acts and so forth go to the moon," and thus the ascent of evildoers to the lunar world is heard, it is nonetheless determined that sinners attain hell according to their own karma. Furthermore, in another Śruti, it is stated that by the command of Yama, the evildoer must experience the fruit [of his actions] before [proceeding further].

By the remainder of that [merit], he goes to the world of mortals day after day; it is not otherwise for evildoers. Just as a doer of good deeds, having been seen by the soldiers of Śamana and by their command, proceeds to the heavenly world through his virtuous karma, so too does the wise man, having reached the Moon, [proceeds] past the soldiers of Vaivasvata.
Having first beheld Vaivasvata, he then indeed proceeds to heaven.
The evil-minded one,
having seen Yama through the gateway of the moon by means of his own cruel deeds that end with the son of Vivasvat, [is led away] according to his own karma.
One falls into a most terrible hell characterized by suffering.
Thus it is heard in the Skanda Purāṇa. Therefore, although both [the doer and the non-doer] attain the moon, the evildoer— according to his own karma—
experiences most terrible suffering in hell in the world of Yama by its command, and subsequently attains a contemptible womb according to the specific nature of his various actions.
Because living beings are designated as the bearers of Yama’s commands, inert *karma* does not possess independence;

for in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*," "One should perform the twilight worship day after day," "Otherwise one goes to hell," and "From merit comes heaven, from sin comes hell," it is *karma* itself that is seen to be the agent of Yama.
Anticipating the objection as to how it is possible for [the Lord] to bestow the experience of the merit and demerit created by living beings, he says regarding that point:
"But for others, after experiencing [their results] in Saṃyamana, there is ascent and descent, because their course is seen [in scripture]. (1.2.13)

Just as in the world a ruler punishes evildoers according to their deeds, so too, by the decree of Yama, those who have performed good and evil deeds are restrained in hell according to their own evil karma. Having experienced that, there is ascent and descent; having first reached hell, one returns again due to the remainder of that karma.

And thus, such ascents and descents must be accepted; why? Because their movement is observed. In passages such as "The son of Vivasvat, the restrainer of people, King Yama," there is the designation that living beings (jīvas) carry out the commands of Yama; therefore, inert karma alone does not possess independence.
Therefore, the doctrine of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, which holds that karma alone is the cause and is primary, is indeed contradicted by scripture, reasoning, and experience.
This is because it establishes Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, as the agent of Vaivasvata and others;
for [it is Śiva who acts] through Vaivasvata himself as the regulator of the merit and demerit performed by individual souls. Thus, [the agency of the Supreme Brahman remains].
Fearing that [the injunction] would be purposeless, he says regarding that point:
"And they remember" (1.3.14).

In such scriptural passages as "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, He alone causes one to perform good deeds," they remember that the quality of being the controller of all beings, beginning with Brahmā, belongs to Śiva alone. Therefore, agency according to the capacity of those individual souls (jīvas) is appropriate for Him alone and not for another. Hence [it is said]: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises."

In such passages as "From fear of Him, fire, Indra, and death as the fifth run away," the state of being the cause of fear for all the gods, beginning with the Wind, is observed. Just as in the world, although ministers and others may possess the capacity to investigate actions performed by people in accordance with the king's commands and to deliver their respective fruits, [they do so only under his authority].

In that same way, although Vaivasvata also possesses the capacity to judge the merit and demerit of all beings and to bestow their respective destinies by the command of Śiva, the agency for those acts is attributed to Śiva alone.
He alone is Viṣṇu, he is the vital breath, he is time, he is fire, and he is the moon;
he alone is everything that has been and all that is to be, the eternal.

"He entered from within to the innermost," as stated in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "He who is Rudra in fire," and so forth; thus, His status as the material cause of all and the inner controller of all is taught.
Likewise, by the command of Śiva, [the powers] named Hari, Brahmā, Rudra, Mṛtyu, Yama, and others [are manifested].
For even through engagement in all activities, the agency therein indeed belongs to Śiva.
The work of a servant who acts solely by the king’s command is not appropriate for him;
the work of one whose mind is focused exclusively on Śiva cannot even be conceived.
Thus, from this scriptural vision, it is established that the status of being the creator of Vaivasvata and the others belongs to no one else.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"Also seven" (sūtra 1.3.15).

It is clearly taught in the Śruti that even the seven hells, beginning with Raurava, were created by the Supreme Lord as the destinations for evildoers. Therefore, it is He alone who, acting as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of Yama, is taught to be the bestower of the fruits of happiness and suffering upon those who have performed good and evil deeds. And so says the Smṛti:
Having fashioned many hells suitable for the residence of sinners,
Mahādeva designated seven among them as the principal ones.
"He created the Raurava and other hells characterized by great suffering"—
from this observation, Śiva’s exclusive authority [over the administration of retribution] is established without obstruction.
Now, one might object that in such passages as "the son of Vivasvat, the restrainer of people, King Yama," and so forth...

Anticipating the objection that, because Yama is established as having the authority to discipline all living beings independently of the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), it would be difficult to avoid the conclusion that Śiva is likewise merciless if he were the agent of that action, [the author] says regarding this:
"In that case too, there is no contradiction, because it is due to His activity. (Sūtra 16)

Even in that case, although Yama acts as the presiding officer over the investigation of the meritorious and non-meritorious actions of all living beings, there is no contradiction with the previously cited Śruti, Smṛti, Āgama, and other texts which establish that the Supreme Lord Parameśvara— Paramaśiva, who is Brahman— is the possessor of all authority, for Yama’s activity is ultimately determined by His.

Just as even a compassionate lord inflicts punishment upon his sons and others for violating his commands, so too does the Supreme Lord, by way of bestowing torments in the world of Yama according to their respective deeds upon those who perform undesirable acts and transgress the path of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama— which constitute His commands— does He indeed [act].
There would be a loss of supreme compassion.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that those who perform desirable and undesirable deeds may experience the fruits of heaven, hell, and so forth; but what is the destiny of the devotees who have attained the knowledge of Śiva? To this, he says:
Because "of knowledge and action" is the subject under discussion [in the preceding sūtra]. || 17 ||

"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; concerning this, it has been declared: 'Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. He who knows that which is hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest ether—he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman.
Thus [it is said]. [One should meditate upon] the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly tranquil.
Having meditated, the Sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness.

"In those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, all are completely liberated"; "He establishes the all-pervading mark; the wise man burns away the bond by the practice of meditation and churning upon the mantra that is the purifier of the hand"; "From meditating upon That, from union with That, and from becoming the reality of That, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion"—in hundreds of such scriptural passages.

For one established in the knowledge of Śiva, because [the practices] of meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), worship (pūjā), and so forth— both external and internal— are established by way of the path of the Suṣumṇā, which is designated as the Brahma-nāḍī;

[this applies] to those householders who are firmly established in the knowledge of Śiva, assisted by the pacification of the three defects of desire and by self-restraint (śama) and tranquility (dama).

Union with Śiva, whose nature is the glory of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), and the threefold liberation beginning with *sālokya*, whose nature is the glory of auspicious manifestation, are designated according to the distinction of qualified aspirants;

[the former] for those distinguished by devotion to Him, and [the latter] for those who rely on rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which take the form of the command of Paramaśiva, via the path of the gods (*devayāna*).

The experience of the bliss of the heavenly world (*svarloka*) for those others who do not transgress the paths of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Āgama*, as well as the experience of terrible suffering in the world of Yama for evildoers according to their respective actions, is thus determined.
Now, one might object: [what of] those performers of rites such as those based on the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, which constitute the command of Paramaśiva?

Anticipating the objection that even for those devoid of the means such as meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and worship (*upāsanā*), the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya* is possible, he states in response to that:
"Not in the third [state], because it is not observed to be so. (Sūtra 3.4.18)

For those who proceed on the third path of liberation, being solely devoted to Śiva, the attainment of heaven or hell resulting from merit or demerit is not possible, because such [attainment] has been perceived [as non-existent for them].
When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman—
Then the wise one, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality.

Since hundreds of such scriptural passages teach that devotees attain only Śiva, who is distinct from merit and demerit, and since even in other Vedas— such as "Thus Viṣṇu, the knower of the Supreme, being born, the Great One, protects the third"— the word "Great" (bṛhat) refers to Ādiviṣṇu, and it is taught therein that he protects Kailāsa, the third [world].
Brahman is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than that which is higher than the highest;
He who is the supreme Lord beyond even that—may my mind be intent upon auspicious resolve for Him.
In such passages as these, the superiority of Maheśvara—the third [deity] in relation to Brahmā and Viṣṇu—is taught.
Likewise, in the Smṛti:
"The primordial Viṣṇu, the great knower, [arose] from Mahādeva Sadāśiva."
Having been born, he attained the supreme abode, the third realm of eternal glory.
Born from a portion of Gaurī’s power, he always protects Kailāsa— the bestower of the fruits of prosperity upon his devotees— through his devotion to Śiva.

Based on this teaching, it is instructed that a devotee of Śiva should always remain established in the state of Śiva— even regarding the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and individual soul— by means of the scriptural wisdom in the form of Śiva’s command, which pervades all times and all conditions.

Some here [hold that] in the statement, "All of them go to the moon alone," the word "all" (*sarva*) must be accepted as having its scope restricted; having thus established that it refers exclusively to those of meritorious deeds, they cite: "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they pass into the light (*arciḥ*); and those who here in the village..."

They say that by such passages as, "Those who worship with the thought, 'Sacrifices and works of public utility are charity'—they pass into smoke," it is established that the path of the gods (devayāna) has knowledge (*vidyā*) as its object, while the path of the fathers (pitṛyāna) is devoted to meritorious works (*puṇyakarman*). Nevertheless, this does not contradict our own position; for according to that view, there is a restriction (*saṅkoca*) of the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, the undesirable consequence of the aforementioned defects, such as the lack of scope for traditional Smṛti texts, would be difficult to avoid.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"And it is also recorded in common worldly usage" (Sūtra 1.3.24).

Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛtis that even in this world, devotees experience the fruits of their meritorious and sinful actions. Previously, those who dedicated their actions to Śiva now experience the unsurpassed bliss of Śiva-yoga and Śiva-jñāna;
and by virtue of having a nature forever distinct from the forest fire of the three types of suffering and the heat of saṃsāra, they [are transformed] through this prior remembrance of Śiva.

It is recorded in the Smṛti that one who possesses good deeds dedicated to Śiva [attains such rewards]. For those who perform meritorious deeds, there is the attainment of elephants, horses, kingdoms, wealth, and grain;
for those who commit evil deeds, there is blindness, deafness, muteness, and so forth.
Therefore, even by the force of worldly convention, this threefold experience is pointed out even by common folk.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 133 || "And because it is observed" || 20 ||

"I am devoted to all of them; this one is meritorious, this one is demeritorious"—this is not mere recollection (smaraṇa), according to the principle that "recollection is knowledge produced by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of prior experience," like the recollection of the experience of bliss in deep sleep;
rather, it is so because it is seen through the statements of the Śruti, verbal testimony, and direct experience, regarding both the devotees and those who perform meritorious deeds.

[It is] the state of being the enjoyer of the fruits of both the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Regarding sinners, however, you know the answer to the question "How is it that this world is not filled? [which is given in the passage]: "Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small creatures that return again and again; 'be born and die'—this is the third station."

Therefore, that world is not filled; so it is heard in the Śruti. Having experienced great suffering in the terrible hells such as Raurava and others due to their evil deeds, those who [worship] Śiva—the Lord with Ambā, the teacher of all worlds, the Supreme—are seen to again initiate a body in anticipation of the fifth oblation.
Having cast off anxiety, he remained deluded by the desire for the three worlds for many days.
He indeed spends his time in vain in this world,
his chest constantly beaten by the servants of Yama with a body known as *yātanā* (torment).
Having seized him in the middle of that path, he, filled with terrible suffering,
[drags him] to the waters of the great Vaitaraṇī in front of the gateway of Yama.
Then, their bodies being tormented in that terrible place crowded with flames of fire,
they reach Yama by his command according to the ordinance of their own karma.
Having experienced suffering again and again in all the hells, beginning with Raurava, they likewise [return] to the surface of the earth by means of the remainder of their karma.
By the very sequence of the wheel’s rim, one is always born and dies;
one attains birth as a womb-born, egg-born, and so forth—of this there is no doubt.

Thus, it is well known even in the Purāṇas that for evildoers there occurs, in the midst of the path to the world of Yama, punishment by his servants with bodies of torment; thereafter, by the command of Vaivasvata, the attainment of most terrible hells; and following that, the attainment of the fourfold collection of beings, such as those born from eggs, according to their own karma.
However, some argue that the word "third" in the Sūtra refers to hell, because they observe the usage of hell as the "third station" in the Śruti passage: "Be born and die—this is the third station.
They maintain this because such a thing is not perceived in the third [station] in that manner.
[They cite: "Thus Viṣṇu, the knower of the Supreme, being born, the great one, protects the third. Likewise, "the knower..."
"Having shaken off merit and demerit, the stainless one attains supreme equality"— in such scriptural passages as these, it is said:
"To those who have been purified through many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śrutis and Smṛtis, who are dispassionate and awakened, Maheśvara becomes gracious."
When [the Lord] is pleased, one shall be liberated; being liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva.
Even for that mortal who possesses but little devotion, after three births at most—

In such Smṛtis and Āgamas as well, the third status of the supreme state—the state of Śiva in the form of liberation—which is distinct from both sin and merit, is clearly taught. As for the phrase "of knowledge and action" (*vidyākarmaṇoḥ*) [in the sūtra], it is because that is the subject at hand; for in the preceding sūtra, the context of knowledge and action was demonstrated, and this is supported by the evidence of position, context, and indicative mark.

Because it would contradict injunctions stating that "the intended meaning of the Śruti and Sūtras must be known," and because in the Purāṇas and other texts the term "Brahman"— characterized by non-return and unsurpassed bliss—
is seen to be situated above the worlds of hell and heaven, the scriptural mention of hell as being "third" is figurative.

It is thus determined. But surely, [this is so] because of the contradiction with the scripture regarding the fifth oblation in the Purāṇas and other texts, and because of the instruction on the threefold classification beginning with "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*), "born from a living being" (*jīvaja*), and "sprout-born" (*udbhija*) in the Śruti, as in the case of the one born from a jar (*kumbhasambhava*).

Anticipating the objection that there is a mutual contradiction between the scripture prescribing the fifth oblation and the scripture teaching the fourfold collection of beings, he says regarding that point:
"The inclusion by the word 'third' refers to that which is born from heat. (2.3.21)
The scriptural authority that prescribes the commencement of the body— namely, the Śruti text stating, "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'"—
and the Purāṇic authority that prescribes the origin of those born from jars and so forth, as well as the injunction "One must not harm any living beings," [are all consistent].

The scripture (*śruti*) possesses a general character because of its utility in all cases. For example, the scripture "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma" has a specific character because it is restricted to that alone; likewise, [the passage] "He whose desire is truth, whose resolve is truth;
from his mind the moon was born, from his eye the sun was born" has a specific character, as does [the passage] "He whose desire is truth, whose resolve is truth; from his mind the moon..."
In such passages as "When [the sun] was born, the sun was born from the eye," the Lord Supreme possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*).

According to the principle that there is no difference between the object of meditation and the meditator, we observe that great beings such as Viśvāmitra and others—who were devotees of Him—possessed true resolve and thereby manifested the diverse creation of the universe. This is evident from the scripture that ordains the fifth oblation (*pañcamāhuti*).
It is determined that [the text] refers to beings who perform meritorious and non-meritorious actions, distinct from the causal Puruṣa.

Furthermore, even regarding the creation of the Supreme Lord, there is no stain of doubt because the four classes of living beings—such as those born from eggs and so forth—are clearly indicated; for those born from moisture and those born from sweat are included within the category of those born from sprouts (udbhijja), thus there are indeed only three [classes].

The term "seeds" (bījāni) does not contradict the scriptural establishment of a threefold classification; rather, it should be understood to include objects such as trees, creepers, mountains, and so forth. Therefore, because the scriptural statement, "All of them go to the moon alone," cannot be restricted in its scope, it applies to all performers of meritorious and non-meritorious deeds who have attained birth as either egg-born or womb-born beings.
Indeed, the instruction regarding the fifth oblation preceded by the attainment of the moon is not contradictory.
The Section on Attaining That Essential Nature (Tatsvābhāvyāpattyadhikaraṇa) || 4 ||
The manner in which those who perform meritorious deeds return from heaven;

previously, how evildoers attain hell in the world of Yama and subsequently reach blindness in this world; in that context, for the sake of discerning sinners, [the text provides] examples according to which there are devotees who are exempt from rebirth.

And a discussion regarding those who perform meritorious deeds has been undertaken. In that context, to resolve the doubt as to how those who perform meritorious deeds return again from heaven, the author states another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) for the purpose of elaborating upon that:
"The attainment of that nature [of the world] occurs because it is logical. (2.3.22)

It has been stated previously that those whose natures are characterized by good deeds descend from heaven along with a subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) produced from the subtle elements, driven by the specific force of their own karma. Here, the manner of that descent is demonstrated:
"Then they return again by this very path as they came—to space; from space, to air; having become air..."

"Smoke arises; having become smoke, it becomes mist; having become mist, it becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, it rains"—from hearing such scriptural passages, those who perform sacrifices and other rites and return again from the heavenly world attain the ether and so forth. Thus, there is the attainment of ether and the subsequent stages.
A doubt arises as to whether the state of [becoming] ether and so forth, like the states of gods, humans, and others, is merely the attainment of similarity to them.

When it is argued that—in passages such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—those whose nature is merit experience the enjoyment of the heavenly world, and therefore they must also possess that very nature during the interval [between lives] and thus experience those [etheric] enjoyments, we reply: [The state of becoming ether and so forth is not a literal transformation, but rather a mere attainment of similarity.]
"Attainment of that nature" means attaining similarity to that; why is this so? Because it is logically consistent.

For in the case of becoming the moon or becoming a human being, one assumes that state for the sake of experiencing pleasure and pain. However, in the case of [becoming] space and so forth, since there is an absence of the experience of pleasure and pain, the assumption of such a state is impossible; therefore, this is the response.

This intends to convey that they have attained a similarity [to the gods] produced by association with them. For those whose merit is exhausted, only their connection [with the body] is logical; enjoyment is not possible for them within those [bodies].
This is an elliptical indication: even in the absence of a gross body until they reach a new birth, they exist by means of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
It is determined that this is because they lack the capacity for enjoyment in the midst of those [worlds]. This concludes the section on "Not Too Long" (Nāticirādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||

In response to the doubt that while [the soul] moves quickly through space and so forth, it experiences a slight delay in grains and the like, and even its stay in places such as the sky is only for a single day per location rather than for many years, he speaks by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
Not after a very long time, because of the distinction. || 23 ||

There arises a doubt as to whether those performers of rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* who act out of desire for rewards, upon descending from heaven, abide for a long time or for a short time while passing through the elements such as space (*vyoman*).
[The opponent's view is: "From space comes air," and so forth; thus, there is a long duration of stay in the elemental stages such as space.

And the attainment of those respective forms is understood— furthermore, in the Śruti passage, "Here rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans are born," the state of being rice, barley, and so forth is shown immediately after the rain; therefore, [this applies] to the individual soul (jīva) in each respective case.
When it is argued that they must remain for a long time, it is replied: "Not after a very long time."

Why? Because of the distinction. Since, with reference to the subsequent attainment of rice, barley, and so forth, there is a specific statement regarding the difficulty of emergence—namely, "From that, indeed, it is more difficult to emerge"—it follows that upon reaching space and the other stages, the emergence is understood to be rapid.
In the phrase "ato vai khalu durniṣprapataram," the elision of the letter *t* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. [The word is] *durniṣprapataram*.

The meaning is that it is the means for more easily escaping from suffering. Therefore, after the connection with space and the other elements, there is a painful exit for those performing ritual actions during the stage of rice, barley, and so forth; through the medium of food, their connection with a person occurs after a lapse of time. The delay lasts from the beginning of the sprout until the completion of the grain.

The intended meaning is understood to be that even immediately after the grain has emerged, there is a slight delay due to its being cast into a granary or similar vessel. Therefore, it is determined that there is rapidity in the case of space and so forth, while there is a slight delay in the case of rice and other grains.
The Section Concerning the Superintendence by Another (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa). || 6 ||
Having experienced the enjoyment of that [state] with a dull body acquired through evil deeds among rice and other [plants], those of meritorious deeds again take up a birth in a virtuous womb;
for it is observed everywhere that the manner of experiencing happiness belongs to the meritorious even among rice, barley, and so forth.

In response to the doubt—namely, whether there might be an experience of bliss there, similar to the experience of the bliss of heaven, because of the designation of its long-term duration—it is said:
"Because of the mention [of it] as being presided over by another, as before. (Sūtra 24)

"In what is presided over by another" means in rice, barley, and other plants which are presided over—that is, assisted—by other individual souls who identify with those plants; for those whose nature is merit, enjoyment consists merely in their remaining there for a long period of time. Why?
Because of the description being as before—as in the case of space and so forth, it is the same regarding rice, barley, and the rest.
For in this scripture, only the mere relationship [of the self to the body] is stated;

thus, the experience of pleasure and pain arising from wind, heat, rain, and so forth belongs only to those living beings who identify with the bodies of stationary things such as rice and barley, and not to those whose nature consists of the merit they have acquired, because they are like travelers [who do not identify with the place].
It is heard in scripture that descending souls are born in the form of rice, barley, and so forth; "having become clouds, they rain down;

these are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. Do these [souls] project rice and the like already presided over by other enjoyers possessing bodies of rice and so forth, or are those enjoyers themselves born with bodies of rice and the like?
A doubt arises:

because of the scriptural observation that "these [beings] are born here as rice and barley" (*ta iha vrīhiyavā iti jāyante*), and because of such passages as "from which these beings are born" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante*) and "Soma flows,
the progenitor of thoughts" (*somaḥ pavate janitā matīnām*), rice, barley, and so forth are indeed merely bodies of gods and humans, just as one says "gods are born" or "humans are born."
When it is argued that "those who have performed good deeds are born [as rice, etc.]," we reply: "Presided over by another" (Brahmasūtra 3.1.24).
Their connection with the bodies of rice and so forth, which are presided over by another living being, is merely one of contact. Why?
Because of the description as before; for, from the ether up to the clouds, there is only a description of their becoming those things, as in the case where—

The state of being an enjoyer is intended there, and the action that serves as its means is described [in the text] as "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct.
