However, in this context, action is not mentioned in the same manner as ether and the other elements; for, once an action such as a sacrifice—which is engaged in the bestowing of the fruit of action—has yielded its fruit to be enjoyed in heaven, it ceases to exist through that very enjoyment in heaven.
Because [the transmigratory state] has already been concluded, because it will be stated later that "those of pleasant conduct" and "those of foul conduct" have not yet begun [their new existence],

and because there is no other intervening karma in the interim, the statement regarding birth in the form of rice and so forth is figurative, just like the statement regarding becoming ether and so forth.

Now, an objection may be raised: since rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma prescribed by the Vedas are seen to involve both meritorious acts and terrible sinful deeds—such as the slaughter of animals and the consumption of meat—they appear to possess a dual nature of both merit and demerit.
Therefore, because it is impossible to experience the suffering of evil deeds in heaven, which is the abode of happiness, those [who go there] must eventually return.

Anticipating the objection that one might experience the enjoyment of those [objects] with a body rendered dull by rice, barley, and so forth, and then— by virtue of a specific previously performed merit (sukṛta)— assume a birth characterized by great sovereignty as a Brahmin or the like, he says:
If it be argued that [the world] is impure, we say no, because of the Word (Śruti).

This is not so: that there is merely an attachment to a body such as rice or other grains presided over by another, and not a birth in the form of rice or the like due to the absence of a cause for being an experiencer. Rather, because the cause for being an experiencer exists, it is precisely the karma of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, which has heaven as its fruit to be enjoyed, that—being impure and mixed with evil—is [the cause], as in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and others.
Because it is associated with violence; and since violence is prohibited by the injunction "one should not harm any living beings," it is indeed a sin.

Furthermore, there is no possibility here of the relationship between a general rule and its exception (utsarga-apavāda), as in the case of the foot and the Āhavanīya fire, because their objects are different.
The injunction for the Agniṣomīya sacrifice makes known that violence serves as an auxiliary to the ritual, whereas the [prohibition] "one should not harm... [prohibits violence in general].

The fact that violence results in demerit (*pratyavāya*). Now, it might be argued: "Since one engages in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and similar rites by virtue of a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), the prohibitory rule does not apply to them, because its scope is restricted to acts prompted by worldly desire (*rāga*). This is not so; for here too, there is no difference in terms of being prompted by desire. Indeed, one engages in such acts as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," and this applies equally to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and the like.

Having understood from the scripture that sacrifices and the like are contributory factors toward those [ends] which constitute the means for attaining the fruit, one engages in them out of passion alone. For even in the case of worldly violence, having understood through some means of knowledge that violence is a means to achieve one's own desired end, one engages in it out of passion; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever. Likewise...

Since it is understood from such statements as "even in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), there is supreme and immeasurable happiness for all castes through the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*)" that these rites are means to a fruit, one engages in them out of mere passion (*rāga*);
thus, they too are characterized by impurity (*aśuddhi*). Therefore, because the *iṣṭi* sacrifices and others are mixed with sin, they are associated with impurity.

Heaven is the fruit to be experienced; having experienced that there, the fruit of the portion consisting of violence is experienced through the state of being an immobile entity such as rice and so forth. And they record the state of being an immobile entity as the fruit of sin in the verse: "By the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of immobility. Therefore, those with residual karma (*anuśayin*) are born in the form of rice and other such things for the purpose of experiencing [the remainder of their retribution].

If it is argued: "From what [source] is there a scriptural statement— namely, from the statement that the slaughter of the Agniṣomīya animal and others is not an act of violence because it is a cause for attaining the heavenly world— for [the scripture] declares that the animal attains the heavenly world by reason of its being slaughtered?"
The scriptures declare: "Possessing a golden body, he goes upward to the heavenly world," and so forth.
An action that serves as a means for attaining superior prosperity, even if it involves slight suffering, is not indeed *hiṃsā* (violence); on the contrary, it is truly protection (*rakṣaṇa*).
And thus says the Vedic mantra:

"Verily, you do not die here, nor shall you perish; you go indeed to the gods by easy paths, where the doers of good deeds go, and not the doers of evil—there may the god Savitṛ establish you. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, those who know the truth declare that even a physician who causes slight, temporary pain is indeed a protector, and they honor him accordingly.
The substitution of a flour-offering (*piṣṭapaśu*) for the animal sacrifice of a goat is not contradictory.

Furthermore, because it is enjoined by such Vedic injunctions as "One should immolate an animal dedicated to Vāyu," the violence involved in the act of renunciation does not produce sin. Therefore, [this applies] to rice, barley, and so forth, which are presided over by living beings, for those whose nature is merit.
It is determined that there is merely a connection [between the self and objects], and not actual enjoyment.
Now, an objection is raised: in Vedic injunctions such as "One should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," the slaughter of an animal is prescribed for ritual acts.
Is this, like the human sacrifice (naramedha) or the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), a case of the direct slaughter of an animal, or is it like the Pitṛmedha and other rites?
Or rather, it is appropriate to accept flour-made animals and the like;

for in such Vedic passages as "One should not harm any living beings," "One should sacrifice a beast at the Agniṣomīya rite," and "Recite the invitatory verse for the omentum of the goat," there is the designation of both prohibitions and non-prohibitions regarding injury, and thus the acceptance of flour-made animals is justified.
It is taught by way of an illustration: "The gods indeed sacrificed a man as an animal. From him, once he had been sacrificed, the sacrificial essence (medha) departed;

it entered the horse, and therefore the horse became fit for sacrifice (*medhya*). Then they abandoned him from whom the essence had departed, and he became a *kiṃpuruṣa*. They then sacrificed the horse."
When the horse was sacrificed, it departed; it entered the cow. Then they abandoned it, its sacrificial essence having departed, and it became the *śarabha*.
They sacrificed the cow; it entered the sheep. Therefore, the sheep became unfit for sacrifice (*amedhya*).
Then they abandoned it, its sacrificial essence having departed, and it became the *gavaya*. They [then] sacrificed the sheep.
It departed from the goat that was being sacrificed; it entered the ram (*aja*); therefore the ram became fit for sacrifice (*medhya*).

Then, when they abandoned him whose sacrificial essence had departed, he became the bull (*vṛṣabha*). They sacrificed the goat; it departed from the goat that was being sacrificed; it entered the rice (*vrīhi*). Thus [it is said] regarding the omentum (*vapā*) even in the *Ṛgveda*.
This is because it is stated, by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa-pramāṇa*), that [the sacrificer] enters into plants such as rice;
likewise, in the *Manusmṛti*:
"In times of distress, one may perform an animal sacrifice with clarified butter, and likewise one may perform an animal sacrifice with flour."
But one should never, under any circumstances, desire to kill an animal in vain.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body,
so many times does the killer of animals undergo death in vain, birth after birth, after passing away.

"He who does not desire to inflict upon living beings the afflictions of bondage and death, being patient toward all and seeking their welfare, enjoys absolute happiness. Thus it is said; and in the Śātātapa [Smṛti] as well:
In rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma,
a Brahmin may indeed take away the life-breaths of an animal by the recitation of its mantra, but never for the purpose of binding it.
He who indeed slays the life-breaths of animals in sacrifices through the power of mantra-attainment should perform a most auspicious sacrifice with a manifest animal.
For ordinary twice-born men who are devoid of mantra-perfection,
the ritual procedure for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices is performed with a goat made of flour.

And because of this scriptural indication: for those who are capable of attracting the life-force (*prāṇa*) of an animal merely by the recitation of mantras and are endowed with purity of speech, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices are prescribed using a conscious goat as the sacrificial animal (*paśu*).

Similarly, for those who lack such capacity, a sacrifice of a flour-animal (*piṣṭapaśu*) alone is appropriate. [This is so] because of the invocation of the life-force into the flour-animal by means of mantra.
Likewise, because the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is possible, there is no contradiction between Vedic and worldly [reality].

Just as the sour creeper (*amlalatā*) is accepted as a substitute for the *soma* plant, similarly, there is no contradiction in the scriptural injunction regarding the flour-animal (*piṣṭapaśu*) as a replacement for the goat animal (*chāgapaśu*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that, because the *soma* creeper is not found here in this world, its acceptance as a substitute (*pratinidhi*) in the form of sour milk-creepers (*amlalatā*) is appropriate?

And since a goat is available here, why is it not prescribed in the same manner? [Reply: No, because for those desiring the *Pitṛmedha*, there would arise the contingency of actually killing one's own father in the *Pitṛmedha*, just as in the case of the *Aśvamedha* and other such sacrifices.

Furthermore, because the *pitṛmedha* sacrifice would be rendered fruitless by the cutting of the *piṇḍas* which have the ancestors as their essence, and because the rite of consecrating rice, cows, and bulls for the cessation of the state of being a *preta*— as well as the injunction to use a flour-effigy (*piṣṭapaśu*) in the passage "animals are indeed the *cāturmāsya* offerings"— would result in a mere gesture of empty-handedness.
Furthermore— since the initiation (*upanayana*) prescribed by the injunctions is the primary means for attaining success in mantras,
therefore it is appropriate to accept a flour-effigy (*piṣṭapaśu*) in sacrificial rites.
Moreover— the penance, knowledge, fame, and [merit] of that person whose self is characterized by good deeds—
Anticipating the objection that [this] is possible, he says:
"Then there is the union with the seed and the womb" (26).
The statement regarding the birth of those whose nature is well-performed (*sukṛtātman*) as rice and so forth is figurative.

Immediately after entering rice and other such plants, they enter the body of a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*) and are transformed into the form of semen. For it is said: "Whoever eats the food, whoever sheds the semen—that indeed he becomes again"; thus, the state of being the shedder of semen belongs to those who linger (*anuśāyin*).
Just as that which is being heard is taught merely as a connection [with a specific state], so too is the state of becoming rice and so forth indicated.
In response to the doubt— how can the production of a body be possible for those performers of meritorious deeds who have entered the heart of a person and are delimited by purity— it says:
The body [originates] from the womb. || 27 ||

When those of virtuous nature who have attained divinity in the heavenly world enter a womb in the form of semen, their body is produced at that very moment. Nevertheless, because they experience the suffering of the womb and so forth,
and because we observe them undergoing various afflictions even during stages such as infancy, [it follows that the self is not newly created].

Having shaken off the veil of bonds by virtue of the descent of power (śaktipāta) obtained through the glance of a teacher who has distanced himself from the suffering of birth and death, and possessing the means of knowledge— namely, the firm seat of the knowledge of the Śiva-principle, meditation, concentration, dispassion, tranquility, self-restraint, fortitude, and faith— he remains until the dissolution of the manifestation of his prārabdha karma.
The sense is that it must be accomplished continuously and with undivided devotion. Likewise, in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"What longing could a person of discrimination have for unstable, momentary pleasure arising from children, wife, and the like, or for heaven which is subject to decay and other such defects?"
"Having always established his mind upon Śiva— the supreme auspiciousness who grants the desired fruits of his devotees— a man possessed of devotion should wander [in the world].
Thus it is said in the Śaiva [scriptures].
One should abandon sons, friends, wives, and so forth— those known as mere semblances of kinsmen—
who are the sole producers of great delusion and the obstructors of the knowledge of Śiva.
Those who desire liberation must abandon their minds from everything else and bestow them upon Śaṅkara.

Thus, from this scriptural teaching, it should be understood that those seeking liberation must abandon the agency of performing meritorious and sinful deeds— which establish the going to and returning from the next world— and instead engage exclusively in the worship of Śiva for the sake of the knowledge of Śiva.
Therefore, it is established that for those of virtuous nature, there is merely union with that [Śiva], beginning with the attainment of the vital breath, space, and so forth.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Meditation," in the Śrīkarabhāṣya composed by the venerable teacher Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of holy ascetics.

The first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter [in the Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya], beginning with "In that interval, upon reaching... and so forth, up to the sixth section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerning "that interval";
[followed by] the second quarter of the third chapter.
The refutation of the view that the world is illusory by means of the analogy of the dream-phenomenon;

the destruction of evil through the performance of meritorious deeds as prescribed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, which are in accordance with the supreme Lord’s command and transcend the [ordinary] system of castes and stages of life; and by the destruction of evil...

Faith in the true scriptures, such as the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama; through inquiry based on that faith, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities; from that discrimination, detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter; through that detachment, the attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama); by the fruit thereof, the grace of the auspicious teacher (śivācārya) through one-pointed devotion to liberation alone; and from that, the relationship of the Lord, the individual soul, and the bonds (pati-paśu-pāśa) conducive to liberation.

Therefore, there is the practice of Śiva-yoga, which is the cause for the direct realization of Śiva and the unification of the mind. Through that practice—and by means of it being the cause for the performance of meritorious deeds preceded by the cessation of the notion of "I" and the intellect of sin—those virtuous people who are steadfast in the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life experience happiness in this world and in the worlds hereafter. Conversely, those others who are sinful undergo the agonizing torments of hell.

And this has been demonstrated. Here, however, some [hold] that because it is impossible for Brahman— which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), devoid of attributes (*nirdharmika*), devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), partless (*niravayava*), and undifferentiated (*nirbheda*) and eternal— to be the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [they explain it] by means of the analogy of the dream-world.
They establish the falsity of all four states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and swoon.

This is the section on the Sandhyā [of the *Sandhyādhikaraṇa*] concerning Pure Non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*), Buddha Non-duality (*buddhādvaita*), Dry Non-duality (*śuṣkādvaita*), and Impure Non-duality (*aśuddhādvaita*). || 1 ||
Since dreams are observed to indicate future auspicious and inauspicious results, the reality of dreams is established;
for indeed, in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other texts, it is stated that "a dream is like a magical illusion (indrajāla), consisting of an inconceivable arrangement," and so forth.

Since the world of manifold diversity (*prapañca*) is stated to be false like a dream, it follows by implication that the experiences of heaven and hell for those who perform meritorious and non-meritorious deeds, as previously mentioned, are likewise unreal. Therefore,
there is no [contradiction] regarding the performance of well-done actions preceded by dedication to the Supreme Lord.
Anticipating the objection that there might be some purpose [for this], he says: "For [the scripture] declares that creation occurs during the intermediate state. (1.3.1)

In the intermediate state—that is, in the state of dream—the creation of the manifold world of moving and non-moving beings following that intermediate state of dream is ultimately real. Why? Because it says:
"There are no chariots there, no draft animals, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads."

Since the phenomenal world of dreams (*svapnaprapañca*) is established in such scriptural passages as these, its unreality is proven; therefore, by means of the analogy of the dream-world, the inference of the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the waking world (*jāgratprapañca*) is primary:
"There are no chariots there, no horses yoked to chariots, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, horses yoked to chariots, and roads. No.

In that state, there are no joys, delights, or raptures; yet he creates joys, delights, and raptures from himself. There are no ponds, lotus-pools, or rivers there; yet he creates ponds, lotus-pools, and rivers from himself. "For he is the agent"—thus it is heard in the Śruti with reference to the dream state. Therefore, in this case...

A doubt arises as to whether the creation of the dream-world, like the creation of the waking world, is produced by the individual soul (jīva) or by the Lord (īśvara), and whether it is real or unreal. [The answer is:
The creation beginning from the act of seeing up to the entry [into the body] is fashioned by the Lord.
The creation beginning with the waking state and ending with deep sleep is imagined by the individual soul (jīva).

From the observation of this statement, it follows that the creation during the intermediate state [the dream state] is by means of the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because the dream state is called "intermediate" (sandhya), according to the scriptural declaration: "The third state is the dream state. Furthermore, that [creation] is created by the soul alone; for the text says, "He is indeed the agent.
Indeed, it is the dreaming soul itself that is perceived here.

Furthermore: since the manifold world of elephants, chariots, and so forth experienced in a dream is seen to be false upon waking, it follows that the waking world is likewise false—just like the snake [imagined] in a rope. To this we reply: the creation in the intermediate state—that is, in the dream—is a manifold, variegated creation of elephants, horses, and so on; for [the scripture] declares [the Lord] to exist as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of the individual soul (jīva).

The Śruti declares that [He is] the all-pervading Supreme Śiva-Brahman; for instance, in numerous Śrutis such as "The Lord of all beings, the Master of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Lord of the Guṇas," [His] status as the controller of all living beings and His agency in the bondage and liberation of all living beings are established.
Furthermore, according to the treatises on dreams (*svapnādhyāya*),

since it is observed that a dream indicates future auspicious or inauspicious results, the dream itself possesses reality. Moreover, by virtue of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of living beings, the Lord alone is the agent of the dream-phenomenon (*svapnaprapañca*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "In the Śruti passage, 'This person who remains awake while others sleep, creating desire after desire,' the agency for the creation of sons, friends, wives, and so forth is attributed to the individual soul (jīva) as an independent agent;
how then is the creation of dreams and the like possible for the Lord (Īśvara)? To this doubt, he says:
And some [hold that the Lord is] the creator, as well as sons and so forth. || 142 || 2 ||

"Some followers of other Vedic branches declare that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the creator of desires in dreams, based on the text: 'While these [senses] sleep, this person remains awake, creating desire after desire. Furthermore, the individual soul's power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) is established in the speech of Prajāpati: 'Ask for all desires according to your wish; choose sons and grandsons with a lifespan of a hundred years.'"

[Objection: "It has been heard [in scripture]; therefore, the state of being a *jīva* alone constitutes the agency within dreams. [Reply: This is incorrect—since the *jīva* is one of the eight forms (*mūrti*) of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the attributes of being the creator of dreams and so forth are logically applicable to the Supreme Lord. For this very reason, it is said: "The ether is Brahman; the air is Brahman; yonder sun is Brahman."

In such scriptural passages as "This Āditya is Brahman," the Śruti establishes that the word *brahman*— which refers exclusively to Śiva— is the creator and fashioner of ether, air, fire, water, and earth. Furthermore, because they are produced in accordance with the will of the Creator, even things such as sons, friends, and wives existing during a dream [are manifestations of Him].

Furthermore, objects must be accepted as being real; for sons and the like are designated by the word "desire" (*kāma*) because they are the objects of desire. This is because, on the view that they are illusory, it would be impossible for them to be dependent upon the will of the agent.
Indeed, in the world, things that are illusory—such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell or a snake in a rope—are never seen to be dependent upon the will of the agent.
It has been observed. Thus, the purport of the Śruti is that the Lord is the agent of the dream-manifold by virtue of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).
By this, it is established that the dream-manifold is indeed taught by the Śruti through its intended meaning. [This is confirmed by the passage: "There are no chariots there... and so forth.

Since the ultimate chariot and other such things were refuted in the preceding statement, it is established that the doctrine of the oneness of Brahman— based on the analogy of the dream-world— is also untenable. Furthermore, neither the insentient *pradhāna*, which is of the nature of a power distinct from Paramaśiva, nor the bound soul (*baddhajīva*) characterized by that [power], [can be the cause].

To the objection— namely, that since the Śrutis such as "the one unborn, red, white, and black" point to the insentient *pradhāna* as the cause of the world, how can the sentient individual soul (*jīva*) be the creator of the dream-multiplicity?— he says:
But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety. || 143 || 3 ||

The word "tu" (but) excludes the individual soul (*jīva*) as the agent. The meaning is that the collection of objects such as chariots and lotus ponds in a dream is merely *māyā*—that is, created by the Supreme Person, Paraśiva; for the word *māyā* denotes something wonderful, as in the phrase "Devamāyā, born in the lineage of Janaka, was fashioned [by him]."
Gaurī, the daughter of Himavat, is Maheśvarī, whose name is Māyā.
She is the eternal bestower of the desires of her devotees, dependent upon Śiva, and of the nature of consciousness;

for this is seen in the Purāṇas, as well as in such Vedic texts as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (Nature), but Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā. Furthermore, in this context, the statement "There were no chariots there, nor yoke-poles, nor roads" refers to its being experienced by the Person who is other than the one possessing all.

The meaning is that they do not exist [in reality]. Then he creates chariots, distinct from the yoking of chariots; he creates them as things to be experienced by the dreamer, which terminate at that very moment. Thus he speaks of its wondrous nature. Such a wondrous creation is possible for the Supreme Person, Śiva, whose resolve is true, but not for the individual soul (jīva). For him—

Even though he possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and other attributes, such a wondrous creation is not possible for the individual soul (*jīva*), because during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), his essential nature is not fully manifested. Furthermore, the Śruti text, "Creating whatever he desires," refers to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) alone as the creator.
That which remains awake while all things sleep—that indeed is the pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal.
Upon it all worlds are supported; there is nothing whatsoever beyond it.

Thus, because the unique nature of Paramaśiva is recognized in both the opening and the conclusion; and furthermore, because of the identity of meaning with the Śruti passage, "He creates ponds, lotus-pools, and rivers, for he is the agent," it points to the Supreme Person alone as the agent. Therefore, [the agency] does not belong to the insentient Pradhāna.

It is untenable that the bound individual soul (*baddhajīva*)— which is of the nature of the power non-different from Paramaśiva, yet consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), is characterized by those [qualities], and possesses limited knowledge (*kiñcijjña*)— should be the creator of the dream-like phenomenal world. This is because the soul is deluded by the bondage of *māyā*, and its liberation from that bondage is dependent upon the Supreme Lord.
The agency of dreaming also does not belong to the other [the individual soul];
furthermore, because in the world the manifestation of the dream-world is not seen to occur in accordance with the will of the individual soul, and because undesirable,
evil dreams are manifested [against his will], there is no [distinction] between the individual soul and the Lord due to their identity in being consciousness.
Anticipating the doubt as to the distinction between these two, he says:
"But [the power] is concealed by the meditation on the Supreme; for from that come its bondage and its opposite. (1.4)
Through scriptural authority, reasoning, and experience— such as the Śruti passage, "The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord"—
and through the established mutual difference between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), comparable to a divine gem and a useless stone,
[the world] consists of the three guṇas distinct from the conscious power (cicchakti) that is non-different from Śiva, due to the meditation upon the Supreme (parābhidhyāna).

Due to the contemplation of the insentient *parā-prakṛti*, which takes the form of a fetter (*pāśa*), and because of being firmly touched by it, the individual soul’s own knowledge is concealed or veiled. Consequently, on account of this concealment, there occurs for him the inversion of bondage and liberation.
Bondage is the conceit of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and so forth.
Through the ripening of merit accumulated over many lifetimes, preceded by one's own knowledge and the knowledge of Śiva—
thus it is heard in the Śaiva tradition:
"In Śiva, the eternal, who is with Ambā and possesses the glory of perpetual auspiciousness..."
Its power is manifested through the distinction of being both supreme and non-supreme.
Another [aspect] is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is all-auspicious;
she manifests within all living beings through the differentiation of the three qualities.
Through the merit produced by the act of offering everything to Śiva, one becomes a recipient of Śiva’s grace;
therefore, Māyā, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), is called the supreme bond (pāśa) and the supreme fetter (khapā).
"The individual soul perishes in that way; otherwise, he becomes Śiva.
Having known the Lord, through meditation upon Him, and having known Śiva, there is faith and devotion—so it is said in the Śruti. Furthermore:
"When indeed one finds fearless support in this invisible, non-self, indefinable, and groundless [Brahman], then..."

"He becomes one who has attained fearlessness when, indeed, he does not perceive even the slightest difference within this [Brahman]; but when he perceives therein even a slight difference, then fear arises for him.
For He alone causes bliss; from fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth in the Śrutis.

Regarding His bondage, some maintain that although the individual soul's possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and other qualities is innate, it is nevertheless concealed by the Māyā of the Supreme Lord.
They say this, but that is incorrect; for it is impossible for one whose essential nature is *satyasaṅkalpa* (one whose resolve is true) to be concealed by *māyā*.

Furthermore, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were inherently and naturally *satyasaṅkalpa* while still unliberated, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), as the attributes of being established in the non-dual *satyasaṅkalpa* of the Supreme Lord and so forth would then apply [inappropriately] to it as well.

Therefore, its concealment by the illusion of the fetters (pāśa-māyā) occurs; and since both bondage and liberation depend upon the Supreme Lord, it is established that even the agency of dreaming does not belong to anyone else.
By the power and majesty of the grace obtained from the Śiva-teacher, the individual soul’s [egoity] which obstructs the knowledge of Śiva—

In response to the doubt— namely, "How is 'I-ness,' 'mine-ness,' and so forth, which obscure one's own knowledge and obstruct the knowledge of Śiva for the individual soul (jīva) whose true knowledge has been concealed by the Māyā of Śambhu, uprooted?"— he says:
Or he too [is called a "knower"] because of his connection with a body. || 5 ||

At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), like deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the soul’s omniscience becomes concealed due to its union with the power of the insentient (*acit-śakti*) and its contemplation of the Supreme as being of the nature of fetters (*pāśa*). Even at the time of creation, through the union with the power of the insentient and the conjunction with gross and subtle bodies, notions such as "I" and "mine" arise even for the discerning. Therefore, [the realization] "I am not... [is necessary].
"The means of accomplishment must be undertaken this very day"—thus it is sung in the Vedas and Vedāntas:

"The person who has a teacher knows. And in such scriptural passages as: "One who stands beyond all stages of life, having restrained all the senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru, should approach that very guru, carrying fuel in his hand—a master of the Vedas (śrotriya) who is established in Brahman."

Liberation is traditionally taught for the individual soul (*jīva*) through its conjunction with a body, by virtue of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) obtained through the grace of a Śiva-teacher who is a reflection of Paramaśiva.
This is the nature of the descent of power.
The procedure for the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) as shown in the Śiva Āgamas is as follows:
"The Śiva-teacher should respectfully perform the descent of power for the disciple, which is the cause for severing the great impurity that has reached full maturity."
Indeed, through the descent of power (śaktipāta), the individual soul attains the nature of Brahman;
and this descent of power is for all beings, unlimited and imperishable.
Or rather, the purpose is characterized by the generation of supreme bliss;
that descent of power (śaktipāta), O Queen of the Gods, occurs through distinctions such as intense, mild, and so forth.
"It is proclaimed to be sixfold, through the distinctions beginning with devotion (bhakta) and ending with oneness (aikya).

Therefore, the definition of the descent of power (śaktipāta) is traditionally taught: "The descent of power is the cause for the uprooting of fully ripened impurity. By means of that, the individual soul (jīva), in its nature as the Supreme Śiva-Brahman—
The purpose, characterized by the manifestation of unsurpassed and unlimited bliss, has been taught.

Furthermore, the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—which reveals the supreme secrets of the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetters (*pāśa*)—is sixfold according to the distinctions of intensity, such as "intense" (*tīvra*) and "mild" (*manda*), and it occurs within the stages beginning with devotion (*bhakti*) and ending with oneness (*aikya*). This is established through the *nigamas*, *āgamās*, and *tantras* which proclaim these truths.

In the first stage of devotion (*bhakta-sthala*), the manifestation of the state of the Great Lord (*maheśvaratva*), which consists of unsurpassed bliss, is indicated as occurring within the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) produced by a sentence of undivided form (*akhaṇḍākāra*).

Similarly, in the second stage (*prapanna-sthala*), there is the manifestation of Sadāśiva, who is a mass of pure consciousness and stainless being (*amala-sattva-cit-dhana*), characterized by the opening up that wipes away the casket of ignorance (*avidyā-sampuṭa-uddhūlana-lakṣaṇa-unmeṣaṇa*).
Having pierced the six chakras via the path of the Suṣumnā by means of Kuṇḍalinī, at the location of the Brahmarandhra, there occurs—
by virtue of the practice of Śiva-yoga— the third [state], characterized by the union of Śiva and Śakti, which was elaborated upon in the section on Prasāda.

Out of an extraordinary desire to favor his disciples, the teacher (deśika) abandons his own body, enters the body of the student, and through the purification of the student's channels, causes the student's kuṇḍalinī to circulate through the seven wheels (cakras). This constitutes the fourth type [of initiation], characterized by the direct demonstration of traveling to all worlds like Śiva, as described in the section concerning the *prāṇaliṅgin*.
By means of the union of the vital winds of prāṇa and apāna,

having attained the auspicious glory consisting of the digit of consciousness (citkalā) that illuminates the center of the suṣumnā nāḍī, he is always endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers beginning with aṇimā; such a one is described as the fifth refuge-place.
Having set aside the state of being distinct from knowledge and ignorance, unsurpassed, stainless, changeless, partless, devoid of all attributes,
and like a camphor lamp placed in a windless spot in the midst of a fierce sun—
[the mind] which is empty of the thorough knowledge of external and internal objects such as the body, senses, mind, and vital breath; [this is the nature of the Self].

In such descents of power (*śaktipāta*), it is taught that [the soul's states] are like those of an ant, a monkey, a bird, a cow, a fish, and so forth. Therefore, the dependence of the individual soul (*jīva*) upon the Lord (*Īśvara*) and the Lord’s role as the creator of the waking, dreaming, and deep-sleep states are unavoidable. In Him all worlds are established; there is nothing else.
In the Smṛti, the phrase "someone" (kaścana) teaches such unique attributes of the Lord of All as remaining awake while all others sleep and being the refuge of all worlds;
for the individual souls (jīvas) remain for only so long as is necessary for them to experience the fruits corresponding to their very limited actions.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [the Lord] produces those objects to be experienced by that [individual soul].
If [your position] were intent on establishing falsity (*mithyātva*), the contradiction with the Śruti and the Sūtras would be unavoidable.
Now, [one might object]: how can there be such a production for Brahman, whose nature is eternal and immutable?

Since it is impossible for [the self] to be the agent of false conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) characterized by perverse transformations, its being the cause of the dream-proliferation is untenable. In that regard, because the collection of things such as sons, friends, and wives does not exist during the waking state, their falsity is unavoidable; likewise, so too is the falsity of the waking proliferation.
Anticipating the objection that [the dream state] is likewise unreal, like a city of Gandharvas and so forth, he says:
"And it is indicative, for so the scripture declares, and those who know it say. (6)

"When one sees a woman in dreams while engaged in rites for specific desires, one should know that there will be success in that dream-vision. Now, as for dreams: "One sees a black man with black teeth; he kills him," and so forth.

Furthermore, those who know the science of dream interpretation declare that a dream is an indicator of both the auspicious and the inauspicious. And this quality of being an indicator would not be possible if [the dream] were dependent upon one's own volition. Thus, since the inauspicious is undesirable, one would have to create only the indicator of the auspicious and then behold it. Therefore, it is determined that the creation of dreams is performed by the Lord alone, and not by the individual soul (*jīva*).

This Sūtra is intended to dispel the doubt that at that time there might arise the manifestation of such qualities as "truthful resolve" (satya-saṅkalpatva), which is useful only for the creation within a dream. Those who know the chapter on dreams—that is, those who know the Vedic passages concerning dreams—maintain that a dream is not false because it provides designations for the attainment of auspicious and inauspicious results. For this very reason, [the same applies to] the phenomenal world as well.
Reality is established by implication.

Here, however, others take the position that the objects of dreams are ultimately real—like the ether and so forth—because they are created by God, and then establish their falsity as the final conclusion on the grounds that they cannot be defined in terms of place, time, and cause. And of these...
The statement that the Self alone creates—that which is said regarding its being the creator—is merely figurative.

The designation of the Self as the agent of dream-objects is figurative, based on its being the agent of good and evil deeds, which are the causes for the perception of pleasure and pain. This refers to the dream-state in the passage: "Having moved about outside his body as an immortal."

And the Śruti, having moved as if outside [the body], in that very context establishes the Supreme Lord and, by showing the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Him, dispels the doubt regarding the soul’s capacity for creation through its power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*). "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over them both by means of the perishable self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10)

In the Śruti text, "From meditating upon Him, from union with Him, and from becoming His very essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion (viśvamāyānivṛtti)," it is taught that the individual soul (jīva) possesses all supreme majesties such as knowledge, sovereignty, and power, and that there is the cessation of the concealment of its bonds (pāśa) through the practice of meditation on Śiva. Therefore, its bondage and liberation are dependent upon Śiva; and that [bondage] is indeed the state of concealment (tirobhāva).

They connect [the section] by saying, "due to the connection with the subtle and gross bodies. In that case, however, both the subject matter following from the previous chapter (*pādānugatārtha*) and its logical consistency (*saṃgati*) are untenable. If the purpose of the chapter were the determination of the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), there would be a lack of connection with the section on the fruit (*phalādhikaraṇa*). Nor is the Lord (*īśvara*) the state of the living soul, since he is merely superimposed upon Brahman.

Because [the dream world] is superimposed upon the individual soul (*jīva*). If the definition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the function of the chapter (*pāda*) were intended, then the statement here that the objects of dreams are false because they have the individual soul as their agent would not be consistent. Furthermore, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is untenable, because it is impossible to establish falsity (*mithyātva*) as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). For falsity is indeed established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.

The falsity of the entire phenomenal world has been established. Since the falsity of even ether and the like is thus proven, the falsity of dream-objects is established *a fortiori*; therefore, this particular section [of the commentary] would be redundant.
For while ether and the other elements possess empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*), that even does not apply to dream-objects, as they do not withstand empirical scrutiny.

If it is argued that this undertaking is for the purpose of demonstrating the difference [of the waking state] from space and so forth, we say no; because at the time of awakening, the non-correspondence of the waking experience with its objects is universally acknowledged by all people, and because the dissimilarity between the two states has already been stated in the sūtra: "And on account of its difference in nature, [the waking state] is not like a dream, etc. (BS 3.2.4).

If it is argued that the commencement [of this inquiry] is for the purpose of dispelling doubts regarding the reality [of the world] produced by Vedic statements, we say no— because the status of the Lord as the creator, which is established by its own natural force through such reasons as being the refuge of all worlds, must not be sublated;
for there is no contradiction in the Lord’s being the creator being compatible with the cessation of its conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*).

This is because you yourself accept that even those dreams— such as those seen by Brahmadatta under the influence of limiting adjuncts— which arise through the grace of higher and lower deities attained via specific forms of worship, lack empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*).
If the absence of empirical reality is what you seek to prove, then even the reliance on the individual soul (*jīva*) as the agent [of such experiences] would be contradictory.
For it would follow that things such as pots, which have the individual soul (jīva) as their agent, would possess empirical reality;
furthermore, since the soul's status as a creator has been refuted by the final two sūtras, its primary agency as a creator is rejected.
Its agency is merely figurative, based on its being the agent of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), which is the root of the manifestation of pleasure and so forth. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction, [we reply] no, because there would follow the consequence that [the world] possesses only empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), just like the creation of bodies, sense organs, and so forth, which are rooted in the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) of individual souls (*jīva*).
Even though they are rooted in the *adṛṣṭa* of individual souls, the creation of bodies and so forth is nonetheless dependent upon Īśvara.

If such dependence on God exists even for the objects of dreams— since you yourself have admitted that they depend upon Him— then the supreme sovereignty of God, which consists in His being seen by all living beings at all times and in all bodies, would not exist. For the existence of both types of phenomenal worlds (waking and dreaming) is equally established through perception.
For the disparity consists in the swiftness or delay of the sublation (*bādha*).

Thus, because the absence of the individual souls' direct agency regarding the objects of dreams has been established as false by the author of the Sūtras through the very mention of what is relevant, it is understood that this falsity is what is to be negated [by the subsequent statement]. This is indicated by the words "and the indicator" (*sūcakaśca*).

Furthermore, we shall explain its contradictory nature due to the composition of sutras that are inconsistent [with the intended meaning]. For in this case, the sutras ought to be applicable to the thesis being proved (*sādhya*), rather than being irrelevant or contradictory. That alone should be the thesis.
If the opponent's argument concerns God’s status as creator, then the portion of the sutra stating "and sons and so forth" would be rendered fruitless.

Because the capacity for being the creator of sons and so forth, which is possible in the case of individual souls (*jīva*), cannot serve as a proof for [the existence of] God; and because the word *māyā* does not denote falsity (*mithyātva*). Furthermore, the sūtra "And [it would be] contradictory to the [meaning of the] syllable" (*sūdhakaśca*) would be contradicted.

The intention is that since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is incompatible with falsity, ultimate reality belongs to the indicator (*sūcaka*)—such as the needle—and not to that which is indicated (*sūcyasya*).
If it be argued that this is not so—[we reply] no, because it is not based on the words [of the scripture].

Furthermore, since it is improper to assume an intention not expressed in the sūtra and thereby postulate something contrary to the Śruti, the need for both ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and a transposition of the syntactical connection (*vyutkramānvaya*) would be all too evident in the interpretation: "By the meditation upon the Supreme, the concealment ceases."

The reflection "so 'pi" (even that) regarding concealment (*tirobhāva*) is also improper, because the word *tirobhāva* has not been introduced in the context; furthermore, when "that which is concealed" (*tirohitam*) is indicated, the pronoun "it" (*tat*)— which is fit to refer back to the mere meaning of the verbal root in the form of concealment—
is unfit to be referred back by the pronoun "he" (*saḥ*), since among masculine nouns employed, some appropriate referent must be reflected upon.

The scriptural statement must also be examined. The primary meaning of the scripture is "they do not exist. Your interpretation—that the term "creates" (*sṛjati*) is used figuratively in accordance with that [primary meaning]—is established as being figurative. Furthermore, the preceding statement is also redundant, because the falsity of dreams is already well-known in the world. For a teaching is purposeful only when its subject matter is not already established. Therefore, it is superfluous.

If it is argued that even the two statements are difficult to reconcile because they involve both literal and figurative senses— namely, that by restating the collection of dream-objects as being false, the statement "He creates" (sṛjati) is shown to be figurative, thereby establishing that [the creation] is rooted in the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) of the individual soul (jīva), and thus there is unity of the statements— this is not so, because [the figurative sense] must conform to the falsity which serves as a qualification of the subject (uddeśya).
Because those learned in logic do not accept the violation of the natural consistency of an acceptable statement,

and because when both [meanings] can be primary, it is improper to resort to making either one secondary; nor is it the case that objects such as chariots seen at the time of dreaming are non-existent upon waking, as there is no perception of the absence of the objects experienced during the waking state.

Because they exist [in that state]. Nor does it refer to the prior non-existence of dream-objects, since the prior non-existence of things imagined in a dream is already established in common worldly experience. Nor is there a statement of mutual non-existence between those seen in dreams and those seen in the waking state, precisely because such a thing is well-known in the world.

Therefore, by negating the well-known existence of dream-objects such as chariots and so forth, their dissimilarity [to waking objects] is established. By this, the distinction consisting in [dream-objects] being experienced by a single subject and persisting only for a specific duration would be stated. Thus, since it is intended to establish that they are created by Īśvara as qualified by this distinction, there is unity of the sentence and no redundancy.

There would be both a lack of appropriateness and a contradiction with logic. Therefore, if [the text] were intent on establishing falsity, the contradiction with the Śruti and the Sūtras would be unavoidable.
This concludes the section on "The Absence of That" (Tadabhāvādhikaraṇa). 2.

If it is argued that since Śiva alone is the cause of going to sleep, let the Lord (Īśvara) be the cause of dreaming; then for whom does the causality of sleep itself arise? To address the doubt as to by whom the forgetting of the gross phenomenal world (sthūla-prapañca) occurs during that sleep, he presents another topical section (adhikaraṇa).
The demonstration of the soul’s similarity to a king;
its absence in the channels and in the self, according to scripture. 147, 7.

Having previously examined the state of dream and established that Paraśiva, the Brahman, is its agent by following the sequence of actions performed therein, it is now determined that the agency of the state of deep sleep and the status of being its controller belong to Him alone. [This is so] because in the waking and dreaming states, there is the sense of "I" and "mine," and so forth.

One who possesses the conceit of identifying with the body, senses, and so forth is "embodied" (*śārīra*). Being devoid of that [conceit] during the state of deep sleep—that is, being one for whom there is an absence of that conceit of body, senses, and so forth—he, being free from the conceit of the body, sleeps within the channels (*nāḍī*), in the Self (the *ātman*), and—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—in the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*). This occurs by way of entering through the gates of the ramparts, namely the channels, the lotus of the heart, and so forth.

Through the aggregate of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), which constitute a portion of the power of Śiva-consciousness delimited by that lotus, [the soul] becomes one with darkness and sleeps within the channels (*nāḍī*). Having withdrawn from the channels, it rests in the pericardium (*purītat*). Having withdrawn from the pericardium, it rests in Being (*sat*). According to the scripture, "Having attained Being, they do not know: 'We have attained Being,'" the embodied self [proceeds] by way of the channels and the pericardium.

It is explained that during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), one rests in the *purītat*—which is delimited by it, which is the primary locus of all, and whose nature is the supreme Śiva-Brahman in the form of Ghoratamas—because of the scriptural mention of "lying down. The meaning of that scripture is as follows: the king known as the individual soul (*jīva*), while wandering through his own two kingdoms of waking and dreaming, [enters] his own city called the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*).

Having entered his own city called the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*), he then enters the channels (*nāḍī*); emerging from the channels, he enters the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*); and emerging from that lotus, he rests in the vicinity of Brahman as delimited by it, in the palace consisting primarily of darkness, which is of the nature of His terrible power (*ghora-śakti*).

Now, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream, then he is asleep in these channels (*nāḍī*). Likewise, when one is in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), when one knows nothing at all—there are seventy-two thousand channels called *hitā* that extend from the heart to the pericardium; by means of them...
"Having withdrawn, he rests in the pericardium"—when a person is said to be "sleeping," my dear, then he has become united with Being.

At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved and he is overcome by darkness, he attains the nature of bliss; dreaming occurs in the pericarp, deep sleep in the stalk, and the fourth state upon the abandonment of the lotus.
In the states of waking and dreaming, the individual soul (jīva) is indeed agitated by passion, hatred, and other such afflictions;
however, due to the absence of these in deep sleep, the soul attains the state of Śaṅkara.
Since such Śruti and Smṛti texts teach that during deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) rests within the seventy-two thousand channels,

in the channel called *purītat* which is their root, in the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), and in Brahman characterized by predominance of darkness (*tamaḥ*), there arises the question whether this is an option (*vikalpa*)— as in "one should sacrifice with rice or one should sacrifice with barley"— or a combination (*samuccaya*).

A doubt arises: now, since the scripture states, "When [he] is in deep sleep," and because this individual soul (jīva) is designated as residing within the palace of the lotus of its own heart, it is indicated that he alone is the agent of sleep.
Furthermore, in hundreds of scriptural passages such as the *liṅga* text, "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being (*sat*)," it is shown that he is present there during deep sleep.
The claim that this consists in possessing the attainment of that Lord is incorrect;
for in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "He does not return again," those who have attained the Lord are declared to be subject to no further rebirth.
Furthermore, the assertion that it consists in the dissolution of the power of ignorance (tamas) as delimited by that Lord is untenable.

Because darkness and light are mutually contradictory by nature, there is a contradiction between the light of Brahman— which is self-luminous and consists of knowledge— and the power of ignorance (tamas) which is of the nature of darkness; furthermore, this contradicts many Vedic scriptures such as "Brahman is one only, without a second" and "Rudra is one alone, he does not stand for a second."

Now, if the purpose is indeed the arrival [of the result], then since multiple [means] cannot operate simultaneously due to having an identical effect, one must resort to the rule of conjunction (*samuccaya-vidhi*) based on the distinction of effects— just as in the case of a palace, a bed, and a couch— which serves to indicate a difference in effects.
This would be analogous to the case of "one sacrifices with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajate*), where the purpose is the production of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

If it be argued that, because the purpose of sleep is to rest, his sleeping occurs sometimes in the channels (*nāḍīs*), sometimes in the heart-lotus (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), and sometimes in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), this is inconsistent; for, due to the absence of a primary rule, there would result the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached that his location during sleep is solely within the lotus of one's own heart, we reply: "The absence of that [sleeping]. *Note: This passage is from Śaṅkara’s commentary on Brahmasūtra 3.2.7.*

"At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved and [the self] is overcome by darkness, it attains the nature of bliss"—from such passages, the combination of these locations—the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), the pericardium (*purītat*), and the Self (*ātman*)—is determined. Why?
Because of that scriptural statement (*tacchruteḥ*); for we observe scriptural texts prescribing those three locations. Therefore, during his sleep...

Even though there is the possibility of attaining the Śiva-tattva delimited by the heart-lotus, because that attainment is rendered impossible by being characterized by the power of the fetter (pāśa-śakti) consisting of *tamas*, repeated return [to saṃsāra] is logically established. This is so because the scriptural passages stating "he does not return again" refer [to those who have attained liberation] by means of knowledge resulting from the practice of meditation, concentration, and other forms of worship directed toward the Supreme Lord.

There is no contradiction because [the scripture] refers to liberated souls (*muktajīva*) characterized by the severance of their bonds (*pāśaviccheda*). Since it is possible for a soul’s own knowledge to be obscured by the power of its bonds at the time of its departure and return, Śiva’s role as the cause of entering into deep sleep (*supti*) is also clearly taught. Therefore:

The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, is the cause of bondage, maintenance, and liberation from saṃsāra; as in the passage "from which indeed these beings are born," He is the cause of creation, maintenance, dissolution, manifestation, and concealment.
Just as light and darkness coexist, there is no mutual contradiction between the Supreme Lord and His power of bondage (pāśa-śakti).

Because it is established by scripture, reason, and personal experience; because its power is self-dependent; and because it is self-generated; [the Self is] the witness of all, beyond darkness, both consciousness and unconsciousness, and both truth and untruth—becoming Truth itself. Thus, in such scriptural passages, there is no contradiction regarding its being beyond darkness and its being the substrate of darkness.

It is established that, unlike the obstruction to entering a palace, entry into the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth— being characterized by the power of the darkness of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)— is not incompatible with proximity to the Supreme Lord. Therefore, during deep sleep, for the individual soul (*jīva*) who has entered into the state of subtle ignorance (*tūlājñāna*),
Śiva alone [acts] through the causal medium delimited by root-ignorance, via the path of the channels and so forth, in order to pacify the exertion of the waking and dreaming states.
It is determined that by placing [the individual soul] in His own proximity, He bestows the state of abiding in His own bliss.

Now, one might object: although the Supreme Lord would indeed grant supreme bliss to the living being through His own proximity, nevertheless, at the time of re-awakening, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of merit and demerit, it is the embodied soul alone who possesses independence.
Anticipating the doubt that there might be a return [to worldly existence], he says:
"Therefore, awakening arises from this. (8)

Since Brahman alone is the direct locus of deep sleep, the awakening of these individual souls (jīvas) from that Brahman is thus indicated; for we hear such scriptural passages as, "Having come back from there, they do not know, 'We have come back,'" and so forth. Therefore, the soul does not possess the agency of awakening by itself. [This occurs] in the lotus of the heart immediately following the state of deep sleep.
In the Supreme Brahman, which is a liṅga consisting of radiant light, the individual soul (jīva)—whose consciousness was previously delimited by the bonds of māyā—attains awakening;
that is, one whose understanding is preeminent. Being characterized by the identification with the body, senses, and so forth, he rises again in order to behold the kingdom known as the waking world.

It goes out from the city called the body through the gate of the heart-lotus, which is the enclosure of the *purītat* vessels. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from that Self all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) go forth each according to its own path; from the vital breaths the deities, and from the deities the worlds.

This scriptural passage has been clearly taught here by the Blessed One: "He, having come back... According to this scripture, a combination (*samuccaya*) must indeed be accepted. And regarding the position of option (*vikalpa*), the venerable Śivācārya Śrīkaṇṭha stated that there are eight defects:

when the individual soul (*jīva*) sleeps in the channels (*nāḍī*), one would have to abandon the established authority of the passages concerning the pericardium (*purītat*) and Brahman, and accept what was not previously established.

And [the other] would have its invalidity accepted. But when [the soul] sleeps in the pericardium (purītat) and Brahman, then the validity previously abandoned by the two passages concerning the pericardium and Brahman would have to be accepted, and the invalidity previously accepted would have to be discarded. This being the case—
There are eight defects:
[the four consisting of] abandonment, acceptance of what was not obtained, acceptance of what was abandoned, and abandonment of what was accepted—this constitutes the tetrad of defects.

When this tetrad of defects is applied both to the category of passages concerning the heart (*purītat*) and Brahman, and likewise to the category of passages concerning the channels (*nāḍī*), there are thus eight defects.
[The meditations] exist [simultaneously]. Therefore, it is established that they do not belong to the category of optional alternatives (*vikalpa*).

Others state the reasoning for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as follows: "Because the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth serve a single purpose, there is an option between them, just as there is between rice and barley.

However, even by those [who hold this view], it is intended that since there is a single purpose through a traditional succession, there would be a combination (*samuccaya*); thus, it is precisely the perception of independence (*nirapekṣatva*) that is meant [in the prima facie argument].

It must be said: it happens in those [channels] in such a way that one who is asleep sees no dream whatsoever. Now, when this breath becomes unified, having descended through them, he rests in the pericardium (*purītat*); thus the reasoning for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) has been stated, showing that the combination of the channels and so forth is demonstrated by scripture. Among those, regarding the channels...

Since it is understood that they merely constitute the path for returning [to the body], there is no perception of them as being combined in their status as the locus of deep sleep; therefore, they are disregarded. Furthermore, the designation of the channels (nāḍīs) and the pericardium (purītat) as the support of the individual soul (jīva) is untenable.
Likewise, it is incorrect to claim that the soul’s support in Brahman—by virtue of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—is what constitutes its identity with Brahman (brahmātmakatva).

This is because of the well-stated sūtra, "By the difference between deep sleep and departure," and because of the lack of natural consistency in those scriptural passages that express a grammatical non-co-ordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya).

Now, as for the two scriptural passages: "Where this one [is] thus in deep sleep... then this person consisting of consciousness, having taken the consciousness of the vital breaths by means of his own consciousness, lies in that space within the heart" and "He lies in the pericardium."

How is there no contradiction here? For others [hold that] "in this space" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); nevertheless, the statement "in the heart" is contradicted by the fact that [the self] lies within the *purītat*.
Therefore, it must be said that there is no contradiction because of the identity of the substratum (*dharmin*) called the *purītat*, which is denoted by the word "space."
Others say that the pericardium (*purītat*) is the measure of the heart's enclosure and serves as the support for the heart; therefore, they claim there is no contradiction.
But that is incorrect, because there is a contradiction between lying in the pericardium—having descended from the heart through the channels (*nāḍī*)—and lying in the heart itself.

Others, however, say that during deep sleep one attains the Supreme Self who is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). That is incorrect, because it is not established by authoritative means that the inner controller is distinct from the Lord (the Supreme Self), and because it contradicts the scriptural text: "He is embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*). Therefore, what was stated previously is the correct view.
The Section Concerning the Recollection of Karma, Words, and Injunctions. 3.

The individual soul (*jīva*), transmigrating during deep sleep, attains the light-linga known as Paraśiva and, having become refreshed, arises again for the sake of experience. Indeed, it is the very same souls from the previous day who, during the state of sleep, are characterized by their internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having entered into a subtle state.

Having become dissolved in the light-linga (jyotir-liṅga) delimited by the heart-lotus, do they become manifested on subsequent days by being delimited by internal organs that have attained a gross state? Or rather,
are the individual souls (jīvas), whose internal organs were known [as merged] on the previous day, entirely in a state of deep sleep (suṣupti)?

In response to the doubt as to whether those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) possess the conceit of truth (satya-abhimāna) arise again as individual souls (jīva) characterized by that conceit during the ultimate dissolution into Brahman, the author provides a determination through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"But he [is the same], on account of work, remembrance, scriptural word, and injunction. (Sūtra 9.3.149)

He who was merged on the previous day into the Supreme Śiva—whose nature is the light-linga delimited by the heart-lotus during the state of deep sleep—is the very same one who becomes manifest on the following day through the attainment of the gross internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Why is this so?

This is stated on account of the recollection of past actions, the hearing of words, and scriptural injunctions. For one remembers on this day the actions performed on the previous day—whether by a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) or a non-scholar; furthermore, there is the hearing of Vedic revelation such as "here [one becomes] a tiger or a lion," and there are injunctive statements such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. It is for these reasons that this is said.

If a different soul were accepted for each successive day, then one soul would be the performer of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice while another would be its enjoyer; consequently, the scriptural injunction prescribing the Jyotiṣṭoma for one desiring heaven would become invalid. Similarly, the statement beginning with "Whether he becomes a tiger or a lion... and ending with "...whatever they become, that they become" would likewise be invalid.

This statement may be explained as follows: it is indicated that the very same living beings who existed on the previous day, characterized by subtle internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) during the state of sleep, become manifest on subsequent days as being characterized by gross internal organs. Otherwise, there would be no recollection on this day of actions experienced on the previous day.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for one person to remember what has been experienced by another, the scriptural passage itself is the subject here: "When this person is said to sleep, my dear, then he becomes united with Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1). A doubt arises as to whether it is the very same sleeper who rises at the time of awakening, or someone else.

"One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed; he does not return again," and so on—since hundreds of such scriptural passages declare that one who has attained the state of Brahman is subject to the condition of non-return. Furthermore, regarding the statement, "My dear, at that time he becomes united with Being," how could the return of those who have reached Brahman and are as if asleep be possible for anyone? For all [who have thus merged], [there is no returning].
Because we observe the sleep and awakening of living beings, it is said that one who has arisen is indeed different [from the one who slept].
However, in the phrase "it is he indeed" (*sa eva tu*), the word "indeed" (*tu*) sets aside that position. It is he himself who arises. Why?

[The soul returns from deep sleep] because of action, remembrance, and scriptural injunctions. First, regarding action: the merit and demerit previously performed by one who has fallen into deep sleep must be experienced by that very same person prior to the attainment of the knowledge of reality. This is also evident from remembrance: "I who was asleep am now awakened. Furthermore, scripture shows that he who was asleep is indeed the same as he who is awakened: "They [return] here as tigers, or lions..."

The injunctions stating, "Whether he becomes a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—whatever he may be, then he becomes that," are for the purpose of liberation. If deep sleep were itself liberation, these [injunctions] would be purposeless. Furthermore, in deep sleep, one has not yet attained the state of Supreme Śiva, which is entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for it is with reference to deep sleep that [the scripture] says, "In this state he is deep asleep."
"Indeed, this one does not thus know himself at present as 'I am this,' nor these beings.
He has only reached destruction; I see nothing enjoyable here," so it is heard in the Śruti. And of the liberated one:
"Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own true form. There he moves about, laughing and playing."

"Delighting, he becomes a self-ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds; for he sees everything as one who sees through [the Lord]; he attains everything in every way. Thus, it is heard that those residing on Kailāsa, who have attained auspicious power and achieved *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sārūpya* [liberations], possess the attributes of the Supreme Lord, such as omniscience and so forth.

Having entered that state of deep sleep while still transmigrating—with all his organs exhausted and incapable of cognition or enjoyment—he reaches the light-liṅga called Paraśiva, the place of rest; then, having regained his breath and become refreshed, he arises again for the sake of experience. This concludes the section on the "Stupefied" (mugdha). 4.
Regarding the statement of the mutual distinction between the states of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and fainting (*mūrchā*):

although the three states within the three bodies are established through scripture, reasoning, and experience, the state of fainting—being similar to deep sleep—is not [explicitly] observed as such. Therefore, in response to the doubt as to whether it is distinct from that [state of sleep] or included within it:
By means of another discussion, he states the mutual distinction between the state of deep sleep and the state of swoon:
"In the case of one who has fainted, there is partial attainment [of death], because of the remainder. (2.1.10)

In the state of fainting, there is only a partial attainment or partial dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is characterized by its identification with the body and so forth—into Brahman, which is like a luminous *liṅga* within the heart-lotus; however, it is not a dissolution of that identification in its entirety, as occurs in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). This is the case for a person who has fainted.

Even in the absence of knowledge of external objects, because there exists a continuity of internal experience of suffering, one must indeed admit, at least in part, the persistence of the identification with the body and so forth. Thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) and because it is distinct from the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], the state of swoon (*mūrcchā*) is indeed different [from those three]. As stated previously:

Having described the various types of living beings while asleep, we now consider the state of the "fainted" person. Since it is observed in the world through universal experience that there is such a thing as a "fainted man," there exists a certain state called fainting (*mūrchā*).
The doubt arises as to whether this state is one of those already mentioned, such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*), or something distinct from them.

Since there is no evidence for postulating a distinct state [other than those already known], and since it is logically consistent to establish fainting (mūrchā) as being one of the states such as deep sleep (suṣupti) and so forth, we respond to the position that "this is one of those states" as follows: The state that exists in a person who is fainting is a half-attainment of death; why? Because of the method of elimination (pariśeṣāt). It is not [one of the other states].

Dreaming and waking are so designated because of the absence of [true] knowledge. Deep sleep and death are not [included here] because of the dissimilarity of their causes and the dissimilarity of their forms.

For the cause of fainting is injury and the like; by process of elimination, fainting is a partial attainment of death. Death, indeed, is the cessation of the connection between all the vital breaths and the body.

Furthermore: because of the dissimilarity of its signs (*nimitta*), it is distinguished from deep sleep (*suṣupti*); because of the dissimilarity of its form (*ākāra*), it is distinguished from death.
Since it is stated that it is neither deep sleep nor death, and because it stands midway between deep sleep and death due to its proximity, the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) has been stated.
Subsequently, when there is a suspicion that it might be included within death, the dissimilarity of its form is explained.

In deep sleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) is most abundant; in a swoon, it is diminished and perceived only slightly; in death, it is not perceived at all. In deep sleep, the vital breath is nourished to the greatest extent by external air;
in a swoon, it is nourished only slightly, because a vital breath that has not been nourished is incapable of being perceived.

Others, however, state that they consider the inquiry: "In the state of fainting, has the supreme self been attained? Or has it dissolved into that [self] as in a dream? Or has it entered into another mode?
Since this inquiry is included within one of the states beginning with waking, there is no purpose in treating it separately; thus, the inquiry is twofold.
This is appropriate; furthermore, it is ordained that the scope of inquiry extends up to the Supreme Self.
Therefore, it is concluded that "fainting" (mūrchā) is the state of remaining connected to the subtle vital breath and body.
This concludes the section on the two-fold characteristics (Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa). 5.
The demonstration of the dual nature— both manifest and unmanifest— of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman,

was previously [stated] for the purpose of generating dispassion, which serves as the cause for crossing over the most terrible saṃsāra that obstructs the knowledge of the Supreme Self regarding the individual soul (jīva), the referent of the term *tvaṃ*.

The author of the Sūtras, having examined the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, swoon, and departure [from the body] with respect to that [individual soul], and having established the Lord's agency therein solely by following its activities, addresses the doubt as to what the referent of the word "That" (tatpadārtha)—the Supreme Self—is like: whether it possesses parts or is partless; and he provides its definition through another topical section (adhikaraṇa).
He explains:
|| 151 || "Even from the standpoint of location, the Supreme has no dual characteristics, for everywhere [it is so]. || 11 ||
The term "ubhayaliṅgam" (the dual-liṅga) refers to the Supreme Śiva, the cause of the universe; this is a designation emphasizing the state of being (*bhāvapradhāna*).

This "dual-liṅga-nature" consists of [Śiva] existing in the form of a *liṅga* within the bodies of Śiva’s devotees at Kāśī and elsewhere, and as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all bodies—such as those of gods and humans—at the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, and so forth.
For the sake of the auspicious manifestations consisting of the threefold liberation beginning with *sālokya*, as well as for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation,
His pervasiveness of the entire universe has been taught by virtue of His partless nature; therefore, both of these [qualities] are indeed inherent to Him.

Some [hold] that while the Supreme's being devoid of qualities and partless is innate, its possession of qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) is adventitious; because of the contradiction between these two in a single locus,

they maintain that for the sake of meditation by those of dull intellect, the possession of qualities— which is illusory— is to be accepted through a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Thus they say. He refutes that view [with the words]: "Not from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānataḥ*). Because it has been established that [Brahman] possesses qualities (*saguṇatva*) due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is indicated that its possession of both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) is indeed natural. As it is said: "Rudra is indeed Agni;
these two are his bodies—the one terrible, the other auspicious"—[and] "O Rudra, that which is yours... [etc.].
