"O Giriśanta, look upon our bodies with that auspicious, non-terrible form which dispels evil—upon us with that most peaceful form!

O Soma and Rudra, place all these remedies within our bodies; be gracious and release [us from harm]"—thus in the Vedas; and "Brahman has space as its body, is enriched by peace, is immortal"—thus in the Vedāntas.
The yogi should contemplate the inner liṅga: resembling gold in the ādhāra, possessing the luster of coral in the heart,
and having the brilliance of crystal between the eyebrows.
The characteristics of a Brāhmaṇa who bears the Liṅga are as follows: the mantra in the mouth, meditation in the heart, bearing the Liṅga on the head,
the Rudrākṣa on the crest-lock, and sacred ash— this indeed is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
In such Smṛtis as these, the wearing of external marks is also taught:
"Whether he is capable of internal [meditative] wearing or incapable, the best of the twice-born,
having consecrated it by his guru, should wear the Śaiva liṅga upon his chest."

"It should be worn by a Brahmin for the sake of liberation; thus it is sung in the Vedas. Therefore, one should constantly wear with devotion the Shiva-linga, which is of the nature of consciousness, both in its gross and subtle forms, for the sake of release from the bondage of worldly existence."

Since this has been extensively elaborated upon in various ways in the Śiva-āgamas as well— due to the natural equality of both [liṅgas]— it is improper to maintain that they belong to a single category, as that would be as ill-famed as the "half-old woman" (ardhajaratī) maxim. Therefore,
by the principle that "the establishment of both follows from the force of both types of injunctions," their possession of both liṅgas is indeed beyond dispute.

The establishment of the Supreme Lord as the object of meditation within the small space (dahara) is stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "That small, stainless lotus, the abode of the supreme, situated in the middle of the city..."
Therein also is a small space; free from sorrow, one should meditate upon that which is within it.
Thus, having prescribed that the Supreme Lord is to be meditated upon as the one within the small space (dahara), [the text addresses] the inquiry "Who is He? with the following:

"He who is declared as the Sound at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda—He who is beyond that which is merged in primordial nature (prakṛti), He is the Great Lord (Maheśvara)."

Having thus clearly taught that Maheśvara is the one to be worshipped there, and having demonstrated the worship of Śiva as delimited by the heart of Nārāyaṇa— using him as an example by virtue of being the most excellent among his devotees in the *anuvāka* beginning with "The thousand-headed god"—
and having declared his nature as the Self of all through the passage beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of Death," [the text continues] with "This [belongs] to Soma, to Sūrya..."
"He establishes all marks; the mantra of the hand is pure"—thus, because of the designation of its being both embodied and unembodied through the distinction between external and internal.
Furthermore, in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure," [it describes] the one accompanied by Umā.

"Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, the sage goes to the source of all beings"—thus [it is said]. "The size of a hair-tip, in the center of the heart, the All-God, the Knower of Beings, the most excellent"—thus in the *Atharvaśiras*.
"A person the size of a thumb, like a smokeless light"—thus in the *Kaṭhavallī*. And: "Now, in this city of Brahman..."

"In the small lotus-palace, there is a small space within; that which is inside it is what must be sought"—thus [it is said] in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. This is that supreme Haṃsa, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns, by whom all this is pervaded; its function is eightfold:
on the eastern petal is the thought of merit, and in the Liṅga is deep sleep—these belong to that which resides within the heart.

The fact that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses the form of a *liṅga* is clearly taught; for it is seen in the *Sāmarudrasūkta* of the Sāma Veda that "the *liṅga* is indeed Brahman alone," and that "the ascetic should always meditate eternally on the *jyotirliṅga* between the eyebrows. Thus, the Supreme [Brahman] may be characterized as having parts, being partless, or possessing both natures.

Furthermore, there arises the doubt: "Is it logical that, as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all living beings, [the Lord] is the enjoyer of the fruits of the merit and demerit performed by those living beings, or not?
This is the demonstration of His dual nature.

If it is argued that the embodied and unembodied nature of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is not supported by the Vedas according to the maxim "that which is established by the force of both types of injunctions [is valid]," that is incorrect. For it is said: "He is without eyes or ears, without hands or feet;
eternal, all-pervading, exceedingly subtle; indeed, without breath or mind, pure, like space, omnipresent, and untainted."

Because its corporeality is prohibited in collections of scriptural passages such as "partless, devoid of qualities, peaceful, irreproachable, stainless, soundless, intangible, formless, and imperishable," because there would be a lack of omnipresence if it were corporeal,

and because it would follow that it would experience the likes and dislikes, pleasure and pain of individual souls— since a body (śarīra) is so called because it perishes (śīryate)— [it cannot be corporeal].

Because we observe a fixed order of things, and because even if [the Lord] possessed a body subject to His own will, it would still be possible for that body not to be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it is possible for the Supreme— who reveals Himself according to the "half-old woman" maxim— to possess both attributes simultaneously. If it is argued that this is established by such passages as "He whose self is the body" and "Who is Rudra in the fire," whereby His being the inner controller of all and having all as His body is logically consistent, that argument is untenable.

Furthermore, because the human goals (puruṣārtha) consisting of various relationships are illuminated [by scripture], and because the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca)— such as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which are distinct from Brahman— is established by implication through the determination of non-duality in such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here," [the world] is like a snake superimposed on a rope, lacking ultimate reality even throughout the three periods of time.
When it is argued that God, as defined by attributes such as having parts and being omniscient, does not exist, we reply: "Even not on account of place" (*asthānato 'pi*).

With the particle *hi*, he refutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). [The sūtra says: "Not even on account of place is there any distinction for the Supreme. This is not the case for the followers of Maheśvara and others.

How can this book be possible? Because it possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*); for everywhere—in the Śruti, Smṛti, Āgama, Purāṇas, and so forth—its nature as possessing both characteristics, that is, its being composed of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), is taught. Therefore, externally, [it contains] Kāśī, Śrīśaila, and...

In locations such as the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, the space between the eyebrows, and the *brahmarandhra*, its formlessness is established by virtue of its nature as the *cidākāśa* (the ether of consciousness), which is the sole cause of the universe. Furthermore, in the *Taittirīyaka*, through the passage beginning with "daharaṃ vipāpam" (the small, stainless [space]), there is the internal wearing of the *liṅga* consisting of the contemplation of the *jyotirliṅga*; this belongs to Soma and Sūrya.

By the mantra, "He establishes all signs; the hand-mantra is pure," the wearing of external signs is also taught. "He who is the bull among the Vedas, whose form is universal, who arose from the nectar of the Vedas—may he, as Indra, strengthen me with wisdom. May I become a bearer of the divine nectar; may my body [be purified]."

"May my tongue be most sweet, my ears wide-hearing; you are the treasury of Brahman, covered by wisdom—protect what I have heard. Thus is the wearing of external marks. [One should contemplate] the mind which delights in truth, the self, and the vital breaths, and finds bliss therein; that which is this space within the heart—in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal.
It is golden. That which hangs down like a breast between the two palates is the womb of Indra, where that limit of the hair (the crown of the head) turns back.
Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "having pushed aside the two halves of the skull," the wearing of the internal *liṅga* is seen.
Moreover: "Being and non-being, the defined and the undefined, consciousness and unconsciousness."

"Truth and falsehood became truth"—thus the state of being both manifest and unmanifest is taught of that One. In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, by the words "from the meditation upon Him" (tasyābhidhyānāt), the internal contemplation of the *liṅga* is indicated; and by the word "from union" (yojanāt), [the external practice is indicated].
The wearing of external marks has also been taught.
The locations for wearing these marks are now defined:
"He whose faces, heads, and necks are everywhere, who dwells in the cave of the heart of all beings."
The Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent.
Thus, in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]: "The wise man should bear the *praṇava-liṅga* on the head, the neck, the armpit, the belly, or even on the chest,
as well as on the palm of the hand."
From this statement, the wearing of external marks [is established]. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "dwelling in the cave of all beings," its internal [wearing] is also taught:
"Those who revile the *tripuṇḍra* revile Śiva himself;
but those who wear it with devotion, they wear Śiva himself."
Thus, in the *Bṛhajjābāla*, having kept in mind the superiority of the wearing of the *liṅga* over all else, the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* is taught as being equal to it.
Furthermore, in the *Kaivalya-śākhā*, regarding the passage "Umāsahāyaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt" (Accompanied by Umā, beyond darkness), [the term] "Umāsahāyam" [is explained].

By such passages as these, its possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) is established; and by such passages as "the witness of all, beyond darkness" (*samastasākṣiṃ tamasaḥ parastāt*), its qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) is likewise established for that same single reality. This is because another scriptural text declares: "The witness, the cognizer, solitary and devoid of qualities" (*sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca*);
thus, the qualitylessness of the supreme Self, which is of the nature of the witness, is taught. Likewise, in the Smṛti also:
Auspicious, profoundly peaceful, immortal, omniscient, facing in all directions,
endowed with true resolve, possessing true desires, and eternal.
Consisting of both form and formlessness, pure, and bestowing the desired fruits upon devotees.
Adorned with jewels, bracelets, armlets, crowns, and other ornaments,
he has a blue neck and odd eyes, and his left side is graced by Umā.
Resembling ten million full moons, more beautiful than ten million gods of love,
liberated from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), and proficient in the fivefold cosmic acts.
And thus it is said in the Purāṇas:

"Śiva is the sole mass of qualities such as splendor, strength, sovereignty, great awakening, heroism, and power; he is higher than the high, his desires are fully realized, all that is to be discarded has been cast off, and he is the Lord of all."

Thus, the supreme state called Śiva, endowed with all such auspicious qualities, is understood from the Śruti and Smṛti to be none other than the Supreme Brahman, characterized by both [auspiciousness and transcendence]. Furthermore, although He is eternally established as the inner controller of all, even while possessing a divine, playful, and auspicious form—

In Paramaśiva, because Māyā has been brought under His own control, there is no blemish of defect whatsoever, as is the case with the individual soul (jīva). If it is argued that [the Lord] attains enjoyment (sambhoga), [the answer is] no, because of His distinction (vaiśeṣya). In passages such as "By abiding and eating," the absence of defects in Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, due to His not being subject to karma, is indeed taught: "This is your Self, free from evil, ageless... and so forth.
"He is free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true;
He is to be sought after, He is to be known"— thus in many such Vedic passages,
there exists a certain Great God who is a mine of beautiful qualities.
The creator of the entire world, distinct from both the bound soul (paśu) and its fetters (pāśa).

He is the Great Lord (Maheśa), whose nature consists of all auspicious qualities; who, by a mere fraction of his own power, sustains the creation of beings; whose designation as possessing both genders is established by his very nature; and who is the Lord of both Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña).
In such passages as these, it should be understood that he is the inner controller of all, the source of all auspicious qualities,
and that ordinary living beings are like poison in his presence.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is designated as both having a natural form and being formless, their mutual difference is established by implication—just like that between a jar and the ether—and thus there arises a contradiction with many Vedic texts such as 'Brahman is indeed one, without a second' and 'Rudra is indeed one'. Anticipating this, the author refutes it:
If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because of the distinction [between the two types of *sāman*], we say no; for each [individual *sāman*] is stated to be other than that. || 12 ||
Just as the state of being an original object and the state of being a reflection are imagined in the sun,
so too are the states of being the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) imagined in the one Brahman.

Since the Smṛtis and Purāṇas understand the individual self (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) to possess a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda), it is logical that the Śruti texts prescribing the embodied (mūrta) and unembodied (amūrta) natures of Brahman refer solely to such a distinction based on limiting adjuncts;
otherwise, there would be a mutual difference between the embodied and unembodied Brahman. If this is argued, we say no—
Because each [of these] is stated to be "not that": "There are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless;
inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite consciousness, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman;
that which is without beginning, middle, or end, the one, all-pervading, formless wonder of consciousness and bliss."

Since hundreds of such scriptural passages declare that He possesses both a formal (mūrta) and a formless (amūrta) nature as His inherent (svābhāvika) characteristic by way of non-difference, one must not accept a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda) established by Smṛtis and Purāṇas which contradict that [scripture].
Furthermore, in passages such as "He who dwells in the earth," in every successive instance, it is said: "He is that... [and so forth].
If it is argued that the passage "the Self, the inner controller, the immortal" indicates that the inner controller Śiva possesses those attributes,

that is incorrect; for even though he has the eight forms beginning with Earth, his distinctness from them is expressly stated in such scriptural passages as, "The witness of all, beyond darkness," and "Rudra, the great seer, who transcends the universe."

If it be argued that, according to such scriptural passages as "possessing all actions, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes," Brahman's having parts and its being endowed with qualities (saguṇatva) are indeed primary—
[we reply: by such passages as "without sound, without touch, without form, immutable," its being partless and devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva) is established.

Some say it is essential (svābhāvikam), while others say that both the qualityless (nirguṇatva) and the qualified (saguṇatva) aspects must be accepted, because otherwise there would be the consequence of mutual contradiction between the scriptural texts. Therefore, an inconsistency is observed due to the absence of a determining factor. Thus, in response to the inquiry as to which among these three is logically tenable, he says:
Moreover, some [hold] this very same view. 13.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the sole authority is the scriptural passage which establishes the primary definitive doctrine resolving all doubts—namely, "Moreover, O descendant of Daiva, there are two forms of Brahman, the embodied and the unembodied"—that is not so.
Why? Because some [scriptures] say thus, and all the scriptures [say thus].

In opposition to this, certain preeminent Vaidikas, such as Vāmadeva, Agastya, and others, declare that the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, possesses both genders; therefore, that alone should be accepted. As stated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*:
"Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata..."
These forms of pride are not to be refuted by logical arguments.
O Mahāmati, the Vedas are the authority for all [schools], including Sāṃkhya and the rest;
it is certain that their preeminence is due to their following the Vedas.
O great sage, it is traditionally held that Pāñcarātra, Yoga,
and Sāṅkhya abide within a single portion of the Veda, whereas the Śaiva system is considered to consist of the Veda in its entirety.

"O great sage, because it conforms to all the Vedas, the Śaiva Tantra is superior to the Sāṅkhya and other systems that reside in only a single portion of the Veda. Thus it is stated in the Vāmadeva-saṃhitā as well.
Śiva is the soul of all, infinite, and accepted by all the Vedāntas;
he consists of both the formed and the formless, eternal, faultless, and stainless.

Thus, from this observation, it is established that its possession of both characteristics is inherent. However, because in such passages as "Verily, he who dwells bodiless," and "For he is without breath and without mind," the qualityless nature and partlessness of Brahman are primarily elaborated upon more extensively, its qualified nature [is secondary].
Anticipating the objection that [the Self] is secondary because it is conditioned and illusory, he refutes it:
"For it is indeed like that which is formless, because it is primary. (1.3.14)

If it is argued that the Śiva-tattva must indeed be accepted as formless, because in numerous Vedic passages such as "the inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite awakening, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the womb of Brahman," the partless Śiva-tattva alone has been established; then [we reply]:

Because that is the primary focus: "Salutations to the one with golden arms, to the golden-colored, to the golden-formed, to the Lord of gold, to the Lord of Ambikā, to the Lord of Umā, to Paśupati—salutations, salutations! [He is] the Law, the Truth, the Supreme Brahman, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny."
Salutation indeed to Virūpākṣa, the one of upward-directed semen, who possesses universal forms.

"Salutations to you, O Rudra, for your wrath, and also to your impetuous speed; salutations be to your bow, and salutations to your two arms," and so forth—in hundreds of such scriptural passages, [the Lord's] possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*), his having parts (*sāvayavatva*), the fact that he is the object of meditation and worship, and his possessing both formal (*mūrta*) and formless (*amūrta*) attributes are established. This is according to the principle that "from the force of both sets of attributes, the existence of both sets of attributes is proven."

It should be understood as being natural by virtue of its equality. For it is said, "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is between these two is Brahman. Even though it enters into everything, since the text establishes only the bringing-forth of name and form without any contact with the effects of name and form, its possession of both characteristics (liṅga) is unavoidable.
Objection: Is it not the case that Brahman is understood from such passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" to have a nature consisting solely of non-differentiated light?

Elsewhere, however, [attributes] such as omniscience, the power of true resolve, having parts, and being illusory in nature are understood. Therefore, how can it be established that Brahman is a mine of auspicious qualities and possesses parts?
Anticipating this objection, he says therein:
"And like light, because [the scripture] is not purposeless. (1.1.5)

Just as there is no redundancy between Vaiśvānara, the lord of the southeast corner, and Vaiśvānara, who exists in all locations such as the *āhavanīya* fire, because they share identical attributes such as self-luminosity, the dispelling of darkness, and the removal of cold;

so too [there is no redundancy] between the formless Brahman established by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," and [the Lord] addressed as "Obeisance to Hiraṇyabāhu."

The golden nature (*hiraṇmayatva*) established by such passages as "To the one of golden color" (*hiraṇyavarṇāya*), and the nature of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—both of these are accepted as being of the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśasvarūpatva*).
Therefore, the fact that the single Brahman possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) has been explained in many ways without contradiction. It is partless (*niṣkala*).

"Actionless, peaceful, faultless, and stainless—then for what reason is he called Mahādeva? Because, having transcended all things, he destroys [evil] and exalts himself through the sovereignty of the yoga of self-knowledge; therefore he is called Mahādeva.
Since such descriptions of both the embodied and unembodied Brahman appear in hundreds of scriptural passages without contradiction, he possesses both characteristics (liṅga).
That it is "intrinsic" (svābhāvika) is beyond reproach.
Furthermore: [He is] omniscience, omnipotence, the cause of all, and the essence of all;
[we worship] Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity, the small, the stainless, the abode of the supreme.

In passages such as "That lotus which is situated in the middle of the city," and others, there are scriptural texts— well-known externally and internally as the *dahara*, *śāṇḍilya*, *upakośala*, and *vaiśvānara* vidyās— which prescribe the attainment of the world of Śiva as their fruit;
yet, by means of one's own fabricated logic, these texts are made to produce fruits such as the attainment of the world of an illusory Lord characterized by His own qualities.

If it is argued that falsity (*mithyātva*) is not contradictory [to the Veda], we reply: according to the maxim "as is the Yakṣa, so is the offering," it is improper to accept only a portion of a position through one's own logic— like the maxim of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīnyāya*)—
because it follows as a matter of course that even the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahman*) taught in the Veda, which is itself qualified and false, must be false.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the Veda to propound a purely attributeless (nirguṇa) reality, that non-Vedic doctrine is indeed charming only so long as it is not subjected to critical inquiry.

Thus, since the Śruti passage, "In this very way, my dear, this Self is entirely within and without, a mass of pure consciousness," teaches that the Self is merely pure, attributeless consciousness, how can there be any primacy for a Brahman possessed of attributes?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
|| 156 || And he says: "It is merely that. || 16 ||

Since the nature of Brahman as both embodied and unembodied is established without doubt in such scriptural passages as "There are indeed two forms of Brahman," and since there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the Śruti, and since statements such as "Now, therefore, the instruction: not this, not this" aim solely at the realization of the inner self after first negating the manifest world of the embodied and unembodied; [therefore, Brahman possesses both forms].

Furthermore, from the understanding that the divine forms— which are eternal, auspicious, and identical in nature with Śiva, the sole cause of the universe, as described in passages such as "With firm limbs, multiform, and fierce"— are eternal,
there arise scriptural texts such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite."
These [scriptural passages] merely establish that Paraśiva is of the nature of self-luminosity;

they do not aim at the negation of the body of the perfected Brahman as characterized by truth, desirelessness, and so forth. For this very reason, the Śruti states that their function is solely to establish those two—the embodied and the unembodied Brahman. And it says:
The meaning is that it establishes [this].

Furthermore, in the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], the state of being both manifest (mūrta) and unmanifest (amūrta) is observed through such passages as "It became the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat). Therefore, there is no doubt.
Now, one might object: let the twofold nature (ubhayaliṅgatva) of Śiva, who is Brahman, be well-known since it is established by scripture; nevertheless...

Having raised the objection—"How can there be oneness [of the Self] when the mutual difference in their attributes is manifested, as in the case of Yajñadatta and Devadatta?"—he says in response: "And it is shown, moreover, it is also recorded in Smṛti. (Sūtra 1.1.17)
The entire collection of Vedāntas demonstrates that Brahman is a mine of auspicious qualities, possesses a divine and auspicious form,
is free from the stain of all defects, is all-pervading, is incorporeal, and is the inner controller of all;
this is also recorded in the Smṛtis, wherein its corporeality and incorporeality are shown to be natural.

It is recorded in the Smṛti: "Of that which consists of all powers, which is all-pervasive like the wind and so forth, formless, and the source of all desires—even though there exists a natural mutual difference [among its powers], non-difference is declared.
Thus it is said: "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among lords..."
We shall worship that god, the supreme deity among deities, the first lord of cattle, the primordial one,
the exalted Parameśvara worthy of praise.
"He is the cause, the lord of the cause of causes; he has no progenitor and no overlord. For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither his equal nor his superior is seen.
Thus it is stated in such scriptural passages as "partless, actionless, and tranquil."
Under my supervision, nature brings forth the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves.
But there is another, the Supreme Person, designated as the Supreme Self—
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
He is omniscient, the doer of all, and possessed of the power of knowledge regarding all capacities; he is neither diminished nor increased, self-dependent, beginningless, and the master of himself.
Free from fatigue, drowsiness, fear, anger, desire, and the like;
blameless, supreme, attained, without support, and imperishable is that sequence.

Since in such Smṛti texts as well, Śiva, who is Brahman, is designated as having the nature of both Liṅgas, the non-difference between the embodied and the unembodied is established despite their difference.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
And for this very reason, there is the analogy of the reflection of the sun and so forth. || 18 ||
In Śiva alone—who is partless and all-pervasive—the states of Sadāśiva, Maheśvara, Kālarudra, and Īśvara are seen;

and although there is differentiation, non-difference is also observed, just as the sun and other luminaries appear distinct when reflected in water, mirrors, and so forth. For this very reason, there is the following analogy:
"Just as the one sky appears separate within jars and other vessels..."
In the very same way, though indeed one, it appears as many, like the sun reflected in various reservoirs of water.
For the single Self of all beings, though established in every being,
is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.

Since the state of possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*)—namely, being both different and non-different (*bhedābheda*)—of the Brahman with form (*mūrta*) and the Brahman without form (*amūrta*) is clearly taught in such scriptural passages as these, there is no occasion for the stain of doubt.
[Objection: But in passages such as "it is seen like the moon in water," [the relationship] is by way of the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).

Even when establishing the difference-in-identity (*bhedābheda*) between the embodied and the unembodied Brahman, one might object that since difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it is ultimately unreal (*apāramārthika*) and thus false; therefore, the purport of the Śruti is always only their difference. Anticipating this, the author refutes it: "But it is not so, because [the soul] is not apprehended like water. (Sūtra 2.3.19)
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Regarding the scriptural statement, "He is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water," just as the sun,

a face, and so forth are perceived in water, mirrors, and the like due to adventitious distinctions (*aupādhika-bheda*), Mahādeva is not perceived in the same way within the locations of the forms such as Sadāśiva.

For in cases such as water and the like, the sun and other luminaries are perceived as if situated therein due to an illusion, but they are not actually situated there in ultimate reality. Here, however, in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "There are indeed two forms of Brahman," the equality of both [the formless and the formed] is stated in terms of their ultimate reality. Therefore, in statements such as "It is seen like the moon in water," that very same status [of ultimate reality] is understood.

Now, one might object: since in such passages as "He whose body is the earth" and "He who dwells within the earth," the Supreme Lord is taught to possess the eight forms beginning with the earth and to be their inner ruler (antaryāmin), how can the established position that Śiva and the other [deities] alone possess those specific forms be justified? To this, he says:

The state of participating in increase and decrease [belongs to the individual soul] because of its being included [within the Lord], because of the consistency of both [theories], and because it is so observed.

Because of being included within— since Sadāśiva and the others are included within Śiva by virtue of being portions of His own innate, non-material, and non-differentiated power of consciousness (cicchakti), they do not undergo increase or decrease,
unlike the eight forms (mūrtis) such as Earth, which consist of the three qualities (triguṇa) and are portions of a power distinct from Śiva.

The state of being the locus of defects such as birth and destruction is not possible; why? Because of the consistency of both—because of the consistency of both difference and non-difference between the two, namely Brahman in its formed (mūrta) and formless (amūrta) aspects. Why so? Also because of scriptural revelation; for in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Two indeed are the forms of Brahman," the difference between Brahman in its formed and formless aspects is established.

Furthermore, because it illuminates the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) among the divisions of the Truths (*satya*), it is determined that Sadāśiva and the others do not possess the nature of those divisions—unlike the eight forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Earth, which are veiled by the insentient primordial matter (*jaḍaprakṛti*) in the form of bonds (*pāśa*). Or rather: "Brahman has space as its body, whose self is Truth, who delights in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and whose mind..."

By the phrase "Bliss," "Space," and "Space is the true Self—the true nature"—the state of being both formed and formless is indicated. In the statement "Brahman has space as its body," its formlessness is established;
whereas in passages such as "delighting in breath" (prāṇārāma), there is the teaching of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) consisting of mind and breath.

Since the gross body is established by implication through the designation of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), and because the activity of the subtle cannot occur without the gross, its corporeality (mūrtatva) is taught. By this, it is understood that Brahmanhood belongs to that which is both corporeal and incorporeal—the sole cause of the universe, eternally stainless, and omniscient. Thus, it is also stated in the Smṛti:
He who consists of both the formed and the formless, who is infinite, whose majesty transcends the phenomenal world,
who is stainless, supportless, and untainted— he is called Śiva.
The Lord, who is the singular mass of infinite and endless auspicious qualities,
is called Śiva by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).

From this observation, they explain that Brahman, which is denoted by the word *Śiva*, possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*). Having described its specific form with such passages as, "The form of this very person is like a saffron-dyed garment," and so forth, [the text continues]: "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*); for there is nothing else higher than this 'not-this,' [which is] Brahman, the subject under discussion, in all its modes."

Having referred to all that by means of the word "iti" (thus) and having negated it all, [the scripture] shows that Brahman is indeed pure Being (*sanmātra*) which is the substratum of all particularities, whereas the particularities are imagined by Brahman through its own nature not knowing itself to be of such a kind. This concludes the section on "The Limitation of What is Under Discussion" (*prakṛtaitāvatvadhikaraṇa*). 6.
Therefore, as to how Brahman possesses both genders, he says here:
"The establishment of the dual gender of Brahman, the Supreme Śiva.
(Sūtra 3.2.11) "For [the scripture] denies the nature of this world as it has been described; thereafter, it speaks further. (Sūtra 3.2.22)

This is not tenable— that Brahman’s possession of specific attributes is negated by the words "not this, not this"— for, were that so, it would be nothing more than the prattle of a madman. For no sane person, having first taught everything unknown through other means of knowledge as an attribute of Brahman, would then subsequently negate those very same things as its attributes.

It is established. Even though some of the entities being pointed out are well-known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their nature as modes (*prakāra*) of Brahman remains unknown. However, the intrinsic nature and the status as modes of Brahman of the others [the words *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*] are indeed known.
[It is] unknown. Therefore, since it is impossible to refer back to those [qualities], they are taught right here. Consequently, the negation of them is not tenable.

Because this is so, this sentence negates the "limitedness" (*prakṛtaitāvatvam*) of Brahman—that is, the "extent" (*iyattā*) by which Brahman is perceived as qualified by those specific attributes that have been introduced. [The phrase] "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) [negates this].
It is negated: "Not this, not this" (neti neti). It does not mean that Brahman is not characterized by the aforementioned modes at all;
rather, the meaning is that the "extent" (iyattā) of Brahman—characterized by those aforementioned modes—is what is referred to here by the word "iti."

And since, immediately after the negation, it speaks further of a multitude of qualities belonging to Brahman, it therefore negates only the connection with the previously mentioned qualifiers. For it speaks of a multitude of qualities: "Not this, not this; there is nothing else higher than this. Its name is 'the Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the truth."
"For them, this is the truth.

The meaning is as follows: there is no other entity superior to this Brahman which has been established as "not this, not this" (neti neti); that is to say, there is nothing else distinct from Brahman that is superior either in its essential nature (svarūpa) or in its qualities (guṇa). And of that...
"Brahman" has the name "the truth of truth. Its etymological explanation is: "The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are indeed truth; of them, this [Brahman] is the truth.

By the word "vital breaths," the individual souls (jīvas) are referred to due to their association with the vital breaths. They, for their part, are "truth" in the sense that they are not like the ether and other elements [which are subject to transformation].

Because there is no modification (*pariṇāma*) consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*), they alone are real; yet even more real than they is this Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*). For while living beings (*jīvas*) possess contraction and expansion of knowledge according to their karma, these two do not exist for the Supreme Person, who is free from all evil (*apahatapāpman*); therefore, he is more real even than they.

And for this reason, because of the connection with the multitude of qualities declared by specific scriptural passages, the statement "not this, not this" does not negate the qualified nature of Brahman;
rather, it negates only the previously mentioned limitations. Therefore, the supreme Brahman possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga).
Since Brahman is not within the scope of other means of knowledge, [the scripture] restates its forms as embodied and unembodied in relation to it.

Since a negation of that [Brahman] itself is impossible, the negation of its specific magnitude (*prakṛti-iyattā*) has been stated; this very point confirms that it is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus he says: || 162 || "For [the scripture] declares that it is unmanifest" (Sūtra 2.1.22).

That Brahman is not manifested by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the Scripture (*śāstra*) says: "Its form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees it with the eye; it is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech;
one who knows not the Veda does not comprehend that Great One; this understanding is not to be attained through logic."
In such scriptural passages as these, it is clearly taught that [the nature of Śiva] is not within the scope of those who lack devotion.
In response to the doubt— “By whom can the nature of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is both with and without form, be known, since it is unlimited and self-luminous?”— it is said:
Moreover, [the existence of God] is established through both perception and inference even during the process of propitiation. || 163 || 23 ||

Moreover, through direct perception and inference, it is established that the direct realization of the deity in both its formal (mūrta) and formless (amūrta) aspects occurs for some during dreams and for others during the waking state— provided there is proper propitiation through external and internal meditation, concentration, worship, and the like— and not otherwise.

This is understood from both Śruti and Smṛti: "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing; it is attained by him whom the Self chooses; to him this Self reveals its own form. Then, with his being purified through the clarity of knowledge, he [attains] Him."
"He beholds the partless one while meditating," and so forth— in such scriptural passages (*śruti*), as well as in the *Smṛtis* and specifically in the *Śātātapa-smṛti*,
there is an etymological definition of the terms "the worshiper" (*ārādhaka*) and "the object of worship" (*ārādhya*):
"Having worshipped with devotion the Great God Sāmba, who is the object of worship and whose face is turned everywhere..."
It is eternal, consisting of both form and formlessness, [attained] through the path of meditation, worship, and so forth.
"Then, for the sake of attaining the grace of Śiva, the procedure for propitiation must be performed by the seeker, both externally and internally. Thus it is stated in another Smṛti as well.
Having propitiated the Lord who has Umā as his companion— the omniscient,
immutable, divine Master, whose nature consists of both form and formlessness, and whose splendor is equal to ten million suns—
Endowed with faith, devotion, and other virtues, the wise person should constantly worship [the deity] who resembles ten million moons and consists of ten million streaks of lightning.
"He who worships Maheśvara in the form of the *liṅga*, both internally and externally, according to the scripture, is worthy of worship on this earth. Thus it is said in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a manner, O Arjuna; only by undivided devotion am I possible to be known.
"To know and to see him in truth, and to enter [him], O scorcher of foes"— thus, in the *Vedapādastava*:
"I bow to that Lord whose *liṅga* [is worshipped] day and night."
The hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, perform sacrifices together with their wives.
Thus, in the Vedapādastava: "I bow to that Lord whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives."
And because this has been explained in many ways, meditation (*dhyāna*) takes on the form of devotion (*bhakti*).
Now, [it is said]: "From which words turn back, not having reached it along with the mind..."
That which the mind does not conceive, that by which they say the mind is known— know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here.

If it be objected: "Since in such scriptural passages as these, Brahman is not shown to be cognizable by mind, speech, or body, how can there be a method for its worship?"—we reply: No; for in such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back," the scripture teaches that Brahman is ungraspable by those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are impure, and thus the direct realization of Brahman is precluded for them. However, through the clarity of knowledge, when the sattva is purified, one then [perceives] Him.

The sense is that there is no contradiction between these two scriptural passages, because the Supreme Lord is perceivable by a purified internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), as stated in hundreds of such Vedic texts beginning with: "He who meditates sees the partless," "But He is seen by the keenest intellect," and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Thus, the Lord is perceived through meditation by one whose mind is purified.

Also in the *Smṛti*: "Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, whose breath is conquered, who are contented and have restrained their senses, perceive as light while practicing yoga."

Thus, the ungraspability of Brahman by means of the impure internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been demonstrated. Therefore, it is determined that such scriptural passages as "that which the mind does not think" have precisely this as their purport.

Furthermore, through the worship of the referent of the word *tat* (the Supreme), the seeker—who is the referent of the word *tvam*—attains the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the referent of the word *tat*.
In response to the doubt as to how the innate state of being a jīva—which constitutes the referent of the term "thou" (tvam)—is removed, he says:
"And there is non-distinctness, like light and so forth; and light [arises] from practice in action. (24)
For this reason as well: the present [text] negates only the state of being the individual soul (*jīvatvam*), and not the possession of attributes such as having form or being formless;

because, like Vāmadeva, Agastya, Upamanyu, and others who have directly realized the nature of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, even while in the state of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukta*), they possess the nature of both form and formlessness, just as they possess the nature of knowledge, bliss, and so forth.

Brahman shines forth. Seeing this very [reality], the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu and the Sun," and so forth. Furthermore, the manifestation of bliss and other qualities identical in nature to Brahman is perceived by those such as Vāmadeva through the practice of the ritual acts of meditation, concentration, worship, and service, which consist of complete devotion (*saṃrādhana*).

In the same way, for those who worship Śiva both externally and internally, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—whether in its embodied or unembodied form—is perceived without distinction as being identical with that [Śiva]. This is the state of supreme grace (*sanprasāda*): having emerged from this body and attained the highest light, by means of one’s own...

In other scriptural passages such as "He manifests in form; he is the Supreme Person," it is observed that for those who practice meditation, concentration, and worship of Paraśiva, there occurs the attainment of Śivatva— preceded by the cessation of their innate state as individual souls (*jīvatva*)— through His grace upon liberation while disembodied (*videhamukti*).

Now, one might raise the objection: since the direct realization of Brahman is understood to arise through hearing and so forth—as in such passages as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"—how can the established rule that the direct realization belongs only to those who worship Him both externally and internally be justified? To this doubt, he says:
Therefore, it is infinite; for such is the mark. || 25 ||

Therefore—from the very worship consisting of meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and so forth upon Śiva—the *liṅga* is indeed the Supreme Brahman itself, by virtue of its being infinite and consisting of the entire manifold of moving and non-moving beings. For instance, just as through meditation there is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is both embodied and unembodied; so too [is the *liṅga*].

Through the power of uninterrupted practice, all that phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) appears to him in its true nature as that Brahman during the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). Here, the particle *hi* is used for the purpose of certainty, signifying a definitive conclusion. Therefore, [the result] does not arise from mere hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth, in the same way as it does from meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).

It is the state of being the cause for the direct realization of that [Self]. By such passages as "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen," the hearing, reflection, and so forth of those who worship It are indicated. Otherwise, [as held by] the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika schools, there would be no difference between the Lord and other objects of meditation. Therefore, the fruit of the hearing, reflection, and so forth undertaken for the sake of worshipping Him is indeed the direct realization of Him.

It is determined that even in such scriptural passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the word *veda* denotes meditative knowledge (*upāsanā-jñāna*) alone, and not merely the knowledge of the scriptures.
It should be understood that mere knowledge of the scriptures serves only as a means for debate, cavil, and fallacious arguments.
Demonstrating that the knowledge of one's own experience is both the cause and the fruit:
"Without direct experience, the fool rejoices in vain regarding Brahman,
like one who rejoices at tasting the fruit reflected on the tip of a branch."
Because in such scriptural passages as these, it is specifically the knowledge born of one's own direct experience that is designated as the cause of the fruit;
furthermore, the preeminence of meditation [is established] through the particular greatness of the worship of Śiva, as seen in the cases of Viśvāmitra, Agastya, Sānandana, and others.
It is observed in the world that for those who worship the mantras of Garuḍa and others, their adversaries— such as serpents and the like—

become possessed by Garuḍa and other [deities] through such contemplation, and thus become submissive, acting under the power of their command. Therefore, the superiority of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*) is beyond reproach.
Those who have attained perfection must maintain the worship of both forms of Brahman, as established by such scriptural passages as, "There are two forms of Brahman," and so forth.
This has been stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Hari placed his *liṅga* upon his chest, while Pitāmaha (Brahmā) wore it upon his head."
Having propitiated me residing in the *liṅga*, you each attained your respective station.
Likewise, having inwardly assumed the linga which is of the nature of knowledge and identical with Śiva, one attains Śiva through the yoga of meditation upon it; not otherwise.
And because of this scriptural vision, it is established that Brahman possesses both characteristics. This concludes the section on the serpent and its coils (Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||

In the first chapter, after stating the three views regarding difference and the nature of difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman— beginning with the words "The sign for the fulfillment of the promise [is found] in Āśmarathya"—
and having refuted two of those three views (which, like the Buddhists and others, accept only a portion of the authority of the Śruti), [the author proceeds].

The final conclusion (*rāddhāntita*) was established by the sūtra "Kāśakṛtsna [holds that] the doctrine of both difference and non-difference alone is superior because it is consistent with all scriptural revelation and because [the other views] lack stability.
And that difference-and-non-difference was established after proving the non-difference of the world from Brahman, like that of a clay pot from its clay.
Having refuted the views of those outside the Vedic fold who do not accept the non-distinct efficient and material causes that serve as the cause of that [world],

this chapter— through the section on the "Two-fold Nature" (*ubhayaliṅga*) beginning with "On account of place also, of the other" (*sthānato 'pi parasya*)— establishes that Śiva, as Brahman, possesses both natures by way of being both different and non-different; therein, the referent of the term *tvam*...

Thus, in this doubt, although there exists a real distinction and non-distinction between those two until the attainment of liberation, [the author] states in another section that, upon the direct realization of Brahman at the stage of liberation by one whose internal organ is completely purified, absolute non-difference alone is logically established, preceded by the destruction of that distinction: [The Sūtra: *parābhidhyānāt tu tirohitaṃ tato hy asya bandhaviparyayau* (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.5). [The Commentary: But [the Self's nature] is concealed due to the meditation on the Supreme; for from that [concealment] arise its bondage and its opposite [liberation]. Just as the sun, though naturally luminous, appears as if devoid of light when covered by clouds, so too the Self, though naturally pure, appears as if impure when its true nature is obscured by the beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) consisting of the impressions (*vāsanā*) of merit and demerit. When that ignorance is destroyed through the grace of the Lord, the Self attains its own innate nature. Therefore, the Self is not eternally subject to transmigration; rather, it is transmigratory only while its true nature remains unmanifest. This is because the scriptures declare that the state of being a transmigrator is merely a superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Furthermore, since the Self is omnipresent, it is not subject to spatial movement. Nor does it undergo transformation, for it is eternal and immutable. Consequently, the Self is neither born nor does it die. It is simply designated as "born" or "dead" based on its association with the body, just as a tree is said to be "burnt" when its wood is consumed. Thus, the Self is distinct from the body, the senses, and the mind, and is characterized by consciousness alone. It is not the agent of action, for the agency belongs to the conjunction of the Self, the mind, and the senses. Since the Self is inherently free from all attributes, it is not the enjoyer of objects; rather, enjoyment arises from its proximity to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the locus of pleasure and pain. Therefore, the Self is essentially pure consciousness, free from all qualities, and identical with Brahman. This identity is established by such scriptural passages as, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*). Although the Self is omnipresent, it perceives only that portion of space within which the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and senses reside, just as the ether within a jar is perceived only within the limits of that jar. Thus, the Self is both all-pervading and yet limited by its adjuncts. This is the conclusion of the inquiry.
But [the relationship between Brahman and the world] is like that of a serpent and its coils, because both designations [of difference and non-difference] apply. || 166 || 26 ||

Because of the designation of both [natures]— due to the realization of difference in such scriptural passages as "Two birds...," and the realization of non-difference in such passages as "Thou art That"— both difference and non-difference must be accepted between the two, like a snake and its coils.
Just as in the case of a snake that has coiled itself and a snake that has straightened out, there is oneness in their nature as snakes, yet they possess distinct forms.

Because the Sāṅkhya doctrine, which emphasizes duality, and the Yoga doctrine, which emphasizes non-duality, are indicated as being one and the same, some say that "dualism is the single doctrine" or "non-dualism is the single doctrine.

That [view] should not be accepted due to such delusion; for, as stated in the first chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras], "But that [is so] because of the harmony [of the texts]" and "because of the uniformity of the way [the texts lead to Brahman]," and so forth.

Because the reconciliation of both the scriptures on difference and the scriptures on non-difference is established in Brahman alone— since difference and non-difference are clearly taught in such scriptural passages as "Just as rivers..."— the ignorant speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as being distinct.
"Not the wise," as stated by Kṛṣṇa in the *Kṛṣṇagītā*, and here also by the Blessed Vyāsa,

this aphorism was taught for the purpose of indicating the difference-in-identity (*bhedābheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, which constitute the referents of the words "that" (*tat-pada*) and "thou" (*tvam-pada*). This is because they possess contradictory dimensions, such as shortness and length.

Difference and non-difference are indeed accepted; likewise, although the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are one in their nature as consciousness (*cit*), they are distinct by virtue of [the soul's] atomic size (*aṇutva*) and [Brahman's] omnipresence (*vibhutva*). This is established by such scriptural passages as: "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious," "Having known the Self as distinct from the Impeller, the Illusionist creates this universe," and "The Lord of all sciences. Thus, there is a distinction between the individual soul and Brahman as the worshiper and the object of worship.
Since the non-duality of existence is always indicated by the designation of the oneness of Brahman in such scriptural passages as "By what means could one see whom? and so forth,

and since the relationship between difference and non-difference is established for those two in such scriptural passages as "That thou art," "I am Brahman," and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," there is either a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman as worshiper and worshipped, or [non-difference].
A doubt arises as to whether there is non-difference or difference-and-non-difference.

Due to the contradiction in the nature of things, there can be no difference-and-non-difference. For in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "One eats the sweet fruit of the fig tree while the other looks on without eating," and "The two, the Knower and the Unknower," the Lord and the individual soul (jīva) are shown to be distinct from one another, just like a jar and a cloth.
It is not so, because cessation [of inquiry] is impossible; because sentences such as "That thou art" would then be merely figurative and intended for praise;

because there is a contradiction between non-difference and the relationship of the object of worship and the worshiper; and because in the scriptural text, "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'," there is a negation only of the limited extent of Brahman in its form as the manifest and unmanifest, sentient and insentient entities.
When it is argued that the non-difference between the object of worship and the worshipper is established at some point, we reply as follows:
"Because of the designation of both."

Just as in such scriptural passages as, "As rivers flowing [into the ocean]," and "This serene being (samprasāda) emerges in its own true form," although there exists a natural mutual distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman— the worshipper and the worshipped— resembling that of a river and the ocean,

yet because of the designation of both difference and non-difference in terms of the relationship between the goal to be attained and the attainer at the stage of liberation, that very [view] is logical.
It is like a serpent and its coil. Why? Because of the designation of both. For in such passages as "All this has that as its self; That is the Truth; That is the Self;

Thou art That," "Brahman indeed is all this," and "The Self indeed is all this," there is a designation of non-difference through identity (*tādātmya*). Yet, because of the designation of difference in the passage, "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*)," it is like the serpent [and its coil].

Just as the states of being a coil and being straight belong to the same object, so too, although the two [states] are one in their nature as consciousness (*jñāna*), they are mutually contradictory in their specific attributes; yet, because there is no evidence to the contrary and because both types of scriptural testimony (*śruti*) possess equal authority, all *bheda* (difference) scriptures pertain to the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), while the *abheda* (non-difference) scriptures refer to the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). [This is established by the rules of] position (*sthāna*) and context (*prakaraṇa*).

It is determined that, according to the maxim "the connection [of meaning] follows from the indicative mark" (*liṅgāt samanvayaḥ*), the meaning consistent with the context (*prakaraṇa*) is to be accepted;
otherwise, it should be understood that the entire scripture would become invalid due to mutual contradiction.
Now, one might object: let there be both difference and non-difference through a distinction of time, as in the cases of falling asleep and waking up.
Anticipating the objection that this is inconsistent because darkness and light are by nature mutually opposed like shadow and light and thus cannot coexist at the same time, he says:
"Or rather, it is like the substratum of light, because it is of the nature of light. (2.2.17)

The word "or" (*vā*) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Just as the light of a lamp and the orb of the lamp which is the locus of that light are one in their nature as fire (*tejas*), despite their difference in pervasiveness—
following many observed examples such as cloth that is contracted or expanded— so too is the individual soul (*jīva*).

Furthermore—although it is established that all individuals such as Brahmins possess a single nature by virtue of their connection to the genus (jāti) of "Brahminhood" and so forth, we nevertheless observe mutual distinctions among them through the states of superior and inferior, as well as through forms such as blue and yellow; likewise is it with the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, the pernicious doctrine that there is both difference and non-difference between the two, which is untenable due to the contradiction of entities, is refuted.

Is it not the case that what was stated—that the non-difference of space and time between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established merely through their belonging to the same genus, like light and its substratum, or an elephant and a horse—is inconsistent? For that [non-difference] pertains only to the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*);

whereas upon the direct realization of Brahman, the identity of essential nature (*svarūpaikya*) is also accepted, as ordained by hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Just as rivers... and so forth.

And because it is impossible for an essential difference to cease, one must accept that the state of being a *jīva* is due to a difference caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), like the space within a jar; in response to this doubt, he says:
"Or as before" (Sūtra 2.3.19).
The word "or" (*vā*) here is intended to refute the two views that accept each of the two individual positions [separately]. As in the previous case (*pūrvavat*):

just as in the preceding section the formal and formless aspects of Brahman were specified by the force of scriptural passages such as "There are indeed two forms of Brahman," so too here, there is a natural distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman during the state of transmigratory existence, and [their non-distinction] in the state of liberation.
In that same way, the natural non-difference has been indicated.

Furthermore, even during the state of transmigratory existence, difference and non-difference must be accepted as existing through the oneness of consciousness (*cit*), just like a lamp and its light. Moreover, this is established by such scriptural passages as: "And because there is a designation of difference [He is] other," and "But there is more, because of the mention of difference."
Just as, by means of the relationship of cause and effect between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman— through such statements as "Moreover, because of the designation of difference"—

the mutual distinction in their intrinsic natures is demonstrated, and then [their] non-difference is established through the proposition "Not different from that" (*tadananyatvam*); so too [is the case here].

Having raised the objection regarding the impossibility of cessation [of difference], in the sūtra *upasaṃhāradarśanāt* (BS 2.1.13), it was shown— just as in the previous chapter— that just as milk, through contact with buttermilk and other substances, first ceases its natural state of being milk and subsequently attains the state of curd, so too, even though there exists a mutual, ultimate difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, non-difference is established at the stage of liberation.
It should be understood that, as was elaborated there, the intended meaning of those two [scriptural passages] is likewise intended here.

Regarding the phrase "as before" (*pūrvavat*) in this context, the intention of the sūtra is that the purport of the mutually contradictory scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference should be grasped according to the logic applied in the previous sūtra, the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*), and the previous chapter (*adhyāya*).

The stubborn claim that difference alone is primary on the basis of the authority of certain portions of the Śruti is entirely unacceptable, as it is non-Vedic, like the doctrines of the Sugatas and others. Now, one might object: just as there are Śrutis such as "That thou art" which enjoin non-difference, there are also Śrutis such as "Two birds... which enjoin duality; therefore, duality is not [negated] here...

In response to the doubt—namely, that since non-duality is illuminated in such passages as "There is no diversity whatsoever" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19) and others, how can both [the Self and Brahman] be non-objects of injunction like the Buddhist view and so forth?—he says:
|| 169 || "Or because of negation. || 29 ||

Because if the Śrutis such as "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) were held as primary solely in their aspect of teaching difference, they would contradict the Śrutis on identity such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); and because if the Śrutis such as "That thou art" were held as primary solely in their aspect of teaching identity, they would contradict the Śrutis that enjoin difference such as "Two birds. This is also evident from Śrutis such as "As rivers... (*yathā nadyaḥ*).
Because of the lack of certainty [regarding the soul's nature], following the analogy [of the body], and because of the relationship between the attained and the attainer,

the contradiction between the various scriptural passages concerning the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman makes it unavoidable that the soul is non-Vedic, like the Buddhists and others. Therefore, just as in the previous section there was the distinction and non-distinction of the embodied and unembodied Brahman, here likewise there is the distinction and non-distinction of the individual soul and Brahman, which constitute the referents of the words "thou" and "that."

In order to reconcile the scriptural texts that establish both duality and non-duality, one must indeed accept that there is ultimate duality and non-duality in the states of bondage and liberation respectively, due to the difference in time; for there is both difference and non-difference.
Furthermore: "Even in the state of worldly existence, [the soul] is a part, because of the various designations, as in the case of light and so forth; it is not otherwise."

Since duality and non-duality are clearly taught in passages such as "the other" (paraḥ) and so forth, their distinction and non-distinction are logical according to the principle of part and whole, like the sun and its rays or the jewel and its light. Therefore, [it is said]: "O gentle one, when that is known, all this becomes known; by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay is known."

In such scriptural passages as, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth," the entire body of scripture—which establishes the proposition that knowledge of the effect arises through knowledge of the cause, which is Brahman—is rendered coherent. Here, it should be understood that the word "truth" (satya) refers to the mere reality of the thing itself.
Topic 8: The Refutation of the Opponent's Position.
Regarding the establishment of the difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman:

since the negation of the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman is understood from such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here" and "There is no other seer or thinker than He," how [can there be difference]?
Anticipating the objection that the doctrine of both difference and non-difference is thus established, he says:
"On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference, [the Brahman] is other than this. (Sūtra 30)

Therefore, Brahman is distinct from and superior to the individual soul (jīva). Why? Because of the reasons consisting of the designations of a "bridge," "measurement," "connection," and "difference. In such scriptural passages as, "This is the bridge, the support, so that there may be no confusion of these worlds," and so forth, [the distinction from] the individual soul is established. Furthermore: "If the tip of a hair is divided into a hundred parts, and each part is again divided into a hundred, the individual soul should be known as one such part."

Since the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established by such scriptural passages as "Space is all-pervading and eternal," which describe their infinitude, and since statements such as "There is no other seer but He" refer to His omniscience and the excellence of His peerless majesty, the non-difference of the individual soul and Brahman is ever-present.

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that even the [theoretical] debate is not to be accepted. Now, the subject matter of this [Sūtra] is precisely such scriptural passages as: "That which is the Self is the bridge, the support"; "Having crossed over this bridge, one then becomes equipped for immortality"; and "The supreme bridge of immortality," and so forth; as well as: "This Self is Brahman"; "Brahman is consciousness"; and "That thou art."

Since there are scriptural passages such as these which teach the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and since there are other scriptural passages such as "Two birds... and "Of these, the Lord is the master of bipeds and quadrupeds" which establish their mutual difference, there arises the doubt as to whether they are non-different or different.

If it is argued that because such scriptural passages as "O gentle one, in the beginning this was indeed Brahman," "In the beginning this was indeed the Self, one only, without a second," and "Rudra is one alone;

he does not stand for a second," demonstrate the negation of difference, whereas the scripture "He is the bridge, the supporter" speaks of a distinction between those two, that is incorrect; for just as in the world, [the term] "bridges" [is used].

Just as the ocean serves as the regulator of its boundaries, so too does Brahman serve as the regulator of the boundaries of the castes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas). Therefore, Brahman is seen to possess the nature of a "bridge" (setu).
Furthermore, until the direct realization of Brahman, there exists an adventitious and illusory difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.

This must indeed be accepted. If it is argued that there is a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman based on the designations of "atomic" (*aṇu*) and "all-pervading" (*vibhu*), that too has already been addressed. For the scripture states: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven," thereby indicating that the consciousness of the individual soul existing within the cosmic egg constitutes one foot, while that which exists outside the cosmic egg [constitutes the other three].
The three-footed nature of Brahman-consciousness was stated for the purpose of distinguishing between the referents of the terms *tvaṃ* (you) and *tat* (that).
Since the knowledge of the non-difference between the referents of *tat* and *tvaṃ* is impossible without first knowing the referents of *tat* and *tvaṃ*,
the [Self] qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is [first taught] for the sake of knowing those two referents, according to the maxim of the "large star" and "Arundhatī."

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic (*aṇu*) while Brahman qualified by *māyā* is all-pervading (*vibhu*). Therefore, since the scriptural texts concerning these two do not intend to establish a real difference—because both the atomic dimension and the all-pervading dimension are false, being merely imagined through *māyā*—and because non-difference alone is the ultimate reality, we reply as follows: [The opponent's position: Since the atomic size of the *jīva* and the all-pervasive size of Brahman qualified by *māyā* have been taught, the scriptural passages concerning them do not have the intention of establishing a real difference. This is because both the atomic dimension and the all-pervasive dimension are illusory (*mithyā*), being constructed by *māyā*; thus, non-difference alone is the true reality. To this, we respond: [The Siddhāntin’s position: ... [the following argument follows]... [Note: The provided text fragment ends here; the full response would typically include the refutation of the opponent's view based on the distinction between the *upahita* (conditioned) and *anupahita* (unconditioned) aspects of Brahman.]

Now, because that Self is designated as a "bridge" and a "support" in the passage, "He is the bridge, the support," and because the word "bridge" (setu) is well-known in common usage as that which causes one to reach the opposite bank, it is understood that there is something else to be reached by this [Self]. Likewise, in the statement, "Having crossed over this bridge, he becomes bound below," that which is to be crossed over is also mentioned. Therefore, there exists something else to be reached.

"This immeasurable [Brahman] is measured as this supreme Brahman, the four-footed Brahman, the sixteen-part [Brahman]"— because of this designation of measurement (*unmāna*), and because this designation of measurement indicates the existence of that immeasurable [Brahman] which is to be reached by means of that bridge (*setu*). Likewise, there is also a designation of relation (*sambandha*) with the bridge.

"Like a fire whose fuel is consumed; this is the bridge to immortality. And for this reason, there exists that which is higher than the high, and it is designated as "higher than the high" by way of distinction, as in: "He attains the divine Person who is higher than the high," and "That which is greater than the great. Likewise: "All this is filled by that Person; what else is higher than that?"

Because this would lead to contradictions with such scriptural passages and sūtras as "That is formless and free from affliction" (referring to the nature of Brahman), and "The unborn one, being one, lies beside her while enjoying her; another unborn one leaves her after she has been enjoyed," as well as "Because birth is impossible" and "But there is a designation of difference," which establish that the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman are not distinct from each other like a pot and a cloth. Therefore, [the relationship] between the individual soul and Brahman from the beginning...

Just as in the case of mercury and iron, even though there exists a natural distinction between them, it is determined that the individual soul (jīva) becomes Śiva through the glance of a true teacher.
Now, one might object: since in such passages as "This Self is Brahman," the very nature of the individual soul is taught to be Brahman, [how can there be] a natural distinction?

Having raised the objection that— since the states of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and being the Lord (*īśvaratva*) are imagined in one and the same Brahman because their cessation is impossible, and since their status as imagined is established in such passages [as those cited]— the difference [between them] must, like a snake in a rope, be merely an object of delusion due to its being caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he says in response to that:
But [the rule applies] because of the commonality. || 31 ||
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. "On account of commonality" (sāmānyāt): the state of being common is "commonality";

it is on account of this commonality, because there is an equal designation of both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—difference from the scriptural texts on distinction such as "Two birds... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and non-difference from the scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Since those two types of scriptural passages are reconciled through a difference in time, there is no contradiction between them; nor is either of those two scriptural passages secondary.

Furthermore, because Śiva is designated as being superior to the entire expanse of the sentient and insentient (*cid-acit-prapañca*) in such passages as "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," the doctrine of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahma-vāda*), namely "I am Brahman," is not tenable. Now, that which is the Self...

If it is argued that this [distinction] is necessary because their difference is designated through such attributes as being a bridge (*setu*), the need for crossing (*taritavyatva*), being limited (*parimitatva*), and being a means of attainment (*prāpakatva*)—as in the passage beginning with "The bridge is the support" (*setur vidhṛtiḥ*)—then that is incorrect. For in the passage, "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; one should meditate upon Him with a calm mind," He is taught to be the non-different efficient and material cause (*abhinnanimittopādānakāraṇa*). From here... [etamitaḥ]... [the text continues].

In another Vedic scripture, the state of being attained is expressed as: "Having departed, I shall fully realize [Him]. By the passage, "Having meditated upon the Sage who is accompanied by Umā, the witness of all, beyond darkness," the fact that Śiva, who is beyond darkness, is the goal to be attained by the liberated soul is demonstrated.
This is further illustrated by the analogy of rivers and the ocean in such scriptural texts as "Just as rivers... and so forth.
Since the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the individual soul's (jīva) condition has been clearly taught,
the authority of both scriptural passages is determined to be equal.
Now, even if the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference refer to different times, they nonetheless pertain to the distinct states of the bound and the liberated.
Anticipating the objection, "How can there be equality given the difference [in nature]?", he says:
"The purpose is for the sake of cognition, as in the case of the feet. (32)

Regarding the statement, "This Brahman has four quarters and sixteen parts; three-quarters of It are immortal in heaven," it is shown that the one Brahman alone possesses three quarters by virtue of being the substratum for the transcendent manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*) beyond the cosmic egg,

and possesses one quarter by virtue of being the substratum for the single-quarter manifestation consisting of the cosmic egg in the form of the expansion of sentient and insentient beings (*cidacid-prapañca*).
