Because they were composed by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), they possess equal authority as means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The word "budhya" means for the sake of certain realization. In the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the attainment of the state of Śiva through the knowledge of one who worships Śiva—who consists of the three-quarters manifestation transcending the cosmic egg—is established. Furthermore, [it is said]: "He who knows Brahman—truth, knowledge, infinite—hidden in the cave of the heart within the supreme sky, he enjoys all [desires]."

By the phrase "together with desires," [it means] together with Maheśvara, who consists of the vibhūti of one quarter, through the knowledge of the worship of Maheśvara residing within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Furthermore, it is heard [in scripture] that [the Self] is the enjoyer of the fruits of all desires.

Moreover, with respect to Maheśvara, who dwells within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there is also seen the designation of speech and other faculties as "feet," such as: "Speech is one foot, breath is one foot, the eye is one foot, and the mind is one foot."
Some say that the designation of the feet of Brahman is for the purpose of meditation; that is incorrect.

It is determined that His status as the substratum of all and His majesty—such as being distinct from everything else—is elaborated for the purpose of teaching the identity between the embodied (mūrta) and unembodied (amūrta) Brahman.

Now, since there is no observation of mutual difference between the embodied and unembodied Brahman— due to their being the inner controller of the universe and being distinct from it, respectively, like a jar and a cloth—
and since both types of scriptural texts that enjoin difference and non-difference convey a meaning of mutual distinction regarding the One; [how can they be reconciled?]
In response to the doubt as to how the reconciliation with the Supreme Brahman (parabrahman) is possible, he says:
|| 173 || "On account of the difference of place, as in the case of light and so forth. || 33 ||

On account of the distinction of abode: in the passage "All beings are one foot of Him," the abode of the single-footed manifestation consists of the entry of the expansion of the conscious and unconscious into the Heart; whereas by the passage "The immortal three feet are in heaven," the abode of Śiva’s three-footed manifestation is shown to be transcendent to that expansion—thus there is a distinction between the two abodes.

Because their difference is designated, as in the case of light and so forth; just as there is oneness between the sun and its light despite their mutual distinction, so too [is there oneness] between that which is qualified by Māyā and that which is distinct from it, with respect to the Śrutis expressing the predominance of qualities— which designate their difference— and the Śrutis establishing non-duality which teach the absence of qualities.

There is no contradiction in their being one, as they convey the means, the goal, and the practitioner. Because meditation on the form of difference is taught for the sake of achieving the experience of non-duality delimited by uninterrupted contemplation,

there is no contradiction between the two scriptural passages— just like the light of a gem and its brilliance— even due to their specific locations, like those of a lower and upper story of a palace.

[The point] is established. Now, one might object: let there be mutual dependence between the Śrutis that enjoin duality and non-duality according to the principle of the relationship between a limb and its possessor (aṅga-aṅgin); nevertheless, regarding both sets of Śrutis—
Anticipating the objection as to how there can be a single birth when there is a designation of different fruits for each, he says: "And because of the possibility [of both]. (Sūtra 3.1.34)

By such statements as "This is the bridge to immortality," and because of the indications that Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) are the goal to be attained in passages such as "I am of the nature of Śiva," "I am Brahman," and "That thou art," as well as because both the scriptural texts concerning difference and those concerning non-difference are logically consistent with respect to Brahman, their mutual contradiction is refuted.

If it is argued that one’s own attainment [of Brahman] occurs through the discernment of one's own tenth state—just as in the case of the union [of breaths] and so forth—we say no. For when the Supreme Person, who is the object to be attained, is attained, it is not logical for one's own self to be the means. As it is said: "This Self is not to be obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing; only he whom this Self chooses, by him is He obtained; to him this Self reveals His own form."
Because of hundreds of scriptural passages such as "His own body," which describe the uninterrupted and unconditioned meditation of the individual soul (jīva) upon Brahman,

and because of the teaching in scriptures such as "knowledge and action combined" that the synthesis of knowledge and ritual action is appropriate, it is logical that all scriptural texts— both those concerning difference and non-difference— are established in Brahman without contradiction.
Likewise, there is the section concerning the negation of others. 9.
The Determination of the Attained and the Attainer in the Case of the Individual Soul (Jīva) and Brahman:
Now, [one might object that] the scriptural texts prescribing duality and non-duality are established as having different goals according to the distinction between the bound and liberated states—
as seen in such passages as "A person is submerged in the tree" and "Two birds, inseparable companions," which speak of the individual soul (jīva).

In response to the doubt— arising from such passages as "the other unborn [Self] having enjoyed its experiences" (*bhuktabhogāmajo 'nyaḥ*), which indicate that those two possess the nature of knowledge and thus imply they are produced, and from such passages as "there is nothing higher than whom," which show merely the refutation of anything superior to Śiva— how can their equality and the relationship of the attained and the attainer (*prāpya-prāpakatva*) be logically established? He says:
Likewise, because of the negation of others. || 35 ||
In the preceding section, having refuted the two systems of Dvaita and Advaita which prescribe only partial aspects of the Śruti,

and having established the concordance of all Śrutis within the primary Vedic doctrine of Dvaitādvaita by demonstrating its status as the cause for reconciling the earlier and later parts of all Śrutis, [the author proceeds] regarding the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas...

Regarding the doubt that "similarity exists merely because of the cognition of similarity," it is shown here by the passage beginning with "tathānyapratiṣedhāt" (likewise, because of the negation of others) that the equality of those such as Nārāyaṇa in his form as a *jīva* with Śiva is in no way possible;
for we observe scriptural injunctions of both kinds, such as "the person is submerged in the same tree" and "Rudra is one alone."

It is considered whether there exists another living being equal to Śiva or not, based on such passages as "There is nothing higher than Him," and so forth; and in the passage "The Person has a thousand eyes, a thousand feet," the fact that a certain Person is characterized by infinite faces and feet,
and that "His foot consists of all beings"— meaning He is delimited by the manifest world of sentient and insentient things— while His three feet are the immortal state in heaven.

Thus, having ascended to the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), from that the Virāj was born; from the Virāj, the Puruṣa. Thus, [the text establishes] his status as the material cause (*upādāna-hetu*) of the unmanifest Hiraṇyagarbha. "Of the color of the sun, beyond darkness" establishes his transcendence of darkness (*tamaḥ-paratva*).
"One who knows him thus becomes immortal here" refers to those who worship him.

Furthermore, the state of being the cause for the absence of rebirth is taught. Then, beginning with "The thousand-headed god... and ending with "...the Lord of the universe," the status of being the Lord of the universe is established; and by the statement "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," it is shown that he who is denoted by the word Nārāyaṇa alone is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, firmly established.
Furthermore, its being the object of meditation as the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is perceived; these attributes are understood to belong to Śiva.

This is evident from the *Mantropaniṣad* in the passage "having all faces, heads, and necks," from the *Mahopaniṣad* in "possessing eyes everywhere and mouths everywhere," from the *Śivasamkalpa*, and from the *Atharvaśiras* in "possessing eyes everywhere and mouths everywhere."

The Supreme Lord is taught to possess many faces, feet, and other limbs; that this entire world is pervaded by what has arisen from His limbs as Māyā; that He has entered into the parts of the universe; that He is the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha, as in the passage "Behold Hiraṇyagarbha being born, who is superior to the universe"; and that He is the witness of all, beyond darkness, and so forth.

The state of being the witness of the universe and the transcendence of darkness are taught [of both]. Thus, the equality of these two—Nārāyaṇa and Maheśvara—in attributes such as having the universe as their form is heard in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth; likewise, the procedure for their worship is heard as being identical. And in the world, regarding both mantras—the eight-syllabled and the five-syllabled—...

We shall now explain the procedure for the worship of both the Śālagrāma stone and the Śiva-liṅga, as well as the rules regarding the sacred water (tīrtha) and the consecrated offerings (prasāda), and the acquisition of Tulasī and Bilva leaves;
likewise, because of the prohibition of others, just as in the Śrutis such as: "There is nothing higher than Him, nor anything else."

There is nothing superior to Paraśiva; likewise, there is no one equal to Maheśvara, the cause of the universe. This is because of the negation of any other [being] in such passages as, "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen," and "Rudra is indeed one, there is no second to him," and "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness, having abandoned everything else."
By such passages as these, it is understood that there is a refutation of any person other than Maheśvara, the cause of the universe. Therefore, there exists no one equal to Śiva.
[This concludes] the demonstration that Viṣṇu is a partial manifestation (aṃśa) of Śiva’s power.
Moreover, the power of Maheśvara is indeed one alone,
yet it becomes fourfold at the time of its application.
In wealth you are Bhavānī, in men you are Viṣṇu, in anger you are Kālī, and in battle you are Durgā.

Thus, because the Sāma Śākhā establishes that Viṣṇu is the Śiva-power (*śivaśaktitva*), there is both difference and non-difference between power and the possessor of power; and although a distinction is designated between Śiva, who is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and Nārāyaṇa, who is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*),
on account of differences in name, form, and so forth, they are nonetheless non-different, as there is no existence apart from their own substrate.

The arising of all phenomena [occurs] from that very source; for by the statement "from him Virāj was born," the Puruṣa's status as the material cause (upādānatva) is taught, while by the verse "the one God, engendering heaven and earth, beheld Hiraṇyagarbha being born," the Supreme Lord's status as the efficient cause (nimittatva) is likewise taught. For this very reason, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
At the beginning of creation, the supreme power Maheśvarī manifests from Śiva, the ultimate cause, who possesses all powers and is accompanied by Ambā.
For at the time when he acts as the enjoyer of primordial matter (pradhāna), he exists under the name of Puruṣa:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet."

Because it is heard [in scripture] thus, "therefore the world consists of Śiva," by this statement the harmony of the various scriptural passages—both those teaching difference and those teaching non-difference—is taught, on the grounds that the manifest universe of sentient and insentient beings is a transformation of the nature of Śiva and Śakti. Therefore, it is said: "All is indeed Rudra."

Having introduced the fact that Śiva is the self of all, a doubt arises as to how the status of being the self of all can be established for the Person Nārāyaṇa, given his nature as the material cause; in response to this, it is stated: "The Person is indeed Rudra;
we know the Person, the thousand-eyed Mahādeva, and meditate upon him. By this, it is shown that even the Person [Nārāyaṇa] is [identical with] the Supreme Lord through His supreme majesty.

It has been shown that [He] has the form of the universe. Because He is omniscient, omnipotent, entirely independent, supreme over all, and the efficient and material cause of the universe, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all scriptural texts is without contradiction.
In the Śruti text, "He desired: 'May I become many,'" it is He alone who, by His own volition, having produced the Puruṣa from His own self...

It is taught that the entire world comes into being through that which is its own distinct portion; this is heard in such passages as, "Having created that, He entered into it," and is understood likewise from such passages as, "But [He projected] Māyā. Therefore, the attributes of the material cause (upādāna) are indeed taught with respect to the instrumental cause (nimitta); nevertheless, because the instrumental cause is superior to the material cause.

The superiority of Śiva over Viṣṇu and others is established. In the Smṛtis and Purāṇas, such as "Vāsudeva is the supreme Prakṛti; you, O Rudra, are the Puruṣa," the nature of Viṣṇu as Prakṛti and Śiva as Puruṣa is clearly taught. Therefore, the non-duality of Śiva is beyond dispute.

In response to the doubt as to how the oneness of Śiva, His being the self of all, His being the controller of all, His being the inner ruler of all, and His being distinct from everything else can be logically established, [the author] says:
"By this [scripture], His omnipresence [is established], because of such words as 'extent' (āyāma) and so forth. (Sūtra 36).

By this, the all-pervasiveness of Brahman and its pervasion of the entire universe—understood from words such as *āyāma* and other terms denoting universal pervasion—is made known to mean that there is nothing superior to it.
The word *āyāma* [is seen in the passage]: "He who has eyes on all sides and faces on all sides... subtler than the subtle and greater than the great..."

The Great Self is hidden in the cave of this living being; by that Puruṣa all this is filled. Free from sorrow, through the grace of the Creator, he beholds Him—the Lord, the desireless, the majesty. Whatever exists as the universe, the world, manifold and born in many ways—all this is indeed Rudra; let there be obeisance to that Rudra. Truth is the Eternal Order (Ṛta).
The Supreme Brahman has faces, heads, and necks everywhere. Indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world;
those gods asked Rudra, "Who are you? He said, "I alone existed in the beginning;
I carry [all] and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me. By that Puruṣa, all this is eternally filled."

"The wise behold the all-pervading, omnipresent, and most subtle source of all beings. "All this, indeed, is Brahman; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. "This whole world has that as its self; this whole world is the Self," and so forth—these and other such scriptural passages are included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). Therefore, just as space is the innermost of all, [so too is the Self].

Thus, it is established that for the one Brahman alone, all-pervasiveness, being distinct from everything, being the cause of wind and other elements, and being the substratum of all are logically consistent; likewise are its omnipresence, consisting of all things, and being the locus of the fruit [of liberation].
This concludes the section on the locus of the fruit (Phalādhikaraṇa). 10.
Refutation of the Mīmāṃsā View:

Now, since Vedic scriptures such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" declare that ritual action alone is the bestower of all fruits, the Lord has no purpose whatsoever. Therefore—

By means of the logic of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, which holds that the deity expressed in the dative case is primary, [the author] refutes Jaimini’s view—which is included among those systems that deny the Lord (nirīśvara) and hold that action alone is the cause of the origin of all beings—as follows:
"Because it is logical, the fruit [comes] from Him (the Lord). (JS 3.2.37)

Therefore, since the attainment of the fruits of action for living beings is possible only from the Lord when He is propitiated by all rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, the status of being the giver of fruit does not belong to ritual action alone; why? Because it is logically consistent (upapatti).

Since it is logically established that only the conscious Lord is the producer of results, and because it is impossible for insentient *karman* to produce results independently, the granting of the fruits of action by anyone other than the Supreme Lord is in no way possible. In the preceding [section], all the scriptural passages enjoining both difference and non-difference have been [shown to apply] to Brahman without restriction.
Having established the concordance [of the Upanishads] and prescribed the worship of the Supreme Lord for the sake of the enjoyment of fruits pertaining to this world and the next for living beings,

and having declared therein that the fruit for those worshippers who are free from desire and whose impure latent impressions have been discarded is the attainment of Śiva-hood— preceded by the cessation of their natural state as individual souls— through sacrifice, charity, and austerity, [the author now states] that in this [world], however, it is from action alone...

Having stated that [the self] bestows all fruits because it perishes in an instant and is insentient, it has been shown that [bestowing fruits] is impossible due to its insentience; for in such scriptural passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "He alone causes one to perform good deeds," both action and Brahman are understood to possess independence.
It is established that it is either the action (*karman*) or the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) who is the giver of the fruit of action.

According to the principle that sound, cognition, and action endure for only three moments, since action is by nature momentary and perishes instantly, its capacity to bestow a fruit at a later time is mediated by the *apūrva* (unseen potentiality) produced by it.
It is possible. For the world is strung together by the thread of its own karma;
a living being is born through karma, it grows through karma alone, and it dies through karma; therefore, karma alone is the deity.
Since agency is observed for action in such Śruti and Smṛti passages as these, and since— just as the movement of a carriage, a cart, or a cloud is superimposed upon mountains,

trees, the moon, and so forth, which are distinct from them— the attribution of being the giver of the fruits of action to the Supreme Lord might arise through delusion, we reply: that [agency] alone is appropriate for Him.

Because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*), its destruction in three moments (*trikṣaṇavinaṣṭatva*), and its being produced (*janyatva*), [the self] does not perform sacrifices, giving, oblations, meditation, or the like.

For in such scriptural passages as, "He indeed causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds," and as in the world it is always the King who [directs] people who have performed meritorious or non-meritorious acts; [so too here].
In accordance with each respective action, it will bestow a corresponding fruit.
In the same way, Maheśvara will eternally bestow the enjoyment of fruits upon beings in higher and lower worlds, in accordance with their individual karma.
The staff that severed Janaka’s head is honored in the world of Śiva.
Dakṣa,
though skillful in performing his ritual duties, obtained the fruit of being beheaded because of his notion that he was the agent of the action.

Since Mahādeva alone is established in such Smṛtis and Purāṇas as the bestower of the fruits of all actions, discerning people should perform acts such as sacrifice, charity, austerity, and worship— which constitute his command— with the intent of propitiating him, for the sake of obtaining his grace.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
"And because it is so heard [in the scriptures]. (Sūtra 3.2.38)
"He indeed is that great, unborn Self, the eater of food, the King of the sacrifice, Rudra, the Hotṛ priest who performs true sacrifice for the two worlds,
the Lord of the ford, and the Lord of the sacrifice"— as stated in such scriptural passages as "May Vāja and Prasava be mine; may Dhātṛ and Viṣṇu be mine," and so forth.
The Lord of all actions, accompanied by Ambā, is the bestower of the fruits of all actions;
therefore, one should worship him constantly for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.

In such Smṛtis as these, it is stated that "there is no sacrifice superior to the Aśvamedha for the propitiation of Rudra"; and because in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts, Śiva alone is heard of as being worshipped through all rites and as the bestower of the fruits of all rites, insentient ritual action possesses no independence. Therefore, at all times—

Now, one might raise the objection that since there is no mention or establishment of the propitiation of the Supreme Lord anywhere in the treatises composed by the teacher Jaimini, such propitiation is not enjoined for the followers of the Vedas; in response to this doubt, he says:
"Jaimini [holds] that dharma [is the goal], for that very reason. (Sūtra 3.4.39)

Since it has been established in the Vedas, Vedāntas, and Āgamas that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is supreme as the bestower of the fruits of all actions and that his worship is the cause of the attainment of all desired objects, for this very reason the teacher Jaimini also—
I bow to that Lord,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives.
By such statements in his *Vedapādastava*, he teaches that the worship of the Śiva-liṅga is the cause of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) and thereby instructs upon its specific duties.

Therefore, even for those Vedic scriptures emphasizing ritual action, such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the intended meaning is that Śiva alone is the bestower of the fruits of those actions. For this very reason, [it is said]: "That state which all the Vedas proclaim..."
The intended meaning of the Śruti has been clearly taught. Therefore, it is established that the capacity of karma to bestow its fruit is in no way possible.
Now, [one might object]: if there is no such intention of the Śruti regarding the independent bestowing of fruits by karma, [how can this be so?]

In response to the doubt— how can the Supreme Lord’s status as the giver of fruits be logically established, given that even Bādarāyaṇa, who possesses knowledge of the meaning of all the Vedas, has not explicitly stated anywhere a formal rule regarding the Lord being the giver of the fruits of action— it is said:
But Bādarāyaṇa holds the former view, because of the designation of a reason. || 180 || 40 ||

By the word "tu" (but), the sense of certainty is established. The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the status of being the bestower of the fruit belongs to Śiva alone, the previously mentioned Supreme Brahman. Why? Because of the designation of a cause (*hetuvyapadeśāt*). [The root] *yaj* is used in the senses of worshiping a deity, forming a connection, and giving.

This is because even in those respective scriptural passages, it is the deities themselves—such as Agni, Vāyu, and others, who are the objects of worship in sacrifices and other rites intended for propitiating the gods—who are designated as the causes of the various fruits. For example: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu;
Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he [the sacrificer] approaches Vāyu with his own share; he (Vāyu) alone leads him to prosperity."

In such passages as these, even the instruction regarding the manner in which the act is the means to achieve the desired result for one who possesses desire is precisely what is required by the injunction; therefore, it is not reasonable to suspect that the text is not intent upon this. Furthermore, when the manner in which the act is the means to the result is understood from the words themselves—despite being required—those who follow authoritative tradition do not tolerate its abandonment or the postulation of an unmentioned *apūrva* (unseen potency) and so forth. This applies to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others as well.

It has already been stated that [words] express the fact that the meaning of the verbal root—such as sacrifice, which consists in the propitiation of a deity—is to be accomplished by the agent's activity; this is established by linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*), sanctioned by the grammatical treatises (*śabdānuśāsana*), and nothing else supernatural.
Thus, from such statements as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," the fact that Vāyu and others are bestowers of results is understood.
It is heard in the Śruti that Śiva alone exists as the object of worship and as the bestower of fruits in the form of Vāyu and the other deities:
"The center of the universe supports the world—the sacrifices and works of public utility, the many things born and being born.
That indeed is Agni; that is Vāyu; that is Sūrya; that is Candramas; that indeed is the pure, the immortal, that is Brahman, those are the waters."

In passages such as "Prajāpati, who is Rudra in fire, who is in the waters, who is in the herbs— he, Rudra, who has entered all beings," the inner rulership of Śiva over everything is taught. Therefore, it is stated that he alone is to be propitiated by all rites and is the bestower of the fruits of all rites,
and no other.

If it is argued that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is postulated for the purpose of establishing that a momentary action can produce a result, and that therefore the statement [of Śiva’s identity] is of secondary importance because it is merely a supplementary part of that [ritual injunction], we say no. For in the *Atharvaśiras*, it is heard that Śiva alone is the essence of all deities such as Vāyu, by such passages as: "He who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed Lord," and "He who knows me [knows all]."

"By knowing the gods," it is taught therein by Śiva that through knowledge of oneself, one gains knowledge of all the deities within one's own self; therefore, Śiva alone is the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of all fruits, the embodiment of all deities, and the one to be propitiated by all rites. Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"He who worships all the deities through devotion by means of every path— Sāmba, being pleased, bestows the fruit in the form of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
Thus [it is said] in the Kṛṣṇagītā:
Whatever form of body each devotee desires to worship with faith,
I make that very faith of theirs firm and unwavering.
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that deity;
and from that [deity], he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone.
For Kṛṣṇa also, through such statements as "I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices," like Vāmadeva and others, by virtue of being a devotee of Śiva and as his inner controller,
[perceives] through the contemplation of Śiva in the form of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which consists of the manifestation of the notion of "I."

He has taught that "I alone am everything. In the world, it is observed that even a king's servant, having accepted wealth and other gifts given by all people as if they were his own property, offers them to the king who resides within him (as the inner controller). Likewise, Śiva, as the inner controller, accepts the worship of various deities such as Viṣṇu and so forth, and [bestows] their respective fruits.
"It will grant [the fruit]"— this is established.
Thus ends the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* composed by the venerable teacher Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of holy ascetics.
The second quarter of the third chapter, which consists of ten topical sections beginning with "Sandhyā," concerning the exposition of *upāsanā*, is completed.
Now begins the third quarter of the third chapter in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*.
The Section Concerning the Uniformity of Knowledge Derived from All Vedānta Texts. || 1 ||

The qualities of the worship of Paramaśiva are set forth in the preceding section; for, by means of the worship of Paraśiva-Brahman— which is the referent of the term *tat*— the supreme human goal, consisting in the attainment of Paśupati preceded by the removal of the bonds (*pāśa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the referent of the term *tvam*, is elaborated, and thus that worship [is described].

In response to the inquiry "How so?", the third quarter (pāda) begins; for some maintain that because the Lord with attributes (saguṇeśvara) is illusory, the hearing of the Vedānta texts— which enjoin meditation on Him as the cause of the direct realization of the eternal, attributeless, partless, all-pervading, and qualityless Brahman— is the means [to that realization].

Since the direct realization of the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*) is impossible through the mere hearing of the Vedānta and so forth— which, like the study of medical science and the like, does not constitute a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*)—

the stainless Brahman is attained only through the meditations on the "small [space]" (*dahara*) and other such practices that enjoin the worship of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma*), as established by the Śruti.
He states this subject matter:
"The exposition of the meditations on the Dahara and others, which have Śiva as their primary object and are of the same nature as those taught in all the branches [of the Veda].
(Sūtra 181) "There is a single cognition [resulting] from all the Vedānta texts, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. (Sūtra 1)

The meditation on the "small" (dahara-upāsana) is one and the same, being established by all the Vedāntas and propounded by all the Upaniṣads found in every recensional branch (śākhā). Likewise, the meditation on Vaiśvānara, well-known in all branches, is also one and the same. Similarly, the Śāṇḍilya-upāsana is also one and the same. Likewise, the Upakośala-upāsana is one and the same. Why? [Because...]

"Because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. By the etymological derivation that "they are enjoined" (*codyante*) means "they are prescribed" (*vidhīyante*), the word *codanā* refers to ritual acts such as the *agnihotra*. Thus, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth—that is, because the meditations on the qualified Brahman are not distinct from, but are equal to, ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* in terms of their injunctions and other characteristics—nevertheless...
Just as the ritual known as the Agnihotra, established in all recensions (śākhās), is one and the same; just as the ritual known as the Jyotiṣṭoma is one;
and just as the ritual known as the Vājapeya, though taught in all recensions, is indeed one—so too is that which is taught in all recensions [one].

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that the meditations on the *dahara* (the small ether) and so forth, which primarily concern Śiva who is of the same class (*sajātīya*), constitute one and the same meditation.

Now, for the purpose of determining whether there is a combination or an option regarding the qualities in the meditations on Brahman, an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of these meditations (*vidyā*) is commenced.
First, regarding a single meditation such as the Vaiśvānara-vidyā found in various Vedic branches (*śākhā*):

A doubt arises as to whether that which is being heard constitutes a single meditation (*ekavidyātva*) or a difference in meditations (*vidyābheda*). Because of the difference in recensional branches (*śākhābheda*), there is indeed a difference in the meditation on Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, across all branches due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*).
In the Taittirīyaka: "That small, stainless lotus which is the abode of the highest..."
"Situated in the middle of the city; there, too, is the small ether (dahara-gagana) which is free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be meditated upon.

In this passage, the meditation on Śiva is taught regarding the small ether (daharākāśa). In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether..."

"Whatever is within that, that is to be sought; that indeed is what one must desire to understand. Because of such statements, the small space (*daharākāśa*) itself is designated as the object of meditation, and thus a mutual contradiction is observed [between this and other passages].
This refers to the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*).

Furthermore, in the Taittirīyaka, the attributes of the Supreme Brahman to be meditated upon as the "small" (dahara)— such as being "black-and-tawny" (kṛṣṇapiṅgala) and so forth— are heard in the passage beginning with "The supreme Brahman is Ṛta and Satya, the Person who is black-and-tawny. In the Chāndogya,
qualities such as being "free from evil" (apahatapāpman) and so forth are heard of that same [Brahman] in the passage beginning with "This is your Self, free from evil."

Therefore, because differences in qualities are observed here and there, a difference in the meditations (*upāsana*) is indeed taught by implication. Likewise, in the *Chāndogya*, specific dharmas are heard in connection with the Pañcāgni, Śāṇḍilya, Upakosala, Udgītha, and Śirovrata meditations: "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those who have performed the Śirovrata."

Since the rule for the instruction of knowledge applies specifically to the followers of the Atharva Veda—those who have performed the "head-vow" (śirovrata) according to the prescribed injunctions—it follows that there is a difference in meditation due to the difference in their religious duties (dharma). Consequently, since there is a difference in meditations based on the difference in Vedic branches (śākhā) and so forth, this being the position reached, we reply: [The full response follows: ...the meditations are not different. Why? Because the form of the object of meditation is the same, as declared by the scriptural texts such as, "The True is Brahman, the Knowledge is Brahman, the Infinite is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1), and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Furthermore, the connection with the fruit is identical, as seen in the passage, "He who knows it thus becomes a fulfiller of desires" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). Moreover, the name is the same, namely, "The science of Brahman" (brahmavidyā). And because the details of the subsidiary elements are identical, the meditations are one and the same. As for the mention of the head-vow, that is merely a specific characteristic of the particular branch of the Atharva Veda and does not constitute a reason for a difference in the meditation itself. Therefore, the meditations are non-different.

On what basis is it said that the meditation is one and the same in all the Vedāntas? Because there is no difference in the injunction (*codanā*) and so forth. First, the injunction—such as "one should meditate" (*upasīta*) or "one should know" (*vidyāt*)—is a prescription regarding the specific meaning of the verbal root. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the Sūtra] refers to the principle from the section on different recensions (*śākhāntara*) in the Karma-kāṇḍa: "Or rather, [the ritual action is one], because there is no difference in the connection, form, injunction, and name."

This very same knowledge is recognized as identical in another Vedic branch. For instance, the injunction "one should meditate upon Vaiśvānara" is uniform in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka. Likewise, the injunction for the Dahara-vidyā in the Chāndogya—"that which is within it is to be sought after"—is equivalent to "that which is within it is to be meditated upon."

Thus it is stated in the Taittirīyaka. In that case, because there is no difference in location and so forth, and because the Brahman to be meditated upon is also non-different, there is no contradiction between the attributes mentioned in both places;
therefore, the meditation (vidyā) is indeed one and the same in the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka recensions. [The sequence is: heaven, rain, earth, food, man, and speech.

The essential nature as it has been handed down is the same in both cases; therefore, it is established that there is no difference between the two forms of knowledge (*vidyā*). In response to the objection that—since different qualities are heard in different recensions (*śākhā*)—it is untenable for meditations of the same kind found in various recensions to be identical, he says:
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not [arise from the object] because of its difference [from it], then [this would apply] even in the case of a single [object].
If it is argued that there is no unity of injunction because of the repetition of the statement without distinction and because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*), [we reply:

even within a single meditation (*vidyā*), the repetition of the statement and the difference in context are justified by the difference among the practitioners. For in this case, both the repetition of the statement and the difference in context pertain to a single practitioner; since they would otherwise be inexplicable, [they must be understood as referring to different levels of realization].

A difference in knowledge arises from a difference in what is to be enjoined; however, when there is a difference in the practitioners, the repetition of the scriptural text and so forth is justified as being for the sake of their comprehension, and thus no further injunction is possible therein. Therefore, it is concluded that the unity of these similar meditations concerning Paramaśiva found in various Śākhās is indeed taught.

Regarding the claim that a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) is perceived because a restrictive rule for the instruction of that knowledge is seen only among the followers of the Atharva Veda who observe the "head-vow" (śirovrata), he says in response: "The determination of the nature of the head-vow."

For the same applies to the private recitation (svādhyāya), because it is included in the rules of conduct (samācāra) and because of its specific qualification; and like the Sava sacrifice, there is a restriction regarding that [recitation].

They do not say this: that the observation of the rule for the instruction of the head-vow (śirovrata) indicates a difference in the knowledge (vidyā), because the head-vow lacks the status of being an auxiliary limb of the knowledge. Rather, the rule for the instruction of the head-vow is for the purpose of establishing the status of the Vedic study (svādhyāya) as such—that is, for the purpose of establishing its participation in the purification produced by that vow—and not for the sake of the knowledge itself. Why is this so?

"Who has not observed the vow does not study this"—because of this connection with study and because of the qualification for the *Samācāra*, this [text] is also explained as being part of the Vedic vow by means of an extension (*atideśa*) to the work called *Samācāra*. In the passage "one should teach this knowledge of Brahman only to them," the meaning is "knowledge of the Veda. And it is like the *Sava* offerings; for just as the *Sava* oblations—
The rites beginning with the seven suns and ending with the hundred pots of rice are connected solely with the single fire (*ekāgni*) of the Ātharvaṇikas;

they do not exist within the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*). Furthermore, because the instruction in the *Ātharvaṇa*—"One should impart this very knowledge of Brahman to such a person"—indicates that even the "Head Vow" (*śirovrata*) is directed toward that same [knowledge], no distinction between different forms of knowledge is designated.

Now, if it is admitted that there is unity among all meditations on the Supreme Śiva-Brahman belonging to all the Vedic branches, then— according to the logic of the sūtra to be cited later, "There is a combination because the meaning is non-different"— the attributes such as *satya-saṅkalpatva* (truthfulness of resolve), *sarvajñatva* (omniscience), and so forth, which are taught in the contexts of all those similar meditations, [would have to be combined].

It must be determined. This being the case, one might ask: since it is impossible for any single individual to study all the Vedic branches (*śākhās*), how can there be a determination regarding the synthesis of the qualities taught in all those branches? If this is raised, we reply: no; for in the scriptural injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied," the term *svādhyāya* refers to one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*), based on the etymological derivation that "one's own study" is *svādhyāya*.

And likewise, because of the principle that "the practice of the teacher is superior by ninefold" regarding the nature of one's own study (*svādhyāya*), since the instruction concerning one's own qualification occurs within the context of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), even if a single person does not study all the recensional branches (*śākhā*), [the authority is established] by those who have studied all the branches, such as Bharadvāja, Atri, and so forth.

Similarly, regarding the determination of the commonality [of attributes] for worshippers, even though it is impossible for them to study all the recensional branches (*śākhā*), they may nevertheless meditate upon the qualities— such as "having true resolve" and "being dark-brown"— found in all the recensions, as practiced by those who have studied all the branches, such as Vemārādhya, Udbhaṭārādhya, Marulasiddha, and others.
It is taught that the determination of oneness is logical;
this constitutes the demonstration that Paramaśiva is the object of worship for all vidyās, such as the Dahara,
as well as for the various meditations found in numerous recensions (śākhās) including the Taittirīya and Kaivalya Upaniṣads, according to those who are omniscient.

In response to the doubt—arising from the fact that although the great sages such as Agastya and others have taught oneness, they are nevertheless seen to differ from one another—how can oneness be established?
[The Sūtra] says: "And it shows. (Sūtra 4)

Furthermore, [the scripture] demonstrates the identity of the knowledge (*vidya-ekya*) across all Vedāntas because the fruit of the worship of Paraśiva is one and the same. In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, beginning with "The lotus of the heart, pure and free from sorrow," up to "accompanied by Umā, beyond darkness," and in the *Taittirīyaka* with "Ṛta, Satya, the Supreme Brahman," [these texts describe] Śiva, the Supreme Person who is the object of worship in the *Dahara* meditation.

And corporeality has already been mentioned. Now, beginning with the passage, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling," and stating, "That which is within it is what must be sought," [the text asks]: "What is there that must be sought?"

It has been stated that, preceded by a series of questions, the Supreme Brahman Śiva— distinguished by the eight qualities such as being free from sin— is the object of meditation therein. Furthermore, in the Taittirīyaka, relying on the corresponding reference found in the Chāndogya, [it is taught] there too that the "small" (dahara) [space]...
"That it should be worshipped" refers to the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, as distinguished by the eight qualities.
Therefore, the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) in all cases is established precisely through the combination of these qualities.
Having thus stabilized that very unity of knowledge—which is proven by the logic of the section concerning different Vedic branches (śākhāntarādhikaraṇa)—its purpose [is now stated].
In response to the inquiry "What [is it]?", he says there:
|| 185 || "The conclusion [of the mantra] is the same because there is no difference in meaning, as in the case of the remainder of an injunction. || 5 ||

Thus, since meditation is the same throughout all Vedāntas, the qualities mentioned in one Vedāntic text must be combined with those mentioned in another Vedāntic text. Why? Because, like the supplementary details of an injunction, there is no difference in the object, just as a quality heard in one Vedāntic text—such as the supplementary details of the Vaiśvānara or Dahara meditations—is connected to that very injunction.

It is practiced for the sake of accomplishing the purpose consisting of that assistance; likewise, even that which is taught in another Vedānta [text] must be integrated, because there is no difference in its assistance due to its connection with that same knowledge (*vidyā*). The word "ca" (and) is indicated here in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
He shows the purpose of the meditation:
"But surely, in the Chāndogya, in the Dahara-vidyā, qualities such as being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth are heard;

since they are not seen in that way in the Taittirīya branch, [how can there be identity] between the qualities of the Taittirīya practitioner, such as being black-and-tawny (kṛṣṇapiṅgala), and [those of the Chāndogya]?"

If it is argued that since this is not seen anywhere in the *Chāndogya*, how can the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedānta texts be established through the principle of the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*), we say: no; for since the designation [of the object of knowledge] is identical everywhere—as in the case of the *Taittirīya* and other texts—the principle of combination is appropriate, because there is oneness of purpose in the form of the assistance rendered to the meditation (*vidyopakāra*).

Just as in the case of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) prescribed as belonging to a single ritual system, such as the Agnihotra and others, it is likewise consistent because the qualities of meditations on the "small space" (*dahara*) and so forth are identical due to the commonality of the injunctions and other factors.
Furthermore, this applies to those qualities propounded within the contexts of the meditations on the Supreme Lord found in various Vedic branches (*śākhā*).
Because qualities such as *satyasaṅkalpatva* (the power of realizing one's intentions) are manifested everywhere, their combination [in a single meditation] is not contradictory.

Since there is no difference in the object—the fruit consisting of the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman being identical for meditations of the same kind qualified by various qualities found in different recensional branches (*śākhā*)—their unity is established by implication. And thus:

The synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*), in the form of a combination, must be performed of those qualities— such as "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpatva*) and so forth— which belong to meditations of a similar nature found in various recensions (*śākhā*) and which serve as the means for attaining the single fruit characterized by reaching the world of Paraśiva-Brahman. Although this sūtra speaks of the synthesis of qualities, [it implies] that of one...

Since it is impossible for a single person to study all the various recensions (śākhās), how can there be a doubt regarding the synthesis of qualities found in different recensions that must later be resolved? Nevertheless, taking for granted the synthesis of qualities that will be explained in the subsequent sūtras— on the grounds that it is impossible to study every single recension— [the objection is raised].
The doubt that the integration of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) is not taught has already been refuted.
Pages 268 and 269 are missing.
[He is] Sāmba, the medicine for the world, situated in the center of the solar orb.
The blue-necked one, the odd-eyed one, the beloved of Viṣṇu, the imperishable.
Thus, in the *Smṛti*, its reference to Sadāśiva is indicated. Therefore, since it is argued that the identity of the *vidyā* is never possible, the following is said in response:
in the first section (*pāda*) of the first chapter (*adhyāya*), under the heading "On account of the teaching of those attributes" (*antastaddharmopadeśādhikaraṇa*), regarding the *Chāndogya*...

Furthermore—since in both cases we hear that the object of meditation is the *udgītha* itself upon which the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been superimposed, there is no distinction in the connection with the fruit, namely the form of overcoming one's enemies, because the injunctions and other factors are identical.

The "form" (*rūpa*) [of the meditation] is also identical, as it is characterized by the oneness of the object of meditation—the *udgītha* upon which the nature of the vital breath has been superimposed—and so forth. And the injunction (*codanā*)...

The various classes of meaning are indistinguishable, and the designation "Udgītha-vidyā" is likewise indistinguishable. Here, having raised an objection based on the shadow of the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), he refutes it with the words beginning "otherwise-ness" (*anyathātva*). That which was stated—namely, the identity of the two knowledges—is not tenable because of the difference in form; for the alteration of form is indeed understood from the sacred word itself. For in the Vājasaneyaka [it says]: "Then, indeed..."

"They said to this breath in the mouth, 'Chant the Udgītha for us. 'So be it,' [said] Prāṇa; and for them Prāṇa chanted the Udgītha. Having thus described the defeat of the Asuras through the vision of Prāṇa in the agent of the act of rising (*utthāna*), the text continues with "He who knows thus. From the word "thus" (*evam*), it is understood that the vision of Prāṇa is to be applied to the agent alone. In the Chāndogya: "Now, he who is this..."

Having stated that the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) performed meditation upon that *udgītha*— thereby describing the removal of the Asuras through the vision of the vital breath (*prāṇadṛṣṭi*) applied to the *udgītha*, which is the action of singing— the text says, "He who knows thus desires evil," and by the word "thus" (*evaṃ*), the vision of the vital breath is enjoined specifically upon the *udgītha* as an action. Therefore, in one instance there is the vision of the vital breath in the agent, while in the other instance it is in the action.

From the words "view of the vital breath" (*prāṇadṛṣṭi*), a difference in form (*rūpānyathātva*) is clear. And if there is a difference in form due to a difference in the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), then the mere lack of distinction in the injunction (*codanā*) and so forth is ineffective; thus, [the opponent argues,] there must be a difference between the two meditations (*vidyābheda*). To this we say: no, because there is no such distinction. For in both cases, at the outset, the subduing of others by means of the *udgītha* is perceived without distinction. In the Vājasaneyaka: "They... [and so on].
In the beginning of the passage, it is heard: "The gods said, 'Come, let us surpass the Asuras by means of the Udgītha in the sacrifice. Likewise, in the Chāndogya:

"The gods, indeed, offered the Udgītha as a call, thinking, 'By this we shall strike them down. Therefore, in order not to contradict the opening statement, the phrase "for their sake this Prāṇa sang the Udgītha" must refer precisely to the Udgītha-singing act in which the Udgītha has had the nature of Prāṇa superimposed upon it.

In cases such as cooking, [the agent] is designated as the "doer" (kartṛ) due to the desire to express an excellence of ease, just like the boiled rice; otherwise, the word *udgītha* occurring at the beginning would have to be taken figuratively in the sense of the agent. Therefore, there is identity of knowledge (*vidyaikyam*).
There is identity of knowledge among the Dahara-vidyā and others because of the identity of their fruits.

Now, if it is granted that there is no difference even between the internal meditations (*antaraṅga-upāsanā*)— such as those on the *dahara*, *śāṇḍilya*, *vaiśvānara*, and *manaḥpradhāna*— which, though belonging to different Vedic branches, have the single fruit of attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman as their goal; then...

Since the mind is predominant even in all external actions, this applies even to rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma mentioned in the sections of the Karmakāṇḍa, such as: "One should worship the twilight daily," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

[Otherwise] the fruit of attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman would result; and if that were the case, the contradiction with the scriptures that prescribe the fruits of various specific actions would be unavoidable. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
|| 187 || "Or rather not, because of the difference in context, as in the case of 'being higher than the high' (parovarīyastva) and so forth. || 7 ||
There is indeed no identity among the various meditations (upāsanās) recited in the sections of the *karmakāṇḍa*. Why?
Because of the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*); that is, because the two contexts of the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *brahmakāṇḍa* are mutually distinct.
This is because Vedic injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" teach the attainment of prosperity as their fruit, whereas [the teachings on] Brahman...

Since the scriptures, such as "He becomes Brahman indeed," establish that meditations on Brahman result in the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) characterized by non-return, [the author] provides the illustration of the *dahara*, *śāṇḍilya*, and other meditations: "Like the 'Supreme' (*para*), the 'More Excellent' (*varīyas*), and so forth. Just as the *agnihotra* and *jyotiṣṭoma* [lead to different results].

What need is there to speak of the even greater distinction found in those passages read within the section on Dharma, such as: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven," "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun," and "Now, this small lotus-palace within this city of Brahman," and so forth? These demonstrate the progressive superiority of the distinctions [of the Self].

Although it is understood from words such as *atha* (now), which indicate a distinction between sections (*prakaraṇabheda*) of the Brahman, that the various meditations on Paraśiva-Brahman are independent of one another and each serves as a means for attaining Brahman, their distinctness is nevertheless not established, because the fruit is one and the same— just as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Jyotiṣṭoma, Vājapeya, and Aśvamedha sacrifices.

In the same way, only those [meditations] read within the context of Brahman are always the direct cause for attaining Brahman. This is so even though there is the scriptural statement: "That state which all the Vedas declare. Furthermore, regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices offered to the Supreme Lord without desire for rewards—moreover, as for the syllable *praṇava*, which is a part of the *udgītha* under discussion in the passage: "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*."

Having introduced this, there follows an explanatory exposition (*upavyākhyāna*) of this very syllable. Beginning with the words, "The gods and the asuras, indeed, once contended," and continuing until, "Then they meditated upon that very vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is in the mouth as the *udgītha*," the followers of the *Chāndogya* study a meditation concerning the *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*. The followers of the *Vājasaneyi*, however, [study it differently].

Since there is no such ancient *prakaraṇa* (contextual section), [the text] introduces the *udgītha* as the task—saying, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras at the sacrifice by means of the *udgītha*"—and then teaches the subject matter of the *udgītha* as a task, beginning with, "Then they said to this breath within the mouth, 'Sing the *udgītha* for us. Therefore, due to the difference in *prakaraṇa*, there is a difference in the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*); and when there is a difference in the object to be enjoined...

And because there is a difference in form (*rūpa*), there is no identity of the knowledge (*vidyā*). Now, as for the statement, "They meditated upon that which is this chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*," for the followers of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is the very *praṇava* (the syllable Om), which is a constituent part of the previously mentioned *udgītha*, that is to be meditated upon as having the superimposed nature of the vital breath. For the Vājasaneyins, however, it is the entire *udgītha*.

"The Udgātṛ priest is to be meditated upon as the vital breath (prāṇa) through the vision of the vital breath. Then, they said to this vital breath within the mouth, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us," and he replied, "So be it"; thus, having pointed out the superimposition of the vital breath upon the Udgātṛ by stating, "This vital breath sang the Udgītha for them," the text enjoins that the Udgātṛ himself—in whom the state of the vital breath has been superimposed—is the object of meditation for one who knows thus. Therefore, there is a difference in form. It is not [the same].

One should not suspect a contradiction with the introduction of the narrative, which states, "When the two forms of meditation were prescribed, we shall surpass [our rivals] by means of the *udgītha*";

for in the meditation on the *udgātṛ*, the *udgītha*—which constitutes the act of singing (*udgāna*)—is necessarily required, as it too serves as a cause for the result known as the humiliation of others. Therefore, despite the lack of distinction in the injunctions and other such factors, there is a difference between the two meditations due to the difference in their forms (*rūpa*).

There is no identity of the meditations (*vidyaikya*). For even though there is a similarity in the injunction to view the *praṇava*—which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*—as the Supreme Self within a single branch (*śākhā*), the injunction to view it as the "Golden Person" and the injunction to view it as characterized by qualities such as "being higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) constitute distinct meditations. Therefore...

If it is argued that the unity of knowledge is thus established, we reply: In all the Vedāntas, such as "The goal which all the Vedas proclaim," "I alone am to be known by the many Vedas," "I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas," and "I ask you about that Person who is described in the Upaniṣads," [the unity of knowledge is evident].

Although in the state of saṃsāra, distinctions such as the object of worship and the worshiper serve to establish duality, it is nevertheless possible for all [Vedic texts] to be harmonized (*samanvaya*) with the Supreme Śiva-Brahman—the reality of the six planes—by means of the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*). This is because the meditations (*vidyā*) on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart), the *śāṇḍilya*, and others share a single ultimate human goal: the attainment of Śiva-nature preceded by the cessation of the notion of being a transmigrating soul (*jīva-bhāva*).
The attainment of Brahman occurs through a succession of stages for rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma when they are performed with a mind dedicated to Śiva and free from desire;
however, meditations on the "small" (dahara) and so forth are the direct cause of attaining Brahman.
Now, one might object: what of the meritorious acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, performed by a person free from desire, which are recited within the context of Dharma?

Anticipating the objection— "Since meditation on the *dahara* (the small space) and other such meditations, as well as meditations on the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, are designated in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and so forth as causes of liberation through the medium of the purification of the mind in a traditional succession, how can it be untenable that they are non-different due to having the single fruit of liberation?"— he says:
If it is argued that [the self] exists as a designation, it has already been stated that even that [designation] exists. || 8 ||
Based on the power of various distinct designations (*saṃjñā*), that which is the distinction between both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—
as stated in such scriptural passages as "Having crossed over death through ignorance, one enjoys immortality through knowledge"—
the duty appropriate to one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) is defined here as ignorance.
By means of that [wisdom], having abandoned past karmas, one attains knowledge.
One attains liberation through knowledge; therefore, one should practice action.
Even he, relying upon knowledge, performed very many sacrifices.
Relying upon the knowledge of Brahman to cross over death through ignorance,
a man should perform the duty prescribed for his own caste as declared in the Vedas.

From the performance of the duty prescribed for one's own caste, as declared in the Vedas and the Smṛtis, there arises for a man the cessation of evil; through that, indeed, comes the purification of the mind.
Through the purification of the mind, confidence in the Śruti and Smṛti arises;
from that, devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, shall arise in men.
Through devotion, there arises a constant perception of the defects of saṃsāra;
from that, there comes detachment from enjoyments both in this world and the next.
Through that [work], the manifestation of the nature of Śiva in the meaning of the Vedānta texts becomes perfect knowledge; by means of that, liberation for the person shall certainly occur.
Therefore, a Brahmin devoted to Maheśvara should not abandon the dharma appropriate to his caste and stage of life, as proclaimed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama, even at the cost of his life.

Since such teachings in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other texts also instruct that dharma must precede the knowledge of Brahman, [the objection] that the dahara-vidyā is not preceded by it is likewise invalid. For it is said: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite; he who knows it as hidden in the secret cave of the heart, in the highest heaven, attains all desires together with Him."
Neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality;
they enter that which shines brilliantly, placed beyond the highest heaven, which the ascetics seek.
Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation and are pure in being—
they all, at the time of their final end, are liberated into the supreme immortality in the world of Brahman.

Since in such scriptural passages there is no mention of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices as being the direct means for attaining Brahman— unlike the Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, and other meditations— even though these sacrifices may serve as causes for the meditations on the Dahara and others through the sequence of devotion, dispassion, tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, which result from the purification of the mind achieved by the fruit of merit accumulated over many births;

Since it is impossible for meditations such as the *dahara* (the small one) to be direct causes of non-attainment— just as in the case of other meditations— and since the scripture, "Knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*),

teaches their mutual distinction by name alone, like a jar and a cloth, there can never be any identity between meditations such as the *dahara*, which are of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), and rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which are of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*).
In every respect, this is untenable.
Regarding the necessity of meritorious actions:
surely, since rites such as the *saṃdhyāvandana* and the *jyotiṣṭoma* cannot have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit, [how can they be necessary for that end?]

Fearing that, because the knowledge of the *dahara* (the small ether) and other meditations is seen to be the cause of their respective fruits, there would follow the non-performance of rites such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*) by both the learned and the ignorant, and the consequent occurrence of faults, he says in this regard:
"And on account of pervasion, [the Smṛti rule] is consistent. (Sūtra 9).

"Also because of pervasiveness": This is because, in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other texts such as "By dharma one dispels sin," meritorious acts like the Sandhyā-vandana performed with desirelessness and dedicated to Śiva possess pervasiveness regarding the fruit of liberation—which consists in the attainment of Śiva-hood preceded by the cessation of innate individuality (jīvatva) through the removal of sin. Thus, they are pervasive with respect to that result.

This is for the sake of the ignorant, through the purification of the mind, for the attainment of liberation— consisting of eternal bliss and characterized by *sālokya* and other states— preceded by the cessation of the bond of *māyā*; and for the sake of the wise, for the purpose of rescuing them from delusion, preceded by the cessation of worldly reproach.

The performance of meritorious acts such as the daily and occasional rites of twilight worship (*sandhyāvandana*) and so forth is entirely consistent, because they are established in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and *Āgamas*. Thus, according to scriptural passages such as "the knower should offer the *agnihotra*," the destruction of evil occurs precisely for one who performs these daily and occasional rites.
Just as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in the world;
therefore, one should possess good conduct and knowledge until the fall of the body.

Thus, because this has been elaborated in many ways in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources, it is established that the performance of all meritorious acts, such as the Sandhyā-vandana, is mandatory. This concludes the section on the non-difference of all [deities]. 3.
And there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā) here, because it is everywhere presided over by Śiva;

for the sake of those seeking liberation in former times, having established the meditation on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart)— which is the root of incomparable, eternal auspiciousness and unsurpassed bliss— as well as the meditation on the *praṇava*, the *sāmarasya* (state of equilibrium), and the *udgītha* and so forth, therein...

Although all meditations on the "small one" (*dahara*) and others appear to be distinct due to differences in their specific qualities (*guṇa*), attributes (*dharma*), and contexts (*prakaraṇa*), they are nonetheless unified because of the identity of their fruit, which is the attainment of that [Brahman]; thus, all the attributes read within those contexts, such as the twilight prayers (*sandhyāvandana*) and so forth, [are connected] through a continuous succession.

And since the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is perceived as being preeminent among all [meditations] in establishing its status as the cause for attaining that [Brahman], and because it is manifested in various ways across different Vedic branches, there arises the doubt: "How can there be a consistent convergence (*samanvaya*) upon Brahman?
In response to this doubt, he introduces another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
|| 190 || These others [are different] because of the non-difference from all. 10.
The knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is introduced in both the *Chāndogya* and the *Vājasaneyaka*: "He who knows the eldest and the best indeed becomes the eldest and the best;

the vital breath, verily, is the eldest and the best," and so forth. Having established there that the vital breath, characterized by the qualities of being the eldest and the best, is the object of meditation, [the text then discusses] speech, sight, hearing, and mind.

Having established the qualities known as being the most excellent (*vaśiṣṭhatva*), being the foundation (*pratiṣṭhātva*), and being the perfection (*sampattva*), and having demonstrated the preeminence of *prāṇa*— on the grounds that speech and the other [senses], as well as the body, exist dependent upon it and perform their respective functions dependent upon it—
he then [reinstates] those qualities such as being the most excellent, which were previously heard in connection with speech and the others.

It establishes [the attributes] as being connected with the vital breath (prāṇa). Thus it is understood in the Chāndogya; however, in the Kauṣītaki version of the Prāṇavidyā, the vital breath is taught as the object of meditation specifically as possessing the qualities of seniority and preeminence, but not the qualities such as "being the wealthiest" (vasiṣṭhatva) and so forth, which are associated with speech and the other organs.
These [meditations] have been presented as being connected with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the meditation (*vidyā*) different here, or not?

What is the correct view? That it is different. Why? Because of the difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*). Although in both cases the vital breath alone, characterized by the qualities of being the oldest (*jyeṣṭha*) and the best (*śreṣṭha*), is the object of meditation, nevertheless, in one case it is also endowed with qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*).

In one place, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is understood as the object of meditation, whereas in the other, it is devoid of that [quality]; thus, due to the difference in the nature of the object of meditation, there is a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*). This being the position reached, we reply:

"Because of the non-difference of all [attributes], they are the same in the others. There is no difference between the meditations here; [the same attributes apply] elsewhere—in the Kauṣītaki school.
These qualities, such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, are also to be meditated upon in the *prāṇavidyā*. Why? Because of the non-difference of everything;

for the entire method of establishing the pre-eminence and superiority of the *prāṇa*, which was promised, is non-different there as well. To illustrate: in the *prāṇavidyā* of the Chandogas and Vājasaneyins, [it is said] "these deities, in regard to the question of who is the best... and so on.
Having begun with the statement, "We were disputing among ourselves as to who was the best," and having demonstrated that upon the departure of each one individually— beginning with speech—

the stability and respective functions of all the sense organs together with the vital breath (prāṇa) and of the body remained intact; and having further declared that upon the departure of the vital breath, the dissolution of all [the organs] and their incapacity to perform their functions ensued— for all of them...

The preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been established through its dependence on the vital breath for its own existence and its dependence on that same breath for its functions. Having thus demonstrated that the functions of speech and the other organs depend upon the vital breath, this is then restated in such passages as: "Then Speech said to him: 'Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent,'" and so forth; likewise in the *Prāṇavidyā* of the Kauṣītakins.

In order to establish the preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) were attributed to speech and the other organs. Then, through the passage beginning with "Then these deities, having approached their father Prajāpati, said: 'Who among us is the most excellent? it was demonstrated that the qualities residing in speech and the others, as well as speech and the rest themselves, and even the body, are dependent upon the vital breath; thus, the preeminence of the vital breath was established.

It is not merely a restatement that speech and the other organs possess their respective qualities—such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*)—in dependence upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Nor does this imply a difference in nature; for by the very demonstration that the functions of speech and the others, endowed with qualities such as excellence, are dependent on the vital breath, it is established that the vital breath is the cause of those qualities of excellence belonging to speech and the rest.

Because it is already established; for that very quality of being endowed with attributes such as being the "most excellent" (vasiṣṭhatva) belongs to the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, since the vital breath is also recognized here as the "eldest" due to its connection with attributes such as being the most excellent, there is no difference in the meditation (vidyābheda).
This concludes the section on Bliss and so forth (Ānandādyadhikaraṇa). 4.
The demonstration that the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, is distinguished by infinite auspicious qualities:

"You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter as Rudra within. He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, he is Fire, he is the Moon. They say that the mark of the mind is within his vital breaths. Prāṇa is Brahman; Prāṇa indeed is the conscious self."

In such scriptural passages as these, just as in the statement "This sun is Brahman," the worship of Prāṇa is presented on the grounds that it has Śiva as its substratum and is identical with Śiva; therefore, let the injunction for its worship be established on the basis of its being identical with Prāṇa. Nevertheless, this designation as being identical with Prāṇa [applies] to Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is the foremost among all deities.
Since the practice of meditation upon Him is possible through His connection with qualities, there may arise the doubt: "Are there qualities that are not shared by others?
In response to this, the author demonstrates the expansion of His infinite auspicious qualities through another topical section:
"Bliss and the rest [belong] to the Principal. (Sūtra 1.3.11)

Immediately following this, another discussion concerning the subject matter of the ancillary attributes of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) will be undertaken. Just as the contemplation of the pre-eminence and excellence of the vital breath is untenable without the contemplation of its being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, [the qualities of] being the most excellent and so on, though not explicitly mentioned, [must be understood].

The meaning to be established here is that those qualities without which the attainment [of the fruit] in the Kauṣītaki Prāṇavidyā, as well as the contemplation on the nature of Paraśiva-Brahman, would not be possible, must be contemplated in all the Brahmavidyās as well.

The qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and others, which are heard in individual recensions—such as "Bliss is Brahman" and "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman"—are to be combined within the single Brahma-vidyā that consists of the one Brahman characterized by bliss, truth, the quality of being dark-and-tawny (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*), and so forth, whether in its manifest or unmanifest form. Why? Because [these qualities belong to] the principal [subject]. Who [is that]? The one who...

The Supreme Brahman Śiva— the primordial Person of the gods, Rudra, the Great Seer who transcends the universe, and so forth, as established by the Śruti— is present in all Vedic branches (śākhās) in both embodied and unembodied forms.

Even though there is a designation of difference, the unity of attributes is not contradicted because of the teaching of non-difference in the same manner. This is because in such scriptural passages as "There are two forms of Brahman," the attributes belonging to the formed and the formless are specified as belonging to this very Śiva;
thus, all the attributes concerning the formed and formless Brahman found in all the Vedic branches reside in that one alone.
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that "concomitance" (samanvaya) is to be understood;

the word "because of non-difference" (abhedāt) is to be supplied as the remainder. For in such scriptural passages as "Bliss indeed is ageless, immortal; he who consists of bliss is the enjoyer of bliss," qualities such as bliss and others are heard in the higher knowledges (paravidyā) as belonging to the primary reality, Brahman. Therefore, in this [context],...
It is now deliberated whether there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the attributes of the nature of Brahman across all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) or not.

Since there is no authority for synthesizing those [attributes] studied outside of a specific context, synthesis should be performed only for those heard within a specific context. For if the one Brahman, Śiva, were characterized by multiple attributes such as bliss and so forth, the contingency of his being manifold would arise.

Since qualifiers convey the meaning of the qualified object, or because meditation on that [Brahman] is possible through the mere qualities mentioned in each respective context— this being the position reached— it is replied:
"Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal," because of the non-difference of the Principal, that is, the possessor of qualities, Brahman, from all meditations.
Because there is no difference—that is, because the qualities are not separate from the possessor of qualities—the qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth must be combined everywhere.

If that is so, then by the very fact of being non-different from the possessor of qualities, attributes such as "having joy as its head" (*priya-śiras-tva*), which are heard in the passage "Joy indeed is its head" (*priyam eva śiraḥ*) and so on as qualities of Brahman, would also necessarily apply everywhere. To this, he says:
