|| 192 || Because [the Self] has the beloved as its head and so forth, there would be no attainment [of liberation]; for increase and decrease occur only where there is difference. || 12 ||

When the attainment of the qualities of the nature of Paraśiva-Brahman is being discussed, qualities such as "having pleasure as the head" (priyaśirastva) and so forth are not attained, because they are not qualities of Brahman; for qualities such as having pleasure as the head are included merely within the figurative representation of Brahman as having a human form. Otherwise, there would be a distinction of limbs such as head, wings, and tail.

Furthermore, increase and decrease would necessarily follow for Brahman as well; and that being the case, the introductory statement, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," would be contradicted. [The text continues:
"His joy indeed is the head; his delight is the right wing."
Joy is the higher part; bliss is its essence; Brahman is the tail, the foundation.

Thus, because the qualities such as "having joy as the head" (*priyaśirastva*) and so forth are designated without ambiguity in the Taittirīya recension, there is an accumulation—that is, a plurality—of qualities; whereas a depletion of qualities would mean their scarcity. In this manner, these accumulations and depletions of qualities pertain to a distinction in the object of meditation (*upāsya*).

These two are possible only with respect to Brahman endowed with qualities (*saguṇa-brahman*). Since an abundance of qualities is utterly impossible in the qualityless and undifferentiated (*nirguṇa-nirviśe�șa*) Brahman, it is established that the relationship of the object of meditation and the meditator exists only with respect to *saguṇa-brahman*.
Now, this very [relationship] consists of the sovereignty, profundity, magnanimity, and so forth belonging to Brahman.
If there were a synthesis even of the Śruti texts, it would follow that all [mantras] would apply everywhere; moreover, there would be no capacity for synthesis due to their infinity.
To this, he says:
|| 193 || "But the others [apply] because of the similarity of the purpose. || 13 ||
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. However, other qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth follow everywhere because they are common to the object;

whereas those qualities which are identical with the object—being attributes that define the very nature of the object and are inseparable from the cognition of the object—follow everywhere just like the nature of the object itself. And these qualities are truth (*satya*), knowledge (*jñāna*), bliss (*ānanda*), purity (*amalatva*), and infinity (*anantatva*).

By the passage beginning with "From which these [beings arise]," Brahman—characterized as the cause of the universe—is defined in its essential nature through attributes such as bliss, as in "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and bliss. Therefore, for the sake of understanding the essential nature of Śiva, who is the Brahman to be meditated upon, attributes such as bliss and so forth recur in all the meditative teachings (vidyās). As for those qualities of Brahman, whose nature has been thus defined, such as compassion and the like—

The qualities have been established; even though they do not exist apart from the possessor of qualities (guṇin), because they lack independence from the cognition [of that possessor], it is certain that those qualities which are heard in a particular context must be combined there.

For if they were not, there would follow the undesirable consequence of increase or decrease [in their number]. Thus, qualities such as "having joy as its head" and so forth belong to Brahman, who is Śiva.

If these [passages] are intended merely for the purpose of describing the anthropomorphic form (*puruṣavidhatva*) and do not [thereby] constitute qualities of Brahman, then for what purpose is Śiva, who is formless Brahman, described as having such a form? For when something is described as being "thus" despite not being experienced as such, there must be some specific purpose behind that description. As it is said: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot."

It has been stated that by such passages as these, the description of the worshiper and his implements as being the charioteer, the chariot, and so forth, is intended for the purpose of bringing under control the body, senses, and other instruments of worship. However, since no such purpose is observed here, [the attributes] must necessarily be understood as qualities of Brahman.
The status of having "the beloved as the head" and so forth must be accepted. Regarding this, he says:
|| 194 || "For the purpose of meditation, because there is no other purpose. || 14 ||
Since there is no other purpose, this instruction regarding form and qualities is given for the sake of *ādhyāna*.

*Ādhyāna*—meaning constant reflection—is what is called "meditation" (*upāsana*). This is for the sake of establishing the realization in the form of meditation as taught in such passages as, "By the practice of churning through meditation, the wise man burns away the bond," and "Know [the Self] through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation."

For the purpose of realizing Brahman as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), Brahman as consisting of bliss is taught by dividing it into the forms of joy, delight, and so forth, and defining it through its head, wings, and other parts. Just as the "person consisting of food" (*annamaya*)— this body— is superimposed upon the intellect by means of its head, wings, and so forth, as in "this is its head," and just as the "person consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) [is similarly treated]...

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and other limbs are superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*). In the same way, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), which is a distinct entity from these [limbs] and is their inner self (*antarātman*), is also superimposed upon the intellect for the sake of meditation, by means of its partial attributes—such as "dear" (*priya*) and "joy" (*moda*)—which are figuratively represented as the head and so forth. Thus, because the "having dear as the head" and the rest are merely indicative of the one consisting of bliss, they do not [apply] at all times.
[The attributes] continue to apply in the cognition of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

In response to the objection— namely, that since bliss is taught as Brahman in passages such as "Food is Brahman," how can it be established that the *ānandamaya*, which is read within the same context, is indeed the Supreme Brahman— he says:
And because of the word "self" (ātman). || 195 || 15 ||

In the *Taittirīya*, in passages such as "From that very Self, space was produced," the Self is taught to be the sole cause of the universe; and in the *Māṇḍūkya*, in the passage "They consider the fourth state to be the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual— that is the Self," the auspicious Supreme Brahman is [described].

Because the word "Self" (ātman) is employed as the cause of conceptual proliferation (prapañca); and because in the *Atharvaśikhā*, starting from "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be expanded upon," and ending with "Śiva alone, the maker of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon," there is the understanding of a prohibition against those in their final bodies who seek liberation meditating on anything other than Paraśiva-Brahman; therefore, [Brahman] is eternal.

The Supreme Brahman alone, which is the cause of both the worlds, is determined by the term "Śiva. Therefore, in the passage "Ṛtam satyam," the practice of meditative worship (*anusandhāna-upāsti*) upon the reality of Brahman is taught through such descriptions as "kṛṣṇapiṅgala" and "virūpākṣa. And so says the Smṛti:
Those men who worship Śiva go to Śiva;
those who worship that which is other than Śiva go to that which is other than Śiva.

From this scriptural statement, it follows that for those whose habit is the practice of devotion to anything other than Śiva, the fruit is inauspiciousness (*aśivatva*). For this very reason, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not anyone else; for it is clearly taught that, because it is instructed as being distinct from the layers beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) by virtue of having unsurpassed bliss as its pinnacle, the one consisting of bliss is none other than Śiva alone who is to be meditated upon.

Furthermore, since the Supreme Self, Śiva— who is designated by the word "Self" in the passage "Another inner Self consists of bliss"— possesses a head, wings, and a tail, it is taught that His having "pleasure as the head" and so forth is a mere figurative description intended for easy comprehension.
The objects are indeed superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects;
the intellect is superior to the mind, and the Great Self is superior to the intellect.
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. Beyond the Puruṣa there is nothing else; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal.

Thus, because the Śruti teaches that the Puruṣa is superior to all—beginning with wealth, mind, intellect, and the self—by stating, "Another inner self is the one consisting of breath (prāṇamaya); another inner self is the one consisting of mind (manomaya); another inner self is the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya)," the word *ātman* has been previously applied even to non-selves; therefore, [it follows that] "another inner self is the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya)."
How is it determined that the word "self" (ātman) has the self as its referent? To this, he says: "The grasping of the self [is established] because of what follows, as in other cases. (Sūtra 1.4.6)
In the passage, "Another inner self consists of bliss," the word *ātman* refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, as in other similar cases.

Just as in other passages—such as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone; He thought, 'Let me create the worlds'" and so forth—the term "Self" (ātman) refers exclusively to the Supreme Self. Why is this so? Because of what follows: from the subsequent passage concerning the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), which begins, "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"If it be argued [that there is no proof] because of positive concomitance (anvaya), [we reply] that it would be so because of the restriction. (197) || 17 ||

If it is argued that because the word "Self" (ātman) is seen to be applied to non-Selfs such as the *prāṇamaya* and others in the preceding sections, the [true meaning] cannot be determined from each subsequent statement, [we reply: "It would indeed be so, because of the definitive restriction. There would certainly be such a determination.
Why? Because of the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). This applies even to the preceding [sections].
For it is from this very Self that space was produced; thus, because the Supreme Self alone has been determined by the intellect.

First, the cognition of the Supreme Self descended into the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) which is within the *annamaya* (consisting of food); immediately after that, into the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) within the *prāṇamaya*, and then into the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness). Thereafter, it proceeded into the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss).
Because there is nothing prior to it and because it follows from the statement "He desired," the notion of the Supreme Self is established;
thus, even at the beginning, the connection is through the word "Self" (ātman) by means of the idea of the Supreme Self applied to the non-Supreme Self, which is beyond reproach.
This establishes the definitive conclusion that for all seekers of liberation, the worship of Śiva alone is what must be performed.

Furthermore: at the commencement of that [treatise], it is said, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and elsewhere, "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace"; and from the passage beginning with "By meditating upon Him, there is cessation [of rebirth]; [meditate on] Him who is accompanied by Umā, the Tranquil One," it continues:
"The Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self."
Beholding this, one goes to the supreme Brahman; it is not by any other cause.

By this much, the definitive meaning— that only those who rely upon meditation (*dhyāna*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) of Śiva are free from rebirth— is established. This is because the attainment of identity with Śiva through the worship of Paraśiva— characterized by truth (*satya*) and so forth, as in the words "the *ṛta* is the truth"— is clearly taught even in other Vedic branches (*śākhās*), just as the bee and the worm [attain their respective states].

It is taught that for the sake of attaining that supreme human goal, an inquiry into it must be performed continuously through hearing, reflection, and so forth. This concludes the section on the non-difference between the effect and the cause (Kāryākhyānādhikaraṇa). 5.

The definitive conclusion that all meditations on the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇopāsanā*) are intended as means for attaining the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇabrahma*) is found in the *Upakośala-vidyā* section— where the fires such as the Āhavanīya, Gārhapatya, and Dakṣiṇāgni are mentioned—
and likewise in the *Pratardana-vidyā* section.

Thus, there are two types of meditations concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*). Likewise, in all the Upaniṣads, there exist meditations on entities other than Brahman—such as those on the vital breaths—which occur in proximity to meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*).
Similarly, there are meditations on the "Full" (*bhūman*) and so forth, as demonstrated in the section on the knowledge of the Full (*bhūmavidyā*). Thus...
Are the various meditations on the individual limbs of Vaiśvānara found in the section on the Vaiśvānara-vidyā auxiliary parts of the Vaiśvānara-upāsanā or not? Likewise,
are the meditations on objects other than Brahman found in their respective sections [auxiliary] by way of purifying the mind?

Are these [meditations] auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) to the worship of Brahman with form, or are they independent means for attaining other fruits? According to the maxim that "whatever is enjoined with reference to something has that very thing as its fruit," and because the scripture stating "there is nothing unmade by what is made" prohibits the attainment of the unmade fruit of liberation through performed actions, [it follows that] all meditations consisting of ritual action [are not independent means].

In response to the doubt that—because it cannot be the cause for becoming the Self of the attributeless Brahman—the world [attained] by one who has accumulated merit must, like the world [attained] through the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices performed with desire, have only impermanent results, he states this in another section:
|| 198 || "Because of the mention of the effect, it is something unprecedented. || 18 ||
Now, that which is supplementary to the previously introduced knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is being considered.

Those fires and other rites enjoined in proximity to the meditations on the various saguṇa (qualified) embodied forms of Brahman are indeed merely ancillaries (*aṅga*) to those meditations on the saguṇa embodied Brahman, and not independent means for attaining other fruits. Thus:

And because of the accomplishment of the effects— namely, from the very performance of the subsidiary meditations (*aṅgopāsanā*) concerning the individual soul, the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, which constitute the effects or duties to be performed— an unprecedented transcendental merit (*apūrva*) arises from that meditation upon the qualified, embodied Brahman together with its limbs. By means of that [merit], [the soul attains] the partless, unsurpassed bliss, full, and undivided [Brahman].

This is not tenable. Therefore, from the very meditation on the "cow" (*gopāsanā*), which is the meditation on Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahmopāsanā*), even a minor fruit arises as a matter of course from the meditations on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are performed as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the meditation on the embodied Brahman with attributes. As stated in such scriptural passages as: "Whatever is the fruit of knowledge, that indeed is the fruit of action."

Furthermore, this is seen even in the Smṛtis, which state that "whatever kind of meditation one has in a given case, such is the success that occurs. Also, from such Śruti passages as "He attains union with Brahman" and "He attains the same world as Brahman," it is understood that the declarations of fruit found in proximity to the meditations on the limbs [of the ritual] have their purport solely in the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman.

It is taught that there is an intermediate intention regarding minor injunctions; for in such scriptural passages as "The Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā," since the attainment of the supreme Śiva— who is partless and of the nature of the Witness— is established through the meditation on the qualified, embodied Brahman,
all meditations on the qualified [Brahman] are means for attaining the unqualified Brahman.
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtras is as follows:

because in both the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka [Upaniṣads], through such passages as "the eldest and the best," all meditations on the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth are taught as means for attaining Brahman, [it follows that] all of them...

Does it serve as a cause for the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) by its own independent power, or does it serve as a means for attaining abundance in that world and auspicious manifestations (*vibhūti*) as an ancillary to the meditation on the Saguna-mūrti-Brahman; and furthermore,
as an ancillary to the meditation on the Saguna-mūrti-Sadāśiva-Brahman, [does it lead to] the formless (*amūrta*)?

A doubt arises as to whether [this practice] is indeed the cause for attaining the Śiva-tattva—which consists of the glory of liberation (kaivalya), whose nature is eternal bliss, which is partless, and which is witnessed by the entire universe whose essence is the supreme light that is self-luminous.
For the scripture states: "All these become possessors of meritorious worlds," [indicating that] all worshippers [attain results] according to their own will.
Because of the instruction regarding the attainment of various respective worlds, and because of the scriptural declarations— such as "the world of one who acts perishes"—

that the fruits of action are impermanent; and because, despite the distinction between external and internal, meditations on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, though they are more intimate, are nonetheless composed of the three *guṇas* just like meritorious rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

The state of having *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good) as its fruit is untenable. Starting from the passage, "Whatever is the fruit of knowledge, that indeed is the fruit of action for one who performs these forty-eight sacraments (*saṃskāras*)," up to the end, "he attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman," [it is shown that] this refers to rites such as *garbhādhāna* performed without desire and dedicated to the Supreme Lord.

If it is argued that, because one understands the attainment of the fruit of supreme beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*) through the grace of that [Supreme Being], actions preceded by the intention for meritorious worlds (*puṇyaloka*) independently bring about those respective worlds— nevertheless, since meditation has qualities as its object and because action is by nature impermanent, [the result would be] Sadāśiva who possesses qualities and parts, and is eternal.
When it is argued that [the attainment of Śiva] is merely the reaching of the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), we reply:
in such scriptural passages as "The world acquired by karma perishes," the subject matter concerns the worlds of merit and demerit produced by ordinary (prākṛta) karma;
whereas in passages such as "With firm limbs, many-formed, and fierce," the subject is the limb of the Brahman Sadāśiva, who possesses parts.

Because its permanence is established, and because that world also possesses characteristics distinct from the qualities of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it is the world of Sadāśiva known as the three-quartered manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*) consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, according to the [scriptural] statement: "All beings are one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven."

Because its eternity is understood, the eternity of that world is also unavoidable. For it is said in the Taittirīya and Kaivalya [Upaniṣads]: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, appears in his own true form," and "But at the time of the final end, all are completely liberated from supreme immortality in the world of Brahman. Thus, for all [beings].

For those devotees who worship the Saguna-Sadashiva-Brahman with desireless devotion, there exists, through His grace, the bestowal of eternal sovereignty consisting of auspicious manifestations, namely: Sālokya (residing in the same world), Sāmīpya (proximity), Sārūpya (similarity in form), and Sāyujya (union); as well as the state of Shiva-hood, which is unsurpassed, unobscured, stainless, incomparable, and bodiless.

The attainment of Brahman as the fruit for all lay practitioners (upāsakas) is established by implication. Furthermore: "When all desires that dwell within his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."

In such scriptural passages as these, it is taught that for those who have abandoned all desires, who are practitioners of the *dahara* and other meditations, who are preeminent in the practice of unwavering and uninterrupted steadfastness in knowledge— like a needle drawn to a magnet— and who, being in their final bodies, have attained the state of oneness with Śiva at all times, there exists in this world a state that is incomparable and stainless.

If it is argued that [the world] is established [as real], [we reply]: "The non-difference of that [effect from its cause] follows from such scriptural statements as 'the originative word' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4): 'The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; clay alone is real. This refers to the Vaiyāsika Sūtras which establish both duality and non-duality.
Furthermore, "name" (*nāmadheya*) and "verbal handle" (*vācārambhaṇa*) refer to that which is the conventional usage of desired purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) by means of speech.
It becomes the producer [of the effect], as the state of being a jar is merely a modification of the substance of clay. Furthermore, the name "jar" and so forth is a transformation;
the jar is a mere matter of verbal designation, a scope for the employment of speech such as "this is a jar.
It is simply another state arising for the sake of establishing conventional usage, and not a different substance from the clay.

"Clay alone is the true name. Since everything such as a pot and the like is merely clay, all names such as "pot" and so forth are truly clay. When there is a real, authoritative object, the means of accomplishment is simply another form of that substance; therefore, because the pot is indeed clay, the effect is non-different from the cause.

However, the distinction in conventional usage regarding causal efficiency and so forth between clay and a jar indeed arises from a difference in their respective designations. Therefore, just as in the case of clay and a jar, there is non-difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) due to their relationship as the pervader and the pervaded. And thus says the Smṛti:
"From Śakti down to Earth, [the elements] arise from the Śiva-tattva;
by that one [tattva], all is pervaded, just as a jar and such are pervaded by clay"— from this teaching,
the wicked doctrine of the Naiyāyikas and others, who claim there is always a difference between the individual soul (jīva), the phenomenal world (prapañca), and Brahman, is refuted.

[This objection] is refuted. If it is argued that, whereas in the case of "the pot is clay" the pervasion by clay is observed in the pot, the pervasion by Brahman is not observed in the world such that one says "this world is Brahman," [we reply: it is indeed observed everywhere that "the pot exists, the cloth exists.
If the world were not pervaded by Śiva in His aspect as *Sat* (Being), then [the cognition of existence would not occur].
How indeed could that which is devoid of both existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*sphūrti*) be seen as "it exists" or "it manifests"?
Therefore, the distinction-cum-non-distinction (*bhedābheda*) between Brahman and the phenomenal world of the sentient and the insentient is a matter of certain proclamation (*ghaṇṭāghoṣa*).
This is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*). 6.
The demonstration that all meditations, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, which have the singular fruit of the direct realization of Brahman, constitute a single unified knowledge (*vidyaikya*):

The Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is recorded both in the *Agnirahasya* and in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*. In one place [the text says]: "One should meditate upon the Self as consisting of mind, having vital breath for its body, whose form is light, whose will is true, and whose self is space. In the other [place],...

"Consisting of mind, this person shines within this inner heart, like a grain of rice or a grain of barley; he is the lord of all, the sovereign of all, and he rules over all this"— with such passages from all the *vidyās*, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others, does the attainment of Brahman occur independently for each *vidyā*, or [is there a single result] for all the *vidyās* collectively?

In response to the doubt that [the knowledge of the subordinate sciences] might be a cause for liberation through a succession of steps according to the "ladder" analogy, he states [the solution] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"And likewise, it is equal because there is no difference. (Sūtra 3.3.19)

In the *Agnirahasya* of the *Vājasaneyaka*, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is recorded: "One should meditate on Brahman as Truth. Then, beginning with "Now, this person consists of will (*kratu*)," it continues: "He should meditate on the Self as consisting of mind, having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for its body, having light for its form, having space for its self, and possessing true resolve," and so forth—thus [the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and the Dahara-vidyā].
A doubt arises as to whether [these meditations] are mutually different or non-different;
for while all the various Vidyās are seen to be distinct from one another, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is further recorded in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"This person consists of mind, is composed of light, and is true; within his heart, like a grain of rice or a grain of barley..."

Or rather, he is this one who is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he rules over this entire universe. And elsewhere [it is said]: "I am that god who enters into all beings, born before them all. I alone am the one born and the one yet to be born. He stands facing inward, with faces on every side; he has eyes on every side. And: "He has eyes on every side..."

With faces on every side, with hands on every side, and likewise with feet on every side, the one God, creating heaven and earth, moves with his arms and wings. Within the center of the heart, no larger than the tip of a hair, is the universal God, Jātavedas, the most excellent.
Those wise ones who perceive that Self attain eternal peace, and no others.
I alone abide within every womb; by me all this, consisting of fivefold forms, is filled.
Having realized me—the Lord, the Puruṣa, the adorable God—one attains unto me, the ultimate peace.
They say that within the vital breaths is the mark of the mind—that wherein there is anger, as well as craving and forbearance.
Having severed craving, the root of the net of causes, and having established the mind in Rudra through the intellect;
Thus, for those who worship me while meditating upon me, there is eternal peace, and not for others.
"He who knows the bliss of Brahman, from which words turn back along with the mind without having reached it, fears nothing whatsoever.
"Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, this Self is hidden in the secret place of this creature.
Free from desire, he beholds Him—the Lord, the Greatness—through the grace of the Creator."
Whether in the *ādhāra*, the heart, or between the eyebrows,
the continuous contemplation of the light-liṅga (*jyotirliṅga*) is known as *dhāraṇā* directed toward that.
The yogi should contemplate the *liṅga* as resembling gold in the *ādhāra*, as having the luster of coral in the heart, and as having the brilliance of crystal between the eyebrows.
The ascetic should always and constantly meditate upon the Jyotirliṅga between the two eyebrows.
Having firmly ascertained through the intellect of Brahman that the self is directly the Self by means of the self,
[one should disregard those] endowed with caste and stage of life due to their connection with the body, birth, and so forth.
One should discard the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas like the dust from one's feet;
then the knot of the heart is broken and all doubts are severed.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen;
or rather, where there is the cessation of the seer, the seeing, and the seen—
there alone vision should be fixed, not in the gazing at the tip of the nose.
Making the self the lower fire-drill, the wise man burns away the bond.

Since hundreds of scriptural passages such as these teach various distinct attributes, it might be argued that the convergence (*samanvaya*) of all meditations (*vidyās*), such as the "Small" (*dahara*) and the "Śāṇḍilya," upon Brahman is appropriate by way of different ascending and descending steps. To this we reply:
"They are the same, and thus there is no difference."

Just as in the *Agnirahasya* the collection of qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomaya*), having breath as the body (*prāṇaśarīra*), consisting of light (*bhārūpa*), and possessing true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*) is heard, so too in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, although the qualities beginning with "consisting of mind" are common to both, there is no difference in the nature [of the object] because of the distinction in the quality of "possessing true resolve," which includes mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth. Therefore, the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikyam*) holds elsewhere as well.

Even though there is a perception of difference due to differences in location and differences in qualities, the unity of the knowledge (vidyā) is not contradicted, because the fruit—the direct realization of Brahman—is one through one-pointedness of mind. This concludes the section on "Connection" (Sambandha-adhikaraṇa). 7.

Having established the identity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and others through the unity of meditation on that which possesses qualities and that which is devoid of qualities, as they are interconnected as mutual limbs and the whole, [the author] now addresses the following doubt: "Even if the identity of knowledge is proven in those cases, how can there be identity of knowledge in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, given that mutual differences are perceived therein? To this, he speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
|| 200 || In the same way, [this applies] elsewhere as well due to the connection. || 20 ||

In other cases, such as the Pratardana-vidyā, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, and the Bhūma-vidyā, the production of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) arises from the worship of the supreme Śiva with attributes (saguṇa), which is assisted by the subsidiary meditations (aṅgopāsana) directed toward the individual soul (jīva), the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), the Vaiśvānara, and the names of His various limbs; it does not arise from the worship of the supreme Śiva with attributes alone. Why is this so?

"Because of the connection. The subtle meaning indicated by this sūtra is that the unity of the two meditations (vidyā) is possible because of their mutual relationship as principal and subordinate through the meditations on the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa).
It is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "That which is the True (satya), that is yonder sun; he who is the person in this orb..."
Having begun with "And that which is in the right eye," [the text states] "Its secret name (upaniṣad) is *Ahar*" with respect to the divine,

and "Its secret name is *Aham*" with respect to the self; thus, having stated that the Brahman of Truth within the solar orb and the eye is to be meditated upon as having the *vyāhṛtis* for its body, two secret names (*upaniṣads*) are given for the purpose of meditation.

When a doubt arises as to whether those two [meditations] are established as restricted to their specific locations as heard in the texts, or whether both are to be practiced in both places without restriction—
the answer is that for the Brahman which is the object of meditation, namely the "Real" (satya) whose body is the phenomenal world, there is [presence] in both locations.

On account of the connection [of the qualities], the identity of the object of meditation, the non-difference of form, and the non-difference of conjunction and so forth, it follows that there is unity of the knowledge (vidyā) and thus no fixed rule [regarding its application]. To this, it is replied: "Because of the connection, it is the same elsewhere as well. Just as, due to the identity of the one qualified by attributes such as consisting of mind (manomaya), there is unity of the object of meditation, non-difference of form, and consequently unity of the knowledge.

Regarding the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*): thus, because the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is associated with the eye and the solar orb, is one in essence as the Truth (*satya*), there is a combination of both [qualities] in both places.
Furthermore, even though a distinction in meditation is designated based on the difference in locations such as the eye and the solar orb, the object of meditation remains the same.

The unity of the knowledge (vidyaikyam) is established through the oneness of Śiva. However, in meditations such as those on the Sun and the Eye, a distinction between specific knowledges is observed due to the difference in locations and the resulting difference in the meditations. Therefore, in response to the doubt as to how there can be unity of knowledge, he says:
Or rather, not so, because there is a distinction.

Indeed, there is no difference in the knowledge (vidyā) here; why? Because of a distinction—namely, a distinction in the form of the object of meditation. Although Paraśiva-Brahman is one, in one case he is to be meditated upon as residing in the solar orb, while in the other he is to be meditated upon as having the eye as his locus. Thus, due to the difference in form arising from the difference in connection with the location, there is a difference in the knowledge. Nevertheless, because the fruit is the same—liberation—there is no difference in the knowledge.

The identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) has been stated. Even though a difference in the location of the object of meditation is seen in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, there is identity of meditation because in both cases it is to be meditated upon as having the heart as its locus; it is the same here as well. Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
And he demonstrates it as well. || 22 ||

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], after teaching that the lotus of the heart (*daharapuṇḍarīka*) is the locus for the worship of the Supreme Lord—stating, "Therein is the small ether, free from sorrow; that which is within it is to be worshipped"—the following arises as a doubt: "Who is the Supreme Self (Paramātman) to be worshipped there? To this, [the text replies]: "He who is declared at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda is Maheśvara."

In that context, the fact that Maheśvara alone is the object of worship has been demonstrated. In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*, having shown the heart-lotus to be the place of worship for the Supreme Lord by stating, "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure," and so forth, when the question arises as to in what form the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is to be worshipped therein, [it is stated]: "The Supreme Lord accompanied by Umā."

By the words "the Lord" (*prabhum*) and so forth, the status of Śiva as the Brahman with form, characterized by attributes such as being accompanied by Umā, is indicated as the object of worship. Likewise, in the *Taittirīya* and *Kaivalya* Upaniṣads, in one instance there is the word "dahara" (the small) along with the word "Maheśvara," and in another instance there is the word "hṛdaya" (heart) along with the word "Umāsahāya" (accompanied by Umā).

Even when there is a designation of mutual difference, since the identity of the underlying reality is understood, the unity of the meditation is established; likewise, he shows that the unity of the Akṣy-vidyā and Aditya-vidyā is unavoidable. The word "ca" (and) is used for the sake of certainty.
Now, an objection: in the Taittirīya, Chāndogya, Kaivalya, and other Upaniṣads, in one place it is said, "This golden person within the sun... [and so on].

"This one is seen as golden," and so forth is heard [in scripture]. Elsewhere, having introduced the golden person (*puruṣa*) as residing within the solar orb in the passage, "This golden person who is within the sun," the text concludes by stating his nature as the self of all and his possession of golden arms, beginning with "Rudra is indeed everything" and ending with "Salutation to the one with golden arms."

Furthermore, the status of being the Lord of Umā (Umāpati) is recorded [in scripture]. In this regard, there is a difference in form: in one place it is "having all limbs golden," while in another it is "possessing much gold.

There is also a difference in attributes: in one place it is "Rudra is indeed everything," indicating his nature as the self of all, while in another it is "he rules over all worlds," indicating his sovereignty over all. Therefore, if it is argued that the knowledge is not identical, we say no; for [the text] says, "within the sun... [and so on].

This demonstrates that identity of location indeed implies identity of the knowledge (vidyā). In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], beginning with "The golden person" (*hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the mention of the arms is intended as an illustration; thus, even in the conclusion, what is intended is that all limbs are made of gold.
This is because Paraśiva, who transcends the universe, is the cause of both the creation and sustenance of the world through His Śakti, and because He enters into it.

Identity is logical. Therefore, since one [entity] is established in both places, the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*) is unimpeded. This concludes the section concerning the "Accumulation" (*sambhṛti-adhikaraṇa*). 8.
The establishment that the meditation on Brahman as distinguished by all attributes is a means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman [is not contradicted] because,
in the Śruti passage beginning with "The powers were gathered, with Brahman as the eldest," those [attributes] reside in a different context and are separated [from the meditation].

In response to the doubt as to how even the meditation on Paraśiva-Brahman, characterized by qualities such as *sambhṛti* (accumulation), *dyu* (heaven), and *vyāpti* (pervasion), can independently be a means for attaining His world, he states another topical section:
"Accumulation, heaven, pervasion, and so forth also [are means], and therefore. (Sūtra 23)

In the *Taittirīyaka*, in the *Khilas* of the *Rājāyanīyas*, it is said: "The heroic powers were gathered with Brahman as the eldest; Brahman first stretched out the eldest heaven. Among those things that have become Brahman, he was born first. Therefore, who is worthy to rival Brahman? Thus, there is the gathering of heroic powers in which Brahman is the eldest.

That which the Supreme Brahman extended and accomplished—namely, the destruction of Tripura, the swallowing of the Kālakūṭa poison, the conquest of the god of love (Manmatha), and the lifting of the mountain [Govardhana]—which are filled with extraordinary qualities; that which is considered the eldest, Hari, and Śiva, as non-dual and the fourth state—that is the Self, that is to be known. This is established in such scriptural passages as these.

"Brahman" was first among them; thus it is clearly taught in such scriptural passages as "one should meditate upon the Lord who is to be meditated upon," and "they are fully produced. He extended—that is, he pervaded and occupied—the station of the supreme ether prior to heaven.
Furthermore, the complete gathering and pervasion of all those great heroic powers occurred everywhere.
A doubt arises as to whether there is a combination [of attributes] from the higher knowledges [regarding Brahman] or not:
"Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun; and that light which shines beyond heaven;
and this small lotus-palace dwelling within this city of Brahman."

In such scriptural passages as these, the word *atha* itself indicates a distinction between sections (*prakaraṇa*). Accordingly, in each respective section on meditation (*upāsanā*), the meditations on the ancillaries (*aṅga-upāsanā*) enjoined separately are subordinate members of the proximate meditation on the Saguna Brahman;
they merely serve to ordain the attainment of that particular world. [They are] "the knowledges whose first-born is Brahman, gathered together, with Brahman as the first-born."

In this *Khila-saṃhitā* verse beginning with "He stretched out the heaven," many qualities such as the accumulation of virility, the pervasiveness of the celestial world, and being the cause of all beings are set forth.

Nevertheless, neither an injunctive statement (*vidhi*) such as "one should meditate" nor the fruit [of such meditation] is heard there. Therefore, regarding those [qualities] propounded in the *Khila-saṃhitā*...

The term *sambhṛtivyāpti* is a singular compound (*ekavadbhāva*) formed from the collective copulative (*samāhāra-dvandva*) "the maintenance [of the world] and the pervasion [of heaven and earth]," which refers to the qualified meditations (*saguṇa-vidyā*) such as the Dahara and Śāṇḍilya, that enjoin these qualities.

Although the "maintenance" and so forth are taught without reference to a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), they must nevertheless be restricted [to specific meditations] precisely because of the difference in location (*sthāna-bheda*).
It must be applied everywhere. How is it that those [qualities] taught as unconnected [to specific meditations] are restricted to particular locations?

We reply: by their own inherent power. First of all, the pervasion of heaven cannot be brought over into meditations whose scope is limited to small places such as the heart; nor can qualities such as "being supported" (sambhṛtatva) and so forth, which are concomitant with that [pervasion], be brought over, as they occupy the same location.

Thus, [the meditation] regarding objects with limited scope is not to be combined. However, passages such as "This space within the heart is like that space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3) can be combined here and there,
for they are intended to establish the majesty of the object of meditation characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind and being free from sin.
Furthermore: "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world; those gods asked Rudra, 'Who are you?

For it is heard in scripture that there is a great abode, denoted by the word "heaven," which, by its nature as supreme bliss, is greater than the stations of Hiraṇyagarbha and others. Therefore, [this applies] to meditations on Vaiśvānara and so forth, which differ from those limited stations.

Since the pervasion of heaven (*dyuvyāpti*) is to be concluded [from the context], its concomitant— the accumulation of great power (*mahāvīryasambhṛti*)— must likewise be concluded in that very same place. Alternatively,

even though neither an injunction nor a fruit is explicitly seen in the *Khila-saṃhitā*, one should supply an injunction such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) and a fruit consisting of the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman, just as in the case of the meditation on the "small" (*dahara*) and other such meditations.
There is no fault even if it is accepted that, in the *Khila-saṃhitās*, the meditation on Brahman as distinguished by all its attributes is a means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman.
This concludes the section on the Puruṣavidyā (Puruṣavidyādhikaraṇa). 9.
The determination that the mental-activity-based Jyotiṣṭoma and [the physical sacrifice] are causes of liberation through a succession mediated by the purification of the mind;

and [the application of this] to the meditator, as stated in such scriptural passages as: "Of this sacrifice whose [performer] knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife," and so forth.

A mental Jyotiṣṭoma, consisting of the well-known limbs of the [physical] Jyotiṣṭoma, has been prescribed with respect to the limbs such as the hands and feet. In this regard, there arises the doubt: does this mental Jyotiṣṭoma function as an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma found in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), or is it independent as a means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman? To address this, he speaks therein by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
204. And because the others are not mentioned even in the Puruṣavidyā. 24.

The meaning is that for others—namely, for the lay follower (*upāsaka*)—the mental auxiliary rites consisting of fuel-sticks, *kuśa* grass, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, which are mentally imagined upon the limbs of his hands and feet, are not prescribed; that is to say, they are not enjoined, just as [they are not found] in the Jyotiṣṭoma consisting of ritual action within the Karma-kāṇḍa, such as in the Puruṣa-vidyā or the mental Jyotiṣṭoma. And thus:
Because the mental Jyotiṣṭoma and the ritual Jyotiṣṭoma are distinguished by their mutually distinct sets of constituent parts (*aṅga*),

it is untenable for the mental Jyotiṣṭoma— characterized by parts imagined by the mind— to be a subordinate part of the ritual Jyotiṣṭoma, which is characterized by real constituent parts; rather, it exists independently.
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that [this knowledge] serves as a means to attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman.

In the Taittirīyaka, the Puruṣavidyā is recorded: "Of this sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass," and so forth. The Puruṣavidyā is also found in the Chāndogya.
It is recorded in scripture: "Man indeed is the sacrifice; those twenty-four years of his," and so forth. Regarding this, a doubt arises:
Is there a difference in the meditation (vidyā) here, or not? [The opponent argues:

There is no difference, because the name is identical—namely, "the meditation on man"—and because the form is identical, as both consist in the same imaginative attribution of the parts of the sacrifice to the limbs of the person.

In the *Taittirīyaka*, because no connection with a fruit is heard— unlike the statement "he lives for one hundred and sixteen years" found in the *Chāndogya*— and since that very fruit of the Puruṣavidyā belongs to the *Chāndogya* scripture, it follows that the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikyam*) results from the non-difference of the connection with the fruit; this being the position reached, it is replied:
Although both meditations taught in the two [texts] are indeed "Puruṣa-vidyās," there is nevertheless a distinction between the two meditations.

Because they are not mentioned in other [recensions]. Since the qualities (guṇas) mentioned in one recension (śākhā) are not mentioned elsewhere—for instance, those beginning with "that which is in the evening, in the morning, and at midday are the pressings" (savanāni) are mentioned in the Taittirīyaka, but they are not recorded as "pressings" (savana-tvena) in the Chāndogya; likewise, the human lifespan divided into three parts...

In the Chāndogya, [the rites] are conceived as the *savana*s (pressings). While the Chāndogya conceives of the *āśis* and other elements heard there as being the *dīkṣā* (initiation) and so forth, this is not done in the Taittirīyaka. Furthermore, the conceptualization of the sacrificer, his wife, and others is different [in the two texts].
Therefore, the form (*rūpa*) differs in both cases, and likewise the connection with the fruit (*phala-saṃyoga*) also differs. For in the Taittirīyaka, in the preceding section...

Having taught the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) with the words, "I unite you, who are Brahman, with Om," and having stated that one attains the majesty of Brahman as its fruit, the Puruṣavidyā is recorded in the passage beginning with "Of him who knows thus.

It is understood that this is a conceptualization of the sacrifice belonging to this very knower of Brahman; therefore, because it is an auxiliary part of the knowledge of Brahman, [it is not separate].

In this case, the attainment of Brahman itself is the fruit, according to the maxim that "when something without a stated fruit is mentioned in proximity to something with a fruit, it is an auxiliary part of that.

Thus, it is understood that the Puruṣavidyā taught in the Taittirīyaka is an auxiliary part of the Brahmavidyā. However, in the Chāndogya, the Puruṣavidyā is said to have the attainment of long life as its fruit. Therefore, because of the difference in form and connection [to fruits], there is a difference between the two knowledges (vidyā).
Thus, there is no transfer of qualities mentioned in one place to another.

Nevertheless, just as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices performed for the sake of the Supreme Lord without desire for rewards, the Chāndogya Puruṣavidyā— when practiced without desire— establishes itself as a cause of liberation through the indirect means of purifying the mind.
The Section on Piercing and Other [Ritual] Bases || 10 ||

The determination of the attainment of the fruit desired by one who wishes for the world of Śiva, which is reached through the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of the two mantras beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*) and "Having pierced the bright [target]" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*);
for indeed, regarding the knowledges (*vidyā*) recited in the *Chāndogya*, *Taittirīya*, *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and other scriptures...

Furthermore, because some rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others possess expectancy, it is stated that they lead, through a succession of stages, to the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman. For instance, since the mantras beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious to us; may He protect us both" are recited at the commencement of the Taittirīya Upaniṣads, those [rites] as well—
It would be an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), because [the passage] "piercing the semen, piercing the heart, piercing the mind, having cut with razors,

he has turned it threefold" and so forth— which consists of the description of malevolent rites (*abhicārakarma*) such as the piercing of the heart— is recited at the beginning of the Upanishads by the followers of the Atharva Veda.
Anticipating the objection that [the result] would not exist, he states it by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth. (Sūtra 25)

The meaning is that because of the difference in purpose and results—such as piercing [the enemy], afflicting the foe, and so forth—and because they lack connection with the meditation on Paraśiva-Brahman as possessing qualities and parts, these mantras do not constitute limbs of that meditation on Brahman.
[As it is said: "All this is indeed Brahman; it is born from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; one should meditate upon Him with a tranquil mind."
Thus, since the Śruti establishes that only one who is tranquil (śānta) possesses the qualification for the worship of Paraśiva-Brahman,
it is impossible for a mantra intended for the death of an enemy to be an auxiliary to such Brahman-worship; therefore, being situated within the Karmakāṇḍa,
it yields only a desired fruit (kāmyaphala), just like an auxiliary to a sacrifice— this is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra.

The followers of the Atharvaveda recite at the beginning of their Upaniṣads the mantras beginning with "Having pierced the bright [heart]," and so forth; the Sāmavedins likewise recite at the beginning of the *Rahasyabrāhmaṇa* the mantra beginning with "O God Savitṛ, impel us";
and the Kāṭhakas, the Taittirīyas, and the Śāṭyāyanins recite the mantra beginning with "May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious."

"Thou art a white horse, thou art a greenish-blue horse," and so forth—thus do the Aitareyins recite the Mahāvrata Brāhmaṇa. "Indra, having slain Vṛtra, indeed became great," and so forth—the Kauṣītakins also [recite] the very same Mahāvrata Brāhmaṇa. "Prajāpati, indeed, is the year..."

Regarding this, the Vājasaneyins [state] in the *Pravargya-brāhmaṇa*: "This is his self which is the Mahāvrata," and so forth, beginning with, "The gods indeed sat down for a sacrificial session. In this regard, there arises a doubt: Are the mantras studied at the commencement of the Upaniṣads—such as "Piercing the bright [sun]," "O Mitra," and so on—as well as ritual acts such as the *Pravargya*, auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), or not?

What is appropriate? That [the mantra] is an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). Why? Because its status as an auxiliary to knowledge is understood from its recitation in proximity (*sannidhi*) to that knowledge.

Although there is no direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) for the application of the mantras such as "The bright one, having known" (*śukram pravidya*) and so forth, nor for rites such as the *pravargya*, nevertheless—because other applications for the mantra "May Mitra and Varuṇa protect us together" (*saṃ naḥ avatu*) and so forth are absent, and because it occurs within the context of knowledge (*vidyā*)—it is concluded that it is an auxiliary to knowledge.
Since being an auxiliary to the Vidyās is unavoidable, it follows that these mantras must be incorporated into all the Vidyās;
this being the position reached, we reply: No, because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth.

Because these [mantras] are understood to be employed in practices such as the study of malevolent incantations (*abhicāra*), based on indicative marks such as "piercing the semen, piercing the heart; I shall speak the *ṛta*, I shall speak the truth; I have spoken the *ṛta*, I have spoken the truth; may our study be radiant; may we not hate each other," they do not constitute an auxiliary part of knowledge (*vidyā*).

This is what is meant: just as, by the power of the mantra beginning with "piercing the heart," it is understood that mantras such as "piercing the semen" are subsidiary to rites of exorcism (*abhicāra*) and the like, even so, by the power of the mantras beginning with "I shall speak the truth" and "May our study be brilliant," the mantra "śanno mitraḥ" is understood to be subsidiary to the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).

This is understood from such mantras as these. Therefore, they do not constitute auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the Vidyā. The recitation here of [mantras] such as *śukraṃ pravidhya* and the Brāhmaṇas concerning the Pravargya rite and so forth is due to their being designated as *divākīrtya* (to be recited by day) or *araṇye'nuvākyā* (to be recited in the forest).
Consequently, for those who recite the mantras beginning with *śanno mitraḥ*, just as for those performing the Sandhyā-vandana, [the same applies].

The means to attain the world of Śiva is through a succession of stages by way of the purification of the mind. However, for those who recite mantras such as "śukraṃ pravidhya," it is taught that they result in fruits desired for specific purposes. This concludes the section on "Loss" (Hānyadhikaraṇa). 11.

Having determined the supreme fruit attainable through the worship of the Saguna Paraśiva-Brahman, a doubt arises as to what the destiny is for those worshippers who possess only mild dispassion: "May the fruit of attaining Śivatva belong to those who are endowed with tranquility, self-control, and other virtues, who are free from passion, and are solely devoted to Śiva; but what is the fate of those worshippers who possess only mild dispassion?"
He states, by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa), that there is a rule for the inclusion of intermediate fruits:

"But in the case of departure [from the body], because of the supplementary nature of the word 'approaching' (upāyana), it is as in the case of the Kuśa grass, the meters, the hymns of praise, and the singing; this has been stated. (Sūtra 26)
"Shaking off evil as a horse shakes off its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu,

having shaken off the body, I— being one whose self is perfected— attain the uncreated world of Brahman," thus [it is said] in the Sāma-śruti regarding those who meditate upon the Saguna Paraśiva-Brahman after death.

It has been stated that there is merely the relinquishment of good and evil deeds, as in: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his sons obtain his inheritance, his friends his good deeds, and his enemies his evil deeds.
However, in the scriptural text of another recension (*śākhā*), following the relinquishment of good and evil deeds by the practitioners (*upāsaka*s), it is said:
In this context, the acceptance of the good and evil deeds of those who are friends of the devotee and those who are enemies of the devotee has been stated. This being the case,

when there is a departure [of the soul], the scriptural passage that teaches only the abandonment consisting of the relinquishment of good and evil deeds must be supplemented by the meditative practice consisting of the acceptance of the good and evil deeds of both the friends of the devotee and the enemies of the devotee.

Why? Because it is supplementary to the word "appropriating" (upāyana). This means that in the scriptural passage, "He shakes off his good and evil deeds," the word *vidhūnana* (shaking), which denotes the act of striking off, is used in association with words denoting appropriation (*upāyana*).
He provides an illustration for this: "As in the case of the *kuśa*-grass, the meters, the praise, and the singing. Just as in a certain Vedic branch (*śākhā*)...

The meaning is as follows: just as among the subsidiary elements of a ritual (*karmāṅga*)—such as the *kuśa* grass, the meters, the hymns of praise (*stuti*), and the chanting (*upagāna*)—which are studied together, when one particular element is heard in a certain branch (*śākhā*), the other elements are to be combined (*upasaṃhāra*). As it has been said: "When one individual element is heard, [the others are to be supplied]."
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that the withdrawal of the limbs [of the body] is appropriate here according to the principles of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā.
The Chandogas record: "As a horse shakes its hairs... and likewise the Atharvaṇikas: "The wise man [shakes off] merit and sin..."

"Having shaken off [all taints], stainless, he attains the supreme equality"—thus [it is said]. But the Śāṭhyāyanins [read]: "His sons inherit his property; his friends, his good deeds; and his enemies, his evil deeds," and so forth.
The Kauṣītakins, however, [state]: "He shakes off both his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen inherit his good deeds..."
"Unpleasant [results] from evil deeds. Thus, it is heard in some places that there is a loss of merit and demerit; in others, that one attains those [results] among pleasant and unpleasant things;

and in yet others, both are mentioned. Although both are heard in each individual meditation (vidyā), they must nevertheless be accepted as auxiliary to all meditations, for even one established in any Brahma-vidyā who attains Brahman [is subject to them].

Because the abandonment of merit and demerit is inevitable, and because the means of attainment has as its object that which has already been abandoned, such reflection, when enjoined, ought to be an auxiliary to all branches of knowledge. In this regard, the following is considered:
should the reflection on abandonment, the reflection on the means of attainment, and the reflection on both be treated as alternatives (*vikalpa*) or as things to be combined (*upasaṃhāra*)? Which...

It is logical that they should be treated as optional alternatives. Why? Because of the force of their separate scriptural injunctions. For if there were a conjunction (*samuccaya*), there would have to be a coordination of both at every instance; and since that is already established by the Kauṣītaki passage itself, the injunction elsewhere would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, the purpose of being enjoined in one place is not merely to provide an option. No.

The fact that [the same teaching] is recorded in multiple places can be resolved by the difference in reciters (adhyetṛ). Indeed, repetition without distinction is to be resolved by the difference in reciters; however, in this case, there is a loss [of the teaching] in two branches and its acquisition in only one.
Nor can it be established by means of a difference in the knowledge (vidyā) itself.

Since it has been stated that this connection [of the two] is the remainder of all [the preceding], the following is said here: "But in the case of abandonment, because of the word 'attainment' being the remainder. The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the previous position.
The phrase "in the case of abandonment" is for the purpose of illustration; [it applies] when either abandonment alone or attainment alone is heard in the scripture.

The mutual conjunction of these two is necessarily established. Why? Because the statement regarding their "taking up" (upāyana) is a supplement to the statement regarding their "abandonment" (hāni). Indeed, it is appropriate that the statement regarding taking up be a supplement to the statement regarding abandonment, because the statement regarding taking up expresses the place of entry for the merit and demerit abandoned by the knower; this is so because [the former] is a passage recited in another location [of the scripture].

Examples are presented to illustrate the status of being a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) prescribed in another location: "like the *kuśā* grass, the meters (*chandas*), the hymns of praise (*stuti*), and the chanting (*upagāna*). The followers of the Kālāpa school recite, "The *kuśā* grasses are of the nature of trees (*vānaspatya*)," whereas the Śāṭhyāyanins recite, "The *kuśā* grasses are made of *udumbara* wood. Thus, the *kuśā* grasses are understood in a general sense as being of the nature of trees.

The word "audumbarī" becomes a supplementary part of that sentence by way of specification. Similarly, when there is a general reference to the meters of both gods and asuras in the passage beginning with "of the gods and asuras by means of the meters," the statement "the meters of the gods first" serves to establish a specific order and thus becomes a supplementary part of that same sentence. Likewise...

When the rule "He begins the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra with gold" is obtained without qualification, the specific statement "He begins the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra when the sun has half-set" serves as its supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*). Likewise,
regarding the general rule "The priests sing along (*upagāyanti*)," the specific prohibition "The *adhvaryu* should not sing along" [serves as its supplement].

A sentence that conveys a meaning pertaining to someone other than the Adhvaryu priest necessarily becomes a subordinate part (*vākyaśeṣa*) of that [primary] sentence. Thus, for those who do not accept the subordinate status of a sentence—which is capable of establishing a general meaning within a specific context—they must resort to an option (*vikalpa*) between those two meanings; and that...
When such a possibility exists, it is not tenable [to assume otherwise], as was stated in the previous section:

"But rather, because they are supplementary to a sentence, and because an option would be improper, they should be parts of the injunctions. Thus, since the statements concerning mere relinquishment and mere acquisition form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), there is no such thing as a mere relinquishment or a mere acquisition.
The alternative view is not tenable. For the Kauṣītakins, the mention of both [the names] is not contradictory, as it is a repetition without distinction due to the difference in the practitioners.
If it is asked, "How can an explanatory passage (arthavāda) depend on an explanatory passage located in another section?"—it is because it serves to establish the meditation on the Name (nāmopāsti).

Regarding the phrase "or twenty-one according to the Śruti," this is because it is observed that the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not definitively establish the number twenty-one on its own, but rather depends upon the explanatory passage found in the *Satvaprakaraṇa* of the Taittirīyas: "Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun—this is the twenty-first. Having thus explained the resolution of the number therein, [the text continues:]

Therefore, even if it is a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), the "taking over" (*upāyana*) must be combined [with the other texts]. For there is an understanding of both "casting off" (*hāna*) and "taking over" (*upāyana*) in a single place;

for in the Kauṣītaki Śruti, it is stated: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take over his good deeds, and those who are not dear take over his evil deeds. Thus, there is consistency between these two.
The section concerning the future life. || 12 ||

At the time of Vīraśaiva initiation, there is the destruction of meritorious and non-meritorious karma accumulated prior to the Śiva-initiation; and after the departure of the vital breath (prāṇotkramaṇa), there is the attainment of the natural merit resulting from the period subsequent to the initiation.
Now, even for those with weak dispassion, through the worship of Paraśiva in all branches of knowledge, [liberation occurs] preceded by the separation from merit and demerit.

The experience of those respective worlds has been taught; nevertheless, in response to the doubt as to whether such experience occurs during the lifetime of that body or at the time of separation [from it], he demonstrates the determination of time by means of another section: || 207 || "At the time of death, because there is nothing further to be crossed; for thus others [hold]. || 27 ||

In this regard, the Śruti texts establish the destruction of both merit and demerit for those divine worshippers whose [bondage] has been severed by Śaiva initiation, immediately after they cross the Virajā river on the Devayāna path— which serves as the cause for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman in the hereafter.

He states the authoritative evidence: "For likewise others. Other followers of different recensions (śākhins) state in the Śruti: "He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it by the mind alone; there he shakes off his good and evil deeds. Thus, they establish the destruction of good and evil deeds immediately after crossing the river Virajā. Nevertheless, at the time of the Śaiva initiation which follows the crossing of the river Virajā—

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that, due to the dissociation from the meritorious and non-meritorious karma performed prior to that [initiation], the entire multitude of evil deeds committed after initiation perishes for the practitioners at the time of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkramaṇa*). It has been stated that the abandonment and acquisition of good and evil deeds must be considered in all meditations (*vidyā*); and that—

Regarding the doubt as to whether the falling away occurs at the time of separation from the body and on the path after the soul has departed from the body, or only at the time of separation from the body—the correct view is that it occurs in both cases, because it is heard in scripture in both ways. For the Kauṣītakins record it thus, beginning with:
"Having entered upon this path of the gods, he comes to the world of Agni," and continuing, "He comes to the Virajā river."

"He crosses that river with his mind; he shakes off his good and evil deeds. In this passage, the destruction of good and evil deeds on the path is understood. However, the Tāṇḍins [read]: "As a horse shakes off its hairs, shaking off evil;
as the moon frees itself from the mouth of Rāhu; having shaken off the body, the self-realized one [attains] the uncreated."

"I am attaining the world of Brahman. In this context, however, it is understood to refer to the time of separation from the body. Furthermore, in the case of Śāṭhyāyanaka, the transfer of good and evil deeds—which is heard to occur simultaneously with the transmission of the inheritance to one's sons—is understood to take place at the time of separation from the body. Therefore, a portion of the good and evil deeds is cast off at the time of separation from the body.
Since it might be argued that "the remainder [of karma] persists on the way," it is replied:

"At the time of departure" (*sāmparāye*). At the very time of departure from the body, the good and evil deeds of the knower perish without remainder. Why? Because there is nothing further to be crossed (*tartavyābhāvāt*). For the knower...
After separation from the body, there is an absence of experience that must be traversed by means of good and evil deeds;

for apart from the attainment of Brahman, which is the fruit of knowledge, there is nothing to be experienced through good and evil deeds—namely, pleasure and pain, which touch one as the pleasant and the unpleasant. "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light..."

In such scriptural passages as, "He manifests in his own form; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall attain [Brahman]," the direct attainment of Brahman is shown even without reaching another world; thus, the entire scripture is consistent.

In response to the doubt that—since the *Śruti* states, "As a horse shakes off its hairs, so shaking off evil" (*aśva iva romāṇi vidhūya pāpam*), and since the *Śruti* also speaks of one who is "free from passion and free from evil" (*virajāvipāpmā*)—it is taught there only that evil (*pāpa*) is destroyed and not merit (*puṇya*), [the author] says:
"According to one's will, because there is no contradiction with either. (2.3.28)

"According to one's wish" means by the power of the opposite side. By the word "evil" (pāpa), merit (puṇya) is also implied through indirect indication (ajahallakṣaṇā). Why? Because there is no contradiction between the two.
When the seer beholds Him who is golden-hued, the Maker, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman;
then the knower, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality.

This is because other scriptural passages are observed that prescribe the destruction of both merit and demerit through such means; furthermore, there are Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas which prescribe the attainment of the world of Śiva by crossing the Virajā river,
as well as those that establish the attainment of the supreme Liṅga of Paraśiva, consisting of supreme light, at this very spot upon the fall of the body.

If it is argued that a mutual contradiction is observed, it should be understood that [the scripture] prescribes a single fruit consisting of devotion solely to the Supreme Lord, whether He appears as detached or non-detached.

According to the principle that the sequence of words in the Veda may be explained according to one's desire, it is proper to investigate the meaning, the purpose, and the underlying state of the revelation. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the liberation from merit and demerit at the time of casting off the body; therefore, after that [point],...

In order to avoid the contradiction between the two scriptural texts regarding the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman, it is established that in the Kauṣītaki passage, the phrase "having reached that path" (*tatsukṛtaduṣkṛte vidhūya...

panthānam āpadya*) must be inserted prior [to the mention of the path]. Now, one might object: is it not more logical that the rule for the destruction of merit and demerit applies here and now to those who have dissolved into the supreme Liṅga consisting of light? As for others distinct from them...

In response to the doubt that for those whose passion has only slightly subsided, the merit and demerit accumulated during their lifetime—which are difficult to ward off—might arise immediately after crossing the river Virajā at the end of the body, [the Sūtra] says:
|| 209 || "The meaningfulness of the movement is twofold; otherwise there would be a contradiction. || 29 ||

If it is accepted that both merit and demerit are destroyed in both ways, then the journey— namely, the travel to the world of Brahman via the path beginning with light— becomes meaningful and fruitful. Otherwise,
if the destruction of meritorious karma were not accepted, [one would remain] for some time in the world of Brahman, which is Paraśiva.

Since it must necessarily be admitted that after the enjoyment of the fruits of worship, there is a return to the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) for the sake of enjoying the fruits of merit (*puṇya*), a contradiction would arise; furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural text (*śruti*) stating, "He does not return. By this, [the phrase] "they do not return to this human whirlpool" which is being propounded [is explained].
The authority of the Śruti would be undermined.
Furthermore, because in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Āgama, the conventional designation "karma" is established exclusively for obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and desire-driven (kāmya) rites.

Because it is impossible to maintain the conventional usage of [the soul] being the instrument of devotion—which arises from His grace—by means of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*) dedicated to Śiva performed throughout many lifetimes without desire; for by such devotion, there would arise in His world a manifestation of auspicious glory (*kalyāṇa-vibhūti*), which is the root of unsurpassed bliss and endowed with all sovereignty, and this would be contradictory [to the nature of the transmigrating soul]. Likewise...
And it is clearly taught in the Śivagītā: "Devotion to Śiva arises through merits accumulated over ten million births;
by means of that [devotion], a human being performs rites such as sacrifices (iṣṭa) and works of public utility (pūrta)."

"Having renounced desires according to the prescribed rule with the resolve of offering everything to Śiva"— having thus established the expansion of the greatness of devotion by such means, [it continues: "By this very path, you shall indeed reach the further shore of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa."
O sages, I shall explain that vow known as the Pāśupata.
Having performed the initiation of Viraja and wearing sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
they recited the thousand names of Śiva known as the *Vedasāra*.
By means of that, having abandoned your mortal state, you shall attain the body of Śiva;
thereafter, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, will be pleased.
Having come within the range of your vision, it will bestow upon you the state of absolute liberation.
I shall relate to you all that which the Pot-born Sage spoke to Rāma in the Daṇḍaka forest; listen, O practitioners of devotion!
Therefore, having resorted to the path free from passion, I shall initiate you;
by that path, having abandoned mortality, one becomes composed of light.
"I shall perform this Pāśupata vow in brief.
Then, on the auspicious Ramagiri mountain, on the bank of the Godāvarī, Rāma [established himself].
Having installed a Śiva-liṅga and having performed the initiation according to the prescribed rule.
With all his limbs adorned with sacred ashes, he was endowed with ornaments made of rudrākṣa beads.
By such statements as these, the pot-born Agastya instructed Śrī Rāma in the ritual procedure for initiation into Śiva, which is synonymous with the Virajā river.
Now, one might object: for devotees who have cast off their bodies, the journey by the path of the gods (devayāna) occurs only when their karma is exhausted at the time of crossing the Virajā river.

If it is argued that [the soul] is the prompter [of karma] because otherwise all karma would be exhausted at the very moment of separation from the body, such that liberation would occur immediately thereafter—this is not so, because the journey by the path of the gods (devayāna) would then be purposeless. For it is said: "Having reached the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form."

There would be a contradiction with the scriptural teaching that immediately upon reaching Brahman by the path of the gods (*devayāna*), one assumes its very form. And so, although the journey by the path of the gods, as well as the wandering through various regions, the dialogue with the Moon, and so forth, are all rendered possible by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*) alone— just as subsequent wanderings are possible even after reaching Brahman— nevertheless, until the actual attainment of Brahman...

Since the persistence of saṃsāra, which consists in the contraction of the intellect (*dhī-saṅkoca*), is not possible through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*) alone, one must necessarily admit the persistence of a trace of karma (*karma-leśa*) that serves as its root. Nor should it be argued that this persistence could arise solely from a specific volition (*saṅkalpa-viśeṣa*) of the Supreme Lord; for that very [volition] is what we...

This is because [the attainment of results] is stated to be rooted in karma. For in this system, there is no intention (*saṅkalpa*) of the Supreme Lord brought about by the performance of prescribed or prohibited actions. Merit and demerit exist independently of His intention. For those solely devoted to Śiva, there is the attainment of the world of Śiva preceded by the eradication of merit, as well as the attainment of the state of Śiva (*śivatva*).
