If it is argued that after attaining Brahman, it is logical for those who desire to go to the world of Śiva to attain His essential nature—which is devoid of mental fluctuations such as expansion—and for them to manifest a divine, auspicious form characterized by the expansion of the intellect and so forth; [we reply:
until that point, there must persist the activity of karma which causes the contraction of that very intellect. Thus:

The destruction of karma is said to occur immediately after crossing the Virajā river. By the phrase "having attained the supreme light," the attainment of Brahman is intended. The Virajā river is not related to Viṣṇu’s abode; rather, it is the boundary of the phenomenal world (prākṛta-prapañca), and its entry constitutes that limit.

Yogis who have exhausted all traces of karma enter the supreme state of Śiva, which is beyond the material world, consisting of ultimate bliss, and situated above the station of Viṣṇu. For thus says the Śruti: "He reaches the end of the paths;
that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu. And so too the Smṛti:
"Brahmā is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than he who is higher than the highest;
and Hīśa is indeed higher than he who is higher than the highest," according to the injunction of the Vedānta.
He who meditates day and night upon Śiva, the Supreme Self, the Lord of Umā, the Creator of the Universe, who is free from both merit and demerit—
Having crossed the river named Virajā, one reaches the supreme state beyond the world of Viṣṇu,
which is endowed with eternal sovereignty and is beyond the reach of mind and speech.
He indeed attains Kailāsa through the power of Śiva’s grace.

From this observation, it follows as firmly as a diamond coating that for those solely devoted to Śiva, the attainment of the world of Śiva and the attainment of the state of Śiva-ness occur after the prior elimination of both merit and demerit.
Now, one might object: if the destruction of all karma is accepted either at the time of separation from the body or immediately after crossing the Virajā river—

There would follow the consequence of the destruction of the subtle body; and that being the case, the departure of the isolated Self (ātman) alone would not be possible. Therefore, in response to the doubt that the complete exhaustion of all karma for the knower at the time of departure is not tenable, [the Sūtra] says: "210.
It is tenable, because its characteristic object is perceived, as in the world. (3.1.30)

The destruction of all karma occurs precisely at the time of departure [from the body]. Why? Because the object characterized by that [liberated state] is perceived: for even one whose karma is exhausted, there is the perception of an object characterized by connection to a body when his true nature has become manifest. "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own form; there he moves about, eating, playing, and rejoicing."

"He becomes his own ruler; for him, there is freedom of movement in all worlds. In such passages as "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold," etc., the meaning known as connection with a body is indeed perceived. Therefore, even for one whose karma is exhausted, travel by the path of the gods (*devayāna*) is possible as long as he is still joined with the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). How so?

If it is argued that the subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) also persists upon the destruction of the karma that initiated it, we reply: it is by the power of knowledge (vidyā). For knowledge, although itself not a cause for the initiation of the subtle body, [destroys] the gross body—which is the means for the experience of natural pleasure and pain—and all karmas.

Even when [the subtle body] has been destroyed without remainder, He establishes this subtle body for the sake of granting the attainment of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, which is its own fruit, by means of the path of the gods (devayāna)— just as in the world,

when a tank or similar structure has been begun for the purpose of increasing crops and so forth, even though the causes of that [construction], such as the intention for it, have perished, [the structure remains].
Those who perform tasks such as the construction of tanks and so forth drink water and perform other activities therein; it is established that it is just like that.

Now, it might be argued: although for the wise—those who have directly realized the supreme Śiva-reality—their karma is exhausted without remainder at the moment of the body's fall, and thus after the body falls, only the subtle body persists for the sake of movement, nevertheless...

As for what was stated— that the experience of pleasure and pain does not exist— that is not tenable. Anticipating the objection that for those who have directly realized the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), there is seen a transition to another body after the fall of the current one, as well as the experience of pleasure and pain caused by events such as the birth of a son or the loss of one, Vasiṣṭha says:
The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their term of office. || 211 || 31 ||
We have not stated that for all knowers there is a destruction of good and evil deeds at the time of the fall of the body; rather,
it is said that for those knowers who attain the path beginning with light (arcirādi) immediately after the fall of the body,
there is the abandonment of good and evil deeds at the time of that bodily fall.

However, for those such as Vasiṣṭha who hold office (*ādhikārika*), there is no attainment of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-gati*) immediately after the fall of the body, because their commenced office has not yet been completed. For them, a specific office is attained through a specific karma; and since karma is exhausted only through experience, the karma that initiated that office for those holding office [persists].
He remains as long as his office lasts. Therefore, for them, there is no attainment of the path beginning with light immediately after the fall of the body.
This concludes the section on the lack of restriction (Aniyamādhikaraṇa). 13.
[This is] the bliss of the play of consciousness (cidvilāsa) attained by those who worship Paraśiva-Brahman in His embodied, non-material, divine form. Now,

in response to the doubt— namely, whether the attainment of Brahman belongs only to those who worship through the Upakośala-vidyā and others, or whether the attainment of Brahman is possible for all worshippers of Brahman whatsoever— the author speaks by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa).
There is no restriction for all [the means of knowledge]; there is no contradiction, as is established by both verbal testimony and inference.

Regarding those meditations on Upakośala and others in which the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi-gati*) is heard of in scripture: is the attainment of Brahman by that path restricted only to those established in those specific meditations, or does it apply to all [meditators], such as those in the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya* vidyās, and those mentioned in the passage,
"And these who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they worship truth as faith"?

Since there is no evidence for the claim that [the path belongs] only to those devoted to all other forms of Brahman-knowledge, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being thus established, it is replied: "There is no restriction. Because all those devoted to any form of worship must go by that very same path, there is no restriction that it belongs only to those devoted to that specific one. For, when it pertains to all, it is so established by both scripture (*śabda*) and inference (*anumāna*).
There is no contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti; otherwise, there would indeed be contradiction—this is the meaning.
As for the Śruti, it is stated in the Taittirīya, Chandogya, Vājasaneyi, Ātharvaṇaśikhā, and other Upaniṣads:
"He who is the bull among the Vedas, possessing all forms, who was born from the nectar of the Vedas—he is Indra."

"May [the Lord] protect me with wisdom; may I become a divine vessel for immortality. This is the *sarvaliṅga* [mantra] of Soma and Sūrya. "The hand-mantra is pure"—thus it is stated in the Taittirīyaka.

For those who are practitioners of the meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and other forms of worship directed toward the Śiva-liṅga—both external and internal—which is a limb of the Pāśupata knowledge, [this applies].
"Immortality is declared for those who know this thus, and for those who, in the forest, worship faith as the Truth;

they attain the light," so it is taught in the *Chāndogya* within the context of the Five-Fire Doctrine (*pañcāgni-vidyā*) that the soul proceeds to the city of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*). In the *Vājasaneyaka*, however, it is stated: "Those who know thus, and those who, in the forest, [worship] faith and austerity..."
"Thus they meditate upon the Real, the Real"— referring to those who know thus,

namely those established in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), and those who, as indicated by the passage beginning "And these," meditate upon Brahman preceded by faith— it is taught that their path is that which begins with light (*arcis*). "The *ṛta*, the truth, the supreme Brahman, the Truth."

"Knowledge is infinite Brahman; truth indeed is what must be sought to be known. Since the word "truth" (satya) is well-established as referring to the supreme Śiva-Brahman, and since the word "austerity" (tapas) has the same meaning as that [word "truth"], it is Brahman alone that is denoted by the two words "truth" and "austerity"—namely, the meditation upon Brahman preceded by faith, as heard elsewhere in scripture.

In the *Atharvaśikhā*, *Śvetāśvatara*, *Bṛhajjābāla*, and other [Upaniṣads], beginning with the passages: "Know [the Self] through the yoga of faith and devotion," "Truth indeed must be sought to be known," and "Faith indeed must be sought to be known"—this is the *Pāśupata* vow; one who desires liberation should practice it so as not to be born again, and so forth.
Furthermore, for those established in the Pāśupata knowledge, the attainment of the supreme Brahman, who is Śiva, from which there is no return, is taught. The Smṛti also states:
"Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice..."
"Those people who know Brahman go to Brahman when they depart from there"—
by this mark, O child, for those whose limbs are joined to the Linga, there is no rebirth;
there shall be the simultaneous attainment of knowledge, and from that, one attains liberation.

And from this observation, a rule is seen to apply to all practitioners of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), namely that they proceed solely by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*).

There are many such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) of a similar kind. Thus, this goal, which is common to all forms of knowledge, having been established, is subsequently restated in the Upakośala-vidyā and other instances.

Now, one might object: "Since liberation is attained by the sun, moon, and other planets, the asterisms such as Aśvinī, and the gods such as Indra and the guardians of the quarters, with this very body, it is not possible for human beings—unlike them—to attain the Śiva-principle preceded by the separation from the gross and subtle bodies. To this, we say: no.
The fifteen parts have reached their foundations; all the gods have entered into their respective deities.
Actions and the self consisting of consciousness become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].
Thus, based on the evidence of the Śruti, it is established that for devotees who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), as well as for the sun, moon, stars,

and other deities such as Indra, following the cessation of their respective offices and prior to the abandonment of the gross and subtle bodies, there occurs a state of unification with Paraśiva-Brahman.
This is designated as disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). [End of] the section on the Imperishable (*akṣaradhyadhikaraṇa*). 14.
The determination of the attainment of bodiless liberation (*videhakaivalya*) for those who have realized the partless Supreme Śiva-Brahman.

Now, [one might ask: for those who worship the embodied Brahman and are devoted to the *dahara* and other meditations, [is there not a state] characterized by a divine, auspicious, non-material form in the Great Kailāsa, which is endowed with all sovereignty?

May there be the experience of the bliss of the play of consciousness, the eternal auspicious majesty consisting of *sālokya* and the other [liberations]. In response to the doubt— arising from the Vedic text, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)," which indicates that Supreme Śiva-Brahman has two forms—
as to what is the destiny of those who worship the formless Brahman, he speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

But there is the inclusion of those [meditations] whose objects are syllables, on account of the commonality and the presence of that [quality], as in the case of the *aupasada*; this has been stated.

In the sūtra "There is no restriction for all," it is stated that all those who worship the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman. However, there is an exclusion— that is, an obstruction to going to the next world— for those possessing the cognition of the Imperishable (akṣaradhiyaḥ), namely those who have attained the direct realization of the partless Paraśiva-Brahman.
The non-existence of going to another world must indeed be accepted; why? Because of "generality" (sāmānya) and "the state of being that" (tadbhāva).

This means that because the destruction of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) is common to all who have realized the formless Brahman, and because of "the state of being that"—that is, due to identity with Brahman through becoming one with it. It is "like the Aupasadins": just as...
Just as all those who perform sacrificial rites such as the *aupasada* attain the heavenly world,

so too, according to the previously mentioned logic of the celestial mansion (*saudha*), there is an equality in the merging into Brahman— along with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)— of all those who possess the direct realization of Brahman in both its qualified (*mūrta*) and unqualified (*amūrta*) aspects.
Regarding this, he states the authoritative proof: "It has been said [in the scriptures]: 'His vital breaths do not depart; they are completely dissolved right there;

in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman], all become one,' and so forth. Thus, the subtle meaning indicated by the aphorism is that for those devotees who have attained direct realization of Paraśiva-Brahman, unity with Paraśiva-Brahman is established along with their subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
By this, the two systems—the dualism that holds the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) as primary and the qualified non-dualism (*viśiṣṭādvaita*)—are also refuted even for those who are liberated;
for, since identity between the insentient and the sentient is impossible, these systems establish the falsity of the individual soul (*jīva*) like a snake in a rope.

Furthermore, they are rejected according to the principal Vedic doctrine known as Non-dualism (*advaita*), which maintains the equal authority of all the Vedas, and thus [these systems] are like the Buddhist and other such views.
This is refuted by the authority of a portion of the Śruti. In the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is heard:

"It is bloodless, unctuous, shadowless, darkless, windless, spaceless, unattached, tasteless, odorless, eyeless, earless, speechless, mindless, lusterless, breathless, blissless, measureless, and without interior."

"It eats nothing that is external. Or, as it is said in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "Under the governance of this Imperishable (*akṣara*), O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. Likewise, in the *Atharva-veda*: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unindicatable, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; eternal and all-pervading."

"The wise perceive that which is all-pervading, extremely subtle, undecaying, and the source of beings; as a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as herbs arise from the earth, and as hair and body-hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe arise here from the Imperishable. Regarding this, there is a doubt: what are these?

Are the attributes such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth—which are heard in connection with Brahman designated by the word *akṣara* and which consist in its nature as the opposite of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—to be meditated upon in all meditations on Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), or only where they are actually heard? What is the correct view? That they apply only where they are heard. Why? Because they constitute the very nature of each specific meditation.

Since there is no evidence that the qualities (*guṇas*) constitute the very nature of other forms of knowledge (*vidyāntara*), and since these [qualities], being negative in form, cannot serve as a means for understanding the essential nature—unlike bliss (*ānanda*) and other such attributes—it follows that when Brahman’s nature is established as distinct from bliss and so forth, cosmic attributes such as grossness (*sthūlatva*) and the like are negated; for a negation without a substratum (*nirālambana-pratiṣedha*) is impossible. Thus...
We state [our position] regarding what has been attained:

by the passage beginning with "But there is the inclusion of the cognitions of the Imperishable" (BS 3.3.33), the meaning is that the cognitions of the qualities of the Imperishable Brahman—such as being "neither coarse nor fine" and so forth—are consistently applicable across all meditations on Brahman; therefore, [there is no contradiction]. Thus...
For devotees who possess the direct realization of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman as the Imperishable (akṣara), there would be no contradiction regarding their attainment of other worlds;

why? Because of the sameness and that state (tadbhāva). Since the Imperishable Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is the object of worship, is identical and one in all meditations, and because of that state—according to the principle that "destruction is dissolution into the cause"—[there is no such contradiction].
And because there exists the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the dissolution of the *liṅga-śarīra*.
For the apprehension of a thing occurs through its unique form;
and [the word "bliss"] does not present the unique form of Brahman, which consists of bliss and so forth, in its entirety.

Since bliss and other attributes also exist in the inner self (pratyagātman), bliss and so forth—which are the opposites of all that is to be abandoned (heya)—constitute the unique, defining form of Brahman. However, although the inner self is by its very nature devoid of anything to be abandoned, it still possesses the capacity for connection with what is to be abandoned. Furthermore, this state of being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned—

It possesses a form contrary to the grossness and other attributes belonging to the phenomenal world composed of consciousness and matter; therefore, by one who meditates upon Brahman through its unique characteristics,
Brahman must be meditated upon in the form of knowledge, bliss, and so forth, as qualified by non-grossness and other such attributes— thus [the text speaks] of non-grossness and the rest.
Since qualities such as bliss are included within the very realization of the nature of Brahman, Brahman should be meditated upon in that same manner in all Brahma-vidyās.
He provides an illustration for the principle that qualities must follow the principal subject: "as in the case of the Aupasadah."

For example, in the *Jāmadagnya-caturrātra* sacrifice, the *puroḍāśī-upasad*, though recited in the *Sāmaveda*, is employed with the low-voiced (*upāṃśu*) intonation characteristic of the *Yajurveda*, because it follows the primary mantra beginning with "Agnir vai hotram.

This has been stated in the first book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]: "In the case of a conflict between a subordinate and a primary element, the primary prevails, because the former exists for the sake of the latter."
It is said that there is a connection with the Vedas.

If one were to accept that Brahman, which is denoted by syllables and words, is exclusively devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) and without distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), there would be a contradiction with its worship. Furthermore, [it is stated] in passages such as: "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable is attained... and so forth.

Having established the partless nature of Brahman by first refuting its possession of color, limbs, ears, and so forth, the text concludes with the statement, "From the Imperishable, this universe arises. Since it is thereby determined that the Imperishable Person alone is the cause of both [the origin and dissolution] of the world— just as in the case of the *lūta* (spider)— it is understood even by children that He possesses distinctions and attributes (*saviśeṣatva* and *saguṇatva*).

In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad as well, starting with the passage "This indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī," the partlessness of that Imperishable Person is established after first negating all natural attributes; then, at its conclusion, it is stated:
"Under the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. Thus, it is of that very [Imperishable] that [the text speaks].
From the designation of attributes such as being the Ruler (*praśāsaka*), its possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) and its having distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) are established by implication.

Now, if this is so, since Brahman alone is the possessor of qualities in all Brahma-vidyās, and since qualities follow the principal [subject], then the entire collection of qualities— such as "possessing all works, all odors, and all tastes"— [would apply everywhere].
Fearing that even for one who is established in each specific realization there might be a lack of fixed determination, he says regarding that point:
"Because of the teaching to this extent" (Sūtra 3.3.34).

*Āmananam* means thinking toward [the object], that is, reflection. On account of this reflection, this entire collection of qualities is established as something to be integrated everywhere. This collection of qualities—characterized by such attributes as "not gross" and so forth, beginning with bliss—is indispensable; for without it, the contemplation of the nature of Brahman, distinguished from all else, would not be possible.

That very point is to be followed everywhere; and the meaning is that it is only this much. As for the others, however—such as "all forms" and so forth—they follow the primary [subject] but are established separately for each *vidyā* (meditative knowledge) because they are to be contemplated. Here, others [hold that] it is intended to establish [the conclusion] by way of negation through both the general rule and its specific application (*sāmānyatadbhāvābhyām*).

They connect [the sūtra] by stating that it is because the syllable is identical [to Brahman] and because of its recognition as non-different from Brahman; however, it is better to take it as having the stated meaning [of bliss]. For such an illustration is appropriate when subordinate elements follow the principal element, due to its conformity with the example. Furthermore, because it concerns attributes in the form of existence and non-existence, [the qualities] beginning with "bliss" (ānanda) are not [exhausted] by that [sūtra alone].
They say there is tautology; that is incorrect, because it is accepted that sentences such as "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*) have the purpose of excluding what is not that, and even in those cases,
no attribute in the form of an exclusion distinct from the essential nature itself is admitted, since the essential nature is already excluded from everything else.
Furthermore, there is no purpose in the cognition of the exclusion of specific things to be excluded for that which has already been understood through statements such as "the Truth" (*satya*).

For once a jewel has been separated from a heap of dust, there is no purpose in repeatedly separating it from each individual grain of dust. The two statements, "The two drinking the *ṛta*" and "Two birds," concern the difference or non-difference of the meditations (*vidyā*).

They state that the sūtra *iyadāmananāt* constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*). Having stated the difference between the two meditations— namely, that in one case both [the individual soul and the Self] are enjoyers,

while in the other case one is the enjoyer and the other is not an enjoyer— they argue that there is no contradiction by means of the "umbrella-bearer" analogy (*chatrinyāya*), and because the purpose of taking the individual soul as the material cause (*upādāna*) is to establish identity (*tādātmya*).

It has been stated that because there is no difference in form, there is oneness of knowledge; however, that is incorrect. This is because the unity of meaning has already been established through the "umbrella-bearer" analogy (*chatrinyāya*) and other such arguments in the Sūtra, *guhāṃ praviṣṭāvātmānau hi taddarśanāt* (1.2.11), and because the words of the Sūtra lack any unique application to that [specific case]. Furthermore, the word *iyat* is common to place, time, essential nature, and numerical quantity.

Furthermore, when it is intended— according to the Paiṅgi-śruti— that the statement "two birds" (dvā suparṇā) refers to the inner self accompanied by *sattva*, then it contradicts [the view] that it refers to the Supreme Self accompanied by the individual soul (*jīva*). Moreover, even if it were intended to refer to the Supreme Self accompanied by the individual soul, the fault of tautology has already been stated.
If it is argued that there is no tautology because this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of elaborating upon that [previous point], we say no;

for the subjects to be determined in other sections are not elaborated here, and thus there is no difference between this [sūtra] and them. Furthermore, the word *iyat* (so much) in the sūtra does not exclusively convey the exclusion of the number two. And therefore—

In passages such as "All this indeed is the Puruṣa" and "The Puruṣa is the Great Lord," why could the Sūtra not be intended to establish the identity of the knowledge [of Brahman], by means of delimiting the world-form? If it were merely stated that there is a delimitation of number,
then [it would refer to texts such as] "This Brahman is threefold" and "Brahman has four quarters."

Why should this not concern sentences referring to Brahman that are delimited by other numbers such as "one" and so forth? Furthermore, reasons for both difference and non-difference can be imagined everywhere; therefore, since the required meaning is established through some manner of interpretation, [the objection is invalid].
The Section on Interiority (Antaratvādhikaraṇa) || 15 ||

This determination that Paraśiva, who is Brahman alone, is the innermost object of worship is established because the state of being Brahman and the state of being denoted by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) are revealed in such Vedic texts as "This Self is Brahman," and in such Smṛti texts as "All perishable beings are the Perishable; the Immutable is called the Akṣara," with respect to the individual soul (jīva) itself.
In response to the doubt that for one's own knowledge, worship of oneself alone is appropriate, he states the following in another section:

"If it be argued that [the Self] is different [from the Lord] because of the internal plurality of the aggregate of elements, as in the case of the body, we say no, because it is like the instruction [of the scriptures]. (Sūtra 3.3.38)

How is it established that the Supreme Self, Śiva, resides within one's own self—the individual soul—specifically in the center of the heart-lotus? It is because of the statement regarding the "group of elements" (*bhūtagrāma*), meaning as in the passage concerning the group of elements. This is based on such scriptural texts as: "The One God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings. etc.
The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.

And since in such Smṛtis as these, the state of abiding within the hearts of all beings is predicated of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, it follows accordingly that both questions— "That which is Brahman, immediate and direct"— [refer to Him]; for,

by the principle of ultimate identity between the object of worship and the worshipper, there exists a relationship of part and whole between the individual self (jīvātman) and the Supreme Self (paramātman).
The Supreme Self is said to be the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all beings.

Now, one might object: "It is more appropriate for the individual soul (*jīva*) to reside within the heart of the individual soul; for in passages such as 'This Self is Brahman,' Brahman is taught as non-different from the individual soul. This is not so, because it is impossible for something to be its own inner ruler.

If that were so, it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that those scriptural and traditional texts which designate the Supreme Self as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all living beings— such as "The one God, hidden in all beings"— would lose their status as valid authority.
This applies even to statements concerning those such as Uṣasti and Kahola who possessed direct realization of Brahman.

The question was indeed posed by the sages for the benefit of the entire world. Thus, in response to the incidental objection that since the welfare of the whole world is accomplished by a single question alone, two questions are redundant, he says:

"Otherwise, without a difference in the object to be seen, a difference [in the result] would be untenable; a difference in questioning is observed in the world [only when there is such a difference]."

And if it is argued that, likewise in the present case, since both questions establish the state of difference and non-difference—namely, the difference between the individual soul (jīva) who is the worshiper and the seer, and Śiva who is the object of vision and the one to be worshipped, as well as the difference between the jīva and [Śiva]—then the two questions are redundant;
[the answer is: "The justification is like that of the instruction."

Just as when Śvetaketu asked nine times, "May the venerable sir explain this to me further," Uddālaka gave the answer "That thou art" nine times to Śvetaketu for the purpose of strengthening the established doctrine that consists of both difference and non-difference; so too here [in the case of Uṣasti]—
Because in mantras such as "Two birds... (dvā suparṇā), Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) are understood to be mutually distinct like a pot and a cloth;

and because in Vedic texts such as "This Self is Brahman" (ayam ātmā brahma), Brahman is designated as non-different from the individual soul; and because in the investigation of all Vedānta, there arises the suspicion of absolute mutual invalidity [of these two positions], it may be that both difference and non-difference exist between the object of worship and the worshipper.

Furthermore, because the knowledge of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)— which reconciles the dualistic and non-dualistic doctrines established by all the Vedānta scriptures— is difficult to comprehend through mere logic, it is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra that the multiplicity of questions and the multiplicity of answers serve a fruitful purpose for the sake of strengthening that knowledge.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, within the *Upastipraśna*, it is thus recorded: "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. The reply to this is: "That which breathes by means of the out-breath (*prāṇa*), that is your Self, which is within all; that which breathes down by means of the in-breath (*apāna*), that is your Self," and so forth. Being unsatisfied with this, he asked again, to which [the teacher] said: "No..."
"You may see the seer of seeing; you may hear the hearer of hearing; you may think the thinker of thought;
you may know the knower of knowing. This is your Self, which is within all; everything else is afflicted.
Likewise, immediately following that, in the question of Kahola, it is similarly recorded: "That which is Brahman, immediate and direct..."

"Explain to me that Self which is within all. And the reply is: "He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death"—thus, having known this Self, [one renounces] the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and so forth, ending with the words, "everything else is afflicted."

In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether there is a difference between these two branches of knowledge or not. What is the correct conclusion? That there is a difference. Why? Because of the difference in form (*rūpa*).
The form differs due to the difference in the answers. For even though the question is uniform in nature, the manner of the answer is perceived to be distinct.
In the former [passage], the agent of breath and so forth is described as the innermost Self of all; in the latter, [the Self] is described as being devoid of hunger, thirst, and the like.

Therefore, in the former, the inner Self (pratyagātman) is spoken of as distinct from breath, body, senses, mind, and vital force; in the latter, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is spoken of as distinct from those and devoid of hunger, thirst, and the like. Thus, the form [of the subject] differs, as does that which possesses the aggregate of elements.
It is also logical that this inner self possesses the quality of being "within all" by virtue of being the inner self of the entire aggregate of beings.

Although the inner self's status as being within all is required only in relation to the aggregate of beings, nevertheless, that alone must be accepted. Otherwise, if one were to accept the supreme self out of a desire to embrace the primary inner self, [the context would be lost].

A distinction in the replies is not tenable; for every reply refers to the inner self (pratyagātman), since the supreme self cannot possess such qualities as being the vitalizer or not being the vitalizer. Furthermore, [the other set of replies] refers to the supreme self, because it transcends hunger and so forth. This is what is being questioned: "As in the case of the group of beings within. Within.
Because He is the innermost of all, the first answer—just like [the case of] the aggregate of beings—is with respect to one's own self;

that is, one's own self, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is called "the innermost of all. Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency in the difference between the answers, such as "He who breathes by means of the vital breath" and "He who transcends hunger, thirst, and so forth. To this, the reply is: "No"—it is not so.
The meaning is that there is a difference in the knowledge [taught], because both the question and the answer have the Supreme as their object. To explain:
the question, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self which is within all," refers exclusively to the Supreme Self.
This is so even though the word *brahman*, while common to the Supreme Self, can also apply to the individual self (*pratyagātman*).

Sometimes, because figurative usage is observed, the qualification "that which is directly Brahman" (*sākṣād brahma*) is employed in order to exclude that [figurative sense] and to establish the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) consists in being connected with all bodies and all times. It is real (*satyam*).

The statement "Brahman is infinite knowledge" is appropriate only for the Supreme Self (paramātman), which is understood as being infinite. Its quality of being the innermost of all is also established in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "He who is in the fire, he who is in the waters, he who is in the plants—he is Rudra. Likewise, in the Atharvaśiras: "I alone existed first, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is no other."
"Someone distinct from me has entered into the innermost of the inner.

This statement, beginning with "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth," and continuing up to "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self," as found in the Kāṇva recension, can apply only to Paraśiva, the Supreme Lord who is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) of all.

The reply, likewise, refers to the Supreme Self. The statement, "He who breathes by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," indicates that the agency of breathing belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self, since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) lacks such agency regarding breathing during deep sleep. Thus, Uṣasti, not knowing this, spoke only of the agency of breathing, thinking [it referred to the individual self].
Considering that the answer regarding the inner self (*pratyagātman*) was too general,

the questioner, being dissatisfied, asks again. In response, [the teacher] speaks of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is distinct from the inner self by virtue of being free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) and is the agent of the act of breathing, using the passage beginning with, "You cannot see the seer of seeing."

Do not think that the inner self (pratyagātman) is described here as the agent of breathing on the grounds that it is the agent of seeing, hearing, thinking, and cognizing—which depend upon the sense organs; for during deep sleep, fainting, and so forth, it is not the agent of breathing and the like. For who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale, were there not this bliss in the ether?

Thus, the fact that the Supreme Self alone is the cause of the sustenance of all living beings is heard elsewhere in the Śruti; therefore, the answer to the preceding question concerns the Supreme Self. Likewise, the subsequent [passages] also concern Him, because the state of being beyond hunger and so forth is unique to the Supreme Self. Consequently, the concluding statement, "Other than this, everything is afflicted," is uniform in both cases.

The repetition of questions and answers, however, is for the purpose of establishing that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who is the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, is beyond hunger and other such needs. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like the instruction.
Just as in the Sadvidyā [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6], having begun with the instruction on the Existent (Sat) with the words, "Have you asked for that instruction?"—
"May the Blessed One indeed speak thus," and "May the Blessed One inform me further"—thus [the student requests]. Then follows the question:

"This subtle essence (aṇiman), this identity of all this, that is the Truth; that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. And there is a repeated recurrence of the answer for the sake of the disciple's realization of the specific greatness of that Being, Brahman.

And it is heard [in scripture] for the purpose of strengthening the realization of both duality and non-duality established by all the Vedāntas. Similarly, here, because of the identity of nature— established through the determination of the single Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who dwells within all beings, as being the cause of the life-breath of all living creatures and as transcending sleep and so forth— the unity of knowledge (vidyaikyam) follows.
Now, it might be argued that even though both the question and the answer concern Paraśiva-Brahman, a difference in the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) is nevertheless appropriate;
for in one case the object of meditation is presented as the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, while in the other it is presented as transcending hunger and so forth.
Thus, there is a difference in form due to the difference in meditative qualities and a difference in the questioner. For in the former instance, Uṣasti is the questioner, whereas in the latter...
Anticipating this objection, [the author] says regarding that point:
"There is an exchange [of attributes], for they distinguish [them], as in the other case. (Sūtra 3.3.36)

There is no difference in the knowledge taught here, because the two questions and their two answers are understood to form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva) through their common subject matter and through the presence of a single injunctive word. First, both questions have as their object the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, characterized as the innermost Self of all. In the second question, that which is "directly perceived and immediate" (sākṣād-aparokṣāt)...
The phrase "Brahman, which is the Self within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.1) establishes that Kahola’s question concerns Brahman as qualified by the attributes previously mentioned;
furthermore, the answer in both instances is identical: "That is your Self, which is within all."

The subject matter is of a single uniform nature, concerning the Supreme Śiva-Brahman as characterized by being the inner Self of all. Furthermore, an injunctive suffix is seen later on: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should remain in a state of childlike simplicity.
Thus, when it is determined that both [passages] have as their object the identity with the Supreme Śiva-Brahman as characterized by being the inner Self of all, [the conclusion follows].

When the single Supreme Śiva-Brahman, characterized as the innermost Self of all, is the object of meditation, there must be an exchange of cognitions between Uṣasti and Kahola. That cognition which Uṣasti possesses regarding the Supreme Brahman—the innermost Self of all—as being the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, must also be formed by Kahola, the questioner. And that [cognition] which belongs to Kahola...

Uṣasti must also cultivate that very cognition regarding Brahman’s transcendence of hunger and other such states. When this exchange has been made, both [Uṣasti and Ajātaśatru] come to understand the exclusion of the individual soul (jīva) from the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is the innermost of all. This is for the purpose of making known this innermost Self as distinct from the individual soul.

Indeed, Yājñavalkya’s replies distinguish [the object of meditation] by demonstrating that it is the cause of the life-force of all living beings and is beyond hunger and other such needs. Therefore, the quality to be meditated upon is precisely the state of being the inner self of all for Paraśiva-Brahman;
whereas being the cause of the life-force and so forth are merely its supporting attributes, not themselves the objects of meditation.

Now, if the quality to be meditated upon is indeed the state of being the inner self of all, then for what purpose is there this reciprocal meditation by the questioner regarding the cause of the vitalization of beings and the transcendence of hunger and so forth?

To this it is said: when Brahman, as the inner self of all, is distinguished from the individual soul (jīva) by its being the cause of the vitalization of all living beings, it is thus determined by Upasti.

Since Kahola had not yet conceived of the specific nature of the individual soul (jīva) as being the inner self of all— which distinguishes it from other souls— he asked his question again. Yājñavalkya,
recognizing his intention, explained that the inner self possesses the inconceivable quality of being the opposite of hunger and other such needs.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the cognition of the exclusion of the object of meditation, an exchange of cognitions between the two must be performed. This is just as in other cases; for instance, in the Sadvidyā, that very Brahman which is Being is delimited through repeated questions and answers, and not by means of a previously apprehended attribute.
In that case as well, since there is a difference between the question and the answer, how can their identity be understood? To this he says:
"For she [the Self] alone [is meant by] 'Truth' and so forth. (3.3.7)

For that very same [deity]—designated by the word "Sat" (Being), the supreme cause, the transcendent deity—is this very deity referred to in the passage, "That deity thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "In the supreme deity, fire was produced," as established in all the preceding sections such as, "As bees, my dear, produce honey from various trees... and so forth; for it is said: "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self."
The truths and other qualities mentioned in the first section are to be applied and concluded in all subsequent sections.

However, some describe the two sūtras— "There is an exchange, for they distinguish [them], as in the case of the others" and "For that very [meditation] consists of truth and so forth"— as constituting two separate topical discussions (adhikaraṇas).
Regarding this, it is said that in the passage, "O venerable deity, you indeed are I; O venerable deity, I indeed am you;

that which is I is that [Supreme], and that which is that is I," the mutual interpenetration (*vyatihāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*paramātman*) is established. Furthermore, they say: "All this is indeed Brahman; all this has that as its self; thou art That."

Since this statement has as its object the realization of the state of being the Self of all, there is nothing novel to be established here; thus, it should not be disregarded. That, however, will be explained [in the sūtra]: "But they approach [the teacher] as the Self, and they cause [others] to grasp it as such. Furthermore, there is nothing in the supreme Brahman beyond the contemplation of its being the Self of all.
The contemplation of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman within that soul are both possible as truths.

Furthermore, by the subsequent Sūtra, [the author] establishes the identity between that which is taught in the passage beginning with "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as the True Brahman"—referring to the meditation on Truth (*satyopāsana*)—and that which is [described as] "That which is the Truth is yonder Sun; he who is in this... in that [Sun].
It is also incorrect to claim that the identity of the meditation taught in the sentence beginning with "The person who is in this [mandala] and the one who is in the right eye" is being established;

for in the subsequent passage, the difference between the two meditations due to the distinction in their locations—the eye and the sun—has already been demonstrated. Alternatively, [it may be argued that they are not different].

Because this has already been established by the word "specifically" (viśeṣāt). Furthermore, there is no separate injunction for the conjunction of two meditations— as in "He who knows thus slays evil and casts it off," referring to these two which possess form through having the vyāhṛtis as their bodies—
such as [the injunction] "He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as the True Brahman conquers these worlds."

Because they possess conjunction, form, and other such qualities, identity with the preceding meditation—which is independent [of these]—is not possible. Furthermore, there is no evidence for the status of this as a separate section concerning the fruits of specific qualities (guṇaphalādhikāra), based on the statements "he destroys evil" or "he abandons it. If it is argued that the evidence for its being a single meditation (ekavidyātva) with the preceding one is the [textual] authority itself—no, because that would involve circular reasoning (itaretarāśrayatva). Only when the status of being a single meditation is established can the fruit of the preceding [meditation] [be extended].

Since the latter two fruits are subordinate fruits by virtue of the primary fruit being principal, and since it is certain that those two are subordinate fruits, there is no difference in their connection [to the meditation]; thus, because of the identity of the connection, there is oneness of the knowledge with the preceding one—this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
By such arguments, it is determined that these two Sūtras indeed follow the manner already described.
The section concerning desire and so forth. 16.

An argument for the fact that Paramaśiva alone is the abode of the Praṇava and so forth: Now, by such passages as "This entire [universe] is this syllable Om," the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad establishes that the Praṇava itself is the Imperishable (akṣara), is the self of all, and transcends all; likewise, in the Taittirīya, beginning with "The small, stainless [space]," the Dahara-vidyā is introduced.

Having elaborated [on this], by stating "the sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda," and so forth, the Praṇava is established as the object of worship; furthermore, in other passages, its supreme status is determined by such statements as "The single-syllabled Brahman is *oṃ*; *oṃ* is that Brahman; *oṃ* is that Vāyu," and because we observe the usage of "Hari, *oṃ*" at the commencement and conclusion of the Vedas and Vedāntas.
The fact that Nārāyaṇa alone is of the nature of the *praṇava* is established by implication;
therefore, it might be suspected that it is he alone who is appropriately the object of worship in all meditations (*vidyā*), such as the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya*.
In response to this doubt, [the author] speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Desire and so forth [are absent] elsewhere, and in that case [they are absent] from the sense-bases and so on. || 38 ||

In the Māṇḍūkya it is heard: "Om is the single-syllabled Brahman; its exposition follows. The past, the present, and the future—all this is indeed the syllable Om. And whatever else is beyond the three times, that too is indeed the syllable Om. For all this is Brahman; this Self is Brahman. This very Self has four quarters: [the first] is the waking state, whose sphere is the external, and who is conscious of the external."
The first quarter is Vaiśvānara, who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and is the consumer of gross objects.

The second quarter is Taijasa, who abides in the state of dream, is inwardly conscious, is the consumer of subtle objects, and is of the nature of light. The third quarter is Prājña, who abides in deep sleep, is unified, is a mass of pure consciousness, is indeed full of bliss, is the consumer of bliss, has the mind as his gateway, and is the knower.

The Foot: "He is the Lord of all, He is the All-knowing, He is the Inner Controller, He is the Source of all; for He is the origin and the dissolution of all beings. And in the Taittirīyaka, it is heard: "That sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda—Om, that is Brahman," and so forth.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: in the injunction concerning the syllable *oṃ*, is that which is to be meditated upon the syllable *oṃ* itself, or the Supreme Śiva who presides over it, or Nārāyaṇa whose essence is that [syllable]? What is the correct view? That there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*). Why?
Because of the difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*).

Having begun with "Om—this entire world is protected by this," and having established through such passages as "This very Self is Brahman; this Self... that the Praṇava itself is the Self of all and is the directly perceived Brahman;
and elsewhere [it is said]: "Om—the single-syllabled Brahman; Om—that is Brahman; Om—that is Vāyu; Om—that is the Self; Om—that is Truth; Om."
Because this is seen in the *Taittirīya* with the words "All that," etc., and because it is stated in the *Muṇḍaka*: "Oṃ! Brahma was the first among the gods to come into being;

the creator of the universe, the protector of the world, he taught the knowledge of Brahman—the foundation of all knowledge—to Atharvan, his eldest son"; and [furthermore], "Oṃ! Then, indeed, him... [the text continues].

Pippalāda Āṅgīrasa and Sanatkumāra said to Atharvaṇ: "Venerable sir, what meditation should one practice at the beginning? What is that meditation which consists of the four Vedas and austerity? Who is the meditator, and what is the object of meditation? To them, Atharvaṇ replied: "The syllable 'Om'—this is the one to be employed at the beginning."

"Meditation is that which is to be meditated upon"—this syllable is the Supreme Brahman; "its feet are four"—thus the syllable *akṣara* is the four-footed Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, because the *Atharvaṇaśikhā Upaniṣad* likewise teaches its status as the source of all, the practice of meditation and concentration on the *praṇava* in the form of *nāda* is [the means], as seen in the statement: "Hari, Om."
When it is argued that those seeking liberation must practice meditation on Viṣṇu as having the syllable Om (praṇava) as his essence, we reply:
"From desire, or otherwise," so [it is said].

In other cases—namely, in the Taittirīya and other texts—the identity of the meditations is established because the attributes of the Supreme Lord mentioned in the injunctions for the "small" (dahara) and other meditations are identical. Why? Because of the repetition of the same attributes and so forth.

The meaning is that the characteristics unique [to this teaching], such as the state of being the abode of the *praṇava*, the status of being the object of worship, the nature of being identical with the Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), and the location within the lotus of the heart, are common to all Vedic branches (*śākhā*). And thus it is said: "He who is of true desire and true resolve—he is to be sought after, he is to be known."
Thus, the qualities such as "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) and others, which are heard in each individual recension (*śākhā*), must be combined (*upasaṃhāra*) in all recensions.
In that very context, the *Māṇḍūkya* states: "It is neither inwardly cognitive, nor outwardly cognitive, nor cognitive of both; nor is it unconscious."
It is a mass of consciousness, neither conscious nor unconscious;
unseen, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indescribable, the essence of the oneness of the Self;

that is the Self which is to be known. This very Self is the syllable *Oṃ* with respect to the imperishable, and it is the measures (*mātrā*). The feet are the measures, and the measures are the feet.

The feet [of the syllable *oṃ*] are the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. Vaiśvānara, who dwells in the waking state, is the letter *oṃ*; he is the first *mātrā* (measure/syllabic unit), because of his pervasiveness (*āpti*) and because he is the beginning (*ādimattva*). He attains [all things] here.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.8.9; 3.12.1)
He who knows this becomes the beginning of all desires. The Taijasa, whose station is the dream state, is the letter *U*, the second measure;

because of its excellence (*utkarṣa*) and its being between both [the waking and deep sleep states]. For one who knows this, there arises here a continuous succession of knowledge, and he becomes equal [to the gods]; no one ignorant of Brahman is born in the family of him who knows this. The Prajna, whose station is deep sleep, is the letter *M*, the third measure.
"By knowing this, one measures (minoti) all this and becomes the measurer (miter); by knowing this, one also becomes the immeasurable (aṣīti).
The fourth is without measure, beyond worldly discourse, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, and non-dual.
Thus, by means of the self, one enters the self through the self—this is for one who knows thus. By this [passage], the identity with the *praṇava* is established.
Because of the specific designation of Śiva alone, and because all attributes such as being the self of all are established for him and not for another;

likewise, in the other [text], the Taittirīya, by the passage "The Lord of all sciences, Śiva," the nature of Śiva as the essence of the Praṇava is demonstrated. Having thus defined the Dahara-vidyā with the words, "That small, stainless [space] is to be meditated upon."

In this regard, when there is the inquiry "Who is he who dwells there?", [the answer is: "He who is proclaimed as the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas, who is the Supreme, that Maheśvara... and so forth.

Thus, [the Lord]—who is denoted by the term *Maheśvara*, who transcends the three forms whose nature is the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and who possesses the dark-and-tawny (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*) complexion—is the cause, and He alone is to be meditated upon, as stated in the conclusion of the *Atharvaṇaśikhā*: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are [His effects]; but He is the Cause, and He is to be meditated upon."

Śambhu, the Lord of all, is eternally present in the midst of space. By meditating for even a single moment upon that reality (tattva) and so forth, one obtains the fruit of seventy-four hundred sacrifices. One attains the goal of the syllable Om and the fruit of all knowledge, yoga, and wisdom. The syllable Om is the supreme Veda, the Lord, or Śiva alone—the one who brings about auspiciousness—who is to be meditated upon; having abandoned everything else.

By this much, having pointed out that Śiva alone is of the nature of the *praṇava*, the exclusion of meditation on anyone other than Śiva for those seeking liberation has been stated. As for the claim that Viṣṇu is of the nature of the *praṇava* in the passage "Hariḥ Oṃ," that is not so, because no direct scriptural authority (*pratyakṣika-śruti*) enjoining that is observed.

Furthermore, there is the demonstration of the identity and essential harmony (*sāmarasya*) between Śakti and Śiva, as well as Viṣṇu and Īśvara; for instance, the nature of Śiva as the *Puruṣa* is established in such Vedic texts as "Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa; we know him as Tatpuruṣa," and the nature of Viṣṇu as the *Prakṛti* is well-known from the *Kṛṣṇa-gītā*: "Vāsudeva is the supreme *Prakṛti*."

"You are Prakṛti, and Rudra is Puruṣa"—thus it is clearly taught in the *Īśvaragītā*. Furthermore, it is specified in the *Skanda*, *Liṅga*, *Kūrma*, and other Purāṇas: "Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff, the beloved of Viṣṇu; I meditate upon Kālabhairava, born from Śiva and Keśava."
At the time of her deployment, by the gracious favor of Śiva, Śiva’s power became fourfold:
Bhavānī among those who enjoy worldly existence, Viṣṇu among men, Kālī in anger, and Durgā in battle.

Thus it is shown even in the Sāma Veda branch. Therefore, in the expression "Hari Oṃ," [the text] designates that Śiva, whose essence is the syllable Oṃ, is qualified by the Māyā-śakti in the form of Hari. The state of *sāmarasya*—the identity with Śakti—is thus declared. Hence, in such scriptural passages as "Obeisance to Rudra, to Viṣṇu; protect me from death," and so forth...
In Smṛtis such as "To Śiva who has the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu who has the form of Śiva," and in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—"Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace;
within this is a small ether (ākāśa); that which is within that is what one should seek to understand"—and likewise in the Vājasaneyaka, he indeed...

"This is the Self that is not born of day (the eternal), which consists of consciousness, which rests within the space inside the heart among the vital breaths—the controller of all, the lord of all," and so forth; and in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:
"One should contemplate the lotus of the heart as stainless, pure, bright, and free from sorrow in its center."
Inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite awakening, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman.
To Him who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; the one, all-pervading Lord, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless and wondrous;
the Supreme Lord, the Master accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly serene.

By such statements, although a distinction is understood— namely, that qualities like "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) and so forth are attributes of the Self, while qualities like "having a blue throat" (nīlakaṇṭhatva) and so forth are attributes of the body— the unity of the injunctions remains due to the oneness of the object of meditation.
This applies to qualities such as "freedom from sin" (apahatapāpmatva) found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, and "mastery" (vaśitva) and so forth found in the Vājasaneyi Śākhā.
Furthermore, all attributes such as existence, consciousness, bliss, and liberation are understood to reside solely within Paraśiva-Brahman;

therefore, because the fruit is identical in its nature as the attainment of Paraśiva-Brahman— as seen in such scriptural passages as "Brahman is indeed fearlessness" and "Having reached the supreme light, he emerges in his own true form"— [the two paths lead to the same goal].
The identity of the knowledge is unavoidable.

Now, it might be argued: "What was stated regarding the Vājasaneyaka—that the existence of qualities such as 'having true desires' is understood along with qualities such as 'lordship'—is not tenable, because in that context, lordship and the other qualities alone [are intended] in the ultimate sense."

Because of the absence of true existence [in the world], and because of that absence, it is said: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is not even the slightest diversity here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. It is to be perceived as one alone—this immeasurable, eternal [Brahman].
By this preceding statement, and by the subsequent passage, "That indeed is this Self, which is 'not this, not this' (neti neti)," [the nature] of the Brahman to be meditated upon is established.

The realization of non-distinction (nirviśeṣatva) is understood. Therefore, qualities such as mastery (vaśitva) and so forth are also to be negated, just like grossness (sthūlatva) and minuteness (aṇutva); this is how they are perceived. For this very reason, even in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, qualities such as "having true desires" (satyakāmatva) are not stated to be the ultimate attributes of Brahman. Consequently, because these types of qualities are not ultimately real, they are omitted from meditations intended for the sake of liberation.
Anticipating this objection, he says therein: "There is no omission because of reverence. (39)
By virtue of being Brahman, these qualities—such as the power of true desire (*satyakāmatva*) and others—which are not established by any other means of knowledge, belong to Him;

for within Him indeed is the Self, described by such passages as: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, the Peaceful, the Auspicious, the Non-dual, the Three-eyed, the Blue-throated, the Tranquil," and so forth.

"Salutation to the golden-armed one, to the golden-hued one; salutation to the blue-necked one and to the white-throated one"—thus, in the *Taittirīya* [Upaniṣad], because attributes such as Śiva’s being the Supreme Brahman, His predominance of pure goodness (*sattva*), His status as the Lord of Umā, and His blue-throatedness are extensively taught in the Vedas and Vedāntas, there is no contradiction. Therefore, "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold and innate."

By the passage beginning with "the power of knowledge and action," its possession of uncreated powers (*alupta-śaktimatva*) due to its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) is stated. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, after describing the knowledge of Brahman as qualified by attributes such as having true desires— stating, "Those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires, for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds"— it continues:

Now, as for those who depart from here without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds; thus, this passage shows the importance of the knowledge of the one pervaded by the qualities (guṇa) as practiced by Atreya. Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka: "The controller of all, the lord of all, he is the lord of all. This...

From the repeated instruction regarding the sovereignty of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman—such as "He is the lord of beings" and "He is the protector of beings"—an esteem for His attributes (*guṇas*) is perceived. The same applies elsewhere. Furthermore, the Scripture, which is more affectionate than even a thousand parents, does not, like a deceiver, present as real those attributes that are actually unreal and merely to be rejected, nor does it teach what is not established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Having taught with great care, it is sufficient [only] to cause those seeking liberation—who were already wandering due to the rotation of the wheel of saṃsāra—to wander even further; for, by establishing that everything is to be viewed as one alone because everything is an effect of Brahman and thus has that as its essence, [the scripture declares]: "There is no diversity here at all."
By means of the state of being non-different from Brahman (*sābrahmakatvena*), it negates the perception of plurality previously established. This meaning has already been explained in detail.

Furthermore, in the passage "That indeed is this Self, which is 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*)," the word "this" (*iti*) refers to the form of the phenomenal world as apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By reflecting that Brahman is not of such a nature [as the world], the transcendence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman who has become the self of all.
"He who is the first among the gods, their source, Rudra the Great Seer, who transcends the universe..."
May He, who in the beginning brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha, endow us with auspicious wisdom.

Thus, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad it is said, "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," and in the Taittirīyaka, "superiority to the universe" is established as the unique defining characteristic of Śiva; and he demonstrates that very point immediately thereafter: "He is ungraspable, for he is not grasped;
indestructible, for he is not destroyed; unattached, for he does not cling; undistressed, for he is not distressed; he shall not perish."
Because it is of a different genus from that which is grasped by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is not grasped by another means of valid cognition.
Because it is of a different genus from that which is subject to disintegration, it does not disintegrate. This should be understood accordingly in what follows.
Also in the *Chāndogya*: "It does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his being slain. This is the true city of Brahman; in this..."

Having established that Brahman is entirely distinct from all other classes of things by stating "the desires are concentrated," the qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth are prescribed with respect to it.
Now, even in this case, [it is said]: "Those who depart from here after having discovered the Self and these true desires—if he..."

Since it is heard that one who possesses knowledge characterized by qualities such as "desiring the world of the fathers" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1) obtains worldly fruits, the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who desires Brahman should not meditate upon Brahman with attributes;
rather, the fruit of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) is precisely this: "Having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).
Anticipating the objection that attributes such as "having truth as one's desire" (satyakāmatva) and so forth need not be combined for one who seeks Brahman, he says in this regard:
"The distinction between liberation as identity (sāmarasya) and liberation as similarity of form (sārūpya);
therefore, [the former] applies when [the state] is present, because of the scriptural statement. (Sūtra 3.3.40)

*Upasthitiḥ*—the act of standing near; *brahmopasampattiḥ*, the attainment of Brahman. *Upasthite*—in the inner self (*pratyagātman*) which has attained Brahman, being liberated from all knowledge and manifested in its own true nature; for this very reason, namely because of that attainment, it is said that in liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*), there is identity with That, while in liberation through similarity of form (*sārūpya-mukti*), Śiva possesses the power to move at will in all worlds.

"Just as rivers [merge into the ocean], so too is this serene being (*samprasāda*); he is the Supreme Person (*uttama-puruṣa*). There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women or with kinsmen; not remembering this body, which is subject to rebirth, he becomes his own lord (*svarāj*), and for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. This will be explained more thoroughly in the fourth [chapter]. Therefore...

Since the fruit to be enjoyed by the liberated soul in all the liberations, beginning with *sālokya*, consists in the freedom to move at will through all worlds, qualities such as being free from desire (*ayakāmatva*) and so forth must be combined [in the meditation] for one seeking liberation; this is because of the observation of many scriptural passages such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," etc., while there are also scriptural texts such as "Partless, actionless, tranquil," etc.

The negation of attributes such as truth, knowledge, and bliss—which constitute His essential nature—is not being asserted; rather, it is established that He possesses a perfection of qualities characterized by a distinction from the natural attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, some maintain that the scriptures refer to the time of creation, while others maintain that they establish the state of maintenance.
Some describe it as the manifestation of majesty (*mahimā*), some as being intent on withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and others as being intent on the remainder (*pariśeṣa*).
The meaning of the term "remainder" (*pariśeṣa*) is as follows:
it refers to the period following the withdrawal of Brahman until the next creation.

Because it exists through the contraction of its own power (*svaśakti*), that state is called "residual" (*pariśeṣa*). Therefore, it should be understood that all the scriptures concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-śruti*) have as their purport that specific time [of dissolution]. For this very reason, in the Sūtra *lokavat tu līlākaivalyam*, it is stated that when the Supreme Brahman Śiva is intent on creation due to the abundance of His own power, He takes recourse in divine play (*līlā*).

Immediately following dissolution, until the next creation, His state of isolation (*kevalatva*) is taught as being due to the contraction of His power (*śakti-saṃkoca*) by His own will. Therefore, those who know the primary meaning of all the Vedāntas have established this distinction: that the *nirguṇa* (attributeless) scriptures concern the expansion of power, while those concerning the contraction of power pertain to the state of isolation.
It has been determined [as follows]: after the scripture beginning with "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire, the mind is the Anvāhāryapacana fire," etc.,

has taught the meditation on Vaiśvānara consisting of the Prāṇāgnihotra, it states, "Whatever food comes first when eaten, that is to be offered as an oblation," regarding the cooked food intended for eating.

If it is argued that because this teaching is merely an instruction on the ritual procedure for the *prāṇāgnihotra*, it is therefore impossible for that knowledge (*vidyā*) to be a means for attaining Paraśiva, we say no. For [the scripture states]: "The Person of the size of a thumb, who dwells in the thumb, is the Lord of the entire world, the Master; as the All-enjoyer, He gratifies [me]. I am food, I am food, I am food."

"O Annāda! You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter me as Rudra the Destroyer," and so forth. Since in such scriptural passages Śiva is designated here as the consumer of food by virtue of being delimited by the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), having thus described this attribute, [the text proceeds] regarding those men who perform the rites of the vital breath-liṅga delimited by the stomach according to the path prescribed by the injunctions.

The means for attaining Śiva is taught through a traditional succession; therefore, the identity of the knowledge (vidyā) is logical. This concludes the section concerning the lack of a rule for determining that [identity]. || 17 ||

The procedure for praying for the liberation of *sāyujya*, which is distinct from the three types of liberation characterized by fear, [is as follows]: Now, regarding the statement, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," the liberated one attains all desires together with the wise (*vipaścit*)—that is, the omniscient Brahman. The word "together" (*saha*) [indicates] the enjoyment of the bliss of Brahman.

And this refers to the intention of simultaneity. Therefore, it is determined that for the liberated, the fruit is indeed liberation characterized by similarity (sārūpya), as seen later in the text: "He attains union with Brahman and residence in the same world" (*brahmaṇaḥ sāyujyaṃ salokatām āpnoti*). Thus, the purport of all such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which establish the identity of Śiva and the individual soul, is this. Hence...
In response to the doubt that the attainment of partless Śiva-nature, preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), is not possible, he states this in another section:
"221. There is no rule regarding the determination of those [meditations], because they are seen as separate; their fruit is the absence of obstacles. (Sūtra 4.1.11)

**The Restriction of Determination.** The determination regarding that [liberation] is the fixed rule that for devotees who worship the *vidyās* such as the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya*, there is only the threefold liberation beginning with *sālokya*. Regarding the non-restriction of that [determination], an absence of such a restriction is observed in the *Śrutis*, *Smṛtis*, and so forth. Why? Because that is seen [in the texts].
The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations, and all the deities have merged into their respective deities;
the works and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable One.

The fruit of the direct perception (*dṛṣṭi*) which effects the attainment of the Śiva-tattva preceded by the dissolution of the *liṅga-śarīra*—as established in such scriptural passages as "and so forth"—is freedom from obstruction regarding liberation from the body. This consists in the absence of fear caused by obstruction, similar to the lack of fear resulting from a king's command; it is the state of being free from the fear of Śiva’s command, like the threefold liberation (*mukti*).

The fruit: Liberation as absolute isolation (*kaivalya*), characterized by unsurpassed bliss and consisting in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the individual soul's conditioned existence (*jīvabhāva*), is accomplished for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who are solely devoted to Śiva.
For those established in the three types of liberation, such as Reṇuka, Dāruka, Nandīśvara, Jaya, and Vijaya—

Furthermore, in the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas, it is sometimes stated that Śivaśarman and others attained birth in the mortal world for a specific purpose. In Vedic texts such as, "O Janaka, you have indeed attained fearlessness; you do not fear anything from any quarter," [it is taught] regarding those distinguished by supreme devotion and the excellence of knowledge.
The fearlessness of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) who desire the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) is proclaimed.

Therefore, the subtle meaning indicated by the aphorism is that only the liberation of union (*sāyujya-mukti*), which is distinct from the three types of liberation associated with fear, is to be prayed for toward Śiva. This is heard in the *Taittirīyaka* [Upaniṣad] beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and so forth. In that regard:

In the opening statement, "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," since Brahman is described as both the object of knowledge and the goal to be attained, while the individual soul (jīva) is described as the knower and the attainer, a doubt arises here as to whether there is a difference between the jīva and Brahman, or non-difference, or both difference and non-difference.
In the phrase, "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman," the word *saha* (together/with) does not tolerate non-difference; for indeed—

In the expression "Devadatta eats together with Yajñadatta," non-duality (*advaita*) is perceived. Nor should it be said that the meaning is "simultaneously with Brahman" in the sense of being of the same nature as Brahman; for the definition of *saha* as "simultaneous" is nowhere established in such works as the *Skānda* and *Laiṅga Purāṇas*.

If it is argued that this is because the attainment of the reality of Śiva—preceded by the cessation of the natural distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—is well-known, we say no;

for those statements are interpolations, and because [the texts] are accepted as authoritative by all disputants. Therefore, even in the passage, "Different from this self consisting of consciousness is another inner self consisting of bliss," duality alone is indicated. This which...

Since the Advaitins themselves have explained in such scriptural passages as "The person consisting of consciousness, the light within the vital breaths," that the one "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya) is the individual soul (jīva), and since the aphorism *ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt* establishes that the one "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is Brahman; furthermore,
there is a clear and ringing proclamation in such texts as "For having obtained this very essence (rasa), he becomes blissful."
The proponent of difference [objects]:
"For when he perceives even a slight difference in this [Brahman], then fear comes upon him"—here, however, the word *tu* (but/however) is for the purpose of embellishing the sentence.
For what indeed is more of an ornament to sweet things than their proper form?

Since indeclinables are seen to function as poetic ornaments even in such works as the *Itihāsas*— for instance, in the phrase "daram alpaṃ daharam" (slightly, little, small)— where the word *dahara* signifies "little": when this individual soul (*jīva*) creates even a slight interval or distinction (*antara*) regarding this Brahman—
that is, if it perceives even a minor difference or some slight distinction between the Supreme Self and the individual soul— then for him there is fear.
