It is shown that for one who always maintains the great distinction— that the Supreme Self is the master and the individual soul (jīva) is the servant— there is no fear.

Furthermore, even in the conclusion, "He attains this Self consisting of bliss," it is shown that Brahman and the individual soul stand in the relationship of the goal to be attained and the attainer.

The distinction is indicated by way of what is to be attained. By the words of the concluding portion of the Vedas, such as "Brahman is consciousness; having departed from this world in this conscious self, and having attained all desires in that heavenly world, he became immortal," it is also shown that "he enjoys all [desires]."

By such statements as these, difference alone is proclaimed. In the conclusion of the Sāmaveda, "That is Truth; That is the Self; That thou art, O Śvetaketu," difference alone is declared. Through the *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication), just as in the phrase "O minister, you are the king" the word "king" implies being dear to the king, so too in "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the word "That" (*tat*) implies being dear to Paramaśiva for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
Since it is precisely this [interpretation] that is logical—that [the Self] is indicated—distinction is clearly established even by the words of the Upanishads, such as "Two birds... (RV 1.164.20).
Now, one might object: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit" (RV 1.164.20). True; however, "the other, not eating, looks on" (RV 1.164.20).

"That which knows this truth by which one sees dreams—this embodied witness is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Indeed, for one who knows thus, no impurity whatsoever remains. By this statement from the Paiṅgi-rahasya Brāhmaṇa, the scripture teaches that the Self is distinct from the internal organ.

Furthermore, if one were to accept an ultimate difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and then also accept a non-difference corresponding to that [difference], then because such non-difference could never be established, it would follow that difference alone is the intended purport of all the Vedāntas. To this we reply:

based on the predominance of the scriptural texts concerning difference, such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), the scriptural texts that establish both difference and non-difference, such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), [are to be understood accordingly].

If, following the *jahallakṣaṇā* [type of secondary indication], one were to accept mere equality with That— similar to the logic of the "Lord and the Minister"— this would be untenable because the Śruti cannot tolerate such a strained meaning and because there is no evidence for deviating from the primary sense. For in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established through the abandonment of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), just as [the rivers become one] with the ocean.
Because it is clearly taught [as such], it is a portion of the Śruti; furthermore, if it were not primarily authoritative, it would follow that it is non-Vedic.

Since the opening statement, "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," teaches the attainment of Brahman by one who possesses knowledge of Brahman, the sentence "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman" refers to the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).

The devotee who, by means of the path of Śiva-yoga, knows Brahman— which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss— situated within the cave of the heart-lotus (*daharapuṇḍarīka*), that devotee [unites] with Brahman in the supreme ether (*parame vyoman*),
that is, in the space of consciousness delimited by that heart-lotus, together with Śiva, who is composed of the supreme light.

The certain meaning is this: until the dissolution of the appearance of *prārabdha* karma, one enjoys all desires right here; immediately thereafter, upon liberation while in the body (videhamukti), one becomes merged in that Supreme Śiva along with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Otherwise—as it is said: "Until I am liberated, then I shall attain [union]; his vital breaths do not depart, they are dissolved right there."
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here.
Thus, the contradiction with all the scriptures that establish liberation while in the body (videhamukti) is difficult to avoid.

As for the doctrine of Viśiṣṭādvaita, it has been refuted in many ways in such passages as "Because of the designation of being approached by the released" (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.2) and "And in this [state], it teaches his union with that" (1.1.7); therefore, it is treated briefly here. Consequently, there is unity of knowledge and no contradiction.
This concludes the section on the offering (Pradānādhikaraṇa). 18.

In the Supreme Śiva, who is Brahman, through the practice of total surrender preceded by the renunciation of the three-fold desires (*īṣaṇā-traya*), the statement "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" may have as its subject matter liberation through union (*sāyujya-mukti*); and the statement "He enjoys all desires together [with Him]" may either be an injunction for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) or have as its purport the threefold liberation. Nevertheless, for some...

Anticipating the objection as to for whom there is *sāyujya* (union) and for whom there is the threefold liberation beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world), he states another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) therein: "It is stated to be like the giving [of a gift]. (Sūtra 4.3.12)

"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality; they are all liberated"—thus it is heard in the Taittirīya Śākhā. The subject here is whether the fruit of attaining *sāyujya* with Śiva—which precedes the cessation of the state of being an individual soul (*jīvabhāva*)—belongs only to those practitioners of the knowledge of Brahman who are attached to desires, or rather to those who are free from desire.

In the Dahara-vidyā, in passages such as, "Those who depart from here having realized the Self and all these desires," there is a mention of desires even for those possessing knowledge of Brahman; because if desires were absent, there would be no purpose for the knowledge of Brahman,
and because even the enjoyment of this world is primarily governed by desire, whatever is the fruit of knowledge is also the fruit of action.

Since such scriptural passages as "The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings," and such Smṛti texts as "The intellect alone is the root of all fruits," establish that the intellect is the source of all results; and since no prosperity or ultimate good is seen for one who is indifferent, it follows that the fourfold liberation is possible only for those possessed of desire. To this, it is replied: "Just like the offering."
As it has been said:

"Pradāna" means giving or renunciation in an eminent sense; likewise, being distinguished by the body, senses, and so forth, one should—like one who has renounced identification with them—abandon the body, senses, and the like, as well as the threefold craving (iṣaṇā) consisting of wife and other such things which are subordinate to them.

By means of this [realization], which removes one's own ego-inflation, all this [universe] produced by Śiva should be offered to Śiva; then, through a state of non-manifestation and with the awareness of dependence, the experience of *prārabdha* residing in the body and senses must be endured. Thus it has been said: "Whatever one perceives with the eyes, one should contemplate that as the Self."
Whatever taste one eats with the tongue, one should contemplate that very thing as the Self.
Just as one perceives whatever is obtained by the nose as "that is the Self," so too the yogi should contemplate whatever he touches with his skin as "that is the Self."
Whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that as the Self;
having made one's vision consist of knowledge, one should perceive the world as consisting of Brahman.
Wherever there may be the cessation of the seer, the seeing, and the seen—
there alone the vision should be fixed, not in the gazing at the tip of the nose.
He who has a wife has the desire for enjoyment; for one devoid of a wife, where is the ground for enjoyment?
Having abandoned woman, the world is abandoned; having abandoned the world, one becomes happy. The mind is the eye for all objects; when that exists, the three worlds exist.
When that is destroyed, the world is destroyed; therefore, it must be treated with diligent effort. Having arisen from sleep, one should contemplate the single Brahman until the end of sleep.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down,
or even otherwise, the wise great sage, delighting in his own self, may dwell according to his own will.
The ascetic should always meditate with perfect stillness upon the luminous liṅga between the eyebrows,
directly perceiving the Self by means of the self through the realization that it is Brahman.
One should cast off all connections with the body, caste, and so forth, as well as those associated with the social classes and stages of life,
and even the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas, like the dust upon one's feet.
One should remain alone and free from desire, for one should not converse with anyone;
since liberation is sought for this mind when it is devoid of sense-objects.
Therefore, those seeking liberation should always make the mind free from objects;
for the mind itself is indeed saṃsāra, so one should purify it with effort.
"Having brought the visible into the state of the invisible, one should contemplate it in the form of Brahman"—
by such scriptural passages as these, [one should offer] the body, the senses, and everything else to Śiva, the Supreme Self.
Having given it with a mind free from pride, his sole thought being that [gift] as a favor.
A practitioner of Śiva-yoga may enjoy all sense objects;
having renounced all dharmas, take refuge in me alone.
I shall liberate you from all evils; do not grieve.
One should abandon both dharma and adharma, remaining equanimous toward praise and blame.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.

And by such Smṛti passages as these, [the state of being a Sannyāsin] is characterized by the renunciation of the three kinds of desire, preceded by the removal of the false identification with the body, senses, and so forth—furthermore:
"Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else, [liberation is attained] neither by ritual action nor by progeny."

In this context, having taught meditation on Śiva by stating that "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon" because the three types of desire act as obstacles due to being intent on meditation on Śiva alone, the injunction is then taught: "renounce everything other than that, such as wealth, grain, sons, houses, gardens, and so forth."

Regarding the characteristics of one qualified by wisdom, the word "action" (*karman*) in the phrase "not by action" refers to rites such as the *agnihotra*. By the rejection of that, the abandonment of one's wife is taught. In the phrase "not by progeny," the delusion of attachment to offspring is dispelled. [And] "not by wealth..."

By this, the delusion regarding wealth is dispelled. Through this, the intended meaning of the desire for wives, the desire for sons, and the desire for worlds is determined. Thus, having cast off the threefold desire through a single renunciation—the abandonment of the delusion of "mineness" (mamatva) toward the body, senses, and all else—the devotees attained immortality, which is union with Śiva.

The meaning is that they attain [this]. In response to the doubt that by this instruction they might instead attain the delusion of "I" and "mine," [the text states] that by means of the supreme knowledge of Śiva, one attains this—[namely] the *nāka*, which is the nature of supreme bliss, shining and self-luminous within the cave of the small lotus (*dahara-puṇḍarīka*). It is situated there.
The meaning is that ascetics (*yatis*), who are habituated to the effort of attaining the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), attain that auspicious state.

Having thus stated the characteristics of the wise practitioner (*prājña-adhikārin*), he likewise states the characteristics of the practitioner of duller intellect (*mandaprajña-adhikārin*): [He] says: [the following].

Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta— being established in the knowledge of the meaning of the three principles (pāśa, paśu, and pati) by means of the sixfold marks of the purport of all the Vedāntas as prescribed by such scriptural injunctions as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon"— and having attained the state of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-yoga*), where *saṃnyāsa* is complete renunciation...

Renunciation, by means of the yoga that consists of the uninterrupted flow of the mind— like a stream of oil— through the practice of the Dahara-aksha-Purusha-vidya, and through the yoga of union with Shiva alone as its sole object of focus; by such practice, those ascetics who are intent on liberation, whose sattva is purified,
and whose inner organs are stainless and free from the three impurities of passion, hatred, and delusion— they, the devotees, [attain] the world of Brahma.
Having remained in the world of Śiva, which is another synonym for Brahman, and having experienced the possession of all sovereign powers there according to their own desire,
then at the time of their final end— upon the exhaustion of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of that world of Śiva— all are liberated from the supreme nectar of Kailāsa.
The meaning is that, casting off the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), they attain union (sāyujya) with the perfect Supreme Śiva right there.

Likewise, it is heard elsewhere in the Dahara-vidyā: "Those who depart from here having known the Self and all these desires"—thus, the attainment of all desires is shown for those who worship Paraśiva while still attached to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the world.
Therefore, for those who worship Śiva free from desire, the attainment of the Śiva-principle occurs right here. As for those devotees possessed of the latent impressions of the world...

It is determined that those who enter the world of Śiva through the latent impression of desire (kāmavāsanā) experience all desires therein and attain union with Śiva (śivasāyujya) from that very world. Therefore, although a distinction in fruits is taught for devotees with and without desire, the unity of the knowledge (vidyaikyam) is taught because the final fruit of union is one and the same.
By the straight and not the crooked path, all sciences have as their ultimate goal the attainment of Brahman.

Now, [one might object that] meditations based on ritual action, such as "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," are perceived as being subordinate members of ritual action. Furthermore, as in the case of the passage: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood..."

Through the medium of the *udgītha* and other elements that constitute parts of the ritual action, or through the medium of the *juhū* ladle and so forth—just like the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood—the connection with the meditation on the *udgītha* and others is indicated by their established practice as constituent parts of those respective rites. Likewise, from such passages as "He who, knowing thus, sings the *udgītha*" and "He who, knowing thus, sings the *sāman*," it is understood that the meditation upon them is connected to the sacrifice (*kratu*). Therefore...

"Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful. By this statement in the present tense, just as in the case of hearing the verse regarding the absence of evil for one who uses *parṇa*-wood [for the ladle], it is impossible to conceive of a separate fruit; therefore, these [elements] must necessarily be employed within the sacrifices. This is because they are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of ritual action.

If it is argued that the contradiction with such scriptural passages as "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim" is unavoidable because [the knowledge of Brahman] has been established as not being a constituent part (*aṅga*) for the attainment of Brahman, it is replied: No,
because of the statement regarding the performance of rites even by one who does not know, namely, "Therefore, both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know."

Since meditation (*upāsana*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*), the lack of a fixed rule regarding its performance is logically established. Thus, when it is determined that meditation is an auxiliary, and the injunction for meditation has a desire for a fruit, it is understood—according to the *Rātrisatra* principle—that "greater vigor" (*vīryavattaratva*) is indeed a fruit distinct from the fruit of ritual action. What is this "greater vigor"?
It is precisely the non-obstruction of the fruit of action that is meant; for the fruit of one action is indeed obstructed by the fruit of another powerful action.

"Obstruction" refers to the absence of that [original] fruit for such a period of time. This is stated as a fruit distinct from the fruit characterized by heaven and so forth. And for one who has offered the fruit to the Supreme Lord, [this occurs] by way of the purification of the mind.
It is understood that liberation is the sole fruit [of action], because of the Śruti which states: "Whatever is the fruit of knowledge, that indeed is the fruit of action.

Therefore, for one whose internal organ is purified, who is freed from the latent impressions of desire, and who is solely devoted to Śiva, ritual actions lead to the attainment of Śiva by means of Śiva’s grace.

It is determined that for those who have performed actions dedicated to the Supreme Lord with a purified internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), these lead to the attainment of Brahman through a gradual process by means of the cessation of evil (*durita*). Therefore, there is no contradiction in all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*)— whether by the straight or the winding path—
leading to the attainment of Brahman.
The Section on the Abundance of Indicative Marks (Liṅgabhūyastvādhikaraṇa) || 19 ||
The demonstration that Paraśiva-Brahman, who is characterized by the abundance of the attributes of the *liṅga*, is the object of worship for all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since all meditations (*upāsanā*) are understood to be mutually distinct—like a jar and a cloth—and since different fruits are taught for them, how can their coordination (*samanvaya*) in the Supreme Brahman be justified? In response to this doubt, he speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
On account of the abundance of indicatory marks, that [scriptural statement] is indeed more powerful; and that too [is so]. || 43 ||

In the Taittirīya it is heard: "Obeisance to the Lord of the Nidhana; obeisance to the one near the Lord of the Nidhana; obeisance to the Upright One; obeisance to the one whose linga is upright; obeisance to the Golden One; obeisance to the one whose linga is golden; obeisance to the Celestial One; obeisance to the one whose linga is celestial;
obeisance to Bhava; obeisance to the one whose linga is Bhava; obeisance to Śarva."
Salutation to the universal linga; salutation to the blazing one; salutation to the blazing linga; salutation to the Self; salutation to the linga of the Self;

salutation to the supreme; salutation to the supreme linga. With the mantra beginning "This linga of Soma and Surya he establishes, the purifier of the hand," and so forth, [the text] establishes that the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, is of the nature of the linga.
The fact that the Great Liṅga is the self of all has also been taught. In that very same place, immediately following the Dahara-vidyā, it is said:
"The thousand-headed God, whose eyes are the universe, who is the source of bliss for the universe—the God Nārāyaṇa, the universe itself, the imperishable, the supreme state."

Beginning with these words and ending with "He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling," since the teaching that Keśava, like Śiva, is the Supreme Self is found here, there arises the question: if one accepts the supremacy of both Śiva and Keśava, would it not result in the collapse of the established order? Therefore, it must be determined whether Śiva alone is the object of worship in all meditations such as the *dahara-vidyā*, or whether it is someone other than him.
A doubt arises:
Is it appropriate that Nārāyaṇa alone is the object of worship in all the meditations (vidyās) beginning with the "small" (dahara), because he is the subject of that context?
And in this very section [of the text], it is stated: "The heart resembles the interior of a lotus bud, and it is downward-facing," and so forth.
This confirms that the Nārāyaṇānuvāka, which refers to the heart-lotus, serves to determine the object of meditation in the Dahara-vidyā.
Furthermore—
Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge, the self of the universe, the supreme refuge;
Nārāyaṇa is the highest light, the Self, Nārāyaṇa is supreme.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the highest reality. Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditator; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme meditation.
Whatever exists in this entire world, whether it is seen or even heard,
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all of that, both within and without.

In such passages, Nārāyaṇa alone is the subject of all scriptural texts— those concerning his being the self of all, his omnipresence, his illumination of all, and his being neither gross nor subtle; therefore, since it is established that Nārāyaṇa alone, who is superior to everything, is the one to be meditated upon in all vidyās, we reply as follows:
Nārāyaṇa is the great object of knowledge, the self of the universe, the supreme refuge;
Nārāyaṇa is the highest light, the Self, and the supreme.

By such statements as these, although the attributes unique to Paramaśiva— such as "You are That" (*tattvam asi*) and so forth— are established in Nārāyaṇa through the non-difference of power and the possessor of power, of the object of worship and the worshipper, and of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa; nevertheless,

because of the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga-bhūyastva*), [the text concludes] with "Salutation to the Upward One" (*ūrdhvāya namaḥ*) and "Salutation to the Upward Liṅga" (*ūrdhvaliṅgāya namaḥ*).

Because of the abundance of attributes belonging to the supreme Śivaliṅga mentioned in such passages, this [interpretation] is more powerful. Therefore, the established conclusion (rāddhānta) is that Śiva alone is the object of worship there—in all the Dahara and other vidyās expounded elsewhere.
This is demonstrated in the section on "Instruction Established Everywhere" (Sarvatraprasiddhopadeśādhikaraṇa) by means of the sixfold marks of purport (tātparya-liṅga).
Since the purport of this Nārāyaṇānuvāka has been clearly taught, it is stated here in brief: through such passages as "All is indeed Rudra;

Puruṣa is indeed Rudra; to Kadrudra, the wise, the most bountiful, the most powerful, we speak for a peaceful heart—for he is indeed all this, Rudra"—it follows that, by virtue of being the supreme Śiva-liṅga, he is the object of worship for all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*).
This is appropriate for that very [text].

For example, in the sentence "All is indeed Rudra," and in the sentence "Puruṣa is indeed Rudra," there is the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the object of meditation in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; therefore, one should meditate with a peaceful mind."

In the phrase "sanmaho namo namaḥ," "sat" is the characteristic mark of the object of worship in the Puruṣasūkta and the Upakośala-vidyā; "mahaḥ" is the characteristic mark of the object of worship in the Sad-vidyā (Chāndogya 6.2.1), as indicated by "That, my dear, was Being"; and "mahat" is the characteristic mark of the object of worship in the Mahad-vidyā (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.22), as indicated by "That is Brahman, that is the Self, and the other deities are its limbs. Furthermore, the phrase "śāntam agne hṛdi" indicates the heart.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the object of meditation in the Dahara-vidyā is shown by the passage beginning with "Obeisance to the golden-armed one, the golden-hued one," which demonstrates his golden nature; the indicative mark of the object of meditation in the Savitṛ-maṇḍala-vidyā is "to Him, the Lord of Umā"; and the indicative mark of the object of meditation in all vidyās is that he is called "Rudra" because he causes the dissolution (*drāvaka*) of saṃsāra—it is Śiva, the Supreme Self alone.

The fact that Umāpati, the Supreme Brahman Parashiva, is the object of worship through supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*) is understood from scriptural passages (*vākya*). Moreover, this indicative mark (*liṅga*) is indeed stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), for it is observed according to the principles of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā that among *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, and *samākhyā*, *vākya* is more powerful than *prakaraṇa*. Thus, [the Lord] accompanied by Umā...
It is determined that the Supreme Brahman, named Śiva, who dissolves the suffering of saṃsāra and is the object of worship for all branches of knowledge, is [the cause].
This concludes the section concerning the previous alternative views (Pūrvavikalpādhikaraṇa). 20.
The demonstration that the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya* is attainable at one and the same time by those who worship Paraśiva:

Now, as for those among the worshippers of the manifest and unmanifest forms of the Supreme Brahman-Paraśiva who were previously mentioned— those endowed with the fortune of dispassion through such [scriptural passages] as "not by action, nor by progeny," and who are possessed of a world-weariness free from desire for other worlds— [it is established that they attain all four liberations simultaneously].

In this very body, the attainment of the state of Śiva occurs; however, since gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) has been taught for those of dull intellect who are different from them, there arises the doubt that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) might be subject to optionality (*vikalpatva*), which would result in the subversion of its greatness.
To address the doubt that it might therefore be appropriate for all worshippers to have a single goal, the author introduces another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The previous alternative [of the opponent] may apply here due to the context, as in the case of ritual action and mental [action]. || 44 ||

Just as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is of two kinds— the ritual Jyotiṣṭoma and the mental Jyotiṣṭoma— so too, by virtue of the context, there is a prior alternative within the context of those with passion and those free from passion;

this prior alternative is the conceptualization for those possessed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the worlds and non-worlds, which indicates the meaning of gradual liberation as pointed out by the Sūtra.

It is heard in the Taittirīya: "Who? What? That Truth, Food, the Immortal, the Living One, the All—what is the Self-existent? This is Brahman, this is the Immortal, this is the Puruṣa; he is the Lord of beings. He attains union with Brahman, the same world as Brahman; he attains union with these very deities, the same form as them, and the same world as them."

By such statements as these, a doubt arises as to whether all those who worship the Supreme Lord attain the states of *sālokya* and so forth at one and the same time through the majesty of that worship, or rather at different times according to the gradations of their respective qualifications;
[the answer is: by the power of the worship of the Supreme Lord, they attain all the states such as *sālokya* simultaneously, just like the gods and others.
He wanders everywhere, laughing, playing, and rejoicing;
for him, there is freedom to move at will in all worlds.

Since another Vedic text declares that liberated souls possess the power to move according to their will—stating, "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman"—and since this also shows that the wise attain the fulfillment of all desires together with Brahman, it follows that the attainment of all states, such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and others, occurs for the wise simultaneously. To this, we reply: "The former alternative would hold, on account of the context."
"Like the ritual and the mental [sacrifice].

This refers to the sacrifices consisting of ritual action— such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, Vājasaneya, Pauṇḍarīka, and Atirātra— as indicated by scriptural injunctions such as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "One desiring prosperity should immolate a white animal dedicated to Vāyu," and so forth.

The fruits are now specified: for that sacrifice of one who knows thus, the self is the sacrificer, faith is the wife, the body is the fuel, the chest is the altar, the hair is the sacrificial grass, the head is the tuft, the heart is the sacrificial post, desire is the clarified butter,
anger is the victim, austerity is the fire, self-control is the pacifier, the sacrificial fee is speech, the Hotṛ priest is the out-breath, and the Udgātṛ priest is the in-breath.

The eye is the Adhvaryu, the mind is the Brahman, and the ear is Agni; heaven is that which is upheld, and that is the consecration (dīkṣā). What he eats is the sacrificial oblation (havis); what he drinks is his drinking of Soma; what he enjoys is the Upasad rites;
what he moves about, sits down, and stands up is the Pravargya ceremony. His mouth is the Āhavanīya fire; whatever offerings he makes are the oblations.

That which is his consciousness, that he offers as the oblation; that which is the morning and evening [libations], those are the fuel-sticks; that which is the morning, evening, and midday [sessions], those are the Soma-pressings; day and night are the New and Full Moon sacrifices;

the half-months and months are the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; the seasons are the animal sacrifices; the years are the multi-day sacrifices (Ahargaṇas), or else they are the gift of all one's possessions (Sarvavedasa).
Death is the sacrificial session (*satra*), and that [death] is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). This *Agnihotra* sacrifice, which lasts until old age or death, is indeed such a session.
He who, knowing this, dies during the northern course of the sun, having attained the greatness of the gods, dies when the sun is in its southern course;
he, having attained the greatness of the ancestors, goes to union with the moon. These two indeed...
"A learned Brāhmaṇa invokes the greatness of the sun and the moon; therefore, he attains the greatness of Brahman.

In that same work, in another section: "Intelligence is the sacrificial ladle, thought is the clarified butter, speech is the altar, what has been studied is the sacred grass, and consciousness is the..."

In such scriptural passages as "The fire-altar is piled up with breath," "piled up with sight," "piled up with hearing," "piled up with action," and "piled up with fire," distinct fruits are declared according to the respective rites of the mental sacrifice. Similarly, the statement "not by action" indicates that the knowledge of Brahman, which is taught in the section concerning dispassion, is the cause of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*). This is the "prior alternative" (*pūrvavikalpa*).

The previous alternative was taught by way of the distinction between those of sharp intellect and those of dull intellect; for that is the context. However, from the context of the passage, "O Death, go along the other path, which is yours and different from the path of the gods," there would be a difference in the fruits for those who meditate upon the Supreme Lord, according to the distinction of their respective qualifications. Therefore...

It is determined that, just as it is impossible for lay devotees (*upāsaka*) residing in various lands to arrive at the divine abode simultaneously, so too it is impossible for those who worship Paraśiva to attain the fourfold liberation—beginning with *sālokya*—all at once.
Now, one might object: because humans possess limited knowledge and short lifespans, they lack the capacity for long-term meditation; therefore, how could [liberation] occur simultaneously?

There would not be a fourfold liberation. In response to the doubt that this [liberation] might occur simultaneously for deities such as Hiraṇyagarbha—given their divine bodies, their preeminent majesty, their long-term practice of meditation, and the firmness of their knowledge—the Sūtra says:
"And because of the extension [of the rule]. (4.3.45)

"Having encompassed the worlds, having encompassed all beings, having encompassed all the intermediate and cardinal directions, Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), by means of his own self, fully realized his own self"— thus, even for the four-faced Brahmā, [realization occurs] not through action,
but through the abandonment of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as indicated in such scriptural passages concerning the detached person.
Because the attainment of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman is extended [to all] and has been taught, it is established that even gods and humans possess distinct bodies.
Now, in the *Vājasaneyi-Agnirahasya-Brāhmaṇa*, it is stated: "The mind-made, the speech-made, the breath-made," and so forth.

Even if one were to demonstrate that this belongs to the section on sacrifices which are ancillary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there would still be an entry into the ritual sacrifice consisting of action— which was previously under discussion in passages such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent"— as a subordinate element of the fire-altar built with bricks. Consequently,
it is logical that those fires should stand in a relationship of option (*vikalpa*) with the fire-altar built of bricks, just as follows:

On the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which is the day called *avivākya*, it is appropriate that even those things whose nature is knowledge (*vidyā*) possess a ritual form (*kriyārūpatva*), by virtue of their entry into the ritual of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*). Furthermore, regarding the statement, "In each case, it is indeed as great as that former one," the power (*vīrya*) of the previously mentioned fire-altar built with bricks (*iṣṭakacita agni*) is extended (*atidiśyate*) to the altars consisting of breaths (*prāṇacita*) and so forth. Because they perform an identical function, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between them.

Then, in response to the doubt that—since the sacrifice is accomplished by piling bricks, the "mind-piled" (manaścita) and other such [piles] which are its constituent parts must enter into the rite consisting of action and thus have no result other than that [of the sacrifice]—the Sūtra says:
"But it is knowledge alone, because of the determination and because of the scriptural vision. (4.1.46)

The word "tu" (but) here has the sense of certainty. As for what was said—that the *manaścit* and so forth are indeed of the nature of ritual action (*kriyārūpa*) by way of entering into a sacrifice consisting of action—that is not so; these are indeed of the nature of knowledge (*vidyārūpa*). The meaning is that they are connected with a sacrifice whose form is knowledge.
Why? Because of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) and because of the observation (*darśana*). First, as for the selection: "Those two, verily, are built of knowledge alone; by knowledge... [and so on].

"Indeed, these very [sacrifices] become piled up for one who knows thus. Although it is established that the activities of speech, mind, sight, and so forth— unlike bricks and the like— cannot constitute a physical piling (*citi*), and that they take the form of knowledge (*vidyā*) by virtue of being an Agni mentally constructed, there is still the restrictive emphasis "only by the *viśvacit* through knowledge indeed do these [become piled up]," because of their connection with the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*).
It is determined that this is for the purpose of knowing the nature of the knowledge (*vidyā*). And here indeed is seen their principal element, the sacrifice (*kratu*) consisting of knowledge:

"By the mind alone they were studied; by the mind alone they were piled up; by the mind the cups were drawn in them; by the mind they chanted; by the mind they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed in the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—even all that was done in them by the mind alone."

Regarding the fires built of mind (*manaścit*), it is said that whatever sacrificial rite is performed upon the fire-altars built of bricks was performed as something consisting of mind (*manomaya*) upon those fires built of mind which are accomplished by the mind alone; from this statement, it follows that even the sacrifice (*kratu*) consists of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*).

Now, one might argue that since no injunctive word is heard here and no connection with a fruit is perceived, these [meditations] should be understood as having the nature of knowledge (vidyārūpatā) through their connection with a ritual consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya-kratu), rather than with the ritual consisting of action (kriyāmaya-kratu) established by the fire-altar built of bricks; to this he says "no":
And because of the superior strength of direct audition (śruti) and the other means of proof, there is no sublation [of the primary meaning]. || 47 ||

Since direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) are stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), the sacrifice understood through these [latter] and their connection thereto cannot be sublated by the weaker context. Direct statement is as follows: "These two, indeed, are built up of knowledge alone" (*te haite vidyācita eva*). He explains this: "For those who know thus, these two become built up by knowledge" (*vidyayā*). By knowledge...
The meaning is that the *manaścita* and other such altars become "built" (*citā*) when they are connected with a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*).
There is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the text: "Indeed, for one who knows thus, all beings always build these very [altars], even while he sleeps.

And there is a syntactical connection (*vākya*): "For one who knows thus, they build. A sentence (*vākya*) is a co-occurrence [of words]. "For one who knows thus" means for one possessed of the sacrifice consisting of knowledge.

The meaning is that all beings always pile [the fire-altar]. This piling, performed by all beings throughout all time and accomplished through the mind, constitutes an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for its inclusion in a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*); for it cannot possibly enter into a sacrificial rite—which has limited agents, times, and actions—by means of a ritual effect constructed with bricks.

Regarding the argument that because no injunctive suffix is heard and no connection with a fruit is perceived, a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya) other than the sacrifice consisting of action (kriyāmaya) is impossible—on this point he says:
"On account of the [mention of] subordinate elements and so forth, as in the case of the distinctness of other cognitions; and it is seen [in scripture]; that has been stated. (Sūtra 3.3.48)

This sacrifice consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya) is understood to be distinct from the sacrifice consisting of ritual action (kriyāmaya) involving the construction of brick altars, on account of the reasons for distinction such as the "connections" (anubandha) and others. The "connections" are the elements associated with the sacrifice, such as the cups (graha), hymns (stotra), and recitations (śastra); [for it is said]: "The cups were taken mentally; they praised mentally; they recited mentally."
These have been established by such passages as these. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the previously mentioned *śruti* and so forth are included. Regarding *śruti*:

"Like the distinctness of other cognitions" (*prajñāntarapṛthaktvavat*). Just as another cognition, such as the Dahara-vidyā and others, is understood through *śruti* and other means to be distinct from a ritual consisting of action (*kratu*), so too is this [the meditation on the Self]. And thus, by means of the "concomitants" (*anubandha*) and so forth...

When the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-yajña*) is understood as distinct [from the ritual sacrifice], an injunction (*vidhi*) is postulated. Furthermore, an injunction is observed to be postulated even in cases that have the form of restatements (*anuvāda*). As it has been said: "But the statements [are injunctive] because they convey what is not previously known" (*vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*). And there is a result [of this understanding], because of the extended application (*atideśa*): "Of each one of those, the power is as great as that of the former."

It is understood that whatever fruit belongs to the fire-altar built of bricks by way of its own sacrifice, that same fruit belongs to the mental fire-altars and others as well by way of their own sacrifices;
for even the mental piling of the fire-altar possesses independence.
Regarding the investigation into the means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman,

as for what was previously stated— that entry into the ritual action-based sacrifices (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) is understood because they are known through extended application (*atideśa*) to have the same effect—
it is replied:
Nor [is there a contradiction] because of perception even through generality, for there is no falling into the world, just as in the case of death. || 49 ||

It is not necessarily the case that because of an extension (atideśa), the intermediate operation must also be identical, such that these [meditations] would enter into the ritual consisting of action; for an extension is observed from some mere similarity or other. Indeed, it is observed: "This very death which is here in this... [and so forth].

In passages such as "the person in the maṇḍala," the extension [of attributes] is based merely on the commonality of being the agent of withdrawal and so forth. For in those cases, there is no falling into that world—as occurs for Mṛtyu with respect to the maṇḍala-person—nor even the attainment of that location. Likewise here, although the fires consisting of mind and so forth are extended as being like the fire built of bricks, they do not consist of the ritual action pertaining to the location of the brick-built fire.

Nor should it be considered as entering into [the sacrificial fire]. Therefore, by means of this extended application (*atideśa*), it is understood that whatever fruit belongs to the fire-altar built of bricks by way of its own sacrifice, that same fruit belongs to the mental fire-altars (*manaścita*) and so forth by way of their sacrifices consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*).
Now, if the mental piling of the fire-altar (*mānasāgnicayana*) were an independent means for attaining the world of Brahman...

The mental piling of the fire-altar (*mānasāgnicayana*), which constitutes an independent form of worship like the mental *Jyotiṣṭoma*, ought to be recited only in the Upaniṣads. Anticipating the objection that its placement in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) in proximity to the actual piling of the brick altar (*iṣṭakāgnicayana*) would otherwise be inconsistent, he says:
And the same nature applies to the subsequent sound; however, due to its greater frequency, it is perceived as a continuous connection.

Furthermore, from the subsequent Brāhmaṇa passage, it is understood that this word—designating the "mind-altar" (manaścit) and so forth—is of such a nature, possesses that character, and is intended to be established within the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya kratu*). For the subsequent Brāhmaṇa states: "This world is indeed this built fire-altar; its enclosing stones are the waters," and so on, concluding with, "He who knows this thus..."
"All this becomes such a Lokampṛṇā"; thus, knowledge itself, possessing distinct fruits, is enjoined. Therefore, the *Agnirahasya* does not have ritual action as its sole subject matter.
If that is so, then the mental fires (*manaścita*) and others consisting of knowledge must be connected with the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.

For what purpose are they connected here? To this it is replied: "But the connection is due to abundance. Because of the abundance of the components of the fire-altar (*agni*) to be constructed in the case of the mind-altars (*manaścita*) and so forth, their connection is made here in their proximity.
Therefore, for that very sacrifice described in such scriptural passages as "The self of this sacrifice is the sacrificer; faith is the wife," and so on—

The meaning is that just as the mental Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*), possesses an independent status as a means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman, so too it is logically established that the mental construction of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) likewise possesses an independent status as a means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman.
Section on the Single Self: 21.
The refutation of the suitability of the individual soul (*jīva*) for the meditation upon Brahman, [which is] like the ultimate distinction and non-distinction between them:
Now, regarding the prior state of the *jīva* and Brahman as the object of meditation and the meditator...

As for the claim that mutual ultimate difference is established through the power of the worship of Paraśiva, and likewise ultimate non-difference [is established], that is not so; for in such passages as "All this has that as its self," "All this is indeed the Self," and "This Self is Brahman," one does not perceive the existence of an Īśvara distinct from the individual soul (jīva), since one meditates upon oneself as being oneself.

In response to the doubt that—since the words of former teachers such as "Salutations, salutations unto me alone" establish only oneself and one's own worship as the object of devotion, that alone must be correct—the author refutes this by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
231. [The Lord is] One, because of the existence [of the Self] in the body. (Sūtra 51)

The Supreme Self, Śiva, is one with the individual soul (*jīva*) because He exists within the body as the space within the heart (*daharākāśa*), existing as the controller of the *jīva*; furthermore, since the scriptures—such as "established in the cave" and "the supreme beyond the half"—teach that Brahman is distinct from the *jīva*, it is improper for one to worship oneself as the *jīva*. This applies to all forms of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*).

Just as the nature of the object of worship is to be known, so too has the nature of the worshipper been taught as something to be known. For it is of these three alone that there is this presentation and inquiry: "Bṛgu Vāruṇi indeed approached his father Varuṇa, saying, 'Venerable sir, teach me Brahman. To him he said this: 'Food, breath, the eye, the ear, the mind, and speech. And so forth.

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], it is heard beginning with "He said: 'From whence indeed these beings... and continuing with "This very knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇa is established in the highest heaven," and so forth. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the Supreme Self is the object of meditation by virtue of being "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), or rather the individual soul (jīva).

Because the scriptures teach that the individual soul itself is Brahman— starting with "This Self is Brahman"— and because they show that there is no worship of a deity distinct from oneself in such passages as,

"He who worships another deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he goes from death to death, like a beast," and so forth, [it is established that] "I am Brahman, I am Brahman, I alone am I."

Since such understandings are found in these and other passages, it follows that the worship of one's own self alone is established by all the Vedānta texts; to this we reply: "The One, because of its existence in the body of the Self. Here, "the One" refers to the Supreme Self, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the master of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (kṣetrajña). Of the Self...

The meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from the living being consisting of the stationary and the moving, because of the existence of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) within the small lotus of the heart inside the body, as stated in such scriptural passages as, "In this world of good deeds, two who drink the fruit of their righteousness have entered the cave, in the highest upper realm," and so forth; for this is established throughout all the Vedāntas. Beginning with, "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa... [and continuing].

Because the attributes of Brahman are taught through both questions and answers, and because the blissful one (*ānandamaya*) is designated as distinct from the living self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), the difference between the living self and Brahman is unavoidable.
Furthermore, in the conclusion: "He who is this in the person and he who is that in the sun, these are one; he who knows thus..."

Beginning with "I am food, I am the eater of food, I eat; I have surpassed the entire world by my splendor, I am the golden light," and ending with "He who knows thus," [it continues]: "Rudra indeed is all; all this is truly Brahman;
the upward-seeded Virūpākṣa; salutations, salutations to the one of universal form; I am golden, I am the form of Śiva."
Salutations to the one with golden arms (*namo hiraṇyavāhave*), and so forth—[this refers to] the one whose nature as the Self of all is established by such scriptural passages.

He who dwells in cognition, of whom cognition is the body; who is stainless, partless, and pure Brahman within the supreme golden sheath; who is the light of lights—that very Self the knowers of the Self recognize. Indeed, the Self is to be seen.

"One should hear, reflect upon, and meditate [on Brahman]; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—since in all such Vidyās (knowledges) found in all the various branches of the Vedas, Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is taught as the object of worship, and the individual soul (jīva) as the worshipper, and because it is clearly taught that through being a worshipper of Brahman, one attains the nature of Brahman; [it follows that] food is Brahman.

Thus, as in the case of the meditation on the *upāsanā* [of the breath] and so forth, even in the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is consciousness as being identical with Brahman, this is taught for the purpose of designating the Supreme Lord as the innermost self of all, and for the purpose of indicating the successive stages of the path leading thereto; for if the mere individual soul were Brahman, [it would be as stated: "Under the sway of the Unruler, he grieves, deluded; but the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."
Because this would contradict numerous scriptural passages such as these, and because it would entail the collapse of the intended meaning of the introduction and conclusion of the *Bhṛguvallī*;

and because statements such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) are intended to indicate the fruit of the identity between the object of worship and the worshipper, just like "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

It is established that for one whose very nature is being scorched by the fire of the threefold suffering— the activity of entering and exiting numerous bodies bound within beginningless, impure saṃsāra— Brahman-hood cannot possibly exist inherently.
[This applies to] the meditation upon Paraśiva-Brahman, which is characterized by uninterrupted practice and single-minded devotion, and is to be performed by those seeking liberation.
The determination that all knowledge is intended [for liberation].
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 232 || "There is no exclusion [of the probans from the vipakṣa], because [the cognition] occurs when that [object] exists, unlike [the case of] perception. || 52 ||

Beginning with "One should meditate on the 'All' as established in space," and continuing until "One should meditate on that as Brahman; he becomes possessed of Brahman," the text teaches that for those who meditate on Brahman, the fruit consists in having Brahman as their self. Therefore, it is not the case that only the aspect of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth is to be contemplated. This is because [the Self] in its state of transmigratory existence...
Furthermore, the distinction (difference) between the state of liberation and the state of worldly existence is as follows:
in the state of worldly existence, there is the repeated entry and exit into various forms such as gods, animals, and humans, according to the fruits of one's own performed karma;
whereas in the state of liberation, there is the manifestation of auspicious glory consisting of an abundance of supreme bliss within the threefold liberation, such as *sālokya* and the others.

In the sovereign glory of liberation known as *sāyujya-mukti*, the fruit of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)— consisting of being transformed into the form of Paramaśiva through the absence of conceptual constructions such as "I" and "mine"— is indicated. Furthermore,
whatever the nature of this [liberated soul] is during the state of liberation, such is its nature [in that state].
The meaning is that the Self must be meditated upon at the time of worship. Why? Because one becomes imbued with its nature; that is, because one attains its form. As it is said:
"In whatever way a person's resolve (kratu) is in this world, so does he become after departing from here; for in whatever way they meditate upon Him, so indeed do they become.
For it is heard in scripture that attainment is exactly according to the mode of meditation. Nor is this [attainment] restricted solely to the supreme nature [of Brahman].

It can be stated that even the inner self (pratyagātman) [is distinct from Brahman], because of the teaching of its difference from the Supreme Brahman which is the object of worship. Therefore, another Śruti says: "The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations; all the gods have returned to their respective deities."
The actions and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

In such passages as these, because the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and so forth are designated as having the Supreme Lord as their goal, it is taught that seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) must constantly practice meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Just as in the case of "as in the perception" (*upalabdhivat*)—in the passage "just as rivers" (*yathā nadyaḥ*)—the teaching of the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is enjoined, like the perception of the river and the ocean. Therefore...

It should be understood that for those desiring liberation, the constant worship of the eternally incomparable Supreme Śiva-Brahman with undivided devotion is intended by all forms of knowledge. This concludes the section on the "Bonds of the Limbs" (Aṅgāvabaddhādhikaraṇa). 22.
The determination that all lay practitioners (upāsakas) are entitled to the practice of all branches of knowledge:

Now, just as in the injunction "one's own Veda should be studied," the study of one's own branch is mandatory for the acquisition of knowledge, so too in the case of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), it might be argued that only the meditation on the knowledge of Brahman prescribed in one's own branch [is required].
Anticipating the objection that [the rites] are primary, he states this in another section:
"But those connected with the limbs are not [restricted] to specific branches, for they belong to each Veda. (Sūtra 2.3.43)

In the preceding section, having established for all that the meditation on the Supreme Śiva-Brahman must be preceded by the rejection of the meditation on [the individual] Brahman as "I," the author now demonstrates here that meditation on the Brahman found in all Vedic branches is necessary for all seekers of liberation: "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha; one should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds."

"Indeed, all this is Brahman. Having taken the ashes with the mantra beginning "The Priyamedhas have praised from of old," and having applied it by rubbing it over the limbs with "O sons, praise Agni," one should touch the limbs.

Therefore, for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), one should perform the Pāśupata vow and draw three lines; so it is stated in the Chāndogya and other Upaniṣads.

Since it is heard in all the Vedic branches (*śākhā*) that the meditations on all forms of knowledge have liberation as their fruit, there arises the question: among all the meditations contained in every branch— such as the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya* vidyās— which serve as injunctions for the factors of liberation, is the meditation on the knowledge belonging to one's own branch primary for those seeking liberation, or is it the meditation on the knowledge belonging to all branches?
A doubt arises:

even though it has been established that there is a single cognition based on all Vedāntas, there is a suspicion that because the *udgītha* and other elements differ according to the specific accentuation (*svara*) in each Veda, they might remain restricted to their respective branches. Is this [suspicion] reasonable? Why should they remain restricted? Because of the injunction: "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*."

Since that [meditation] is heard in a general sense as being connected with the *udgītha*, it is logical that it should terminate in that specific variety of *udgītha* endowed with a particular tone, due to its proximity within that very same branch (*śākhā*).
Thus, when the prima facie view is reached that these [meditations] should be restricted to those very branches, we reply as follows.
"But those [mantras] bound to the limbs," it says.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. For meditations connected with constituent parts such as the *udgītha* do not remain restricted to those very branches alone;
rather, they should be connected to all branches within each Veda. The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason.

Since they are connected to the constituent parts of the *udgītha* and so forth by the scripture itself, therefore they should be connected everywhere wherever the *udgītha* and other such parts occur. Even though individual instances of the *udgītha* differ according to variations in accent, nevertheless, by virtue of the general term *udgītha*, all individual instances are brought into proximity; thus, there is no authority for any restrictive limitation in any particular case.

And according to the principle that "the sacrifice is one and the same across all recensions" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), the ritual act (*kratu*) is identical in all recensions. Therefore, since the single ritual is present in all recensions, its constituent parts—such as the *udgītha* and so forth—are also present; thus, there is no specific distinction of proximity for any one part, and consequently, no restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*). Therefore, all meditations (*upāsanā*) have competence (*adhikāra*) within all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*).
This is appropriate:
an exposition on the suitability of all practitioners of Brahman for the qualification to perform the meditations on the knowledge of Brahman found in all Vedic branches.

Now, an objection may be raised: since in the *dharmakāṇḍa* (the section on ritual duty) it is declared that all persons are bound by the necessity of performing the duties prescribed in their own specific Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*), how can it be justified that in the *brahmakāṇḍa* (the section on Brahman), all persons equally possess the qualification for meditation (*upāsanā*) in all the various meditative teachings? To this, he says:
Or rather, there is no contradiction, as in the case of mantras and the like. || 54 ||

The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and" (*ca*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), sequence (*krama*), substance (*dravya*), and action (*karman*) are included. For example, although mantras and so forth are recited in individual branches (*śākhā*) [of the Veda], because the sacrifice (*kratu*) which is their subordinate element (*śeṣin*) is one and the same across all branches, they are applied to all branches as appropriate through direct statement (*śruti*) and other means.

Furthermore, it is contradicted by the fact that even in the case of Smārta rituals, the mantras for the *puṇyāhavācana* found in the Ṛgveda are respected by followers of the Yajus and Sāman branches;

likewise, the mantras such as the *Śatarudrīya* found in the Yajus branches are accepted by followers of the Ṛk and Sāman branches, just as the mantras concerning sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and *kuśa* grass contained within their own respective branches are used by all.

Just as [certain rites] accepted in all recensions [are combined], so too, because of the understanding of the Vedāntic injunction— "That state which all the Vedas proclaim"— it is determined that it is appropriate for all practitioners of the meditation on Brahman to have the qualification for the practice of the Brahma-vidyā found in all recensions.
The section concerning the superiority [of the *bhūman*] due to its being like the *kratu*, [number] twenty-three.

The propriety of meditating on the totality [of attributes] and the investigation into the superiority of the meditation on Brahman known as the "Full" (bhūman) in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: After prescribing many meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*) such as "One should meditate on Name as Brahman," "One should meditate on Speech as Brahman," and "One should meditate on Mind as Brahman," it subsequently states: "But the Full alone is what one should desire to understand; wherein..."

"He sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and knows something else—that is the finite. Since this scriptural passage establishes that the meditation on Brahman known as the Infinite is superior to all other meditations, it is that alone which [leads] those seeking liberation...

Anticipating the doubt that [the meditation on the parts] is mandatory, he states another section: || 235 || "The preeminence of the Whole (bhūman) is superior, as in the case of a sacrifice; for thus the scripture shows. || 55 ||

The Vaiśvānara-vidyā is taught beginning with the words, "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava. In that [passage], Vaiśvānara is heard of as the Supreme Self (paramātman) to be meditated upon, having the three worlds as his body, and consisting of the constituent parts of the heavenly world, the sun, the wind, space, water, and earth. And therein, heaven is his head, the sun his eye, and the wind...

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is space (*ākāśa*); "the chest" (*sandeha*) means the middle part of the body; water is the bladder; and earth is the feet—these are the specific limbs. In this regard, there arises a doubt: should the meditation on this body of the three worlds be performed by taking its parts separately, or as a unified whole?

Regarding the phrase "of the whole" (*samastasya*) and "or rather, of the whole alone" (*atha samastasyaiva*): what is correct? That it is separate (*vyasta*). Why? Because at the beginning, there is instruction on separate meditations (*upāsanā*). For it is taught as follows: Aupamanyava and others, having been questioned by Uddālaka, approached Aśvapati Kekaya and said, "You are indeed now teaching us that very Self which is Vaiśvānara."

"Tell us," they asked. And he, having told them each their respective objects of worship—Heaven and the others—and having explained the meditation upon those [deities] when distributed among the head and other parts of the body, as well as the fruit for each, said:
"One sees food in abundance; what is dear comes to him; there is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family."

"One who worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus [thinks]: 'This is indeed the head of the Self,'" and by such statements as "This Vaiśvānara Self is indeed the one with excellent splendor," he declares that the object of worship in each of those various meditations is Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, the meditation must be performed upon him alone in his distributed form. As for the other passage: "But he who [worships] him thus... [it refers to the same].

It should be understood that the statement, "one meditates on Vaiśvānara, the Self, as the measure of a span and as all-pervading," is a summary conclusion regarding the meditation on the head and other limbs taught in reference to Vaiśvānara as delimited by specific regions such as the sky and so forth. Another teacher says: "In this very way, there is also meditation on the whole [Vaiśvānara]."

"It is an effect" [is the objection]. Because of the separate mention of the fruit—namely, "But he who meditates on this Vaiśvānara thus eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves"—there is a division of the sentence. This is just as in the introduction to the Bhūmavidyā, where, after stating the meditation on Name and so forth and its fruit, it is said: "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who..."

Having taught the knowledge of *bhūman* with the words "He surpasses by his being," and so forth, [the text] declares its fruit: "He becomes self-ruling; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. In that context, although the sentence is devoted to the knowledge of *bhūman*, the meditations on name and so forth, along with their respective fruits, are treated as subordinate members (*aṅga*). So it is here as well.

This being the case, it is replied: "The superiority of the *bhūman*. This means that the superiority—namely, the authoritative validity—belongs to the *bhūman*, which is vast and comprehensive as a whole; for it is understood that [the passages] constitute a single coherent statement (*ekavākyatva*). To illustrate: having begun with "Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava," [it continues] "Uddālaka Āruṇi, O venerable sirs... and so forth.
"Now we shall approach this very Self, Vaiśvānara; come, let us go to him.
With the desire to know the Vaiśvānara-Self, the five great sages, beginning with Aupamanyava, approached Uddālaka.
Not finding there anyone who knew the Vaiśvānara-Self, they went together with him to Aśvapati Kaikeya.
Having approached one who knows the Vaiśvānara Self and asked, "You are currently studying this very Self as Vaiśvānara; tell that to us," he understood from him that the Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara,
has the sun-world and so forth down to the earth as His body, and [he understood] the fruit of that meditation.

From the concluding statement, "They have realized the experience of Brahman, which has become the food residing in all worlds, all beings, and all selves," it is understood that the passage constitutes a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*). When this unity of the sentence is thus established, it is determined that the mention of meditations on specific parts and the specification of results are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of portions of the meditation on the whole.

"Like a sacrifice"—just as the constituent parts of a specific sacrifice enjoined by the rule, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," are restated by such passages as, "When it consists of eight potsherds," and so forth; likewise, meditation on the whole alone is logical, not meditation on the parts. For this Śruti demonstrates this very point by declaring that there is misfortune in meditating on the parts.

"Your head would have fallen apart had you not come to me," "You would have become blind had you not come to me," and so forth. Therefore, this [objection] is also refuted—that which was stated regarding the similarity between the meditations on Name and so on;
for in those meditations on Name and so on, no evil consequence is heard [in the scriptures]. From the meditations on Name and so on...

The fact that the meditation on the *bhūman* yields a superior fruit is heard in scripture: "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly by means of the Truth. For this very reason, even though the passage is devoted to the knowledge of the *bhūman*, there is an intention to describe the meditations on Name and so forth along with their fruits;
otherwise, it would be impossible to praise the knowledge of the *bhūman* by means of the "speaking surpassingly" which is caused by its superior fruit. Therefore...
The practice of meditating on [the Lord] as a whole alone is logical.
This concludes the section concerning the distinction based on various words and other factors. || 24 ||

The demonstration of the systematic unity (*samanvaya*) of all meditations (*upāsanā*), which have liberation as their sole fruit: Now, it may be argued that meditations on the Sāman chants and similar passages do not possess an intermediate purport (*avāntaratātparya*), because passages such as "One should meditate on the Name as Brahman" are understood to have the meditation on Brahman as their ultimate purport, according to the maxim of the "gross Arundhatī" (where one first points out a nearby star to lead the eye to the actual, subtle Arundhatī). And so it is said:

In response to the doubt as to how all these meditations on names and so forth can constitute an independent meditation on Paraśiva-Brahman, he establishes the answer through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"On account of the difference of words and so forth, [they are] manifold" (Sūtra 4.1.56).

Various and manifold forms of worship—such as those directed toward Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Indra, Āditya, and others—must also be accepted. Why? Because of differences in names and so forth. [The scriptures state: "One should worship Name as Brahman," "One should worship Speech as Brahman," "One should meditate on Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman," and "One should meditate on the Lord, the Ruler, accompanied by Umā."

In hundreds of scriptural passages such as "That sun is Brahman," the fact that numerous terms denoting meditative worship (*upāsti*) are heard according to the distinction of qualified aspirants— following the maxim of the flow of water before one's eyes— is established as their mutual difference. Nevertheless,
because they constitute a series of steps for ascending by following a gradual sequence, at the end of many births, the possessor of knowledge [realizes] Me.

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that, because of the observation of such statements as "he attains" (prapadyate) and because all meditations are heard to have liberation as their sole fruit, it is entirely appropriate that all forms of knowledge (vidyā) possess a common purport. [Now follow] the various classifications of knowledge.

In this context, all the knowledges of Brahman (brahmavidyās)— which have as their sole fruit liberation in the form of attaining Brahman— include the knowledge of Being (sadvidyā), the knowledge of the Earth (bhūmavidyā),

the knowledge of the Small (daharavidyā), the knowledge of Upakośala, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, the Ānandamaya-vidyā, the Akṣara-vidyā, the Pratardana-vidyā, the Udgītha-vidyā, the Akṣipurusha-vidyā, the Pāśupata-vidyā, and so forth.

And there are others that have as their fruit the single object consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Here, a doubt arises as to whether there is identity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) or a difference of knowledge (*vidyābheda*). Since the mutual difference among these has already been established in this very context, the question is whether it is appropriate to apply the principle of "recognition across all Vedāntas" (*sarvavedāntapratyaya*) to a single knowledge, such as the Dahara-vidyā; that is, is identity of knowledge the correct conclusion? Why? Because the object of knowledge (*vedya*), Brahman, is one. For the object of knowledge is...
The form of the knowledge is the same; therefore, because of this identity of form, there is an identity of the knowledge. This being the position reached, it is replied: "Not so."

The meditative knowledges (*vidyā*) are distinct. Why? Because of the difference in words and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the causes for distinction—such as repetition, number, quality, and the difference in what is enjoined—are seen to be connected with the distinctions [of the meditations]. Although words such as "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) denote mental modifications (*pratyaya*), and these mental modifications have Brahman as their sole object, nevertheless...

The meditations (*vidyās*)— which consist of the repetition of cognitions directed toward Brahman as qualified by attributes such as being the sole cause of the world and being free from sin, as declared in their respective contexts— distinguish themselves [from one another]. Furthermore,
the sentences that designate specific meditations connected to the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman are each complete in themselves (*nirākāṅkṣāṇi*).

It is determined that [these texts] denote the universe in its various distinct forms according to each respective section. Although this point is established by the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā sūtras such as "In the case of another word, there is a difference of action" (PMS 2.2.1), it is presented here once again for the purpose of dispelling the false view that the Vedānta passages are concerned solely with knowledge that is not subject to injunction. Therefore, there is a distinction between the meditations (*vidyā*).

It is pure. It is determined that there is no contradiction among the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), because they are designated as having a single fruit—liberation consisting in the attainment of Paraśiva-Brahman—despite differences in their specific results. This concludes the section on Option (*vikalpādhikaraṇa*). 25.
Among the meditations on the "small one" (dahara) and others,
it is determined that each individual person should perform one specific meditation according to their own preference, practicing it without interruption.

Now, an objection may be raised: regarding all meditations such as "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," does each have as its fruit the attainment of Paraśiva by virtue of being subordinate to the supreme knowledge of the "small ether" (dahara) and so forth, or do they possess independence?
In response to this doubt, the matter is determined through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
|| 237 || The conceptual construction [is not distinct from the non-conceptual], because the fruit is not different. || 57 ||

An option (vikalpa) among the meditations involving the identification with the self (*ahaṃgrahopāsanā*), which have as their fruit the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman such as those beginning with the "small one" (*dahara*), is possible. Therefore, their combination (*samuccaya*) should not be accepted. Why? Because their fruits are non-distinct (*aviśiṣṭaphalatvāt*).

Since meditations involving the grasping of the self (*ahaṃgrahopāsanā*)— such as those concerning the "Person within the small lotus" (*dahara*) and others— result in the attainment of Paraśiva-Brahman through the sequence of *sālokya* and other states in all such vidyās,
each individual, according to their own preference among these meditations, should practice one specific meditation without interruption until death.

The diversity of various forms of knowledge— such as the Sadvidyā and the Daharavidyā— which have as their fruits the attainment of Brahman through fear, devotion, faith, dispassion, compassion for all beings, tranquility, self-control, and so forth, has been stated; now,
it must be considered whether a combination (*samuccaya*) of these knowledges is also possible, given that each serves a specific purpose within a single person.
Is it that there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a doubt (*saṃśaya*) due to the absence of a purpose? What is correct? It is possible that there is also a combination (*samuccaya*). Why?

Because a combination is observed even among different scriptural injunctions that have a single result; for indeed, a combination of the means for that very same [result], such as heaven, is seen in the case of the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and so forth.

Just as there is a combination [of means] in one person with respect to the greater abundance of heaven, so too here, with respect to the greater abundance of the experience of Brahman, a combination is also possible. Why? Because the fruit is not distinct. For all these knowledges (*vidyā*), the fruit—the experience of Brahman as an infinite and unsurpassed bliss—is undifferentiated.

It is heard from such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed," that the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya* (residing in the same world) is possible for the supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is unsurpassed bliss.
For since heaven and the like are limited in terms of space, time, and essential nature, there is a dependence upon space and other factors therein.

Because there is no possibility of [the qualities] existing in greater measure, a combination of means is possible for one who seeks them; however, since Brahman here has a nature contrary to that, such a combination is not possible for you. Furthermore, all forms of knowledge have as their fruit the attainment of Brahman by way of dispelling the beginningless karma and ignorance that are opposed to the realization of Brahman.
Thus, because their fruits are indistinguishable, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) among all [meditations].

However, those meditations whose fruits are distinct from the attainment of Brahman—such as those having heaven and so forth as their fruit—may be combined (*samuccīyeran*) or optionally chosen according to one's desire, like ritual acts that have heaven as their fruit; for since their fruits are limited, there is the possibility of desiring more. To this, he says:
But optional rites may be combined according to one's desire, or not, because of the absence of the aforementioned reason.
