Desires other than the direct realization and experience of Paraśiva-Brahman— namely, the meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*) consisting of viewing inert objects such as the solar orb and so forth as Paraśiva-Brahman, which serve as various distinct means for attaining sovereignty and other powers— may indeed be combined according to time and circumstance; for there is no [contradiction] regarding these meditations on symbols.
One must accept that there is no fixed rule as to whether there is a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*). Why? Because of the absence of the previously stated reason;

it is taught that the reason previously mentioned—namely, the fact of having equal results—is absent here. Having become a god, one goes to the gods; therefore, it is understood that the direct attainment of the state of a god occurs while still alive, by virtue of the intensity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

In the case of the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) consisting of meditations involving the grasping of the self (*ahaṅgrahopāsana*), it is not so; for there is no evidence whatsoever that meditations on Name-Brahman (*nāmabrahma*) and the like—which are performed with a view to specific desires—result in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Furthermore, since those [meditations] lack such a fruit, and because they involve different spheres of experience, their combination (*samuccaya*) alone is appropriate, as they do not possess unity like Brahman; therefore, one [should practice them].
The conclusion is that [the practice] is to be performed by relying upon many [auxiliaries]. Likewise, it is established that this is because there is an absence of unlimited results.
This concludes the section concerning the existence of the state of being based on the auxiliaries (*aṅga*). 26.

Regarding the meditations on the *annamaya* and other sheaths which constitute limbs for the attainment of Brahman, there is the determination that these lead to liberation through a succession of stages, like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others—
just as in the case of the meditations on the *dahara*, *śāṇḍilya*, the person in the eye (*akṣi-puruṣa*), *upakośala*, *udgītha*, and so forth.

In response to the doubt—namely, "Could meditations connected with the members [of the sacrifice], such as 'Food is Brahman,' not be direct causes of liberation?"—the author states this in another section:
"Regarding the members [of the sacrifice], there is the state of being according to their substrate. (Sūtra 3.3.59)

Regarding the limbs [of the body]: in the case of the auxiliary practices for liberation (*mokṣopāsana*), such as "Food is Brahman, breath is Brahman, mind is Brahman, name is Brahman," there is a state of conformity with their respective substrates. This applies to the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who consists of the supreme bliss that transcends all, as in the passage: "He understood that bliss is Brahman."

It is inconsistent to claim that meditations on the "small" (dahara) and the "Great" (bhūman), etc., are direct causes of liberation by virtue of being means for attaining [Brahman] or means for its meditation—just as one might argue for other practices—because passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman" reveal a mutual distinction between them. This is heard in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: therein...
From the mutual distinction understood from such statements as "Food is Brahman," "Prāṇa is Brahman," "Mind is Brahman," and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge,

and Infinite," and because [food and the rest] are established as Brahman by virtue of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe, [the question arises: is it food and the others [that are Brahman], or...?

A doubt arises as to whether the nature of Brahman belongs to the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), or to the meditations on the "small" space and so forth, or to the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and others which are meditations on the limbs [of the body], or whether these are the direct causes of liberation.
Just as in the statement, "He understood that bliss is Brahman," [it is said here] that "He understood that food is Brahman" by virtue of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world.
Because of the instruction on their equality and because they are read within the same context, no disparity is established.

Furthermore, even in other Vedic branches (śākhās), all [of these] are designated as Brahman with equal status through such statements as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," and "One should meditate on name as Brahman. Thus, [the same applies to] the Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, Bhūma, etc. [vidyās].
There is no distinction [between them]. Therefore, since all meditations (*upāsanā*) are equal, it follows that they can all directly cause liberation; this being the position reached, we reply:
in the passage "Another inner self is the one consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), the *ānandamaya* is characterized by having unsurpassed bliss as its culminating point.
Because the status of Brahman is established [therein], and because in the passage "He who knows Him hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3),
it is stated that meditations on the Supreme Self within the small space (dahara-ākāśa) consisting of the cave are the direct cause of liberation—

beginning with the words "The lotus of the heart, stainless and pure," and continuing up to "the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, accompanied by Uma"— [it is concluded that the Supreme Self is the subject].

Having meditated, the sage goes to the source of beings; for even in other Vedic branches, there is instruction that through the worship of the Supreme Lord within the small lotus, one attains liberation as union with Śiva without delay.
Likewise, in both one's own branch and other branches, it is observed that there is no direct attainment of liberation through the worship of the self as consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth.

It is determined that, in the meditations on the *annamaya* and other sheaths which serve as limbs for the attainment of Brahman, these lead to liberation through a successive sequence—just like the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices when offered to the Supreme Lord.
Now, to the objection: "What is the proof that the *ānandamaya* is the Supreme Brahman, which is superior to all? he says:
|| 240 || And because of the conduct of the learned. || 60 ||

*Śiṣṭiḥ* means instruction, command, or ordinance. For it is said: "From fear of Him the wind blows; from fear the sun rises; from fear of Him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on. In this passage, because the quality of being the cause of fear for all—which belongs to the one who governs all—is predicated of Śiva alone, who is the Supreme Bliss (*ānandamaya*) and superior to all.

It is determined that its identity with the [self] consisting of food and the others is not possible, even though it is read within the same section; for it is heard in that very way in another passage: "The Teacher who has entered within, the Self of all beings."
The Section on Combined Aggregation (Samāhārādhikaraṇa) || 27 ||
The realization of Śiva through Śiva-yoga is possible only for those of firm mind who seek liberation.

Now, since the mind is possessed of many volitions, and because without the cessation of the mind it is impossible to accomplish the practice of any of the vidyās such as the Dahara-vidyā, by what path [is this realization attained]?
Anticipating the doubt as to how stability of mind—which is the cause for the experience of the direct realization of Śiva—might come to be, he shows another supporting argument:
|| 241 || "From the withdrawal [of the senses]. (Sūtra 61)

In the Vedāntic texts such as the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, the attainment of the direct experience of the realization of Śiva is possible for those seeking liberation through the practice known as Śivayoga; this is achieved by the integration— meaning the union— of the sight, mind, and vital breath, which constitute the constituent parts of the individual soul's bliss, following the cessation of the mind's fluctuations.

"Oṃ! The exponents of Brahman say: 'What is the cause? What is Brahman? From what have we been born? By what do we live? And upon what are we established? Controlled by whom do we abide in pleasure and pain? O knowers of Brahman, tell us the settled truth regarding Brahman. Beginning thus—"
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities;
within that Great One, who abides in all as the individual soul, the swan (the individual soul) wanders upon the wheel of Brahman.
"Having perceived the Self as distinct from the Impeller, and being favored by Him, one thereafter attains immortality.

Thus it is heard in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, a jewel among the Vedānta texts. A doubt arises as to whether the experience of the direct realization of Śiva through the meditations on the "small space" (*dahara*) and so forth occurs by means of yoga that is an ancillary to the Pāśupata knowledge, or whether it is possible even without that.

In the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], in passages such as "The small, stainless [space]," "Accompanied by Umā," "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," since the direct realization of Brahman is designated as occurring through knowledge alone, it might be argued that there is no purpose for the science of Yoga. To this, we reply:
"From meditating upon that, however, there arises the third [state]: 'Upon the dissolution of the body, universal sovereignty, absolute, with all desires fulfilled'"; beginning thus, [it continues]:
"Where fire is churned, where wind is churned, where Soma overflows—there the mind is born.
Having attained a body that is even and elevated at three points, one should withdraw the senses into the heart along with the mind.
Let the wise man cross over the terrifying, serpent-like currents by means of the raft of Brahman.
Having restrained his vital breaths through disciplined effort, he should breathe through the nostrils when the breath is exhausted;
for the mind, O wise one, is like a vehicle yoked to vicious horses—thus should he hold it steady, remaining vigilant.
Beginning thus:

"When the body composed of the five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and life— has arisen and is set in motion with its five qualities, for one who has attained a body consisting of the fire of yoga, there is no disease, no old age, and no death."

Lightness of body, health, freedom from greed, clarity of complexion, gracefulness of gait, a pleasant fragrance, and scantiness of urine and feces— they say these are the first signs of the onset of yoga.
Just as a statue coated with clay shines forth when it is thoroughly purified and filled with light,
so too the embodied soul, having clearly perceived the reality of the Self, becomes solitary, fulfilled, and free from sorrow.

Thus, from the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, it is understood that only for one who is engaged in yoga is there the realization of the direct perception of Paraśiva-Brahman. Elsewhere it is said: "While listening to the Vedānta, one should commence yoga;
by the contraction of Kuṇḍalinī, having opened the door-panel, one should break through the gate of liberation."
The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the intellect (jñāna), and restrain that [intellect] in the Self (ātman).
If a person should know the Self as "This am I," desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he suffer with this body?
Having understood that very Dharma, a Brahmin should cultivate wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is merely the exhaustion of speech.
Well-restrained by the *yamas*, the *niyamas*,
and the *āsanas*, and having first performed the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*), one should practice *prāṇāyāma*.
Having abandoned all thought with an attentive mind,
one who is free from conceptual construction and serene in soul should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should constantly practice the discipline of the breath (marut) with a concentrated mind;
the wise person should not apply the mind to anything else.
And because of the statement in passages such as these— that among all forms of worship, whether external or internal, the science of Yoga (*yogavidyā*) is preeminent—

it follows that wherever the injunction for worship is taught in the *Taittirīya* Upaniṣad, beginning with "The small, stainless [space]" and continuing with "That which is within it is to be worshipped," etc.,
the suitability for Yoga is established by implication even without an explicit statement of the means.

According to the maxim that "the goal cannot be accomplished [without the means]," there is no stability of the mind without yoga, and in its absence, there is no direct realization of Brahman. Therefore, the necessity of the science of Śiva-yoga— which consists of the unification of the eyes, mind, and breath— is pointed out for those seeking liberation.
Likewise, even in the meditation on the "small" (dahara) within the context of isolation (kaivalya), from the passage beginning with "the lotus of the heart" up to "having meditated,
the sage goes to the source of beings," we see that the realization of Paraśiva-Brahman belongs only to one who is engaged in the yoga of meditation;
thus, in such scriptural texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the word "knows" (veda) is taught to be in accordance with the yoga of meditation and concentration.
The knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is not like that of medical treatises and the like; therefore, a synthesis of all the scriptures is indeed appropriate.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"And because of the scriptural teaching on the commonality of the qualities. (Sūtra 62)
Thereafter, having known that supreme Brahman, the Great One, who is hidden in all beings according to their respective classes,
the one enveloper of the universe— that Lord— they become immortal.
The Pradhāna, the Field, and all else—He has faces, heads, and necks everywhere; His hands and feet are on every side, and He has eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, He stands pervading everything.
Manifesting the qualities of all the senses yet devoid of all senses,
the unmanifest Lord of all, the refuge and friend of all.
His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one sees him with the eye.
Those who know him thus as dwelling in the heart by means of the heart and the mind, they become immortal.
Having performed that action and turned away from it again, one attains the union of reality with reality—
whether by means of one, two, three, or eight [qualities], as well as through disposition and the subtle qualities of the self.

He who, having ascended, directs all actions endowed with qualities and all states of being—when those [qualities] are absent, there is the destruction of performed action; upon the exhaustion of action, he goes to that which is other than reality.
Let us know that God, the Lord of the world, worthy of praise— the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the highest divinity among deities, and the first lord among lords from of old.
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither his equal nor his superior is seen.
Because of such passages and because of the scriptural declarations regarding the unique attributes of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman—
since his qualities are heard to be uncommon to any other— the practice of meditation conjoined with yoga is prescribed for those who desire the direct realization and experience of him.
Or rather, there is no locus for their coexistence. || 28 ||

Now, a determination that even the meditations on the limbs (*aṅga-upāsanās*)— just like the meditations on symbols (*pratīka-upāsanās*) such as the "small ether" (*dahara*)— cannot logically be combined:
indeed, in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]—
"This Udgītha is indeed the supreme Brahman; in it are the three, as well as the self-established syllable.
Having realized the distinction within this, those who know the Veda, being devoted to it, merge into Brahman and are liberated from the womb.
Thus, in the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad], beginning with "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," it continues: "Whatever one performs with knowledge..."

Because the *praṇava* itself is established as the Supreme Self through such passages as "By means of faith and the Upaniṣad, that very [syllable] becomes more powerful," and because the Udgītha-vidyā must necessarily be adopted within the sacrifices as a subordinate element (*kratvartha*) of the sacrifice,
its being directed toward Paraśiva-Brahman is inconsistent. Therefore, regarding the meditations (*upāsanā*) bound to subordinate parts such as the Udgītha...
Anticipating the objection that a combination [of meditations] with the Dahara-vidyā and others is untenable, he states another section:
"Or rather not, because there is no scriptural statement of their coexistence. (Sūtra 63)
Nor is there a rule for the mandatory combination even of meditations connected with subordinate members such as the *udgītha*. Why?

Because there is no scriptural statement of their coexistence. For there is no hearing—that is, no mention—of a coexistence or combination (*samuccaya*) of those meditations connected with the constituent parts (*aṅga*), such as the *udgītha*, with the *dahara*-vidyā and others. As for the statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge," that establishes the status of meditations connected with the constituent parts as being auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*).

Since the status of [meditation] as an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*) has been rejected in the Sūtra— "There is no restriction regarding that determination, because it is seen [in scripture]; there is no obstruction [to the fruit], for it is distinct"— it follows that when one performs the ritual action preceded by meditation conjoined with its auxiliaries,
there is an immediate cessation of those sins which obstruct the arising of worlds such as heaven.

The scripture, in the passage "Whatever one performs with knowledge," teaches only this much: that the production of the fruit occurs. And thus, even for meditations connected with the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), just as in the case of meditations on symbols (*pratīka*) such as the "small ether" (*dahara*), their combination (*samuccaya*) is untenable. This applies to such passages as "One should meditate on the syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*," and so forth.

A doubt arises as to whether the sciences (vidyās) must necessarily be undertaken within the sacrifices for the sake of the sacrifice—like the *udgītha* chant and so forth—or whether they are for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), to be undertaken according to one's desire—like the *godohana* vessel and so forth. It has been stated that they must be undertaken as a rule.
But has it not been established that there is no such rule because they are for the sake of the person?

Regarding the rule of determination [of the agent] in that case, it is true that the fruit is the absence of obstruction [to the action] when that [agent] is seen separately; however, in order to confirm that very point, it is challenged by certain observations of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and by reasoning. For in that context, because of the observation of the lack of a restrictive rule in the statement "by means of that, both perform [the sacrifice]," the fact of separate fruits has been stated.

There are many reasons found for the lack of a rule regarding the adoption [of specific meditations], since the meditations themselves are taken as subordinate members (*aṅga*)—just like the *udgītha* and so forth—which serve as the locus for worship. For instance, in the passage "One should meditate on the *udgītha*," meditation is taught precisely as being connected to the *udgītha* and other such elements;
and likewise, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful."

For the connection with the fruit arises from another sentence in the form of an instruction regarding the present. If the status of being a subsidiary element of the sacrifice were already determined by its own sentence through its connection with the *udgītha* and so forth— which are invariably connected to the sacrifice—
then the mention of a connection with a fruit in the present tense found in another sentence would be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Since the hearing of the "fame of the sinless" (*apāpaśloka*) follows from that, and since the *udgītha* and other such elements—which serve as the bases for meditation—are invariably employed as constituent parts of the sacrifice by the injunction of performance, there is a rule of mandatory inclusion; this is because meditation is enjoined as an auxiliary to the *udgītha* in the passage, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha. At that time, it is like the case of the injunction, "One desiring cattle should lead [the water] with a milking vessel," and so forth.

Since no other qualification is heard in the injunctive sentence, it is understood that the status of being a subordinate member (*aṅga*)—such as the *udgītha* and so forth—is indeed what is to be enjoined.
Furthermore, a rule for the mandatory combination (*samuccaya*) of meditations is seen in the passage: "One should indeed rectify a poorly performed *udgītha* even from the Hotṛ's seat."

Moreover, because of the qualities of the object of meditation, the support of the meditation—the *praṇava*—and the meditation itself, it is understood that there is a combination of meditations, according to the Śruti: "By means of this [the *praṇava*], this triple knowledge proceeds; saying 'Om,' they cause [the Adhvaryu] to announce; saying 'Om,' they recite the *śastra*; saying 'Om,' they chant the *udgītha*.

Furthermore, because of the reference to the subject under discussion by the word "by that" (*tena*), it is the *praṇava* together with its meditation that moves everywhere. Therefore, regarding the meditation...

And since we observe a rule of coexistence with the *praṇava*, it follows that the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth must necessarily be undertaken just like the *udgītha* itself; to this we reply: "Not so, because there is no scriptural statement of their coexistence."

It has already been clearly taught that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is both identical with the *praṇava* and transcendent of the *praṇava*. Nor is it the case that there is a rule for the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth within sacrifices, similar to the [performance of] the *udgītha* and other such rites. Why? Because their coexistence is not heard [in scripture].
The meaning is that there is no mention of the *udgītha* being a subordinate member (*aṅga*). For when something is a subordinate member, there is a rule of concomitance.

Although no separate injunction (*adhikāra*) is perceived within this collection of words, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," nevertheless, immediately following that, [the text says], "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," thus [indicating] the role of knowledge.

The status of being a means toward the greater potency of the ritual (*ṛtu*) is what is being established. Therefore, since meditation is understood as a means to a result distinct from the fruit of the ritual, its application as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *udgītha*—which itself is a subordinate part of the ritual—is not tenable. Consequently, when there is a requirement for a basis (*āśraya*) for the introductory statement (*upanyāsa*), the proximate *udgītha* serves merely as that basis.

Since the *udgītha* is a constituent part of the sacrifice (*ṛtu*), this other qualification— undertaken for the purpose of making the sacrifice more powerful— is restricted only to those qualified for the sacrifice regarding the meditation based on the *udgītha* and so forth that are employed by the sacrifice; thus, there is no rule that such meditation must be performed during the sacrifices themselves.

And it has been stated that "greater vigor" (*vīryavattaratva*) means the non-obstruction of the fruit of the *ṛtu* by the fruit of another powerful karma; that is to say, the *ṛtu* yields its fruit without delay. However, in the case of the "leafiness" (*parṇatā*) and so forth, [the text says]: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more vigorous. Thus, just as knowledge is a means to the fruit, [the leafiness] is [a means] toward fruits such as hearing the "famous verse of the sinless" (*apāpaśloka*).
Since it is not heard that [the *juhū*] functions as a direct means of accomplishment, and because it is enjoined as a subordinate part of the *juhū* and other such subsidiaries,

it is determined that it is impossible to conceive of those things which are themselves subordinate parts as being means for attaining a separate result; therefore, the mention of a result in that context must be merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 244 || "And because it is observed" || 64 ||

It should not be argued that the performance of meditations connected with the ritual subsidiaries (*aṅgāvabaddhopāsanā*) would be useless for men;

Thus ends the third chapter, known as the Sādhanādhyāya, in the Śrīkarabhāṣya composed by the venerable teacher Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of holy ascetics.

The third quarter (pāda) of the third chapter, consisting of sixty-four sūtras beginning with "The cognition [of Brahman] derived from all Vedāntas is one, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth," is completed.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya, titled "The Section on the Purpose of Man" (Puruṣārthādhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

An exposition of the duties of the four stages of life, beginning with the student life (*brahmacarya*): in the preceding section, it was stated that some meditations (*upāsanā*) lead to liberation through a traditional succession, while others lead to liberation directly; here, however, [the focus is on] one who is fit for the enjoyment of fruits such as the heavenly realm (*svarga*) belonging to the next world, which occurs at a later time.

Since it is impossible for discerning persons to engage in ritual acts— which require the expenditure of great wealth as a means for enjoying fruits such as heaven that occur in other worlds and at other times— without knowledge of Śiva, who is the controller of the individual soul (jīva) characterized by the body, senses, and so forth, [there must be] knowledge of Śiva.

It must be stated that [this knowledge] is a constituent factor for the performance of all rituals, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others. And thus, because the subsidiary (aṅga) and the principal (aṅgin) share a single means of achieving a fruit, whatever fruit belongs to the subsidiary rites—such as heaven—that very same fruit belongs to the principal, which is the knowledge of Śiva who is distinct from the expansion of the sentient and insentient universe; this is established independently.

Anticipating the objection of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā— that the commencement of all Vedāntic knowledge would be useless because it is impossible for it to have any result other than liberation as its sole characteristic— the author states this subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*) in order to refute that objection: —
The impossibility of the knowledge of Brahman being an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma-aṅga*).
"Therefore, the human goal [is attained] from the Word; thus says Bādarāyaṇa. (2.1.245)
Therefore, from the direct realization of Sadāśiva-Brahman preceded by meditations on the Day-maker (Ahar) and other deities in accordance with Yoga, the supreme human goal is attained:
the state of Śiva, which is preceded by the cessation of the innate condition of being a limited individual (jīvatva)—a state that is eternal, unsurpassed, natural, and free from rebirth.
As it is said: "He who knows Brahman reaches the ultimate peace; he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself; the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable *praṇava* the upper fire-drill,
the wise man burns away the fetter through the practice of churning with meditation.

Based on scriptural passages such as "Know [the Self] through faith, devotion, meditation, and yoga," the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that those seeking liberation must perform uninterrupted contemplation of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, being free from the stain of the mire of all karmic impressions (vāsanās).

"We shall explain the Śikṣā. "Phoneme, accent, measure, strength, and continuity—thus the chapter on Śikṣā has been described. "May our fame be together, may our spiritual luster be together; now, therefore, we shall explain the Upaniṣad of the Saṃhitā," and so forth, is heard in the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka]. [It continues: "By sacrifice, by giving..."
Because scriptural passages such as "by austerity, by fasting," and so forth, declare that sacrificial rites and the like are limbs of liberation;

and because [texts] such as "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, a Brahmin should attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] through what is created," and "For the sake of realizing That, he should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand, one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman," [demonstrate] the role of action—

Since the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad] denies that [ritual action] is a constituent part of liberation and reveals that both ritual action and knowledge are equally predominant, there arises a doubt: does ritual action, by its own independence, serve as a means to achieve the supreme human goal which is free from rebirth, or does it do so by being a subordinate part of knowledge?

Since there is no evidence for the existence of a Lord distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), and because in such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "one should perform the twilight worship daily," it is understood that the body alone is the agent— just as in passages such as "he whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood [attains immortality]" or "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity, when the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are joined"— consciousness [is attributed to the body].
Statements such as "I am Brahman," "Brahman am I," and "That thou art" are intended merely as praises of the Vedānta.

Furthermore, since even in the Vedānta texts one observes the application of knowledge (*vidyā*) to ritual acts—as in "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful"—its status as an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*) is unavoidable. [The text continues: "Knowledge and action..."
The phrase "they both undertake" shows the conjunction of knowledge and action in a single person, as seen in such passages as:

"Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rules, and having performed the duties for the teacher as a remainder, one should return home; living in a pure place within the family, reciting his own sacred study and establishing others in righteousness," and so forth.
The injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) applies to one who has studied it up to the point of understanding its meaning;
likewise, when enjoining ritual acts, [the scripture] enjoins them only for one who has studied up to the point of understanding their meaning.
It has been established that the injunction to study extends precisely until the comprehension of the meaning. "One should desire to live here performing rituals alone."

Since the statement "a hundred years" applies to the entire lifespan of a person who knows the Self, and because this is employed as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding all ritual acts, it is understood that the fruit results from the performance of the rites themselves. Therefore, the objection that the knowledge of Brahman is merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action stands. Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached.
We shall explain—[the means] "for the sake of the human goal."

"May I become a sustainer of the nectar of immortality for the gods; he who knows Him thus becomes immortal here," and so on— in hundreds of such scriptural passages, since liberation is taught as resulting solely from the injunctions regarding meditation, concentration, and knowledge of Paraśiva-Brahman, and because no logical basis is seen anywhere for the independent efficacy of ritual action, this alone is the virtuous deed.

In such Vedic texts as "He causes [the soul] to act," and in such Smṛti passages as "Causing all beings to revolve by His Māyā, as if they were mounted on a machine," it is stated that even the individual soul (jīva), who is the agent of action, is dependent upon Śiva, and that Śiva alone is the liberator from all sins committed by the soul.
Furthermore: One should not abandon actions as long as knowledge has not yet arisen;
one should abandon both dharma and adharma, and both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon.

Since passages such as these in the Śrutis indicate that those who possess the desire for the knowledge of Brahman are prohibited from ritual action (*karman*), it is untenable that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action. Therefore, the opinion of Jaimini—that the deity denoted by the dative case is the primary object—is unexamined. [Objection: But surely even the teacher Jaimini, the source of the understanding of the four Vedas, [acknowledged] the primacy of ritual action...
In response to the doubt—how can the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) be considered supreme if its status as subordinate to knowledge (*jñāna*) has been established—he says:
|| 246 || "Because it is a subsidiary element, it is a statement of human purpose (*puruṣārthavāda*), as in other cases; so [says] Jaimini. || 2 ||

For from such scriptural passages as, "What one conceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech, and that one performs with action; whatever is the fruit of knowledge, that indeed is the fruit of action," it is understood that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the principal beneficiary (*śeṣin*) and ritual action (*karman*) is subordinate (*śeṣa*). Thus, the "statement of human purpose" (*puruṣārthavāda*)—the discussion of the purpose or goal of the person, namely the individual soul—is established through the presentation of such statements.
Because it is a remainder of karma and because it is a part of that [karma] by virtue of being produced by the living being; "as in other cases," so says Jaimini.

When there was darkness—neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—then Śiva alone existed. That is the Imperishable; that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ; from Him, ancient wisdom has issued forth.

Just as the scriptures, such as "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellect," demonstrate that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the impeller of the intellect, so too Jaimini maintains in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the impeller of action. Therefore, since even in his view the primacy of knowledge is established by implication, [the inquiry] pertains to the *Brahmakāṇḍa*.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers that it goes without saying that knowledge is predominant with respect to the fruit of liberation.

Furthermore, since even the teachers such as Jaimini have accepted that the duties established in the Vedānta— such as "Speak the truth" and "Practice righteousness"— are causes of liberation, [this is evident] from scriptural passages such as, "The world acquired through action perishes."

Because the impermanence of the fruits of karma is understood from such texts as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed; he does not return again," and the permanence of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is understood from such texts as "One should perform the twilight worship day by day," [the injunction] "The Self,
my dear, is to be seen" implies that one should engage in the hearing of the Vedāntas and commence yoga by means of the contraction of Kuṇḍalinī.

Furthermore, because injunctions are observed in such passages as, "Having opened the door-panel, one should break open the door of liberation; may I become a divine upholder of immortality," it is improper to claim that the Vedāntic texts such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) are merely explanatory eulogies (arthavāda). This is also seen in the Śruti regarding Vasiṣṭha, addressed by Kekeya: "O Blessed One, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice."

From the understanding that Brahmins devoted to ritual action seek the knowledge of Vedānta for the sake of liberation, and from the indication in the Purāṇas that the most eminent Brahmins, such as Śuka and Ātreya, sought the knowledge of Brahman from the Kṣatriya Janaka, it is understood that the knowledge of Brahman is the highest of all.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason: || 248 || "Because [the sages] are seen to follow [specific] conduct. || 3 ||
"Space is the body of Brahman; its self is truth; it delights in the vital breaths; its mind is bliss;
it is enriched by peace and is immortal"—thus, O Prācīnayogya, do thou worship.

Since, in this passage, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is established for those seeking liberation as being independent of ritual action (*karman*), it is improper to regard that knowledge as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action.

Furthermore, it has already been established that the one who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), the agent of actions, is taught in the Vedāntas as the object to be attained by those seeking liberation and as the object of knowledge; for this is so according to such sūtras as: "Not the other, because of impossibility" (1.1.16); "And because of the designation of difference" (1.1.17); "But not the embodied [soul], because of impossibility" (1.2.3); and "If it be said that he [is the soul] on account of the reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility" (1.2.12). That very Brahman is [the subject].

In the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), Śiva is taught to be distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of being that which the soul is to attain. Furthermore, the doctrine of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmavāda*) is refuted by such statements as "But [Brahman is] greater, because of the mention of difference" (*adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt*). Through passages such as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*), "Rudra indeed is all," and "Salutations, salutations to the one of universal form" (*viśvarūpāya vai namo namaḥ*), the world is shown to have Śiva as its material cause (*upādāna*).

The nature of being Śiva has been stated. Having refuted the views of partial difference and non-difference through the two sūtras, "A sign for the fulfillment of the promise" (B.S. 1.4.20) and "Because of the state of one who is about to depart, so says Auḍulomi" (B.S. 1.4.22), [the author proceeds] with "On account of the abiding, so says Kāśakṛtsna," and so forth.
It has been established that the doctrine of both duality and non-duality, as proven by all the Vedāntas, is precisely what must be sought by those desiring liberation.

Therefore, for that purpose, the words of the Vedānta result in being intent upon teaching the true nature of the self, which is the agent in ritual acts; thus, it is demonstrated that knowledge is an auxiliary part of ritual action.
He states another reason:
"Because of the scriptural statement of that [fact]. (Sūtra 4)
For scripture itself declares that the meditation upon Brahman alone is the means to liberation for those seeking release:
"This space within the heart—in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal, golden-hued;
between the two palates is that which hangs down like a nipple; that is the source of Indra, where the hair-parting turns."

Having removed [the breaths] at the time of the head, one becomes established in fire with "bhūḥ," in wind with "bhuvaḥ," in the sun with "suvaḥ," and in Brahman with "mahaḥ. Furthermore, the attainment of all desires through the meditation on Brahman is taught by the Śruti: "He who knows it as hidden..."
"In the cave, in the highest heaven; he attains all desires together with Brahman. Thus it is said.
In another passage as well, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is taught to be the attainment of all actions:
"For one fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous."
Or else, he is born into a family of wise yogins themselves.

Thus, in the Smṛti, it is observed that those who have fallen from yoga while practicing the meditation on Brahman are born even in another life in the mortal world in the house of a wealthy person characterized by good conduct due to their latent desire (*kāma-vāsanā*); whereas for those who are free from desire and are yogins devoted to the meditation on Brahman, birth occurs in the house of such [a practitioner]. Therefore, regarding this knowledge of Brahman...
Its status as the most excellent is beyond reproach.
Furthermore, regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 249 || "Because of its being undertaken together" || 5 ||

Since it is established in the Śrutis that the undertaking of virtuous rites serves as an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), it is improper to claim that the knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma*). [As it is said: "Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: 'Speak the truth; practice dharma;
do not neglect your private study of the Veda; having brought wealth pleasing to the teacher, do not cut off the lineage of progeny.'"

"You must distinguish [the true from the false]. One must not neglect the truth; one must not neglect dharma; one must not neglect what is wholesome; one must not neglect prosperity; one must not neglect study and teaching;
one must not neglect the rites for the gods and the ancestors. Thus it is clearly taught here.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
|| 250 || Because it is enjoined for one who possesses that [quality]. || 6 ||
"Be one for whom the mother is a god; be one for whom the father is a god; be one for whom the teacher is a god; be one for whom the guest is a god.

Those actions which are blameless should be practiced by you, not others. Those well-performed deeds of ours should be emulated by you, not others"—by such statements, [these duties] are established as auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman for one who possesses that knowledge.
Since it is understood that the injunctions regarding devotion to one's mother, father, and others are prescribed, the knowledge of Brahman does not have ritual action as its subordinate member.
He states another reason:
"Because of necessity" (niyamāt). || 7 ||

"Whosoever are our superiors, those are the Brahmins; you must not exhale upon their seats. One should give with faith, one should not give without faith; one should give out of modesty, one should give out of fear, one should give out of a sense of obligation," and so forth—by such means, through the prescription of rules, it is established that all ritual actions (*karma*) are auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
The manifold meaning is appropriate.
Thus, having established through the Taittirīya Śruti that ritual action is a subsidiary part of knowledge (vidyā), he demonstrates his own position that this alone is the truth:
But because of the superior instruction of Bādarāyaṇa, it is so seen from that [work]. || 8 ||

The word "tu" (but) here signifies certainty. Why is it that the human goal [puruṣārtha] arises from knowledge alone? Because of the teaching of a superior [entity]. For, among the ritual acts, there is taught as the object of knowledge Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, who is a distinct entity superior to the individual soul (jīva), the agent of actions, by virtue of being a mine of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, and being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned. Thus, [the human goal arises] from the Blessed Lord.
The view of Bādarāyaṇa is precisely this: that [the fruits of knowledge and austerity] belong to the agent; let the indicative marks stand aside.
However, the teaching regarding the object of knowledge refers only to the inner self (pratyagātman) as distinct from the agent. How so? Because of the perception of that [distinction].
In the inner self— which, though impure, is [the locus of] the Knowable, who is worthy of honor, a mine of infinite qualities impossible even to conceive of as existing in the pure [self],

from whom all taints of evil have been dispelled, whose sport consists in the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe effected by His own volition, who is omniscient, omnipotent, whose bliss is beyond the reach of speech and mind, and who is superior to the individual soul— [therein lies] the entirety [of reality].

Because [these qualities] are seen in the scriptural statements teaching the knowledge of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, the Ruler: "He is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst; His desires are true, His resolves are true. "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. "The knower of the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere. "He is the Lord of all. He...

He is the lord of beings, he is the protector of beings; he is the bridge, the sustainer, the cause, and superior to the lord of causes. Of him there is no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him. By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart. By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, out of fear of him the wind blows.

In such passages as these, among the words "feeling" (*vedanā*) and "instruction" (*upadeśa*), there is not even a trace of the notion that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the agent who experiences [it] for itself, nor is there any possibility of its connection with things to be abandoned such as ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, the immortality consisting in the attainment of Him, which is heard of here and there as the fruit of the knowledge (*vidyā*) whose object is the Supreme Person Śiva, constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) arising from that knowledge.
This is incorrect.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"But [the cognition] is equal because of the perception [of the object]. (2.1.25) || 253 || 9 ||
As for the claim that knowledge (vidyā) is a subsidiary part of ritual action (karma) because we observe the performance of rituals by those who know Brahman—that is not so;

for even if knowledge is not a subsidiary part, such observation remains the same. The meaning is that the observation of the performance of rituals by those who know Brahman is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since there is also the case of non-performance.

Because [it is] seen. Indeed, the renunciation of ritual action by those who know Brahman is observed—such as in the case of the Kāvaṣeya sages: "We have studied the Vedas; why should we perform sacrifices? What shall we do with offspring? and so forth. Therefore, since the renunciation of ritual action is seen among those who know Brahman, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action.
How is this consistent? For those who know Brahman, there is both the performance and non-performance of ritual action;

for a sacrifice and other such acts performed without desire for fruit constitute an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, whereas an act of that nature which is not so [performed] is opposed to the knowledge of Brahman whose sole fruit is liberation. Therefore, the observation of their non-performance is more appropriate.

If knowledge were an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), the renunciation of action would not be possible in any way. In response to the objection that the scriptural statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," makes known that knowledge is an auxiliary part of ritual action, [the author] says:
"It is not universal" (Sūtra 4.1.10).
This scriptural passage does not have all subjects—such as the young Śāṇḍilya, Vaiśvānara, Upakośala, and Bhūman—as its scope;

rather, it has only the Udgītha-vidyā as its subject. This is because the word "whatever" (*yat*) in the phrase "whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yad eva vidyayā karoti*), being unspecified, must refer specifically to the Udgītha that was introduced in the statement "one should meditate upon the Udgītha" (*udgītham upāsīta*). For [the word] "whatever" [does not apply to everything].
This is connected with the word "by knowledge" (*vidyayā*). Having indicated by the word "that" which is performed by knowledge, its greater potency (*vīryavattaratva*) is stated.
And as it is said in the Śruti: "Both knowledge and action take hold of him, as does his prior cognition."

Raising the objection that it is improper to claim that knowledge of Brahman is an independent means to liberation—since it has been stated that the combination of self-knowledge and action, in the relationship of principal and subordinate, is the means for attaining the heavenly world—he says:
"The division is like that of a hundred [coins]. (Sūtra 4.1.11)

According to the principle stated in the passage, "Knowledge and action both accompany him," one must observe the distinction that knowledge and action have different fruits: knowledge accompanies [the soul] for its own fruit, and action accompanies it for its own fruit.
Furthermore, by the word "knowledge" (vidyā), either the knowledge of the formless Supreme Śiva or the knowledge of the embodied Supreme Śiva is expressed.
For those who know the reality of the partless [Self], their actions and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

Since it has been established here that unity with Paraśiva-Brahman occurs right here, preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body, there is no possibility of going to another world; therefore, by the word "knowledge" (vidyā), only the worship of the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman is being proclaimed.

This being the case, the distinction is determined by the scriptural statement: "Knowledge and action both accompany him. For that worshiper of the embodied Brahman who proceeds by the path of the gods to the world of Paraśiva-Brahman, knowledge—specifically the worship of Śiva in his embodied form—accompanies him; that is, it follows him as he goes. Him...

How is this distinction understood—that for the performer of ritual action who goes to the heavenly world by way of the path beginning with smoke, it is his specific action, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, that "samanvārabhate," meaning it follows and accompanies him? It is like the case of "the hundred [coins]"; just as when it is said that two hundred coins follow a seller of land and jewels, it is understood that one hundred follow for the sake of the land and one hundred for the sake of the jewels.
Just as a division is understood there, so too should it be understood here.
Furthermore, in the sentence "A hundred leaves for two Brahmins," the division is such that fifty leaves are to be given to one Brahmin and fifty leaves are to be given to the other Brahmin.

Just as it is thus determined, so too, given that both meditation (*upāsanā*) and ritual action (*karman*) are independently stated to be means for attaining, respectively, the world of the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman and the heavenly world (*svargaloka*),
there arises a doubt as to whether these two together constitute the means for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman.

For those who practice rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, there is the experience of the heavenly world (svargaloka); for those who worship the Supreme Śiva-Brahman in His embodied form, there is the attainment of the auspicious glory of the supreme realm of Śiva, which consists of unsurpassed bliss, eternity, and incomparable non-duality.
Now, [it may be argued]: "Knowledge and action both accompany him—the performer of ritual action as he goes to the heavenly world."

In the statement "knowledge and action," by the word "knowledge" (vidyā) is meant the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva), which is distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and so forth that constitute the limbs of action; for,
following the scriptural passage "he goes along following the path," it is understood that there is no difference between the two, as both action and knowledge are perceived as one.

To this it is replied: Since the knowledge of the *jīva* as distinct from the body, senses, and so forth, constitutes an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the worship of Śiva, the practice of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma is said to result in the attainment of the heavenly world by following the knowledge of the identity of the *jīva* with the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and soul. Therefore, it is the knowledge of the *jīva* as the one who identifies with the body, senses, and so forth, that serves as an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma*).
It is determined as follows:

Furthermore, regarding what was stated— that because the scripture says, "He who, knowing thus, performs sacrifice," there is an audition of the eligibility for ritual action even for those possessing knowledge of Śiva, and therefore knowledge of Śiva is merely an auxiliary to the performance of ritual action— [this is refuted].
In order to dispel this doubt, he says: || 256 || "For one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]. || 12 ||
As for the claim that knowledge is an auxiliary to action because the injunctions regarding action apply to one who possesses knowledge, this is not tenable;

for the injunction "having studied the Veda" prescribes [the rites] for one who has merely completed the study. Furthermore, the injunction for study does not itself impel one toward the comprehension of the meaning, because—just like the ritual of consecrating the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—study culminates solely in the acquisition of the mass of syllables, and [only after] what has been acquired...

Since it is observed that the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) leads to the comprehension of fruitful ritual actions, a person spontaneously engages in the inquiry into its meaning—the result of which is the definitive determination of that [Veda]. Consequently, one who seeks ritual action engages in the knowledge of ritual action, while one who seeks liberation engages in the knowledge of Brahman;
thus, knowledge is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action.
Even though the injunction for Vedic study itself impels one toward the comprehension of the meaning, nevertheless, knowledge (*vidyā*) is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of ritual action,

because knowledge is a different thing from the mere understanding of the meaning; just as [knowledge] is distinct from the cognition of the essential form of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which serves as the means to the fruit.
The performance of various ritual acts is a different thing,
and likewise, meditative reflection (*dhyāna*) is indeed a different thing from the realization of the nature of Brahman, which consists in the knowledge of reality;
there is not even a trace of a connection with ritual action in that [meditative reflection].

The word "learned" (*vidvat*) in such scriptural passages as "he who, knowing thus, sacrifices" and "the learned one should offer the *agnihotra*" refers to a person who knows the meaning of the Veda as studied within the context of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). It does not, however, refer to a person who possesses knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, [it applies] to one who has studied the Veda, such as a follower of Pāṇini...
However, it is enjoined that the performance of actions performed over many lifetimes, offered to the Supreme Lord, is the cause of liberation through a traditional succession;
for in the Śruti passage, "Performing indeed here [only] actions," [this applies] to all persons, both those who possess knowledge of Śiva and those who do not.

Raising the objection that because it is stated that the performance of ritual action is necessary until the fall of the body, the knowledge of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman cannot be the independent cause of liberation, he states the refutation of that:
"Not so, because there is no distinction" (Sūtra 1.1.25).

As for the claim that the passage beginning with "Performing here indeed the works... turns away the knower of the Self from knowledge and restricts him to the performance of ritual action for as long as life lasts—that is untenable, because there is no distinction made; for this restriction does not concern independent ritual actions that serve as means to a result.
Thus, there is a specific reason [for this distinction], as it is also logically consistent that [the passage] refers to ritual action (karman) which serves as an auxiliary to knowledge (vidyā).

For in the verse, "Janaka and others, having relied on action alone, attained perfection," it is understood that through action, Janaka and the others obtained the purification of the mind, which is the primary auxiliary to liberation.

A twice-born person who is associated with the Liṅga and its wearer, being free from desire, should perform the desireless actions prescribed for them— the Dharma proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti, which consists of obligatory and occasional rites.
From the performance of actions prescribed by the injunctions, purification of the mind will certainly arise;
from the purification of the mind, devotion arises, and that too shall be unswerving.
Through that [knowledge], wisdom is born, and there is no ignorance for the Self;
therefore, liberation arises from that, and one should properly perform the action prescribed by the injunctions.
Thus, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, it has been established that ritual action is the primary limb of liberation.
Having thus resolved the objection by means of the nature of the subject matter, he states the meaning of the passage "performing actions here indeed" [BhG 3.5]:
"Or it is for the sake of praise, or it is a permission. (Sūtra 4.1.14)
The word *vā* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). "All this is to be pervaded by the Lord—whatever moves on earth;

by that [wealth] renounced may you enjoy; do not covet the wealth of anyone. Since this occurs in the context of knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*), this is an authorization for the performance of ritual action at all times for the sake of praising knowledge. Because of the majesty of knowledge, even while performing action at all times, one is not [bound].

For it is said that "one is stained by actions," and thus knowledge is praised; and the remainder of the passage shows this very point: "In you, O man, there is no other [thought] heard, nor is action stained.
Through the contemplation of Śiva, all [rites], whether obligatory, occasional, and so forth—
Even while acting, the great yogi is not bound by virtues or faults.
Thus it is heard in the Siddhāntāgama. Therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma*).
[Objection:
But as the ignorant act while attached to action, O Bhārata...
Thus, even though he is attached, the wise man should act while desiring to bring about the welfare of the world.
Even when knowledge has been perfected, action is still enjoined for the wise;
therefore, one should not abandon action that is free from desire for its fruits.

In response to the objection— arising from the fact that many such Smṛtis state that even for the learned (vidvān), the performance of all obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites is necessary— how can the performance of ritual action be intended merely as a praise of knowledge (vidyā-stuti)? He says:
And some [hold that there is no fault] by acting according to one's own will. || 15 ||
Moreover, certain followers of particular Vedic branches record the abandonment of the householder's state by one established in the knowledge of Brahman through the exercise of free will.

This statement— “What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world?”— which declares the abandonment of the duties of the householder at will for the wise man who has become dispassionate, demonstrates that the knowledge of Brahman is not a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*).

In such scriptural passages as "not by action," it is said: "The Great Lord is pleased with those who have been purified through many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, who are dispassionate, and who are awakened."
When [the deity] is pleased, one becomes liberated; once liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva.
Even for that mortal who possesses but little devotion, after three births—

In these and other such cases as well, since [the texts] establish that knowledge is an auxiliary part of rituals such as sacrifice, the abandonment of the householder’s life by one established in knowledge according to his own will is not possible.
Therefore, knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action.

Because the knowledge of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is an auxiliary part of the performance of ritual action, it is an auxiliary part of the fourfold liberation (*mokṣa*).

This has been established. Now, in response to the objection that since the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) concerning the knowledge of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman destroys all karma, how could indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) concerning the difference between the *jīva* and Brahman not be an auxiliary to ritual action (*karmāṅga*), he says:
"And [there is] sublation" (Sūtra 3.4.16).

The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. This [vision] destroys the root of worldly suffering— the merit and demerit arising from the activities of entering and exiting many bodies.
The space of the mind, the space of consciousness, and the third, the [outer] space—
know, O Great Sage, that the space of consciousness is more empty than the other two.
Meditating within the space of the heart by means of the flow of the wheel of consciousness, kill the mind without hesitation; then enemies will not bind you.
Having abandoned the sole latent impression of worldly enjoyment, abandon the impression of duality;
then, having relinquished both existence and non-existence, remain firm in the state free from conceptual construction.
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
When the Self has transcended, or when the nature of the Self is all-pervading, what is bondage and what is liberation? Root out such thinking entirely.
Since all this is suffering in its beginning, middle, and end,
therefore, O sinless one, renounce everything and remain established in reality.
Without giving any occasion for sleep, worldly talk, sounds, and so forth, one should contemplate the Self within the self, remaining unmindful of the self [to external objects].
One should spend the time from birth until death in contemplation upon Vedānta;
one should not grant even the slightest opportunity to desire and other such passions.
One should wander the earth like a blind man, like a dullard, and like a mute;

for from such scriptural passages (*śruti*) as these, and from Smṛti texts such as "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes," it is understood that knowledge is the most excellent because it is not subordinate to ritual action, and because it is the cause of the dissolution of all duties. Therefore, that alone is logical.

Nor can it be argued that although the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman does not require the performance of all ritual acts as its constituent part, the subsequent knowledge of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—which is a mediate cognition (*parokṣajñāna*) following upon hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*)—does indeed serve as a constituent part of the performance of ritual acts; for [the scripture states]: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of the Vedānta are liberated."

Since scriptural passages such as "all" and so forth reveal that even the knowledge of that [Brahman] is a cause for gradual liberation, its status as a subordinate element of ritual action (*karmāṅgatva*) is not established.
This concludes the section concerning those whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*). 2.

The Determination of Wearing the Liṅga by Those in the Four Stages of Life according to the Śaiva Āgamas: Now, since scriptural texts such as "He who extinguishes the sacred fire is indeed a slayer of the gods" indicate that there is sin in the non-performance of rites such as the Agnihotra, even for those like Vasiṣṭha and Janaka who were established in Brahman—

In response to the doubt as to how it is untenable for the knowledge of Brahman to be a subordinate part of ritual action—given that the performance of rituals is observed—the author states another section (adhikaraṇa) to refute that objection:
"Moreover, among those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), [the knowledge of Brahman exists], for so says the scripture. (Sūtra 3.4.17)

"Renunciation (nyāsa) is indeed superior to Brahman; for Brahman is supreme, yet these other ascetic practices (tapaḥ) are inferior, and renunciation alone surpasses them—so says the Upanishad. Thus, in the *Taittirīya*, it is said: "The wise call renunciation 'Brahman' and 'the Supreme' (*brahma*)," and so forth. This refers to those whose inner organs have been purified by the ripening of the mass of merit accumulated over many births.

Because of the instruction on the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*) preceded by the rejection of rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and because the lifelong obligation for the *Agnihotra*, *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and other rites is established through the presence of sin (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance— as seen in passages such as "One who extinguishes the sacred fire is a slayer of the heroes of the gods"— and because of the example of Vāmadeva... [the text continues].

Because the designation "Nirābhāra" (the supportless) indicates a distinction in the stage of life (*āśrama*), there arises a doubt among all people and Brāhmaṇas as to whether the renunciation known as the fourth stage (*caturthāśrama*) must be performed or not.

[The conclusion is: even for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), renunciation must indeed be performed, according to such injunctions as, "One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice as long as one lives."

Since the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites are seen to be obligatory for as long as one lives, and since in passages such as "There are three branches of dharma" only the three stages of life (āśramas) are taught, the statements prescribing a fourth stage— such as "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality," "The wise call renunciation [brahman]," and "Brahman is [the goal]"— are here treated as mere explanatory eulogies (arthavāda).

Furthermore, because the passage, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," is devoted to the injunction regarding the path of the gods (*devayāna*), even there an injunction for another stage of life (*āśrama*) is not possible.
Moreover—

In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: mounting a horse, mounting a cow, renunciation (of worldly life), offering ancestral oblations with cooked food, and procreating a son through the husband's brother.
Thus, because the prohibition of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is understood from the *Pārāśara-smṛti*,
it is said: "The law of Manu applies in the Kṛta age, the *Gautama-smṛti* in the Tretā,
the [law of] Śaṅkha and Likhita in the Dvāpara, and the *Pārāśara-smṛti* in the Kali age."
Thus, because it is taught therein that the Pārāśara-smṛti is more authoritative than all other smṛtis,
a Śaiva should avoid these five: [performing] penance, fasting, renunciation, and saluting ascetics.
A follower of Śiva should avoid these five things when undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā).

Thus, since it is taught in the Śaiva Āgamas and likewise in other [texts], it follows that for Vaidikas, the fourth stage of life (caturthāśrama) must not be undertaken under any circumstances; to this we reply:
knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action (karmāṅga).

Because the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is observed among those in the stages of life where the vital energy is directed upward (ūrdhvaretas), the Agnihotra and other rites are indeed seen in those very Vedic texts: "There are three branches of duty; and those who in the forest worship through faith and austerity, as well as those wandering mendicants who, desiring that world, renounce the world—[they reach] this world [of the Vedas] and that world."

"Having abandoned that world, one should seek the Self; these three become possessors of the worlds of merit. Since there is no injunction for the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* for those established in the stage of the ascetic (*yati*)—as seen in passages such as "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality" and "Having renounced, one should engage in hearing [the scriptures]"—it is said: "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as life lasts."

Thus, it is established that the injunction for the lifelong Agnihotra, as proven by such scriptural passages, pertains exclusively to those who are not yet dispassionate. Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
"The mendicants are to be known as fourfold, according to the distinction of their modes of life."
Now, O best of sages, I shall fully declare renunciation;
indeed, mendicants are to be known as fourfold according to the differences in their modes of life.
O best of sages, I shall describe to you the way of life for the Kuṭīcaka, as well as the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsa.
The *kuṭīcaka*, however, having renounced the world, should always take alms from his own house or from the house of his own kinsmen and eat.
Wearing a topknot and the sacred thread, carrying a triple staff and a water-pot, equipped with a purifier and clad in ochre robes, he should constantly recite the Gāyatrī.
One should smear all the limbs with ashes and apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) at the three junctions of the day;
one should worship the Śivaliṅga with faith indeed day after day.
But the Bahūdaka, having renounced and being devoid of kinsmen, sons, and so forth,
should wander for alms at seven houses and avoid eating food from a single source.
A triple staff connected with a cow-hair rope, a marvelous sling,
a water-vessel, a water-strainer, a loincloth, and a water-pot.
Likewise, he should provide clothing, sandals, and a wonderful umbrella;
a sacred antelope skin, a needle, a bird-feathered fan, and a rosary.
One should wear the yogapaṭṭa as an outer garment, the staff as a sword,
and likewise bear ashes as a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) for the dusting of all one's limbs.
Devoted to the worship of the deity, one who is intent on meditation should always abandon the topknot, the sacrificial thread, and the practice of Vedic recitation.
At the time of twilight, one should perform the rite of reciting the Sāvitrī mantra;
likewise, [one should carry] the haṃsa-staff, the water-pot, the sling, and the alms-bowl.
He should always respectfully carry a patched garment to cover his private parts, a cloth for the body, an outer robe, and a single staff made of bamboo.
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and smear ashes, worship the Śiva-liṅga,
eat only eight morsels once a day, and keep one's topknot intact.
At the time of twilight, one should perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra, meditate upon the inner self,
visit sacred fords, and likewise perform penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
Acting according to the rule of a single night in a village,
the Parahaṃsa should carry a triple staff and a rope made of cow-hair.
A carrying-net, a water-strainer, a purifier, a water-pot,
a bird-feather, an antelope skin, a needle, a small axe, and a small knife.
One should permanently renounce the topknot, the sacred thread, and all obligatory rituals;
as well as the loincloth, the covering garment, and the patched rag that wards off the cold.
One should take up the meditation-belt, the outer garment, the sandals, the wonderful parasol,
the rosary, and the flawless staff made of bamboo.
One should joyfully perform the smearing with the mantras beginning with "Agni," while constantly uttering "Oṃ Oṃ"; thus the Haṃsa should perform the triple-staff (tridaṇḍaka).

One should take a vessel of clay, or a vessel of bell-metal, or a vessel of wood, or one of bamboo, or even the hollow of the hand as a bowl; having sipped water (ācamya), one should then take that water.
For swans that drink much water, the hand is their vessel;
water from such a source is not prescribed for a bronze vessel, for the Śruti declares it must be in an earthen vessel.
One should practice eating like a bee or eating only once a day, or one should act as a supreme swan (living on alms).
Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all.
Therefore, the Parahaṃsaka should eat in accordance with his yogic practice; having avoided food from one accused of a grave sin, he should accept alms from all castes.
Upon obtaining each successive stage, one should relinquish each preceding one;
through constant service to the guru, one should thoroughly practice self-knowledge.
One who, having relied upon the highest mode of conduct, resorts to a base mode of conduct,
should be known as one who has fallen from his elevated status (ārūḍhapatita) and is excluded from all religious rites.
Seeing a twice-born man departing for the forest life, the sun moves from its place;
for he, having pierced through the solar orb, goes to the world of Brahmā.
The deity is said to be of two kinds: the immobile and the mobile;
the mobile is the form of renunciants, while the immobile consists of clay images and the like.
O best of sages, for one whose delight in the ascetic life is constant,
there is nothing whatsoever difficult to attain within the three worlds.
Whether of evil conduct or good conduct, whether a fool or even a wise man,
by the mere utterance of his name he is to be honored like the Lord of All.
For those in the stage of the student (brahmacarya), the god Brahmā is proclaimed;
for householders (gṛhastha), Vaikuṇṭha; and for forest-dwellers (vanastha), Ravi is remembered.
"Śaṅkara is to be known as the highest of the high among all ascetics"—
from this [scriptural] vision, it follows that two sacred threads (yajñopavītas) should be worn during both Śrauta and Smārta rituals.
A third is for the purpose of an upper garment; if there is no clothing, four [robes] are required.
The fifth [type of person] is one desiring offspring, and likewise one desiring wealth;
there are ten or eight for the householder, four for the forest-dweller,
and one sacred thread each for the ascetic and the student.

Thus, since the prescription for a single sacred thread (*ekayajñopavīta*) for ascetics has been elaborated by the venerable Bādarāyaṇa in the *Pārāśara-smṛti*, the scriptural passages prohibiting those who have renounced (*saṃnyāsī*) mentioned therein must be understood as referring specifically to the tonsured renunciants (*muṇḍasaṃnyāsī*). Furthermore,
there is the injunction for Śaivas belonging to the four stages of life (*caturāśramin*) regarding the practice of wearing the sectarian mark (*liṅgadhāraṇa*).
Whether a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic—
whoever is endowed with the [proper] signs and limbs, he alone shall be a true member of the stage of life (āśramin).
Because of such passages in the *Vātūla-tantra* and other Āgamas, there is instruction for Śaivas belonging to the four stages of life (*āśrama*) regarding the wearing of the *liṅga*.

Now, one might raise the objection: "Among the four types of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), such as the *kīṭaka*, *cañcuka*, and so forth, which is prescribed for Vaidikas in the Kali age, and which is prohibited?
In response to this doubt, he shows another traditional practice:
Jaimini [maintains that] there is no [independent injunction for the study of the Vedas], because it is not an injunction; moreover, he refutes [the notion of] "grasping" (parāmarśa). || 18 ||

"Not by action," [it is said] in the Taittirīya; "having completed the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having become a householder, one should go forth; or else, in another way, one may go forth directly from studenthood, or from the household, or from the forest. And in the Jābāla [Upaniṣad]: "On whatever day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth."
With his hair, nails, and beard clipped short, and carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot,
he should wander constantly with self-restraint, never causing pain to any living beings.
Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation.
Thus, in the *Manusmṛti*,
the etymological definition of the term *ekarāma* is given:
"One who is beneficial to all beings, peaceful, carrying the triple staff and the water-pot."
Having become a wandering mendicant, he should resort to a village for the sake of alms.
Thus, according to Vijñāneśvara:
"The single staff or the triple staff, the tuft of hair, the sacred thread,
the water-pot, the saffron robe, the tuft of hair, the patched garment, the sacred thread, and the water-pot."
"A renunciant should wear these according to the injunctions of their respective mantras.
Thus it is stated in the Gautama Smṛti:
"Clad in smooth saffron robes, wearing the topknot, and possessing a parasol and sandals."
Then, having slung a beautiful staff and water-pot over his left shoulder,
he followed after Vaidehī in the guise of a wandering mendicant.
Thus, although the duties of the stage of life for those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) are seen in the *Rāmāyaṇa*,

Jaimini— the teacher Jaimini— refutes them as being established through the error of a blind tradition regarding the topknot (*śikhā*), the *Gāyatrī*, and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), based on direct *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Sūtra*, and *Purāṇa* texts. He thus establishes [this refutation].
