Therefore, in accordance with the Śruti and Smṛti, it is proper for these ascetics (yatis) of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) to undertake renunciation (saṃnyāsa) without contradicting the binding of the Sāvitrī-tuft (śikhā) and the sacred thread (sūtra), which are primarily the religious duties (brahmadharma) of Brahmins.

Having thus shown another practice according to his own doctrine—the determination that the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is to be undertaken only by celibates (brahmacārins) who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas)—he likewise states his own doctrine:
"Bādarāyaṇa [holds that it] is to be performed, because of the scriptural statement of equality. (Sūtra 3.4.19)

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that after the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*) and the others, the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) must be practiced by those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*). Why? Because of the scriptural statement regarding equality: "There are three branches of dharma; seeking this very world [of Brahman], mendicants renounce" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.22.6). Thus, for those who have sublimated their vital energy, it is like the stage of studenthood.
For it is heard that even the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) possesses the primary cause for attaining the Supreme Brahman, which is the highest of all;

furthermore, from the passage beginning with "The realm of Prajāpati belongs to the Brāhmaṇas" up to "The realm of Brahmā is ordained for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*"), [it is shown] that for both the castes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*) taken individually, there is attainment of the world of Brahmā.
Having described the fruit:
"For those yogis who are single-mindedly devoted and constantly meditate upon Brahman,
that supreme abode belongs to them, which indeed the wise perceive."
Thus, by the Blessed Pārāśarya, who declares that those established in Brahman attain Brahman within those very [stages],
it was clearly stated: "In that same context, regarding ascetics (yatins), there is to be only one sacred thread (upavīta), even with effort, for the religious student (brahmacārin)."

Because the *Manu-smṛti* and other legal codes state that there is only one sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for those who observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacārin*), it follows that the *Bhārata*, *Bhāgavata*, and other Purāṇas do not contradict this.
Now, an objection may be raised: "In the case of Rāvaṇa, Dharmarāja (Yudhiṣṭhira), Arjuna, and others, their renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) was artificial;

therefore, it is appropriate for them to wear the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*sūtra*). However, that [wearing of the tuft and thread] should not be accepted as the practice of natural renunciants. If this is argued, we say: No. In the world...

Since in the images of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, as well as in men who have assumed their dress, one observes precisely those primary marks and signs fixed upon them, how can the abandonment of such attributes be taught if the definition of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) consists in being characterized by the relinquishment of the topknot (*śikhā*) and the sacred thread (*upavīta*)?

Could there not be a similar power in the non-appearance of the topknot and sacred thread in Rāvaṇa— who, while previously possessing ten faces, was now characterized by the appearance of a single-faced ascetic lord— or in Yudhiṣṭhira and others who had obtained boons from the deities of Dharma?
Furthermore, [this is supported] by the Smṛtis of Manu, Parāśara, Yājñavalkya, and others cited previously.
One should join the palms in *añjali*. Likewise, in the *Vṛddha-Śātātapa*, it is stated: "Rudra is the crest (*śikhā*), the earth is the womb (*yoni*)," based on the vision of the *Taittirīya*.
By the uprooting of the crest, one would certainly become an enemy of Śiva in this world.
The status of a Brahmin is defined by the topknot and the sacred thread.
In the absence of these two, one becomes a Śūdra; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, the topknot and the sacred thread belong likewise to those in all four stages of life.
And that must be upheld with effort by those who rely on the path of the Vedas.

Thus, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā, the nature of the renunciants who bear the *liṅga* is described: "The one who has transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramī*) is connected to the *prāṇaliṅga* and wears the *bhasmaghuṇṭikā*."
One should carry a patched garment, a water-pot, an alms-bowl, and a staff;
for wherever these five great seals (mahāmudrās) reside, [there one dwells].
Having approached each of those as a refuge, one should worship them with one's whole being;
for from them, O child, the Dharma endowed with the five mudrās proceeds.
"Having attained [this state], one is always to be worshipped by those endowed with the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Thus, in that very same [text], the *Mukuṭāgama* teaches that renunciants who bear the *liṅga* must wear the five insignia (*pañcamudrā*):
"The staff, the water-pot, the patched garment, the sacred thread, and likewise the topknot."
The vital-organ liṅga, the saffron robe, the alms-bowl, and the sandals.
Always devoted to the highest stage of life, he should wear the ash-mark on his forehead and carry the umbrella;
having become one who has conquered his senses, he should practice the yoga of Śiva.
Either in the presence of a Śiva-yogi, or in the vicinity of a Śiva-liṅga,
or near a Śiva-āgama, one should take refuge in the state free from objective support (nirābhāra).

Since the specific importance of the *śikhā* (topknot) and *brahmasūtra* (sacred thread) is seen in many ways in numerous *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, and *āgamas*— such as those cited above— and since this is precisely what the chief disciple of Vyāsa intended, that alone is mandatory for the learned. For those seeking liberation (*mumukṣus*), there is the instruction to carry the *brahmadaṇḍa* (staff of Brahman), just as one wears the desired *liṅga*.

Now, an objection may be raised: since in certain Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and other texts, it is determined that for the Bahūdakas and Paramahaṃsas there is an injunction to not carry a staff—as in "the Bahūdaka, indeed, is a Paramahaṃsa; he should carry three staffs," and so on—and for some there is the determination of carrying a single staff, which rule of the Brāhmaṇas should be followed? To this doubt, he says:
Or rather, it is a rule, like the rule regarding the wearing [of the sacred thread]. 20.

The word *vā* here has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Just as [in the texts] such as "May I be a bearer of the nectar of the gods like the bearer of the *dhāraṇā*," "May my body be full of vision," "Salutation to Brahman; may there be for me *dhāraṇā*, non-rejection, and may I be a bearer,"—therein, the wearing of the *liṅga* of Supreme Śiva by those seeking liberation according to the prescribed rule, so too [is it] in that injunction, together with the *svāhā*.

Since it is heard in the scripture that "one should carry the staff of Brahmā with the mantra 'gopāya' (protect)," it is determined that for celibate Brahmins belonging to the four types of ascetic orders, such as the *kuṭīcaka* and others, there is only the single staff (*ekadaṇḍa*) prescribed.
For those three— the staff of speech, the staff of mind, and the staff of action— are indeed [the true staffs].
He in whom these punishments are thus established is remembered as a true ascetic.
If it is argued that this alone is correct— because the *Bodhāyana-smṛti* highlights the possession of the three-fold staff (*daṇḍatraya*) as the primary characteristic of ascetics (*yatis*),

and because even in works such as the *Mahābhārata* and *Rāmāyaṇa*, we observe the conduct of Arjuna, the great king Raghu, and others adopting the three-fold staff— then that is incorrect. For in that very same [text]:
The staff for Brahmins is single; for Kṣatriyas, it is triple-staffed;
and for Vaiśyas, it is likewise declared to be provided with a cord and a knot.
Inner knowledge is indeed truth, while the staff of speech is proclaimed [to be the second];
one's own duties pertaining to the stages of life are called the staff of action.
Meditation on Śiva, beginning with tranquility (śama), is declared to be the mental staff (manodaṇḍa).
Having taken up the single bamboo staff known as the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa), the ascetic (yati) should conduct himself.
Thus says Śātātapa:
"Whether he has a topknot, matted hair, or a shaven head, a Brāhmaṇa who is most learned in the Vedas should carry the single staff of Brahmā; ascetics of undivided mind [should likewise do so]."
The Kuṭīcaka and other ascetics are remembered as Vasiṣṭha and others;
the Bahūdaka and other ascetics are Vyāsa, Śveta, Upamanyu, and so forth.
For them as well, there is the state of carrying a single staff, along with the topknot and the sacred thread;
by the mere sight of him, he is considered a Brāhmaṇa in the world, and he should carry only one staff.
Thus, the Bahūdaka renunciant carries one staff and a water-pot.
One should wear the topknot, the sacred thread, the saffron robe, the deerskin, and so forth.

This is also evident from the *Vṛddha-Śātātapa*: "The staff of speech (*vāg-daṇḍa*) is restraint of speech; the staff of mind (*manas-daṇḍa*) is control of the mind; the staff of action (*karman-daṇḍa*) is steadfastness in the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). Because of this instruction, having abandoned the staffs of speech and the others in the form of bamboo, the staff of Brahman (*brahma-daṇḍa*) alone is prescribed by rule for the Brahmins who are perpetual celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*).
It is determined that [the vow] must be maintained until the fall of the body.

Furthermore, if it is argued that the right to hear the Vedānta belongs exclusively to ascetics (*yatins*) because of the observation of injunctions such as "having renounced, one should listen to the Vedānta," it is replied:
The determination that even a teacher must necessarily take refuge in the state of a householder is established here:
"Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brāhmaṇa should attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created [transient].
For the sake of realizing That, he should approach a teacher alone—with fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and firmly established in Brahman. Thus it is said.
By demonstrating that the disciple has fuel in his hand, it is taught that the teacher also belongs to the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*).

By the instruction regarding his being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), the teacher’s avoidance of prohibited actions is indicated; and by the phrase "established in Brahman," his preeminence in being solely devoted to Śiva—preceded by the refutation of the wicked doctrine of the non-duality of speech—is stated. For this very reason:
Even for those in the stages of life beginning with the student (brahmacarya), hearing, reflecting, and so forth upon the Vedānta is not contradictory.
Therefore, it is logical that karma, which consists of ignorance, serves as an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman.
This concludes the section on "Mere Praise" (Stutimātra). 3.
Indeed, the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*) cannot be enjoined like the celibacy (*brahmacarya*) that is a constituent part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*),
because Vedic statements such as "one who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality" lack the status of authoritative proof for you, even for those who are dispassionate.
In response to the doubt that only those duties recited in the section on Dharma (Dharmaprakaraṇa) are mandatory, he presents another topical section (adhikaraṇa) to refute that view: "265.
[Sūtra 21: 'If it be argued that it is mere praise because of its inclusion, we say no, for it is like the previous case.'"

In the Taittirīya, it is heard: "Not by action. Here, a doubt arises as to whether these sentences negating action are intended solely for the purpose of praising the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), or whether they are intended as injunctions. [The opponent argues: Because injunctions such as "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives" are more powerful, and because no specific injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is observed within those [renunciatory] passages.

Since even for the wise, such as Janaka and others, the necessity of performing rites like the *agnihotra* is demonstrated, it follows that the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) is merely a figurative praise; to this we reply:
[we shall explain] the scriptural, traditional, and authoritative texts (*śruti-smṛti-āgama*) that enjoin renunciation for those who have sublimated their vital energy.

If it be argued that this is merely a commendatory statement (*stuti*) because it is based on a reference to something else, we say no; for it has been previously explained in an unambiguous form as an injunction in earlier *śruti* and *smṛti* texts such as the Jābāla:
"Having completed his student life (*brahmacarya*), he should become a householder; from the household, having become a forest-dweller, he should renounce;
or otherwise, he may renounce directly from student life. Thus it is stated in the Jābāla.
Manu has declared that when one has fallen into imminent, terrible danger, such as being in the range of thieves, tigers, and the like, one who has encountered fear may undertake renunciation.
In the case of those who are ill, there is neither formal procedure nor ritual action for renunciation;
having merely uttered the *praiṣa* (the call), one should complete the renunciation therein.
When the eleventh day has arrived, the pārvaṇa rite is prescribed;
one should not perform any rite other than the pārvaṇa for a mendicant who has become one with Brahman.
Whether he is diseased, devoted to knowledge, a yogi, or even weak,
such a person deserves to eat almsfood from his sons, friends, and wife.

Thus, since the prescription of that [renunciation] has been elaborated without ambiguity even in the Smṛtis of Śaunaka, Bṛhad-Śātātapa, and others, it is established that the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsāśrama), like the student life (brahmacarya) which is an auxiliary to ritual action, is something to be performed by the force of scriptural injunction.
On this point, he states another reason:
|| 266 || "And because of the word 'bhāva'. || 22 ||

"Having abandoned these Vedas and both this world and the next, one should seek the Self"— thus [it is said] in the Śrutis and in the Hārīta-smṛti: "Kaśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Gautama..."
Kapila and Amaṇḍapāla were those who took refuge in the path of the Kuṭīcaka.
Śveta, Upamanyu, Durvāsas, Vyāsa, Nārada, Śaunaka, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Dadhīci are remembered as the Bahūdakas and the Pathas.
Śāṇḍilya, Puliha, Anata, Gārgeya,
and likewise Muṇḍaka are declared to be Haṃsa-saṃnyāsins, who are solely devoted to the meditation on the Vow (vow of silence).
Yājñavalkya, Jābāla, Kaṇva, and Maitreya—
these are declared to be Parahaṃsas, wearing matted hair and bark garments.

From such passages as these, and from the observation of the nature, terminology, and conduct of the four types of renunciants beginning with the *kuṭīcaka*, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is ordained even for those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*) during the Kali age. Nevertheless:
"The student (*baṭu*) has one sacred thread (*upavīta*); likewise, two are held for the other two [the *kuṭīcaka* and *bahūdaka*]."
"For ascetics there should be only one [robe]; such is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures."
He who eats or voids excrement or urine without the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) should be known as a heretic, excluded from all religious rites.
The renunciation prescribed by the Śruti is intended for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
whereas for Śūdras, women, and those of mixed caste, there is a renunciation known as "non-Śrauta."
"Being endowed with the topknot and the sacred thread, and marked by the staff and the saffron robe—
this is declared to be the Śrauta-sannyāsa, according to the words of Vyāsa."
Renunciation is recorded as being of two kinds, distinguished by the Vedic (śrauta) and non-Vedic (aśrauta) methods.
The former is characterized by the possession of a patched garment, saffron robes, a staff, a topknot, sacred threads, and so forth.
What is called Śrauta-saṃnyāsa is declared to be the direct and sole means for achieving liberation;
the Śrauta-saṃnyāsa for Brahmins is extolled by Vyāsa as the [appropriate path] in the Kali age.
Therefore, a Brahmin endowed with dispassion should take recourse to the Śrauta-saṃnyāsa;
for them, that recitation of the Vedas and Vedāntas is prescribed.

This is determined by the consensus of Hārīta, Śātātapa, Śaunaka, Gautama, Pārāśara, and others through such statements as: "From the worship of the Gāyatrī, which is perfectly established as the single Brahmasūtra," and so forth;
for here there is no intent merely to praise renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), as in the injunction: "One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice as long as one lives."
It should be understood that words have a scope exceeding [their literal meaning]. This concludes the section concerning the *pāriplava* (the revolving narrative). 4.

Having established, through this collection of sūtras, that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is conducive to the knowledge of Brahman, [the author] now proceeds to demonstrate that even the subsidiary narratives (upākhyānas), though read within the section on the knowledge of Brahman, are likewise conducive to the knowledge of Brahman.

Having raised an objection regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning those passages situated within the Upaniṣads—specifically the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī—he refutes it by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*):
"Should it be argued that [these stories] are for the purpose of the *pāriplava*, we say no, because of their being specified. (Sūtra 23)

The *pāriplava* is a specific ritual act that constitutes a subsidiary part of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). In that rite, the mantras belonging to all the constituent parts of rituals such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* are to be recited. This being the case, narrative compositions in the form of dialogues such as the conversation between Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī must also serve the purpose of the *pāriplava*.
If it is argued that [these stories] are merely subsidiary parts of the ritual known as *pāriplava* belonging to the *karmakāṇḍa*, we say no; for they are specifically qualified.
It has been stated with specific qualification that "the mantras that are subsidiary parts of all rituals found in the *karmakāṇḍa* are to be recited during the *pāriplava*.
And thus, [this does not apply] to the narratives situated in the *jñānakāṇḍa*.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that there is no possibility of these [narratives] being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the *pāriplava* rites belonging to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). Regarding the narratives in the Vedāntas, such as "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, approached the beloved abode of Indra" and "Śvetaketu, the son of Varuṇa, was [present]," are they intended for the performance of the *pāriplava*, or...?
There is a doubt as to whether these [passages] are intended for the instruction of specific branches of knowledge.

What, then, is the prima facie view? Since they "recite the narratives" (*ākhyānāni śaṃsanti*), the narratives are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the circumambulatory recitation). In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, having seated the king together with his household before him, the Vedic narratives [are to be told].
The duties to be recited by the *adhvaryu* are as follows: this ritual act known as the *pāriplava* is enjoined by the statement, "One should recite the *pāriplava*";

furthermore, because of the application (viniyoga) stating, "They recite all the narratives (*ākhyāna*) during the *pāriplava*," it follows that the introductory stories such as the *Āpya-ākhyāyikā* found at the beginning of the Upaniṣads are for that purpose alone; therefore, it is argued that it is not logical to maintain that knowledge (*vidyā*) is the primary subject matter. To this, it is replied:

"Not so, because they are specified. Thus, those [narratives] do not have the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the daily recitation). This is because the narratives intended for the *pāriplava*—such as "On the first day, King Manu Vaivasvata;

on the second day, King Yama Vaivasvata," and so forth—are specifically distinguished from the narratives of the Upaniṣads. When there is syntactic unity with ritual actions, then [the connection] is through knowledge (*vidyā*) and the like.

There is syntactical unity [of purpose]. Therefore, it is determined that the narrative passages (ākhyāna-śruti) found in all the Vedāntas do not serve the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitations, but rather serve the purpose of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
And likewise, because of the connection within a single sentence. || 24 ||

Furthermore, because they are connected as a single syntactical unit with injunctions such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," it is understood that these narratives have the purpose of supporting the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyā*). For instance, [the narrative] beginning with "He wept" serves the purpose of an injunction for ritual action (*karman*).
This being the case, since the narratives do not function as subordinate elements of the *pāriplava* recitations, they are understood through their connection as a single syntactical unit.

It has been stated that [the story] is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). It is now explained that when the teaching of Brahman is presented preceded by such a narrative, the knowledge of Brahman arises with ease even for those of dull intellect, since the entire process is complete.
This concludes the section concerning fire, fuel, and so forth (Agnīndhanādyadhikaraṇa). 5.
The notion that rites such as the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) are the primary cause for the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) is inconsistent;

for in the *Manusmṛti*, through passages such as "Having discharged the three debts, one should fix the mind on liberation," it is indicated that even for those devoid of passion (*virāgin*), rites like the *ādhāna* are mandatory. Furthermore, this is evident from the preceding context of the scriptural text beginning with "Not by action" (*na karmaṇā*).

Since it is established by implication that [liberation] depends on rituals such as the laying of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), one might ask: "How can even those devoid of passion (*virāgin*) be exempt from the necessity of depending on the laying of the fires and other rites? Anticipating this doubt, he presents another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*):
And for this very reason, there is no dependence on fire, fuel, and so forth. || 25 ||

Since it was previously indicated that the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)— consisting of the limbs of hearing, reflection, and so forth, accompanied by meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and the like— belongs primarily to those who have shaken off the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the desire for wife, the desire for sons, and the desire for wealth, and who are "upward-seeded" (*ūrdhvaretas*), it follows for this very reason that there is no dependence on the kindling of fires and other such ritual requirements.
The subtle meaning of the Sūtra is that it is inconsistent [to claim] that [ritual action] is the primary cause for the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*).

Although in the preceding section it was established that even though ritual action is subordinate to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), the latter has Brahman as its ultimate goal; here, however, [it is shown] that for those in the stage of asceticism (*yatyāśramin*) who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), [action] serves as a subsidiary limb (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman.
It is doubted whether [the soul] is appropriately or inappropriately dependent on rituals such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires).
"He who knows both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—he indeed knows both.
Having crossed over death through ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge."
Thus it is said in the Śruti:
"Relying upon knowledge and established in the science of Brahman, he too performed very many sacrifices in order to cross over death by means of ignorance."

Since the Smṛti also teaches that ritual action is an auxiliary limb of the knowledge of Brahman, it follows that even for those of sublimated sexuality (ūrdhvaretas) who possess such knowledge, rituals such as the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) must indeed be performed as an auxiliary to that knowledge. To this we reply: because the stages of life belonging to those of sublimated sexuality are embraced by Śruti as being connected with knowledge.

"Established in Brahman, one attains immortality; those who, in the forest, worship with faith and austerity—they, being renunciants, depart from home desiring this very world; and desiring that, they practice the life of celibacy," and so forth. For this very reason, among those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), knowledge does not depend upon the kindling of fires and the like. "Kindling of fires" (*agnīndhana*) means the installation of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*).

It is said that knowledge (vidyā) depends solely upon the duties prescribed for its own specific stage of life (āśrama), without requiring rituals such as the Agnihotra or the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are preceded by the formal establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna). The scriptural passage, "Knowledge and ignorance" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12), refers to those who lack dispassion.
This concludes the section on the dependence on all [works] (Sarvāpekṣādhikaraṇa).
How is it that [the means]— purity of mind, dispassion, devotion, compassion for living beings, hearing, reflection, and meditation—
are established as the causes for the direct realization of Paraśiva-Brahman,
given that in the scriptural passage beginning with "By sacrifice, by charity," etc., sacrifices and the like are understood to be the causes for the direct realization of Brahman?
Anticipating the objection that it is untenable for rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma to be auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, he states another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"And there is dependence on all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse. (Sūtra 3.4.26)

By the force of the scriptural statement, "by sacrifice and by charity," it is understood that all forms of expectation—namely, the expectation of all [works] performed daily as offerings to the Supreme Lord—are means [to liberation] through a traditional succession. This is taught to be like a horse:
just as a horse is the cause for reaching a village through a succession of steps in the act of walking, so too is it taught here. And thus, him who...

The meaning of the Sūtra is that there is no lack of authority [in the scriptures], because, according to the Śruti— "Brāhmaṇas desire to know [Brahman] through the study of the Vedas"— rites such as sacrifice, performed for the sake of mental purity, dispassion, devotion, and knowledge, are causes for the direct realization of Paraśiva-Brahman. In the preceding section, it was established that for those who have conquered their senses and possess purified internal organs, there is no requirement for rites such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires).
It is established that [liberation] is possible. Here, it is considered whether or not householders possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
One should renounce and engage in the hearing of the Vedāntas; "there is nothing unattained by means of what is attained"—for the sake of realizing That...

If it is argued that— on account of such injunctions as "one should approach the teacher with fuel in hand," which indicate both [the necessity of a teacher and the performance of rites], and on account of the maxim "one should not perform fruitless action"— it is appropriate for householders as well to require rituals such as the kindling of fire for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*),
we reply: no, because it is impossible for those [rites] to be invariably auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*).

As for the inference that "the knowledge under dispute depends on ritual action as its constituent part, because it accepts such dependence, like the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices which depend on the Prayāja offerings," in that case, what kind of "constituent status" (aṅgatva) is to be proven regarding the fire-installation (ādhāna) and so forth? Is it being a subsidiary that assists toward the result, like the Prayāja offerings; or is it like threshing (avaghāta) and so forth?

Or [is it] being an auxiliary to its own nature? Not the first, because if liberation were produced by that [action], it would be non-eternal. In the second case, the illustrative example would lack the probandum.
Therefore, action is not an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). Consequently, since knowledge does not depend on action even for householders, this being the position reached—
We explain:

by such passages as "The Brāhmaṇas seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through charity," and so forth, sacrifices and the like are indeed heard of as being auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). Through sacrifice and the rest they "seek to know" (*vividiṣanti*), meaning they desire to know; that is, through sacrifice and the rest, [they attain] knowledge.

The meaning is "they desire to attain. It is only when sacrifices are means for attaining knowledge that the designation "they desire to attain knowledge through sacrifices and so forth" becomes logical. Just as there is the designation "they wish to kill with a sword" only when the sword is a means for killing, so too it is understood that sacrifices and the like are means for attaining knowledge. And knowledge—

Distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, it is denoted by such terms as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsana*); it possesses the nature of an extremely vivid direct perception, is of the form of revealed scripture (*śruti*), is unsurpassedly dear,
and is characterized by an excellence that is to be acquired through daily practice until the moment of death.

We have already stated previously that this is the means for liberation, and [the author] will state further: "There is repetition because of the repeated instruction," and so forth. And such meditation is performed daily through obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites.

It is established by the scripture that [knowledge] arises through the propitiation of Śiva, by means of Śiva’s grace; thus, it is taught that "those who desire to know [Brahman] do so through sacrifice and other such acts.
Therefore, for householders engaged in ritual action, knowledge depends upon all obligatory and occasional rites such as sacrifice.
Just as a horse, which serves as a means of locomotion, requires the binding of its harness and grooming, so too [is it with knowledge].
Even knowledge, which serves as the means to liberation, requires the support of obligatory and occasional ritual acts. Regarding this, Kṛṣṇa himself has said:
"Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—action is not to be abandoned; it must indeed be performed."
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed the purifiers of the wise.
Since He is the source from which all beings proceed and by whom all this is pervaded,
a human being attains perfection by worshipping Him with his own prescribed duty.

Thus, from this observation, it is logical that for householders knowledge depends on sacrifices and the like, and for those in all stages of life (āśramas), it depends on the duties prescribed for their respective stages; this concludes the section concerning tranquility and other qualities (Śamādyadhikaraṇa). || 7 ||

The determination that tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth must necessarily be practiced by those in all stages of life (*āśrama*) as auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*),

because of the observation of scriptural passages such as "This very [Self]... by the recitation of the Vedas" (*tam etam vedānuvacanena*), which show that they are auxiliary limbs to knowledge even for householders.

The necessity of performing rituals such as sacrifices is logical; for the Śruti states, "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self in the very Self," and from this it is understood that tranquility and the like alone are the primary causes for the direct realization of Brahman. Thus, for all those in the various stages of life (āśramas), knowledge is paramount.
To address the doubt as to how this is so, he states another topical section (adhikaraṇa):

"Nevertheless, one should be endowed with tranquility and the rest, because they are enjoined by that [injunction] as its constituent parts, and therefore they too must necessarily be practiced. (Sūtra 27)

For all those belonging to the stages of life (āśramins) who possess the direct realization of Sadāśiva-Brahman, there must be the possession of tranquility and other qualities as internal means (*antaraṅgasādhana*).
Why? Because they are qualified by tranquility and the rest; for [tranquility etc.
are prescribed as the direct means toward the direct realization of Sadāśiva-Brahman by virtue of being its internal means. Thus it is with respect to them.
Because tranquility, self-control, and so forth are enjoined by the scriptural statement "one who is tranquil and self-controlled," these means— tranquility, self-control, and the rest—

which are internal instruments for the direct realization of Supreme Śiva, must necessarily be practiced; therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is that tranquility and the other qualities must invariably be accomplished by all possessors of Brahma-vidyā.

Based on the scriptural statement, "He is peaceful and self-controlled," it is deliberated whether tranquility and the like are enjoined for all stages of life (*āśrama*) or specifically for the stage of the ascetic (*yati*):
[the opponent argues] that tranquility and the like do not pertain to the student (*brahmacārin*) and others, because in the case of the student...

Because the mental faculties of householders are distracted by activities such as the study of the Vedas, and because tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities have no opportunity due to the labor involved in performing the rites prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*; and because it is understood that for forest-dwellers (*vanin*),
[the path] abounds in many hardships such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances— by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa-pramāṇa*).

For ascetics who are free from objective support (nirābhāra), tranquility and the like are indeed appropriate; it has been taught that such qualities as "being tranquil" and "being self-controlled" refer precisely to them.
Tranquility (śama) is the pacification of internal passion and hatred, while self-control (dama) is the cessation of the activity of all the sense organs.

*Uparati* is the cessation of engagement in prohibited and desire-driven actions; *samādhāna* is one-pointedness of mind toward pleasure, pain, enemies, friends, and so forth; and [the abandonment of] evil scriptures preceded by steadfastness in the Vedas and Agamas, which are the source of unsurpassed bliss.

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the practice of virtuous conduct (*sadācāra*) consisting of hearing, chanting, and service to Śiva according to the Vedas, preceded by a turning away from all other deities through the actions of mind,

speech, and body; it is born from the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal realities, which serves as the basis for being beheld by the glance of the Goddess of Liberation, who is characterized by constant and unsurpassed bliss.

When it is argued that such qualities—because they do not pertain to other subjects—are appropriate only for ascetics (*yatis*), we reply: tranquility (*śama*) and the rest must be adopted by those in all stages of life (*āśrama*) as auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman, because there is an injunction for them as being limbs of that knowledge. Therefore, "one who knows thus, having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should perceive the Self within the Self alone."

One should see [the Self]—since the arising of knowledge consists in the concentration of the mind, tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] are its necessary prerequisites; therefore, they must necessarily be practiced for the cessation of ignorance. Furthermore, there is no contradiction, because their spheres of operation are distinct: the operation of the instruments [of action] pertains to what is enjoined, whereas their cessation pertains to what is not enjoined and to that which is devoid of purpose.

Nor is it impossible for one engaged in actions consisting of the operation of the instruments [of body and mind] to adopt tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for prescribed actions, being forms of propitiation of Śiva, serve as the cause for the eradication of all contrary latent impressions by means of His grace. Therefore, for those belonging to all stages of life (*āśrama*),...
Peace, self-control, and other such qualities must also be practiced as auxiliary elements of the knowledge of Brahman. Section on the Permission to Eat All Food (Sarvānnānumati-adhikaraṇa). 8.
Is it not the case that even for those who know Brahman, permission to eat all kinds of food is prescribed only when there is a threat to life?

Should it not rather be that for all those in the various stages of life (āśramas), the injunction to practice tranquility and other virtues through the knowledge of Śiva remains, while their adherence to the duties of their caste and stage of life is also enjoined— given that by the majesty of that knowledge, they become equal to Śiva?
Anticipating the objection that it might be appropriate to act according to one's own will, he presents another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"And there is permission for all food in case of danger to life, because that is seen [in scripture]. (2.3.28)

In the *prāṇavidyā* of both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas, it is proclaimed that for one who knows the *prāṇa*, "nothing whatsoever becomes non-food that has been eaten, nor does anything become non-food that has been accepted"; thus, permission regarding all food is declared for the knower of the *prāṇa*. Does this [apply] to one established in the *prāṇavidyā*?
There arises a doubt: does the permission to eat all food apply at all times, or only in the event of a life-threatening emergency?

This is because the scripture states, "The vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the conscious self (*prajñātman*), having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise," thereby describing the vital breath itself as the conscious self; furthermore, in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*, the preservation of the vital breath is declared to be conducive to the highest good.

Since there is scriptural testimony regarding the transgression incurred by the drying up of the vital breaths (prāṇa), it follows that for the sake of preserving life, the consumption of all kinds of food by noble-souled knowers of Śiva belonging to all stages of life (āśrama) is appropriate due to the absence of injunctions and prohibitions; to this, it is replied: "And in case of danger to life."
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis, meaning "only in the event of a life-threatening emergency. Why? Because that is seen [in scripture].

For it is observed elsewhere that even for those who know Brahman, permission to eat all kinds of food is granted only in the event of life-threatening danger; how much more so, then, for one who knows the Prāṇa? It is said that Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa, a preeminent knower of Brahman, while living in Ibhyagrāma during a famine that had devastated the Kuru country with hailstorms, fell into a state where his life was in danger due to fasting.

Desiring the non-depression of his vital breaths for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman, he begged from a wealthy man who was eating *kulmāṣa* beans; having been told by him, "There are no others than these leavings," he replied again,
"Give me some of these," and from that wealthy man, he received the *kulmāṣa* beans which had been taken from the leavings and given to him.

Having accepted the gift of water for drinking when requested by the wealthy man, Cākrāyaṇa said, "I would have been drinking what is left over. When questioned by the wealthy man, "Are these beans not left over? he replied, "I shall certainly not live on pride; my desire was for the water."

Thus, having said that drinking the leftover water would constitute an act of willful transgression for him— since he had faced a threat to his life while eating the *kulmāṣa* beans and had preserved his life by eating only that much— he gave the remainder of what he had eaten to his wife; and when she had preserved it, on the following day, wishing to go out again with the desire to acquire knowledge, he set forth.

In a situation where his life was in danger, he ate food that had become the leavings of a wealthy man, as well as food that had become his own leavings and food that was stale. Therefore, since the permission to eat any kind of food is seen even for knowers of Brahman only when there is a threat to life,
it is determined that the knower of Prāṇa’s capacity to eat all kinds of food— though mentioned here specifically— is restricted solely to the occurrence of a life-threatening emergency.
Regarding this point, he states another reason: || 273 || "And because there is no contradiction" || 29 ||
The Śruti and Smṛti are my very command; therefore, one should follow that path.
He who acts by transgressing them is a violator of my command and a traitor to me.
A wise person should not transgress Vedic conduct even in thought.

When food is pure, the inner being (sattva) becomes pure; when the inner being is pure, mindfulness becomes firm. Through the attainment of mindfulness, the knot of the heart of all beings is severed.

Thus, when these [scriptures] are spoken, it follows by implication that for all those in the various stages of life (*āśrama*), the performance of the duties of their respective stages is established through the instruction of the supreme Lord’s command. Likewise, although the purification of food is enjoined for the knower of Śiva through such passages as "When food is pure," [it applies] specifically to those who are preeminent in their steadfastness in Śiva-yoga and the knowledge of Śiva.
The practice of eating all kinds of food is understood to apply only in times of distress, not as a matter of free will in ordinary circumstances.
To this point, he states another reason:
"It is also recorded in Smṛti. (Sūtra 30)
The righteous conduct of the castes and stages of life was taught by Śiva in the past;
those who act in violation of these are transgressors of Śiva’s command.
Just as punishment is meted out to men who violate the king’s command,
so too is hell the punishment for those who violate Śiva’s command.
If one abandons the Dharma commanded by Śambhu through Sāmba and worships Śiva [instead],
Śambhu becomes angry with him on account of the violation of his own command.
He who worships Śaṅkara— who has been commanded by Śiva to revere Dharma as characterized by Vedic injunction— becomes gracious toward him, together with Ambā.

Even in such passages as these, which teach that the primary duty consists in performing the actions appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) preceded by the command of the Supreme Lord—
[it is said]: "He who, when his life is in danger, eats food with effort, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water."

Thus, because of the observation of this specific injunction, it is established that the rule for partaking of all kinds of food applies only to those who possess the knowledge of Śiva and belong to any of the stages of life (āśrama) when they are in a state of distress, and not at other times. Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
And from this [it follows] that sounds [are produced] without volitional effort. || 31 ||

Since the eating of all kinds of food by those who know Brahman and others is restricted solely to times of distress, for this very reason the scriptural statement regarding "not acting according to one's desire" (*akāmakāra*) exists as a prohibition against acting according to one's desire (*kāmakāra*). Indeed, there is a scriptural statement in the *Kaṭha Saṃhitā* that prohibits acting according to one's desire: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor, [lest he be] defiled by evil."

The meaning is that a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor, thinking, "Lest I become joined with evil. Even at the cost of losing one's life, one must subsist on mere alms among the four castes; otherwise, by practicing what is forbidden, one would become a traitor to the command of the Supreme Lord—this is certain.
The Section on Being Established by Injunction (Vihi-tattvādhikaraṇa) || 9 ||

The practice of the combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*) is prescribed for all those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*). Although internal means such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), worship (*pūjā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) are ordained for all stages of life as the direct causes for the direct realization of Paraśiva-Brahman, what are the external limbs corresponding to them?
Anticipating the objection that [these works] do exist, he determines [the matter] by means of another scriptural passage:
"And because they are enjoined, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed. (Sūtra 3.4.32)

It has been stated that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) has the performance of sacrifices and other rites as its ancillary. Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether those rites, such as sacrifices, are to be performed by those seeking liberation—even by those belonging solely to the [ascetic] stages of life (āśramas)—or not.

This is based on the scriptural passage: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created [transient]."

Since it has been stated that the fruits of actions are impermanent and that there is no liberation through action, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities is observed. Therefore, it is appropriate that rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma have as their domain those who lack knowledge; for in injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it is understood from scripture that the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites are objects of voluntary desire.

When it is argued that [the fire-sacrifices] cannot belong exclusively to the stage of life (āśrama), we reply: even the duties of the stage of life must be performed, because they are understood through injunctions such as "one should offer the Agnihotra for as long as one lives"; thus, the duty of the stage of life also exists. For those who possess only the stage of life, the mere performance of the stage of life is to be practiced as a subordinate part (aṅga) of the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, because [these actions] are performed with the intention of offering them to the Supreme Lord, and because they were also performed by knowers of Brahman such as Janaka and others,
it is determined that the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarmāṇi*) must be performed by both the learned and the unlearned who are established in the Vedas and Smṛtis. By this,
it is established by implication that the duties of their respective stages of life are prescribed for those belonging to the fourfold stages, beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*).

And likewise, because they are prescribed as auxiliary to knowledge in such passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth, they must be performed even as subordinate elements of knowledge;
thus he says: "And as being cooperative. (Sūtra 3.4.33)
From such passages as, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together," and "He is to be attained through truth,

for this Self is indeed reached through austerity, perfect knowledge, and perpetual celibacy," it is understood that liberation results from the cooperation of both dharma and Brahman; thus, there is the practice of the combination (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action.
This is to be observed by all those belonging to the stages of life (āśrama). Therefore, just as in the case of the Agnihotra and other rites,

for all those established in right conduct (sadācāra) across all stages of life, the wearing of external and internal marks and the performance of worship and so forth are irreproachable, provided they possess the qualification for living [according to the rules].
Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that for both the learned and the unlearned, the performance of duties prescribed for their respective stages of life (*āśrama*) is a limb of liberation.
However, since wearing external and internal marks (*liṅga*) as a limb of liberation is not mandatory for the learned," in response to this doubt, he says:
|| 278 || In every respect, they alone [are the objects of knowledge], because of the twofold characteristic. || 34 ||

In every way, even by a thorough investigation of all the scriptures, through the performance of the rites prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti—such as "one removes evil by means of dharma"—the seeker of liberation whose mind is purified becomes a devotee who establishes the universal form (*sarvaliṅga*) from the dual-form; [this is expressed in the mantra]: "May I become the purifier of the hand, the mantra, the vessel of immortality, and the sustainer of the gods."

They say that the internal mark (*liṅga*) of the mind resides within the vital breaths (*prāṇas*); the waking state is in the filaments (*kesara*), the dreaming state in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), deep sleep in the *liṅga*, and the fourth state (*turīyā*) upon the abandonment of the lotus. This is because, according to hundreds of such scriptural passages, Śiva—the Supreme Brahman—by His own will, for the sake of delivering His devotees, is understood to possess both external and internal forms as the desired object and as the vital breath.
Just as for all members of the various stages of life (āśramins), the duties prescribed for their respective stages are mandatory, so too is meditation on those two forms [of the Lord].
I shall describe the practice of bearing the insignia (liṅga) in accordance with the *caraṇa* and *śruti*,
as it is well-known in the *Smṛtis*, *Tantras*, and *Purāṇas*, and is equally valid for all.

A twice-born man who possesses the primary and secondary marks of his lineage should perform, free from desire, those actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti that pertain to the obligatory and occasional rites.
From the performance of actions prescribed by the injunctions, purification of the mind will certainly arise;
from the purification of the mind, devotion arises—devotion that is unwavering.

Through that [knowledge], wisdom is born and the ignorance of the self perishes; therefore, liberation results from that. Consequently, one should properly perform the action prescribed by the injunctions.
Therefore, a person endowed with good conduct should, with devotion and vigilance, worship the chosen *liṅga* of Maheśvara given by the Guru.
With a pure mind, one should constantly perform this three times a day while seated upon a lotus-like hand.

By such statements, because instruction is given in that manner, the meditation on both [types of] emblems, their wearing, worship, and so forth, are irreproachable for all those in the stages of life who are established in good conduct.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
And he demonstrates non-overpowering. || 35 ||

O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible and free from the appearance of evil—with that most peaceful form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us. May I become a vessel for immortality, O God;
through meditation on Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of all worldly illusion.

Such scriptural passages as these demonstrate that by means of the meditation on Śiva, one attains a body free from sin that manifests Śiva, and that through the concentration on Śiva, the bond of Māyā is brought to an end. Therefore, for those seeking liberation,
the performance of duties prescribed for their own stage of life (*āśrama*) and the meditation on Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, both externally and internally— [are essential].
This must indeed be performed by one who is either a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic;
whoever is endowed with the marks and limbs [of this practice] is truly one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī).
Nevertheless, having performed the duties of one's own stage of life according to the injunctions of the scriptures,
one should practice all [duties], such as the worship of Śiva, throughout one's entire life.
Since this is also seen in the Smṛti, [the conclusion follows]. This concludes the section concerning those who are destitute (vidhurādhikaraṇa). 10.

The determination of the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) for all seekers of liberation, irrespective of whether they belong to a stage of life (āśrama) or are without a stage of life (anāśrama):
Now, it may be argued that their eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman should be established through the performance of the duties of the four types of stages of life prescribed by the Śruti.

In response to the doubt as to how the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) can possibly exist for those who are destitute (*vidhura*), since they lack a stage of life (*āśrama*), he states [the answer] in another section:
"But even in the case of those between [the stages], because that is seen. (Sūtra 3.4.36)

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: when separation from one’s wife occurs due to destiny—that is, by the force of previously accumulated *prārabdha* karma—one may practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*) in the interim; for it is understood that those who possess the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman in this world have the qualification (*adhikāra*) for such practices as meditation (*dhyāna*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), worship (*pūjā*), salutation (*namaskāra*), hearing (*śravaṇa*), and so forth, directed toward the Supreme Śiva-Brahman.
A doubt arises as to whether all those belonging to the stages of life (āśramas) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), or not.

It is argued that those who do not belong to a stage of life—such as the widower (vidhura), the student who has completed his studies (snātaka), and others—certainly lack the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, because in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and other texts, no one outside a stage of life is seen to possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. In the absence of a stage of life...

Since the Smṛtis, such as "A twice-born man may remain [in his order] even for a moment," indicate the rejection of being without an āśrama, and since there is an injunction that for all those in the āśramas, [the pursuit of knowledge] is an auxiliary to Vidyā, it follows that only those in the four āśramas have the qualification for Brahma-vidyā; to this we reply: [The full argument continues: Although the Smṛtis state that one must not remain without an āśrama and enjoin that the practice of the āśramas is an auxiliary to knowledge, we maintain that even those outside the four āśramas possess the qualification for Brahma-vidyā. This is because the Smṛtis themselves acknowledge the existence of other orders, such as the "forest-dweller" (vānaprastha) and the "renunciant" (saṃnyāsin), who are distinct from the four traditional āśramas. Furthermore, the Śruti speaks of the "knower of Brahman" (brahmavid) without specifying any particular āśrama, and the Smṛti declares that "one who has renounced all actions attains the highest peace. Moreover, the fact that the Smṛtis prescribe specific duties for those who have fallen away from their respective āśramas implies that they do recognize the possibility of such a lapse. Therefore, since the Smṛtis do not absolutely exclude those outside the four āśramas, and since the Śruti does not restrict the qualification to any specific stage of life, we conclude that the qualification for Brahma-vidyā belongs to all seekers, regardless of their formal status in the āśramas.
"But even for those in between, because that is seen. Here, the word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the previous position;

the word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of restriction. It is appropriate that even those who exist in the interval—those who do not belong to any stage of life (*anāśramin*)—have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.
Why? Because that is seen. For it is observed in the case of Raikva, Bhīṣma, Saṃvarta, and others.

Even those who do not belong to any stage of life (*anāśramin*) can be devoted to the knowledge of Brahman. Nor can it be asserted that the grace of knowledge is obtained through the duties of the stages of life alone; for it is heard in scripture that even acts such as giving—which are not restricted to the stages of life—are means of grace, as in the passage: "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting. This is just as in the case of those whose semen is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*).

Because we observe that one is established in knowledge (*vidyā*), the support of knowledge is provided by means other than the *agnihotra* and other such rites. Likewise, since we observe the existence of Brahma-knowledge even among those who do not belong to any stage of life (*āśrama*), [knowledge] is supported by practices such as recitation (*japa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and the like, which are not restricted to any particular stage of life.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
It is also recorded in tradition: 37.
Moreover, it is recorded in the Smṛti that even for those not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramin), knowledge is favored by means of recitation (japa) and other such practices:
"A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection even through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
He may perform other rites or he may not; one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa."
For those who are widowed or not widowed, as well as for those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātakas),
knowledge is said to arise from the performance of recitation, fasting, worship, and other such rites.

Based on this observation from the Smṛti, it is determined that even those who are widowed or otherwise deprived must always perform the inquiry into Paraśiva-Brahman through hearing, reflection, and so forth— characterized by a pure internal organ attained through constant single-mindedness and the perfection of virtuous conduct.

Anticipating the objection—namely, how knowledge can arise for those who do not belong to any stage of life (āśrama), such as widowers and others, since they lack the performance of rituals that serve as the means for attaining knowledge—the author says:
"And because of the special favor [of the Lord]. (Sūtra 3.4.38)

Since the Śruti states, "One should seek the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge," and since it is heard that knowledge is aided by specific dharmas not restricted to the [four] stages of life (āśrama), it is determined that even those such as the widower (vidhura) possess an incontestable eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.
Regarding this matter, he states another reason:
"But for this reason, the other is superior, and because of the indicative mark. (Sūtra 3.1.39)

Since, through such passages as "May I become a bearer of the nectar of the gods; may my body be most excellent," the wearing of the *liṅga* (emblem) is shown— just like the duties of the four *āśramas*— to be common to both those in *āśramas* and those not in *āśramas*, it follows that the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is superior for all seekers of liberation, regardless of whether they belong to an *āśrama* or not.

It is the most excellent. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Having stated that the indicative mark possesses the nature of the universal self by beginning with "Obeisance to the Lord of the Nidhana," the Śruti declares: "This is the all-pervading form of Soma and Sūrya; he establishes it as the purifying mantra upon the hand.

Thus, because the supreme Brahman in the form of the *liṅga* is described as purifying, it is [the goal] for those in the stages of life (*āśramiṇaḥ*) as well as for those not in such stages (*anāśramiṇaḥ*).
The qualification for the knowledge of Brahman is beyond reproach:
"A twice-born man should not remain even for a single day without belonging to an āśrama;
if he remains so out of delusion, he is not touched by merit."

This statement should be understood as referring to the domain of those who have not yet attained dispassion (*avirāga*). This is because in such scriptural passages as "Know [it] through the yoga of faith, devotion, and knowledge," faith, devotion, and so forth are taught as the primary means for attaining Śiva; furthermore, in all the scriptures, it is understood that specific knowledge (*viśeṣavidyā*) overrides general scripture (*sāmānyaśāstra*).
"From one stage of life he should go to another; otherwise, he would not attain liberation"—since such statements are general in nature, their relative weakness is appropriate.
This concludes the section on "That Being" (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa). 11.

Regarding the question of whether those who have performed expiation— specifically those outside the stages of life such as the *snātaka* and the widower (*vidhura*), as well as those who have fallen from their own stage of life (*svāśramabhraṣṭa*) and the perpetual celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*)— possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) on account of their self-control, charity, austerity, and so forth, Jaimini maintains that they do indeed possess such qualification.
To dispel that doubt, he shows another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"But for one who has become that [state], there is no non-becoming of that state, according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rule and because of the absence of that form. (Sūtra 4.1.40)

For a person who has become such—that is, one who has entered the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*)—the state of "not being that" (i.e., falling away from the stage of renunciation) is not something unenjoined by the scriptures; on the contrary, it is indeed prohibited by the scriptures. Why? Because of the restrictive rules (*niyama*) and because of the absence of those [worldly] forms. After having attained the stage of renunciation, there are restrictive rules (*niyama*).

One must remain in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa-āśrama) until the end of life and not return from it; for this reason, as well as due to the absence of contrary statements— that is, the absence of any statements contradicting the injunctions of Manu and others that establish this rule— there is no falling away from the stage of life.

It is said that this is prohibited by the scriptures. Therefore, since there is no other stage of life (*āśrama*) superior to that, one must remain in that very state for as long as one lives; such is the meaning of the Sūtra.
"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they [dwell] in the world of Brahman."

"At the time of the final end, all are completely liberated through the supreme nectar. [And] "Having renounced [worldly ties], one should engage in the hearing of the Vedānta," and so forth— in such passages, although the qualification for the uninterrupted inquiry into Brahman is heard to belong primarily to ascetics (*yatis*) among all those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramas*), nevertheless, as in the case of the widower (*vidhura*) and others, this applies even to those who have fallen from their stage of life or to those firmly established in their own stage of life.
The subject matter is the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Since it is understood from such passages as "Having renounced, one should engage in the hearing of the Vedānta" that those who have fallen away from renunciation lack the qualification, [the sequence is: having completed the stage of studenthood (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller.

Just as the rule for ascending to the stages of life (*āśrama*) has been shown— namely, "having become a forest-dweller (*vanī*), one should go forth [as a mendicant]"— since no such rule is seen regarding descending from them, their dependence on personal choice must be established through inference. Therefore, like those who are incapacitated (*vidhura*) and so forth, those who have fallen away from the stages of life are qualified for the knowledge of Brahman.

When it is argued that [the renunciate] is thus [bound by rules], we state the reply to that: "But for one who has become that, there is no non-becoming of that. The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the previous position. For one who has "become that"—that is, one established in a lifelong stage of life (naiṣṭhika) and so forth—there is "no non-becoming of that.
That is to say, the state of not being such, namely remaining in a state of homelessness, is not possible. Why? Because of the absence of the characteristics of that [state].

"By rule from their forms": the forms of those such as the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong student) are their dress and duties; the absence of these is "the absence of their forms. From these, by rule, according to the scripture. For the scriptures do indeed restrict the establishment in the stages of life (*āśrama*) of the *naiṣṭhika* and others by means of the cessation of the duties of their own respective stages. [As it is said: "The religious student (*brahmacārin*) shall dwell in the teacher's household."
"The third [type of student] is one who, having exhausted himself completely in the teacher's family, should go to the forest and never return from there;

he should renounce the sacred fire and not return. Therefore, because it is impossible for those such as the *naiṣṭhika* (lifelong celibates) to remain in a state of being without an āśrama—just like widowers and others—the knowledge of Brahman does not qualify them. This is also the consensus of Jaimini.
Showing what has been stated, he confirms his own position:

"Now, it might be argued that for perpetual students (*naiṣṭhika*) and others who have fallen from their vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), eligibility [for the path] is possible through expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

And there exists such an expiation, as established in the definition of eligibility: 'And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and likewise [others]'. Therefore...

Since an expiation is possible for one who has fallen away from the life of a religious student (brahmacarya), it might be argued that such a person, having performed the expiation, will be qualified for the knowledge of Brahman; to this, he says:
"Nor [is there qualification] even for one who holds an office, because of the inference of falling away, as that [expiation] is impossible. (Sūtra 3.4.41)
Even the expiation (prāyaścitta) described for those qualified [for it] is not possible for lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and others who have fallen from their state,
because there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding the downfall of such lifelong celibates and the impossibility of that expiation for them:
"That twice-born man who, having ascended to the duty of a lifelong celibate, falls away..."
"I see no expiation by which that self-killer might be purified. Thus,
one who, having relied upon the highest mode of life, resorts to a new (lower) mode of life,
is to be known as one who has fallen from his elevated state and is excluded from all ritual acts.

Based on the understanding of numerous such Smṛti texts, it should be known that the expiation (prāyaścitta) pertains to other types of religious students (brahmacārins). Regarding the determination of the scriptural validity of expiations for mental and dream-state sins committed by ascetics (yatis), as well as the cessation of expiation for sins arising from the egoistic gross body committed by them themselves: [The following verses provide this determination: "Even for one who has fallen from his vow, there is no loss of merit; he remains a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and is not a sinner. He is not subject to the rules of the world, nor does he incur sin through actions performed with the mind, speech, or body. "For the sake of the welfare of the world, the Lord established the fourfold order of life (āśrama). One should follow that very path; there is no other way. "The wise man should not abandon the duties of his own stage of life (svadharma); even if they appear difficult, he should practice them with devotion. By performing his own duty, he attains perfection. "One should not abandon the duties of one's own stage of life out of delusion or laziness. Even a low-caste person, by performing his own duty, attains the highest state. "Whether he be a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant, one should perform the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life according to the scriptures. "Even if one has fallen from the vows of his stage of life, he is purified by repentance and austerity. There is no destruction of dharma for one who acts according to the scriptures. "By the performance of one’s own duty, one attains the supreme goal. There is no higher path than this for the liberation of the self. Thus, it is established that while expiation is required for those who have transgressed the specific rules of their stage of life, for ascetics, there is no expiation for mental or dream-state faults, nor for those arising from the identification with the gross body, as these do not constitute a fall from the essential nature of their renunciation. This is the scriptural conclusion.
In this regard, he shows another reason: || 286 || "Some say that even when preceded by 'upa', it denotes a state (bhāva), like eating; so it has been said. || 42 ||

The teachers maintain that for perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, the falling away from celibacy is a minor offense (*upapātaka*), since it is not enumerated among the great sins (*mahāpātaka*); therefore, they consider that there exists a penance (*prāyaścitta*) for it, just as there is for eating honey and so forth— just as there is a prohibition against eating honey and the like, so too is there a penance for it.
This applies equally to those who provide assistance, such as lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) and others. As it has been stated by the authors of the *Smṛtis*:

"And this is not in conflict with those who follow the subsequent stages. The meaning is that whatever has been prescribed for those dwelling in the teacher's house (*gurukula*) applies to the practitioners of the subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*) provided it does not conflict with their own specific stage. The same principle holds here as well.

Since there is the possibility of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for lapsing from celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one also possesses the fitness for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Nevertheless, it is determined that while expiation such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance may apply to mental sins and sins committed in dreams, no expiation is possible for sins committed by the gross body through egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
Thus it is stated by Śātātapa: "For ascetics who are solely devoted to Sadāśiva and possess the luster of Brahman,
[attachment] toward women and wealth arises due to a single sin committed in a previous life."
If a firm attachment to sons and others has arisen in an ascetic,
he should constantly perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the sole purpose of removing that fault.
If a mendicant should experience union with a wife in a dream,
he must perform a hundred ablutions with clay for the pacification of that fault.
If a renunciant, through acting according to his own whims, becomes greedy for women, wealth, and the like, he indeed falls immediately; there is no atonement for him.
This has been elaborated upon in many ways through such passages.
Regarding the prohibition of ascetics who have fallen from their vows from having the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman,
he states another reason for this point:
|| 287 || But outside [the village], it is in both ways, because of Smṛti and custom. || 43 ||

The word *tu* here signifies certainty. Whether they are guilty of minor offenses (*upapātaka*) or major sins (*mahāpātaka*), these persons are indeed excluded from those qualified for the knowledge of Brahman; the meaning is that they are disqualified for the knowledge of Brahman. Why? Because of traditional scripture (*smṛti*).

Although, based on the aforementioned Smṛti texts concerning falling [from caste], there exists for some an eligibility for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) through certain statements for the removal of defilement, nevertheless, an expiation that serves as a cause for purification corresponding to the eligibility for ritual action (*karmādhikāra*) is not possible; for the Smṛti states: "I see no expiation by which that self-slayer might be purified."
And because of [the evidence of] conduct. For cultured people (śiṣṭas) avoid lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhikas) and others who have fallen from their vows even after they have performed penance;
they do not impart to them the knowledge of Brahman and so forth. Therefore, they have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman. This concludes the section on the Master (svāmin). 12.
An exposition on Śiva alone being the bestower of the fruits of ritual action and the worship of Brahman:
"Indeed,
for those who violate the king's command, hell is the punishment" (Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi).

In such Smṛtis as these, the punishment of Yama is indicated for all those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas), even including those who have fallen away from their own stage through violation of Śiva’s command. Nevertheless, because the Sūtra "sarvāpekṣā ca" (and there is dependence on all) declares that sacrifices and other duties are limbs of liberation independently— like a horse [reaching] a village— the punishment for falling from one's own stage of life is prescribed here.

In response to the doubt as to how [the status of being the Lord of Sacrifice] is possible for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, he demonstrates that even the state of being the Lord of Sacrifice belongs to Śiva alone through another scriptural section:
"Because the fruit is declared for the master; thus says Ātreya" (Sūtra 3.4.44).

In the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], the following and other passages are heard: "Viṣṇu indeed [performed] the two sacrifices; he protected the king of the sacrifice, Rudra, the Hotṛ priest who truly sacrifices for the two worlds; Paśupati is the lord of animals, both four-footed and two-footed. Regarding this, there is a doubt as to whether the Lord of Sacrifice is Nārāyaṇa or Śiva, who is the form of the Supreme Brahman.

Because of the teaching that Nārāyaṇa alone is the essence of sacrifice in passages such as "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu," and because of the statement of Nārāyaṇa’s supreme preeminence over all in texts such as "That one Viṣṇu is the highest; there was only Nārāyaṇa, neither Brahmā nor Īśāna," [He is to be worshipped] in all Smārta rituals, including the preliminary mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth.

Since he is to be propitiated by means of ritual action preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu’s names, it follows by implication that this [propitiation] belongs to Him alone. Therefore, when it is argued that His being the essence of sacrifice, His being the Lord of sacrifice, and His being the giver of the fruits of sacrifice are appropriately attributed to Him alone, we reply: "Because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit."

Regarding the passage "ā vo rājānam," Ātreya maintains that because of the mention of the fruit [of the rite]—namely, "Rudra, the king and lord of the *adhvara* sacrifice"—Lord Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the object of worship for all branches of knowledge (*sarvavidyopāsya*).
Furthermore, by such passages as "We worship Tryambaka," His very status as the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñeśvaratva*) is taught. He who indeed...

"He sacrifices beyond his own deity; he falls away from his own deity and does not reach the higher one; he becomes worse," because of such scriptural declarations regarding the sin incurred by sacrificing to a deity other than one's own. This is seen in such Vedic texts as: "That syllable, that which is to be sought through the splendor of Savitṛ, and from which ancient wisdom has issued forth."

Since it is observed that Śiva alone is the referent of the Gāyatrī mantra, which upholds all Vedic rites, it is not possible for anyone else to be the object of worship in rituals such as sacrifices.
"The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."
The supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.
May that God— who is the first to arise among the gods, who transcends all, who is Rudra the great seer— unite us with auspicious understanding;
he who is the sovereign of the gods, upon whom the worlds are supported.
To him who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to that god let us do honor with an oblation.
By such passages in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, since it is taught that He alone is the presiding overseer of all actions and is superior to the universe,
it is determined that Śiva alone is the bestower of the fruits of all actions, by virtue of His superiority over all karma and being propitiated by all karma.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"Auḍulomi [holds that] the office of the officiating priest [belongs to the disciple], for he is hired for that purpose. (Sūtra 3.4.45)
