"O Lord of animals, I bind this animal for you today at the beginning, in the midst of the well-performed rite; grant your consent, O Sacrificer, as we sacrifice.

May this offering be pleasing to the gods. At this point, the officiating priest's function related to the *ṛc* verses, the ritual acts involving the binding of the animal, and the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) are performed as an offering to Paramaśiva.

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that it is Śiva alone who is appropriately the object of worship for all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), because he is established as being worthy of the gods. Why? Because in passages such as "To him [is offered] service, who is Rudra in the fire," his status as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all is shown;
in "All is indeed Rudra," his nature as the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*) is shown; and in "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to the universe," his transcendence over the entire world is shown.

In such passages, His being superior to the universe is established by the very teaching [of this text]; this is appropriate for Him alone, and not for another, such as Indra, Upendra, Dinendra, or Mahendra.

Furthermore, by the scriptural injunction that "he chooses the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*) and "he gives the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests" (*ṛtvigbhyo dakṣiṇāṃ dadāti*), the agency belongs to the officiating priests.
It is understood that the ritual action, together with its constituent parts, which serves as the means for attaining the fruit, is to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Although the physical and mental actions included therein have the priests as their agents, the fruit nevertheless accrues to the owner of that [action].

Similarly, even the enjoyment of fruits such as heaven granted to deities like Indra, mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of a sacrifice, is logically possible only for Śiva, who is their inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and their regulator. Therefore, although in injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the Jyotiṣṭoma has heaven as its fruit, and although that heaven primarily belongs to the deity Indra—
"Indra is the performer of sacrifice and Lord of Speech is the author of the Vedas;
I alone am the creator of the world, while Maheśvara is my creator"—
even though in the Skanda Purāṇa it is thus established by Viṣṇu that Indra alone is the performer of sacrifice, [there remains] Śiva, who is distinct from Pākaśāsana (Indra).

There is no contradiction in the authority of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas which establish that the Supreme Brahman is the performer of sacrifice. In the passage "Sacrifice is indeed Viṣṇu," Viṣṇu, who consists of both Śiva and Śakti, is shown to be the embodiment of sacrifice. Furthermore, in the verse "To you, the King of the sacrifice, Rudra... (RV 1.43.1), Rudra is designated as the Lord of sacrifice and other rites without any limitation.
It is established that it is improper for one whose nature is the sacrifice to be the lord of the sacrifice.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
"And because of scripture" (4.1.4).

From such passages as, "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda— may Śiva be my auspiciousness, Sadāśiva," it is understood that Śiva alone is the controller of all knowledge and all living beings;
thus, it is established that Śiva alone is the bestower of the fruits of ritual action and the meditation upon Brahman.
The Section Concerning the Injunction of Another Auxiliary Means (Sahakāryantaravidhyadhikaraṇa) || 13 ||
The determination that scholarship, silence, and so forth are auxiliaries to knowledge, like tranquility (śama) and self-restraint (dama): Now,

for those meditators on Brahman whose internal organs have been purified by sacrifices, gifts, austerities, worship, and the like offered to the Supreme Lord, is there not a necessity for steadfastness in silence, just as there is for tranquility and self-restraint?

Anticipating the objection that this work might primarily consist of rhetorical flourish, like the grammatical treatises of Pāṇini or the philosophical systems of Kaṇāda and others, he presents another topical section:
"An injunction for another auxiliary is stated as a third alternative for one who possesses [the knowledge], as in the case of Vidyā and so forth. (Sūtra 4.1.47)

Just as in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), where for one belonging to a household stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) many rites such as the *agnihotra* are prescribed with heaven as their intended fruit, so too, for a person possessing that [knowledge]—namely, one possessing the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—there is an injunction regarding another auxiliary factor in the scriptural text of the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*), namely: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having discarded scholarship... (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*). This is like the case of knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth.

In relation to tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, among the three auxiliary means— listening (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)— both listening and reflection must be practiced for a long duration by all who desire the direct realization of that [Reality]. As for the third, meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), it depends on the ripening of time.

This must be practiced. Even after hearing and reflecting, for practitioners, the identification with the body—such as "I am a Brahmin," "I am lean," "I am the doer," and "I am the enjoyer"—remains firm.
Therefore, they must perform *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) in order to pacify that [identification]. For those...

The meaning of the Sūtra is that for those whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are exceedingly pure, their identification with the body and so forth has been loosened precisely through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*); since the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Truth is possible for them through nididhyāsana for only a short time, prolonged nididhyāsana need not be performed.

In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa it is heard: "Therefore, a brāhmaṇa, having discarded scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), should abide in childhood (*bālya*); and having discarded both childhood and scholarship, he then becomes a sage (*muni*). In this passage, just as childhood and scholarship, so too is sagehood enjoined. Or rather, is scholarship the form of determining the purport of many Upaniṣads?

Having accomplished "childlikeness" (*bālya*) in its specific sense—because it is free from passion, hatred, and so forth—one should abide in another state that resembles childlikeness. Then, having fully accomplished both scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and childlikeness, there arises the question: in the phrase "then [he becomes] a sage" (*atha muniḥ*), is sagehood (*mauna*) also enjoined, just as scholarship and childlikeness were? Or is it not?
There is a doubt:

since the words "silence" (*mauna*) and "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*) have the sense of knowledge, that very knowledge which was enjoined by the phrase "having become disillusioned with scholarship" (*pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*) is here restated in the phrase "then he is a silent sage" (*atha muniḥ*). For no word of injunction is heard here. This being the position reached, we reply as follows.
The injunction regarding another auxiliary means (*sahakāryantaravidhi*) is enjoined for one who possesses that [knowledge], just as knowledge and so forth are.

By the word "injunction" (*vidhi*), all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) such as sacrifice, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so on, are denoted. By the word "and so on" (*ādi*), hearing and reflection are included. In the expression "injunction regarding another auxiliary," it is called an "injunction" (*vidhi*) because something is enjoined (*vidhīyate*).

The term *sahakāryantaravidhi* means "the injunction regarding another auxiliary. This is what is intended: just as in passages such as "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity," and so forth, as well as "one who is tranquil, self-controlled," and so forth, auxiliary factors such as sacrifice and tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*) are enjoined; and just as in the injunction "it should be heard, it should be reflected upon."
Hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), which follow as a matter of course, are understood to be auxiliaries to knowledge;

likewise, by the passage beginning "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become learned... (*tasmād brāhmaṇaḥ pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya*), a triad consisting of scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), childhood (*bālya*), and silence (*mauna*) is enjoined as another auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman—thus, silence (*mauna*) as well.

He states that "sagehood" (*mauna*) is something distinct from "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*): "By way of an alternative" (*pakṣeṇa*). Because the word *muni* is seen to be used in reference to Vyāsa and others who possess the habit of superior reflection, sagehood is the third [stage] following scholarship and childhood.
Although no injunctive suffix is heard in the phrase "then the sage," nevertheless, since sagehood has not been previously established [as a duty], [it is enjoined].

The state of being subject [to practice] must be accepted; thus, "one should become a silent sage" (*muni*). And this silence (*mauna*) is something distinct from reflection (*manana*), which serves to establish what has been heard; it consists of the repeated cultivation of the object of meditation, taking the form of its constant contemplation (*bhāvanā*). This alone is the meaning of the sentence here.

The Brāhmaṇa, possessing knowledge, having become indifferent to mere scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), and having realized the pure and perfect reality of Brahman which is to be meditated upon— meaning he has attained the realization acquired through hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*)—

and that [realization] being brought about by the increase of the quality of goodness (*sattva*) produced through devotion to the Blessed Lord, as stated in the passage beginning with "I am not [to be known] by the Vedas... and so forth.
"But by unswerving devotion alone am I able to be reached in this way, O Arjuna. And the Śruti says:

"He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine so for the Guru—for that Self is not to be obtained by mere instruction," and so forth. The nature of *bālya* (childlike state) will be explained immediately hereafter in the words, "One should remain in a state of childlikeness. Having realized both *bālya* and *pāṇḍitya* (scholarship), then...

A sage (*muni*) should become one whose nature is contemplation (*mananaśīla*) upon the supreme Śiva-Brahman, which is completely pure and perfect, having duly acquired both childhood and wisdom (*bālya-pāṇḍitya*). To exclude [the mere practice of] knowledge in the form of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), he says that by thus acquiring this triad, one becomes possessed of knowledge: "Having fully mastered both non-silence and silence... (*amaunaṃ maunañ ca nirvidyātha*).

"A Brahmin"—"amauna" refers to the collection of auxiliary factors other than silence. Taking up both that [non-silence] and silence according to the rule, one should take hold of the pinnacle of knowledge, which is exclusive devotion to that alone; this is the meaning. When asked, "By what means would he be such a Brahmin?"—as if asking whether there is anything else to be produced beyond the aforementioned means—the answer is: "By whatever [means], he would be exactly like this. By whatever...

It was stated that "one should be a Brahmin who is preeminent in silence" (*maunivarya*); this was answered by the point that one should be such [a Brahmin] and not by any other means. Therefore, for the knower situated in any of the stages of life (*āśrama*), silence—consisting of scholarship and so forth—is enjoined as a third auxiliary to knowledge, just like the duties of one's own stage of life, such as sacrifice and the rest.

Now, it might be argued: if for those wise ones established in all the stages of life (āśramas), knowledge accompanied by silence as its third assistant—acting in conjunction with the specific duties of each respective stage—is said to be the means for attaining Brahman, then how is it that in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "Having returned home, studying his own Veda in a pure place in the family," it continues: "He indeed, in this manner..."?

"Practicing this for as long as life lasts, one reaches the world of Brahman and does not return again"—this establishes that remaining in the dharma of the householder for the duration of one's life is possible. Therefore, he says:
"The determination that there is no contradiction regarding the eligibility of those in the stages of life beginning with studentship (brahmacarya) for the knowledge of Brahman."
And [there is] the etymological definition of the word "guru.
But because of the totality [of the stages], the conclusion is made with the householder.

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt. Since the knowledge of Brahman exists within all the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma), it exists even for the householder; therefore, the conclusion is made by means of the householder. Thus, the intention is that the conclusion with the householder is for the purpose of demonstrating the duties of all the stages of life.

Is it not the case that, because of the instruction regarding the rule for the yoga of renunciation for those who possess knowledge of the meaning of the Vedānta in the passage, "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of the Vedānta," and because of the teaching that the yoga of meditation is a duty belonging to those beyond the stages of life (atyāśrama) in the passage, "He who stands beyond the stages of life," [it follows that this applies] to celibate students (*brahmacārin*s)?

Because householders are occupied with the performance of Vedic vows and other duties, as well as the burden of maintaining their families; because forest-dwellers are engaged in fasts, *kṛcchra* penances, and so forth;
[the inquiry into Brahman] belongs only to ascetics (*yatins*), who approach a teacher with fuel in hand for the sake of that knowledge.

If it is argued that [the householder] possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), we say no; for in the passage, "To understand that, one should approach a guru alone, with fuel in hand,

a *śrotriya* who is established in Brahman," the student’s state of having fuel in hand establishes the teacher’s status as a householder, while the word *śrotriya* indicates his adherence to the proper conduct of his own stage of life (*āśrama*), and "established in Brahman" indicates his realization of the Absolute.

Thus, since even the status of being a knower of Brahman is indicated here as being unrestricted, it is established that while the ascetics (*yatis*) possess the primary eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman, the knowledge of Brahman is not precluded for those in any of the other stages of life (*āśramas*), such as the student (*brahmacārin*).
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "In his family, in a clean place, studying his own Veda," and concluding with "He, indeed,

conducting himself thus for as long as he lives, attains the world of Brahman," because it is heard that the state of being a knower of Brahman applies to all those who take refuge in the entire [Vedic way of life], and because the conclusion is made with the householder, this is for the purpose of indicating [the inclusion of] all [stages of life].
It should be understood that it is appropriate for members of all stages of life (*āśrama*) to have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).

Indeed, even if householders (*gṛhastha*) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, [they should not perform fruitless action] according to the maxim: "One should not perform fruitless action."

The state of the *atyāśrama* (the highest stage of life) is devoid of purpose [as a distinct stage], because there is no contradiction with the Vedic injunction, "One should perform the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and because the *smṛtis* and *purāṇas* designate the householder’s stage (*gṛhasthāśrama*) as the most superior of all as the foundation for everyone; thus, one established in the *atyāśrama* restrains all the senses.

Having bowed with devotion to one's own guru, and based on the observation of the Smṛti stating that "the wise know [this] as the renunciation of the ultra-ascetic order (atyāśrama-saṃnyāsa) established by such Śruti," the truth is that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the abandonment of fruits. Since the rule "a *yati* is one who is diligent" implies that the effort for liberation (*mokṣaprayatna*) can exist even among householders, [renunciation] belongs to all those in the stages of life (*āśramins*).
That is possible.
[This concludes] the section on silence (mauna). 14.
Regarding the definition of the *atyāśramin*: he who is joined with the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* is indeed the *atyāśramin*.
The *liṅga* is Śiva, the *kṣetra* is the *aṅga*, and their union is the *āśraya*.

Therefore, because the term *atyāśrama* is designated in the *Vātula-āgama* spoken by Śiva as being common to all stages of life (*sarvāśrama-sādhāraṇa*)— as in passages such as "one who is endowed with the [proper] marks and limbs shall be an *atyāśramin*"—
the ascetic stage (*yati-āśrama*) which prescribes silence and other such practices is not appropriate for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
Anticipating this objection, he states another topical section (adhikaraṇa) therein:
"As in the case of the sage, so also for others, because of the teaching [of them]. (Sūtra 49)

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having established the exclusive dharma of wandering mendicancy (pārivrajya) through the passage, "A Brahmin, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then leads the life of a mendicant," it is further stated in that very same context by the words, "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship... and so forth.
Having demonstrated the prescription of the third [type of] silence as an auxiliary cause for remaining established in the dharma of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrajya*), and likewise,

by teaching the knowledge of Brahman even to householders and others through the passage beginning with "having returned there to his own family in a pure place," words such as *saṃnyāsa* and *yati* are established in that very sense through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), just like the word *paṅkaja* ("lotus").

Therefore, among the hundred [paths], the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is primary; for those other than them, rituals such as the Agnihotra are primary. In the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* and other texts, the term "atyāśrama" (the state beyond the stages of life) is used with reference to one who is connected to the *prāṇaliṅga*, who carries the ash-mark (*bhasmaghuṭṭikā*), a patched garment (*kanthā*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), an alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*), and a staff (*daṇḍa*), and so forth.

Although [the practice] is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*), since it is understood that ascetics (*yati*) are primary— just as in the case of "silence" (*mauna*) being [prescribed] for others— it is demonstrated that the ascetic possesses the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) by virtue of being primary. Then, by means of the analogy of the ocean and the pond, following the maxim *samudravattaṭākam*, the teaching of the knowledge of Brahman to others is also established, thereby demonstrating their subordinate status.
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the state] of ascetics (yatins) is irreproachable;
for, from the statement "one who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality," it is understood that liberation belongs to the person devoted to Brahman,
and from the statement "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it is taught that liberation belongs only to those who know Brahman.

In passages such as "By the practice of churning through meditation, the wise man burns away the fetter," the injunction for meditation is stated with the description of its characteristic result, which is the severance of the fetters. Furthermore, in the *Atharvaśiras*: "Having conquered craving, the root of the web of causes, and having contemplated with the intellect and then established [the mind] in Rudra, the eternal Rudra..."

"One should restrain the ancient, desired, and vigorous [power] through austerity; one who desires liberation should practice this Pāśupata vow for the sake of non-rebirth. Since liberation is established as being attained specifically through the Pāśupata vow, and because it is observed likewise in the Purāṇas, it follows that immortality belongs either to those possessing the knowledge of Brahman alone or to those solely devoted to the Pāśupata vow.
A doubt arises:
since the Pāśupata vow is included among the [four] stages of life (āśrama) because it is mandatory for those in all stages of life,
and because its duration in time is observed, [one might think that] for the sake of obtaining a wife, sons, and other such means, Rāma...

Since it is understood that the Pāśupata vow does not depend on any other means of accomplishment, even though it is established by Śruti, it follows that its fruit is merely optional (kāmya). To this we reply:
for those who observe the Pāśupata vow, liberation alone is the fruit, as well as the attainment of knowledge of Rudra, the Supreme Brahman.

Since other practices of liberation—such as the mendicant’s life, tranquility, and so forth—are also prescribed within the Pāśupata vow alongside the sage’s duty of inquiry, those who are devoted to that vow are said to be "one with Rudra. Having taken ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni," one should rub them on and touch the limbs; this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).

Since it is understood that the fruit of the meditation on Rudra is liberation in the form of the severing of bonds (*pāśa*), for those who observe the Pāśupata vow for as long as they live, liberation alone is the result.
[This concludes] the nature of the former Pāśupata and Mahāpāśupata [systems].

Furthermore— because this stage of life, known as the "Beyond-Stage" (atyāśrama), is endowed with the duties of an ascetic such as celibacy for the practice of knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*) found in the *Pāśupata-vrata* and *āśrama*, it is the cause for attaining independent Paraśiva.
[This lasts] either until the fall of the body or for twelve years.
One should perform the divine Pāśupata rite for the sake of the cessation of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu).
The Pāśupata system is to be known as twofold, distinguished by its earlier and later divisions;
it consists of the wearing of ashes and rudrākṣa beads in accordance with the Śaiva initiation.
Having obtained Śiva, the Great God, the Lord of Umā in the form of the Liṅga,
whoever indeed worships him at the three times of day— that is truly the ancient Pāśupata.
According to the ritual procedures for Śiva-initiation (dīkṣā) based on the reconciliation of the Nigamas and Āgamas,
one should hold the Śivaliṅga in the hand, around the neck, or upon the chest.
He who worships with devotion three times a day is indeed a Mahāpāśupata;
he is declared to be of two kinds, distinguished as Śrauta and Aśrauta.
He who, having performed the dharma appropriate to his caste and stage of life in accordance with the Vedas and the Bhārgava [Smṛti],
worships Śambhu, is called a Śrauta-Śaiva.
He who, having abandoned the dharma appropriate to his caste and stage of life,
worships the Lord of the Universe through the Tantric path, is called a Tantra-Śaiva.

Thus it is heard in the Śiva-āgama. Therefore, it is determined that the Pāśupata vow observed for a duration of twelve years has as its cause the attainment of desired, optional fruits, whereas the lifelong Pāśupata vow has as its eternal fruit the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of bonds (pāśa).
For it is determined that the lifelong Pāśupata vow has the attainment of the state of Śiva— preceded by the cessation of bonds (pāśa)— as its eternal fruit.
[This concludes] the definition of the Nirābhāra Vīraśaiva.

He is one who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī), free from worldly burdens (nirābhāra), the moving embodiment of the six sacred sites (ṣaṭsthalī), a wandering ascetic, a hero of Śiva-yoga; he never finds delight in others.

This is because it is seen thus in the Vīrāgama. Although the term *atyāśrama* refers generally to all four stages of life as defined by Śaiva initiation, it is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) in the sense of Vīraśaivism, which is free from the three types of desire and devoid of worldly appearances.
For students (*brahmacārins*), the uncommon duty (*asādhāraṇadharma*) consists of studying the Vedas preceded by eating as much as desired;

for householders (*gṛhins*), it is the performance of daily rites such as the *agnihotra* preceded by eating what is appropriate; and for forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*), it is residing in the midst of five fires and so forth, which serves as the cause for emaciating the body through fasting and other primary practices.

It is appropriate that members of all stages of life (*āśrama*) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), provided they have engaged in hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*) conducive to the practice of yoga preceded by the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*). There is a mutual contradiction between the statements of the *Brahmavids* and the *Pāśupatas* regarding the injunctions for the teaching of liberation; for these [latter] hold that Paśupati is the Lord (*īśa*).

In such scriptural passages as these, the fact that Śiva-Brahman is the sovereign lord of all living beings is established through the traditional authority (āgama) regarding his being the cause of their bondage and liberation; since the attainment [of Brahman] is impossible in the absence of his grace, the direct realization of him by those who worship him— following the instructions for initiation and the injunctions concerning the knowledge of Brahman— is taught by implication.
The Section on Non-Confession. 15.
The possession of the majesty of secret Śiva-knowledge by Śiva-yogins, like that of children and others, is indeed innate.

Now, although all those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas) may have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, there arises the inquiry as to what their specific mode of conduct (vṛtti) is; in response to this, the author demonstrates its defining characteristics through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
|| 294 || Not manifesting [it], because of the logical sequence. || 50 ||

Without manifesting [his spiritual attainments], like a child, he should remain constantly engaged in hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, meditation, concentration, and focused attention upon his own established devotion, knowledge, dispassion, tranquility, self-restraint, and equanimity. Why? Because of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the Śiva-yogins.

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: because one’s own mental activity is always in constant union with Śiva—preceded by the removal of the misconception of the body, senses, and so forth—one possesses the natural majesty of the knowledge of Śiva as Pure Consciousness (*jñapti-śiva*), just like a child and others. Therefore, it is said: "A Brahmin, having discarded scholarship, should not remain in a state of childishness."
The ascetic should always and perpetually meditate upon the Jyotirliṅga between the eyebrows,
clearly perceiving the Self by means of the self through the firm conviction that it is Brahman.

One should discard the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas— along with the distinctions of caste and stage of life arising from the body's connection to childhood and other states— as if they were mere dust on one's feet.
Free from desire, the sage should remain amidst these [worldly things] but not dwell with them; clad in a loincloth or even naked, he should be intent on meditation,
seated with his intellect turned inward, indifferent and free from longing.
Seeking happiness, one should wander here with oneself alone as a companion,
free from the doubts of all beings and devoid of the distinctions of caste and stage of life.
One should wander the earth like a blind man, like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is mute;
whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or otherwise.
The wise sage, ever delighted in his own self, may dwell according to his will;
he should move among the world with the conduct of a fool, a madman, a ghost, or an idiot.

A Brahmin, having become composed in mind, should effect the very identity of the words *tattvam* and *asi*. "Clad in space (naked), there is no salutation, no utterance of *svāhā*, no utterance of *svadhā*, no censure or praise; he should be one who acts according to chance"—by such passages, those possessing the knowledge of Śiva are heard in the Śruti as being acceptable like children and the like. Here, "like a child" refers to the absence of conduct driven by desire or ritual action, and so forth.
There is a doubt as to whether everything should be accepted by the wise, or only that which is free from hypocrisy and the like.

Since it is taught that the conduct of knowers of Brahman is like that of a child, a madman, or a ghost—being devoid of the distinction between what is fit and unfit—the performance of meritorious and non-meritorious actions [in such a state] is what should be accepted. Therefore, the Self...

Or rather, the knower should abide adopting that action which consists in not manifesting one's own nature—namely, the "childhood" (*bālya*) prescribed by such Śruti passages as "The Self is to be seen," which involve hearing, reflection, and so forth on the Vedānta.

Why? Because of "concomitance" (*anvaya*). It is appropriate because of the mental concomitance with the supreme steadfastness of the mind fixed solely upon Sadāśiva; [this is] by means of "childhood."
In this injunction, "one should desire to abide [in Brahman]," it is logical that the connection applies only to that wise person, because for others,
there is scriptural testimony of their being opposed to knowledge:
"Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not concentrated."
Nor can one whose mind is not tranquil attain this through wisdom alone.

In passages such as "When food is pure, the being (sattva) becomes pure; through the purity of the being, mindfulness becomes firm," the observances (*niyamas*) of those established in Brahman are heard. By the maxim that "everything is possible through an illustration," it is merely stated that they are free from hypocrisy, like children and so forth. This applies to those who possess the knowledge of the Perfect Śiva (*pūrṇaśiva*).

For those whose state of being the self of all that is auspicious (*sarvaśivātmatva*) is uninterrupted, the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth is unnecessary. However, for those of duller intellect who possess knowledge of Śiva, hearing and so forth serve to strengthen their realization of the self-nature of all as Śiva.
[As it is said: "Whether one remains immersed in *samādhi* and performs no ritual acts, or whether one performs them, [it matters not]."
In his heart there is no doubt; he is called one liberated while living.

Thus, in such passages of the Vedānta, it is taught that only the ignorant are performers of actions enjoined by injunctions, whereas the wise act according to their own will. This concludes the section on "The Present World" (Aihikādhikaraṇa). 16.

For those possessed of worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*), liberation occurs after a period of time, as in the case of Jaḍabharata and others; for those free from latent impressions and solely devoted to Śiva, liberation occurs in this very life, as in the case of Vāmadeva and others.
Now, [one might ask] regarding those persons who possess the direct realization of the reality of Śiva (*śivatattva-sākṣātkāra*) aided by hearing, reflection, and so forth...

In response to the doubt as to whether those who possess full qualification attain the state of Śiva—preceded by the cessation of the sense of being a transmigrating soul (jīvatva)—in this very life, or whether they attain it through gradual liberation via the stages of *sālokya* and so forth in another birth, he states [the following] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
**"That [liberation] occurs in this life, provided there is no obstruction of what is not yet commenced; for that is seen [in scripture]."** (JS 3.4.51)

In the case of the absence of obstacles (*aprastutapratibandha*)—that is, when there are no impediments such as attachment to worldly objects, lack of dispassion, lack of tranquility, and so forth—knowledge pertaining to this life arises. In this very birth, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Paraśiva-Brahman arises.

However, if there exists an obstacle consisting of a firm identification with the body and other such things, then [realization occurs] again in another birth through hearing, reflection, and meditation.

Because it is accepted in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*— through such passages as "perfected over many births, he then attains the supreme goal"— that Jaḍabharata attained liberation through three births, or Vāmadeva attained the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of bonds in a single birth due to the fruition of previous lives, [it follows that this applies] to those possessing powerful identification with the body and so forth.

For those who possess only a slight conceit regarding their own bodies, yet have been favored by the Lord through meditation, retention, worship, prostration, hearing, and recitation performed over many lifetimes—for them, the devotion to Śiva accomplished in a single lifetime [is sufficient].
As stated in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known? To him—

He said: "There are two kinds of knowledge to be known," as the knowers of Brahman declare; beginning thus and ending with "he who knows the supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," [the text describes] that which is designated as *abhyudaya* (prosperity), the fruit produced by meritorious actions performed by those attached to the desire for prosperity—namely, tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth.
It is designated as *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good). Regarding this, a doubt arises: for those established in the knowledge of Śiva, does liberation occur in this very birth or in another birth?
Since it is taught that "there the knower attains Brahman," implying the attainment of Brahman occurs right here, [one might object] that if a delay in time were accepted as the result...

Because it would follow that the greatness of knowledge is destroyed; for if that were so, since it could not be a primary means like the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and other rites, it would follow that the fruit of liberation is appropriate for those possessing the knowledge of Brahman only in this very birth. To this objection, we shall reply as follows.

Meditation (*upāsana*) which has prosperity in this world (*aihika*) as its fruit is immediate when no powerful intervening karma acts as an obstacle; however, when such an obstacle exists, there is no fixed rule regarding the time [of its fruition], namely that it occurs after that obstacle. Why? Because that is seen [in scripture]. For it is indeed seen in the Śruti that the fruition of action is admitted to be obstructed by another powerful karma, as in the passage: "Whatever one performs with knowledge... (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.1.10).

"Through faith and the Upaniṣadic knowledge, that very same [action] becomes more powerful," because we hear of the non-obstruction of the fruit for action joined with the Udgītha-vidyā; and because, in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, we understand the means of crossing over past obstructions, present obstructions, and future obstructions.

Because it demonstrates the means for the removal of future obstacles, Bharata’s attainment of liberation in another birth— like that of Jaḍabharata and others— is not contradictory, even though he was liberated across three lifetimes. In this case, the statements regarding liberation in this very life refer to those who are already liberated from future obstacles, like Vāmadeva and others.
O Brahman, the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called liberation;
liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor upon the surface of the earth.
When all parts [of the mind] have ceased, the cessation of the mind is declared to be liberation;
for one is bound by being bound by latent impressions (vāsanā), while liberation consists in the destruction of those impressions.

In such passages, since liberation is taught for one who is endowed with the absence of latent impressions (*nirvāsanā*) and is already filled with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) even in this very birth, there is no contradiction.
This concludes the section concerning the fruit of liberation (Sūtra 17).
Now, regarding the exposition of how those who practice the knowledge of Brahman attain both liberation with a body and liberation without a body according to their own will:
indeed, for those possessing the knowledge of Brahman yet still joined with worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*), liberation occurs after a period of time, as in the case of Jaḍabharata and others.

"For those who are established in silence free from latent impressions and whose minds are fixed solely on Śiva, let there be the fruit of liberation in this very life, as in the case of Vāmadeva and others;

nevertheless, regarding the doubt as to whether those possessing the knowledge of Brahman through the *dahara* and other meditations attain liberation while embodied or disembodied, he speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*):"
|| 296 || Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is determined; because that state is determined. || 52 ||

Previously, it was stated that for those possessed of worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in former lives, who have now become established in the knowledge of Śiva free from such impressions, the fruit of liberation—consisting of the attainment of Śiva—occurs in this very life. Nevertheless, there is no fixed rule that the fruit of liberation must be identical for all those who possess such direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of Śiva; for it is said: "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman."

Since the Śruti reveals that for those who know Brahman there is the attainment of all desires together with Brahman, there is no fixed rule that for all knowers of Brahman liberation consists solely of the state known as disembodied liberation (*aśarīra-mukti*) or absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). Rather, for those favored by Śiva and endowed with tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth— [liberation occurs in this manner].

For those who are liberated from the latent impressions of the world beyond, there exists here itself— in this very linga of the light of the small space (daharākāśajyotiḥ)— the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), wherein they experience eternal and unsurpassed bliss with a bodiless form until the exhaustion of their prārabdha karma, like the pleasure of deep sleep; and during the time of that samādhi, they remain like a camphor lamp extinguished when placed in the midst of a scorching sun.
At the time of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), oneness with the Supreme Śiva in the Supreme Space occurs according to the analogy of a river merging into the ocean.

For those who are distinct from that [state] and still possessed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment in the worlds of the embodied Supreme Śiva and Brahmā, at the cessation of their vital breaths, there arises— by means of a divine,
auspicious form suitable for residence in the world of Śiva— the fourfold liberation consisting of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*.

Why is there no fixed rule regarding liberation with a body or liberation without a body? Because that state is determined [by one's final thought]. Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, that very state one attains as the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of action.
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end..."
The knower of reality, constantly permeated by that state of being, goes to that very thing alone.
He who, at the time of death, having been awakened by a friend or even by his own intellect,
meditates single-mindedly upon Śiva, attains the supreme goal.
Meditating upon the form whose essence is Sadāśiva, one releases the vital breaths;
at that time, one attains the state of Śiva—there is no other path, so says the Śruti.

Because such instructions are found in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Āgamas, and other scriptures, there is no difference in liberation between the two states: for during the stage of meditating on the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman, the mind of the devotee is held by that embodied Brahman and is thus fashioned into the form of the embodied Brahman;
whereas during the meditation on the unembodied reality of Paraśiva, the mind of the devotee is held by the unembodied Śiva-reality. Therefore, there is no distinction in the resulting liberation.

The meaning of the Sūtra is that [the two paths] are contradictory. For from the passage "In that case, the vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right there," one understands immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*);

whereas from the passage "But those who reach the world of Brahman at the time of their final end are liberated through the supreme immortality," there is the teaching of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*). Thus, there is a contradiction.
For those who worship Paraśiva-Brahman, there is liberation without a body known as immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*), and liberation through stages known as gradual liberation (*kramamukti*).

This is because the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is similar to the fruits of prosperity mentioned in the sections on *dharma*, such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "One desiring sovereignty over heaven should sacrifice with the Vājapeya."
The presence of excellence [in the means] is faultless; for, in the *Dahara* and *Śāṇḍilya* Śrutis,

there is the understanding that action performed [as mere ritual] is excluded as a cause of liberation, and because in passages such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," it is established that only the knowledge of That produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*) is a constituent part of liberation, and not through meditation (*upāsanā*).
To the objection that the attainment of Brahman is not possible, we reply:

just as for those who meditate on the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices mentioned in the context of ritual duties (*dharma-prakaraṇa*), so too for those who meditate on the Dahara-vidyā and other such meditations mentioned in the context of Brahman (*brahma-prakaraṇa*), a result other than immortality should not be proclaimed.

Because no such scriptural statement enjoining that [attainment] is seen. In the Taittirīya, in the passage "He attains all desires together with Brahman," there is observed for those who meditate on the *dahara* (the small space) while still possessed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), a manifestation of glory consisting of the threefold vibhūtis beginning with *sālokya*. Furthermore, in the Taittirīya, starting from "The small, stainless, supreme abode," the lotus of the heart is described.
Beginning with the words "dustless and pure," and having meditated upon the Supreme Lord accompanied by Umā, "the sage goes to the source of all beings"— thus,

in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad, the manifestation of bodiless liberation (*aśarīrakaivalya*) is established for those who meditate on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart) and are steadfast in the meditation on Paraśiva, which is free from all latent impressions (*nirvāsana*).

Because hundreds of such scriptural passages as "Know [Brahman] through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation; from its contemplation, from union with it, and from the realization of its true nature, there occurs at the end the cessation of the entire cosmic illusion" teach that those who practice the knowledge of Brahman attain two types of liberation— a permanent, incomparable embodied state and a disembodied state— therefore, [this is the case] regarding the knowledge of Brahman.

The status of being the most preeminent is unavoidable. If meditations and other forms of worship were designated as "action" (*karman*), it would follow that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest would also be actions. In the passage, "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," hearing and the like are taught as the means for attaining the fruit, which is the direct realization of Paraśiva, after that fruit has been restated. In that regard:

It has been taught that only *upāsana* (meditative worship) in the form of *nididhyāsana* (intense contemplation), assisted by hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth, is the primary cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*); it is not the mere knowledge of the meaning of the words, as is the case with medical treatises and the like.
Now, one might object: since in the world all people perceive the stars situated in the sky, when their merit (*puṇya*) is exhausted—

If it is argued that disembodied liberation (*aśarīramukti*) is not an object of experience because liberation while still embodied (*saśarīramukti*) occurs on Kailāsa— as inferred from the cases of Upamanyu, Dadhīci, and others who were seen there— and because the relationship between the worshiper and the worshipped exists even there, as evidenced by the attainment of the world of Śiva along with Bhallāṇa, Cirutuṇḍa, and others— then [we reply] no, for it is just like liberation while embodied.
Because the liberation of the bodiless state is established through scripture, reasoning, and experience— given that in deep sleep and meditative absorption (samādhi), the gross body ceases to exist—

and because one experiences the state of being bodiless and is subsequently instructed in that experience; furthermore, it is not as in the case of those who have attained heaven, where there are bodies of light such as stars, that even for great souls who have reached the world of Śiva [there is a physical body].

There is a repeated return [to the world]. However, because the Śruti states, "But at the time of their final end, all those in the world of Brahman are completely liberated through the supreme immortality," it is taught that for those who meditate upon the knowledge of Brahman, there are two types of liberation— with body and without body— whose nature is eternal, unsurpassed bliss, and non-duality, according to their own will, arising from that very world.
It is obtained. Therefore, it is determined that the restriction that "liberation is not for one alone" is possible.
Thus ends the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* composed by the venerable teacher, the lord of the illustrious Yati community, the scholar Śrīpati Bhagavatpāda Svāmī.

The third chapter, known as the *Upāsanādhyāya*, consists of fifty-two sūtras beginning with "Puruṣārtha ataḥ śabdāt" (Brahma Sūtra 3.4.1), which comprise seventeen topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) starting from the section on the human goal (*puruṣārthādhikaraṇa*).
The fourth chapter is completed.
Now begins [the commentary] composed by the venerable teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda,
which elucidates the meaning of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā Sūtras.
The First Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya.
The Section on Reversion (Āvṛtyadhikaraṇa) || 1 ||

The description of the fruit of all knowledge; the necessity of performing that worship which is accomplished through hearing, reflection, and so forth, followed uninterruptedly by an exclusive state of being— this is the subject of the third chapter.

The contemplation of the Dahara-vidyā and other meditations—which establish the meaning of the words *tat* and *tvam*, and which elucidate the relationship between the object of worship and the worshipper, or Śiva and the individual soul (jīva)—has been completed.

Now, in the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, the fruit of all these meditations is treated; in the second, the specific fruit regarding the departure of the jīva, who constitutes the referent of the term *tvam*; in the third, the fruit consisting of the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi*) and so forth; and in the fourth, [the fruit of the attainment of Brahman].

And it demonstrates the fruit of the supreme human goal, which consists in the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the natural state of being a living soul (jīva). Therefore, this constitutes the statement of the fruit for this chapter [of the scripture],
following upon the injunctions of the Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, and other meditations in the preceding chapter.

For the sake of accomplishing the attainment of the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of bonds, when [this] is described along with its common characteristics, it shall bring about all perfections for those who have surrendered even once— merely through a single remembrance.
One should perform the domestic fire ritual (aupāsana) once for the sake of removing the bond of illusion (māyā-pāśa).

In such Smṛtis and Purāṇas, the attainment of Śiva-hood preceded by the cessation of the state of being a transmigrating soul (jīva-bhāva) occurs through worship performed only once; for there is no evidence that it requires repeated worship. Thus, one might raise the objection that the scriptural injunctions prescribing the worship of Brahman—such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—refer to a single instance of time.
To refute that [objection], he states another section:
|| 297 || "There is repetition, because of the instruction being given more than once. || 1 ||

In such scriptural passages as "The Self, indeed, should be seen; by meditating upon It, by concentrating upon It," although there is no fixed rule regarding whether the vision occurs once or repeatedly, one must perform repetition—the practice of meditation, remembrance, reflection, and so forth, upon Paraśiva—repeatedly, that is, many times, without forgetting. Why? Because of the instruction.
One should spend the time from sleep until death in contemplation on Vedānta;
one should not grant even the slightest opportunity to desire and other such passions.
Arising from sleep, one should contemplate the unity with Brahman until the end of that sleep;
whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or even otherwise.
"According to his will, the wise sage, ever delighting in his own Self, may dwell [anywhere].

In accordance with this *smṛti*, perceiving everywhere only his own true nature (*svarūpa*), he attains liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and shall dwell in contemplation of his true nature until the dissolution of the appearance of the residual karma (*prārabdha*). Contemplation of the true nature...
Without this, one should not become intent on improper conduct; that wise person, while listening to the Vedānta, should undertake yoga—such is stated in the Śrutis.
Furthermore, reflecting upon that, meditating upon that, and awakening others to that [truth] are prescribed.
And the wise know that single-minded devotion to this is the practice of Brahman.
With their intellects fixed on That, their very selves absorbed in That, established in That, and intent upon That,
they [attain liberation] through the daily hearing of the Vedānta accompanied by devotion.
Having always attained devotion to the Guru, they worship the imperishable Śiva.

The subtle meaning of the Sūtra is that, since even in such Smṛtis constant remembrance, reflection, meditation, concentration, and absorption upon Śiva are enjoined— and because the mind lacks the nature of being identical with Him— one must always perform His worship through non-forgetfulness.

In such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman," "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace," there arises a doubt among devotees as to whether worship— which consists of the knowledge of Brahman— should be performed once or repeatedly, since there is no definitive criterion [in the texts] to determine between once or more than once.

Since the text "One who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" enjoins only the act of knowing, and since there is no evidence for its repeated performance, it cannot be argued that repetition is required until the effect is achieved— as is the case with threshing and the like— because knowing is not a perceptible means (*dṛṣṭopāya*) toward the direct realization of Brahman.

Just like rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, the knowledge enjoined by the Vedānta is of the nature of worshiping Śiva; and from the Supreme Person thus worshipped, there is the attainment of the four aims of human life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—as stated in the sūtra: "For this reason [the fruit arises] from Him, because that is logical" (Phalamata Upapatteh).

This has been established. Therefore, as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, it is determined that the purport of the scripture is fulfilled by performing [the rite] only once, according to the literal word;
for there is the principle from the Nyāya system that "when it has been done once, the purpose of the scripture is accomplished," just as in the case of the Prayāja offerings and others.
When it is argued that [the practice] should be performed only once, we reply:

"Repetition is not once" (āvṛttirasakṛt). Knowledge that has been repeated more than once is indeed the meaning of the scripture. Why? Because of the teaching regarding the constant meditation on Paraśiva-Brahman.
This is because it is taught and declared that the attainment of the state of Śiva is rooted in the prior cessation of bondage:
"When a human being shall wrap space like a hide, then,
without knowing Śiva, there will be an end to suffering."
Since all this is suffering in its beginning, middle, and end,
therefore, O sinless one, renounce everything and be established in reality.
Without yielding an opportunity at any time for sleep, worldly talk, sound and other such things, or the forgetting of the Self, contemplate the Self within the self.
In such Smṛtis as these:
"I bow to that Lord,
whose linga the hosts of Maruts, with Indra as their chief, worship day and night together with their wives."

Thus, even in the *Vedapādastava* composed by the teacher Jaimini, because the injunction for repeated meditation (*upāsanā*) is understood from various passages, it is intended that the aforementioned Smṛtis—which state that those who have surrendered (*prapanna*) once alone are granted immediate liberation—are solely devoted to the recollection of its (the Lord's) majesty. [As it is said: "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman; it shines and it heats."

"By fame, by glory, and by Brahman-splendor [he prospers] who knows thus; what he knows—that has been told to me by him. Through such scriptural passages, which teach the interchangeability of the injunction (*vidhi*) and the object of meditation (*upāsya*) in both the introduction and the conclusion, [it is established that] knowledge (*vedana*), which is the means to liberation, [is intended].

Because it is understood to be of the nature of *upāsana* (meditative worship), and because the word *upāsana* denotes a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-santāna*), that which was said—that it is like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—is not correct; for since those have unseen results (*adṛṣṭa-phala*), their performance once is appropriate. Likewise, in sentences having the same meaning as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and so on, such as "The Self, my dear, is to be seen," and thereafter...
In passages such as "He sees Him, partless and striving," the verb *dhyāyati* denotes cognition. And *dhyāna* is reflection;

that, moreover, consists of a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*), not mere memory alone. *Upāsti* (meditative worship) has the same meaning, for it is observed in usage to mean the uninterrupted continuity of one-pointed mental activity. This is because both terms share the same sense.

In passages such as "He whose memory is repeatedly turned toward the continuous [tradition] here knows Brahman; having become Brahman itself, he is liberated from all bonds once he has known the God," the term *vedana* (knowing) and others denote precisely *upāsana* (meditative worship).
To this point, he states another reason:
And because of an indicative mark. || 298 || 2 ||
Having established that the *liṅga* is the soul of all, beginning with "Salutation to the upward-facing one; salutation to the upward-facing *liṅga*," and so forth,

[the text] states, "He establishes this [liṅga] of Soma and Sūrya as the *sarvaliṅga*," and by the sentence "He establishes it here with the *pāṇimantra* as a purifier (*pavitra*)," it is seen that the injunction for the establishment of the *liṅga* is in every respect common to both the earth and the body.

Likewise, at all times— whether going or standing— the wise man, with joy and devotion, should hold the Shiva-linga, which consists of pure consciousness, within his external and internal bodies through recitation, worship, prostration, listening, and meditation.
Just as devotion prevails in the world through hearing and chanting, so too does [the medicine for] Saṃsāra—
namely, Sāmba— arise from hearing, worshipping, and meditating upon Him.
The wise one should contemplate this constantly; otherwise, he shall not attain liberation.
From this observation, it is determined that one must perform that meditation as a means consisting of hearing, reflection, and so forth, continuously and with undivided attention.
This concludes the section on the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa). 2.

The direct realization of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) produced by the continuous contemplation of Śiva, as well as the inquiry into its attainment—surely, let there be repeated worship of Śiva for those seeking liberation; nevertheless, by what path should that worship be performed?
In response to the doubt as to whether it should be done with a sense of duality or non-duality, he demonstrates [the answer] through another topical section (adhikaraṇa).
But they do indeed accept [the existence of] a self and cause others to grasp it as such. || 3 ||

The self—the individual soul—attains the direct realization and attainment of Paraśiva-Brahman through continuous inquiry; this is the subtle meaning: that seekers of liberation, having known [the Self] through the Vedānta and other means, cause the Supreme Self to be grasped by means of meditations such as the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya*, and thus they know, approach, and attain It. Indeed.
The word "atra" (here) has the sense of certainty.
When the seer perceives the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman— then the wise man, having shaken off merit and demerit, attains the stainless, supreme equality.
Just as flowing rivers disappear into the ocean, casting off name and form,
even so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high.
Thus, in the *Mundaka*, it is shown that those who worship Brahman possess both the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman and the attainment of Brahman.

This is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "The lotus of the heart, stainless and pure," and ending with: "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness, the sage goes forth."
In the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), the attainment of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is heard of for those seekers of liberation who practice meditation on the "small" (*dahara*).
Regarding the demonstration of the threefold nature of meditation:

meditations are of three kinds—meditations involving identification (*ahaṃgrahopāsanā*), meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsanā*), and meditations bound to the limbs [of the ritual] (*aṅgārabaddhopāsanā*).
And so it is said.

Among those, the meditations involving identification (*ahaṃgrahopāsanā*)—namely, the Dahara, Śāṇḍilya, Vaiśvānara, Upakośala, and Madhu vidyās—are taught as meditations upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). In certain other vidyās, however, because of the mention of difference, [the object of meditation] is superior to the universe (*viśvādhika*).

In accordance with scriptures such as "Rudra is the great seer" (*rudro maharṣiḥ*), although Brahman is superior to the individual soul (*jīva*), the meditation upon Brahman is shown to be performed by identifying oneself with it; that very practice is known as *ahaṃgraha-upāsanā* (meditation through the grasping of "I"). This is evident in Vedic texts such as "Brahman is Ka, Brahman is Kha," and in the case of images made of copper, clay, stone, and so forth.

The meditation on Brahman by means of viewing non-sentient objects such as names and so forth as Brahman— based on passages such as "One should meditate on this [breath] as Brahman, not as Śiva, Keśava, or others"— is called *pratīkopāsana* (meditation on symbols). Similarly, the viewing of Brahman in objects such as the *udgītha* and in ritual acts that are limbs of sacrifice is also included.
This is called "meditation bound to the limbs" (*aṅgāvabaddhopāsanam*).
Therefore, in this context, does the meditation consist of the worshipper—the individual soul (*jīva*) in its conscious form—worshipping his very own self as Śiva;
or is it the worship of Brahman by means of viewing objects distinct from oneself that are insentient as being Brahman; or [is it] regarding the *dahara* (small) space and so forth?
A doubt arises as to whether one should perform the worship of Śiva alone;
for, since in such passages as "This Self is Brahman" and "I am Brahman," the status of the individual soul (jīva) itself as Brahman is established,
the worship of one's own very self as Brahman is unavoidable.

In passages such as "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," "One should meditate on name as Brahman," "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," and "One should meditate on the vital breath as Brahman," because Brahman-hood is taught with respect to insentient entities like speech and so forth, meditation on Brahman as being identical in essence (*tadātmakatva*) with them is also appropriate. Therefore, [Brahman] is distinct from both sentient and insentient entities in contexts such as the "small" (*dahara*) space and others.
When it is argued that those seeking liberation must never perform the worship of Śiva, the following is stated:

Having begun with "The small, stainless [space], the supreme abode," and having taught the worship of the Supreme Self as being within that small space by saying "that which is within it is to be worshipped," then, in response to the inquiry "Who is He?"—

That which is declared as the primal sound at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas— He who is beyond that [sound] when it has dissolved into its source is the Great Lord (Maheśvara).

By such passages as these, the worship of the Śiva-tattva is elaborately expounded in many ways for those seeking liberation in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad as being distinct from both the sentient and the insentient. In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad, beginning with "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure," [it describes] the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā.

By the passage beginning with "the three-eyed, blue-throated, peaceful one," it is taught that seekers of liberation should worship the auspicious form of Līlā, which consists of the nature of consciousness, within the small lotus of the heart.

This has been shown in such passages as: "Brahman has space for its body; it is the Self of truth, delighting in vital breath, whose essence is bliss, enriched by peace, and immortal. Therefore, it is concluded that seekers of liberation must practice the worship of Paraśiva, who is distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious.

"Indeed, all this is Brahman; indeed, all is Rudra; [He is] the eternal and the truth," and so forth—in these passages, the nature of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, as the Self of all is established. "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal. To that Rudra who has entered into the fire, [I bow].

In passages such as "Let there be obeisance to Rudra," because he is designated as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, the meditation on Brahman within conscious and unconscious beings is not contradictory.
Furthermore: "But [He is] greater, because of the designation of difference; and because of the declaration of difference, Paśupati is other than these."

Based on the observation of direct scriptural statements such as "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all beings," the Supreme Brahman known as Śiva is indeed greater than the individual soul (*jīva*). Nevertheless, because non-difference is designated in sentences that establish both difference and non-difference— such as "That thou art"— at the final stage for those who possess the relationship of worshipper and worshipped, [one realizes] "I am Brahman."

By such great sayings (*mahāvākya*) as "I am Śiva," the practice of meditation is not contradictory. As stated in passages such as, "Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, the wise man burns away the fetters through the practice of the friction of meditation," liberation is indeed the attainment of the state of Śiva, which is unsurpassed supreme bliss and distinct from the phenomenal world of consciousness and the unconscious.

Even through the instruction on the established conclusions of all the Vedāntas, the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) and the severance of the fetters (pāśa) are not possible in the absence of meditation in the form of its worship. Since that [cessation] is impossible without it, and because the attainment of the Śiva-principle is unattainable otherwise,
one must perform the uninterrupted and continuous worship of Śiva.

Beginning with "One should meditate upon the Lord who is to be meditated upon" and ending with "Having abandoned everything else, one should meditate upon Śambhu alone, the one Śiva in the midst of space, the maker of auspiciousness," there is an understanding of the prohibition against the worship of other deities for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). Therefore, [the term "all"] refers to the sentient and insentient world, whether consisting of individual souls (*jīva*) or the insentient phenomenal universe (*jaḍaprapañca*).

It is determined that the continuous contemplation of Śiva is the cause for attaining the state of Śiva. In the sūtra, "The non-difference [of the world] from That [Brahman], on account of the words regarding its being a mere beginning and so forth," the fact that the phenomenal universe, which has Śiva as its material cause, is of the very nature of Śiva is indicated by way of its non-contracted [all-pervasive] character. Regarding this, some [hold that]: "[Śiva is] the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual."

Because the use of the word "Self" (ātman) is observed for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, in hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "They consider the fourth to be that Self," Śiva alone is the Self who is to be constantly meditated upon by those seeking liberation in all the Brahmavidyās, such as the Dahara and Śāṇḍilya vidyās; thus says Upamanyu.

It is understood that through the practice of hearing, reflecting, chanting, remembering, and so forth, they cause one to grasp and know [the Lord]; by the word "grasp," it is determined that meditation on other deities is excluded. This too is entirely logical. Thus ends the section on the Pratīka (the Symbol). 3.
Regarding the fact that the meditation on the vision of Śiva within those whose consciousness has arisen from Śiva is the cause for the direct realization of Śiva:

[one might object] that in such scriptural passages as "He is the Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas, the cause of bondage, existence, and liberation from saṃsāra; having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct... and so forth, [the distinction between] the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is taught.

In response to the doubt as to how the individual soul (jīva) is to be meditated upon as being of the nature of Brahman—given that the injunctions for meditating on [Brahman] as distinct [from the self] have been understood—the author states, by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa): "Neither in a symbol (pratīka), for he is not that. (4)

The meditation on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*) is heard in the *Taittirīya*: "Bhṛgu Vāruṇi indeed approached his father Varuṇa and said, 'Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman. To him he spoke this: 'One should meditate upon food, breath, sight, hearing, mind, and speech as Brahman,' and so forth—thus, through the meditation on symbols such as food and the rest as being Brahman."

If it is argued that the worship of food and so forth must be performed, we say no. Why? Because Śiva alone, who is all-pervasive, abides within food and other things as their inner controller (antaryāmin). Therefore, for those seeking liberation, the possibility exists that such worship serves as a cause for mutual liberation—functioning like the maxim of the "large Arundhatī star" (where one first identifies a nearby star to find the true Arundhatī). This is the intended meaning indicated by the Sūtra.

Since food and other such things are taught to be Brahman by virtue of being the cause of the world's birth and so forth, there arises the doubt: should one perform meditation upon food and the like— though they are limited and insentient in nature like jars and cloth— as being Brahman, or not?

Although the father Varuṇa taught his son Bhṛgu that food and other such things should be meditated upon as Brahman, even so, that is not something to be enjoined because they are insentient. In the world, one does not see the fruits [of meditation] for those who have cultivated the notion of elephants and the like in artificial elephants, horses, and so forth; therefore, the meditation on the True and Auspicious (Satya-Śiva) within perishable food and other such things is entirely appropriate.
When it is argued that this is not possible, we reply:

according to the principle that "the accomplishment of the goal occurs even in the absence of the means," we observe in the world that those desiring to ascend a palace must first ascend the stairs; likewise, for those of dull intellect who are unable to practice meditations on the "small ether" (dahara) and so forth, there are [meditations] upon food and other such things.

It is determined that meditation upon Paraśiva as Brahman is, through a succession of stages— by way of the analogy of the water in front [of the moon] and the analogy of the gross Arundhatī— the cause for the direct realization of Brahman. In the world, the honoring of servants and others with the thought that they are the master is the cause for the master’s favorable glance.

It is observed that the status of being a servant toward a king is a cause for punishment. Similarly, it is determined that meditating upon all sentient and insentient beings produced by Śiva—such as food and other things not specifically prescribed by scripture—with the vision of Śiva (śivadṛṣṭi) is the cause for the direct realization of Śiva.
Therefore, he who worships another deity, thinking "He is one and I am another," does not know [the Truth], for this [Brahman] is indeed the Whole.

"One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'. "O Venerable One, I am indeed you, the deity; O Venerable One, you are indeed me, the deity"—by speaking thus in mutual exchange, there is perfect consistency among all forms of meditation. Similarly, in the *Chāndogya*: "All this is indeed Brahman, for it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; one should meditate with a tranquil mind."
It teaches the meditation upon the entire manifold of the conscious and the unconscious as being Brahman.
It is taught that "everything is Brahman" because [the world] is born from That, dissolves into That, breathes in That, is governed by That, and has That as its inner controller.
Here, it states another reason:
|| 301 || The view of Brahmā [arises] from [the notion of] superiority. || 5 ||
Because of His preeminence, there is only one Rudra; He does not stand for a second, for Rudra is superior to the universe, Rudra is indeed the Puruṣa, the Great Being.
Whatever is the manifold world—past, present, and wonderful, born and being born—all this is indeed Rudra.
From hundreds of such scriptural passages, Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is designated as being superior to the entire universe of sentient and insentient beings.

The supreme preeminence [of Rudra] is beyond dispute; nevertheless, because texts such as "Rudra indeed is everything" declare that he alone is the self of all, it is appropriate to view food and other things as Brahman. Starting from "Salutation to the Lord of the End" up to "This belongs to Soma and Sūrya," [the reference is] to Sūrya—that is, the one residing within the solar orb—and to Soma, who is accompanied by Umā.
Having explained the procedure for the worship of the *liṅga* based on limited vessels and hands for the sake of delivering devotees,

[the author] states that because the excellence of that [limited form] is designated by means of the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, the worship of the all-pervading Śiva within limited objects such as food is not contradictory.

If it is argued that because of such scriptural indications as "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," and "One should meditate on the sun as Brahman"—which designate speech and so forth as Brahman—one must therefore perform meditation on Brahman by viewing speech and the rest as Brahman, we say no; for we do not find any supporting scripture, reasoning, or experience for such an injunction. [As the scripture says: "That to which [the word] 'namas' refers is its head."
In the description of the Self as the *śiśumāra* (the porpoise-shaped cosmic being), through such passages as "Dharma is the head, Brahman the upper jaw, Yajña the lower jaw, Viṣṇu the heart,
and the year the offspring," [He is established] as distinct from Viṣṇu and the others who constitute the heart and other parts, precisely because He is the most exalted of all.

The fact that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, has the form of the primary head is stated by way of restating it through the very definition of the object of salutation—namely, "salutation to that which is his head. Furthermore, at the conclusion, it is said of him alone: "You are the lord of beings; you are also the most excellent among beings."
Having declared His sovereignty over the domain of all beings and His preeminence with the words, "Salutation to You, salutation to You,
salutation to You in everything," it is established that because He is superior to all beings, He is the ultimate ground for the culmination of all acts of homage.
Furthermore, in passages such as "Salutation to You, O Rudra, in Your wrath," it is repeatedly stated that homage is due to Him precisely because of His supreme excellence over all.

It is applied [as follows]: for in the world, people bow down more deeply to one who possesses sovereignty and other such qualities; therefore, Virūpākṣa accompanied by Umā—who is the object of all salutations, the supreme Brahman denoted by the word "Īśvara," and the most excellent—is perceived through the vision of pervasion within all things, including the mind, the sun, and so forth, which are themselves the objects of universal homage. This [vision] belongs to that which is most excellent and worthy of all salutation.

The status of the limbs as objects of meditation follows from this very point; for this reason, even in cases such as "Obeisance to you, the dogs and the dog-keepers," the Śruti employs the word "obeisance" by viewing even the most debased beings as pervaded by the Supreme Brahman.
Therefore, because of the connection with that which is superior, we observe the use of figurative designation (*upacāra*) toward inferior things through the vision of Brahman, who transcends all.

The status of the mind and other [faculties] as objects of meditation is established. However, viewing speech and the others as being in the relation of master and servant toward Brahman causes a transgression.
This concludes the section concerning the meditations on Āditya and the rest (Ādityādimaty-adhikaraṇa). 4.

In the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, it is taught that one should meditate upon the sun as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Since we observe instances where meditation involves superimposing a superior entity upon an inferior one, the claim that viewing a servant as a king brings about demerit while viewing servants as kings yields the fruit of prosperity is incorrect.
Anticipating this doubt, he states [the following] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"And the notions of the sun and so forth [are to be applied] to the limbs, because it is logical. (Sūtra 6)
In meditations connected with the limbs of the ritual, such as "One should meditate on the sun as Brahman," although the sun and others are taught to be Brahman,
there are nevertheless conceptions of the sun and others as the sacrificial post (yūpa) and so forth,
in accordance with Vedic injunctions such as "One should meditate on the sun as the sacrificial post"; and all these are indeed limbs [of the ritual].

They are indeed auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Why? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*): from such passages as "One should meditate on the *udgītha* as Brahman," it is understood that the *udgītha*-knowledge directly leads to the realization of Brahman;

therefore, since the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is an auxiliary part of that [ritual], is mentioned within the context of Brahman, and because the sun and others are superior [to the ritual elements], one should meditate on the sun as the sacrificial post.
There is no contradiction because of the logical consistency of the statements;
