for instance, in passages such as "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance, he [knows] both," there is the characterization of the Veda that teaches ritual action (*karman*) as being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), and the Veda that teaches Brahman as being of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Because of the direct instruction [in the scriptures]; and because, in passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the knowledge of Brahman has as its fruit the supreme human goal consisting in the attainment of Paraśiva preceded by the cessation of bonds, its preeminence is unavoidable. Therefore, [this applies] to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) included within the Udgītha-vidyā recited in the context of Brahman.

The subtle meaning is this: because the sun and other luminaries are superior when delimited by the manifold of ignorance (*avidyā-prapañca*), the doctrine of superiority and inferiority—such as that between a master and a servant—is indeed untenable.
This is because, in passages such as "This sun is Brahman," the sun is heard to have Brahman as its self; therefore, one should meditate upon the sun as the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

In passages such as these, because of the designation of the sun as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a doubt arises as to whether or not the cognition of a sacrificial post and so forth can occur with respect to the sun and other such objects.
For instance, in texts such as "This sun indeed shines as this orb," and "He who glides along, blue-necked and deep red," [the sun is described].

Because his status as Śiva is established directly, and because the supreme Brahman Śiva is taught to reside within the solar orb in such Vedic passages as "This golden person within the sun" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6) and in such Smṛti texts as "The one with Ambā [Pārvatī], situated in the center of the solar disc, the medicine for the disease of transmigratory existence," it is improper to equate him with the sacrificial post (yūpa) and other such objects.
We state [our conclusion] regarding what has been presented:
"And the conceptions of the sun and so forth. The word "and" (ca) is used for emphasis.

The conceptions of the sun and so forth—namely, the cognitions of sacrificial posts and other elements belonging to the mental sacrifice (*mānasa-kratu*) directed toward the sun and others—are indeed limbs of the knowledge of Brahman itself. Why? Because they are directly auxiliary to it.

Because of its logical consistency; for it is logically consistent that the sacrificial post and other elements which are limbs of the mental knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) are superior to external objects such as Brahman, the sun, and so forth. Regarding this, they say: "Within the vital breaths, they call the mind the indicator (*liṅga*);
the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings."
When the mind has moved from one place to another, that which is the form of the consciousness in the interval [is the true nature].
"Non-inertness, consciousness, and reflection— that is called the nature of consciousness.

Since such scriptural passages establish that the mental form, which is subtler than gross things like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), possesses supreme excellence, [it follows that] the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and other elements, which are constituent parts of the mental knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), [are superior] to the sun and other [celestial objects].
Regarding "supremacy":
the claim that the sun possesses supremacy because of statements such as "This sun is Brahman," which describe the sun as being of the nature of Brahman,
is incorrect— given statements such as "Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman, food is Brahman, and breath is Brahman."

It has been stated that "everything is Brahman" for the purpose of meditation because Śiva is the material cause [of all]. However, the claim that the Sun possesses supremacy over all because the Supreme Self resides within the Sun— as in passages such as "This golden person within the sun"—
is also untenable, given that in texts such as "He who is Rudra, he who is in the fire, he who is in the waters," it is Śiva [who is thus described].

Because it is established that [the Self] is the inner controller of all; therefore, there is no contradiction in the superiority of the mental Udgītha-vidyā, the sacrificial accessories, the sacrificial post, and so forth. This concludes the section on "Sitting" (Āsīnādhikaraṇa). 5.
The determination that only one seated upon a seat is fit for single-minded meditation on Śiva—
[is it not so? whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or even otherwise?
The wise sage, ever delighting in the Self, may dwell according to his own will.

In such passages, since no rules regarding the time for sitting and so forth are observed for one who meditates on Brahman, there arises the doubt that those who meditate on the Dahara-vidyā and other such meditations have no need for sitting and the like; in response to this doubt, he shows another section [of the Sūtras]:
|| 303 || "He should sit, because that is possible" (Sūtra 4.1.7).
Having made the body even with three parts raised, and having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind,
let the wise man, by means of the boat of Brahman, cross all the fearful streams.
Thus, in the Śvetāśvatara [Upaniṣad]: "But in a secluded place, seated comfortably, pure, with neck, head, and body held erect, having transcended the stages of life (āśrama),
having restrained all the senses, and having bowed with devotion to one's own guru..."

Thus it is heard in the *Kaivalya*: "Seated in a comfortable posture, one should perform single-minded meditation on Śiva in the form of the meditation upon the *dahara* (the small space) and so forth.

Why? Because of possibility (*sambhavāt*). The subtle meaning indicated by this sūtra is that mental one-pointedness is possible only for one who is seated in postures such as the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others.

Here, there arises a doubt: is the knowledge consisting of meditations such as the *dahara* (the small ether), which serves as a means to liberation, to be practiced repeatedly until it takes the form of constant mindfulness (*smṛti*) preceded by the practice of *āsana*, or is it something distinct from that?
[The sage says: "Whether walking or standing, the sage is always delighted in his own Self."
The ascetic should always and constantly meditate upon the Jyotirliṅga situated between the eyebrows.
Because in such [scriptural passages] regarding the meditation on Brahman, no restrictive rules such as the lotus posture (padmāsana) are observed;
because there is no purpose for prescribing bodily postures like the svastika for meditation on the form of Manu;

and because of the instruction that for all practitioners of ritual action, the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation, stating: "The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings."
Since it might be argued that for those seeking liberation there is no rule regarding posture (*āsana*) during meditation, we reply:

because the Upaniṣads, such as the Śvetāśvatara and Kaivalya, teach the injunction for the meditation of those desiring the knowledge of Brahman as being preceded by the practice of posture; thus, although there is no rule of posture for those who have already ascended [to higher stages], [it remains necessary for beginners].

For those desiring to ascend [to the goal], there is no contradiction in the rule regarding the practice of postures (*āsana*), gestures (*mudrā*), the object of focus (*lakṣya*), and discipline (*niyama*).

This is according to the maxim: "Without the means, the goal cannot be accomplished. Since both staying still and moving require effort, and since sleep may occur while lying down, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) arises only for one who is seated. Therefore, being seated...

Since it is understood from the scriptural injunction that "one should practice the meditation upon Brahman," seekers of liberation must perform meditations such as that on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart) preceded by the assumption of a [proper] posture.
Regarding this, he states another reason:
And because of meditation. || 8 ||

For in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, through the instruction on the method of meditation for one who is indeed seated— expressed as "from meditating upon that, from union with it, and from becoming its true nature"— and likewise in the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad* through the passage beginning "in a secluded place,
pure, seated comfortably with neck, head, and body erect," it is taught that for one who is seated, the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*) is stainless and pure.

Beginning thus: "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, who has Umā as his companion, the sage goes to the Source of Beings; making the Self the lower fire-drill and the Praṇava the upper fire-drill."
Through the practice of churning with meditation, the wise man burns away the fetter.
By such statements as these, it is established that for one who is indeed seated, the practice of meditation (*dhyāna*) in the form of the worship of Brahman is appropriate.
Meditation is precisely the mental state whose sole object is Śiva, preceded by the renunciation of all other objects.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
|| 305 || And with reference to immovability || 9 ||
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities—
that One who presides over all those causes joined with Time and the Self.
By such statements as these, the meaning is that one should perform meditation on the Supreme Lord while remaining seated, with reference to— and having in view— immobility and stillness.
He states another reason further:
And they remember it as well. || 10 ||
For one who has attained this body composed of the fire of yoga, there is neither disease, nor old age, nor death;
rather, there is lightness, health, freedom from greed, clarity of complexion, and excellence of voice.
With these and other passages, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad commemorates in many ways the greatness of one who is seated, steadfastly devoted to the yoga of meditation on Śiva.
Here, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of certainty. [As it is said:
"Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place..."
Neither too high nor too low, it should be covered with cloth, a deerskin, and kuśa grass, each placed upon the one before.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained,
let him sit upon his seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
By such statements, it is taught in the Smṛti as well.
Furthermore, he states another reason: || 307 || "Wherever there is one-pointedness [of mind], there [is yoga], because there is no distinction. || 11 ||

One who knows Brahman should dwell in a temple, at the foot of a tree, or in a cave, free from attachment and characterized by virtuous conduct; like a flame without fuel, he is utterly tranquil and does not feel agitation in this world.
A wise person, though distracted, maintains the mind as if it were a difficult horse to control;
[he does so] on a level, clean spot, free from pebbles, fire, sand, and the like, and devoid of noise, water, and other such distractions.
One should employ [the practice] in a place that is agreeable to the mind, not painful to the eyes, and providing shelter from wind in a cave or a windless spot.

By such statements as these, it is determined in the scriptures that one should resort to specific places and times conducive to one-pointedness; for whatever place and time are conducive to one-pointedness, those alone are established as the proper place and time for worship (*upāsana*). Therefore, on a riverbank, in a temple, or in a cave, where the mind is serene, one should perform meditation characterized by uninterrupted worship of Śiva. Why? [Because...]

Because there is no distinction; it is determined that for one whose internal organ is purified, the clarity of the mind is equal in all respects. In response to the inquiry as to how many years those seeking liberation (mumukṣu) should perform meditation on Śiva through the practice of postures (āsana), gestures (mudrā), and the focal point (lakṣya), he says:
|| 308 || For even there, it is seen until death. || 12 ||

Indeed, by practicing in this manner for as long as life lasts, one attains the world of Brahmā; according to the scriptural vision, meditation on Śiva must be continued until the final departure—that is, until death. Why? Because it is seen even there.
O Lord, having known this, one is freed from all bonds; with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Through the contemplation of that [knowledge], upon the dissolution of the third body, one attains absolute sovereignty over the universe, having all desires fulfilled.
By such passages as these, the worship of Śiva is seen to extend from the cessation of the darkness of ignorance— known as the third body— up to the direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of Śiva.
"Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end..."
The knower of reality, constantly permeated by that state, goes to that very thing.

Thus, in the *Smṛti*, the identity with Śiva for the worshippers of Śiva at the fall of the body is taught. Since the gross body is not seen to fall many times, by the statement "one should abandon the body at the end," it is understood that only the fall of the causal body (*kāraṇadeha*) is intended. Therefore, for the purpose of severing the bonds known as the causal body, one should practice through the disciplines of hearing, chanting, worship, and so forth.
It is pointed out that the practice of Śiva-yoga is necessary for those seeking liberation. This is the section concerning the attainment thereof (Tadadhigamādhikaraṇa). 6.

For the wise who are possessed of worldly tendencies (*vāsanā*), there is the destruction of *prārabdha* karma through experience following the exhaustion of future and accumulated karma; however, for those devoid of worldly tendencies, there is the contemplation on the destruction of the four types of karma—
just as for one lying down there is the affliction of sleep and so forth, and for one standing there is the obstruction of thorns and the like regarding walking.

It has been stated that for one seated [in meditation], the worship of Sadāśiva is necessary because it generates the sensation of bliss in the feet; nevertheless, as the Smṛti declares: "The performed action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced; action is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas without being experienced," what then of the practitioner?
In response to the inquiry as to what the fruit of karma is, he refutes [other views] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof. (Sūtra 4.1.13)
Upon the attainment of that—that is, upon the realization of that Supreme Śiva through meditation and worship—there occurs the non-clinging and the destruction of subsequent and prior sins;
that is, there is non-contact with future sin and the destruction of accumulated sin. Why? Because of the scriptural declaration thereof.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf,
and just as a tuft of cotton-wool thrown into a fire is consumed by it.
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, [so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes].
In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.
The meaning is that in such Smṛti texts, there is a designation of the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of both future and accumulated karma (*sañcita-karma*).
Karma is fourfold, distinguished as accumulated (*sañcita*), commenced (*prārabdha*), past (*atīta*), and future (*āgāmi*).
Among these, [accumulated karma] consists of actions performed in previous births that are capable of producing a future body, or those performed with a view toward results such as heaven.
Karmas have been accumulated;
with great effort, hearing, chanting, and reflection have been undertaken.
Past actions are those performed either in this life or in another previous birth with the aim of attaining the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*).
Future actions are those performed in this life subsequent to the direct realization of Brahman.

In that regard, among the four kinds of karma, those accumulated [in past lives] perish without having produced their fruit in the form of a succession of future bodies. Furthermore, as for future karma, because it has been performed while the identification with the body has fallen away, the capacity to produce a fruit is not possible. And thus says the Smṛti:

Prārabdha karma perishes through experience; accumulated (sañcita) karma perishes through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna); and future karma (āgāmi) of both kinds perishes for one who speaks what is pleasing to those who hate him.
Just as the sun enjoys all flavors and the fire consumes everything, so too the yogi enjoys sense objects; pure, he is not stained by merit or sin.

In passages such as these, since it is understood that for those who meditate upon Brahman there is the fruit of the destruction of all karma, the subtle meaning of the Sūtra is that Smṛti texts stating "the performed karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced" have as their object only ignorance (*ajñāna*). Having thus clarified the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*) in the preceding section, [the present section addresses this point].

This section is commenced for the purpose of investigating the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman, it is heard in scripture that there is both non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of a person’s subsequent and prior sins. As water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus.
"Having known that very Self as both the high and the low, one is not smeared by evil action"—this is the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) of future sin.

"Just as a tuft of cotton flung into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed; and his actions are worn away when He, the High and the Low, is seen"—this is the destruction (*vināśa*) of past sin. Such are non-clinging and destruction.

There arises the doubt as to whether the two fruits of knowledge arise or not. What is the correct position? That they do not arise. Why? Because it would contradict such scriptural authorities as, "Karma that has not been experienced does not perish even in hundreds of millions of aeons. As for the designations of "non-clinging" (aśleṣa) and "destruction" (vināśa), [they refer to future karma].

It is also possible that it occurs within the supplementary portions (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the injunctions for the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation, since it can somehow be understood as an expression of praise for that knowledge. Furthermore, knowledge is not enjoined as a penance for the prior and subsequent sins [of the soul].

If it be argued that this is merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the destruction and non-clinging of sin, on the grounds that the means for attaining Brahman is enjoined by such texts as "Through knowledge, indeed, one who knows Brahman reaches the further shore," "Having known Śiva, he goes to ultimate peace," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself"—therefore, the mention of the destruction and non-clinging of sin is merely figurative—then we reply as follows: [The text continues: ...by which expiation (*prāyaścitta*) the destruction of evil is said to occur. Knowledge is indeed enjoined as the means for attaining Brahman. Thus, when this [objection] has been raised, it is stated in response: *na hyadhikārikamapi patanānumānāt tadayogāt ||* (Sūtra 3.4.40) "For even that which pertains to one holding an office does not [save him], because of the inference of his fall; for that [knowledge] is incompatible with that [fall]. This is the meaning: Even the knowledge pertaining to one who holds an office (*adhikārika*) does not prevent his fall from grace. Why? Because of the scriptural inference of his fall, as seen in passages such as, "Having fallen from here, he reaches the worlds of the virtuous" (*chāndogya-upaniṣad* 5.10.5). Furthermore, that knowledge is incompatible with such a fall, since it is the very cause of liberation. Therefore, the expiation mentioned in the text—"By this expiation, the destruction of evil is declared"—is indeed a real expiation. This is because, although knowledge is the primary means for attaining Brahman, it is not impossible for other means of purification to exist alongside it. Just as a man who has reached the top of a tree might still be struck down by a thunderbolt, so too one who has attained knowledge may still suffer a fall due to the force of previously accumulated karma. Consequently, the expiation prescribed for the destruction of evil is a valid and necessary injunction. Thus, the claim that this is merely a commendatory statement is refuted.

Regarding the phrase "upon the attainment of that": upon the acquisition of knowledge, due to the majesty of that knowledge, there is a non-clinging of subsequent and prior actions for the person—meaning sinful karma does not adhere [to him]. Thus, "indeed, all his evils are consumed. "Then the knower, having shaken off both merit and sin, attains the stainless supreme equality," and so forth; such is seen in numerous scriptural passages.

Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural teaching that "karma is not exhausted without being experienced," because their subject matters are different. For that [scripture] concerns the firmness of the capacity of karmas to produce results, whereas this [present teaching] concerns the power of knowledge, once arisen, to destroy the capacity of past sins to produce results, and [to prevent] those yet to arise.

It establishes both the capacity to produce an effect and the capacity to obstruct the production of that effect; thus, there is a distinction between the two objects. Just as heat and the capacity to ward it off belong to two distinct objects, so too, in the case of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their validity arises from the difference in their respective objects. It is the same here as well.
There is no contradiction.

The prevention of the attachment of sin (*agha*) consists in obstructing the production of that power which is the cause of transgression (*pratyavāya*), namely the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of fitness for Vedic action. For when sins are committed, they produce in a person unfitness for Vedic action, a lack of inclination toward undertaking other similar actions, and transgression. [End of section on] Sin.
The "cause of destruction" refers to the destruction of that power once it has arisen. Furthermore, this power is nothing other than displeasure toward the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa).

Thus, for one who knows through knowledge, because the object of knowledge is dear, knowledge itself becomes supremely dear; it takes the form of worshiping Śiva, the Supreme Person, who is the unknowable ground of being.

It destroys the supreme Lord’s displeasure produced by the accumulation of sins committed in the past; that same knowledge also prevents the arising of the Lord’s displeasure caused by sins occurring after its own origination.
This statement regarding non-attachment (aśleṣa) should be understood as referring to sins committed through negligence.

From the passage beginning with "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct," it is understood that knowledge— which arises day by day until death and is characterized by progressive excellence— is to be accomplished through the renunciation of evil conduct; therefore, for the wise who still possess worldly impressions (*vāsanā*), once the future and accumulated karma have been exhausted, they abandon only the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma through experience.

It is determined that for those whose worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been eliminated—whose minds have been made to take on the form of eternal Śiva according to the analogy of the magnet and the needle—the destruction of the fourfold karma occurs. Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The knower of Brahman, out of devotion, [performs] all actions, whether prescribed by the Vedas (*śrauta*) or the Smṛtis (*smārta*)."
Having performed the optional rites and having renounced them, he proceeds like one still involved in worldly existence.
But the foremost yogi among the knowers of Brahman, having always abandoned all rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti,
engages in the contemplation of Vedānta through the attainment of perfect dispassion.
Having attained the supreme culmination of meditation, the knower of Brahman known as Varīyas, renouncing all worldly activities, should consume a measured amount of alms-food.
Through the awakening resulting from steadfast practice in the uninterrupted meditation on Śiva,
one attains the forgetting of the universe and, like one asleep, the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Having consumed food, drink, and other things given by others, one should dwell without expectations,
remaining intent on a single place by virtue of the nature of eternal bliss.
The one known as Variṣṭha, a knower of Brahman, having dissolved his mind continuously into the Śiva-principle through meditation, lives like one whose body has been cast off.
Having abandoned the path of rising again through both one's own intellect and the intellect of others,
the yogi should dwell eternally in the attainment of identity with Śiva.
Although there is but one liberation for all four [types of practitioners], a gradation is clearly observed;
for the first and the second, *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma) always persists.
"But for the third, there is indeed the experience of the fruits of past actions (*prārabdha*);
however, for the fourth, the *prārabdha* neither touches nor stains him. Thus ends the section on "The Other" (*itarādhikaraṇa*). 7.
The subsequent merit and demerit of actions resulting from the greatness of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and culminating in the knowledge of Śiva—[an objection is raised]:

surely, for one who is most excellent among the knowers of Brahman, since the mind is void and there is an absence of action following knowledge, it is logical that he is untainted by karma; for all actions performed through ignorance by those such as the knowers of Brahman are [dissolved] by knowledge.
In response to the doubt as to what becomes of future karma performed after the knowledge of Śiva—even though [past karma] has been destroyed—the author presents another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"But for the other as well, there is likewise non-attachment; however, upon falling away [from that state]. (Sūtra 4.1.14)

But when the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has been obtained through the Guru’s heavy glance, there occurs a non-attachment and non-contact with the meritorious and non-meritorious karma that follows the knowledge of Śiva. This occurs even in the absence of initiation following the descent of power,
by virtue of the greatness of firm Śiva-yoga preceded by the Guru’s instruction.

This same characterization should be understood as applying even to those persons whose causal bodies consist of the nature of darkness— known by such names as *vicchinnapāśa*, *avidyā*, *ajñāna*, and *māyā*— as indicated by the subtle meaning of the Sūtra;
[this applies] to those persons who possess the knowledge of Śiva and whose bonds have dissolved.
A doubt arises as to whether the cessation of future karma— consisting of merit and demerit performed subsequent to that knowledge— is possible or not;
[the same applies to] the karma consisting of merit and demerit performed prior to the time of that knowledge.

Let cessation [of karma] occur by virtue of observing the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti; however, it is not possible for actions generated after the attainment of knowledge to be destroyed. For, as for this destruction, does it apply to meritorious actions or to sinful actions? Not the first, because meritorious actions are not opposed to knowledge and because they take the form of the command of the Supreme Lord. Nor the second—
Since no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for sins committed intentionally is seen in the scriptures, and because the performance of sinful acts would entail the destruction of knowledge,
it follows that in no way can the destruction of actions performed after the attainment of knowledge occur for the wise; to this we reply:
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both transcendent and immanent is seen.
The fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes, O Arjuna;
that which has been accumulated is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, while that which is already commenced perishes through experience.
The two future karmas belong to the one who speaks with malice and the one who speaks kindly.

Since the exhaustion of all karma for the wise is understood from such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*), and since no restrictive evidence (*vinigamaka*) is seen to the contrary, the knowledge of Śiva— which possesses extraordinary greatness— possesses the power to destroy the meritorious and non-meritorious karmas accumulated over many previous births.
Why should it not be that [the knowledge of Śiva] destroys even actions performed after the attainment of that knowledge? Since there is no evidence for restricting the scope of the Śruti and Smṛti,
and since merit, like sin, acts as an obstacle to the knowledge of Śiva,
it is logical that those who have performed meritorious deeds while maintaining the state of identifying with the all-pervading Śiva are untainted, owing to their lack of agency regarding those acts.

Even for the ignorant and the learned, although there may be an absence of sinful conduct due to their own egoism, they remain untouched and unopposed by sins born of negligence arising from the force of *prārabdha*. As it is stated in the Siddhāntāgama:
"Everything, including the daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, [is performed] through the contemplation of Śiva."
Even while acting, the great yogi is not stained by virtues or faults.
From this observation, it is established that, like Śiva, even the Śiva-yogins are untouched by all karma.
This concludes the section concerning actions whose effects have not yet begun (Anārabdhakāryādhikaraṇa).

The statement that the fruit of liberation— which arises at a later time and is attained through the knowledge of Śiva produced by the study of the scriptures— is not touched by future-born karmas for the wise, is inconsistent.

If it is questioned why the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) of Jaḍabharata and others—which, though their effects have not yet begun and have not yet commenced to bear fruit—are not destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*), [the author] states another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) to address this doubt:
"But only those prior [deeds] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is the limit. (4.1.15)

Prior to the arising of the knowledge of Śiva—that is, before the attainment of that knowledge—the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛte*) of pure souls who have not yet aspired [to liberation] perish through *vidyā* (knowledge) even while their effects have not yet begun and their fruits have not yet manifested. Why? Because of that limit [stated in scripture]: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united" (*tasya tāvadeva ciram yāvan na vimokṣye 'tha sampatsye*), which refers to the point until the complete perfection of the knowledge of Śiva.

Just as with a bound soul (*baddhajīva*), the delayed attainment of liberation by pure souls (*śuddhajīva*) is understood from the fact that Jaḍabharata and others lacked the realization of Śiva-knowledge preceded by the removal of latent impressions (*nirvāsana*); thus,
there is no contradiction in that those such as Vāmadeva, who were established in the knowledge of Śiva free from latent impressions, attained liberation without delay.
The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtras is as follows:

there arises a doubt as to whether for all those possessing the knowledge of Śiva, there is immediate liberation (sadyomukti) preceded by the cessation of the experience of future fruits, or whether delayed liberation is possible depending on the gradations of their respective qualifications (adhikāra).

As long as knowledge has not arisen, so long must ritual actions be performed; however, since the Śruti teaches that upon the mere arising of knowledge all ritual actions are to be abandoned, liberation is possible through knowledge alone.
Were this not accepted, it would contradict the scriptural statement: "From knowledge alone comes isolation (kaivalya); there is no other way to liberation."
To the objection that this would entail the consequence of contradicting the scriptures of those who possess great learning (*bahuśruti*),

we reply: without the attainment of the knowledge of Śiva, the attainment of the state of Śiva— preceded by the severance of the bonds (*pāśa*)— is not possible through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), just as [the mastery of] medical science and other fields [does not lead to liberation].
Without direct experience, the fool rejoices in Brahman in vain,
like one who delights in the imagined taste of fruit at the tip of a reflected branch.
Since scriptural passages such as these do not mention a censure of the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by the scriptures,

and since the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*)— used here as a synonym for "desire"— cannot constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because that desire itself is not the goal, it is understood from scriptural passages such as "as long as knowledge arises" that the word "knowledge" refers to the attainment of the practice of Śiva-yoga.
"Know the Self through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation, making the lower fire-drill [the body] and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill," and so forth.

Since in such passages the attainment of the state of Śiva—preceded by the cessation of bonds—is taught only for those who have achieved knowledge through worship (*upāsanā*), it follows that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) in the form of perfected wisdom alone is the cause of liberation. "Brahman exists."

It is thus determined that the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by such scriptures has liberation as its fruit at a later time. This is because the Śruti states: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [in Brahman]. The meaning of this Śruti passage is that for one who possesses the indirect experience of the knowledge of Śiva along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the delay until absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) lasts only for that duration.

There is a delay of time. As long as one is not liberated, and as long as the *prārabdha* karma is not exhausted, so long shall one remain; "then" (*atha*) one will attain [liberation]. This teaches that immediately after the destruction of *prārabdha* karma, one attains *videhakaivalya* (bodiless liberation). By this, it is shown that for those practitioners who possess the practice of the knowledge of Śiva arising from the scriptures, the fruit is liberation at a later time.

It is determined that for those who have attained the knowledge of Śiva preceded by the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), their very physical body becomes identical with the supreme Śiva-principle (*paraśivatattva*) following the cessation of bonds (*pāśa*). This concludes the section concerning the Agnihotra sacrifice. 9.

Now, a determination regarding the propriety of singing [the hymn] to the Reality even for those who worship Śiva—whose inner organs are purified by being perfumed with the state of being free from latent impressions (nirvāsanāvāsita) and who have attained the state of Nirābhāra-Śiva—is as follows:
Indeed, it is stated in the Śruti: "This Agni is indeed Rudra; he has two bodies—one terrible and the other auspicious."

Because Agni is designated as being the body of Śiva, injunctions such as "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives" and "He who, knowing thus, should perform the Agnihotra," are understood to apply necessarily to both the learned and the unlearned; for it is said: "O Bhārata, just as the ignorant act, being attached to action..."
Thus, the wise man, being unattached, should act while desiring the welfare of the world.

In response to the doubt—arising from the fact that such a rule is established in the Smṛti as well—namely, how it could be that rites such as the Agnihotra are not mandatory, he states [the answer] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"But the Agnihotra and so forth are indeed for the sake of that [liberation], because it is seen [in scripture]. (Sūtra 3.4.16)
Agnihotra and other such rites performed with the aim of the knowledge of Śiva lead to that very effect, which is the effect consisting of knowledge itself.

Why? Because of the scriptural evidence (*darśana*). For in such scriptural passages as, "Brahmins seek to know this very [Self] through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting," Agnihotra and the rest are shown to be the means for the knowledge of Śiva; thus, the knowledge of Śiva...
It is taught that because [the world] is to be subsisted upon, it is not something to be destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman. As it is said in the *Śivagītā Upaniṣads*:
"Devotion to Śiva arises through merits accumulated over ten million births."
The rites of sacrifice and charitable works which a human being performs;
Having renounced desires according to the prescribed rule, with the intention of offering everything to Śiva.

This has been elaborated upon in many ways through such passages. Although it is indeed true that karma is destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman— which is itself the fruit [of spiritual practice] since karma is destroyed by its own fruit— nevertheless, the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that the knowledge of Śiva destroys karma precisely in its capacity as a fruit, and not merely in its capacity as knowledge.
In the preceding section, it was established that those who possess perfect steadfastness in the knowledge of Śiva attain immediate liberation;

likewise, it was demonstrated that for those possessing indirect (parokṣa) scriptural knowledge of Śiva, as well as those endowed with tranquility, self-control, dispassion, cessation from ritual activity, and faith, there is the lifelong worship of Śiva. However, in this [section], it is stated that "the man of knowledge should perform the agnihotra," and not...

Regarding such passages as "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth," a doubt arises: since the injunction for the Agnihotra and other rites is understood to have its scope [restricted] by these [renunciatory texts], should the performance of the Agnihotra and other rituals be enjoined until the fall of the body, or until the arising of knowledge?

Since many scriptural passages— such as "One should offer the Agnihotra for as long as one lives" and "One should perform the twilight worship day after day"— teach the injunction that [rites] must be performed throughout one's life,
it follows that the performance of rituals, which cause prosperity as their fruit, is obligatory for both the learned and the unlearned; to this, the following is stated:
As long as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three types of craving for the body are observed,

so long [must there be] the performance of action dedicated to the Supreme Lord, free from desire for fruits, for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Śiva which is liberated from all latent impressions— [this being] for those who possess the knowledge of Śiva and are desirous of ascending [the path].

It is necessary. Thus, because it is firmly rooted by the knowledge of Śiva, the means for attaining that very knowledge—such as the recitation of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting—are established through passages such as "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting," and so forth; this applies to the Agnihotra and other rites, as well as to knowledge, which requires the cultivation of excellence through practice until the moment of death.

Since [the body] must be produced day after day, the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*) must indeed be performed for the sake of that production with the understanding that they are offered to Śiva;

otherwise, if the duties of the stages of life were neglected, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) would become defiled, and the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) would not occur at all. In the passage "This very [Self] by the recitation of the Vedas," "recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacana*) refers to the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*).

The practice of reciting Vedic mantras by those who advocate the internal path (*adhyātmavādin*) is a means for attaining the fruit of reaching Supreme Śiva. Regarding the greatness of the recitation of the *Śatarudrīya*, it is stated in the *Jābālopaniṣad*: "Then the students said to him: 'Tell us, what should one recite to attain immortality?'"

Yājñavalkya said: "By means of the Śatarudrīya," and so forth; "these indeed are the names of the Immortal; by these one indeed becomes immortal. In the Kaivalya [Upaniṣad]: "The Brāhmaṇa who constantly studies the Śatarudrīya becomes purified by fire, he becomes purified by wind, he becomes purified from the drinking of liquor, and [purified] from the theft of gold."

One becomes purified of the murder of a Brahmin; one becomes purified; therefore, one should take refuge in Avimukta. One who has transcended the stages of life (atyāśramī) should recite this always or even once; by this, one attains the knowledge that carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. Having thus understood this, one attains the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya). Here [are the mantras] known as the Śatarudrīya.

Although the Veda is shown to be identical with Śiva and dependent upon Śiva—both through the recollection of mantras that awaken one to Brahman, which leads to the realization of the injunction for generating the knowledge that crosses over saṃsāra, and through Smṛtis such as "The Veda is Śiva; Śiva is the Veda; he who studies the Veda is Sadāśiva," and Śrutis such as "The Lord of all sciences"—nevertheless...

The superiority of mantras such as the Śatarudrīya and the Pañcabrahma, which directly establish the principle of Śiva, is not contradicted [by this]. Even having drunk liquor, gone to the wife of one's guru, committed the theft of gold, and perpetrated the killing of a Brahmin—
Covered in ashes, reclining on a bed of ashes, and reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.

Because the *Sāma-śākhā* also states the superiority of the *Śatarudrīya* with the words "Thus... and so forth; and because in the *Jābāla* it is recorded that by reciting the *Śatarudrīya*, one is freed from all sins, on the grounds that these are indeed the names of Amṛta—that is, of Śiva, who is eternally liberated (*anādimukta*).
Moreover: "Even if a Caṇḍāla should utter the word 'Śiva,' one should dwell with him and eat with him;

for here, by the mere pronunciation of the word 'Śiva' which denotes Brahman, supreme purification is ordained even for an utterly impure sinner. This begins elsewhere with the passage: "The Brāhmaṇa who constantly studies the Atharvaśiras," and so forth.
Having taught that the fruit of practicing this is the destruction of all evils, it is understood that by reciting it once, one becomes purified and fit for action (*karmaṇya*);

by reciting it a second time, one attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas; and by reciting it a third time, one enters into the very deity—thus the fruit of liberation (*mokṣa*) is understood. This refers to the practice of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose essence is Śiva, as in passages such as "making the self the lower fire-drill" (*ātmānam araṇiṃ kṛtvā*).
The definition of the "severer of bonds" (pāśavicchedaka) is now stated; it should be understood in this same way elsewhere as well.

Therefore, since it is understood that for those devoted to Śiva, the Vedic mantras are a means to liberation by virtue of being the cause of the knowledge of Śiva through the destruction of sin, their practice must be undertaken by those possessed of wisdom.

For those who are free from the ultimate state of perfect enmity [toward worldly life], the lifelong performance of sacrifices such as the *agnihotra*— which have their fruits offered to Paraśiva and are established by His command and consist of the nature of His worship— must be practiced like the Vedas. The same applies to charity and other such acts.

Therefore, while the renunciation of action is appropriate for those who are free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and who rely upon the reality that is devoid of false appearances (*nirābhāsa*), it is improper for householders who worship Śiva but are bound by the three worldly desires.
This is because rites such as the *agnihotra* are for the sake of generating knowledge (*vidyā*), and merit acquired prior to the arising of that knowledge must likewise be maintained.

If [the soul] has perished through the experience of having dwelt until the exhaustion of its karma—according to the text "having dwelt as far as the point of exhaustion" (Chāndogya Up. 5.10.5)—then what is the subject matter of the statement "his good deeds also go with him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.6)? To this, he says:
"Moreover, there is another [kind of action] for some; indeed, for both. (Sūtra 3.1.17)

Therefore, even apart from the "good deeds" consisting of the Agnihotra and other rites performed for the sake of the arising of knowledge, it is indeed possible that there exist infinite good deeds—both prior and subsequent to the attainment of knowledge—whose fruits are obstructed by more powerful karma. This statement of certain followers of particular recensions (śākhins) refers to that very point. Of that...
"Children inherit the estate, while friends inherit the merit of good deeds"— thus, the scriptural texts concerning non-attachment and destruction refer to that [merit].
Therefore, for those who perform Vedic dualistic rituals such as the Agnihotra dedicated to Śiva, according to the analogy of the bumblebee and the worm:

It is determined that [the study of Mīmāṃsā] is necessary for those seeking liberation, as it serves as a limb of the spiritual attainment (*siddhi*) consisting in the acquisition of Śiva-nature preceded by the cessation of the state of being a living soul (*jīva-bhāva*), and because it is the repository of the knowledge of the meaning of all Vedāntas. By this...

It should be understood that the doctrine of the falsity of the world and of duality—based primarily on fallacious scriptures and prescribing superimposition and negation (adhyāropa-apavāda)—is in no way to be resorted to by those seeking liberation.

Now, [one might object]: "But surely, for all [seekers], there are such scriptural passages as, 'The Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas' (*tam etaṃ vedānuvacanena brāhmaṇā vividiṣanti*)," and so forth.

As for the claim that it is possible for ritual actions (*karman*) to serve as means to knowledge (*jñāna*) because they are understood through scriptural injunctions (*codanā*) as such for those performing meritorious deeds— that is incorrect. This is because the scriptures, in passages such as "partless, actionless, and tranquil," as well as the Sūtra "and thus upon the attainment of that [Brahman]," establish that Brahman is devoid of all distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*).
|| 314 || "For it is by knowledge alone" (Yadeva vidyaya iti hi) || 18 ||

Regarding the Vedic statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," the phrase "whatever action [one performs] with knowledge" refers here to rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma dedicated to the Supreme Lord, which are devoid of meditations on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart) and other such practices— [meditations] which are the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman— and which, due to the delay of time, [would otherwise lack potency].
It is taught that [Brahman] becomes the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman. The particle *hi* signifies certainty.

Since it is declared in the passage, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action," that the power of Brahman is innate, the possibility of its being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) and so forth is not tenable. Nevertheless, [it is described as] "without parts" (*niṣkala*) and "actionless" (*niṣkriya*).

It has already been stated, in accordance with such sūtras as "Like the world, [His] sport alone [is the cause]," that scriptural passages such as "Thus, etc. refer to the state when His powers are contracted, whereas passages such as "The Lord of the Pradhāna and the Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas" refer to the state when His powers are expanded. Therefore, the sūtra "Upon the attainment of That... does not have the attributeless Brahman (nirviśeṣa) as its subject matter.
It is determined:
[the body] is the substratum for enjoyment. 10.

Having determined that liberation is attained immediately after the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit, [the author] now addresses the following doubt: "Even so, how is the destruction of the *prārabdha* karma—consisting of merit and demerit—possible for those wise ones who meditate on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart) and other such objects? In response to this, he speaks by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
But having exhausted the others through experience, he then attains [the state of liberation]. || 19 ||

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is as follows: the wise devotee, through the experience of *bhoga*— that is, the experience of the *prārabdha* karma consisting of pleasure and pain— exhausts and destroys future merit and demerit which cause the production of future bodies by the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), and thus attains the fourfold liberation according to his own will.

For those who possess full qualification, liberation occurs directly here in this very body; for those of dull intellect who have dedicated their Vedic rituals solely to the Supreme Lord, knowledge arises merely through a succession of many births over three lifetimes. This was stated in the preceding section, because there it was declared that knowledge is the cause for the destruction of both merit and demerit.
Regarding those men possessed of knowledge, it is held that their knowledge will bear fruit either in this very body or in another body. On this point, a doubt arises:

since the scripture states, "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released," and because it is heard that liberation concludes with the release of the body, it follows that for all possessors of knowledge, liberation is possible only at the end of this present body.

If one accepts the assumption of many bodies for the purpose of exhausting the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma, it follows that knowledge (*vidyā*) would fail to achieve its status as a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*).

Just as in the case of prior knowledge, whatever action a person performs even during subsequent states of knowledge necessarily results in the experience of its fruit. Therefore, since the continuity of the succession of births cannot be severed, liberation is in no way possible—this being the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
We say:

the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "by means of experience" (*bhogena tu*) serves to exclude the [previous] position. Others hold that one attains Brahman after exhausting the merit and demerit whose effects have already begun by experiencing their results, and immediately following the completion of that experience.

If merit and demerit were to yield their fruits within a single body, then upon its conclusion one would attain Brahman, because those two types of karma whose fruits have already begun must be exhausted through experience alone; for it is said, "For him, the delay is only so long," and thus liberation from those two karmas occurs through experience.

Since there is no scriptural injunction for a restriction based on the body as a limit, thus, that very karma consisting of merit and demerit— which was performed prior to the knowledge of Brahman, whose fruit has not yet been experienced, which has not begun to bear fruit,
which has been accumulated since beginningless time, and which is infinite— is destroyed through the majesty of knowledge.

Furthermore, that which is performed after the commencement of knowledge does not adhere [to the knower]. In this regard, it has already been stated previously: "In that state, all merit is taken by the knower’s friends, and evil is taken by his enemies.
Thus ends the *Pañcapādikā* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics.
In the Śrīkarabhāṣya, which elucidates the meaning of the Vaiyāsika Brahmamīmāṃsā Sūtras that establish the doctrine of Viśeṣādvaita,
[this is] the section beginning with the Āvṛttyadhikaraṇa of the fourth chapter, known as the Phalādhyāya.
The first quarter (pāda), consisting of nineteen sūtras beginning with "āvṛttirasakṛdupadeśāt" [sūtra 1.1.1] and ending with "daśādhikaraṇāvacchinna," is completed.
Now begins the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya: The Section on Speech (Vāg-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

You [are the one who] demonstrates the specific fruits of the state of the soul's departure (utkrānti) when it has become the object of the feet [of the Lord]. In the previous section, liberation was declared only for those who practice meditation (*upāsaka*). There are two states for those practitioners: death and departure.

Regarding departure, there is the attainment of the world of Śiva—which consists of unsurpassed bliss, sovereign power, and auspicious majesty—by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*).

For those of meritorious deeds, there is attainment of the heavenly world (*svargaloka*) by way of the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārga*). For sinners, there is attainment of the world of hell (*narakaloka*) by way of the third path. However, for those who possess the direct realization of the supreme Śiva-tattva, which consists of the partless supreme light, through the power of the *dahara* and *bhūman* vidyās, there is dissolution right here in the *jyotirliṅga* of Paraśiva.
First, he shows the state of death common to all by saying:
"Because speech [is seen] in the mind, and because of sound. (Sūtra 3.1.1)

An examination of the state of death common to all: why does the organ of speech merge into the mind? Because that is observed; for in the world, even after the cessation of the activity of speech among those seeking liberation, the activity of the mind is seen to persist, and because of the scriptural statement regarding this departing soul: "His speech merges into his mind."

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is as follows: based on the scriptural statement, "Speech merges into the mind; the mind into breath; breath into the presiding deity (the individual soul); and the presiding deity into heat; and heat into the supreme Deity," it is understood that even in the state of death, as in deep sleep, the organ of speech merges into the mind, because of the designation of its connection with the mind.

Now the author begins to consider the manner of the departure of a wise lay follower (*upāsaka*). First, the process of departure (*utkrānti*) is considered. In this regard, the following is recorded in scripture: "O gentle one, when this person is departing, speech merges into the mind," and so forth. Here, regarding the phrase "speech merges into the mind" (*vāṅ manasi sampadyate*), [the merging] of speech into the mind...

Regarding the doubt as to whether the mention of "attainment" (*sampatti*) refers merely to the functioning (*vṛtti*) of speech or to the essence (*svarūpa*) of speech itself: it is logical that it refers merely to its functioning. Why? Because the mind is not the material cause (*prakṛti*) of speech; since the attainment of the essential form of speech is impossible here, [the attainment of speech] occurs through its dependence upon the mind.

The scriptural statement regarding the perfection of their functions is somehow possible; for, as in the world, it is understood that an effect dissolves into its material cause—just as a clay pot [dissolves] into clay—and since speech and the other organs have Brahman as their material cause, it is logical that they should dissolve independently into that very [Brahman] alone. To this, we reply:

Regarding the phrase "speech and mind": speech itself merges into the mind. Why? Because it is observed as such. For it is observed that even when the organ of speech has ceased its activity, the mind continues to function. If it is argued that this is possible through a mere merging of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the author replies: [this refers to] the merging of the mere functions (*vṛtti*). For at that time, when the function has ceased, the organ of speech [does not exist].

That by which something is perceived through another means of knowledge is said to "become merged" (*sampadyate*) as mere function. As for the objection that because the mind lacks the activity of speech, the merging of speech into the mind is not tenable— that must be refuted by the statement "speech merges into the mind," which implies that speech is joined with the mind rather than being dissolved therein.

Furthermore— because of the statement, "O gentle one, for this person who is departing, speech merges into the mind; the sense organs merge into the mind," and because it is observed that at the time of departure,
speech and the other organs cease first, speech merges into the mind first, and thereafter all the sense organs merge into the mind.

As for the statement that "the effect dissolves into its material cause (*upādāna*)," that is not possible, because only the dissolution of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) depends upon a material cause.
Therefore, it is not said that speech and the other organs dissolve into the mind in their entirety; rather, it is the dissolution of their functional activity (*vṛtti*) that is meant.
Just as the functional activities such as illumination cease in a spark of fire cast into the midst of water, so too [do they cease] in the mind, which is not their material cause.

The dissolution of the functions of speech and the other organs is also indicated, because even when there is a distinction between the function and that which possesses the function, the realization of their non-difference is observed.
Here he states another reason: || 317 || "And for this very reason, all [the functions] follow... || 2 ||

Since "attainment" (*sampatti*) is merely the conjunction of speech with the mind and not its dissolution (*laya*), for this very reason the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of all the senses in the mind following speech is logically consistent; thus [it is said]: "one whose vital heat has subsided [attains] rebirth through the senses as they attain the mind."

Furthermore, even in the context of the path of creation (*sṛṣṭimārga*), the primacy of the mind is heard in scripture: "Whatever one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech; that one performs through action. In the section on the *samādhi* of Śiva-yoga:
"The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the peaceful Self."
One should place that knowledge within the Great Self, and that [Great Self] within the Tranquil Self.

By such passages as these, the superiority of the mental organ (*mānasa*) over speech and the other organs is understood. Therefore, even at the time of death, the dissolution of the organ of speech into the mind is not contradictory. This concludes the section on the Mind (*mano'dhikaraṇam*). 2.
Consideration of the dissolution of the mind (*manas*) into the vital breath (*prāṇa*):

Now, since the mental faculty is superior to the organs such as speech, let the function of speech dissolve into the mind, given the scriptural authority, reasoning, and experience that "the mind is the lord of the senses" and so forth. Nevertheless, into what does the mind itself [dissolve]?
Anticipating the doubt that there might be rebirth in the state of a householder (layopapatti), he states another section:
|| 318 || "That mind [goes] to the breath, on account of the subsequent [text]. || 3 ||
In the scripture stating "the mind merges into the vital breath," the mind is the master of the senses, while the vital breath (māruta) is the master of the mind;
when the vital breath moves through the center, stability of the mind arises.

Thus, from the understanding that the mind is dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in this statement, the mind dissolves into the vital breath. Why? Because of what follows—that subsequent statement. From the passage beginning with "the mind [dissolves] into the vital breath," the dissolution of all the senses, such as speech and the rest, into the mind is understood; and since the state of the mind's dissolution into the vital breath is understood therefrom, the senses such as speech dissolve into the vital breath through the mind, which is their material cause (*upādāna*).
There arises the doubt as to whether there is the dissolution of the mind’s own nature (*svarūpa-laya*) or the dissolution of its function (*vṛtti-laya*).

For in the scriptural passage, "The mind, my dear, consists of food; breath consists of water; speech consists of fire," the mind is understood to have food as its material cause (*prakṛti*). And regarding food, [it is said] in such passages as, "They created that food."

It is also perceived that water is a material cause of food; therefore, in the statement "the mind merges into breath" (prāṇa), if one were to argue that the word "breath" refers to the waters— which are the primordial material of breath— and thus establishes the merging of the mind into them, thereby implying a merging into its own ultimate cause through a succession of causes, we reply as follows.

As before, here too there is merely the dissolution of the function (*vṛtti*) of the mind into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), not the dissolution of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). This is because we see the subsequent statement, "The mind merges into the vital breath," and because it is impossible for the mind to have the vital breath as its material cause (*upādāna*). For it is said, "O gentle one, the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), and the vital breath consists of water (*apomaya*)," whereby the nourishment of the mind and the vital breath by food and water is expressed, but not [their identity].

It is determined that the term "prāṇa" refers to water through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), because the mind is derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the vital breath (prāṇa) is a modification of space (ākāśa).
This concludes the section on the presiding deity (adhyakṣādhikaraṇam). 3.

Regarding the inquiry into the dissolution and attainment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the living self (*jīva*): although the dissolution of the mental [breath] into the vital breath might occur because the vital breath can have the mind as its substrate, nevertheless, when the expectation arises as to where the nourishment of the vital breath is appropriate, he states another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
|| 319 || That [Self] is perceptible, because of such things as its approach to that [body]. || 4 ||

That [speech] merges into the individual soul (jīva), which is the presiding deity of the vital breaths (prāṇa). Why? Because of the reasons consisting of its "approaching" that and so forth. For in the scripture—namely, "When he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him; when the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it"—it is heard that the vital breaths and the rest go to the next world together with the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña); therefore, [the soul] is the presiding deity of the vital breaths.
The meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that, in every respect, this does not contradict the nature of the individual soul (jīva).
For in the Śruti, "the vital breaths (prāṇas) do not depart there; they are merged right there," the merging of the prāṇas into the Supreme Self is understood;
and in the Śruti, "as he departs, the prāṇa departs after him," the prāṇas are heard to follow the soul.
There arises the doubt: does [the soul] undergo nourishment in the Supreme Self, or does it follow after the individual soul (jīva)?

For, while the scripture states, "From this [Self] is born the vital breath" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*), indicating that the vital breaths are produced from the Supreme Self, and while elsewhere it says, "You are the knot of the vital breaths; enter me, O Rudra, the destroyer," indicating that the vital breaths have Him as their substratum, it is also said, "The vital breaths do not depart from there; right there... [they remain].
In the phrase "they merge," because the state of these [elements] merging into that [prāṇa] is indicated, the dependence of prāṇa upon the Supreme Self alone is pointed out.
Furthermore, in accordance with the statement, "Speech merges into the mind; the mind [merges] into prāṇa," just as the mind...

Since there is a statement that "speech and mind merge into breath," and likewise "breath merges into heat," it follows that breath merges into heat alone; to this we reply: "It [merges] into the presiding [self].
That breath merges into the presiding self—the individual soul (jīva), the lord of the instruments. Why? Because...

Because of its approaching [the soul] and so forth. First of all, the approach of the vital breath (prāṇa) to the living soul (jīva) is heard in scripture: "In this very way, at the time of my end, all the vital breaths gather around my self. Likewise, the departure of the vital breath together with the living soul is heard: "As he departs..."

It is recorded that the vital breath (prāṇa) departs along with the individual soul (jīva), and its support (pratiṣṭhā) is likewise remembered [as departing] together with the soul: "Upon whose departure shall I depart?

Upon whose being established shall I be established? Thus, having joined with the soul, its merging into fire (tejas) is expressed here as "the vital breath [merges] into fire," just as the Yamunā merges into the Gaṅgā after joining it.
Just as the statement "the Yamunā goes to the ocean" is not contradicted even though [its waters] also go to the sea,

so too there is no contradiction among the statements such as "the vital breaths do not depart from there. Furthermore, the fact that the Supreme Self is established as the cause of all— through passages such as "from Him the vital breath is born"— is consistent with their intent being the sequential creation.

Since Śiva alone is the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe by virtue of being its inner controller (*antaryāmin*), it is not contradictory that everything is established in Him; nevertheless, because the existence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) apart from the individual soul (*jīva*) is untenable, their following after the *jīva* is ordained.
Therefore, both systems of doctrine are consistent. Section on the Elements (Bhūtādhikaraṇa). 4.

Regarding the attainment of absorption (laya-sampatti) of the individual soul (jīva) into Śiva, who is the self of all beings— an objection being raised that since the scripture "the vital breath (prāṇa) [merges] into heat" indicates the merging of the vital breath into fire, how can it be appropriate for it to enter the Supreme Self along with the individual soul? Anticipating this doubt and in order to refute it, he states another topical section (adhikaraṇa).
|| 320 || [The soul exists] in all beings, because that is heard in scripture. || 5 ||

And that presiding deity (adhyakṣa) merges into the elements, that is, the five great elements (pañcamahābhūta). Why? Because of the scriptural statement (śruti): "The Imperishable (akṣara) [merges] into light" (tejas). Since it is entirely appropriate for Śiva, the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all, to possess the nature of being the imperishable, his designation by the word "light" (tejas) is not contradictory in the case of Śiva. As it is said: "He is the God who is the light of lights; there the sun does not shine."

In passages such as "There is no moon or stars," because it is seen that Śiva alone consists of supreme splendor; in passages such as "Rudra is indeed all," because his nature as the self of all is designated; and in passages such as "He who is Rudra in the fire," because he is described as the inner controller of all—therefore, he who dwells within all beings, who is the self of all, possesses the status of being denotable by the word "all."
The subtle meaning indicated by the aphorism is as follows:
since the word *tejas* (splendor/heat) is observed to be used for fire in both the Vedic scripture— “Space, air, light, water, and earth, the supporter of the universe”— and in common worldly usage,
[it refers here to] that stainless, partless Brahman within the supreme golden sheath, which is pure and [consists of] the light of lights.

Since Śiva is designated as consisting of light in passages such as "Light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), and since it is understood from the statement "the breath merges into heat" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5) that the vital breath, conjoined with the individual soul (jīva), merges into heat, there arises a doubt: does the word "heat"— which serves as the substratum for the vital breath and the individual soul— refer to fire, or does it refer to the Supreme Lord?
Since the word *tejas* (splendor) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as referring specifically to the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), and there is no evidence for abandoning its primary meaning,

[the term refers to fire] in such passages as "Agni is the first among the deities," "He who, knowing thus, should offer the Agnihotra," and "One offers the Agnihotra as long as one lives," where all the deities are [otherwise] predominant.

Since the injunction for the lifelong performance of the *agnihotra* and *aupāsana* sacrifices is stated as being common to both the learned and the unlearned, and since the oneness of all worshippers regarding the object of worship is established in the Vedānta texts such as "Thou art That" (*tattvamasi*), it follows that the nourishment of individual souls (*jīva*) within the fire—another synonym for light—is not contradictory; this being the position reached, we reply: [The remainder of the argument follows: ...because the fire is a mere instrument for the sake of the sacrifice, and because the soul's nourishment occurs through its connection with the body, the nourishment of the soul by the fire is not possible. Furthermore, the scriptural statement "He who offers the *agnihotra* [is nourished]" refers to the sacrificer who performs the ritual, not to the fire itself. Moreover, the term "fire" here denotes the sacrificial fire, which is distinct from the elemental fire. Therefore, the nourishment of the soul by the sacrificial fire is untenable. Consequently, the statement that the soul is nourished by the fire is figurative, intended to praise the excellence of the *agnihotra*. Thus, there is no contradiction. ||| 1.3.12 || [End of Sūtra] ||| 1.3.13 || [End of Adhikaraṇa] ||| 1.3.14 || [End of Pāda] ||| 1.4.1 || [Beginning of Pāda 4] ||| 1.4.2 || [Beginning of Adhikaraṇa]
