Because in all the Vedāntas—through such passages as "Brahman is consciousness," "I am Brahman," and "That thou art"—it is taught that those seeking liberation who meditate upon Brahman have Paraśiva-Brahman as their very self.
"There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Him alone..."
Everything shines after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.

Since, in such passages, Brahman is understood to possess a radiance that culminates in unsurpassed excellence, and since the merging of a conscious individual soul (*jīva*) into fire— which is insentient by nature— is impossible, the term "light" (*tejas*) mentioned in the Śruti is appropriately applied only to Paraśiva-Brahman.
Now, even if the merging occurs sequentially into light and the other elements one after another, there is still the Śruti statement, "consisting of earth," and so forth.
How is this established? To this he says:
"Because [the Lord] does not show [the world] as being in one [place]. (6)
It is not [the case that] each one [of the elements] individually is capable of performing the function [of creation], for the Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate their incapacity:

"Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms; let me make each of these threefold, threefold. Thus, the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is taught so as to render them fit for the evolution of names and forms.
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create living beings without a collective union, as they had not come together in their entirety.
Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent,
those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas indeed produce the cosmic egg.

Thus, in the passage "the breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇas tejasīti*), the word "heat" (*tejaḥ*) denotes precisely that light which is of the nature of Paraśiva and is intermingled within all beings.
This concludes the section on the commencement of the journey (*āsṛtyupakramādhikaraṇam*).

[This refers to] the unsurpassed *sālokya* and other [liberations] obtained by liberated souls whose individual subtle bodies (*liṅgaśarīra*) have departed after they worshipped Brahman in its embodied form (*mūrtabrahma*).

Now, one might object: "Granted that the word 'light' (*tejas*) refers to the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, even so, what is the difference at the time of departure between those who worship the principles of Śiva in both embodied and unembodied forms (*mūrtāmūrta-śivatattva*), and those who perform meritorious and non-meritorious actions?"

Anticipating this doubt, he states another topical section (adhikaraṇa): "And [the meditation] is the same up to the departure from the body, and immortality is attained without having burned away [the remainder of karma]. (Sūtra 4.2.7)
This state of death, from the commencement of the departure [of the vital breath]— excluding the commencement of the departure—
is the same for those who possess the direct realization of the partless, sixfold Śiva-Brahman, for those who worship the Śiva-tattva with parts,
and for those engaged in ritual action (karmis). The "commencement of the departure" refers to that which resides in the lotus of the heart.

For the king called the *jīva*, who is surrounded by the fourfold army consisting of the five great elements, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the senses, and the mind, "departure" (*utkrānti*) consists in his exit from the inner apartment known as the body through the gateway of the channels (*nāḍī*) in order to behold the kingdoms of heaven, hell, the world of Śiva, and so forth.

Thus, it is stated that even for those who possess the knowledge of Śiva, the state of death—consisting of the gathering of the entire retinue of the individual soul (jīva), such as the senses and so forth, without the departure [of the soul]—is identical to that of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra). For those who possess the knowledge of Śiva, the subtle body, having gathered within the lotus of the heart, does not burn away; rather, it proceeds to another world while remaining delimited by the lotus of the heart.
Immortality and liberation exist only in Paraśiva-Brahman; dissolution into the causal reality of Paraśiva does not result in unreality.

According to the etymological derivation *liṅga* from "that which causes [the soul] to go to what is dissolved" (*līnaṃ gamayati*), it causes that which is dissolved in Śiva, the Supreme Self, to reach its state of being dissolved within Him.
It is called *liṅga* because it leads [to liberation]; it is called *śarīra* because it perishes (*śīryate*). That which is both *liṅga* and *śarīra* is the *liṅga-śarīra*.

The sense is that when this *liṅga-śarīra* dissolves into Brahman, the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is limited by it, becomes identical with the principle of Śiva (*śivatattvamaya*). Thus, the scriptural passage, "The fire [is merged] into the supreme deity," refers exclusively to one who possesses knowledge of Śiva.

Therefore, the subtle meaning is that the scriptural text prescribing the departure of the soul (*jīvotkrānti*) preceded by the dissolution of the previously mentioned subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is common to all.
Regarding this departure, there is a doubt: is it the same for both the knower (*vidvat*) and the ignorant (*avidvat*), or does it apply only to the ignorant?

This [departure] must belong only to the ignorant. Why? Because for the knower, immortality is stated to be right here, and thus there is no departure; for it is heard that the knower attains immortality right here:
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are released..."
Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains equality with Brahman.
This being the position reached, it is replied:

"And [the departure] is the same up to the beginning of the path" (samānā cāsṛtyupakramāt). For both the knower and the ignorant, the departure is the same up to the beginning of the path—that is, up to the beginning of the journey, meaning prior to entering the channels (nāḍīs). For even in the case of the knower...
The scripture declares that departure occurs by means of a specific channel:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Ascending by that, one attains immortality; the others serve for departing in various directions."

Thus, since the departure [of the soul] is heard of as occurring through a specific channel, the departure of even the knower is unavoidable. Furthermore, prior to entering that channel, no distinction is heard of, so that departure is common to all. However, at the stage of entering it, a distinction is heard:
"By that light, this self departs—either from the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body."
Thus, because of the identity of purpose with the scriptural statement, "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart," the departure through the crown of the head pertains to the knower.
As for what was said—that immortality is heard to belong to the knower right here—it is replied to there by the words, "And immortality without having burned [the body]. And.

The word "eva" (indeed) is used for emphasis. "Without having burned up"—that is, without having burnt away the connection with the body, senses, and so forth—the immortality that is attained, which consists in the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, is what is being stated; this is the meaning according to the Śruti passage beginning with "When all desires are liberated. And here [it is said], "he attains equality with Brahman."

It teaches that the departure [of the soul] pertains to the learned who meditate upon the partless Supreme Śiva-Brahman, and it also instructs regarding the experience of Brahman at the time of their meditation; furthermore, for those who perform meritorious and non-meritorious deeds,
there is the attainment of the worlds of heaven and hell as the locus for the enjoyment of pleasure and pain, just as for worldly people who meditate upon the embodied Brahman.

Even though there is an exit [of the soul] together with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), the threefold vibhūti consisting of *sālokya* and so forth—the abode of unsurpassed, eternal auspiciousness—is attained.
Now, one might object: is not the scriptural text, "The fire [is merged] into the highest deity," also common to all [souls], just like the preceding scriptural texts?
Anticipating the objection that there is no indicator of a distinction [between the two states], he says:
"Because of the designation of transmigratory existence until the absorption into That. (Sūtra 8)

That subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) persists until the "drinking" [of the final dissolution], that is, until the attainment of the Śiva-principle preceded by the cessation of the natural state of being an individual soul (jīva). Why?

Because of the scriptural designation of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). For those who worship the embodied Brahman and for ritualists (karmiṇaḥ), there is the world of Śiva, heaven, and so forth.
It is thus determined that the purport is the knowledge of the partless Supreme Śiva.
Furthermore: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released;
then, having shaken off evil like the hairs of the body, he is freed like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu."
Having shaken off the uncreated body and having perfected the self, I shall attain the world of Brahman.

And thus, having raised the objection— namely, that for those who worship the principle of Paraśiva as either partless or with parts, liberation through union (sāyujya-mukti) occurs; yet, if the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) exits from the physical body at the time of death, why is it not seen by those standing near the dead body?— he says:
And [the atom] is subtle by measure, because it is perceived as such. || 9 ||

The subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is subtle—ungraspable by the senses according to its measure—and it is subtle even in terms of its dimension. Why? Because it is perceived as such; for it has been established that the subtle body is beyond the reach of the senses in embodied beings.
Thus, even when that body exits from the gross body, its invisibility to all is not contradictory.

Furthermore—the *kṣetrajña*, even when having departed from the gross body, continues to follow the subtle body; otherwise, because movement would be impossible, there would be the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of the dialogue with the Moon and so forth. For it is heard in the *Paryaṅka-vidyā* regarding the path of the gods that there is a dialogue between the knower and the Moon: "Those who depart from this world go indeed to the Moon."

They all go there. Having introduced this with the words, "This moon is indeed the door to the heavenly world," [the text continues]: "He who releases [the water] when it has been struck back down, having become rain here, rains; he becomes here a worm, or a moth, or a bird, or a tiger, or a lion, or a fish, or a boar, or a man, or indeed something else."
In those [fires], one is born after death according to one's karma and according to one's nature; when he has arrived, you ask, "Who are you?"—to him one should reply, and so forth.
By such passages, the journey via the path of light (arcir-ādi-gati) for the knower who has departed from the body is heard in scripture.
This refers to the exit of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) from the gross body for knowers other than the devotees of the partless Śiva.
Anticipating the question "What is the reason?", he says:
"Therefore, not by suppression. (10)

Therefore, because the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) exits from the gross body immediately after death, there is no experience of suffering in the gross body through its destruction—such as by means of burning or other forms of affliction. The sole cause for its departure is one's own past karma. For those who are liberated from all desires, that subtle body [merges] right here into the Supreme Self alone.
It becomes dissolved in the body. Thus it is heard in scripture: "In this [body], one attains Brahman.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 326 || "And because of this very same reasoning, there is warmth" (Sūtra 3.1.11).

Because the existence of this subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) in some location is logically established, the warmth of a learned person (*vidvan*) who has begun the process of dying is perceived in certain parts of the gross body prior to death. Nor is this warmth that of the gross body alone, because it is not perceived elsewhere. Therefore, the perception of warmth in specific locations belongs to the learned person.

It is understood that [the departure] is based on the departure of the subtle body. Therefore, it is well said that even for one who has attained the state of *suṣupti* (deep sleep), the process of departure remains the same until the commencement of the journey.
As long as the connection between the subtle body and the gross body persists, warmth remains in the gross body.

Heat, touch, and so forth are observed everywhere. Since it is understood that after separation from the subtle body, the gross body undergoes other properties such as coldness, the departure of the subtle body is inferred.
Furthermore, having raised the objection that the departure of the liberated (vidus) is not possible, it is refuted as follows:
If it is argued that [the soul is not eternal] because of a scriptural prohibition, we say no; for in some [scriptures], the departure [of the soul] from the body is clearly stated. || 327 || 12 ||
As for what was stated—that the departure [of the soul] is the same for the knower as well—that is not tenable, because the departure of the knower is prohibited. For it is said:
having begun with "Taking these particles of light, he descends into the heart itself," it continues, "By that radiance, this Self departs; as he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after him."

Having thus described the manner of departure for the ignorant person, and having further described the assumption of another body with the words, "he makes for himself another newer and more beautiful form," [the text continues]:
"Having reached the end of that karma, whatever this one does here..."
From that world, he returns again to this world for the sake of action.

Having thus concluded the section concerning the ignorant with the words, "But he who desires," the text then addresses the one who desires: "Now, as for him who does not desire—who is without desire, whose desire has departed, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—his vital breaths do not depart. Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman.
In this way, the departure of the knower is negated; likewise, in the earlier question of Ārtabhāga, there too the departure of the knower was negated.

Having introduced the wise man who has transcended death, [Janaka] said, "O Yājñavalkya, when this person dies, do his vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart from him, or do they not? Being thus questioned, Yājñavalkya replied, "No.
"They merge right here," he said. "He swells, he becomes bloated; bloated, the dead man lies there. Therefore...

If it is argued that "the knower attains immortality even here," that is not so; for in this context, the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) from the embodied inner self (*śārīraḥ pratyagātmā*) is prohibited, not from the body.
In the passage, "His vital breaths do not depart," the word "his" (*tasya*) refers precisely to the body, as established by the preceding phrase, "Now, he who does not desire."

The body is not what is referred to [as the point of departure]. By means of the genitive case in the word "tasya" (of him), the body is indicated as being related to the vital breaths (*prāṇānām*), and not as the point of departure for their departure. If it is argued that the body alone is indeed the point of departure for the departure, we say no; for when there is a requirement for a point of departure, it is the Self (*ātman*)—which is heard in scripture as being related [to the breaths]—that must be understood, rather than the body which is not so heard.
Because it is to be grasped as an ablative by virtue of its proximity;

furthermore, since the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are already known to be connected to the individual soul (*jīva*), there is no purpose in stating that connection again; therefore, it is determined that when the genitive case expresses mere relation, the ablative itself is the specific sense intended.

As in the case of "one hears the actor," there is no room for dispute here. For it is clear to some—specifically in the Mādhyandina recension—that the embodied soul (*śārīra-jīva*) itself is the point of departure (*apādāna*), as stated: "He who is without desire, free from desire, whose desires are fulfilled, whose desire is the Self—from him the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart. This is because there is no possibility of the vital breaths departing from the body [in that context].

If it is argued that the negation of that [departure] is not tenable, we say no; for by the statement "for him there is delay only so long," which declares the attainment of Brahman at the time of the knower's separation from the body, it follows that even the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) depart from the body of the ignorant person at that same time.
Consequently, the attainment of Brahman via the path of the gods would not be possible [if the breaths remained]. Therefore, "his vital breaths do not depart."

It is stated that by means of the path of the gods (*devayāna*), even for a wise person (*vidvat*), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not separate from the living self (*jīva*) prior to the attainment of Brahman. Even the question of Ārtabhāga, when it concerns the wise person, has this very same answer; however, when it concerns the ignorant person, it does not. For in that case, no connection with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is observed in either the question or the reply. Indeed, in that instance:
The essential nature of the sense organs and their objects as the "graspers" (graha) and "over-graspers" (atigraha);

the state of water, fire, and food for the living being at the time of death; the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇa) of the dying soul; the persistence of the name and reputation of the deceased; and the attainment of a destination by that soul in accordance with its merits and demerits—these are the matters [discussed].

These have been answered by means of questions. In that context, the statement "he conquers death again" refers to the conquest of fire itself as the conquest of death, based on the knowledge that water has fire as its food; therefore, this does not apply to the knower. However, the statement regarding the non-departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) for the non-knower means that the *prāṇas* do not leave him, just as they do not leave the gross body.
It is irreproachable that this establishes that the individual souls (*jīva*) travel after having embraced the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), like [the soul] does.

In this regard, for those pure souls who worship the embodied Supreme Śiva-Brahman, having reached the world of Śiva (*śivaloka*) and experienced unsurpassed bliss there, the sovereign glory of liberation consisting of union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya-kaivalya*) is subsequently attained.
To the question "What is the proof? he says:
|| 328 || And it is recorded in tradition. || 13 ||

"In the world of Brahman, at the time of the final end, they are all liberated through the supreme immortality," and so forth in such scriptural passages. Among them, there is one who goes upward; having pierced the solar orb and transcended the world of Brahman, he goes by that path to the supreme goal.

This is also recorded in such Smṛtis as: "Therefore, for the wise who are free from all desires and meditate upon the partless [Brahman], as well as for those who meditate upon the embodied Brahman, immediate liberation and gradual liberation are not contradictory.
This concludes the section on the "Possession of All Perfections" (Sarvasampattyadhikaraṇa).
Regarding the faultlessness of the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman:
some who maintain the doctrine of distinction between the conjoined and unconjoined states— likening the relationship of the *jīva* and Brahman to that of a body or to a jar and a cloth—
hold that within one’s own body, in the subtle ether (*daharākāśa*), there is no identity of essential nature for the *jīva* with the Supreme Śiva, along with its subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

They establish that [liberation] is possible. Certain proponents of the doctrine of "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃbrahmavādin*), who seek to prove the falsity of the world, refute the departure of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) at the time of the soul's exit for the wise. Therefore, in order to refute the partial views of those like the Buddhists who accept only a portion of the authority of the Śruti, [the text discusses] both gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) and immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*).
Having thus instructed [on the identity], some, according to the analogy of water and sugar, claim that the unity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is not possible.
To refute that view, he states another section:
"Those [fires] are in the Highest, for so it says. (1.1.4) || 329 ||
These—the elements, the senses, the vital breaths, and the internal organs—dissolve into the Supreme Śiva, who is beyond the individual soul (jīva).
Why? For it is said thus: "These sixteen parts have the Puruṣa as their goal; having reached the Puruṣa, they set.
The fifteen parts that have returned to their foundations, and all the gods, return to their respective deities."
The actions and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here.

The meaning is that scriptural passages such as "the knot of the heart is broken" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8) establish the dissolution of the ten sense organs, the five vital breaths, and the mind— belonging to the knower of Śiva—

into the Supreme Self. Although, in the Sūtra "And because of the commonality from the commencement of the departure" (Brahma Sūtra 4.2.7), the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) of the knowers into Brahman [is discussed]...

It has already been stated; nevertheless, the very meaning that was to be explained in the sūtra "tathāpi tāni pare" (But those [elements] are merged in the Supreme) is restated here for the sake of easy comprehension and to refute the views of certain scriptural schools. Thus, there is no tautology—this is the meaning of the sūtra.

For instance, in such scriptural passages as "Just as rivers flow... and so forth, the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is presented as that of the attainer and the goal to be attained.

A doubt arises as to whether, at the time of liberation, there is an identity of nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) between the liberated soul, mind, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, and Brahman—based on the teaching of unity during the state of liberation—or whether they simply remain silent and motionless, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*).

[The opponent argues: There can be no identity of nature whatsoever between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, because there is no Supreme Self distinct from the individual soul, and [the soul] would otherwise be insentient by nature.
Because the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) cannot be one with Brahman, whose nature is consciousness;
for this individual soul (jīva) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), while the Lord (īśvara) has the cause as His limiting adjunct.
Having abandoned the states of being effect and cause, pure, perfect consciousness remains.

In accordance with such established doctrines of the ancient teachers, the Vedāntic texts that enjoin the identity of the individual soul and Brahman— such as "I am Brahman" and "That thou art"— employ the method of *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning and not abandoning [part of the primary meaning]) according to the maxim "this is that deity," like the relationship between an original object and its reflection, or between the space within a jar and the great cosmic space.

It is logical to speak of the unity of consciousness preceded by the abandonment of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, because the cessation of ignorance—which serves as the limiting adjunct for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—is impossible, and because that which is real cannot otherwise be altered, the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) must be eternal, just like the Supreme Lord. If it were not so, the liberated souls could not exist separately, and thus [the subtle body] would be subordinate.

Since this would contradict all the scriptures that enjoin service and other duties characterized by dependence, it follows that the natural difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and likewise their non-difference during the state of liberation (*mukta*), are untenable; to this, it is replied: [The objection continues: Because it contradicts all the scriptures that prescribe dependence, service, and so forth, the natural difference between the *jīva* and Brahman during the state of *saṃsāra*, and similarly their non-difference during the state of liberation, are inconsistent. To this, it is said:

"Those [elements] in the Supreme" means that those living beings, together with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), merge into the Supreme Self. Why? Because the scripture says so: "The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations, and all the deities have returned to their respective deities," and so forth;

in hundreds of such scriptural passages, it is stated regarding the living beings. Since the identity of the conscious and the insentient is impossible, one must accept [the use of] figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
What was stated is incorrect, because there is no sublation of the primary meaning. Just as in many Śrutis such as "The rivers...

and so forth, [the identity] is beyond doubt; likewise, because of the designation of the essential identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, in the world we observe humans and others who have attained perfection through gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs assuming various forms such as tigers and the like.
It has been seen [in scripture]:

for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, the repository of all sciences, who is the locus of attributes such as the power of will and the capacity to bring about the impossible, [there exists] [grace] toward his own worshippers and devotees.
There is nothing to prevent [this teaching] from bestowing the realization of identity with the Self preceded by the cessation of the state of being a living individual (jīva).

Following numerous examples such as the bee, the worm, and the metallic essence (loharaśa), the cessation of one's natural condition has already been explained. This applies to living beings even in their state of liberation, just as it does in their bound state.

Because accepting a subtle body would entail the consequence of remaining in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), in the state of liberation there is no possibility of experiencing full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*); for, like the maxim of the king and his servant where the master-servant relationship and hierarchy prevail, the servant is a cause of fear. Thus, one who knows the Brahman as bliss has no fear from anything whatsoever; indeed, it is fearless.

The statement "O Janaka, you have arrived" contradicts hundreds of scriptural passages establishing the fearlessness of the liberated; furthermore, since there is no evidence for restricting the meaning of such scriptures as "Just as rivers [merge into the ocean]," the identity of the essential nature of the individual soul and Brahman, established by all the scriptures, is beyond reproach.
Section on Non-Differentiation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) || 7 ||
The determination of the non-difference between the individual soul established in the knowledge of formless Śiva and Paraśiva is like that of water and its reflection. Now,
it may be argued that the attainment of the Śiva-principle by individual souls occurs through the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*),
as in the cases of deep sleep, departure [from the body], cosmic dissolution, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that [the soul] is merely the negation of its gross state, he refutes it by means of another topical section:
|| 330 || "There is no differentiation, because of the scriptural statement. || 15 ||

For those who possess the knowledge of Śiva, the non-separation [of the soul from the Self] is established as the absolute destruction of the subtle body. Why? Because of scriptural authority. For in such Vedic texts as, "He leads one across to the further shore of ignorance; he does not return again," it is clearly taught that for those firmly established in the reality of Śiva, there is the cessation of the bonds consisting of ignorance and the absence of any return to worldly existence.

The subtle meaning is that the absolute destruction of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), which is produced by ignorance in the form of a snare, must indeed be admitted. "The one God rules over the perishable and the imperishable; through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, [one attains liberation] again at the end."

Reality is the cessation of *māyā*; for in such scriptural passages as "When that which is both high and low is seen, the knot of the heart is severed," there is instruction regarding the severance of the knot of the heart—which consists of the fetter of ignorance—for those who possess knowledge of Śiva.
Thus, identity with one's true nature occurs through the prior cessation of that ignorance which constitutes the fetter and serves as the material cause of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).

A doubt arises as to whether [the soul] merges with the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*), which is of the nature of a fettered transformation, like water dissolving into water— as occurs in states such as deep sleep or cosmic dissolution—
or whether it remains with the subtle body even during the state of liberation for living beings, like gold dust within honey or grain within a granary.

It is logical that their attainment of Brahman occurs simultaneously; for in such passages as "The one unborn, delighting [in her], lies by her; another unborn leaves her whose enjoyment has been experienced," and "The two, the Knower and the Unknower," the non-born nature of the individual souls (*jīva*) is established. Furthermore, since a conscious self cannot undergo dissolution, and because in the absence of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) the experience of the bliss of the Supreme Self would be impossible, [the liberated remain] entirely within the water even when they are liberated.

When it is argued that identity of essential nature (*svarūpaikya*) like that of water is untenable, we reply: just as a streak of gold in honeyed flour, the identity of the essential natures of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman as distinct entities is not possible. Rather, non-distinction (*apṛthagbhāva*) is logical, like fire in fire or water in water. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "Just as rivers... [and so forth].
From scriptural statements such as, "Flowing, she approaches the divine Person," identity of essential nature (*svarūpaikya*) and non-distinction (*avibhāga*) are indicated.

Since there is no cause for the existence of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) in the state of liberation—as in the case of the bound state—the absence of the effect follows from the absence of the cause;

by this logic, the persistence of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of a bond, which is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of that subtle body, is implied by implication. Upon accepting that [point]:

Otherwise, the futility of Brahmā’s knowledge of the seat (*pāsanajñāna*) would follow as a logical consequence. If it is argued that liberated souls possess a non-material body (*aprākṛtaliṅga*), that is inconsistent, because it would entail a contradiction with all the Vedāntas; for it is impossible for a non-material entity to serve as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of a subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). Regarding the subtle body...

Furthermore, because it is well-established in all the scriptures that [the subtle body] consists of seventeen principles produced from the five elements, the five qualities (rajas), the three qualities (sattva), and the self (ātman),
that which was stated previously is indeed what must be accepted by the learned. Thus ends the section concerning the blazing of the tip of its dwelling-place (tadoko'grajvalanādhikaraṇam).
The certainty that Śiva resides within the lotus-heart of all living beings and is the object of meditation for those seeking liberation is as follows:

for those established in the knowledge of formless Śiva, by the power of that knowledge of Śiva in this very body, they pierce the veil of ignorance in the form of bonds and attain liberation through union with Śiva (śivasāyujya), becoming indistinguishable from Him like a river merging into the ocean.

In order to establish [this], when the doubt arises as to by which path those wise ones who meditate upon the embodied Brahman proceed at the time of their final departure so that they may attain the experience of the threefold auspicious manifestations such as *sālokya*, he elaborates upon its majesty through another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*):

Then, having consumed that fierce flame at the door by means of the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), and through the application of recollecting the path remaining from that [knowledge], he is favored by the one dwelling in the heart (*hārda*) and departs by the artery that exceeds the hundred.

"Tadokograjvalanam" means the upward flaming of its abode; "its abode" (tadoka) refers to the heart-lotus, which is the dwelling place of that individual soul (jīva) surrounded by the vital breaths and senses. "Upward flaming" (agrajvalanam) means that the upper portion of that abode becomes expanded.
"Tatprakāśitadvāraḥ" means that, by means of that expansion, the path of the gods (devayānamārga) is revealed. Thus, being one for whom the way is shown by that expansion—

The devotee who worships the embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahmopāsaka*) exits from the body through the *suṣumnā* channel. He states two causes for the upward entry and expansion of the heart-lotus (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*): by the power of knowledge—that is, by the power of meditating upon the embodied Brahman—and by the yoga of recollecting the path leading to Him. Of that—
Through the practice of the remembrance of the path (*gatyanusmṛti*), which is a subsidiary to the meditation on the embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahmopāsanā*)— that is,
through the contemplation of the path of the gods (*devayānamārga*) and the connection with *śivayoga*— the top of his dwelling place (the heart) is set ablaze;
being thus illumined at the door, the meditator, favored by the one within the heart (*hārdānugṛhīta*), [proceeds] by means of that which resides in the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*).

The meaning is that, being favored and impelled by the Supreme Śiva-Brahman accompanied by Umā, he goes out from the body through the hundred-and-first *suṣumnā* channel, which is in excess of— that is, distinct from— the hundred principal channels.
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends upward to the crown of the head.
Ascending by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing [from this world].
Thus, the subtle meaning indicated by the aphorism is "by the force of scripture.

Previously, the characteristic of the departure [of the soul] (*utkrānti*) was described for those established in knowledge free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) who worship the partless Supreme Śiva. Here, however, it concerns those great souls who worship the embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahma*) and those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*).
Regarding the doubt as to whether there is a distinction between those who have departed [from the body] or not, this is recorded in the scripture:
"There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upward by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for the purpose of departing."
Thus [it is said]. The meaning of this scriptural passage is as follows: there are one hundred and one channels connected with the lotus of the heart.

Among them, one channel called Suṣumṇā has emerged toward the head, pervading as far as the aperture of Brahman (brahmarandhra). By means of that [channel], "going upwards through the door"—that is, departing from the body—[one proceeds].

The lay follower (upāsaka) attains immortality, the world of Supreme Śiva. The meaning is that the other channels existing in the four directions of the heart-lotus serve as the gateways for the departure of those engaged in ritual action (karmiṇaḥ). Through the path of smoke and so forth, and through the third path, the righteous and the unrighteous attain heaven, hell, and other realms respectively.

Since it has already been stated that [the soul] moves by means of the feet, it is not discussed here. However, there arises a doubt as to whether or not this restriction— that the knower proceeds by means of the single channel at the crown of the head (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*) among these more than a hundred channels, while the ignorant proceed by other channels— is logically tenable.

What is correct? That the restriction is not tenable. Why? Because, due to the great number of the channels (*nāḍī*) and their subtlety, they are difficult to discern and impossible for a person to grasp. The scriptural statement, "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality," merely restates a departure that occurs by chance.

Furthermore, from the scriptural statement, "The light [merges] into the highest deity," it is heard that both the knower and the ignorant, having dissolved along with the elements into the Supreme Cause—the Supreme Brahman which is of the nature of the Supreme Space and self-luminous—rest for a moment in a state of non-distinction; thus, the departure of all is indeed the same. Of this very one...

When it is argued that the superiority of the wise is in no way possible—given the scriptural vision that "the heart shines forth at its own peak; by that light this Self departs, either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body"—we reply: [The following is the response: "But [it is] from the body, on account of the going. (BS 4.2.17) It is not the case that the soul departs from the eye or the crown of the head; rather, it departs from the body. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "Having mounted the breath, he departs from this body" (BṛU 4.4.2). Furthermore, since the soul is atomic in size, it cannot depart from all parts of the body simultaneously. Therefore, it departs from a specific part of the body. And because the soul is connected to the entire body through the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is said to depart from the body as a whole. Thus, there is no contradiction with scripture. Moreover, the departure from the eye or the crown of the head is mentioned specifically for the sake of those who possess knowledge, whereas the departure from the body is stated as a general rule. Therefore, the superiority of the wise is established. Furthermore, the mention of the heart shining forth is intended to indicate the point of departure, not the actual location of the soul's exit. Hence, the superiority of the wise is indeed possible. Thus it is concluded.

"By that which exceeds a hundred": the knower departs by means of the single channel that passes through the crown of the head (*mūrdhanya*). Nor is it difficult to explain this for the knower; for the knower, by virtue of the power of that knowledge—which is exceedingly dear as it constitutes the worship of Śiva, the Supreme Person—the knowledge [itself]...

Because he has become a remnant [of the Supreme] and because of his practice of recollecting the path that is exceedingly dear to the Self, he becomes graced by the serene Supreme Brahman dwelling within the heart.
And consequently, that "abode"—the heart, which is the station of that individual soul—undergoes a "flashing forth at the front" (*agrajvalanam*). "Flashing forth at the front" means...

This illumination is the "flame at the top" (*agrajvalana*). Through the grace of the Supreme Person Śiva, the wise man, having had the door revealed, knows that channel; thus, the departure of the wise man by way of it is logically established.
Therefore, for the ignorant, there is no departure of the individual soul (*jīva*) from the heart along with the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) through the *suṣumnā* channel.
This very distinction is stated in another Śruti as well: "Rudra is seated in the heart of those who know;
having meditated upon the lotus of the heart as stainless and pure, [one perceives Him] in its center, luminous and free from sorrow."
Inconceivable, unmanifest, infinite awakening, auspicious, tranquil, immortal, the source of Brahman.
Thus, in hundreds of such scriptural passages, it is said:
"O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings;
seek refuge in Him alone with your whole being, O Bharata."
Seated in a clean place upon a properly prepared seat,
with his senses subdued and his anger conquered, he should meditate upon the imperishable Śiva.

One should meditate upon the Great Lord, who is composed of supreme bliss, seated within the lotus of the heart, pervading the expanse of the sky with his own splendor, beyond the reach of the senses, subtle, infinite, and primordial.

"Having shaken off all bonds of karma through meditation, his mind remains long immersed in the bliss of consciousness"—in such Smṛtis as these, it is determined that Śiva alone resides within the lotus of the hearts of all living beings and is the object of meditation for those seeking liberation. Furthermore, in such Śrutis as, "In the Liṅga [the Self], O gentle one, there is deep sleep; at that time, he becomes united with Being," [this is established].
Through the functions of all the senses, this body leads one to Sadāśiva along with the evil concealed within itself during deep sleep.
Rudra is superior to the universe, the great seer; indeed, all is Rudra. They speak of the oneness of Rudra; Rudra is indeed the eternal, ancient one.
"The Unborn"—thus does a certain fearful person take refuge. O Rudra, by that face of yours which is turned to the south, protect me.

"Protect us always; Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the bringer of auspiciousness; having abandoned everything else, by knowing the Lord they become immortal"—from such scriptural passages as these, it is understood that Śiva alone is the material cause of all and the bestower of the fruit of universal liberation.

Therefore, it should be understood that for those seeking liberation, there is no object of knowledge other than Śiva. For it is said that at the time of the departure of this living being's vital breaths, Rudra teaches the *praṇava*, the saving Brahman.

Thus, by describing the teaching of the *tāraka-brahma*—which is the *praṇava* itself and which reveals one's own true nature—at the moment of the departure of the wise, its quality of bestowing liberation is established.
It is not established for the other:

"The first divine physician, Dadhivaktar, has spoken [this] for you. O Rudra, do not provoke us with your anger, nor with your mental afflictions, nor with ill-praise, nor with an assault upon the bull."

"O Unnī, deliver the hero with medicines; I hear that you are the most skilled physician among physicians"—by such verses, Śiva alone is seen to be the physician who has liberated [beings] from the disease of *saṃsāra*. In passages such as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā," the entirety...

It is heard in the scriptures that Śiva alone is the sole cause of the universe, by virtue of being delimited by the power of *māyā*, whose characteristic is the creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Therefore, the Supreme Person, Śiva— the Lord of Umā who dwells within the lotus-heart of all—
[is the object of] those rites consisting of His own worship, such as the *śrauta* and *smārta* rituals enjoined by the Vedas which are the form of His own command.

Having caused the destruction of the impurity of ignorance in the form of bonds— by means of His special grace toward His devotee who has abandoned egoism and is devotedly engaged in the duties pertaining to his own caste and stage of life— He reveals the light of the Self; then,
having drawn that soul up through the channel at the crown of the head, He leads him by the path beginning with light to His own supreme abode, which is non-material and unsurpassed.
Having caused [the soul] to attain its own nature of bliss, it leads it to its own eternal, unsurpassed, and pure innate bliss in its own form.
Therefore, the difference in the destination for the ignorant and the wise is thus determined. This concludes the section concerning the following of the rays (Raśmyanusārādhikaraṇa). || 9 ||
An explanation of how a devotee of Śiva, following the rays consisting of unbroken light, attains the world of Śiva through the illumination of Śiva:
the wise devotee of Śiva, at the conclusion of his *prārabdha* karma, having emerged by means of the *suṣumnā* channel through the crown of the head, [proceeds] by what support?
In response to the doubt that [the soul] goes to the world of Supreme Śiva, whose nature is non-material and unsurpassed bliss, he states [the following] by means of another topical section:
"It follows the rays" (Sūtra 4.2.17).

When, through the grace of the Supreme Śiva, one has emerged from the body via the *suṣumnā* channel at the crown of the head, at that moment one's own self-luminosity is perceived extending from one's eyes up to the Great Kailāsa; then, as a worshiper of Śiva,
following the rays consisting of undivided light and being sustained by those rays, one passes through the gateway of that Śiva-light.
He goes to the world of Śiva, which is the eternal abode of auspiciousness and possesses unsurpassed splendor;

for previously, the practitioner— the Śiva-yogin who has been graced by Paraśiva, the illuminator of his own heart— has done so by means of the hundred-and-first channel at the crown of the head, through the majesty of the manifestation of Śiva consisting of great light.
The attainment of Mahākailāsa by way of the solar orb has been taught.
Furthermore, in the Śruti it is recorded that the departure of the wise to the other world occurs by means of rays: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by these very rays."

In this regard, it is considered whether the departure [of the soul] occurs solely by following the rays of light or otherwise; for in such passages as "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "Having meditated,

the sage goes to the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness," and "When the seer sees the golden-colored one," those who worship that [Brahman] are described as departing in a manner other than [following the rays].

This restriction of the path—that it occurs only by following the rays—is not possible. Furthermore, since it would be impossible for one who dies at night to follow the rays, the conclusion would be that there is no fixed rule; to this we reply: [The full response follows: "But [the rule] applies to all times, because of the statement 'until the rising of the rays'. This means that the phrase "until the rising of the rays" indicates that the connection with the rays continues until they rise again. Therefore, even for one who dies at night, the connection with the rays persists until sunrise. Consequently, the rule regarding the path remains valid for all times. Furthermore, the scripture speaks of the soul's departure through the artery called *suṣumṇā*; and since that artery is open at all times, the soul’s departure is possible at all times. And as for the objection that the mention of the day and so forth would be purposeless, we say: it is intended to show that for those who die during the day, the journey is more certain, whereas for those who die at night, the journey depends on the persistence of the connection with the rays until sunrise. Therefore, the rule regarding the path is established for all times. And as for the statement that the soul departs through the *suṣumṇā* artery, that too is possible at all times. Thus, the rule regarding the path is established for all times. And as for the objection that the mention of the day and so forth would be purposeless, we say: it is intended to show that for those who die during the day, the journey is more certain, whereas for those who die at night, the journey depends on the persistence of the connection with the rays until sunrise. Therefore, the rule regarding the path is established for all times. And as for the statement that the soul departs through the *suṣumṇā* artery, that too is possible at all times. Thus, the rule regarding the path is established for all times. And as for the objection that the mention of the day and so forth would be purposeless, we say: it is intended to show that for those who die during the day, the journey is more certain, whereas for those who die at night, the journey depends on the persistence of the connection with the rays until sunrise. Therefore, the rule regarding the path is established for all times. And as for the statement that the soul departs through the *suṣumṇā* artery
The knower goes upward by following the rays alone; why? Because of the restrictive particle "eva" in the phrase, "by these very rays.

For if this were merely optional, the particle *eva* would be redundant. As for the objection that for one who dies at night, travel by following the rays is impossible because rays are absent—this is not so; for even at night, there is a following of the sun's rays.

This is possible; for even during the night in the summer season, the existence of rays is perceived through the experience of heat, whereas in winter and similar seasons, heat is not perceived due to its being overwhelmed by frost, just as on a cloudy day. Moreover, it is heard that there is a constant mutual connection between the channels (nāḍīs) and the rays.

"Just as a great highway, being stretched out, goes to both villages—this one and that one—even so these rays of the sun go to both worlds—this one and that one. They extend from yonder sun; they are merged within these channels. They extend from these channels; they are merged in yonder sun."

Therefore, because rays exist at night, it is certain that even for the wise who die at night, there is attainment of the supreme Śiva-Brahman by following those very rays; for, since scriptural passages such as "the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself" are not seen to enjoin the process of departure, they are explained as merely indicating the result.
The section concerning the night. || 10 ||
The demonstration of the non-differentiation between the channels of day-and-night and rays:
Now, [it is said that] day, the bright fortnight, and the northern course [of the sun]...
For those on the verge of death, these are praised; the opposite, however, is censured.

Thus, there is heard a censure of death at night. Therefore, in response to the doubt as to how the attainment of the world of Supreme Śiva can be possible for Upāsakas who die at night, he presents another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"‘Not at night,’ if it be so argued, [we say] no; because that connection lasts as long as the body exists, and scripture shows this. (Sūtra 3.1.28)
This is now considered: whether or not there is attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman for the knower who dies at night.
Although a journey by following the rays is possible even at night because the sun's rays exist during the night, nevertheless, death at night is prohibited by the scriptures.

The attainment of Paraśiva-Brahman, characterized as the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), is not possible for one who dies at night. In the scriptures, dying during the day is praised, whereas dying at night is the opposite. Furthermore, through such statements as "the day and the bright fortnight," the superiority and inferiority of dying by day and dying by night are established as the causes for attaining the higher and lower paths (*gati*).

[Objection: These two [conditions] may exist; therefore, it follows that dying at night is a cause for rebirth in the lower worlds. To this we reply: "If it be argued that [there is no attainment] because of 'at night,' we say no. This means: if it is argued that because dying at night is understood to be a cause for the lower worlds, those who have committed sins do not attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman when they die at night—this is not so, because of the connection [of the qualification].

Because the light connected to the *suṣumnā* channel, which has Rudra as its deity, persists as long as the body exists, and because the connection between the rays and the channels exists both by day and by night, the scripture declares: "In these channels the rays have entered. Thus, the Śruti establishes the connection between the rays and the channels at all times. Furthermore—

Because for the wise person, the connection with karma persists as long as the body exists. This is what is meant: there is no destruction whatsoever of those karmas that have not yet begun their effects—which serve as the cause for downward rebirth—due to the connection with knowledge; nor is there attachment to subsequent karmas, and [the same applies] to the karma whose effects have already begun.

Because the final body serves as the limit [for liberation] and because there is an absence of causes for bondage, the attainment of Brahman by the knower—even if death occurs at night—is indeed established.

This is evident from the scriptural passage: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united. Furthermore, it is determined that scriptural passages such as "by day" and "during the bright fortnight" pertain to those who lack knowledge.
The section concerning the southern course [of the sun]. 11.

An inquiry into the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman even for one who dies during the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), as if for one who has died at night: "Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern course—
departing therein, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman."
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight, and the six months of the sun's southern course—
attaining the lunar light there, the yogi returns.

Thus, in the *Bhagavadgītā* and other *smṛtis*, it is understood that only those practitioners (*upāsakas*) and ritualists (*karmis*) who die during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*) or the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman or the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). Therefore, how [could there be such attainment] for practitioners who die during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the southern course, the night, or similar times?
Anticipating the doubt that [the deceased] might attain the world of Brahmā, he refutes it by means of another topical section:
"And therefore, even during the southern course. (Sūtra 3.1.21)
Since it is heard in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" that those who know Brahman attain Brahman and, together with Brahman,

obtain all desires, one must consider whether or not it is possible for those practitioners who die during the southern transit of the sun (dakṣiṇāyana) to attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman along with Him, obtain all desires, and achieve identity of form with Him.
A doubt arises:

"Now, he who dies during the southern course, having gone to the greatness of the ancestors, attains union with the moon. Since it is heard that one who dies during the southern solstice attains the moon, and since those who have attained the moon [are subject to return]...

Since there is the scriptural teaching of return—“Having dwelt there until the exhaustion [of their merit], they return again by this very same path”—and since we observe that even those such as Bhīṣma, who were devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, waited for the northern solstice, it follows that for the wise who die during the southern solstice, attainment of Brahman is in no way possible; to this, it is replied: [The answer is: It is not so. For it is stated: “But those who depart from here after the rains, during the smoke-colored [southern] night, proceed by the path of the fathers to the moon” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.4). And having explained that the moon is the gateway to returning, the text says: “From there they do not return” (ibid. 5.10.8), thereby distinguishing those who do not return from those who do. Furthermore, the scripture teaches that the path of the gods is open to all who possess knowledge: “Fire, light, the day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice—the ones who know this go by this path after death to Brahman” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5). Moreover, the Smṛti declares: “Whether one departs at the time of death when the sun is in the north or in the south, one attains the fruit of knowledge” (Mahābhārata, Śāntiparvan 236.17). Therefore, the wise attain Brahman regardless of whether they die during the northern or southern solstice. As for the waiting for the northern solstice seen in the case of Bhīṣma and others, that was merely for the sake of setting an example for the world. Thus, the conclusion is that the wise attain Brahman through both paths.

In the Sūtra, the particle *hi* signifies certainty. Since it has been stated that for a learned person who dies at night there is the cause for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman, for that very reason (*hetoḥ*), the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman by one who dies during the southern solstice (*dīkṣiṇāyana*) is established. This is because in such Vedic passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," [the attainment of the Supreme is affirmed] for those who know Brahman.
Because no restriction of time is observed:
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."
In such passages, since it has been elaborated that when the wise abandon all worldly latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they attain Brahman at that very moment,
it follows that only the ignorant return again by way of the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*) through reaching the moon;
for even those among the wise who reach the moon, [the text states] "from there he attains the greatness of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.6), as indicated by the remainder of the sentence.
It is understood that for those who have died during the southern course of the sun, the attainment of the moon is merely a cause for rest for those persons who desire to go to the world of Brahman;
this is so even in the absence of an explicit supplementary statement, because— as previously stated— there is an absence of the causes of bondage for the wise.
Even if there were the possibility of attaining the world of the Moon, the attainment of the world of Paraśiva-Brahman remains unavoidable:

"Those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta, who are self-controlled, whose being is purified by the yoga of renunciation, they all, at the time of the final end, are liberated from the supreme immortality in the world of Brahman. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6)
Thus, because all Vedāntins teach gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by means of reaching the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*),

and because in such passages as "one who desires the abode of Brahman should practice the knowledge of Brahman; he does not return again," it is taught that only those who know Brahman attain union with Śiva free from rebirth— even for those knowers of Śiva who die during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).

It is a matter of public proclamation that [the goal] is indeed the attainment of the world of Śiva. It is determined that such conduct on the part of Bhīṣma and others— who possessed the power of yoga and could die at will— was intended for the purpose of promoting righteousness and demonstrating the excellence of the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
But is it not observed that for those who know and are about to die, there is an injunction regarding specific times as the cause for non-return or return?
As it is said: "In which time, however, yogis attain non-return, and in which [time] they attain return..."
O bull of the Bharatas, I shall describe that time when those who have set out proceed.
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—
departing there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight and the six months of the sun’s southern course—
having attained the lunar light during that time, the yogi returns.
These two paths, the bright and the dark, are considered to be eternal for the world;
by one a man goes to non-return, by the other he returns again.
Having raised the doubt as to how all those who die during either of the two solstices attain Brahman based on this scriptural vision, he says in response:
"And these two [paths] are recorded in Smṛti with reference to yogins; they are indeed of the nature of Smṛti. (Sūtra 4.2.20)

In this context, no specific time of death is prescribed for those who are about to die; rather, the two paths known as the Devayāna and Pitṛyāṇa—which are objects of recollection—are taught for yogins established in yoga, so that they may be recollected daily as an auxiliary to yoga. For thus is the concluding statement: [The text continues: "Therefore, O Arjuna, at whatever time one departs, having fixed the mind on Me alone, with devotion to Me, one attains Me. (Gītā 8.5) "Thinking of whatever object one leaves the body at the end, to that alone one goes, O son of Kuntī, by that thought being ever held in mind. (Gītā 8.6) And likewise: "Remembering whatever state of being one departs from this world at the final end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, possessed by its nature. (Gītā 8.7) And: "Therefore, at the end, with a mind focused on Me alone, with a heart surrendered to Me, thinking of Me, you shall come to Me, having been liberated from all difficulties. (Gītā 8.8) And: "But he who, with the mind fixed on the Supreme Self, departs, casting off the body at the final end, while the breath is held between the eyebrows—he attains the highest goal. (Gītā 8.13) And: "Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice—departing then, the knowers of Brahman go to Brahman. (Gītā 8.24) "Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern solstice—departing then, one reaches the lunar light and returns again. (Gītā 8.25) "By these two paths, white and black, the world is led. By the one it goes to the state of non-return; by the other, it returns again. (Gītā 8.26) And: "Knowing these two paths, O son of Pṛthā, no wise man is deluded. Therefore, at all times, be established in yoga. (Gītā 8.27) Thus, the instruction regarding the time of departure is intended for yogins, not for those facing imminent death. It is taught so that yogins may daily recollect these two paths as objects of meditation, making such recollection an integral part of their practice. This is confirmed by the concluding summary.
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.

Thus, "Agni is the light, smoke is the night" and so forth, the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths are recognized. Furthermore, at the beginning, in the phrase "But at what time," the word *kāla* (time) refers to the presiding deities of time who act as guides (*ativāhika*), since Agni and the others cannot themselves be time. Therefore, the recollection of the Devayāna path prescribed in the passage "they reach the light" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*) is intended here.

The injunction applies to those established in knowledge (*vidyā*), not to those on the verge of death; for it is understood from scripture that "for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall attain [the goal]. Therefore, for the wise at all times, there is no distinction between night and the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) regarding the attainment of the supreme Śiva-Brahman.
It should be understood that the words found in the *Bhagavadgītā* and other *smṛtis*— namely, the word "night" (*rātri*), the word "bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*), and so forth—

refer to the presiding deities of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-devatā*) and cannot possibly refer to time. Furthermore, even if this *śruti* refers exclusively to those who worship the embodied Supreme Śiva-Brahman, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Thus ends the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*, composed by the venerable Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpādācārya, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics; a work that elucidates the meaning of the *Vaiyāsika-Brahma-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtras* and establishes the doctrine of non-dualism with difference (*viśeṣādvaita*).
The fourth chapter, known as the *Phalādhyāya*,
consists of twenty sūtras beginning with "vāṅmanasi darśanācchabdācca" (Vāyu 4.1.1–20), which are divided into eleven topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) starting from the section on speech (*vāk*).
The second quarter is completed.
Now begins the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śrīkarabhāṣya: The Section Concerning the Path Beginning with Light (Arcirādyadhikaraṇa) || 1 ||
The fruit of the path beginning with light was previously described: one who possesses meritorious karma, through the ripening of his own timely rites, leaves the gross body,
departs by means of the superior openings such as the mouth and eyes, and reaches the moon by way of the path of the fathers (pitṛyāna).

Immediately thereafter, having experienced the heavenly realms and other worlds from that world, one attains birth in an excellent womb— such as that of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) or a Brahmin— by means of the remainder of that merit.
One who possesses sinful karma, at the conclusion of the gross body, [departs] through the lower apertures such as the anus, in accordance with those respective karmas.

Having departed from Dhūmāgati and experienced the terrible hells such as Kumbhīpāka in the world of Yama, one attains birth in inferior wombs such as those of a donkey or a pig in the mortal world once that sin has been destroyed.
Likewise, here, through the specific practice of worshiping the partless supreme Śiva-tattva, the wise person [attains liberation] right here.

Accompanied by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) consisting of sixteen constituents, he goes to the Śiva-principle. The devotee who worships the embodied Brahman in the form of Umāmaheśvara, upon the abandonment of the gross body, ascends by the path of light— the flame at the tip of the *suṣumnā* nerve— through the power of that worship, in accordance with the path beginning with the *arciḥ*, during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).

By following the orb of light during the southern solstice through the gateway of the lunar orb, one becomes a possessor of the experience of incomparable, eternal, auspicious, and unsurpassed prosperity such as the world of Śiva;
this is the teaching for those who know it thus, and for those here in the forest who worship faith and truth.
Beginning with "They attain the flame," and continuing with "After six months they reach the world of the gods;

from the world of the gods to the sun; from the sun to lightning," and so forth, since the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* establishes that performers of meritorious deeds attain the worlds of Vāyu, Varuṇa, Indra, and others, [the text states] "they attain the flame."

Having raised the objection as to how the scriptural injunctions— such as the Chāndogya Śruti— which prescribe the attainment of His world and so forth for those who meditate upon the embodied Brahman (mūrtabrahma) via the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga), can be justified, he begins the third pāda to determine that the wise indeed attain the world of Paraśiva-Brahman solely by way of the path beginning with light.
|| 336 || Because that [attainment] is well-known to occur by way of the path beginning with light (arcis). || 1 ||

In the preceding section, it was stated that for the worshiper of the Supreme Śiva— who has had the door opened by the grace of the Supreme Śiva residing in the heart-lotus— the commencement of the journey occurs via the specific *nāḍī* at the crown of the head upon his departure, due to the grace of the one within the heart. Now, the path traversed by him as he proceeds is being determined.

In that regard, various alternative paths are taught in manifold ways within the Śrutis. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, for instance, after beginning with the passage, "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf," and having instructed the knowledge of Brahman, it is further taught: "Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him here or not, they pass into the light; from the light, into the day."
From the fortnight of the waxing moon, through the fortnights of the waxing moon, they go to those six months during which the sun moves northward;
from the months, to the year; from the year, to the sun; from the sun, to the moon; from the moon, to the lightning.
There, a person who is not human [waits]. He leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. By this [path]...
"Those who practice thus do not return to this human whirlpool. Likewise, in this very same [text], in the eighth [chapter]: "Then, by these very rays, he ascends upwards.
And the Kauṣītakins recite the path of the gods differently: "Having entered upon this path of the gods..."

"He goes to the world of Agni, then to the world of Vāyu, then to the world of Varuṇa, then to the world of Āditya, then to the world of Indra, then to the world of Prajāpati, and then to the world of Brahmā.
Likewise, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, worship truth with faith..."

"They attain the flame. Furthermore, in that very same context, it is stated otherwise: "Just as a person departs from this world, he goes toward the wind; for him, the wind parts there like the hole of a chariot wheel.
By that [opening], he ascends upward. He reaches the sun; for him, the sun parts there like the hole of a drum."

By that [path], he ascends upwards; he reaches the moon; there, for him, the door opens like the opening of a drum-skin. Regarding this and so forth, there is a doubt: is it the case that a single path beginning with light (*arci*) is taught by these scriptural passages, and by that very [path] alone?
It is recorded in the Smṛti that "the wise man goes to Brahman, and others go by other paths from him.

There is no fixed rule that the attainment of the world of Supreme Śiva for the wise occurs solely by way of the path beginning with the rays of light (arcir-ādi). In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad it is said:
"That which is this space within the heart; in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden."
Between the two palates, that which hangs down like a breast is the birthplace of Indra.

Where this parting of the hair occurs, having pushed aside the two skull-halves, one establishes oneself in the *bhūḥ* [world] in the limbs, in the *bhuvaḥ* [world] in the wind, in the *suvaḥ* [world] in the sun, and in the *mahaḥ* [world] in Brahman. Thus one attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Thus [it is said] in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Therefore, since it might be argued that the attainment of that world occurs otherwise, we reply:

for the wise, the attainment of the realm of Supreme Śiva occurs only by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*). Why? Because of its renown; for in the *Pañcāgni-vidyā* and other texts, the path beginning with light is well-known as the means of reaching Brahman, through such statements as "they proceed toward the light" (*te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*).

By the passage beginning with "He stands firm in fire through *bhūḥ*," etc., the path for attaining the world of Paraśiva-Brahman is not being described in relation to the various meditations (*vidyās*) and so forth; rather, what is taught is the attainment of His manifestations (*vibhūtis*). Therefore, the attainment of that world is understood to be nothing other than this. Because He is recognized as the Lord (*pati*), that very same path is set forth everywhere according to a relative gradation of deficiency or excellence, just as there is a combination of the qualities of the meditations elsewhere.
The elements previously mentioned are combined elsewhere.
In the Chāndogya, for instance, in both the Upakośala-vidyā and the Pañcāgni-vidyā, they are recorded as being of one and the same form.
Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the path beginning with light (arcis) is recorded in exactly that manner. Therefore, it is so even there.
Thus it is understood. Elsewhere, too, in all cases, Agni, Āditya, and others are recognized [as identical].
The section concerning Vāyu. 2.
Regarding the consideration of one's entry into the world of Vāyu after a year has passed:
Now, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śruti, it is stated, "He [goes] to the world of Vāyu, he [goes] to the world of Varuṇa, he [goes] to the world of Indra, he [goes] to the world of Prajāpati";
thus, four worlds—those of Vāyu, Varuṇa, and so forth—are mentioned. Where, then, does his entry into these take place?
Anticipating this doubt, he states [the solution] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"The air [is reached] after the year, on account of both non-distinction and distinction. (Sūtra 2)

After a year—that is, beyond the year—he enters the world of Vāyu. Why? Because of both the general and the specific. From the general statement, "He [goes] to the world of Vāyu," it follows that he must enter the world of Vāyu somewhere; since there is no specific mention of a particular location, his entry must occur at some point.
In this regard, because of the specific relationship between the forms of Vāyu and Āditya, [his entry occurs] between the year and Āditya.

It is determined that there is an entry into the wind, because the scriptural text "He [reaches] the world of wind" (vāyuṃ lokaṃ) indicates the world in general and lacks any indication of a specific sequence; thus, it should be understood as a non-specific statement—this is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra.
It has been stated that the knowers proceed by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi). Regarding that path beginning with light, the Chāndogya...
Between the month and the sun, the year is studied; from the months to the year, and from the year to the sun—this is the sequence beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*).
In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, it says: "When a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind; for him, the wind makes way there."
It is heard [in scripture]: "As the hole of a chariot wheel, by that he ascends upwards; he reaches the sun.

However, according to the Vājasaneyins, because of the teaching—"Between those two [the worlds] is the world of the gods; from the months to the world of the gods; from the world of the gods to the sun"—Vāyu is heard as being situated between the year and the sun. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: should he (Vāyu) be inserted there or not?

He is not to be inserted [at this point]. According to the principle of the inclusion of what is heard elsewhere (*śravaṇādguṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya*), Vāyu is to be inserted after the year and before Āditya.
Since the path is identical in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, both [deities] are to be included in both places.

In this regard, although the fifth [term] mentioned in both the year and the deities— namely, the Vedic sequence— is identical, yet because "from the light to the day, from the day to the waxing fortnight,
from the waxing fortnight to the six months when the sun moves northward" refers to longer durations than the shorter ones, they follow in successive order.

Because the year is perceived immediately after the month in the mental sequence, it is determined that the year itself must be placed after the month; therefore, it is concluded that "the world of the gods" (*devaloka*) follows after that.
Elsewhere, however, the Vājasaneyins state: "When a person departs from this world, he goes to Vāyu; to him, he [Vāyu]..."
There he glides forth; as the hole of a chariot wheel, so does he. He ascends upwards and reaches the sun.
Thus, before the sun, they study [the arrival at] Vāyu.
But the Kauṣītakins [read]: "Having entered upon this path of the gods, he reaches the world of Agni. He...

The phrase "the world of wind" (vāyuloka) refers to the wind that comes after the flame designated by the term "the world of fire" (agniloka). In this regard, although according to the textual sequence of the Kauṣītakins the wind is reached as being beyond the flame, for the Vājasaneyins, by the scriptural sequence indicated by the word "upwards" in the passage, "He ascends upwards; he reaches the sun," [the wind is placed before the sun].

Because it is more powerful than the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), entry [into the world of the gods] is determined to occur prior to that of the sun. Therefore, since the world of the gods and the world of wind are designated before the sun, they are understood to be distinct. And since they have distinct referents, both are established by the sequence of the scripture (*śruti*) as being situated between the year and the sun—by means of the word "above" (*ūrdhva*) and the ablative case-ending (*pañcamī*) respectively—and because there is no further distinction [between them].
When it is argued that [the soul proceeds] according to its own desire, it is said in response: "Vāyu after the year.

It should proceed to Vāyu after the year. Why? Because of both the general and the specific; Vāyu alone has been specifically indicated. For the term *devaloka* (world of the gods) is used generally as "the world of the gods" without specification.

By means of the word *rūpa*, it denotes *vāyu*; thus, "he goes to that *vāyu*," and for him there [is that], the word *vāyu* denotes *vāyu* specifically. Therefore, since *vāyu* alone is denoted by both the general term *devaloka* and the specific term *vāyu*, one should go to *vāyu* itself after the year, according to the Kauṣītakins.
