The term *vāyuloka* (the world of wind), like the term *agniloka* (the world of fire), denotes the wind itself through the etymological derivation "that which is the wind and is a world. Furthermore, it is heard elsewhere that the wind serves as the abode for the gods, as seen in the scriptural passage: "He who blows here—he is the houses of the gods. Thus, there is no contradiction.
The Section on Varuṇa. 3.
An investigation into the soul’s entry into the world of lightning from the world of wind:

Now, in response to the doubt as to from which world beyond the world of wind the world of Śiva arises for the knowers who follow the path beginning with light, [the author] shows this by means of another topical section:
Varuṇa is superior to Taṭita because of their connection. || 3 ||

After the world of Vāyu, the soul enters the world of lightning (taṭilloka). From the world of lightning, it goes upward to the world of Varuṇa, presided over by Varuṇa. Why? Because of their connection; due to the mutual relationship between lightning and Varuṇa, [the world of Varuṇa follows], according to the principle that "those remaining are placed at the end of those already mentioned," as in the case of the worlds of Indra and Prajāpati.

The subtle meaning is that immediately after the world of Varuṇa is the world of Indra; from there, one reaches the world of Paraśiva by way of the world of Prajāpati. According to the Kauṣītakins: "Having entered this path of the gods, he goes to the world of Agni; he [goes] to the world of Vāyu; he..."
In the passage "the world of Varuṇa, the world of Āditya," the primacy of the word *agni-loka* (world of fire) as a synonym for *arcis* (flame) is undisputed.

Furthermore, the entry of Vāyu after the year has been stated. Regarding Āditya as well, here the established order of the textual sequence must be set aside, as it is said: "from the world of the gods to Āditya, from Āditya to lightning."

The placement [of Vāyu] above the world of the gods (devaloka), which is designated by the term "world of the gods," is established according to the sequence of the Śruti text as recited by the Vājasaneyins.

Now, there is an inquiry regarding Varuṇa, Indra, and the others: should these, Varuṇa and the rest, be placed above Vāyu according to the order of the text, or rather above the lightning? Regarding this doubt—

Since there is no scope for [the soul] to go anywhere else due to the contradiction with the sequence of the scriptural text beginning with "From the flame to the day" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5) and so forth, and because of the hearing that the person beyond the lightning is the one who leads them to Brahman—
"The person beyond the lightning, who is non-human, he leads them to Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.5)—
[the soul] does not reach [any other destination].

In order to avoid the futility of the instruction, since something must necessarily be sublated, Varuṇa should be placed immediately after Vāyu in accordance with the order of the recitation; for the sequence between Vāyu and Āditya has been sublated, [leaving] Indra and Varuṇa as the pair to be considered.
First, Varuṇa should be placed above lightning. Why? Because of their connection.
The connection between lightning and Varuṇa is well known in both the world and the Vedas because of their common nature as "water-rollers" (clouds).

What is meant is this: since Varuṇa and the others must be placed somewhere so that their instruction is not rendered meaningless, and given that the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is stronger than the sequence of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), Varuṇa must be placed after lightning.

From this, it is understood that the role of the non-human being as a conductor is capable of tolerating an interval. Because he can tolerate such an interval, and because Indra and the others— who have been taught [as conductors]— must necessarily be inserted [in the sequence], and because those who are adventitious (āgantūnām) are to be inserted at the end, [the non-human being] is placed above Varuṇa.
It should be understood that Indra and the others are to be made to enter [the body]. Thus ends the section concerning the *ātivāhika* (conveying) deities. 4.
An investigation into the process by which the subtle body (ativāhika-deha), impelled by Paraśiva, leads the person who worships all the vidyās such as Dahara to Mahākailāsa;
[an objection]: when the liberated soul travels via the path beginning with the Radiance (arcir-ādi) to the worlds of Vāyu, Lightning, Varuṇa, and so forth, by what assistance is he accompanied?
In response to the doubt that [the soul] goes as far as the world of Śiva, the author provides a resolution through another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"The conducting deities [lead it], because of its characteristic mark" (Sūtra 4).

In those worlds beginning with the world of light (arciḥ), the gods residing in each preceding world act as guides for the meditators until they reach each subsequent world; they are the *ātivāhika* (conveying) helpers and no others. Why?
Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the scripture: "He leads them to Brahman," which refers to a superhuman person appearing immediately after reaching the world of lightning.

The subtle meaning is that, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the presentation of [the deities] as leaders, it must be accepted—even by way of analogy—that in the previous worlds as well, there are no other leaders.
Now this is being considered: are the paths beginning with *arciḥ* (light) signposts, or are they places of enjoyment?

Or rather, [the view] that they are "the bearers of the understanding for the wise who desire to reach Brahman. What, then, is the more reasonable position? That they are "signs of the path. Why? Because such is the nature of instruction. For in the world, such instruction is seen from teachers given to those traveling toward villages and the like: "Having departed from here, [you will see] a certain tree, a certain river, and a certain..."
"Go to such-and-such a village after reaching the side of the mountain.

Alternatively, these may be "lands of enjoyment" (*bhogabhūmi*). For it is impossible for well-known temporal divisions such as days and so forth to serve as markers of a path, and because none of these [terms] denotes anything else that could function as a marker of the path.
[The soul attains] the state of being a ground for enjoyment. It is precisely these worlds that are referred to when days and nights, years, months, sacrifices, and years are mentioned;

thus, the statement that days and so forth are subordinate to the worlds becomes logical. For this very reason, the Kauṣītakins recite the stages beginning with light (arcis) in accordance with the word "world" (*loka*), stating:
"He goes to the world of fire," and so on. This being the case—
We shall explain: "They are the conductors" (Ātivāhikāḥ).

These specific deities, beginning with Light (arcis) and so forth, are the conductors appointed by Śiva, the Supreme Person, for the purpose of conducting the wise (vidus) along the path. Why? Because of that indicative mark—namely, the indicative mark of conducting. For conducting is indeed [the function] of the threads.

The state of being a "conductor" (*gamayitṛtva*). And this—being heard in the concluding passage, "A non-human *puruṣa* leads them to Brahman"—indicates that he alone is the one connected to all the preceding [passages] as well, since they are heard without distinction. They say:
it is like [the statement], "The earth spoke."
Furthermore, in this Sūtra, according to the *Laghusūtravṛtti* composed by the sage Agastya-Sārvabhauma, regarding the passage "in the Liṅga is deep sleep" and so forth,

since the words *brahman* and *liṅga* are understood from many Śrutis to be synonyms— just like the words *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*— they, being impelled by that *Liṅga*, which is Paraśiva, the object of worship in all the aforementioned *Vidyās* such as the *Dahara* and others, [proceeded].

It has been explained that the *ātivāhika* deities— divinities residing in the interval between the mortal world and the world of Śiva— lead the person who meditates upon all the Brahma-vidyās, such as the *dahara*, by means of the analogy of ascending the steps of a palace staircase, gradually to Mahākailāsa, which possesses incomparable bliss and eternal majesty.
That too is not contradictory;

for since the scripture states, "A person who is not human leads them to Brahman," it is the very person belonging to the lightning who is heard to be the one who leads them to Brahman. How, then, could Varuṇa and the others who are beyond the lightning be connected as *ativāhika* (conveying) agents?
To this he says: "Therefore, [he goes] by the lightning alone, because of that being heard [in scripture]. (5)

Then, from the lightning upwards, the journey of the knowers until the attainment of Brahman is by means of the "lightning-like" one—that is, the superhuman *ativāhika* (conductor) alone. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "He leads them to Brahman.
Since scripture declares that he alone is the leader (*gamayitṛ*), Varuṇa and the others are his assistants; thus, they too are connected as *ativāhikas*.
It certainly exists.

Since there is the teaching that for some liberation occurs right here, while for others it occurs in another world, one must accept only one of these two positions; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting those scriptural passages which establish the uniformity of the fruit for all practitioners of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
Anticipating this objection, he says:
|| 341 || "Because that [cognition] is established through the delusion of both. || 6 ||

This is due to the delusion of both those who follow the dualistic path— which achieves merely the attainment of another world— and those proponents of non-duality who establish liberation as the ornament of their own necks,
resulting from their failure to fully comprehend the primary meaning established by all the Vedas.
The two partial views regarding the authority of only a portion of the Śruti should not be accepted by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

Why? Because that [liberation] is established [by scripture]: "The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not depart from there; they are merged right here. But at the time of their final end, in the world of Brahman, they are all completely released through supreme immortality. This refers to the transition between this world and the next world.
It is correct.
The section on legal proceedings. 5.

Indeed, even according to the view of Pādari, there is consideration of the task of going to the world of Śiva for the individual soul (jīva) who has entered the path of liberation obtained through the worship of the Supreme Brahman;
for in such scriptural passages as "Consciousness is Brahman," the identity of the individual soul with Brahman itself is directly established.
Is the scripture that establishes the relationship of the attained and the attainer between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman merely figurative? Or [is it not so], as in:
"And like space, He is omnipresent and eternal; that is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises"?
Taking the fullness from the full, only fullness remains.

Furthermore, since it is understood from such passages that Brahman is all-pervasive, traveling by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga) for the sake of attaining the Supreme Brahman would be purposeless.

Moreover, because the individual soul (jīva) has Brahman as its very self, it is impossible for it to be produced by Brahman; therefore, its "attainment" of Brahman is logically untenable. Consequently:

In response to the doubt that the Śrutis prescribing the attainment of Brahman refer exclusively to Hiraṇyagarbha, he states [the solution] by means of another topical section (adhikaraṇa): "Or rather, it is the effected state (kārya), according to Bādari, because the going [to it] is logically possible. (Sūtra 7)

The effect [of Brahman]: because in such scriptural passages as "from which these beings are born," although the individual souls (*jīva*) are not produced [in the sense of being newly created], they are designated as manifestations of the Supreme Brahman; therefore, Bādari indicates that this soul is an effect of Brahman. Why? Because of the logical consistency of the journey [to Brahman]. This is because, in the passage "into which they enter when they depart," it is understood that the souls are absorbed into Brahman.
Therefore, the subtle meaning is that it is logical for the knower to proceed to the world of Paraśiva-Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

It has been stated that the knower goes by means of light and the others, and that the group of conductors beginning with light and ending with the non-human (*amānava*) leads the knower to Brahman. Now, this point is considered here:

In this regard, there arises a doubt: does this group beginning with light lead those who meditate upon Hiraṇyagarbha to the effect [the conditioned Brahman], or does it lead those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman,
or else those among the meditators on the Supreme Brahman who meditate upon the inner self as being identical in nature with Brahman?
It is determined that [the conductors] lead only those who worship the effected Brahman (kāryabrahman). Why? Because in such passages as "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning;

having been born, he alone was the Lord of all that exists," and "Brahman indeed was this in the beginning," the four-faced Hiraṇyagarbha is described as being supreme over all; therefore, the conductors lead only his worshippers to his world. Not [others].

Indeed, for a worshiper of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman—which is perfect, omniscient, omnipresent, and the self of all—movement to another place is not required for the attainment of that [Brahman], precisely because it has already been attained. For the effect of supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*) consists solely in the cessation of ignorance regarding the eternally attained Supreme Brahman. As for the effect [of action]:

For one who meditates upon Brahman in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, travel is appropriate for the purpose of reaching a goal situated within a limited space; therefore, since it is established that the group of conducting deities beginning with Light leads him to that very place, we reply: Bādari maintains that for this meditator on the Supreme Brahman, there is a task to be accomplished—namely, the task of proceeding to the world of Paraśiva.

Why? Because in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme; he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman," and "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," we observe that only those who worship the Supreme Brahman attain the fulfillment of all desires along with Him. This is evident from worldly practice regarding the worship, salutation, temples, recollection, mantras, tantras, and the like, directed toward Śiva and Keśava.
The Kinnaras are devotees of Indra, while the Rākṣasas are devotees of Brahmā;
the Gandharvas are devotees of Viṣṇu, and the Siddhas are devotees of Śaṅkara.
Nevertheless, Bali, Prahlāda, Vibhīṣaṇa, and Surāntaka are declared to be devotees of Viṣṇu, as are the Asuras Bāṇa and Daśānana.
These two are declared to be devotees of Śiva, while others are devotees of Druhiṇa (Brahmā).
Since Hiraṇyagarbha is a deity belonging to the class of Rākṣasas, the path beginning with the "arcis" (flame) is not possible for those seeking liberation through his worship.

Furthermore: "From this very Self (Ātman), space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the person"—by such passages as these, the creation of the individual soul (jīva) is heard to have occurred even prior to Hiraṇyagarbha. Just as [from sparks] from a well-kindled fire...
"Just as sparks of the same nature issue forth by the thousands from a fire, so, O gentle one, do various beings arise from the Imperishable,

and into that very same [source] they also enter"— by such passages, the manifestation of individual souls (*jīva*) from the Supreme Brahman and their dissolution back into that very same [source] is established.

Since their oneness is established in the state of liberation (*muktidaśā*), no other meaning is appropriate. For instance, by such passages as "There are only two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless," and "Salutation to the golden-armed one, to the golden-hued, to the golden-formed, to the lord of gold, to the lord of Ambikā, to the lord of Umā, to the lord of creatures—salutation, salutation! [it is shown that] this belongs to Śiva alone.

Since it is understood through the determination of its having both embodied and unembodied forms, there is no contradiction in that all-pervading entity possessing both embodied and unembodied states, just like the wind and other elements.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 343 || And because of being specified. || 8 ||
I, seeking liberation, take refuge in Him who alone creates Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him— Him, the light of the Self and of the intellect of the gods.

Thus, since the Śruti reveals that the four-faced one (Caturmukha) was born from Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, and that he is the bestower of the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and so forth, it is in no way possible for Hiraṇyagarbha to possess supremacy over all or to be the bestower of immortality.

Now, one might raise the objection: since in such passages as "The non-human person leads them to Brahman," it is understood that those seeking liberation reach the world of Hiraṇyagarbha and even reach Hiraṇyagarbha himself, his status must therefore be the highest of all; in response to this doubt, he says:
But that designation [of the soul] occurs due to proximity. || 9 ||
The word "tu" (but) here serves to dispel doubt. For in such passages as, "He who is the source and origin of the gods,

Rudra the Great Seer who transcends the universe— may He, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha being born, endow us with auspicious understanding," it is established that Hiraṇyagarbha originates from Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, and that [Śiva] is the impeller of the intellect of the worshipper.

Because of this specific instruction; and because, in that very same passage, the status of being the object of meditation for one seeking liberation is established for Śiva alone—through the determination that He is the Lord of whom it is said, "He who [is the Lord] of the gods," and through His being the observer of Hiranyagarbha in His own proximity and the cause of auspicious memory—and not for anyone other than Śiva, as stated: "He who knows Him hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven, he enjoys all [desires]."

In the passage, "He [attains] all desires together with Brahmā the All-knowing," it is likewise established that for one who meditates upon Paraśiva-Brahman, there is the attainment of all desires along with Him. This is precisely what is proven by such scriptural texts as, "His person is non-human; he alone leads him to Brahman," and so forth, through which Śiva alone is understood. Śiva is the One.

Because in passages such as "Having abandoned everything else, Śiva, the bringer of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon," we observe the prohibition of anything other than Śiva as an object of meditation for those seeking liberation.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 345 || Because, when the task is completed, he departs together with its supervisor; this is stated in the subsequent [sūtra]. || 10 ||
The fifteen parts that have their foundations, and all the gods within the respective deities,
as well as actions and the self consisting of consciousness— all these become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman].

From this scriptural statement, it follows that at the time of liberation from the body (*videhamukti*)— when those seeking liberation who possess their final bodies have transcended all effects and all things consisting of effects, such as the vital breaths and sense organs, have perished—
their departure is described as being together with the presiding deities, beginning with Brahmā.
Because of the designation of becoming one with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the meditation on Hiraṇyagarbha is not to be undertaken by those seeking liberation.
Therefore, this is the path of the gods (*devapatha*) and the path of Brahman (*brahmapatha*); those who proceed by means of this do not return to this human world.

The claim that the scriptural passages teaching the attainment of immortality—such as "Going upwards by that, one attains immortality"—refers to Hiraṇyagarbha is untenable. Furthermore, by the designation of "non-return," Cit-Kailāsa alone is indicated.
This is because, in such Smṛtis as "O Arjuna, all worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return," the realms of Brahmā and others [are shown to be transitory].
Upon hearing of impermanence,

when there is neither darkness nor day, neither night nor existence nor non-existence, Śiva alone remains; that is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom has issued forth.

Thus, because it is taught that even after the dissolution (*pralaya*), at the primordial state of the world, there is only the persistence of Śiva, it follows that in such passages as "The *ṛta* is the true, the supreme Brahman," His alone is the status of being *ṛta* by virtue of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, he states another reason: "And because of memory. (11)
The worship of Śiva is prescribed for those living beings who are portions of Śiva;
indeed, solely through the grace of Śiva, they are always [like] worms and insects.
Having attained the nature of Śiva, there is no further rebirth.

Thus, since even in the *Smṛtis* it is declared that only the worshippers of Śiva attain the nature of the reality of Śiva, which is free from rebirth, the worship of any other deity is not prescribed for those seeking liberation.
Regarding this point, another teacher also says:
But Jaimini [holds that it refers to the Supreme], because of its primary significance. || 347 || 12 ||
Because in such scriptural passages as "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman, the Person, dark and tawny;

the Lord of Brahman, the Overlord of Brahman—may that Brahman, Śiva, be mine; Sadāśiva Om," there is the indication that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is of the nature of the Praṇava and possesses supreme sovereignty over all.

The teacher Jaimini maintains that the *ativāhikas* lead those who worship the Supreme Brahman known as Śiva to the heavenly world (*svarloka*) by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*). Why? Because of the primary sense of the word. Since in passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the word *brahman* has its primary meaning only with respect to the Supreme Brahman—and not in the case of the four-faced Hiraṇyagarbha.

Furthermore, because of the contradiction with the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introduction and conclusion, it is determined that in passages such as "That person who is non-human— he leads them to Brahman," the word "Brahman" refers exclusively to Śiva.
He states another reason:
And because it is seen [in scripture]. || 13 ||

This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the supreme light, manifests in its own true form; just as rivers flowing along reach the ocean, casting off their names and forms.
In the same way, the wise man, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high.

Because in such scriptural passages, the difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman are seen without doubt through their relationship as the attainer and the attained, one must not accept that the individual soul is eternally identical with Brahman nor that it is eternally distinct from Brahman.
Furthermore, he states another reason:
And there is no intention directed toward the effect. || 14 ||

Based on the observation of such scriptural passages as, "Rudra, the great seer, superior to all, generated Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning," the liberation consisting of the attainment of the state of Śiva— preceded by the cessation of the state of being an individual soul (*jīva*)— is not prescribed with respect to Hiraṇyagarbha as an effect. There is no other path.

Because in such scriptural passages as "There exists [a path] for going," liberation characterized by identity (*sāyujya*) is designated as resulting solely from the knowledge of Śiva alone; and because among those who worship the Four-faced One (Brahmā), no attainment of liberation free from rebirth is observed in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Purāṇas, or Āgamas—as in the verse: "Having shaken off evil like the horse shakes its hair, like the moon... [freed from clouds].

It should be understood that the "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) specified in such scriptural passages as, "Having been released from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, being self-perfected, I attain the uncreated world of Brahman," refers to the world of Śiva (*śivaloka*).
Thus, according to the maxim "many [things] also [are accomplished] by a single effort," the doctrine of another teacher is adopted in accordance with one's own established tenet.
Having thus demonstrated [the opponent's view], he reveals his own position:
"Badarāyaṇa holds that [the Lord] leads those who do not rely on symbols; for there are faults in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve (tatkratu). (Sūtra 4.3.15)

The venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the group of conducting deities, beginning with Light (arciḥ), leads those who do not have the parts [of the body] as their support—that is, those distinct from those whose support is the parts.
This is what is meant: the position that these deities lead those who meditate upon the phenomenal world of effects (kāryaprapañca) is not tenable.

If this is argued, we say no; for from such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; one should meditate on it with a calm mind," and "Thou art That, Thou art That," it is understood that through meditation on the fivefold aggregate of sentient and insentient beings—which are the effects of Brahman—as having Brahman as their self, one attains the reality of Brahman. Furthermore, there is a fault in either case [if one were to deny this]. [As stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Two birds..."

Because adopting the mere difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman would entail the fault of contradicting numerous Vedic texts that enjoin non-duality, such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi), and because asserting the primacy of non-duality would entail the fault of contradicting hundreds of dualistic scriptures, [the truth is established] in accordance with many illustrations such as the worm in dung.

One must accept both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; for in such scriptural passages as, "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own true form," we understand that partial positions [of absolute difference or absolute identity] are refuted. Furthermore, the rule "according to his resolve" (tatkratuḥ) means that one attains exactly what one meditates upon.

According to the scriptural injunction, "As is one's resolve in this world, so does one become after departing from here; in whatever way one meditates upon [the object]," it is observed everywhere that meditators attain the very object of their meditation. Therefore, the establishment of both difference and non-difference in all the Vedānta texts is indeed unavoidable.
Now, since various deities such as Viṣṇu and others are understood from scriptural passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," one might raise the doubt:

for the sake of removing the possibility of rebirth for those seeking liberation, what is the actual reality characterized by the severing of the bonds of Māyā that should be meditated upon in all the vidyās, such as the Dahara-vidyā? In response to this doubt, he says:
And he shows the distinction: || 16 ||

The letter *ca* here signifies certainty (*niścayārtha*). It demonstrates—that is, illuminates—the distinction of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman known as Paśupati, among the individual souls (*jīvas*) such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu who possess the nature of bound creatures (*paśus*), within the Ṛgveda and other Vedas as well as in the Vedāntas: "People seek him, Rudra, beyond their thought; they seize him with their tongue as he eats."
This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [hand] of mine is the more blessed one.
This is my universal medicine; this is the auspicious touch.

By these and other verses in the Ṛgveda: "O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not reveal evil— with that most peaceful form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor."

This should be understood from such passages in the Yajurvedic tradition and elsewhere as well. Furthermore, the determination that this [abode] belongs to Paraśiva alone is established in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad by the passage beginning with "daharaṃ vipāpam" (the small, stainless [lotus]), which refers to the heart-lotus (*daharapuṇḍarīka*) for those seeking liberation.

Having prescribed the meditation on the Supreme Self, when the inquiry arises as to "who is He?", [the scripture] determines that Maheśvara alone is the object of meditation there, stating: "He who is the sound proclaimed at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda—He who is beyond that which is dissolved in primordial nature (prakṛti), He is Maheśvara. Thus, for those who are detached and have renounced the desire for wives and other such things, [it is taught] by the verse beginning with "Not by action" (*na karmaṇā*).

Having taught the means of attaining that [state], and in response to the inquiry as to which among all the gods possesses the qualification for the worship of that Śiva, the text introduces Nārāyaṇa with the verse beginning "The thousand-headed God" (*sahasraśīrṣaṃ devam*), and then,
starting from "resembling the interior of a lotus bud" (*padmakośapratīkāśam*), concludes that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established within the center of His crest-lock (*śikhā*).

By this much [of the text], having taught that He is the self of all through His omnipresence, as well as His limited nature and His manifestation as the world in the form of both the embodied (mūrta) and the unembodied (amūrta) liṅgas,
and having expressed the praise of Śiva in His embodied and unembodied forms by means of the five Brahma-mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, [the text continues]: "Obeisance to Hiraṇyavāhu."

Having thus proclaimed his nature as having a body composed of light (*jyotirmaya-vigraha*) and his being worthy of worship by all because he is distinguished by the power of Umā (*umā-śakti*), [the text] describes his dark-brown color (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*), his three-eyed nature (*virūpākṣa*), and his universal form (*viśvarūpa*) through the passage beginning with "The Truth, the Reality, the Supreme Brahman. In the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad*: "The lotus of the heart is stainless and pure..."

Having thus begun by describing the worship of Śiva within the small lotus (daharapuṇḍarīka), and in response to the inquiry "Who is He?", [the text says]: "The one, all-pervading, wondrous Lord, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, consisting of consciousness and bliss,
formless, accompanied by Umā, the Supreme Lord, the Master, three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful."
Having thus taught its nature as both embodied and unembodied by these and other means, [the scripture says]:
"Beholding the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self, one attains the supreme Brahman; there is no other cause."
By such statements as these, liberation is taught exclusively for the worshiper of Śiva.
Furthermore, in the *Śivasamkalpopaniṣad* and in the *Bodhāyanasūtra*, it is said: "Beyond the Supreme is Brahman; beyond that Supreme is Hari."
May that which is the Lord beyond the supreme, may my mind be intent upon Śiva’s resolve.

Thus, because Maheśvara is designated as the supreme over all, it is taught in the passage "The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ*) that the wise— the learned— always behold with the vision of knowledge that supreme abode of Śiva known as Kailāsa belonging to Viṣṇu. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Those wise ones always behold that supreme, divine abode of Viṣṇu known as Kailāsa, by means of even a fraction of Śiva’s compassion.
Thus it is said in the Māṇḍūkya [Upaniṣad]: "They consider the fourth state (turiya) to be the cessation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual."
From the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, beginning with "That Self is to be known": "Rudra is indeed one; he does not stand for a second.

He is the first origin of the gods, Rudra, the Great Seer who transcends the universe. He brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning. One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (Nature), and the wielder of Māyā as Maheśvara."
This entire world is pervaded by that which arises from its constituent parts; the perishable is *pradhāna*, while the imperishable is *hara*.
The one God enters through the perishable self.
Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature, there occurs at last the cessation of the universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*).
Him, the supreme Maheśvara among the lords, and the supreme deity among the gods.
May we know the Lord of lords, the supreme one in the beginning, the divine Ruler of the world, worthy of praise;
for him there is neither action nor instrumentality, and no one equal to him or superior to him is seen.
"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of innate knowledge, strength, and action.

He has no master in the world, nor is there any ordainer of him, nor indeed any mark of him. Thus, in the *Atharvaśiras*, it is said: "The gods, indeed, went to the heavenly world; those gods questioned Rudra."

"Who are you? he asked. He replied: "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is no other whatsoever distinct from me. And in the *Atharvaśikhā*: "One should meditate upon the Lord, who is to be meditated upon; this entire world—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—is produced from Him," beginning thus, [it concludes that] Śiva alone [is the cause].

Because in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "Having abandoned everything else, Śiva alone, the maker of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon," liberation is taught specifically for those who worship Śiva directly; and because [liberation is also taught] for those who worship speech, mind, and so forth— such as in the scripturally established texts, "One should meditate on speech as Brahman," "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," and "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman"— [it follows that all these lead to the same goal].
Thus, liberation is determined. Therefore,

for those who worship the embodied Supreme Śiva-Brahman, at the conclusion of the body, by means of the Suṣumṇā channel and the path beginning with light (arcis) consisting of incomparable, self-luminous, and undivided splendor— known as the *ativāhika*— [they proceed].
The established conclusion is that the supreme state, which is the root of supreme bliss and the Kailāsa of consciousness, comes into being.
Thus ends the Śrīkarabhāṣya composed by the venerable master, the teacher Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpāda, the preeminent leader of the assembly of holy ascetics.
The third quarter of the fourth chapter, known as the *Phalādhyāya*,
consisting of five sections beginning with the section on the *arcirādi* (the path of light), starting from "attained by the *arcirādi*," etc.,
is completed.
Now begins the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śrīkara-bhāṣya: The Section on Manifestation upon Attainment (Sampadyāvirbhūtādhikaraṇa). || 1 ||

The determination of the fruit of the supreme human goal, which consists in the attainment of Śiva-hood following the cessation of the state of being a transmigrating soul characterized by its own nature,
was established previously for those who worship various deities such as Indra according to their varying degrees of qualification, as well as for those free from desire.

Having demonstrated that through the worship of Śiva over time, one attains the reality of Śiva preceded by the cessation of the bonds (pāśa) from which there is no return, the nature and method of liberation for those seeking release (mumukṣu) are now considered.
Regarding the contemplation on the vision of Brahman within the small lotus (*daharapuṇḍarīka*) here itself for those who worship the Śiva-principle:
indeed, for those who possess the delusion of self in the body, senses, and so forth— which are not the Self— and who worship Śiva as non-different from themselves,

let there be the attainment of the world of Śiva by way of the staircase of Indra’s world through the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*), by means of the sustained application of the discernment of the tenth state.

When the question arises as to whether liberation consists in attaining such a nature through the majesty of meditating upon the five elements, the five sheaths, and the three bodies, or whether it consists in abiding in proximity to Him in a state of servitude, dependence, and being a subordinate (śeṣatva) along with the risen divine sages (udgatadivya-sūris): [The following verse is provided: pañca-bhūta-pañca-kośa-tri-tanu-nija-mūrtayaḥ | tad-upāsti-mahimnā tu tat-sārūpyam athāpi vā || divya-sūri-gaṇair yuktaḥ kaiṅkarya-paratantratām | bhajann eva hi sāyujyam iti kecit pracakṣate || Some declare that liberation is indeed Sāyujya, while remaining subject to service (kaiṅkarya) accompanied by the hosts of divine sages.
The Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa reveals his own intention—the primary Vedāntic doctrine—for those seeking liberation:
"Upon attaining [the Supreme], there is manifestation [of the self] by its own nature, because of the scriptural word. (Sūtra 4.4.1)

Based on the scriptural vision, "There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*)," for those who worship Śiva as the formed, there is a distinction between gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) and immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*). Consequently, at the stage of final liberation, having attained and become one with the luminous Śiva-reality (*jyotirmaya-śivatattva*), they abide by their own nature as omniscient and omnipotent.

Manifestation consists in having one’s true nature revealed. Just as copper and other metals become gold through the process of alchemical transmutation (*rasavedha*), so too, by the power of meditating upon the Brahma-knowledge of the "small ether" (*dahara*) and so forth, the embodied individual soul (*jīva*) becomes directly manifest in the form of Sadāśiva. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "This serene being (*samprasāda*), having risen up from this body... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is as follows: from the observation of such scriptural passages (śruti) as, "In this very way, this serene being (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having attained the highest light, manifests in its own true form. Does it rise up from this body?

When there arises a doubt as to whether this sentence teaches that one who has attained the supreme light becomes connected with a form to be accomplished— such as the form of a god— or rather that it is simply the manifestation of one's own natural essential nature,
it is determined that liberation is the manifestation of the natural essential nature, just as in the case of the *Daśamīviveka* and the *Sandhāna*.

If [the plurality] were adventitious and merely grasped, the qualification "in its own form" would be meaningless. Therefore, even though it is non-distinct [from Brahman], its status as its own inherent nature is established. Furthermore, since the plurality of individual souls (jīva) is adventitious—like the heat of water—it follows that, like that, it would be subject to impermanence; this consequence is difficult to avoid.

Alternatively, since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is established through their mutual difference in numerous Śrutis such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), and because an inherent difference cannot be sublated, does one remain in the next world in a state of subservience, service, and dependence alongside the Supreme Lord who is worshipped? Or...

Alternatively, there may be an existence characterized by a state of independence identical in form to that [of Brahman]. Therefore, the doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman possess ultimate difference during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and likewise possess ultimate difference in the state of liberation (*mukti*),
belongs to the schools of Dvaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, and Vaiśeṣika.
We explain:

"Manifestation upon attainment. This inner self, at the conclusion of its *prārabdha* karma, attains the supreme light (*parañjyotis*) and reaches this particular state, according to the analogy of the bee and the insect.

It is a specific state consisting in the attainment of the Śiva-principle preceded by the cessation of the state of being a living soul (jīva), and it does not take the form of the previous modes. Why?
"By its own [nature], because of the word 'own'. By the qualification "in its own form," it is like a river and the ocean; that is, [the soul's] essential nature [is not lost].

By this, the false doctrine of the soul (jīva) being like a rope-snake is refuted, as well as the doctrines that the soul is always [different from Brahman] like a pot and a cloth, or like a limb and the body.
Therefore, the doctrine that through the power of the knowledge of Brahman, the soul attains the state of Śiva preceded by the cessation of its innate ignorance is logical.

Otherwise, the scripture on liberation would fail to communicate a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because the essential nature [of the self] is not seen to be a human goal in itself. Indeed, when the activities of the body and senses have ceased in deep sleep, no connection with a human goal is observed for the mere essential nature of the self. Nor is it merely the cessation of suffering [that constitutes the goal].

For one who has attained the supreme light, the goal of human endeavor is such that the manifestation of one's own true nature is called liberation. This is because of scriptural passages such as "That is one Brahman-bliss; and the bliss of a learned Śrotriya who is free from desire," and "Having obtained this very essence, he becomes blissful," which declare that for the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), there is no difference from happiness. Nor is it the case that...

Its true nature is consciousness itself, whose form is undivided bliss; it can be said that this [nature], which is concealed by ignorance during the state of transmigratory existence, becomes manifest upon attaining the supreme light,
because concealment is impossible for that which has knowledge as its very essence— knowledge being synonymous with luminosity.
For it has already been stated previously that concealment (*tirodhāna*) is indeed its destruction.
Furthermore, the state of bliss (*ānandatā*) cannot belong to mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*). Indeed, the nature of bliss is the nature of joy (*sukha*);
and the nature of joy is being experienced as something favorable to the self. For one who maintains that there is only mere luminosity, to whom [would this favorability belong]?

The idea that "light" means "to be experienced as agreeable" is difficult to establish. Furthermore, if the goal were merely the attainment of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then since that essential nature is eternally accomplished, the statement "he is manifested in his own form" would be meaningless.
Therefore, it must be connected with the form previously established through meditation. And thus, the expression "is manifested" [is justified].
It refers precisely to the primary sense. The phrase "in its own form" also accords with the statement "it manifests itself," meaning by means of its own unique nature consisting of pure bliss.
Now, one might object that even for the knowers who meditate upon the partless Paraśiva, as stated in the passage "this serene being (samprasāda) is exactly thus... [there is no such manifestation].

Raising the objection as to how there can be attainment of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, delimited by the heart-lotus, preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) given that the subtle body has already exited from the physical body, he says in response:
"The one who is liberated [attains it], because of the scriptural promise" (Sūtra 4.2.2).

Regarding the phrase "having risen up from this body," although [the subject] exists within the body, he is called the pure *jīva* who is liberated from the conceit of the body. Why? Because of the declaration. This is because in the subsequent statement, "he manifests in his own form," there is the teaching that the *jīva* attains the reality of Śiva—becoming one with the nature of Śiva like water in water or fire in fire.

By the statement regarding the identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), it is taught that for those who worship Śiva-tattva— the partless supreme ether and the supreme light— there is attainment of Him right here in this very small lotus (*dahara-puṇḍarīka*), preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*).

Some maintain that surrender (*prapatti*) is the cause for attaining the world of Viṣṇu known as Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode, and that this surrender consists of five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*). These five sacraments are: branding (*tāpa*), the sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), the name (*nāma*), the mantra (*mantra*), and sacrifice (*yāga*) as the fifth.
O Sudarśana of great flames, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
O Lord, show the path to me, who am blinded by ignorance, O Viṣṇu.
O Pāñcajanya, by whom the accumulation of sins has been destroyed through your own meditation,
protect me, a terrible sinner fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should likewise burn the left arm;
by this very procedure, one should bear the conch and the discus.
Such statements, which emphasize the primacy of tantric mantras, are not to be respected, as they lie outside the Veda. Furthermore,

even regarding the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*), there is no mention of them within their own context— unlike the five *prayāja* offerings or the sequence beginning with the *āgneya* sacrifice— and they are not set forth by the authors of the Sūtras in the Vedāṅgas or the Kalpasūtras.

Furthermore, since the *Rāmāyaṇa*, *Bhāgavata*, *Mahābhārata*, *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, *Padmapurāṇa*, and *Hārītasmṛti*— which expound Vaiṣṇava dharma— are not accepted by all people and are therefore unworthy of trust,
the procedure for the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*) prescribed therein is to be disregarded; for those who have strayed from the path of the Vedas enter the way of Tantra.

This is because of the traditional scripture of the established doctrine of Vyāsa’s son (Vaiyāsika-siddhāntāgama). Furthermore, even in the Vaiṣṇava system, although the five sacraments alone serve as the cause for the purification of the person, there is no authoritative evidence (pramāṇa) to enjoin that a purified person is directed toward the goal known as liberation, which consists in the attainment of the supreme state; thus [it was said] by Rāvaṇa.

Because there was no provision for the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*) for Vibhīṣaṇa— who was expelled from the midst of the assembly and immediately sought refuge with Rāmacandra— and because it is impossible to postulate even a change of name for him due to contradiction with authoritative evidence, [the same applies to] Draupadī when she was immediately [rescued by] Kṛṣṇa while being assailed by her enemies.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of the five sacraments (*pañcasaṃskāra*) for one who has taken refuge [in the Lord], and because of the statement in the *Gītā*: "I take refuge in that very First Person from whom the ancient course of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) proceeded," and because even in the case of Kṛṣṇa we observe activity directed toward other objects, those five sacraments are not the cause of such activity. Therefore, regarding this activity...
For even without [intense] meditation, the *Bhāgavata* establishes that Gopikā and others attained Viṣṇu through mere thought alone:

"O King, the Gopīs [attained Him] out of desire, Kaṃsa out of fear, and kings such as Citraketu out of hatred; Vijaya [attained Him] through kinship, you through devotion, and we, O Lord, through [our service]."
And elsewhere:
"O King, those very lords of men who were slain by Janārdana, the wielder of the discus and lord of the three worlds, have gone to that abode; even the anger of Kṛṣṇa is equal to the Supreme."

Thus, since liberation is established even without [further] purification (*saṃskāra*), there is no contradiction; for it is understood from scriptural statements that even one who has surrendered once attains fearlessness, implying that their activity in a previous birth was already present. As it has been said:
To one who has surrendered but once and entreats me, saying "I am yours," I grant fearlessness from all beings; this is my vow.

If this is argued, it is not so; for even in the case of those who have taken refuge, if they were to obtain births as Daityas and the like, their taking of refuge would be rendered futile. As it has been said: "Abandoning all duties, come to Me alone as your refuge.
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve."
Thus, due to the doubt regarding *prapatti* in a previous birth, no one at all would engage in spiritual practice. Furthermore,

since even for those such as Jaya and Vijaya it is difficult to attain Vaikuṇṭha without *prapatti*, when even they have attained subsequent births as Daityas, what hope is there for other *prapannas*?

What hope is there that there will be no further saṃsāra? [The answer is: "Through faith, devotion, knowledge, and yoga. Just as there are Vedic passages enjoining devotion to Śiva—such as "Worship! Worship well! We sacrifice to Tryambaka; he establishes the universal liṅga; the mantra in the hand is purifying"—there are likewise [passages] enjoining devotion to Viṣṇu...

Now, it may be argued that in the statement "having attained the supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotir upasaṃpadya*), the word "light" (*jyotis*) refers to the solar orb; therefore, for those established in the knowledge of the partless Supreme Śiva who worship the embodied Śiva,
there is only the attainment of the world of Śiva by way of the solar orb, and not liberation right here.
In response to the doubt that the attainment of the all-pervading, formless Supreme Śiva-Brahman—preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)—is not possible, he says:
"The Self [is meant], because of the context. (Sūtra 3.2.354)

By the word "light" (*jyotis*) here, the Supreme Self alone is meant, and not the orb of the sun. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇāt*). For the introductory passage of Prajāpati’s discourse begins thus: "That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true. And this context has the Supreme Self as its subject matter.

If [it is argued that this is] from the subsequent passage, it has already been established in the verse beginning "But he whose nature is manifested" (*āvirbhūtasvarūpas tu*). Otherwise, how could the qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) be possible for a *jīva* who is bound by beginningless fetters? Furthermore, in the verse "The two unborn ones, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord," regarding the *jīva* and the *Īśvara*—

Having attained the supreme light— just as rivers [merge into] the ocean— the one who possesses innate omniscience (*nādisiddhasarvajñatva*) and limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) becomes the supreme Śiva, whose nature is that very supreme light. Thus, in hundreds of scriptural passages such as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," there exists both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
It has been clearly taught.
Section on Non-Differentiation (Avibhāgādhikaraṇa) || 2 ||
An inquiry into the state of non-difference from Brahman for those who worship the formless Supreme Śiva:

Now, since the attainment of all desires together with the wise Brahman is seen in the passage, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," [one might ask] regarding the statement, "Having reached the supreme light... [is there not a contradiction?]
In response to the inquiry as to whether for those possessing the knowledge of Śiva only a connection with Śiva is ordained and not identity with Śiva, he shows another topical section (adhikaraṇa):
"Because [they] are seen as undivided. (Sūtra 4)

Like a river merging into the ocean, the liberated soul exists as both non-different and different from the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, yet not by way of being related to Brahman; for in such passages as, "When he finds fearlessness in that which is invisible, bodiless, indefinable, and supportless, then he becomes free from fear," this is stated regarding the state of liberation.

The subtle meaning is that the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is "seen"— that is, perceived— by those who have attained the state of Śiva, whose souls have reached the reality of Śiva through steadfastness in the knowledge of the meaning of such Vedic texts as "Having attained the supreme light" and "That thou art. For them, [the world] is like grain in a granary, like the flour of sacrificial animals, like particles of gold dust, and so forth.
Or is there a state of non-separation like that of a river and the ocean? Such is the doubt.
"When the seer beholds the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person, the source of Brahman;
then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains the supreme equality."
In such scriptural passages as these:
"Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."
Maheśvara is pleased with those who have been purified through many births, who follow the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, who are dispassionate, and who are awakened.
When [the mind] becomes serene, one is liberated; being liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva.

Since such Smṛti texts state that even after liberated souls have attained Brahman, they remain distinct from it— like sesame seeds and rice grains, or like grain in a storehouse— and yet obtain all desires just as Brahman does, it is concluded that liberated souls exist in a state of similarity to Brahman. To this, the following is said:
"Without distinction."
The state of those living beings who have attained the nature of Śiva as abiding in non-difference from Brahman is taught. Why? Because it is observed [in scripture].

For in such scriptural passages as "I am golden," "I am the form of Śiva," "That thou art," "Rudra indeed is all," and "All this is indeed Brahman," the liberated soul is observed to be non-different from Brahman.

Just as in the state of bondage, one must not accept a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman in the state of liberation; for this is in accordance with such scriptural passages as, "The stainless one attains the highest equality," and "He enjoys all desires," which refer to the stage of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) through the power of meditations on the "small [space]" (dahara) and other such practices.

It should be understood that this refers to the state of experiencing the supreme light-liṅga (paraṃjyotirliṅga) shining within the pericarp of one’s own heart. This is because the preceding passage— “He who knows Brahman, which is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite, as hidden in the secret cave in the highest heaven” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)— teaches the realization of the Supreme Self within the small space (daharākāśa).
This samādhi, known as *asaṃprajñāta*, is dear to yogis; it is a wondrous state of quiescent activity that illuminates supreme bliss.
In that samādhi, the great yogi, having attained Śiva— whose characteristics are truth and the like—
in the supreme space of the heart, rejoices in that very form.

In this way, the experience of Śiva has been elaborated upon in many ways within the Smṛtis and Āgamas. Therefore, it is not contradictory for there to be a state of abiding in non-differentiation from Brahman during the time of meditative absorption (samādhi), at the conclusion of prārabdha karma, and in liberation as bodiless isolation (videhakaivalya). Now, an objection may be raised: in passages such as "Obeisance to the golden-armed one, to the golden-hued one," Brahman is described as having parts; yet [elsewhere] it is said to be "bodiless" (aśarīra).
In passages such as "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells [in this state]," there is the witness of the bodilessness, the state of being without distinction, and so forth;

in passages such as "The mind alone is solitary and devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), partless, actionless, and peaceful," there is the witness of the qualitylessness (nirguṇatva); and in passages such as "He consists of bliss, he is the enjoyer of bliss, whose desires are true and whose resolve is true," there is the witness of the possession of qualities (saguṇatva).
Since this is observed, the mutual contradiction among all the Vedāntas is unavoidable.

If one were to accept two Brahmans in order to establish the harmony of all the Śrutis, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "Brahman is indeed one, without a second" and "Rudra is one alone; he does not stand for a second."

Furthermore, some maintain that through the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (indication by abandoning and not abandoning) of such scriptural texts as "That thou art," there is oneness between Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*)— just as there is oneness between a reflection and its original object upon the removal of the limiting adjuncts of Maya and Avidya which create the distinction between Śiva and the soul's adjuncts;
or just as there is oneness of space upon the removal of the adjuncts of a jar or a cloth— this being the oneness of Śiva and the soul with respect to Brahman.

Since it is impossible for there to be causality regarding the creation of the universe and so forth in the absence of a body, sense organs, and the like; since there would be no purpose in the absence of a motivator; and since there is no evidence for the existence of a featureless reality—therefore, in the state of liberation, the worshiper of that [Lord], possessing a divine and auspicious form, remains in a state of being a subordinate servant, characterized by dependence and the performance of service.
In these and various other ways, those who follow the views of the ancient teachers (pūrvācāryas) speak.
Therefore, raising the objection as to how the lack of consistency among the views of the Vedāntic ancient teachers can be avoided,
[the author] presents the view of another distinguished teacher, characterized by the authority of a specific portion of the Śruti.
The venerable Bādarāyaṇa demonstrates his own position regarding the authority of all the Vedas:
"Jaimini [holds that the soul is] of the size of the body, on account of the introductory statements and so forth. (Sūtra 3.2.5)
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born.
Since the birth of the Brāhmaṇas and others is understood from such passages as those concerning the mouth and other limbs of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman—

and since the conceptualization of the world by one who is bodiless and devoid of senses is impossible— it is established by such scriptural texts as "He is without breath, without body, and pure" that there exists for Him a non-material, incomparable body, sense organs, mind, and vital breath.

The teacher Jaimini maintains [that the liberated possess bodies]. Why? Because of the introductory statements and so forth. In the discourse of Prajāpati beginning with "That Self which is free from evil," the fact that the liberated possess bodies is understood through the presentation of attributes such as having true volitions (*satya-saṃkalpa*), just like the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in scriptural passages such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing," [these attributes of the liberated are established].

The worldly activities of those who have attained the state of Brahman are observed; therefore, based on these instances such as the introductory narratives (*upanyāsa*), the doctrine that [the individual souls] possess bodies of Brahman is indeed logical—this is the view of the teacher Jaimini.
Having thus presented the view of those who maintain that Brahman consists solely of parts (*sāvayava*):
He states the view of those who maintain that Brahman is partless, actionless, and devoid of distinctions:
|| 357 || "Because it consists of that [Brahman], it is consciousness alone; thus says Auḍulomi. || 6 ||

Because in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," "Verily, in the beginning this was the Self alone," "Verily, in the beginning this was Brahman alone," and "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," there is taught the negation of any entity other than Brahman and the fact that Brahman is pure consciousness; and since that which is of the nature of consciousness cannot logically be the cause of an insentient phenomenal world.

The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that Brahman alone exists throughout the three periods of time as pure consciousness, by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness alone (*caitanyamātra*). Why? Because it has that as its essence (*tadātmakatvāt*).

"Unseen, beyond conventional discourse, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet—eternal and all-pervading; that which they consider the fourth, the peaceful, the auspicious, the non-dual—that is the Self, that is to be known.
Thus, that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal and all-pervading.
Since the scriptures, beginning with the passage "all-pervading and extremely subtle," teach that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman,

consists solely of pure consciousness after first negating [the existence of] a body, senses, and so forth, it is logical that the nature of the Supreme Self is eternally partless. The phenomenal world of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so on, exists there through delusion, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
"It is indeed so," says Auḍulomi.

Having thus examined the view of the proponent of parts (*sāvayavavādin*)— who relies on the authority of certain portions of scripture— and the view of the proponent of partlessness (*niravayavavādin*),
he states his own position, which constitutes the essence of all Vedānta:
|| 358 || Even so, because of the mention [of the soul] existing prior [to the creation], Bādarāyaṇa maintains there is no contradiction. || 7 ||
"Verily, there are two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless.
From such introductory statements [it follows]: "That which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, one, all-pervading, consciousness-bliss, formless, and wonderful;
the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful."

Because in hundreds of such scriptural passages, Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is presented as having both a formal (mūrta) and a formless (amūrta) aspect—just like the wind—it is the teacher Bādarāyaṇa, who is skilled in the established conclusions of all Vedānta, who maintains that it is not contradictory for the one Brahman to consist of both the formal and the formless. Why? Because of prior existence (pūrvabhāvāt).
Because of existence—that is, because of being present—both are established by the force of the injunctions for both;

by the force of the scriptural texts enjoining both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), both must be accepted. If one were to rely solely on the authority of scriptural texts concerning the formed Brahman, such as "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth," [one would overlook that] "He is omnipresent and eternal like space."
Full within and full without, like a jar of wool in the ocean;
empty within and empty without, like an empty jar in the sky.
Space, wind, light, water, and the earth which sustains the universe;
that which is the Supreme Brahman, the Self of all, the great abode of the universe.
Because [the position that Brahman has parts] contradicts many scriptural passages that establish its all-pervasiveness,

and because that which possesses parts would be limited like a jar or similar objects, how could the status of being the cause of all-pervasive, formless entities such as space— as indicated by scriptural texts such as "From this very Self, space was produced"— be logically justified?

Moreover, its being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all is inconsistent, and its being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the world is not tenable. "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. "Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), without breath..."

According to such scriptural passages as, "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is bodiless or dwelling in the body," and so forth, if one accepts that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is partless, devoid of distinctions, and pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), then [one must reconcile this with] the texts: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate'; having created that, He entered into that very thing," and "From which indeed these beings are born, by which..."

Furthermore, contradictions with numerous scriptural passages, such as "From which all beings are born, by which they live when born, and into which they enter when departing," would be difficult to avoid.

Therefore, its nature as both manifest (mūrta) and unmanifest (amūrta) is logical; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with those texts that prescribe the fruits of meditating upon the manifest Supreme Śiva, such as: "Eating, playing, and rejoicing..."
Regarding these and other such statements that demonstrate the fruit of meditating upon the formless Supreme Śiva:
"If a person should know the Self, thinking 'I am this,' desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he wander about following after a body?"

Furthermore, there would result a mutual contradiction between such scriptural passages as, "But where everything has become his very Self, who should see whom, and by what should one speak what? and [the description] of the nature of the embodied Brahman as being impermanent,
such as, "With firm limbs, he is many-formed and fierce."
Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with such scriptural passages as establish the stability of the embodied form of Brahman, for instance:

"He is without hands or feet, possessed of inconceivable power; I see without eyes, I hear without ears," and so forth, from which it is understood that he, being independent, is the creator of all through his lack of dependence on a body or senses.
Thus it is established that everything is logically consistent.
This concludes the section concerning volition (saṅkalpādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||

Having thus established that for those who worship the Brahman as the manifest Paraśiva, there is the manifestation of the glory of unsurpassed bliss, and that for those who worship the Brahman as the unmanifest Paraśiva, the fruit is non-difference from Him— now,
in response to the inquiry as to what the fruit is for those who worship the Brahman as the manifest Paraśiva, [the author proceeds] by means of another topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).
He shows that result:
"Because of the scriptural statement 'by mere volition' alone. (Sūtra 8)

Having previously established that those who are steadfast in the knowledge and meditation upon the pervasive, formless Paraśiva-Brahman attain identity with Him through freedom from all desires— and having thereby proven His nature as both manifest and unmanifest— the author now elaborates upon the unsurpassed glory of bliss for those who worship the manifest Paraśiva-Brahman.
For lay devotees (*upāsaka*), the attainment of all objects of sense—such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women—occurs through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) alone. Why is this so?

Because of that scriptural statement: "By his mere will, the ancestors arise"—the subtle meaning of this scripture is that for those who worship the embodied Paraśiva, the gods, ancestors, Gandharvas, and others become attendants like servants.
This is also evident from the scripture: "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or with youths, or with kinsmen."

The scriptures record the activities of one who meditates upon Brahman with form (mūrtabrahmopāsaka), which are brought about by his power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva). Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether the liberated soul (muktajīva) possesses a body and sense organs or not, or whether he possesses [faculties] such as resolve; furthermore, does his adoption of a resolve occur through his own independence, or does it occur solely through the resolve of the Supreme Lord?
If a person were to know the Self, realizing "I am this," then desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he wander about with a body?
For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant;
but for one dwelling in the bodiless state, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him.

Thus, having stated that suffering is unavoidable when there is a connection with a body, the Śruti declares the bodilessness of the liberated one in the passage: "Having risen from this body and having attained the highest light... Therefore, the possession of volitional power is not possible [for one who is bodiless].

Furthermore: since in the world, even for kings and others who are described as having "true resolve" (*satya-saṃkalpa*), we observe that the accomplishment of their effects depends upon other efforts, it follows that this [resolve of the liberated soul] must also depend upon them. To this, it is replied:
"By his mere resolve, his ancestors arise," for it is indeed from resolve alone that the arising of the ancestors and so forth occurs.

It is heard [in scripture]. Nor is another scriptural passage heard that speaks of the dependence on another effort, by which the restriction "from his own resolve alone" (*svasaṅkalpād eva*) could be established—just as [the restriction] is established in the case of "a mass of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*).
In such scriptural passages as "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold," etc., [it is said] of the Self...
Because that which is one and indivisible is designated as having manifold states, it is understood that its threefold existence and so forth are connected to the body.

The statement regarding the absence of a body refers to those who meditate upon Brahman as being without parts. Furthermore, the statement concerning bodilessness has as its purport the absence of a body caused by karma; for it is precisely such a body that is the cause of pleasure and pain.
It is established that the body of a devotee who has attained the state of Kailāsa, being composed of non-material light like the body of the Supreme Lord, is not a cause of suffering.
Now, [one might ask] regarding those devotees who have attained the state of Mahākailāsa...

Since there exist injunctions regarding subservience (*śeṣatva*), dependence (*pāratantrya*), and service (*kaikarya*) to the Supreme Lord, there is a state of being caused by fear, according to the analogy of a king and his servant. Therefore, anticipating the objection that this would result in a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing at all," he says:
And for this very reason, he has no other lord. || 9 ||

Since he is liberated and possesses true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*), for that very reason he is also one who has no other lord (*ananyādhipati*). For "having another as lord" consists in being subject to injunctions and prohibitions; indeed, if one were subject to injunctions and prohibitions, one's true resolve would be obstructed. Therefore, by the scriptural statement of "true resolve" itself, "having no other lord" is also established. For this very reason, he is a self-ruler (*svarāṭ*).

It has been stated [that he] "becomes. For this very reason, by the worship of Śiva alone, who is endowed with all powers, the worshiper becomes one for whom there is no other lord (*ananyādhipati*). This is because, through the attainment of all desires dependent upon his true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), he has no other superior. From the hearing of the Vedic revelation, "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," it follows that there exists no other lord besides Śiva; thus he is "one for whom there is no other lord. Another [being] would be one subject to control (*niyāmya*).

Therefore, he is indeed independent, like Śiva. As it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "What evil deed can there be for the servants of Śaṅkara, who are renowned for their exclusive devotion to Śiva, who prohibit meditation on anything other than Śiva, and who treat even Brahmā and Indra as mere blades of grass?"

By the designation of having no other as a sovereign, the independence of the liberated one is taught; by that, it is indicated that he is never subject to *karma*. Since *karma* has a nature that is destroyed, there is no other supreme Lord as a regulator, because [the liberated one] transcends the path of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions consisting of the commands of Śiva obtained through the stream of birth and death. Why?

Because of the exclusion of the state of being a bound animal (paśutva), it is logical that those characterized by the defects of the three desires bound by the impressions of beginningless ignorance are subject to karma in the form of Śiva’s command;
for in those who possess the likeness of Śiva— whose nature is eternal, unsurpassed, and auspicious— the qualities such as omniscience exist just like Śiva’s.

There is no contradiction in [the Lord’s] sovereignty, because He is characterized by being distinct from old age, death, sorrow, and fear, and because He finds delight in the Self alone through the experience of unsurpassed bliss.
But surely—
When all desires that dwell within his heart are utterly released,
then the mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman even here.
For bondage is bound by latent impressions; liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
O Brahmin, the attenuation of latent impressions is designated as liberation.
Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor within the elements;
when all desires have perished, the dissolution of the mind is declared to be liberation.
Because such scriptural passages as these demonstrate that for the liberated one all desires have ceased; and in the scripture describing the experience of liberation:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I take up? What shall I abandon?
By me the entire universe has been filled, as if by the waters at the time of the great dissolution."

Thus, the prohibition against going to other regions and so forth is prescribed for him. Therefore, how can the state of possessing worldly activity— as indicated by such scriptural passages as "therefore he moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing with women, or with his kinsmen"— be logically consistent for one who has been liberated?
Furthermore, regarding Vādari’s presentation of the doctrine of absolute non-duality (*kevalādvaita*):

in such passages as "There is nothing else whatsoever that blinks; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth; everything else is perishable," and "But there is no second," the negation of any entity other than Brahman is observed.

Likewise, in another place, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is understood from such scriptural passages as: "He who, dwelling within the self, is internal to the self, whom this self does not know, whose body is the self, and who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal"; and "He has entered within, the ruler of people"; and "Two birds [of beautiful plumage]," "the knowing and the unknowing," and "two unborn ones. Through these and other such Śruti texts, the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is apprehended.

In response to the objection that— since the Vedāntas would lack the capacity to provide certainty because sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) convey non-difference, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of indeterminacy— the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) itself would be untenable— the author presents three views.
Bādari says that there is non-existence, for it is thus stated.

Since it is understood from such passages as "Brahman is one only, without a second; wherein one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and knows nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā); herein there is no diversity whatsoever," that difference is denied throughout the three periods of time, the entire manifestation of the world, including the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), is unreal despite its appearance like a snake in a rope.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa considers [the world] to be non-existent and merely false, like the horn of a hare and so forth;

therefore, for the sake of instructing his disciples, following the maxim that "the non-differentiated is made manifest through superimposition and negation," even when teaching the conceptualization of the world and so on by way of scripture, reasoning, and experience—
The view of Bādari is that [the opponent’s position] is determined to be nothing but falsehood, like a description of the royal splendor of the son of a barren woman.
