As for Jaimini, he presents the reality of the world and the mutual difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara);
thus, there is the predominance of fallacious scriptures (*śrutyābhāsa*), the authority of only a portion of scripture, and the nature of the world as being illusory.
He shows [the view]:
|| 362 || Jaimini [maintains] the existence [of the soul], because of the consideration of the various alternatives. || 11 ||

In such scriptural passages as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," "One desiring prosperity should immolate a white animal dedicated to Vāyu," and "By sin one becomes blind, mute, deaf, or a dog; by merit one becomes possessed of noble lineage, wealth,
and enjoyments," there is the [prohibition of] killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) preceded by the rejection of meritorious actions that constitute the commands of the Blessed One.

For it is seen without doubt in the Śruti that through the performance of evil deeds such as drinking liquor and the like, one experiences the hells and other states of suffering, while through the performance of meritorious deeds consisting of the commands of the Blessed One, one experiences the bliss of the heavenly worlds and so forth—as stated in such scriptural passages as: "Not by sacrifice, nor by gift, nor by austerity, nor by food-restraint... and so on.

Furthermore, since it is understood that rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, when performed without desire and dedicated to the Supreme Lord, serve as means for attaining knowledge of Brahman by way of removing the mire of sins established within the individual's internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the teacher Jaimini maintains that the "bhāva"—the reality—of the entire manifold of the individual soul, the Lord, the Vedas, the Āgamas, and so forth, is true. Why? Because [these are the means].
Because of the non-mentation of conceptual construction.
"Vividha" means manifold; "kalpa" means conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); "vicāra" means reflection (*āsamantānmanana*) or thorough consideration (*āmanana*).

From that "consideration of conceptual construction" (*vikalpāmananāt*): if the world were false, then—just as in the case of the Buddha and others—the possession of enjoyments in this world and heaven through rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, as well as the state of being incorporeal through acts such as the killing of a Brahmin, would not be possible. Therefore...

Otherwise, the faults of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would arise. Furthermore, since that [doctrine] would entail contradictions with such scriptural passages as "He becomes one-fold, three-fold, five-fold, seven-fold," and so forth, the proponents of difference (*bhedavādinaḥ*) must accept that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and so on, is eternal, and that there is a mutual difference between the individual soul and the Lord.
This is the view of Jaimini,
which is also approved by Bādarāyaṇa;
for in this way, between the two systems that rely on the authority of only a portion of the Śruti, there arises the contingency of mutual invalidity.
In order to refute both those views, he states his own position—which consists of both duality and non-duality as established by all the Vedas, Vedāntas, and Āgamas—without restriction:
"Therefore, Bādarāyaṇa [holds it] to be of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice. (Sūtra 3.3.55)

Because there is a mutual contradiction between the doctrine of absolute non-duality (*kevalādvaita*), which holds that mere knowledge—which constitutes a single portion of the Vedas—is predominant, and the doctrine of duality (*dvaita*), which maintains that [knowledge] is realized solely through the yoga of ritual action and devotion; for this reason, that which is intended as the primary purport of all the Vedas and Upanishads is established by such scriptural texts as "Just as rivers... and so forth.
Bādarāyaṇa considers the doctrine of duality-cum-non-duality (*dvaitādvaita*) to be of two kinds, consisting of both knowledge and action.

This "two-fold" nature means that during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—the object of worship and the worshipper—possess ultimate reality; however, in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), they become one, like a river merging into the ocean or an insect entering a bee-hive.
It is determined that [the Self] is the pervasive, partless Brahman, preceded by the cessation of the state of being an individual soul characterized by its own nature.
This is like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*): "Those desiring prosperity should undertake it," or "One should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite."

Thus, by the force of two means of knowledge—the injunctions "it approaches" and "he sacrifices"—the nature of a *satra* and the nature of an *ahīna* are accepted through a distinction in intention (*saṅkalpa*) and a distinction in performance (*prayoga*).
Similarly, in mantras such as "Two birds... and others, the mutual distinctness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman [is established].

Since the identity of those two is established in statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), one must indeed accept that there is both ultimate difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman;
for it is observed in the words of many Śruti texts, Purāṇas, and former teachers that the Śruti speaks the truth, and thus there would be a contraction of the Śruti [if this were not accepted].

Because there is an absence of evidence [for non-duality] and because it would follow that [the Upanishads] are other than Vedic, in the earlier section—starting with "But the additional [attributes], on account of the mention of difference" (BS 3.3.8)—the reality of duality is established by determining the mutual difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. Furthermore, in the sūtra "Non-difference from That" (BS 2.1.14), the reality of non-duality is likewise indicated. And in the sūtra "But like the world, His sport alone" (BS 2.1.33), regarding the Supreme Lord...
By means of the designation "divine play" (līlā), it is stated that all dualistic scriptures refer to the state of differentiation at that specific time;

and by the term "isolation" (kaivalya), because it designates his state of absolute oneness, it is clearly taught that non-dualistic scriptures such as "There is no diversity here whatsoever" refer to his residual state.

If it is asked what purpose is served by the embodiment of Śiva— the all-pervading, omniscient Supreme Brahman— the answer is that his sole purpose is the sport of ferrying his devotees across the ocean of existence. Therefore, Śiva himself, assuming an auspicious form through his divine play (līlā) like the solidification of ghee, brought forth the collection of Vedas which reveal his own true nature.

Immediately thereafter, through Hiraṇyagarbha, he caused the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas to circulate throughout all the worlds. Therefore, one who desires liberation, by following the path of the Vedas and worshipping the reality of Paraśiva—both with and without form—attains the auspicious liberations beginning with *sālokya* up to *videha-kaivalya*; otherwise, by what means could the knowledge of the reality of Śiva be attained?
Therefore, no stain of doubt is incurred.

By stating, "The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct," Kṛṣṇa has shown that the very doctrine of non-duality-in-duality (*dvaitādvaita*) is his own view. Consequently, the doctrine of partiality (*pakṣaikadeśa*) is inconsistent.
The Section on Twilight Devotions (Sandhyā). 4.

The demonstration that Śiva is the cause of the world by means of the analogy of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*): Now, one might raise the objection that even if the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference is consistent with all the Vedas, it is nonetheless subject to logical sublation because difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory, like darkness and light; in response to this doubt, [the author provides] the analogy of difference-and-non-difference.
He demonstrates that [Brahman] is the cause of the world through another topical section (adhikaraṇa): || 364 || "Because its existence is possible as in the case of the twilight. || 13 ||

Just as it was taught in the *Samanvaya* section that all Vedānta texts establish Brahman and enjoin the knowledge of Brahman, so too, by the logic of "the accomplishment of both through the force of both injunctions" using the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha-yajña*) as an illustration, the Śruti is a speaker of truth regarding all Vedānta texts.
Thus, following this reasoning, it has been established that his own view is precisely that the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman possess both difference and non-difference.

By this, it is indicated that the meditation upon Brahman as having parts leads the wise to the attainment of the partless Brahman by means of the fulfillment of all desires. [It is] the cessation of the phenomenal world, peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual.

They consider the fourth [state] to be that Self; He is to be known as Śiva, non-dual. In such scriptural passages as "Rudra is indeed one, without a second" and "One only, without a second," although the Supreme Brahman—which is non-dual—possesses such qualities as the fulfillment of true resolves, yet in the context of its manifestation, there are scriptural texts such as "From this very Self, space was produced. It is in this sense of its existence [that the world arises].

At the time when the primary state of the power called *acic-chakti*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), prevails, He possesses the agency of creating the web of the world consisting of beings and their material elements through His divine play (*līlā*); however, at the time when that power is contracted, He does not create the web of the world Himself, even though He possesses true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*).

Therefore, the creation of the world is not contradictory through the simultaneous presence of Brahman as non-dual and as having a second, with Pradhāna as the primary factor. Why? Because it is logically possible, like the state of twilight;
that is, because it is possible in the same way as the state of dreaming, which exists between the states of waking and deep sleep.
Because the status of being the cause of the world is logically established;
just as [the scripture] begins with "Now, he creates chariots, horses for chariots, and roads in a dream," and continues, "Then he creates ponds and lotus-pools; for he is the creator."
While these sleep, it remains awake, according to its desire, free from pride.
That alone is the Pure, that is Brahman, that alone is called the Immortal.
In it all worlds are supported; nothing whatsoever exists outside of it.
Thus, in the Śruti as well, it is taught that even in dreams, the Supreme Lord creates chariots and other objects with the assistance of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the individual soul (jīva).

Therefore, just as there is no contradiction between [different states] occurring at different times, so too it is taught that difference and non-difference are not contradictory even at the same time. By this teaching, even for one who is liberated—

The very nature [of the individual] is permeated by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of past actions (*prārabdha*). It has been shown that just as there is the experience of unsurpassed bliss in the world of Śiva, when there is liberation from all impressions, then there occurs the experience of the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of oneness with Śiva alone.

In this context, [the distinction is made between] the non-dual Śiva, the Supreme Brahman whose essence is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), and the insentient [world] which possesses duality.
It is doubted whether the Pradhāna can possibly participate in the creation of the world.
Since Pradhāna and Śiva possess mutually contradictory natures— being insentient and sentient, like darkness and light— the non-dual Śiva has no dependence whatsoever upon the dualistic Pradhāna.

This is also an indicative mark for the liberated one (*mukta*). If [the Lord] were thus dependent, there would follow the consequence of a violation of His independence, such as the possession of "true desires" and "true resolves" established by scriptures like "He whose desires are true, whose resolve is true. For in scriptural passages such as "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper," that independent Being is shown to possess a preeminent majesty through His own greatness, being independent of any other means.

The state of being the creator of all has been demonstrated. Therefore, since it follows that Śiva, his worshiper, and the liberated soul are at times necessarily dependent upon *prakṛti*, it is said in response to this:
there is no mutual contradiction between Śiva and *pradhāna*, whether they are considered non-dual or dual, any more than there is between darkness and light.

In the passage, "From that very Self, space was produced," the words "from that" (*tasmāt*) and "from this" (*etasmāt*) have a cumulative sense, referring to the Pradhāna and this [Self] respectively. As it is said: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā."
This entire world is pervaded by that which has arisen from its constituent parts.

Because in such scriptural passages as "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; it is innate, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action," the dependence of *māyā* upon Śiva, its status as the cause of the universe, and the innate nature of that power are taught;
therefore, in the phrase "in its existence" (*tasya bhāve*), which refers to the actual state of the expansion of *pradhāna* dependent on Śiva, the word "twilight" (*sandhyā*) is used [by analogy].

The subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), understood as being within the three bodies, is designated as the state of dream (svapnāvasthā). Just as the stage of the deluded seeker after liberation is the cause of latent impressions (vāsanā) for all Vedāntic inquiry, and doubt is the seed of both the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta), so too is the subtle body itself [the cause] of the activity of the gross body (sthūlaśarīra).

And it is the cause of the knowledge of Śiva, which severs the ignorance of the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*). Therefore, by that analogy, the creation of the world by Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, has been described.

Furthermore, at the time of the specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), [the creation occurs] through the intellect alone, independent of the external senses and so forth.

Śivānanda is experienced by the Śiva-yogins; sporting in the Self, delighting in the Self, he becomes the self-ruling one who experiences the bliss of the Self. "He enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman"—by this, the attainment of Kailāsa as the cause, as well as the maintenance of the state of having the same form (sārūpya), is also implied.
From this it follows: Brahman has space as its body; it has truth as its self, breath as its delight, and the mind as its bliss.

Even for Sadāśiva, who dwells on the great Kailāsa, there is the experience of supreme bliss through independence from the external senses; thus, in the phrase "mind-bliss" (*mana-ānanda*), he is one whose bliss is in the mind (*manasi ānandaḥ*). He delights completely (*prāṇeṣu āsamantāt*) in the vital breaths.

It is ascertained through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). By the passage beginning with "the nectar enriched by peace" (*śāntisamṛddhamamṛtam*), the reality (*satyatva*) of that body, its quality of bestowing peace (*śāntikaratva*), and its immortality (*amṛtatva*) are taught. Here too, the same characteristics are taught for the worshiper of that [body] as well.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
|| 365 || "In the case of existence, it is like being awake. || 14 ||

Just as, during the state of manifestation, the waking state caused by merit and demerit arises for the gross body while it exists within the subtle body, so too, when the expansion of His own power and primordial nature (prakṛti) is present, the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of the universe arise for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman.

By this, it is indicated that even for one liberated from the bonds (*pāśa*), the experience of fruits appropriate to various worlds is possible only if the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) exists in this world and the next; in its absence, the attainment of all [remaining] karmas is not possible—this is the meaning regarding the fruit.
For the sake of the fruit, the Supreme Person...
Mahādeva also [performed] the destruction of the demons Vyāghra, Gaja, Tripura, and others, as well as the removal of poison and so forth;
[this is supported by] such scriptural passages as: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then he attains Brahman here."
It should be understood that [this state] pertains to the learned who possess firm dispassion and are established in the supreme Śiva-tattva, which is partless and all-pervasive.
Like the Supreme Lord, the liberated one also possesses the power to create various worlds.
Now, one might object: "Surely the liberated one becomes equal to Śiva," as in such passages as, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman.

Even though these texts teach that the worshipper of the embodied Śiva attains equality with Śiva and shares the same enjoyments, it is not possible for him to travel simultaneously to multiple bodies in various locations at one and the same time, in the manner of Maheśvara.
In response to the doubt that this is because of the presence of the body of the adventitious Śiva, he says:
"The penetration is like a lamp; for thus [the scripture] shows. (3.2.15)

Just as a lamp situated in one place pervades other places by means of its own radiance, so too, it is not logically untenable that the Self, though residing in only one part [of the body], pervades the entire body by means of consciousness (*caitanya*), which is its very nature. And just as in a single body, although [consciousness] resides in only one part such as the heart, it pervades the whole body through the extension of consciousness.

The conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) is likewise. This much, however, is the distinction here: for one who is not liberated, whose knowledge is contracted by karma, pervasion corresponding to the self across various bodies is not possible; but for the liberated one, whose knowledge is uncontracted, it is so.

The pervasion [of the self] is in accordance with one's own conceit (*abhimāna*) as it is intended, while the impossibility [of such a conceit] is in accordance with the apprehension of "this" [the object].
For it shows this thus:
"Of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred parts..."
That portion of the living being is to be known; and it leads to infinity.

Thus: for one who is not liberated, karma is the regulator; but for one who is liberated, like the Supreme Lord, it is possible through his own will to be the creator of bodies and so forth in the world of Brahmā, as well as to enter multiple bodies simultaneously. "He becomes onefold."

Since scriptural passages such as "He becomes threefold, he becomes thousandfold" demonstrate that those who worship the Supreme Lord can, by the power of that very worship, create multiple bodies through mere volition (saṅkalpa), it is concluded that the scriptures prescribing the atomicity (aṇutva) of the soul refer specifically to bound souls (baddha-jīva).

If it is argued that there is no difference between the bound and the liberated regarding the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—since for the liberated one, just as for the transmigrating soul, the body, senses, and so forth are established, and the perception of the phenomenal world is likewise designated—we say no. This is because for the liberated one, there is an absence of the perception of the phenomenal world in the form of an object of personal human purpose (*puruṣārtha*); rather, for the liberated one, the phenomenal world, which is an effect of Brahman, is [perceived] as being Brahman itself.

And because it is manifest: in the scriptural passage beginning, "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman)," the experience of the liberated is taught.
Furthermore: "This becomes that: Brahman, whose body is space, enriched by peace, immortal."

In the preceding [verse], it was stated that "the yogi attains self-sovereignty (svārājya) and attains the Lord of the Mind (manasaspati)," meaning he attains the state of Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, whose sole essence is the bliss of self-sovereignty, and who, as the Lord of the Mind, serves as the presiding authority through his power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti). Now, in response to the inquiry as to what specific qualities he possesses at that time, [it is said]: "He is the Lord of Speech (vākpati), the Lord of the Eye (cakṣuṣpati)."
The term "Lord of Hearing" (śrotrapati) and "Lord of Consciousness" (vijñānapati) refers to his sovereignty over speech and the other organs when they are under the control of his own will.

For one who has ascended to the state of Śiva known as Mahākailāsa and possesses such pure instruments of speech and so forth governed by his own will, this entire web of the universe [arises] after the attainment of that state.
What comes to be? It becomes the very Brahman whose body is space (*ākāśa-śarīra*).

For the Supreme Power (*parama-śakti*), which is of one flavor (*samarasa*) with the light and bliss of the supreme existence that is the nature of the Supreme Nature (*paraprakṛti*), is called the Supreme Space (*paramākāśa*) because it constitutes the body of the Supreme Brahman; she who belongs to both the liberated ones and Śiva.

That [Brahman] is the cause of direct purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), whereas that which is different from it is so through a mediated succession. For thus it is heard in scripture that this [Brahman] is the object of all experience: "For who indeed could inhale, who could exhale, if this Ākāśa were not bliss? For he alone is bliss; he is indeed the essence (*rasa*);
for having obtained the essence, one becomes blissful. And at that time, he is one.

Beginning with "The human bliss, O Ānanda," and culminating in "That is one [unit] of the bliss of Brahman," the scriptures declare that the manifestation of bliss occurs in varying degrees due to the obscuration caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). However, in its unconditioned state, it exists in its full perfection within Brahman and the liberated soul, as indicated by the Vedic mantra: "That is one [unit] of the bliss of Brahman, and of the learned Śrotriya who is untouched by desire."

The bliss of one who possesses the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), who is a *śrotriya* untouched by desire, and who has performed the *agnihotra* and other rites without desire through the realization that they are an offering to Brahman—
he who is liberated even while living— his bliss is indeed equal to that of Brahman. For him,
who has ascended to various stages through the excellence of yoga, the practice of the preceding stage is minimal.
In accordance with this, there is no contradiction in the scriptural statement that the manifestation of bliss on each respective level is incomparable to human bliss (*mānuṣyānanda*).
Therefore, one understood: "This alone is the supreme bliss; it is the supreme primordial nature (*parā prakṛti*); it is the bliss of non-difference from the Supreme; it is Brahman."

It is heard in the scriptures that [Brahman] exists as the essence of Brahman and as the cause of the world. Its manifestation is this very knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇi, which is established in the supreme ether. Therefore, for those who are liberated, the body—which is of the nature of supreme bliss and the supreme ether—is Brahman; thus, for these [liberated ones] who have entered into supreme bliss, it is Brahman.
The absence of any connection with suffering has been shown.
But does not the Śruti demonstrate the cessation of external knowledge immediately after attaining similarity (*sārūpya*) with the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, stating:
"Embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), he knows nothing external, nor anything internal"? How then [can it be said that the liberated one possesses knowledge]?
Regarding the statement that [the Lord] possesses omniscience, the reply is as follows:
"It refers to either the state of deep sleep or the state of union; for this has been made manifest. (Sūtra 3.2.9)
This statement does not refer to liberation (*mukti*), but rather depends on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or death (*sampatti*).

Deep sleep is *suṣupti*, and death is *sampatti*, because of the scriptural passage beginning with "Speech merges into the mind" and ending with "heat [merges] into the supreme deity. And in those two states, there exists both the attainment of the Prājña (the conscious Self) and the absence of consciousness.

Therefore, this statement refers to one or the other of those two states. For the Śruti has revealed that deep sleep and death consist in a lack of consciousness, whereas liberation consists in omniscience: "Indeed, I do not now know myself as 'this is I,' nor indeed these beings; he has gone to utter annihilation; I see no object of enjoyment here."

Having stated the state of non-cognition during the time of deep sleep with the words "I see [nothing]," that very same text, referring to the liberated one, declares omniscience: "He, indeed, with the divine eye, the mind, sees these desires and rejoices in them—those which are in the world of Brahman. Likewise, it is explicitly stated: "The seer sees all; he attains all."

Omniscience is thus described; likewise, at death, there is a state of non-cognition. It has been stated: "Arising from these elements, one perishes after them. To "perish" means "one does not see. Therefore, the expression "by the conscious self" (prājñenātmanā) refers to either deep sleep (svāpyaya) or union with the Supreme (sampatti).

Now, an objection may be raised: since scriptural passages such as "He moves at will in all worlds, wandering through these worlds according to his desire and assuming forms at will" indicate that the worshiper of the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman possesses limited dimensions and thus undergoes movement through all worlds, [the Brahman] cannot be all-pervasive.
Therefore, if it is argued that [the soul] does not act simultaneously like the Supreme Lord because of the transition through the entry into various bodies, we say no:
"He is our kinsman, he is the progenitor, he is the ordainer; he knows all abodes and all worlds, wherein the gods attained immortality and reached the third realm. (RV 10.64.2)
In an instant, they traverse the earth, the heavens, the worlds, the quarters, and the intermediate spaces;
having sustained the outspread thread of cosmic order (*ṛta*), they beheld that [truth], and it became manifest among living beings.

Thus, in the Śruti, it is shown that upon the release from the bond of ignorance (*avidyā*), the worshiper of that [deity] attains a pervasive immersion (*āveśa*) into the universe, just like Him; this is demonstrated in the context of the passage beginning with "This indeed is the God" (*eṣa hi devaḥ*). This refers to Mahādeva, the creator of the universe who possesses a cosmic form (*viśvarūpa*).
He—Mahādeva—is our kinsman (*bandhu*), our progenitor (*janitā*), our father; He is the Ordainer (*vidhātā*).

The creator of all auspicious things knows the *dhāman*—the non-material worlds whose nature is splendor—and indeed all universes; therein, the purpose of the connection with kinship and so forth, as well as the knowledge of the *dhāman*, is stated:
"wherein"—in which God here—those whose minds hope for the glory of immortality (*amṛta*), namely liberation (*kaivalya*), having attained it, experience it.

The gods—by virtue of that state—being playful by nature, in that third station known as *dyu*, which transcends *māyā*, they attained (*abhyairayanta*) their desired abodes (*dhāmāni*), which consist primarily of splendor (*tejas*).
This is what is meant: by Mahādeva, who acts for the welfare of all like a kinsman or a father, being well-pleased...

Having been released from the bonds of the fetters of the *dalita* (the bound), they have attained the state of immortality and are liberated; in the third sphere, characterized as the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), they have reached the stations and established their abodes in their own place. Therefore, their supreme pervasion is described: "They go around heaven and earth"—the liberated souls go around heaven and earth with the rays of their own power.
They attain the higher worlds—even attaining the worlds of Hiraṇyagarbha and others—and they pervade the quarters;
thus they exist as those who pervade the entire universe. For instance:
being omniscient, they have severed the vast thread of enjoyment belonging to *ṛta*—that is, ritual action—having held it fast.
Being liberated from merit and demerit, the virtuous beheld that very reality called Mahādeva within all living beings.
Because it is the self of all, they became that; they became of its very nature. Therefore, for those who are liberated and whose sole essence is Śiva, there is indeed omnipresence.

These liberated souls, possessing the same nature as Mahādeva and denoted by the word "deva," are heard of in the Sāman hymns known as the *Devavrata* as pervading the heavens and other realms, beginning with the verse: "Those gods who dwell in heaven," and so forth. And in the Purāṇa: "For they are indeed the manifest dwellers in heaven, as well as the dwellers in the intermediate space."
These gods, who dwell upon the earth, have been praised in the Devavrata hymn.

Thus: "Earth" refers to the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); "the intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*) is the second state, which is *māyā*; and the third, synonymous with the supreme ether (*paramākāśa*), is said to be the state of Śiva, whose nature is pure power (*śuddhaśakti*). Therefore, the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the liberated ones is not contradictory.

Furthermore, as for what was stated—that according to the Śruti passage, "Embraced by the wise Self, he knows nothing that is external, nor anything internal," there is a contraction of the powers of the liberated souls (muktas) regarding the knowledge of the world other than Śiva—that is not so. This [passage], rather, concerns the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) and so forth of bound individual souls (baddha-jīvas). Alternatively, it may be intended to negate the knowledge of the world other than Śiva and the like [in that specific context].
The Topic Concerning the Agency of the World's Activity. 5.

[This concerns] the sovereignty consisting of the effortless experience of Brahman, which is free from the fivefold cosmic functions such as creation—which are [only] to be attained by those who are liberated.

Now, regarding the doubt: "Would not those who worship the Supreme Śiva-Brahman likewise possess true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) and omnipresence (*vyāpakatva*)?"—to this doubt, [the answer is: it would indeed be so.
He states the distinction between the liberated soul and the Supreme Lord by means of another topical section:
"Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context and because of non-proximity. (Sūtra 4.4.17)
In the former case, it was established that the partless Supreme Brahman, Śiva himself, is all-pervasive and omnipresent like space,
and that his worshippers attain that state; whereas in the latter case, it was established that the embodied Brahman is pervasive like a lamp,
and that his worshippers likewise possess independence and the power to traverse all worlds.

Having taught [the Lord's] possession of the attainment of all desires and so forth, he now demonstrates the distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper: "Excluding the activity of the world."

For the practitioners (*upāsakas*), there is only the capacity to determine the manifestation of a multitude of bodies (*kāyavyūha*) and so forth that serve as the means for their own enjoyment, setting aside the activity of creating the elements and elemental beings such as gods, *gandharvas*, and humans.
However, the activity of creating gods, *gandharvas*, and so forth belongs to Śiva alone. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore...
"From this Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth;
from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the person. From which indeed these beings are born—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra—they are all produced," and so forth.

This is because it is established that [the Lord] is the creator of the bodies of gods and others, both sentient and insentient; furthermore, in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas, there is no mention of His worshippers being the creators of all the bodies of gods and others beyond their own.
Moreover: "Because of His non-proximity [to the individual soul], Rudra, the great seer who is superior to the universe, is he who creates Brahmā."

Because, in passages such as "He who indeed imparts the Vedas to him," Hiraṇyagarbha is established as being born directly from Paraśiva-Brahman during the prior state of all living beings— including gods and Gandharvas— and because he is thus proximate to Paraśiva and constitutes His inner circle.

The subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra is that, because at that time there is no creation of a living being distinct from Him, and because liberated souls are not present, it is impossible for them to be the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, just as the Supreme Lord is.

This is because [the status of] being the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe, as pointed out by such scriptural passages as "From which indeed these beings are born," [cannot apply to others].
The doubt arises as to whether [this state] occurs for both the object of worship and the worshipper—namely Śiva and the individual soul—or whether it occurs for Śiva alone;

for in such passages as, "When the seer sees the golden-hued one, he attains supreme equality," the attainment of equality with the Supreme Person, Śiva, by the liberated souls is heard, and [the nature of the liberated soul is described] in such texts as, "The Self which is free from sin... and so forth.

Because there is instruction regarding attributes such as having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*) similar to those of the Supreme Lord; because in passages such as "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," the capacity to create the world of the fathers and so forth through mere resolve is heard; and because in the passage "Moving about at will among these worlds, assuming any form at will," his activity everywhere is indicated—there is equality with the Supreme Lord.

And since contraction is impossible, it follows that even for the liberated one, the status of being the cause of the creation and so forth of the world is possible, just as it is for the Supreme Lord. To this we reply: "With the exception of the activity regarding the world."

The activity of the world (*jagadvyāpāra*) consists of the regulation of the nature, maintenance, and various functions of all sentient beings. "Excluding that" refers to the primary sovereignty (*mukhyaiśvarya*), which consists of the unmediated experience of Brahman for one whose every veil has been removed. Why is this so?

On account of the context. For the governance of the entire universe is indeed recorded in scripture as being the nature of Paraśiva-Brahman. Since the status of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the universe—as indicated by such scriptural passages as "From which these beings are born," "The one God generating heaven and earth," and "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts"—is common to liberated souls as well, [the definition of Brahman] would not [apply uniquely].

This is consistent. For only a unique (asādhāraṇa) property constitutes a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. "It thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate. "That is the Imperishable. "That is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ. "When there was darkness, neither day nor night existed. "Though being one, it became manifold. "It emitted that form which is superior—the Kṣatra."
In passages such as, "These are the divine constellations: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna;
nothing else even blinks," the fact that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, is the controller of the entire universe is heard.
In all contexts concerning the governance of the entire universe and so forth, there is no presence of the liberated soul (mukta) by which he could [be considered] the agent of the world's activity.

That too would be the case. For indeed, [it is said] in such passages as: "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; the Creator fashioned [the worlds] as before"; "Nārāyaṇa alone existed; from Nārāyaṇa Brahmā is born; from Nārāyaṇa Rudra is born"; and "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed."
Since Hiranyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, and others are understood from direct Vedic scriptures to be the cause of the universe,
how can the status of Śiva alone as the Supreme Brahman and the cause of the birth and so forth of the world be possible?
Therefore, in response to the doubt that the causality of the world's birth and so forth might not be inconsistent even for liberated beings, he says:

If it be argued that [the soul's departure] does not occur because of the teaching of direct perception, we say no; for there is a statement concerning those situated within the mandala who possess specific authority.

If it be argued that because the direct Vedic texts beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning" teach that Hiraṇyagarbha and others are the cause of the universe, it is impossible for Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, alone to be the cause of the universe—[we reply:
this is not so, because in many such Vedic texts, it is established that Śiva, Hiraṇyagarbha, Nārāyaṇa, and the rest cannot be the cause of the cause [of the universe]. Therefore, their...

Equality with that [Brahman] is not possible. Why? Because of the mention of those residing in the spheres of authority (*ādhikārika-maṇḍala*). For it is taught that Indra, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others abide in limited worlds such as Satya and Vaikuṇṭha—worlds granted by the grace of Śiva—which is stated in the passage: "With that [Brahman], the gods, the Sādhyas, and the ṛṣis sacrificed."
Since the Śrutis beginning with "He who... directly teach that Paraśiva alone is the creator of all beings, including the gods,

even though Hiraṇyagarbha and others are understood to be the causes of the intermediate creation, it is established that the Supreme Lord alone is their cause by virtue of being their inner controller (antaryāmin).

If it be objected that in such scriptural passages as, "He becomes his own ruler; for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds," the activity of governing the universe is taught for the liberated soul just as it is for the Supreme Lord—this is not so. For the liberated one, whose intellect is no longer obstructed by karma, experiences the various worlds which are the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Brahman-Śiva, and having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire, he remains satisfied.
It is taught that they attain those worlds according to their desire; therefore, the activity of creating the world does not belong [to the liberated soul].

If one were to object: "If the liberated soul, like one still in saṃsāra, enjoys enjoyments existing within the realm of transformation, then for the liberated soul—as for the bound—the collection of objects of enjoyment would be finite and limited," the author says this in response:
And it does not participate in modifications, for thus it declares its state. || 19 ||

The liberated one experiences the Supreme Śiva-Brahman—along with its manifestations (savibhūtikam)—which does not abide in transformations such as birth and so forth, which is free from all modifications (nirdhūtanikhilavikāram), which is the sole embodiment of auspiciousness opposed to everything that is to be abandoned, and which is unsurpassed bliss; it is endowed with all auspicious qualities. Likewise, [he experiences] those things that abide within transformations by virtue of being included within those manifestations.

The worlds, too, have their objects of enjoyment already experienced. For instance, the Śruti declares that the liberated one abides as the experiencer within the supreme Brahman—which is changeless, infinite, and unsurpassed bliss: "When indeed he finds support in this that is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode, then he has attained freedom from fear."

"He is indeed the essence (rasa). For having obtained this very essence, one becomes blissful," and so forth. Furthermore, the world, which is His manifestation, exists within Him alone; for the Śruti declares: "In Him all worlds are supported; there is nothing else whatsoever.
Therefore, experiencing Brahman along with His manifestations, [one realizes] that which exists within the modifications...

It is stated that one enjoys even those enjoyments situated within the presiding mandalas, such as "moving at will through all worlds," and so forth; thus, the identity with Śiva (śivasāmarasya) is established. Furthermore, [it applies] to the wise ones who dwell on Kailāsa, who are eternally liberated and wander according to their own will.
In such passages as "moving through the worlds of desire and the worlds of form," the term refers to the state of identity with Śiva—

which consists of the power of will free from the conceit of possessing bodies such as those of humans in the desire and form realms, and which is composed of the manifestation of self-luminous glory, the root of eternal sovereignty and supreme bliss— and which possesses the same nature as that [Śiva].
Scripture reveals this through such passages as: "I am food, I am food, I am food;
I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food, I am the eater of food. Likewise, in another scripture, the experience of the liberated is clearly taught:
Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes—
I am Sadāśiva, the pure consciousness, the witness distinct from them all.
Everything has arisen in me alone; everything is established in me;
everything goes to dissolution in me; therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman.
I am the subtlest of the subtle, and likewise I am that; I am the Great One, this manifold universe.
I am the ancient one, I am the Puruṣa, I am the Lord; I am the golden one, I am the very form of Śiva.

By these and other such [passages], this scripture serves as an illustration— like Vāmadeva and others— of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), who possess the knowledge of Śiva and are established in the yoga and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Śiva, which is the experience of bliss through Śiva’s all-pervasive nature like space. It refers to those who have attained identity with Śiva (*śivasārūpya*).

Even for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), despite their firm abidance in the singular knowledge of Śiva, they do not possess the causality for the birth of the world and so forth, just like Śiva himself.
In this regard, the ego of the liberated one is not of the nature of worldly transmigration (*sāṃsārika*).

Because He is distinct from the transmigratory ego limited and circumscribed by the divisions of gods, humans, castes, and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), and because He is all-pervasive due to encompassing the entire manifold of consciousness and the unconscious; here, by the word "I" (*aham*), Śiva alone is denoted.
Regarding this point, he states another reason:
And thus, he demonstrates both perception and inference. || 20 ||

Out of fear of him the wind blows; out of fear of him the sun rises;
out of fear of him Agni and Indra, and Death as the fifth, run on.

Thus [it is said]: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (akṣara), the sun and the moon stand held apart," and so forth. Likewise, the Śruti says: "He is the Lord of all, He is the Sovereign of beings, He is the Protector of beings, He is the Bridge, the Sustainer, for the sake of the non-confusion of these worlds. And in the Manusmṛti:
In the beginning, He created the waters alone; into them He cast His seed.
Everything produced by Śiva is protected by Śiva;
again, all that is moving and unmoving dissolves into Mahādeva, Śiva.

Thus [it is said]. And in the Śātātapa [Smṛti]: because it is taught that Śiva alone is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, and because in such passages as "the stainless one attains supreme equality" and "the liberated one becomes equal to Śiva," although the mere equality of the liberated ones with Śiva is taught, their lack of agency over the world is indeed logical, since they are not seen to possess the causality of the world like Śiva.

Based on the scriptural statement, "Viṣṇu alone is the Great Being, appearing as manifold separate beings," in the passage "one foot of his is all beings" (*viśvābhūtāni*), the word *viśva* (all) refers to infinite millions of Brahmāṇḍas,
while the word *bhūta* (beings) refers to the entities such as Nārāyaṇa, Hiraṇyagarbha, Indra, and so forth; these constitute one foot of Śiva, the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*).
From the statement, "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven," it is determined that [Brahman] is characterized by the attributes of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
Therefore, in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*, it is said: "They consider the non-dual Śiva to be the Fourth; He is the Self, and He is to be known."
That which is declared as the sound at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas— He who is beyond that [sound] when it has dissolved into its source is Maheśvara.

Thus, according to the Taittirīya [Upaniṣad], although those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) possess equality with the Supreme Lord Maheśvara— consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who are composed of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*, and possessing such qualities as the power to realize their true intentions (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)— it is not contradictory that they exclude themselves from the activity of creating and maintaining the world (*jagadvyāpāra*).

Now, one might object: "Since it is impossible for liberated souls to be the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe like the Supreme Lord, the contradiction with the supreme equality indicated by such scriptural passages as 'The stainless one attains the highest equality' and 'The liberated one becomes equal to Śiva' is unavoidable. Anticipating this, he says in response:
|| 372 || And because there is a mark indicating equality in respect of enjoyment alone. || 21 ||

Because the equality of the liberated soul with Brahman is established even regarding mere enjoyment, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that the cause of the entire world is devoid of worldly activity, there is no contradiction [in this]. In passages such as "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," the equality of the liberated one with the enjoyment of Paraśiva is demonstrated.

On this point, some [maintain]: since it is taught that there is equality only in respect to enjoyment between the embodied Paraśiva and the liberated soul who worships Him— both being derived from the Śiva-tattva, which is the cause of the world's birth and so forth, and is perfect and partless— therefore, like the eternally liberated embodied Supreme Śiva, the intermediate liberated souls possess the status of being the cause of the world.

Furthermore, they argue that the conceptualization of various bodies such as those of gods and humans is not possible, because in passages such as "He alone causes bliss," one observes a hierarchy between the object of worship and the worshiper, characterized by the states of being the goal to be attained and the means of attainment.
This too is not contradictory; for it is heard thus in the Skanda Purāṇa:
O Sāmba, although you belong to me when enjoyments are present, you do not belong to me when they have departed;
for a wave belongs to the ocean, but the ocean does not belong to a wave.
When all are completely liberated, one attains Brahman right here;
his vital breaths do not depart, but are absorbed right there.

This is because, in such passages, it is taught that those who are established in the knowledge of the partless Śiva-tattva and are liberated from all desires attain the Śiva-tattva preceded by the dissolution of the *liṅga-śarīra*;
and because there is the prohibition of the return of the liberated as indicated by such scriptural texts as, "He does not return, he does not return."
It is pointed out that this refers precisely to being intent upon That.

Since the embodied form of the all-pervading Brahman is imagined for the sake of meditation—like a snake [superimposed] on a rope—and is therefore illusory, liberation cannot result from meditating upon an illusory object; thus, for the sake of establishing the validity of the Śruti, [it is said]:

For those who worship the Brahman with form (*mūrtabrahmopāsaka*), liberation occurs right here through the knowledge of the supreme Śiva-Brahman, which is devoid of qualities and distinctions, by means of returning [to the world] again.
This is the section concerning the non-return based on scriptural testimony (*anāvṛttiśśabdādhikaraṇa*).
Regarding the certainty of non-return for both those who worship the embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahma*) and those who worship the unembodied Brahman (*amūrtabrahma*):

furthermore, in passages such as "He attains" (*so 'śnute*), since the fulfillment of desires is seen for those worshippers who have attained states such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) like bound souls (*baddhajīva*), there arises the doubt that their freedom from returning is inconsistent.
At the conclusion of the scripture, he demonstrates his own intended conclusion of all Vedānta as being unrestricted:
"No return, on account of the scriptural statement; no return, on account of the scriptural statement. (4.4.22)

In the preceding [section], it was taught that [the Self] is the source of all auspicious qualities, eternally satisfied, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, free from all defects, and characterized by unique attributes such as being the cause of the universe;
whereas here, [it is taught]: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself," "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow."

Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace; for through such scriptural statements as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), there is the designation in the Śruti that those who meditate upon Brahman—which is without parts—are of the nature of Brahman itself. Consequently, by the power of that meditation—according to the analogy of iron being transformed by mercury—the innate state of being a limited individual soul (jīva-bhāva) ceases, and the attainment of the reality of Śiva becomes possible.

Like a living being bound by a snare, there is no returning. According to the Śruti: "Having meditated upon Umāsahāya, the sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness"—this refers to the wise ones who worship the embodied Paraśiva-Brahman as distinct from Prakṛti, which is the state of equilibrium of the three qualities denoted by the word *tamas*.

"Until the end of their life-span, they attain the world of Brahmā and do not return, do not return," and so forth; according to such scriptural passages, those who worship the embodied Maheśvara attain all desires together with Him in that world,
and immediately thereafter, from that very world, by means of the fullness of the knowledge of Śiva— following the analogy of the bee and the worm— [they proceed].

Furthermore, because the attainment of *sāyujya* (union) with the all-perfect Śiva is revealed [in scripture], it follows that even for those who worship the embodied Paraśiva, a return to worldly existence—like that of bound souls (*baddhajīva*)—is impossible; such is the subtle meaning indicated by the Sūtra.
This is evident from passages such as "the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā," which concern those who worship the embodied Brahman.

Because of the instruction on the attainment of the Śiva-tattva, and because in such passages as "the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," it is understood that for those who meditate upon the formless Brahman there is the cessation of the suffering of saṃsāra— which consists of the continuous flow of birth and death—
it is doubted whether those who meditate upon the formed [Brahman] or those who meditate upon the formless [Brahman] are likewise free from rebirth.
For in such passages as, "He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman," it is heard that those who worship the embodied [Brahman] attain their desires just like bound souls; and:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are liberated..."
Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman.
If a person were to discern the Self, thinking "This am I," then desiring what, or for whose sake, would he wander about following this body?
Furthermore, because the cessation of all desires is taught for those who know Brahman in passages such as this,
the return of those who worship the embodied (mūrta) Brahman is not possible.
Moreover, in passages such as "eating whatever he desires and assuming whatever form he desires, he moves about," [it is shown that] for those who worship the embodied Brahman...

From the understanding that one enters various bodies fashioned according to one's own will, and from the observation of all types of experiences, the status of being the agent of merit and demerit is established by implication. This is evident in such scriptural passages as: "When merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals"; "The world accumulated through merit perishes; what is accumulated through action perishes"; and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma."

Just as there is the designation of "return" for those established in states such as heaven obtained through the fruit of merit, so too is the return of even those devotees who have ascended to the state of Śiva’s abode, Mahākailāsa, unavoidable; this is because [such attainment] is accomplished through karma and has its cause in one's own agency. As it is said: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a Brahmin should attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated."

In the passage beginning with "kṛtena," there is seen the refutation of liberation for those seekers of release who have performed ritual acts (*kṛtakarmāṇām*). Furthermore, in passages such as "But at the time of their final end, they [attain] the world of Brahman," the word "Brahman" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the four-faced one (Brahmā);
therefore, the attainment of that world is declared for his worshiper. In passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," [the term refers to] Nārāyaṇa.
Because it is established as the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) and because the word "Bhagavat" is conventionally rooted in that alone,
it is logical that the status of being denotable by the word "Brahman" belongs to Him alone. For the sake of fulfilling the path of those scriptural texts,
[this applies] to those who worship the embodied forms of the four-faced Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and others, who have attained perfection through many births.

Through the purification of the mind preceded by the cessation of all the mire of sin, and by means of the knowledge of one's own true nature—which is eternal, partless, and free from phenomenal proliferation—the attainment of non-return is established. This being the position reached [by the opponent], we reply: "Non-return, on account of the scriptural word; non-return, on account of the scriptural word. [The analogy of] the rope-snake does not apply here, because that [error] is possible [in the case of the rope-snake], whereas this [attainment of the Self] is not so. Thus it is concluded.
There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the manifest and the unmanifest.
That [Brahman] is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; it is one, all-pervading, consciousness-bliss, formless, and wonderful.
It is the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful.

In such scriptural passages as these, the fact that Śiva, the Supreme Brahman, possesses both partlessness (*niravayavatva*) and possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*) is established as appropriate; likewise, in the *Śatarudrīya*— through such verses as "Salutations again and again to you who are formless and to you who possess universal forms"— the twofold nature of devotees is observed, specifically those who worship the embodied (*mūrta*) Brahman.

And for those who worship the embodied Brahman (*mūrtabrahmopāsaka*), there is no return, because of the scriptural authority (*śabda*) of the Veda; for instance, by such passages as "Having meditated, the sage goes to the source of beings," and "Just as rivers [merge into the ocean]," and "This serene being (*saṃprasāda*),
having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form."
From such words as these, it is determined that for those who worship the formless, there is non-return—that is, no returning again.

In the passage "He enjoys," the distinction from the bound soul is shown by the scriptural hearing of the attainment of all desires together with Brahman. In passages such as "He becomes one whose desires are attained, whose desires are fulfilled, who is free from desire, and whose desires have perished," [this refers to] liberated selves.

The characteristic of Brahman has been taught as the state of having all desires under one’s own control like that of Brahmā. If it were admitted that even the wise are bound merely by the presence of desire, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because in such passages as "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" Brahman itself is heard to possess desire. [As it is said: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are released..."

The passage beginning with "they remain" (*sthitāḥ*) and so forth refers to the time of attaining supreme Śiva— preceded by the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*)— at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma for those wise ones who follow the scriptures on desirelessness; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as "Vāmadeva [attained it] while still in the womb" and "Śuka [attained it] while still in the body."

Because it is accepted as being intent upon liberation characterized by the eternal, unsurpassed, and auspicious glory of *sālokya* and other states attained through the *liṅga-śarīra*, one should take faith, devotion, and meditation as the fire-drill (*araṇi*) for the Self;

[thereby] Hara [reveals] the perishable *pradhāna* and the immortal imperishable. Through the intense contemplation (*abhidhyāna*) of that, there arises the divine sustaining power (*dhāraṇā*) of the immortal.
Because the worship of Paraśiva— recited in the context of Brahman in passages such as "We worship Tryambaka" and "The Self, verily, my dear"— is taught as the direct means for attaining Paraśiva,
it is stated that only those rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are recited in the context of Dharma, lead to rebirth for as long as one lives.

In passages such as "He attains the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) and does not return," the term *brahmaloka* does not refer to the Four-faced One (Brahmā). This is because in common usage, as well as in the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other texts, no such practice of meditating upon the Four-faced One is observed; furthermore, that world cannot be attained without such meditation upon him.

Because Smṛtis such as "Śiva is the deity of the Brāhmaṇas, while Mādhava is the deity of the Kṣatriyas" designate Viṣṇu as the deity of the Kṣatriyas, it is not logical [to claim] that he is the cause of the cause. In passages such as "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman," it is understood that Śiva, who is superior even to Nārāyaṇa, is indeed Brahman.

It is thus determined. Furthermore, in such passages as "May Śiva, who is Brahman, be ever auspicious to me" (sadā śivo me astu) and "The supreme Brahman is the eternal Truth" (ṛtaṃ satyaṃ paraṃ brahma),
the synonymy of the terms *Śiva* and *Brahman* is clearly taught, much like the relationship between *ghaṭa* and *kalaśa*.

"In the *Māṇḍūkya*, it is said: 'They consider the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which is peaceful, auspicious, and non-dual, to be the Fourth (*turya*); that is the Self; that is to be known. And in the *Kaivalya*, beginning with 'Accompanied by Umā' [it says]: 'He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Hiraṇyagarbha, he is Indra, he is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Sovereign Lord. Thus, because the teaching is given that Śiva alone transcends the three forms, so too in the *Atharvaśiras*:"

Starting from "One should meditate upon Īśāna" and ending with "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," there is an understanding of the prohibition against the worship of deities other than Śiva for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). In the term *śivaṃkara*, by the etymology "he who makes [one] auspicious" (*śivaṃ karoti*), the bestowing of one's own true nature upon devotees is shown, according to the maxim of the bee and the worm (*bhramarakīṭanyāya*).
Although the word *bhagavat* is observed in common worldly usage for [deities] such as Indra, in the *Pitṛmegha* it is said: "May the Lord Īśāna, Mahādeva, Maheśvara,
the Blessed One (Bhagavān), the Sovereign (Īśa), the Supreme Self (Paramātman), Sadāśiva, be pleased in the form of the ancestors."

Thus, in the *Brahmakāṇḍa* of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "The Blessed Lord has all faces, heads, and necks; He is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. And in the *Atharvaśiras*: "He who is Rudra is the Blessed Lord, as well as he who is Brahmā and he who is Viṣṇu," and so forth.
By such passages, the term "Blessed Lord" (*bhagavat*) is repeatedly and in many ways proclaimed of Śiva.

In the Śatarudrīya, it is taught thus: "Salutations be unto you, O Blessed One, the Lord of All, the Great God. Because scriptural injunction (*śrautavidhi*) is more authoritative than worldly usage, the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*) does not primarily refer to anyone else.
This is because, at the commencement of the scripture with the words "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," Brahman is taught as the object of inquiry for one who seeks liberation.

The doctrine of a Brahman devoid of distinctions has been refuted right there [in that very text]. For, according to the logical principle that "the establishment of a real entity depends upon its definition and means of valid cognition," regarding the establishment of the reality whose nature is Brahman, there are the aphorisms prescribing the definition and the means of valid cognition— namely, *janmādy asya yataḥ* and *śāstrayonitvāt*— as well as those texts illuminating their meaning, such as *yataḥ vā imāni* and *tasmād vā*.

In such passages as "From this Self, space was produced," "The Vedas are His breath," and "I ask you about that Person who is known through the Upanishads," the production of the world from Brahman is indicated;
for since the production of a non-existent entity— such as a hare's horn— is impossible, it is established that only an existent entity can be produced.

If it is argued that [the world] is non-existent, we say no, because [the objection] consists of a mere negation; for in passages such as "like a cloth," it has been elaborated that even during dissolution, the phenomenal world (prapañca) persists in a subtle form—according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout—just as a cloth remains folded, whereas at the time of creation, the world unfolds like the expansion of that same cloth. Therefore, [this applies to] the existent entity.

In the Śruti passage, "Of the eternal, the Eternal," it is taught that at the dissolution of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca), it persists in the form of its cause, and that individual souls (jīvas) are eternal by their very nature as conscious entities, just like the Supreme Self (paramātman). Likewise, in another Smṛti,
the reality of the phenomenal world is taught to be like a continuous flow.
For the reality of sentient beings is indeed established by way of their own intrinsic nature.
For the reality of Śiva’s non-obscuration is indeed established by itself.

From this observation, the doctrine that Brahman is a featureless pure consciousness is not pleasing to the wise. If the Lord’s body were designated as being illusory in nature— like a snake superimposed on a rope— then how could the state of being seized by fear, as indicated in the scripture, "From fear of Him the wind blows, and death runs as the fifth," be possible for the learned who perceive the sun and other celestial bodies?
In the passage, "Indra, through his powers of illusion (māyā), is multiform and fierce," although even Śiva— who is distinguished by supreme sovereignty—
is seen to assume many bodies characterized by having a blue throat and so forth due to his power of illusion (māyā-śakti), he remains "multiform and fierce" with his stable limbs.
Furthermore, regarding those of non-material nature who possess divine and auspicious forms embraced by the Supreme Lord, [there is the state of] Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).

Moreover, in such passages as, "When there was darkness, neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone existed," the witnesshood of Śiva during the Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is established. Thus, one who is fearful resorts [to Him], thinking, "He is the Unborn. O Rudra, [seek] the right [path].

"By that [face], protect me always"—in such passages, the unborn nature (*ajātatva*) of the Supreme Lord is heard; furthermore, His transcendence over the universe, His status as the Great Seer (*maharṣi*), and His supreme power are declared in various ways, such as: "One should know Māyā as Nature (*prakṛti*)," and so forth.
Thus, His transcendence over the universe, His omnipotence, His being the cause of all, and other attributes belong to Him alone.

"Rudra does not stand for a second; neither his effect nor his instrument is found; neither his equal nor his superior is seen"—in such passages, his state of being without a second is established. "Puruṣa indeed is Rudra; to him, the Great One, salutations again and again!
All that has been, all that is becoming, and the manifold world—all this is indeed Rudra; let there be salutation to that Rudra; salutation indeed to the one of universal form."

In passages such as "namas" and others, his nature as the soul of the universe is taught; and in passages such as "namo hiraṇyavāhave," his luminous nature is also taught. If it is asked how the word *hiraṇya* can denote light, [the answer is that] in the scriptures, the nature of gold (*hiraṇya*) as being essentially fire is well-established everywhere. If one were to accept the literal sense of "gold" for the word *hiraṇya*, [it would contradict this].

The contingency of unreality would be unavoidable for the golden body of Śiva residing within the solar orb, due to its susceptibility to liquefaction like gold situated in the midst of fire. In the *Atharvaśiras*, there is the word of the Blessed One:
"I am the lotus, I am the pure, I am the foremost, the middle, the exterior, and the front."
"I alone am the light, and all are indeed I; he who knows me knows all.
Likewise, in the Śiva Purāṇa:
"The primordial abode of Umāpati is resplendent like ten million suns."
Endowed with all desirable things, it is pure, eternal, and imperishable.
Having attained that divine state, they are thereafter freed from afflictions;
they become omniscient, eternally pure, and perfectly fulfilled.
Having accomplished their pure tasks and endowed with supreme sovereignty,
they become both embodied and disembodied again according to their own will.
Those men who have reached the supreme state and are devoted to the yoga of knowledge shall not return again to this terrible cycle of worldly existence.

Since the state of Mahākailāsa, the abode of Paramaśiva, is established as being like ten million suns by such passages, there is no stain of doubt regarding its nature as consisting of light (*jyotirmaya*). If it is argued that in the verse, "He reaches the end of the path; that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu," the status of Viṣṇu’s station as the "supreme station" is also understood—
Brahman is higher than the highest; Hari is higher than that which is higher than the highest;
may my mind be intent on Śiva, who is the supreme lord beyond even that which is higher than the highest.

Thus, because the state of Maheśvara is meditated upon as being superior to Viṣṇu and others in the Bodhāyana-sūtra and the Śivasaṅkalpa, it is stated here that the supreme station of Śiva is higher than Nārāyaṇa— that is, it is beyond and transcends such a path.

"Therefore, he attains the world of Brahman and does not return"— in this passage, the state of non-return is designated by the term "world of Brahman" as the very station of Śiva. In such texts as "Salutation to you who are formless and who possess all forms," the state of being devoid of form (*vigatarūpatva*) refers to the devotees of Śiva who have attained the partless Lord.

For those who worship the nature of Paraśiva as possessing form, his possession of manifold forms is indicated by the term "Viśvarūpa" (the Universal Form). In passages such as "The blue-necked, the white-throated Śarvas, moving upon the earth below," it is shown that when devotees assume bodies, their bodies possess characteristics such as having a blue throat, exactly like the bodies of the Lord.
These [qualities] arise for those devotees who are similar to Him.
Regarding the statement "There is no return, because of the scriptural word," some say that the repetition [of the phrase] is intended to indicate the completion of the chapter;

however, that is incorrect—because of the designation of both [aspects], like a serpent and its coils, and because of the fault [that would arise] in either case, [it is not so] even from the standpoint of location.

Although [the author] has indicated, through such sūtras as "The other [is] possessed of both characteristics everywhere" (*parasyobhayaliṅgaṃ sarvatra*), "But there is a further distinction because of the mention of difference" (*adhikantu bhedanirdeśāt*),

and "Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the word 'originating' and so forth" (*tadananyatvamārambhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ*), which in every way condense all the Vedānta texts, that his own intended position is the doctrine of duality-in-non-duality (*dvaitādvaita*); yet...

Because of such an introductory statement, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] there is no contradiction due to their prior existence; "Bādarāyaṇa [holds it to be] of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice"— thus, for those established in the path of the Vedas, his own intended view is that the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman are naturally distinct during the state of saṃsāra, yet [unified] in the state of liberation.
Likewise, because the non-difference of Brahman from its formed and formless aspects, as well as the dual nature for those devotees who worship Him,
is explicitly stated and introduced in the previously mentioned sūtras,
it is determined that the statement "non-return, on account of the word; non-return, on account of the word" refers specifically to the devotees who worship both the formed and the formless aspects.
Therefore, it is a proclamation as clear as the ringing of a bell that the view of the author of the Sūtras is indeed one of dualistic-nondualism (dvaitādvaita).

Thus ends the section comprising the six topical discussions beginning with "Manifestation upon Attainment" (*sampadyāvirbhūtādhikaraṇa*) within the fourth chapter, known as the *Phalādhyāya*, of the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* composed by the venerable Svāmī Śrīpati Paṇḍita Bhagavatpādācārya, the preeminent leader of the assembly of ascetics.
It is finished.
Salutations to the venerable Guru Śiva.
The fourth chapter is completed.
